title: Structural Plasticity
text: Structural plasticity refers to physical changes in the architecture of neural circuits - in contrast to just changing synaptic strength, it involves altering the wiring itself. This encompasses processes such as the growth of new synapses (synaptogenesis), elimination of existing synapses, sprouting or retraction of dendritic and axonal branches, and even the birth of new neurons (neurogenesis). Unlike synaptic weight changes, which tweak the gain of existing connections in milliseconds to hours, structural plasticity remodels the network topology itself on timescales of hours to years, providing a slow but powerful substrate for learning, memory allocation, and circuit homeostasis. It begins with exuberant growth and pruning in development, persists throughout adulthood at a lower rate, and declines with ageing-yet can be re-opened by salient experience, injury, or neuromodulation Micron-scale remodeling The most dynamic structural element in the adult cortex is the dendritic spine. Two-photon imaging shows an ongoing turnover of  3-5% of spines per week in young adult mice; learning transiently doubles local formation rates, and new spines appear in spatial clusters that later stabilize and correlate with memory strength 1 . Spine growth is driven by actin polymerization, regulated by small-GTPases (Rac1, RhoA, Cdc42) and adhesion molecules (cadherins, integrins). Enlargement of a spine (’structural LTP’) typically follows the induction of functional LTP within seconds, whereas shrinkage or elimination accompanies LTD, linking synaptic and structural forms of plasticity. Dendritic shafts themselves also remodel: segments can sprout new branches or retract entire arbors, altering input integration zones and computational capacity. Mesoscale remodeling Presynaptic structures are equally labile. New axon collaterals and en passant boutons can sprout after minutes of heightened activity or after injury, while disused branches are pruned. Recent primate V1 imaging shows perceptual learning induces waves of axonal sprouting and bouton stabilization that mirror skill acquisition, whereas ageing reduces bouton persistence and learning-related growth 2 . The axon initial segment (AIS) can also shift position or change length within hours, tuning neuronal excitability to restore firing-rate homeostasis after prolonged perturbations. Oligodendrocyte lineage cells remain surprisingly plastic. Action-potential trains raise OPC calcium, biasing them toward differentiation and de-novo myelination of active axons; conversely, blocking adolescent oligodendrogenesis in mouse visual cortex re-opens ocular-dominance plasticity in adulthood, indicating that myelin acts as a brake on circuit malleability. Developmental structural plasticity The developing brain exhibits a remarkably high degree of structural plasticity. Young brains generate an excess of axons, dendrites, and synaptic connections and later eliminate a large fraction of them in an experience-dependent pruning process 3 . Neural activity and sensory experience guide which synapses, dendrites, and axons are preserved; for example, altering visual input during a critical early-life period causes a dramatic reorganization (and loss) of synapses in the developing visual cortex 4 . Glial cells contribute significantly to this refinement: microglia, the brain’s immune cells, actively engulf weaker or excess synapses as part of developmental synaptic pruning. Meanwhile, astrocytes release factors (such as the protein Hevin) that promote the formation and stabilization of appropriate synapses during development 5 . Together, these processes ensure that by the end of childhood the neural circuitry is pruned and tuned to the organism’s environment, retaining the most useful connections and removing redundant or maladaptive ones. Perineuronal nets (PNNs) are lattice-like structures of extracellular matrix that enwrap certain neurons as the brain matures, and they have a crucial regulatory role in structural plasticity. PNNs are composed largely of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) and form around neuron cell bodies and dendrites, particularly of fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons, toward the end of developmental critical periods. Their emergence signals the closure of high-plasticity windows in the cortex. By physically surrounding synapses and dendrites, PNNs stabilize existing connections and restrict new growth - essentially acting as a molecular brake on structural remodeling in the adult brain. The negatively charged CSPGs in PNNs inhibit synaptic change and axon sprouting, which is one reason why plasticity declines with age. For instance, in the visual cortex the maturation of PNNs coincides with the end of the ocular dominance critical period, locking in the synaptic configuration established during development. If PNNs are experimentally dissolved (e.g. with the enzyme chondroitinase ABC), the adult brain can regain a juvenile-like plasticity: previously stable circuits become susceptible to rewiring and recovery of function after injury improves. Adult structural plasticity In adulthood, the rate of structural change is much lower than during development, but it does not cease. The majority of synaptic connections (dendritic spines) in the mature cortex are long-lived and stable - often persisting for months or even a lifetime in the absence of perturbations 3 . This stability provides continuity for stored knowledge (long-term memories), yet the adult brain retains a fundamental capacity for synaptic remodeling: small numbers of spines are continually formed and eliminated over time. Experience and learning can transiently increase this synapse turnover. For instance, novel learning experiences can induce a burst of dendritic spine formation (on the order of  5% new spines on affected neurons within a day or two) 3 . While most of these nascent spines are pruned within a few weeks, a very small fraction (on the order of 0.04% of all synapses) survive and become long-lasting synapses; these stable new connections are thought to encode the learned information as a persistent memory trace in the network. Notably, learning-driven structural changes involve both addition and removal of synapses - as new spines form, some pre-existing spines may also be eliminated - effectively rewiring certain microcircuits to store new knowledge. Axonal arbors are far less malleable than during development, yet they are not frozen in place. Both intensive experience and tissue damage can drive the emergence of new axon collaterals or the rerouting of existing branches, although the distance they grow and the number of new synapses they form are tightly constrained by intrinsic growth programs and the inhibitory extracellular milieu 6 . Adult axonal growth is usually local and requires either strong activity-dependent signals or a permissive molecular environment. Long-distance regeneration comparable to development is rare without experimental interventions that lift myelin-associated inhibitors, neutralize chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, or re-activate embryonic growth programs. A striking form of structural plasticity is the generation of new neurons in the adult brain. For decades, neuroscience dogma held that no new neurons are born in adulthood, but we now know there are exceptions to this rule 7 . In mammals, active neural stem cell niches persist in specific regions - most notably the hippocampal dentate gyrus and the olfactory bulb - producing new neurons throughout life. These adult-born neurons become integrated into existing neural circuits and can take on functional roles. For example, new granule cells in the dentate gyrus participate in forming memories (e.g. they have been implicated in pattern separation and spatial memory tasks), and new olfactory neurons in the bulb help in learning new odors. Adult neurogenesis thus adds entirely new circuit elements, providing a unique form of plasticity beyond modulating existing connections. However, the extent of adult neurogenesis varies greatly across species and brain regions. Rodents and some other animals exhibit robust adult neurogenesis, but in humans it appears far more limited - neurogenesis drops to very low levels after childhood, and its existence in the adult human hippocampus has been a topic of debate. Some studies suggest adult human neurogenesis is extremely sparse or even absent, while others find evidence for continued neuron birth at a low rate 8 . Across these scales, structural plasticity follows a set of recurring design rules: (1) Activity tags and growth factors (e.g., BDNF, NGF, IGF-1, neuregulins) bias where growth or pruning occurs; (2) Competition and resource constraints ensure that net connectivity remains sparse, maximizing energy efficiency; (3) Homeostatic feedback couples average firing and connectivity, preventing runaway excitation; (4) Multi-timescale coupling with synaptic weight plasticity enables rapid encoding followed by slower structural consolidation; (5) A stable structural core is complemented by a dynamic fringe throughout life. Theoretical work shows that allowing both synaptic weights and structural rewiring dramatically increases memory capacity and noise robustness compared with weight change alone, at the cost of slower convergence-mirroring the brain’s stability-plasticity trade-off. title: Neuromodulators
text: Neuromodulators as broadly-acting gain control and state switches Diffuse projection systems that globally modulate computation Timescales: fast phasic signals vs slow tonic states Computational roles: learning rates, precision, exploration, consolidation "Neuromodulatory systems serve a special meta-processing role in the brain. Due to their anatomical privileges of having massively extensive arborization patterns throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems and to their physiological capacity of finely controlling how other neurons communicate with each other and plasticize, they are ideally positioned to regulate the way information is acquired, processed, utilized, and stored in the brain." title: Dopamine
text: Neuroanatomy of substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area dopaminergic, and dorsal raphe serotonergic circuits in the human brain using T1-weighted and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging: A morphometric pilot study with estimate of reliability include TD/RPE details and how evolution shaped dopaminergic circuits Overview, machinery, and pathways Dopamine is the brain’s all-purpose "currency of significance." A mere  400,000 dopaminergic neurons–0.0006% of the 70 billion neurons in the human brain–send widely ramifying axons that make an estimated 1-2 million synapses apiece, allowing a single spike volley to broadcast a global "pay attention to this" signal. Most somata reside in two midbrain nuclei-the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and ventral tegmental area (VTA)-with a smaller contingent in the arcuate nucleus and dorsal raphe. From there five major ascending pathways emerge: the nigrostriatal tract (SNc -> dorsal striatum) that underwrites action selection and motor vigor; the mesolimbic (VTA -> ventral striatum, amygdala, hippocampus) and mesocortical (VTA -> PFC, ACC) tracts that shape motivation, decision-making and cognition; the tuberoinfundibular tract (arcuate -> median eminence) that gates pituitary hormone release; and a sparsely studied thalamic/habenular projection implicated in arousal and aversion 2 . Dopamine is synthesized from tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase, packaged into vesicles by VMAT2, and cleared mainly by the high-affinity dopamine transporter (DAT). Dopamine’s temporal dynamics span multiple timescales: phasic bursts lasting 100-500 milliseconds encode reward prediction errors with firing rates jumping from baseline 3-5 Hz to 15-30 Hz, while tonic dopamine levels fluctuating over minutes to hours set motivational tone and response vigor. Postsynaptically, D1-like receptors (D1, D5) elevate cAMP/PKA to gate long-term potentiation, whereas D2-like receptors (D2, D3, D4) depress cAMP and favor long-term depression or presynaptic autoinhibition. Because most dopaminergic varicosities lack classical synapses, transmitter often spreads by volume diffusion, granting a spatiotemporal footprint of hundreds of microns and seconds 3 , 4 . Crucially, brief D1 surges also serve as synaptic tags: in motor cortex and hippocampus they mark a small subset of newly formed dendritic spines that happened to encode a rewarded action or novel context, allowing late-phase LTP proteins to consolidate those spines and thereby bind dopamine signals to skill acquisition and memory persistence through a tag-and-capture mechanism. Recent single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have shattered the myth of a monolithic dopaminergic system. At least a dozen molecularly distinct subtypes differ in projection target, intrinsic electrophysiology, receptor repertoire, and disease vulnerability 5 . For example, a 2025 eLife study resolved three broad families that tile the SNc and VTA in partially overlapping gradients and exhibit subtype-specific degeneration in Parkinson’s models 6 . Such diversity explains why some dopamine neurons signal reward while neighboring neurons encode novelty, effort, or aversion. Signaling prediction errors The canonical computational role of dopamine is the reward-prediction error (RPE): when an outcome is better (or worse) than expected, dopaminergic bursts (or pauses) teach downstream cortico-striatal synapses to update value estimates-a biological instantiation of temporal-difference reinforcement learning. This biological TD signal updates synaptic weights throughout the basal ganglia and cortex, with spike-timing-dependent plasticity windows aligned to dopamine’s arrival latency of 50-100 milliseconds after pre-post spike pairs. The precision is remarkable: dopamine can encode reward magnitudes over at least three orders of magnitude and temporal predictions down to 100-millisecond resolution. The dopamine system also implements credit assignment through eligibility traces. Synapses throughout striatum and cortex maintain molecular traces of recent activity for 1-10 seconds, allowing dopamine signals to retroactively strengthen connections that led to unexpected outcomes. This solves the temporal credit assignment problem; the brain can learn which actions caused rewards even when those rewards arrive seconds later. The mechanism involves cascades of calcium-dependent kinases and phosphatases that maintain synaptic "tags" until dopamine arrives to consolidate changes. Modern work extends this framework in three ways. First, recent work shows that VTA/SNc populations jointly encode a full probability surface over reward amount and delay, rather than just a one-dimensional distribution of returns. Sousa et al. (2025) trained mice on variable-magnitude, variable-timing rewards and uncovered a "time-magnitude RL" (TMRL) code: neighbouring dopamine neurons span a grid of discount factors and magnitude tunings whose population activity, read out 450 ms after a cue, reconstructs a two-dimensional density map of future pay-offs. This code predicts anticipatory licking and improves foraging in silico, showing that downstream circuits can exploit multidimensional uncertainty when deciding both what and when to act 7 . Second (related to the first point), dopamine neurons compute reward-prediction errors in a way that leverages the brain’s complex world- and value-modeling machinery: the update depends not only on the sensory cue you can see but also on the brain’s internal beliefs about hidden variables that might have produced and are implied by that cue. Third, when this global, scalar RPE reaches the striatum, dopaminergic axon terminals can reshape it into feature-specific prediction errors linked to particular sensory or motor channels–evidence that significant local computation happens inside the striatum itself 8 . Yet RPEs are only half the story. Distinct midbrain ensembles broadcast action-prediction errors (APEs)-the gap between the action just executed and the one the basal ganglia expected-reinforcing value-free repetition of sensorimotor mappings 9 . In mice, dopamine in the tail of the striatum encodes APEs and causally drives sound-action learning, while sister populations scale burst magnitude almost linearly with reach velocity, dynamically tuning movement vigor 10 . These fast motor-domain signals close cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamic loops on a 50-200 ms timescale-far faster than classical reward learning-and thus act more like an adaptive gain controller than a slow critic. The same teaching logic recurs higher in the abstraction hierarchy. When an outcome violates an abstract rule, category boundary, or reward identity, midbrain neurons emit feature-specific prediction errors even though scalar value is unchanged; disrupting the orbitofrontal-midbrain loop (where OFC learns abstract maps/rules of state spaces) abolishes these identity-prediction signals and blocks category learning in humans 11 . Optogenetic boosting of the VTA->hippocampus pathway accelerates schema acquisition and contextual generalization, whereas silencing it impairs flexible inference 12 . In primates, dopaminergic firing flips in lock-step with hippocampal and prefrontal rule codes as animals master new task grammars, indicating that dopamine synchronizes abstraction updates across distributed cortico-hippocampal networks 13 . Together these findings imply that dopamine delivers a hierarchy of error signals-from muscle twitches to latent causal structure-allowing the brain to learn what happens, how it unfolds, and why it matters through a single neuromodulatory broadcast. - Such hierarchical error signals reflect an anatomical and kinetic gradient that stretches from the ventral to the dorsolateral striatum: phasic dopamine in nucleus accumbens integrates reward history over seconds to tens of seconds and discounts future pay-offs slowly, whereas bursts in dorsomedial striatum compress that window to a few seconds, and dorsolateral transients sharpen further into sub-second spikes that emphasise instantaneous sensorimotor contingencies. This temporal spectrum arises because dopamine is cleared  2-3 x faster and DAT expression is markedly higher in dorsal than in ventral regions, while astrocytic ensheathment and receptor composition vary in the same direction, collectively shortening the effective eligibility trace as one moves laterally. Reinforcement-learning models that simply assign progressively steeper trace-decay and discount parameters to adjacent striatal compartments reproduce the empirical ramp-to-pulse transition in dopamine and explain why habits crystallise first in dorsal loops even while ventral value coding remains flexible. From an engineering standpoint, the brain’s striatal gradient functions like a bundle of parallel critics-long-horizon, mid-horizon, and reflexive-all driven by a common error signal but tuned to different temporal kernels 14 , 15 . In prefrontal cortex, dopamine modulates the stability-flexibility tradeoff of working memory representations-D1 receptor activation stabilizes current representations while D2 activation promotes updating; an inverted-U relationship governs PFC working-memory fidelity, with too little or too much dopamine degrading sustained activity. By biasing local circuit gain, dopamine dynamically toggles PFC between stabilization (maintenance) and flexibility (updating) modes, creating a gating mechanism where surprising events (signaled by dopamine bursts) update internal models while expected events maintain current states. The hippocampus uses dopamine to tag memories for consolidation, with novel experiences triggering VTA projections that enhance both encoding and subsequent replay during sleep. Coordinating exploration vs exploitation Dopamine biases an animal toward exploration through a set of nested mechanisms that operate on different time-scales and circuit motifs, all of which tip the brain’s cost-benefit calculus in favor of sampling the (specific) unknown rather than exploiting the familiar. First, phasic "novelty bursts" from VTA and SNc act as a rapid incentive for trying new options. When a cue or context has little prior association history, midbrain neurons fire brief, high-amplitude volleys that travel chiefly to the ventral striatum, orbitofrontal cortex (abstract rules), and hippocampus (episodic memory). In the nucleus accumbens these bursts transiently boost D1-receptor signaling on direct-pathway spiny projection neurons, raising the effective action value of the novel choice by what behavioural economists would call an "uncertainty bonus". Optogenetically augmenting these bursts accelerates exploration, while chemogenetically damping them makes animals stick with the status quo 16 . Second, tonic dopamine directly sets the exploration-exploitation "temperature." Basal-ganglia models and rodent work show that baseline (2-10 nM) dopamine tunes how strongly cortical value estimates gate the motor output channel: lower tonic levels keep indirect-pathway D2 neurons more active, softening choice policies and letting low-value or even random actions (and working memory contents) leak through. Conversely, pharmacologically elevating tonic dopamine (e.g., in DAT-knock-down mice or with L-DOPA in humans) tightens gating, increasing the probability of selecting whichever action has the highest learned value and thus favouring exploitation 17 , 18 . Computationally, the striatum behaves like a soft-max sampler whose inverse temperature is set by ambient dopamine concentration. Third, dopamine carries an uncertainty representation in its burst amplitude and variance. Recent recordings in head-fixed mice show that burst size scales with the posterior standard deviation of expected reward, not just the mean. A biophysically grounded model in which the direct pathway tracks the mean and the indirect pathway tracks the variance reproduced both the neural data and exploratory choice patterns better than classical upper-confidence-bound algorithms, implying that dopamine converts statistical uncertainty into a directed drive to gather information 19 . Fourth, local striatal computations reshape the global burst into feature-specific "novelty-prediction errors." Axon-terminal recordings reveal that even when a midbrain neuron carries a scalar burst, dopamine release hotspots can be confined to those striatal columns that encode the currently uncertain sensory or motor channel. This creates a map of where exploration is needed without broadcasting noise everywhere, and it depends on cholinergic interneuron gating as well as striosome-to-dopamine feedback loops that veto release in over-learned channels 20 . Fifth, fronto-striatal loops harness dopaminergic signals to regulate cognitive flexibility. In the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), phasic dopamine bursts-often routed through basal ganglia gating mechanisms-can transiently destabilize working memory attractor states, loosening the grip of currently active task rules and facilitating the generation of novel hypotheses 21 . This flexibility stands in contrast to the stabilizing influence of tonic dopamine, which supports sustained representations through D1-mediated strengthening of recurrent microcircuits 22 . In the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), similar dopamine transients appear to "tag" latent state representations for re-evaluation, particularly when the identity (rather than magnitude) of expected rewards becomes uncertain. 23 , 24 . Finally, dopamine works in concert with a larger neuromodulatory "control panel" that converts its novelty- and uncertainty-weighted bursts into overt exploratory acts. Dorsal anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and anterior insula-regions that light up whenever subjects abandon the safe option-are the cortical read-outs of these dopaminergic salience tags, dynamically computing when the expected marginal value of a patch or hypothesis has dipped below some threshold 25 . Via dense reciprocal projections, the same ACC drive toggles the locus-coeruleus noradrenergic system between low-tonic/high-phasic "exploit" mode and high-tonic "network-reset" mode; the latter floods cortex with noradrenaline, loosening attractor basins and initiating broad foraging once dopaminergic precision falls-exactly the adaptive-gain switch described by Aston-Jones and Cohen 26 . Basal-forebrain cholinergic neurons then fire sub-second transients that synchronize with these state shifts, sharpening sensory gain and lowering detection uncertainty so that the organism can interrogate the newly chosen stimulus or idea with high fidelity 27 . Serotonergic bursts from dorsal raphe to orbitofrontal and medial PFC add yet another layer, accelerating reversal learning and thereby preventing dopamine-driven novelty seeking from collapsing into perseveration 28 . Computationally, this division of labor maps neatly onto Doya’s extended actor-critic framework in which dopamine supplies the reward-prediction-error term, acetylcholine controls the speed of memory update, and serotonin controls the temporal discounting of reward predictions, together ensuring that chemical nudges in the midbrain blossom into the flexible foraging and hypothesis-testing behaviours observed across species 29 ; an extended account proposes that the noradrenergic system controls the rate of learning 30 . In sum, dopamine encourages exploration by (i) tagging novelty with instantaneous bursts that confer a value bonus, (ii) dialing basal-ganglia gating thresholds via tonic levels, (iii) scaling burst size with statistical uncertainty, (iv) locally steering that burst toward the most uncertain features, and (v) partnering with cortical and neuromodulatory systems that translate these chemical nudges into concrete foraging and hypothesis-testing behaviour. By modulating the relative expected value and uncertainty of candidate actions, these dopaminergic signals drive prefrontal-striatal arbitration that decides when to stick with cached, model-free habits versus invoking computationally expensive, model-based planning and exploration. Dopamine’s multiplexed error repertoire suggests upgrading standard RL algorithms along three fronts: (i) distributional critics that learn full return distributions rather than expectations; (ii) dual critics that separate value-centric RPEs from value-free action-prediction errors, enabling simultaneous learning of "what pays" and "how to do it"; and (iii) meta-controllers that tune learning-rate and exploration drive as a function of uncertainty and novelty. Crucially, dopamine illustrates how a tiny, slow channel can steer a vast, fast network by modulating plasticity thresholds and circuit excitability instead of encoding content directly–an engineering pattern worth emulating in large-scale world-model agents.

title: Acetylcholine
text: Overview, machinery, and pathways Acetylcholine is the brain’s most ancient neuromodulator, yet a surprisingly small contingent of cells creates its influence. In the human forebrain only about 400,000 cholinergic projection neurons-barely 0.002% of all cortical neurons-arise from four basal-forebrain nuclei (Ch1-Ch4) and nevertheless blanket the neocortex, hippocampus, and amygdala with arborisations that branch thousands of times before terminating; equally sparse populations in the pedunculopontine/laterodorsal tegmentum (PPN/LDT) innervate thalamus and midbrain, while a single giant interneuron class provides the striatum’s intrinsic cholinergic tone. This "wire-by-volume" organisation means that a single spike volley from one nucleus basalis neuron can modulate on the order of one square millimetre of cortex, setting the gain of tens of thousands of local pyramids and interneurons 1 , 2 . The acetylcholine system operates through two fundamentally different receptor architectures that provide complementary computational capabilities. Nicotinic receptors function as ionotropic ligand-gated ion channels, assembled as pentameric structures that open within milliseconds of acetylcholine binding, allowing rapid sodium, potassium, and calcium flux 3 . The neuronal nicotinic receptor family includes multiple subtypes formed from combinations of α \alpha 2- α \alpha 10 and β \beta 2- β \beta 4 subunits, with α \alpha 7 homomeric receptors showing particularly high calcium permeability and rapid desensitization kinetics-properties that make them ideal for detecting transient acetylcholine signals. Muscarinic receptors, by contrast, operate as G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) with five subtypes (M1-M5), where M1/M3/M5 couple to Gq proteins to increase intracellular calcium via phospholipase C, while M2/M4 couple to Gi/o proteins to decrease cAMP. This dual signaling architecture allows acetylcholine to simultaneously mediate fast synaptic transmission and slower, more sustained neuromodulatory effects across different spatiotemporal scales. Astrocytes express both receptor families and, when activated, alter local blood flow and glymphatic clearance, linking cholinergic tone to metabolic homeostasis 4 . The brain’s cholinergic system is organized into two major projection systems with distinct anatomical origins and functional specializations. The basal forebrain cholinergic system, originating from the medial septum/diagonal band of Broca (MS/DB) and the nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM), provides the primary cholinergic innervation to the entire neocortex and hippocampus 5 . Recent evidence reveals this system is far more topographically organized than historically appreciated, with specific cholinergic cell populations targeting distinct cortical areas and layers. The MS/DB neurons specifically innervate the hippocampus via the septo-hippocampal pathway and are critical for spatial memory, while NBM neurons project to cortical areas and support object recognition and working memory 6 . The second major system consists of brainstem cholinergic neurons in the pedunculopontine tegmentum (PPT) and laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT), which project both rostrally to the thalamus and basal forebrain, and caudally to the pontine and medullary reticular formation. Signaling expected uncertainty In cortical circuits, acetylcholine increases the influence of feedforward sensory input while suppressing intracortical and feedback connections, effectively increasing the signal-to-noise ratio and making neurons more responsive to external stimuli rather than internally generated patterns 7 , 8 . This mechanism, demonstrated through both slice physiology and computational modeling, suggests acetylcholine acts as a network state switch between externally driven "encoding" modes and internally driven "consolidation" modes. Computationally this corresponds to signalling "expected uncertainty," complementing noradrenaline’s "unexpected uncertainty." In the hippocampus high cholinergic tone during exploration biases the network toward pattern-separation and encoding, while low tone during quiet wake or non-REM sleep favours retrieval and consolidation; medial-septal bursts are phase-locked to theta, timing synaptic plasticity windows across the trisynaptic loop. PPN/LDT bursts gate REM sleep and reset locomotor microstates, whereas their tonic activity tracks vigilance. In striatum, single-spike cholinergic "pauses" or "waves" sculpt sub-second dopamine release, adjusting the credit assignment landscape for habit learning and behavioural flexibility 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 . Microdialysis studies in behaving animals show acetylcholine release in prefrontal cortex increases by 140% during sustained attention tasks, with transient acetylcholine release specifically signaling the detection of behaviorally relevant cues 13 , 14 . The basal forebrain cholinergic system appears to implement a hierarchical attention control system, with prefrontal cortex detecting task-relevant stimuli and then enhancing sensory cortical processing through cholinergic modulation (among other mechanisms) 15 . Seen through a world-modeling lens, acetylcholine switches the brain between two computational regimes: an externally oriented, high-plasticity "model-updating" mode and an internally oriented, energy-efficient "model-exploiting" mode. By modulating sensory gain, hippocampal encoding, and cortico-striatal learning thresholds, this single molecule orchestrates when organisms should trust their generative models, when they should revise them, and how strongly new evidence is written into synapses 9 . Several engineering principles emerge from the cholinergic system’s design. First, the dual receptor system (ionotropic vs metabotropic) allows multiplexing of fast and slow signals through the same neurotransmitter, maximizing information bandwidth. Second, the topographic organization combined with local and volume transmission enables both specific and broadcast signaling modes. Third, the rapid enzymatic degradation provides precise temporal control while the spatial distribution of degrading enzymes creates structured acetylcholine gradients. Fourth, the system implements gain control through multiple mechanisms: presynaptic autoreceptors, receptor desensitization, and activity-dependent synthesis. Finally, acetylcholine’s interaction with other neuromodulators (particularly dopamine) creates a multi-dimensional control space for behavioral states, with different combinations producing distinct computational modes optimized for encoding, consolidation, attention, or action selection. But how did evolution "bake in" this ACh function (as an architectural bias)? Topology: a small cholinergic system with diffuse, targeted projections gives a single global variable ("this context is learnable but noisy") the ability to reconfigure many cortical areas simultaneously–a cheap control channel with high leverage. Receptor diversity = pathway-selective gating: fast nicotinic effects can amplify feedforward thalamo-/cortico-cortical input, while muscarinic effects can reshape recurrent dynamics and plasticity windows, letting "precision" be applied selectively (e.g., to sensory evidence vs. internal recurrence) rather than as a blunt arousal signal. More specifically, muscarinic (M1, M2) and nicotinic receptors are distributed with higher density in cortical layer IV (the thalamocortical input layer) than in upper layers carrying lateral/feedback connections 16 . This means ACh release preferentially amplifies feedforward sensory signals while relatively suppressing recurrent top-down predictions. Phasic signaling for moments of learnability: brief cholinergic transients aligned to cues/outcomes let the brain mark exactly when information is worth incorporating ("this bit is diagnostic"), enabling time-local learning-rate spikes instead of slow, global modulation. Hard-wired inputs to ACh nuclei: basal forebrain receives convergent inputs from prefrontal cortex (task statistics, uncertainty estimates), amygdala (salience signals), and brainstem arousal nuclei (novelty/salience), enabling a genetically scaffolded estimator that can then be tuned by experience. In terms of the ACh system’s training data (what trains basal-forebrain ACh release policies): Inputs (features): convergent streams that summarize cue reliability, attentional demand, and current context 17 , 15 , 18 , including (i) sensory/cortical evidence about whether a cue is present and how diagnostic it is (salience, SNR, ambiguity), (ii) cortical performance-monitoring / uncertainty proxies (e.g., sustained conflict, unstable cue-outcome mappings, rising residual error despite effort–signals that "more evidence + plasticity might help"), and (iii) motivational/state variables (arousal, threat, hunger, reward expectation) routed via limbic/hypothalamic and related afferents into basal forebrain. Outputs (actions): region- and moment-specific phasic cholinergic transients (plus slower tone) that (a) boost bottom-up impact / cue detectability, and (b) open local plasticity windows–i.e., "allocate precision + learning rate here, right now." 19 , 20 , 5 Error signals (credit assignment / what counts as ’good’ ACh deployment): the cleanest empirically supported "label" is reinforcement feedback / reinforcement surprise : identified basal-forebrain cholinergic neurons show rapid, phasic responses to reinforcement feedback (including unexpected outcomes) 21 , 22 , consistent with a broadcast that marks moments when updating is valuable. That reinforcement-linked teaching can then shape–via plasticity within basal forebrain circuits themselves –which sensory/contextual patterns should trigger future ACh pulses (including cases with delayed reinforcement , where basal forebrain learns to bridge cue -> later outcome). Under this view, basal forebrain is not "given" learnability labels; instead it is trained to emit ACh when doing so increases future reward and/or future error-reduction , making reinforcement-surprise and task-improvement act as an implicit proxy loss for "deploy precision/plasticity where prediction error is compressible."

title: Norepinephrine
text: Overview, machinery, and pathways Norepinephrine (NE) represents one of evolution’s most elegant solutions to a fundamental computational problem: how to rapidly adapt neural processing when your model of the world fails. The locus coeruleus (LC), a tiny bilateral nucleus containing just 20,000-50,000 neurons in humans, manages to modulate virtually the entire brain through an extraordinarily divergent projection system. Recent findings support the idea that the locus coeruleus signals several types of prediction error and integrates them to compute global model failures 1 , 2 , serving as the brain’s "rapid response" state-switch neuromodulator. Anatomically,  90% of ascending NE originates in the bilateral LC (A6 cell group). Smaller clusters (A1-A5, A7) in the medulla and pons project to hypothalamus, amygdala, brain-stem autonomic nuclei, and spinal cord, knitting arousal with visceromotor control. LC axons are unusually thin, varicose, and energy-efficient, releasing transmitter extrasynaptically ("volume transmission") so that a single spike volley can flood entire cortical columns within  200 ms. Modern viral-tracing and Ca2+-imaging show that LC neurons are not a uniform sprinkler system: discrete ensembles preferentially innervate sensory, limbic, or fronto-parietal circuits, implying projection- and task-specific codes rather than a single global signal 3 , 4 . From a synthesis perspective, NE follows a remarkably efficient pathway. Starting from tyrosine, the rate-limiting enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase converts it to L-DOPA, which is then decarboxylated to dopamine. The critical step occurs when dopamine β \beta -hydroxylase converts dopamine to norepinephrine within synaptic vesicles. In the peripheral nervous system, chromaffin cells can further convert NE to epinephrine via phenylethanolamine-N-methyl transferase 5 . This compartmentalized synthesis allows for precise control - you can’t accidentally flood the system with NE since the final conversion happens in vesicles ready for release. Five G-protein-coupled adrenoceptor subtypes orchestrate the downstream effects. α \alpha 1 (Gq) receptors depolarise pyramidal and thalamic relay neurons, sharpening sensory throughput; α \alpha 2 (Gi/o) receptors serve as somatodendritic and axonal autoreceptors that curtail further release and, postsynaptically in prefrontal cortex, dampen cAMP-HCN currents to stabilise working-memory ensembles. β \beta 1-3 (Gs) receptors boost cAMP/PKA signalling, lowering plasticity thresholds and amplifying network excitability. The nuanced mixture-and local receptor ratios-means NE can simultaneously enhance signal-to-noise in sensory cortex yet suppress distractors in PFC [ α \alpha 1-Adrenergic Receptors in Neurotransmission, Synaptic Plasticity, and Cognition; Noradrenergic dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease]. LC neurons release NE to control arousal, but also in the context of a variety of sensory-motor and behavioral functions 1 , with phasic bursts (3-15 Hz) signaling salient events requiring immediate attention, while tonic activity (0.1-5 Hz) modulates overall arousal and learning rates. This creates a hierarchical control system where rapid phasic signals can interrupt ongoing processing for urgent updates, while slower tonic changes adjust the brain’s overall operating mode. For example, as behavioural utility degrades (e.g when rewards dwindle) tonic firing drifts upward, suppressing phasic peaks and driving exploration, a principle formalised as the "adaptive-gain" theory 6 , 7 , 3 . At the network level, NE raises membrane conductances, suppresses slow oscillations, and synchronises gamma rhythms, thereby increasing the mutual information between stimulus and cortical response. LC responses to behaviorally relevant sensory stimuli promote visual discrimination in a spatially selective way 8 , demonstrating that this isn’t just global arousal but targeted enhancement of task-relevant processing. β \beta 1 receptors increase heart rate and contractility through cAMP-dependent pathways, while β \beta 2 receptors in the brain enhance synaptic plasticity. This creates a coordinated response where the same neuromodulator simultaneously prepares the body for action while enhancing the brain’s ability to learn from the current situation. Plasticity is where NE converts momentary salience into durable memory. β \beta -adrenergic activation transforms early-LTP into protein-synthesis-dependent late-LTP in hippocampus and cortex; concomitant α \alpha ₁ signalling can promote structural spine growth, whereas α \alpha 2 receptor engagement biases toward LTD and pruning-yielding a bidirectional "save or erase" dial controlled by arousal. Such adrenergic gating explains why emotionally charged experiences imprint so vividly [ β \beta -Adrenergic receptor signaling and modulation of long-term potentiation in the mammalian hippocampus; β \beta -Adrenergic Control of Hippocampal Function: Subserving the Choreography of Synaptic Information Storage and Memory]. In the amygdala-hippocampal complex, NE interacts with glucocorticoids to prioritise threat-laden or appetitive episodes for consolidation, while co-release of dopamine from some LC terminals further biases spatial and contextual learning 9 , 10 . Spatial organisation within the LC itself adds another computational layer. Rostro-ventral ensembles preferentially drive prefrontal and parietal cortices to reset task-sets, whereas caudo-dorsal cells bias toward autonomic and cerebellar targets, coordinating somatic readiness with cognitive shifts. Gradients of dendritic innervation by CRF, orexin, and GABA interneurons tune these modules on sub-second timescales, enabling the LC to multiplex stress, metabolic state, and behavioural context 3 . Signaling unexpected uncertainty NE release approximates a threat prediction error signal under temporal uncertainty, combining cognitive and affective information into a predictive signal that links time with the anticipation of danger 11 . Unlike dopamine’s reward prediction error, NE appears to encode unsigned prediction errors - it doesn’t care whether you predicted too much or too little, just that your prediction was wrong. This is in line with the LC signaling unexpected uncertainty, which can be computed by summating prediction errors and subtracting their expected rate 12 . The LC-NE system implements what we might call a "model failure detector" that operates across multiple timescales. LC activity is triggered by errors in prediction and the subsequent release of noradrenaline alters the rate of learning about the environment, describing an LC-cortex feedback loop promoting behavioural flexibility in times of uncertainty. When your predictions consistently fail (high prediction error rate), the LC ramps up NE release, effectively telling the entire brain: "our current model is broken, increase learning rates and explore new strategies." But how did evolution "bake in" this NE function (as an architectural bias)? Single nucleus, global broadcast: The locus coeruleus (LC) contains only  30,000 neurons in humans yet projects to virtually the entire forebrain via highly branched axons. A single LC neuron can simultaneously modulate millions of synapses across cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, and thalamus. This makes it an ideal one-to-many interrupt line –a fast, energetically cheap way to push the whole brain into a "reassess" mode. Phasic/tonic operating modes: built-in dynamics support both (i) phasic interrupts for abrupt surprises and (ii) tonic gain control for longer exploration/exploitation shifts, matching the two time-scales of unexpected uncertainty (instant change-point vs. drifting volatility) 13 , 14 . Receptor affinity gradients : Moderate NE release in prefrontal cortex preferentially engages high-affinity postsynaptic α 2 A \alpha_{2A} -adrenergic receptors, strengthening task-relevant recurrent firing and improving signal-to-noise (e.g., working memory) 15 , 16 . At higher NE levels (stress or high arousal), lower-affinity α 1 \alpha_1 and β \beta receptors are increasingly recruited, which tends to disrupt prefrontal working memory and top-down control 15 , 16 . At the systems level, the locus-coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) adaptive gain framework links moderate tonic LC activity with strong phasic responses to focused task engagement (exploitation), and high tonic LC activity to disengagement, distractibility, and exploratory behavior, producing an inverted-U relationship between tonic LC activity and task performance 6 , 17 . Input wiring optimized for surprise: LC receives afferents from anterior cingulate cortex (conflict/error signals), orbitofrontal cortex (outcome prediction errors), and the paragigantocellularis nucleus (autonomic state). This input architecture positions LC as a "surprise detector" that fires when prediction errors exceed what the current model can explain. Receptor placement supports rapid reconfiguration: adrenergic receptor subtypes and autoreceptors allow both quick gain changes and stabilization of NE tone, giving an evolutionarily convenient mechanism for switching between "keep exploiting the current model" and "break glass, explore." Coupling to arousal and autonomic systems : LC-NE is also central to fight/flight responses. Evolution thus co-opted circuits that already needed to detect "the world has changed in important ways" (predator appearance, resource discovery) for the more general function of volatility detection. The measurable correlate–pupil dilation–provides a non-invasive readout of this system. Training data / "teacher signals" for the LC-NE controller (what trains norepinephrine release policies): Inputs (features): convergent streams that summarize whether the current internal model or latent-state hypothesis is invalid , rather than merely noisy: (i) unexpected prediction-error structure (oddballs, violated temporal expectations, abrupt contingency changes) consistent with a change-point rather than stochastic variance 18 , 19 , (ii) performance-monitoring and conflict signals (errors, response conflict, escalating cost of continued exploitation) indicating that the current policy is failing 6 , (iii) interoceptive and stress-related channels (autonomic perturbations, effort, threat) that reliably co-occur with environmental regime shifts and task breakdowns 20 , plus (iv) reward-rate context (drops in expected utility under the current strategy), which determines whether switching is advantageous 21 . Outputs (actions): phasic LC bursts that act as a rapid, global interrupt / reorient / reset signal–temporarily increasing neural gain, breaking ongoing attractor dynamics, and biasing the system toward alternative state hypotheses–and tonic LC levels that modulate longer-timescale exploration-exploitation tradeoffs and task engagement 22 , 23 . Error signals (credit assignment / what counts as "good" NE deployment): LC-NE is effectively trained by downstream behavioral value : NE transients and tonic shifts are reinforced when they lead to rapid recovery of performance (successful identification of a new rule, context, or latent state) and suppressed when they cause unnecessary or destabilizing switching. In other words, the implicit loss is "did interrupting now increase future reward rate or reduce future prediction error under a new model?"–a biologically cheap proxy for change-point detection wrapped around utility maximization 23 , 18 . This architecture implements an inductive bias toward maximizing learning progress: the brain preferentially allocates metabolic resources (attention, synaptic plasticity) to situations where learnable structure exists, while avoiding both the waste of trying to learn from pure noise (low-ACh disengagement) and the danger of perseverating on a failed model (NE-triggered reset). The result is a system that implicitly seeks out the "sweet spot" of reducible uncertainty–exactly the regime where compression progress is possible.

title: Serotonin
text: Overview, machinery, and pathways Serotonin (5-hydroxy-tryptamine, 5-HT) is forged from tryptophan in ∼nine bilateral raphe nuclei that straddle the midline of the pontine and medullary brain-stem. The dorsal (B7) and median (B8) raphe nuclei together supply most forebrain serotonin, while more caudal groups carpet the cerebellum, spinal cord, and autonomic nuclei. Although serotonergic somata number only on the order of 200,000, each cell grows beaded, extraordinarily ramifying axons so that a single spike volley can wet millimetres of cortex with transmitter in a few hundred milliseconds-a design that allows 5-HT to re-weight whole-brain dynamics on the fly. Modern single-cell transcriptomics and viral tracing reveal that the raphe is anything but monolithic: plate-based single-cell RNA-sequencing generated a dataset comprising eleven transcriptomically distinct serotonin neuron clusters subtypes 1 , with these transcriptomic clusters differentially express a rich repertoire of neuropeptides, receptors, ion channels, and transcription factors; subtypes also project with surprising specificity to sensory, limbic, basal-ganglia, or prefrontal targets, implying parallel "micro-circuits" rather than one global spray 2 , 3 . The computational power of serotonin emerges from its diverse receptor mechanisms operating across multiple timescales. The 7 general serotonin receptor classes include a total of 14 known serotonin receptors, each implementing distinct computational operations through specific G-protein coupling patterns. The 5-HT1R and 5-HT5R subtypes couple with Gi/o protein, leading to the inhibition of adenylyl cyclase (AC) activity and a reduction in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels 4 , while 5-HT2R couples with Gq/11 protein, stimulating phospholipase C, which leads to elevated levels of inositol triphosphate and calcium ions (Ca2+). This diversity enables serotonin to implement both fast synaptic transmission and slower paracrine signaling, with some projections form classical chemical synapses while many do not, thus contributing to the so-called paracrine or volume transmission 5 . At the synaptic level, 5-HT gates plasticity in receptor-specific ways: Gs-coupled 5-HT4/6/7 receptors raise cAMP/PKA, lower LTP thresholds, and accelerate dendritic spine maturation, whereas 5-HT1A autoinhibition or postsynaptic activation can stabilise working-memory ensembles by damping HCN-mediated noise currents. Serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe fire tonically at low single-digit rates (∼1-5 Hz on average, state-dependent) and exhibit phasic, task-locked modulations to salient events, including expectancy violations. Optogenetic fMRI shows that brief activation of DRN 5-HT produces widespread BOLD increases across medial prefrontal cortex, striatum, and VTA in awake animals, whereas under isoflurane these effects are markedly reduced or inverted-consistent with projection- and receptor-specific bidirectionality (e.g., stronger 5-HT₁-mediated inhibition) 6 , 7 , 8 . Signaling long-horizon cost-benefit tradeoffs Recent work refines Doya’s (2002) proposal that serotonin tunes temporal discounting by showing that subsets of dorsal raphe 5-HT neurons carry slow, predictive signals that approximate discounted state value over multi-second horizons in waiting/foraging tasks, while other subsets exhibit fast, mixed-signed responses to appetitive and aversive events 9 , 10 . Behaviorally, lowering central 5-HT (e.g., tryptophan depletion) reliably steepens temporal discounting and, in several RL fits, leaves learning rates and choice stochasticity comparatively less affected-consistent with a relatively specific influence on the discount parameter, though not an exclusive one. Framed as a "meta-decision variable" 11 , serotonergic tone appears to encode (or regulate in proportion to) long-horizon value calibrated by resource availability and costs (time, effort, metabolic load, risk), thereby adjusting patience, persistence, quitting thresholds, and the propensity to engage model-based over model-free control. This picture, however, is mechanistically heterogeneous: receptor class (5-HT1A/1B vs 5-HT2A/2C), target circuit (PFC, striatum, accumbens, hippocampus), and timescale (phasic vs tonic) all matter, and some DRN neurons carry aversive or RPE-like components. Thus, serotonin is best viewed as a family of meta-decision control signals that bias planning depth and opportunity-cost accounting, rather than a unitary, purely ’slow value’ channel. In support of these computations, serotonergic neurons in the DRN and median raphe receive unusually rich context about both future payoffs and the costs of getting there: Hypothalamic AgRP/POMC, leptin/ghrelin, insulin, orexin, and other interoceptive channels project (directly or via parabrachial nucleus/BNST/insula routes) to raphe, letting 5-HT "know" whether you can afford to wait, work, or explore. Low energy or high internal threat should compress the horizon (steepen discounting). The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and supplementary motor areas (SMAs)-which encode subjective effort, sunk costs, and time-on-task-send dense projections to DRN. These signals can down-weight protracted plans when predicted control costs are high. Amygdala, BNST, periaqueductal gray (PAG), and habenula-RMTg pathways convey threat, pain, and negative surprise. These inputs let 5-HT factor prospective harm into the long-horizon estimate, often by raising patience for safe plans and lowering it when the tail risk is fat. OFC, vmPFC, hippocampus, striatum, and VTA DA neurons provide slowly varying predictions of expected value and context/state identity. Empirically, many DRN 5-HT neurons ramp ahead of expected rewards and track discounted state value over multi-second windows, complementary to dopamine’s fast, derivative-like RPE bursts. Locus coeruleus (NE) and basal forebrain ACh gauge the price of time (what else you could be doing) and the precision of beliefs. High tonic NE (high opportunity cost) can bias 5-HT systems to truncate horizons (switch sooner), while low NE enables the serotonin system to support long, persistent policies. Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) and other chronobiological inputs give serotonin a very literal clock, modulating the affordable horizon across the day (and across sleep pressure). On top of its access to rich value, cost, threat, and interoceptive signals, serotonin’s position as a long-horizon state-value estimator reflects three additional specialties: Slow biophysics: 5-HT neurons exhibit prominent after-depolarizations, calcium-dependent plateau potentials, metabotropic receptor kinetics, and recurrent raphe->raphe loops that naturally low-pass filter inputs. That turns fast cortical/striatal value signals into slow ramps that look like multi-second discounted value traces. Metabotropic, diffuse, extrasynaptic signaling: 5-HT is often volume-transmitted; its receptors are mostly slow GPCRs. That pushes it toward setting global control knobs (discount, patience, planning depth, quitting thresholds) rather than encoding moment-to-moment spikes of information. Division of labor with dopamine: It’s metabolically and computationally efficient to let DA carry the derivative (error/novelty/uncertainty) while 5-HT carries the integral (sustained value/persistence), solving a classic control problem (PD vs. I terms) at the algorithmic level. Even if DRN computes a broadly similar "long-horizon value" signal, spatial gradients in projections, receptors, and transporters make its effects highly region-specific: Medial/ventral DRN neurons preferentially project to limbic cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, whereas lateral "wing" DRN neurons target basal ganglia and sensorimotor territories. Thus, patience/persistence signals can be stronger for cognitive/affective control vs. action selection, or vice versa, depending on context. 5-HT2A receptors are enriched in association cortex (especially layer V pyramidal neurons), promoting excitation and cognitive flexibility, whereas 5-HT1A density is high in mPFC/hippocampus, producing inhibition and stability. A single ramping 5-HT waveform can therefore stabilize long-range planning circuits (via 1A) while loosening over-confident local attractors to encourage model-based reevaluation (via 2A). 5-HT1B receptors presynaptically modulate glutamate and dopamine release with a dorso-ventral gradient, letting serotonin tune exploration/exploitation differently in dorsal (habitual/model-free) vs ventral (goal-directed/model-based) striatum. Regions with higher densities of serotonin transporters (SERT) will experience briefer, sharper 5-HT transients; low-SERT territories will see longer, more integrative signals-effectively spatially varying time constants for the same raphe output. Mood Phenomenologically, mood looks like the low-pass, circuit-weighted integral of serotonin’s long-horizon value estimates: when tonic 5-HT-especially in mPFC/hippocampus via 5-HT1A and 5-HT4/6/7-signals that future returns exceed opportunity costs, networks settle into an "optimistic, patient" attractor; when tone falls, or LC-NE/habenular/SCN inputs truncate the affordable horizon, the running estimate of future value collapses and mood drifts negative, yielding impatience and impulsivity. Phasic 5-HT rides on this baseline as micro-updates, but slow GPCR kinetics, somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptor feedback, and raphe->raphe recurrence set a long averaging window-explaining why SSRIs raise extracellular 5-HT rapidly yet improve mood only after weeks, when autoreceptors desensitize and downstream plasticity (e.g., BDNF upregulation, spine remodeling, hippocampal pattern separation) retunes priors away from pessimistic predictions. Spatial/receptor gradients let the same waveform stabilize cognition (5-HT1A-heavy mPFC) or promote flexible reappraisal (5-HT2A-rich association cortex), aligning psychedelic 5-HT2A agonism’s acute emotional lability with its longer-term antidepressant plasticity. Trait-level variation in SERT expression, raphe-amygdala coupling, and metabolic/interoceptive inputs effectively lengthen or shorten serotonin’s temporal integration window, shifting baseline mood by biasing how far ahead-and how hopefully-the system looks. Social cognition Dense 5-HT projections blanket canonical social hubs-anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), orbitofrontal cortex, amygdala, hippocampus CA2, nucleus accumbens and medial septum-where phasic bursts or slow ramps re-weight how these nodes integrate social cues. In awake humans, sub-second microdialysis in substantia nigra shows that serotonin tracks the current value of offers during an ultimatum game, while neighbouring dopamine encodes rapid prediction-errors-evidence that 5-HT supplies a slowly integrating "state value" channel even for abstract, strategic exchanges with other people 12 , 13 . A century of ethology already hinted that the raphe sets the pecking order: elevating central 5-HT in vervet monkeys flips subordinates into alpha-like behaviour, whereas depletion has the opposite effect. Modern PET-fMRI in humans extends the story: individuals with low serotonin-transporter (SERT) availability in dorsal raphe show larger ventral-striatal signals when computing opponents’ ranks, implying that higher extracellular 5-HT dampens the neural salience-and perhaps the emotional sting-of losing status. More broadly, 5-HT1B signalling in orbitofrontal/violence circuits restrains impulsive aggression, while 5-HT2C activity in lateral habenula biases surrender when the cost of further conflict outweighs potential gain 14 , 15 . Prosociality is not a monolith, and serotonin’s bidirectional control becomes obvious when one parses the behaviours. In rodents, activating dorsal-raphe -> ACC fibres via 5-HT1A/2A receptors promotes consolation grooming after a cage-mate’s distress, yet the same manipulations can blunt vicarious freezing (an empathy-like read-out), suggesting parallel channels for "soothing" versus "feeling" the other’s pain. Chemically forcing a massive 5-HT surge with MDMA shifts the balance toward affiliative approach: nucleus-accumbens release potentiates oxytocin-driven circuits and produces measurable empathy-like behaviours even in mice. Conversely, raising tonic 5-HT in the ACC can reduce empathic responses in observational-fear paradigms, underscoring receptor- and circuit-specific polarity 12 . Social memory-remembering who a conspecific is-also leans on serotonin. Median-raphe terminals that release 5-HT onto medial-septal neurons gate plasticity at septum->CA2 synapses via 5-HT1B receptors; optogenetically amplifying this signal stabilises the memory trace for familiar individuals, whereas suppressing it hastens forgetting. Such circuitry places serotonin as a molecular "notary" that certifies social encounters worth storing, dovetailing with CA2’s unique role in identity coding 16 . Finally, serotonin shapes the computations that let us navigate norms, fairness and cooperation. Acute tryptophan depletion famously makes people reject almost any unfair split in the ultimatum game; the 2024 microdialysis study reveals the flip side-higher in-situ 5-HT flattens sensitivity to inequity by keeping the integrated value signal lofty when offers are stingy. This slow, context-aware coding is well-suited for adjusting long-horizon strategies such as tit-for-tat reciprocity, and it interacts with oxytocin in nuanced ways-baseline 5-HT4-receptor binding predicts who will (or will not) show oxytocin-induced shifts in affective bias 13 , 17 . In sum, serotonin supplies a suite of social control knobs: it tempers aggression and dominance drives, stamps social encounters into memory, toggles consolation versus empathy, and biases moral-economic choices toward patience and cooperation-all via projection- and receptor-specific computations layered atop the long-horizon value code detailed in the preceding section.

title: Oxytocin & Vasopressin
text: Oxytocin Froemke Overview, machinery, and pathways Oxytocin (OXT) and arginine-vasopressin (AVP) are evolutionarily ancient nonapeptides synthesized primarily by magnocellular neurons in the paraventricular (PVN) and supraoptic (SON) nuclei of the hypothalamus, with additional parvocellular populations projecting within the CNS. They are released both peripherally (from the posterior pituitary into blood) and centrally (from axons, dendrites, and even somata), where they act as slow neuromodulators that reshape large-scale network dynamics governing homeostasis, reproduction, stress, and-most famously-social cognition and attachment. A central theme that has replaced the simplistic "oxytocin = prosocial hormone" story is context-, circuit-, sex-, and species-specific modulation of social salience: OXT and AVP bias which stimuli are emphasized, how long they are tracked, and what control policies are expressed, rather than directly causing "trust" or "love." 2 , 3 , 4 Magnocellular OXT/AVP neurons fire high-frequency bursts to eject peptide into the bloodstream, but they can also release peptide locally from dendrites 5 and somata, creating local neuromodulatory fields that operate on different spatiotemporal scales than synaptic transmission. Dendritic release is activity- and state-dependent (e.g., "primed" by prior depolarization or intracellular Ca2+ mobilization), can auto-excite neighboring OXT cells, and produces volume transmission that bathes millimeter-scale territories for tens of seconds to minutes-timescales that are orders of magnitude slower than classical fast synaptic transmission. Central peptide can also move along perivascular spaces, raising the possibility of BBB-adjacent transport routes that complicate "intranasal oxytocin" pharmacokinetics 6 . Oxytocin (OXTR) and vasopressin (V1aR/V1bR/V2R) receptors are class-A GPCRs with biased, context-sensitive signaling. OXTR couples predominantly to Gq/11 -> PLC β \beta -> IP3/Ca2+ and DAG/PKC, but can also recruit Gi/o and β \beta -arrestin scaffolds that drive ERK/PI3K-AKT. Depending on cell type and state, oxytocin rebalances excitation-inhibition-often via interneurons-can potentiate NMDA currents, and can facilitate LTP, but it does not uniformly "disinhibit" circuits. Vasopressin V1aR (the most abundant CNS receptor) is likewise Gq/11-coupled, engaging Ca2+/PKC, ERK, and Rho/ROCK pathways to increase neuronal excitability and glutamate release, and is implicated in social memory and vigilance/aggression in a region- and sex-dependent manner (e.g., lateral septum, hippocampal CA2). V1bR (also Gq/11) amplifies CRH->ACTH release in pituitary and modulates stress-linked hippocampal/PFC plasticity. V2R is Gs->cAMP/PKA, canonically mediating AQP2 trafficking in kidney and is sparsely expressed in brain, where limited evidence suggests it can influence ion channels and plasticity thresholds. All four receptors desensitize via GRK/ β \beta -arrestin, and OXTR-V1aR heterodimerization has been reported to bias G-protein usage, offering a molecular foothold for the striking region/sex/state dependence of oxytocin/vasopressin effects. Parvocellular OXT/AVP neurons project widely to limbic, striatal, and brainstem targets (e.g., amygdala, BNST, nucleus accumbens, VTA, PAG), while magnocellular cells mainly project to the posterior pituitary but still communicate centrally via dendritic release. On the postsynaptic side, species- and strain-specific receptor maps-especially V1aR and OXTR densities in regions like the lateral septum, nucleus accumbens, anterior hypothalamus, and prefrontal cortex-predict social organization (e.g., monogamy vs. promiscuity, paternal care, territorial aggression) in voles and other mammals. These spatial gradients are a large part of why translational claims from rodent OXT/AVP studies to humans routinely overfit 7 , 8 , 9 . Signaling social salience, among other functions Peripherally, OXT drives uterine contractions and milk let-down; AVP (a.k.a. antidiuretic hormone) controls water retention and vascular tone via V2 and V1 receptors, respectively. Centrally, both peptides also tune feeding, energy expenditure, thermoregulation, nociception, and autonomic output via hypothalamic and brainstem targets 10 , 11 . PVN parvocellular OXT and AVP co-regulate CRH neurons, sculpting HPA axis gain. AVP often amplifies CRH actions during chronic stress (via V1b receptors), whereas OXT can buffer anxiety and dampen amygdala reactivity-but again, effects are sex-, state-, and circuit-dependent. In males, AVP pathways to the extended amygdala and hypothalamus are particularly implicated in defensive aggression and vigilance 12 , 10 . Classic vole work tied pair bonding to nucleus accumbens OXTR and to AVP V1aR expression patterns, with OXT/V1aR manipulations biasing partner preference, paternal care, and selective aggression in pair-bonded males. However, CRISPR OXTR-knockout prairie voles still form pair bonds, upending the "OXTR is necessary for bonding" dogma and suggesting redundancy/degeneracy in peptide-dopamine circuits-or developmental compensation. Follow-ups show nuanced, sex-specific deficits (e.g., consoling behavior disrupted in male but not female OXTR-KO voles), reframing OXT’s role as modulatory and developmentally plastic rather than strictly causal. AVP in the anterior hypothalamus remains a key driver of mate-guarding aggression after bonding 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 . Human intranasal OXT (IN-OXT) studies originally reported boosts in trust, empathy, and emotion recognition, but effect sizes are small, heterogeneous, and strongly moderated by task, sex, personality/clinical phenotype, and phase of reward processing (larger during "liking"/consummatory phases). The Social Salience Hypothesis proposes that OXT heightens the informational weight of socially relevant cues, whether positive (affiliation) or negative (threat, envy, in-group bias), by acting in mesolimbic and salience networks. Large-sample, longer-duration IN-OXT imaging studies increasingly show circuit-specific modulation (amygdala, insula, ACC, striatum, salience and attention networks) rather than uniform behavioral effects, and several meta-analyses question whether appreciable peptide reaches the brain at typical doses 4 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 2 . OXT and AVP interact with dopamine in the nucleus accumbens and VTA to tag social cues with value, biasing credit assignment and plasticity in cortico-striatal loops during attachment formation and social learning. In hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, OXTR/V1aR signaling can shift E/I balance and cAMP/PKA pathways, altering stability of working memory ensembles and gating plasticity in ways that mirror other neuromodulators (DA, NE, ACh) but with strong selectivity for socially inferred latent states 9 , 12 . AVP systems are typically more sexually dimorphic (and often male-biased) than OXT, with V1aR-rich circuits in hypothalamus, BNST, and amygdala linked to male aggression and territoriality. Aging, pubertal hormones, and early-life adversity remodel receptor expression and coupling, contributing to age-dependent and sex-dependent behavioral effects of IN-OXT observed in humans. Developmental knockouts (and compensation) warn against simple one-gene/one-behavior mappings 15 , 10 , 19 . Overall, oxytocin and vasopressin are state-dependent neuromodulators that bias the gain, plasticity thresholds, and E/I balance of circuits that compute social value, vigilance, and attachment, while coupling those computations to bodily budgets (energy, osmolality, lactation/parturition). In predictive-processing terms, they likely tune the effective precision of social prediction errors (i.e., social salience), and-largely through interactions with dopamine, noradrenaline, and the HPA axis-shift exploration/exploitation, persistence, and learning in affiliative vs. defensive regimes. Their control is robust and partially degenerate: disrupting a single receptor (e.g., OXTR) can leave core social behaviors like pair bonding partly intact via compensatory AVP or other circuit mechanisms, even though quantitative phenotypes change.
