title: Computational Integration
text: The individual stories above (DA = RPEs, NE = unexpected uncertainty/adaptive gain, ACh = expected uncertainty/encoding mode, 5-HT = long-horizon value & cost, OXT/AVP = social precision & homeostatic coupling) are only locally true. In vivo, these systems talk constantly-through direct synapses, reciprocal hypothalamic/brainstem loops, heteroreceptor complexes, shared second-messenger pathways, and common targets (PFC, striatum, hippocampus, amygdala). The result is not six independent "knobs," but a low-dimensional control manifold that continuously retunes a high-dimensional world-model. A useful way to see this manifold is to map each transmitter to a small set of algorithmic hyperparameters and then watch how they co-regulate them as contexts, internal states, and horizons change. In reinforcement-learning terms, dopamine mostly carries and gates error terms (derivatives of value and action expectations), serotonin biases the discount factor / planning depth and opportunity-cost accounting, noradrenaline sets learning rates and policy temperature in proportion to unexpected uncertainty, acetylcholine sets Kalman-like gains under expected uncertainty and flips the cortex between encoding and retrieval regimes, and oxytocin/vasopressin apply precision weighting to the "social slice" of the generative model, while coupling these computations to bodily budgets and life-history phase. Multiple recurrent motifs make these systems interdependent: First, descending cortical control: medial and orbital PFC, ACC, and insula project densely to VTA/SNc, LC, DRN/MRN, and basal forebrain, allowing high-level beliefs about task demands, costs, social context, and model adequacy to bias the entire neuromodulatory panel. Second, brainstem/hypothalamic hubs (PVN, LH, PAG, BNST, habenula/RMTg) integrate interoception, stress hormones, circadian signals, and nociception, and then co-drive LC, raphe, and VTA-explaining why energetic scarcity, inflammation, or chronic stress simultaneously steepen discounting (reduced 5-HT function), raise opportunity-cost signaling (increased tonic NE), and flatten dopaminergic exploration bursts. Third, striatal convergence: cholinergic interneurons, comprising only  1-2% of striatal neurons, exert outsized influence by directly shaping dopamine release dynamics. When these giant aspiny interneurons pause their tonic firing ( 5-10 Hz), the resulting dip in nicotinic receptor activation on dopaminergic terminals creates a brief window of enhanced dopamine release probability. This pause-triggered dopamine surge can occur even without changes in VTA/SNc firing, effectively allowing the striatum to locally compute its own teaching signals 1 . The temporal precision is remarkable: cholinergic pauses lasting 50-200ms can triple dopamine release within specific striatal compartments while leaving neighboring regions unaffected. This cholinergic gating becomes even more sophisticated through muscarinic signaling. M4 receptors on spiny projection neurons suppress cAMP when acetylcholine is high, effectively raising the threshold for dopamine-dependent plasticity. When cholinergic interneurons pause, this brake releases just as dopamine surges, creating a narrow temporal window where learning is maximally enabled-a molecular implementation of an AND gate for credit assignment. Push-pull dynamics in PFC In prefrontal cortex, dopamine and norepinephrine implement complementary control over working memory dynamics despite both originating from catecholaminergic precursors 2 . The inverted-U relationships governing their effects operate at different set points: optimal dopamine levels for working memory stability occur at moderate D1 receptor occupancy, while norepinephrine’s sweet spot for sustained attention requires lower tonic levels with preserved phasic responsiveness. Crucially, these systems cross-regulate each other’s effects. High tonic norepinephrine (via α \alpha 2A receptors) can functionally oppose D1 signaling by strengthening HCN channel conductances, effectively raising the bar for dopamine to stabilize persistent activity. This creates a push-pull dynamic where stress-induced norepinephrine release not only signals model uncertainty but actively destabilizes working memory representations-adaptively favoring cognitive flexibility when current strategies fail 3 . Temporal hierarchies and dependencies Interactions are stratified by kinetics. Fast, phasic NE (tens to hundreds of ms) can momentarily override cortical attractors ("network reset"), after which sub-second ACh transients sharpen sensory gain to re-sample the world with high fidelity. Phasic DA (100-300 ms) then labels the surprising sample with an error signal for synaptic credit assignment. Over seconds to minutes, tonic DA biases vigor/exploitation, tonic NE sets the organism’s learning rate and exploration drive, tonic 5-HT integrates value and cost to determine patience and quitting thresholds, and minutes-to-hours OXT/AVP fields weight social cues and link policy to bodily budgets. The LC-NE system acts as a critical state switch in this hierarchy. When tonic norepinephrine rises (signaling persistent model failure), it not only increases cortical gain but also modulates both dopaminergic and serotonergic signaling. High NE suppresses dopamine neuron firing via α \alpha 2 receptors while simultaneously truncating serotonin’s temporal integration window-effectively telling the brain to abandon long-term plans and focus on immediate model revision. This creates a natural progression from patient, model-based planning (high 5-HT, low NE) through focused execution (balanced DA/ACh, moderate NE) to exploration and model updating (high NE, suppressed 5-HT). The whole stack sits on even slower steroid and peptide backgrounds (glucocorticoids, leptin/ghrelin, cytokines) that reshape receptor densities, intracellular cascades, and even cell-type abundance-slowly moving the operating point of the control manifold. In engineering terms, the brain implements a hierarchical PID/meta-controller: DA supplies largely derivative-like (error/change) terms, 5-HT contributes an integral-like persistence/value term, NE adjusts the adaptive gain and step size, ACh tunes the Kalman gain / observation model, and OXT/AVP reweight a socially restricted precision channel. Convergent Modulation of Shared Effectors Multiple neuromodulators often converge on the same molecular targets, creating rich combinatorial effects. Both dopamine (via D1) and norepinephrine (via β \beta receptors) activate PKA signaling, but with different spatial patterns and temporal dynamics. In hippocampal CA1, the coincidence of dopaminergic novelty signals and noradrenergic arousal signals synergistically enhances LTP through PKA, but only when acetylcholine is low (permitting strong Schaffer collateral transmission). This three-way interaction ensures that memories are preferentially strengthened when they are both novel (DA), behaviorally significant (NE), and arriving via external input rather than internal retrieval (low ACh). Precision, uncertainty, and arbitration Framed in predictive processing/active inference, the core computation these systems share is precision control-i.e., setting the gain on different prediction errors and priors. NE inflates precision on sensory PEs when the model fails unexpectedly; ACh inflates precision on sensory channels when high noise is expected (encoding mode) and deflates top-down predictions; DA sets precision on value/state-transition PEs; 5-HT calibrates the precision of long-horizon value estimates vs. opportunity costs; OXT/AVP set precision on social prediction errors and on the interoceptive priors that couple social policies to bodily budgets. Arbitration between model-free vs. model-based control, or between exploitation vs. exploration, is therefore naturally a chemically implemented precision game: high tonic NE + low 5-HT shortens horizons and heats policies; high 5-HT + moderate DA + low NE cools policies and deepens planning; high ACh with low DA locks the system into externally driven encoding; high OXT/AVP with DA/OFC engagement increases the precision of conspecific-related latent states, biasing credit assignment toward social cues. To summarize, the neuromodulators do not form six orthogonal axes but a coordinated, partially redundant, partially specialized control sheet that lies on top of cortex-basal ganglia-hippocampus loops. It allocates precision, time, energy, and social weight; it partitions surprise into kinds (expected vs. unexpected, appetitive vs. aversive, private vs. social); and it ensures that a tiny number of slow, low-bandwidth channels can steer a vast, fast, content-rich world model without ever needing to encode that content themselves Example Behavioral States and Their Neuromodulatory Signatures Treat the following "neuromodulatory cocktails" as coarse heuristics, not laws. Active Exploration/Foraging High tonic NE: Elevated LC firing increases arousal and sampling behavior Low-moderate tonic DA: Permits exploration rather than exploitation High phasic DA: Responds to novel stimuli and unexpected rewards Low 5-HT: Reduces behavioral inhibition and patience Moderate ACh: Balances external attention with memory retrieval Focused Task Learning Moderate tonic DA: Maintains motivation without compulsive focus High phasic DA: Strong RPE signaling for learning Low-moderate tonic NE: Optimal for working memory stability High phasic ACh: Enhanced sensory processing during cue presentation Moderate 5-HT: Balances immediate rewards with future costs Acute Stress/Threat Response Very high phasic NE: Massive LC activation, network reset Suppressed DA: Reduced reward seeking Low 5-HT: Shortened temporal horizons High ACh: Enhanced sensory vigilance Elevated AVP: Defensive aggression, territoriality Suppressed OXT: Reduced social approach Focused exploitation/Consummatory Behavior High tonic DA: Sustained motivation and vigor; sits near the D1 "inverted-U" optimum in PFC to stabilize task rules Low tonic / high phasic NE: boosting moment-to-moment gain without globally heating policy temperature High 5-HT: Behavioral persistence Moderate ACh: supporting selective attention without fully flipping cortex into an encoding-dominant regime Context-dependent OXT: Elevated during social feeding Chronic Stress/Learned Helplessness Chronically elevated tonic NE: Persistent hypervigilance Blunted DA responses: Anhedonia, reduced RPEs Depleted 5-HT: Loss of behavioral inhibition Dysregulated ACh: Impaired attention switching Altered OXT/AVP: Often reduced OXT, elevated AVP

title: Neural Representations
text: Defining "neural representation": neural dynamics that carry information about internal or external states Hierarchical Flows of Human Cortical Activity Overview The brain’s ability to construct world models relies fundamentally on how information is encoded and represented in neural populations Representations must balance multiple constraints: metabolic efficiency, computational flexibility, noise robustness, and behavioral relevance Neural representations exist at multiple scales: from single neurons to population codes to large-scale network states The format of representations constrains what computations can be performed and what behaviors can be supported Neurons, the primary signaling units of the nervous system, communicate through sequences of electrical impulses known as action potentials, or spikes. The information carried by these spikes is thought to be encoded through several principal mechanisms. Rate coding posits that the frequency or rate of action potentials conveys information, with a higher intensity of stimulus typically eliciting a higher firing rate. This scheme, while robust to noise due to its reliance on an averaged signal, may be less efficient in conveying rapidly changing or precise information. In contrast, temporal coding emphasizes the precise timing of spikes, or the intervals between them, as carrying significant information. Furthermore, population codes involve the combined activity of many neurons, where information is represented by the pattern of activity across an entire ensemble rather than by any single neuron alone The brain does not rely on a single coding scheme but employs a flexible combination of these strategies, adapting to the specific informational demands of different contexts, brain regions, and the nature of the information being processed. For instance, rapid and precise information required for fine motor control or the early stages of sensory processing might leverage temporal codes, allowing for swift and detailed representation. Conversely, more stable, abstract concepts that form the enduring components of a world model might be effectively represented by the average firing rates in specific, dedicated neural populations. Moreover, the choice of neural code likely co-evolved with the types of synaptic learning rules most effective for modifying and refining those representations. Information encoded primarily by firing rates might be more amenable to Hebbian-like plasticity, where synaptic strengths are adjusted based on the co-activation of pre- and post-synaptic neurons. In contrast, representations relying on the precise timing of spikes would necessitate learning rules sensitive to these temporal relationships, such as spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). This suggests a synergistic relationship: the manner in which information is encoded influences which learning algorithms are most effective for updating the world model, and conversely, the available learning mechanisms might favor or constrain the adoption of certain coding schemes for particular functions within the model. Slow and fast representational dynamics: Sub-second activity states in primary sensory cortices track rapidly changing signals, whereas vmPFC, posterior medial cortex, and hippocampus exhibit multi-second to days-long drifts that knit together scenes into narratives. These nested time-scales align with anatomical hierarchies, enabling the simultaneous representation of the immediate present and broader situational context.

title: Basic Representational Mediums
text:
Neural population activity for memory: Properties, computations, and codes Silences, spikes and bursts: Three-part knot of the neural code Rate Coding and temporal coding Rate coding Information encoded in firing rates averaged over time windows ( 50-500ms) Robust to noise but limited temporal precision Often associated with the intensity of a stimulus or the strength of a represented feature Most common in cortical areas for stable feature representation Energy-efficient for sustained representations Temporal Coding Information in precise spike timing, not just the rate Includes spike synchrony, phase-of-firing (e.g., relative to neural oscillations like theta or gamma), and specific inter-spike intervals Phase-of-firing coding: spikes locked to oscillatory phases (theta, gamma); synchronized circuits Spike timing dependent plasticity (STDP) suggests temporal precision matters Population Coding and Cell Assemblies Noisy single neurons become reliable when pooled across tens-thousands of cells. Population-vector and probabilistic-population-code formalisms describe how stimulus features reside in the geometry of ensemble activity, while Hebbian plasticity binds repeatedly co-active neurons into enduring "cell assemblies" that can later be reactivated during recall or planning, supporting attractor dynamics, error correction, and pattern completion Basis for most modern decoding approaches Sparse vs distributed representations Overall: only  1-5% of neurons active at any given time, enabling high representational capacity while minimizing metabolic costs and interference Early sensory areas favour dense codes that maximise fidelity under wiring constraints, whereas hippocampal and higher association areas adopt sparse codes ( < 5 % <5\% of neurons active at a time) that minimise interference between memories, facilitate pattern separation, and economise metabolic cost. Biological systems span five orders of magnitude in coding density, trading energy cost for noise robustness, generalization, and rapid readout Enables smooth generalization The degree of sparsity also depends on how novel a stimulus is; novel stimuli will have sparser codes due to less resonance with the existing conceptual mesh, which is mitigated through gradual integration Neuromodulators control sparsity: During states of focused attention and waking exploration, cholinergic input from the medial septum raises the threshold for recurrent excitation within CA3 and CA1 networks. This heightened threshold reduces the likelihood that overlapping populations of place cells fire together, enforcing a sparse code that’s ideal for encoding new spatial experiences. Conversely, when acetylcholine levels drop during slow-wave sleep, CA3 recurrent collaterals become more excitable, promoting dense, synchronized bursts (sharp-wave ripples) that facilitate memory consolidation. In essence, acetylcholine dynamically gates the transition between dense replay (sleep) and sparse encoding (wake), controlling how many neurons coactivate and thus modulating representational sparsity on the order of seconds to minutes. Dopamine, too, exerts control over sparsity, particularly in the prefrontal cortex and striatal circuits. By binding to D1 versus D2 receptors, dopamine shifts the balance between excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons, adjusting overall network gain. Under high-dopamine conditions-such as during reward anticipation-prefrontal neurons adopt a higher excitability state but also sharpen their tuning curves, meaning each neuron responds more selectively to its preferred input. That selective tuning yields a sparse code: fewer neurons respond strongly to particular task-relevant cues, bolstering signal-to-noise and improving working memory robustness. When dopamine levels drop, tuning broadens, allowing a denser ensemble to participate but at the cost of decreased selectivity. Thus, dopamine dynamically alters sparsity to match behavioral demands-tight, sparse representations during high-reward or high-attention situations, and more distributed representations when flexibility is needed. Point attractors: Stable memories, categorical decisions Line/ring attractors: Working memory, head direction Chaotic attractors: Flexible computation, exploration Oscillations and phase locking Neural traveling waves in cortex: Network mechanisms and potential roles in neural computation Prefrontal cortex temporally multiplexes slow and fast dynamics in value learning and memory Resonant hierarchies: a multiscale framework for oscillatory dynamics in the brain Oscillatory control of cortical space as a computational dimension Cortical traveling waves in time and space The neocortex exhibits rhythmic activity at multiple frequencies: Gamma (30-100 Hz): Local computation, attention, binding Beta (12-30 Hz): Motor control, status quo maintenance Alpha (8-12 Hz): Inhibition, sensory gating Theta (4-8 Hz): Memory encoding, navigation Delta (0.5-4 Hz): Sleep, long-range coordination These aren’t noise-they serve functional roles in: Gating information flow between regions Temporal binding of distributed representations Multiplexing multiple computations Memory consolidation during sleep Definitions and functions Neural oscillations are rhythmic fluctuations of neural activity, occurring across a wide range of frequencies. Classic electrophysiology defines bands such as delta (∼0-4Hz), theta (∼4-8Hz), alpha (∼8-12Hz), beta (∼12-30Hz), and gamma (>30Hz) 8 . These oscillatory patterns are observed at multiple scales - from local field potentials to EEG - effectively bridging micro-level neuron spiking and macro-level brain dynamics 9 . Far from being mere epiphenomena, oscillations are increasingly recognized as playing integral roles in brain function. Mechanistically, they stem from circuit interactions (e.g. recurrent excitation/inhibition loops) that produce rhythmic cycles of neural excitability. In essence, oscillations modulate when neurons are closer to or farther from firing threshold, creating repeating windows of high and low spiking probability. This means oscillatory phase is deeply tied to neuronal excitability: "they move the membrane potential towards and away from the spiking threshold." 10 . In other words, oscillations provide a temporal scaffolding that organizes neural firing in time. Beyond shifting single-cell excitability, population rhythms create spatially patterned electric fields that coordinate large ensembles almost instantaneously, aligning windows of high gain across millimeters of cortex-an emergent property not reducible to individual spikes 11 . Phase locking refers to the synchronization of oscillation phase across different neurons or regions - effectively aligning their high-excitability periods. This synchronization is thought to be crucial for communication in neural networks. According to the "communication through coherence" hypothesis, coherent oscillations enable selective information routing: inputs arriving at a target area’s excitable phase (i.e. when its oscillation is at the optimal phase) are transmitted most effectively 12 . For two neural groups to exchange signals reliably, their oscillations must be appropriately phase-locked so that spikes from the sender arrive during the receiver’s peak excitability. Empirical evidence strongly supports this idea. For example, synchronized gamma-band oscillations between visual cortex areas V1 and V4 have been shown to improve visual processing - when the two areas’ gamma rhythms are in phase prior to a stimulus change, animals detect the change faster, whereas misaligned phases correlate with slower reaction times 13 . This suggests that inter-area phase alignment gates effective connectivity: coherence does not just time when signals pass; alpha/beta coherence also sculpts where they can pass. Under the "spatial computing" paradigm, top-down control is implemented as spatial patterns of alpha/beta that transiently veto or permit local gamma bursts, effectively laying a stencil over cortex so only selected columns express content during their optimal phase. This converts cortical space itself into a computational dimension for selective routing and gating 14 , 6 , 11 . High coherence between brain regions often predicts better performance on cognitive tasks, consistent with the view that oscillatory phase locking underlies attention and neural communication. Neural oscillations also contribute to how information is represented and grouped in the brain. A prominent example is feature binding in perception: neurons encoding different features of the same object can oscillate in synchrony (particularly in the gamma range), effectively "tagging" those features as belonging together. Classic studies found that neurons in visual cortex synchronize their gamma oscillations when an animal perceives a coherent object, suggesting gamma synchrony is a mechanism for binding distributed features into one percept 8 . In practice, feature binding rides on where alpha/beta releases cortical patches from suppression; the spatial pattern of that release determines which assemblies can synchronize in gamma at a given moment 11 . Oscillatory timing may also help segregate distinct representations: by assigning different phases or frequencies to different information streams, the brain can avoid interference between concurrent signals. In the prefrontal cortex, for instance, neurons have been observed to use phase-specific firing to encode multiple items in working memory. In primate PFC, information about multiple items is time-division multiplexed: item-specific spikes ride on distinct gamma bursts locked to different phases of a slower carrier, while intermittent beta bursts gate which cortical patches are allowed to express those gamma packets 15 . The first item’s spikes were concentrated at an earlier phase of the cycle and the second item at a later phase, implying a phase-of-firing code that multiplexed two memory representations without confusion. By oscillatory phase-locking of spikes, the brain can thus disambiguate multiple pieces of information held at once. This principle - using oscillation phase as an extra coding dimension - appears to be widespread, allowing temporal ordering of spikes to signal different content even if average firing rates are similar. This regime enables rapid remapping by changing the spatial pattern of beta without relearning the content itself. Oscillations across different frequency bands often interact to support complex cognitive operations. Cross-frequency coupling provides a way to link fast, local processes with slower, broad coordination. In the hippocampus and cortex, for example, high-frequency gamma bursts (which accompany local neuronal ensembles firing) are often nested within slower theta oscillation cycles 16 . The slower rhythm (theta,  6-8Hz) can modulate the amplitude or timing of the faster gamma, effectively organizing sequential neural firing within each theta cycle (a phenomenon important for episodic memory encoding) 16 . Such theta-gamma coupling is hypothesized to underlie the neural coding of sequences - e.g. during navigation, successive places along a route may be activated on successive gamma sub-cycles of each theta wave (more on this later!). More broadly, many brain regions share a common set of rhythms (delta, theta, gamma) that appear during specific behavioral states to orchestrate memory operations 16 . During active wakefulness (and REM sleep), the "fast" mode of network oscillations emerges: hippocampal and cortical circuits engage theta and gamma rhythms which are associated with effective encoding and retrieval of memories. By contrast, in slow-wave sleep the brain switches to a "slow" oscillatory mode (dominant delta waves and sporadic bursts) that supports memory consolidation. In all cases, oscillations serve as a timing infrastructure to coordinate memory systems - they constrain when neurons fire and thereby help organize the flow of information for encoding, consolidation, or recall. Notably, gamma oscillations are found in hippocampus, cortex, and striatum alike, where they compress neural spiking into brief bursts, while slower oscillations (theta, delta) modulate these bursts and align activity across regions. In summary, oscillations and phase locking appear to be fundamental organizational principles of the brain’s computations. By synchronizing neuronal activity in time, oscillations enable efficient communication, selection, and integration of information across neural circuits. Synchronized rhythms can flexibly route signals between regions (by opening and closing communication channels via phase alignment) 12 . They can group neurons into coherently firing assemblies that represent perceptual objects or memories, and can segregate different assemblies by assigning them different phases or frequencies. Oscillatory timing thus provides a multiplexing scheme for the brain’s encoding of information, adding a layer of temporal coding on top of average firing rates. How rhythms arise from circuit motifs, intrinsic cellular physics, and neuromodulation At the microcircuit level, the most ubiquitous generator of cortical rhythm is the excitatory-inhibitory loop. In PING (pyramidal-interneuron gamma), local excitation transiently drives fast-spiking PV+ interneurons; the resulting perisomatic GABAA inhibition silences the population and, as it decays, the cycle repeats. In ING (interneuron-network gamma), mutually coupled interneurons (helped by gap junctions) can oscillate with minimal excitatory drive. The dominant clock in both cases is set by synaptic kinetics and delays: the decay time of GABAA currents ( 6-12 ms in vivo) plus axonal/dendritic conduction times places the natural frequency in the  30-90 Hz gamma range, while slower inhibition (GABAB), NMDA currents, and longer loops push networks toward beta/alpha. Stronger tonic excitation typically raises gamma frequency and lowers its power; weaker drive does the opposite-classic PING behavior. These principles, worked out in theory and slice/optogenetic work, now anchor most mechanistic accounts of fast rhythms 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 . Perisomatic PV+ inhibition gives gamma its precision, but electrical coupling between interneurons further boosts phase-locking and speed. PV-basket cells and chandelier cells are richly coupled by connexin-36 gap junctions; blocking these junctions degrades interneuron synchrony and weakens fast oscillations. In hippocampus, the sharp-wave ripple ( 140-200 Hz) exemplifies an extreme: tightly timed recurrent inhibition among PV basket cells can pace pyramidal populations at ripple frequencies; cutting PV-PV connections or perturbing their GABAA time constant desynchronizes the ripple 21 , 22 , 23 . Rhythmogenesis is not only a network property; single-cell intrinsic dynamics supply resonant preferences and rebound mechanisms that circuits recruit. Subthreshold membrane resonance arises when restorative currents (notably Ih and M-current IM) counteract capacitive lag, endowing neurons with band-pass impedance that peaks in theta-alpha or beta ranges depending on channel densities and dendritic morphology. These same currents bias spike timing to preferred phases when the cell sits in an oscillatory field. Separately, post-inhibitory rebound-driven by T-type Ca2+ channels, often in concert with Ih-turns inhibition into precise timing pulses; this is central to thalamic bursting and to thalamocortical alpha-like rhythms. Persistent Na+ currents and dendritic Ca2+ conductances can sustain or amplify subthreshold oscillations, further shaping local frequency content 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 . Specific long-range motifs favor particular bands. The septohippocampal loop (GABAergic and cholinergic neurons in medial septum entraining hippocampal interneurons and pyramids) acts as a theta-rate metronome; cooling the septum slows hippocampal theta with preserved phase lags, consistent with a pacemaker/organizer role 29 . Thalamocortical circuits, with low-threshold Ca2+ spikes in thalamic relay cells and inhibitory gating from the thalamic reticular nucleus, readily generate alpha and spindles and impose phasic inhibition onto cortex 30 . Cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamic loops naturally express beta, especially under dopaminergic control; in sensorimotor systems, beta power/coherence scales with maintenance or withholding of action and can become pathologically exaggerated in Parkinsonism 31 . Cortex itself is spectrally laminated. Superficial layers tend to express gamma (driven by feedforward input and PING-like microcircuits), whereas deep layers favor alpha-beta that broadcast feedback predictions and top-down control. Models and laminar recordings show deep-layer alpha/beta phasically suppress superficial gamma/spiking, yielding a multiplexed channel 32 , 33 , 34 . Beyond zero-lag synchrony, anatomical delays and spatial coupling make rhythms travel. Alpha, theta, and beta often propagate as traveling waves across cortex, sequencing distant columns by phase and turning space into a timing dimension for routing 35 , 36 . Connectome-constrained models and ECoG show that structural gradients steer wave direction and speed; in behaving primates, beta traveling waves in frontoparietal networks track recent reward history and working-memory demands 37 . In effect, traveling waves instantiate a spatiotemporal form of communication-through-coherence: with finite conduction delays, only particular phase offsets let inputs arrive during a target’s high-gain window, and the wave’s phase gradient supplies those offsets to open selective channels between areas. Finally, neuromodulators retune the whole dynamical substrate. Acetylcholine suppresses Im and some intracortical inhibition, increasing excitability and biasing networks toward high-frequency packets; in hippocampus, muscarinic drive can scale gamma power and septal cholinergic input promotes theta while suppressing ripples-consistent with an encoding-mode shift 38 , 39 . Norepinephrine flattens low-frequency synchronization and desynchronizes cortex during arousal surges, while sustained tone sets longer-lived gain states; pupil-linked LC activity tracks these shifts 39 . Dopamine in cortico-basal-ganglia loops modulates beta-band propensity and coherence, reshaping temporal control of movement and working memory 40 . By dialing channel conductances and E/I balance, neuromodulators move circuits across attractor regimes-altering not only which rhythms appear but their phase relations, cross-frequency coupling, and effective connectivity.

Methods like MARBLE capture local flow fields on the manifold, revealing that task switching corresponds to traversals along nearly orthogonal axes, minimizing interference. PFC representations Encodes task rules in low-dimensional subspaces; rather than hard-switching between task-specific encodings, brains seem to implement low-rank perturbations of population activity (see Rule et al., 2020; Aevermann et al., 2023). This allows for flexible reuse of shared representational axes with minimal interference During the delay of a sequence-reproduction task, activity in thousands of lateral-prefrontal neurons collapses into three nearly orthogonal, ring-shaped manifolds-one for each ordinal position-so that each item rotates within its own low-dimensional subspace without perturbing the others, revealing a factorised and flexible code for sequence working memory. Same idea: subspace coding; spiking activity is restricted to a low-dimensional subspace of the full high-dimensional population space (1D for each neuron) 15 Mixed selectivity: Cellular computations for complexity Optimally Structured Mixed Selectivity. A Normative Theory of Control in Neural Circuits Non-linear mixed selectivity: some neurons (especially those in control and associative regions) exhibit nonlinear tuning to mixtures of features (e.g stimulus, context, rule, reward; for example, a neuron that only responds to "butterfly" when it is first in the sequence 15 ). Such mixed selectivity inflates representational dimensionality so that simple linear readouts can realize a combinatorial explosion of possible policies. . A Review of Normative Grid Cell Theory Cells in the entorhinal cortex that tessellate space into a hexagonal coordinate system Hierarchical ring attractors; populations of grid cells organize as toroidal structures where two circular coordinates encode 2D position 22 Found in EC, primary input to HPC Spatial and semantic codes remain largely segregated through entorhinal cortex and only converge in hippocampus Place cells Mark discrete, context-dependent locations and replay trajectories during rest Include information on tasks and future states (SR) Discovery of spatial view neurons in hippo in the 80s/90s suggested allocentric map learrning Object-vector and boundary cells Landmark-vector cells encode allocentric distance-direction vectors to salient objects Boundary cells spike near environmental borders, supplying basis functions for path-planning Remapping and abstraction. Partial map remapping can occur in < 1 s after context change, while hippocampal ensembles preserve topological continuity across morphed environments-evidence for graph-like rather than metric storage 23 Models CSCG (Clone-Structured Cognitive Graph) Allocates multiple "clone" states to the same sensory cue so that identical observations can belong to distinct sequential contexts Learning splits/merges clones to minimise ambiguity, producing a higher-order transition graph that captures laps, routes, and task phases Naturally explains splitter cells, lap-specific place fields, landmark-vector and boundary tuning, and rapid context-specific remapping Supports probabilistic inference and flexible sequence generation; replay and prospective sweeping emerge from graph traversal Successor Representation (SR) Stores a matrix of discounted future-state occupancies under the current policy; rows correspond to predictive place fields, eigenvectors resemble grid cells The eigenvectors of SRs resemble grid cell firing patterns, even recapitulating hexagonality under biologically plausible constraints Tomov et al. (2021) tested whether humans use successor features (SFs) and generalized policy improvement (GPI) for cross-task transfer. Participants learned tasks sharing transition structures but differing in reward functions, then faced a novel task. Results showed "policy reuse" - participants favored training policies that performed better on the new task even when suboptimal, a key signature of GPI that couldn’t be explained by pure model-based or model-free approaches. The influential Temporal Context Model 24 of episodic memory can be re-expressed in a manner that resembles learning of a SR, with a temporal context vector serving as an eligibility trace 25 ; the resulting model spans the continuum between the vanilla SR and full model-based search. The degree to which vanilla SR vs model-based search is being used is determined by a scalar context drift parameter 25 Can be learned with a TD-like eligibility trace, enabling rapid value recomputation when reward locations (or task representations in general) shift Accounts for field skew opposite running direction, theta-sequence look-ahead, and grid-to-place transformations, but struggles with repeated cues because it assumes one latent state per observation Proposed as a middleman between the two canonical extremes of RL (model-free and model-based); supports lightweight planning in reasonably in-distribution scenarios by caching transition dynamics Fully model-based RL transcends the SR limitation where states that are not frequently visited under the policy (which the SR was learned with) are not fully accounted for Evidence for non-spatial SR-like representations in HPC-EC activity Much of the existing neuro work on SR-activity correspondences use the discrete SR; need to scale up to naturalistic experiments and expressive models Hybrid view DG/CA3 recurrent circuitry builds the CSCG-like higher-order graph; CA1/entorhinal layers can sum over that graph online to compute an SR when needed Combines context separation (clones) with efficient predictive evaluation (SR), reconciling fast remapping with stable predictive fields Predicts grid-cell eigenvectors arise from spectral decomposition of the clone graph, and that SR read-outs will shift when policy or context changes even if the underlying graph is unchanged Provides a unified explanation for both rapid context switching and habitual value-based navigation, matching a wide range of hippocampal and entorhinal data There isn’t (yet) a single, canonical "CSCG + SR" paper, but several papers lay out the two halves and then explicitly point to how they can be combined: The original predictive-map work-Stachenfeld, Botvinick & Gershman’s "The hippocampus as a predictive map"-shows how CA3-like recurrence can learn a successor-representation that CA1 can read out for planning and value learning. Gershman’s earlier temporal-context paper even sketches the circuit idea that CA3 provides an SR-like prediction that is compared against entorhinal sensory drive in CA1. On the higher-order-graph side, George and colleagues introduced the clone-structured cognitive graph (CSCG) and emphasised that its latent-state graph naturally overcomes the one-state-per-cue limitation of SR while still allowing an SR-style matrix to be computed over the clones for evaluation. The most explicit bridge is in the recent theory paper "Space is a Latent Sequence" (Raju & Guntupalli, 2024). They argue that a CSCG-like model is the underlying data structure and that an SR emerges as a summary statistic-essentially the "read-out" you get when you integrate future clone occupancy. Taken together, these papers provide the ingredients of the hybrid view even though no single article packages it under that label: CA3/DG circuitry can implement a clone-structured, higher-order graph; CA1 (and downstream cortico-striatal targets) can pool over that graph to produce the familiar successor-representation used for prediction, value transfer and planning. How a CSCG or SR could be learned in CA3 Review paper; ask o3 for full math and verify Several works have learned SFs with biologically plausible learning rules. Two notable examples: learning SFs with STDP; shown to be equivalent to TD with an eligibility trace. Learning SFs with STDP and theta sweeps leads to place cells that mirror biological behavior (also showed dorsal-ventral hippocampal gradient of place field sizes matches gradient of discount factors over SFs) The former shows that STDP mathematically implements temporal difference learning with an eligibility trace, where the eligibility trace is dynamically determined by the behavioral timescale T (states traversed slowly -> T=0 ; quickly, T=1) During normal behavior, place cells fire at constant rates for  100ms when the animal is in each location. The relatively long duration means the network performs TD(0) updates - learning through bootstrapping where each weight update depends on the next state’s predicted value. This allows learning connections across behavioral timescales (seconds) using millisecond STDP windows. During replay events, place cells fire precisely timed single spikes separated by  7ms intervals. These fast sequences correspond to TD(1)/Monte Carlo learning, which samples entire trajectories and averages the discounted state occupancies without bootstrapping. Synaptic weights converge to the successor representation matrix, where each element wij represents the expected future occupancy of state j starting from state i. Learning predictive cognitive maps with spiking neurons during behavior and replays - PMC The network automatically handles the bias-variance tradeoff: replay-based learning provides quick initial learning with low bias, while behavioral learning provides stable convergence with low variance. This means the same STDP rule automatically switches between these learning modes based purely on timing, without needing separate eligibility trace mechanisms. The biological timescales naturally implement the algorithmic distinction between bootstrapped and sampled learning. Replays can learn trajectories never directly experienced, enabling offline policy refinement and shortcut discovery. The framework naturally explains why replay frequency decreases in familiar environments - you need the low-bias Monte Carlo updates most when your initial estimates are poor. This bridges three levels of analysis: STDP at the implementation level, TD(λ) at the algorithmic level, and predictive cognitive maps at the computational level. Goal of the theta model is to make a biologically plausible model of HPC-EC that accounts for both path integration and sensory prediction 26 They model the HPC as a Helmholtz machine that uses theta rhythms to determine whether the model is in the "wake" (model learns to infer latents from sensory data) or "sleep" (model learns to generate sensory data from latents) phase; uses local learning rules and runs theta sweeps at 5-10Hz, both of which are biologically plausible Recent work shows that place fields follow a 3D hyperbolic geometry instead of Euclidean geometry; this results in an exponential number of small place fields relative to large place fields, given the same number of neurons. This representation far outpaces the capacity of a linear alternative and naturally supports a multiscale, deformable representation that expands dynamically with exploration experience 27 Dynamically expands in proportion to time spent exploring the environment Schemas (higher-order relational priors) Schema-based active inference supports rapid generalization of experience and frontal cortical coding of abstract structure By "schema" I mean an abstract, reusable model of relations among entities and events that the brain learns across many episodes and then uses as a prior when interpreting, storing, and retrieving new experiences. Classic examples are scripts like "restaurant" or "airport" (ordered subevents, role relations, typical contingencies), spatial layouts such as "grid-like apartment" or "four-way intersection," and task structures like "odor sequence -> choice -> outcome." Schemas speed learning (including one-shot assimilation), guide segmentation of continuous experience into events, bias attention toward expected relations, and provide scaffolds for recall and inference. In rodents, once a flavor-place "paired-associate" schema has formed, a single new pairing can be learned and consolidated rapidly; in humans, schematic knowledge boosts encoding of narrative details that fit the script. These effects place schemas squarely as priors over relational graphs-they encode expected node types (roles, states), edge types (temporal/causal/contingency links), and transition statistics that new data are fit into 29 , 30 . Schema congruence typically enhances memory and accelerates systems consolidation (faster hippocampal->neocortical integration), while controlled novelty against a schema can also stand out and be remembered well-resolving the apparent "schema vs. novelty" paradox. Schemas also support transfer: a previously learned task graph enables rapid re-learning when surface features change, and they enable state inference when observations are ambiguous by supplying hidden-state structure. At retrieval, schemas supply organized cues that steer memory search and reconstruction, improving recall of story details when schema representations were strong at encoding 31 , 32 , 33 . Mechanistically, schemas emerge from interactions among medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC/vmPFC), hippocampus/entorhinal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and posterior-medial default-mode hubs (posterior cingulate/precuneus, angular gyrus, parahippocampal and retrosplenial cortex). The posterior-medial (PM) pathway supplies contextual/situational/relational structure; the anterior-temporal (AT) pathway supplies item/semantic structure; both converge in the hippocampus and interact bidirectionally with mPFC during learning and consolidation. Thalamic nucleus reuniens forms a key conduit coordinating hippocampal-prefrontal coupling, including during sleep and extinction 34 , 35 , 36 , 33 . Human fMRI with naturalistic narratives shows that anterior mPFC carries schema representations (e.g., "restaurant" vs. "airport") whose strength at encoding predicts later recall of story details; during retrieval, a partly distinct network (including parahippocampal and angular gyrus) carries schematic information. This fits the view that mPFC provides a scaffold at encoding onto which hippocampus and posterior cortex bind specific content 33 . In the classic rodent paradigm, once a schema exists, new pairings become hippocampal-independent rapidly-yet hippocampus still supplies event-specific detail and prediction. Single-unit and imaging work shows both schema-like generalization (including "schema cells" in primate hippocampus) and detail-specific coding, often organized along the long axis (anterior = coarser/general; posterior = finer/detail) and interacting with mPFC during assimilation and replay 29 , 37 , 30 . OFC represents the latent state space of tasks-the abstract rules linking observations, hidden states, and outcomes. In rats, OFC ensembles develop schema representations that compress across superficially different problems, converging onto a low-dimensional code for shared task structure; OFC populations also encode value-based schemas and contextual states that guide retrieval. Recent causal work indicates OFC schema cells can form even when one hippocampal output (ventral subiculum) is inactivated, and may form faster when hippocampal output is suppressed during transfer-highlighting complementary (and sometimes competitive) roles across the circuit 38 , 39 , 40 . Across PFC and OFC, learning typically reduces representational dimensionality as populations align around task-relevant latent variables; in the OFC schema studies this appears as manifold compression and cross-problem alignment. More generally, prefrontal geometry supports abstraction-neural state spaces factorize rule-informative variables that generalize to novel instances, whereas hippocampal geometry tends to preserve specificity. In vmPFC, even value is coded along a curved manifold whose geometry predicts patterns of context-dependent "irrational" choice, emphasizing that schemas instantiate nonlinear priors over relational variables rather than simple axes 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 . Under naturalistic viewing/listening, posterior medial cortex, mPFC, and superior frontal areas express schematic event patterns that generalize across subjects and across modalities; disrupting the temporal order of events weakens these schematic patterns, consistent with schemas encoding expected temporal relations among subevents 44 . Rodent and human work converge on: slow accrual of a schema in neocortex; accelerated assimilation of congruent information once the scaffold exists; mPFC engagement and gene-expression changes as schema-congruent material is encoded; and hippocampal-prefrontal coordination (via direct/entorhinal routes and nucleus reuniens) during encoding, replay, sleep, and retrieval. These dynamics reconcile complementary learning systems with schema-driven "fast" consolidation 45 , 30 , 35 . Schemas sit "above" cognitive maps: maps encode metric/topological relations within a context, while schemas encode classes of contexts and their typical transition/causal structure. Predictive representations like the successor representation (often linked to hippocampus/entorhinal) provide building blocks; PFC/OFC then recode these building blocks into abstract, policy-relevant state spaces (state abstractions) that are reusable across tasks-i.e., relational priors 46 .

title: Embodied Representations
text: Biological representations are fundamentally embodied and action-oriented; the prime directive of the brain is to map sensory input to control outputs Body schemas The brain encodes a "body schema" through somatotopic maps in primary sensory and motor cortices. Classic studies by Penfield revealed an orderly "homunculus" mapping of the body on these cortices, with body parts that have finer sensation or require dexterity (e.g. fingers) occupying disproportionately large cortical areas 1 . These maps are plastic and update with experience or injury. A preserved latent manifold supports wrist, reach-to-grasp, and motor imagery, implying that new skills repurpose existing "neural modes" rather than invent new ones 2 Forward models The motor system constantly generates internal predictions of sensory outcomes for planned movements. The cerebellum and associated circuits are thought to implement forward models that transform motor commands into fine-grained expected sensory feedback 3 , which can be contrasted with actual outcomes during learning (more on this later). A striking example is our inability to tickle ourselves: when you attempt to self-tickle, the brain (via a copy of the motor command, an efference copy) predicts the tactile outcome and cancels it out 4 Image schemas An image schema is a recurrent, dynamic sensorimotor pattern-things like containment (in/out), force dynamics (push/pull), paths (source-goal trajectories), and balance/equilibrium states-abstracted over thousands of episodes and later "re-used" by language and abstract thought. Lakoff & Johnson’s original philosophical formulation is now backed by fMRI and lesion data showing that reasoning about these patterns re-activates premotor, parietal and posterior-temporal regions that code underlying actions and spatial relations Within  150 ms of viewing a potential action-scenario the dorsal fronto-parietal network instantiates containment, path or force dynamics as low-dimensional manifolds that feed forward to prefrontal and temporal cortices where they scaffold semantic and linguistic inferences. The brain seems to use them as a layer between low-level kinematics and high-level symbolic reasoning, placing them in the hierarchical region where mid-level action representations (e.g "move arm to mug handle" or "jump into the water") reside Embodied semantics Abstract or high-level cognitive representations, like language and concepts, show evidence of sensorimotor grounding in the brain. According to the embodied cognition view, understanding a concept or word involves partial re-activation of the sensory and motor circuits associated with that concept. Empirical studies support this: for example, reading action verbs like "kick," "pick," or "lick" preferentially activates motor cortex regions corresponding to feet, hands, or mouth respectively - mirroring the body part used in the described action Similarly, brain imaging has shown that thinking about or listening to descriptions of, say, the taste of cinnamon can engage olfactory and gustatory regions, or hearing a sentence about a texture can engage somatosensory areas. Moreover, transiently disrupting motor cortex with magnetic stimulation can selectively impair people’s understanding of action-related words, suggesting those motor circuits contribute functionally to language comprehension. These findings indicate that the brain’s semantic representations are not amodal symbols but are grounded in modality-specific systems. General intelligence and parietal affordance maps Affordance maps In macaques and humans, single-unit, LFP, and fMRI work all converge on the idea that posterior parietal cortex (PPC) does not passively list the world’s contents-it maps how the body could interact with what is out there. Area V6A, for example, dynamically recodes a graspable object as soon as it becomes the goal of an arm movement; nearly half of the neurons flip their firing depending on whether the animal will reach, grasp, or merely look, even when the retinal image is unchanged. That "visual-for-action" code persists through movement execution and is updated online by proprioceptive error, giving PPC the flavour of a forward state-estimator tuned for affordances rather than for neutral object identity. The same dorsal codes feed forward into prefrontal regions that maintain, rank and inhibit candidate actions. Overlap with P-FIT theory and general intelligence measures The Parieto-Frontal Integration Theory (P-FIT) argues that individual differences in general intelligence reflect the efficiency with which this fronto-parietal loop integrates perceptual evidence with candidate motor programs and evaluates them against task goals. A landmark meta-analysis found that Brodmann area 7 (superior parietal) was engaged in >70% of reasoning tasks and that dorsolateral PFC, anterior cingulate and angular gyrus co-activation explained roughly 40% of the variance in full-scale IQ across 37 neuroimaging studies. White-matter integrity of the superior longitudinal fasciculus-the main parietal-frontal highway-predicts fluid intelligence as robustly as grey-matter volume. So the intraparietal sulcus and superior parietal lobule that correlate most strongly with IQ scores are exactly where the brain computes spatial transformations, object manipulability, and action sequences. When you’re solving Raven’s Progressive Matrices (the gold standard IQ test), you’re literally using the same neural machinery that computes "how do I grasp this object?" The parietal cortex is performing spatial rotations, transformation sequences, and relational mappings - whether you’re mentally rotating shapes on an IQ test or planning how to pick up a coffee cup. Synthesis Fluid reasoning may amount to running rapidly-refined internal motor simulations under executive control. Three lines of evidence reinforce this interpretation. First, mental-rotation, visuomotor imitation, and even matrix-reasoning tasks all recruit dorsal parietal voxels whose tuning curves look indistinguishable from those engaged by actual reach-to-grasp movements, suggesting that "spatial" reasoning recycles motor primitives. Second, disrupting these parietal sectors with TMS or lesion selectively impairs both tool-use kinematics and abstract reasoning scores, implying a shared causal substrate. Third, developmental expansions of BA 7/40 correlate with the emergence of complex tool use and the steepest gains in fluid intelligence across primate evolution, fitting Cisek’s "affordance-competition" framework in which ever-richer action repertoires drive selection for larger fronto-parietal loops. Assuming a definition of intelligence as one’s ability to produce predictive models, the centrality of affordance-computing parietal regions in general human intelligence suggests that the human ability to model and manipulate the environment is fundamentally based on representations of potential actions and their consequences; this form of learning and representation is fundamentally distinct from leading A.I training recipes This convergence suggests that abstract reasoning emerges from embodied spatial computation rather than being a separate "higher-order" process. The brain doesn’t have distinct systems for thinking versus acting - thinking IS a form of internalized action simulation. Even when you’re doing pure mathematics, you’re leveraging neural circuits evolved for navigating and manipulating the physical world. Cortical population codes that evolved to predict the sensory consequences of candidate movements now serve as the proto-symbols that higher-order cognition manipulates. Contemporary AI systems that learn static embeddings from disembodied data streams are missing this affordance-first substrate; closing the gap will likely require models that keep an online, parietal-style action manifold tightly coupled to their perception and planning modules. Neural recycling of spatial systems Evolutionary co-option of navigational mechanisms (e.g grid cells and place cells) for representing non-spatial relationships and abstract knowledge From an AGI engineering perspective, this suggests that spatial reasoning might be the fundamental substrate for all abstract cognition. The key transferable principle is that abstract reasoning emerges from concrete spatial computation rather than being a separate higher-order process.

title: Representing Uncertainty
text: Representing confidence and uncertainty is a key goal for biological world models; comes quite naturally and is an instance of meta-learning Metacognitive representations gate learning rates, direct information seeking and attention, and arbitrate between model-based and model-free control Confidence representations serve multiple timescales of behavioral control, from momentary economic decisions to longer-term learning and adaptation. Confidence builds as trajectories approach stable attractor states, with high-confidence trials showing faster convergence to stable manifold regions. The brain distinguishes between confidence and certainty, even though both relate to probability. One proposal defines confidence as the estimated probability that a specific decision or belief is correct, whereas certainty refers to encoding the full probability distribution of a variable (the overall predictability of the situation). This distinction implies different neural representations: confidence is a single-value assessment about a choice, while certainty involves representing spread or variance of possible states. Probabilistic population codes and metacognitive hubs Neural circuits appear to represent uncertainty by coding probability distributions across populations of neurons. In Bayesian brain models, each neuron’s activity can represent a "vote" for a certain stimulus value, and the overall pattern (tuning curve spread, firing variability) reflects uncertainty. For example, when sensory information is unreliable, population responses become broader or more variable, signaling low certainty about what was sensed. Conversely, sharply peaked activity patterns indicate high certainty. The brain can decode these population patterns to estimate confidence or uncertainty about stimuli. An alternative proposal is that the brain may not explicitly construct full distributions at all times, but instead samples possible interpretations in parallel. In one neural model, many semi-independent modules each integrate evidence noisily; if their conclusions agree (low dispersion), confidence is high, whereas disagreement (high dispersion) signals uncertainty. In this view, confidence emerges from consensus across redundant neural processes. This sampling-by-ensemble mechanism can explain why confidence usually correlates with stimulus clarity and decision speed Generative-model decoding of human visual cortex shows that each trial’s voxel-pattern contains a full likelihood function over stimulus orientation; the decoded width predicts subjects’ expressed confidence, directly tying distributional spread to subjective certainty 1 , 2 Similar reconstructions during working-memory delays reveal that parietal and occipital ensembles maintain both content and precision of remembered items 3 . These findings generalize the probabilistic-population-code (PPC) idea: the intrinsic noise in a population’s firing simultaneously encodes what is represented (the mean) and how sure the system is (the variance). Metacognitive hubs There are dedicated metacognitive neural substrates; it is not all bottom-up Two canonical criteria for metacognition: ongoing monitoring of internal processing and strategic control based on that monitoring Pulvinar The pulvinar nucleus of the thalamus stands out as a key metacognitive hub. Because the pulvinar is the only thalamic nucleus that receives reciprocal, topographically organised projections from virtually every tier of the visual and fronto-parietal hierarchy and can rhythmically gate their interactions, it is uniquely placed to fuse the many local "proto-confidence" traces that exist in cortex (e.g. evidence strength in V1, choice-related drift in LIP, value precision in vmPFC) into a single global variable. Electrophysiology, inactivation, and network-level recording all show that the pulvinar then pushes this summary out to the very circuits that set learning rates, attentional gain, and opt-out behaviour-ultimately resulting in rhythmic control of inter-areal communication and biasing downstream computations in proportion to certainty Sensory reliability: estimate of how informative a given sensory stream is about some latent variable of interest (e.g. object location, motion direction, body position, internal states like pain or hunger). More formally, it reflects the inverse of uncertainty or variance in the mapping between sensory input and the hidden state it’s trying to infer By collapsing heterogeneous uncertainty cues into one thalamic firing-rate variable, the pulvinar lets disparate cortical regions compare their epistemic states on the same scale-crucial for deciding whether to exploit, explore, or delegate a choice These same neurons that encode confidence participate in large-scale alpha/low-beta synchrony that determines which cortical areas can exchange information at a given moment Opt-out and neglect phenomena after inactivation show the pulvinar can abort actions when integrated certainty falls below threshold-something that neither LIP nor rlPFC can accomplish on their own Because layer-5 driver axons hit granular cortical layers, confidence-weighted prediction-error information can update sensory cortices before slower neuromodulatory systems arrive, aligning plasticity with reliability in near-real time Overall, the pulvinar decides which cortical nodes can talk to which others, at what gain, and for how long, according to the certainty of the current belief state. This mechanism turns a local, modality-bound confidence trace into a global control variable that tweaks perception, learning rate, motor gating, and conscious report-all within a few tens of milliseconds rlPFC (right rostrolateral prefrontal cortex) The rlPFC sits at the apex of the prefrontal gradient, receiving convergent inputs from posterior sensory, parietal, temporal-memory, and value areas and projecting to anterior cingulate and thalamic hubs; this position lets it pool already-processed "proto-confidence" traces into an explicit, domain-general certainty variable that humans can consciously interrogate or report. Domain-general confidence code: multivariate decoding shows that a common population pattern in rlPFC predicts trial-by-trial confidence across perception, memory, and value tasks, in contrast to neighbouring mPFC which carries task-specific codes. By integrating heterogeneous certainty cues into a single, autonoetic firing-rate/distributed-pattern signal, rlPFC enables disparate cortical and subcortical systems to compare their epistemic states on a shared scale, a prerequisite for flexible arbitration between exploitation, exploration, and memory retrieval strategies fMRI and intracranial recordings show that rlPFC activity correlates with reported confidence even when accuracy, reaction time, and stimulus reliability are held constant, proving that it encodes metacognitive certainty rather than low-level evidence strength Lesion and TMS evidence: focal damage to anterior/rostrolateral PFC or continuous theta-burst stimulation selectively impairs meta-d′/d′-the coupling between confidence and accuracy-without degrading first-order performance, demonstrating a causal role in metacognition rlPFC tracks relative uncertainty in explore-exploit tasks: the higher its BOLD, the more likely participants are to sample the less-certain option, indicating a strategic control signal that adjusts behaviour when evidence is ambiguous. Functional connectivity analyses reveal strengthened rlPFC-vmPFC and rlPFC-ACC coupling on high-confidence trials; this network appears to set learning-rate and credit-assignment parameters by forwarding precision-weighted teaching signals to dopaminergic and cingulate circuits. Trial-resolved MEG-fMRI work places the emergence of the rlPFC confidence signal  250-350 ms after parietal evidence accumulation finishes but  200 ms before overt report, positioning it as a late but still online evaluator that can adjust decisions on the fly. 4 Overall, rlPFC transforms distributed reliability signals into a consciously accessible, broadcast-ready confidence estimate that calibrates strategy selection, learning-rate modulation, and verbal report OFC (orbitofrontal cortex) Sitting on the ventral prefrontal surface, OFC receives convergent inputs from multimodal sensory cortices, amygdala, hippocampus and basal ganglia and projects back to limbic, striatal and mediodorsal-thalamic hubs, positioning it to marry perceptual evidence to motivational context and predicted outcomes. Behavior- and modality-general confidence code: single-unit recordings show that OFC neurons encode statistical decision confidence independent of the sensory modality (olfactory vs. auditory) that generated the choice and predict both trial-by-trial waiting time and cross-trial strategy updating. By integrating heterogeneous uncertainty cues with momentary value and elapsed time, OFC converts raw reliability signals into a value-weighted, temporally extended confidence estimate that answers "how long is it worth persisting in this choice?"-a computation essential for temporal wagering, foraging and credit assignment. Causal evidence: reversible inactivation or lesion of OFC abolishes appropriate waiting-based confidence reports while leaving primary choice accuracy intact, proving that OFC supplies a dedicated metacognitive signal rather than duplicating sensory evidence. Human fMRI reveals that lateral OFC BOLD tracks subjective confidence after controlling for reward magnitude and reaction time, and transiently signals unexpected outcomes to primary sensory cortex-delivering top-down "teaching" signals that help re-learn stimulus-outcome mappings when confidence drops Functional connectivity and optogenetic work show that OFC communicates confidence-weighted value signals to dorsal striatum; disrupting this loop biases economic choices without affecting sensory discrimination, underscoring a role in translating certainty into action value. Meta-reinforcement learning: slow-timescale plasticity in OFC supports meta-RL-optimising the policy that sets learning-rate and exploration as a function of accumulated confidence; silencing CaMKII-dependent plasticity in OFC blocks this meta-learning while sparing within-session RL. Population decoding indicates that OFC encodes both expected value and confidence in orthogonal subspaces, allowing downstream circuits to extract either variable as needed; variability in the confidence subspace predicts trial-to-trial adjustments of persistence and exploration. Across subjects, grey-matter thickness and OFC-striatal connectivity correlate with calibrated confidence in value-based decisions, linking anatomical variation to economic metacognition Overall, OFC transforms distributed reliability signals into a value- and time-coupled confidence estimate that governs persistence, credit assignment and meta-RL dACC Reads the certainty signals packaged upstream (sensory reliability from pulvinar, domain-general confidence from rlPFC, value-weighted confidence from OFC) and combines them with the current action set and motivational landscape to decide how much cognitive control and effort a particular course of action deserves. It therefore sits at the interface between abstract certainty representations and concrete motor or cognitive "affordances." Theoretical and empirical work converge on the view that dACC computes the expected value of control (EVC): it integrates (i) the probability that ongoing behaviour will fail-closely related to low confidence or high uncertainty-and (ii) the prospective benefit of expending extra resources (time, attention, working-memory, motor vigour) to reduce that failure risk. Neural activity in dACC tracks this cost-benefit quantity across a wide range of tasks, from Stroop-like conflict to exploration-exploitation dilemmas and volatile reinforcement-learning environments Causal evidence strengthens the bridge model: recent TMS and tDCS studies show that perturbing dmPFC shifts metacognitive bias and changes how much effort people choose to invest, without altering first-order accuracy-exactly what you would expect if dACC were reading confidence/value signals and turning them into control allocations. Intracranial EEG and fMRI work further reveal that dACC engagement is highest when rlPFC-encoded confidence is low and the stakes encoded in OFC are high, suggesting a conjunctive "low-certainty/high-value" trigger for ramping up control. Functionally, then, dACC closes the loop: Monitoring. It receives certainty/uncertainty summaries from pulvinar, rlPFC and OFC, along with performance feedback and error signals. Computation. It estimates the marginal payoff of deploying more control-effectively asking, "Given how unsure we are and how big the reward is, is extra effort worth it?" Control broadcast. When that payoff is positive, dACC drives adjustments in dorsolateral PFC, basal ganglia and neuromodulatory nuclei, scaling working-memory maintenance, attentional focus, learning rate and action vigour In short, dACC does not generate new confidence estimates; instead, it bridges existing certainty representations to the brain’s control and policy systems, ensuring that effort is spent only when low confidence and high stakes make it worthwhile. The brain’s overall representation of uncertainty A multi-tier, hierarchical certainty pipeline Pulvinar (sensory reliability). Fast sub-cortical circuits in the pulvinar compute a moment-by-moment reliability tag for each incoming sensory stream. When that tag is low, pulvinar firing drops, monkeys "opt-out," and cortical traffic is throttled-even though raw discrimination accuracy is unaffected-making the pulvinar a global router that gates information on the basis of stimulus precision. Right rlPFC (domain-general confidence). rlPFC reads sensory reliabilities plus higher-order and mnemonic traces to construct an explicit, task-agnostic confidence signal. This abstract code predicts subjective ratings even when difficulty and reaction time are matched, and disrupting rlPFC selectively flattens meta-d′ while sparing first-order performance. This form of confidence is explicitly inferential, informed by an agent’s internal models of the world and its own cognitive system. OFC (value-weighted confidence). OFC binds rlPFC-style certainty to expected reward and the opportunity cost of time. Its neurons ramp with the subjective probability that continued waiting will pay off; silencing OFC leaves choice accuracy intact but abolishes the finely tuned willingness-to-wait that normally tracks confidence. dACC / dmPFC (expected value of control). dACC receives the certainty signals packaged by rlPFC and OFC, combines them with action costs and available affordances, and computes the expected value of deploying additional cognitive control. When confidence is low but stakes are high, dACC activity rises and drives top-down adjustments in attention, learning rate, and effort allocation; perturbing dACC shifts effort investment without changing raw accuracy. Complementary codes, complementary control Pulvinar: low-dimensional rate and oscillatory signals deliver a rapid go/hold veto on cortico-cortical communication. rlPFC: abstract population patterns yield a consciously accessible, domain-general confidence "common currency" that calibrates exploration, learning, and verbal report. OFC: value- and time-weighted confidence subspace governs persistence, credit assignment, and meta-reinforcement learning. dACC: control-demand signals translate combined certainty and value into dynamic adjustments of cognitive effort, ensuring resources are deployed only when low confidence and high stakes warrant it. Together, these four layers let the brain compare, broadcast, and act on uncertainty at the appropriate timescale and level of abstraction-from millisecond sensory gating to strategic effort investment-turning raw sensory noise into well-calibrated, goal-directed behaviour. Two complementary neural-coding schemes recur across areas: (i) graded rate codes where firing magnitude monotonically maps to posterior probability (LIP, OFC, pulvinar), and (ii) population probability distributions where the shape of activity across a neural ensemble encodes a full probability distribution (sensory cortex, grid cells, working memory). The brain appears to mix these codes, using graded certainty for fast action selection and full distributions when precision matters for future inference. Detecting risk vs ambiguity Risk describes a decision-making scenario where the probabilities of different outcomes are explicitly known. For example, choosing to bet on a lottery with a stated 50% chance of winning is a decision under risk. This corresponds to a situation of pure aleatoric uncertainty. Ambiguity describes a scenario where the outcome probabilities are unknown or imprecisely specified. The classic example is the Ellsberg paradox, where individuals are asked to bet on drawing a colored chip from an urn with an unknown composition of red and blue chips. Behaviorally, risk aversion and ambiguity aversion are distinct traits that are largely uncorrelated across individuals. Neurobiologically, these two forms of uncertainty recruit both distinct and overlapping neural systems. Neurobiologically, these two forms of uncertainty recruit both distinct and overlapping neural systems. Studies comparing choices under ambiguity versus risk have found greater activation in regions such as the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), and posterior parietal cortex for ambiguous options. Other work has dissociated subjective value tracking, linking risk to the ventral striatum and superior parietal cortex, and ambiguity to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and superior temporal gyrus. EEG studies have also revealed distinct patterns, with ambiguity engaging a broader fronto-parietal network compared to risk. At the same time, a common valuation system involving the striatum and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) appears to encode subjective value under both conditions, suggesting a point of convergence in the brain’s valuation circuitry. The brain’s differential processing of risk and ambiguity provides strong evidence for its capacity to distinguish between irreducible randomness and knowable unknowns. This reframes ambiguity aversion not as an irrational bias, but as an adaptive response from a system designed to motivate the resolution of epistemic uncertainty. Episodic memory for contextual uncertainty and asserting epistemic authority Episodic memory allows us to assert epistemic authority; corresponds to strength of episodic trace and/or operational mode of HPC (e.g imagination mode or retrieval mode)? Neuromodulator systems At the whole-brain level, diffuse neuromodulator systems encode different forms of uncertainty. Acetylcholine (ACh) release is thought to signal expected uncertainty - situations where the unreliability of cues is known in advance (e.g. a noisy environment). In contrast, norepinephrine (NE) from the locus coeruleus signals unexpected uncertainty, spiking when the world suddenly violates expectations (a flash of surprise). According to this theory, ACh and NE adjust cortical gains: under high expected uncertainty, ACh biases the brain toward bottom-up information (since top-down predictions are less trusted), while NE surges act as an "alert" to rapidly revise beliefs after a surprising event. These neuromodulatory systems thus provide a global representation of uncertainty that modulates processing throughout the brain. Even reward-processing neurons carry uncertainty information. Midbrain dopamine neurons, famous for encoding reward prediction errors, also exhibit a distinct signal for uncertainty about rewards. In one study, dopamine cells showed a sustained ramping activity when reward probability was 50% (maximal uncertainty), which was absent at 0% or 100% probability. This ramping signal covaried with reward uncertainty and suggested that dopamine not only reports expected value but also signals risk or variance. The presence of an uncertainty-related dopamine response points to a role in guiding learning and exploration - for instance, higher dopamine during uncertainty might encourage information-seeking or risk-taking behavior.
