title: Broad Subdivisions and Evolutionary Layering
text: What is the "steering" versus "learning" subsystem in Byrnes’ work? Where is each sensory modality "wired in?" This dictates cortical organization (the spatial distribution of representations (e.g abstraction gradients and cross-modal hubs)). Structure-function coupling in the human brainstem Evolution didn’t replace the old predictive systems (cerebellum for forward models, BG for value-based selection), it added a third prediction engine that operates at a different timescale and level of abstraction. The cerebellum predicts immediate sensory consequences of actions (microsecond-to-second range), the cortex builds hierarchical models of the world structure and long-term contingencies, and the BG sits in between, using both to steer behavior toward rewarding states. By the time you get to primates around 50-60 million years ago, cortex has exploded to dominate brain volume–humans are  75% cortex by mass. That’s the system doing the heavy lifting on abstract world modeling in modern mammals. Evolution built the vertebrate brain by accretion rather than replacement. The hypothalamus and brainstem are the ancient core that keeps an animal alive, coupling interoceptive signals to autonomic, endocrine, and instinctive behavioral responses; their circuitry integrates peripheral state and sets homeostatic goals such as thermoregulation, energy balance, and arousal 2 , 3 . In mammals, these nuclei remain small in volume but disproportionately powerful levers on behavior, coordinating visceral reflexes with motivated action. They are the control room for set-points, not a relic, and they still dictate the "why now?" of behavior. Layered on top is the telencephalon’s dorsal pallium, which in mammals expanded into the six-layered neocortex-an evolutionary novelty that scaled dramatically in primates. Strip away the folds and the human cortex is only a few millimeters thick (roughly 2-4 mm, mean  2.5 mm) 4 , yet-depending on method and sample-its sheet spans on the order of 1,600-2,500 cm² when flattened; the exact figure varies with how much buried sulcal surface you count. What matters for computation is the sheet’s repeating microcircuit theme 5 : thalamic "driver" inputs preferentially target layer IV; layers II/III broadcast cortico-cortically; layers V/VI drive subcortical targets. The motif is conserved but not rigid: primary motor cortex is famously agranular or near-agranular (weak layer 4) 6 , yet recent physiology shows a small, functionally bona fide L4-like relay there. Across areas, the "canonical" circuit is less a blueprint than a grammar that supports specialization through changes in input-output statistics and interneuron composition. Cortex does not operate in isolation; it is wired around thalamus. A core organizational principle is the cortico-thalamo-cortical loop, which comes in two flavors. First-order relays (e.g., LGN) carry subcortical drivers to cortex; higher-order relays are driven by cortex itself (often from layer 5 "driver" neurons) and route messages between cortical areas via the thalamus ("trans-thalamic" communication). The pulvinar-enlarged in primates alongside visual and association cortex-illustrates the point: it synchronizes and gates traffic among connected cortical maps according to attentional demands, acting as a flexible switchboard rather than a passive relay 7 , 8 . These laminar and thalamic asymmetries implement a directional grammar: supragranular-heavy feedforward pathways convey sensory evidence up hierarchies, while infragranular-heavy feedback conveys predictions, context, and goals back down. The large-scale picture of cortex is often caricatured as "uniform," but "uniformly reconfigurable" is more accurate. The sheet uses the same laminar parts list to build distinct mesoscale specializations 5 -granular primary sensory areas dominated by thalamic drive; intermediate association zones that remix multimodal features; and agranular premotor/prefrontal zones that emit deep-layer commands and predictions. This graded architecture explains why feedforward/feedback dynamics and oscillatory regimes change smoothly across space and task, without appealing to different learning rules per area 9 . By contrast, subcortical systems are anatomical one-offs-compact, deeply conserved "coprocessors" with idiosyncratic algorithms that the cortex recruits via re-entrant loops 10 . The basal ganglia concentrate massive cortical and thalamic convergence into a small set of tonic output channels that can disinhibit brainstem controllers and motor thalamus; their parallel, partially segregated cortico-BG-thalamo-cortical loops implement selection and dopaminergically gated credit assignment 11 , 12 . The canonical architecture-motor, associative, limbic loops running in parallel with a ventral-to-dorsal "ascending spiral" via midbrain dopamine-provides a literal pathway for value to bias policy and for habits to crystallize. The cerebellum is the timing/forecasting counterpart to the basal ganglia’s selection/valuation machinery. It is neuron-dense ( 69-70 billion neurons,  80% of all brain neurons, mostly granule cells 13 ) yet small in mass, and it connects to cortex through closed-loop cerebro-cerebellar circuits via the pons and thalamus 14 , 15 . These loops are topographically matched: the same cortical fields that send a mossy-fiber copy of their commands receive refined predictions back, enabling rapid calibration of sensorimotor sequences and, in association territories, the timing of cognitive operations such as working memory and planning. Two allocortical (the phylogenetically oldest part of the cerebral cortex, characterized by fewer than six cell layers) systems round out the telencephalic toolbox. The hippocampal formation (archicortex) is optimized for rapid relational binding and episodic indexing, enabling one-shot learning of who-did-what-where-when and the recombination of those relations during simulation and planning 16 . The amygdala (especially BLA) attaches valence/arousal to stimuli and events and recruits neuromodulatory systems (basal forebrain ACh, locus coeruleus NE) to increase gain and plasticity for behaviorally important inputs 17 . These systems are not "limbic add-ons"; they are bidirectionally coupled with multimodal cortex and subcortical drivers and reshape processing on the fly. If you step back, the brain’s broad subdivisions form a three-tier information-flow hierarchy that evolution has tuned rather than redesigned. The homeostatic and orienting tier (hypothalamus-brainstem-superior colliculus) provides the organism’s internal objectives and fast reflexive reorienting. The valuation/selection/timing tier (basal ganglia, cerebellum, amygdala) assigns priorities, selects policies, and calibrates temporal structure. The representational/predictive tier (cortex with its thalamic relays, plus hippocampal indexing) builds and queries compositional world models under those priorities. What makes primate-and especially human-brains distinctive is not a brand-new module, but the scale and coupling 18 : a massively expanded cortical mantle ( 75-84% of brain mass, depending on inclusion of white matter) riding on conserved subcortical loops, with an enlarged pulvinar and association thalamus to orchestrate long-range cortical communication 19 . That combination buys depth, bandwidth, and flexible arbitration without discarding the reliable, fast machinery underneath.

Has been called the seventh layer of the cortex by Numenta Acts as a nexus between sensory inputs, cortex, and subcortex ’Core’ thalamic nuclei route precise sensory/motor content to specific primary cortical layers, while ’matrix’ (higher-order) nuclei project diffusely to superficial cortex to coordinate widespread activity Thalamic gating mechanisms provide temporal coordination across distributed cortical networks, enabling synchronized processing of multimodal sensory information and top-down predictions from higher-order areas Higher-order thalamic nuclei (pulvinar, mediodorsal, etc.) act as dynamic switchboards, routing context-dependent information between cortical areas and synchronizing their rhythms to support cortical cooperation and flexibility. For instance, the pulvinar nucleus (greatly expanded in primates) interconnects visual cortical areas in parallel loops, implementing attention by modulating gain and synchrony Anatomically, every major cortico-cortical pathway tends to have a parallel cortico-pulvinar-cortical route ("replication principle"), which allows the thalamus to adjust the precision of inter-area signals and bind distributed cortical representations. In effect, cortico-thalamo-cortical loops enable iterative processing: cortical predictions drive thalamic neurons and thalamus feeds back integrative signals to cortex, essential for sensory gating, attention, and evidence accumulation Overall, thalamus can be though of as a global cortical coherence operator; think of it like a distributed system coordinator - while each node (cortical area) handles its specialized computation, the thalamus ensures the overall system reaches coherent, globally consistent solutions. More in "Loops" section Brief Recap of Cortical Architecture The cortical column–a vertically organized ensemble spanning roughly 300 – 600 μ m 300–600\mu m in diameter and all six cortical layers–has long been proposed as the fundamental repeating computational unit of cortex 12 , 13 . Though the degree of columnar discreteness varies across areas and species–and the concept remains debated 14 , 15 –there is broad agreement that the laminar microcircuit constitutes a canonical motif that is replicated, with quantitative variations in cell density, layer thickness, and connectivity ratios, across nearly all cortical areas 16 , 3 , 17 . For the purposes of understanding cortical learning, the key architectural features of this microcircuit are the following (readers should refer to the "Whole-Brain Architecture and Information Flow" section for full anatomical detail): 1. Laminar segregation of signal types. Thalamic and lower-area feedforward input arrives predominantly in the granular layer (L4), where it is relayed upward to superficial layers (L2/3). Feedback projections from higher areas target preferentially the superficial layers (especially L1) and deep layers (L5/6), largely bypassing L4 18 , 19 , 20 , 17 . This laminar separation means that, at each stage of the hierarchy, bottom-up data and top-down contextual or predictive signals are anatomically segregated before being integrated–a structural prerequisite exploited by nearly every computational theory of cortical learning, from predictive coding 21 , 22 to biased competition 23 . Layer 1 in particular functions as an integration and control plane: it is a major termination zone for long-range feedback and higher-order thalamic input onto apical tufts, and it is densely innervated by neuromodulatory fibers and specialized inhibitory circuits that gate whether top-down signals actually influence somatic output and plasticity 24 . 2. Excitatory recurrence dominates. The majority of excitatory synapses onto a cortical pyramidal neuron originate from other cortical pyramidal neurons within the same area or from feedback projections, rather than from feedforward thalamic or lower-area inputs 25 , 26 , 27 . The cortex is thus predominantly a recurrent prediction machine rather than a feedforward feature-extraction pipeline. This architectural fact has profound implications for learning: the majority of synaptic weights that must be tuned are those mediating lateral and top-down recurrent dynamics, and the dominant "input" to any given neuron is the cortex’s own ongoing internal model, not the external world directly. Moreover, synaptic efficacies (and their spine-size correlates) in cortex are heavy-tailed and well-described by log-normal-like distributions, implying that cortical computation/learning is often dominated by a minority of strong synapses embedded in a sea of weak ones 28 , 29 . 3. Feedback connections vastly outnumber feedforward (but are often weaker per pathway). Quantitative tract-tracing shows that feedback projections are typically more numerous and more diffuse than feedforward projections, both in the number of source areas and in the fraction of labeled neurons per connection 30 , 31 . However, detailed analyses of laminar connection rules suggest a complementary nuance: feedforward pathways tend to have higher weights , cross fewer hierarchical levels, and are less numerous than feedback pathways, and the hierarchy is constructed from supra- and infragranular counterstreams in which both bottom-up and top-down signals can be point-to-point in supragranular layers while infragranular streams are more diffuse 20 . This asymmetry remains exactly what one would expect of a predictive hierarchy: rich high-dimensional expectations must be broadcast downward and compared locally against sparser ascending data streams. This anatomical counterstream organization has a physiological correlate: in human visual cortex, directed inter-areal influences consistent with feedforward signaling are strongest in the gamma band, whereas feedback influences are strongest in the alpha–beta range, supporting the idea that cortex can multiplex predictions and prediction-error–like traffic in distinct spectral channels 32 , 33 . 4. The pyramidal neuron as a multi-compartment learning unit. The principal excitatory neuron of the cortex–the pyramidal cell–is far more than a simple integrate-and-fire point neuron. Its elaborate dendritic arbor is functionally compartmentalized into at least two semi-independent integration zones: the basal/proximal dendrites, which primarily receive feedforward and local recurrent input, and the apical tuft dendrites in layer 1, which receive feedback, contextual, and modulatory input from higher areas and nonspecific thalamic nuclei 34 , 35 . When sufficiently strong basal (bottom-up) and apical (top-down) inputs coincide, the neuron can generate dendritic calcium spikes that dramatically boost its firing rate–a coincidence-detection mechanism sometimes called backpropagation-activated calcium spike firing (BAC firing) 35 , 36 . This architecture means that individual pyramidal neurons can, in principle, use dendritic nonlinearities to implement powerful context-sensitive gating of bottom-up drive by top-down input 37 , 38 . However, it is often safer to treat apical feedback not as a literal subtractive "error" input but as a contextual/precision signal that can nonlinearly gate which bottom-up patterns win and which synapses are eligible for strengthening; recent causal work shows that cortico-cortical feedback can recruit branch-specific apical dendritic events consistent with nonlinear integration of top-down signals 39 . 5. Distinct pyramidal cell classes serve distinct computational roles. Deep-layer pyramidal neurons are not a monolithic population. Layer 5 contains at least two major classes: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons projecting to other cortical areas and striatum, and extratelencephalic (ET, or pyramidal tract) neurons projecting to subcortical targets including thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord 40 , 3 , 41 . Layer 6 contains corticothalamic (CT) neurons that provide modulatory feedback to thalamic relay nuclei. These distinct output channels mean that the "predictions" and "errors" computed within a column can be routed to qualitatively different targets–subcortical motor systems, thalamic relay and modulatory circuits, other cortical areas–each of which may use the signal differently for its own learning. Recent single-cell transcriptomic and connectomic studies have further revealed that even within these broad classes, there exist finer-grained subtypes with distinct connectivity, gene expression, and likely plasticity profiles 42 , 43 . 6. Interneuron diversity enables flexible error computation. Cortical circuits contain a rich repertoire of GABAergic interneuron types–parvalbumin-expressing (PV) basket and chandelier cells, somatostatin-expressing (SST) Martinotti cells, vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing (VIP) interneurons, and others–each of which targets distinct compartments of pyramidal neurons and is embedded in distinct circuit motifs 44 , 45 . PV interneurons provide powerful perisomatic inhibition that regulates gain and timing; SST interneurons preferentially target apical dendrites, gating top-down input; VIP interneurons predominantly inhibit SST interneurons, creating a disinhibitory motif (VIP->SST->pyramidal) that can selectively "open the gate" for feedback signals when attention or surprise is high 46 , 47 , 48 . For cortical learning, this interneuron diversity is not a complication–it is the machinery through which the cortex flexibly computes, gates, and routes error signals across dendritic compartments, layers, and behavioral states. 7. Thalamocortical and cortico-subcortical loops. Each cortical area is embedded in reciprocal loops with the thalamus–both through "first-order" relay nuclei (receiving ascending sensory input) and "higher-order" nuclei such as the pulvinar and mediodorsal nucleus (receiving cortical layer 5 input and projecting back to cortex), which have been proposed to function as a flexible routing and gain-control substrate for cortico-cortical communication 49 , 50 . Cortical areas are also embedded in parallel loops through the basal ganglia (via striatal input and thalamic return) and the cerebellum (via pontine nuclei, cerebellar cortex, deep nuclei, and thalamic return) 51 , 52 . The learning implications are twofold: first, the thalamus is not a passive relay but an active partner in cortical learning, capable of gating plasticity and mediating inter-areal credit assignment; second, the cortex never learns in isolation–its representations are continuously shaped by reinforcement signals from the basal ganglia, predictive error signals from the cerebellum, and memory-replay signals from the hippocampus, as outlined in the introduction to this section. 8. A note on areal variation. While the canonical microcircuit provides a useful common framework, it is important to acknowledge that cortical areas differ quantitatively in ways that affect their learning dynamics. Primary sensory areas have a thick, neuron-dense L4 (granular cortex), reflecting their role as the main recipients of thalamic feedforward input, whereas agranular cortex (e.g., primary motor cortex, anterior cingulate, orbitofrontal cortex) has a diminished or absent L4 and expanded deep layers, reflecting a shift from sensory reception toward output and top-down control 53 , 54 . Importantly, this granularity gradient correlates with gradients in plasticity: agranular and dysgranular areas in the prefrontal and limbic cortex exhibit markers of higher synaptic turnover and plasticity (e.g., higher expression of growth-associated proteins, lower myelination, and higher spine density turnover), whereas heavily myelinated primary sensory areas show greater synaptic stability after critical-period closure 55 , 56 . The implication is that the learning rate and plasticity regime of the cortical optimizer are not spatially uniform but are graded along the cortical hierarchy–a theme we return to when discussing cortical learning across development. 9. The Principal Gradient and Hierarchy of Timescales. The cortex is organized along a continuous macroscopic gradient of connectivity and gene expression, stretching from primary sensory/motor regions to transmodal association areas (e.g., the default mode network) 57 , 58 . This structural gradient imposes a corresponding hierarchy of temporal receptive windows . Lower areas (e.g., V1, A1) possess strong intrinsic inhibition and fast membrane time constants, optimizing them to learn rapid, transient sensory fluctuations. As one ascends the gradient, excitation/inhibition ratios shift and recurrent connection strengths increase, lengthening the intrinsic integration window 59 , 60 , 61 . This forces higher areas to "ignore" high-frequency noise and instead learn slow, invariant, and abstract regularities (e.g., social narratives or long-term goals) 62 , 63 . Thus, the "optimization horizon" is not uniform; the cortical architecture enforces a spectral decomposition of the learning problem, with different areas theoretically "assigned" to minimize prediction error over different timescales. 10. Small-World Topology and "Rich Club" Hubs. Beyond the laminar microcircuit, the global connectivity of the cortex exhibits a "small-world" topology : high local clustering (supporting specialized, modular learning) combined with short path lengths (supporting global error propagation) 64 , 65 . Crucially, this network possesses a "rich club" of densely interconnected high-degree hubs (e.g., precuneus, superior frontal cortex, insula) that serve as a high-capacity backbone for integrating information across modules 66 , 67 . For an optimization system, this topology represents a trade-off between segregation and integration: local modules can update their weights to minimize local prediction errors without causing catastrophic interference elsewhere, while the rich club provides a high-capacity backbone for rapid global coordination when model updates must be system-wide 68 , 69 . 11. Topographic interfaces. Many cortical and cortico-subcortical projections preserve topography (retinotopy, tonotopy, somatotopy, and related continuous maps), which constrains learning by making prediction errors spatially local and credit assignment more tractable: nearby units share receptive fields and can update coherently without global rewiring 70 . Topographic precision is also cell-type- and area-dependent in major learning loops (e.g., corticostriatal projections), implying that what the basal ganglia can reinforce is constrained by the geometric alignment between cortical representational space and striatal input channels 71 . In sum, the cortical architecture reviewed here–laminar segregation of feedforward and feedback signals, massive recurrence, feedback-dominated connectivity, multi-compartment pyramidal neurons, diverse inhibitory interneuron types, embedding in thalamocortical and cortico-subcortical loops, and genetically-specified macroscopic cortico-cortico connectivity motifs–is not merely a substrate on which learning happens. It is an architecture designed for a particular kind of learning: the continuous, hierarchical comparison of internally generated predictions with externally and internally driven signals, and the use of resulting mismatches to refine a deep generative model of the world. The sections that follow examine how this architecture realizes each step of the optimization loop–what the cortex is optimizing, how errors are computed and propagated, how credit is assigned, and what plasticity mechanisms implement the resulting weight updates. See "The Cortex" in the "Optimization Architecture" section.

title: Cortical Subdivisions and White Matter Highways
text: Anatomical white matter tracts span the cortical hierarchy to support cognitive diversity The cerebral cortex is organized into distinct functional areas or "subdivisions" that emerge during development under graded morphogen and transcription factor (TF) patterns 2 . These early molecular gradients (e.g. anterior FGF vs posterior Wnt/BMP sources) set up opposing gradients of TFs (such as Pax6 anteriorly and Emx2 posteriorly) that impart positional identity to cortical progenitors (cells that are pre-differentiation). As a result, the adult cortex contains four canonical "primary" areas - visual (V1), auditory (A1), somatosensory (S1) and motor (M1) - each tied to a specific modality and its corresponding thalamic relays. In broad strokes, the occipital cortex is specialized for vision, the superior temporal lobe for audition and language-related processing, the postcentral gyrus and adjacent parietal lobe for somatosensation and spatial processing, and the frontal lobe (including premotor and prefrontal regions) for motor control, executive function and higher cognition. These lobar and areal subdivisions are reflected in cytoarchitectonic differences and in the patterns of long-range connections that interlink them. The flow of information into and out of the cortex follows "highway" pathways in the white matter. All sensory modalities project via the thalamus into specific cortical areas: for example, the optic radiations carry visual signals from the lateral geniculate nucleus to V1, the acoustic radiations from the medial geniculate nucleus to A1, and dorsal column/medial lemniscus projections from the ventral posterolateral thalamus to S1. In fact, the thalamus is the major hub sending axons to the entire cortical mantle, establishing modality-specific projection tracts early in development 3 . Motor output pathways (e.g. corticospinal fibers via the internal capsule and corona radiata) likewise leave frontal motor cortex and descend to subcortical and spinal targets. These projection fibers - sometimes called the corona radiata, internal capsule, and specific radiations - define the feedforward sensory streams and feedback motor streams. Commissural fibers in the corpus callosum provide the main interhemispheric highway, linking homologous regions of the two hemispheres and enabling bilateral integration of sensory and motor maps. Together, thalamocortical, corticofugal, and commissural tracts form the core "subcortical highways" for sending raw sensory data into the cortex and distributing cortical output, while respecting the functional layout of cortical subdivisions. Within each hemisphere, long-range association tracts interconnect cortical areas according to functional streams. Prominent dorsal-stream tracts (often termed the superior longitudinal system) run anteroposteriorly: for example, the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) and its arcuate fasciculus branch link frontal regions with parietal and occipital cortices 4 . These dorsal pathways underlie spatial "where" processing and coordinate fronto-parietal attention and sensorimotor integration. In contrast, the ventral-stream or inferior longitudinal system carries information between occipital/temporal and frontal lobes. The inferior fronto‑occipital fasciculus (IFOF) and uncinate fasciculus (UF) run beneath the insula, connecting anterior temporal and occipital regions to frontal cortex. Likewise, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF) courses ventrally to join occipital visual areas with anterior temporal cortex, supporting object and face recognition ("what" pathway). Medial association tracts include the cingulum bundle, which arches within the cingulate gyrus to interconnect medial frontal, parietal and hippocampal regions, supporting the limbic and default-mode networks. (In parallel, short U-fibers link neighboring gyri, and multiple parallel sub-branches of these major systems fan out to diverse targets.) In sum, each cortical subdivision tends to exchange information with appropriate partners via these large fasciculi: for instance, visual cortices connect to parietal (dorsal) and temporal (ventral) cortices via SLF/AF, ILF and IFOF; auditory and language areas in superior temporal lobe connect to inferior frontal (Broca’s) regions via the arcuate; somatosensory areas connect to motor regions via local U-fibers and the SLF; and prefrontal areas receive convergent inputs from many of these streams. The overall architecture ensures that unimodal sensory regions feed into higher association cortices, while distributed frontal and parietal regions can rapidly communicate through the dorsal "belt" and the ventral "ventral belt" of fibers. These pathways are not random but emerge from developmental patterning. The genetic protomap of the cortex sets up a scaffold of areal identity 2 , and axon guidance molecules (ephrin gradients, netrins, semaphorins, etc.) steer fibers into the correct white‐matter highways. For example, retinotopic maps form in concert with graded Eph/ephrin signaling in both retina-to-LGN and LGN-to-V1 projections. Similarly, corticothalamic and thalamocortical fibers navigate through the internal capsule under the influence of "handshake" interactions and gradient cues 3 . In effect, early molecular gradients and midline patterning centers anchor the broad topology of cortical subdivisions, and subsequent chemoaffinity and activity-dependent processes refine the specific tracts between them. The result is a genetically-guided organization in which chemical gradients foreshadow the adult functional layout: e.g. anterior‐posterior gene gradients align with frontal-vs-occipital specializations, which in turn align with the course of major association fascicles. Over time, ongoing activity and plasticity further sculpt these highways (e.g. via pruning or myelination) so that the structural connectivity faithfully maps the information flow demands of vision, audition, sensation, and higher cognition across the cortical sheet.

title: Streams
text: Anatomical white matter tracts span the cortical hierarchy to support cognitive diversity The superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) is a massive association fiber bundle running anterior–posterior parallel to the cortical sheet, linking frontal cortex with parietal, occipital, and temporal association areas. It exemplifies the long-range corticocortical wiring that allows distributed cortical models to exchange information without routing through subcortical hubs. Relationship with ventral stream? A stream refers to a major, relatively segregated pathway through which information flows across different regions of the brain, typically from primary sensory areas toward higher-order association areas. Each stream is usually defined by its anatomical connections, the kind of information it processes, and its functional roles in perception, cognition, or action. Streams are not just highways for information-they are partially parallel, often recurrent, and interact with one another and with other brain systems. Modern research increasingly views them as dynamic, flexible networks that route and transform information according to current goals and contexts, rather than as rigid, linear processing lines. The classic examples are the dorsal ("where/how") and ventral ("what") visual streams, but similar stream-based architectures have been identified in auditory, somatosensory, and even language domains. In these systems, streams can be thought of as distinct but interacting circuits that handle complementary aspects of sensory input. For instance, in vision, the ventral stream processes object identity, while the dorsal stream processes spatial location and guides movements. The auditory system, likewise, splits into a ventral stream for recognizing sounds and a dorsal stream for mapping sounds to actions or locations. Two visual processing streams The primate visual cortex routes information through two major, partially overlapping highways that spring from primary visual cortex (V1). The ventral stream arcs along the inferior temporal lobe (V1 -> V2 -> V4 -> inferior temporal cortex) and builds increasingly invariant, high-dimensional representations of "what" is in view-objects, faces, textures, written words, scene categories, and their semantic associations. The dorsal stream rises dorsally through the parietal lobe (V1 -> V2 -> MT/MST -> posterior parietal cortex) and emphasizes "where" and "how": motion, depth, spatial layout, eye and limb position, and the real-time transformations needed to guide actions such as grasping or saccades. Classic neuropsychology, single-cell recordings, and neuroimaging established this functional dichotomy in the 1980s-1990s and it remains a central organizing principle of vision science today 2 . Over the last decade, the picture has shifted from two neat, serial hierarchies to a pair of densely interconnected, recurrent heterarchies embedded in widespread cortical and subcortical networks. The dorsal and ventral streams are not rigid pipelines that progressively refine information in a fixed order; instead, they consist of regions whose responses are shaped by context, goals, and cross-stream interactions. Many areas once thought to belong exclusively to one stream are now known to communicate extensively with the other, and both are directly influenced by inputs from memory systems, motor structures, and prefrontal areas. Rather than building a single unified percept, each region contributes a partial, task-relevant interpretation that may be used independently or in coordination with others depending on behavioral demands. 2 . Two somatosensory streams Somatosensory processing is done through at least two largely parallel ascending streams: a medial "lemniscal" channel that relays fine-grained proprioceptive and cutaneous position signals through dorsal column nuclei (in the spine) and VPL thalamus to S1 and on into parietal areas supporting sensorimotor control; and a more lateral/paralemniscal channel that carries multimodal object and affective touch information toward S2, insula and temporal operculum for haptic object recognition and affective valuation. Dense axonal reconstructions show distinct projection motifs all the way to cortex, supporting genuine stream-like segregation 3 . Somatosensory Dorsal Stream Starting in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and coursing through posterior parietal cortex (especially intraparietal areas) to premotor cortex, this stream represents the body’s configuration and object location. It encodes spatial and postural information (proprioception and tactile cues) in an egocentric reference frame, and projects this to motor planning areas. Functionally, it forms a "body-in-space" map used to guide actions (e.g. reaching, grasping) and sensorimotor coordination 4 Somatosensory Ventral Stream From S1 through secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) and insula into medial temporal areas (including hippocampus), this pathway encodes the intrinsic properties of touched objects. It builds invariant representations of object shape, texture and identity through touch. Anatomically, it connects to limbic/hippocampal regions (via S2 and insula) to support haptic object memory and recognition. In effect it underlies tactile "what" processing, forming memory traces of objects felt (akin to (and interacting with) visual ventral stream but via touch) 4 . Two auditory streams The auditory cortex is now widely accepted to host a "what/where-how" split that mirrors the visual dorsal-ventral dichotomy. A ventral route courses from primary A1 through the middle and anterior superior temporal gyrus into anterior temporal pole and inferior frontal areas; it builds increasingly invariant spectro-temporal templates for identifying voices, phonemes, words and environmental sounds, essentially mapping acoustic patterns onto meaning. In parallel, a dorsal pathway arcs posteriorly into the parietal operculum and premotor cortex, where sensory traces are mapped onto articulatory or spatial motor codes-essential for vocal imitation, phonological working memory and sound-source localisation; it supports sensorimotor integration in speech and music: learning to produce sounds, guiding vocal tract movements, and real-time feedback control of articulation. Lesion patterns such as conduction aphasia and modern tractography of the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculi clinch the dissociation between the dorsal and ventral streams. Two language streams The dual stream model of language processing follows the same fundamental architectural principle as the general auditory system - a ventral "what" stream for recognition/comprehension and a dorsal "how" stream for sensorimotor transformation; language piggy-backs on exactly the same scaffold but adds a layer of linguistically specific computations, especially combinatorial semantic processing in the ventral stream. The core insight-traced all the way back to Wernicke- is that the auditory word representation in posterior superior temporal gyrus (STG) simultaneously feeds two diverging routes: an auditory-to-conceptual (A -> C) branch for comprehension and an auditory-to-motor (A -> M) branch for production/monitoring. Hickok & Poeppel formalised these as the ventral and dorsal language streams. Ventral Stream (Comprehension) After bilateral spectro-temporal analysis in primary auditory cortex, activity flows along mid/posterior STG and the upper STS where phonological features are extracted. From there it fans antero-ventrally into posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG)-a "lexical interface" that maps sound patterns onto distributed semantic memory-and further into the anterior temporal lobe, which supports combinatorial conceptual processing. The network is almost bilateral, with only a mild ( 60/40) leftward bias. Functionally it answers the questions what word is that? what does it mean? In your auditory map this is the linguistic specialisation of the ventral "what" stream. Dorsal Stream (sensorimotor integration & production) Phonological representations in STG/STS project posteriorly to a Sylvian-parietal-temporal hub called area Spt in the planum temporale; Spt transforms auditory codes into articulatory ones and stays active both when you listen and when you silently rehearse speech or hum a melody. From Spt the signal ascends the supramarginal gyrus to premotor cortex and into the inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis, BA 44) and dorsal M1, completing a loop that compares predicted and heard speech to fine-tune articulation. This stream is strongly left-lateralised ( 90% of right-handers), mirroring your auditory "how" tract but specialised for the rapid, learned articulatory gestures of language. Two attention and executive streams The dorsal attention network (intraparietal sulcus <-> frontal eye fields) is bilaterally organized and implements sustained, goal-directed orienting and sets gain on modality-specific cortices, while the ventral attention network (temporo-parietal junction <-> ventral frontal cortex) is strongly right-lateralized acts as an interrupt/reset circuit that re-orients the system to unexpected but behaviorally relevant stimuli. Contemporary fMRI/MEG work shows dynamic coupling between the two nets rather than a simple hierarchy, underscoring their stream-like but interactive nature. 5 . At the level of prefrontal cortex itself, a dorsal-ventral axis of functional specialization mirrors these attention streams. Petrides and colleagues have shown that mid‐dorsolateral PFC (areas 46 and 9/46) underlies higher‐order monitoring and manipulation of information-holding abstract representations "on line" and comparing them against goals-whereas mid‐ventrolateral PFC (areas 45 and 47/12) mediates first‐order executive processes such as the active selection, comparison, and judgment of mnemonic and perceptual inputs 6 . Anatomically, this aligns with the finding that the dorsal visual stream (spatial/action information) projects preferentially to dorsolateral PFC, while the ventral visual stream (object/feature information) projects to ventrolateral PFC 7 . Thus, PFC itself is not a homogeneous executive control center but rather comprises parallel "streams" tuned either for abstract, spatially organized monitoring (dorsal) or for the selection and comparison of concrete stimulus features (ventral). Two episodic memory streams Episodic memory research has converged on two cortico-hippocampal "medial temporal lobe streams"-the anterior-temporal (AT) and posterior-medial (PM) systems-that feed the hippocampal formation from opposite ends. The AT stream (perirhinal -> anterior temporal pole / ventrolateral PFC) emphasizes item identity, emotion and social semantics; the PM stream (parahippocampal / retrosplenial -> precuneus / vmPFC) conveys contextual frameworks (space, situation, self). Effective-connectivity analyses during naturalistic recall show the two systems exert separable influences on the subjective vividness and content of memory, vindicating Ranganath & Ritchey’s dual-stream proposal. 8 , 9 Multiple value/reward streams The macroscopic picture starts with four largely parallel dopaminergic projection systems. The nigrostriatal tract (substantia nigra -> dorsal striatum) biases vigor and habit formation; the mesolimbic tract (VTA -> ventral striatum, amygdala) encodes incentive motivation and appetitive learning; the mesocortical tract (VTA -> prefrontal and cingulate cortices) carries a slower, state-value and cognitive-control signal; and the tuberoinfundibular tract modulates hypothalamic endocrine set-points. Anatomically these bundles share a midbrain origin yet remain largely non-overlapping up to their cortical or striatal termini, and functional imaging or fiber-photometry confirms that each stream carries a distinct "flavor" of reward information. 10 Zooming in, even the mesolimbic axis fractures into finer sub-streams. Medial VTA cells projecting to nucleus accumbens shell emit textbook reward-prediction-error bursts, whereas lateral VTA neurons projecting to accumbens core or dorsolateral striatum fire more transient salience or movement-gain signals and can be optogenetically separated in both rodents and primates. Single-cell sequencing and connectomics now map these populations onto discrete molecular lineages, arguing that the "dopamine RPE" is only one branch of a broader, parallel value architecture 11 , 12 . Opponent valence rides its own tracks. The lateral habenula-rostromedial tegmental ("anti-reward") stream suppresses VTA firing when outcomes are worse than expected, while medial habenula and specific hypothalamic-VTA pathways convey positive or homeostatic value. Recent stress-induction studies show that hyperactivity of the negative-valence stream can globally re-weight cortical processing within minutes, underscoring its independence from the classical reward pathways 13 , 14 Downstream, cortico-basal-ganglia loops are themselves arranged in parallel limbic, associative and sensorimotor circuits that feed into ventral, dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum, respectively. Each loop implements a distinct cost-benefit calculus-motivation, goal-directed planning, or habitual efficiency-yet they all reconnect to cortex through thalamus, giving the organism multiple, simultaneously running value estimators that can be blended or weighted according to context 15 , 16 . Other neuromodulators furnish additional streams: serotonergic raphe projections encode punishment expectancy and temporal discounting; noradrenergic locus-coeruleus fibers broadcast surprise and arousal; endogenous-opioid hotspots in nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex register consummatory "liking". These systems interdigitate with, but do not collapse into, the dopaminergic tracks, reinforcing the idea that the brain maintains multiple, parallel value channels tuned to different statistics of the environment and body.

title: Loops
text: Loops are topographically organized cortico-subcortical-cortical circuits in which a cortical territory sends a copy of its state to a specialized subcortical module, that module transforms it according to its own objectives and learning rules, and thalamic or direct output returns the result to the same-or functionally allied-cortical field. Because different hubs optimize on different timescales and signals, the brain runs many such loops in parallel. The effect is to interleave evaluation (basal ganglia), prediction and timing (cerebellum), routing/attention and working-memory stabilization (thalamus), and episodic indexing and sequence generation (hippocampus) directly into ongoing cortical computation. Rather than a one-way pipeline, cortex operates inside a reentrant heterarchy where loop outputs continuously shape the next cortical step. Basal ganglia loops implement context-sensitive gating and policy learning: direct/indirect/hyperdirect channels regulate which motor or cognitive program is released, how vigorous it is, and when to withhold action under conflict. Dopamine conveys reward-prediction errors that retune corticostriatal synapses, solving temporal credit assignment with eligibility traces and, over repetition, compiling habits. Cerebello-cortical loops function as forward-model predictors and timing regulators. Their massively expanded granule cell code and climbing-fiber teaching signals support precise, millisecond-scale calibration of movements and, in association territories (e.g., Crus I/II), the automation and smoothing of cognitive sequences. Thalamo-cortical loops provide the brain’s dynamic I/O and coordination fabric. Core relays deliver precise feedforward drive while matrix-type nuclei (pulvinar, MD) send broad, layer-1 feedback that carries context, attention, and predictions. These bidirectional exchanges naturally implement predictive-coding style computations-gamma-dominated feedforward channels emphasize unexpected input; alpha/beta-dominated feedback carries priors and top-down suppression-while MD<->PFC circuits stabilize delay activity for working memory and flexibly set decision thresholds. Hippocampo-cortical loops supply the complementary memory operations: dentate/CA3 separate overlapping inputs and complete sparse cues; theta sequences and ripple-time replay generate and evaluate prospective or past trajectories; repeated replay trains long-term cortical schemas. Across systems, the common motif is a reentrant transform-and-return: cortex proposes, specialized modules evaluate/predict/index on their preferred objective and timescale, and the refined signal re-enters cortex to update perception, cognition, and action. This architecture yields three system-level advantages. First, it distributes learning across mechanisms tuned to different feedback (dopamine RPEs, climbing-fiber errors, cortico-thalamic context), improving sample efficiency and robustness. Second, it enforces flexible control-global "stops" and local "goes," attentionally gated routing, and stability of task sets when needed. Third, it supports multi-horizon computation: cerebellar timing (ms), thalamo-cortical maintenance (hundreds of ms to seconds), basal-ganglia policy shaping (seconds to days), and hippocampal consolidation (hours to years). In short, loops are the brain’s integration pattern: the reason evaluation, prediction, memory, and action selection stay coupled yet modular, giving biological agents both speed and adaptivity. More on these specific loops in the in Systems-Level Architecture section. Covering thalamo-cortical loops here since they show up in every subsystem. Thalamocortical architectures for flexible cognition and efficient learning A thalamocortical circuit encoding deviations from sensory history Thalamo-Cortical Loops Thalamo-cortical loops are recurrent circuits connecting the thalamus and cerebral cortex, forming bidirectional pathways that underlie much of the brain’s information processing. Unlike many brain region interactions that are one-directional, the cortex and thalamus send massive excitatory projections to each other, engaging essentially all cortical areas and thalamic nuclei in loops. These loops have long been implicated in fundamental neural functions - from generating brain rhythms (sleep spindles, alpha oscillations) to enabling sensory attention and inter-areal communication. Historically, the thalamus was viewed as a simple relay for sensory signals, but modern evidence reveals a more complex, interactive architecture: specific thalamic nuclei connect with defined cortical layers and regions, and feedback from cortex profoundly modulates thalamic transmission. Anatomy Each thalamic nucleus has a reciprocal relationship with specific cortical areas, forming distinct thalamo-cortical loops. First-order (relay) nuclei (sometimes called core-type nuclei) receive direct sensory or subcortical input and project mainly to primary cortical areas. Examples include the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) for vision (projecting to V1), medial geniculate body (MGN) for audition (to A1), and ventrobasal complex (VB; comprising VPL/VPM) for somatosensation (to S1). These core nuclei typically project topographically to layer 4 of cortex and nearby layers, providing a focused, point-to-point relay of sensory information. In contrast, higher-order (association) nuclei (often matrix-type nuclei) receive a significant driving input from cortex itself (via descending layer 5 pathways) and project more diffusely to higher cortical areas. Examples are the pulvinar and lateral posterior (LP) nuclei in visual systems (connecting to parietal and temporal cortex), the mediodorsal (MD) nucleus connecting with prefrontal cortex, and the ventral medial (VM) nucleus connecting with frontal premotor areas. These matrix-type nuclei tend to project to superficial cortical layers (layers 1 and 2/3) over broad areas, often influencing apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons and coordinating activity across cortical regions 3 . Thalamo-cortical loops are usually named by the corresponding thalamic nucleus and its cortical target. For example, the visual loop comprises retina -> LGN -> visual cortex (V1) -> back to LGN; the auditory loop involves cochlea -> MGN -> auditory cortex; and a somatosensory loop links dorsal column nuclei -> VPL/VPM -> somatosensory cortex. Importantly, association loops connect higher-order thalamic nuclei with frontal and parietal cortices; for instance, the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus <-> prefrontal cortex (PFC) loop and pulvinar <-> visual association cortex loops are critical for cognition and attention. Beyond sensory pathways, the thalamus also participates in motor and limbic loops: e.g. the ventrolateral (VL) thalamus relays signals from cerebellum and basal ganglia to motor cortex, closing a motor loop; the anterior and midline thalamic nuclei connect with cingulate and hippocampal regions, forming loops involved in memory and emotion. Thus, virtually every cortical area is part of a specific thalamic loop, underscoring that cortex and thalamus function as an integrated circuit rather than isolated processors. Each loop exhibits reciprocal connectivity: the thalamic relay neurons send excitatory afferents to cortex, and in turn cortical neurons (primarily deep-layer pyramidal cells) send excitatory feedback projections back to those same thalamic neurons. This reciprocity creates a closed loop that can sustain reverberant activity. The feedforward (thalamo->cortical) pathway often carries rapidly time-locked information (e.g. a visual stimulus onset), while the feedback (cortico->thalamic) pathway can modulate the gain, context, or timing of thalamic relay, rather than simply echoing the input. Indeed, the feedback projections far outnumber the feedforward inputs in many cases: for example, in the LGN as little as  5-10% of synapses come from retinal fibers, whereas up to 95% of inputs are from cortical feedback, local GABAergic interneurons, the thalamic reticular nucleus, and brainstem modulatory systems. This anatomical fact highlights that the thalamus is not a passive relay - it is a convergence hub where cortical and subcortical signals intermingle to shape what is ultimately sent to cortex. Within each cortical area, thalamic inputs and cortical outputs are arranged in a precise laminar pattern. Core-type thalamic neurons (often parvalbumin-positive in primates) project to the middle cortical layers (layer 4 and lower layer 3), forming dense terminal arbors often called "thalamo-recipient layers". These projections create the initial feedforward drive in cortical columns and also excite local inhibitory interneurons, producing feedforward inhibition that sharpens spatial and temporal response properties. Matrix-type thalamic neurons (often calbindin-positive) project more to layer 1 and upper layers (1-2), spreading more diffusely. A given cortical area can receive a mix of core and matrix inputs: for instance, primary visual cortex (V1) gets core input from LGN (to layer 4) and also matrix input from the pulvinar/LP (to layer 1). Higher-order association cortices (e.g. prefrontal, temporal) often receive predominantly matrix-type input to layer 1 from association thalamic nuclei like MD or pulvinar. The functional consequence is that core inputs deliver precise sensory details to cortical circuits, while matrix inputs provide a more modulatory, context-carrying signal to the distal dendrites of pyramidal neurons (in layer 1), influencing how cortex interprets or prioritizes information. From the cortical side, there are discrete classes of pyramidal cells that participate in thalamo-cortical loops. Layer 6 corticothalamic (CT) neurons project almost exclusively to the thalamus (with a collateral to the inhibitory thalamic reticular nucleus), and provide the main feedback pathway to first-order thalamic relays. These layer 6 cells typically make small, modulatory synapses on thalamic relay neurons and often target the distal dendrites, implying they modulate thalamic responsiveness rather than driving it strongly. Layer 5B pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, in contrast, are large output cells that send one branch down to subcortical structures (e.g. forming the corticospinal or corticopontine tracts) and another collateral branch up to higher-order thalamic nuclei 4 . These layer 5->thalamus projections are thought to act as drivers for higher-order thalamic relays (like pulvinar, MD, LP, etc.), in a similar way that retinal afferents drive the LGN. Indeed, many higher-order thalamic nuclei essentially sit in between cortical areas: a PT neuron in one cortical area can send a driver signal to a thalamic nucleus, which then projects to another cortical area - forming a trans-thalamic cortico-cortical circuit. This provides an indirect route for cortical areas to influence each other via the thalamus (in addition to direct cortico-cortical fibers). Meanwhile, intratelencephalic (IT) neurons are the typical cortico-cortical pyramidal cells (located in layers 2/3, 5A and 6) that project within the cortex and to striatum, but notably do not project to the thalamus. IT cells instead form local recurrent networks and long-range cortical pathways. They help "close the loop" on the cortical side by integrating thalamic input and feeding activity back into deep layers or to other cortical regions. Importantly, IT neurons often mediate the connection between cortico-thalamo-cortical (CTC) loops and pure cortico-cortical (CC) circuits: they receive thalamic input and can broadcast it to other cortical areas. This means the thalamic loop doesn’t function in isolation - it’s interwoven with cortical networks via these IT neurons acting as hubs. In summary, a "core loop" (first-order) might involve a layer 6 CT neuron projecting to a relay nucleus, which in turn projects to layer 4 of the same cortical area, and an IT neuron in layer 4/5 completes the loop by connecting back to layer 6 or locally. A "higher-order loop" might involve a layer 5 PT neuron driving a matrix-type thalamic nucleus, which projects broadly to layer 1 and 5A of higher cortical areas, and then IT neurons propagate that activity within cortex and perhaps back to layer 6 of the originating area. Researchers distinguish "simple" vs. "complex" CTC loops: simple loops consist of a direct reciprocal pair (one population of cortical neurons monosynaptically connected to one thalamic population), whereas complex loops include additional cortical interneurons or IT neurons that create multi-synaptic chains closing the loop. Many higher loops are complex, engaging a web of intracortical connections. Even within a single cortical area, multiple loop types may coexist (for example, S1 has a first-order loop via VPM and a higher-order loop via posterior thalamic nucleus PO). Operation A thalamo-cortical loop has distinct feedforward and feedback streams that together form a recurrent circuit. Feedforward flow generally refers to signals originating in the periphery or lower areas, ascending through the thalamus into cortex. For instance, when a visual stimulus appears, retinal ganglion cells fire -> LGN relay cells transmit bursts to V1 (layer 4) -> V1 neurons process and forward signals to higher visual cortices. Such ascending drive is often rapid and time-locked to stimuli, initiating cortical responses. Feedback flow denotes signals from cortex back to thalamus (and also from higher cortical areas back to lower ones). These descending signals can carry contextual information, predictions, or attention-related modulation. In the visual example, V1 sends axons back to LGN (mostly from layer 6 CT cells) and even higher visual areas send feedback to V1 and LGN (via higher-order thalamus like pulvinar). Feedback typically is not a simple mirror of feedforward content; instead it can sharpen or suppress certain inputs and synchronize thalamic neurons. In fact, corticothalamic fibers outnumber incoming drivers in many relays, and they terminate broadly (often on distal dendrites or inhibitory interneurons), consistent with a modulatory role. This recurrent architecture allows iterative refinement of neural representations. A classic hypothesis by David Mumford (1991) suggested that each cortical area and its thalamic partner form a "comparison loop" that implements a form of predictive coding: the cortex sends an expectation of incoming features down to the thalamus, where it is compared with the actual incoming signal, and any mismatch (error) is sent back up to cortex. In this view, feedforward inputs carry error signals (novel or unpredicted information) while feedback conveys predictions or context, and the loop continually adjusts cortical activity to minimize error. Whether literally true or not, this concept aligns with the observation that cortico-thalamic feedback can suppress predictable inputs or amplify unexpected ones. For example, if an expected stimulus is suddenly omitted or altered, thalamic relay cells often respond with burst firing (due to a release from cortical inhibition) signaling a "surprise." Conversely, focused attention from cortex can pre-depolarize specific thalamic neurons, putting them in a tonic mode that relays information faithfully while filtering out irrelevant signals (see Attention and Gating below). Thus, information flow in the loop is bidirectional and dynamic: cortex influences what thalamus relays, and thalamus gates what cortex perceives. The directionality also maps onto distinct frequency channels. Fast oscillations (gamma  30-80 Hz) are often prominent in feedforward pathways (superficial cortical layers to thalamus and onward), whereas slower oscillations (alpha/beta  8-20 Hz) are seen in feedback (deep cortical layers projecting to thalamus). This spectral separation is thought to help organize the hierarchy: high-frequency synchronized bursts can drive the next stage, while lower-frequency rhythms convey contextual modulation. For instance, attending to a stimulus increases gamma coherence between LGN and V1 or between V1 and V4, tightening feedforward coupling, whereas feedback signals from higher areas to lower might ride on alpha oscillations associated with expectation or top-down suppression. Thalamo-cortical loops thus operate with a temporal coding scheme where feedforward and feedback streams interact but retain some distinction in timing and frequency domain 5 . The net result is a loop that can resonate - supporting sustained activity (working memory states, oscillatory rhythms) - but also remain responsive to new inputs. Functions Sensory Relay and Preprocessing At the most basic level, thalamo-cortical loops handle sensory signal transmission from the outside world to the cortex. But rather than a passive relay, the loop performs preprocessing such as filtering, sharpening, and timing control. The thalamus can emphasize novel or significant inputs by switching into burst mode for a transient, high-salience signal. It can also suppress transmission when appropriate: e.g. during sleep or inattention, strong TRN inhibition causes relay neurons to oscillate among themselves (spindles) rather than forwarding input to cortex. Even in waking, the thalamus contributes to adapting sensory processing. A classic example is the lateral geniculate nucleus in vision: LGN cells receive not just retinal input but also feedback from visual cortex and brainstem (e.g. locus coeruleus, dorsal raphe). This allows state-dependent gating - for instance, under high arousal, LGN throughput is increased (tonic mode, less surround inhibition), improving visual sensitivity, whereas under relaxed conditions, more surround inhibition or burst firing might enhance detection of only the most salient changes. Additionally, receptive field properties of thalamic neurons can shape cortical responses. Many relay cells already exhibit center-surround organization (enhancing contrast), and some higher-order relays integrate inputs (e.g. the pulvinar integrates signals from superior colliculus and cortex, potentially combining retinal and cortical motion information). Thus, the loop’s initial feedforward pass is a processed version of raw sensory data, conditioned by the organism’s internal state. The cortical side of the loop further sharpens tuning through intracortical circuits, but notably much of that sharpening involves thalamic input driving feedforward inhibition. For example, a whisker deflection in rodents triggers thalamic VB neurons that excite layer-4 fast-spiking interneurons in barrel cortex, which in turn laterally inhibit neighboring barrels - leading to a crisp spatial encoding of which whisker moved. This is an emergent property of the TC loop: only the connections present enable this computation (VB->PV interneuron->silence adjacent columns). If the thalamus simply broadcast uniformly, the specificity would be lost. Therefore, one computational role of TC loops is sensory feature selection and enhancement - highlighting important inputs and localizing them in space and time for the cortex. Attention and Gating Thalamo-cortical loops play a pivotal role in selective attention - dynamically gating the flow of sensory or cognitive information. The pulvinar (in visual and association loops) is often described as an "attentional spotlight" or hub that coordinates cortical areas. When attention is directed to a visual target, pulvinar neurons not only increase their firing rates but also synchronize their activity with the cortical circuits processing that target. By phase-aligning oscillations in those cortical areas, the pulvinar loop effectively boosts effective connectivity between them. Attention-related gating is not unique to pulvinar. Modality-specific loops also exhibit attention modulation. In the LGN, when a subject attends to a visual stimulus, responses of LGN neurons to that stimulus are enhanced (an effect likely mediated by feedback from visual cortex and cholinergic basal forebrain inputs). Similarly, the MD thalamus in cognitive tasks can gate prefrontal cortex processing (discussed below). A unifying principle is that thalamo-cortical loops allow top-down signals to intervene at an early stage of processing. Working Memory and Executive Loops Growing evidence indicates that working memory - the temporary holding and manipulation of information - relies on thalamo-cortical loops, especially involving the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus and prefrontal cortex. Classical models of working memory often focused on persistent recurrent activity in cortical circuits alone (e.g. PFC maintaining a trace of a cue). However, recent optogenetic and electrophysiological studies in rodents show that disconnecting or silencing the MD thalamus profoundly disrupts PFC working memory function. In one study, during a spatial working memory task, MD->PFC activity was required to sustain persistent firing of PFC neurons during the memory delay, and inactivation of MD caused those delay-period representations to fade, leading to errors 6 . Interestingly, the reverse pathway (PFC->MD) was needed later, at the choice period, suggesting a loop: the thalamus helps keep information online in cortex, and then the cortex instructs the thalamus when to clear or use that information for decisions. These findings paint the thalamus as an "amplifier" or stabilizer of cortical activity in service of working memory. Because the MD thalamus has diffuse connectivity with PFC (matrix-type projections to superficial layers and even to inhibitory interneurons), it is well-placed to influence network excitability. Predictive Coding and Error Signaling Predictive coding theories propose that the cortex constantly generates predictions of incoming sensory inputs and compares them with actual inputs, with only the mismatch (prediction error) being propagated forward. Thalamo-cortical loops have been hypothesized to implement this comparison and error gating. Classic ideas (Mumford, 1991; later Friston, 2010) envisioned the thalamus as an "active blackboard" where cortical feedback (predictions) are written and then updated by sensory input differences. Recent experimental evidence provides concrete examples of this principle in action. A 2024 study by Furutachi et al. demonstrated a circuit for prediction-error generation in mouse visual cortex that crucially involves the thalamus. When mice were trained to expect a certain visual pattern in a virtual reality setup, neurons in V1 responded normally if the pattern appeared as predicted. But if an unexpected stimulus appeared instead, a specific subset of V1 neurons (those tuned to the unexpected feature) showed a selectively boosted response, as if signaling "this feature was not predicted". This selective amplification of unpredicted input was traced to a cooperative thalamo-cortical disinhibitory circuit: the higher-order thalamus (the pulvinar/LP in this case) provided a supplementary input to V1 when the surprise occurred, and at the same time, VIP interneurons in V1 became active to silence SST interneurons, thereby lifting inhibition from the pyramidal cells that prefer the unexpected stimulus 7 . In other words, breaking a prediction engaged a loop where the thalamus + local cortical circuit worked together to enhance the error signal (the unexpected feature). If either the thalamic input or the VIP interneuron activity was experimentally blocked, this selective amplification did not happen - showing that the thalamus was required for robust error signaling. Another way to frame this is through active inference - the idea that the brain not only passively predicts but also takes actions to fulfill predictions (minimize surprise). Thalamo-cortical loops are positioned to influence action selection via their connections to motor circuits (basal ganglia, cerebellum loops) and to sensorimotor cortex. For example, the higher-order loops through the pulvinar and MD might signal when an outcome deviates from the internal model, and this could engage frontal-striatal circuits to adjust behavior. Some theories propose that the intralaminar thalamus (central lateral nucleus and others) broadcast prediction errors widely (as part of a "global workspace") to update multiple cortical areas and possibly drive exploratory behavior. While direct evidence for thalamic involvement in active inference is still emerging, the known anatomy fits: thalamic outputs reach broad cortical territories and can rapidly alter cortical states, which is what a global error broadcast or belief update requires. Notably, the anterior cingulate loop through midline thalamus might convey reward prediction errors or context changes that motivate policy shifts. In rodents, inactivating the medial thalamus impairs the ability to use contextual cues for behavior (which can be seen as a deficit in inferring the correct context). All these points converge on the idea that thalamo-cortical loops compute "differences" and "updates" - whether it’s sensory surprise, cognitive set shifting, or a violation of expectation, the loops kick in to signal the rest of the brain that an update is needed. This contrasts with the cortex alone, which might settle into a predictive state; the thalamus is a node that can inject a disruptive corrective signal when reality and prediction diverge. Decision-Making and Action Selection Thalamo-cortical loops are also integral to circuits that underlie decision-making. Here, the loops often involve interactions with the basal ganglia. A canonical pathway is the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex loop, where cortex projects to striatum (input of BG), BG output nuclei (like GPi) inhibit thalamus, and thalamus projects back to cortex. The thalamus in these loops (e.g. ventroanterior and ventrolateral nuclei for motor, MD for executive) serves as the final gateway that either allows a cortical command to be executed or not, depending on BG disinhibition. Thus, one can think of the thalamus as the "gate that opens" when a decision is made - for example, when the basal ganglia decides to initiate a movement, it releases the VL thalamus from inhibition, and VL then drives motor cortex to generate the action. In decision tasks under uncertainty, cognitive thalamic loops also contribute. We saw earlier that MD has distinct circuits for handling uncertainty (low signal vs high noise). In practical terms, during a difficult decision with conflicting evidence, the thalamus might dampen impulsive cortical activity (via one pathway) until enough signal accumulates, and then amplify the chosen direction’s cortical ensemble (via another pathway) once confidence is higher. Animal studies support this: if MD is lesioned, animals often have decision-making deficits, such as being unable to adjust choices based on changing rules or probabilities (they perseverate or get distracted easily). This mirrors PFC lesions, suggesting the loop as a whole is required. Another intriguing role is in active sensing: the thalamo-cortical circuits (particularly those involving higher-order thalamus and layer 5 PT neurons) might help decide where to sample information next. For instance, the circuit from frontal eye field (FEF) cortex -> thalamus (pulvinar or MD) -> back to visual cortices could influence where to move the eyes by highlighting particular stimuli. Some experiments in primates show that microstimulating the thalamus can bias choices or attention, indicating a causal role in guiding decisions. There is also emerging evidence that thalamic loops contribute to conscious decision processes. The central lateral thalamus has been called a "higher-order state" nucleus that might reflect the current rule or plan and broadcast it (some have tied this to conscious awareness of actions). While these ideas are still speculative, it’s clear that beyond sensory gating, the thalamus collaborates with frontal cortex and basal ganglia to implement the computations underlying voluntary decisions and action selection. One can conceptualize it as follows: cortex proposes, basal ganglia disposes, and thalamus gates the disposition back to cortex for execution. In computational terms, the thalamo-cortical loop in decisions might compute a "commitment function" - holding cortical plans in check until a threshold is met, then allowing full activation once the decision is made, thereby ensuring a definitive rather than wavering response. AGI Design Principles Forward-model separation. Cerebellar loops highlight the value of maintaining a parallel supervised simulator that learns dynamics rapidly and hands predictions to the slower policy network. In practice, this argues for a lightweight system-identification module sitting alongside a heavier policy/value learner. Offline generative rehearsal. Hippocampal loops demonstrate how experience replay can be context-dependent, compositional and goal-directed, not just random sampling. Incorporating a replay controller that triggers targeted roll-outs when expected value of information is high can dramatically cut sample complexity. Hierarchical gating rather than monolithic back-propagation. BG-style loops show how action and memory updates can be gated by local reinforcement signals without global credit transport. An AGI architecture can approximate this with striatal-like sparse gating modules that decide when downstream subnetworks update. Thalamic routing for dynamic modularity. Thalamus teaches us that routing traffic between expert subnetworks can itself be an active, trainable process. Attentional transformers and mixture-of-experts schemes are early steps; a fuller analogue would add a learned gating matrix that can switch entire cortical areas on-the-fly. Attractor-based working memory. Embedding shallow recurrent attractor micro-loops inside a deep feed-forward backbone can give an AGI stable latent states without constant refresh traffic, reducing energy and enabling long-horizon temporal credit assignment.

title: Macroscale Gradients and Intrinsic Neural Timescales
text: Across cortex-and mirrored in several subcortical systems-organization is better captured by smooth gradients than by sharp borders. The dominant cortical axis ("principal gradient") runs from unimodal sensorimotor areas to transmodal association cortex (default-mode and frontoparietal zones). Along this path, myeloarchitecture thins, pyramidal dendrites lengthen, receptive fields broaden, and connectivity shifts from short-range, topographically precise links to long-range, integrative projections. Functionally, this same axis separates fast, stimulus-locked processing from slow, model-based inference. Diffusion-map embeddings of resting connectivity first made this explicit, placing primary visual/auditory/somatomotor cortex at one end and default-mode cortex at the other, with higher association zones in between. T1w/T2w myelin maps and multimodal parcellations recapitulate the same sensorimotor->association gradient, tying the functional axis to a structural substrate 1 , 2 , 3 . Temporal organization follows this geometry. Electrophysiology across primate cortex shows a monotonic increase in intrinsic timescales-from tens of milliseconds in early sensory areas to hundreds of milliseconds or more in prefrontal and midline association cortices-consistent with a hierarchy that integrates over progressively longer windows as one ascends the gradient. Naturalistic fMRI pushes this further: "temporal receptive windows" expand from word/phoneme-scale in early auditory cortex to sentence/paragraph-scale in superior temporal, angular gyrus, and medial prefrontal cortex, supporting narrative-level inference and event segmentation. Together these data argue that the cortex is wired to accumulate evidence over time in proportion to its position on the sensorimotor->association gradient: posterior/lateral regions compress immediate input; anterior/medial regions stabilize context over seconds to minutes 4 , 5 , 6 . Hippocampus exhibits a homologous long-axis gradient. Posterior hippocampus couples to posterior-medial, perceptual networks and emphasizes precise spatial/contextual coding and pattern separation; anterior hippocampus couples to anterior-temporal/ventromedial networks and emphasizes coarse, affect- and schema-laden representations and pattern completion. This posterior->anterior sweep aligns with a short->long horizon in mnemonic integration and abstraction, positioning hippocampus as a bridge between fast sensory maps and slow, schema-driven simulation 7 , 8 . Comparable gradients appear outside neocortex. In cerebellum, a principal functional gradient runs from sensorimotor lobules to DMN- and control-network-coupled territories, with a secondary axis differentiating task-focused from task-unfocused cognition; this mirrors the neocortical principal gradient and suggests that cerebellar forward models operate over short horizons in motor zones and longer, more abstract sequences in cognitive zones. Thalamus, too, shows low-dimensional gradients that align with cortical hierarchies, offering a substrate for routing information across timescales via core (driver) and matrix (modulatory) channels. These parallel gradients imply that hierarchical timescales are not a cortical curiosity but a whole-brain design principle implemented across loops 9 , 10 . Mechanistically, gradients and timescales co-vary with three families of constraints. First, cyto/myeloarchitectonics: lightly myelinated, homotypical (eulaminate) association cortex with long apical dendrites (DMN, anterior PFC) supports slower membrane and network dynamics and stronger feedback, lengthening integration windows; heavily myelinated heterotypical granular cortex (V1/A1/S1) favors fast feedforward drive and short windows. Second, wiring geometry: as geodesic distance from primary landmarks increases, long-range associative tracts and hub participation rise, boosting recurrent mixing and temporal stability. Third, neuromodulatory/thalamic tone: association cortex receives denser higher-order (matrix-type) thalamic input and neuromodulatory afferents that tune gain and plasticity over seconds-to-minutes, effectively stretching the ’temporal kernel’ of inference. The resulting system implements hierarchical inference in time: lower tiers encode rapidly changing causes; mid-tiers integrate over episodes; top tiers carry slowly drifting latent states, goals, and schemas that regularize lower levels via feedback." 2 , 11 , 12 , 13 . !!!
