title: Hub-and-Spoke Architecture and Rich-Club Organization
text: Hippocampus, BG, and thalamus as supreme hubs At the mesoscale, the cortex is a modular graph overlaid by a sparse, high-bandwidth core of hubs that are unusually well connected to one another-the "rich club.". These hub-to-hub edges are longer, thicker, and more heavily myelinated than average, so they are costly in wire and energy but buy global efficiency: a disproportionate fraction of shortest paths traverse the rich-club core, keeping average path length near  3 steps while most day-to-day traffic stays within modules 1 , 2 , 3 . Two hub classes matter computationally. "Connector hubs" have high participation coefficients: they bridge multiple modules and switch partners with task demands. Canonical examples include posterior cingulate/precuneus on the medial wall (DMN anchor with long temporal receptive windows), anterior insula and dorsal ACC (salience/control switches), lateral frontoparietal cortex (multiple-demand system), superior parietal/intraparietal areas (sensorimotor-attention nexus), and temporoparietal junction/anterior temporal cortex (semantic/conceptual convergence). "Provincial hubs" are highly connected within a module (e.g., early visual or auditory association zones) and stabilize local processing. Rich-club hubs are densely interlinked with each other (hub-hub "backbone") and spoke outward via major association tracts-the superior longitudinal/arcuate fasciculi (dorsal frontoparietal and language dorsal stream), inferior fronto-occipital and inferior longitudinal fasciculi (ventral object/semantic stream), uncinate (orbitofrontal-anterior temporal), and cingulum (medial wall DMN). Dynamics reflect this geometry. Across primate cortex, feed-forward influences are preferentially expressed in faster gamma-band activity, whereas feedback/predictive signals are carried in slower alpha-beta rhythms; this frequency split is clearest in laminar recordings and inter-areal interactions along the visual hierarchy and generalizes to other cortices 4 , 5 . Inter-areal propagation times are on the order of a few to a few tens of milliseconds: the fastest callosal routes conduct in <5 ms, with many long cortico-cortical paths yielding effective delays of  3-20 ms that, together with synaptic and circuit latencies, set the phase relations that enable frequency-specific coupling across hubs 6 , 7 . Association-cortex hubs operate on longer intrinsic timescales-hundreds of milliseconds in single-unit and mesoscale measures-with network-level integration unfolding over seconds during naturalistic cognition, consistent with a temporal hierarchy from sensory to transmodal regions 8 , 9 , 10 . In practice, the system behaves as a small-world, core-periphery network: segregated work is handled within modules and spokes, while brief, selective, frequency-aligned bursts through the rich-club backbone support global integration; "cortical architecture" therefore is a two-tier interconnect: many specialized spokes doing cheap, local computation, stitched together by a thin, expensive, and highly plastic core that enables rapid, goal-dependent integration across modalities, timescales, and cognitive domains.

title: Large-Scale Networks
text: Beyond individual modules, fMRI and tractography reveal functionally cohesive networks that link distant regions to perform complex cognitive functions. The default-mode network (DMN; medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate/precuneus, hippocampus) is engaged during rest, introspection, and episodic simulation - supporting internal scene construction and memory recall. The frontoparietal control (executive) network (dorsolateral PFC, lateral parietal) sustains task rules and goals during cognitive effort, integrating sensory input with working memory. The salience network (anterior insula, dorsal ACC) detects behaviorally relevant cues and acts as a switch: it suppresses DMN and engages executive regions when novel or salient events occur. In practice, these networks reflect core architectural motifs: the DMN overlaps hubs for multi-modal memory and affect, the executive network overlaps regions receiving BG-thalamic feedback, and the salience network overlaps areas receiving subcortical arousal/reward input. Together they coordinate global information flow - e.g. shifting between exploration (DMN-driven model updating) and exploitation (executive-driven action) - essential for adaptive world modeling. Dense within-module connectivity (clustering coefficient  0.5-0.7) and sparse between-module connections ( 0.1-0.2) Many tasks involve competition between networks. A classic example is the competition between FPN and DMN in attention tasks: stronger FPN activity suppresses DMN, enabling focus. However, there are also cooperative interactions: e.g. the hippocampus (DMN) and FPN co-activate when retrieving memory-guided rules. Neuromodulators provide a coarse level of coordination: e.g. dopamine and noradrenaline shifts can globally increase gain in FPN/SN or in sensory areas depending on motivational state However, interactions are not solely competitive. Cooperative dynamics also occur, where different networks co-activate and synchronize their activity to support complex cognitive functions. For example, tasks that require retrieving memory-guided rules or engaging in creative thought can involve co-activation of the FPN and DMN. The Salience Network is believed to play a pivotal role in orchestrating these inter-network dynamics, particularly in switching the brain’s dominant processing mode between internal focus (DMN engagement) and external task-orientation (FPN/CEN engagement) based on the perceived relevance of internal or external stimuli. This "triple network model" (SN, DMN, CEN) highlights how the brain flexibly allocates its processing resources. Dynamic Network Switching These networks are not static anatomical entities but are better understood as dynamic coalitions of brain regions. The specific regions participating in a network and the strength of their interactions can vary depending on the ongoing cognitive state, task demands, and even individual differences. Despite this variability, a set of core, consistently identified networks forms the backbone of the brain’s functional organization. This leads us to a broader principle: thia dynamic reconfiguration of functional circuits is a highly efficient mechanism for allocating limited neural resources. Instead of maintaining all possible processing pathways in an active state simultaneously-which would be metabolically exorbitant and could lead to widespread interference-the brain flexibly "wires up" the necessary circuits on demand. This allows a finite anatomical structure to support an impressively vast repertoire of cognitive functions and adaptive behaviors. Brain alternates between segregated states (modules operating independently) and integrated states (increased between-module communication) based on task demands State transitions occur on 100-500ms timescales, orchestrated by subcortical neuromodulators Flexibility of network reconfiguration correlates with cognitive performance (r = 0.4-0.6)

title: Broader Characteristics
text: Redundancy Modular Organization and Hierarchical Structure Modules exhibit hierarchical organization across  5-7 octaves of temporal scales: from millisecond cerebellar predictions to multi-year schemas in ventromedial PFC Enables parallel processing; some theories of modularity, such as Fodor’s, propose that certain modules operate with a degree of "informational encapsulation," meaning they can perform their specific computations without extensive reference to other psychological systems, further enhancing processing speed for dedicated tasks; this further leads to extensibility (evolvability; no need for complete redesign, just modular extension and broad scaling) and robustness (damage to one specialized module may not necessarily lead to a catastrophic failure of the entire system) Each level of hierarchy shows characteristic timescale ratio of  5-7× relative to adjacent levels, suggesting fundamental engineering regularities Ascending the hierarchy roughly corresponds to increasing the timescale of representation learning, increasing inference-time representational stability? 1 , and the potential for top-down influence Types of invariance Spatial: translation, rotation, scale Temporal: speed, phase Categorical: within-class variation Context: background, lighting Functional connectivity among networks is dynamic and context-dependent. Modularity enables flexible reconfiguration of processing networks based on task demands, allowing the same anatomical substrate to support diverse world modeling contexts through dynamic connectivity changes Two visual streams, one spatial and one semantic Anterior-posterior processing gradients organize temporal abstraction, with posterior regions processing immediate sensory information and anterior regions handling extended temporal contexts and future-oriented prediction. This principle is evident in sensory pathways that ascend from primary cortices to higher-order association areas, and also within specific cortical regions. For instance, the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) exhibits a functional hierarchy where caudal (posterior) areas are more involved with concrete, present-oriented information and task details, while rostral (anterior) areas handle more abstract, future-oriented information and overarching goals. This ascent in the processing hierarchy often corresponds to an increase in the timescale of representation learning and an enhancement in the stability of representations during inference Types of abstraction Prototype/Entity Extraction Statistical centers of categories Stored in anterior temporal lobe Rapid generalization to new instances Coexists with exemplar memories Relational Abstraction Relations independent of specific entities Prefrontal and parietal substrates Enables analogical reasoning Structured like language Specific brain regions or neuronal populations are highly specialized for representing particular types of information (e.g., fusiform face area for faces, parahippocampal place area for scenes) Small-World Organization and Efficiency Human brain networks exhibit small-world topology: high local clustering (0.4-0.6) combined with short average path lengths ( 3 steps between any two regions), enabling efficient information transfer at minimal wiring cost. This optimizes the trade-off between local processing efficiency and global integration capacity, enabling rapid information transmission while maintaining modular specialization for different aspects of world modeling This architecture achieves  35% reduction in wiring length compared to random networks while maintaining similar communication efficiency. Small-worldness (σ = clustering/path-length ratio) typically ranges 1.5-3.0 in healthy brains, declining with aging and neurological disorders Rich-Club Organization and Network Hubs: top 15-20% of highly connected regions form a "rich-club" backbone consuming  80% of the brain’s communication capacity Hub nodes link networks, modalities, conceptual subspaces, timescales, and cognitive domains; hubs are essential for complex cognitive functions that necessitate drawing upon and synthesizing information from multiple, often disparate, sources. For example, constructing a unified episodic memory of an event requires binding together visual, auditory, spatial, emotional, and conceptual information, a process heavily reliant on hub regions like the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. The structural connectivity provided by white matter pathways forms the anatomical backbone that enables this functional integration across the brain. Convergence zones and integrative hubs, such as the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) for semantic memory, exemplify this principle, bringing together information from various modality-specific areas to form supramodal concepts. Energetic and Spatial Constraints Brain consumes  20% of body’s energy despite being  2% of body weight Wiring minimization principle:  60-70% of connections are to spatially adjacent regions Across mammalian cortex the probability (or weight) of a cortico-cortical projection falls off roughly exponentially with Euclidean distance. Tracer data show a decay length of λ 5-10mm for macaque inter-areal links and an even steeper fall-off for microscopic intracortical axons. Simulations using this single-parameter rule reproduce rich-club hubs, small-world efficiency and overall wire-length minimisation. 2 , 3 Recent work proves that for any system optimizing relevance versus compression, power laws emerge automatically in the frequency distributions of optimal representations, suggesting that neural connectivity patterns encoding these representations would also exhibit power-law distributions. 4 Lognormal weight rule - synaptic strengths and inter-areal weights span 4-5 orders of magnitude and are well fit by a lognormal distribution, producing a "skeleton of strong links in a sea of weak ones." 5 Trade-off between minimizing wiring cost and maximizing topological efficiency drives modular organization Structural wiring and myelination follow an economy-efficiency trade-off: long-range axons consume ∼60% of the brain’s metabolic budget yet occupy only  5% of volume, enforcing sparse high-bandwidth highways atop dense local recurrence. Hemispheric Specialization and Integration Hemispheric specialization emerges from the minimization of wiring costs and the need for parallel processing Interhemispheric connections via corpus callosum ( 200 million axons) predominantly link homotopic regions Left hemisphere shows denser local connectivity for language regions; right hemisphere shows longer-range connectivity for spatial attention Callosal connections show specific developmental timing critical for establishing lateralized functions Network Robustness and Degeneracy Multiple overlapping pathways between any two regions provide robustness to damage Cognitive functions map to distributed networks rather than single regions - lesion of any single node rarely eliminates function completely Developmental plasticity allows alternative network configurations to support similar functions (degeneracy principle)

title: The Episodic Memory System
text: The neural basis of imagination: an evolutionary perspective Episodic memory is best understood as a constructive, self-referential system for simulating particular events situated in space and time. Its signature is autonoesis-a first-person sense of "re-living"-implemented by hippocampal pattern completion over distributed cortical features, coordinated with posterior-medial (context/scene) and anterior-temporal (items/people/concepts) systems and embedded in the default mode network. Rather than storing veridical records, the system flexibly recombines stored elements to reconstruct or preconstruct episodes, which explains both the vividness of recollection and its systematic distortions, as well as the large overlap between remembering the past and imagining the future. Neuropsychology and neuroimaging converge here: hippocampal damage impairs both recollection and the ability to imagine new experiences; classic PET/fMRI show common recruitment for past and future event simulation; and contemporary accounts treat episodic memory as a generative engine for event models, not a tape recorder. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 . For an intelligent agent, episodic memory serves rapid, data-efficient inference over events. In the explicit mode, it can run detailed simulations that bind sensory, conceptual, contextual, and affective features into a coherent scene; in a leaner mode, it can supply key relational constraints or values without full-blown imagery. Functionally, this enables model-based decision making (via prioritized or generative replay, hippocampal-prefrontal loops, and control-DMN coupling), supports counterfactuals and planning, seeds semantic abstraction through consolidation, and underwrites social communication by letting agents present reasons for belief grounded in first-person event models. The system usually appends a reality-monitoring tag-supported by anterior medial PFC and parietal hubs-that helps distinguish experienced from merely simulated events. Emerging "barcode" results suggest a neural mechanism for assigning event-unique indices that can be reactivated at retrieval; compelling animal data and modeling exist, with human generalization an open, exciting frontier 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 . The episodic system appears capable of spanning the full spectrum of inference-time control. In a model-free episodic control mode, the system can retrieve "what worked last time" and directly bias choice-effectively a fast, nonparametric cache over state-action-return tuples that excels when decisions are time-pressured or environments are near-deterministic. This idea is formalized in model-free episodic control algorithms and maps naturally onto hippocampal replay mechanisms that stamp back high-return sequences. At an intermediate grain, hippocampal/entorhinal codes often look successor-like: predictive, policy-dependent state embeddings that cheaply generalize values yet are limited when transition structure changes. At the deliberative end, hippocampal-prefrontal loops use prioritized replay and prospective sweeps to support model-based planning when time and control resources allow, with lesion and fMRI work tying hippocampus to model-based choice. Together, these modes explain why EM can sometimes feel like a one-shot "do what worked," sometimes like a fuzzy but efficient look-ahead, and sometimes like explicit multistep planning 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 .

title: The Trisynaptic Loop
text: Perceiving and simulating worldly events is an "all hands" effort, drawing on hierarchical representations of spatiotemporal relationships among agents, objects, and environments; this results in interactions between otherwise isolated networks 1 . EM network largely corresponds to the default mode network Episodic memory is implemented by a cortico-hippocampal loop that takes richly structured input from the medial temporal cortex, performs aggressive sparsification and binding in the hippocampus, and broadcasts an indexed trace back to cortex and to control circuits. Within the hippocampus, information flows through a highly organized circuit known as the trisynaptic loop, which sequentially connects distinct subfields - the dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1 - each performing specialized computations essential for episodic memory encoding and retrieval 2 . Hippocampal Circuitry and the Trisynaptic Loop At the system level, the hippocampal formation is largely organized as a feedforward excitatory circuit. Unlike most cortical networks which are highly recurrent, the hippocampus routes information in a mostly unidirectional manner through its subfields 3 . Sensory inputs from multiple modalities are first processed in hierarchically organized cortical pathways and funneled into the entorhinal cortex (EC), specifically the superficial layers (II/III) of the EC 4 . The entorhinal cortex serves as the gateway to the hippocampus: neurons in layer II of EC project via the perforant path to the dentate gyrus (and also to CA3), while layer III fibers (the temporoammonic pathway) project directly to CA1 and subiculum; deep EC (layer V/VI) receives hippocampal/subicular output, closing the loop. This layer-specific organization is conserved in humans and is measurably engaged in encoding versus retrieval, with superficial EC more active during encoding and deep EC during retrieval. These anatomy-function correspondences give the system two input routes-an indirect trisynaptic path EC->DG->CA3->CA1 optimized for separation/binding, and a monosynaptic EC->CA1 path optimized for fast comparison to current input 4 , 5 , 6 . Within the classical trisynaptic loop, the information flow is as follows: (1) Entorhinal layer II axons (perforant path) synapse onto dentate gyrus granule cells (first synapse); (2) Dentate granule cells activate CA3 pyramidal neurons via mossy fiber axons (second synapse); (3) CA3 pyramidal cells project to CA1 pyramidal neurons via the Schaffer collateral pathway (third synapse). CA1 in turn sends output to the subiculum and back to the deep layers of entorhinal cortex (which project out to neocortical association areas), effectively closing the loop; highly processed multimodal inputs from many cortical areas converge onto the hippocampus (especially into a single integrated network in CA3), and after hippocampal processing, the output diverges back to many cortical and subcortical targets via EC, subiculum, and fornix projections. Such architecture places the hippocampus in a pivotal position to bind distributed inputs into a unified memory trace (during encoding) and later reinstate or index that trace across the cortex (during recall) 7 . Dentate Gyrus and Mossy Fiber Pathway: Encoding New Patterns The dentate gyrus (DG) is the first processing stage in the trisynaptic loop and plays a critical role in encoding new episodic memory representations. Anatomically, the DG receives the bulk of cortical input to the hippocampus: entorhinal layer II perforant path fibers form synapses on the dendrites of dentate granule cells in the DG’s molecular layer. This is a densely convergent projection - in rodents, roughly a million granule cells receive projections from the EC. Only a small fraction of granule cells are active at any given time, however, reflecting extremely sparse coding in the DG. Such sparse activity (on the order of a few percent or less of neurons active in any environment) is a hallmark of the DG and is believed to underlie pattern separation - the process of orthogonalizing or decorrelating input patterns so that similar experiences are stored as distinct memories. This makes overlapping inputs (e.g. two similar contexts or events) produce more divergent neural representations, reducing interference between memories. Consistent with this idea, empirical studies have shown that small changes in input (for example, slight alterations in the environment) can lead to large changes in DG granule cell activation patterns, indicating separation of representations. After processing by the DG, information is relayed to area CA3 via the mossy fibers, the axons of dentate granule cells. The mossy fiber (MF) pathway is distinctive in both its anatomy and function. Unlike the diffuse perforant path input, each granule cell makes only a few, but extremely powerful, synapses onto CA3 pyramidal neurons. In the rat, a single CA3 cell receives on the order of  40-50 mossy fiber contacts (out of hundreds of thousands of granule cells) 7 , yet each individual mossy fiber synapse is giant and efficacious. These synapses have been termed "detonator synapses" because a single presynaptic burst can reliably trigger a postsynaptic spike in CA3 8 . Indeed, mossy terminals form multiple active zones and release a large glutamate volume, producing an unusually large excitatory postsynaptic potential in CA3. Moreover, short-term plasticity at the mossy synapse is dominated by frequency facilitation: repetitive spikes from a granule cell lead to progressively larger transmitter release, enhancing the postsynaptic impact by up to  1200% during theta-frequency bursts 3 . In practice, this means that isolated DG spikes have relatively little effect on CA3, but if a granule cell fires a high-frequency burst (as might happen when a salient or novel input strongly drives the DG), the later spikes in the burst can "ignite" the CA3 neuron. This conditional high-pass filter property prevents CA3 from being overactivated by noise or minor cues, while ensuring that a strongly activated DG cell (or small set of cells) can rapidly trigger a new memory engram in CA3. Functionally, the sparse and strong DG->CA3 connections impose a form of random orthogonalization: by connecting to only a random tiny subset of CA3 cells, each active granule cell helps produce a new, largely uncorrelated pattern of CA3 activity (compared to other memories). This randomness, combined with DG’s sparse coding, is thought to maximize the ability of CA3 to encode many distinct memories with minimal overlap 9 . Biologically, the DG has several special features that support these functions. In addition to its sparse activity, the DG is one of the few brain regions with adult neurogenesis - new granule cells are generated throughout life. Newborn granule cells are highly excitable and plastic, which some theories suggest may contribute to pattern separation by introducing more variability and flexibility in encoding new memories (e.g. new neurons can rapidly integrate into circuits and potentially encode subtle differences in experiences). The DG also contains feedforward inhibitory circuits (via interneurons in the hilus) that tightly control when and which granule cells fire, preventing runaway excitation and further decorrelating inputs 3 . CA3 Recurrent Network: Autoassociation and Pattern Completion Area CA3 lies at the heart of the hippocampal memory system. It is often described as an autoassociative network or attractor network because of the extensive recurrent connections between its pyramidal neurons 9 . In CA3, each pyramidal cell not only receives feedforward input from DG (mossy fibers) and EC (perforant path), but also sends out collateral axons that synapse on other CA3 cells. Anatomically, this recurrent collateral system is remarkably well-developed: in the rodent CA3 there are on the order of 300,000 pyramidal cells, and each one makes recurrent synapses onto thousands of other CA3 cells. Estimates suggest  12,000 recurrent synapses per CA3 neuron in rats, implying a  2-4% probability of connection between any two CA3 neurons (with near-complete connectivity when considering the network as a whole). These recurrent projections span the entire CA3 region (not just locally), effectively linking all CA3 neurons into one integrated network. By comparison, estimates indicate that each human CA3 subregion contains on the order of 1.7 million pyramidal neurons, reflecting a substantial scaling-up relative to the roughly 300,000 neurons observed in rodents 10 . Such widespread recurrent coupling means that once a subset of CA3 neurons is activated (by an input or cue), they can excite each other in a positive feedback loop, tending to drive the entire network into a coherent activation pattern. The computational significance of the CA3 recurrent network is profound. It provides the substrate for rapid one-shot learning and pattern completion in episodic memory. Because CA3 plasticity is strong and rapid (in part due to NMDA receptor-rich synapses), even a single exposure can "wire together" the active neurons, fulfilling the need for one-trial episodic learning. Later, if a partial or degraded cue of that event is received (for instance, only some elements of the original experience are present), the recurrent CA3 network can complete the pattern: the subset of neurons activated by the cue will reactivate their interconnected partners, reconstructing the full original activity pattern representing the entire memory (a hallmark of episodic recall). Studies have shown that disrupting CA3 (or blocking CA3-specific NMDA receptors required for plasticity) impairs the ability to recall memories from partial cues, confirming that CA3’s recurrent synapses are critical for pattern completion in vivo 7 . Importantly, the CA3 network does not act in isolation; it operates in concert with the feedforward inputs. The dentate gyrus and mossy fibers provide what could be called the "encoding drive," while the entorhinal cortex perforant path provides context and cues for retrieval. Theoretical models (e.g. by Treves & Rolls) posit a division of labor: During learning, the sparse but extremely strong mossy fiber inputs from DG dominate CA3 activity - effectively "forcing" a new pattern to be stored in the recurrent synapses regardless of prior activity. During retrieval, however, the direct perforant path input from EC (which is much more numerous in synapse count, though individually weaker) serves as the initial cue to trigger recall. Even a partial cue coming from EC can activate some of the originally stored CA3 cells, and then the recurrent collaterals take over to complete the full pattern of activation. In this way, the system uses EC inputs to probe CA3 for a stored memory, and CA3’s autoassociation to reignite the full memory. Consistent with this, experimental lesions have shown that disrupting the perforant path input to CA3 impairs memory retrieval, whereas blocking the mossy fiber input impairs new learning but not recall 7 . From another perspective, CA3’s recurrent network also endows it with capacity for temporally extended representations. Episodic memories often involve sequences of events unfolding over time, and CA3 is thought to link events across temporal gaps. The attractor dynamics, with inherent reverberatory activity, can maintain a memory active for a short period and form associations not just in space (what happened where) but also in time (what happened when/in what order). Modeling and recordings have suggested that CA3 neurons can encode sequential relationships (e.g. "time cells" that fire at specific moments in a temporally structured experience), supporting memory for the flow of events 11 . In short, CA3 provides the associative glue for the episodic memory system, rapidly binding together the who/what/where/when of an episode into a single representation, and allowing that representation to be stored, maintained, and completed when needed. CA1 and Output Pathways: Integration, Sequence Ordering, and Memory Retrieval The final relay in the trisynaptic loop is area CA1, which performs an integrative role and serves as the primary output node (together with subiculum) from the hippocampus. CA1 pyramidal neurons receive a dual input: one set of excitatory inputs comes from CA3 (the Schaffer collateral synapses), and another comes directly from entorhinal cortex layerIII (the temporoammonic pathway). These two inputs carry somewhat different information - the CA3 input conveys the outcome of hippocampal processing (pattern-completed representations, sequences generated internally, etc.), while the direct EC input carries current cortical activity (often reflecting the external sensory context or ongoing experience). By combining these, CA1 is thought to act as a comparator or associator that checks whether the hippocampus’s reconstruction (from CA3) matches the current input from the environment. If there is a mismatch (for example, the expected pattern from CA3 doesn’t align with what EC is signaling), CA1 neurons can detect this novelty or discrepancy - essentially flagging that the current situation does not match a known memory. This mismatch detection function of CA1 has been hypothesized in several models 12 , 13 and is supported by evidence that CA1 is particularly sensitive to changes in input patterns and can signal prediction errors (a critical component for learning when an outcome is unexpected). Thus, CA1 may contribute to episodic memory by ensuring that retrieved memories are compared against reality, and by driving learning of new representations when mismatches occur. Beyond novelty detection, CA1 also temporally refines and outputs the hippocampal code. Some theories propose that CA1 "orders" or sequences the information it receives from CA3, helping to organize the elements of an episode in time. In rodent studies, CA1 place cells and time cells can represent sequences of locations or temporal intervals, respectively, and CA1 is known to exhibit sharply timed firing relative to network oscillations (like theta phase precession) which could underpin a timeline for events. By receiving input from CA3 (which may contain partially formed sequences) and the EC (current context), CA1 might align these inputs to produce a coherent spatio-temporal representation - essentially a timeline of events within a context 2 . Anatomically, CA1 pyramidal neurons project to the subiculum and back to the deep layers of the entorhinal cortex (layers V/VI). From entorhinal deep layers, the information is sent out to various cortical areas (including the parahippocampal and perirhinal cortices and then to widespread association cortices) as well as other targets such as the medial prefrontal cortex. In this way, CA1/subiculum serve as the main output relay of the hippocampus, communicating the result of hippocampal processing (e.g. a retrieved memory or a newly encoded pattern) back to the rest of the brain. This hippocampal-neocortical feedback is essential for memory retrieval: it allows a reactivated hippocampal memory to reinstate the corresponding pattern of cortical activity that represents the details of the episode (often referred to as the hippocampus acting as an index to retrieve distributed cortical engrams). Over time (during systems consolidation), repeated reactivation via these outputs may strengthen direct connections among cortical areas so that the memory becomes gradually less hippocampus-dependent (and more abstract/generalized). Putting this together, the episodic system is a set of coupled modules with complementary inductive biases: EC supplies structured coordinates over items, contexts, and experienced time; DG generates ultra-sparse, interference-resistant patterns; CA3 stores and completes indices with attractor dynamics; CA1 computes prediction error and orchestrates retrieval versus updating; subiculum/EC and thalamo-prefrontal loops distribute and regulate the trace.

title: Modular Architecture and Supporting Cortical Regions
text: The episodic system is built from a set of semi-segregated cortical-MTL modules that specialize for complementary ingredients of an event-the "who/what," the "where/when/context," and the control signals that determine when to construct, retrieve, or reshape an episode. A useful organizing principle is the anterior-temporal versus posterior-medial (AT-PM) framework: an AT network centered on perirhinal cortex (PrC), anterior temporal lobe, and lateral orbitofrontal cortex emphasizes item-, person-, and concept-centric features, whereas a PM network centered on parahippocampal cortex (PHC), retrosplenial/precuneus, and posterior cingulate emphasizes scene and extended contextual structure 1 . These streams converge on the entorhinal cortex (EC) and hippocampus but remain partly segregated up to specific hippocampal subfield zones, enabling the system to bind item and context without collapsing their codes. In humans, anterior-lateral EC (alEC; homologous to rodent LEC) preferentially carries nonspatial information, providing information about objects, features, and the temporal context of events, while posterior-medial EC (pmEC; homologous to MEC) carries spatial/path-integration information, providing a multimodal spatial map of one’s environment; their projections target largely distinct sectors of CA1 along the proximodistal axis (LEC->distal CA1/subiculum, MEC->proximal CA1), preserving the division of labor as information enters the hippocampus 2 , 3 . Perirhinal and parahippocampal cortices form the principal cortical interfaces to EC. PrC supports highly specific, object-centric and concept-rich representations and is well positioned to "unitize" features of an entity, often carrying learned value/affect through its amygdala connectivity. PHC (and the parahippocampal place area) emphasizes scenes, landmarks, and broader situational context, providing a scaffold for event location and environmental structure. Together these streams deliver entities and roles into EC, where they can be indexed by the hippocampus during encoding and reinstated during recall 4 , 5 , 6 . A prominent gradient runs along the longitudinal (posterior-anterior) axis of the hippocampus and adjacent MTL, mirroring an abstraction/scale gradient in the computations that support episodes. Posterior hippocampus (dorsal in rodents) is biased toward fine-grained spatial detail, precise sequences, and smaller spatiotemporal scales; anterior hippocampus (ventral in rodents) emphasizes broader, gist-like, schematic, and affect-laden context, and is preferentially engaged when tasks are open-ended, prospective, or demand flexible recombination rather than cue-driven recall constrained by sensory specifics. Thus, the hippocampus is not monolithic: it embodies a multiscale memory system wherein the posterior end encodes the specific "episodes" with rich detail and the anterior end encodes more abstracted "situations" or schemas spanning episodes - a design that permits both episodic specificity and cross-episode generalization within a single circuit. This gradient maps onto entorhinal subdivisions and large-scale network coupling, with posterior sectors aligning more strongly to PM scene networks and anterior sectors to AT/valuation networks 7 , 8 , 9 . Beyond MTL, the "core recollection network" supporting vivid episodic remembering overlaps extensively with the default mode network (DMN), with special emphasis on its midline core: anterior medial prefrontal cortex (amPFC) and posterior cingulate/precuneus (PCC). These hubs sit high in the cortical semantic hierarchy and maintain event context during both on-line perception and recall, projecting schematic event models onto new input to generate predictions. The amPFC (including ventromedial PFC) is strongly engaged when memories have personal relevance or schematic structure - it may inject self-referential and schema-based information into the reconstruction of a scene, encoding one’s goals, identity, and prior knowledge into the remembered event. This region is also implicated in scene construction and imagination, as neuroimaging shows amPFC activity when people envision novel experiences or place themselves in hypothetical scenarios, in concert with hippocampal activation. Meanwhile, the posterior cingulate cortex (encompassing PCC proper and retrosplenial areas) serves as a hub linking hippocampal outputs to widespread cortical regions. The PCC is believed to support the spatiotemporal context and vivid re-experiencing of memory scenes; for example, damage to retrosplenial cortex impairs the ability to mentally navigate familiar places or recall rich contextual details. During recollection, PCC shows increased connectivity with the hippocampus and parietal cortex 10 , and it may help integrate egocentric (self-centered) perspective with the allocentric (world-centered) representations coming from the hippocampus, grounding recalled events in a coherent viewpoint or "scene" from the autobiographical self. The angular gyrus (a lateral parietal region) has emerged as a critical locus for integrating the content elements of a memory into a single conscious experience. Cognitive models propose that AG functions as an "episodic buffer" or convergence zone, where the various components of an event - sights, sounds, people, places, emotions - are bound together and brought to awareness as a unified memory 11 , 12 . Consistent with this, high-resolution fMRI multivariate analyses have shown that during episodic retrieval (especially after memories have been consolidated), different feature-specific representations reconverge in the angular gyrus 10 . The AG is also strongly associated with the subjective sense of recollection - patients often report less vivid or "complete" recall when the lateral parietal cortex is disrupted, despite being able to recognize or know that something happened. Causal evidence for AG’s role in memory vividness comes from brain stimulation studies: applying inhibitory TMS to left angular gyrus prior to retrieval selectively reduces the vividness of recollected memories without affecting objective accuracy or metacognitive confidence 13 . This indicates that while the hippocampus provides the core content (and can support basic recognition even if AG is offline), the angular gyrus contributes critical multimodal integration and rich re-experiential detail - effectively painting the full scene and embedding it in our awareness. Along with parietal hub regions, primary and premotor cortices can be recruited when episodes involve planned or simulated actions, reflecting the embodied, interactive nature of event construction 14 . Remembering is not always a passive replay; often it is a goal-directed act of retrieval guided by the prefrontal cortex (PFC). Both medial and lateral prefrontal regions are recruited to initiate memory search, apply learned schemas, and monitor the products of retrieval. The medial PFC, especially the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), interacts closely with the hippocampus during encoding and recall of schema-related memories. This region encodes high-level contextual or schematic representations - abstract frameworks that organize knowledge - and can use these to bias hippocampal retrieval toward schema-consistent information 10 . Studies have shown that vmPFC activity can precede and drive hippocampal activity when a person starts to recall an autobiographical memory: in MEG recordings, vmPFC activation was seen to lead hippocampal reinstatement at the onset of memory retrieval, suggesting the PFC provides an early cue or "trigger" that kicks off hippocampal pattern completion 15 . The vmPFC likely carries a summary of one’s current goals and prior knowledge, which helps instigate and coordinate hippocampal-dependent recall processes. During encoding, strong hippocampal-vmPFC coupling has been associated with the schema effect - better learning of new information that fits an existing schema - supporting theories that the PFC actively assimilates new episodes into organized knowledge networks 16 . During retrieval, the vmPFC also plays a role in reality monitoring and selection: patients with vmPFC damage can retrieve many details from memory but are prone to confabulation, weaving together pieces that don’t belong or endorsing false memories, presumably because the control processes that evaluate and constrain retrieved information are compromised 17 . This highlights that medial PFC normally helps ensure that the recalled scenario is coherent and relevant to the query, suppressing extraneous associations and filling gaps with plausible elements (often based on schemas or semantic memory) rather than false blends. Complementing the medial PFC, the lateral prefrontal cortex (especially dorsolateral PFC) provides executive control over search and verification operations during episodic recall. The lateral PFC is engaged when we must intentionally search our memory (e.g. "recall everything that happened at last week’s meeting"), maintaining task cues and systematically probing memory stores. It helps formulate effective retrieval strategies (such as initiating recall by time or place cues), and it dynamically focuses hippocampal retrieval by inhibiting irrelevant memory traces. The dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC), in particular, is associated with post-retrieval monitoring - checking whether the content retrieved is what was sought and is veridical. If the hippocampus produces partial or ambiguous results, the DLPFC can cue another attempt or cross-check details against expectations (analogous to an internal query refinement loop). Together, these prefrontal mechanisms impose a hierarchical control on episodic recall: high-level goals and semantic constraints (often represented in anterior/medial PFC) guide the general direction of retrieval, while mid-ventrolateral PFC may retrieve specific cues or semantic seeds, and dorsolateral PFC evaluates and edits the output. Recent computational models formalize this idea, positing that the PFC generates "queries" to the hippocampus in a top-down manner - effectively encoding a cue or key that will trigger hippocampal pattern completion of a relevant memory - and then gates the retrieved memory for use in decision-making 18 . The PFC also works in concert with the hippocampus for episodic simulation - assembling elements from past events to imagine novel futures (more on this later) - by enforcing constraints so that imagined scenarios remain realistic and in line with one’s goals. In summary, the medial and lateral PFC together form an executive layer that queries, guides, and validates the hippocampal memory retrieval, enabling episodic memory to function not just as a recording device but as a flexible, queryable database for decision-making and planning. The effectiveness of memory encoding and retrieval is profoundly influenced by reward, emotion, and other salience signals, implemented via interactions between the hippocampus and subcortical neuromodulatory centers. One important pathway is the hippocampus-midbrain dopaminergic loop, which links novelty and reward evaluation to memory formation. When the hippocampus detects something novel or unexpected in the environment, it can trigger a burst of dopamine from the ventral tegmental area (VTA); this dopamine release, in turn, enhances synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus, prioritizing the encoding of that event 19 . Individual differences in the integrity of this loop (for example, structural connectivity between midbrain and hippocampus) correlate with how well people remember rewarded information. Complementing dopamine’s role, emotional arousal engages the amygdala - another key subcortical player - which modulates episodic memory via stress and arousal hormones. The amygdala-hippocampus interaction is known to boost memory for emotionally charged events: during emotional experiences, the amygdala can influence hippocampal circuits both directly and through neurochemical cascades (such as norepinephrine release from the locus coeruleus) 20 , with recent intracranial work showing amygdala-theta to hippocampal-gamma coupling that predicts subsequent memory for aversive scenes 21 . Finally, the hippocampal system interfaces with the basal ganglia to translate memory into action, particularly via the nucleus accumbens (NAc) in the ventral striatum. The hippocampus->NAc pathway (largely from ventral subiculum) provides the striatum with contextual and spatial information about experiences, effectively informing the reward system of "where" and "what" has happened 22 . The NAc, in turn, is a motivation hub that helps select behaviors based on expected rewards. Animal studies show that this pathway is necessary for linking memories to motivated behavior: if hippocampal outputs to NAcc are silenced, animals cannot learn or express place-reward associations (e.g. remembering a location where food was found).

title: A Modern View of the Hippocampus
text: General purpose sequence generator and predictive model The contemporary understanding of the hippocampus casts it as a content-agnostic, general-purpose sequence generator that underlies our capacity to construct, store, and imaginatively recombine experiences. In contrast to older views that emphasized a dedicated "spatial memory module" or a temporary memory buffer, modern evidence indicates the hippocampus implements a singular algorithm for organizing experience: it produces sequential, "content-free" structural codes that can bind and index arbitrary cortical contents 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . In essence, the hippocampus furnishes a generative skeleton (a predictive, sequential scaffold) on which the specifics of any event - spatial or non-spatial - can be hung. This architecture makes it "input-agnostic" (equally adept at processing spatial layouts or abstract sequences) and positions the hippocampus as a world-modeling engine for flexible episodic simulation in the brain. Consistent with this, hippocampal ensemble activity in rodents and humans has been shown to organize incoming information into predictive models of the environment; for example, when mice learn structured tasks, their CA1 neurons gradually stabilize into a model that predicts upcoming events, integrating new experiences into an existing framework 2 . Likewise, computational models of the hippocampal circuit (with CA3 as a recurrent predictor and CA1 as a comparator) exhibit hallmark hippocampal phenomena - one-shot place learning, fast sequence encoding, theta phase precession, and replay - when trained to predict incoming inputs 4 . These lines of evidence support the idea that the hippocampus is fundamentally a predictive auto-associator: it rapidly encodes sequences (of locations, events, actions, etc.) and continually attempts to predict the future, using mismatch signals (especially in CA1) to flag prediction errors. This predictive coding scheme dovetails with the hippocampus’s role in imagination and planning: it can generate trajectories or event sequences internally, effectively running simulations to explore possible outcomes. During active navigation, for instance, hippocampal place cells fire in sequences that anticipate an animal’s future path on a sub-second timescale (within each theta cycle), representing past, present, and impending locations in order 5 . Such "pre-play" and prospective firing patterns are observed even before an animal enters a new place, hinting that internally generated sequences (not just learned ones) can model novel routes 6 . During pauses or sleep, the hippocampus emits sharp-wave ripples that replay past experiences and potential future paths, effectively rolling out possible scenarios in a compressed format - a mechanism thought to support planning and consolidation. Specific, one-shot memories One immediate consequence of this modern view is that the hippocampus is not a transient store that invariably hands off memories to the cortex and then disengages. Instead, the hippocampus’s unique inductive biased lead to it retaining a role in memories indefinitely when vivid, detail-rich recollection is needed. Recent neuropsychological findings show that even very old "semanticized" memories (e.g. famous public events) continue to rely on the hippocampus for retrieval of precise details, despite the passage of decades 7 . Patients with hippocampal damage exhibit subtle but reliable deficits in the accuracy and precision of remote memories (for example, mis-dating public events), indicating that the hippocampus supports high-fidelity, fine-grained representations no matter a memory’s age. In other words, episodic memories do not automatically become fully hippocampus-independent - especially when an exact, contextual recollection (the where and when and how of an event) is required. The hippocampus appears to continuously provide the "index codes" or pointers that can reactivate detailed cortical representations on demand. This aligns with the classic index theory and is dramatically illustrated by recent single-neuron recordings: when food-caching birds store thousands of locations, their hippocampal neurons emit brief, unique burst patterns - essentially barcode-like activity signatures - for each individual caching event, and reliably reactivate the matching pattern when the bird later retrieves that specific cache 8 ; these barcodes remain distinct even for two events at the same place or close in time. Generalization Crucially, the hippocampus balances this ability to preserve particulars with a capacity to generalize and extract structure across experiences. It does so via its intrinsic circuitry and dual input streams. On one hand, the trisynaptic path through the dentate gyrus (DG) and CA3 imposes extremely sparse, pattern-separated codes that keep memories orthogonal - "distinguishing examples" so that even similar events are stored with minimal overlap. On the other hand, the direct entorhinal cortex->CA3/CA1 inputs carry more dense, integrative codes that can link related experiences - essentially "building concepts" by emphasizing shared features across memories; a recent computational and empirical study formalized this idea, showing that CA3 can store complementary encodings of the same events: a decorrelated DG-driven representation that remains unique for each instance, and a more correlated EC-driven representation that gradually merges commonalities across instances 9 . As more events are stored, the correlated codes in CA3 tend to converge on mutual features (forming a rudimentary concept or schema), while the sparse codes stay distinct for specifics. In rat data, this was evident as CA3 place cells showed more differentiated (sparser) firing during network states associated with pattern separation, and more overlapping firing when the network state favored integration 9 . Functionally, this means the hippocampus can simultaneously support specificity and generalization. It can encode unique one-off episodes without interference and abstract the underlying structure spanning multiple episodes. For example, as an animal explores many environments, some hippocampal neurons become selective for the orientation or broader geometry of contexts (independent of exact location) - effectively tagging common structure - which biases the network toward recognizing a familiar layout in a new setting 10 . Initial representations of each new context are actually quite generic (reflecting past similar contexts), which aids rapid learning, and only with repeated experience does the hippocampus decorrelate them into highly discriminable, unique maps. This strategy provides a high-capacity coding scheme: by first generalizing and then gradually differentiating, the hippocampal network achieves an optimal discrimination-generalization balance that maximizes storage while minimizing confusion. Moreover, having generalized codes for prior experiences improves the network’s ability to predict novel situations - in the study, hippocampal patterns that were common to multiple past contexts enabled better anticipatory coding when a new but related context was encountered. In line with its predictive mandate, the hippocampus thus seems to encode common regularities (for inference) alongside distinct details (for veridical recall), matching its aforementioned longitudinal abstraction gradient. Supporting this dual mandate is the hippocampus’s extraordinarily broad connectivity, which gives it access to multimodal information and enables it to bind disparate inputs into a single simulation or memory. Anatomically, the hippocampus sits at the nexus of the medial temporal lobe, converging inputs from "where/when" pathways and "who/what" pathways that remain partially segregated up to the point of hippocampal entry. The lateral entorhinal cortex (alEC, input from perirhinal/temporal areas) conveys information about items, agents, and features (the elements of an episode), while the medial entorhinal cortex (pmEC, input from parahippocampal/retrosplenial areas) provides spatial, contextual, and temporal scaffoldings 11 . These streams target different zones of the hippocampus, preserving a distinction between content and context that the hippocampus can exploit to form combinatorial codes. In essence, the hippocampus can independently vary "tokens" (specific people or objects from the anterior-temporal stream) within "slots" defined by the situational context (from the posterior-medial stream), somewhat like a generative grammar for events 12 . This combinatorial capacity (which aligns with the "language of thought" hypothesis that suggests that roles and entities are independently represented in the brain, similar to in language 13 ) allows novel episodes to be constructed by recombining familiar elements 14 . It also aligns with evidence that hippocampal codes are factorized or disentangled when supporting inference: in humans, once people learn a structured task, hippocampal neurons come to represent multiple task variables in an abstract, orthogonalized format 15 . This means the hippocampus can encode, say, the context and the item independently (rather than conflating them into a single pattern), which is precisely what one would expect if it were assigning elements to roles (e.g. "place = kitchen" + "person = Alice" + "action = cooking"). Such a representation is optimized for generalization, since the learned components (kitchens, Alice, cooking actions) could be flexibly recombined in imagined or future scenarios.

title: Network Dynamics
text: Theta-gamma during active behavior and REM During movement, attentive exploration, and REM sleep, the hippocampus enters an "online" regime dominated by 6-10 Hz theta whose cycles organize local spiking and the nesting of faster (30-150 Hz) gamma bursts. Medial septal GABAergic pacemaker cells entrain hippocampal interneurons and pyramidal cells at theta, while hypothalamic inputs (notably the supramammillary nucleus) modulate theta frequency and gain-together setting the temporal backbone for hippocampal computation 1 , 2 , 3 . Causally, suppressing septal GABAergic drive selectively during REM reduces hippocampal theta and impairs consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memories, establishing the behavioral importance of this state 4 . A hallmark of this regime is phase precession: as an animal traverses a place field, a place cell fires at progressively earlier phases of the ongoing theta cycle. Population-wise, this compresses a seconds-long trajectory into a  100-150 ms theta window, effectively time-ordering the recent past and near future within each cycle 5 , 6 , 7 . Phase precession, first reported in rodent CA1 and then generalized across hippocampal-entorhinal circuits, has now been demonstrated in humans (including for non-spatial, goal-related representations), supporting a domain-general role in sequencing 7 . These within-cycle orderings manifest as theta sequences-rapid sweeps of place-cell activity that span positions just behind and ahead of the animal. At decision points, CA3 and CA1 ensembles transiently represent alternative future paths, and theta sequences bias toward current goals when choices must be made 8 , 9 . Coordinated hippocampal and prefrontal sequences at multiple timescales link these within-theta "micro-simulations" to behavioral planning 10 . As tasks become stereotyped, theta sequences become less exploratory, consistent with a transition from deliberation to habit 9 , 11 . Theta provides a phase-structured clock that both aligns spikes for Hebbian updates and sets the sign of those updates. Because theta sequences and theta-gamma nesting compress seconds of behavior into  100-150 ms cycles, presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes repeatedly fall within the  10-50 ms windows required for STDP. Moreover, the phase of theta gates plasticity: brief bursts at one CA1 theta phase drive LTP, whereas the opposite phase favors LTD, yielding alternating epochs of encoding vs. weakening within each cycle 12 , 13 . In models constrained by hippocampal physiology, STDP operating on phase-precessing inputs forms directed chains-and even successor-like predictive maps-within a handful of traversals 14 . Within each theta cycle, gamma-nested "item packets" segment assemblies into discrete subevents. Critically, CA1 couples to different afferents at different gamma sub-bands and theta phases: "slow" ( 30-50 Hz) gamma synchronizes CA3->CA1 interactions associated with retrieval of stored associations, whereas "fast" ( 60-100 Hz) gamma aligns entorhinal cortex->CA1 drive associated with current sensory input 15 , 16 , 17 . Human and animal work shows that assigning different items or positions to distinct theta phases (via theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling) supports sequence encoding and order memory 18 . Theta also synchronizes hippocampus with neocortical partners to broadcast and read out these sequences. Hippocampal-mPFC theta coherence increases at choice points and during rule acquisition; prefrontal units can show theta phase relationships and even phase precession tied to spatial variables. Across trials, coherent theta supports a shared positional code between CA1 and mPFC, linking hippocampal simulation to executive selection 19 , 20 , 21 . A key subcortical coordinator is thalamic nucleus reuniens, which reciprocally connects mPFC and hippocampus. Reuniens manipulations modulate mPFC-hippocampus theta coherence and extinction retrieval 22 , and can transiently impose synchronized beta bursts for memory-guided decisions-evidence that thalamus flexibly switches interareal channels on top of the theta scaffold 23 . Broader midline thalamic circuits help align the timing of hippocampo-prefrontal interactions during working memory and spatial tasks 24 , 25 . Finally, theta in REM appears to re-use the same temporal code under different neuromodulatory conditions. Selective disruption of REM theta impairs contextual memory consolidation without abolishing REM per se 4 , and convergent reviews argue that NREM ripples and REM theta play complementary roles-ripples for sharp, compressed reactivation; REM theta for integrative, schema-updating plasticity under high acetylcholine. Reports of theta-sequence-like organization during REM suggest that online sequence machinery is redeployed offline, albeit with different coupling to cortex than during wake 26 . In summary, theta provides the millisecond-precision temporal scaffold that turns distributed hippocampal activity into ordered sequences, gates plasticity through phase-specific STDP, and multiplexes input-output streams via gamma nesting. By synchronizing with prefrontal, entorhinal, and thalamic partners, the theta-gamma code binds items into episodes during exploration and reprocesses them during REM. Sharp-wave ripples during pauses, quiet wakefulness, and NREM sleep Sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) are brief, highly synchronous population events generated when a CA3 population burst produces a large "sharp wave" in CA1 dendrites while fast ( 140-200 Hz in rodents;  80-120 Hz in humans) ripple oscillations ride in the CA1 pyramidal layer for  30-120 ms. Mechanistically, SWRs start as a build-up in the recurrent CA3 network; the CA3 surge drives CA1, where perisomatic PV-basket-cell-mediated inhibition phase-locks sparse pyramidal spiking at ripple frequency 27 , 28 , 29 . This interneuron-pyramidal loop accounts for the striking temporal precision and for the fact that only a small subset of CA1 pyramids fire on any given cycle. SWRs occur most frequently in NREM sleep, less during quiet wake/immobility, and least during brief pauses in locomotion-precisely the "offline" windows that isolate plasticity from ongoing sensorimotor drive 30 . Content-wise, SWRs compress recent or predictive experience into time-ordered "replay" sequences. In awake immobility, replay runs in reverse after rewards (assigning credit to the just-traveled path) and forward before movement (prospective planning), often depicting routes from the current position to a known goal 31 , 32 . Across tasks, awake hippocampal-prefrontal replay during SWRs distinguishes correct from incorrect choices, and its prevalence shifts from reverse->forward with learning, linking replay to evaluation and planning rather than mere recapitulation 33 . Notably, some datasets emphasize that replay can reflect previously important but currently unattended paths, underscoring that replay content is not a simple mirror of the next action 34 . Several lines of causal evidence put SWRs on the critical path for memory. Disrupting ripple-locked spiking during post-learning rest or sleep impairs spatial learning 35 , whereas prolonging naturally occurring long-duration ripples enhances memory 36 . At the synaptic level, place-cell reactivation during ripples drives potentiation in downstream CA1, providing a mechanism for "stamping in" recent experience 37 . Together, these results argue that SWRs are not epiphenomenal but instructive for consolidation and decision support. SO-spindle-ripple cascades during NREM sleep During NREM, sharp-wave ripples are embedded in a slow-oscillation->spindle->ripple hierarchy with clearly defined generators and timing. Slow oscillations (SOs) are <1 Hz alternations between cortical down-states (neuronal quiescence/hyperpolarization) and up-states (widespread depolarization), originating largely in neocortex and often propagating as traveling waves; the SO up-state increases cortical excitability and provides the coarse timing frame for memory transfer 38 , 39 , 40 . Sleep spindles are brief waxing-waning sigma bursts ( 11-16 Hz,  0.5-2 s) generated by reciprocal loops between thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) interneurons and thalamocortical relay cells, with "slow" ( 9-12 Hz, frontal-dominant) and "fast" ( 12-15 Hz, centro-parietal) subtypes that occupy slightly different SO phases 41 , 42 , 43 . Human intracranial and scalp work shows the canonical nesting: SO up-states group spindles, and the troughs of those spindles, in turn, cluster hippocampal ripples ( 80-100 Hz in humans;  140-200 Hz in rodents), providing millisecond-precision "transfer slots" for compressed hippocampal content 44 , 45 . The directionality of this chain has been resolved at subcortical nodes: convergent cortical down-states lead thalamic down-states, which hyperpolarize thalamic cells and trigger spindles that are projected back to cortex on the down-to-up transition-exactly when ripples are most likely to be nested 46 . Causally, boosting the phase alignment within this triad improves memory: closed-loop auditory stimulation that delivers sounds in-phase with impending SO up-states amplifies SOs/spindles and enhances next-day recall, and optogenetically timing thalamic spindles in-phase with the SO up-state increases triple coupling and hippocampus-dependent memory; out-of-phase timing is ineffective or detrimental 47 , 48 , 49 . Beyond mere coincidence, spindles appear to mediate hippocampal-neocortical communication most strongly during long-duration ripples and when prefrontal spindles are themselves locked to local SO up-states, linking the strength of nesting to the efficiency of systems consolidation 50 . Quantitatively, human depth recordings demonstrate that ripple probability rises within the spindle window and that ripple power is phase-locked to spindle troughs while spindle power climbs toward the SO up-state, confirming a precise SO->spindle->ripple phase-amplitude cascade in hippocampus and cortex 45 . Finally, prefrontal cortex is not a passive recipient: iEEG shows that prefrontal slow-waves and spindles can organize ripple-locked information transfer-consistent with a thalamo-cortical "gate" that schedules hippocampal broadcasts into cortico-cortical networks at the exact SO phase when plasticity and effective connectivity are maximal 51 . Together, these results elevate the SO-spindle-ripple triad from a correlational motif to a mechanistic clocked bus for systems consolidation: SOs set the frame, thalamic spindles carve high-gain channels, and ripples deliver compressed episodic content to targets poised for synaptic change 52 . In humans, ripples are not confined to hippocampus: brief  90 Hz cortical ripples appear across association cortex in sleep and quiet wake, often co-occurring with hippocampal ripples and increasing during successful recall. These widespread events frequently recruit default-mode-network hubs and track memory demands, suggesting that SWR-time broadcasting reaches cortex via both thalamocortical spindles and locally generated cortical ripples that bind distributed assemblies during reactivation 53 , 54 . SWRs also interact with control systems. The thalamic nucleus reuniens, which links hippocampus and mPFC, modulates prefrontal-hippocampal coherence around offline states, positioning midline thalamus as a switchboard that helps route ripple-time content to executive networks 25 , 55 . Intriguingly, recent work in rodents shows brief prefrontal cortical ripples that can top-down suppress hippocampal reactivation-evidence that cortex is not a passive recipient but can gate or veto hippocampal outputs during offline computation 56 . A central organizing principle is prioritization. Replay frequency and direction are shaped by salience and learning stage-reverse replay scales with reward magnitude at the goal 57 , while forward replay forecasts planned paths; normative models formalize this as prioritized memory access, where the utility of a replayed transition depends on predicted performance gain 58 . New experiments show that awake SWRs preferentially sample informative fragments of experience, consistent with these theories 59 . Neuromodulators gate when the brain enters the SWR regime. Acetylcholine, high during online encoding, suppresses ripples; elevating septal cholinergic drive reduces SWR incidence and impairs working-memory performance, while ACh drops during ripple-rich offline periods. This state control helps segregate "write" and "replay" modes across the day-night cycle 60 , 61 . Event Boundaries and Segmentation Dynamics Continuous experience is parsed into events by detecting when the current situation model stops predicting incoming data and must be updated. In humans, these "event boundaries" elicit transient increases in hippocampal and default-mode network (DMN) activity during naturalistic viewing and listening, and boundary-evoked responses in posterior hippocampus predict later memory detail, especially in younger adults 62 , 63 , 64 . Boundaries are not only detected when the sensory stream changes; similar boundary-like responses appear at internally generated context shifts during unguided recall, implying a common neural "context switch" signature for external and internal transitions 65 , 66 . Computationally, boundary probability correlates with Bayesian surprise derived from language-model predictions during narrated stories 67 , supporting the idea that segmentation tracks model mismatch rather than low-level surprisal alone. Together, this work formalizes boundaries as update points in an online generative model, aligning perceptual segmentation with memory formation. Hippocampal dynamics at boundaries are both selective and functional. fMRI and EEG show that boundaries trigger rapid reinstatement of the just-ended event, plausibly "packaging" it before a new model is initiated, and hippocampal offset responses scale with subsequent memory for the preceding episode 68 , 69 . In naturalistic studies, boundary strength modulates the magnitude of cortical pattern shifts and the hippocampal response 70 ; boundary-evoked hippocampal-PMN coupling at event offsets is especially predictive of durable memory for central narrative content 64 . These observations converge on a boundary-centric consolidation step in which reinstatement and hippocampal-cortical interaction at the end of an event stabilize its representation. Segmentation has structured consequences for how memories are organized. A consistent behavioral pattern is strengthened ordering and binding within events but impaired ordering across events; these cross-boundary costs are malleable and can reverse when retrieval cues reinstate the right context 71 . The Event Horizon account and modern reviews integrate this by proposing that boundaries create separate situation models that facilitate access to cohesive "chunks," with context reinstatement determining whether items straddling a boundary integrate or dissociate 72 . Recent work also indicates that goal shifts and task-set switches are sufficient to impose boundaries, emphasizing the agent- and goal-centric nature of event structure 73 , 74 . Importantly, boundaries are not only "cuts" but also integration points. During ongoing narratives, the brain selectively reactivates context-specific past information at event boundaries, retrieving only the prior episodes needed to interpret the present 66 . Hippocampal mechanisms that support this "event conjunction" likely leverage theta-gamma organization to reconstruct a high-level model from the just-ended event and append new details as a related event begins 75 . In line with this, the hippocampus contributes to constructing cross-event narratives, with posterior medial network partners supplying schematic structure 76 . Event structure also has a graph-theoretic footprint. When movies are converted into event networks, nodes with higher centrality-defined by denser semantic and causal linkages-are better remembered, elicit larger hippocampal boundary responses at encoding, and drive stronger DMN recruitment at recall 77 . These central nodes function as hubs that knit local event segments into a global memory graph. Complementing this, behavioral modeling demonstrates that people search memories by "skipping" from boundary to boundary, using these hubs as access points, which explains efficient retrieval of long naturalistic episodes 78 , 77 . What prompts boundaries? Beyond prediction error in perception and language, salient reward prediction errors create mnemonic boundaries that disrupt temporal integration across them 79 ; arousal-linked boundary effects track pupil-indexed locus coeruleus engagement at environmental changes 80 . Boundaries also arise at subtask switches 73 , environmental/scene changes 81 , 74 , and goal shifts, underscoring that segmentation is causation- and control-centric rather than purely sensory 82 . Theoretical and empirical updates nuance classic prediction-error accounts by showing that contextual stability (and prospective knowledge about imminent changes) can also generate boundary-like segmentation even without surprise. At the mesoscale, segmentation dovetails with systems-level coordination and replay. During naturalistic movie watching with intracranial recordings, human hippocampal ripples concentrate at event boundaries while cortical ripples occur preferentially within events, suggesting a division of labor in which hippocampus tags segment ends and cortex processes intra-event content 83 ; coordinated ripple timing across temporal-hippocampal-frontal sites supports encoding 84 . More broadly, replay-triggered activations seen at rest highlight that the same circuits enlisted at boundaries for online model-updating are reused offline to refine the event graph. Finally, the "engram" perspective reframes boundaries as times when membership in cell assemblies can be retuned. Across DG, CA3, CA1, mPFC and sensory cortices, engram composition is dynamic across consolidation and retrieval, with inhibitory plasticity shaping which neurons remain in the trace. Models with coordinated hippocampal-thalamic-cortical timescales reproduce engram turnover and predict that coupled reactivations at boundaries accelerate systems consolidation-linking segmentation, reinstatement, and long-term remodeling of memory substrates 85 , 86 , 87 . In summary, boundaries are algorithmic "commit-and-integrate" points where the brain (i) detects a model change via Bayesian surprise or goal/context shifts; (ii) rapidly reinstates relevant recent episodes and schema fragments to integrate them with the just-arrived evidence into an updated situation model; (iii) gates hippocampal-cortical communication to bind this integrated content-selectively strengthening central nodes and writing new cross-event links (causal, semantic, and goal-related) into the event graph; and (iv) schedules ripple- and spindle-coordinated interactions that both package the completed segment and propagate the newly integrated inferences to long-term stores. Framed this way, boundaries do not merely segment experience-they are constructive junctions that stitch episodes into narratives, update schemas and policies, and allocate fresh indices/pointers so future retrieval can flexibly jump from boundary to boundary for goal-directed inference over a hierarchical, causal network of events.
