title: The Semantic Memory System
text: Semantic memory, as used here, is the brain’s long-horizon statistical model of the world: a store of decontextualized, recombinable knowledge that supports rapid generalization across tasks and modalities. As said by Binder et al: "semantic memory is one of our most defining human traits, encompassing all the declarative knowledge we acquire about the world. A short list of examples includes the names and physical attributes of all objects, the origin and history of objects, the names and attributes of actions, all abstract concepts and their names, knowledge of how people behave and why, opinions and beliefs, knowledge of historical events, knowledge of causes and effects, associations between concepts, categories and their bases, and on and on ... humans use conceptual knowledge for much more than merely interacting with objects. All of human culture, including science, literature, social institutions, religion, and art, is constructed from conceptual knowledge. We do not reason, plan the future or remember the past without conceptual content - all of these activities depend on activation of concepts stored in semantic memory." 1 . Contemporary accounts converge on a two-system view-rich, transmodal representations plus control processes that shape retrieval to current goals-while also emphasizing that these functions are distributed, graded, and embedded in the cortex’s macroscale organization 2 . Natural-speech fMRI shows semantic information tiling large swaths of temporal, parietal, and prefrontal cortex, overlapping substantially with the transmodal apex of the principal connectivity gradient (the default-mode end) 3 , 4 , rather than any single "language" area 5 . Evidence from neuropsychology, stimulation, and ATL-optimized fMRI supports a "hub-and-spoke" organization in which modality-biased spokes (visual, motor, affective, linguistic) project to a graded semantic hub centered in ventral/anterior temporal cortex; the hub’s subregions show smooth shifts in bias rather than sharp boundaries 6 . This view accommodates both "semantic tiles" observed with voxelwise encoding models 5 and transmodal integration demanded by concept combination and generalization, and it explains classic semantic dementia phenotypes 7 . Debates continue over additional hubs (e.g., angular gyrus), but current syntheses place AG as a heteromodal integrator/buffer interfacing DMN with language-perceptual systems rather than a sole amodal store 8 . This cortical schema rides on long-range white-matter "highways." Ventral pathways-the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (occipito-temporal), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (occipito-frontal), and uncinate fasciculus (temporal-orbitofrontal)-link perceptual areas with anterior temporal and prefrontal hubs; dorsal streams (superior longitudinal/arcuate) and the cingulum bind semantic regions with control and mnemonic networks. Lesion mapping, intraoperative stimulation, and diffusion imaging converge on these tracts as the structural backbone enabling fast access to distributed conceptual content during comprehension and production 9 , 10 , 11 . Functionally, the control side of the system is left-leaning and includes inferior frontal gyrus and posterior middle temporal cortex, among others; meta-analyses and surface-based state-space work show that network configuration shifts with association strength and task demands, flexing along the principal gradient from sensory-coupled to transmodal states. During retrieval, humans exhibit "semantic foraging"-cluster-and-switch search through conceptual space-supported by frontoparietal control and DMN-adjacent buffers. Over learning timescales, hippocampal-neocortical complementarities and schema effects help explain how episodic traces are distilled ("semanticized") into durable cortical structure, with schema-consistent knowledge integrating more rapidly.

title: Hubs and Spokes Along a Principal Cortical Gradient
text: Semantic memory is organized along a macroscale principal connectivity gradient that runs from modality-specific sensory-motor cortices to transmodal integration hubs 1 . At one extreme of this gradient lie the unimodal "spokes" - specialized cortical regions devoted to processing a particular type of information (visual, auditory, motor, etc.). At the opposite end lie heteromodal "hub" regions (notably the anterior temporal lobes, angular gyrus, medial prefrontal cortex, and posterior cingulate/precuneus) which sit atop the cortical hierarchy and integrate inputs across modalities 1 . This arrangement enables increasingly abstract, multimodal representations to emerge as one moves from the peripheral spokes toward the transmodal hub apex. In essence, the brain’s default mode network (DMN) - which includes these high-level regions - occupies the gradient’s transmodal end, whereas primary sensory and motor areas anchor the low-level end, with intermediate association areas in between 2 . This gradient topography is thought to facilitate memory-guided and conceptual cognition, allowing heteromodal DMN regions to represent information in a format less tied to immediate sensory inputs and more grounded in stored knowledge 3 , 2 ; however, the DMN should not be equated with the semantic network: while there is substantial anatomical and functional overlap (especially in ATL, AG, and mPFC), semantic cognition also relies on control regions outside the DMN, and DMN nodes participate in many other functions unrelated to semantics, including episodic memory, scene construction, and social cognition 3 . The two systems dynamically couple or decouple depending on task demands, rather than forming a fixed one-to-one mapping. Within the principal gradient, semantic knowledge can be understood via a "hub-and-spoke" architecture 4 . Modality-specific "spokes" in visual, auditory, somatosensory, olfactory, and motor association cortices encode the raw features and instances of experience-for example, the sound of a waterfall in auditory cortex, its visual cascade of motion and color in occipito-temporal cortex, or the feel of its cool mist in somatosensory areas. These distributed representations converge via long-range connections onto bilateral, graded transmodal "hub" regions in the anterior temporal lobe (ATL), especially the ventrolateral and temporal pole zones, where unified, modality-invariant concepts of "waterfall" are synthesized 4 . Crucially, when the ATL hub is damaged-most starkly in semantic dementia with bilateral ATL atrophy-the deficit is not merely naming: patients show a category-general, cross-modal degradation of conceptual knowledge, with impaired single-word comprehension, poor picture naming and word-picture matching, reduced knowledge of object features and use, and semantic errors for stimuli presented as words, pictures, and even environmental sounds; speech output and repetition are relatively spared early, yielding fluent but empty discourse 5 , 6 . Left-predominant ATL disease accentuates verbal semantic impairments (naming, single-word comprehension, exception-word "surface" dyslexia/dysgraphia reflecting over-regularization), whereas right-predominant disease disproportionately disrupts person-specific knowledge-recognizing familiar faces/voices and retrieving proper names and biographical facts-reflecting graded specializations across the bilateral hub 7 , 8 . The overall severity of the semantic deficit scales with the extent of bilateral ATL degeneration, and transient disruption of lateral ATL with TMS in healthy participants mimics the same amodal, category-general impairment profile 9 , 10 . White-matter tractography in semantic dementia further shows that multiple "module-to-hub" routes carrying written word, lexical, and face/object information into ATL are selectively compromised, and disconnection along these routes predicts semantic impairment severity 9 , 11 . Another transmodal convergence zone is the angular gyrus (AG) at the temporo-parietal junction-part of the DMN’s heteromodal apex along the principal connectivity gradient, far from unimodal sensory-motor cortices 1 . fMRI, lesion, and stimulation work converge on the view that AG encodes high-level, combinatorial situation meanings-event schemas and thematic relations that bind who-did-what-to-whom across modalities (e.g., the structure of "a wedding," "hammer hits nail," or "ordering coffee") 12 , and it supports semantic integration/buffering that makes retrieval of well-learned associations feel effortless 13 , 14 . High-definition tDCS and patient work show a causal role for AG in integrating meanings during conceptual combination, while other recent studies link AG specifically to event-centric semantic structure rather than object-feature coding, which is stronger in ATL. In contrast, posterior MTG contributes more to controlled retrieval of weak links; disrupting AG selectively harms automatic retrieval of strong, highly related knowledge 14 , 15 . Consistent with this computational profile, the AG’s position at the transmodal end of the principal gradient (with ATL/mPFC/PCC) equips it to pool inputs from multiple ’spokes’ and stabilize abstract, generalized situation models during comprehension and memory. Hub regions are densely connected to widespread cortical modules by major white-matter "highways," enabling the hub-and-spoke integration. For instance, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF) connects occipital visual areas to anterior temporal cortex, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) links occipital and temporal regions to frontal cortex, and the uncinate fasciculus (UF) connects the ATL with orbitofrontal/vmPFC areas - all providing direct routes for modality-specific information to reach transmodal hubs. Likewise, dorsal pathways such as the arcuate fasciculus bridge temporal and inferior parietal regions with frontal cortex (supporting language and action-related semantics), and the cingulum bundle interconnects medial parietal, hippocampal, and frontal hubs along the DMN. Recent tract-tracing and neuroimaging studies have identified specific fiber pathways that implement this module-to-hub network: for example, direct tracts link the ATL to category-specific posterior areas (such as face-responsive fusiform cortex and word-form areas), effectively funneling visual and lexical information into the semantic hub 11 . Damage to these hub-centered tracts in semantic dementia correlates with semantic impairment, whereas damage to more general ventral tracts (e.g. ILF or UF) has comparatively less impact. These findings reinforce a core principle of the hub-and-spoke model: semantic coherence is achieved by robust anatomical connections that allow distributed feature processors (the spokes) to converge on a central integrative network (the hubs). The semantic "hub-and-spoke" system is graded rather than monolithic: domain-biased spokes specialize by content yet stay tightly coupled to a shared, transmodal hub instead of operating as sealed modules. A left-lateralized fronto-temporo-parietal circuit (classically left inferior frontal gyrus, left posterior middle temporal gyrus, and intraparietal sulcus) comes online for tools and action semantics when you decide whether a wrench or pliers is better for loosening a bolt, simulate the grip sequence to use a corkscrew, or plan the hand trajectory to thread a wire through a tight space 16 , 17 , 18 . Social and mentalizing semantics recruit a medial prefrontal-temporo-parietal network spanning mPFC, precuneus/posterior cingulate, and bilateral TPJ/pSTS when you infer a character’s hidden motive while reading a short story, detect sarcasm in a friend’s remark, or predict a teammate’s next move from gaze and body cues 19 , 20 . Scene and contextual knowledge are supported by a posterior-medial network centered on parahippocampal and retrosplenial cortex when you choose a route through an unfamiliar building, reorient using a distant landmark after taking a wrong turn, or recognize your street at night from its spatial layout and stable cues 21 , 22 . Together, these content-biased systems interface with the common hub to yield flexible, modality-invariant concepts that can be redeployed across tasks and contexts 23 ; in practice, they interact with transmodal integrators like the ATL and angular gyrus to enrich semantic representations with domain-specific detail. For instance, the PHC-RSC "place network" provides spatial context information that can be bound to more general event or object representations in the ATL or midline hubs. Similarly, the tool/action network in the left hemisphere contributes motor-pragmatic features of tool concepts, but it links into the ATL/temporal hub to integrate those features with an object’s visual and functional properties. The default mode network (DMN) - encompassing many of these heteromodal hub areas - plays a central role in orchestrating this integration. The DMN is often associated with internally driven cognition (e.g. episodic memory, imagination, narrative comprehension), and accumulating evidence indicates it is intimately involved in semantic processing 1 . One proposal is that DMN regions collectively coordinate and synchronize activity across multiple modality-specific areas, effectively binding their features into a coherent, higher-order representation 3 . In this view, the DMN acts as a global convergence zone that momentarily recruits local ensembles from visual, auditory, language, and other systems into a unified "neuronal ensemble" representing a situation or concept. The result of this large-scale synchrony is an integrated simulation of phenomenological experience - essentially, an embodied situation model that the brain constructs on the fly from diverse memory traces. For example, understanding a sentence or story involves the DMN weaving together word meanings, sensory contexts, and personal memories into a holistic mental scene. Such situation models are thought to be invaluable not only for semantic tasks like language comprehension but also for many cognitive functions not traditionally considered "semantic," such as imagining future events, navigating social interactions, or moral reasoning 3 . By creating a richly textured simulacrum of experience, the DMN-driven hub network allows us to transcend the here-and-now, integrating what we know with what we perceive or imagine. This account finds support in neuroimaging studies showing DMN activation during semantic retrieval at sentence and discourse levels, and in the overlap between DMN regions and those engaged by autobiographical memory, theory-of-mind, and other high-level tasks (suggesting a common reliance on situation-modeling). Within these integrated representations lie structured knowledge schemas - higher-order associative frameworks that capture abstract commonalities across our experiences 24 , 25 . In cognitive theory, schemas (a concept dating back to Bartlett 1932 and Piaget 1954) are mental models of the world that summarize typical patterns in a given context (for instance, the layout of a standard European city, the expected sequence of events at a neuroscience conference, or the characteristic behaviors of a sheriff in Wild West folklore). Schemas can be viewed as complex semantic memories: they organize concepts, relationships, and rules into a abstract templates that can guide our understanding and expectations in new situations; they represent information at a higher level of abstraction than single concepts - often encoding contextual and relational structure (who, what, where, when typically goes together) within a certain domain 26 , 27 - and are highly flexible and generalizable. Once a schema is formed (e.g. a "restaurant schema" for the sequence of events in dining out), it can be applied to interpret or predict new instances (a meal at a brand-new restaurant) by filling in missing details with educated guesses 28 , 29 . This makes schemas powerful tools for directing attention to relevant details, facilitating memory encoding and retrieval (by providing an organized scaffold for new information), and even guiding problem-solving or exploration (by suggesting likely outcomes and strategies based on past patterns) 30 , 25 . Neuroanatomically, schema processing centers on an mPFC/vmPFC-hippocampal axis that interfaces with posterior‐medial scene/context machinery (RSC/PHC) and parietal integrators (AG). mPFC/vmPFC expresses "schema templates" that bias encoding and retrieval toward prior structure and dynamically couple with the hippocampus; when vmPFC is damaged-especially in confabulators-patients fail to reinstate the correct script and over-accept schema-consistent lures (e.g., endorsing out-of-place "doctor’s office" details when judging a bedtime script), despite otherwise fluent behavior 25 , 31 , 32 . Cross-species work shows that once a relevant schema is established, consolidation of new consistent information accelerates and shifts neocortical, vmPFC/ACC-dependent: rats with a learned flavor-place schema acquire new pairings in a single trial, and pharmacologically disrupting ACC/vmPFC plasticity abolishes this rapid assimilation-predicting that humans with medial prefrontal damage should show blunted schema benefits even when hippocampus is intact 33 , 34 , 35 . The angular gyrus contributes the combinatorial "situation model" layer that stitches concepts into event schemas; perturbing AG causally slows or distorts conceptual combination (e.g., parsing "wet leaf," "wedding toast"), consistent with patients’ deficits on integrative semantic judgments when this node is compromised 12 , 36 . Finally, posterior‐medial cortex supplies the spatial-contextual scaffold that many schemas rely on: RSC/PHC lesions yield classic topographical/heading disorientation-patients become lost in familiar neighborhoods or can’t use landmark layout-reflecting a failure to instantiate the "place" component of situation models that would normally anchor scripts for wayfinding, scene construction, and narrative comprehension 22 , 37 .

title: Graph-Theoretic Properties of Semantic Memories
text: Semantic memory can be conceived as a vast network of concepts (nodes) connected by associations (edges), and analyses show it has a pronounced small-world topology 1 . In a small-world network, most concepts are not directly connected, yet any concept can be reached from any other via only a few steps through the network. In practical terms, semantic knowledge is organized into densely interlinked clusters of related concepts (e.g. animals, tools, emotions) with short-cut links bridging across clusters via more universal or polysemous concepts 1 . This architecture yields high local clustering (concepts within a category share many interconnections) alongside short global path lengths (even concepts from very different domains can be connected through surprisingly few associative hops). Such a small-world arrangement is thought to balance specialized processing with efficient integration: closely related ideas form substructures that promote context-specific priming and inference, while the overall network remains globally integrated, enabling far-flung analogies and fast knowledge transfer across domains 2 . these network properties appear to be an intrinsic feature of semantic organization: studies have found small-world characteristics in semantic networks built from diverse sources (word association norms, thesauri, WordNet) and across languages, suggesting a universal architectural principle for how human knowledge is structured 3 . Alongside small-world clustering, semantic networks exhibit a heavy-tailed (approximately scale-free) degree distribution, meaning a minority of nodes serve as highly connected hubs linking many concepts, while most nodes have fewer connections 1 , 4 . In essence, some ideas (often very abstract or general ones, like "time," "person," or "move") act as major hubs with disproportionate connectivity, whereas more specific concepts are richly interlinked with their close kin but sparsely connected outside their niche. Graph-theoretically, this yields a network with hub nodes that greatly reduce the degrees of separation between any two concepts. These hubs form part of a high-connectivity backbone or "rich club" that promotes global integration: they tend to be interconnected with each other as well, creating a core subnetwork through which much information flow passes 5 . In the brain’s semantic system, this graph structure is mirrored by transmodal integration hubs like the anterior temporal lobes, angular gyrus, and medial prefrontal cortex. Connectome analyses show that heteromodal default-mode regions (including key semantic areas) often rank among the most globally connected and central nodes in the whole-brain network 2 . This hub architecture confers efficiency and robustness: it ensures any two distant cortical regions (or concepts) can communicate quickly via hub-mediated shortcuts, and it economizes wiring by funneling information through central highways. However, it also implies a vulnerability to hub disruption. Just as removing a highly connected node in a scale-free graph can fragment the network, damage to semantic hub regions or their white-matter connections (for example, bilateral ATL degeneration in semantic dementia) produces disproportionate deficits, effectively disconnecting many modality-specific "spoke" areas and collapsing conceptual coherence across domains 6 . By contrast, damage to a peripheral spoke or a single category tends to have more circumscribed effects. Thus, the graph-theoretic lens helps explain why focal hub lesions yield generalized semantic impairments while leaving other cognitive functions intact - the network’s high-degree nodes are singularly important for holding the knowledge web together. The semantic network shows modular structure with community organization aligning to meaningful subdomains. Graph analysis reveals that concepts naturally cluster into communities corresponding to thematic or categorical groupings (e.g. living things vs. artifacts, social concepts, spatial navigation concepts, etc.) 2 . These modules can be thought of as the cognitive equivalent of "neighborhoods" in the semantic graph - sets of nodes with dense internal connections and shared contextual features. For instance, tools and manipulable objects form a tightly knit subnetwork linked by shared action and shape attributes, whereas social concepts cluster via person-related knowledge, and spatial landmarks via scene and place associations. This community structure is consistent with the domain-biased subnetworks observed in neuroimaging (e.g. a tool-use network, a social reasoning network, a spatial navigation network) and with classic category-specific semantic effects (such as selective impairments for living vs. nonliving things in some brain injuries); however, these communities are not isolated islands: the hub nodes (both certain high-level concepts and integrative cortical regions) serve as bridges between modules, allowing information from one domain to inform another. For example, the concept "restaurant" might link a social script module (people, roles, intentions) with an object module (food items, tools like utensils) and a spatial module (the layout of a dining area). Such cross-talk is enabled by the network’s long-range connections (edges that link nodes in different communities) and by hub regions that anatomically connect to multiple specialized areas; graph-theoretic measures of modularity and connectivity thus map neatly onto cognitive structure: high modularity underlies distinct conceptual realms, while inter-module links and low characteristic path lengths underlie our ability to combine concepts across realms (e.g. to apply social knowledge to a tool-use scenario or blend metaphors between unrelated domains). The topological properties of the semantic network have direct consequences for how we retrieve and generate knowledge. Spreading activation in a small-world, hub-supported network can quickly reach remote nodes, accounting for how a single cue can trigger far-ranging associations or creative insights. At the same time, the clustering of related concepts means that memory search tends to yield groups of similar items - a phenomenon well documented in verbal fluency tasks. When people list as many exemplars of a category as possible ("name all the animals you can"), they naturally produce items in clusters (e.g. a streak of farm animals, then a bunch of ocean creatures) and occasionally make sudden switches to a new cluster 7 . Graph-theoretic models explain this as a byproduct of network topology: because related concepts are tightly interconnected, an initial probe (say, "cow") activates its neighbors ("horse," "pig," "goat"), leading to a local run of farm animals; but to avoid repetition or diminishing returns, the search process must then jump along a weaker link to a different region of the network (from "farm" cluster to "sea creatures" cluster, for example). This "semantic foraging" strategy - exploit locally, then explore globally - can emerge even from a random walk on a small-world semantic graph, and it closely resembles optimal foraging in physical space. In cognitive terms, the network’s structure itself affords an efficient search: high clustering yields rich local neighborhoods that can be thoroughly mined for related ideas, while short path lengths and hubs allow relatively effortless leaps to new contexts when needed. This helps resolve the puzzle of how human memory retrieval is both focused (sticking to a context for a time) and flexible (able to shift context and find distant associations) without an exhaustive, serial scan of our entire knowledge store. Functional brain studies show that task demands can transiently shift network topology: for instance, under high semantic workload or when making unusual associations, the brain’s connectivity may become less segregated and more integrated (reducing modularity and increasing long-range communication), effectively flexing along the spectrum from localized to distributed processing. Such dynamic reconfiguration aligns with the idea of a "flexible semantic workspace" that can globally broadcast conceptual information when required (engaging a broad default-mode/semantic network), or conversely, tighten into context-specific loops for automatic retrieval of well-known facts. Pathological states also illustrate the graph dynamics: in Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, progressive loss of associative links and node degradation leads to a less small-world-like network (more random or lattice-like), which corresponds to patients’ slowed retrieval and impoverished clustering. Schemas and task representations can be viewed as mesoscale motifs embedded in the semantic graph. A schema effectively "adds" structured shortcut edges among otherwise distant communities (roles, objects, places, causal relations), reducing path length and increasing local clustering around event- or script-nodes (e.g., "restaurant") so that inference can proceed with minimal search. vmPFC/mPFC appears to index and reinstate these templates, biasing traversal toward schema-consistent subgraphs and coupling with hippocampus during encoding and post-encoding rest; when vmPFC is damaged, people over-accept schema-consistent lures and fail to apply the appropriate script, consistent with degraded control over which subgraph is activated 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 . In this graph-theoretic framing, semantic control networks select and transiently reconfigure subgraphs to meet task goals, while schemas provide pre-wired "network macros" that compress search and enable one-shot assimilation of consistent information.

title: Representational and Control Subdivisions
text: Ventrolateral prefrontal cortex in macaques guides decisions in different learning conditions ; Working Memory as Programmable Fast Weight Computation WM relies more on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, whereas maintaining information in mind but not manipulating it 3 does not need involvement of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (D’Esposito et al. 1999, Eldreth et al. 2006, Smith & Jonides 1999). Imaging studies show frontal activation only in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex for memory maintenance that is not suprathreshold. 4 A compact way to organize the system is: representational hubs encode long-horizon, amodal regularities; control circuits tune access, competition, and task alignment. On the representational side, a graded, transmodal core spans bilateral anterior/ventral temporal cortex, angular gyrus (ventral PGp), medial prefrontal cortex, and posterior cingulate/precuneus. These regions lie at the apex of the principal connectivity gradient and support content-rich, modality-invariant concepts and situation models that can be recombined across contexts. By contrast, a left-leaning semantic control network (SCN) comes online when retrieval must be shaped to context, cues are weak, or competitors are strong. Meta-analyses and causal perturbations highlight left inferior frontal gyrus-subserving controlled retrieval in anterior/ventral BA45 and selection among competitors in more dorsal/posterior IFG/IFS-together with posterior middle/inferior temporal cortex, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex/pre-SMA, and dorsal parietal control zones (dorsal AG/IPS). These areas bias access to non-dominant associations, resolve competition, and reformat conceptual outputs into a task-appropriate code. Critically, pMTG sits at the anatomical "middle ground" between DMN and the multiple-demand (MD) executive system (which is implicated in domain-general control), coupling to ventral IFG during control-heavy semantic judgments and to IFS/IPS when selection demands rise-consistent with its role as a nexus linking representational hubs to control machinery 5 , 6 , 7 . The SCN is not a carbon copy of the MD network, nor is it simply an extension of the DMN. Topographic and connectivity analyses place it in an intermediate zone between the two, allowing it to dynamically recruit resources from either end of the cortex’s principal connectivity gradient 8 , 9 . When a task involves strong, well-learned associations, SCN activity shifts toward the transmodal end of the gradient-functionally coupling with DMN hubs like ATL, AG, and mPFC to exploit automatic, richly integrated representations. When the task instead demands retrieval of weak or novel associations, or selection of atypical features, SCN regions shift their coupling toward the sensory-coupled, executive-control end of the gradient-aligning more with MDN regions such as IFS and IPS to impose stronger top-down constraints. This ability to "flex along the principal gradient" means the SCN can reconfigure its network position to favor either automatic, knowledge-driven processing or effortful, control-driven processing as needed-a dynamic now directly observed in surface-based "informational connectivity" analyses during semantic search tasks. Two cortical interfaces are particularly important. First, a language interface maps conceptual content to lexical and syntactic forms via a temporal-frontal pathway: mid/anterior STS-MTG and temporal pole support lexical-semantic access and combinatorics along a ventral stream, while left IFG parcels implement unification, selection, and morpho-syntactic operations; a complementary dorsal stream supports sensorimotor mappings for articulation. This architecture explains how the same conceptual representation can be verbalized under varying constraints, and why linguistic difficulty recruits adjacent MD control regions while core language regions remain functionally distinct 10 , 11 , 12 . Second, a working-memory/attention interface recruits MDN (IFJ/IFS, dlPFC, IPS) proportionally to semantic processing difficulty, stabilizing intermediate goal states and sequencing multi-step inferences; in naturalistic tasks, language, DMN, and MDN remain dissociable yet coordinative, with MDN providing domain-general control that scaffolds semantic selection when demands escalate 13 , 14 . Value and goals modulate semantic access via a vmPFC/OFC interface. vmPFC carries a domain-general subjective-value code that can weight candidate interpretations or inferences, while OFC represents a cognitive map of task/state space, supplying the currently relevant state features that semantic control should target. This arrangement links abstract knowledge to goal-directed behavior: vmPFC/OFC bias which meanings are worth pursuing and which features of the situation should be integrated next 15 , 16 , 17 . Subcortical partners close the loop. Pre-SMA/ACC interact with basal ganglia and mediodorsal thalamus to gate retrieval, update task sets, and broadcast the selected interpretation to cortical workspaces 18 , 19 , 20 . Word-generation and semantic retrieval studies implicate a pre-SMA-caudate-anterior thalamic loop during access to stored lexical-semantic knowledge, while converging human and primate data assign MD thalamus a regulatory role in prefrontal-dependent cognition, including selection among lexical-semantic alternatives. These cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits provide the control dynamics-initiation, maintenance, and switching-that the cortical SCN exploits 21 . Putting this together: the representational core (ATL/ventral AG-PGp/mPFC/PCC) furnishes amodal, recombinable structure over long horizons; the SCN (LIFG/IFJ, pMTG/ITG, dmPFC/pre-SMA, dorsal AG/IPS) tunes entry into, traversal of, and readout from that structure to meet task goals; language and MDN interfaces render the content in communicable form and manage difficulty; and vmPFC/OFC plus fronto-striato-thalamic loops supply goal/value signals and control gating. This fractionation explains classic dissociations: representational damage (e.g., bilateral ATL degeneration) yields degraded knowledge across modalities, whereas control-network lesions ("semantic aphasia") spare stored content but produce context-inappropriate retrieval that is disproportionately impaired under weak cues or high competition.

title: Dual-Process Models and General Retrieval Ability
text: A long tradition in cognitive science frames memory search as the interaction of two families of processes: fast, associative dynamics that spread activation through an attractor-rich knowledge space, and slower, capacity-limited control operations that steer, select, and evaluate what rises to mind. Contemporary dual-process accounts refine this into hybrid models in which intuitive (Type 1) and deliberative (Type 2) operations often run in parallel, with conflict detection and rational arbitration determining when effortful control should override default outputs. In reasoning, this shift is captured by "default-interventionist" and "hybrid" revisions of classic System-1/System-2 theory, and the same logic maps cleanly onto semantic retrieval: associative activation propagates rapidly along learned links, while fronto-basal ganglia control systems bias access toward task-relevant neighborhoods and gate entry into working memory for evaluation. Meta-analytic and theoretical treatments emphasize that the point is not two monolithic "systems," but multiple algorithms grouped by speed, automaticity, and reliance on executive resources, coordinated by monitoring processes that detect conflict or low confidence and trigger controlled search 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . On the associative side, spreading activation and random-walk formalisms explain the hallmark structure of semantic fluency: people emit items in tight clusters (e.g., farm animals) and then jump to a new region (e.g., sea creatures) when local returns diminish. Optimal-foraging analyses show that this "exploit-then-explore" rhythm emerges naturally in small-world semantic graphs and can be approximated by random walks constrained by learned similarity structure. Neural data complement the behavior: during foraging-like retrieval, switching epochs recruit control nodes compared to within-cluster exploitation, consistent with a supervisory role 5 . Strategic retrieval policies make the control contribution concrete. Classic diary and protocol studies show that people deliberately seed search with organizing cues-recalling high-school classmates by scanning extracurricular groups, alphabet, or yearbook pages 6 ; or restarting a stuck search by switching to a new subcategory. More recently, computational work demonstrates that model-based cue selection measurably boosts recall by choosing reminders predicted to activate regions of memory space that still contain unretrieved items 7 . This links metacognitive monitoring ("what is likely to work next?") to control of cueing and termination decisions. Across tasks, individual differences reveal a domain-general retrieval ability (sometimes labeled broad retrieval, Gr): latent-variable work finds that factors derived from semantic and autobiographical fluency load on a higher-order construct correlated with working-memory/attentional control but only weakly with vocabulary 8 . This dovetails with executive-attention theories of working memory that attribute variance in complex cognition to goal maintenance and interference control-precisely the ingredients needed to sustain exploitation within a cluster, shield against competitors, and then pivot to a new cluster when returns fall 9 , 9 . People lower on this control dimension are less likely to report using structured strategies and benefit less from them.

title: Episodes and Semantics: Their Overlap, Cooperation, and Distinctions
text: Recent research increasingly suggests that episodic and semantic memory are not separate, isolated systems, but rather points along a continuum of declarative memory that engage a common core network to different degrees. Neural evidence shows a substantial overlap in the brain regions involved in both episodic and semantic retrieval. All types of long-term memory - from impersonal facts to personal facts to rich recollections - activate a shared "core memory network" including the medial temporal lobes (hippocampus and associated structures), medial prefrontal cortex, and posterior parietal cortex. The distinction between simulating an event versus knowing a fact appears to arise from quantitative differences in the magnitude and pattern of activation within this common network, rather than entirely different circuits. For example, retrieving a unique, vivid event (classic episodic memory) elicits a stronger ramp-up of activity in hippocampal, posterior parietal, and medial prefrontal regions compared to recalling a general piece of knowledge, with intermediate levels of engagement for "in-between" cases like memories of a repeated routine. This continuum perspective calls into question the once-standard view of completely distinct systems, instead indicating that the distinction between semantic and episodic inference is more or less a distinction resulting from the activity of similar components across time: the 5D (3D space, 1D time, and 1D activity) activity profile of the system’s components determines the location of the psychological product on the semantic-episodic continuum. In operational terms, the system defaults to semantic retrieval when the cue sits in a dense, well-learned region of conceptual space and/or the cost of latency is high: vmPFC and anterior temporal hubs return a compressed prototype or rule that is ’good enough’ without reinstating context. It recruits episodic simulation when expected gains from reinstating spatiotemporal structure outweigh the costs-when cues are novel or ambiguous, when the query requires WWW binding or counterfactual recombination, or when the transition model may have changed. Formally, arbitration follows an expected-value-of-computation policy in which semantic memory provides fast, low-variance estimates and episodic memory provides slower, high-fidelity samples that reduce uncertainty or expose edge-cases. Strong schemas push the balance toward semantic reuse and rapid integration; weak or violated schemas shift weight to hippocampal construction. This rule explains everyday behavior: you answer ’What’s the capital of France?’ semantically; you answer ’Would I enjoy a sauna after heavy deadlifts?’ by simulating specific episodes; you choose a restaurant in your home city semantically (scripts, prototypes), but in a new country by sampling episodes, reading off WWW details, and updating the semantic map. One key hub in the unified memory network is the hippocampus. Long known for its role in episodic recollection, the hippocampus is now understood to be deeply involved in semantic memory as well. It is critical for encoding new semantic information and can be recruited during semantic retrieval, especially when relationships or context must be processed 1 . In fact, recent reviews reaffirm that both episodic and semantic memories are relational and (re)constructive, relying on the hippocampal formation to bind together elements into coherent representations. The rich associations that give semantic knowledge its structure (e.g. how concepts link to one another) and give episodic events their situational detail (who, what, where, when) both depend on hippocampal-dependent coding of relationships. Damage to the hippocampus tends to impair not only the ability to re-experience past events, but also the acquisition of new factual knowledge - underscoring that hippocampal computations support both kinds of memory content. Still, there are differences in degree: during a truly episodic memory task (say, recalling a specific birthday party), hippocampal and related "internal mentation" regions often show greater activity than during a purely semantic task (e.g. recalling what the capital of France is). At a representational level, mounting evidence suggests that both episodic and semantic memories are organized in brain networks as cognitive maps or graphs, and that retrieving a memory involves a process akin to navigation. The hippocampo-entorhinal system famously supports spatial navigation, and an emerging view is that this system also encodes abstract relationships among experiences and concepts in a map-like format 2 . In other words, neurons that map physical space (place cells, grid cells, etc.) may similarly map conceptual "spaces," allowing us to mentally wander through knowledge just as we would wander through a landscape. This idea is consistent with the aforementioned studies of human semantic retrieval, where people are shown to "forage" through semantic space: remembering episodes and retrieving facts might leverage a common spatial-navigation-derived mechanism - effectively moving along paths in an internal cognitive map 3 . Episodic recollection can be seen as a journey through the time and place of a past event, and semantic recall as a journey through a network of related concepts. In both cases, the trajectory our mind takes (traversing associative links or spatial-temporal context) reflects a shared computational heritage. Despite these deep commonalities, there are clear qualitative distinctions between an episodic memory and a semantic memory in terms of phenomenological detail and format. Episodic memories are often described as being "re-experienced" rather than just known. They contain richly bound What-Where-When (WWW) elements - the specific persons, objects, places, and the temporal sequence of events - all embedded into a single mental reconstruction 4 , 5 . Such memories have an internal spatiotemporal structure: one can say that in an episodic recall, you know not just what happened, but where each element was relative to others ("next to") and when things occurred ("before/after" something else), and you often recall the event from a particular perspective (usually your own) with accompanying sensory details and emotions. In other words, episodic recall attempts to reinstate the multidimensional context of an experience - yielding a "holistic" representation with the feel of mentally traveling back in time. By contrast, semantic memory stores more decontextualized knowledge. A semantic memory might be the fact "saunas are hot, steamy, and relaxing", divorced from any particular time or personal experience. An episodic memory, on the other hand, would be "I remember the Friday night when I won a dare to stay the longest in a sauna - it was so hot and we celebrated afterward with cucumber water". The latter is singular, tied to a specific when and where, and laden with perceptual detail (the heat, the taste of the water), whereas the former is a general truth accumulated from many instances. Indeed, neuropsychology has long noted that patients can lose the ability to vividly re-live events (episodic impairment) while still knowing facts, and vice versa, highlighting that the presence of contextual detail is a key differentiator. Modern views, however, stress this is a difference in degree and kind of information represented, not a wholly separate memory store - episodic memory simply sits at the extreme end of high-detail, high-context "episodicness," whereas semantic memory lies at the other end of low-context, generalized knowledge. Crucially, episodic and semantic memory cooperate during both learning and retrieval, each supporting the other. During learning, episodic experiences are a primary source of new semantic knowledge. Recalling or replaying specific episodes can lead to the extraction of general principles or facts - a process sometimes dubbed "semanticization." For example, a person who vividly remembers a series of individual chemistry experiments (episodic) may over time abstract from them the general scientific concepts or rules (semantic). In cognitive neuroscience, this idea is captured by consolidation theories: initially, new information is encoded episodically with hippocampal involvement; with repeated reactivation of the memory (e.g. recalling or reflecting on the event), the hippocampal-cortical network gradually distills the common elements and stores them in the cortex as semantic knowledge. Empirical evidence supports this gradual gist abstraction: repeatedly recalling a past event tends to reinforce the central ideas while certain contextual details fade, resulting in a more schematic version of the memory. For instance, over months or years you might forget exactly which day a particular meeting took place (episodic detail) but remember the outcome or knowledge gained from it (now part of your semantic memory). In neurological patients, we see the other side of this coin: damage that prevents forming new episodic memories (e.g. hippocampal amnesia) also severely impairs the learning of new facts, unless alternative pathways are leveraged. Likewise, there is often a gradual transformation of memories from episodic to semantic form. Initially, a memory of a learning event is rich in context, but with time and repeated exposure, it becomes "known" independent of the original context. This can happen slowly or, if the new information fits an existing schema, quite rapidly. Research indicates that when new information is schema-consistent (fits prior knowledge), the brain can integrate it into semantic memory very quickly - sometimes bypassing the need for prolonged hippocampal replay. On the other hand, schema-inconsistent information (truly novel structures) usually requires more hippocampal engagement and consolidation time to become integrated. Thus, episodic memory provides a training ground or "gateway" for semantic learning, and having a rich base of semantic schemas in turn can accelerate new episodic experiences being generalized. During retrieval and inference, the two forms of memory are likewise interwoven. Remembering a specific episode often requires semantic support to fill in gaps and guide the search. Our semantic knowledge about the world provides context that helps us reconstruct events: for example, knowing typical scripts or schemas ("what usually happens at a birthday party") will guide and scaffold the retrieval of a particular birthday party memory. If semantic memory is compromised, episodic recollection suffers. In semantic dementia (a neurodegenerative disease that erodes semantic knowledge), patients can often recall recent experiences to some extent, but their ability to retrieve older, more remote autobiographical episodes degrades in tandem with their loss of general knowledge 5 . They might remember isolated sensory fragments of an event but struggle to place them in a coherent narrative, effectively "falling back" on over-general memories of the sort "something usually happens" without specifics. This happens because without the semantic framework (e.g. understanding who people are, what typical contexts mean, the narrative structure of events), the hippocampal pattern completion has little scaffold on which to hang the retrieved perceptual details. Conversely, semantic memory retrieval can be enriched or supported by episodic simulation. We often answer ostensibly semantic questions by mentally simulating episodes. For instance, to answer a question like "Do I like saunas?", one might remember a particular sauna visit (an episode) and derive the answer from it (concluding "Yes, because in that episode I felt great"). In this way, episodic memory can produce on-the-fly "semantic" information - effectively extracting general knowledge from a specific reconstruction. Researchers have termed such on-demand abstraction as episodic memory enabling "prototypically semantic" inferences 6 . Even when we think we are using pure semantic memory, subtle experiments show that we often tap into episodic traces (especially for personal or experiential knowledge) to inform our judgments. Neuroimaging reveals that tasks requiring flexible inference or novel combination of knowledge (like figuring out a puzzle) activate episodic retrieval networks alongside semantic areas, indicating the brain recruits episodic simulation to supplement semantic reasoning. Personal semantic memory occupies a middle ground in this interplay. Personal semantics refers to one’s store of factual knowledge about their own life - e.g. "I have a gym membership" or "I used to go jogging every Sunday." These are facts (thus semantic-like) but also personal and derived from repeated episodes (thus episodic-like). Conceptually, personal semantic memory lies between general semantic and fully episodic memory. Its neural correlates reflect this: for example, remembering an autobiographical fact (like your first phone number) engages the core memory network less than recalling a unique event, but often more than impersonal facts 7 . Some personal semantics (especially repeated-event memories, like "my Sunday jogging routine") recruit brain activity very similar to recalling a generic episode, whereas other personal facts (like your own street address) behave more like pure semantics in the brain. Functionally, personal semantic knowledge can serve as a powerful retrieval cue for episodic memory. Knowing the general schema of your life - e.g. that "I usually do stretches before a workout" - can help trigger a memory of a specific instance ("that time last week at the gym when I stretched and then tried a new exercise") by providing a scaffold to search within. Studies indeed suggest that having rich personal semantics (like well-developed life schemas or narratives) is associated with better access to detailed autobiographical episodes. Moreover, personal semantic memories themselves often originate through the repeated replay of episodic events until they lose their context - a process sometimes observed during memory consolidation when frequent experiences (like going to the gym every week) blur into a generalized memory of one’s habits. The tight coupling between semantic scaffolds and episodic details becomes especially apparent in prospective memory - imagining or planning for the future. Episodic future thinking (EFT), the ability to construct plausible future scenarios, draws on both systems. To imagine a novel event (say, a future vacation), one must flexibly recombine bits of past episodic memories (sights, sounds, places one has been) and incorporate semantic knowledge about the world (what typically happens on vacations, what one knows about the destination, etc.). Semantic memory provides the semantic and schematic context that keeps an imagined scenario coherent. Individuals with semantic memory loss dramatically illustrate this: patients with semantic dementia can often describe past events they lived through, but when asked to imagine a new event, they struggle greatly. Lacking general knowledge of people, objects, and schemas, their attempts at future simulation often degrade into disjointed "replays" of actual past events or a collection of unconnected fragments; one study found that  80% of the "future" events described by semantic dementia patients were essentially replays of previously experienced events 5 . This phenomenon supports the semantic scaffolding hypothesis, which posits that conceptual semantic knowledge provides a necessary framework for building both richly detailed memories and novel imagined scenarios 5 . Without that scaffold, episodic details - no matter how vivid - cannot be bound into a coherent, chronological narrative. On the flip side, when the episodic system is compromised (as in some cases of amnesia), people can still often imagine general future events in semantic terms (e.g. "I will probably eat dinner, because I know I usually do"), but they cannot envision them with the specificity of a real episode. Thus, both past- and future-oriented mental time travel rely on an interplay: episodic memory supplies the experiential building blocks, while semantic memory ensures those blocks fit into a sensible structure. In sum, episodic and semantic memory are deeply interdependent, each providing material and constraints for the other: episodic recollection lets us relive and recombine raw experience, but semantic frameworks knit those experiences into organized knowledge and plausible imaginings. One compelling application of this episodic-semantic synergy is in creative thinking. Creativity - generating ideas that are both novel and useful - turns out to be a memory-intensive process, drawing on our stores of knowledge and experiences and recombining them in new ways. A recent framework called MemiC ("Memory in Creative Ideation") 8 makes the episodic-semantic continuum operational for creativity by carving ideation into four interactive stages - search, construction, novelty evaluation, and effectiveness evaluation - and by specifying how controlled and associative processes recruit semantic and episodic memory at each step. In the search stage, semantic memory is the workhorse for rapid, breadth-first access to concepts - broad retrieval ability strongly predicts the fluency and originality of ideas - but episodic memory adds crucial, high-variance samples that widen the search frontier. Brief "episodic specificity" inductions that train people to unpack concrete event details boost idea fluency on divergent thinking tasks, and when hippocampal-DMN nodes are perturbed with TMS or direct cortical stimulation, fluent idea production drops, indicating a causal contribution of episodic retrieval to candidate generation. Practically, people mix strategies: they query semantic neighborhoods (category/property cues, remote associates) while also "walking around" remembered scenes to harvest candidates (for example, mentally touring a zoo during animal fluency). The upshot is cooperative: semantic search raises recall probability for many relevant items; episodic search injects distinctive, recombinable particulars. Construction turns what search finds into candidate solutions via two partially dissociable mechanisms that nonetheless share substrates. On the semantic side, construction forges new links among weakly related concepts (remote associations, multiply-constrained search), and people higher in creative ability are better at generating such bi-associations. On the episodic side, construction runs mental simulations that recombine multimodal fragments into plausible scenes or object manipulations. Neurocognitively, construction draws on hippocampus-anchored default-mode circuitry while engaging control regions to keep the recombination goal-directed; the same system that supports episodic simulation also ramps during the creation of novel semantic links, underscoring the shared, relational machinery behind both "knowing" and "imagining." Novelty evaluation then compares the constructed candidate against what is already known or experienced. Here, semantic knowledge provides a fast familiarity metric (is this association in the graph?), while episodic memory checks it against lived instances. Imaging work isolates a left supramarginal gyrus signal that tracks novelty judgments over and above usefulness, suggesting a dedicated comparator that feeds back to generation when an idea looks familiar. Functionally, novelty checks prune obvious, overlearned outputs and push search toward remoter regions of both the semantic network and the episodic archive. Effectiveness evaluation is a different beast: instead of "have I seen/thought this before?" the question is "would this actually work?". Semantic memory supplies prototypes, affordances, and constraints that let you quickly reject infeasible constructions; episodic memory supplies the simulator to run mental feasibility tests under context and dynamics. Across tasks, effectiveness judgments elicit stronger engagement of hippocampus, angular gyrus, and posterior cingulate - the same episodic-simulation network - and, tellingly, effective ideas drive more activation than ineffective ones, consistent with simulation-based "stress testing" of the candidate. This stage is where the systems are most complementary: semantics frames the evaluation criteria; episodes supply counterfactual rollouts that expose hidden failure modes or reveal a path to implementation. Looping these stages yields the practical algorithm of creative cognition: controlled cues bias memory search; semantic and episodic construction synthesize candidates; novelty vetoes the cliché; effectiveness vetting, powered by episodic simulation but guided by semantic constraints, selects for useful originality. MemiC’s contribution is to show that this is not a hand-off between two separate stores but a coordination of shared, relational machinery tuned across tasks and timescales - exactly what a continuum view predicts. In closing, the interplay between episodic and semantic memory is best understood not as a meeting of two isolated faculties, but as a dynamic, bidirectional exchange within a shared relational architecture. They trade in different currencies-episodic memory in richly contextualized reconstructions of specific experiences, semantic memory in abstracted, generalized knowledge-but each continually seeds, constrains, and reshapes the other. This mutual scaffolding is evident in learning, retrieval, imagination, and creative ideation: episodes provide the raw, detail-rich building blocks that keep knowledge grounded in lived reality, while semantic structures offer the organizing principles, schemas, and inferential shortcuts that keep recollection and invention coherent. This synergy enables not only accurate remembering and efficient knowledge use, but also the recombinative leaps that underpin planning, problem-solving, and creative thought.

title: Low-Level Motor Representations and Action Output Substrates
text: Figure 1. Brain motor circuits 1 At the bottom of the control hierarchy sit the substrates that actually build and issue motor commands: primary motor cortex (M1), the premotor complex on its anterior bank (PMd/PMv), supplementary and pre-supplementary motor areas (SMA/pre-SMA), and cingulate motor zones (areas in the mid-cingulate sulcus: rostral CMA 2 and caudal CMA 3 ). These fields are agranular, projection-heavy cortex whose layer-5 pyramidal-tract neurons drive brainstem and spinal circuits. In primates, M1 is distinguished by cortico-motoneuronal synapses onto distal pools, and its neurons carry rich, movement-centric codes: classic cosine tuning for reach direction across the full 360°, speed/velocity signals that scale with peak hand velocity, load/force tuning that predicts compensatory torques under perturbation, and muscle-like synergy weights that linearly reconstruct EMG patterns (e.g., selective post-spike facilitation of FDI vs EDC in forelimb). Many M1 units also encode grasp aperture and wrist pronation/supination during object manipulation, and population activity evolves along low-dimensional manifolds whose rotational components forecast time-varying EMG at millisecond resolution across effectors. Anatomically and computationally, M1 is thus the final common cortical controller: a fast, movement-trajectory generator with direct access to the spinal plant. Premotor cortex supplies the conditional "if-this-then-act-like-that" scaffolding that shapes those M1 trajectories, with distinct representational niches across its sectors. PMd carries intention and kinematic plans for reaching, including delay-period codes for the chosen target, hand- or eye-centered spatial coordinates, probability distributions over multiple potential targets before commitment, obstacle-aware path biases, and urgency/commit signals that precede movement. PMv (area F5) encodes hand shaping and object-specific grasp synergies-neurons distinguish precision pinch vs power grip, track 3-D object features relevant for affordances, and exhibit mirror responses that map observed goal-directed acts onto the agent’s own motor repertoire. SMA represents internally generated sequence structure, with neurons selective for ordinal position in a sequence, chunk boundaries, and interval timing; pre-SMA emphasizes rule identity, set-switching, and the rapid engagement of a stop/switch policy that interfaces with the hyperdirect pathway. Cingulate motor areas couple skeletomotor plans to value and state, multiplexing action choice with effort cost, expected vigor, and outcome/error feedback while co-modulating autonomic variables (pupil, heart rate) that energize the forthcoming movement. Causally, long-train stimulation across precentral and premotor cortex elicits whole-limb, ethological action fragments (defensive postures, hand-to-mouth, grasp-and-bring), consistent with these regions caching compositional policies; in behavior, their outputs set the initial conditions for the M1 dynamical "engine" and bias which spinal subcircuits will be recruited. From cortex to muscle, the human motor outflow runs through a handful of well-characterized descending pathways that differ in speed, gain, and the granularity of control. The lateral corticospinal tract (CST)-arising from M1, premotor, and somatosensory cortex-decussates in the pyramids and terminates on spinal interneurons and, in primates, directly on motoneurons innervating intrinsic hand muscles, enabling independent finger forces and fractionated grasp. Parallel corticobulbar fibers target cranial motor nuclei for face, tongue, larynx, and orofacial gestures. Corticoreticular projections descend to the pontomedullary reticular formation and, via reticulospinal tracts, provide fast, large-gain adjustments of posture and multi-joint synergies; in humans, reticulospinal output contributes substantially to proximal arm drive and becomes up-weighted after CST injury, where it supports coarse recovery at the cost of fractionation. Rubrospinal contributions to hand control are modest in humans compared to other mammals but participate in upper-limb kinematics via the dentato-rubro-thalamic loop; vestibulospinal tracts stabilize head/eye/body posture; and tectospinal outputs mediate orienting. Taken together, CST supplies high-bandwidth, fractionated control, while reticulo-/vestibulo-/rubrospinal channels supply posture, gross synergies, start/stop and orienting-an arrangement that lets cortex "write" fine structure on top of robust brainstem controllers. (Riddle et al., 2009; Krimmel et al., 2025; Baker, 2011; Akalu et al., 2023; Rho et al., 2023). Those brainstem controllers are not passive relays: the mesencephalic locomotor region (cuneiform + pedunculopontine nuclei) forms an executable interface for gait, speed, and posture, with cell-type-specific subcircuits that differentially command locomotor modes and feed ascending state back to basal ganglia and cortex. Superior colliculus stacks rapid visual/multisensory salience with premotor commands for gaze-head redirection, and basal-ganglia output nuclei (GPi/SNr) tonically inhibit these brainstem effectors so that disinhibition selects when an orienting or locomotor program is allowed to run. This subcortical "actuator layer" is therefore both a target of cortical commands and a gate controlled by value-informed loops. (Noga, 2022; Ferreira-Pinto et al., 2021; Ryczko & Dubuc, 2024; Basso & Wurtz, 2011; Fee, 2012; McElvain et al., 2021). Below the brainstem, spinal circuits transform descending drive into coordinated muscle activity. Identified premotor interneuron classes (e.g., propriospinal relays at C3-C4 for reaching; dorsal interneuron dI3 populations for grasp) route cortical and reticulospinal commands into motoneuron pools while enforcing task-dependent reflex gains via presynaptic inhibition of Ia afferents. Central pattern generators and long propriospinal chains supply rhythmic and multi-segment coordination that descending tracts can start, stop, and shape on the fly. This organization explains why the same cortical pulse can yield context-appropriate motor output: the spinal cord is an adaptive, state-dependent transformer that composes learned synergies under descending and sensory control. (Takei et al., 2010; Isa et al., 2013; Bui et al., 2013; Pierrot-Deseilligny & Burke, 2012). Critically, low-level motor substrates are not isolated from "control" regions; they are embedded in re-entrant thalamo-cortico-basal ganglia-cerebellar loops that determine when a prepared motor population is allowed to drive effectors, how forcefully, and with what timing. Motor thalamus (VA/VL/VM) is the nexus: it receives powerful excitatory drive from deep cerebellar nuclei and layer-5 motor cortex, modulatory inhibition from GPi/SNr, and projects back to premotor/M1 where it can amplify, time-lock, or redirect population trajectories. Recent anatomy in mice and humans shows overlapping cerebellar and cortical terminals in motor thalamus with BG outputs interdigitated through the same territories-exactly the geometry for rapid thresholding and timing control-while human neurophysiology demonstrates short-latency facilitation of M1 from dentate stimulation (consistent with cerebellar "forward-model" timing). Hyperdirect PFC/pre-SMA input to STN can raise BG output and transiently clamp thalamo-cortical throughput ("global brake"), whereas direct- and indirect-pathway balance tunes movement vigor; in parallel, cerebellar dentato-thalamo-cortical signals set subsecond timing and predictive corrections. In practical terms, PFC decides "what/when," BG sets the gate and gain, cerebellum sets timing/trajectory corrections, and premotor/M1 instantiate the selected plan on the spinal interface. (Koster et al., 2024; Alonso-Martínez et al., 2023; Conner et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Dautan et al., 2021; Basso & Wurtz, 2011). Putting it together, the motor stack is a layered control fabric. Premotor/SMA/cingulate encode conditional action fragments and internal sequence policy; M1 compresses these into movement-centric population dynamics that directly drive spinal controllers; descending tracts select among brainstem executors with different gains; spinal microcircuits compose synergies and reflex gains to meet the current state; and thalamo-basal-ganglia-cerebellar loops modulate access, vigor, and timing based on goals, conflict, and prediction error. For robotics, the translation is literal: keep a movement-centric "plant" that runs low-dimensional dynamics to emit torques; front it with a library of action fragments conditioned on context; route outputs through multiple executors with distinct bandwidth/gain (fine vs. gross control); and interpose a centralized gate (BG-like) plus a predictive timing corrector (cerebellum-like) that together decide when the plant is allowed to run and how forcefully it should express the chosen plan.

title: Control Primitives
text: We define control primitives as the reusable algorithmic operations that coordinate behavior under uncertainty, goals, and context. These include basic subroutines for selectively loading information into working memory, maintaining or clearing it, monitoring and adjusting competing demands, and routing information through neural circuits. For example, fronto-striatal "gating" circuits implement working-memory update and maintenance: cortical inputs are allowed into active prefrontal representations only when striatal "Go" signals disinhibit corresponding regions of the thalamus. Computational models show that nested prefrontal-basal ganglia loops can implement distinct input and output gates, as well as a "reset" to clear outdated contents 1 . Recent neural-network models confirm that dorsolateral PFC populations can re-use the same neurons to store multiple items by strategic gating, trading off slot-like capacity for precision under dopamine-modulated learning 2 . In these models, striatal D1/D2 circuitry (go/no-go pathways) controls fronto-thalamic gating, while phasic dopamine (reward-prediction errors) adaptively tunes which items are gated or maintained. This cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop effectively acts as a control primitive for selective updating of working memory, and will be covered in greater depth in Section X. Other primitives govern switching and stopping of actions or rules. Task-set switching engages frontoparietal and basal ganglia loops to reconfigure task rules and contexts, analogous to motor set switches. By contrast, action stopping taps a well-characterized hyperdirect pathway: when an unexpected stop signal appears, right inferior frontal cortex (rIFC, sometimes called rIFG) and pre-SMA rapidly drive the subthalamic nucleus (STN), which in turn excites globus pallidus output to globally inhibit thalamocortical circuits. This PFC-STN "brake" can halt ongoing motor plans. Human ECoG and stimulation studies show that potentials in rIFC precede STN activation during stopping, and individuals with stronger rIFC-STN coupling stop faster 3 . In rodents, optogenetic excitation of STN (or of the dmPFC->STN pathway) causally delays or interrupts responses, confirming its key role. Notably, stopping is associated with transient frontal beta-band bursts (in rIFC/preSMA and STN), suggesting that brief oscillatory events implement the top-down "stop" command. Thus, the stop primitive is instantiated by a PFC-basal ganglia loop that can globally suspend output. Conflict monitoring and uncertainty are also treated as control primitives: medial frontal cortex, especially dorsal ACC, signals when processing conflicts or errors rise, triggering adjustments in control. Theoretical models propose that ACC computes the "expected value of control" by integrating anticipated rewards, required effort, and uncertainty, then biasing when and how much to engage executive mechanisms 4 . Empirically, ACC activity correlates with conflict levels, error likelihood and volatility, and predicts the need to upregulate lateral PFC control. Thus, a conflict-monitoring primitive may reside in ACC, detecting when parallel responses or surprising outcomes demand increased top-down control. Another primitive is decision-threshold modulation: adjusting response speed-accuracy tradeoffs. Here the basal ganglia again play a role. For example, activity in the STN can raise decision thresholds during conflict (through diffusely inhibiting motor output) 5 , 6 , whereas striatal Go/No-Go balance can shift the threshold of gating 7 . Dopamine likewise influences threshold: high tonic dopamine can bias faster decisions (lower effective threshold), whereas dips can induce caution 8 . These mechanisms allow flexible control of when to commit versus continue deliberating. A related primitive is meta-control, the arbitration between decision systems (e.g. model-based vs. model-free, or goal-directed vs. habitual) based on uncertainty or task demands. Here cortical-striatal loops again are key. Ventromedial circuits (OFC, ventral striatum) tend to encode predicted reward outcomes (model-based planning) 9 , whereas dorsolateral striatal loops execute learned habits 10 , 11 , 12 . Some evidence (e.g. from neural decoding in primates) suggests higher PFC areas monitor reliability of each system and gate which one drives action 13 , 14 , 15 . In effect, meta-control might be implemented by gating which striatal loop is currently dominant, influenced by dopamine (and perhaps serotonin) context signals 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , though the precise "arbitrator" circuitry is still under study 20 . Finally, a fundamental primitive is information routing and shielding. Prefrontal networks must selectively broadcast current goals or rules to task-relevant modules while protecting them from interference. Recent work highlights the role of the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus 21 , 22 : MD nuclei form recurrent loops with PFC and can transiently amplify or redirect PFC representations. In rodents, disrupting MD input to PFC impairs flexible working memory and set-shifting 23 , 24 . Theoretical and empirical studies suggest MD acts like a dynamic switchboard, enabling a given PFC population to drive its targets when needed. In short, thalamocortical loops provide primitives for gating communication between cortical areas and for holding information "in the blackboard" against distractors 25 .
