title: Control Gradients and Regional Specializations
text: Control primitives are organized along multiple brain gradients. The principal cortical gradient of connectivity runs from unimodal sensory-motor areas to transmodal association cortex (especially default-mode areas) 1 . Unimodal regions handle immediate sensory-driven control (fast stimulus-response gating), whereas at the transmodal apex (e.g. frontopolar, DMN) lie abstract, context-rich representations. In practice, this means that simple reactive control operations predominate in peripheral cortex, whereas high-level rule integration and counterfactual reasoning occur in frontopolar/dorsomedial PFC. Gradients of neural timescale parallel this axis: primary sensory and motor areas have very short intrinsic timescales (rapid dynamics), while PFC and other association areas integrate information over seconds or longer 2 . These gradations shape control: a top-down signal from frontopolar cortex can modulate a very slow-changing goal context, whereas a sensory cortex only can sustain fast-varying cues. In other words, cortex has a built-in hierarchy of time constants, so that control primitives operating at different levels naturally inherit different temporal resolutions. Within frontal cortex, multiple orthogonal gradients shape what is represented and controlled. Along the rostro-caudal axis, evidence supports a hierarchy of abstraction: caudal premotor and posterior lateral PFC carry concrete sensorimotor plans and stimulus-response mappings (e.g., effector- and spatially specific codes used to implement a learned rule), mid-dlPFC encodes conditional/task rules and context-dependent mappings (e.g., "if color then compare, if motion then ignore"), and the most anterior territories (rostrolateral/frontopolar cortex) integrate across time and tasks, representing pending subgoals, alternative strategies, and higher-order relations among rules 3 , 4 , 5 . For example, frontopolar/RLPFC tracks the value of unchosen options and supports exploratory strategy switches-representations that sit "above" the immediate rule set and bias "policy" over "policies"-whereas mid-dlPFC activity scales with the need to bind currently relevant cues to a chosen rule and suppress competitors 6 . This posterior->anterior progression is supported by converging fMRI, lesion, and perturbation data, meta-analytic gradients, and formal accounts of hierarchical control. Overlaid on this is a dorsal-ventral (and partially medial-lateral) specialization that clarifies the content of control. Dorsal LPFC is biased toward spatial/executive control and maintenance of spatial relations (e.g., oculomotor working memory, spatial selection), whereas ventrolateral PFC-especially left IFG/VLPFC-implements controlled retrieval and selection among competing semantic or feature representations (e.g., choosing the task-relevant meaning of an ambiguous word or feature dimension when competition is high) 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 . Medially, dACC/mpFC carries signals related to conflict, effort, and the expected value of deploying control, providing a motivational "meter" that tunes how strongly lateral PFC implements a chosen rule. On the ventral/medial side, vmPFC/OFC represents integrated subjective value 11 and OFC carries a cognitive map of latent task states-representations of "where you are" in an abstract state-space that guide flexible choice when the state isn’t directly observable. Together these gradients mean that a given task can recruit, in parallel, caudal sensorimotor codes to implement an S-R mapping, mid-lateral codes to maintain the current rule and suppress distractors, frontopolar codes to manage pending subgoals or explore alternatives, VLPFC codes to select among competing semantic/features, dACC signals to up- or down-regulate control intensity 12 , and vmPFC/OFC state/value codes to bias choices under uncertainty. These representational gradients align with macroscale connectivity. Along the brain’s principal connectivity gradient, anterior/medial PFC sits near the transmodal apex with the default‐mode network (DMN) 13 , 1 , while sensorimotor cortex anchors the opposite end; this arrangement predicts that anterior PFC will couple with memory/scene-construction machinery to support long-horizon goals, latent task states, and contextual priors. That’s what you see: during episodic retrieval and multi-step reasoning, anterior/rostrolateral PFC increases its functional coupling with hippocampus and DMN nodes, and overall network modularity drops as memory and control systems interlock-precisely the pattern you’d expect if PFC is binding a world-model to a control policy 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 . At the other end of the hierarchy, caudal lateral PFC coactivates with dorsal attention (a "spotlight operator" network) and sensorimotor networks and is wired for concrete stimulus-response specifications and moment-to-moment selection 18 . Bridging these poles, frontoparietal "flexible hubs" dynamically retune their connectivity-tightening links to DMN when internal models must be consulted, or to attention/sensorimotor systems when external constraints dominate-so the control system can route information through the right partners at the right time 18 . Large meta-analytic gradient work in LPFC, together with flexible-hub studies, nails this picture: rostral bins lean DMN-ward, caudal bins lean DAN/sensorimotor-ward, and hub regions pivot between them as task demands shift 19 . Subcortically, similar axes organize control. The striatum exhibits a ventral-to-dorsal gradient: limbic and ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) process reward prediction and goal valuation, whereas the posterior dorsolateral putamen (with contributions from caudate tail for over-learned visual habits) subserves learned stimulus-response habits 20 , 21 . Dopaminergic midbrain projections follow this scheme: the VTA predominantly innervates ventral/associative striatum while the SNc feeds dorsal striatum. Neocortical dopamine also shows gradients, with prefrontal cortex receiving dense modulatory input that tunes gating thresholds and plasticity 22 , 23 . MD-PFC connectivity is topographic: anteromedial (’rostral’) MD links to frontal pole/medial PFC, lateral/parvocellular MD to dorsolateral PFC, and a caudodorsolateral MD sector to ACC/medial frontal cortex 24 , 25 ; MD thus supports higher-order prefrontal state maintenance and routing. In parallel, VA/VL motor thalamus projects to premotor/motor cortex, and first-order sensory nuclei project to sensory cortices. The cerebellum shows a homologous gradient: anterior lobules couple with sensorimotor cortex, whereas Crus I/II and lobule VII couple with prefrontal association networks and support executive timing/prediction 26 .

title: Cortico-Basal Ganglia-Thalamo-Cortical Loops
text: The CBGTC architecture is phylogenetically ancient : the full complement of basal ganglia nuclei, their intrinsic direct/indirect pathway organization, dopaminergic innervation from the midbrain, and segregated parallel loop topology are identifiable in lampreys–among the most basal extant vertebrates–indicating conservation over > > 500 million years 1 , 2 . The parallel, segregated loop organization itself (skeletomotor, oculomotor, dorsolateral prefrontal, lateral orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate/limbic channels) is an architectural prior that partitions the action-optimization problem into semi-independent subspaces: rather than searching over a monolithic joint distribution p ( a 1 , a 2 , … , a n ) p(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) for the full action vector, the system can approximately factorize the optimization across loops, each handling a lower-dimensional action subspace 3 . This factorization is a biologically instantiated form of dimensionality reduction on the optimization itself–converting an intractably large channel-capacity problem into a collection of coupled but smaller subproblems. Cortico-Basal Ganglia-Thalamo-Cortical Loops Anatomy The CBGTC system is organized into parallel, functionally segregated loops. Each loop originates from a particular cortical area, projects to a specific region of the striatum (caudate/putamen), then through basal ganglia nuclei to the thalamus, and finally back to the same cortical area. Classic models identify multiple loops - often grouped into motor, associative (cognitive), and limbic circuits (with finer distinctions such as oculomotor or prefrontal sub-loops). For example, a motor loop runs from motor and premotor cortex to the putamen, then via GPi/SNr to the ventrolateral thalamus and back to motor areas, maintaining a consistent somatotopic organization throughout. Similarly, there are loops centered on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (associative/cognitive), orbitofrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex (limbic), each engaging distinct striatal and pallidal territories and thalamic targets. These loops are largely parallel and segregated, processing different functional domains with minimal convergence 4 . However, some cross-communication exists - studies show that limbic regions of the striatum can influence motor circuits via dopamine projections forming an ascending "spiral" from ventral to dorsal striatum. In essence, the basal ganglia loops are modular yet hierarchically arranged, allowing motivation and context (limbic loop) to ultimately bias cognitive decisions (associative loop) and action execution (motor loop). The striatum-the input nucleus of the basal ganglia-receives dense excitatory input from cortex and modulatory dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta (with VTA especially to ventral striatum). Striatal projection neurons segregate into a direct (D1) pathway and an indirect (D2) pathway. In the direct pathway, GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs) inhibit the output nuclei (GPi/SNr); because GPi/SNr neurons are tonically active, this disinhibits thalamus and facilitates thalamocortical drive for the selected action. In the indirect pathway, D2 MSNs inhibit GPe; the resulting reduction of GPe output both disinhibits the STN (allowing its glutamatergic excitation of GPi/SNr) and removes GPe’s direct inhibition of GPi/SNr, increasing thalamic inhibition and suppressing competing actions. A third, hyperdirect pathway projects from cortex to STN, providing a rapid, relatively broad increase in GPi/SNr activity that acts as a fast brake/threshold-raising signal; this transient suppression can then be selectively lifted by the direct pathway as the chosen action wins the competition, while the indirect pathway helps contain alternatives. Each CBGTC loop maintains a high degree of topographic specificity - neuronal channels for distinct functions remain largely separate through the striatum, pallidum, and thalamus. This supports parallel processing (e.g. motor vs. cognitive information) without interference. At the same time, the loops are reentrant: after processing in basal ganglia and thalamus, the information returns to the originating cortical area, where it can influence the next cortical activity. The basal ganglia also send outputs to brainstem centers (e.g. pedunculopontine nucleus for locomotor regulation, superior colliculus for eye movements) in addition to the thalamocortical route, implying a role in both cortical and subcortical motor control. In healthy function, these loops work in concert to smoothly select and execute behaviors; in disease states (like Parkinson’s or Huntington’s), imbalances in pathway activity (due to dopamine loss or neuron degeneration) lead to characteristic movement disorders by altering the normal loop dynamics. A few diseases are worth mentioning. In Parkinson’s disease, degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta disrupts the balance between the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia, leading to excessive inhibition of thalamocortical circuits and resulting in bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor. In Huntington’s disease, early degeneration of D2-expressing indirect-pathway MSNs in dorsolateral striatum removes the surround brake on competing programs, reducing GPi/SNr output and yielding choreiform, unwanted fragments of movement; with progression, direct-pathway and cortical loss produce akinetic phases. In hemiballismus, focal lesions of the subthalamic nucleus collapse the hyperdirect "global stop," cutting excitatory drive to GPi/SNr and producing violent, proximal flinging movements contralateral to the lesion-an object lesson in threshold control. In primary dystonia, abnormal pallidal output and loss of surround inhibition in sensorimotor territories cause co-contraction and overflow; GPi deep-brain stimulation often restores a more normal balance of gain and selectivity. In Tourette syndrome and OCD, dysregulation of associative/limbic loops is central: excessive gain in sensorimotor striatum plus weak prefrontal control yields tics, while over-weighted OFC-ventral striatal valuation and habit circuits drive compulsions; both improve when fronto-striatal gating is strengthened or pallidal output is modulated. Addiction exploits the ventral-to-dorsal "spiral": drug-induced phasic/tonic dopamine surges stamp in cue->action associations in nucleus accumbens and, with repetition, control shifts to dorsolateral striatum as rigid habits. More broadly, disorders like schizophrenia (elevated associative-striatal dopamine that mis-teaches credit assignment and destabilizes working-memory gating) and ADHD (low tonic catecholamine, low signal-to-noise, premature responding, excessive exploration) can be read as loop gain mis-setting. Across these conditions, the symptom profiles line up with principled perturbations of the same controller-too much global inhibition (Parkinson’s), too little surround (Huntington’s/dystonia), loss of the hyperdirect brake (hemiballismus), or maladaptive habit/valuation signals (OCD/addiction)-which is precisely what the CBGTC computations predict. Computations Action Selection and Motor Control The canonical view still helps: basal ganglia (BG) circuits implement a center-surround scheme for action selection in which activity in a task-relevant direct-pathway channel transiently disinhibits its thalamocortical target ("center"), while indirect-pathway engagement increases inhibitory tone on competing channels ("surround"). The hyperdirect cortico-STN route adds a fast, global brake by exciting BG output (GPi/SNr) with minimal synaptic delay, forestalling premature actions until more evidence accrues. This architecture explains why unwanted movements are suppressed and why rapid stopping is possible 5 , 6 . Modern data, however, show that BG computations are not a binary winner-take-all gate but a continuous, history-dependent control system layered on top of selection. Direct and indirect pathways often co-activate around movement onset, jointly shaping timing and structure rather than acting as pure Go/No-Go opponents 7 . Moreover, pathway activity can bidirectionally scale movement kinematics (speed/"vigor"), consistent with the idea that BG output provides a learned gain on ongoing motor programs rather than merely permitting them 8 . A converging synthesis is that BG circuits select and suppress actions while also tuning their vigor via a "history-dependent gain" computation informed by recent outcomes and dopamine 9 , 10 . In parallel, the hyperdirect pathway is especially handy under conflict or surprise: STN activity transiently raises the decision threshold-the proverbial "hold your horses"-buying milliseconds for cortex/striatum to evaluate alternatives; disrupting this mechanism with STN-DBS reduces that cautious slowing 11 . On net, CBGTC loops embed decision and control inside the motor system: they bias which action proceeds, when it proceeds, and how forcefully it is expressed. Reinforcement Learning and Temporal Credit Assignment CBGTC loops provide a biologically plausible substrate for reinforcement learning. At a computational level, the system is well described by an actor-critic decomposition in which dorsal striatal loops shape policy and ventral striatum/midbrain dopamine provide a teaching signal. Many midbrain dopamine neurons emit bidirectional, trial-by-trial reward-prediction-error (RPE) signals, 12 and selectively driving or suppressing these transients is sufficient to imprint learning, establishing dopamine as a causal teaching signal rather than a mere correlate 13 . At striatal synapses, learning obeys a three-factor rule: cortical activity plus postsynaptic spiking write a short-lived "eligibility trace," and a subsequent DA burst or dip converts that trace into LTP/LTD within a seconds-wide window 14 , 15 . This implements temporal-difference-like credit assignment and is supported by in vivo and spine-level experiments that precisely delimit the timing window for DA-gated plasticity 14 . Although the canonical D1=Go/D2=No-Go heuristic remains useful, modern data show that direct and indirect pathways are often coactive during movement and jointly regulate movement vigor and suppression; plasticity rules are opponent on average (D1 favors potentiation with high DA; D2 favors depression) but are gated by local state, endocannabinoids, adenosine, and interneuron/thalamostriatal control 16 . Together, these mechanisms let BG circuits reinforce recently active channels when outcomes are better than expected and suppress them when worse, gradually shaping policy and consolidating skills and habits. Habit Formation and Procedural Learning Repeated reinforcement and practice can lead to behaviors becoming habits, which are actions executed automatically with little deliberation. The cortico-basal ganglia loops are critical for this transition from goal-directed action to habitual response. Early in learning, the associative/limbic loops (including the ventral striatum and dorsomedial striatum) are heavily involved - actions are goal-directed and sensitive to outcomes. But with extensive repetition, control shifts toward the sensorimotor loop centered on the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) 17 ; the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) has been linked to goal-directed actions (flexible, outcome-sensitive), whereas the DLS is linked to habitual actions (inflexible, stimulus-driven). Lesion experiments show that destroying the DLS leaves goal-driven behavior intact, while lesioning the DMS makes animals resort to habits more quickly. During habit learning tasks, neurons in the DLS start to exhibit characteristic "task-bracketing" activity, firing at the beginning and end of action sequences - essentially marking the routine’s boundaries. This pattern grows stronger with over-training, indicating the DLS is encoding the learned chunk of behavior. Concurrently, neural activity in the DMS (which was high during initial learning) subsides as the behavior becomes automatized. Thus, the locus of control shifts from cortical and associative BG circuits to more embedded sensorimotor circuits as habits form. Computationally, this can be seen as the BG "compiling" frequently used action sequences into efficient subroutines. This has the benefit of efficiency and speed - habitual responses deploy quickly without engaging higher cognitive circuits - but at the cost of rigidity, since habits are hard to override. Dysfunctions in this system are thought to underlie disorders of compulsivity (e.g. OCD or addiction), where maladaptive habits persist due to abnormal striatal plasticity. In summary, CBGTC loops not only learn which actions to choose, but with repetition they also automatize action selection, handing control to deep motor circuits that can execute behaviors with minimal conscious input. Decision Uncertainty, Exploration vs. Exploitation, and Cognitive Control Another important computational aspect of the basal ganglia loops is how they help regulate decisions under uncertainty - essentially balancing exploration vs. exploitation. The subthalamic nucleus (STN), via the hyperdirect pathway, plays a key role in this domain. When a decision is difficult or conflictual (multiple options have similar expected values), the STN is thought to emit a "hold your horses" signal that raises the decision threshold. In practice, cortical detection of conflict (e.g. in anterior cingulate or prefrontal areas) leads to increased STN activity, which globally increases inhibition via GPi, buying more time for the system to accumulate evidence before committing to a choice 11 . In reinforcement learning terms, the basal ganglia can thus adaptively tune between exploitation (deciding based on the current learned policy) and exploration (stalling or trying alternative actions when uncertainty is high). Besides the STN’s role in gating decision speed, the tonic level of dopamine in the striatum may also influence exploration-exploitation balance. Higher tonic dopamine tends to lower the perceived cost of effort and delay, which can make the agent more likely to exploit known rewarding actions (and less sensitive to negative feedback), whereas a dopamine dip might promote exploration of new strategies (this is evidenced in conditions like ADHD, where low baseline dopamine is thought to produce excessive exploration and impulsivity in the form of difficulty maintaining focus on delayed rewards). Furthermore, basal ganglia loops contribute to cognitive control by acting as a gate for working memory and task switching. The same Go/No-Go mechanism that selects motor actions is believed to operate in frontal loops to select which information is maintained in working memory or which rule to apply. Dopamine bursts to the frontal-striatal loop can signal a gating of working memory (allowing new information in), whereas No-Go pathway activity can lock the gate to protect ongoing maintenance. In summary, the CBGTC circuits provide a context-dependent regulation of decision thresholds and cognitive gating: they prevent rash decisions by increasing inhibition when needed, and conversely can facilitate quick choices or updates when a clear best option is present. Why is this architecture necessary/effective? Can’t cortical regions receive dopaminergic reinforcement, select actions, and implement gain control? Cortex can learn from dopamine, bias competition, and scale gains, but it is not wired to solve the whole control problem which loops are solving. The basal ganglia (BG) exist because animals need a single, fast, value-informed arbiter that 1) can halt everything in a few synapses, 2) can precisely stamp credit on the last-active action channel on a sub-second clock, and 3) sits at the one place where a decision actually opens or closes the gates to thalamus and brainstem effectors. That combination-centralized bottleneck + rapid global brake + dopamine-timed three-factor plasticity + direct access to effectors-is unique to the cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamo-cortical motif. Cortex on its own doesn’t have that geometry or those kinetics. First, the wiring: the BG concentrate massive cortical/thalamic convergence onto a tiny output set in GPi/SNr-a literal computational bottleneck compared with the striatum’s population size. Because GPi/SNr neurons fire tonically and project straight to motor thalamus and key brainstem controllers (e.g., superior colliculus for eye movements, pedunculopontine/MLR for locomotion), they can release or suppress whole motor subsystems by disinhibition in a single place. This is why saccades don’t trigger until SNr pauses and why subthalamic lesions unleash ballistic movements: the "valve" is subcortical and centralized. A distributed cortical competition lacks that single choke-point into the thalamo-brainstem machinery. Now the timing: credit assignment in the striatum is specialized for reinforcement learning in ways that cortex generally isn’t. At corticostriatal synapses, conjunctive presynaptic->postsynaptic activity sets a short-lived eligibility trace that must be converted by a phasic dopamine transient within a seconds-wide window ( 0.3-2 s); if DA misses that window, the trace decays-essentially a hardware implementation of TD learning with eligibility traces 14 . In parallel, centromedian/parafascicular thalamostriatal input drives the characteristic burst-pause in cholinergic interneurons, which gates when cortical spikes are ’heard’ by spiny neurons and synchronizes with phasic DA, aligning plasticity to salient events 18 , 19 . By contrast, an equally tight, seconds-locked DA teaching signal hasn’t been established for neocortex: prefrontal DA axons have low DAT, so clearance relies largely on NET and COMT, producing slower, more spatially diffuse signals that are well suited to modulating persistent activity and tuning signal-to-noise rather than stamping second-scale credit at specific synapses. Cortex can show DA-gated plasticity, but the timings are broader and less precisely yoked to RPE transients than in striatum. Anatomically, the actor-critic split is instantiated by complementary striatal compartments and their downstream targets: striosomes ("patch"), heavily aligned with limbic and prefrontal inputs, project to midbrain dopamine cells through distinctive striosome-dendron bouquets and can directly sculpt the teaching signal, whereas the surrounding matrix, dominated by sensorimotor inputs, projects through the canonical direct/indirect routes to GPi/SNr to shape the policy over body-part-specific channels 20 , 21 . Recent circuit work sharpens this division: striosomes house dual, D1- and D2-expressing pathways that parallel the classic basal-ganglia architecture yet target SNc/VTA dopamine neurons rather than BG output, giving patch a bidirectional lever on dopamine transients; activating striosomal circuitry suppresses striatal dopamine and locomotion in vivo, demonstrating causal control of the critic signal. In contrast, matrix-mediated cortico-BG-thalamic loops carry the bulk of corticostriatal drive for moment-to-moment action selection and long-run policy tuning. Critic-to-actor transfer is wired in by Haber’s striatonigrostriatal "ascending spiral," a feed-forward chain in which ventral (limbic) striatum biases progressively more dorsal (sensorimotor) territories via midbrain dopamine projections-an anatomical route for value and motivation to migrate into habits and skills with training. The upshot is that cortex can implement actor-critic-like computations, but the BG supply a literal projectional separation between "critic-shaping DA" and "actor-shaping output," with a dedicated ventral->dorsal conduit that couples motivational state to the consolidation of automatized policies. Finally, this architecture is older than cortex. Lamprey and other basal vertebrates, which have no neocortex, still have BG that select and sequence behaviors by disinhibition of brainstem pattern generators. Evolution kept the same subcortical arbitration layer and then let cortex grow around it; we plugged model-based, high-dimensional planning into a conserved gate that turns plans into actions safely and economically. That is a strong argument that this division of labor solves a fundamental control problem, not just a historical accident. So could cortex "just do it"? Cortical dopamine certainly modulates working memory, exploration/exploitation, and effort allocation, and cortical circuits run winner-take-all competitions. But cortex lacks (i) a single output bottleneck into thalamus and brainstem, (ii) an ultra-fast global brake that raises the decision threshold across all actions, (iii) precise sub-second, DA-gated eligibility at the main action synapses, and (iv) an intrinsic actor-critic geometry with a limbic-to-sensorimotor transfer line. Those are precisely the ingredients you need for safe, fast, value-informed arbitration over many effectors. That is why the CBGTC architecture is not redundant-it’s the only place where all four constraints are met in one circuit. For AGI/robotics design, the translation is direct. Keep a centralized action gate with a real bottleneck and direct access to actuators; give it a fast global "stop/threshold-up" line separate from the slower evidence channels; make its plasticity explicitly three-factor with tight temporal windows; and keep a distinct critic signal that can be steered by "limbic" valuation toward the "sensorimotor" policy as habits compile. You can distribute planning across cortical-like modules, but the last mile-the arbitration that decides what actually runs-should look like the basal ganglia. That’s the part you really don’t want to scatter.

title: Cerebello-Thalamo-Cortical Loops
text: forward-model prediction, subsecond timing, and error-driven adjustment of control policies Mapping Connectomic Structure to Function(s) in Cerebellar-like Networks using Kernel Regression The cerebellar microcircuit is conserved across all vertebrate classes with remarkably little structural variation–unlike the dramatic expansion and laminar reorganization seen in neocortex across mammalian lineages–suggesting that it represents a deeply optimized evolutionary solution to a domain-general computational problem: learning high-dimensional mappings with limited training data 2 . That the same microcircuit can serve as a forward model (predicting sensory consequences of commands, as discussed under (2)), an inverse model (recovering commands from desired transitions), and–in cerebellar contributions to cognition–an abstract “prediction machine” for non-motor domains 3 , is consistent with its role as a generic function-approximation module that can be recruited for whichever component of the empowerment computation a given cortico-cerebellar loop demands. Cortico-Cerebellar Loops Anatomy The cortico-cerebellar system is organized into reciprocal loops linking widespread cerebral cortical areas with the cerebellum. In the cortico-pontine-cerebellar pathway, axons from the cerebral cortex (especially motor, premotor, prefrontal, and parietal areas) descend and synapse in the pontine nuclei of the brainstem. Pontine neurons send massive projections (20+ million fibers in humans) across the midline into the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle. This provides the cerebellar cortex with a "copy" of cortical motor commands and cognitive signals. In turn, the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway carries the cerebellum’s output back to the forebrain: Purkinje neurons of the cerebellar cortex inhibit neurons of the deep cerebellar nuclei, whose axons exit via the superior cerebellar peduncle and decussate to reach the contralateral thalamus (primarily ventrolateral and ventroanterior nuclei). Thalamic relays then project to the original cortical areas, completing a closed loop 4 . These pathways are predominantly contralateral (each cerebral hemisphere connects to the opposite cerebellar hemisphere), consistent with functional studies showing that activity in left cortical regions correlates with right cerebellar regions and vice versa. These cortico-cerebellar loops are topographically organized. Classic tracer studies in monkeys demonstrated that each neocortical region projects to a specific, localized region of the cerebellar cortex, and that same cerebellar region projects back (via deep nuclei and thalamus) to the same cortical area. This one-to-one mapping created the notion of parallel, functionally segregated "closed loops" between cerebellum and cortex. Human resting-state fMRI connectivity has reinforced this view by revealing distinct cerebellar networks aligned with known cortical networks - for example, cerebellar Crus I/II functionally connect with prefrontal-parietal (executive) networks, whereas anterior cerebellar lobules connect with sensorimotor cortices. The human cerebellum contains multiple mapped representations of the entire cerebral cortex: at least two (and possibly three) complete homotopic maps exist, with the anterior lobe and lobule VIII representing sensorimotor areas and lateral posterior lobules (Crus I/II, lobule IX) representing association networks. In other words, the cerebellum is not exclusively a motor structure but is anatomically interconnected with virtually all cortical regions, arranged in repeating topographic loops. Recent high-resolution tracing and imaging studies have refined this anatomical picture. Divergence and convergence are now recognized as key features of cortico-cerebellar wiring, rather than strictly one-to-one loops. For example, viral tracing from a small region of mouse frontal cortex (ALM, anterior lateral motor area) showed that this single cortical locus sends divergent inputs to multiple distributed sites across the cerebellar cortex via the pons. Likewise, a given cerebellar output nucleus (fastigial nucleus in that study) collected inputs from wide swaths of cerebellar cortex and projected back to the original cortical area, closing the loop only in a diffuse way 5 . The cerebello-thalamo-cortical projection was not perfectly aligned topographically with the input projection, indicating that cortico-cerebellar loops are largely open-loop and divergent, with only partial overlap between input and output zones. In primates and humans, evidence for convergence has emerged from functional MRI: models that allowed each cerebellar region to receive convergent input from multiple cortical areas best predicted cerebellar activity patterns 6 . Notably, the highest degree of convergence was found in cerebellar regions associated with higher cognitive functions (language, working memory, social cognition), whereas primary sensorimotor cerebellar regions showed more segregated (one-to-one) connectivity. This suggests that cognitive cerebellar circuits integrate information from multiple cortical sources, whereas motor cerebellar circuits may be more modular. Overall, the anatomical connectivity of cortico-cerebellar loops is organized into recurrent, contralateral circuits linking specific cortical areas to specific cerebellar modules, but with a many-to-many mapping that enables broad integration across the loop. Computations The cerebellum has long been theorized to function as an internal model system for the brain’s motor and cognitive commands. Two principal types of internal models are discussed in cerebellar theory: forward models and inverse models. A forward model takes a copy of the current motor command (an efference copy) and predicts the expected outcome - for example, the future position of a limb or the sensory feedback that should result 7 . The cerebellum is thought to continuously compute such forward predictions of movement outcomes based on ongoing motor commands and the context, effectively simulating the body’s dynamics. These predictions can be used as a rapid substitute for actual sensory feedback, which is delayed, thus allowing for smoother real-time control. The cerebellum’s forward model output can be compared to incoming sensory feedback to compute a prediction error - any mismatch between expected and actual sensation. This error signal (often carried by climbing fibers from the inferior olive) is then used to update the cerebellar model via synaptic plasticity, refining future predictions. Empirical support for the forward model hypothesis comes from behavioral and neurophysiological studies: for instance, humans with cerebellar damage exhibit movement discoordination and lagging error correction consistent with a loss of predictive feedforward control 7 . In contrast, an inverse model works in the opposite direction, computing the motor command needed to achieve a desired outcome. Some theories (notably by Kawato and colleagues) have proposed that the cerebellum, together with cerebral circuits, may implement paired forward and inverse models for motor learning. However, current evidence more strongly implicates the cerebellum in forward model computations; any inverse modeling might emerge through the cerebellum’s integration into larger control loops (e.g. a forward model used within a cortical feedback loop can function as an inverse controller) 7 . In summary, the cerebellum is widely viewed as a predictive simulator, using internal models to anticipate the consequences of commands and thus enable fast, coordinated action. Beyond motor control, contemporary theories emphasize the cerebellum’s role in predictive coding and error-driven learning across many domains. In the predictive coding framework, the brain constantly generates predictions at multiple levels and compares them with actual inputs, adjusting on the basis of prediction errors. The cerebellum fits neatly into this scheme as a specialized processor of predictions and errors. Classic models by Marr (1969) and Albus (1971) cast the cerebellum as a supervised learning machine: mossy fiber inputs provide the contextual signals, Purkinje cells produce the output, and climbing fiber inputs act as a teaching signal that conveys errors when predictions fail to match reality 8 . According to the Marr-Albus theory, each Purkinje cell learns to associate specific patterns of parallel fiber input (which reflect particular combinations of cortical signals and sensory context) with the appropriate output, and climbing fiber activity during errors adjusts the strength of those parallel fiber synapses (e.g. via long-term depression) to improve performance. Recent findings reveal that cerebellar error signals are more complex than a simple "wrong vs right" binary feedback, and instead carry nuanced predictive information. For example, recordings of inferior olive activity (climbing fiber signals) in learning tasks have shown properties consistent with temporal-difference (TD) reinforcement learning models 9 , allowing our view of the cerebellum to expand beyond supervised learning. Altogether, modern computational perspectives describe the cerebellum as a "neuronal prediction machine" that not only fine-tunes movements through supervised learning, but also generates predictions about reward, timing, and other non-motor events and updates these predictions through experience. This expanded view accounts for cerebellar involvement in cognitive functions: the cerebellum may apply similar internal modeling and error-correction principles to support predictive processing in domains like language, working memory, or social interaction. It continuously tests forward models of both motor and mental sequences against reality and helps adjust behavior and thought for smooth, coordinated performance. Functions Motor coordination and control The cerebellum’s most classic role is in the fine-tuning and coordination of voluntary movements, as well as the maintenance of balance and posture. While it does not initiate movement, it ensures that actions are smooth, precise, and accurately timed. This capability arises from its unique architecture: a massive feedforward network with an enormous expansion of inputs via granule cells, and a sparse, high-fidelity error signal conveyed by climbing fibers from the inferior olive. These climbing fibers encode discrepancies between intended and actual movement outcomes-sensory prediction errors-and trigger plastic changes at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapse to adapt future motor output. The cerebellum integrates proprioceptive and vestibular inputs to stabilize posture and continuously adjusts muscle activity in response to perturbations (a function starkly revealed in patients with cerebellar lesions, who exhibit broad-based, unstable gait and postural instability). It coordinates multi-joint movements by sequencing and scaling the activity of muscle groups (e.g., aligning shoulder and elbow during a reach), such that motor commands are properly timed and shaped. When the cerebellum is impaired, movement becomes erratic and decomposed (ataxia), with hallmark symptoms like dysmetria (overshoot/undershoot), intention tremor (worsening as a target is approached), and poor performance on rapid alternating tasks-all pointing to deficits in timing, prediction, and dynamic calibration. The cerebellum also modulates eye movements, including the vestibulo-ocular reflex and saccades, for stable and accurate visual tracking. In short, the cerebellum is uniquely positioned-both structurally and computationally-to monitor, refine, and calibrate ongoing behavior via tightly looped circuits with the motor cortex and brainstem, enabling real-time error correction and the acquisition of expert motor skills. Cognition and language Over the past few decades, it has become clear that cortico-cerebellar loops extend into prefrontal and other association cortices, giving the cerebellum roles in cognition, emotion, and language in addition to motor control. Functional neuroimaging has revealed cerebellar activation during a wide variety of cognitive tasks that have minimal motor demands. For example, different parts of the cerebellum are engaged during tasks involving working memory, attention shifting, planning and executive control, language processing, music perception, and even social cognition. Specifically, the lateral cerebellar hemispheres (Crus I and II) show activity during verbal working memory tasks and language processing (syntax, word generation), while medial posterior cerebellum (vermal regions of lobule VII-IX) have been implicated in emotional processing and the "default mode" network (internally directed thought) 10 . The cerebellum’s cognitive contributions are subtle but observable: for instance, cerebellar involvement in language might manifest in fluent articulation and grammar processing, and cerebellar activation in prefrontal loops is seen during planning or abstract reasoning tasks. Clinical observations support these findings: patients with cerebellar damage can exhibit a "cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome", characterized by impairments in executive function (poor planning, set-shifting), spatial cognition, linguistic difficulties (agrammatism or dysprosody), blunted affect or dysregulated emotion, and even autism-like features in some cases. These deficits, which go beyond pure motor symptoms, illustrate that the cerebellum contributes to the automation and fluidity of mental processes analogously to how it refines movements. Essentially, the cerebellum is thought to provide an internal modeling and predictive function for non-motor domains: it helps predict the next element in a thought or sentence, checks for errors, and aids in correcting the course of cognitive operations in real-time, much as it does for physical movements. Learning and memory The cerebellum is a critical substrate for certain types of motor learning and adaptation. A classic example is eyeblink conditioning, a form of associative learning in which an initially neutral tone (conditioned stimulus) is paired with an eyeblink-eliciting air puff (unconditioned stimulus). The cerebellum (specifically the interposed nucleus and overlying cortex) is necessary for acquiring and timing the conditioned eyeblink response. Through repeated trials, the cerebellar circuit learns to produce a well-timed blink in response to the tone before the air puff arrives - effectively learning the predictive relationship. If the cerebellum (or its input from the inferior olive) is lesioned, animals cannot learn this anticipatory response. This is a prime example of supervised learning: climbing fibers from the inferior olive signal the error (the unexpected air puff or timing mismatch), and the cerebellar synapses adjust to gradually eliminate that error by producing an appropriately timed blink. Beyond classical conditioning, the cerebellum is integral to adaptive motor calibration. When you put on prism glasses that displace your visual field, it is the cerebellum that drives the gradual adaptation of your hand-eye coordination to counter the shift; individuals with cerebellar lesions struggle to adjust and exhibit persistent endpoint errors. Similarly, the gain of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) - which stabilizes gaze during head movements - is fine-tuned by the cerebellum (flocculus): if visual feedback indicates that eye movements are too small or too large, cerebellar circuits adjust the VOR gain over time to improve accuracy. While declarative memory (facts, events) is a cerebral cortex and hippocampus specialty, the cerebellum excels at procedural memory - the subconscious fine-tuning of motor and cognitive routines through repetition and feedback. Specialized cerebellar architecture How does a cerebellar circuit achieve these remarkable feats of prediction, timing, and coordination? A key lies in its microcircuit architecture, which is highly uniform across the cerebellar cortex. This circuit is designed to take diverse inputs, expand them into a high-dimensional representation, and compute precise, well-timed outputs. The major input pathway, the mossy fibers from pontine and other sources, carries a wide array of information: copies of motor commands, sensory context from the periphery and spinal cord, proprioceptive feedback, and even signals from association cortex (e.g. about a task rule or linguistic context). These mossy fibers terminate in the granular layer of the cerebellar cortex, where they synapse onto granule cells - the most numerous neurons in the brain (the human cerebellum houses 5̃0 billion granule cells, more than half of all neurons). Each granule cell receives only 4-5 mossy fiber inputs, a very sparse input sample, but there is an enormous divergence: a single mossy fiber will spread and synapse onto hundreds of granule cells. Granule cells then send their outputs up into the molecular layer as parallel fibers - long T-shaped axons that fan out and form synapses onto the dendrites of Purkinje cells. On the order of 100,000 parallel fiber connections converge onto a single Purkinje neuron. In this way, the cerebellum creates a massive combinatorial expansion of the input space: any given pattern of mossy fiber activity is transformed into a much larger vector of granule cell/parallel fiber activity. This high-dimensional encoding is thought to facilitate pattern separation - making similar input patterns more distinguishable - and to provide a rich basis for learning. Indeed, experimental studies have shown that granule cells can exhibit extremely sparse, selective firing, and that inputs from different sources (e.g. somatosensory vs. motor cortex vs. visual) can converge onto individual granule cells, effectively combining multiple modalities or cortical signals at the single-cell level. By activating unique subsets of granule cells for each context or command, the cerebellum ensures that the downstream Purkinje cells can discriminate fine differences and associate the appropriate outputs to each scenario. In essence, the cerebellum functions as a predictive feed-forward controller: mossy fiber inputs tell it the current state and intended action, the cerebellar cortex computes an anticipated outcome or required adjustment, and the deep nuclei send the adjustment to the upper motor centers or cortex at just the right time. This architecture is why the cerebellum is especially important for tasks requiring fine timing and coordination. For example, during a rapid motor sequence (like playing a piano scale), the cerebellum ensures each finger strike is correctly timed relative to the others and with the appropriate force. It also helps coordinate timing across different brain regions - acting like a metronome that can synchronize cortical processes. Experiments have shown that neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibit ramping or predictive activity during waiting intervals, such as the delay period of a planned movement 7 . These cells gradually change their firing rate leading up to an expected go-signal, effectively counting down time. If the cerebellar output is inhibited, the corresponding cortical area (like the frontal motor cortex) loses its ramping activity and the animal’s timing of movement initiation becomes erratic. This demonstrates that the cerebellum is broadcasting timing signals that shape cortical dynamics during motor planning. Similarly, cerebellar output has been shown to encode the timing of periodic stimuli: certain cerebellar neurons fire in an oscillatory pattern that predicts when the next stimulus should occur, and if the stimulus timing is altered, these neurons specifically signal the unexpected timing error. Disrupting the cerebellum’s communication with cortex (via thalamus) impairs tasks like rhythmic tapping or interval timing. Thus, temporal coordination is a fundamental mechanistic contribution of cortico-cerebellar loops. Another mechanistic insight is how the cerebellum can integrate information from diverse cortical areas and coordinate their activity. Because of the convergence in mossy fiber inputs, a single cerebellar region might receive signals related to, say, an upcoming movement from motor cortex, the current visual scene from visual cortex, and a goal or context from prefrontal cortex. The cerebellum can combine these into a prediction like "given the goal and visual feedback, the current motor command will result in error unless adjusted." It can then output a corrective command that appropriately coordinates the motor response with the sensory context. In cognitive terms, if the cerebellum connects to both prefrontal and parietal regions, it might help align working memory (prefrontal) with attentional or sensory information (parietal) at the right moment. The loops are bidirectional: while the cortex sends an efference copy to the cerebellum, the cerebellar output in turn influences cortical processing. Studies have shown that cerebellar output can enhance or gate cortical neuron firing in a task-specific manner. For instance, during motor planning, the cerebellum’s input to frontal cortex via thalamus was necessary for sustaining preparatory neural activity (the "ramping" that encodes a pending action). In a broader sense, the cerebellum ensures that different parts of the brain work in synchrony - it "tunes" cortical circuits by providing timing cues and predictive feedback. This integration is dynamic: as one learns a task, cortico-cerebellar interactions become more coordinated. In fact, recordings of activity have shown that as animals learn a goal-directed task, the correlation between cortical activity and cerebellar granule cell layer activity increases, implying the two are developing a tighter functional coupling. In summary, the mechanistic hallmarks of cortico-cerebellar processing are: (a) massive parallel processing and feature expansion in the granule cell layer enabling integration and pattern separation of inputs; (b) utilization of precise timing mechanisms (parallel fiber delays, pacemaker activity of inferior olive, and intrinsic dynamics) to generate temporally specific outputs; (c) a powerful error-learning rule via climbing fiber instructive signals driving synaptic plasticity to fine-tune connections until the output matches the desired performance; and (d) a modular architecture of repeating microcircuits (microzones) each handling a particular set of inputs and outputs, which collectively allow the cerebellum to contribute to a wide array of behaviors using the same computational principles. This design enables the cerebellum to serve as the brain’s predictive coordinator, ensuring that whether it’s muscles or thoughts, the commands issued by the cortex are properly calibrated, timed, and adjusted for optimal execution.

title: PFC-Hippocampal Control Over Episodic (Re)construction
text: Prefrontal default-mode network interactions with posterior hippocampus during exploration Flexible prefrontal control over hippocampal episodic memory for goal-directed generalization Fronto-Hippocampal Synchronization in Rapid Spatial Learning in Humans The hippocampal formation supplies a fast, recombinable code for episodes and relations-a substrate for scene construction, counterfactuals, and prospective imagination-while the prefrontal cortex (PFC) provides goal-directed control over when and how those internal models are consulted. A robust macro-level regularity is that hippocampus couples with the default-mode network (DMN) during retrieval and simulation and decouples during externally focused encoding 4 , 5 , consistent with a control policy that engages internal models when they help and suppresses them when sensory-driven control is required. What is exchanged between hippocampus and PFC during "imagination" is not raw sensory replay but brief, structured trajectories over a learned state-relation graph. Hippocampal sharp-wave ripples and theta-nested sequences compress experience into forward and reverse rollouts; these events recruit distributed control networks and can bias upcoming choices 6 . In humans, magnetoencephalography (MEG) reveals sub-second replay of candidate paths that ramps up before decisions when planning is beneficial; across rest and task, replay bursts co-activate hippocampus with DMN hubs 7 , suggesting a system-level channel for internal evaluation 8 . When-and how strongly-PFC queries the hippocampal "world model" appears to follow an expected-value-of-computation (EVOC) principle. Normative accounts predict that agents prioritize the memories whose evaluation most improves reward rate; hippocampal replay in rodents and humans follows this prioritization, emphasizing reward-salient or task-relevant paths, and human replay strength scales with planning demand 9 , 10 . This yields a concrete control objective for PFC: regulate access to hippocampal simulation based on opportunity cost and expected utility 11 . Circuit anatomy makes this gating feasible. Ventral CA1/subiculum conveys contextual state directly to medial PFC (mPFC) and amygdala, supporting valuation and control over behaviorally significant contexts 12 . In the top-down direction, the thalamic nucleus reuniens (RE) is a key relay from PFC to hippocampus and entorhinal cortex; perturbing RE alters PFC-hippocampal synchrony and memory performance, and, during memory-guided decisions, RE can drive transient beta-band coupling that appears to "bind" PFC and hippocampus into a single control loop 13 , 14 . Functionally, PFC->RE->HPC acts as a broadcast channel for turning simulation on/off and for routing which memories are sampled. Beyond glutamatergic relays, there is a direct long-range GABAergic projection from PFC to hippocampus 15 . Activating these PFC->HPC inhibitory axons increases feedforward inhibition and improves hippocampal signal-to-noise for location coding, providing a rapid, cell-type-specific lever for top-down suppression or sharpening of hippocampal activity during externally anchored tasks-essentially, a concrete circuit for "retrieval stopping" and noise gating 15 . Timing gives PFC additional control surfaces. During NREM sleep and quiet wake, sequential slow-oscillation->spindle->ripple cascades orchestrate hippocampal-cortical dialogue; spindles provide the temporal window in which ripples convey reactivated content to cortex, and replay-locked events can propagate cortex-wide 16 . New intracranial work in humans shows that brief prefrontal "cortical ripples" can impose top-down modulation of hippocampal reactivation, suggesting a fast timing-based veto when reactivation would be maladaptive 17 , 18 . A practical design lesson is to decompose fast hippocampal rollouts from slower prefrontal timing controllers that gate when-and for how long-simulation runs. PFC also suppresses hippocampal output when attention must remain sensorimotor-locked or when intrusive traces 19 threaten performance. Think/No-Think studies show that lateral PFC down-regulates hippocampus to stop retrieval, with concomitant amygdala down-regulation for aversive content 20 ; related rodent work indicates that RE-mediated synchrony helps suppress extinguished fear 21 . Together with the long-range GABAergic pathway, these findings specify multiple levers-oscillatory timing, thalamic gating, and direct inhibition-by which PFC enforces task-appropriate access to internal simulations. Functionally, PFC and hippocampus bring complementary inductive biases. The hippocampus is optimized for rapidly encoding and recombining specific episodes (it "knows" where you are in a rich state-space and can imagine novel arrangements on the fly). PFC, by contrast, is geared toward abstract, goal-oriented control and working memory. A recent theory formalizes PFC working memory as controllable, structured activity "slots" that interface naturally with hippocampal cognitive maps-an algorithmic duality between activity-based WM and synaptic episodic memory 22 . In practice, PFC can retrieve an episode, hold and transform it within slot-like subspaces, bind it to current goals/values, and then decide whether more rollouts are worth the compute 23 . This synergy lets an animal generalize from a single experience: PFC can "plug in" an episodic memory into its current goal context, recombine it with other memories, and thus plan new behavior without extensive new learning. Empirical studies highlight this benefit. For example, hippocampal replay-PFC coordination supports both recalling useful past routes and exploring new shortcuts in a maze 24 , and models predict that this interplay can explain flexible transfer to novel tasks (compositional generalization) 25 . Overall, we can treat the PFC-hippocampal system as a controller-simulator pair. Represent the world as a hierarchical predictive graph (SR-like) in the simulator; let the controller learn an EVOC policy that gates rollouts via (i) a thalamic-like broadcast (RE) that sets when simulation is allowed, (ii) timing windows that schedule rollouts into oscillatory "slots," and (iii) a direct inhibitory path that suppresses or sharpens retrieval when external demands dominate.

title: Dorsal and Ventral Attention Networks
text: The brain’s attentional machinery splits into two tightly coupled, largely supramodal systems 1 . A dorsal fronto-parietal network (DAN) implements sustained, goal-directed selection and sampling; a ventral fronto-temporo-parietal network (VAN) acts as a right-lateralized interrupt/reorienting system that detects behaviorally relevant changes and rapidly resets the dorsal controller. This division is supported by converging lesion, neurophysiology, and imaging results: damage to right ventral frontoparietal cortex (including TPJ/IFG) yields classic spatial neglect 2 and broader deficits in reorienting and vigilance 3 , while dorsal lesions impair voluntary orienting and priority mapping. Functionally, DAN supplies the "spotlight operator" that amplifies task-relevant channels, and VAN detects behaviorally relevant violations of expectation and rapidly resets DAN’s priorities to reorient sampling 1 . DAN is anchored in intraparietal sulcus/superior parietal lobule (IPS/SPL) and in frontal eye field / superior precentral sulcus (FEF/sPCS). The intraparietal sulcus (IPS) is anatomically a crossroads and functionally a Swiss army knife-exactly what you want for building and maintaining a supramodal priority map. Its subdivisions tile distinct effector and sensory interfaces: LIP encodes gaze-centered spatial priority for saccades 4 ; MIP/PRR (PRR = "parietal reach region") codes reach targets 5 , 6 ; VIP integrates vision with tactile and vestibular signals to represent peripersonal space 7 ; and AIP specifies object shape, orientation, and grip postures for hand use and tools 8 . This mosaic lets IPS fuse "where" with "how" across effectors and modalities and project that synthesis to downstream controllers. The same territory also carries abstract magnitudes-hIPS responds to amodal numerosity and quantity 9 -illustrating how IPS sits high enough in the hierarchy to host amodal control variables yet remains topographically organized for spatial selection. This blend of multisensory convergence, effector specificity, and topographic coding is what makes IPS the natural substrate for a manipulable, task-coupled priority map 10 , 11 . Frontal eye field (FEF; in humans centered around the superior precentral sulcus, sPCS) is wired to read out the parietal map into sampling policies and to write precise, retinotopically aligned gain commands back into sensory cortex. Subthreshold microstimulation at a given FEF locus boosts V4 responses at the corresponding visual-field location and reproduces classic signatures of voluntary attention 12 , 13 ; concurrent TMS-fMRI in humans shows the same causal direction of influence from FEF/sPCS to early visual cortices with perceptual consequences 14 . Anatomically, FEF has privileged two-way lines to the superior colliculus and receives a corollary-discharge loop via mediodorsal thalamus, giving it online access to where the eyes are going next and enabling predictive updates ("remapping") of attention pointers so perception stays stable across saccades 15 . Functionally, this means FEF can schedule the next fixation, pre-amplify the corresponding sensory channels, and confirm execution through subcortical loops-tight, millisecond-scale control that a pure parietal node lacks on its own. Long-range white-matter scaffolding explains why these nodes act as a single controller even when they compute different pieces of the problem. The dorsal branches of the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF I/II) link IPS to dorsal frontal cortex (including FEF/sPCS), supporting fast bidirectional exchange between map maintenance and readout modules; where these tracts are compromised, voluntary orienting suffers and neglect risk rises, matching the clinical asymmetries seen after right-hemisphere lesions 16 . Retinotopic mapping confirms the architectural logic: IPS and sPCS contain attention-driven visual-field maps whose coupling to V1 varies with the locus of attention 17 , 18 , consistent with a controller that dynamically "opens" communication channels to the currently prioritized sector of sensory cortex. Putting it together: IPS maintains the continuously computed, multisensory priority landscape and translates it into effector-specific coordinates (eyes, hands, body), while FEF turns the current peak into a timed sampling policy and precision-gated sensory gain-backed by subcortical loops for rapid execution and corollary discharge for predictive stability. This division of labor is why DAN can both "think ahead" (goal-biased maps in IPS) and "act now" (FEF-driven gain and saccade scheduling) with latencies compatible with real-world behavior like reading a road sign at speed, catching a tossed object, or switching from a wrench to pliers mid-repair. VAN’s core lies in right temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and ventral/lateral prefrontal cortex (often IFG/MFG). TPJ is a heteromodal convergence zone bordering posterior STS and inferior parietal lobule, perched near the transmodal apex of cortex along the principal gradient from sensory to abstract processing 19 , 20 . That location and its broad connectivity to control and default-mode systems make TPJ ideal for computing model-level surprise: integrating context, expectations, and multisensory evidence to decide when ongoing sampling should be interrupted. White-matter anatomy explains the rapid TPJ-to-PFC handshake: the ventral branch of the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF III) links inferior parietal (TPJ) to ventral frontal cortex (IFG) 21 , and exhibits strong rightward lateralization that tracks individual differences in spatial attention bias and neglect risk. IFG/MFG translate detection into enforcement. Right IFG has a hyperdirect projection to subthalamic nucleus (STN), giving VAN a monosynaptic brake on basal-ganglia output that can halt ongoing motor and cognitive programs while priorities are recomputed 22 , 23 . MFG sits at the handshake with the dorsal attention network (DAN): it routes the interrupt so DAN can retarget the priority map, and-during sustained focus-helps DAN suppress VAN’s chatter. Thalamic partners (especially pulvinar) provide timing that opens and closes communication windows between sensory and control cortices, and LC-norepinephrine bursts supply the state switch that makes the reset global. Net effect: while you’re locked on a phone number, a siren or your name from behind spikes TPJ, IFG slams the brake via STN, MFG hands the new locus to DAN, and pulvinar/LC orchestrate the system-wide flip-typically within a couple hundred milliseconds. DAN’s top-down control is largely carried on slow alpha-beta rhythms that bias cortical excitability and open phase-aligned "communication windows" for fast, feedforward gamma activity; when a salient event engages VAN, it triggers a rapid phase reset of these slow rhythms so the windows reopen at the new locus 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 . The pulvinar functions as the timing switchboard for this exchange: during selection it synchronizes and phase-aligns nodes such as FEF, LIP, and V4/TEO-predominantly in theta/alpha-low-beta bands-to route information among the right cortical partners at the right moments 28 , 29 . In humans and macaques, feedback-like influences preferentially ride alpha-beta while feedforward signals ride gamma, providing a frequency-multiplexed channel structure that the pulvinar can gate 30 . By modulating interareal coherence (rather than only mean firing rates), this thalamic brokerage enables swift, low-latency handoffs between goal-directed (DAN) and stimulus-driven (VAN) modes and couples top-down setpoints to bottom-up sensory flow in a behaviorally advantageous way 31 . Beneath the cortical controller sits a fast, phylogenetically old subcortical layer that both seeds and shapes what DAN and VAN will deal with in the first place. The superior colliculus (SC) is a stacked sensorimotor map: superficial layers receive direct retinal and early cortical input; intermediate/deep layers integrate visual, auditory, and somatosensory cues with motor commands for gaze, head, and body turns. In primates, SC neurons signal salient onsets within  50 ms and even show short-latency category preferences (e.g., faces) 32 , giving the system an ultra-rapid, coarse priority sketch that can bias covert selection before cortex has finished its recurrent work. Causally, inactivating SC degrades covert attention and the selection of task-informative signals without requiring eye movements 33 , while dorsal fronto-parietal outputs pre-tune SC: FEF/sPCS can sharpen or damp SC visual bursts on a tens-of-milliseconds timescale, aligning subcortical orienting with current goals 34 . Through the inferior/mediodorsal pulvinar, SC routes these "first pass" salience estimates to extrastriate cortex and to the amygdala, forming a quick subcortical conduit that can flag biologically urgent events even when V1 pathways are compromised 35 . Zooming in on the amygdala clarifies why an "ancient" structure is still indispensable to human attention control. The basolateral complex (BLA) sits at a convergence of fast, coarse subcortical input and rich, high-level cortical descriptions: in primates it receives a rapid magnocellular-biased stream routed via superior colliculus -> pulvinar (a pathway that is present anatomically and functionally in humans) 36 , 37 while also ingesting detailed ventral-stream signals from inferotemporal/perirhinal cortex 38 . Within  74 ms of a threat-like image, human intracranial recordings show the amygdala firing before visual cortex, consistent with that subcortical route and low-spatial-frequency sensitivity 39 . From this hub, the BLA sends feedback to visual cortex-including V1 and TE-via synapse-forming, layer-targeted projections that up-weight behaviorally important features 40 ; lesion/inactivation work in humans and macaques shows that without the amygdala, the usual "emotional boost" of extrastriate responses disappears and perceptual sensitivity to biologically relevant cues is blunted 41 . Computationally, single-unit studies reveal neurons that multiplex value with space 42 , 43 , tracking which location is currently worth sampling and biasing gaze toward reward-predictive or ethologically salient stimuli; when the amygdala is silenced, value/context-driven facilitation of saccades is diminished, an effect that can be mediated by amygdalo-nigral access to basal ganglia output channels controlling eye movements 44 . The amygdala also has privileged levers on global state: it can recruit basal forebrain cholinergic 45 and locus-coeruleus noradrenergic systems, producing arousal-biased competition that selectively amplifies high-priority representations (and, via NE "hotspots," potently suppresses distractors 46 ), thus handing VAN a system-wide reset while boosting DAN’s gain at the newly prioritized locus. Finally, its coupling to posterior STS/TPJ and ventral/lateral prefrontal territories links social/affective relevance to reorienting control, with task-dependent amygdala-rTPJ connectivity changes in humans underscoring this ventral network handshake 47 . In short, the amygdala’s unique combination of speed, associative plasticity, bidirectional sensory links, and direct access to arousal and oculomotor gates makes it the brain’s affect-weighted "priority injector" into DAN/VAN rather than a redundant relic.
