title: Frontoparietal Control (Multiple-Demand) Network
text: The frontoparietal control (FPN; also called "multiple-demand" (MD) or "central executive" (CEN)) network is best understood as a domain-general operating system for cognition: a set of reusable, parameterizable control routines instantiated in lateral PFC and posterior parietal cortex, positioned mid-way along the principal cortical connectivity gradient-between unimodal sensorimotor systems and the transmodal apex occupied by the default-mode network-so they can flexibly couple outward to DAN or inward to DMN as goals dictate 1 , 2 . Across tasks, these regions are the first to ramp with load and the ones whose whole-brain coupling patterns change the most, supporting rapid instructed task learning and novel rule composition. Recent syntheses argue that cognitive flexibility arises from shifts in "network activity flows" driven by these hubs, rather than from isolated, task-specific modules-a framing that unifies decades of "MD" findings under a single control-flow mechanism 3 , 4 . Anatomically, the network’s cortical core spans mid-to-rostral middle frontal gyrus (BA 9/46), inferior frontal gyrus, and dorsomedial premotor/pre-SMA, coupled to intraparietal and inferior parietal sectors. Importantly, it is not content-free: multivariate decoding in 2024 shows robust task and stimulus codes within MD core, with mixed selectivity that scales with difficulty-exactly the representational profile needed to bind abstract rules to concrete inputs and actions 5 . Within the frontoparietal complex, there is reliable internal heterogeneity: one subnetwork preferentially aligns with the default-mode system and another with the dorsal attention system, reflecting the FPN’s ability to flexibly interface with networks handling both internal simulation and attention to concrete external stimuli 6 . The parietal arm of the system computes compact, short-horizon affordance maps-the space of immediately available actions over millisecond-second horizons-while prefrontal sectors condition these maps on longer-horizon goals. Work from the "affordance-competition" framework shows parallel representation and selection among potential actions across parietal and premotor fields, with prefrontal and basal ganglia biases resolving the competition as task demands evolve 7 , 8 ; for instance, LIP/IPS may encode saccade-biased spatial priority while AIP codes grasp postures for object shape while prefrontal and basal ganglia biases resolve the competition. This account fits the MD system’s role in moment-to-moment control and clarifies why parietal nodes are so tightly coupled to scene structure and the "now," while prefrontal nodes carry the rule and policy context. The wiring that makes this possible is specific. SLF II links angular gyrus/IPS to mid-lateral PFC (MFG/dlPFC), SLF III links inferior parietal regions to IFG, and long tracts like the arcuate and IFOF bridge temporal/occipital content stores to prefrontal control 9 . These routes concretize how rules in PFC reach parietal affordance maps and, when needed, how stored lexical/semantic or visual knowledge is pulled into the control loop. Diffusion and dissection work in 2022-2025 sharpens these trajectories, and intraoperative stimulation confirms causal contributions of SLF II/III segments to task performance 10 , 11 . Subcortically, mediodorsal (MD) thalamus is a peer partner. Closed MD<->PFC loops regulate recurrent PFC dynamics, stabilize task set under uncertainty, and coordinate inter-areal coupling for flexible cognition. A 2024 review and 2025 modeling work converge on a picture where MD adjusts prefrontal gain and uncertainty-dependent gating, complementing basal ganglia loops that gate what is updated 12 , 13 . This division of labor makes thalamus indispensable for the sustained, context-sensitive stability that complex tasks require. At the network level, the MD/FPN’s operation is best captured along two coupled axes-spectral composition and intrinsic timescale. As control demands rise, fronto-parietal hubs reliably ramp low-frequency phase coordination, especially midfrontal theta that synchronizes distributed nodes and tracks the need for control across paradigms; large-sample EEG/MEG and reviews in 2024-2025 consolidate this picture, while also noting that scalp theta topographies don’t map one-to-one onto the MD atlas, cautioning against naïve localization 14 , 4 , 15 . Separating periodic from aperiodic signals shows that broadband (aperiodic) power/slope/intercept shifts are the most general neural signature of load, generalizing across tasks and sometimes locking to events 16 , 17 . Because these aperiodic shifts index aggregate spiking and E-I balance, they provide a task-general, modality-bridging readout of how hard the frontoparietal system is working and when control/learning signals are updating policies. In parallel, intrinsic neural timescales (INT) lengthen in prefrontal cortex as engagement and training increase 18 , and recent causal evidence indicates that parietal inputs can selectively dilate prefrontal/FEF timescales 19 , providing a concrete mechanism by which task context and long-range biasing tune the integration windows used by control circuitry; population-level fMRI/MEG analyses and modeling converge on plastic, state-dependent timescale gradients spanning cortex 20 . Taken together, these results explain both the ubiquity and the burden of MD engagement: the system expands temporal integration to stabilize rules and policy over seconds while coordinating distal regions via slow phase-coupling and broadband upshifts-a powerful, general-purpose control regime that is effective across tasks precisely because it is spectrally and temporally generic. The cingulo-opercular network (CON)-which recently saw a compelling reframing as the Action-Mode Network (AMN) 21 -sets the brain’s global operating context for goal-directed behavior: dACC and anterior insula/fronto-operculum initiate and sustain a high-arousal, externally oriented "action mode" that readies sensorimotor circuits, with the network extending into SMA, aPFC, and supramarginal sectors more broadly than the original CON label implied. In mixed block/event designs, these hubs show the classic start-cue transient followed by block-sustained set activity, consistent with a role in establishing and maintaining the task context across many seconds, while the frontoparietal control network flexibly reconfigures within that context at the trial scale 22 , 23 . Converging invasive electrophysiology and modeling indicate that anterior insula exerts directed influence over frontoparietal and default-mode systems at control transitions-functioning as a switching hub that helps allocate resources between externally and internally focused modes 24 , 25 . The AMN’s tonic control is tightly coupled to arousal apparatus: pre-stimulus CON/AMN activity predicts faster responses and sustained alertness, and dACC/insula interact with noradrenergic (LC-NE) and thalamic (including intralaminar) nodes that stabilize the action mode and set overall gain 26 , 27 . Functionally, cingulo-opercular subnetworks can motivate or "energize" frontoparietal implementations under ambiguity or effort, with late CO signals carrying performance-monitoring and adjustment information that feeds back to FPN to update control policies 28 , 29 . Pharmacology reinforces the mechanism: α2A-adrenergic stimulation enhances error-based updating in ACC/dlPFC circuits, linking neuromodulatory state to the quality of the action mode 30 . In short, the AMN runs upstream in time and upstream in state: it establishes and sustains the arousal-aligned task set and arbitrates large-scale network switching, while the frontoparietal hubs perform rapid, within-mode recombination of rules and adjustments-resolving "who does what" in control and explaining why dACC/insula show onset transients plus block-sustained activity even as FPN keeps reshaping within trials. Interactions among control and non-control networks are goal-contingent, not hard-wired. During externally focused, high-demand tasks the frontoparietal/MD system rises while the default-mode network (DMN) is actively suppressed, a canonical pattern linked to better control performance; when the problem benefits from internal simulation-autobiographical planning, hypothesis generation, creative search-frontoparietal and DMN co-activate and couple, and time-resolved analyses show that the capacity to dynamically switch between these systems predicts divergent-thinking ability at scale (with evidence for an inverted-U dependence on switching), rather than a simple monotonic anti-correlation 31 , 32 , 33 . Within frontoparietal cortex this flexibility is scaffolded by heterogeneity: one subnetwork aligns more with the DMN (supporting introspective, memory-guided control) and another aligns with the dorsal attention network (DAN) (supporting world-facing selection), a division replicated and sharpened in recent perturbation and neuromodulation work 6 , 34 . When problems are perceptually anchored, DAN-FPN coupling implements precise sensory gating and orienting; when they are model-anchored, DMN-FPN coupling integrates stored knowledge and simulation into the control loop-consistent with emerging naturalistic and creative-task data and with reports that DMN subnetworks differentially couple to control and language systems 35 , 36 , 37 . Energetically, this network is expensive and must be stabilized. Simultaneous PET-fMRI shows that task-positive control responses coincide with heightened glucose metabolism, and whole-brain analyses tie increases in control energy (time-averaged control costs) to oxygen metabolism 38 . Large-sample work in 2024 indicates that metabolic costs concentrate in hub regions and rise with task-driven reconfiguration-exactly where frontoparietal and salience hubs sit-offering a physiological reason the system is both potent and fragile under fatigue or pathology 39 , 40 . Development and individual variation make the same point from another angle. Mapping individual-specific MD nodes shows pronounced selectivity increases with executive function during development 41 , and adolescence is marked by concurrent maturation of aperiodic/E-I signatures and working-memory capacity 42 . These changes are what you would expect if the control "OS" is coming online: longer timescales, more selective codes, and more efficient hub reconfiguration. The network architecture of general intelligence in the human connectome Why does the MD/FPN so tightly index general intelligence? The core of P-FIT still holds-individual differences in reasoning and "g" emerge from a distributed parieto-frontal system-but the last few years sharpen the picture from where to how. Large-sample and multi-task work shows that people with higher ability more readily occupy a task-optimal MD state shared across diverse paradigms, and the occurrence and stability of this state predict control performance; in other words, smarter brains get to (and stay in) the right control regime with less fuss 44 . Converging dynamic-connectivity studies report that higher g is associated with more typical, efficient, and stable macroscale dynamics, and with less unnecessary reconfiguration between rest and multiple task states-consistent with an architecture already closer to task demands 45 , 46 . At the same time, when problems require internal modeling, high performers exhibit selective FPN-DMN cooperation and flexible switching, a pattern now tied to complex cognition and creative search at scale; what differentiates ability is not chronic anti-correlation but the capacity to engage the right coupling at the right time 32 . Causally, lesions and perturbations keep the arrow pointed at the multiple-demand network rather than perisylvian language cortex 47 : focal damage within MD hubs degrades fluid intelligence 48 , graph-lesion mapping localizes the deficit to fronto-parietal nodes/edges 49 , and neuromodulatory or stimulation manipulations over parietal/dlPFC move reasoning and goal coding 50 . White-matter scaffolding matters, too: bridging tracts-especially SLF II/III and long fronto-temporal/parietal pathways-support executive functions, working memory, and flexible control, providing the substrate on which flexible-hub dynamics ride 51 . Finally, updates from systems neuroscience elevate the associative thalamus (notably mediodorsal) from relay to regulator: MD thalamus helps stabilize set, resolve uncertainty, and shape prefrontal dynamics, offering a mechanism for set stability under volatility that generalizes across tasks and species 12 , 13 . A modern "P-FIT-plus" therefore has three load-bearing parts. (i) Structure: integrity of fronto-parietal nodes and their connecting tracts (e.g., SLF), which provide bandwidth for relational integration. (ii) Dynamics: a flexible-hub operating mode that minimizes gratuitous reconfiguration yet selectively retunes coupling and spectral/timescale properties to meet the problem-including context-dependent FPN-DMN teaming. (iii) Subcortical orchestration: thalamocortical loops (MD<->PFC and partners) that coordinate set control and uncertainty, allowing the system to enter and hold the task-optimal state. Together these features explain why the MD/FPN is the best single neural predictor of complex cognition today: it is the brain’s general-purpose control fabric, and general intelligence reflects how well that fabric is wired, tuned, and coordinated.

title: Salience Network
text: The salience network (SN) is a large-scale paralimbic-limbic system whose cortical anchors are the anterior insula/fronto-operculum and the dorsal/anterior mid-cingulate cortex, with a robust and often right-lateralized emphasis, especially in the anterior insula 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . Subcortical affiliates are reliable and behaviorally interpretable: amygdala and ventral striatum (valuation and action vigor), mediodorsal thalamus and related thalamic relays, and arousal nuclei in the brainstem (notably the locus coeruleus and neighboring neuromodulatory complexes) that couple interoceptive state to whole-brain gain control 1 , 5 , 6 , 7 . Functionally, the SN performs rapid context appraisal and relevance signaling and, via the right anterior insula in particular, initiates network-level switches that up-regulate frontoparietal control while suppressing default-mode activity when salient events demand action 8 , 9 . This circuitry is closely allied with-but separable from-the cingulo-opercular (CON) "set-maintenance" network: across datasets, CON tracks tonic alertness and stable task set over extended epochs, whereas SN is optimized for detecting change and triggering mode shifts, together forming a complementary controller axis centered on insula-cingulate hubs 10 , 11 , 12 . The salience network’s distinctive contribution is to govern state transitions between internally focused cognition and externally oriented control. In the "triple-network" framework, SN activity-centered on anterior insula and anterior/mid-cingulate-detects behaviorally relevant change and biases large-scale dynamics away from default-mode processing and toward frontoparietal and dorsal-attention engagement. Convergent evidence supports this switching role: fMRI effective-connectivity shows the right anterior insula exerting causal influence that suppresses DMN while recruiting executive circuitry; replications with dynamic causal modeling recover the same SN->DMN and SN->CEN directions; and intracranial electrophysiology reveals that task-evoked high-frequency activity peaks earlier in attention/control networks than in the DMN, with the SN’s response timing intermediate and consistent with an initiating role 8 , 13 , 14 , 15 . Mechanistically, anterior insula and cingulate signals ramp at salience detection and error, propagate to dorsolateral/frontoparietal nodes, and are accompanied by deactivation in core DMN hubs; perturbation and stimulation studies add causal weight by showing that modulating anterior insula alters conflict handling and attention reallocations 16 , 15 , 17 . In the absence of salient external demands, SN drive relaxes and the DMN reasserts its baseline dominance for self-referential/internal mentation, consistent with longstanding observations of DMN activity at rest and its anticorrelation with task-positive systems 18 , 19 . Taken together, the SN orchestrates a context-appropriate balance-dampening introspective modes when action is required and releasing them when the environment permits-so that the agent pivots efficiently between internal simulation and outward, goal-directed control. Salience computation begins with what these cortical hubs are built to represent. The posterior dorsal insula is the brain’s primary interoceptive sensory cortex: it receives high-fidelity thalamic relay of lamina-I signals for pain, temperature and visceral state, and its activity tracks graded pain intensity during sustained noxious stimulation 20 , 21 , 22 . From there, information is relayed forward into dysgranular/anterior agranular insula where interoceptive maps are merged with exteroceptive and motivational context-taste and oral somatosensation in the mid/anterior insula, vestibular and motion cues in posterior/mid insula, and limbic value signals via dense amygdala and striatal connectivity 22 , 23 . This posterior->anterior gradient equips the anterior insula with a multimodal "state estimator" that can represent risk, surprise, and decision uncertainty (e.g., risk-prediction errors that update within a trial 24 ), rather than just raw bodily input 25 . Microstructurally, the agranular fronto-insular cortex and dorsal ACC are enriched in large von Economo "spindle" neurons-thought to support rapid long-range broadcast-positioning these nodes to issue fast "global relevance" updates that bias processing elsewhere 26 . On the cingulate side, the dorsal ACC/mid-cingulate carries precisely the computations needed to turn those relevance estimates into control. Single-unit and imaging work shows that dACC neurons encode response conflict 27 , learned error likelihood 28 , prospective foraging value 29 , and the cost-benefit "expected value of control," 30 consistent with a role in deciding when control is worth paying for and of what kind. Anatomically, dACC nests cingulate motor zones with outputs to premotor/M1 and even spinal targets, and it couples tightly to autonomic effectors; this lets relevance signals translate into immediate adjustments of attention, sampling, arousal, and action. In concrete terms, when the anterior insula infers a high-precision deviation-say, a sudden siren while driving-dACC can hike control demand and prepare skeletomotor and autonomic responses in the next beat 31 , 32 . Computationally this division of labor fits predictive-coding accounts in which attention is the tuning of "precision," i.e., synaptic gain on prediction-error units 33 , 34 , 35 . The anterior insula carries precision-weighted surprise signals in multiple domains (pain, value, risk) and sits at the apex of a network that can up-gain sensory and control circuits while down-regulating distractors 36 ; neuromodulatory coupling to the locus-coeruleus/noradrenergic system provides a plausible fast channel for these gain shifts during salience hits 37 . Put together, the insula-dACC axis implements a relevance->control transform: insula computes that an event matters (because it perturbs the organism’s predicted internal/external state with high precision), and dACC decides and implements the control policy to handle it. Seen alongside the other control networks, the salience network (SN) is best characterized as a supervisor of when and where control is needed, rather than a system that represents what the current rules or contents are. The multiple-demand/frontoparietal network (FPN/MD) carries the parametric, content-specific representations that implement task rules and working memory, whereas the SN monitors the unfolding environment and internal state to decide if control should be intensified, relaxed, or reallocated. In contrast to the dorsal attention network (DAN; IPS/FEF), which maintains a continuous, top-down spatial priority map and selection policy, the SN is phasic and event-driven: it flags unexpected or urgent changes and biases DAN to "point the spotlight" and FPN to update or switch the active policy. Within SN, the dACC/aMCC implements the cost-benefit calculus for deploying control-coding conflict, error likelihood, and the expected value of control-providing a principled trigger for upshifts in top-down regulation when the payoff outweighs the effort. The anterior insula supplies the complementary "why it matters" signal: by integrating interoceptive/body-state cues with exteroceptive and affective value, it confers urgency and motivational significance on candidate events and helps initiate large-scale switches, especially from its right fronto-insular sector. Overall, a purely frontoparietal controller can execute a chosen rule set, but the SN biases whether to persist, escalate, or abandon that set in light of pain, threat, reward opportunity, uncertainty, or conflict-functionally operating as a high-level action selector that modulates DAN and FPN according to a holistic relevance assessment. The centrality of the salience network (SN) shows up most starkly when it breaks. Because the SN sits high in the control hierarchy-as a gatekeeper for when to engage top-down systems-its disruption propagates through cognition. In schizophrenia, the classic "aberrant salience" account links dysregulated mesostriatal dopamine to misassignment of significance, with downstream insula-cingulate dysfunction producing unstable belief updating and the intrusion of internally generated content as externally meaningful; structural and functional evidence implicates anterior insula and dACC within the SN as core loci of this failure mode 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 . Anxiety and PTSD show the complementary problem: lowered thresholds in SN hubs yield hypervigilant, threat-biased appraisal, with anterior insula and dACC over-engagement, stronger stress-sensitive SN coupling, and difficulty disengaging once aroused 42 , 43 , 44 . Disorders marked by switching failures further reveal the SN’s role as a mode selector. In ADHD, deficits cluster around poor attenuation of the default-mode network (DMN) during task engagement and impaired cross-network coordination, consistent with an SN that fails to efficiently flip the system from internal mentation to externally driven control 45 , 46 , 47 . Major depression shows a different imbalance-hyperconnected DMN with weakened SN coupling and perturbed insula-anchored interactions-which tracks rumination and blunted reactivity to behaviorally relevant change; effective-connectivity work and meta-analysis converge on this triple-network signature 48 , 49 , 50 . Finally, degeneration of the very neurons that likely enable the SN’s rapid, broadcast control-von Economo and related fork cells in fronto-insular and cingulate cortex-produces the apathy, inertia, and loss of initiative that headline early behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia, a clinicopathologic demonstration that when the SN’s motivational monitor goes offline, goal-directed behavior collapses 51 , 52 . In summary, the salience network provides an indispensable layer of control that complements other brain systems. It detects what matters most at each instant and tilts the entire cognitive apparatus accordingly - toggling between world-model introspection and environment interaction, mobilizing effort when needed and recovering idle mode when possible, and infusing executive commands with affective and interoceptive context.

title: The Linguistic System
text: Mapping the neuronal building blocks of human language with language models A language network in the individualized functional connectomes of 1199 human brains doing arbitrary tasks Phonological loop? Human language rides on a set of cortical-subcortical circuits that are highly specialized for mapping signals to structure and meaning while remaining deeply integrated with more general control, memory, and sensorimotor systems. The best top-down description is a pair of large-scale pathways: a left-dominant dorsal stream that maps sound to articulation and an often bilateral ventral stream that maps sound to meaning (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Saur et al., 2008; Friederici, 2011/2012). The dorsal stream originates in posterior superior temporal cortex and area Spt at the temporo-parietal junction and projects via supramarginal/angular parietal cortex into premotor and inferior frontal articulatory regions; the ventral stream runs from mid/posterior superior temporal sulcus/gyrus into middle/anterior temporal lobe and onward to ventrolateral prefrontal cortex. White-matter anatomy supporting these streams includes long and indirect segments of the arcuate fasciculus and SLF dorsally, and the extreme capsule, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), and uncinate fasciculus ventrally (Catani et al., 2005; Saur et al., 2008; Makris et al., 2009; Dick et al., 2012). In right-handed populations, dorsal long-segment asymmetry is common ( 82.5% leftward), consistent with left-lateralized phonological-articulatory control and bilateral but left-biased semantics (Catani et al., 2007; Binder et al., 2009; Friederici, 2011). At the representational level, posterior-mid superior temporal regions host phonological codes and sublexical sequence structure, anterior temporal lobe functions as a transmodal "semantic hub" that integrates distributed conceptual features, and inferior frontal cortex supports unification operations over phonology, syntax, and semantics (Hagoort’s MUC model) (Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Binder et al., 2009; Hagoort, 2013/2016). The ATL hub view explains broad semantic deficits in semantic dementia and converges with a "semantic control" network comprising left IFG and posterior middle temporal cortex that modulates retrieval when meaning must be shaped by task goals or context. Angular gyrus and anterior temporal pole contribute to multimodal integration at sentence/discourse scales, consistent with their long intrinsic timescales and coupling to default-mode subsystems during narratives (Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2013; Humphreys & Lambon Ralph, 2015). During speaking, cortical processing unfolds in a repeatable temporal cascade. Meta-analyses and chronometric studies estimate that lemma selection begins by  200 ms after cue onset, phonological code retrieval by  275 ms, syllabification by  350 ms, and phonetic/motor encoding  450-600 ms, mapping onto mid/posterior temporal, inferior parietal, and inferior frontal/premotor territories, with left anterior insula and ventral premotor cortex contributing to articulatory planning (Indefrey & Levelt, 2004/2011; Dronkers, 1996). The dorsal stream’s sensorimotor interface, area Spt, supports phonological working memory and auditory-motor transformations; its disruption yields conduction-aphasia-like phonological output errors and impaired nonword repetition, highlighting the role of dorsal buffers in on-the-fly sequence assembly (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007). These temporal-anatomical correspondences ground a mechanistic account: lexical access and morphosyntactic selection in temporal cortex feed dorsal phonological encoders and frontal unification/motor programs, with online self-monitoring via auditory predictions of one’s own speech. Comprehension engages bilateral auditory cortex at phoneme-syllable timescales but rapidly recruits left mid/posterior STG/STS for phonological-to-lexical mapping and ventral temporal-frontal circuits for semantics and combinatorics (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Saur et al., 2008; Friederici, 2011). Two high-precision signatures constrain models of inference-time dynamics. First, cortical oscillations are organized by speech rhythms: delta-theta bands align with prosodic/ syllabic structure, while gamma relates to phonemic encoding, and cross-frequency coupling supports hierarchical parsing and prediction (Giraud & Poeppel, 2012; Ding et al., 2016). Second, event-related potentials index stages of meaning and structure building: N400 amplitudes track contextual predictability and semantic access (peaking  400 ms) and the P600 often reflects reanalysis or conflict at the form-meaning interface; both can co-occur when surprisal propagates across levels (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Kuperberg, 2007). Together these data support predictive, multi-level inference in which ventral circuits instantiate priors over lexical semantics and combinatorics while dorsal circuits maintain phonological items and serial constraints. The production-perception loop is stabilized by forward models. During speaking, auditory cortex exhibits "speaking-induced suppression" and selective error responses when feedback is perturbed, consistent with corollary discharge from motor to sensory cortex that predicts self-generated sounds and gates error signals (Houde & Nagarajan, 2011). Intracranial and neuromodulatory studies refine the picture: suppression peaks in early auditory fields at utterance onset, prediction errors emerge when formants are shifted, and pathological alterations of this mechanism are implicated in auditory verbal hallucinations (Ford et al., 2001; Ozker et al., 2022; Khalilian-Gourtani et al., 2024). These principles mesh with "analysis-by-synthesis" accounts in which motor-invertible generative models propose candidate parses that are tested against incoming acoustics, enabling rapid recovery from noise and coarticulation (Bever & Poeppel, 2010; Hovsepyan et al., 2020). Orthography piggybacks on ventral visual pathways via a reproducible "visual word form" zone in left ventral occipito-temporal cortex that becomes tuned through literacy, then couples to phonology and semantics along dorsal and ventral language tracts (Dehaene & Cohen, 2011; Price, 2012). This "neuronal recycling" view predicts modality-invariant higher language circuits with culture-specific front ends-the data broadly support that reading recruits the same inferior frontal and temporal-parietal combinatorial/lexical systems that support speech and sign. Signed languages recruit left perisylvian cortex-including classical temporal and inferior frontal territories-despite visuomotor input/output, demonstrating that the combinatorial/semantic core is largely modality independent. Additional recruitment of dorsal parietofrontal visuomotor circuits reflects effector-specific demands (MacSweeney et al., 2008). This convergence constrains computational theories: linguistic composition and semantic mapping are properties of a fronto-temporal network that tolerates different sensorimotor interfaces. Natural stories reveal a cortical gradient of temporal receptive windows: early auditory areas integrate over tens to hundreds of milliseconds, mid-level language areas over seconds, and default-mode subsystems (angular gyrus, posterior cingulate/precuneus, medial PFC, anterior temporal pole) integrate over tens of seconds to minutes, tracking paragraphs and situation models (Lerner et al., 2011). Information flow lags during narrative comprehension are consistent with feedforward accumulation of context followed by top-down constraint, elucidating how meaning is maintained and updated across long spans (Chang et al., 2022). Neural similarity across listeners in DMN predicts shared interpretations, quantifying when high-level priors converge. These findings situate language within the brain’s hierarchy of intrinsic timescales and explain why semantic hubs and DMN nodes are essential for inference beyond the sentence. Language-selective fronto-temporal regions dissociate from the multiple-demand (MD) network: MD regions scale with task difficulty and executive demands but do not closely track linguistic content during passive comprehension; the adjacent language-selective territories in IFG and temporal cortex do (Fedorenko et al., 2012; Blank et al., 2014; Diachek et al., 2020). This dissociation clarifies how attention and control shape language without implementing core composition: MD and salience systems gate when/where resources are deployed, whereas the language network computes structure and meaning. For algorithmic models, this argues for a dual-route controller that modulates, but does not replace, specialized parsing/unification machinery. Beyond cortex, cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic loops contribute to chunking and serial order selection-functions that map naturally onto morpho-phonological sequencing and prosodic timing-while cerebellar circuits provide forward-model predictions and event-based temporal calibration for speech perception and semantic expectations (Kotz & Schwartze, 2010/2016; Moberget & Ivry, 2016; Lesage et al., 2017; Jin & Costa, 2014). These loops are engaged even in the absence of overt movement, consistent with internal modeling roles; they intervene when language demands fast, precise temporal control (e.g., parsing time-compressed speech or maintaining meter), aligning with broad evidence that BG and cerebellum implement complementary timing/sequence control regimes. A synthesis across EEG/MEG suggests a working division of labor: theta power tracks lexical/episodic retrieval; beta indexes maintenance of the current syntactic/semantic state and top-down predictions; gamma reflects local binding and mismatch repair, with task-/context-dependent variability (Bastiaansen & Hagoort, 2006; Lewis & Bastiaansen, 2015; Prystauka & Lewis, 2019). This is consistent with predictive-coding views in which beta carries top-down priors within the language network and gamma carries bottom-up error, coordinating dorsal buffers with ventral semantic composition in sentence/discourse processing. For comprehension of a spoken sentence, bilateral auditory cortex entrains to prosodic and syllabic rhythms, chunking the stream; left posterior STG/STS and Spt transform acoustic features into phonological items while a dorsal phonological buffer maintains order; ventral temporal cortex maps items onto lexical-semantic candidates; IFG/ATL unify these into structured meaning; DMN nodes carry the situation model over long spans; and MD control engages when ambiguity, noise, or task rules require extra effort. Forward models from frontal-premotor speech systems send predictions to auditory cortex to cancel self-generated or expected input; deviations drive error signals that update lexical and structural hypotheses. During production, the same representational substrates are traversed in reverse: conceptual intent in DMN/temporal hubs selects lemmas; IFG unifies morpho-syntax; dorsal stream retrieves phonology and sequences syllables; motor cortex issues articulatory programs; auditory cortex compares expected and actual feedback and corrects online. This loop-level account explains rapid robustness in noise, human-like error patterns under dorsal lesions (phonological), and deep-semantics deficits under ATL damage, providing algorithmic constraints for AGI-scale language systems that must operate under uncertainty, across timescales, and with tight perception-action coupling (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Hagoort, 2013; Giraud & Poeppel, 2012; Ding et al., 2016; Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Blank et al., 2014; Diachek et al., 2020). The linguistic system achieves data efficiency and reliability by combining a specialized, composition-first representational substrate (fronto-temporal language network) with multi-timescale priors (temporal integration gradient reaching into DMN), error-driven prediction (auditory-motor loops with corollary discharge), and executive gating (MD/salience). For engineering, that suggests language modules that (i) implement explicit composition and long-context situation modeling, (ii) are embedded in active generative loops that predict and compare sensory consequences of candidate parses, (iii) maintain dorsal-style phonological buffers for serialization, and (iv) coordinate with domain-general controllers that regulate effort rather than perform parsing. These constraints are borne out by convergent anatomy, timing, and perturbation data and align with predictive-coding and analysis-by-synthesis frameworks that already scale in machine systems.

title: Superordinate Objectives
text: When we ask "what objective does the brain optimize?", the most productive answer is not a single scalar but a stack of drives, constraints, and learned goals layered across phylogeny, physiology, development, and culture. Evolution does not hand the organism an explicit utility function; it bakes objective priors into anatomy and plasticity rules by making survival-critical variables (glucose, temperature, hydration, tissue damage, social inclusion, etc.) matter to circuitry. Day-to-day behavior then looks like partially observed control over hidden bodily and environmental states: keep the organism inside a viability manifold (hard constraints) while opportunistically improving future prospects (soft preferences) under time/energy/computation limits. Formal homeostatic RL makes this explicit: seeking "reward" is equivalent to defending physiological variables, and even classic temporal discounting can be derived as the shortest path back to setpoints in homeostatic space 1 . This framing dissolves the apparent tension between "reward maximization" and "survival": rewards are not arbitrary hedonic bonuses but proxy signals for restoring viability, and the effective discount factor reflects the dynamics of physiological drift (how fast the system departs from setpoints) rather than being a free parameter. This section describes the objectives that most fundamentally guide the evolution, development, and everyday operation of the human brain ( superordinate objectives ). These forces determine the curriculum that emerges across evolutionary and individual timescales. Later sections (especially the "Dense, Chronological Account of Human Learning" section) will enumerate the concrete, domain-specific objectives (e.g. "navigate to the kitchen", "perform addition", "earn a degree") and the sequence of training recipes that optimize against them. A compact taxonomy of superordinate objectives: Viability regulation: keep interoceptive variables in safe ranges (homeostasis/allostasis; pain/avoidance as constraint signals). Epistemic control: reduce uncertainty that matters for control (hidden state, dynamics, parameters, other agents). Control / option value: maintain and expand reachable futures (controllability/empowerment; skill acquisition as channel expansion). Social-normative value: status, belonging, attachment, reputation, fairness, identity; internalized norms as learned constraints. Cognitive economy: trade decision quality vs time/energy/computation (bounded rationality/resource rationality).

title: Definition and Relationship with EFE
context: Intrinsic Motivation: The Drive for Compression Progress
text: Intrinsic motivation is a broad term in psychology and adjacent fields: it denotes self-generated value –the tendency to engage in activities for their own sake (play, mastery, exploration, social games, art, sports) even when there is no immediate extrinsic or homeostatic payoff. In computational neuroscience and ML, this broad idea is typically operationalized more narrowly as an endogenous objective that assigns value to experiences because they are expected to improve an internal model or skill . In computational neuroscience and machine learning, this diffuse psychological concept has been sharpened into a specific formal principle: the drive for compression progress . Rather than seeking novelty per se (which would trap agents in noise) or minimizing prediction error per se (which would favor boringly predictable environments), intrinsically motivated agents seek experiences where their ability to compress–equivalently, to predict or explain–is improving. This formulation, originating with Schmidhuber’s "curiosity as compression progress" framework 1 , 2 , can be read as an online minimum description length (MDL) principle: the agent is driven to reduce the total code length needed to represent its experience, where model quality is not just data fit but fit plus complexity . Concretely, if L t L_t denotes an MDL-style description length (e.g., negative log-evidence/likelihood plus a complexity penalty for the current model class/parameters), intrinsic reward is the temporal derivative of that description length, r t i n t = δ L t ≡ L t − 1 − L t , r_t^{\mathrm{int}} = \delta L_t \equiv L_{t-1} - L_t, capturing the idea that curiosity is satisfied by progress in compressing the world. For continuous-time formulations, this becomes r i n t ( t ) = − d L d t r^{\mathrm{int}}(t) = -\frac{dL}{dt} . Importantly, sustained MDL improvement generally requires structured models : to keep shrinking L t L_t the agent must discover a disentangled internal model organized around approximately independent causal factors (separable mechanisms that can be recombined), since entangled representations tend to plateau in compression and generalization. In embodied settings this same drive is often expressed in a more behavioral currency as competence progress : intrinsic value tracks improvements in skill/goal performance (e.g., rising success rates on self-chosen subgoals), such that the agent is drawn to tasks in the "learnable" band where Δ Success ( g ) \Delta\,\text{Success}(g) is largest–an operational link between compression progress and the familiar phenomenology of mastery, practice, and the zone of proximal development. The compression-progress drive is closely related to, but not identical with, the ambiguity term in expected free energy. EFE’s ambiguity term (the expected entropy 𝔼 [ H [ P ( o τ | s τ ) ] ] \mathbb{E}[H[P(o_\tau|s_\tau)]] ) rewards policies that visit states where observations are diagnostic–it is an epistemic drive over state inference within a fixed model. Compression progress, by contrast, is an epistemic drive over parameter learning –it rewards experiences that improve the model itself. The two can be unified under extended active inference formulations that treat model parameters as random variables to be inferred: expected information gain about parameters (sometimes called "novelty" or "salience" in the active inference literature) then emerges as a third term in the EFE decomposition, and compression progress is its empirical, online approximation. Mathematically, both drives descend from the same variational principle. Minimizing variational free energy F F over time involves both (a) improving the approximate posterior Q ( s ) Q(s) given a fixed model (perception/state estimation) and (b) improving the generative model P ( o , s | θ ) P(o,s|\theta) itself (learning). The ambiguity term in EFE handles (a) at the policy-selection level; compression progress handles (b) at the learning level. Together they ensure the agent (i) seeks informative states given its current model and (ii) seeks experiences that make the model better–two facets of a single imperative to maximize long-run model evidence.

title: Curriculum
context: Intrinsic Motivation: The Drive for Compression Progress
text: The formal definition of intrinsic motivation as the time-derivative of description length ( r t int = − ∂ L t / ∂ t r_t^{\text{int}} = -\partial L_t / \partial t ) offers a normative explanation for the structured developmental trajectories observed in biological agents. If an agent is driven to maximize the rate of compression, it will naturally gravitate toward stimuli of intermediate complexity –the so-called "Goldilocks Zone" 1 , 2 , 3 or "Zone of Proximal Development" 4 . This preference is not a heuristic but an optimality condition relative to the agent’s current model class, priors, and capacity : totally predictable stimuli yield no new compression ( L t L_t is already minimal), while chaotic or wholly alien stimuli yield no progress ( L t L_t cannot be reduced). Thus, the agent’s attention is sequestered in the narrow band of the "learnable," where Δ L \Delta L is maximized. Formally, let Δ L ( π , θ t ) \Delta L(\pi, \theta_t) denote the expected description-length reduction from following policy π \pi given current model parameters θ t \theta_t , and let C ( π ) C(\pi) denote the cost (time, energy, risk, opportunity cost). The optimal curriculum policy maximizes compression rate per unit cost: π * = arg ⁡ max π Δ L ( π ; θ t ) C ( π ) , \pi^* = \arg\max_\pi \frac{\Delta L(\pi; \theta_t)}{C(\pi)}, where C ( π ) C(\pi) aggregates time, metabolic expenditure, and opportunity costs. The Goldilocks zone emerges because 𝔼 [ Δ L ] \mathbb{E}[\Delta L] is a concave function of task complexity relative to current competence–near-zero for tasks that are already solved under the current representation, near-zero for tasks that exceed the agent’s effective capacity/priors, and maximal near the boundary where errors are frequent but systematically reducible. This dynamic generates an emergent curriculum without explicit programming. Because the physical world is compositionally structured (e.g., edges form shapes, shapes form objects, objects form scenes), the "learnable frontier" moves hierarchically. The agent initially focuses on simple sensorimotor primitives; once these are compressed (mastered), the marginal return on attending to them vanishes (phenomenologically experienced as boredom ). This frees cognitive resources to attend to correlations between these now-compressed primitives, effectively "leveling up" the internal model to more abstract representations. The developmental progression from facial recognition -> object permanence -> chunked actions -> language -> abstract knowledge is therefore the trajectory of a locally-optimal learner whose reward landscape endogenously reshapes as skills saturate. This yields a characteristic developmental dynamic: Early : many domains offer large Δ L ̂ ( π ) \widehat{\Delta L}(\pi) → \to broad exploration and rapid acquisition of reusable primitives. Middle : progress concentrates at the current frontier → \to sustained practice, skill chaining, and compositional growth (new goals formed from mastered subskills/options). Late : as local progress saturates, the system restores learning progress by (i) switching domains/environments (novelty), or (ii) changing representational level (chunking, abstraction, new latent factors), enabling a new round of compression. Importantly, this framework presupposes that agents can estimate expected compression gain 𝔼 [ Δ L | π ] \mathbb{E}[\Delta L|\pi] for candidate policies. This metacognitive capacity itself requires a second-order model: a model of how the first-order world model changes under different experiences. Several mechanisms have been proposed: 1. Proxy signals : Using prediction error variance, gradient magnitude, or ensemble disagreement as heuristic estimators of Δ L \Delta L . 2. Memory-based extrapolation : Storing a history of ( π , Δ L ) (\pi,\Delta L) pairs and generalizing via function approximation. 3. Structural inference : Estimating task complexity from observable features (e.g., dimensionality, stationarity) and comparing against current model capacity. Developmental evidence suggests this metacognitive capacity is itself learned–young children notoriously overestimate their competence in novel domains (poor calibration), while adults show systematic biases (e.g., the Dunning-Kruger effect).

title: Tensions and Failure Modes
context: Intrinsic Motivation: The Drive for Compression Progress
text: A tension arises between depth (continued compression in the current domain) and breadth (sampling new domains). Formally, this is an exploration-exploitation tradeoff at the meta-level of curriculum selection: the agent must balance the diminishing returns of further practice against the uncertain but potentially high returns of novel domains. This can be addressed via upper confidence bound (UCB)-style heuristics. Let Δ L ̂ ( π ) \widehat{\Delta L}(\pi) be the mean estimated compression gain and σ ( π ) \sigma(\pi) its uncertainty (e.g., posterior standard deviation). A UCB-style policy scores each option as: U ( π ) = Δ L ̂ ( π ) + α σ ( π ) , U(\pi) = \widehat{\Delta L}(\pi) + \alpha \, \sigma(\pi), where α > 0 \alpha > 0 controls the exploration bonus. Large α \alpha favors breadth (exploring uncertain domains); small α \alpha favors depth (exploiting known high-yield domains). Another complicating factor is the need to account for analogical mapping: deep compression in one domain can yield representations that transfer to others, meaning the true value of depth is not just local Δ L \Delta L but the expected compression gain across all domains sharing latent structure. An agent that masters music theory may find physics more compressible; one that learns chess may compress strategic reasoning generally. This transforms the depth-breadth tradeoff from a simple bandit problem into a structured one where the reward function itself depends on the similarity kernel over domains–favoring depth in "hub" domains with high transfer potential over isolated curiosities. This leads us to failure modes; the compression-progress drive is not always adaptive. Pathological cases include: Novelty addiction : Over-weighting exploration ( α → ∞ \alpha \to \infty in the UCB formulation above) prevents sustained engagement; the agent "surfs" novelty without deep compression. Compulsive systematizing : Over-investment in domains with high local Δ L \Delta L but low transfer value, i.e., Δ L local ≫ 0 \Delta L_{\text{local}} \gg 0 but 𝔼 [ Δ L transfer ] ≈ 0 \mathbb{E}[\Delta L_{\text{transfer}}] \approx 0 . Boredom intolerance : Some skill acquisition requires tolerance of the low- Δ L \Delta L consolidation phase; agents with steep temporal discounting on r i n t r^{\mathrm{int}} may abandon skills prematurely. These failure modes suggest that the raw compression-progress signal must be modulated by higher-order objectives–pragmatic value, social relevance, long-term goal structure–to produce adaptive behavior

title: Phenomenology
context: Intrinsic Motivation: The Drive for Compression Progress
text: We can map distinct phenomenology to specific regimes of the loss landscape: Boredom and Frustration: These states represent the vanishing of the intrinsic reward signal ( r t int → 0 r_t^{\text{int}} \to 0 ), acting as "interrupts" that force policy exploration. Boredom occurs when model evidence is high and stable (the domain is fully compressed/mastered). Frustration occurs when model evidence remains low despite computational effort (the domain is irreducible noise or requires priors the agent does not yet possess). Frustration bifurcates into two computationally distinct cases: (i) stochastic frustration , where H ( o | s ) H(o|s) is genuinely high, signaling the agent should disengage; and (ii) structural frustration , where compression would be possible given appropriate priors, signaling the agent should backtrack to prerequisite subskills. Distinguishing these requires second-order inference about model class adequacy–a metacognitive capacity that itself develops. Flow and the Learning-Performance Paradox: The phenomenon of "Flow" 1 presents a theoretical tension: it is characterized by "effortless" action and high performance (suggesting a fixed, perfected model), yet it is driven by challenge and complexity (suggesting active learning). This is resolved by synthesizing Schmidhuber’s compression drive with Friston’s active inference 2 . Schmidhuber’s principle provides the drive : the agent seeks high-complexity regimes to maximize compression velocity. Active inference provides the mechanism : to remain viable in these high-entropy regimes without experiencing "surprise" (a spike in free energy), the agent must adopt a state of maximal precision weighting on its current policy. In this state, counterfactual planning and self-referential monitoring are suppressed because the path of error minimization is unambiguous. Thus, Flow is not static perfection, but the phenomenological signature of "surfing the gradient"–deploying high-precision priors to successfully assimilate a complex, high-entropy data stream that is on the verge of becoming unmanageable. Aesthetics as Sudden Compression: Experiences of humor, insight, or aesthetic appreciation can be modeled as "structured violations"–inputs that initially spike prediction error but allow for a rapid, global re-encoding of the latent state. The resulting sudden drop in description length (a "Eureka" moment) generates a high-magnitude pulse of intrinsic reward. Formally, aesthetic pleasure can be modeled as r t i n t = L t − ϵ − L t r_t^{\mathrm{int}} = L_{t-\epsilon} - L_t where ϵ → 0 + \epsilon \to 0^+ but Δ L \Delta L is large–a high-bandwidth compression event. This explains why effective jokes require setup (establishing a high-entropy prior) followed by a punchline that retroactively compresses it, and why repeated exposure kills humor (the prior is no longer high-entropy). This framework also reframes social learning (Vygotsky’s scaffolding) as cooperative loss-landscape smoothing . A teacher or caregiver acts as an auxiliary controller that actively reduces environmental variance, keeping the student within the high-gradient regime of learning and preventing them from falling into the local minima of boredom or the plateaus of frustration. More specifically, effective scaffolding can be understood as the teacher performing active inference on the student’s model , selecting demonstrations and hints that: 1. Lie within the student’s current zone of positive Δ L \Delta L (comprehensibility), 2. Maximize the student’s compression progress (informativeness), and 3. Sequence exposures to respect prerequisite structure (curriculum design). Interestingly, this teacher-objective is itself a form of compression: the teacher seeks the minimal intervention sequence that induces maximal model improvement in the student. Language acquisition exemplifies this–caregiver speech ("motherese") is systematically simplified and structured to track the child’s current model capacity, a phenomenon termed "fine-tuning" by developmental linguists.

title: Thermodynamic Constraints
context: Intrinsic Motivation: The Drive for Compression Progress
text: In biological neural networks, information is metabolically expensive. Action potentials and synaptic transmission consume significant ATP; consequently, the brain is under valid evolutionary pressure to represent the world using the minimum number of active neurons. This physical constraint naturally enforces a sparse coding regime 1 , which is a proxy for model complexity. A "good model" in the brain is literally a "cheap model"–one that explains sensory variance with the fewest spikes (lowest description length L L ). Thus, the minimization of variational free energy is not merely a statistical goal but a thermodynamic one: by compressing representations, the agent minimizes its metabolic load.
