title: Circuit-Level Biases
context: Intrinsic Motivation: The Drive for Compression Progress
text: It is therefore clear that evolution favors brains that are intrinsically motivated; but how did this materialize in the human brain, mechanistically? What are the actual mechanisms in the brain that drive it towards more-compressed representations over time? Fundamental mechanisms Pyramidal neurons act as multi-layer processing units rather than point neurons. By segregating inputs (distal apical vs. proximal basal), the dendrite can perform local "error detection." This architecture allows a single cell to learn specific non-linear features (compression) without interfering with the rest of the network’s weights, serving as a micro-scale mechanism for efficient feature extraction. Long term depression and pruning of redundant synapses (i.e those between neurons with low resonance); evolution has tuned the brain for a certain degree of selectivity when it comes to which neurons are connected. Lateral inhibition , which further enforces sparse, non-redundant representations. Sparse coding in V1 (driven by lateral inhibition / "competitive learning"), for example, produces Gabor-like receptive fields that optimally compress natural image statistics 1 . Evolution has also instantiated a curriculum on the neural level, with regions being successively "frozen" (i.e synapses stabilized, white matter myelinated) according to their level in the cortical abstraction hierarchy (low-level regions frozen first), allowing each stage of compression to proceed in a focused manner with stable representations as their inputs. Some systems look like they come with representational basis sets that make the world compressible: Entorhinal grid / head-direction / border cell system: a low-dimensional structured basis for space that massively compresses navigation and generalizes across environments. Hexagonal coding implements factorized spatial representation (frequencies at different scales). Topographic maps (retinotopy/tonotopy/somatotopy) + locality constraints: strong priors that reduce hypothesis space (a compression prior at wiring level). Cortical architecture (hierarchical generative model) The remarkably uniform structure of the neocortical column across different functional areas (visual, auditory, motor) is perhaps the brain’s greatest inductive bias. By using a "universal" circuit template, the brain assumes that all sensory data–regardless of modality–shares the same underlying statistical structure (hierarchical, temporal, and spatial correlations). This uniformity forces the brain to seek "compression" using a singular algorithmic language, perhaps making it easier for meta-learners to evaluate learning progress across different domains using a unified "currency." The cortical column and, especially, cross-cortical wiring implement predictive coding, a hierarchical compression scheme where each cortical level maintains predictions about the level below; only prediction errors (residuals) propagate upward 2 . This is exactly online MDL: Lower levels compress raw sensory data Higher levels compress the residuals Each level reduces L t L_t by finding regularities in its input This means that, across development, the cortex is constantly trying to "lift" representations to the next level of the hierarchy, producing lower-dimensional engrams that cancel out otherwise lower-order, high-dimensional, distributed, and costly codes. This results in a temporal abstraction gradient , where early sensory areas encode fast timescales and prefrontal regions encode slow, abstract timescales (see "Whole Brain Architecture" section). This implements hierarchical chunking: fast primitives are compressed into slower "options" or "schemas"–matching the developmental trajectory (primitives -> chunks -> abstractions). The centrality of thalamo-cortical loops can also be seen as a driver of intrinsic motivation. The restricted bandwidth of the thalamo-cortical interface forces a computational bottleneck . You cannot attend to everything. To pass the bottleneck, data must be compressed into a high-level representation. The "drive" here is instantiated by the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), which helps the brain ignore the "already-compressed" (predictable) and focus on the "compressible" (novel/progress-inducing). The thalamus appears to learn its routing functions at least partially through RL, speaking to the power of the (relatively miniscule) dopaminergic system, which is perhaps the most critical component of any "neural mechanisms of intrinsic motivation" discussion (keep reading). Subcortical regions Often overlooked, but the cerebellum is arguably the brain’s most dedicated compression engine: Climbing fiber error signals from inferior olive provide precise prediction error (akin to TD error, but for sensorimotor predictions) Mossy fiber -> Granule cell expansion followed by Purkinje cell compression is literally an encoder-decoder architecture (what does this mean and why is it relevant?) Optimizes for minimizing sensory prediction error over motor commands Basal ganglia as chunking / option discovery machinery You already cite DA broadly, but BG loops give you something more "architectural": a system biased toward discovering reusable action/state chunks. Cortico-striatal gating can turn repeated sequences into automatic policies (options), compressing control. Habitization isn’t just "mindless repetition"–it’s model compression of policy space: fewer degrees of freedom for common routines. Neuromodulatory systems If intrinsic reward is proportional to compression progress r t i n t ≈ L t − n − L t r_t^{int}\approx L_{t-n}-L_t , the nervous system must implement a progress estimator and a global allocator . Prediction errors are locally available throughout a predictive-coding hierarchy, but error magnitude alone cannot define intrinsic value: incompressible noise yields large prediction errors with no learnable structure. Neuromodulatory systems represent and broadcast this meta-statistic as global gain factors that regulate (i) attention to prediction errors, (ii) synaptic plasticity, (iii) policy switching, and (iv) memory tagging for offline replay–effectively implementing "spend metabolic budget where the model is improving." Dopamine Dopamine (which promotes pursuit ) has been shown to encode domain-general information gain 3 , 4 . Furthermore, curiosity states upregulate VTA-hippocampus connectivity and boost hippocampus-dependent learning 5 ; human fMRI shows caudate/NAcc activation scales with epistemic drive during trivia-style tasks 6 . This means compression progress comes to gate plasticity and working memory and shape exploration-exploitation tradeoffs (see "Neuromodulators" section). But how is this learned by / instantiated in the dopaminergic system? How did evolution accomplish the feat of having neurons that reward information gain (in a way that is independent (per se) of extrinsic rewards)? Overall, the dopaminergic encoding of information gain can be understood as a learned meta-objective that emerges from the interaction of evolutionary-specified factors: Temporal difference learning dynamics During development, exploratory behaviors and information-seeking states reliably precede reward acquisition (infants who explore more efficiently find food, comfort, and social reinforcement). Standard TD learning then backpropagates value to these states: δ t = r t + γ V ( s t + 1 ) − V ( s t ) \delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t) Over thousands of such episodes, the value function V ( s ) V(s) comes to assign high value to "curious states" even before any primary reward is delivered–the information gain is the reward, because it predicts future reward. Connectivity VTA/SNc neurons receive convergent input from: Prefrontal cortex (goal representations, counterfactual predictions) Hippocampus (novelty/familiarity signals) Superior colliculus and sensory association areas (salience, prediction errors) Evolution tuned this connectivity such that cortical prediction errors reliably modulate dopamine release . The DA system doesn’t "know" it’s encoding information gain–it’s simply responding to the signals it receives, which happen to correlate with model improvement. Acetylcholine and Norepinephrine Acetylcholine (ACh) (basal forebrain → \rightarrow cortex/hippocampus) and norepinephrine (NE/NA) (locus coeruleus → \rightarrow nearly everywhere) can be treated as a paired meta-learning controller : dedicated hardware for estimating whether prediction error is worth learning from , and for routing computation accordingly. In the "compression / learning-progress" view, they implement a fast, evolution-installed approximation to a learnability test : ACh biases the system toward sustained sampling + plasticity when errors are consistent with learnable structure under known noise (keep updating your model; increase sensory evidence and attention). NE biases the system toward interrupt + reset + exploration/switching when errors look like model failure under context change (stop trusting the current explanation; reorient, change policy/state, or search for a new compressible regime). A useful computational interpretation is that ACh tracks expected uncertainty : within a context, cues are known to be unreliable (noisy likelihoods, partial observability, stochastic outcomes), so additional bottom-up evidence is valuable and learning should continue rather than immediately "explain away" error via top-down expectations 7 , 8 . Mechanistically, ACh functions like a precision-weighting knob on sensory and associative inference: it boosts the influence of afferent input and cue detection, sharpens attention, and gates synaptic plasticity (controls the "learning rate" parameter)–all of which reflect the probability that residual error reflects compressible signal 9 , 10 , 11 . Viewing the system as an inductive bias, high ACh effectively biases cortical/hippocampal dynamics toward encoding mode (data assimilation) rather than retrieval/attractor completion (hallucinating the past into the present). This is exactly what you want if your objective is compression progress: keep the model plastic when there is structure left to be captured, and prevent overconfident top-down completion from masking learnable residuals 12 , 13 , 9 . See the "Acetylcholine" section of "Neuromodulators" for an account of how evolution "baked in" these ACh functions through architectural biases and specific training data. A complementary interpretation is that norepinephrine (NE) reports unexpected uncertainty : outcomes that are too surprising under the current context/model (change-points, rule switches, latent-state transitions). The correct response is not "increase precision and keep integrating," but " interrupt the current inference/policy and consider that you’re in the wrong state" 7 , 14 . In control terms, NE is a state-switch / exploration trigger . Phasic LC bursts can rapidly reconfigure network gain and responsiveness ("network reset"), while tonic LC levels are often modeled as shifting the explore/exploit regime and global task engagement 15 , 16 . Viewed as an inductive bias, NE implements a prior that the world is piecewise-stationary : most of the time you should compress within a stable regime (ACh-dominated), but occasionally the regime changes and the right move is to abandon the current codebook and search for a new one (NE-dominated). This is the architectural analog of change-point detection wrapped around a learning-progress objective. See the "Norepinephrine" section of "Neuromodulators" for an account of how evolution "baked in" these NE functions through architectural biases and specific training data. The default mode network: the offline compression engine The default mode network (DMN) functions as the brain’s offline compression engine and generative simulator . While sensory networks process the high-dimensional "ground truth" of the immediate present, the default mode network DMN maintains the compressed latent state of the organism’s history and future. It is responsible for semanticization –converting high-entropy episodic data (specific, noisy memories) into low-entropy semantic schemas (generalizable rules/concepts) 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 . Essentially, this is where the brain performs model-based reinforcement learning : running internal rollouts ("what if?" simulations) to update value estimates without the cost of real-world trial and error. Essentially, the DMN represents the organism’s Bayesian priors . It houses the autobiographical narrative and abstract concepts that predict sensory inputs before they arrive (and contextualize new experiences), serving as a major locus where cortex expresses high-level generative structure –latent causes that are (i) abstract, (ii) slow-changing, and (iii) useful for simulating and interpreting situations. It integrates ongoing input with stored context to produce "sense-making" representations rather than stimulus-locked feature maps. 21 When the brain is "at rest" (i.e., not engaged in externally-directed tasks), the DMN becomes highly active precisely because it is performing offline compression work: consolidating recent experiences, integrating them with existing knowledge structures, and–in information-theoretic terms–maximizing mutual information between previously disconnected (especially salient ) experiences (or, more accurately, between "representational states") 22 . What "compression" means here (mechanistically): Episodic -> schematic transformation : repeatedly re-instantiating episodes (or fragments) to extract invariants (who/what/why), reducing storage from many idiosyncratic traces into fewer higher-level factors and rules. 23 , 24 , 25 Generative recombination ("simulation as data augmentation") : constructing counterfactual scenes and future events by recombining stored elements–effectively generating new training samples that share structure with past experience. 26 , 27 , 28 Semanticization (compression into concept space) : integrating across instances to build meaning at word/sentence/discourse scales, i.e., compressing sensory particulars into conceptual codes that support inference. 29 How did evolution instantiate this network? Hierarchical Distance (The "Untethering" Hypothesis) Across the cortex, there is a macroscale sensory/motor -> transmodal gradient; DMN regions sit at the transmodal apex and are maximally separated (in a geometric/topographic sense) from primary systems. This is a real, measurable "placement prior": DMN computations are structurally biased away from immediate sensory drive. 30 . The tethering hypothesis frames how expanding association cortex (including DMN territories) could become "untethered" from direct sensory anchor points during evolution and development, enabling increasingly abstract, combinatorial cognition. Essentially, evolution didn’t just scale up cortex; it expanded the depth of the hierarchy, allocating territory for internal model compression that is less yoked to momentary inputs 31 . Intrinsic Bias for Long Temporal Integration : Hierarchies in cortex are also hierarchies of intrinsic timescales: association/prefrontal regions exhibit longer temporal integration windows than early sensory cortices. DMN regions exhibit the longest intrinsic timescales in the cortical hierarchy–on the order of hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, compared to tens of milliseconds in primary sensory cortex 32 , 33 . This temporal receptive window hierarchy means that while V1 responds to moment-to-moment luminance changes, DMN regions integrate information across extended temporal windows. This is precisely what is needed to discover slow-moving, abstract causal structure (social relationships, physical laws, narrative arcs) that cannot be detected from instantaneous sensory snapshots. Broad and Genetically-Specified Connectivity : DMN hubs (especially PCC/precuneus and mPFC) are positioned to integrate widely distributed information, which is exactly what you want for global compression: pulling together multimodal evidence to infer a smaller set of latent variables that explain it. 18 , 19 Furthermore, DMN connectivity patterns are present early in development and persist even under anesthesia, suggesting they reflect genetically-specified architectural priors rather than purely experience-dependent organization 34 . Evolution "pre-wired" this network topology, betting that an offline compression system would be universally useful across environments. DMN Can Interface with Control Networks : A critical architectural feature is that DMN can be selectively coupled to frontoparietal control systems during planning and other internally oriented goal-directed tasks. This gives you a clean computational story: DMN generates and compresses candidate world-model hypotheses; control networks gate which internal rollouts are pursued, evaluated, written back, or suppressed. 35 , 28 See "The Episodic Memory System" and "The Semantic Memory System" for more What is the training data / training pipeline of the DMN?: Complementary learning systems and online/offline learning regimes The learning problem, stated cleanly: the DMN is not trained on a continuous sensory stream. It is trained on a curated , temporally restructured , value-tagged set of internal samples whose job is to transform a long tail of idiosyncratic episodes into a small set of predictive latent variables (schemas, narratives, social models) that generalize. Importantly, this offline "dataset" is not only replay–it also contains strategically synthesized pseudo-episodes : counterfactual variants, prospective rollouts, and recombined fragments that let the brain learn from experiences it did not literally have, in the same sense that many model-based RL agents learn from both real and model-generated transitions 36 , 37 , 28 . "Rest" and sleep are not idling–they are the brain’s dataset construction + optimization loop for high-level generative structure (select -> edit/augment -> train -> renormalize). The DMN’s signature computation is directed self-generated thought (simulation, narrative construction, social inference), so the most important offline training samples are often scene-level simulations rather than veridical replays 28 , 38 . The brain implements a dual-store architecture codified in the Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) framework 39 : The Fast/High-Complexity Store (Hippocampus): Rapidly encodes episodic experiences with high fidelity via pattern separation . This minimizes immediate prediction error but carries a high "description length" or complexity cost. The Slow/Compressed Store (Neocortex/DMN): Over time, hippocampal traces are replayed and interleaved with prior knowledge to extract invariants and to train a generative model that can simulate (i) likely futures, (ii) alternative pasts, and (iii) other agents’ hidden states. The endpoint is not just "stored facts," but a simulator that can produce useful synthetic data on demand 37 , 26 , 40 . Systems consolidation is the offline process that distills episodic logs into the compressed cortical model 24 . We can frame learning through an online/offline regime split: Online (wake): Hippocampus indexes episodes; neuromodulators tag priority (reward, novelty, uncertainty) for later replay–implementing "importance sampling" for the offline learner 41 Offline (rest/sleep): Replay-driven compression. Sharp-wave ripples during rest trigger DMN activity–ripples act as "commit events" writing minibatches into DMN representations 42 . Replay is selective, prioritizing high-utility memories 43 Importantly, offline "replay" is not mere "playback"–it is strategic synthetic data generation . The hippocampal-cortical system functions as a generative world model that constructs novel training trajectories the organism never actually experienced: Counterfactual rollouts : Replay sequences routinely combine fragments from different episodes, traverse paths in reverse, and generate trajectories through never-visited state-space regions 44 , 45 . This is not noise–it reflects model-based simulation of alternative pasts and possible futures. Preplay and trajectory stitching: Before novel experiences occur, hippocampal sequences can "preplay" routes through environments, suggesting the system generates training data by composing learned transition dynamics into novel rollouts 46 , 47 . Why synthetic data? Real experience is expensive, sparse, and temporally autocorrelated. Generative replay enables the brain to (1) densify coverage in undersampled state-space regions, (2) break temporal correlations that cause catastrophic interference, and (3) explore counterfactual branches that refine causal and predictive models without costly real-world sampling 48 , 49 . This mirrors the logic of Dyna-style architectures in model-based RL, where learned world models generate "imagined" rollouts to augment real data 36 . REM sleep as hyperassociative generation: During REM, the neuromodulatory environment (high ACh, absent NE) biases the generative model toward distal, low-probability associations –producing the recombinant imagery of dreams. This can be understood as sampling from the tails of the learned distribution, stress-testing schemas against edge cases and promoting generalization 50 , 51 . Implications for the DMN: If the DMN encodes compressed, schema-level world models, then its training distribution consists heavily of internally generated counterfactuals –not raw sensory logs. This positions the DMN as the brain’s equivalent of a latent variable model trained on synthetic rollouts from a hippocampal "world simulator." Distinct oscillatory profiles scaffold consolidation and synthesis through temporal multiplexing: Sharp-wave ripples (hippocampus): time-compressed sequence activation (the "seed sequences" for both replay and rollouts) Slow oscillations (cortex): gate plasticity windows (when cortex can be updated without runaway interference) Thalamocortical spindles: facilitate hippocampal -> cortical transfer and long-range coordination This nesting (ripples -> spindles -> slow-oscillation up-states) maximizes transfer while preventing interference 52 . Distinct neuromodulatory climates change the brain’s "optimizer settings" (and, importantly, its search strategy) 41 , 53 : Wake (high ACh / higher NE / higher 5-HT): encoding, externally anchored attention; SWR-driven offline sequences are comparatively suppressed NREM (low ACh / low NE / low 5-HT): high-fidelity consolidation + controlled interleaving (good for stable distillation) REM (high ACh with very low NE & 5-HT): associative expansion / recombination–a chemistry consistent with broader, more "creative" search over memory fragments (good for synthetic recombinations and unusual counterfactual links) 54 . NREM sleep and REM sleep are interleaved across the slumber. Sleep also implements cortex-wide synaptic downscaling –a complexity penalty that removes low-utility potentiation while replay + rollouts write back high-utility structure 55 . See the "Offline Learning" section for a much more detailed account. Prefrontal "metacognitive" signals (self modeling / meta-learning / meta-RL) and learned exploration policies Some higher-order regions quickly learn that maximizing long- and short-term rewards entails maximizing learning/compression progress in general ; they store learned estimates of expected error reduction per unit cost, with these estimates of "expected learning progress" being based on the complex, branching simulations that are characteristic of higher-order cortex. Metacognitive state variables relevant for intrinsic motivation: Expected value of deploying control (is it worth paying effort/compute now?)–a quantity formalized as the expected value of control (EVC) and strongly associated with dACC control allocation. 56 Explore/exploit value in option space (try a new arm/strategy vs harvest current one), including dissociable directed exploration (information-seeking bias) vs random exploration (noise-driven sampling). 57 , 58 Metacognitive confidence / self-evaluation (how good is my policy/model right now?), supported by rostrolateral/frontopolar PFC contributions to metacognitive monitoring. 59 Latent state / context hypotheses ("what task am I in?"), which is critical because "learning progress" is only meaningful within a latent regime; surprise that implies regime change should trigger switching rather than continued integration (bridging naturally to the NE/change-point story). It behaves like a flexible hub that can rapidly rewire its coupling to other systems based on goals. 63 . Essentially carries the learned exploration policy and the meta-value of information in a form that can actually steer action sequences (directed exploration, hypothesis tests, curriculum choice). The "multiple demand" property (activation across diverse cognitive tasks) reflects a domain-general compression engine that extracts task-invariant control structure 64 The dorsal attention network Think of it as "active sensing" machinery. It executes where to look / sample next under top-down control (overt attention, gaze, feature selection) 65 Contains priority maps (FEF, IPS) that flexibly encode "informativeness" alongside salience 66 , 67 The rostrolateral prefrontal cortex (Broddman area 10, "frontopolar cortex") Can be seen as a strategy-space explorer : evaluates alternative rules/policies, supports directed exploration, and tracks long-horizon opportunities to learn at the level of task structure rather than immediate actions 68 Phylogenetically newest cortex, suggesting selection pressure for long-horizon meta-learning 69 , 70 The rostro-caudal organization of PFC may constitute an architectural bias for hierarchical compression 71 , 72 , 73 : Posterior PFC: Concrete, immediate prediction errors (concrete actions) Mid-lateral PFC: Rule-level, task-set prediction errors Frontopolar (BA10): Abstract, long-horizon "meta-prediction errors" (am I learning the right kind of thing?) This gradient wasn’t learned–it’s anatomically specified, with systematic variations in laminar structure, temporal integration constants, and connectivity patterns that evolution installed to enable compression at multiple timescales simultaneously. How did evolution instantiate these networks? Salience Network Anterior Insula as an Integrative Hub The anterior insula sits at a unique anatomical crossroads, receiving convergent input from visceral/interoceptive systems, limbic structures (amygdala, ventral striatum), and higher cognitive regions (PFC, ACC). Evolution positioned this region to integrate "body state" with "world state," enabling it to compute whether current physiological resources justify cognitive expenditure 74 , 75 . Von Economo Neurons (VENs) as Rapid Broadcast Architecture The anterior insula and dACC contain distinctive von Economo neurons –large, spindle-shaped projection neurons with simple dendritic arbors found almost exclusively in these regions (and, phylogenetically, only in species with complex social cognition: great apes, elephants, cetaceans) 76 , 77 . VENs have long-range axons and fast conduction properties, positioning them as rapid relay cells that can broadcast salience/switch signals across distributed networks faster than typical pyramidal neurons. This is exactly what you want for a "circuit breaker" that must quickly shift the brain between processing modes. 0 Their late development (emerging postnatally and maturing through adolescence) suggests they are shaped by experience within an evolutionarily-specified template–consistent with a meta-learning system that requires both innate structure and developmental tuning 78 . dACC Cytoarchitecture Optimized for Conflict/Error Integration dACC has a unique laminar profile with dense reciprocal connections to both limbic (emotional valuation) and lateral prefrontal (cognitive control) systems. This positions it as a hub for computing expected value of control (EVC)–integrating information about task demands, error likelihood, and reward prospects to decide whether increased cognitive effort will pay off 79 , 56 . Evolution installed this as a "worth it?" calculator: before committing resources to a learning opportunity, dACC estimates whether the expected compression progress justifies the metabolic investment. Frontoparietal Control Network Lateral PFC Expansion in Primates The lateral prefrontal cortex underwent massive expansion in the primate lineage, particularly in humans. This isn’t just "more cortex"–it reflects selection for circuits that can maintain abstract, temporally-extended representations in working memory despite interference and delay 80 , 81 . The granular prefrontal cortex (with well-developed layer IV) is essentially a primate innovation, enabling the kind of sustained recurrent activity patterns that implement working memory and sequential rule-following. Laminar Microcircuitry for Persistent Activity LPFC neurons exhibit sustained firing during delay periods–the neural substrate of working memory. This persistent activity emerges from recurrent excitatory connections (primarily in layers II/III) balanced by inhibition, creating attractor dynamics that can maintain information "online" 82 , 83 . Evolution tuned the excitation/inhibition balance and NMDA receptor density in PFC to support this bistability, creating an architectural prior for maintaining compressed task representations (rules, goals, context) across time. Cortico-Basal Ganglia Gating PFC doesn’t work alone–it’s tightly coupled to basal ganglia circuits that implement selective gating of what enters and exits working memory 84 , 85 . This PFC-BG loop implements a "bouncer" mechanism: not all information gets maintained, only that which passes a learned relevance threshold. The threshold itself is trained by dopaminergic RPE signals, meaning the gating policy is shaped by reward history–an architectural substrate for learning what’s worth learning about. Multiple-Demand Property as Domain-General Compression The same FPN regions activate across wildly different cognitive tasks (math, language, spatial reasoning, social inference). This "multiple demand" property suggests these circuits implement domain-general operations–task-set maintenance, variable binding, structured composition–that constitute a universal compression vocabulary 86 , 87 . Evolution installed a general-purpose "cognitive algebra" rather than task-specific modules, allowing the same circuits to compress structure across domains. Dorsal Attention Network Direct Sensory Modulation Pathways The frontal eye fields (FEF) and intraparietal sulcus (IPS) have direct, retinotopically-organized projections back to visual cortex (V4, MT, V1). This gives the DAN the anatomical capacity to directly bias sensory processing in favor of task-relevant locations or features 88 , 89 . This is "active sensing" hardware: the ability to sculpt incoming information before it’s fully processed, implementing directed exploration at the level of perception itself. Priority Maps for Flexible Sampling FEF and LIP maintain priority maps –topographic representations where activity reflects the behavioral relevance of spatial locations, combining bottom-up salience with top-down goals 66 , 90 . Importantly, these maps can be rapidly reconfigured by task demands , allowing the brain to dynamically redirect sampling toward high-information regions of the environment. Evolution installed coordinated retinotopic architecture across multiple areas to enable this flexible, goal-directed sampling. Oculomotor Coupling FEF is directly connected to brainstem oculomotor nuclei, and IPS connects to FEF. This means priority map activity can be directly converted into eye movements and shifts of covert attention –the primary mechanisms by which primates actively sample their environment 91 , 92 . The tight coupling between "where to attend" representations and motor output ensures that meta-learned sampling policies can be immediately executed. Rostrolateral PFC Phylogenetic Novelty BA10 is the most recently evolved region of prefrontal cortex, with disproportionate expansion in humans relative to other primates. The allometric scaling suggests strong selection pressure specifically for whatever BA10 computes 93 , 94 . Unique Cytoarchitectonic Features BA10 has exceptionally low neuronal density and the highest proportion of dendritic spines per neuron of any cortical region, suggesting capacity for massive integration of diverse inputs 95 , 96 . Its granular layer IV receives inputs predominantly from other prefrontal regions rather than sensory thalamus, architecturally "insulating" it from immediate sensory drive and biasing it toward abstract, internally-generated representations. Longest Intrinsic Timescales BA10 sits at the apex of the cortical timescale hierarchy, with intrinsic fluctuations on the order of seconds–far longer than sensory cortex 97 . This temporal integration constant is suited for tracking slowly-evolving, abstract variables like "which learning strategy am I using?" or "is my current approach working over the long run?" Connectivity Pattern Supporting Cognitive Branching BA10 has dense connections with mid-lateral PFC (rule maintenance), orbitofrontal cortex (outcome evaluation), and anterior temporal regions (semantic knowledge), but sparse direct sensory input. This positions it to perform cognitive branching: maintaining a background goal or strategy while executing a foreground task 70 , 98 . This is exactly the architecture needed for meta-learning: tracking whether a current learning policy is working while simultaneously executing that policy. Inter-Network Dynamics as Evolutionary Architecture The key evolutionary insight isn’t just the individual networks–it’s that evolution installed the interaction dynamics between them: The triple-network model (Menon, 2011) describes how the salience network arbitrates between DMN and FPN 99 This switching architecture implements a fundamental explore/exploit tradeoff: DMN consolidates (exploits current model), FPN actively samples (explores) The anticorrelation between DMN and FPN is itself an architectural prior–evolution shaped connectivity such that you can’t simultaneously consolidate and actively explore 100 , 18 The Rostro-Caudal Gradient as Hierarchical Compression Architecture: Posterior PFC: Concrete, immediate prediction errors (stimulus-response mappings) Mid-lateral PFC: Rule-level, task-set prediction errors (if-then contingencies) Frontopolar (BA10): Abstract, long-horizon "meta-prediction errors" (am I learning the right kind of thing? Should I switch strategies?) This gradient wasn’t learned–it’s anatomically specified, with systematic variations in laminar structure (increasing granularization rostrally), temporal integration constants (increasing rostrally), and connectivity patterns (increasingly prefrontal-prefrontal vs. sensory-prefrontal) that evolution installed to enable compression at multiple timescales simultaneously 101 , 102 . Hierarchical Control via Nested Gating : The rostro-caudal gradient implements hierarchical policy abstraction : rostral regions set context for caudal regions, which in turn constrain motor output. This cascade architecture allows abstract meta-policies ("explore until error drops") to shape specific behaviors without micromanaging them 103 , 104 , 105 . The gating at each level is learned (via cortico-striatal loops), but the hierarchical organization itself is an evolutionary prior on the structure of good policies. What are the inputs and outputs of prefrontal meta-learners? Inputs (features): what the meta-learner can observe in real time Uncertainty and ambiguity proxies from perceptual and associative hierarchies (distributional uncertainty, conflict, cue reliability), including attention-demand signals routed through salience/control systems. 65 Performance-monitoring signals (errors, response conflict, volatility indicators) that summarize when the current policy is failing or costly 56 Learning-progress statistics that are locally computable: not just | ϵ t | |\epsilon_t| but | Δ ϵ t | |\Delta \epsilon_t| over a window (did error shrink after I sampled/attended?), plus novelty/familiarity and replay-worthiness tags (your DA/ACh/NE sections already lay the broadcast channels). Opportunity-cost / reward-rate context (is staying worth it?), framing exploration as foraging in policy space: leave a depleting patch (current strategy) when expected returns fall below alternatives. 106 , 107 Outputs (actions): what the meta-learner actually controls Control allocation vectors: increase WM maintenance, tighten attention, engage planning, or conversely drop control and allow habitual policies 56 Sampling / exploration policies: directed exploration (choose high-information options), random exploration (increase stochasticity), and structured hypothesis tests (e.g., sample the feature/action that disambiguates task structure fastest). 58 Network-mode switches: couple/decouple DMN<->FPN and bias toward internal simulation vs external sampling, mediated by salience-network switching dynamics. 60 What is the training data / training pipeline of these networks? The meta-learning networks face a fundamentally different credit assignment problem than sensory or motor systems: they must learn not just "what predicts reward" but "what learning processes lead to future reward across diverse situations." This requires training signals that evaluate the quality of learning itself. The Meta-RL Framework Core Insight: Slow Weights Train Fast Dynamics: A powerful framework for understanding prefrontal meta-learning comes from the meta-reinforcement learning perspective: dopaminergic reward prediction errors slowly tune synaptic weights in prefrontal circuits, and these weights configure recurrent dynamics that implement a fast, flexible learning algorithm in the space of neural activity 108 , 109 . In other words: DA trains the weights; the weights implement the algorithm; the algorithm learns within episodes. The "training data" for the meta-learner is the entire distribution of tasks/environments encountered over development, not any single task. What Gets Encoded in Prefrontal Weights: After training on many related tasks, PFC weights come to encode: Task structure priors: What kinds of state spaces, transition dynamics, and reward functions are common in this organism’s niche? Efficient exploration strategies: What information-gathering policies tend to work across tasks? Credit assignment heuristics: How should outcomes be attributed to earlier actions/states? These are exactly the ingredients of a compression-oriented meta-learner: priors that make new tasks "instantly compressible" because the PFC has learned what structure to expect. The Recurrent Network as "Inner Loop" Learning Algorithm: PFC recurrent dynamics–sustained activity, attractor states, sequential transitions–implement a learned algorithm that can update task representations within an episode based on observations and outcomes, without any weight changes 110 , 111 . The training objective for these dynamics is implicit: configurations that lead to better cumulative reward across episodes are reinforced via slow synaptic updates. Over evolutionary and developmental time, this shapes PFC dynamics to implement efficient Bayesian inference (or approximations thereof) over task-relevant latent variables. Training Signals for Meta-Learning Networks Dopaminergic TD error as the outer-loop supervisor: even if "information gain" is not innately rewarded, the consequences of good information seeking (higher future reward-rate, fewer costly errors, safer policies) generate RPEs that reinforce the internal states and actions that preceded them–training an intrinsic-motivation proxy via standard TD backup across time 3 , 6 . This is the core meta-RL story for PFC. 108 . The anatomical targeting of DA to PFC (especially to layers that support sustained activity) makes it particularly well-positioned to serve this function 112 , 113 . Control-value prediction errors: dACC (and related loops) learns not only "was I right?" but "was deploying control worth it?"–a meta-error comparing predicted EVC vs realized payoff after paying effort/time costs. 56 , 114 Exploration-value prediction errors: frontopolar + intraparietal circuits learn when exploration paid off (found a better arm / improved model), consistent with neurocomputational accounts of exploratory decisions. 57 Metacognitive prediction errors: discrepancies between predicted confidence/competence and actual outcomes tune rlPFC "self-model" variables that gate whether to persist, switch, or seek more evidence. 59 Outcome Prediction Errors from OFC: The orbitofrontal cortex tracks the specific sensory features of expected outcomes and generates prediction errors when outcomes differ from expectations in identity (not just value) 115 , 116 . These outcome identity prediction errors provide a training signal for learning about task structure (what leads to what) rather than just task value (is this good or bad). For meta-learning, this helps train the "world model component" of PFC representations. Salience / interoceptive prediction errors from right anterior insula (rAI): rAI computes: (i) salience prediction errors when ongoing sensory/cognitive streams violate short-horizon expectations, and (ii) interoceptive prediction errors when predicted arousal/effort/body-state consequences mismatch actual state (a fast "this policy/model is off" signal). These rAI error signals act as a training/gating label for the meta-learner, marking moments where the agent should upweight updating or switch hypotheses because the current compression codebook is failing. 117 , 118 , 119 , 60 Surprise/Novelty Signals from Hippocampus: The hippocampus generates novelty and mismatch signals when observations violate predictions from the current model 120 . Via hippocampal -> PFC projections (through medial PFC and orbital regions), these signals inform the meta-learner that the current task model is inadequate–a signal that should trigger either increased learning rate (ACh) or model switching (NE). Offline augmentation: The DMN/hippocampal simulator supplies counterfactual and prospective rollouts that let PFC evaluate "what would happen if I explored X?" without paying real-world cost; this creates a second training stream where meta-control policies are refined against imagined outcomes. Hierarchical Bootstrapping (The Developmental Curriculum) The training pipeline follows a rostral-caudal maturation gradient: Infancy/Childhood (Posterior PFC): The system is trained on immediate sensorimotor loops. The "policy" learned is simple curiosity: "if I move my hand, visual input changes." Adolescence (Mid-LPFC & dACC): The system is trained on rule-based feedback. Pruning of redundant synapses refines the "switching cost" parameters, tuning the balance between perseverance (concentration) and distractibility (flexibility) 121 . Adulthood (Frontopolar/RLPFC): The apex of the hierarchy comes online last. It is trained on long-horizon "life outcomes." It learns to value abstract exploration–seeking new categories of knowledge (e.g., "I should learn a new language") rather than just new sensory states, because it has meta-learned that expanding the "basis set" of the internal model yields the highest long-term compression 122 . Overall, the prefrontal meta-learning system represents evolution’s solution to a challenging optimization problem: how to build a brain that learns how to learn across the enormous diversity of tasks an organism might face. Architectural priors (network topology, timescale hierarchies, neuromodulator targeting) constrain the hypothesis space such that good meta-policies are learnable within a lifetime, training signals (DA RPE, ACC EVC-PE, hippocampal novelty, interoceptive prediction errors) provide feedback about the quality of learning effort and exploration choices, and training data consists of the structured stream of experiences across development, augmented by self-generated play, culturally-transmitted heuristics, and offline counterfactual simulation. The result is a system that, over development, comes to represent and pursue compression progress as an intrinsic goal–not because evolution directly installed "seek compressible domains" as an objective, but because the architecture and training regime reliably shape networks that find such domains and allocate resources to learning from them. The prefrontal meta-learner is, in essence, a learned approximation to the optimal solution of the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in a world where the value of information derives from its capacity to improve the organism’s predictive model. title: Relationship with Previous Objectives
text: There is a striking theoretical convergence between empowerment and expected free energy (EFE) minimization. While EFE minimizes the divergence between predicted and preferred outcomes, empowerment maximizes the channel capacity of the agent’s actuation. However, inspection of the decomposition reveals that empowerment is effectively a limit case of EFE minimization under specific priors. The conditional entropy term in empowerment, − H ( S t + k | s t , A t : t + k ) -H(S_{t+k}|s_t,A_{t:t+k}) , is analagous to the ambiguity term in EFE: both metrics drive the agent to minimize noise in the action-outcome mapping, penalizing policies where the consequences of control signals are uncertain. The divergence arises in the second term: empowerment explicitly maximizes the entropy of reachable states ( H ( S t + k | s t ) H(S_{t+k}|s_t) ), whereas EFE constrains outcomes to match a phenotypic prior P ( o τ ) P(o_\tau) (and when that distribution is sharp, it effectively favors low-entropy, "stasis-like" outcomes). This tension is resolved by recognizing that for a biological agent, the "preferred prior" P ( o τ ) P(o_\tau) is not a point-mass on a single stasis state, but a broad distribution over a viable phase space. Under a sufficiently flat prior over survival-compatible states, minimizing EFE requires the agent to "fill" the available state space (maximizing entropy within the viable set) to avoid overfitting to a specific, potentially fragile niche. This leads us to the idea of intrinsic motivation as constrained entropy maximization 1 . Thus, empowerment can be viewed as the pure exploration / option value component of EFE: it is the objective function that dominates in proportion to how "flat" external reward signals (i.e risk) are, driving the agent to seize the "high ground" of the causal landscape where the agent can realize many distinct futures reliably . The convergence of expected free energy, compression progress, and empowerment reveals that each framework captures a distinct but complementary facet of adaptive behavior–and that the brain’s apparent "objective function" is best understood as the dynamic arbitration among all three. EFE provides the overarching decision-theoretic scaffold: it specifies how to select policies that satisfy homeostatic and learned preferences (the risk term) while reducing state-level uncertainty (the ambiguity term), yielding a principled account of why organisms both exploit and sample even when sampling has no immediate reward 2 , 3 . However, EFE’s ambiguity term operates within a relatively fixed generative model–it rewards visiting diagnostic states but does not directly incentivize improving the model’s parameters. This is precisely what compression progress supplies: a learning-level objective that assigns intrinsic value to experiences that shrink description length, ensuring the generative model continually refines its structure and not just its state estimates. Meanwhile, empowerment captures something neither EFE nor compression directly addresses: the option value of a state independent of any currently active goal. An agent minimizing EFE with sharp preferences might converge on a narrow behavioral repertoire that satisfies current priors but leaves it vulnerable to distributional shift; an agent maximizing compression might obsessively model domains with no practical relevance. Empowerment provides a corrective prior toward states that preserve future flexibility–effectively a "strategic reserve" of controllable futures that hedges against model misspecification and goal change. Essentially, all three objectives are useful precisely because human behavior is a mixture of (1) constraint satisfaction under deep priors (stay viable, stay socially acceptable), (2) model improvement (learn compressed causal structure and skills), and (3) option preservation (maintain autonomy, resources, and controllable degrees of freedom), with different terms dominating depending on deprivation, uncertainty, and available affordances.

title: Behavioral and Developmental Manifestations
text: If empowerment is a drive to maximize the reliable causal influence of action on sensation, then its behavioral signature is not "novelty seeking" per se, but a persistent preference for contingency : organisms will choose situations where (i) their actions produce detectable changes and (ii) those changes are lawfully coupled to specific action choices. In classic motivational language, this is the "effectance/competence" motive : an intrinsic pull toward experiences that yield a feeling of efficacy even when no primary deprivation is in play 1 . Newborn behavior is dominated by reflex arcs and low-dimensional control; empowerment is initially near-zero because the actuator → \rightarrow sensor channel is weak, noisy, and poorly calibrated. Across the first months, infants rapidly allocate attention toward and learn from events that are response-contingent, treating contingency itself as valuable (and its violation as salient) 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 . The mobile conjugate reinforcement paradigm provides the canonical demonstration: infants whose ankle is tethered to an overhead mobile dramatically increase their kick rate and display sustained positive affect, while yoked controls receiving identical but non-contingent visual stimulation do not 9 , 10 . The reinforcing signal is the contingency itself –the mutual information I ( A ; S ′ ) I(A;S') –not the sensory richness of the mobile’s motion. This interpretation is strengthened by the finding that when a previously learned contingency is extinguished, infants as young as 2 months display anger rather than mere disinterest 11 , suggesting that the expected empowerment signal functions as a reference point whose violation elicits aversive arousal–a primitive "empowerment prediction error." Developmental milestones (reaching, sitting, crawling, walking, speech articulation) can be read as successive bandwidth expansions of the action channel: each newly controllable degree of freedom increases the size of the reachable future state set H ( S t + k ! ∣ s t ) H(S_{t+k}!\mid s_t) , while practice/refinement reduces H ( S t + k ! ∣ s t , A ) H(S_{t+k}!\mid s_t, A) by making outcomes more deterministic. On this view, "practice" is empowerment optimization: repetition is not mere motor babbling but an intrinsic program to tighten the action → \rightarrow outcome mapping while broadening the controllable manifold 1 , 2 . Piaget’s taxonomy of circular reactions tracks an orderly expansion of where empowerment is sought (and at what level of abstraction) across the first 18 months 12 : Primary circular reactions ("motor babbling"; 1-4 months): discover controllable contingencies within the body itself (proprioceptive empowerment) Secondary circular reactions (4-8 months): extend controllability to distal objects and simple tool-like interactions Tertiary circular reactions (12-18 months): systematically vary actions to map the causal geometry of the action-outcome channel–effectively probing its local channel capacity via intervention. There is evidence that social empowerment is present from early infancy: even before robust object control, infants are sensitive to social contingencies and preferentially engage in interactions where their actions (vocalizations, gaze, affect) reliably elicit responses from caregivers. These early turn-taking loops constitute a high-gain social control channel, supporting the idea that empowerment over other agents is not a late add-on but an early, evolutionarily prepared target of intrinsic control-seeking 5 , 13 . The ubiquity of play across mammals and birds provides perhaps the most direct behavioral evidence for empowerment as an intrinsic motivation. Play is metabolically costly, carries non-trivial injury risk, and by definition yields no immediate instrumental payoff–yet it is a robust developmental invariant across altricial species 14 . The empowerment framework offers a unifying account: each major category of play maps onto a distinct component of the channel-capacity objective. Object play (manipulating, dropping, mouthing, and disassembling novel items) systematically probes the dynamics of the action-outcome mapping, reducing the conditional entropy H ( S t + k | s t , A t : t + k ) H(S_{t+k}|s_t, A_{t:t+k}) by building forward models of object physics–how things break, bounce, roll, and deform under varied forces. Locomotor play (running, jumping, climbing in varied and exaggerated patterns) expands the effective motor repertoire, increasing the "alphabet size" of the action channel and thereby the achievable diversity of reachable futures H ( S t + k | s t ) H(S_{t+k}|s_t) . Social play –particularly rough-and-tumble play 15 –involves learning to influence non-stationary agents, arguably the highest-dimensional empowerment challenge, as the "channel" now includes another adaptive system whose (partially observable) transition dynamics must be simultaneously modeled and controlled. Several features of play are specifically predicted by the empowerment framework but are puzzling under purely curiosity-driven or skill-practice accounts. First, play is preferentially performed under low-risk, "relaxed field" conditions –satiated, in familiar territory, in the proximity of attachment figures 16 –precisely the conditions under which the risk term of EFE is slack and the empowerment term would dominate the agent’s objective. Second, play is characteristically repetitive with variation : animals repeat action sequences but introduce small perturbations, consistent with an agent that is not merely sampling novelty (which would favor maximal variation) but is refining its estimate of the local channel capacity [Intrinsically Motivated Learning of Real World Sensorimotor Skills with Developmental Constraints]–iteratively testing how reliably distinct actions yield distinguishable outcomes. Third, play peaks during the juvenile period 17 when the organism faces the greatest gap between its current motor/social competence and the full affordance structure of its ecological niche–i.e., when the marginal return on empowerment investment is highest. Moreover, play is not randomly directed across the difficulty spectrum but is preferentially targeted at challenges just beyond current mastery–the same "zone of proximal development" discussed for compression progress (see "Intrinsic Motivation" section), but measured in a different currency. Where compression progress peaks at the frontier of learnability , empowerment gain peaks at the frontier of controllability : tasks where the agent has partial but incomplete command of the action-outcome mapping, so that marginal effort yields the largest increase in ℰ \mathcal{E} . Fully mastered contingencies offer zero marginal empowerment; wholly uncontrollable dynamics offer zero as well. Csikszentmihalyi’s flow state 18 may mark the joint optimum where both gradients are steepest–the task is simultaneously learnable-but-not-yet-learned and controllable-but-not-yet-controlled. The empowerment framework makes strong predictions about what happens when the action-outcome channel degenerates, and these predictions are borne out across species. Learned helplessness 19 , 20 provides the paradigmatic case: organisms exposed to inescapable aversive stimulation–where I ( A ; S ′ ) ≈ 0 I(A;S') \approx 0 by experimental design–subsequently fail to learn avoidable escape, exhibit dramatically reduced exploration, and display depression-like symptomatology including anhedonia, passivity, and appetite disruption. In information-theoretic terms, persistent experience of a zero-capacity channel causes the agent to update its generative model such that empowerment is near-zero across the state space, collapsing the motivational gradient that would normally drive action selection. The connection to clinical depression is well established: the reformulated helplessness theory’s emphasis on attributional style–global, stable, internal attributions for uncontrollable events 21 –can be read as the agent’s generative model overgeneralizing the zero-empowerment estimate from one context to the entire state space, a catastrophic prior update that renders all actions equally futile. At the trait and cognitive level, empowerment surfaces as stable beliefs about controllability that modulate behavioral engagement. Bandura’s self-efficacy construct–the belief that one can execute the actions required to produce desired outcomes 22 –predicts whether coping behavior is initiated, how much effort is expended, and how long the agent persists under difficulty; in channel-capacity terms, self-efficacy is a meta-estimate of one’s own empowerment, and low self-efficacy functions analogously to a low estimated ℰ \mathcal{E} that preemptively suppresses policy search. Rotter’s locus of control 23 captures a similar dimension: whether the agent models outcomes as contingent on its own actions (internal locus, high estimated I ( A ; S ′ ) I(A;S') ) versus determined by luck, chance, or powerful others (external locus, low estimated I ( A ; S ′ ) I(A;S') ). Langer’s (1975) illusion of control findings–where subjects behave as if they exert causal influence over demonstrably chance events 24 –suggest the empowerment computation is systematically biased toward overestimation, consistent with an asymmetric loss function in which underestimating controllability (risking learned helplessness) is more fitness-costly than overestimating it; the bias is strongest when situational cues resemble skill contexts (choice, competition, familiarity), indicating that the system defaults to an agency-assuming prior that must be actively overridden by strong evidence of uncontrollability. Self-determination theory identifies competence (perceived effectance over the environment) and autonomy (perceived self-causation of behavior) as two of three basic psychological needs whose satisfaction is necessary for wellbeing and whose frustration reliably impairs intrinsic motivation 25 , 26 . The overjustification effect –the well-replicated finding that tangible external rewards undermine pre-existing intrinsic motivation 27 , 28 –is particularly telling: when the perceived locus of causality shifts from internal to external, the agent’s estimate of its own channel capacity decreases (it models itself as a passive conduit for externally specified behaviors rather than an autonomous source of causal influence), and intrinsic motivation collapses accordingly. Collectively, these phenomena suggest that organisms continuously monitor and defend their empowerment, and that sustained deprivation of controllability produces motivational and affective pathology that is not reducible to the absence of reward. Across taxa, organisms exhibit strategies for amplifying channel capacity beyond the limits of their native actuator-sensor loop, and these strategies scale from concrete sensorimotor extensions to abstract institutional design. Tool use –documented in corvids, primates, cetaceans, and other lineages 29 –literally expands the set of physically reachable states: a chimpanzee wielding a stick probe can access food items that are unreachable without it, directly increasing H ( S t + k | s t ) H(S_{t+k}|s_t) , and the drive to acquire, cache, and iteratively refine tools is consistent with an agent that assigns intrinsic value to states of higher empowerment independent of any single consummatory goal. Territorial behavior can be similarly reframed: maintaining exclusive access to a spatial domain ensures continued access to a diversity of resource patches and microhabitats (preserving high reachable-state entropy) while excluding competitors whose presence would inject stochastic disruption into the action-outcome mapping (increasing H ( S t + k | s t , A t : t + k ) H(S_{t+k}|s_t, A_{t:t+k}) as a noise source). Similarly, niche construction can be viewed as the externalization of empowerment: by building nests, roads, or writing systems, organisms restructure the physical world to lower the conditional entropy of future interactions ( H ( S | A ) H(S|A) ). A paved road, unlike a chaotic forest floor, ensures that a specific motor command ( a s t e p a_{step} ) results in a highly predictable displacement ( s l o c s_{loc} ), thereby increasing the reliability of the agent-environment channel. In humans, the empowerment drive appears to generalize far beyond sensorimotor contingencies. The robust preference for choice –demonstrated even in non-human animals such as pigeons 30 and monkeys and rats 31 –persists even when additional options do not improve expected outcomes, reflecting valuation of the state-space entropy term itself rather than any particular reachable state. Langer’s (1975) illusion of control findings–where subjects behave as if they exert causal influence over demonstrably chance events 24 –suggest the empowerment computation is systematically biased toward overestimation, consistent with an asymmetric loss function in which underestimating controllability (risking learned helplessness) is more fitness-costly than overestimating it. At the largest scale, distinctly human capacities for cumulative culture and institutional design can be read as mechanisms for abstract empowerment preservation : the accumulation of resources and skills beyond immediate need, the invention of property rights that formalize exclusive state-access, financial instruments that convert current assets into diversified future options, and political freedoms that protect the individual’s channel capacity against coercive reduction–all suggest that empowerment maximization, once liberated from concrete sensorimotor channels by model-based cognition, becomes a dominant organizing principle of human behavioral ecology.

title: Computational Requirements and Neuro-Evolutionary Implementation
text: Realizing empowerment as a real-time intrinsic drive imposes a demanding set of computational requirements. Unlike a simple reward signal that can be read off a scalar afferent (e.g., blood glucose), empowerment is a derived information-theoretic quantity: it requires the agent to internally represent a causal model of its own action-outcome channel , estimate entropies over high-dimensional future state distributions, and solve an optimization over action distributions–all before empowerment can even serve as a motivational signal to guide policy selection. The core computational primitives can be decomposed as follows.

title: (1) An intrinsic motivational signal
text: (1) An intrinsic motivational signal: empowerment as a dopaminergically encoded drive. Empowerment cannot shape behavior unless the organism has some way to value increases in control: the system must convert "this state affords many reliably distinct futures" into an intrinsically appetitive signal that biases attention, exploration, and action selection. Classical motivation theories propose that organisms are not only driven by homeostatic deficits but also by an "effectance/competence" tendency to seek mastery and causal efficacy, and later work frames autonomy/competence as basic psychological needs–suggesting an evolution-installed preference for being an effective cause in the world, even when immediate extrinsic reward is absent 1 , 2 . Empirically, infants rapidly learn action → \rightarrow outcome contingencies in paradigms like the mobile conjugate reinforcement task and show physiological/affective reactivity when contingency is violated (nonreinforcement), consistent with an early-emerging valuation of controllability (though this does not, by itself, resolve whether it is present "from birth" versus learned extremely quickly) 3 , 4 . Importantly, even if the initial bias is weak or purely "curiosity-like," dopaminergic TD learning can rapidly bootstrap empowerment into a proxy for long-run reward : states and policies that expand controllable futures tend to (i) increase the chance of encountering extrinsic rewards, (ii) enable flexible switching when goals change, and (iii) reduce the expected cost of adverse events–so repeated experience causes value to back up onto high-empowerment regions of state space (see "Neuromodulators" for TD/RPE details and how evolution shaped dopaminergic circuits) 5 , 6 . Recent evidence that dopamine can carry value-free action -prediction errors (teaching which actions reliably produce which outcomes, not only which outcomes are rewarding) further supports a mechanistic bridge from "learn the channel" to "value the channel" 7 , 8 .

title: (2) A forward (generative) model of transition dynamics
text: (2) A forward (generative) model of transition dynamics, P ( s t + k ∣ s t , a t : t + k ) P(s_{t+k} \mid s_t, a_{t:t+k}) . Empowerment is defined over the actuator-sensor channel , which means the agent must possess an internal model that predicts how the sensory state will change as a function of actions emitted from the current state. This is the same generative/forward model required by EFE minimization and model-based planning more broadly, but empowerment places a specific demand on its interventional fidelity: the model must accurately capture how outcomes differentially change across the full action repertoire, not merely predict the most likely next state under a default policy. In causal-inference terms, empowerment requires a model of P ( s ′ ∣ d o ( a ) , s ) P(s' \mid \mathrm{do}(a), s) –an interventional distribution–rather than the merely observational P ( s ′ ∣ s ) P(s' \mid s) that suffices for passive prediction 1 . In realistic partially observed settings, this requirement lifts to the agent’s inferred state: the forward model must propagate a latent/belief representation (e.g., P ( z t + 1 ∣ z t , a t ) P(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,a_t) with an observation model P ( o t ∣ z t ) P(o_t\mid z_t) , or directly P ( b t + k ∣ b t , a t : t + k ) P(b_{t+k}\mid b_t,a_{t:t+k}) ), since controllability estimates are otherwise confounded by hidden variables and perceptual aliasing 2 . For the multi-step case ( k > 1 k>1 ), this all requires either an explicit k k -step rollout through the transition model (compounding approximation errors at each step 3 ) or a learned "jumpy" model that directly predicts P ( s t + k ∣ s t , a t : t + k ) P(s_{t+k} \mid s_t, a_{t:t+k}) without intermediate unrolling–a substantial function-approximation challenge given the exponential growth of the action-sequence space. Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior? The brain implements action-conditional forward models at multiple hierarchical levels, with architecturally distinct systems covering different temporal horizons and abstraction scales. At the fastest timescale, the cerebellum functions as a dedicated forward model for sensorimotor dynamics, acquiring paired inverse-forward controller modules (learned as internal models of limb/plant dynamics) that predict the sensory consequences of motor commands on the order of tens to hundreds of milliseconds 4 , 5 . Critically, the interventional character demanded by empowerment–prediction under do(a) rather than passive observation–is secured by the efference copy / corollary discharge architecture : motor commands routed to the periphery simultaneously send an efference copy to predictive circuits (via cerebellum, thalamus, and sensory cortex), allowing the system to distinguish self-caused from externally caused state changes and thereby maintain a genuinely action-indexed transition model 6 . This wiring is an evolutionary architectural prior–corollary discharge pathways are phylogenetically ancient, identifiable in invertebrates and conserved across vertebrate taxa 6 –meaning that the brain does not need to learn that actions have causal consequences on sensory input; only the specific parameters of those consequences require experience-dependent calibration. For longer-horizon, more abstract forward modelling, the hippocampal-entorhinal system and prefrontal cortex jointly support multi-step rollout through mental simulation. Hippocampal "preplay" and replay sequences sweep through place- and concept-cell assemblies in compressed time, effectively unrolling candidate action trajectories through a learned cognitive map of state space 7 , 8 , while prefrontal networks maintain and evaluate the predicted outcomes of these trajectories in working memory. The hippocampal system naturally operates over latent/belief representations rather than raw sensory input–place cells, grid cells, and object-vector cells encode allocentric spatial and relational structure abstracted away from immediate sensory particulars 9 , 10 –satisfying the requirement for forward modeling over inferred states P ( z t + 1 ∣ z t , a t ) P(z_{t+1}∣z_t,a_t) . Evolutionarily, the entorhinal-hippocampal loop architecture, the fixed theta-phase organization that temporally structures look-ahead sequences 11 , and the grid-cell lattice geometry itself 12 all constitute architectural priors that scaffold rapid acquisition of structured world models without specifying their content. The brain thus addresses the multi-step rollout problem not through a single mechanism but via a hierarchy: fast, precise cerebellar forward models for immediate sensorimotor consequences, and hippocampal-prefrontal simulation for more abstract, temporally extended (k>>1) action-contingent prediction–with evidence suggesting that the latter may also learn "jumpy" abstractions at the level of temporally extended options or subgoals rather than exclusively performing step-by-step unrolling 13 , 14 .

title: (3) Entropy estimation over continuous, high-dimensional state spaces
(4) Channel-capacity optimization
text: (4) Channel-capacity optimization: maximizing I ( A ; S ′ ) I(A;S') over the action distribution p ( a ) p(a) . Empowerment is not mere mutual information but the supremum of mutual information over all possible input (action) distributions–it is formally a channel capacity 1 . This is a constrained optimization problem: find the p * ( a ) p^*(a) that maximizes I ( A t : t + k ; S t + k ∣ s t ) I(A_{t:t+k}; S_{t+k} \mid s_t) subject to the constraint that p ( a ) p(a) is a valid distribution. In classical information theory, this is solved by the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm, an iterative alternating-maximization procedure that converges to the capacity-achieving input distribution 2 , 3 . For continuous action spaces, variational lower bounds on mutual information provide a tractable alternative: variational information maximization replaces the intractable marginalization with a learned "planning" distribution q ϕ ( a t : t + k ∣ s t + k , s t ) q_\phi(a_{t:t+k} \mid s_{t+k}, s_t) that approximates the true posterior over actions given the achieved outcome, yielding a lower bound ℰ ( s t ) ≥ 𝔼 p ( a ) p ( s ′ | s , a ) [ log ⁡ q ϕ ( a ∣ s ′ , s ) ] + H ( A ) \mathcal{E}(s_t) \geq \mathbb{E}_{p(a)p(s'|s,a)}[\log q_\phi(a \mid s', s)] + H(A) that can be optimized end-to-end via gradient ascent 4 . This variational formulation is significant because it factorizes the empowerment computation into two learnable components: a source model p θ ( a ∣ s ) p_\theta(a \mid s) that proposes actions (playing the role of the capacity-achieving input distribution), and a planning/inverse model q ϕ ( a ∣ s ′ , s ) q_\phi(a \mid s', s) that "decodes" which action sequence was responsible for a given state transition (playing the role of the optimal receiver in the channel-coding analogy). Biologically, this decomposition maps naturally onto the distinction between a policy generator ("what actions are available from here?") and an inverse model ("what action would produce that outcome?")– both of which have well-attested neural substrates in premotor and cerebellar circuits 5 , 6 . Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior? The most "direct" biological substrate for channel-capacity optimization is the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical (CBGTC) loop architecture, which evolution appears to have specialized as a generic distribution-shaping engine over actions. Rather than selecting a single motor command, basal ganglia circuits implement competition, normalization, and gating over action candidates proposed in cortex–exactly the kind of machinery needed to approximate an optimizer over p ( a ) p(a) under constraints ( ∑ a p ( a ) = 1 \sum_ap(a)=1 , nonnegativity). Striatum can represent many candidate policies in parallel from high-dimensional cortical state/context, while pallidal output and thalamic gating determine which channels are disinhibited, effectively reallocating probability mass over actions instead of executing a rigid argmax 7 , 8 , 9 . In the variational empowerment view, capacity optimization factorizes into a source/proposal policy p θ ( a t : t + k | s t ) p_\theta(a_{t:t+k}|s_t) and an inverse "decoder" q ϕ ( a t : t + k | s t + k , s t ) q_\phi(a_{t:t+k}|s_{t+k},s_t) that measures how uniquely an action sequence can be inferred from the resulting state (i.e., "decodability"). Neuroanatomically, p θ p_\theta is naturally implemented by fronto-premotor policy manifolds (PMd/SMA/M1, plus parietal affordance maps) feeding into striatal channels that compete for gating. The key missing piece is q ϕ q_\phi : the brain needs circuitry that can rapidly answer "what action would have produced that outcome from this state?" and do so with graded uncertainty. That inverse-model role is plausibly realized by a cerebellum + cortical inverse-model stack . The cerebellum is well-suited to act as an inverse/forward model workhorse because of its massive expansion of granule cells, supervised error-driven plasticity, and tight coupling to motor and premotor targets; classic sensorimotor-control accounts explicitly frame cerebellar modules as learning internal models that support both prediction and inversion (command inference) 6 , 10 , 5 . But inverse modeling is not purely cerebellar: cortical circuits–especially posterior parietal cortex (PPC), premotor cortex, and prefrontal cortex–encode action goals, effectors, and action-effect mappings in a way that supports "goal->motor command(s)" transformations (e.g., reach-to-target transforms), providing a higher-level inverse model over abstract actions and outcomes, while cerebellum supplies fast, calibrated inversion at the fine-grained motor level 6 , 5 . Inverse modeling matters because the variational lower bound contains 𝔼 [ l o g q ϕ ( a | s ′ , s ) ] \mathbb{E}[logq_\phi(a|s',s)] : it rewards policies whose outcomes make the responsible action easy to decode. Biologically, that "decodability reward" can be instantiated as inverse-model confidence/precision . When cerebellar + parietal/premotor inverse models return a sharp posterior over actions (high certainty about which command produced the transition), the system is implicitly detecting low conditional entropy H ( S ′ | s , A ) H(S'|s,A) ’ when the inverse model is uncertain (many actions could have produced similar outcomes), conditional entropy is high. Thus, empowerment-relevant gradients can be supplied not by explicit MI computation but by how confidently the inverse stack can attribute outcomes to actions . The basal ganglia then provide the optimization substrate that can use this signal. Cortico-striatal plasticity–shaped by dopamine–can reinforce action channels that yield transitions with high inverse-model confidence while maintaining diversity via neuromodulatory control of exploration "temperature." The STN-GP system (see "Cortico-Basal Ganglia-Thalamo-Cortical Loops") offers a stabilizing prior (global inhibition / threshold control) that prevents premature collapse of p ( a ) p(a) onto a single mode when multiple distinct futures are available, functionally resembling normalization/regularization in distributional optimization 11 . In parallel, LC-NE (and tonic dopamine) can modulate gain and stochasticity, acting as the biological knob that trades off sharp exploitation vs high-entropy coverage 12 , 13 . In sum, the evolutionary "architectural prior" is a three-part motif: (i) CBGTC loops that maintain and reshape a distribution over actions, (ii) a cerebellum + cortical inverse-model stack (cerebellar microcomplexes plus PPC/premotor goal-to-command transforms) that supplies a fast, graded decodability/precision signal approximating the l o g q ϕ logq_\phi term, and (iii) neuromodulatory temperature control that keeps the optimizer from collapsing, enabling the system to approximate channel-capacity optimization without explicitly running Blahut-Arimoto in neural tissue 7 , 6 , 12 .
