title: (5) A cached empowerment landscape
text: (5) A cached empowerment landscape, ℰ ̂ ( s ) \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) . Computing empowerment from scratch at every encountered state via forward-model rollout and channel-capacity optimization is computationally prohibitive for real-time decision-making. A more plausible architecture maintains a learned value map ℰ ̂ : 𝒮 → ℝ \hat{\mathcal{E}}: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} that caches empowerment estimates across the state space, updated incrementally as the agent explores and refines its forward model. This cached landscape then serves as a pseudo-reward or intrinsic value function that can be queried rapidly during action selection: the agent can evaluate candidate next states by looking up ℰ ̂ ( s ′ ) \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s') rather than re-solving the channel-capacity problem de novo . Such a representation is analogous to the successor representation (SR) 1 , which caches expected future state occupancy. Just as the SR allows rapid recomputation of value under changing reward functions by separating "what states will I visit?" from "how rewarding are they?," a cached empowerment map separates "how controllable is this region?" from the current goal, enabling the agent to navigate toward high-empowerment states as a background policy even when the primary objective is defined by other terms (e.g., EFE risk minimization). Maintaining this landscape requires ongoing calibration: as the agent’s motor skills improve (expanding the action repertoire) or as the environment changes (altering transition dynamics), previously cached ℰ ̂ \hat{\mathcal{E}} values become stale, necessitating a mechanism for empowerment prediction errors –discrepancies between expected and experienced controllability–that trigger local re-estimation, much as reward prediction errors trigger value function updates in temporal-difference learning. Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior? The neural substrate for a cached empowerment landscape requires three things: (i) a state-indexed memory that covers the environment and supports smooth generalization to unvisited states, (ii) a mechanism for associating controllability values with state representations, and (iii) a prediction-error signal for incremental re-estimation when cached values become stale. The hippocampal-entorhinal system provides a natural scaffold for (i). Beyond encoding a cognitive map, hippocampal place-cell representations exhibit properties consistent with the successor representation (SR): place fields are distorted by transition statistics under the agent’s policy, encoding expected future state occupancy rather than mere location 2 . This is significant because the SR at state s s implicitly encodes reachability structure–the diversity, depth, and probability of states accessible from s s under the current policy–which is precisely the substrate from which empowerment can be read. The rank and entropy of the SR row vector at s s reflect how many distinct futures the agent’s policy explores from that state; regions of state space with high-rank, high-entropy SR rows are exactly the high-empowerment regions. Grid cells in entorhinal cortex supply a multi-scale periodic basis set whose spatial frequencies correspond to eigenvectors of the SR 2 , 3 , providing a compressed, smoothly interpolable representation that enables generalization of cached ℰ ̂ \hat{\mathcal{E}} to states the agent has never physically occupied–the neural analogue of function approximation over a continuous value landscape. For (ii), the hippocampal formation projects densely to ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) and to orbitofrontal / ventromedial prefrontal cortex –regions canonically associated with state-value representation and model-based evaluation 4 , 5 . These projections supply the anatomical pathway for linking state representations to cached empowerment estimates: ventral striatum can store ℰ ̂ ( s ) \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) as a pseudo-reward value function via standard dopaminergic TD learning (see “Neuromodulators”), while OFC/vmPFC can maintain a more flexible, model-based empowerment estimate that updates when the agent’s world model is revised (e.g., after discovering that a door is now locked). The convergence of hippocampal state representations and midbrain dopaminergic teaching signals onto striatal medium spiny neurons is a phylogenetically ancient wiring motif, conserved across amniotes, that evolution has repurposed for caching many forms of state value–empowerment included. Maintaining ℰ ̂ \hat{\mathcal{E}} across a large state space requires offline propagation to states the agent has not recently visited. Hippocampal sharp-wave ripple (SWR)-associated replay provides exactly this: compressed reactivation of trajectory sequences during rest and sleep drives simulated “experience” at distant states, enabling TD-like updates to propagate empowerment estimates across the cognitive map without physical traversal 6 , 7 . Evidence that replay is prioritized toward trajectories with large unsigned prediction errors or high information gain 7 suggests a natural mechanism for concentrating ℰ ̂ \hat{\mathcal{E}} re-estimation on regions where cached controllability values are most likely stale–e.g., near recently changed environmental affordances or newly acquired motor skills. For (iii), the empowerment prediction error –the discrepancy between cached ℰ ̂ ( s ) \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) and controllability as actually experienced upon arrival–can be carried by dopaminergic RPE signals if empowerment contributes to intrinsic value (see bullet 1 above). But a more specific controllability-monitoring circuit exists in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly prelimbic / anterior cingulate regions. Maier and Seligman’s revised learned-helplessness model argues that mPFC actively detects when outcomes are controllable (instrumentally contingent on actions) and, upon such detection, inhibits default passivity and anxiety-like responses originating from dorsal raphe serotonergic projections and amygdala 8 . This mPFC circuit is functionally a controllability monitor : it signals whether the current state affords causal influence, which is exactly what empowerment measures. Discrepancies between mPFC’s real-time controllability assessment and the cached landscape value could thus serve as the trigger for re-estimation of ℰ ̂ \hat{\mathcal{E}} in the relevant region of state space, analogous to how RPEs trigger value-function updates in reward-based TD learning. The evolutionary architectural priors are therefore: (i) the hippocampal-entorhinal cognitive map (place cells, grid cells, boundary cells) supplying a structured, SR-like state scaffold over which controllability values can be smoothly cached and generalized; (ii) the hippocampal → \rightarrow ventral striatum and hippocampal → \rightarrow OFC projection motifs that wire state representations to value-caching circuits; (iii) SWR-replay machinery for offline, prioritized value propagation; and (iv) the mPFC controllability-detection circuit for generating empowerment prediction errors. All four are phylogenetically conserved–the hippocampal formation is homologous across mammals (with antecedents in reptilian medial pallium), the mesolimbic dopamine system is ancient, and mPFC controllability circuitry appears shared across mammalian orders 8 . The organism thus arrives equipped not with a pre-computed empowerment landscape but with the architectural scaffold to rapidly construct, cache, maintain, and update one through experience–converting a computationally prohibitive on-line optimization into an incrementally refined lookup.

title: (6) An action-outcome repertoire
text: (6) An action-outcome repertoire: representing a hierarchical skill library Channel capacity depends critically on the size and structure of the input "alphabet"–the set of distinguishable actions the agent can emit. Empowerment computation therefore requires the agent to maintain an inventory of its available action primitives and, crucially, to represent which actions are functionally distinct in their state-space consequences (since two motor commands that produce identical outcomes contribute nothing to channel capacity). This connects empowerment to the concept of option discovery in reinforcement learning 1 : acquiring new temporally extended action primitives (options, skills, macro-actions) that produce reliably distinct outcomes effectively increases the alphabet size of the control channel, directly boosting the achievable empowerment. On this view, skill acquisition is channel expansion : each new reliably executable skill adds a new "symbol" to the action alphabet, increasing ℰ \mathcal{E} by enabling the agent to reach states that were previously inaccessible or indistinguishable. The hierarchical organization of motor control–from low-level muscle synergies to high-level action plans 2 –can then be understood as a multi-resolution encoding of the action channel: low-level primitives provide fine-grained but local controllability, while high-level skills ("go to the kitchen," "build a shelter") provide coarse but far-reaching causal influence over temporally distant states, and empowerment at different planning horizons k k is maximized by operating at the appropriate level of the hierarchy. Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior? The brain’s action repertoire is organized as a genetically scaffolded hierarchy of motor representations, each level contributing a distinct "alphabet layer" to the control channel. At the base, spinal central pattern generators (CPGs) and brainstem motor nuclei define a set of phylogenetically ancient, largely innate motor primitives–locomotor rhythms, postural synergies, orofacial patterns, reaching-and-grasping coordination–that constitute the organism’s factory-installed action alphabet 3 , 4 . Muscle synergies –low-dimensional patterns of co-activation across muscles that can be recombined to produce a wide range of behaviors–provide one influential description of this compression: many natural motor outputs can be approximated by combinations of a modest set of such patterns rather than independent control of each muscle 5 . However, the extent to which synergies should be interpreted as discrete, hardwired control "units" versus emergent regularities shaped by biomechanics, task constraints, and learning remains an active debate; a conservative statement is that early spinal/brainstem circuitry provides strong structural constraints on coordination, while development, exploration, and practice refine and reshape the effective basis over time 4 , 5 . Thus, the channel’s lowest-level "alphabet" is available very early, but it is not purely fixed: it is progressively tuned by experience as cortical and subcortical learning systems come online 3 , 4 . Above this base layer, primary motor cortex (M1) and a premotor/medial motor hierarchy (PMd, PMv, SMA, pre-SMA) participate in control at longer timescales and higher levels of abstraction, as established by genetically specified areal boundaries, laminar connectivity motifs, and corticospinal projection patterns 6 , 7 . While the precise mapping is not strictly one-to-one (each area is multifunctional and highly interactive), a broadly supported functional division is: M1 is most tightly linked to movement execution and relatively fine-grained parameters (force, velocity, direction for specific effectors); dorsal/ventral premotor areas (PMd/PMv) contribute to action preparation and selection in terms of goals, targets, and grasp/hand configurations (actions in the behavioral rather than muscular sense); SMA is especially implicated in internally generated actions and the organization/ordering of learned action sequences; and pre-SMA and rostral prefrontal areas are more strongly recruited when selecting or switching action sets under abstract task demands ("which kind of action policy to engage") 6 , 7 . In this framing, each level provides a progressively more abstract "alphabet" (from fast coordination patterns to action plans to sequence structure to task-level control), and higher-level selections bias and constrain lower-level motor release through dense corticocortical and cortico-subcortical interactions rather than a purely serial top-down chain 6 , 7 . A key mechanism for effective channel expansion –in the sense of creating new, distinguishable, reusable action units that can be selected as if they were single primitives at a higher temporal grain–is action-sequence chunking in dorsal striatum (dorsolateral striatum in rodents; putamen in primates). With repetition, cortico-striatal circuits come to treat a multi-element sequence as a unitized behavioral object: neural activity in sensorimotor striatum evolves from broadly tracking many elements to exhibiting characteristic boundary or "bracketing” signals (selective responses at sequence initiation/termination), consistent with a learned delimiter-like representation of the chunk 8 , 9 , 10 . This phenomenon is strongly dopamine-linked, reinforcing the view that chunk formation is shaped by reinforcement-modulated plasticity in BG loops 9 , 11 , 12 . Functionally, once a sequence is chunked it can be gated, competed over, and released by cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuitry more like a single temporally extended action than a chain that must be re-planned element-by-element 13 , 8 . This is the neural instantiation of skill acquisition as channel expansion –each consolidated chunk adds a new entry to the action alphabet at its hierarchical level, enabling causal influence over more temporally distant states without requiring step-by-step planning through the primitive action space. Cerebellar learning plays a complementary role. The cerebellum is strongly implicated in acquiring and refining predictive internal models (forward/inverse computations) that support fast, low-latency, feedforward calibration of movement dynamics and error-based fine-tuning of execution 14 , 15 . In human sequence-skill learning, extended practice often shows a network reweighting in which early learning recruits cerebellar-cortical components more strongly, whereas later, well-learned performance increasingly engages sensorimotor putamen/striatum and shows reduced cerebellar cortical involvement (with phase-dependent changes in deep cerebellar contributions), consistent with a division of labor: BG contributes to selection/serialization and chunk-level control , while cerebellar circuitry supports predictive execution and refinement 16 , 17 , 18 . On evolutionary timescales, the disproportionate expansion of the cerebellum in anthropoid primates and especially humans is well supported, and this expansion includes cerebellar regions coupled to prefrontal systems rather than being purely "motor" 19 , 20 . A conservative interpretation consistent with these data is that cerebellar enlargement reflects an evolutionary investment in scalable predictive modeling and automatization across large repertoires of sensorimotor (and likely cognitive) skills–increasing the brain’s capacity to deploy well-calibrated, rapidly executable control policies once they are learned, while BG loops remain available for continued acquisition and selection of new chunked action structures 15 , 20 . For empowerment, what matters is not the raw cardinality of the motor command set, but the functional discriminability of actions in their induced outcome distributions–i.e., whether different actions lead to reliably distinguishable future sensory states. This follows directly from the definition of empowerment as a channel capacity between actions and future states: actions that induce the same (or highly overlapping) conditional outcome distribution contribute little new information, whereas actions that induce separable outcome distributions increase the effective capacity of the action-outcome channel 21 , 22 , 23 . A plausible neural substrate for tracking this discriminability is the brain’s system for action-effect bindings (ideomotor "event files"): actions are represented together with their anticipated sensory consequences, enabling selection and learning in terms of what an action will cause rather than only the motor command itself 24 , 25 , 26 . Consistent with this framing, frontoparietal planning circuits can encode actions in terms of their expected/desired sensory outcomes: both posterior parietal cortex and dorsal premotor cortex carry information about the visual consequences of upcoming actions during preparation, and intraparietal regions are recruited when action preparation is organized around explicit effect representations 27 , 28 , 29 . In this view, two actions that are predicted (in a given context) to yield indistinguishable outcomes will be informationally redundant at the level of empowerment, even if their motor commands differ, because they map to overlapping outcome codes; conversely, a newly acquired skill that produces a reliably novel outcome distribution effectively adds a new distinguishable action-outcome mapping and thus increases the channel’s effective alphabet at that abstraction level 21 , 27 . Posterior parietal cortex (especially intraparietal sulcus) is well positioned for this computation because it lies at the convergence of sensory state representations and motor-intention/planning signals, and is centrally implicated in parietal-frontal circuits for intention, sensorimotor decision-making, and state estimation–the kinds of representations needed to evaluate the diversity/structure of the action → \rightarrow outcome mapping that governs channel capacity 30 , 31 , 32 . The evolutionary architectural priors for the action-outcome repertoire are therefore: (i) spinal CPGs and brainstem nuclei providing a (more or less) genetically specified base alphabet of motor primitives and synergies; (ii) the cortical motor hierarchy (M1 → \rightarrow PMd/SMA → \rightarrow pre-SMA → \rightarrow PFC) establishing a graded abstraction axis with genetically specified areal differentiation and hierarchical connectivity; (iii) the parallel CBGTC loop architecture supporting simultaneous maintenance and competitive selection of action repertoires at multiple temporal scales; (iv) cortico-striatal chunking plasticity rules (dopamine-gated Hebbian learning at cortico-striatal synapses) enabling experiential expansion of the alphabet through sequence consolidation; (v) massive cerebellar circuitry for automating consolidated skills and thereby freeing BG capacity for continued hierarchical repertoire growth; and (vi) premotor-parietal action-effect binding networks that track the functional discriminability of the repertoire. The organism is thus born not with a fixed action alphabet but with an expandable, hierarchically organized channel architecture whose initial symbols are genetically installed (reflexes, synergies, CPGs) and whose capacity for alphabet growth–the rate and depth at which new skills can be chunked, consolidated, and stacked–is itself the key evolutionary prior that determines the ceiling on achievable empowerment across the lifespan.

title: (7) A controllability monitor
text: (7) A controllability monitor: online estimation of I ( A ; S ′ ) I(A;S') and detection of channel degradation. The behavioral evidence reviewed above–the anger response to contingency extinction in infants, learned helplessness, the defense of autonomy–implies that the agent does not merely compute empowerment prospectively for planning purposes but also monitors it retrospectively as a running diagnostic. This requires a mechanism that continuously tracks the realized mutual information between recent actions and observed outcomes, compares it against an expected baseline ℰ ̂ ( s t ) \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s_t) , and generates an empowerment prediction error signal δ ℰ = I ̂ ( A recent ; S recent ′ ) − ℰ ̂ ( s t ) \delta_{\mathcal{E}} = \hat{I}(A_{\text{recent}}; S'_{\text{recent}}) - \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s_t) when the experienced controllability deviates from expectation. A positive δ ℰ \delta_{\mathcal{E}} ("I have more control than expected") would reinforce the current state and policy, while a negative δ ℰ \delta_{\mathcal{E}} ("I have less control than expected") would signal alarm and motivate either (a) a change in policy to restore controllability, (b) a revision of the forward model (perhaps the dynamics have changed), or (c) retreat to a previously known high-empowerment state. This dual prospective/retrospective architecture mirrors the structure of reward processing in dopaminergic circuits, where anticipated value guides policy selection while temporal-difference errors drive learning–suggesting that empowerment monitoring may piggyback on (or operate in parallel with) the same neurocomputational machinery. Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior? The controllability-monitoring requirement is functionally distinct from the cached-landscape update described in (5): rather than offline re-estimation of ℰ ̂ ( s ) \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) , it demands a real-time, retrospective diagnostic that tracks whether recent actions are exerting a causal influence on subsequent outcomes. Computationally, this corresponds to continuously accumulating evidence for the action-dependent component of state transitions–e.g., comparing an "actor" model P ( s ′ ∣ s , a ) P(s' \mid s,a) against a "spectator" model P ( s ′ ∣ s ) P(s' \mid s) to form a running controllability statistic that is closely related to transfer entropy / conditional mutual information (a graded estimate of how much knowing a a reduces uncertainty about s ′ s' beyond s s alone) 1 , 2 . When this statistic drops (outcomes become increasingly action-independent), the system should generate graded motivational/affective signals and bias policy selection toward information-gathering or control-restoring actions 1 . The architecture can be decomposed into (a) a contingency-tracking circuit for controllability inference, (b) a fast sensorimotor agency-detection layer, (c) signed update/error pathways that drive the running estimate, and (d) behavioral/affective readout. (a) Core contingency tracker: medial PFC-centered, with ACC contributions. Evidence suggests that online controllability inference is implemented by a distributed medial network rather than a single locus: medial prefrontal regions are repeatedly implicated in estimating controllability/causal influence, with convergent support for additional nodes (e.g., temporoparietal and salience-network contributions) that carry controllability update signals. Within this network, dACC is strongly supported as a controller of control allocation –computing an expected value of control by integrating the expected payoff of exerting control against its costs, and adjusting control intensity accordingly 3 . Separately, contingency-learning work shows that medial prefrontal/ACC circuitry is causally involved in sensitivity to instrumental contingency (e.g., deficits in adapting behavior when action-outcome contingencies are degraded), consistent with maintaining a running dependence measure that cannot be reduced to single-trial prediction errors 4 , 5 . Finally, dACC/adjacent medial regions encode volatility/uncertainty signals and relate to dynamic learning-rate adjustment, which is consistent with (though not uniquely diagnostic of) maintaining and updating a temporally smoothed controllability statistic over a recent window 6 . Taken together, a parsimonious interpretation is that medial PFC supports controllability inference (actor-spectator divergence / TE-like accumulation), while dACC additionally translates inferred controllability into control-demand and allocation signals (how much control to exert, and when) 3 , 6 . (b) Sense-of-agency circuitry as fast, lower-level contingency detection. Below the level of deliberative controllability inference, the brain implements a rapid, largely automatic mechanism for estimating whether sensory consequences match action-generated predictions. In classical forward-model terms, an efference-copy / corollary-discharge signal generates predicted reafference, and a comparator evaluates the match between predicted and observed sensory input; systematic prediction error attenuates the feeling that "I caused this" 7 , 8 . Critically, sense of agency is well-described as multilevel : low-level sensorimotor prediction errors contribute to a pre-reflective feeling of agency , which then informs higher-level, context-sensitive judgments of agency 9 , 8 . Neuroimaging and perturbation paradigms repeatedly implicate the angular gyrus / temporoparietal junction (TPJ) in agency attribution, especially under conditions that reduce self-agency (e.g., visuomotor delays/perturbations) and promote external attribution; angular gyrus activity tracks awareness of action–outcome discrepancies and supports the interpretation of events as self- vs other-caused 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 . In an empowerment framing, persistent comparator mismatch constitutes a fast, graded indicator that the local action-outcome channel has degraded at the sensorimotor level, providing evidence that can be integrated by slower, higher-level contingency/controllability monitors (e.g., medial prefrontal systems jointly implicated with TPJ in controllability estimation) rather than requiring a full offline re-estimation of ℰ ̂ ( s ) \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) . (c) Signed empowerment-prediction-error pathways. Translating a controllability deviation signal δ ℰ \delta_{\mathcal{E}} into motivational output plausibly recruits multiple neuromodulatory systems, with partially dissociable roles for valence versus change detection . While "empowerment prediction error" is a computational synthesis, the underlying ingredients are well-supported: (i) circuits that detect loss of control and induce passive/avoidant states, (ii) classical dopaminergic prediction errors that reinforce unexpectedly valuable states/actions (which can include perceived control), and (iii) LC-NE responses to unexpected environmental change that upregulate gain/attention irrespective of sign 15 , 16 , 17 . Negative δ ℰ \delta_{\mathcal{E}} (loss of control). A central, causally supported pathway linking stressor controllability to behavioral shutdown is the vmPFC/mPFC → \rightarrow dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) circuit emphasized in modern learned-helplessness neuroscience. Under controllable stress, vmPFC is engaged and (via inhibitory microcircuits within DRN) suppresses stress-induced activation of serotonergic output; disrupting vmPFC engagement during escapable stress abolishes the protective effect and yields DRN activation and helplessness-like outcomes 15 , 18 . Conversely, when experienced controllability is low (or fails to recruit vmPFC control), DRN activity contributes to a syndrome of behavioral inhibition/passive coping and anxiety-like responding, with downstream influence over canonical defensive/affective targets (including midbrain and limbic effector systems) 15 , 19 . In parallel, the lateral habenula (LHb) provides a phylogenetically conserved aversive-signal hub that can suppress reward-related midbrain activity and couple uncontrollable stress to negative motivational states. Electrophysiology in primates supports LHb firing to worse-than-expected outcomes and downstream inhibition of dopaminergic neurons (notably via habenula → \rightarrow RMTg → \rightarrow VTA/SNc pathways) 20 , 21 . Moreover, LHb has direct functional influence on the DRN (including inhibitory effects on putative serotonergic neurons) and has been causally implicated in uncontrollable-stress phenotypes: LHb activation during uncontrollable stress predicts/mediates subsequent helplessness-like behavior, and inhibiting LHb output (including LHb → \rightarrow DRN projections) can reduce passive coping under high-stress conditions 22 , 23 , 24 . Finally, comparative neuroanatomy supports the habenula as a deeply conserved vertebrate forebrain relay, identifiable across jawed vertebrates, consistent with a "channel-degradation alarm" role that long predates mammalian cortex 25 . Positive δ ℰ \delta_{\mathcal{E}} (unexpected control). Discovery of greater controllability than predicted can, in principle, be reinforced if control carries intrinsic value: canonical phasic dopamine prediction errors in VTA/SNc reinforce unexpectedly better-than-expected states/actions and can train cached values and policies 26 . Human fMRI work further supports that perceived control/choice is intrinsically valued and engages corticostriatal valuation circuitry (ventral striatum, vmPFC), providing a plausible bridge by which increases in controllability could be treated as appetitive and thus dopaminergically reinforced 27 , 28 , 29 . Sign-indifferent channel-change detection (LC-NE). Independently of valence, sudden shifts in the action-outcome channel (controllability changes in either direction) constitute unexpected environmental change . The locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC–NE) system is strongly linked to phasic responses to salient/unexpected events and to global "network reset" / adaptive-gain modulation that elevates neural gain and reallocates attention to support rapid updating 30 , 31 , 32 . In this framing, LC-NE supplies a fast broadcast signal that mobilizes resources for re-estimation, while the signed motivational valence (appetitive vs. aversive) is primarily carried by dopaminergic versus stress/serotonergic (and habenular) pathways respectively 30 , 15 , 26 . (d) Behavioral/affective readout. The proposed circuitry predicts a characteristic phenomenology of controllability change. A sustained negative empowerment-prediction error (experienced controllability falling below expectation) shifts the organism toward aversive arousal, behavioral inhibition, and eventual passivity: in the learned-helplessness framework, controllability-sensitive mPFC regulation of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) gates the transition from active coping/exploration to inhibition-dominated responding under uncontrollable stress, while parallel habenula-centered "anti-reward" signaling tracks adverse outcome statistics and can promote helplessness-like shutdown when persistently engaged 18 , 33 , 15 . Consistent with this, plasticity and activity changes in the lateral habenula (LHb) are repeatedly observed in learned-helplessness paradigms and correlate with helplessness-like outcomes, positioning LHb as a convergent "channel degradation / negative value" node that can bias downstream monoaminergic systems toward withdrawal-dominant policies 34 , 35 . At shorter time scales, abrupt loss of expected contingency often manifests not as passivity but as protest/frustration : in the mobile / contingency learning literature, infants show an extinction burst (increased responding) and predominantly anger expressions when an expected response-contingent outcome is withdrawn–i.e., when an established action->outcome channel suddenly collapses 36 , 37 , 38 . This pattern aligns with "frustrative nonreward" as an aversive motivational state triggered by blocked expected outcomes, which is associated (in human and translational work) with recruitment of ACC/dACC-linked control/conflict systems and amygdala-linked affective salience systems during frustration/reward-omission tasks–plausibly an early, fast readout of negative δ ℰ \delta_{\mathcal{E}} that can precede (and, if prolonged, transition into) slower helplessness-like adaptations 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 . Finally, the "defense of autonomy" described in psychological reactance can be interpreted as a policy-level compensatory response to perceived channel restriction: freedom-threats reliably elicit motivational pressure to restore the constrained action options 43 , 44 . Neurocomputationally, this is naturally implemented by prefrontal-striatal valuation/control circuitry that treats having choice as intrinsically valuable (and scales engagement when choice is threatened), consistent with evidence that the opportunity to choose recruits ventral striatal and related corticostriatal systems, and that self-determined choice modulates performance-relevant control networks 45 , 46 . Evolutionary architectural priors (phylogenetic layering + "hard-wired" connectivity). A plausible evolutionary installation story is that controllability monitoring was not invented de novo in cortex, but assembled by stacking newer cortical inference on top of older vertebrate control machinery . Early nervous systems already required a fast distinction between self-caused versus external sensory change to stabilize movement and perception; this selects for efference-copy / corollary-discharge pathways and comparator-like circuits (brainstem/cerebellar-tectal sensorimotor loops) that flag persistent action–outcome mismatch as "loss of agency," providing the ancestral seed of the fast agency-detection layer (later elaborated into temporoparietal association cortex/TPJ–angular gyrus as multisensory agency attribution expanded in primates). In parallel, the vertebrate habenula → \rightarrow midbrain/raphe control axis is deeply conserved and is naturally suited as an ancient channel-degradation alarm : when outcomes become worse-than-expected or uncontrollable, it can rapidly bias global motivational state by suppressing dopamine (via RMTg/VTA pathways) and modulating serotonergic stress effector systems. Brainstem monoamine nuclei then provide the broadcast "operating modes" required by a monitor: LC–NE as a fast, sign-indifferent change detector / network reset that upregulates gain during contingency shifts, and DRN as a controllability-sensitive switch that (when not top-down regulated) promotes passive coping under sustained uncontrollability. Mammalian cortical expansion then adds the missing computational sophistication by building medial prefrontal–ACC circuits into pre-existing cortico–striato–thalamo–cortical loops : these loops are an evolutionarily convenient scaffold for (i) maintaining paired "actor vs. spectator" transition models, (ii) accumulating a temporally smoothed controllability statistic (TE/CMI-like), and (iii) converting it into control allocation via dACC’s cost–benefit machinery. Critically, evolution can "compile in" empowerment prediction errors by wiring these cortical inference nodes into the old neuromodulatory hubs (mPFC/vmPFC projections to DRN; ACC/striatal and habenular access to VTA/SNc; salience-network access to LC), so that loss of controllability automatically recruits aversive arousal/frustration (amygdala/salience + ACC) and, if prolonged, helplessness-like shutdown (DRN/LHb influence), while unexpected gains in control are treated as intrinsically valuable via dopaminergic reinforcement of the policies/states that restored contingency. Finally, the "defense of autonomy"/reactance phenotype becomes plausible once expanded prefrontal association cortex can represent counterfactual action sets and social constraints; evolution can then bias the system toward restoring threatened option sets by coupling those representations to the same prefrontal–striatal valuation circuitry that already assigns incentive value to opportunities for control and choice.

title: (8) A meta-cognitive self-model
text: (8) Meta-cognitive self-model: beliefs about one’s own channel capacity. The psychological constructs reviewed earlier–self-efficacy, locus of control, perceived autonomy–are not raw empowerment values but beliefs about empowerment : generalized, context-abstracted estimates of the agent’s capacity to influence outcomes. This implies a hierarchical representational structure in which the agent maintains not only state-by-state empowerment estimates ℰ ̂ ( s ) \hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) but also higher-order summary statistics: a trait-level prior P ( ℰ ) P(\mathcal{E}) reflecting the agent’s generalized expectation of controllability across contexts, and domain-specific priors P ( ℰ ∣ domain ) P(\mathcal{E} \mid \text{domain}) (e.g., "I am generally effective in social interactions but not in athletic contexts"). These meta-estimates function as priors on empowerment that modulate the agent’s willingness to engage with a new context before any direct empowerment estimation has occurred: an agent with a strong prior of high self-efficacy will enter novel situations and begin "probing the channel," while an agent with a helplessness-shaped prior ( P ( ℰ ) ≈ δ ( 0 ) P(\mathcal{E}) \approx \delta(0) ) will avoid engagement entirely, foreclosing the possibility of disconfirming evidence and creating the self-perpetuating motivational collapse observed in depression 1 . This meta-cognitive layer also introduces a learning rate problem: the prior must be responsive enough to update from new evidence of controllability (allowing recovery from helplessness via mastery experiences 2 ) but stable enough to resist transient fluctuations in experienced I ( A ; S ′ ) I(A;S') –and pathological states may correspond to miscalibrated learning rates (too fast → \rightarrow fragile confidence; too slow → \rightarrow entrenched helplessness). Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior? Maintaining hierarchical beliefs about one’s own channel capacity–a trait-level prior P ( ℰ ) P(\mathcal{E}) and domain-specific priors P ( ℰ ∣ domain ) P(\mathcal{E} \mid \text{domain}) –requires three architectural ingredients: (a) a self-referential representational substrate that encodes stable, context-abstracted properties of the agent itself (not just the current state of the world), (b) a hierarchical abstraction mechanism that distills episode-level empowerment experiences into progressively more general summary statistics, and (c) precision-weighted updating that controls how rapidly these meta-estimates revise in light of new controllability evidence. The neural substrate most consistently implicated in trait-level self-referential representation is medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) , particularly ventromedial and dorsomedial subdivisions. A large convergent literature–spanning fMRI self-referential judgment paradigms, lesion studies, and meta-analyses–supports that mPFC is preferentially recruited when subjects evaluate enduring self-attributes (personality traits, generalized competence beliefs, autobiographical identity) as opposed to other-referential or semantic judgments, and that damage to mPFC impairs the coherent organization of self-knowledge 3 , 4 , 5 . This positions mPFC as the natural locus for a generalized empowerment prior P ( ℰ ) P(\mathcal{E}) : it is the same region that (i) monitors real-time controllability (vmPFC → \rightarrow DRN gating, per bullet 7), and (ii) encodes generalized state value (vmPFC value signals in model-based decision-making), making it architecturally efficient for trait-level controllability beliefs to be stored within the same cortical territory that computes and acts on controllability signals online. mPFC does not operate in isolation but as the anterior midline hub of the default mode network (DMN) –a large-scale network (mPFC, posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus, angular gyrus/TPJ, hippocampal formation, lateral temporal cortex) that is reliably active during internally directed cognition: self-reflection, autobiographical memory retrieval, prospective simulation, and mentalizing 6 , 7 . The DMN’s functional profile is significant because constructing and maintaining a generalized self-model of controllability requires exactly the operations this network supports: retrieving episodic evidence of past control successes and failures (hippocampal autobiographical retrieval), simulating counterfactual scenarios to evaluate what one could have done (prospective/counterfactual simulation in mPFC–hippocampal circuits), and integrating these into context-abstracted summaries (midline convergence zones) 8 , 9 . The DMN thus provides the network-level scaffold for the meta-cognitive self-model: hippocampal episodic stores supply the evidence base (specific episodes of experienced controllability), while mPFC and posterior midline structures abstract across episodes to maintain and revise the trait-level prior. The hierarchy between trait-level and domain-specific priors maps onto the well-documented rostro-caudal abstraction gradient in prefrontal cortex: more posterior prefrontal regions (premotor, caudal lateral PFC) represent concrete, context-bound action-outcome contingencies, while progressively more anterior regions (rostral lateral PFC, frontopolar cortex, and medial PFC) represent increasingly abstract, temporally extended, and context-general rules and policies 10 , 11 , 12 . In a hierarchical Bayesian framing, domain-specific empowerment priors P ( ℰ ∣ domain ) P(\mathcal{E} \mid \text{domain}) would be maintained in mid-level prefrontal and cingulate representations (encoding controllability expectations for specific task contexts or skill domains), while the most abstract trait-level prior P ( ℰ ) P(\mathcal{E}) –corresponding to generalized self-efficacy or locus of control–would reside in the most anterior/medial prefrontal representations, consistent with frontopolar and anterior mPFC involvement in the most abstract levels of self-referential and metacognitive evaluation 13 , 14 . For (c), the learning rate / precision-weighting problem –how readily the trait-level prior updates from new controllability evidence–is governed by the same hierarchical precision mechanisms that operate throughout the predictive-processing hierarchy (see “Representing Uncertainty,” “Neuromodulators”). In hierarchical Bayesian terms, the trait-level prior updates slowly when it is held with high precision (strong confidence → \rightarrow low learning rate) and rapidly when precision is low (uncertainty about self-efficacy → \rightarrow high learning rate). Neuromodulatory systems exert direct control over this: serotonergic signaling from DRN –the same system gated by vmPFC’s controllability assessment in bullet (7)–modulates the balance between perseverative and flexible behavioral strategies and is strongly implicated in setting affective priors on environmental controllability (with chronic serotonergic dysregulation linked to the “learned helplessness” phenotype and depressive attribution styles) 1 , 15 . Noradrenergic (LC-NE) modulation of network gain controls how much novel evidence “breaks through” existing priors–phasic NE responses to unexpected controllability changes (per bullet 7c) can transiently increase the learning rate of the meta-estimate, while tonic NE levels set the background balance between prior-dominated and evidence-dominated inference 16 , 17 . The pathological extremes described in the parent bullet follow naturally: depression/learned helplessness corresponds to an excessively precise (low-learning-rate) trait prior P ( ℰ ) ≈ δ ( 0 ) P(\mathcal{E}) \approx \delta(0) , maintained by serotonergic/habenular dysregulation that renders the prior resistant to disconfirming evidence 1 , 18 , while fragile/unstable self-efficacy corresponds to an imprecise prior with excessive learning rate, vulnerable to collapse from single negative episodes. The evolutionary architectural priors are: (i) the medial prefrontal cortex as a phylogenetically conserved midline structure (mammalian mPFC/vmPFC has homologues–though with debated functional equivalence–across rodents, and medial pallial territories are identifiable in non-mammalian vertebrates) that is genetically wired to integrate controllability-monitoring outputs with self-referential encoding and value computation 19 , 5 ; (ii) the DMN-like resting-state architecture , which has been identified (with appropriate caveats about cross-species functional interpretation) in non-human primates and rodents, suggesting that the large-scale network topology linking midline self-referential hubs with hippocampal memory systems is a conserved mammalian connectivity blueprint rather than a human novelty 20 , 21 ; (iii) the rostro-caudal prefrontal gradient , whose laminar and connectivity organization is established by genetically specified molecular gradients during development, providing the structural scaffold for hierarchical abstraction without specifying the content of any particular prior 22 ; and (iv) the neuromodulatory wiring (vmPFC → \rightarrow DRN, LC projections to PFC, habenula → \rightarrow monoamine nuclei) that couples controllability-monitoring circuits to the precision-control machinery governing meta-estimate update rates. The organism thus arrives with the representational format and update architecture for a hierarchical self-model of controllability–not with any particular belief about its own efficacy, but with the structural guarantee that experienced controllability will be abstracted, cached at multiple levels of generality, and maintained with neuromodulatorily regulated confidence, enabling the rapid developmental emergence of self-efficacy beliefs from early contingency-learning episodes.

title: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: The preceding sections have treated the environment as if it were composed primarily of physical objects whose dynamics, while complex, are governed by stable causal laws amenable to compression and control. But the single most consequential feature of the human ecological niche is that it is saturated with other agents –entities whose behavior is generated by hidden generative models of approximately the same complexity as the observer’s own. Other agents are unique among environmental dynamics in being simultaneously (i) the highest-dimensional prediction targets (their behavior is driven by beliefs, desires, emotions, plans, and social commitments that are only partially observable), (ii) the most non-stationary (they learn, deceive, update, and strategically adapt to the observer’s own actions), and (iii) the highest-stakes (they are the primary source of both the greatest fitness benefits–cooperation, mating, alloparental care, coalition defense, cultural knowledge transfer–and the greatest fitness costs–aggression, exclusion, exploitation, reputational destruction). This convergence of inferential difficulty and fitness relevance means that natural selection has imposed enormous pressure on human brains to build, maintain, and deploy rich generative models of other minds –and, reflexively, a generative model of one’s own mind as it appears to other minds . The result is a suite of social-cognitive capacities (mentalizing, empathy, reputation management, norm internalization, identity construction) that are not epiphenomenal add-ons to a fundamentally asocial optimization engine but constitute a superordinate objective in their own right : the drive to maintain accurate, predictive models of the social world and to occupy a viable position within it.

title: Formal framing: social cognition within the EFE / compression / empowerment stack
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: Within the formal architecture developed above, social cognition does not require new first principles–it is the application of the same EFE-minimizing, compression-seeking, empowerment-maximizing machinery to a domain whose generative structure happens to be recursive and reflexive . Consider the problem facing an agent i i that must select policies in an environment containing agent j j . To minimize expected free energy, agent i i needs a generative model P i ( o τ i , s τ i , s τ j ∣ π i ) P_i(o^i_\tau, s^i_\tau, s^j_\tau \mid \pi^i) that includes the hidden states of agent j j –crucially, j j ’s beliefs, goals, and policy. But j j ’s policy is itself a function of j j ’s model of i i : π j = f ( P j ( s τ i ) ) \pi^j = f(P_j(s^i_\tau)) . This yields the characteristic recursive embedding of social cognition: i i must model j j modeling i i (and, in principle, j j modeling i i modeling j j , ad infinitum ). In practice, this recursion is truncated–human adults appear to reliably handle approximately two to three levels of recursive mentalizing ("I believe that you believe that I intend...") before performance degrades 1 , 2 –but even truncated recursive inference over hidden mental states is a compression problem of extraordinary depth. Each "other-model" is itself a generative model (with latent variables for beliefs, desires, temperament, knowledge states, and social commitments) that must be learned, maintained, and updated from sparse, noisy behavioral observations–and the number of such models scales with social group size, imposing the representational demands that have been argued to drive primate neocortical expansion 3 , 4 . Compression progress in the social domain takes a distinctive form: because other agents are partially observable systems generating behavior from hidden generative models, "compressing" social experience means discovering the latent trait and state variables (personality dimensions, attachment styles, social roles, cultural identities, moral commitments) that render others’ behavior predictable across contexts. A good social model is one that achieves low description length over the behavioral stream of a social partner–explaining their choices, utterances, and emotional displays as the output of a compact set of stable dispositions modulated by contextual states. This is why humans spontaneously construct character models of familiar others (trait attributions, narrative identities, relational schemas) and why violations of expected character ("that’s so unlike her") generate large social prediction errors that demand model revision. The same compression logic applies reflexively to the self-model : the agent’s representation of its own dispositions, values, and social commitments functions as a generative prior over its own future behavior, and maintaining a coherent self-model is equivalent to maintaining a low-complexity, high-predictive-accuracy model of oneself–an identity. Empowerment in the social domain– social empowerment –is the capacity to reliably influence the behavior and internal states of other agents. Formally, it is the channel capacity of the agent’s social action repertoire (utterances, gestures, facial expressions, favors, threats, reputation signals) with respect to others’ future states (beliefs, emotions, cooperation decisions, resource allocations). Social empowerment is uniquely challenging because the "channel" is non-stationary (the other agent adapts) and partially adversarial (the other agent may resist influence or attempt counter-influence)–making other agents simultaneously the highest-value and highest-difficulty targets for empowerment maximization. Critically, social empowerment is bidirectional : the agent’s capacity to influence others depends on others’ willingness to be influenced, which in turn depends on the agent’s reputation , trustworthiness , group membership , and perceived alignment with shared norms . This creates a fundamental interdependence: maximizing long-run social empowerment requires the agent to constrain its own short-run behavior (honoring commitments, adhering to norms, investing in relationships) in ways that build and maintain the social capital upon which future influence depends. In other words, social norms and relational bonds are not merely external constraints on the agent’s optimization but are instrumentally optimal strategies for sustained social empowerment –and, through internalization, they become part of the agent’s own preference landscape (entering the P ( o τ ) P(o_\tau) term of EFE as learned priors over social outcomes). The risk term of EFE is also profoundly reshaped by social embedding. For a hypersocial, obligately cooperative species like Homo sapiens , social exclusion is not merely unpleasant but constitutes a viability threat comparable in severity to starvation or predation: across ancestral environments, loss of group membership meant loss of access to shared food, cooperative defense, mating opportunities, and cultural knowledge, making exclusion tantamount to a death sentence 5 , 6 . Evolution has accordingly installed social exclusion as a deep viability prior –social rejection activates neural circuitry (dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, anterior insula) that overlaps substantially with circuits processing physical pain 7 , 8 , and the threat of exclusion is sufficient to override other motivational signals (hunger, fatigue, personal gain) in favor of socially conforming behavior 9 . This means that a substantial portion of the human preference distribution P ( o τ ) P(o_\tau) is allocated to social outcomes: being included, being valued, being seen as trustworthy and competent, occupying a recognized role in a social group. The "risk" that human EFE minimization works to avoid is not only physiological (hypoglycemia, hypothermia) but deeply and irreducibly social (rejection, humiliation, reputational collapse, norm violation and its punitive consequences). Identity, attachment, and norm compliance are therefore not luxuries pursued after survival needs are met; they are themselves survival-relevant variables that occupy privileged positions in the organism’s viability manifold.

title: I. Modeling Other Minds: The Core Inference Problem
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: The most computationally demanding inference problem a human brain faces is not modeling turbulent fluids or predicting weather–it is modeling other brains . Each socially relevant agent j j in the environment is a partially observable system whose behavior is generated by hidden variables–beliefs b j b^j , goals g j g^j , emotional states e j e^j , knowledge states k j k^j , stable dispositions θ j \theta^j , and a current policy π j \pi^j – that are accessible to agent i i only through a narrow, noisy, and strategically filtered observation channel: j j ’s actions, utterances, facial expressions, gaze direction, prosody, and posture. The inference problem is to maintain an approximate posterior Q i ( b j , g j , e j , k j , θ j , π j ∣ o 1 : t j ) Q_i(b^j, g^j, e^j, k^j, \theta^j, \pi^j \mid o^j_{1:t}) that is accurate enough to predict j j ’s future behavior and select policies that successfully influence j j . This is a hierarchical Bayesian inference problem with (at least) two timescales: fast state inference (what does j j currently believe, want, and feel?) updated within episodes from behavioral cues, and slow parameter learning (who is j j –what are j j ’s stable traits, values, and relational tendencies?) updated across episodes as evidence accumulates. The agent must maintain many such models simultaneously–one per socially relevant individual (and animal)–imposing representational demands that scale with social network size and that have been argued to constitute the primary selection pressure driving primate neocortical expansion 1 . What makes social inference qualitatively harder than physical-world modeling is the recursive and adversarial structure of the problem. Agent j j ’s policy depends on j j ’s model of i i : π j = f ( P j ( s i ) ) \pi^j = f(P_j(s^i)) . Accurate prediction of j j therefore requires i i to model j j ’s model of i i –and in strategic settings (negotiation, deception, courtship, coalition politics), j j modeling i i modeling j j , yielding a recursion that is formally equivalent to interactive POMDPs or cognitive hierarchy models 2 , 3 . Empirically, human adults can sustain approximately two to three levels of such embedding ("I believe that you believe that I intend X X ") before performance degrades 4 , 5 , suggesting a capacity-limited approximation to the full recursive solution. Additionally, observations of j j are not passively generated: j j engages in impression management , strategically selecting which behaviors to display and which to conceal–meaning i i ’s observation model must account for the fact that j j ’s emissions are themselves policy-selected actions designed to shape i i ’s posterior. This transforms social inference from standard filtering into an adversarial/cooperative signaling game where the likelihood model P ( o j ∣ s j ) P(o^j \mid s^j) is itself agent-controlled and context-dependent. Evolution’s answer to this inference problem is a genetically scaffolded mentalizing network – a set of cortical regions with characteristic cytoarchitecture, long-range connectivity, and functional biases that collectively implement hierarchical generative modeling of other minds. The network’s major nodes map onto distinguishable computational roles: Posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS): The network’s primary likelihood model . pSTS is selectively responsive to biological motion, gaze direction, and intentional action kinematics – the observable signals from which hidden intentions and goals must be inferred 6 , 7 . It encodes how an agent is behaving in a format that downstream regions can decode into why . Damage to pSTS impairs the ability to interpret others’ actions as goal-directed, while sparing lower-level motion perception 8 . Developmental onset is early: preferential tracking of biological motion is present in neonates 9 , suggesting that pSTS-region biases toward animate-motion statistics are at least partly experience-expectant rather than fully learned. Temporoparietal junction (TPJ): The network’s belief-state inference engine . TPJ is consistently and selectively activated when subjects must represent another agent’s belief as distinct from their own or from reality – the hallmark of "decoupled" mentalizing 10 , 11 . Functionally, TPJ performs the key computation of maintaining a representation of j j ’s epistemic state b j b^j that is dissociated from i i ’s own belief b i b^i , which requires active inhibition of the default egocentric perspective. Right TPJ in particular has been implicated in reorienting attention when social predictions are violated (a "social prediction error" signal) 12 , consistent with a role in updating the posterior Q i ( b j ∣ o 1 : t j ) Q_i(b^j \mid o^j_{1:t}) when new evidence arrives. Medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), especially dorsomedial PFC: The network’s trait inference and person-model hub . While TPJ tracks fast-changing belief/desire states, dmPFC is preferentially engaged during inferences about stable dispositions – personality traits, moral character, social roles, and long-run relational tendencies 13 , 14 . This division mirrors the fast-state / slow-parameter hierarchy: TPJ infers what j j currently thinks; dmPFC infers who j j is . dmPFC also supports explicit self-other comparison, which is required whenever the simulation route (see below) must be corrected for known self-other differences 13 . Its position within the DMN means that offline social compression–ruminating about others’ character, integrating social episodes into updated person-models–recruits the same architecture used for non-social model consolidation. Temporal poles (anterior temporal lobes): Person identity and person-specific semantic memory –a modality-bridging "person file"/person-identity representation that supports access to biographical facts and semantic knowledge about individuals upon recognition 15 . High-level perceptual person cues (faces in fusiform face areas; voices in STS/superior temporal regions) converge onto anterior temporal representations that can trigger identification and enable retrieval of person-specific semantic information (a putative "person identity node") 16 . Person knowledge is distributed: anterior temporal regions provide a key hub/access point, while mPFC/dmPFC is strongly engaged for trait/mental-state models and the hippocampus contributes episodic details. Lesion and atrophy studies show that anterior temporal damage can selectively disrupt familiar-person recognition in a lateralized manner (right: familiarity/person-specific information from faces; left: proper-name retrieval), whereas more extensive/bilateral ATL degeneration (e.g., semantic dementia) typically produces broader semantic impairment that includes person knowledge 17 . Posteromedial cortex (precuneus / PCC): Scene scaffolding and perspective transformation –supporting the construction of an egocentric, imageable situation model that social simulation can operate over. Across autobiographical recall, imagination, and perspective shifts, the precuneus is consistently implicated in visuospatial/embodied imagery and in flexibly transforming viewpoint (e.g., first- vs third-person), while PCC acts as a DMN hub that helps integrate internally generated content with self-relevance and broader contextual constraints 18 , 19 . In this framing, posteromedial cortex helps provide the spatiotemporal scaffold (the "scene model"), while TPJ and mPFC supply the mental-state variables and social-causal structure used for mentalizing. These nodes are linked by genetically specified long-range white-matter tracts (including segments of the arcuate fasciculus, cingulum bundle, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus) that establish the mentalizing network as an anatomically coherent system early in development, before extensive social experience has occurred 20 . Functional connectivity among these regions is detectable in infancy 21 , and the network’s topological organization–heavily overlapping with the DMN–means that offline social cognition (remembering, simulating, and planning social interactions) draws on the same architecture as non-social generative modeling and consolidation. This overlap is not accidental: it reflects the evolutionary insight that the most important "world model" for a social primate is a social model, and the general-purpose offline compression engine (DMN) was either co-opted for or co-evolved with social-cognitive demands 22 , 23 . A critical feature of the system’s training data is that it is not passively received but actively generated through social interaction. From the earliest months, infants preferentially attend to faces 24 , track gaze direction 25 , and are sensitive to social contingency (turn-taking, communicative ostension) 26 – a suite of innate attentional biases that functions as active data curation , ensuring the developing mentalizing system is trained on maximally informative social observations. Joint attention episodes (triadic interactions where infant, caregiver, and object are coordinated) serve as particularly rich training events because they provide simultaneous evidence about the other’s attentional state, referential intent, and emotional evaluation of an object 27 . As communicative competence develops, the child gains access to an even richer channel: explicit mental-state discourse ("What do you think?", "She doesn’t know that...", "He’s pretending"), which provides direct supervision on the mentalizing model by labeling hidden states that would otherwise require many behavioral observations to infer 28 , 29 . Social pretend play provides a further training regime: by jointly constructing counterfactual scenarios ("let’s pretend the block is a cake"), children practice decoupled representation–maintaining a model of the play-partner’s pretend-state alongside their own and alongside reality–which is structurally identical to the recursive state-tracking required for mature mentalizing 30 , 31 . Simulation vs. Inference: The Dual-Route Architecture The brain implements (at least) two computationally distinct routes for inferring others’ mental states, corresponding to different tradeoffs in the speed-accuracy-flexibility design space: The simulation route ("like-me" / embodied simulation): Use one’s own generative model as a proxy for the other agent’s: given a representation of j j ’s situation and observable cues, run i i ’s own affective, motor, and decision-making circuits "as if" i i were in j j ’s position, and read off the resulting internal states as predictions of j j ’s states. This is computationally cheap (it reuses existing self-model infrastructure rather than maintaining a separate model for each agent) but egocentrically biased : it assumes j j ’s generative model resembles i i ’s, which fails when j j has different beliefs, knowledge, preferences, or cultural background. The neural substrate includes the mirror/shared-representation system : ventral premotor cortex (PMv) and inferior parietal lobule (IPL) show overlapping activation when performing, observing, and imagining actions 32 , 33 ; anterior insula shows analogous shared activation for affective states (observing pain, disgust, or pleasure in others activates the same insular regions as experiencing those states firsthand) 34 , 35 ; and somatosensory cortex contributes to embodied simulation of others’ tactile and nociceptive experience 33 . Rather than requiring dedicated "mirror neurons" as a distinct cell type, these shared representations likely emerge from Hebbian association during self-observation: executing an action and simultaneously perceiving its sensory consequences binds motor and sensory representations, such that later perception of similar sensory patterns automatically co-activates the motor representation–a developmental learning process that operates over a connectivity prior linking sensory and motor areas for corresponding action classes 36 , 37 . The inference route (decoupled / "theory-theory"): Explicitly model j j ’s hidden states using a dedicated representational system that can maintain self-other divergence . This route is essential when j j ’s perspective is known or likely to differ from i i ’s: false-belief reasoning, strategic deception, cross-cultural interaction, or any context where egocentric projection would yield inaccurate predictions. The key neural substrates are TPJ and dmPFC –regions that are engaged specifically when self-other perspectives must be distinguished 10 , 13 . The decoupled route carries a higher computational cost (maintaining a separate state representation and actively inhibiting the default egocentric model) and matures later in development, but it provides the accuracy needed for strategic social reasoning. The two routes can be modeled as a Bayesian / uncertainty-sensitive mixture : embodied simulation / mirroring yields a fast self-model-based initialization (a "first guess" for action-goal/intent), while mentalizing / decoupled inference supplies an evidence-driven correction when self-projection is unreliable. Under time pressure, cognitive load, or low incentives for accuracy, the initial anchor tends to dominate and egocentric biases are larger; when accuracy is incentivized, stakes are high, or there are explicit cues that j ≠ i j \neq i , controlled adjustment is upweighted and TPJ-linked self-other distinction / perspective correction is more engaged 38 , 39 . At the network level, evidence suggests both mirroring and mentalizing systems can be co-recruited during social understanding, with context determining reliance on each; salience/attention control may act as a gating influence on whether situations trigger deeper mentalizing (hypothesis-level claim) 40 , 41 .
