title: II. Emotion Recognition and Empathy: Fast Affective Inference
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: The mentalizing system described above operates over relatively abstract latent variables (beliefs, goals, traits) on timescales of hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. But social interaction also demands a faster, lower-level inference channel dedicated to reading others’ affective states from perceptual cues–facial expressions, vocal prosody, body posture, autonomic signals (flushing, pupil dilation, trembling)–and converting those inferences into motivationally relevant internal signals that can bias the observer’s own policy in real time. This is the domain of emotion recognition and empathy , which together constitute a specialized, high-throughput likelihood model P ( o affect j ∣ e j ) P(o^j_{\text{affect}} \mid e^j) mapping observable displays to hidden emotional states, plus a mechanism for generating corresponding affective states in the observer that serve as fast proxy-value signals for social prediction and action selection. The computational distinction between emotion recognition and full mentalizing is important: recognizing that j j is afraid can be accomplished by pattern classification over facial and vocal features without representing j j ’s beliefs or goals (a two-year-old can detect fear in a face long before passing false-belief tasks). Emotion recognition is thus more akin to perceptual categorization over a biologically constrained signal space than to recursive latent-variable inference–but it interfaces tightly with the mentalizing system, providing fast affective priors (" j j is angry") that constrain the slower inference (" j j is angry because j j believes I violated a commitment"). This layered architecture–fast affect detection feeding into slower intentional inference–mirrors the general predictive-coding motif of rapid bottom-up signals being contextualized by slower top-down models. Empathy extends emotion recognition by generating a partially shared affective state in the observer: not just "I infer that j j is in pain," but " j j ’s pain induces an aversive/concern-related state in i i that covaries with it." This affective resonance is computationally useful because it converts another agent’s hidden state into a fast first-person value signal that can bias i i ’s policy without fully deliberative perspective-taking or explicit belief inference 1 , 2 . Importantly, this does not imply a single motivational logic: shared affect can recruit either (a) egoistic aversive-arousal regulation (act to reduce one’s own vicarious discomfort) or (b) genuinely other-oriented motivation (act to improve j j ’s welfare), depending on how the elicited state is appraised and regulated 3 , 4 . Empathy-related responding is therefore not monolithic; it is often decomposed into dissociable processes with distinct computational roles and partially distinct substrates: (i) affective resonance / emotional contagion (automatic affect sharing; very early in development, with neonatal "contagious crying" as a canonical precursor), (ii) empathic concern / compassion (other-oriented care/approach motivation that requires self-other distinction and can be strengthened by training), and (iii) personal distress (self-oriented aversive overarousal that tends to motivate avoidance/withdrawal and can be maladaptive for prosociality when dominant) 5 , 1 , 6 . Adaptive social behavior thus requires regulated empathy : maintaining enough shared affect to generate prosocial motivation while preserving self-other boundaries and control to prevent empathic overarousal–computationally, a gain/precision-allocation problem over the simulation route’s output 1 , 7 . Neural Implementation and Architectural Priors The face-processing cascade. Faces are the highest-bandwidth channel for social affective information, and evolution has invested in dedicated cortical territory for their processing. A hierarchically organized set of face-selective regions–the occipital face area (OFA) for early part-based processing, the fusiform face area (FFA) for holistic identity recognition, and face-selective patches in pSTS for dynamic facial features (expression changes, gaze shifts, mouth movements)–constitutes a genetically scaffolded processing pipeline 8 , 9 . Evidence for genetic scaffolding includes: neonatal preferential tracking of face-like configurations within hours of birth 10 ; proto-FFA activation in infants before substantial visual experience 11 ; the face inversion effect (disproportionate disruption of face perception by inversion, reflecting holistic processing strategies specific to upright faces); and congenital prosopagnosia, in which heritable deficits in face individuation occur without detectable cortical damage, implying the underlying circuit specialization has a genetic component 12 . The developmental trajectory–early coarse face detection (likely mediated by a subcortical route through superior colliculus and pulvinar 10 ) refined into adult-level face expertise over years of massive exposure–exemplifies an experience- expectant architecture: evolution installs the region-level bias and connectivity scaffold, then relies on the guaranteed environmental input (faces are ubiquitous in the infant’s visual diet) to tune the fine-grained feature detectors. Rapid threat and salience detection via the amygdala. The amygdala provides a fast, low-threshold detector for socially salient and threat-relevant affective displays. Amygdala neurons respond to facial expressions–particularly fear and anger–with short latencies, and a phylogenetically ancient subcortical route (retina → \rightarrow superior colliculus → \rightarrow pulvinar → \rightarrow amygdala) enables coarse affective categorization even before detailed cortical face processing is complete 13 , 14 , 15 . This pathway prioritizes speed over resolution: it can detect "threat-relevant face present" within ∼ \sim 100 ms, providing a fast prior that biases subsequent cortical processing toward threat-consistent interpretations. The amygdala’s role is not limited to fear or threat–it responds broadly to social salience and ambiguity (unpredictable faces, novel social stimuli, faces with direct gaze) 16 , 17 , consistent with a more general function as a relevance detector that flags social stimuli warranting further processing. Architecturally, the amygdala’s dense bidirectional connectivity with sensory cortex (especially temporal face/voice areas), prefrontal valuation circuits (OFC, vmPFC, mPFC), and hippocampus positions it as a social salience hub that can simultaneously bias perceptual processing (top-down enhancement of threat-relevant features), trigger autonomic/endocrine stress responses (via hypothalamic and brainstem projections), and tag social episodes for preferential memory encoding 18 . This multi-output architecture is deeply conserved across amniotes, with homologous structures identifiable in reptiles and birds–suggesting that rapid detection of conspecific threat signals is among the oldest social-cognitive functions. Anterior insula: the empathic bridge. The anterior insula (AI) serves as the critical neural substrate for converting observed affective states into felt bodily experience–the core mechanism of empathic resonance. AI is activated both when subjects experience first-person pain, disgust, or visceral affect and when they observe these states in others 19 , 20 , 21 , consistent with a shared representational code where another’s affective display is mapped onto the observer’s own interoceptive predictive model. In the active-inference framework, this can be understood as the observation of j j ’s distress cues generating a vicarious interoceptive prediction error : i i ’s generative model predicts what it would feel like to be in j j ’s inferred state, producing a simulated body-state deviation that enters the same affective processing pipeline as genuine interoceptive signals 22 . The precision (gain) on this vicarious signal determines whether the observer experiences mild cognitive awareness of the other’s state vs. intense shared affect–and this precision is modulated by contextual factors (relationship closeness, perceived similarity, attentional focus, group membership) and by neuromodulatory state (oxytocin enhances empathic resonance; stress and self-protective states reduce it) 19 , 23 . AI’s position at the convergence of interoceptive afferents (from brainstem and hypothalamus), social perceptual inputs (from STS and face-processing areas), and evaluative/motivational circuits (connections to ACC, OFC, and ventral striatum) makes it architecturally optimized for this bridging function. The von Economo neurons (VENs) concentrated in anterior insula (and ACC)–large, fast-conducting projection neurons found almost exclusively in species with complex social cognition 24 –likely support the rapid broadcast of empathic/salience signals to distant cortical and subcortical targets, providing the speed required for empathy to influence social decision-making in real time. ACC: affective evaluation and social pain. The anterior cingulate cortex , particularly its dorsal (dACC) and subgenual (sgACC) subdivisions, contributes to the evaluative component of empathy and to the detection of social-affective threats. dACC activation during the observation of others’ pain scales with the observer’s reported empathic distress 19 , and dACC/AI activation during social exclusion (Cyberball paradigm) overlaps with physical pain processing 25 –a convergence that reflects the evolutionary co-option of pain-monitoring circuitry for social viability tracking. Functionally, ACC provides the motivational output of the empathic inference: whereas AI generates the felt quality of vicarious affect, ACC translates this into control signals–"this situation demands a response"–linking affective resonance to behavioral adjustment via its dense projections to motor planning and autonomic effector systems. Somatosensory cortex and embodied simulation. Beyond the insula, primary and secondary somatosensory cortices (SI, SII) contribute to emotion recognition through what has been termed "embodied simulation" of others’ bodily states. Observing touch, pain, or facial expressions in others activates somatotopically appropriate regions of the observer’s somatosensory cortex 26 , 27 , and lesions to right somatosensory cortex impair the ability to recognize emotions from facial expressions 27 . This suggests that part of how the brain "reads" another’s emotional expression is by covertly simulating the somatomotor pattern that would produce that expression–running the facial musculature model in reverse to infer the underlying affective state, an instance of inverse-model inference applied to the social domain. In sum, the emotion recognition and empathy system is built on a stack of evolutionary architectural priors: (i) dedicated face-processing cortical territory with neonatal onset, ensuring the highest-bandwidth social channel is prioritized from birth; (ii) a subcortical fast route (SC → \rightarrow pulvinar → \rightarrow amygdala) for rapid threat-relevant affective detection, conserved across amniotes; (iii) anterior insula positioned at the interoceptive-social convergence zone, with VENs for fast broadcast, implementing the empathic bridge between observed and felt affect; (iv) shared sensorimotor representation architecture (PMv, IPL, SI/SII) that repurposes self-model circuitry for social inference via Hebbian binding during development; and (v) neuromodulatory gating (oxytocin, endogenous opioids – detailed in Section IV) that tunes empathic precision by social context. Cross-cultural universality of basic emotion production and recognition 28 –while debated in its specifics and likely more gradient than categorical 29 –is at minimum consistent with a shared evolved architecture for the production of affective displays (facial action units, vocal affect bursts, postural configurations) and a corresponding perceptual system tuned to detect them, forming a co-evolved sender–receiver system whose broad strokes are genetically specified even as cultural display rules and contextual modulation are layered on during development. Regulation: From Resonance to Adaptive Empathy Raw affective resonance is a double-edged computational mechanism. Unregulated, it produces personal distress – overwhelming self-oriented aversive arousal that paradoxically impairs prosocial behavior by motivating withdrawal and self-protection rather than other-directed help 30 . Adaptive empathy therefore requires a regulatory layer that maintains the useful motivational signal (empathic concern) while dampening the self-destabilizing component (personal distress). This regulation involves: Self–other distinction: Maintaining a clear boundary between vicarious affect (this is j j ’s pain, represented in my model) and genuine self-affect (I am in danger). TPJ and dmPFC contribute to this distinction–the same circuits that decouple self- and other-perspectives in belief attribution also decouple self- and other-affect in empathic processing 7 , 31 . Failure of this distinction (as in alexithymia, or under extreme stress) collapses empathy into personal distress. Precision modulation via prefrontal control: dlPFC and vlPFC exert top-down modulation of AI and amygdala activation during empathic processing, adjusting the gain on vicarious affect signals based on context (e.g., downregulating during surgical procedures, upregulating when a close other is in distress) 32 . Compassion as a trained policy: Contemplative training paradigms (e.g., loving-kindness meditation) shift the neural empathic response from AI/ACC-dominated personal distress toward mPFC- and ventral striatum-engaged compassionate concern , with measurably different affective quality (warm, approach-oriented rather than aversive) and behavioral consequences (increased prosocial action) 33 , 34 . This demonstrates that the mapping from vicarious affect to motivational output is not hardwired but learnable –the architectural prior provides the resonance mechanism, but the policy over that resonance (distress vs. concern vs. detachment) is shaped by experience and training. The developmental trajectory reflects this layered architecture. Emotional contagion is present from birth (neonatal crying in response to others’ cries 35 ), reflecting the most basic shared-representation mechanism. Emotion recognition from faces and voices develops rapidly over the first year, supported by the genetically scaffolded face-processing cascade and amygdala pathways. Empathic concern –other-oriented helping motivated by another’s distress, requiring self-other distinction–emerges in the second year as prefrontal regulatory circuits mature and self-recognition develops. Sophisticated empathic regulation –flexibly modulating resonance by context, relationship, and strategic demands–continues to develop through adolescence and into adulthood, tracking the protracted maturation of prefrontal control networks. This progression recapitulates the evolutionary layering: ancient resonance mechanisms (conserved across social mammals–rodents show contagious distress and approach behavior toward distressed conspecifics 36 ) are progressively wrapped in newer cortical regulation, with the human-specific contribution being not empathy per se but the flexible, context-sensitive control over empathic processing that enables empathy to serve strategic as well as automatic prosocial functions.

title: III. The Self-Model: Identity as Reflexive Social Modeling
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: The capacity to model other minds has a necessary reflexive consequence: an agent that can represent "what j j believes about the world" can also represent "what j j believes about me ." Once this representational capacity is in place, evolution can–and did–exploit it to construct a self-model : a generative model P i ( s i , θ i ) P_i(s^i, \theta^i) of one’s own stable dispositions, values, social roles, competencies, and relational commitments that functions simultaneously as (a) a prior over one’s own future behavior (reducing planning costs by constraining the policy search space), (b) a prediction about how others will model oneself (enabling strategic self-presentation and reputation management), and (c) a social signal (communicating to others what kind of agent one is, thereby facilitating coordination and trust). What we call identity is, computationally, this self-model–and its maintenance, defense, and strategic deployment constitute a superordinate objective that pervades human cognition and motivation. Why Identity Coherence is Valuable The value of maintaining a coherent self-model can be derived from all three superordinate objectives discussed previously: Compression: A compact self-model dramatically reduces the computational cost of planning. Instead of evaluating the full policy space Π \Pi at every decision point, the agent can constrain search to the much smaller subset Π θ i ⊂ Π \Pi_{\theta^i} \subset \Pi consistent with its self-model parameters ("I am the kind of person who does X X and does not do Y Y "). Internalized values, moral commitments, and role-based expectations function as learned priors over policy space P ( π ∣ θ i ) P(\pi \mid \theta^i) that prune the decision tree before deliberation begins–yielding faster, less effortful, and more consistent action selection. In description-length terms, a coherent identity compresses behavioral history into a low-dimensional trait vector from which specific actions can be reconstructed (predicted), rather than requiring independent explanation for each choice. Empowerment: A consistent, predictable identity is a prerequisite for sustained social empowerment. Other agents will cooperate with, invest in, and grant influence to i i only insofar as they can predict i i ’s future behavior–and predictability requires that i i ’s behavior be generated by stable parameters θ i \theta^i rather than shifting capriciously. Trust, which is at root a confident prediction that the other will honor commitments, depends on the perceived stability and coherence of the partner’s self-model 1 . An agent with an incoherent or rapidly shifting identity is a noisy channel from the perspective of social partners: their actions are unpredictable, their promises unreliable, and investment in them is high-risk. By maintaining identity coherence, the agent reduces H ( S social ′ ∣ A i ) H(S'_{\text{social}} \mid A_i) for social partners–making itself a reliable, decodable element in others’ generative models–and in return receives the cooperative benefits (trust, alliance, resources, status) that constitute social empowerment. EFE risk minimization: Because social exclusion and reputational collapse are viability-level threats (see opening paragraphs), maintaining alignment between self-model and others’ models of self is directly risk-reducing. Large divergences between P i ( θ i ) P_i(\theta^i) ("who I think I am") and 𝔼 j [ P j ( θ i ) ] \mathbb{E}_j[P_j(\theta^i)] ("who others think I am") create vulnerability: if the agent’s behavior suddenly deviates from what social partners expect, the resulting social prediction errors in others trigger suspicion, withdrawal, or punishment. Identity coherence minimizes the expected KL divergence 𝔼 j [ D K L [ P j ( θ i ) ∥ P i ( θ i ) ] ] \mathbb{E}_j[D_{KL}[P_j(\theta^i) \| P_i(\theta^i)]] between self-model and others’ models, keeping the agent within the social viability manifold. Identity as a Learned Constraint on the Preference Landscape A critical insight is that identity does not merely describe the agent’s dispositions–it actively constrains them. Once a self-model P i ( θ i ) P_i(\theta^i) is established and socially communicated (through behavior, explicit declarations, group affiliation, and narrative), deviation from it becomes costly: internally through cognitive dissonance (aversive prediction error against the self-model), and externally through reputational damage (others’ models of i i are violated, triggering trust revision). These costs function as a regularizer on the policy space, penalizing actions that are inconsistent with stated/inferred identity even when those actions would be locally reward-maximizing. In EFE terms, identity commitments enter both P ( o τ ) P(o_\tau) (preferred outcomes include "behave consistently with my values") and P ( π ) P(\pi) (prior over policies concentrates mass on identity-consistent action plans), effectively converting a learned self-description into a normative constraint. This is the computational mechanism underlying the common observation that people will sacrifice material payoffs to maintain identity consistency–refusing to "sell out," honoring commitments at personal cost, punishing identity-inconsistent behavior in themselves and others–behaviors that are puzzling under narrow reward maximization but follow naturally from a system that treats self-model coherence as a high-weight objective. Identity Threat and Defense If the self-model functions as a high-precision prior, then evidence contradicting it will generate large prediction errors–and the system will be strongly motivated to minimize these errors, either by updating the model or by discounting / reinterpreting the evidence . In practice, because the self-model is both deeply entrenched (trained over a lifetime of behavioral evidence) and costly to revise (triggering downstream changes in social commitments, group memberships, and others’ models of self), the system is generally biased toward evidence discounting over model revision –the computational basis of ego-defense mechanisms. Cognitive dissonance 2 is the phenomenological signature of a large self-model prediction error: the aversive arousal generated when one’s behavior or outcomes contradict one’s self-model. The resolution strategies documented in the dissonance literature–rationalization, selective attention, post-hoc attitude change, trivialization of the inconsistency–are all instances of approximate posterior maintenance : adjusting auxiliary beliefs and interpretive frames to reduce the apparent prediction error without revising the core self-model parameters θ i \theta^i , analogous to a generative model that explains away surprising observations through changes in context variables rather than deep structural revision. Self-serving attributional biases (attributing success to internal/stable factors and failure to external/unstable ones) serve the same function: they maintain the precision of the self-efficacy component of θ i \theta^i by routing negative evidence away from the self-model. Self-affirmation effects–whereby reminding individuals of valued aspects of their identity buffers against threatening information in unrelated domains 3 –are consistent with a system that evaluates threat relative to overall self-model coherence: bolstering one facet of the model increases the effective prior precision, rendering the system more tolerant of local prediction errors elsewhere. Neural Implementation and Architectural Priors Cortical midline structures (CMS) as the self-model substrate. The neural substrate of the self-model is anchored in the cortical midline structures (CMS) –medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC, both ventromedial and dorsomedial), posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), and precuneus – regions that form the anterior and posterior hubs of the default mode network and show a reliable activation signature during self-referential processing across dozens of paradigms and meta-analyses 4 , 5 , 6 . When subjects evaluate trait adjectives for self-relevance ("Am I honest?"), recall autobiographical memories, imagine their personal future, or reflect on their own preferences and attitudes, CMS activation consistently exceeds that observed during matched other-referential or semantic control conditions 7 , 8 . Within this system, a functional division is evident: Ventromedial PFC (vmPFC): evaluative self-representation–integrating self-relevant information with affective value; vmPFC damage produces impaired social decision-making and flattened self-evaluation without loss of self- knowledge per se, consistent with a role in computing the "value of being me" rather than storing self-descriptive content 9 , 10 . vmPFC also supports the representation of personal values and moral identity 11 , 12 , positioning it as the locus where identity commitments interface with the valuation system. Dorsomedial PFC (dmPFC): reflective self-representation and explicit self-other comparison; dmPFC is engaged when subjects explicitly evaluate their own traits, compare self to others, or consider how they appear from a third-person perspective 8 , 6 . This is the region that most directly supports the reflexive function–modeling oneself-as-modeled-by-others–and it overlaps heavily with the mentalizing network (Section I), consistent with the claim that self-modeling is architecturally parasitic on other-modeling. Posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) / precuneus: autobiographical integration and self-continuity–providing the temporal "backbone" of the self-model by linking current self-representation to the remembered past and imagined future 13 , 14 . PCC shows the highest baseline metabolic rate of any cortical region and is a major DMN hub, reflecting its continuous role in maintaining the contextual frame ("who am I, where have I been, where am I going") against which current experience is interpreted. The heavy overlap between the self-model system and the DMN is not incidental–it reflects the deep architectural relationship between identity and offline compression. The DMN’s core function, as discussed in the "Intrinsic Motivation" section, is generative simulation and schema extraction: converting episodic experience into compressed latent structure. The self-model is one such schema–the compressed representation that renders the agent’s own behavioral history predictable from a small number of trait parameters–and its construction and maintenance are core operations of the DMN’s offline consolidation engine. During rest, mind-wandering, and sleep, a substantial fraction of DMN activity is self-referential : spontaneous thought is disproportionately self-focused, autobiographical replay is biased toward identity-relevant episodes, and prospective simulation preferentially explores futures relevant to personal goals and social commitments 15 , 16 . This architecture means the self-model is continuously "retrained" offline, with priority given to experiences that update trait-level self-knowledge–explaining why identity-threatening events (social humiliation, moral failures, achievements that exceed expectation) produce intense offline rumination (high-salience training data demanding model revision) and why disruption of DMN consolidation (sleep deprivation, chronic stress) can destabilize the self-model. Hippocampal–mPFC circuits: autobiographical memory as the evidence base. The self-model is not built from current sensory input but from the accumulated autobiographical evidence base : the corpus of remembered episodes that, once compressed, yields the trait-level parameters θ i \theta^i . The hippocampus provides the episodic component–encoding specific events with their spatiotemporal and affective context–while mPFC extracts the invariants across episodes that constitute stable self-knowledge 17 , 18 . This division mirrors the CLS framework (Section on the DMN): hippocampus as fast, high-fidelity store; cortex (including mPFC) as slow, compressed, schema-level store. A critical implication is that autobiographical memory is not a neutral recording system but a self-model-maintaining reconstruction engine: memories are recalled not veridically but in a manner biased toward consistency with the current self-model 19 , 20 . Memory distortion in the service of identity coherence–remembering oneself as more consistent, more virtuous, more competent than the raw data would support–is not a "bug" but a feature of a system whose primary objective is to maintain a low-complexity, high-predictive-accuracy self-model that supports effective social functioning. The well-documented reminiscence bump (disproportionate recall of events from adolescence and early adulthood 21 ) is consistent with this framework: the self-model’s foundational parameters are installed during the identity-formation period (see developmental trajectory below), and episodes from this critical window receive priority encoding and retention because they contributed most to defining θ i \theta^i . Insular cortex: the interoceptive self. The self-model is not exclusively a cognitive/narrative construction–it includes a somatic component representing "how I characteristically feel." The anterior insula , as the cortical terminus of interoceptive processing, maintains a representation of current and predicted body states that contributes to the subjective sense of self as an embodied, feeling agent. Individual differences in interoceptive accuracy (the ability to accurately detect one’s own heartbeat, respiration, etc.) correlate with the stability and clarity of self-concept 22 , 23 , consistent with the idea that the self-model is anchored in interoceptive prediction as well as social/narrative construction. Disruption of insular processing (as in depersonalization/derealization disorder) produces the phenomenological experience of estrangement from one’s own body and identity–a self-model prediction error at the somatic level that the system cannot resolve 24 . Right-lateralized fronto-parietal circuits: body ownership and self-other boundary. At the most basic sensorimotor level, the self-model must specify which body belongs to "me" and which sensory events are self-caused versus externally generated. Right-lateralized fronto-parietal regions –including right TPJ, right inferior parietal lobule, right premotor cortex, and right insula–support this bodily self-model by integrating multisensory signals (visual, proprioceptive, vestibular, interoceptive) into a coherent estimate of body ownership and agency 25 , 26 . The rubber hand illusion (in which synchronous visuotactile stimulation shifts perceived hand ownership to a prosthetic hand 27 ) and full-body illusions (in which vestibular-visual conflict produces out-of-body experience phenomenology 28 ) demonstrate that body ownership is inferred from multisensory evidence rather than given a priori –it is a posterior estimate that can be manipulated by altering the likelihood model. This bodily self-model provides the foundation layer of identity: before there can be a narrative self ("I am a kind person") or social self ("I am a member of group G G "), there must be an embodied self ("this body is mine and these actions are mine"), and this foundation is constructed from phylogenetically ancient multisensory integration circuits that are already functional at birth, albeit imprecisely calibrated. Social Identity and Group-Level Self-Models In humans, the self-model extends beyond individual traits and dispositions to include group memberships as core identity components. Social identity theory 29 and self-categorization theory 30 document that categorizing oneself as a member of a group ("I am a [member of G G ]") triggers a suite of automatic consequences: activation of group-prototypical norms as behavioral priors, favoritism toward in-group members, derogation or homogenization of out-group members, and willingness to sacrifice personal interests for group welfare. From a computational perspective, social identity functions as a hierarchical extension of the self-model : when G G -membership is activated, the agent’s policy priors shift from purely individual parameters P ( π ∣ θ i ) P(\pi \mid \theta^i) to group-level parameters P ( π ∣ θ G ) P(\pi \mid \theta^G) , importing the group’s norms, values, and behavioral expectations as constraints on one’s own action selection. This is a powerful compression heuristic in social environments: rather than learning an individual policy for every social context, the agent can index into group-level policies that encode the accumulated cultural knowledge of G G about appropriate behavior in context C C . In-group favoritism and out-group homogeneity bias are explained within this framework as a model-selection economy : in-group members are modeled using the shared θ G \theta^G prior (cheap, often accurate given genuine within-group similarity in norms and values), while out-group members are modeled using a coarser, less differentiated prior (fewer training episodes, lower motivation to invest in individual-level modeling) 31 . The minimal group paradigm 32 –in which mere arbitrary categorization (e.g., preference for Klee vs. Kandinsky paintings) is sufficient to produce in-group favoritism and out-group discrimination–demonstrates how readily the social identity system can be activated, suggesting low thresholds and strong default priors. The neural correlates include: differential mPFC activation when processing in-group vs. out-group targets (more individuated, self-like processing for in-group 8 , 33 ); ventral striatum activation for in-group reward and cooperation (in-group coordination is intrinsically rewarding 34 ); amygdala response modulation by racial and group-category cues (with magnitude influenced by implicit bias and modulated by individuation goals 35 , 36 ); and ACC/AI activation when observing in-group members’ suffering (empathic resonance is amplified for in-group, attenuated for out-group, absent deliberate regulatory effort 37 , 38 ). This in-group empathy bias is a direct consequence of the simulation route’s egocentric default: in-group members are perceived as more "like me," hence the self-model is a better proxy, and simulation is more readily engaged. The evolutionary basis for social identity is likely rooted in coalitional psychology : across the hominin lineage, between-group competition created intense selection pressure for mechanisms that facilitate rapid coalition detection, in-group coordination, and out-group vigilance 39 , 40 . The ease with which social identity biases are activated (minimal groups), their early developmental onset (in-group preference by ∼ \sim 5 years [The development of implicit intergroup cognition]), and their cross-cultural ubiquity suggest that the architecture for group-based self-categorization is genetically specified–evolution installed a "group membership slot" in the self-model that is ready to be filled by whatever cultural group structure the developing child encounters. The content (which groups, which norms, which boundaries) is learned, but the capacity to define oneself in terms of group membership and to automatically activate group-level behavioral priors upon categorization is an architectural prior. Developmental Trajectory The self-model develops through a sequence that recapitulates the layered architecture, with each level depending on the maturation of its neural substrate: Bodily self (0-18 months): Multisensory self–other discrimination, sense of agency over motor outputs, proprioceptive body schema. Supported by early-maturing right-lateralized fronto-parietal circuits and somatosensory cortex. The mirror self-recognition milestone ( ∼ \sim 18 months 41 ) marks the point at which the visual body image is integrated into the self-model with sufficient coherence to support recognition of one’s own reflection. Categorical/objective self (18 months - 3 years): Emergence of self-referential language ("I," "me," "mine"), self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, shame–requiring a model of how others evaluate the self 42 ), and early self-description in terms of observable attributes (age, gender, physical features). This stage depends on the development of representational capacity in mPFC and temporal-pole person-knowledge circuits, and on the linguistic tools that enable self-referential encoding. Narrative/trait self (middle childhood): Self-description shifts from concrete attributes to psychological traits ("I am shy," "I am good at math"), reflecting the abstraction of behavioral regularities into stable dispositional parameters θ i \theta^i 43 . This development tracks the maturation of dmPFC trait-inference circuitry and the expansion of autobiographical memory networks (hippocampal-mPFC consolidation of self-relevant episodes into schematic self-knowledge). Identity exploration and commitment (adolescence): The self-model undergoes its most substantial reorganization, driven by the convergence of (i) prefrontal maturation (synaptic pruning and myelination in mPFC and frontopolar cortex, enabling more abstract and temporally extended self-representation 44 ), (ii) pubertal neuroendocrine changes (gonadal hormones reorganize social-motivational circuits, shifting reward sensitivity toward peer approval and status 45 ), and (iii) social-ecological transition (expanded peer networks, reduced parental supervision, identity-relevant choices about education, values, and group affiliation). Erikson’s identity crisis 46 corresponds, in this framework, to a period of high-variance, high-learning-rate exploration over self-model parameter space: the system temporarily relaxes the coherence prior to test alternative identity configurations before committing to a stable adult θ i \theta^i . Heightened adolescent sensitivity to social evaluation, self-consciousness, and peer influence reflects the increased precision weighting on social feedback signals during this calibration period–exactly what an optimal meta-learning system would do when the self-model is undergoing substantial revision and external validation is informative. Adult identity maintenance and revision: The mature self-model operates with a relatively high-precision prior over θ i \theta^i , supporting rapid and consistent action selection but resisting revision. The self-model is continuously but slowly updated by ongoing experience (career outcomes, relationship feedback, aging, life transitions), with major revisions occurring during identity-disrupting life events (divorce, bereavement, job loss, religious conversion, immigration) that generate self-model prediction errors large enough to overcome the coherence prior. The balance between stability and plasticity is modulated by the same neuromodulatory systems that govern learning rate elsewhere: noradrenergic signals that detect "regime change" can transiently increase the self-model’s learning rate, enabling faster identity revision when circumstances demand it, while serotonergic and oxytocinergic modulation of social confidence and relational security influence the baseline precision of the trait-level prior (see Sections IV and V). In sum, the self-model system is built on: (i) CMS architecture – phylogenetically conserved midline cortical structures (with homologues across mammals) genetically wired to integrate multimodal evidence about the organism’s own states, traits, and values; (ii) DMN connectivity – long-range white-matter connections linking anterior (mPFC) and posterior (PCC/precuneus) midline hubs with hippocampal memory systems and lateral temporal person-knowledge stores, establishing the network topology for self-referential processing before experiential content is available; (iii) right-lateralized multisensory integration circuits for the bodily self-model, providing the foundational layer of self–other distinction; (iv) a social identity slot – the coalitional-psychology architecture that allows group memberships to function as identity components, modulating empathy, norm compliance, and intergroup behavior; and (v) a rostro-caudal developmental gradient in which the self-model is built bottom-up across ontogeny (bodily self → \rightarrow categorical self → \rightarrow trait self → \rightarrow narrative/ideological identity), with each layer depending on the maturation schedule of its prefrontal substrate and the availability of appropriate social training data. Evolution does not install a specific identity – it installs the representational architecture and developmental program that guarantees a self-model will be constructed from the organism’s particular social embedding, and that once constructed, it will function as a high-inertia prior that simultaneously compresses one’s own behavioral complexity, signals reliability to social partners, and constrains future policy in identity-consistent (and therefore socially predictable) directions.

title: IV. Attachment: The Deep Prior for Reliable Social Partners
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: For an altricial species with the longest juvenile dependency of any primate, maintaining proximity to specific reliable caregivers is not a social preference but a viability-level constraint : in the ancestral environment, separation from the caregiver is near-certain death. Evolution has accordingly installed attachment at the same priority level as core homeostatic variables–"proximity to attachment figure j j " enters P ( o τ ) P(o_\tau) with weight comparable to glucose and temperature, and its violation triggers distress of corresponding intensity. Bowlby’s foundational insight 1 was that attachment is an independent behavioral control system with its own activating conditions (threat, novelty, separation), set-goal (proximity), and terminating conditions (felt security)–a homeostatic loop operating over a social variable. The Internal Working Model as a Generative Prior The lasting computational product of attachment is the internal working model (IWM) : a generative model encoding (i) the expected availability and responsiveness of attachment figures ("will they come when I need them?") and (ii) the expected worthiness of the self as a care recipient ("am I worth investing in?") 2 . The IWM functions as a relational hyperprior –a trait-level expectation about close-relationship dynamics–that biases interpretation of ambiguous social signals, selection of relational policies, and precision weighting on social feedback across the lifespan: Secure attachment : high expected availability, high self-worth. Functions as a safe base for exploration : because proximity restoration is expected to succeed when needed, the system can allocate resources to empowerment and compression drives (curiosity, play, skill acquisition) rather than vigilant monitoring of the attachment figure 3 . Also installs an emotion-regulation template : reliable co-regulation (caregiver soothes distress → \rightarrow distress resolves) trains mPFC-amygdala circuits to treat negative affect as controllable 4 . Insecure-avoidant : low expected availability → \rightarrow compensatory self-reliance and affect suppression . The system learns that the social channel has near-zero capacity ( I ( A bid ; S response ′ ) ≈ 0 I(A_{\text{bid}};S'_{\text{response}}) \approx 0 ) and redirects control-seeking toward non-social domains. Cost: impaired co-regulation and muted social-reward signaling 5 . Insecure-anxious : high variance in expected availability → \rightarrow hypervigilant monitoring and amplified distress signaling . The caregiver’s availability is modeled as stochastic, so the system maintains costly high precision on attachment-relevant cues and escalates bids to increase detection probability in a noisy channel 5 . Disorganized : the attachment figure is simultaneously the source of safety and threat, producing a representational paradox . The caregiver’s behavior is incompressible under any single model , and the resulting failure of model fitting predicts downstream psychopathological associations (dissociation, borderline features, fragmented self-representation) 6 , 7 . IWMs are not merely retrospective summaries–they actively shape future social data acquisition . A securely attached individual makes confident bids that elicit responsiveness, confirming the prior; an anxiously attached individual monitors and escalates in ways that push partners toward inconsistency, also confirming the prior. This prior-data feedback loop explains the well-documented stability of attachment across the lifespan 8 : the prior shapes the training distribution from which it would need to be updated, creating self-reinforcing inference resistant to disconfirmation without targeted intervention. Neural Implementation and Architectural Priors Neurochemical bonding substrate. Attachment is implemented through a neurochemical architecture that converts social proximity into intrinsic reward and separation into visceral distress: Oxytocin (OT): Hypothalamic OT, released both centrally and peripherally, functions as a social precision enhancer –biasing the system toward increased salience of social cues (enhanced face processing, gaze detection, vocal affect discrimination 9 ), increased trust and approach 10 , and reduced amygdala reactivity to social threat 11 . In the mother-infant dyad, OT creates a bidirectional positive feedback loop : maternal OT promotes caregiving; infant OT (released during contact and contingent interaction) promotes bonding; each partner’s release facilitates the other’s 12 . OXTR distribution–genetically specified high densities in ventral striatum, hippocampus, and mPFC–is the architectural prior ensuring that social proximity is automatically tagged as rewarding and preferentially encoded. Endogenous opioids ( μ \mu -opioid): Mediate the hedonic component–the warmth of social contact. Social separation activates the same withdrawal circuitry as opioid deprivation 13 , 14 , creating a homeostatic drive loop (contact → \rightarrow opioid release → \rightarrow maintain contact; separation → \rightarrow withdrawal → \rightarrow seek reunion). The PAG generates species-typical separation distress vocalizations from birth, requiring no learning–a genetically installed alarm for attachment violation 13 . Dopamine (VTA → \rightarrow ventral striatum): Supplies the motivational/wanting component. Attachment figures become conditioned incentive stimuli through repeated pairing with OT- and opioid-mediated consummatory reward, such that their faces and voices acquire dopaminergic incentive salience 15 . Adult romantic attachment activates VTA and ventral striatum in patterns resembling early-stage drug reward 16 . Cortical circuits and emotion regulation. Secure attachment trains robust mPFC → \rightarrow amygdala top-down regulation through thousands of co-regulation episodes, installing autonomous emotion regulation that progressively replaces external co-regulation 17 , 18 . Early adversity and insecure attachment are associated with reduced prefrontal regulation and heightened amygdala reactivity–a calibration toward environments where threats are frequent and uncontrollable 18 . Subgenual ACC provides the cortical alarm for attachment-system violation, overlapping with physical pain circuits 19 –consistent with the viability-level status of social separation. Sensitive period. Attachment formation is temporally constrained to the first ∼ \sim 1-3 years by genetically timed maturational processes: heightened OT receptor expression in limbic circuits 20 , a period of relative amygdala independence from prefrontal damping (enabling high-intensity bonding) 18 , and experience-expectant plasticity in mPFC-hippocampal circuits optimized for relational encoding 21 . The window is not a hard cutoff–IWMs remain revisable (e.g., "earned security" through consistently responsive partners or psychotherapy 22 )–but revision requires concentrated counter-evidential experience to overcome the high-precision prior installed during the initial period. Phylogenetic depth. The attachment system’s core components are conserved across mammals: separation distress vocalizations modulated by opioid/OT systems across rodents, ungulates, and primates 13 ; pair-bonding circuits dependent on genetically specified OT/vasopressin receptor distributions in ventral striatum 23 ; imprinting-like sensitive-period mechanisms across birds and mammals 24 . Humans elaborate on this substrate by (i) extending the sensitive period (matching extended juvenile dependency), (ii) layering cortical mentalizing onto subcortical bonding circuitry (enabling representationally rich IWMs that go beyond approach/avoid), and (iii) generalizing attachment beyond the parent-infant dyad to romantic partners, friends, groups, institutions, and symbolic entities–the representational flexibility afforded by cortical expansion applied to an ancient motivational system.

title: V. Belonging and Social Inclusion: The Group Membership Imperative
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: Attachment secures dyadic bonds with specific individuals; belonging extends the social viability constraint to the group level. For an obligately cooperative species whose ancestral survival depended on shared defense, cooperative foraging, alloparental care, and cumulative cultural knowledge, loss of group membership was functionally equivalent to a death sentence. Evolution has accordingly installed inclusion status as a continuously monitored viability variable : the brain maintains a running estimate of "am I a valued member of my group?" and generates graded alarm signals–from mild social discomfort to acute social pain–when that estimate drops below threshold 1 , 2 . Sociometer Theory: Self-Esteem as a Cached Inclusion Estimate Sociometer theory 3 , 4 reframes self-esteem not as an end in itself but as a gauge –a cached, real-time estimate of relational value: P ̂ ( included ∣ recent social feedback ) \hat{P}(\text{included} \mid \text{recent social feedback}) . Like a fuel gauge that summarizes a complex physical variable into a single readable signal, self-esteem compresses diverse social feedback (approval, rejection, status cues, performance outcomes, social comparison) into a scalar that can rapidly bias policy selection. When the sociometer reads high (confident inclusion), the system can pursue other objectives (exploration, status competition, skill acquisition); when it reads low (exclusion threat), it triggers corrective social behavior–conformity, affiliation-seeking, self-presentation, appeasement–aimed at restoring inclusion probability above the viability threshold. Trait self-esteem corresponds to the slowly updating prior P ( inclusion ) P(\text{inclusion}) shaped by accumulated relational history; state self-esteem corresponds to the fast-updating likelihood-driven posterior that fluctuates with immediate social feedback. The system’s asymmetry–drops in self-esteem are more motivationally potent than equivalent increases 5 –is consistent with an asymmetric loss function appropriate for a viability variable: the cost of failing to detect exclusion threat far exceeds the cost of a false alarm. Neural Implementation Social pain as co-opted physical pain. The neural signature of social exclusion overlaps substantially with circuitry processing physical pain. The Cyberball paradigm (in which participants are excluded from a virtual ball-tossing game) reliably activates dorsal ACC and anterior insula –the same regions engaged by nociceptive stimuli–and the magnitude of dACC activation correlates with self-reported social distress 6 , 7 . This overlap is not metaphorical but reflects genuine architectural co-option: evolution repurposed the phylogenetically ancient pain-monitoring system to track social viability, ensuring that exclusion threats receive the same affective urgency and motivational priority as tissue damage. Supporting evidence includes the finding that acetaminophen (which reduces physical pain via central COX-mediated mechanisms) also attenuates social pain reports and associated dACC activation 8 , and that individuals with greater pain sensitivity show greater exclusion distress 9 –consistent with shared underlying circuitry rather than merely shared phenomenology. Social reward circuitry. The converse of social pain is social reward : positive social feedback (acceptance, praise, being chosen, cooperative success) activates ventral striatum and vmPFC with a profile similar to non-social reward 10 , 11 . Social approval generates dopaminergic RPE signals that reinforce the behaviors and self-presentations that elicited approval, and social conformity–aligning one’s judgment with group consensus–recruits ventral striatum reward signals even when the conforming judgment is objectively incorrect 12 . This means that the brain’s standard reinforcement-learning machinery is recruited for belonging maintenance: socially approved behaviors are stamped in by the same RPE mechanism that reinforces any other rewarding outcome, and norm-conforming behavior is literally rewarding–not merely instrumentally useful but intrinsically valued at the level of mesolimbic circuitry. Self-esteem as a cached value in mPFC-striatal circuits. The sociometric estimate is maintained by circuits linking mPFC (self-referential evaluation) with ventral striatum (reward/value representation). mPFC encodes self-relevant social evaluation signals and projects to striatum where they can be integrated with ongoing value computations. Social feedback generates RPE-like update signals: unexpected social acceptance produces positive striatal RPE; unexpected rejection produces negative RPE and dACC/AI alarm activation. Trait self-esteem corresponds to the tonic baseline of this mPFC-striatal value representation–a slowly updating prior shaped by the cumulative history of social inclusion/exclusion experiences, with the same neuromodulatory learning-rate dynamics discussed for the empowerment meta-estimate (Section on Empowerment, bullet 8): noradrenergic and serotonergic modulation set the balance between prior-dominated stability (resistant to transient social setbacks) and evidence-dominated plasticity (responsive to genuine shifts in relational value). Conformity and Belonging Maintenance Conformity, compliance, and norm adherence can be understood as inclusion-maintenance policies –behavioral strategies selected to keep the sociometric estimate above threshold. When subjects discover their opinion diverges from group consensus, ACC and anterior insula generate conflict/error signals proportional to the degree of divergence 12 , 13 –effectively a "social prediction error" signaling that the agent’s current behavioral trajectory threatens group alignment. The resolution of this conflict by adjusting one’s expressed (and sometimes genuinely held) opinion toward the group mean represents a policy correction aimed at minimizing social risk. Importantly, this conformity circuitry is modulated by group membership: divergence from in-group generates stronger conflict signals and more robust conformity than divergence from out-group 14 , consistent with the social identity framework (Section III) in which group-level self-models selectively amplify the belonging-maintenance drive for identity-relevant collectives. Evolutionary Priors and Development The belonging system is built on phylogenetically deep foundations: separation distress circuits (PAG-mediated vocalizations, opioid-modulated, shared with the attachment system) are the ancestral alarm for social isolation, present across social mammals 15 . The co-option of physical pain circuitry for social exclusion monitoring has been argued to reflect the evolutionary transition from solitary to obligately social living, where pre-existing nociceptive "viability alarm" architecture was the most efficient substrate for a new threat category (exclusion) that carried comparable fitness costs 16 , 17 . Developmentally, sensitivity to belonging cues is present from infancy (distress to social isolation, preferential attention to social inclusion/exclusion events in puppet shows by 6-10 months 18 ) but undergoes a dramatic amplification during adolescence . Pubertal neuroendocrine changes–rising gonadal hormones that reorganize dopaminergic reward sensitivity and heighten the salience of peer evaluation 19 , 20 –create a sensitive period during which the belonging system is recalibrated from family-centered to peer-centered inclusion. Adolescents show exaggerated dACC/AI responses to peer rejection, heightened conformity, and increased risk-taking in the presence of peers 20 , 21 –all consistent with a system that has temporarily increased the precision weighting on peer-social feedback to support the critical developmental task of establishing a viable position in the adult social landscape. This adolescent recalibration is not pathological but is an evolved sensitive period: the transition from family to peer group is the most consequential social-niche shift in the human lifespan, and increasing the learning rate on peer-inclusion signals during this window is the computationally appropriate response.

title: VI. Status, Reputation, and Dominance Hierarchies
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: In any group of cooperating agents with partially aligned interests, asymmetries in influence inevitably emerge–some individuals’ preferences disproportionately shape collective outcomes, resource distribution, and norm enforcement. The resulting status hierarchy is a latent variable that every group member must continuously track, because one’s position in it determines access to resources, mates, allies, and–critically– tolerance for behavioral deviation (high-status individuals can violate norms at lower cost). In empowerment terms, status is a social empowerment multiplier : higher rank increases I ( A i ; S social ′ ) I(A_i; S'_{\text{social}}) by expanding the set of social states the agent can reliably bring about (more influence over others’ behavior, greater resource access, more cooperative partners willing to follow the agent’s lead). Evolution has accordingly installed status-tracking and status-seeking as core components of the social objective. Dual Routes to Status Human status hierarchies are organized along (at least) two dissociable dimensions 1 , 2 , each posing distinct computational demands: Dominance: Status derived from coercive capacity –the ability to impose costs on others. Tracking dominance requires a threat-estimation model : inferring physical formidability, coalition size, willingness to aggress, and capacity to withhold resources. Dominance cues are largely phylogenetically conserved (body size, low voice pitch, direct gaze, expansive posture, aggressive display) and are processed rapidly via subcortical pathways. The appropriate behavioral response to a dominant individual is submission/avoidance –deference motivated by fear rather than admiration. Prestige: Status derived from competence, knowledge, or skill that others value and wish to acquire. Tracking prestige requires a competence-estimation model : inferring who possesses useful information or expertise, who has a track record of success, and who is worth learning from. Prestige cues are more cognitively mediated (demonstrated skill, third-party testimony, informational generosity) and the appropriate response is voluntary deference and proximity-seeking –motivated by the learning opportunity the prestigious individual represents. Prestige is arguably a human-specific (or at least human-elaborated) status dimension, enabled by cumulative culture: in a species that depends on socially transmitted knowledge, individuals who possess and share valuable compressed models become high-value social partners, and the capacity to identify and preferentially associate with them is a powerful social-learning heuristic 1 . The two routes can be dissociated behaviorally (dominance elicits fear and gaze aversion; prestige elicits admiration and gaze attraction 2 ), neurally (see below), and developmentally (dominance-based hierarchies emerge earlier in childhood and are more prominent in non-human primates; prestige-based hierarchies require the mentalizing and cultural-learning capacities that mature later). Reputation Management Status is not merely tracked but actively managed . Because one’s status position is a function of others’ models– rank i = f ( { P j ( θ i ) } j ≠ i ) \text{rank}_i = f(\{P_j(\theta^i)\}_{j \neq i}) –the agent faces a continuous multi-audience signaling problem : selecting behaviors that maintain or enhance the status-relevant latent variables that others are tracking, while managing potentially conflicting impressions across different audiences (e.g., displaying toughness to rivals while displaying warmth to allies). Reputation management is computationally expensive because it requires recursive mentalizing (modeling what j j will infer about θ i \theta^i from observing action a a in context c c ) and multi-step planning (current actions affect future reputation which affects future social empowerment). The well-documented audience effect –people behave more prosocially, more generously, and more norm-compliantly when observed 3 , 4 –reflects the system’s sensitivity to the reputational channel: when others are modeling you, the reputational consequences of behavior are upweighted in policy evaluation. Neural Implementation Serotonergic system as a status neuromodulator. Central serotonin (5-HT) levels covary with social rank across primates: dominant vervet monkeys show elevated whole-blood 5-HT, and experimentally increasing 5-HT (via SSRIs) in subordinate males promotes social confidence and ascent in rank, while decreasing it promotes subordination 5 , 6 . Serotonin modulates the behavioral repertoire relevant to status maintenance–inhibiting impulsive aggression (which risks costly conflict), promoting social confidence and affiliative signaling, and calibrating risk tolerance in status-relevant contexts. This positions the serotonergic system as a status-state neuromodulator : high 5-HT signals "you are in a secure status position" and enables the confident, prosocial behavioral profile that maintains prestige; low 5-HT signals "you are in a precarious position" and shifts the system toward either anxious submission or impulsive status-challenge. The evolutionary conservation of 5-HT-status linkages across vertebrates (including crustaceans–serotonin modulates dominance posture in lobsters and crayfish 7 ) indicates an ancient architectural prior for neurochemical status-state tracking. Striatal status-reward signals. Learning one’s own status position activates ventral striatum with RPE-like dynamics: status gains produce positive reward signals; status losses produce negative ones 8 , 9 . Being perceived as higher-ranking than a comparison target activates ventral striatum even in the absence of material payoff 8 , confirming that status is intrinsically rewarding at the level of mesolimbic circuitry–not merely instrumentally valued for the resources it provides. The dorsal striatum is additionally engaged during decisions about whether to challenge or defer to others in competitive contexts 10 , consistent with its role in action selection based on learned values. mPFC: social comparison and status representation. The dmPFC is engaged during explicit social comparison – evaluating one’s own performance, competence, or traits relative to others 11 , 12 . vmPFC encodes the subjective value of one’s own social standing and integrates status information with broader self-evaluative processing 13 . Together with the mentalizing network (dmPFC, TPJ), these circuits support the recursive computation required for reputation management: simulating how one’s actions will affect others’ models of one’s competence and character. Testosterone-cortisol interactions. The dual-hormone hypothesis 14 proposes that status-seeking behavior is jointly regulated by testosterone (T) and cortisol (C): high T + low C promotes dominant, status-seeking behavior (the motivational drive is present and not inhibited by stress reactivity), while high T + high C attenuates status-seeking (the drive is present but suppressed by anxiety about the costs of competition). This interaction positions the HPG and HPA axes as a joint gating mechanism for status-relevant policy: testosterone sets the motivational gain on status-seeking; cortisol sets the threat-sensitivity that modulates whether that motivation is expressed as approach (compete, display, challenge) or avoidance (defer, withdraw, appease). Pubertal testosterone surge drives recalibration of status-seeking circuitry, particularly in males, creating an adolescent sensitive period for status-hierarchy entry that parallels the belonging-system recalibration described in Section V. Evolutionary Priors Hierarchical social organization characterizes virtually all gregarious primate species, and the neural circuitry for rank-tracking is deeply conserved. Monkeys and apes rapidly learn dominance hierarchies via observation alone, track transitive rank relations (if A > B A > B and B > C B > C , then A > C A > C ), and adjust their behavior by rank with minimal trial-and-error 13 , 15 . The human-specific contribution is the prestige dimension : the capacity to acquire status through demonstrated competence and knowledge-sharing rather than (or in addition to) coercive capacity. This dimension depends on the mentalizing network (evaluating others’ competence and intentions), social-learning circuits (identifying who is worth copying), and temporal-pole person-knowledge stores (maintaining individual-level prestige profiles over time)–all components of the expanded cortical architecture described in previous sections. The result is a dual hierarchy system in which the ancient dominance-tracking circuitry (subcortical, fast, cue-driven, shared with other primates) operates alongside a newer prestige-tracking system (cortical, deliberative, mentalizing-dependent, human-elaborated), with context and cultural norms determining which dimension is weighted more heavily in a given social ecology.

title: VII. Fairness, Norms, and Moral Cognition
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: Stable cooperation among self-interested agents requires behavioral constraints that prevent defection from unraveling cooperative equilibria. These constraints are norms : context-dependent rules specifying what actions are permitted, obligatory, or forbidden–functioning computationally as prior constraints on policy space P ( π ) P(\pi) that narrow the set of admissible behaviors before any deliberation about instrumental value. An agent that has internalized the norm "don’t steal" does not evaluate theft as an option and reject it on expected-value grounds at each decision point; instead, theft is excluded from the policy search space by a learned prior, dramatically reducing both computational cost and the probability of defection under temptation. Norms are thus the social analogue of viability boundaries: just as homeostatic constraints define the region of physiological state space the agent must remain within, norms define the region of behavioral state space the agent must remain within to avoid social punishment and exclusion. Fairness Computation A critical subset of norms concerns fairness –the expected relationship between contributions, costs, and outcomes across cooperating agents. The brain must compute whether resource distributions and behavioral exchanges conform to equity/reciprocity expectations, using inputs about one’s own and others’ contributions and outcomes. Multiple fairness models coexist (equality, proportionality, need-based allocation, earned entitlement), with context determining which is applied 1 , 2 . The Ultimatum Game –in which responders reject materially advantageous offers they perceive as unfair, at cost to themselves–provides a clean behavioral readout of fairness-norm enforcement: the responder’s rejection is not payoff-maximizing but norm-enforcing, sacrificing immediate gain to punish a perceived violation 3 . Cross-cultural universality of Ultimatum Game rejection (though rejection thresholds vary with local cooperative norms 4 ) confirms that fairness computation is a species-typical capacity, even as its calibration is culturally tuned. Moral Emotions as Error Signals The motivational force behind norm compliance and enforcement comes from moral emotions , which function as specialized prediction-error signals within the social generative model: Guilt: Self-generated norm-violation detection–a prediction error against the self-model ("I did something inconsistent with who I am / what my group expects"). Guilt is prospectively useful because it motivates reparative action and deters future violation; it is the affective mechanism by which externally imposed norms become internal policy constraints 5 . Shame: A self-model update reflecting others’ negative evaluation–"I am seen as a norm violator." Where guilt is private and action-focused ("I did a bad thing"), shame is public and identity-focused ("I am bad"), making it a social-exclusion threat signal that recruits the belonging-maintenance circuitry of Section V 5 . Moral outrage / indignation: Other-directed norm-violation detection–triggering punishment motivation and reputation-damage behavior toward the violator. Outrage is the emotional substrate of third-party punishment : even uninvolved observers are motivated to sanction norm violators, maintaining the cooperative equilibrium at personal cost 6 . Gratitude / admiration: Positive social prediction errors–others exceeded cooperative expectations–generating relationship-strengthening signals that reinforce prosocial partners and promote future cooperation 7 . Neural Implementation Norm representation and enforcement. vmPFC/OFC integrates norm-compliance costs and benefits with goal-directed value in a context-dependent manner; bilateral vmPFC damage produces "acquired sociopathy"–intact knowledge of norms but catastrophic failure to weight them appropriately in decision-making 8 , 9 . DLPFC supports deliberate norm enforcement via cognitive control: TMS disruption of right DLPFC increases selfish behavior in economic games (subjects know the norm but can no longer override the selfish impulse) 10 , establishing a causal role for prefrontal control in norm-compliant policy execution. Anterior insula generates the aversive signal to unfairness–its activation predicts rejection of unfair Ultimatum Game offers 11 –functioning as the visceral alarm that translates norm-violation detection into motivational urgency. Dorsal striatum shows reward-like activation during altruistic punishment (punishing defectors at personal cost) 12 , indicating that norm enforcement is not merely grudging compliance but is intrinsically rewarding–evolution has wired the punishment of free-riders into the same reward circuitry that reinforces food and sex, ensuring that cooperative equilibria are actively maintained. Moral emotion circuits. Guilt and shame recruit subgenual ACC , anterior insula , and mPFC –the self-evaluative circuits that generate aversive arousal when behavior violates the self-model 13 , 14 . These overlap with the social-pain network (Section V), consistent with norm violation being processed as an exclusion-risk signal. Moral outrage activates amygdala , anterior insula , and lateral PFC –the threat-detection and motivated-action pathways–while simultaneously engaging the mentalizing network (TPJ, dmPFC) for attribution of intent and responsibility to the violator 15 , 16 . This dual-network recruitment (affective alarm + mentalistic attribution) is what distinguishes moral anger from non-social frustration: the system must both feel the violation and understand the violator’s culpable mental state. Innate Proto-Moral Biases and Developmental Curriculum The norm system is not built from a blank slate. Converging evidence identifies innate proto-moral biases that function as inductive priors constraining the hypothesis space from which cultural norm content is acquired: Neonatal distress to others’ crying (rudimentary empathic resonance, present from birth 17 ) Preference for prosocial over antisocial agents in pre-verbal infants ( 18 ) Sensitivity to unequal resource distribution by ∼ \sim 15 months 19 Early protest against norm violations and tattling on violators by age 3 20 , 21 These biases do not constitute innate moral rules but rather architectural priors –they make certain norm-contents (harm avoidance, fairness, reciprocity) easier to learn and more resistant to extinction than others, while leaving the specific calibration (how much inequality triggers protest, which violations merit punishment, who counts as a rights-holder) to be filled in by cultural transmission. The developmental trajectory proceeds from authority-based compliance (early childhood: "because the caregiver says so") through peer-norm internalization (middle childhood: reciprocity, rule-following, fairness among equals) to abstract moral reasoning and identity-linked moral commitment (adolescence: questioning conventions, integrating moral principles into the self-model) 22 , 23 . This sequence tracks the maturation of the underlying circuitry: early compliance depends on amygdala-mediated fear of punishment; peer-norm internalization depends on striatal reward-for-conformity and developing mentalizing capacity; abstract moral reasoning depends on the prefrontal maturation and identity-formation processes described in Sections III and V. Gene-culture coevolution. The architecture is designed for norm learning , not for specific norm content. Genetic evolution installed the capacity to detect violations, feel guilt and shame, compute fairness, and punish defectors; cultural evolution fills in the specific rules, transmitted via social learning, narrative, ritual, and observed punishment 24 , 25 . The two inheritance systems co-evolved: populations with stronger norm-psychology architectures could sustain more complex cooperative institutions, which in turn created selection pressure for even more sophisticated norm-learning capacity–a ratchet that produced the extraordinary human capacity for culturally variable yet psychologically constrained moral systems. Neuromodulatory gating ensures context-sensitivity: oxytocin amplifies norm compliance and trust within group boundaries while potentially sharpening inter-group competition 26 ; serotonin modulates harm aversion and patience in moral judgment (SSRIs shift decisions toward harm-avoidance in trolley-type dilemmas 27 )–confirming that moral cognition is not a unitary "module" but an integration of multiple neurochemically gated systems whose relative weighting is tuned by social context and internal state.
