title: VIII. Communication and Language: The Social Channel
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: The social-cognitive systems described in Sections I-VII all depend on a communication channel through which agents exchange information about internal states, intentions, norms, and world models. While non-human primates communicate through gestures, vocalizations, and facial displays, human language represents a qualitative expansion of channel capacity: a discrete combinatorial system capable of transmitting arbitrary propositional content–including content about absent entities, hypothetical scenarios, others’ mental states, and abstract norms–with a bandwidth and precision unmatched by any other biological signaling system. Language is not merely a tool used by a social mind; it is a co-evolved component of the social-cognitive architecture, and many of the systems described above (recursive mentalizing, norm transmission, reputation management, narrative identity, cultural learning) could not function at human scale without it. Pragmatic Inference: Communication as Recursive Mentalizing The computational core of linguistic communication is not grammar but pragmatic inference : recovering the speaker’s intended meaning from an utterance that underdetermines it. Grice’s cooperative principle 1 –the expectation that speakers are informative, truthful, relevant, and clear–is a shared generative model of communicative behavior that enables listeners to infer intended meaning by reasoning about why the speaker chose this utterance rather than alternatives . This is explicitly a mentalizing computation : the listener must model the speaker’s beliefs, goals, and knowledge state to recover meaning. "Can you pass the salt?" is decoded as a request (not a question about ability) only by inferring the speaker’s communicative intention via the mentalizing system. Bayesian models of pragmatics formalize this as recursive social reasoning: the listener reasons about a speaker who reasons about a listener 2 , engaging the same recursive modeling architecture described in Section I. The tight coupling between language comprehension and mentalizing is confirmed by neuroimaging: pragmatic inference recruits the mentalizing network (dmPFC, TPJ, temporal poles) over and above lexico-semantic processing 3 , 4 , and individuals with impaired mentalizing (e.g., autism spectrum) show corresponding pragmatic deficits even with intact syntax 5 . Language as a Reputation and Norm-Transmission Channel Language dramatically amplifies the social systems described in previous sections: Reputation via gossip: Language enables third-party reputation transmission –agents can learn about others’ past behavior without direct observation. Gossip (which likely constitutes the majority of spontaneous conversation 6 ) functions as a distributed reputation-tracking system: norm violations and cooperative acts can be broadcast through the social network, making reputation consequences extend far beyond the dyadic encounter. This massively increases the cost of defection (one act of cheating can be reported to the entire group) and the returns to prosociality (one act of generosity can enhance reputation network-wide) 6 , 7 . Norm transmission: Explicit instruction, narrative, and moral discourse allow norms to be transmitted with propositional precision –specifying not just "don’t do X X " but the conditions, exceptions, justifications, and punishments associated with X X . This enables the culturally cumulative norm systems described in Section VII: each generation inherits not only behavioral norms but the rationale structure behind them, allowing selective modification rather than wholesale reinvention 8 . Narrative identity: Language enables the construction of a narrative self-model (Section III)–a temporally extended, causally structured account of "who I am and how I got here"–that goes far beyond the trait-level self-representation available to non-linguistic creatures. Narrative identity integrates episodic memories into a coherent life story that can be communicated to others, evaluated against cultural templates (redemption arcs, contamination sequences 9 ), and used to coordinate mutual expectations in relationships. Neural Implementation The dual-stream language architecture and its social interfaces. The perisylvian language network– left IFG (Broca’s area) for hierarchical structure building and articulatory planning, left posterior STG/STS (Wernicke’s area) for phonological and lexico-semantic processing, connected via arcuate fasciculus and other dorsal/ventral pathways 10 , 11 –provides the syntactic-semantic processing engine. But crucially, this engine is densely interconnected with the social-cognitive networks described throughout this paper: Anterior temporal lobes / temporal poles: The convergence zone for semantic person-knowledge, social concepts, and narrative comprehension–providing the interface between linguistic representations and the person-model database (Section I) 12 . Mentalizing network (dmPFC, TPJ): Recruited during pragmatic inference, irony/sarcasm comprehension, indirect speech acts, and narrative perspective-taking–all cases where recovering meaning requires modeling the speaker’s mental states 3 . STS voice-selective regions: Analogous to face-selective areas, voice-selective cortex along bilateral STS provides a dedicated processing channel for paralinguistic social cues–vocal identity, emotional prosody, speaker confidence, and deception markers 13 –that are processed in parallel with and inform the interpretation of linguistic content. Evolutionary and developmental trajectory. Language acquisition follows a genetically timed sensitive period with well-characterized milestones (babbling ∼ \sim 6 months, first words ∼ \sim 12 months, grammar explosion ∼ \sim 18-36 months 14 ) and depends on both domain-specific architectural priors (lateralized perisylvian cortex, vocal tract anatomy, statistical learning biases) and obligate social input (contingent interaction with speakers; language cannot be acquired from passive exposure alone 15 ). The social gating of language learning –infants learn phonemes from live social interaction but not from equivalent audio/video exposure 15 –demonstrates that the language faculty is architecturally embedded within the social-cognitive system: the learning mechanism itself requires the ostensive communicative cues (eye contact, contingent turn-taking, joint attention) that signal "this is addressed to you" and that depend on the social-attention and mentalizing circuits described in Section I. Language is not a general-purpose computational tool that happens to be used socially; it is a fundamentally social technology whose acquisition, processing, and deployment are gated by social-cognitive architecture at every level.

title: IX. Integration and Conclusion
context: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships
text: The preceding sections have described a suite of social-cognitive systems–mentalizing, empathy, self-modeling, attachment, belonging, status, norms, and communication–that are often studied independently but are best understood as components of a single integrated architecture organized by the three superordinate objectives introduced in the theoretical framework: compression (building efficient generative models of self and others), empowerment (maximizing the agent’s causal influence over social outcomes), and expected free energy minimization (keeping the organism within its social viability envelope). Every system described here serves at least two of these objectives simultaneously, and their neural implementations share overlapping substrates precisely because they draw on common computational primitives–prediction error computation, precision weighting, recursive generative modeling, and homeostatic-style regulation over social variables. The Architecture in Summary The core architectural claim is that evolution has installed a layered social generative model whose structure reflects the computational demands of human ultra-sociality: Layer 1 – Social perception (STS, FFA, voice-selective cortex, biological motion areas): rapid extraction of social signals from faces, voices, bodies, and gaze, providing the sensory likelihood terms that drive all downstream inference. Layer 2 – Agent modeling (mentalizing network: TPJ, dmPFC, temporal poles; mirror/simulation circuits): constructing generative models of other agents’ beliefs, desires, intentions, traits, and likely actions–the computational engine for prediction in a world populated by intentional beings. Layer 3 – Self-modeling (cortical midline structures, DMN, hippocampal–mPFC circuits): the reflexive application of agent-modeling to oneself, producing the identity representation that compresses one’s own behavioral complexity and signals predictability to social partners. Layer 4 – Relational regulation (OT/opioid bonding circuits, mPFC–amygdala regulatory pathways, social pain/reward networks): maintaining the dyadic bonds (attachment) and group memberships (belonging) that constitute the social viability envelope, with dedicated neurochemical systems (oxytocin, μ \mu -opioid, serotonin) that convert social variables into homeostatic-format signals. Layer 5 – Social structure tracking (striatal status-reward circuits, norm-enforcement networks in AI/dACC/DLPFC, fairness computation in vmPFC): monitoring and navigating the hierarchical and normative structure of the social environment – who has power, what rules apply, whether exchanges are fair. Layer 6 – Communicative interface (perisylvian language network interfaced with mentalizing and person-knowledge systems): the high-bandwidth channel that enables propositional exchange, gossip-based reputation tracking, norm transmission, and narrative identity construction–amplifying every lower layer’s reach and precision. These layers are not independent modules but form a deeply interactive hierarchy : social perception feeds agent modeling, which feeds self-modeling (via reflected appraisal), which feeds relational regulation (via IWM-based expectations), which feeds social-structure navigation (via status and norm computations calibrated by attachment security and belonging state), which feeds communication (whose pragmatic content presupposes all lower layers). Disruption at any layer cascades upward and downward–explaining why social-cognitive deficits rarely present in isolation, and why conditions affecting early layers (e.g., autism spectrum: atypical social perception and mentalizing) produce pervasive downstream consequences across the entire social-cognitive architecture. Evolutionary Priors vs. Learned Content A recurring theme across all sections is the distinction between genetically specified architectural priors and experientially acquired content . Evolution does not install specific social knowledge–it installs the representational format, learning biases, sensitive-period timing, and neurochemical gating that guarantee the right kind of social knowledge will be acquired from the organism’s particular social embedding. The mentalizing network is genetically wired but the specific models of specific people are learned; the attachment system’s neurochemistry is innate but IWM content depends on caregiver behavior; the norm-learning architecture is species-universal but norm content is culturally transmitted; the status-tracking circuitry is phylogenetically ancient but the dimensions of status valued in a given ecology are culturally shaped. This format-content distinction is the key to understanding both the universality of human social cognition (same architecture everywhere) and its cultural variability (different content installed by different social environments) without retreating to either nativist or blank-slate extremes.

title: From Implicit, Hard-Coded Objectives to Explicit, Learned Goals
text: Every objective described so far–viability regulation, compression progress, empowerment, attachment, belonging, status, fairness, identity coherence–is, in the first instance, implicit : it is realized not as a proposition the organism entertains but as an architectural bias –a wiring pattern, a receptor distribution, a neuromodulatory gain schedule, a genetically timed sensitive period–that shapes computation without ever being "represented" in the format that would allow the organism to inspect, verbalize, or deliberately revise it. A newborn whose separation-distress circuit fires upon loss of skin contact is not pursuing the goal "maintain proximity to caregiver"; a toddler whose dorsal striatum chunks a reach-grasp sequence is not pursuing the goal "expand my action-channel capacity"; a teenager whose ventral striatum fires to peer approval is (probably) not pursuing the goal "maximize social empowerment." These objectives are enacted by the architecture but not tokened in any workspace where they could be deliberated over, traded off against one another, or communicated to others. Yet adult humans routinely do all of these things: they set explicit goals ("finish the dissertation by June"), rank-order competing objectives ("career vs. family"), report their motivations to others ("I want to feel more in control of my life"), and adopt culturally transmitted purposes ("reduce global poverty") that bear no resemblance to anything evolution could have directly installed. How does the implicit objective stack described above give rise to the explicit, linguistically structured, culturally scaffolded goal representations that characterize human agency? This subsection traces the computational and neural bridge between the two regimes and argues that explicit goals are best understood not as replacements for implicit objectives but as learned, compressed, communicable re-descriptions of policy-relevant subproblems discovered by the implicit stack operating over a lifetime of structured experience. A useful operational criterion: a goal is explicit to the extent that it is (i) represented in a format accessible to working memory and deliberative planning (i.e., tokened as a discrete state in prefrontal-parietal workspace circuits rather than embedded only in synaptic weights or neuromodulatory set-points), (ii) encodable in a compositional symbolic medium (paradigmatically natural language, but also imagery, diagrams, or formal notation–any medium that supports combinatorial recombination), and (iii) selectable and revisable by the agent’s own meta-cognitive control system –the agent can choose to adopt, abandon, or modify the goal in response to changing circumstances, new information, or competing objectives. On this definition, explicit goals are data structures in working memory that function as target states for model-based planning : they specify a desired region of (latent) state space, and the planning system searches for policies π * \pi^* such that Q ( s τ ∣ π * ) ≈ P goal ( s τ ) Q(s_\tau \mid \pi^*) \approx P_{\text{goal}}(s_\tau) . Implicit objectives, by contrast, shape behavior through architectural constraints on the learning and inference process itself –they bias which policies are explored, which prediction errors are attended to, and which state transitions are reinforced, without needing to be represented as target states in any explicit planning computation. The distinction is not binary but graded: an objective can be partially explicit ("I feel restless and want to do something" registers a drive without specifying a target state) or situationally explicit (the thirsty organism may represent "find water" as an explicit subgoal while the deeper homeostatic regulation of osmolality remains implicit). The computational bridge: how implicit objectives generate explicit goals The bridge from implicit to explicit proceeds through three inter-dependent mechanisms, each scaffolded by architectural priors and refined by experience: (1) Interoceptive and affective "surfacing": implicit drives become felt states. The first step is that implicit viability constraints generate interoceptive prediction errors and affective valence signals that are accessible to cortical inference. When blood glucose drops, the hypothalamic-brainstem homeostatic controller does not merely adjust insulin and glucagon; it also generates an ascending signal that is registered by insular cortex as a felt state (hunger) and by anterior cingulate as a motivational urgency signal. This "surfacing" converts an implicit set-point deviation into a phenomenologically accessible datum –a prediction error that the agent’s generative model can attempt to explain and resolve via deliberate action. Active inference formalizes this: interoceptive prediction errors that cannot be resolved by autonomic reflexes (the "interoceptive inference" route 1 ) are "passed up" the hierarchy until they reach levels capable of active inference–generating actions ("go to the kitchen") rather than merely adjusting internal parameters. The felt state is thus an interface representation : it translates an architectural constraint (glucose < < set-point) into a format compatible with the explicit planning machinery of prefrontal cortex. Importantly, not all implicit objectives surface equally well. Viability-level drives (hunger, thirst, pain, thermal discomfort, social distress) generate strong, identifiable felt states because their rapid resolution is fitness-critical. But subtler objectives–compression progress, empowerment, long-run social-capital maintenance–generate weaker, more diffuse affective signals (curiosity, restlessness, vague dissatisfaction, ennui) whose correct interpretation requires substantial meta-cognitive development. Much of the developmental trajectory from childhood to adulthood involves learning to read these subtler signals accurately: recognizing that the restlessness one feels is a compression-progress signal ("I need a harder challenge"), or that the vague unease in a social situation is an empowerment signal ("I have no influence here"), or that chronic low mood reflects a belonging deficit rather than a personal failing. (2) Model-based decomposition: felt needs become subgoal structures. Once an implicit drive has surfaced as a felt state, the prefrontal-hippocampal planning system can decompose it into a structured subgoal hierarchy via prospective simulation. The hungry organism does not simply emit random foraging behavior; it simulates candidate action sequences ("open the fridge → \to retrieve leftovers → \to heat them → \to eat"), evaluates each against the felt need, and selects the plan whose terminal state best resolves the interoceptive prediction error. Each node in this plan is an explicit subgoal –a target state representation maintained in working memory and monitored by ACC/frontoparietal control circuits. The decomposition process is itself a compression operation : a high-dimensional, continuous drive ("restore glucose homeostasis") is compressed into a discrete sequence of achievable waypoints, each expressible in a compact representational format. This is where the hierarchical option/skill architecture described in the Empowerment section becomes critical: the agent can only plan in terms of actions it can already execute as chunked units . A skilled cook decomposes "make dinner" into a few high-level steps; a novice must plan at a much finer grain. The available option library thus determines the resolution at which explicit goals can be formulated–another instance of empowerment constraining the effective goal space. (3) Linguistic encoding: subgoals become communicable propositions. The qualitative leap from primate-level subgoal pursuit to human-level explicit goal representation is catalyzed by language . Once a subgoal can be encoded in a compositional symbolic format ("finish the dissertation by June"), it acquires properties that no purely sensorimotor goal representation possesses: Displacement: The goal can refer to states that are spatiotemporally remote, counterfactual, or abstract–"reduce global carbon emissions," "become the kind of person who keeps promises"–transcending the reach of sensorimotor simulation 2 . Compositional generativity: Goals can be combined, negated, conditioned, and embedded ("if the weather is good, hike; otherwise, finish chapter 3") using the same syntactic machinery that structures sentences, enabling goal structures of unbounded complexity. Social shareability: A linguistically encoded goal can be communicated , enabling coordination ("let’s both aim for X X "), delegation ("your job is Y Y "), negotiation ("I’ll do X X if you do Z Z "), and cultural transmission ("our community values W W "). This transforms goal pursuit from an individual to a collective computational process, vastly expanding the effective planning horizon and resource base. Reflective accessibility: A verbalized goal can become an object of the agent’s own meta-cognitive scrutiny ("is this really what I want?"), enabling deliberate goal revision, prioritization, and abandonment–the operations that distinguish human agency from stimulus-driven or habit-driven behavior. The neural interface between goal representation and language is supported by the dense connectivity between prefrontal goal-maintenance circuits (especially left DLPFC and frontopolar cortex) and the perisylvian language network (left IFG, posterior temporal cortex) via dorsal and ventral white-matter pathways 3 , 4 . Inner speech –the covert linguistic rehearsal that accompanies much of human planning and self-regulation–may be the primary vehicle through which subgoal representations are maintained in working memory in linguistic format, leveraging the phonological loop as a goal-maintenance buffer 5 , 6 . Vygotsky’s observation that children progress from overt self-directed speech ("now I put the red block on top") to covert inner speech during problem-solving 7 documents the developmental moment at which linguistic encoding is internalized as a planning tool–the point at which the child gains the capacity to hold explicit, compositional, revisable goal representations in a format that can also be externalized for social coordination. The relationship between implicit and explicit: alignment, scaffolding, and conflict The relationship between implicit objectives and explicit goals is best characterized not as replacement but as hierarchical scaffolding with imperfect alignment . Explicit goals are generated in the service of implicit objectives–they are the plans that the organism’s deliberative system constructs to satisfy the drives that the implicit stack has surfaced–but the mapping is neither one-to-one nor guaranteed to be faithful. Several systematic patterns of alignment and misalignment are worth distinguishing: Faithful instrumentality. In the simplest case, explicit goals are accurate instrumental decompositions of implicit drives: "drink water" faithfully serves hydration homeostasis; "practice the piano piece" faithfully serves compression progress in the musical domain; "apologize to my friend" faithfully serves attachment/belonging maintenance. Here the explicit goal is a well-calibrated proxy for the implicit objective, and pursuit of the explicit goal reliably reduces the implicit drive. Most everyday goal-directed behavior falls in this regime–the implicit-to-explicit translation is straightforward because the agent’s world model is accurate, the relevant drive has surfaced clearly, and the available options are well-matched to the problem. Approximate proxies and Goodhart drift. More commonly, explicit goals are approximate compressions of implicit objectives that sacrifice fidelity for tractability. "Get a high GPA" is a learnable, measurable proxy for the deeper objectives of compression progress (learning), social empowerment (career options), and belonging (meeting parental expectations), but it can diverge from all three: a student who optimizes GPA by memorizing rather than understanding sacrifices compression; one who chooses easy courses over challenging ones sacrifices empowerment (skill expansion); one who cheats risks social exclusion if discovered. This is the social-cognitive analogue of Goodhart’s Law 8 : once a proxy is adopted as an explicit target, the optimization process can exploit the gap between proxy and true objective 9 . In the brain, such divergence manifests as a conflict between explicit goal pursuit and implicit affective signals : the student who is "succeeding" by GPA metrics but not learning may experience persistent dissatisfaction, boredom, or anxiety–interoceptive/affective prediction errors from the compression and empowerment drives signaling that the explicit goal is not resolving the underlying implicit need. Whether the agent heeds these signals depends on meta-cognitive capacity (can it recognize the source of the discomfort?) and on the relative precision weighting of explicit goal-monitoring circuits vs. implicit affective feedback–a balance that is itself developmentally and contextually modulated. Culturally transmitted goals with no direct biological grounding. Human explicit goals frequently have no straightforward mapping to any single implicit objective. "Prove Fermat’s Last Theorem," "achieve enlightenment," "write the great American novel," "end factory farming"–these are goals whose content is specified by cultural models rather than biological drives, and whose pursuit may require sustained effort against multiple implicit drives (physical discomfort, social isolation, opportunity cost to empowerment in other domains). Yet they are pursued with an intensity and commitment that rivals or exceeds biologically grounded drives. Two complementary mechanisms explain this: Goal adoption via social-identity integration. As described in "Theories of Minds", the self-model includes group memberships and cultural role commitments as core identity components. When an agent identifies as a "mathematician," "Buddhist," "novelist," or "animal rights activist," the goals associated with that identity enter P ( π ∣ θ i ) P(\pi \mid \theta^i) –the prior over policies conditional on the self-model–and deviation from them generates identity-threat distress (cognitive dissonance, shame). The implicit belonging and identity-coherence drives thus provide motivational fuel for culturally specified goals that would otherwise lack biological grounding. The goal is "explicit" in content but is powered by implicit drives that care not about the specific content but about maintaining coherence between behavior and self-model. Learned intrinsic value via compression/empowerment bootstrapping. A domain that initially offers high compression progress (mathematics is deeply compressible; artistic creation generates high Δ L \Delta L ) or high empowerment gain (mastering a complex skill dramatically expands the action-outcome channel) can become intrinsically valued through standard value-learning: dopaminergic RPEs reinforce the states and policies associated with the domain, and over time the domain itself–with all its culturally specific goal structures–acquires cached value that persists even when the marginal compression/empowerment returns diminish. This is the mechanism by which the implicit drive for learning progress "hands off" to an explicit, culturally structured goal: the initial engagement is driven by r t int r^{\text{int}}_t ; the sustained commitment is maintained by learned value, social identity, and the sunk-cost dynamics of expertise investment. From the outside, the mature expert pursuing a culturally defined goal looks like an agent with a "terminal value" for that goal; from the inside, it is the endpoint of a developmental trajectory in which implicit drives discovered, engaged with, and ultimately delegated sustained motivation to, a learned objective. Explicit goals that conflict with implicit objectives (akrasia, self-destructive goal pursuit, ideological override). The most consequential misalignment arises when explicit goals actively oppose implicit drives. Classic akrasia (weakness of will)–eating the cake despite the explicit goal of dieting–reflects a failure of prefrontal goal maintenance to override subcortical/habitual policy selection when the implicit drive (caloric homeostasis in an energy-scarce-adapted system) and the explicit goal (long-run health in an energy-abundant environment) point in opposite directions. The converse pattern, where explicit goals override implicit welfare signals, is equally important and often more consequential: religious ascetics suppress hunger, sexual desire, and comfort drives in pursuit of identity-congruent spiritual goals; political ideologues sacrifice personal safety and social bonds for abstract causes; perfectionists pursue explicit achievement targets well past the point where compression and empowerment drives have saturated, driven by identity-threat/shame avoidance rather than positive learning progress. In these cases, the explicit goal has captured the motivational system by engaging the identity-coherence and belonging drives at high precision while suppressing or overriding the affective signals from other implicit objectives. The capacity for such override is a distinctively human feature–enabled by the prefrontal control architecture’s ability to maintain abstract goal representations with sufficient precision to dominate subcortical valuation–and it is simultaneously the source of humanity’s greatest achievements (sustained pursuit of goals requiring decades of effort against biological drives) and its most spectacular pathologies (ideological fanaticism, self-destructive perfectionism, addiction to culturally defined status metrics). Cultural amplification: how explicit goals transcend individual biology The capacity for explicit, linguistically encoded, socially shared goals is the mechanism by which human motivation escapes the bounds of individual biology . Three features of cultural goal systems merit emphasis: Goal inheritance and cumulative refinement. Culturally transmitted goals can persist across generations, accumulating refinements that no single individual could achieve. The goal "understand the fundamental laws of physics" has been pursued across centuries by successive communities of scientists, each inheriting the compressed models (theories) and explicit subgoal structures (open problems) of predecessors. This is inter-generational compression progress : each generation’s contribution is a Δ L \Delta L that reduces the description length of physical phenomena, but the accumulated L 0 − L T L_0 - L_T over generations dwarfs anything achievable within a single lifespan. Cultural institutions (universities, journals, professional societies) function as external memory and coordination infrastructure that maintains explicit goal structures, accumulated knowledge, and quality-control norms across the temporal horizon that biological memory cannot span. Institutional goal structures. Human societies construct institutional goals –the objectives of organizations, governments, religions, and social movements–that are super-individual : they are pursued by collectives of agents, persist beyond any individual’s lifespan, and can coordinate behavior at scales (millions of agents, decades of time) that no individual goal representation could. Institutional goals are "explicit" in an extended sense: they are encoded in constitutions, mission statements, legal codes, and strategic plans–external representations that function as shared priors over policy space for all members of the institution. Individual agents adopt institutional goals via the social-identity mechanism described above: identifying as a member of institution I I imports I I ’s goals into one’s own policy priors, powered by belonging and identity-coherence drives. The result is a multi-scale goal hierarchy : individual implicit drives → \to individual explicit goals → \to group/institutional goals → \to civilizational aspirations, with each level scaffolded by the one below and enabled by the cultural technologies (language, writing, institutions) that support goal representation and coordination at that scale. Normative goal structures and moral progress. Cultural goal systems include not only instrumental objectives ("build a bridge") but normative ones ("create a just society"). As described in "Theories of Minds", the norm-learning architecture installs sensitivity to fairness, harm, and reciprocity, but the scope of these norms is culturally specified. The historical expansion of moral concern–from kin to tribe to nation to (in some modern frameworks) all sentient beings 10 –can be understood as a culturally driven expansion of the set of entities included in P ( o τ ) P(o_\tau) ’s preference distribution: each expansion redefines "preferred outcomes" to include welfare states of a larger circle, generating new explicit goals (abolish slavery, extend suffrage, reduce animal suffering) that would have been unrepresentable in earlier cultural contexts. These goals are "explicit" in the strongest sense: they require compositional linguistic encoding, abstract moral reasoning, and institutional coordination to pursue, and they often conflict with implicit drives (in-group favoritism, status competition, resource hoarding) whose architectural biases must be deliberately overridden. Synthesis: the full objective stack The full picture of human motivation is therefore a multi-layered objective stack in which each layer emerged through a different mechanism, operates on a different timescale, and is represented in a different neural format: Layer Origin Neural format Timescale of change Viability constraints (homeostasis, pain) Phylogenetic (genetic specification of set-points & alarm circuits) Brainstem/hypothalamic set-points; interoceptive prediction error Evolutionary ( 10 5 10^5 - 10 6 10^6 years) Implicit learning drives (compression, empowerment) Phylogenetic architecture + ontogenetic meta-learning Neuromodulatory gain schedules; intrinsic reward signals; architectural biases (sparse coding, hierarchical prediction) Architectural: evolutionary; tuning: developmental ( 10 0 10^0 - 10 1 10^1 years) Implicit social objectives (attachment, belonging, status, fairness) Phylogenetic architecture + sensitive-period calibration Neuropeptide/neuromodulatory circuits (OT, opioid, 5-HT); social-pain/reward overlap; IWMs Architectural: evolutionary; calibration: infancy-adolescence Explicit personal goals Ontogenetic: model-based decomposition of implicit drives PFC working-memory representations; hippocampal-PFC prospective simulation; linguistic encoding Minutes to years (adopted, revised, abandoned within lifespan) Identity-level commitments Ontogenetic + cultural: self-model integration of roles, values, group memberships CMS (mPFC/PCC) self-model; DMN consolidation; identity-affect circuits Years to decades (high-inertia learned priors, revisable under strong evidence) Cultural/institutional goals Cultural transmission via language, narrative, institutions External representations (texts, laws, norms) internalized via social-identity mechanisms Generations to centuries (cumulative cultural evolution) These layers do not operate in isolation but form a coupled dynamical system . Implicit drives generate the felt states that motivate explicit goal formation; explicit goals, once adopted, reshape the training distribution for implicit learning (a student who explicitly commits to studying physics exposes their compression drive to physics-structured data, biasing future intrinsic motivation toward that domain). Identity commitments constrain explicit goal selection (goals inconsistent with identity are filtered before deliberation); cultural goal systems shape the identities available for adoption (one cannot identify as a "scientist" in a culture without science). Upward causation (implicit → \to explicit) and downward causation (cultural → \to identity → \to explicit → \to implicit training distribution) operate simultaneously, producing a co-constructive dynamic in which no single layer has absolute priority. The question "what objective does the human brain optimize?" now has a layered answer: At the architectural level (fixed within a lifetime): minimize long-run variational free energy, subject to viability constraints–which decomposes into risk minimization (preference satisfaction), ambiguity reduction (state estimation), and model improvement (compression progress), with empowerment as the option-value prior and social objectives as deep viability-level priors on the preference landscape. At the meta-learning level (tuned across development): the implicit stack’s operation over structured experience generates a meta-learned exploration/exploitation policy (see "Intrinsic Motivation") that implicitly approximates: "allocate resources to domains and experiences where model improvement, skill expansion, and social capital accumulation are jointly maximized per unit cost." At the explicit goal level (revised within episodes to years): the agent pursues a portfolio of linguistically structured, culturally informed, identity-constrained goals that are best understood as locally optimal compressions of the implicit stack’s demands given the agent’s current world model, option library, social context, and identity commitments. These explicit goals are the "conscious objectives" that the agent would report if asked "what are you trying to do?"–but they are shadows cast by a much deeper, wider, and older objective structure that operates largely below reflective awareness. The practical consequence is that human behavior cannot be predicted or understood from explicit goals alone, because explicit goals are (a) incomplete compressions of the full implicit stack, (b) subject to Goodhart drift under optimization pressure, (c) in chronic low-grade tension with implicit drives that surface as affect, and (d) embedded in a social/cultural context that shapes which goals are available, valued, and identity-consistent. Equally, behavior cannot be predicted from implicit drives alone, because the explicit goal layer–enabled by prefrontal control, language, and cultural scaffolding–can sustain behavioral programs that override, redirect, and even counteract implicit drives for extended periods. Understanding human motivation requires modeling the full stack and its interactions : the ancient implicit objectives that generate the energy for action, the learned explicit goals that give it direction , and the cultural institutions that extend both scope and horizon far beyond anything a solitary biological optimizer could achieve.

title: Honorable Mentions
text: Some other proposed superordinate objectives Criticality: The Entropic Brain A growing body of work suggests that the brain does not merely optimize what it computes but also the dynamical regime in which it computes, self-tuning toward a narrow operating point– criticality –at the boundary between ordered (low-entropy, rigid, highly predictable) and disordered (high-entropy, labile, noise-dominated) dynamics. Criticality, borrowed from statistical physics, refers to the phase transition between these regimes: a system poised at this edge exhibits spatiotemporal activity patterns that follow power-law (scale-free) statistics rather than the characteristic scales expected of either phase alone. The landmark observation of neuronal avalanches –cascades of spiking activity whose sizes and durations follow power-law distributions with exponents matching those predicted by critical branching processes–provided the first direct cortical evidence for near-critical dynamics in vitro and subsequently in vivo 1 , 2 . Complementary signatures at larger scales include long-range temporal correlations and 1 / f 1/f -like spectral structure in EEG/MEG and fMRI signals 3 , 4 , scale-free functional connectivity fluctuations, and maximal dynamic range and susceptibility of cortical populations near the critical point 5 , 6 . Why would this matter as a candidate superordinate objective? The theoretical motivation is that criticality simultaneously optimizes a constellation of information-processing desiderata: maximal dynamic range (the range of input intensities a network can discriminate is maximized at criticality, because the network is sensitive enough to amplify weak signals without saturating on strong ones) 5 , maximal information transmission and storage (mutual information between inputs and outputs peaks at the critical point, as do measures of information capacity) 6 , 7 , maximal computational flexibility (the repertoire of distinguishable network states–and transitions among them–is largest at criticality, enabling the system to rapidly reconfigure for diverse tasks without requiring structural rewiring) 8 , 9 , and optimal balance between integration and segregation (critical networks support both local specialized processing and long-range coordination, precisely the regime needed for hierarchical generative modeling) 6 . In the language of the preceding sections, criticality can be understood as the dynamical regime that jointly supports the objectives already discussed: compression progress is fastest when the network’s representational repertoire is maximal (criticality maximizes the number of distinguishable activity patterns available for encoding); empowerment is highest when the system can flexibly generate many distinct output trajectories; and EFE minimization is most effective when the generative model can both propagate precise predictions (requiring some order) and remain responsive to surprising evidence (requiring some disorder). The entropic brain hypothesis 10 , 11 synthesizes these observations into a unifying framework, proposing that the quality of conscious states can be placed on an axis of neural entropy (closely related to criticality), with the ordinary waking state representing a near-critical regime that has been finely tuned by evolution, development, and moment-to-moment neuromodulatory regulation. Deviations toward subcriticality (excessive order)–associated with reduced entropy, stereotyped dynamics, and over-weighted priors–are linked to psychopathologies of rigidity such as depression, addiction, OCD, and anorexia, where behavior and cognition become trapped in narrow, self-reinforcing attractors 11 . Deviations toward supercriticality (excessive disorder)–associated with elevated entropy, weakened top-down constraints, and flattened priors–characterize psychedelic states, early psychosis, and certain acute stress responses, where the model "loosens" and normally suppressed hypotheses flood awareness 12 , 10 , 13 . This is more than analogy: serotonergic psychedelics (which agonize cortical 5-HT 2 A _{2A} receptors concentrated in layer V pyramidal neurons) measurably increase neural signal entropy, reduce the strength of top-down predictions, and flatten the precision hierarchy–temporarily pushing cortical dynamics toward supercriticality and producing subjective loosening of prior beliefs that can, under controlled conditions, enable therapeutic "model revision" in previously rigid psychopathological states 13 , 14 , 15 . Mechanistically, the brain appears to maintain proximity to criticality via homeostatic tuning of the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance: cortical circuits actively regulate synaptic strengths, intrinsic excitability, and inhibitory gain to keep network dynamics near the critical point, recovering from perturbations on timescales of minutes to hours 16 , 17 , 18 . Neuromodulatory systems–particularly tonic serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, and acetylcholine–act as global criticality regulators , shifting the operating point along the order-disorder axis by modulating E/I ratio, gain, and precision weighting across cortex 14 , 11 , 19 . An important caveat: while the theoretical case for criticality as an organizing principle is compelling, empirical claims remain debated. Power-law distributions are notoriously difficult to distinguish from alternative heavy-tailed distributions with finite data 20 , the brain may operate slightly subcritically rather than exactly at the critical point (which would offer robustness against runaway excitation while retaining most computational benefits) 21 , and the relationship between mesoscale neural criticality and the macroscale "entropic brain" measures remains to be fully bridged 9 . Criticality did not receive a full subsection here because it is arguably better understood as an emergent consequence of the superordinate objectives already treated–a dynamical-regime property that results from optimizing compression, empowerment, and flexible inference under metabolic constraints–rather than an independent objective with its own dedicated motivational circuitry. The brain does not "seek criticality" the way it seeks food or social inclusion; rather, critical dynamics are what you get when a metabolically constrained, hierarchical, precision-weighted generative model is well-tuned for the joint optimization described in the preceding sections. Resonance Maximization: The Brain as a Coupled Oscillator An alternative–and arguably deeper–way to state what the brain "wants" is that it seeks to become structurally isomorphic to the causal architecture of its environment : to mirror, in its internal connectivity and dynamics, the statistical and causal regularities of the world it must predict and control. This idea has roots in cybernetics (Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety : a controller must have at least as much internal variety as the system it regulates 22 ), in Conant and Ashby’s Good Regulator Theorem (every good regulator of a system must be–or contain–a model of that system 23 ), and in the free-energy principle’s implication that a system that persists in exchanging signals with its environment will, over time, come to mirror the statistical structure of that environment in its internal states 24 , 25 . The resulting framework treats the brain not as an input-output device that happens to predict well, but as a coupled dynamical system whose internal structure is progressively sculpted–by evolution, development, and learning–until its state-space geometry resonates with (i.e., is homeomorphic to) the causal manifold of its ecological niche. "Resonance" here is not merely metaphorical: when two dynamical systems are coupled and one comes to mirror the other’s attractor landscape, they exhibit generalized synchronization –the internal trajectory of the "model" system becomes a smooth, invertible function of the "target" system’s trajectory–meaning that the model’s states reliably track (and can be decoded into) the target’s states with minimal lag and error 26 , 27 . In information-theoretic terms, resonance corresponds to maximizing the mutual information I ( S brain ; S env ) I(S_{\text{brain}}; S_{\text{env}}) between internal and environmental state trajectories, subject to a complexity/capacity constraint on the internal model–precisely the rate-distortion tradeoff that compression-based accounts formalize 28 . In dynamical-systems terms, it corresponds to the brain’s attractor landscape acquiring the same topological structure (number, type, and connectivity of attractors and saddle connections) as the environment’s latent causal dynamics, so that transitions in the world map onto corresponding transitions in the brain with preserved adjacency and direction 23 , 25 . Several lines of evidence support the claim that the brain converges toward structural isomorphism with environmental dynamics rather than merely learning input-output mappings. Neural representational geometry increasingly mirrors task and stimulus geometry: in trained animals and humans, the population-level geometry of neural activity in relevant cortical areas (measured via representational similarity analysis or manifold-learning techniques) comes to reflect the metric and topological structure of the stimulus or task space–e.g., the ring topology of head-direction cells mirrors the rotational symmetry of heading 29 , grid-cell lattices mirror the translational symmetry of Euclidean space 30 , tonotopic and retinotopic maps preserve the neighbourhood structure of frequency and visual space, and object-category representations in inferotemporal cortex arrange along axes that mirror ecological similarity rather than arbitrary labeling 31 , 32 . More strikingly, hippocampal and entorhinal "cognitive maps" generalize spatial coding motifs to abstract relational structures: grid-like hexagonal coding has been observed during navigation of conceptual spaces parameterized by non-spatial stimulus dimensions 33 , 34 , and hippocampal representations of social hierarchies and abstract task graphs exhibit geometric structure that mirrors the latent relational topology 35 , 36 , 37 . These findings suggest that the brain does not merely learn what predicts what (a correlation structure) but installs internal dynamics whose geometry and topology recapitulate the causal/relational geometry of the domain–a stronger condition than predictive accuracy alone. At the network level, the hierarchical laminar architecture of cortex (with distinct feedforward, lateral, and feedback connection classes) can be interpreted as an architectural prior that makes it efficient to mirror hierarchically structured generative processes in the world: the factorized, layered connectivity of the cortical sheet is itself a structural "pre-resonance" with the compositional, multi-scale causal structure of natural environments 38 , 39 . The resonance view clarifies a feature of neural coding that is otherwise puzzling: why the brain appears to invest heavily in preserving relational and geometric structure in its representations rather than adopting maximally compressed, but geometrically arbitrary, codes. A lookup table or hash function could in principle achieve zero prediction error with no structural resemblance to the environment, but such representations would fail catastrophically under distribution shift, novel recombination, or transfer–precisely the conditions that biological agents face continuously. Representations that are structurally isomorphic to environmental dynamics support zero-shot generalization : if the internal geometry mirrors the external causal geometry, then novel inputs that occupy unexplored regions of the environmental manifold will map onto the correct region of internal state space by geometric interpolation , without requiring new training data 32 , 40 . This is the representational analogue of the good-regulator theorem’s implication: a structurally isomorphic model is not merely accurate on trained data but robust and compositionally generalizable , because new situations are handled by the same structural relationships that governed old ones. Viewed this way, the compression objective described in the "Intrinsic Motivation" subsection and the resonance objective are not competing accounts but two faces of the same imperative : compression seeks to minimize description length, which (for structured environments) is achieved precisely by discovering and internalizing the causal factors and symmetries of the data-generating process–i.e., by becoming isomorphic to it 41 , 42 . Empowerment, similarly, is maximized when the agent’s internal model accurately mirrors the controllable degrees of freedom of the environment, because only a veridical causal model supports reliable action-outcome differentiation across the full action space. This framework was not given a full subsection because, like criticality, resonance maximization is arguably not an independent objective with dedicated motivational circuitry but rather the representational endpoint that the brain converges toward when it successfully minimizes free energy, maximizes compression progress, and expands empowerment in a structured world. The good-regulator theorem guarantees that a system coupled to an environment and minimizing prediction error over sufficient time will come to mirror that environment’s structure–making isomorphism a consequence of the objectives already treated rather than a separate drive. Nevertheless, the resonance framing adds explanatory value that pure prediction-error or compression language sometimes obscures: it foregrounds geometric and topological fidelity as the relevant notion of model quality (not just scalar loss reduction), it explains why the brain preserves structure that is "wasteful" from a pure minimum-code-length standpoint but essential for robustness and transfer, and it connects neural representation learning to deep results in dynamical systems theory and cybernetics that ground the entire enterprise of biological modeling in physically principled terms 23 , 25 , 24 . Neural Darwinism: Goal-Directed Agents All the Way Down A recurring motif in the preceding sections is that the brain’s global objectives (compression, empowerment, EFE minimization) are realized not by a central optimizer issuing commands but by distributed, competing, locally goal-directed elements –neurons, synapses, neural groups, cortical columns, large-scale networks–whose interactions produce globally adaptive behavior as an emergent population-level outcome rather than a top-down design. This perspective finds its most explicit formulation in Edelman’s Neural Darwinism (the Theory of Neuronal Group Selection, TNGS), which proposes that the brain implements a genuinely selectionist process–variation, competition, differential amplification–operating over populations of neuronal groups, analogous in logical structure (though not mechanism) to natural selection over organisms 43 , 44 . TNGS identifies three stages: (i) developmental selection , in which genetically guided but stochastic processes (axon pathfinding, dendritic arborization, activity-dependent refinement) generate a vast, partially random primary repertoire of neuronal groups with diverse connectivity patterns–an anatomical "population" over which selection can act 43 , 45 ; (ii) experiential selection , in which postnatal experience differentially strengthens or weakens synaptic populations via Hebbian and reward-modulated plasticity, amplifying groups whose response properties are functionally useful and allowing others to atrophy–producing a secondary repertoire adapted to the organism’s actual environment 43 , 44 ; and (iii) reentrant signaling , in which reciprocal connections among selected groups create synchronized, mutually reinforcing ensembles that bind distributed features into coherent percepts and action plans–the mechanism by which local "winners" of selection are integrated into globally coherent function 44 . Critically, this framework was paralleled and in some respects anticipated by Changeux’s selective stabilization theory, which proposed that an initial exuberance of synaptic connections is pruned by activity-dependent competition: synapses that participate in functional circuits are stabilized while redundant or non-functional ones are eliminated, implementing a Darwinian logic at the synaptic population level 45 , 46 . The empirical reality of this overproduction-and-pruning dynamic is now well established: human cortex overproduces synapses by roughly 50% during early postnatal life and then selectively eliminates them through adolescence in a region- and layer-specific maturational sequence 47 , 48 , and this pruning is not random but activity-shaped –a selection process whose "fitness criterion" is functional participation in viable circuits. The deeper theoretical insight–and the reason for the subtitle "goal-directed agents all the way down"–is that selectionist logic is not confined to neurons or synapses but operates at every spatial and temporal scale of neural organization, producing a nested hierarchy of competent agents each pursuing local objectives whose alignment produces (but does not guarantee) globally adaptive behavior. At the molecular/synaptic scale , individual synapses can be modeled as autonomous reinforcement learners that adjust their own transmission probability to maximize a local reward signal (postsynaptic depolarization, neuromodulatory reinforcement, retrograde signaling): Seung’s formalization shows that stochastic synaptic transmission combined with a global success signal is sufficient for individual synapses to implement a REINFORCE-like policy gradient, converging on transmission policies that maximize reward without any synapse "knowing" the network’s global objective 49 . Loewenstein and Seung extended this to show that Hebbian synapses performing operant matching–distributing synaptic resources in proportion to experienced reinforcement rates–behave optimally under assumptions analogous to foraging theory, treating synaptic "weight" as a depletable resource allocated competitively among afferents 50 . At the neuronal scale , individual neurons compete for metabolic resources, trophic factors (the classical neurotrophic hypothesis: target-derived NGF/BDNF is produced in limited quantities, and only neurons that secure sufficient trophic support survive developmental apoptosis 51 , 52 ), and representational territory: cortical map expansion following increased use of a body part or sensory modality reflects competitive Hebbian displacement at the population level, with "winning" neurons literally expanding their receptive fields at the expense of less-active neighbours 53 , 54 . At the assembly/group scale , Calvin’s "cerebral code" hypothesis and related Darwinian neurodynamics proposals argue that spatiotemporal firing patterns (cell assemblies, synfire chains, cortical hexagonal mosaics) compete for replication across cortical territory in a process isomorphic to clonal selection: a pattern that "works" (generates accurate predictions, drives successful actions, receives neuromodulatory reinforcement) is copied to adjacent cortical columns via lateral excitatory connections, while patterns that fail are overwritten–implementing a rapid, intra-lifetime "evolution" of neural codes on timescales of hundreds of milliseconds 55 , 56 . At the network/coalition scale , global workspace and ignition models treat large-scale conscious access as the outcome of competition among neuronal coalitions : multiple assemblies vie for entry into a capacity-limited prefrontal-parietal workspace, and the "winning" coalition suppresses competitors via lateral inhibition, broadcasts its content globally, and thereby shapes downstream processing and memory consolidation 57 , 58 . The "goal" of each coalition is local (sustain its own coherent activation), but the competitive dynamic ensures that only the most contextually relevant coalition achieves global influence–a selectionist mechanism for attentional prioritization. A powerful modern generalization of this multi-scale selectionist view comes from Levin’s multi-scale competency architecture , which argues that goal-directed problem-solving is not a property that emerges only at the level of whole-brain neural computation but is a scale-free property exhibited by biological systems at every level of organization–from ion channels and individual cells through tissues, organs, and organisms to swarms and societies 59 , 60 . Individual cells navigate transcriptional, metabolic, and morphogenetic spaces using local signaling and bioelectric gradients; cell collectives solve anatomical problems (regenerating limbs, correcting developmental perturbations) by coordinating toward target morphologies encoded in bioelectric pattern memories; and neural networks implement the cognitive competencies discussed throughout this document–each level constituting an agent with its own "cognitive lightcone" (the space of states it can sense, represent, and act upon) that is nested within and partially controlled by agents at higher and lower scales 61 . This multi-scale agency perspective reframes the brain not as a single optimizer but as a society of nested optimizers –a coalition of goal-directed subsystems at every spatial grain from single synapses to whole-brain networks–whose alignment is mediated by the architectural priors (shared neuromodulatory broadcasts, hierarchical connectivity, common metabolic constraints) that evolution installed to ensure that local competitions produce globally coherent behavior. Czegel, Szathmary, and colleagues formalize one key linkage, showing that replicator populations (competing, differentially amplified entities at any scale) performing selection naturally implement Bayesian inference : the population distribution over variants converges toward the posterior distribution over hypotheses given data, with fitness playing the role of likelihood 62 . This result provides a principled bridge between the selectionist and inferential framings: Neural Darwinism and predictive processing / active inference are not competing theories but dual descriptions of the same underlying dynamic–selection is inference, performed by populations of competing elements whose differential survival embodies belief updating. This framework did not receive its own subsection because, at the level of global brain objectives, Neural Darwinism and multi-scale competency are best understood as accounts of the implementation mechanism – how the brain realizes compression, empowerment, and EFE minimization–rather than as independent objectives. No neuron "wants" to minimize whole-organism free energy; it "wants" (in a minimal, non-sentient sense) to secure trophic support, maintain its membrane potential, and strengthen synapses that predict its inputs. But the nested competitive architecture ensures that these local wants, filtered through genetically installed connectivity priors and shaped by neuromodulatory reinforcement that reflects organism-level outcomes, collectively approximate the global objectives treated above–much as firms pursuing profit in a well-regulated market can collectively approximate efficient resource allocation without any firm representing the social welfare function. The selectionist framing nonetheless adds explanatory value that pure top-down optimization language misses: it explains why neural representations are diverse and redundant (variation is the fuel of selection), why pruning and competition are as important as growth (selection requires elimination), why neuromodulatory broadcast is so architecturally central (it is the "fitness signal" that aligns local competitions with global objectives), and why the brain is so robust to damage (a selectionist system degrades gracefully because surviving elements can be re-selected for new roles 43 , 54 )–properties that are natural consequences of a Darwinian architecture but require special explanation under a centralized-optimizer view.

title: Optimization Architecture
text: The learning problem confronting the brain is remarkable not only in scale but in heterogeneity. The system must simultaneously acquire hierarchical generative models of high-dimensional sensory streams, calibrate precise sensorimotor transformations requiring millisecond-scale temporal fidelity, discover behavioral policies that maximize reward over horizons ranging from seconds to years, and encode episodic records of individual experiences with sufficient specificity to support one-shot inference. These demands impose fundamentally different constraints on learning rate, memory persistence, representational format, and error signal structure. A fast learning rate that enables single-trial memorization of an episode would be catastrophic for the slow, interleaved statistical learning needed to extract stable sensory representations 1 , 2 , 3 . The cerebellum’s comparatively explicit teaching channel (climbing fibers) supports rapid calibration and timing-sensitive prediction learning–classically framed as supervised error-driven learning, but now understood to include broader predictive and outcome-related teaching signals 4 , 5 , 6 –whereas cortical learning is often hypothesized to rely more on locally generated self-supervised/predictive errors under modulatory gating. No single set of plasticity parameters can satisfy these demands simultaneously. Throughout this section, an optimizer refers to any neural circuit motif that repeatedly implements the following loop: Propose : generate internal activity patterns representing predictions, candidate actions, or inferred latent causes. Compare : evaluate those proposals against constraints (sensory observations, motor outcomes, rewards and punishments, social feedback, homeostatic set points), producing an error-like signal –a message that reflects the discrepancy, though not necessarily in the form of an explicit gradient 7 . Assign credit : attribute the mismatch to particular parameters–often only approximately, locally, or with substantial temporal delay 8 . Update : modify synaptic weights, intrinsic excitability, or network structure so that future proposals better satisfy the constraints 9 , 10 . Not every system implements each step with equal fidelity or explicitness. The cerebellum’s climbing-fiber-driven complex spikes provide a comparatively explicit instructive channel that supports rapid calibration and relatively precise credit assignment, classically framed as supervised error-driven learning but now known to carry broader predictive and outcome-related teaching signals 4 , 11 , 12 , 6 . In contrast, the basal ganglia’s dopaminergic signal is a low-bandwidth, temporally sparse broadcast that conveys value- and outcome-prediction errors, requiring synaptic eligibility traces and three-factor learning rules to bridge temporal gaps between action and feedback 13 , 14 , 8 . The hippocampus emphasizes rapid associative binding rather than incremental optimization: novelty and mismatch signals bias the system toward encoding, while dendritic plateau potentials enable large, single-trial synaptic updates (BTSP) that support one-shot learning; nevertheless, hippocampal subfields–particularly CA1–exhibit match-mismatch / mnemonic prediction-error responses that may regulate when memories are written or updated 15 , 16 , 17 . These differences in how the optimization loop is realized–and where it is approximate, compressed, or bypassed–are among the most informative features of the brain’s learning architecture. The brain’s solution is to partition the learning problem across multiple, anatomically distinct optimization systems, each embodying inductive biases appropriate to its subdomain. Doya influentially formalized this decomposition by mapping three major brain systems onto machine learning paradigms 18 : the cerebral cortex performs unsupervised learning through redundancy reduction and self-organization; the cerebellum performs supervised learning using climbing fiber signals from the inferior olive as explicit teaching inputs 19 , 20 , 21 ; and the basal ganglia perform reinforcement learning using dopaminergic reward prediction errors–classically characterized as a scalar signal, but increasingly consistent with a heterogeneous, multi-dimensional teaching signal: population diversity can be interpreted in distributional-RL terms (different neurons behaving like different "optimism/expectile" channels), and dopamine responses can also reflect prediction errors about specific task variables / sensory features, with the effective dimensionality depending on which projection/striatal subnetwork reads the signal out 22 , 23 , 24 . In predictive-coding / predictive-processing accounts 25 , 7 , 26 , 27 , the cortical paradigm is now more accurately described as self-supervised –the cortex generates its own targets by predicting incoming input and learns from structured, high-dimensional prediction errors propagated across its hierarchical layers 28 . To these three systems, the hippocampal formation adds a fourth optimizer: a fast, one-shot relational memory system that binds conjunctions of cortical activity patterns into retrievable episodes through behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity and Hebbian auto-association 29 , 1 , 17 , 30 . This four-system decomposition is not merely a pedagogical convenience–it reflects deep differences in neural architecture, connectivity, cell-type composition, and plasticity mechanisms, all of which have been detailed in the preceding systems-level sections. Table 1 summarizes the key computational characteristics of each optimizer. Several features of this landscape deserve emphasis. The brain’s four major optimization systems compared across key computational dimensions. Abbreviations: CF = climbing fiber; IO = inferior olive; PF = parallel fiber; PC = Purkinje cell; RPE = reward prediction error. Cerebral Cortex Cerebellum Basal Ganglia Hippocampus Learning paradigm Self-supervised/predictive Supervised Reinforcement One-shot relational binding Error / teaching signal Cortical prediction errors (hierarchical, feedback-mediated) Climbing fiber signals (IO) Phasic dopamine RPEs (VTA/SNc); distributional and feature-aware Novelty / mismatch; dendritic plateau potentials Signal format Structured, high-dimensional, topographic Structured, temporally precise Compressed at the synapse; population-/projection-structured Sparse, conjunctive Routing Point-to-point cortical feedback connections Point-to-point synaptic (IO → \to CF → \to PC) Broad neuromodulatory projections with topographic organization (projection-specific readouts) (Mostly) local circuit (EC → \to HPC → \to EC) Primary update rules Hebbian, STDP, homeostatic; neuromodulator-gated (3-factor) PF->PC LTD/LTP + plasticity in deep nuclei (and intrinsic plasticity) Three-factor (pre × \times post × \times DA) BTSP, Hebbian LTP Learning timescale Slow-dominant (statistical, across sessions) with fast adaptation in some regimes Fast-moderate (across trials) Moderate (across episodes) Fast (single exposure) What is learned World model, perceptual and conceptual representations Forward models, timing, calibration Policies, value functions, habits Episodes, relational/cognitive maps First, the error signals driving these systems differ not only in what they encode but in bandwidth, format, and routing, which strongly constrains what each system can learn. In predictive-coding / predictive-processing accounts, cortex relies on high-dimensional, topographically organized error-like signals generated by hierarchical feedforward/feedback interactions, providing rich information about what and where predictions failed for updating generative models 25 , 28 . Cerebellar learning is distinguished by an explicit instructive channel: climbing-fiber events from the inferior olive deliver sparse but powerful, temporally precise teaching signals (classically framed as error-driven supervision, though their content can be broader than simple motor error) 31 , 32 , 4 . By contrast, basal ganglia learning is driven by dopamine as a compressed neuromodulatory teaching signal: dopamine responses are heterogeneous across neurons/projections and are consistent with distributional/value 22 and task-variable (feature) prediction-error components 23 , 33 , but any given synapse effectively receives a low-bandwidth modulatory factor–so temporal/synaptic credit assignment depends heavily on eligibility traces and repetition 8 , 34 . Finally, hippocampal rapid encoding emphasizes gated one-shot storage: novelty/mismatch can control "write" state, and dendritic plateau potentials drive BTSP over behavioral timescales (seconds), enabling episodic traces to form in a single pass through experience 17 . Second, these four optimizers do not operate in isolation. In the online loop, cortex supplies rich state representations and prediction errors, while basal ganglia and cerebellum sit in parallel cortico-subcortical-thalamo-cortical loops that act on cortical activity as well as plasticity : basal ganglia implement a value-weighted gating/selection mechanism that stabilizes chosen cortical action plans into habits under dopaminergic teaching, whereas cerebellum provides fast forward-model predictions and temporally precise error-corrective feedback that refines ongoing control and can serve as an instructive signal for cortical (and downstream) representations 18 , 4 , 13 , 8 . The hippocampus complements these incremental learners by binding episodes and latent context, then re-injecting that context into cortex (to condition inference) and into striatum (to disambiguate state and sharpen credit assignment), with dopamine additionally coupling systems by regulating both striatal updates and hippocampal encoding "write" policies 1 , 15 . Coordination is then achieved by (i) neuromodulatory meta-control , which sets a brain-wide learning regime (plasticity gain, exploration/arousal mode, encoding-retrieval bias) appropriate to uncertainty and utility 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 , and (ii) replay-mediated inter-system teaching , where hippocampal sharp-wave ripple replay–coordinated with neocortical slow oscillations/spindles and modulated by reward circuitry–trains slower cortical models while also imprinting value-sensitive regularities into striatum and motor circuits 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 . Third, the multi-optimizer architecture entails a system-level arbitration problem: when systems produce conflicting behavioral recommendations, control is typically allocated gradedly via reliability- (and effort-) weighted meta-control rather than an all-or-nothing switch. Along with the emergent competitive dynamics that pervade the entire brain, computational theory and human neuroimaging support an uncertainty-based scheme in which each controller tracks the reliability of its predictions from recent state/reward prediction errors, and an inferior lateral PFC/frontopolar-rostral cingulate arbitration circuit adjusts their mixture weights–down-weighting dorsolateral striatal / posterior putamen model-free valuations when model-based predictions are reliable, but reverting toward cached/habitual control when deliberative models become unreliable or too costly 45 , 46 , 47 , 48 . This arbitration is modulated by neuromodulatory and hormonal state, but the updated picture is nuanced: acute stress effects on goal-directed vs habitual balance show substantial task- and individual-dependent boundary conditions (with mixed replications), whereas chronic/recent stress history more consistently disrupts action-outcome learning and promotes inflexible habits via identified amygdala-striatal pathways 49 , 50 , 51 . The remainder of this section examines each of these optimization systems in detail (characterizing its error signals, learning rules, and the nature of the representations it acquires) before turning to the inter-system coordination mechanisms that bind the ensemble into a coherent learning architecture.

title: The Cortex: Heterarchical Generative Modeling
text: The cerebral cortex is the brain’s largest and most expansive learning substrate. In the human brain, approximately 16-20 billion neurons are distributed across a roughly 2000 c m 2 2000\,cm^2 sheet (often reported in the ∼ 2000 \sim 2000 - 2500 c m 2 2500\,cm^2 range depending on method), folded into gyri and sulci yet remarkably uniform in its basic circuit motifs 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . As detailed in the "Whole-Brain Architecture" section, this sheet is organized into a hierarchy of areas–e.g., 180 per hemisphere in the HCP multimodal parcellation 5 –interconnected by a dense web of white-matter projections whose aggregate wiring length dwarfs that of any other brain structure. Here we revisit this architecture only to the extent needed to frame the cortex’s central learning problem: how does a recurrent, hierarchical, massively parallel network generate, propagate, and exploit error signals to build increasingly accurate generative models of the world?
