title: Cortical Error Signals
text: Intro, relating back to previous section and giving an overview of what’s in store We have normative, cortex-scale loss functions, now onto the actual hardware that computes and routes error signals The preceding section established the form and structure of the cortical loss; we now turn to the neural machinery that computes, weights, and routes the error signals that this loss implies.

title: Laminar Error Signals
text: The normative framework defines prediction errors over abstract "levels" and "nodes," but the cortex is built from columns, layers, and cell types. Mapping error computation onto this laminar architecture is not merely an implementation detail; it determines which populations must perform the comparison between prediction and input, which axonal projections carry the resulting mismatch signal, and how the precision-weighting mechanisms described above gain access to the right signals at the right processing stage. We address this mapping at two scales: first at the level of cortical layers, then at the level of cortical neurons. At the level of cortical layers , the most influential attempt to assign specific error-computation and prediction-generation roles to identified laminar populations is the canonical microcircuit for predictive coding proposed by Bastos et al. 1 . Starting from the Douglas and Martin canonical microcircuit and the message-passing requirements of (generalised) predictive coding, they associate specific neuronal populations with specific computational roles in generating and routing prediction errors and predictions: Superficial pyramidal cells (L2/3) are the principal error-computing population. These neurons compare the current-level representation (relayed via L4 from below and via local recurrence) against top-down predictions arriving from higher areas (via L1 apical dendrites and deep-layer feedback); their output encodes the residual mismatch ε l \varepsilon_l (top down inhibition minus feedforward drive) and is transmitted upward via feedforward projections to the next hierarchical level. Under this mapping, the signal carried by each superficial-pyramidal population is the precision-weighted prediction error at that level: 𝚷 l 𝜺 l \boldsymbol{\Pi}_l\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_l , where 𝜺 l = 𝒙 l − 𝒙 ̂ l \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_l = \boldsymbol{x}_l - \boldsymbol{\hat{x}}_l . Deep pyramidal cells (L5/6) are the principal prediction-generating/output population. They encode the conditional expectations (posterior means) 𝝁 l \boldsymbol{\mu}_l —the cortex’s current best estimate of the latent causes at level l l —and send descending feedback projections that deliver these predictions to lower cortical areas (where they serve as the comparison target for the error-computing superficial neurons one level down) and modulate the thalamus. Their connectivity is well suited to this role: deep pyramidal cells receive converging input from local L2/3 error populations (providing the ascending mismatch signal that drives belief updating), from other deep-layer neurons via recurrent collaterals (supporting the integration and maintenance of predictions), and—via elaborate apical dendrites extending into L1—from long-range feedback carrying higher-level contextual priors; they in turn issue the principal descending corticocortical projections to lower areas, corticothalamic projections (L6 CT neurons to first-order thalamus; L5 ET neurons to higher-order thalamus), and—in the case of L5 extratelencephalic (ET) neurons—projections to subcortical motor structures (brainstem, spinal cord), providing a direct route by which cortical predictions can be enacted as actions 1 , 2 , 3 . L4 spiny stellate (and related granular excitatory) neurons act as the principal recipient of ascending drive from lower areas (and thalamus in primary sensory cortex), distributing that drive into superficial circuits. Because the ascending projections often originate from L2/3 error populations in the level below, the drive arriving in L4 is itself prediction-error-like under the canonical mapping, providing one of the two terms that the superficial error neurons must compare. Inhibitory interneurons supply the circuit operations that make the comparison physically possible. SST + ^+ interneurons can deliver the inhibitory component of the top-down prediction–effectively subtracting descending expectations from bottom-up drive at the dendrites of superficial pyramidal cells–while PV + ^+ interneurons provide the divisive gain control that implements precision weighting on the resulting error signal (connecting directly to the precision mechanisms detailed in the preceding subsections). The resulting signal flow instantiates the hierarchical error-correction loop implied by the free-energy decomposition (Eq. 2 in "Cortical Loss Functions"): L2/3 error populations compute 𝜺 l \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_l and route it upward; this ascending error drives updates in the L5/6 prediction populations at the next level, which in turn refine the descending predictions sent back down–closing a recurrent loop whose convergence reduces the mismatch at every level simultaneously. Bastos et al. further predicted a spectral asymmetry in the routing of these complementary signals: feedforward prediction-error signals are carried predominantly by gamma-band ( ∼ \sim 30–80 Hz) oscillations (driven by PV-interneuron networks in superficial layers), whereas feedback predictions are carried by alpha–beta ( ∼ \sim 8–30 Hz) oscillations (originating in deep layers). This spectral tagging provides a useful (but not universal) heuristic for dissociating the predominant direction and functional identity of inter-areal signals; linking these frequency bands uniquely to "error" versus "prediction" messages remains an active area of investigation 4 , 5 . A direct multi-area, multi-laminar test of these spectral-asymmetry predictions was provided by Bastos, Lundqvist, Waite, Kopell, and Miller, who recorded spikes and LFPs with laminar resolution across five cortical areas (V4, LIP, area 7A, FEF, and PFC) while monkeys performed a working memory task in which stimulus predictability was manipulated blockwise 6 . The results supported the core laminar-spectral mapping: unpredictable stimuli evoked stronger spiking and gamma-band ( ∼ \sim 40-90Hz) power, preferentially in superficial layers, and enhanced feedforward Granger-causal connectivity across the hierarchy; predictable stimuli were associated with enhanced alpha/beta ( ∼ \sim 8-30 Hz) power, preferentially in deep layers, and enhanced feedback Granger-causal connectivity–strongest from deep layers of PFC to the rest of the network. Importantly, these modulatory effects were stimulus-specific : gamma/spiking increases to unpredicted stimuli, and alpha/beta increases to predicted stimuli, were strongest at recording sites whose spiking preferred the specific stimulus being predicted–with gamma selectivity concentrated in superficial layers and alpha/beta selectivity concentrated in deep layers (with area 7A exhibiting elevated high-beta power for unpredictable stimuli, highlighting area-specific deviations from the canonical pattern). Furthermore, alpha/beta power in higher-order areas (LIP, FEF, PFC) negatively coupled to spiking in deep layers of V4 on a trial-by-trial basis, consistent with top-down rhythmic inhibition of sensory cortex by higher-order predictions 6 . Importantly, this negative coupling was strongest for deep-layer V4 spiking, and the authors explicitly propose that local deep->superficial inhibitory pathways could translate this deep-layer modulation into suppression of superficial gamma and feedforward output. These findings motivated a refinement of the canonical predictive-coding microcircuit that Bastos et al. termed predictive routing 6 . In the standard account, superficial-layer "error units" explicitly compute a subtraction between bottom-up input and top-down prediction, and the resulting signed prediction error is forwarded via gamma. In predictive routing, by contrast, there need not be specialized circuits that compute a literal subtraction. Instead, feedback alpha/beta oscillations from higher-order areas selectively prepare (i.e., functionally inhibit) the specific sensory pathways–down to the level of stimulus-specific columns–that would process the predicted input. Deep-layer alpha/beta suppresses deep-layer spiking and gamma, and–via local interlaminar inhibitory circuitry–reduces superficial-layer gamma and feedforward output in the "prepared" pathway; as a result, predicted stimuli are attenuated at source while unpredicted stimuli, whose pathways have not been prepared, pass through with full gamma/spiking strength and are fed forward–constituting a prediction error not because a subtraction was computed, but because inhibitory preparation was absent 6 . This reframes how error signals are generated in an important way: the "error" routed up the hierarchy need not be the output of a dedicated comparator circuit but can emerge from the differential gating of feedforward pathways by top-down oscillatory inhibition. The functional consequence for the hierarchical error-correction loop is the same–unpredicted inputs produce larger ascending signals and therefore drive stronger updates at higher levels than predicted ones–but the mechanistic implementation is pathway-selective gain modulation rather than point-by-point subtraction. Notably, this mechanism is naturally graded : the strength of alpha/beta preparation can vary continuously with learned predictability, producing a continuum of effective prediction-error magnitudes rather than an all-or-none gate–a property consistent with the precision-weighted scaling of error signals described in the preceding subsections. A complementary proposal by O’Reilly, Wyatte, and Rohrlich– Deep Predictive Learning (DPL) –offers a laminar mapping that prominently involves the thalamus, shifting the locus of error computation partly outside the cortical sheet 7 . In their framework, the pulvinar nucleus of the thalamus serves as a temporal comparator that alternates between two functionally distinct states on an alpha-frequency cycle ( ∼ \sim 100 ms period). During the prediction phase , numerous weak (modulatory) projections from layer 6 corticothalamic neurons–originating across multiple cortical areas and levels of abstraction–converge on the pulvinar to generate a composite top-down prediction of the expected next cortical state: the pulvinar acts, in O’Reilly et al.’s metaphor, as a "projection screen" onto which the cortex’s current generative model is rendered. This prediction state is then briefly overwritten during the outcome phase , when sparse but powerful (driver) inputs from layer 5 intrinsic bursting (5IB) neurons fire a phasic burst that imposes a high-fidelity snapshot of the actual cortical activity pattern onto the same pulvinar neurons. Because the prediction and outcome states occupy the same neural substrate but are separated in time, the transition between them constitutes an implicit temporal-difference prediction error : the change in pulvinar activity from one phase to the next encodes the mismatch between what the cortex expected and what it observed. This error signal is then broadcast back to cortex via thalamocortical return projections, where it drives synaptic changes throughout the hierarchy. A key claim is that this scheme can approximate error backpropagation using only local activation signals—specifically because these temporally separated activation states encode the same error gradients as explicit backprop when propagated through shared forward and feedback connectivity 7 . Importantly, the same L5-driver / L6-modulator architecture that computes the content of each error signal also determines its effective gain —making the pulvinar simultaneously a comparator and a channel-selective precision gate. This dual role arises because the L6 modulatory predictions do not merely set a passive reference state for comparison; they actively shape the excitability landscape of pulvinar relay populations. Pulvinar channels whose L6-predicted state closely matches the subsequent L5 driver burst undergo a small temporal-difference transition, producing a weak return signal to cortex—effectively suppressing that error channel. Conversely, channels where the L5 outcome departs strongly from the L6 prediction produce a large transition and a correspondingly powerful return volley— amplifying that error channel. The L6 prediction thus functions as a channel-specific gain setting : it suppresses throughput for predicted content and leaves gain high for unpredicted content, implementing precisely the differential gating that the predictive routing framework describes at the cortical level 6 , 7 , 8 . This gain modulation is further sharpened by the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) : L6 corticothalamic axons send collaterals to the TRN en route to the pulvinar, and TRN neurons project inhibition back onto pulvinar relay cells, providing a prediction-dependent inhibitory gate that raises the threshold L5 drivers must exceed to produce a significant output—so that well-predicted channels face stronger TRN-mediated suppression while novel signals pass through with less resistance. Finally, the laminar targeting of thalamocortical return projections adds a further dimension: pulvinar projections terminating in cortical layer 4 deliver more driver-like error content into the feedforward input stream, whereas projections terminating in layer 1 act in a more modulatory capacity, adjusting the gain on apical dendrites—the same compartment-level precision mechanism described in the preceding subsections 9 , 10 . In sum, the pulvinar does not first compute an error and then separately decide how to weight it; the prediction-dependent gain structure of the L6-modulator / L5-driver / TRN circuit is the mechanism by which errors are both computed and routed with appropriate precision. Recent empirical work provides direct support for this active thalamocortical role in error-signal generation. Furutachi et al. demonstrated that prediction-error responses in mouse V1 layer 2/3 require a cooperative mechanism involving both pulvinar input and VIP-interneuron-mediated cortical disinhibition: the pulvinar does not merely relay a pre-computed error but actively participates in amplifying responses to unexpected stimuli–selectively boosting the neurons most tuned to the violated prediction 11 . Complementarily, Varela et al. proposed that L6 corticothalamic feedback enables thalamic relay cells to detect deviance from cortical predictions by controlling firing mode: burst firing selectively flags inputs that depart from the L6-conveyed expectation, casting the thalamus as an active deviance detector rather than a passive relay 12 . Together, these findings reinforce the DPL picture in which the thalamocortical loop is not an ancillary relay but an integral component of the cortex’s error-computation and error-routing architecture. More recently, a machine-learning-inspired approach has proposed a self-supervised predictive architecture that assigns each major laminar population a specific role in computing and routing error signals, deriving these roles from the requirements of temporal prediction rather than from top-down Bayesian reasoning 13 . In this framework, L2/3 integrates higher-order feedback (arriving via L1) with feedforward drive from L4 (which transforms thalamic/sensory input) to generate a prediction of L5 activity at the next timestep. L5 activity at time t + 1 t+1 –which itself reflects a distinct transformation of thalamic input and recurrent cortical activity–serves as the prediction target, and the mismatch between the L2/3 prediction and the L5 target constitutes the error signal that drives synaptic updating across the column. Notably, this model inverts the laminar role assignment of canonical predictive coding: whereas Bastos et al. cast L2/3 as the error-computing population and L5/6 as the prediction-generating population, Costa et al. cast L2/3 as the predictor and L5 as the target against which errors are evaluated. Despite this inversion, the two frameworks converge on several architectural principles relevant to error-signal routing: both assign L4 the role of feedforward relay, both identify L2/3 as the laminar site where feedforward and feedback streams must converge to enable comparison, and both require that an error signal–however computed–be generated within the column from the discrepancy between these streams. This partial convergence from an independent starting point reinforces the general principle that the cortical column’s laminar architecture is organized around the computation of temporally predictive error signals, even as the precise assignment of "predictor" versus "error" roles to specific layers remains an open question that different normative frameworks resolve differently. The preceding proposals all address how the column computes error signals from mismatches between sensory predictions and sensory inputs. Hawkins, Ahmad, and Cui introduced an additional dimension: the error signals computed within each column are conditioned not only on the current sensory state but also on a continuously updated allocentric location estimate ("location" in the broadest sense; i.e location in some latent space ) 14 . In their "Thousand Brains" framework, each cortical column contains a repeating two-layer input–output motif that they map onto cortical anatomy in at least one–and possibly two–instances per column: Primary instance (L4 → \rightarrow L2/3). L4 serves as the input layer : it receives feedforward sensory drive from thalamocortical afferents on its proximal dendrites and receives a location signal from L6a on its basal (distal) dendrites, which acts as a modulatory input representing the current allocentric position on the sensed object. The conjunction of these two inputs causes a specific subset of L4 cells to become active, forming a sparse representation that encodes not just "what feature" but "what feature at what location on the object ." L4 projects upward to L2/3, which serves as the output layer : L2/3 pools over the successive feature-at-location representations delivered by L4 as the sensor moves across an object, converging on a stable sparse pattern that represents the object’s identity. Importantly, L2/3 cells form long-range lateral connections within their layer, both within and across columns–these carry the inter-columnar "voting" signals by which columns with overlapping receptive fields (or "cognitive lightcones") share partial evidence and reach consensus on object identity. Feedback from L2/3 back to the apical dendrites of L4 cells enables top-down prediction: once the output layer has narrowed down the set of candidate objects, it biases L4 cells corresponding to the feature-location pairs consistent with those objects into a predictive (depolarized) state, so that expected sensory inputs are processed preferentially while unexpected inputs–those arriving at non-depolarized cells–constitute an implicit error signal that triggers model updating 14 . Possible second instance (L6a → \rightarrow L5). Hawkins et al. note that a second copy of the same input-output motif may exist in the sub-granular layers: L6a receives direct thalamic input with driver-like properties (paralleling L4’s role), projects to L5 (which, like L2/3, forms long-range intralaminar connections and constitutes a major cortical output–in this case projecting to thalamic relay cells and other subcortical regions rather than making direct corticocortical connections), and receives feedback from L5. However, they acknowledge that this mapping is less secure: empirical evidence shows that L5 cells can fire simultaneously with or even before L6 cells in response to sensory stimulation, which is inconsistent with a strict input → \rightarrow output flow 14 . A distinctive feature of this model is its use of dendritic compartmentalization as the mechanism for combining the signals that enter the error computation. Their "hierarchical temporal memory (HTM)" neuron model distinguishes three integration zones on pyramidal cells: proximal dendrites carry feedforward driving input (capable of directly eliciting spikes), basal (distal) dendrites carry contextual/modulatory input (including the location signal in L4 and lateral object-identity signals in L2/3) that depolarizes the cell into a "predictive" state without directly triggering a spike, and apical dendrites carry feedback from the output layer. Prediction errors emerge implicitly from this dendritic logic: when an input arrives at a mini-column in which no cell has been depolarized by the appropriate location context, all cells in that mini-column fire (a “bursting” response), signaling a novel or unpredicted feature-location conjunction; when the predicted cell is depolarized, only that cell fires, producing a sparse, confirmatory response. The transition from bursting to sparse activation is the column’s error signal–functionally analogous to the predicted-vs.-unpredicted gating described in the predictive routing framework above, but implemented via dendritic depolarization states rather than oscillatory inhibition. The location signal itself–proposed to originate in the sub-granular layers (L5/6) of each column, drawing on grid cell-like computations analogous to those in the entorhinal cortex 15 –fundamentally restructures what counts as a prediction error at every level of the column. The column does not merely ask "was this feature predicted?" but "was this feature predicted at this location on this object ?"—making every columnar error signal inherently sensorimotor (consistent with the active predictive coding principle that action terms enter the generative model at every cortical level (covered next)). Lateral excitatory connections in L2/3 (and potentially L5) provide a mechanism for inter-columnar error resolution : columns sensing different parts of the same object share their partial evidence via these long-range intralaminar projections, allowing the network to reach consensus on object identity more rapidly than any single column’s sequential error-driven convergence could achieve–a form of spatial message passing that complements the temporal error-correction loops described in the preceding proposals 14 , 16 . Hawkins et al. further propose that this same location-conditioned error-computation motif operates across all cortical regions, including those processing non-spatial modalities, where "location" generalizes to an abstract reference frame and the error signal becomes a mismatch within that frame 14 . Rao’s active predictive coding (APC) model extends the columnar error-signal architecture by placing action prediction errors on equal footing with state prediction errors , yielding two complementary error channels within each cortical area 17 . In APC, each cortical area is hypothesized to implement two coupled recurrent networks within its laminar structure: a state-transition network f ̂ s \hat{f}_s , which predicts the next latent state s ̂ t \hat{s}_t given the previous state s ̂ t − 1 \hat{s}_{t-1} and the previous action a ̂ t − 1 \hat{a}_{t-1} , and a policy network f ̂ a \hat{f}_a , which maps the current state estimate to an action (or abstract goal). Rao proposes the following laminar mapping for these networks and the error signals they generate: L2/3: state-transition network. Recurrently connected superficial-layer neurons receive filtered sensory lower cortical input from L4 and efference copies from L5, using these inputs to implement f ̂ s \hat{f}_s (predictions of the next latent state). State prediction errors–mismatches between predicted and observed states–are conveyed upward via feedforward pathways, consistent with the ascending error channel described in standard predictive coding. L5 (motor-output class): action/policy network. Recurrently connected L5 neurons whose axons target subcortical motor centers implement f ̂ a \hat{f}_a , generating action outputs that are simultaneously sent as efference copies to f ̂ s \hat{f}_s to predict the sensory consequences of each action. Importantly, such motor-targeting L5 neurons exist in all cortical areas, not only traditional motor cortex 18 , making the action error channel a canonical feature of cortical computation. L5 (corticocortical class) A second population of L5 neurons–those projecting to other cortical areas and the striatum–maintains the current state estimate s ̂ t \hat{s}_t by integrating the state prediction from L2/3 and correcting it with prediction errors arriving via feedforward thalamic inputs to layers 4 and 5/6. L6: top-down prediction generation. Layer 6 neurons, receiving input from state-estimating L5 neurons, compute predictions for the level below: at the lowest hierarchical level, they predict sensory input directly; at higher levels, they predict the cortical state of the lower area. Higher-order thalamus: action error computation. L5 motor-output neurons send axon collaterals to higher-order thalamic nuclei (for example, the pulvinar) and these nuclei also receive information from subcortical motor centers (for example, the superior colliculus) regarding actually executed actions. These thalamic nuclei are therefore positioned to compare the cortical action prediction a ̂ t \hat{a}_t with the actual executed action a t a_t , and to convey the resulting action prediction error back to cortex (especially to L5 and L1)–enabling the state network f ̂ s \hat{f}_s to correct its state prediction and the action network f ̂ a \hat{f}_a to correct its policy. The columnar error-signal architecture in APC therefore comprises (at least) two channels: a state-prediction-error channel driven by the mismatch between predicted and observed sensory consequences, routed via feedforward cortical pathways; and an action-prediction-error channel driven by the mismatch between intended and executed (or feedback-reported) actions, routed via higher-order thalamocortical pathways. Both channels are corrected through the same predictive-coding machinery of local error computation and iterative relaxation. It is worth noting that this laminar mapping assigns L2/3 the role of state-prediction generator rather than error-computing population –inverting the canonical predictive-coding assignment of Bastos et al., where L2/3 encodes prediction errors and L5/6 encodes predictions. APC instead distributes error computation across the circuit: state prediction errors arise wherever the L6-generated prediction meets ascending sensory drive (primarily at L4 and the feedforward thalamocortical interface), action prediction errors are computed in the thalamus, and both error types converge on the L2/3 state network and L5 action network to drive corrective updates. A critical feature distinguishing APC from the models above is its account of how top-down feedback reshapes the error signals computed at lower levels . In standard predictive coding, feedback connections carry predictions (expected values) that are subtracted from bottom-up representations to yield error signals. In APC, feedback from higher cortical areas goes further: higher-level state and action vectors s ̂ ( i + 1 ) \hat{s}^{(i+1)} and a ̂ ( i + 1 ) \hat{a}^{(i+1)} are transformed by top-down networks H s ( i ) H_s^{(i)} and H a ( i ) H_a^{(i)} , respectively, into modulatory signals that change the functions f ̂ s ( i ) \hat{f}_s^{(i)} and f ̂ a ( i ) \hat{f}_a^{(i)} being computed at the lower level–either through multiplicative gain modulation of the recurrent network’s input-output function, or through additive contextual ("embedding") inputs that bias the recurrent dynamics toward a task- or context-appropriate regime 19 , 20 , 21 . This is equivalent to a "hypernetwork" architecture in which a higher-level network generates the effective parameters (or gain configuration) of a lower-level network, and it provides a concrete neural mechanism for how the cortex can compose novel sensory-motor programs on the fly: different higher-level state vectors instantiate different lower-level dynamics without requiring separate hardwired circuits for each. The consequence for error-signal computation is that the nature of what a lower-level column treats as a prediction error is not fixed: it is conditioned on the higher-level context, which determines both what state transitions the column is trying to predict (by setting f ̂ s \hat{f}_s ) and what actions it should produce (by setting f ̂ a \hat{f}_a ). A mismatch that constitutes a large error signal under one top-down context may not register as an error at all under another, because the prediction function itself has been reconfigured. This dynamic reconfiguration of error computation complements the precision-weighting mechanisms described in the preceding subsections: whereas neuromodulators and oscillatory gating scale the gain on a fixed error signal, APC’s top-down modulation changes the content of the prediction against which incoming signals are compared. APC’s hierarchical structure also provides a specific mechanism for the temporal organization of error signals discussed in the "Cortical Loss Functions" section: at each level of the APC generative model, a higher-level state-action pair generates (via the top-down H s H_s and H a H_a networks) the transition and policy functions at the level below, and a lower-level sequence executes for a characteristic temporal interval (a "macro-step") before control returns to the higher level for a new state transition. Error signals therefore operate on different timescales at different levels : lower-level state and action prediction errors are generated and corrected at the fast micro-step rate (for example, individual eye fixations or movement primitives), while higher-level errors–reflecting mismatches between predicted and observed outcomes of entire lower-level sequences –are generated and corrected at the slower macro-step rate. This temporal nesting of error signals naturally reflects the kind of timescale hierarchy observed empirically across cortex. Rao demonstrates that this same architecture can perform active visual perception (recognizing objects through sequences of simulated "eye movements," with predicted glimpses maintaining perceptual stability despite discontinuous sampling), hierarchical planning (navigating large environments by composing reusable high-level actions from low-level primitives), compositional part-whole learning (parsing objects into parts and subparts with nested reference frames), and even abstract concept formation–all using the same canonical module, differing only in the content of the state and action spaces (sensory features and eye movements for vision; locations and movement primitives for navigation; symbols and relational transitions for abstract reasoning) 19 . The proposals discussed so far all operate in the regime of continuous latent variables, where error signals take the form of signed prediction errors—differences between predicted and observed continuous values—encoded in firing rates or membrane potentials. George, L’ a zaro-Gredilla, Lehrach, Dedieu, Zhou, and Marino’s Bio-RCN (the biological implementation of Recursive Cortical Networks) offers a fundamentally different starting point by deriving a cortical microcircuit from the message-passing requirements of Bayesian inference over discrete latent variables, validated on real-world vision benchmarks 22 , 23 . Rather than predictive coding’s subtraction of a continuous prediction from a continuous input, Bio-RCN implements belief propagation (BP) on a probabilistic graphical model in which each cortical column represents a binary random variable —a feature that is either ON or OFF (e.g., an oriented edge in V1, the letter B” in inferotemporal cortex)—and the functional equivalent of error correction emerges from iterative forward, backward, and lateral message passing, including a form of competitive inference called explaining away , distributed across cortical layers and the thalamus. In this framework, neurons in different laminae do not encode separate quantities ("prediction" versus "error") as in canonical predictive coding; instead, each lamina performs a specific stage of the inference computation that determines the posterior belief about the column’s single binary state, integrating evidence along lateral, hierarchical, and feedback dimensions 22 . The laminar mapping that George et al. derive for this discrete-BP architecture assigns the following roles: Layer 4: feedforward evidence computation. L4 stellate cells compute the feedforward evidence for the column’s feature ( FF_feat ) by summing bottom-up messages arriving from the thalamus (or from L2/3 of the lower cortical area via the thalamic pathway). The signal computed is a log-likelihood ratio–quantifying the bottom-up support for the feature being ON versus OFF–rather than a raw sensory representation or an explicit prediction error. This role is consistent with L4’s assignment as the "feedforward entry point" in all the preceding proposals, but the interpretation of the signal it carries is different: it is one term in a larger inference computation, not a sensory input awaiting comparison with a descending prediction. Layer 2/3: lateral propagation and pooling (feedforward output). L2/3 pyramidal neurons serve two distinct computational roles. First, a subset implements contour-continuity lateral connections : these neurons receive the FF_feat signal from L4 via interlaminar axons and exchange lateral messages ( FF_lat ) with neurons in neighboring columns, enforcing higher-order spatial consistency (e.g., that activated contour features form smooth, continuous curves) and allowing cross-column normalization/inhibition. Clonally related neurons within each column–sharing identical bottom-up selectivity but differing in their lateral connections–encode the column’s participation in different lateral contexts, providing a parsimonious mechanism for representing higher-order dependencies via what George et al. term "cloned" copies of the feature variable; FF_lat neurons also send "long distance" axons to other columns. Second, a subset of complex pyramidal cells implements pooling ( FF_pool ): these neurons transform lateral (cross-column) and feedforward input to compute a maximum over locally transformed versions of the same feature (e.g., small translations), yielding position-invariant representations (similar to L2/3 in Thousand Brains Theory) that constitute the direct feedforward output to the next cortical area/level. L2/3 in Bio-RCN is neither the dedicated error-computing population of canonical predictive coding 1 nor the dedicated prediction-generating population of APC 17 or self-supervised predictive learning 13 . Instead, it performs lateral consistency enforcement and invariant feature extraction–operations that refine the evidence supporting the column’s binary state and prepare a feedforward signal for the next level. Layer 5: feedback-modulated beliefs and column output. L5 pyramidal neurons integrate feedforward evidence (especially from L2/3) with top-down feedback (arriving via apical dendrites in L1) and lateral messages to compute three quantities: (i) feedback-modulated lateral propagation —analogous to the L2/3 lateral computation but incorporating top-down priors, so that lateral consistency is enforced under the constraint of higher-level hypotheses; (ii) pool beliefs ( BEL_POOL_FF )–the combination of feedforward pool ( FF_pool ) likelihoods with feedback messages, representing the column’s current estimate of its pool membership (pool=categorical variable) given all available evidence, which is sent to the thalamus via L5 corticothalamic projections (which is an additional feedforward pathway beyond the cortico-cortical L2/3), where they take part in "explaining away" computations (combining feedforward and feedback) and gating, before projecting to the next level in the hierarchy; and (iii) feature beliefs ( BEL_feat )–the summary output of the column, incorporating all evidence (bottom-up, lateral, and top-down) about whether the column’s feature is ON or OFF. These feature-belief neurons project to subcortical structures, consistent with the principle that motor actions should be driven by posterior beliefs rather than raw likelihoods or partial error signals. Layer 6: feedback generation to child regions. L6 neurons generate the descending feedback messages to lower-level areas by “unpacking” the column’s belief into its component sub-features and sending these to the corresponding child columns, establishing the top-down side of the hierarchical inference loop. Layer 1: feedback arrival. Top-down messages from higher cortical areas arrive in L1 as horizontally extending axons, accessible by the apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons across multiple laminae—particularly the L5 neurons that must combine feedforward and feedback evidence to compute posterior beliefs. The most consequential feature of Bio-RCN’s laminar architecture–and its most significant departure from the other proposals reviewed here–is its account of how error correction is achieved without dedicated error-computing neurons . In predictive coding, error signals are explicit: a specific neuronal population computes ε l = x l − x l ̂ \varepsilon_l=x_l-\hat{x_l} and transmits this signed residual to the next level. In Bio-RCN, no such subtraction occurs. Instead, the functional equivalent of error correction emerges from two interacting mechanisms: Iterative message passing. Forward, backward, and lateral messages are passed through the cortical hierarchy in multiple rounds. Each round updates the beliefs at every column based on the messages arriving from its neighbors (other columns in the same area via lateral connections, lower-level columns via feedforward pathways, and higher-level columns via feedback pathways). The convergence of this iterative process corresponds to the network settling on the maximum a posteriori (MAP) explanation of the input–the joint assignment of ON/OFF states to all feature variables that best explains the sensory evidence. The "error" at any given column is implicit in the discrepancy between its current belief state and the messages arriving from its neighbors; this discrepancy drives the next round of updates, but it is never isolated in a dedicated neuronal population. Explaining away in the thalamus. The thalamic circuit–involving relay cells in the LGN (for V1) or pulvinar (for higher areas), the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), and cortical L5 and L6 projections–implements the Noisy-OR factor nodes of the graphical model, which encode how multiple parent features at a higher level interact to generate the same child components at a lower level. In this circuit, L5 neurons from the lower cortical area send driver (feedforward) projections carrying pool-belief messages to thalamic relay cells; L6 neurons from the higher cortical area send modulatory (feedback) projections that pass through the TRN en route to the same relay cells, encoding top-down certainty about which higher-level features are ON; and TRN neurons, excited by L6 axon collaterals, inhibit the thalamic relay cells, providing a context-dependent gate on the feedforward evidence. The net effect is contextual gating of feedforward evidence via competitive inference : when a higher-level feature b b sends a strong top-down signal that it is ON, the thalamic circuit diminishes the feedforward evidence flowing to alternative parent features a a and c c that would explain the same child components–because b b ’s presence already "explains away" those components. Conversely, when no parent feature claims the evidence, the full bottom-up signal passes through to all potential parents, driving them toward activation. An initial forward pass activates all features compatible with the bottom-up evidence; subsequent backward-forward iterations produce explaining-away competition until the network settles on a stable solution–constituting Bio-RCN’s equivalent of predictive coding’s iterative error-correction loop 22 . This thalamic explaining-away mechanism converges with the DPL proposal that the pulvinar is an active comparator rather than a passive relay, and with the predictive routing framework’s emphasis on differential gating rather than literal subtraction 6 , 7 . However, the computational logic is distinct in each case: in DPL, the pulvinar computes a temporal-difference error between L6-predicted and L5-observed cortical states; in predictive routing, alpha/beta oscillations selectively inhibit predicted feedforward pathways; in Bio-RCN, the thalamic circuit implements a specific probabilistic operation (the Noisy-OR factor) in which feedforward evidence is redistributed among competing hypotheses based on top-down certainty signals, with the TRN providing the requisite inhibitory competition. George et al. further note that top-down object-based attention falls out as a special case of the same mechanism: clamping a parent feature node to ON via top-down signals automatically suppresses evidence flow to competing parents through the explaining-away dynamics, implementing attentional selection without requiring a separate attention circuit—a form of attention that standard predictive coding models, which lack multi-cause explaining away, do not naturally support 22 . Bio-RCN also provides a computational rationale for the existence of two parallel feedforward pathways between cortical areas. The direct cortico-cortical pathway (originating from L2/3 pooling neurons and projecting to L4 of the next area) carries feedforward likelihoods —fast, prior-free evidence that provides an initial, approximate estimate of feature presence without any top-down modulation. The indirect cortico-thalamo-cortical pathway (originating from L5 pool-belief neurons and gated through the thalamic explaining-away circuit) carries beliefs that incorporate both feedforward and feedback evidence, and is subject to explaining-away competition. George et al. propose that the direct pathway enables rapid, bottom-up-driven responses—potentially advantageous for detecting novel, out-of-context stimuli—while the thalamic pathway enables context-sensitive, iteratively refined inference. This dual-pathway architecture resonates with the predictive routing observation that unpredicted stimuli generate stronger feedforward signals (here because explaining-away has not suppressed them), and with empirical observations of fast feedforward sweeps followed by slower recurrent processing in visual cortex. A further notable feature is Bio-RCN’s derivation of specific dendritic computations from the requirements of BP message passing. The equations governing the Noisy-OR explaining-away transfer function require nonlinear operations—including exponentiation, division, logarithm, and context-dependent routing of excitation and inhibition—that George et al. propose are implemented in the dendritic trees of the excitatory and inhibitory neurons within the thalamic and cortical factor nodes. Different dendritic branches receive feedforward evidence and top-down contextual signals, and their interaction through compartmentalized nonlinear integration computes the outgoing BP message. This proposal aligns with the broader theme (developed in the Hawkins et al. and APC discussions above) that dendritic compartmentalization is a key mechanism for combining the multiple information streams that enter the error computation—but derives the specific dendritic operations and nonlinearities from the mathematical requirements of probabilistic inference in a discrete graphical model, rather than from temporal prediction or sensorimotor control. George et al. demonstrate that Bio-RCN reproduces several visual phenomena—subjective contour formation, neon-color spreading, and superior recognition under occlusion versus deletion—with predictions at the level of specific laminar populations and their temporal dynamics. For subjective (illusory) contours, L4 neurons in retinotopic locations lacking bottom-up contour evidence remain silent during the initial forward pass; only after top-down and lateral messages propagate (requiring feedback from higher levels that have identified a globally consistent shape hypothesis, and lateral propagation through L2/3 contour-continuity circuits) do these “hallucinated” contour features activate in L5 and L6, producing the percept of illusory contours with a temporal delay relative to real-contour responses—matching the physiological dynamics observed in V1 and V2. This observation is significant for the present discussion because it demonstrates that a model without explicit error-coding neurons can produce the laminar-specific, temporally structured response dynamics (feedforward-driven early responses followed by feedback-modulated late responses) that are often interpreted as evidence for predictive coding’s subtraction-based error signals. Bio-RCN suggests that such dynamics may be signatures of iterative Bayesian inference more generally—whether the underlying variables are continuous (as in predictive coding) or discrete (as in BP)—rather than of any particular error-signal architecture, reinforcing the point that the functional requirement of hierarchical error correction can be met by multiple distinct computational mechanisms 22 . In synthesis, the proposals reviewed in this subsection converge on a core architectural principle–that the cortical column’s laminar organization exists to compute, route, and gate hierarchical error-correction signals using only locally available quantities–while diverging, sometimes sharply, on precisely which laminae perform which operations. The most striking disagreement concerns the computational identity of L2/3: canonical predictive coding casts it as the error-computing population whose output is the ascending residual ε l \varepsilon_l ; APC and self-supervised predictive learning cast it as the prediction-generating population whose output is compared against a target elsewhere; the Thousand Brains framework treats it as a pooling and consensus layer that accumulates object-level evidence across sequential sensory samples; and Bio-RCN assigns it the role of lateral consistency enforcement and invariant feature extraction within a discrete belief-propagation scheme. Deep layers (L5/6) are similarly contested: they generate descending predictions in canonical predictive coding, maintain state estimates and action policies in APC, supply the driver signals that define the "outcome" phase of the pulvinar’s temporal-difference comparison in DPL, and compute posterior beliefs integrating all evidence streams in Bio-RCN. Despite these divergences in role assignment, several robust points of agreement emerge. First, all frameworks require that feedforward and feedback streams converge within the column–whether at L2/3 apical dendrites, at the L4-L6 interface, or in the thalamus–so that a comparison (explicit subtraction, differential gating, or competitive explaining away) can occur. Second, all assign L4 the role of principal feedforward entry point, transforming ascending input into a format suitable for intracolumnar processing. Third, all invoke dendritic compartmentalization as a key mechanism for combining the multiple information streams that enter the error computation–proximal dendrites carrying driving input, basal/distal dendrites carrying contextual or location signals, and apical dendrites carrying top-down feedback–though each framework derives different specific operations from this shared substrate. Fourth, the thalamus is increasingly recognized not as a passive relay but as an active participant in error computation: the pulvinar serves as a temporal comparator in DPL, a site of explaining-away competition in Bio-RCN, and a locus of action-prediction-error computation in APC–roles that are mechanistically distinct but functionally convergent in positioning thalamocortical loops as integral to the cortex’s error-correction architecture. Fifth, all frameworks accommodate the observation that error signals need not arise from literal point-by-point subtraction: predictive routing achieves the same functional outcome through pathway-selective oscillatory gating, Bio-RCN through iterative message passing and competitive redistribution of evidence, and the Thousand Brains framework through the contrast between sparse (predicted) and bursting (unpredicted) columnar responses–suggesting that "prediction error" in cortex is best understood as a functional category (any signal whose magnitude scales with the discrepancy between expectation and observation) rather than as a commitment to a single biophysical mechanism. The deepest invariant across these otherwise competing accounts is therefore not any particular laminar wiring diagram but the requirement of local computability: each column must be able to evaluate, using only signals available at its own synapses and dendrites, whether its current representational state is consistent with the messages arriving from its hierarchical, lateral, and thalamocortical neighbors–and to generate a corrective signal whose propagation, aggregated across the full cortical sheet, reduces a shared variational objective.

title: Neuromodulators as precision weighting machinery
text: The precision matrices Π l \Pi_l in the hierarchical free-energy decomposition act as multiplicative gain fields over prediction-error units: they amplify mismatches deemed reliable and suppress those attributable to noise. Implementing this operation requires mechanisms that can multiplicatively rescale neural input-output functions in a context-dependent, rapidly adjustable manner. The ascending neuromodulatory systems–acetylcholine (ACh), norepinephrine (NE), dopamine (DA), and serotonin (5-HT)–are natural candidates, sharing three properties that distinguish them from fast synaptic transmission and that map directly onto precision-weighting requirements 1 , 2 : (i) broad but topographically organized projections from compact source nuclei, enabling a single modulatory signal to set different effective precisions across areas via area- and layer-specific receptor distributions; (ii) slow, often metabotropic signaling (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds) that modulates on the timescale of contextual state–arousal, volatility, attentional set–rather than individual spikes; and (iii) multiplicative (gain-like) effects on neuronal input-output functions, achieved through modulation of leak conductances (e.g., ACh (via muscarinic receptors) often suppresses M-type (Kv7) K+ currents, increasing input resistance and excitability, while NE often modulates neuronal gain through receptor-specific effects on intrinsic conductances and inhibitory circuitry that can either enhance or suppress excitability), suppression of spike-frequency adaptation (extending linear dynamic range), alteration of synaptic conductance states (shifting normalization set points), and modulation of dendritic Ca2+ and NMDA nonlinearities that gate compartment-specific regenerative events 3 . The theoretical link to predictive coding was made explicit by Friston: in the cortical hierarchy, superficial pyramidal neurons encoding prediction error ε l \varepsilon_l have their postsynaptic gain set by neuromodulatory input; a neuromodulator that multiplicatively increases this gain is, formally, increasing the precision Π l \Pi_l –causing the same physical mismatch to exert greater influence on both perceptual inference and synaptic learning 4 , 5 . Conversely, reducing gain on error units is equivalent to declaring those errors unreliable, allowing other synapses/neurons to dominate. This framing unifies classical observations of neuromodulatory sensory enhancement with Bayesian inference: "turning up the volume" on a sensory area is increasing sensory likelihood precision relative to prior expectations. Each neuromodulator controls a distinct axis of the precision landscape: ACh – sensory likelihood precision . Yu and Dayan formalized ACh as signaling expected uncertainty–the known unreliability of top-down predictions–boosting the weight of bottom-up evidence relative to descending priors 1 . Mechanistically, β 2 \beta2 nicotinic receptors (often α 4 β 2 \alpha4\beta2 -containing) expressed on thalamocortical afferents in granular layers (e.g., L4) potentiate feedforward drive, while muscarinic receptors (via subtype- and circuit-specific mechanisms, often involving presynaptic modulation and inhibitory interneurons) suppress intracortical recurrent and feedback transmission that carries lateral and top-down predictions 6 , 7 –a coordinated shift that raises sensory precision and lowers prior precision. Empirically, sustained attention elevates cortical ACh and improves detection 8 ; optogenetic basal-forebrain ACh activation enhances visual cortical gain and perceptual sensitivity 9 ; cholinesterase inhibition enhances the mismatch negativity (MMN), with dynamic causal modeling localizing the effect to increased gain on forward prediction-error connections 10 . Cholinergic tone also controls cortical state: high ACh decorrelates population activity, reducing shared variability and increasing effective coding precision 11 ; low ACh (non-REM sleep) allows synchronized, prior-dominated dynamics suited to consolidation rather than inference. See the "Acetylcholine" section of "Neuromodulators" for a detailed account of how evolution "baked in" these ACh functions through architectural biases and specific training data. NE – volatility and global gain reset. NE from the locus coeruleus (LC) encodes unexpected uncertainty (volatility)–the degree to which the generative model itself has become unreliable 1 , 12 . Phasic LC bursts deliver a transient, brain-wide precision boost that amplifies whichever prediction errors are currently active, forcing rapid belief updating (consistent with the P3/P300 scalp potential scaling with surprise 13 ). Tonic LC mode sets baseline gain and the exploitation-exploration trade-off: intermediate tonic NE sharpens gain selectively on task-relevant representations (exploitation); high tonic NE elevates gain uniformly, washing out differential precision and promoting disengagement and exploration 12 . At the cellular level, moderate NE engages high-affinity α 2 A \alpha2A receptors, strengthening prefrontal recurrent dynamics (e.g., via inhibition of cAMP signaling and closure of HCN channels on spines), whereas high NE release during stress recruits lower-affinity α 1 \alpha1 and β 1 \beta1 receptors that weaken PFC network persistence and impair working memory–yielding the classic inverted-U dose-response for prefrontal function 14 , 15 , 16 . See the "Norepinephrine" section of "Neuromodulators" for a detailed account of how evolution "baked in" these NE functions through architectural biases and specific training data. DA – prior/policy precision. Mesocortical DA modulates the gain of prefrontal representations–the confidence assigned to abstract goals and rules maintained in working memory. Intermediate D1R stimulation stabilizes and sharpens persistent PFC representations (improved signal-to-noise/selectivity/precision) via multiple synaptic and intrinsic mechanisms, producing an inverted-U optimum 17 , 18 . Insufficient D1 stimulation yields imprecise priors (distractible, stimulus-bound inference); excessive D1 stimulation aberrant precision control (e.g., maladaptive weighting of priors vs prediction-errors)–a leading computational account of psychotic positive symptoms 19 , 20 and THC effects 21 . D2-dominated regimes reduce attractor stability and facilitate rapid switching/updating (lower ‘policy commitment’), supporting flexibility 22 , 23 . In active inference, the policy precision parameter γ \gamma governing the softmax over policies has been formally identified with dopaminergic signaling, linking parkinsonian akinesia to low γ \gamma and impulsivity/mania to high γ \gamma 24 . See the "Dopamine" section of "Neuromodulators" for a detailed account of how evolution "baked in" these DA functions through architectural biases and specific training data. 5-HT – temporal depth and prior-likelihood balance. Serotonin’s 14+ receptor subtypes resist a single computational gloss, but convergent evidence supports roles in modulating the temporal horizon of the loss (high 5-HT promotes patience / low discounting, effectively increasing the weight assigned to distal outcomes / long-horizon errors (a temporal-depth meta-parameter 25 , 26 ) and the learning rate under volatility 27 . High 5-HT2A expression in deep-layer pyramidal populations and (apical) dendrite-rich compartments (notably layer V/Va) in prefrontal/association cortex positions serotonin to gate the gain on top-down feedback at the dendritic level 28 , 29 . 5-HT-2A agonists (psychedelics) profoundly disrupt prior-likelihood balance, producing states interpretable as collapsed or chaotically fluctuating prior precision: the REBUS model (Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics) formalizes this as a flattening of the precision hierarchy, releasing sensory processing from the constraint of high-level priors 30 . See the "Serotonin" section of "Neuromodulators" for a detailed account of how evolution "baked in" these 5-HT functions through architectural biases and specific training data. Much of the cortex’s fine-grained spatial specificity in neuromodulatory gain control is achieved not only by direct action on pyramidal neurons, but also–and often more selectively –through differential recruitment of inhibitory interneuron subtypes , providing the circuit-level mechanism by which a diffuse broadcast can yield compartment- and pathway-specific gain adjustments. VIP + ^+ interneurons (many within the 5-HT 3 _{3} -expressing interneuron class and strongly excitable by nicotinic ACh) can act as neuromodulatory relay switches: when recruited, they suppress SST + ^+ dendrite-targeting inhibition (the VIP → \rightarrow SST disinhibitory motif), thereby disinhibiting pyramidal distal/apical dendrites and increasing dendritic responsiveness–an arrangement consistent with a state-dependent "opening of the gate" for signals that preferentially impinge on apical compartments (including, plausibly, feedback/contextual inputs) 31 , 32 . PV + ^+ basket cells, by contrast, deliver fast perisomatic inhibition that strongly shapes spike output and population gain; neuromodulators that alter PV excitability and PV-driven E/I balance can therefore shift cortical responses in a manner consistent with divisive gain control/normalization , even if normalization itself is implemented by multiple interacting mechanisms 33 , 32 . SST + ^+ neurons provide the complementary handle, targeting dendritic compartments (often distal/apical) more directly and thereby modulating apical integration itself 32 . Taken together, these subtype-specific targeting rules (PV: perisomatic output control; SST: dendritic/apical inhibition; VIP: dendritic disinhibition via SST) furnish a concrete substrate by which neuromodulators can differentially reweight feedforward-dominated drive (often impacting spike output via perisomatic control) versus feedback/contextual influences (often impacting apical integration), enabling a partially dissociable tuning of effective likelihood- vs prior-related precision in hierarchical predictive coding (the dendritic mechanisms are elaborated in the next subsection). Overall, the four neuromodulatory systems implement a multi-dimensional state space over the cortex’s precision landscape. No single neuromodulator "is" precision; each controls a different axis (sensory likelihood, volatility/global gain, prior/policy confidence, temporal depth), and these axes interact through dense inter-nuclear connectivity and receptor co-expression. The joint neuromodulatory state is coordinately reshaped across behavioral contexts–from drowsy rest (low ACh, low NE -> low sensory precision, prior-dominated) to alert focused attention (high ACh, moderate phasic NE, optimal DA -> high sensory precision, sharp policy precision) to acute stress (high tonic NE, high DA, low 5-HT -> uniformly high but poorly differentiated gain, shallow temporal horizon)–tuning the effective cortical loss function to the demands of the moment (see the "Computational Integration" section of "Neuromodulators" for more). Importantly, these gain changes do not themselves compute prediction errors; they weight them. In machine-learning terms, neuromodulators are not part of the forward pass that computes the loss but part of the optimizer–they set the effective learning rate and the relative weighting of loss terms, moment by moment, across the cortical hierarchy.

title: Other precision weighting mechanisms
text: Neuromodulators provide a powerful global and state-dependent handle on gain, but they are only one layer of the precision-control stack; the cortex also implements precision weighting through several other mechanisms: Apical dendritic gating: compartment-level precision switching. The finest-grained precision control can occur at the single-neuron level via the functional compartmentalization of pyramidal dendritic trees. Driving sensory/feedforward inputs tend to impinge more strongly on basal dendrites and perisomatic circuits, whereas cortico-cortical feedback /contextual signals are especially enriched in layer 1 and preferentially target the apical tuft–a segregation that provides a natural substrate for differentially reweighting evidence-dominated vs context/prior-dominated influences in hierarchical predictive architectures. Rather than acting as a separate "error computer," the apical compartment can be viewed as a gain-control channel whose effective influence on somatic output spans a wide dynamic range: when apical depolarization is weak, its impact on spike output is often modest and primarily modulatory; when sufficiently strong apical drive coincides with basal drive and backpropagating activity, regenerative dendritic events (e.g., BAC firing via apical Ca 2 + ^{2+} electrogenesis) can supralinearly amplify somatic output, effectively increasing the leverage of feedback/context on the neuron’s response 1 , 2 . This amplification is, however, not an all-or-none "precision bit": the probability, timing, and amplitude of apical Ca 2 + ^{2+} events vary continuously with the balance of apical excitation, basal drive, dendritic nonlinearities, and inhibition, yielding a graded control of how strongly apical information shapes output. This apical gain is strongly regulated by dendrite-targeting inhibition, including SST + ^{+} Martinotti cells that innervate the apical tuft and can raise the threshold for (or suppress) apical regenerative events; conversely, VIP → \rightarrow SST disinhibition can release this brake, biasing the circuit toward greater apical influence and thereby providing a pathway by which behavioral state and neuromodulatory context can tune feedback efficacy at the dendritic level 3 . Disruption of apical integration (for example, via NMDA hypofunction and impaired dendritic nonlinearities) has been proposed as a precision-control failure contributing to core cognitive deficits in schizophrenia 4 . For learning, apical Ca 2 + ^{2+} spikes can also gate and shape plasticity by generating large, prolonged dendritic calcium transients that bias the induction of LTP/LTD at co-active feedforward synapses, coupling precision-weighted inference with precision-weighted learning at the level of single cells (also covered in "Cortical Plasticity") 1 , 2 . Oscillatory synchrony: temporal windowing of error propagation. Neural oscillations provide an intermediate-timescale control channel for effective connectivity, adjusting cycle by cycle which populations can influence one another . In the communication-through-coherence (CTC) framework, inter-areal transmission is most effective when sender and receiver rhythms are phase-aligned such that presynaptic spikes arrive during high-excitability phases of the receiver; misalignment reduces the postsynaptic impact of the same spike trains 5 , 6 . Coherence can therefore be treated as a temporal gate on pathway gain (and, in predictive-coding terms, can be interpreted as scaling the effective precision of signals along that pathway), although an important alternative view is that some forms of coherence may arise as a consequence of communication rather than its cause 7 . A large body of work supports a spectral asymmetry in cortical routing: feedforward-directed influences are often strongest in higher-frequency bands (gamma, and in some analyses theta/gamma), whereas feedback-directed influences are strongest in lower-frequency bands (alpha/beta) 8 , 9 , 10 . Consistent with this, attention increases gamma-band synchronization/coherence between lower and higher visual areas, strengthening effective feedforward drive 10 . Conversely, increased alpha power over task-irrelevant/unattended regions predicts worse perceptual performance and is well modeled as rhythmic inhibitory pulsing that reduces local excitability and sensory throughput 11 . This "gamma-up / alpha-down (or alpha-up in suppressed regions)" pattern naturally supports spectral multiplexing : ascending error-like signals and descending context/prediction-like signals can be differentially gated–even along the same anatomical pathways–by shifting coherence and power in the corresponding bands 6 , 12 . Theta-range rhythms (~4-8 Hz) further organize processing over longer windows, and theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling can nest fast, high-gain processing epochs inside slower control cycles 13 . These oscillatory gates interact with slower precision channels: neuromodulators can bias the global oscillatory regime (e.g., cholinergic engagement often promotes gamma and theta-gamma coupling and reshapes low-frequency rhythms in a task- and region-dependent manner); the net result is a multi-scale temporal precision architecture in which neuromodulators set the slow envelope and oscillatory synchrony supplies rapid, cycle-by-cycle gating 13 , 11 , 6 . Population variability as intrinsic gain control. Trial-to-trial variability in neural population responses is not merely a nuisance that obscures a separately computed precision signal–it directly implements precision weighting through its effect on gain. When shared variability is high (elevated Fano factors, strong low-dimensional noise correlations), the population’s net drive to downstream targets is inconsistent across repetitions: the same nominal prediction error produces a noisy, temporally smeared volley whose postsynaptic impact is effectively attenuated by the incoherence of its constituent spikes. A high-variance error representation is, by simple biophysics, a low-gain error representation–and therefore a low-precision one. Conversely, stimulus onset, attention, and confident perceptual states are all associated with a suppression of shared variability 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , which tightens the population response around its mean, increases the reliability and temporal coherence of the output volley, and thereby raises the effective gain with which that population’s prediction errors influence downstream inference and plasticity. In this view, precision need not be represented as a separate scalar quantity and then multiplicatively applied to error units; rather, the statistical structure of the error-coding population itself determines how heavily that error is weighted in the global loss. Thalamocortical precision gating. Every cortical area participates in reciprocal thalamocortical loops, and a growing body of work supports the view that thalamus is not a passive relay but a reconfigurable gain/routing node that helps determine which signals are amplified and broadcast to and between cortical areas–and when. The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) –a GABAergic shell that receives excitatory collaterals from both corticothalamic (especially L6) projections and thalamocortical relay axons–projects inhibition back onto thalamic relay neurons, providing a circuit substrate for state- and context-dependent inhibitory gating that can act like gain control over thalamocortical throughput (often approximating divisive effects depending on operating point and network state) 18 , 19 . Consistent with an attentional "mask" implemented upstream of cortex, TRN activity can decrease for attended stimuli (disinhibiting relay) and increase when attention is directed elsewhere, shaping relay responses early in the sensory stream and plausibly contributing to cross-channel suppression before cortical attentional effects fully emerge 20 . Beyond first-order relays, higher-order thalamic nuclei (e.g., pulvinar, mediodorsal nucleus) receive driver-like input from cortical L5 and return projections to superficial layers across multiple cortical areas, creating transthalamic corticocortical pathways that can regulate directed inter-areal communication rather than merely retransmitting peripheral input 21 , 19 . In the visual system, the pulvinar has been shown to coordinate attention-dependent inter-areal coupling–particularly in the alpha band–such that pulvinar activity is consistent with a coordinating (and not purely reflective) role in shaping cortical synchrony and effective connectivity across visual areas 22 , 23 . Within predictive-coding/active-inference framings, this naturally invites an interpretation in which higher-order thalamus helps set the effective precision/gain of inter-areal message passing (e.g., amplifying attended channels and down-weighting unattended ones via corticothalamic control of transthalamic gain) 24 . These thalamic precision/routing mechanisms dovetail with other gain channels: cholinergic input can depolarize many relay neurons and exerts receptor-specific (nicotinic/muscarinic) control over TRN excitability, reshaping TRN-mediated inhibition and thus relay throughput; noradrenergic input from locus coeruleus tends to bias relay neurons toward tonic, relay-competent firing and reduce rhythmic bursting, altering both linear fidelity and salience sensitivity 21 , 19 . More generally, thalamocortical loops are deeply intertwined with cortical oscillatory regimes (including alpha/beta generators and state-dependent synchrony), making thalamus a plausible convergence point where neuromodulatory state, oscillatory coordination, and feedback control jointly determine which signals enter cortex and which inter-areal channels dominate moment-to-moment computation 19 , 22 , 23 . The five precision-weighting mechanisms operate at different spatial scales (single dendritic compartments local populations inter-areal thalamic routing brain-wide modulatory broadcasts), different temporal scales (single oscillatory cycles at 1̃0-25 ms neuromodulatory state changes over seconds), and on different aspects of the precision tensor (compartment-specific gating, mean gain, temporal windowing, covariance structure, inter-areal routing). Their joint action implements the full Π l \Pi_l field: neuromodulators set the slow, state-dependent envelope; the thalamus gates which inter-areal channels are open; oscillatory coherence provides cycle-by-cycle temporal gating; apical dendritic mechanisms control compartment-level prior-likelihood integration; and population variability quenching reflects the aggregate precision achieved by the ensemble. The result is a deeply layered precision architecture that allows the cortex to continuously reshape its effective loss function in response to attention, arousal, uncertainty, and task demands, without altering the synaptic weights that define the generative model itself.

title: Cortical Plasticity
text: The preceding subsections covered (i) the objectives the cortex implicitly minimizes—both overarching intrinsic goals and their neuron-/synapse-local decompositions—and (ii) the mechanisms by which error-like signals are computed, represented, precision-weighted, and routed through cortical circuitry. The remaining question is the one that turns an abstract optimization story into a physical one: given these error signals, what cortex-specific plasticity rules actually implement the update step? In other words, how does neocortex convert moment-to-moment mismatches into lasting changes in synaptic efficacy, intrinsic excitability, and circuit wiring, while remaining stable, metabolically viable, and continuously online? At the foundation are the synaptic and structural plasticity primitives already developed in "The Fundamentals." Here we will not re-derive those mechanisms in detail, but we will explicitly build on them. In cortex, Hebbian rules and spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) supply the canonical local substrate for credit assignment: synapses are biased to strengthen when presynaptic activity reliably contributes to postsynaptic depolarization (and to weaken when it does not), with millisecond-scale spike timing (or more generally, local voltage trajectories) shaping the sign and magnitude of change. These two-factor rules, however, are only the entry point. The cortex rarely learns from a single, clean teaching channel; instead, it learns under a superposition of constraints and teaching pressures that must be integrated without destabilizing the network. The key bridge from error signals to weight change is that cortical neurons are simultaneously subject to multiple concurrent "error" terms. Some are explicitly instructive in a dendritic-computation sense: apical-basal voltage mismatches can encode a local disagreement between top-down feedback and bottom-up drive, providing a compartment-specific teaching signal for synapses that contributed to the mismatch. Others are predictive and temporal : self-predictive errors track whether a neuron or microcircuit correctly anticipated its own near-future activity, enabling learning rules that are locally self-supervised. Still others enforce viability constraints : homeostatic rate errors penalize sustained deviations from target activity regimes; metabolic cost gradients favor sparse, low-energy solutions; and neuromodulatory reinforcement-learning (RL) signals provide low-bandwidth, state- and outcome-dependent teaching that gates when locally eligible synapses are actually modified. In cortex, these heterogeneous pressures do not remain separate all the way down to the synapse. They converge on a shared biophysical currency: dendritic voltage and Ca 2 + ^{2+} dynamics with a strongly compartment-specific spatiotemporal structure 1 , 2 , 3 . The "meaning" of an error signal, in practice, is therefore expressed as a deformation of the neuron’s dendritic voltage landscape, and as a corresponding pattern of Ca 2 + ^{2+} influx and buffering across spines, branches, and apical tufts. The job of this section, then, is to track the transduction chain: error signals → \rightarrow voltage/Ca 2 + ^{2+} landscape → \rightarrow synaptic and structural change . Concretely, we will focus on the cortical implementation details that determine which plasticity rules dominate where and when . The underlying synaptic and structural mechanisms remain those reviewed in “The Fundamentals”; the emphasis here is on why cortex, given its dendritic geometry, laminar wiring, and modulatory meta-control, instantiates them in a way that looks like a unified optimizer despite being implemented as many local, partially gated learning rules operating in parallel.
