title: Voltage-Dependent, Compartment-Specific Plasticity
text: Perhaps the most useful way to write cortex-specific plasticity laws is in a voltage-first form: local synaptic change is driven by presynaptic input timing interacting with the postsynaptic dendritic voltage trajectory at or near the synapse. Under this framing, apparently distinct empirical traditions–pair-based STDP, rate-dependent plasticity, and dendrite-centered plasticity–are not separate rule families so much as different operating regimes of the same underlying state variable, namely local membrane potential V m ( t ) V_m(t) . What matters for a synapse is not whether the neuron emitted a spike in some abstract sense, but what voltage waveform the synapse actually experienced, on both fast and slower timescales, as presynaptic input arrived. A canonical realization of this idea in cortex is the family of voltage-dependent STDP rules associated with Clopath and related models 1 , 2 . In these models, synaptic updates depend jointly on presynaptic spike arrival and postsynaptic membrane potential , typically through a combination of an instantaneous voltage term and one or more low-pass filtered voltage traces, often alongside a presynaptic eligibility trace. Pair-based STDP then appears not as the fundamental rule, but as a special case that emerges under particular voltage trajectories induced by pre/post spike pairing. This reframing is important because it replaces a spike-centric description with a biophysically closer one: the effective control variable for plasticity is the local postsynaptic state, not the symbolic occurrence of a pre-post spike pair. Mechanistically, the rule says that potentiation requires a sufficiently strong and fast depolarizing event–for example, coincidence between an EPSP and a backpropagating action potential, or between clustered synaptic input and a local dendritic spike–embedded within a permissive longer-timescale depolarization context captured by a filtered voltage trace 1 . Depression, by contrast, is favored when presynaptic activation occurs in more moderate depolarization regimes that are insufficient to cross the potentiation boundary but still drive a plasticity-relevant postsynaptic state. In this way, a single voltage-based formulation reproduces many of the nonlinearities that historically made the plasticity literature look fragmented: timing-window asymmetries, frequency dependence, voltage-clamp dependence, and the classical LTP/LTD induction protocols can all be understood without treating somatic spikes themselves as the primitive variable 1 . This is why voltage, rather than spikes, is the right control variable . The proximate gate on synaptic change is the voltage experienced locally at the synapse and in its parent dendritic compartment. Somatic action potentials and their backpropagation are only one source of such depolarization. Others include summed EPSPs, NMDA spikes, dendritic Ca 2 + ^{2+} spikes, and plateau-like regenerative events, all of which can provide the local depolarization needed to trigger plasticity even when the soma does not emit a conventional output spike 1 . A voltage-based rule therefore generalizes naturally beyond simple spike pairing and is better matched to the compartmental structure of pyramidal neurons, where different dendritic domains can experience qualitatively different voltage landscapes during the same behavioral event. Once the rule is local in this sense, dendritic location dependence falls out almost automatically . The same phenomenological plasticity rule can yield different outcomes at proximal versus distal synapses because the voltage waveform differs with dendritic location: backpropagating action potentials attenuate with distance from the soma, branch-specific nonlinearities such as NMDA or Ca 2 + ^{2+} spikes are easier to trigger in some compartments than others, and ion-channel densities vary systematically across the arbor. Modeling work shows that many seemingly paradoxical findings–including LTP without somatic spikes, frequency-dependent inversions of timing rules, and apparent reversals of the sign of plasticity with dendritic location–can be explained as lawful consequences of differences in local V m ( t ) V_m(t) rather than as evidence for fundamentally different plasticity mechanisms 3 . A complementary, more explicitly dendrite-centric framework extends this logic further by introducing multiple post- and presynaptic pathways in a biophysically realistic pyramidal neuron and showing that a range of landmark “contradictory” protocols can be reconciled once dendritic propagation and synapse location are modeled directly 4 . From this perspective, calcium-threshold models are best understood as a downstream biophysical implementation of the same principle . Local voltage dynamics determine NMDA conductance, activation of voltage-gated calcium channels, regenerative dendritic events, and calcium release from intracellular stores; the resulting Ca 2 + ^{2+} transient then determines whether the synapse crosses an LTD-like or LTP-like induction threshold 5 . Voltage-based rules thus provide the phenomenology, while calcium-threshold rules provide the more explicit biophysical substrate. The two are not competing accounts so much as different descriptive levels of the same update machinery. In the same spirit, normative dendritic-prediction schemes in which apical-basal mismatch encodes an error signal can be read as specifying which voltage configuration should occur if learning is to happen , while voltage-dependent plasticity rules specify how that configuration is converted into synaptic change. Recent in vivo work strongly supports the idea that a unified voltage/calcium-dependent plasticity machinery can nevertheless produce compartment-specific effective rules within a single cortical pyramidal neuron 6 . In mouse motor cortex during naturalistic learning, Wright et al. found that potentiation in apical dendrites is best predicted by local coactivity among nearby spines : plasticity events tend to cluster spatially along apical branches, consistent with a cooperative, branch-local rule. In basal dendrites , by contrast, potentiation is better predicted by synaptic activity coincident with postsynaptic output , i.e, a more classical output-referenced Hebbian rule. This dissociation is especially telling because it occurs within the same neuron. It implies that cortical pyramidal cells do not implement a single homogeneous learning rule across their arbor; instead, the effective rule depends on the dendritic compartment in which the synapse is embedded and on the voltage/calcium regime that compartment typically inhabits during behavior. The causal asymmetry is equally informative. When postsynaptic spiking is blocked, basal potentiation is selectively disrupted, whereas apical plasticity is much less affected 6 . Apical plasticity is therefore not simply “ordinary STDP with a weaker backpropagating spike.” It is mechanistically distinct and can be largely output-independent , relying instead on branch-local cooperativity and dendritic nonlinearities. In computational terms, basal synapses appear to learn mainly from features that successfully contributed to the neuron’s emitted code, whereas apical synapses appear to learn from the co-occurrence structure of contextual or feedback inputs at the branch level. A direct biophysical mechanism for this apical cooperativity is provided by calcium-based heterosynaptic interaction among neighboring spines 7 . Bhatt et al. show that calcium influx at an active spine can diffuse to nearby unstimulated spines, with the sign and magnitude of the induced heterosynaptic plasticity depending on inter-spine distance, timing, spine-neck geometry, buffering, and store-mediated amplification. This provides a concrete mechanism for the clustered apical rule seen in vivo : an active spine can generate a local calcium plume that effectively tags neighboring spines on the same branch for potentiation or depression, even if those neighbors were not driven by precisely coincident presynaptic spikes. In distal apical compartments, where somatic backpropagation is attenuated and plasticity depends more heavily on local NMDA- and Ca 2 + ^{2+} -dependent dendritic events, this kind of diffusion-mediated coupling creates a genuine branch-level credit-assignment mechanism . Inputs that are nearby on the dendrite and roughly co-timed become bound into a functional cluster, regardless of whether the cell fired an output spike. The computational interpretation is therefore a clean one. Basal plasticity approximates credit assignment to the neuron’s emitted code: synapses are strengthened when they help drive the output that the neuron actually produced. Apical plasticity , by contrast, approximates credit assignment to a branch-local latent cause or context model: co-active inputs are bound together into dendritic subunits that can later act as nonlinear contextual features or top-down hypotheses 6 , 7 . The important point is that these are not two unrelated learning systems. They are two emergent operating regimes of a common voltage/calcium-dependent plasticity machinery, expressed through different compartmental biophysics. Overall, these results resolve much of the long-standing apparent conflict between “Hebbian,” “non-Hebbian,” “spike-based,” and “dendritic” accounts of cortical plasticity. Cortex does not need a proliferation of qualitatively unrelated rules to explain its phenomenology. A single local voltage- and calcium-dependent update framework, when embedded in the real geometry of pyramidal dendrites and the compartment-specific propagation of signals through that geometry, is sufficient to produce very different effective plasticity laws across synapses, branches, and layers. The apparent diversity of cortical learning rules is therefore, to a substantial extent, the visible consequence of a unified underlying mechanism operating in different dendritic regimes.

title: Three-Factor Learning and Synaptic Consolidation in Cortex
text: Three-factor learning is the natural next step after voltage- and calcium-dependent coincidence rules. The previous subsection described how cortical synapses compute a local eligibility trace from presynaptic timing, postsynaptic voltage trajectories, dendritic nonlinearities, and compartment-specific Ca 2 + ^{2+} dynamics. The three-factor formalism adds a second stage: a synapse first writes an eligibility trace e i e_i , and only later is that trace converted into lasting change if an additional modulatory or circuit-level factor M ( t ) M(t) arrives, so that Δ w i ∝ e i M ( t ) \Delta w_i \propto e_i M(t) . In molecular terms, this second stage can be implemented through mechanisms such as CaMKII-dependent tagging, cAMP/PKA signaling, and synaptic tagging-and-capture (STC), while neuromodulator receptor pharmacology determines how a given modulatory input reshapes STDP windows, plasticity thresholds, and consolidation probability. This formalism relates closely to the precision-weighting story from predictive coding: the third factor does not merely “permit” learning, but helps determine which locally computed errors are important enough to be converted into persistent synaptic change. An important feature of cortical three-factor learning is that the eligibility trace is not a signless memory of “something happened.” Cortical synapses can preserve which direction of future change is currently eligible–for example, whether the stored trace is poised for LTP-like strengthening or LTD-like weakening 1 . Moreover, the same pre-existing eligibility trace can be converted with opposite signs depending on which neuromodulator arrives: in visual cortex, norepinephrine transforms such traces toward potentiation, whereas serotonin transforms them toward depression 2 . The “third factor” also need not be a diffuse monoamine in the narrow sense. Interneuron-mediated disinhibition can play an equivalent gating role by determining whether dendritic coincidence signals are allowed to produce a plasticity-permissive voltage/Ca 2 + ^{2+} state. This provides a bridge back to dendritic credit-assignment models such as Sacramento et al.: the local voltage and apical–basal mismatch machinery writes the synaptic eligibility trace, but whether that trace is ultimately expressed depends on additional modulatory or circuit-level state. This is why cortex needs three-factor learning rather than Hebbian coincidence alone. Purely Hebbian rules are too myopic: they can register local covariation, but they cannot by themselves solve delayed credit assignment, distinguish salient from irrelevant coincidences, or regulate when transient errors should be committed to long-term storage. Three-factor learning is a general biological motif, but its cortical implementation is unusually shaped by laminar architecture, pyramidal-cell dendritic geometry, feedback pathways, and local disinhibitory motifs. In cortex, the eligibility trace written at a synapse is already compartment-specific: apical tuft synapses may encode local coactivity and branch-level context, whereas basal synapses may encode output-referenced coincidence. The task of this subsection is therefore to show how cortical architecture–its lamination, dendritic compartmentalization, interneuron motifs, and regionally varying neuromodulator distributions–determines which three-factor rules operate where, when, and under what precision regime. Cortical eligibility traces are themselves tuned to cortical computation. In cortex, experimentally inferred eligibility windows are on the order of ∼ 5 \sim 5 – 10 10 s, substantially longer than the ∼ 1 \sim 1 – 2 2 s windows typically demonstrated in striatum 3 , 1 , 4 , 5 . That longer window is well matched to cortical working memory, multi-step sensory inference, and planning, and it also compensates for the fact that cortical dopamine and other modulators often arrive through slower and more diffuse volume transmission than the tightly timed dopaminergic signals seen in striatal microcircuits. In prefrontal cortex, recurrent activity may extend the functional credit-assignment window even beyond the molecular lifetime of the trace itself, creating a hybrid mechanism in which a labile molecular eligibility trace is sustained or re-instantiated by persistent network activity 6 . The regional distribution of third-factor control across cortex is best understood not as a set of simple spatial gradients, but as a multidimensional receptor-and-innervation landscape. The cleanest way to summarize that landscape is as follows: Dopamine Cortical dopamine is not organized by a single “more anterior = more dopaminergic” rule. Rather, it varies along partly dissociable maps of axonal innervation density, receptor density per neuron, and degree of behavioral dependence on dopaminergic third-factor gating 7 . In primates, dopaminergic fiber density is especially high in agranular cortex—including motor cortex, anterior cingulate, and insula—whereas more granular regions such as dorsolateral PFC and occipital cortex often show lower density and more bilaminar patterns of innervation 8 , 9 . D1 receptors are the dominant cortical dopamine receptor class in macaque neocortex, with D1 density far exceeding D2 density overall, although D2 receptors remain widespread and are not restricted to frontal cortex 10 , 11 , 12 . Functionally, dopamine is sparse or episodic rather than absent in early sensory cortex, where it can gate salience- and value-weighted remapping and consolidation 13 , 14 , 15 . In motor cortex, dopamine is one of the clearest cortical examples of an RL-style third factor, required for motor-skill acquisition and learning-related reorganization of local circuits 16 , 17 . In lateral PFC and ACC, dopamine shifts from an occasional consolidation gate to an online regulator of learning state, flexibility, effort allocation, and self-initiated action control 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 . Acetylcholine Cortical acetylcholine is broadly available across neocortex, but its distribution is also not captured by a simple gradient. Cholinergic innervation is biased toward limbic/paralimbic and downstream association territory, whereas primary visual cortex is relatively cholino-poor 23 , 24 . The receptor map is, however, partly dissociable from the raw supply map: some muscarinic receptor classes peak in sensory cortex in absolute density, but when normalized per neuron, cholinergic receptor expression generally increases from sensory to higher-order cortex 25 . In early sensory cortex, acetylcholine often acts as a major online teaching signal that converts attentional selection into map reorganization and perceptual learning 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 . In prefrontal and cingulate cortex, by contrast, acetylcholine functions less like a scalar reward signal and more like a state-setting gate 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 . Serotonin Serotonergic axons are broadly distributed across primate cortex, so cortical specialization appears to arise more from receptor topology and receptor-specific sign than from whether serotonin reaches a region at all 36 , 25 . A particularly important receptor gradient is 5 -HT 1 A 5\text{-HT}_{1A} , which is enriched in anterior cingulate, default-mode, and salience-network territory and relatively weak in motor and visual cortex 25 . Meanwhile, 5 -HT 2 A 5\text{-HT}_{2A} is concentrated on pyramidal-cell apical dendrites, especially in layers II/III and V/VI, giving serotonin direct access to the same dendritic compartments that carry top-down and error-like signals 37 . A parallel route runs through interneurons, as 5 -HT 3 5\text{-HT}_{3} receptors are largely confined to cortical GABAergic interneurons 38 , 39 . Functionally, serotonin is one of the clearest examples of a neuromodulator that can set the sign of plasticity: in visual cortex, delayed serotonergic input converts eligibility traces into LTD-like weakening, opposite to norepinephrine’s potentiating effect 2 , 1 . Primate V1 is a notable sensory exception with unusually prominent serotonergic receptor machinery, whereas frontal and orbitofrontal cortex use serotonin more strongly as a flexibility- and contingency-switching gate 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 . Norepinephrine Noradrenergic fibers are broadly distributed across cortical layers, with especially high innervation in primary sensorimotor cortex and more uniform innervation across limbic/paralimbic cortex 46 , 8 . The sharper specialization comes from which locus coeruleus (LC) subpopulation is recruited, in what firing mode, and onto which receptor-defined microcircuit 47 , 48 . In prefrontal cortex, α 1 \alpha_1 , α 2 \alpha_2 , and β \beta receptors occupy different laminar compartments, giving noradrenergic modulation different access to apical, associational, and feedforward-recipient strata 49 . Norepinephrine can also act in a compartment-specific way within a single area, as in auditory cortex where it differentially regulates apical versus basal inhibition onto pyramidal dendrites 50 . Functionally, NE is a strong third factor for salience- and novelty-gated potentiation in sensory cortex, a task-timed plasticity gate in motor cortex, and a precision- and state-setting signal in PFC 2 , 51 , 52 , 53 , 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 . Mu-opioid receptors Mu-opioid receptors are relatively enriched in cingulate, insular, and prefrontal cortex, where they modulate reinforcement, valuation, and affective processing. They likely provide an additional third-factor signal for pain- and reward-related plasticity, especially in circuits where motivational salience is tightly coupled to affective state 59 . These neuromodulator-specific maps are not arbitrary. Large-scale receptor mapping shows that cortical receptor landscapes form principal gradients aligned with the unimodal-to-transmodal hierarchy, while additional gradients capture modality-specific and circuit-specific specializations 60 , 61 . The implication is that the third factor at a cortical synapse is not a single scalar neuromodulatory variable but a composite vector : which modulators arrive, at what concentration, onto which receptor subtypes, in which laminar and dendritic compartments, under which local inhibitory state. That composite vector determines whether an existing eligibility trace is converted into potentiation, depression, consolidation, or no lasting change at all. Cortical three-factor learning is also implemented through disinhibitory circuit motifs . The canonical example is the VIP → \rightarrow SST → \rightarrow pyramidal-dendrite motif. Across neocortex, VIP interneurons preferentially inhibit SST interneurons; SST cells provide major dendritic and apical inhibition onto pyramidal neurons; and long-range feedback, behavioral-state, and reinforcement-related signals can recruit VIP cells 62 , 63 , 64 , 65 , 66 , 67 . The net effect is a transient removal of the SST-imposed dendritic veto, increasing the probability that coincident feedback and feedforward input will generate the dendritic voltage and Ca 2 + ^{2+} signals required for associative plasticity. This is not merely a theoretical possibility: activating VIP cells or silencing SST cells is sufficient to open associative LTP in mouse olfactory cortex, and engaging the same motif enhances adult plasticity in V1 62 , 63 , 68 . It is therefore useful to regard dendritic disinhibition as a circuit-level third factor : not the eligibility trace itself, but a context-specific gate on whether locally written eligibility is allowed to become lasting plasticity (but also whether eligibility will be computed in the first place). Related cortex-wide gradients in interneuron composition further bias which kinds of three-factor rules dominate in different territories. Across human and macaque cortex, the most consistent tradeoff is not total inhibition but a relative SST ↔ \leftrightarrow PVALB balance: SST is relatively enriched in orbitofrontal, medial prefrontal, anterior insular, and temporal association cortex, whereas PVALB is relatively enriched in unimodal somatomotor, parietal, and visual cortex 69 , 70 , 71 . Since PV interneurons primarily target the soma and perisomatic compartment, they are well suited for fast gain and temporal-precision control, whereas SST interneurons preferentially target distal and apical dendrites, where they regulate top-down input, dendritic nonlinearities, and plasticity 72 , 73 , 74 , 75 . This suggests a cortex-wide plasticity bias: PV-richer unimodal cortex is biased toward fast somatic precision control, whereas SST-richer association cortex is biased toward dendritic and apical gating of integrative plasticity. Synaptic consolidation is the slower selection stage of this cortical plasticity process. Here, the story is not just “strong events consolidate, weak events do not.” Rather, early voltage/Ca 2 + ^{2+} - and three-factor plasticity write a labile tagged state at recently active cortical synapses, and persistence depends on whether those tagged synapses can capture sufficient plasticity-related products (PRPs) within the relevant temporal and spatial window 76 , 77 . Strong events usually persist because they both set tags and drive PRP synthesis; weak events may still set tags, but are stabilized only if PRPs are supplied by nearby strong events, neuromodulator-dependent protein-synthesis signals, or later reactivation (e.g through spaced repetition) that refreshes tags and recruits additional PRPs. Consolidation is therefore a selection, capture, and reinforcement process, not a simple threshold: tagged synapses can cooperate or compete for limited stabilizing resources, and repeated/spaced reactivation can increase the probability of persistence by re-opening effective capture windows 77 , 78 , 79 . This capture can also be branch-local rather than neuron-global, consistent with local dendritic protein synthesis and branch-specific persistent plasticity 80 , 81 , 82 . The computational consequences are substantial. First, cortical storage is precision-weighted : the third factor does not merely allow plasticity, but helps decide which cortical prediction errors are worth committing to long-term change. In humans, cortical unsigned prediction errors are precision-weighted in a dopamine-dependent manner, and in auditory cortex acetylcholine sharpens prediction-error responses 83 , 84 . Second, three-factor rules solve temporal credit assignment on cortical timescales : second-long eligibility traces, supplemented in PFC by persistent activity, allow delayed outcomes to update the synapses that were actually causal 1 , 3 , 6 . Third, branch-local consolidation supports low-interference memory allocation , because different latent causes or task variables can be stabilized on different dendritic branches rather than indiscriminately across the whole neuron 80 , 82 . Finally, in frontal and especially motor cortex, reward- and outcome-gated three-factor rules can be interpreted as approximations of policy gradient updates 85 , 86 , 17 . The overall picture is consistent with the rest of the cortical optimization architecture developed so far. The previous subsection explained how cortex writes compartment-specific eligibility traces through local voltage and Ca 2 + ^{2+} dynamics. This subsection shows how cortex decides which of those candidate updates should count: through neuromodulator-specific receptor landscapes, laminar and dendritic specialization, disinhibitory circuit motifs, and branch-local consolidation machinery. Cortex does not invent a qualitatively new biochemistry for each region. Instead, it overlays a shared molecular eligibility system with a multidimensional receptor-and-interneuron landscape whose principal axes track the cortical hierarchy and whose local deviations implement modality- and circuit-specific specializations. The result is a cortex-wide family of three-factor learning rules in which the “third factor” is best understood not as a single scalar broadcast, but as a structured, regionally tuned control vector that converts local cortical errors into selective long-term change. See "Neuromodulators" for a broader treatment of what variables each neuromodulatory subsystem may encode (and how evolution purpose-built each subsystem).

title: Inhibitory Plasticity and E/I Balance
text: The voltage/Ca 2 + ^{2+} -dependent and three-factor mechanisms introduced above were developed mainly in the context of excitatory plasticity, but cortical learning is not stabilized by excitation alone. In cortex, inhibitory synapses are themselves plastic, excitatory drive onto interneurons is plastic, and both are required to keep learned changes from saturating or destabilizing the circuit 1 , 2 , 3 . Inhibitory synapses are therefore not passive scaffolding; they are part of cortical credit assignment and part of the machinery that keeps learned representations usable rather than runaway. It is useful to separate three levels of claim. First, the canonical theoretical principle is well established: inhibitory plasticity can homeostatically restore E/I balance and stabilize cortical dynamics, as in the Vogels-type framework where inhibitory weights adapt to maintain sparse, asynchronous, stable activity 4 . Second, specific cortical rules have been demonstrated for particular pathways, including I → \to E and E → \to I synapses with pathway- and cell-type-specific LTP, LTD, and STDP 2 . Third, and importantly, there is no single cortex-wide inhibitory learning rule analogous to the simplified textbook picture often given for excitatory STDP; the effective rule depends strongly on interneuron subtype, postsynaptic target compartment, induction protocol, and modulatory context. The cleanest theoretical starting point is therefore the homeostatic inhibitory-plasticity picture , not a claim that every cortical inhibitory synapse literally obeys one symmetric STDP law. In recurrent-network models, inhibitory plasticity provides negative feedback that can establish and maintain balanced excitation and inhibition, yielding stable asynchronous states while preserving learned structure 4 , 5 . This is the right organizing principle for cortex: inhibitory plasticity is the main anti-runaway mechanism that lets excitatory learning occur safely. At I → \to E synapses , a useful unifying point is that inhibitory plasticity is often gated by postsynaptic pyramidal-cell Ca 2 + ^{2+} arising from excitatory mechanisms such as NMDAR activation, voltage-gated Ca2+ channel recruitment, and backpropagating spikes, rather than from the GABAergic synapse alone 6 . This makes inhibitory plasticity inherently context-dependent on the surrounding excitatory state. But beyond that shared dependence, cortical I → \to E rules are highly diverse: cortical inhibitory synapses can show timing-dependent bidirectional change, burst-triggered potentiation, and heterosynaptic reweighting rather than one uniform iSTDP law 2 , 3 . A strong empirical anchor is the D’Amour and Froemke result in mouse auditory cortex. Pairing presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes potentiated inhibition within an approximately ± 10 \pm 10 ms window regardless of precise order , whereas co-recorded excitatory inputs followed a more classical asymmetric STDP window 7 ; both depended on NMDAR activation, and together they adjusted the E/I ratio, tightened the E-I lag, and improved spike-timing fidelity. The symmetry of the inhibitory rule makes functional sense: if the job of inhibitory plasticity is to rapidly bring co-active inhibition into register with the excitatory events that drive postsynaptic spiking, then any inhibitory input that reliably participates in that narrow peri-spike window should strengthen whether it slightly leads or slightly follows the spike. That is best read as a timing-alignment and gain-normalization rule , not as a mirror image of excitatory Hebbian STDP. Another major cortical result is PV/perisomatic LTPi in neocortical layer 5. Postsynaptic depolarization or brief bursts in pyramidal neurons can selectively potentiate perisomatic inhibition from PV basket cells without changing nearby glutamatergic input; this plasticity depends on postsynaptic Ca 2 + ^{2+} , NMDARs, L-type Ca 2 + ^{2+} channels, and retrograde nitric-oxide signaling, increases presynaptic GABA release, and narrows the temporal integration window of the pyramidal neuron 8 . This is another clear example of inhibitory plasticity implementing gain normalization and temporal precision control. The broader I → \to E (inhibitory → \to excitatory) frontier is that different inhibitory projection classes almost certainly obey different effective rules matched to their circuit roles. PV → \to pyramidal synapses are positioned to regulate perisomatic gain and spike timing; SST → \to pyramidal synapses gate distal and apical dendrites; chandelier cells target the axon initial segment; and disinhibitory motifs change whether dendritic coincidence is even allowed to matter. The reviews are quite clear that the field does not yet support a single settled cortex-wide taxonomy for all of these pathways, so the safest summary is diversity constrained by compartmental function 2 , 3 , 9 . Plasticity at E → \to I synapses is the other half of cortical E/I balancing: learning changes not only how much inhibition pyramidal neurons receive, but how strongly excitation recruits each interneuron class. Here the dominant empirical principle is extreme target-cell specificity . In L2/3 somatosensory cortex, pyramidal → \to LTS synapses (LTS=low-threshold spiking cell; often SST) show bidirectional STDP, whereas pyramidal → \to FS synapses (FS=fast-spiking cell; often PV) show only LTD under the same pairing protocols 10 ; mechanistically, LTP at pyramidal → \to LTS depends on postsynaptic NMDARs, whereas LTD depends on mGluRs. So even when the presynaptic cell is the same pyramidal neuron, the plasticity rule depends sharply on interneuron identity. Additional E → \to I results reinforce this picture. In mouse V1, theta-burst stimulation paired with depolarization preferentially induces LTP at excitatory synapses onto fast-spiking interneurons, but this LTP is NMDAR-independent and voltage-gated Ca2+ channel-independent, instead requiring postsynaptic Ca 2 + ^{2+} elevation via mGluR5-driven release from internal stores 11 . By contrast, excitatory synapses onto neocortical SST interneurons can express a strong-stimulation LTP that is presynaptic in expression, NMDAR-independent, insensitive to postsynaptic Ca 2 + ^{2+} chelation (suppression), and dependent on cAMP/PKA signaling 12 . So the main lesson of cortical E → \to I plasticity is not a universal postsynaptic Ca 2 + ^{2+} rule, but extreme subtype-specificity in how plasticity is induced. Some interneuron classes use postsynaptic Ca 2 + ^{2+} rises reached through distinct routes, whereas others can express LTP that is NMDAR-independent and insensitive to postsynaptic Ca 2 + ^{2+} chelation 11 , 12 . In general, the strongest modern framing is thus not “excitation learns first, inhibition compensates afterward,” but that local excitatory and inhibitory synapses are often co-trained . In mouse auditory cortex, pairing protocols can modify both paired excitatory and paired inhibitory inputs while also inducing heterosynaptic changes at the strongest unpaired inputs; these coordinated changes require dendritic Ca 2 + ^{2+} signaling and set a cell-specific E/I correlation set-point 13 . Complementing that, work in visual cortex shows that inhibitory plasticity can directly alter the sign and capacity of excitatory plasticity at the same postsynaptic neuron 14 . So inhibition is not merely downstream stabilization; it actively helps determine the admissible regime for excitatory learning. A useful theoretical synthesis is therefore the co-dependent plasticity picture: excitatory and inhibitory synapses should be treated as a coupled local learning system rather than two separate subsystems 6 . In that view, inhibitory strength gates whether excitatory potentiation is possible, neighboring excitatory interactions shape LTP magnitude, and heterosynaptic redistribution stabilizes the result; together these mechanisms allow fast learning without long-term instability 6 . That specific formalism is theoretical rather than a direct experimental law, but it captures the direction in which the cortical data point: a dendritic branch or local input ensemble is often best treated as a coupled E/I learning unit. Inhibitory plasticity also operates across slower timescales. Transient disinhibition often opens a cortical plasticity window, whereas slower inhibitory reweighting helps close that window again and restore a stable operating point. In adult neocortex, inhibitory circuits are structurally plastic as well as electrophysiologically plastic: chronic imaging and review work show experience-dependent branch remodeling, bouton turnover, and circuit-specific restructuring of inhibitory connections 15 , 16 , 17 . At an even slower "metaplastic" scale, activity-dependent transcriptional programs such as NPAS4 promote inhibitory synapse formation onto excitatory neurons and, through cell-type-specific gene programs, can also increase excitation onto inhibitory neurons 18 , 19 ; BDNF-related pathways are likewise major regulators of inhibitory-circuit maturation and critical-period timing 20 . Overall, inhibitory plasticity makes cortical learning selective, stable, and precise : it does not simply oppose excitation, but co-defines which excitatory changes are allowed, how sharply they are expressed, and in what dynamical regime they remain usable 4 , 14 , 7 .

title: Short-Term Plasticity (Dynamic Gain at the Synapse)
text: The preceding subsections have focused on mechanisms that produce lasting changes in cortical synaptic efficacy—voltage/Ca2+-dependent rules, three-factor consolidation, and inhibitory plasticity. But cortical signal transmission is also continuously reshaped on much faster timescales by short-term plasticity (STP) : the rapid, reversible, use-dependent changes in effective synaptic strength that occur with every spike and recover within tens of milliseconds to seconds, with augmentation and post-tetanic potentiation extending into the seconds-to-minutes regime. The core biophysical mechanisms of STP—facilitation (residual presynaptic Ca2+ enhancing release probability on subsequent spikes), depression (vesicle depletion, release-site refractoriness), augmentation, post-tetanic potentiation, and postsynaptic receptor desensitization—are developed in detail in "The Fundamentals" and are not recapitulated here. The emphasis in this subsection is cortex-specific: which cortical pathways depress, which facilitate, which postsynaptic targets they differentially recruit, how neuromodulatory state retunes these temporal filters, and what this means for the moment-to-moment flow of predictions, prediction errors, recurrent context, and inhibition through cortical circuits. STP is not a durable memory mechanism; it does not store the cortex’s generative model. Its importance is that it determines the momentary transfer function of every pathway through which cortical computation flows 1 , 2 . A strongly depressing synapse transmits the first spike in a train faithfully but progressively attenuates subsequent spikes; a facilitating synapse does the opposite, transmitting early spikes weakly but amplifying later ones. In practice, most cortical synapses exhibit a mixture of facilitation and depression, producing a characteristic net transfer function (net facilitating, net depressing, or mixed/biphasic) that depends on initial release probability ( p 0 p_0 ), vesicle pool size, calcium dynamics, and receptor desensitization kinetics. The effective STP phenotype is therefore not a binary label but a continuous, tunable filter 3 . The cortex-specific question is how this filter is distributed across the canonical pathways of cortical computation—feedforward, recurrent, feedback, and inhibitory—and how it dynamically retunes the effective gain of each pathway from one spike to the next 4 , 5 . The best-studied sensory-cortex example is thalamocortical and closely related feedforward excitation. When probed from rest, core thalamocortical synapses onto layer-4 cortical neurons (e.g those transmitting retinal data) are typically strong and strongly depressing, and this depression contributes directly to rapid sensory adaptation in vivo 6 , 7 . However, this should not be stated as a universal fixed law. In mouse barrel cortex, lemniscal thalamocortical synapses are indeed depression-dominated when stimulation begins from rest, but during ongoing stimulation they show a continuum of interval tuning, including facilitation after prior depression; the effective cortical filter therefore depends on recent history, not just synapse class 8 . A closely related intracortical feedforward example is the L4 → \to L2/3 pathway in V1: it shows robust short-term depression, and recent in vitro/in vivo work argues that this depression is sufficient to explain a substantial part of stimulus-specific visual adaptation and temporal integration in awake cortex 9 . The safest cortical summary for this motif is therefore: sensory feedforward pathways often begin in a depressing regime that suppresses sustained or redundant drive and emphasizes changes, onsets, and pattern irregularities—but the realized filter can become richer under ongoing activity, with the effective transfer function shifting as a function of the recent stimulus history rather than remaining fixed by synapse class alone 6 , 8 , 10 . In contrast to core thalamocortical and many local intracortical excitatory synapses, long-range corticocortical projections are not exclusively depressing and in several cases show robust short-term facilitation during repeated activation. Using selective optical stimulation, Martinetti et al. found strong facilitation in reciprocal vS1 ↔ \leftrightarrow vM1 projections as well as in the sensory-sensory vS1 → \to vS2 pathway 11 . In mouse auditory cortex, direct A1 ↔ \leftrightarrow A2 corticocortical connections have been shown to comprise two response classes, one of which showed smaller initial EPSPs together with paired-pulse facilitation and metabotropic glutamate receptor recruitment 12 . An analogous mixed organization was reported for reciprocal V1 ↔ \leftrightarrow V2 connections in mouse visual cortex, where corticocortical inputs again included a facilitating/Class-2 subtype alongside a depressing/Class-1B subtype 13 . Thus, facilitation recurs across multiple interareal corticocortical pathways, although often as one component of a heterogeneous projection rather than as a uniform property of every synapse. Computationally, facilitating corticocortical channels preferentially transmit sustained or repeated evidence, allowing ongoing activity in one cortical area to accumulate influence over another across the course of a train 11 , 12 , 13 . A related association-cortex motif appears in prefrontal recurrent excitation. In rat and ferret medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), recurrent pyramidal subnetworks include strongly facilitating synapses with pronounced augmentation and post-tetanic potentiation; these subnetworks are distinct from more sensory-like depressing subnetworks and are plausible contributors to sustained activity and working-memory-related temporal integration 2 , 14 . Computational modeling supports this link: facilitating recurrent excitatory synapses, particularly when combined with augmentation-timescale dynamics, can sustain delay-period activity and support robust working-memory representations without requiring fine-tuned attractor parameters—providing a synaptic substrate for temporal integration that complements classical persistent-activity models 15 , 16 . From these two motifs, one potential cortex-specific contrast emerges: sensory and feedforward cortex often uses STP to attenuate repeated input (emphasizing transients and novelty), whereas association and prefrontal subnetworks more often exploit facilitation and augmentation to preserve or amplify long-range and/or temporally extended context 2 , 14 , 11 . Another one of the most important cortex-specific findings is that STP depends strongly on the postsynaptic target cell . In classic paired recordings from neocortical L2/3, the same class of pyramidal neuron produced facilitating EPSPs onto bitufted/SST-like interneurons but depressing EPSPs onto multipolar/PV-like interneurons 5 . Related work in layer-4 neocortex suggests that STP can depend strongly on the identity of the postsynaptic inhibitory target: synapses involving fast-spiking (FS)/PV cells were reported to more often show relatively reliable, depressing transmission, whereas pathways involving low-threshold spiking (LTS)/SST-like cells more often showed weaker initial responses with facilitation 17 . Thalamic recruitment shows the same logic. During behaviorally relevant thalamocortical trains, PV/FS interneurons are activated rapidly but only transiently because their thalamic inputs depress strongly, whereas a subset of SOM/SST interneurons are recruited with a delay through facilitating and summating EPSPs, producing a shift from early perisomatic/feedforward inhibition toward later dendritic inhibition 18 . More recent auditory-cortex work formalizes this computational implication: excitatory input to PV neurons generally depresses, whereas excitatory input to SST neurons facilitates, and this differential STP can account for temporal-context effects such as rapid adaptation versus delayed facilitation of cortical responses 19 . STP should therefore be understood not merely as "synapses weaken or strengthen briefly," but as a microcircuit routing rule that determines whether a spike train first recruits fast perisomatic veto (via depressing PV pathways), delayed dendritic gating (via facilitating SST pathways), or recurrent amplification—and how this recruitment sequence evolves over the course of a stimulus 5 , 17 , 18 . Neuromodulation adds to the picture: in cortex, neuromodulators do not simply multiply synaptic amplitudes; they can change the train dynamics themselves–the effective STP rule. Acetylcholine can modulate synaptic transmission in a pathway- and receptor-dependent manner rather than acting as a uniform gain signal: in mouse visual cortex, cholinergic modulation differed across stimulated pathways and could either facilitate or depress responses depending on ACh concentration and muscarinic receptor subtype, consistent with the idea that cholinergic state dynamically reweights cortical input streams 20 . Norepinephrine shows equally pathway-specific effects. In auditory cortex, NE changes inhibitory train dynamics differently for apical versus basal pathways onto L2/3 pyramidal cells: it selectively enhances facilitation in layer-I-evoked inhibitory responses while increasing depression in layer-II/III-evoked inhibitory responses during high-frequency trains 21 . Available cortical evidence suggests that dopamine can also interact with short-term synaptic dynamics in a pathway-, receptor-, and cell-type-specific manner. In prefrontal cortex, D1/D5 receptor activation has been reported to slightly reduce initial non-NMDA transmission while enhancing the sustained NMDA component during 20 Hz trains, effectively favoring persistent over isolated excitatory input 22 ; complementary work found that D1 activation at excitatory inputs onto fast-spiking interneurons selectively reduced the first EPSP in a 20 Hz train while sparing later responses 23 ; and a further study showed that D2 activation in layer-V PFC pyramidal neurons altered spike-train dynamics in a subtype- and frequency-dependent manner 24 . The takeaway is therefore that neuromodulators reparameterize the temporal filters implemented by local cortical synapses , often in a pathway-, compartment-, and cell-type-specific manner, thereby changing which streams dominate over the course of a burst or behavioral state 25 , 21 , 26 . STP and long-term plasticity are not independent layers. STP shapes the actual voltage and Ca2+ trajectories seen during induction trains, so it changes the effective pairing statistics that downstream LTP/LTD mechanisms experience; conversely, presynaptic forms of long-term plasticity can alter the subsequent STP profile of the synapse 10 , 27 . A useful example is layer-5 neocortex, where long-term changes have been shown to include a presynaptic component identifiable through altered coefficient of variation and altered short-term plasticity dynamics, implying that some "long-term learning" rewrites the synapse’s future short-term filtering properties 27 . The correct framing is therefore that STP is part of the induction state for cortical long-term learning, and it is itself one of the variables that long-term plasticity can tune; in that sense, some long-term learning may act by rewriting the synapse’s future short-term temporal filter, not only its baseline efficacy 27 , 28 . The cortex-specific STP motifs reviewed above converge on several computational functions that are directly relevant to the optimization architecture developed in the preceding sections: Rapid adaptation and novelty/transient sensitivity in sensory cortex. Depression at thalamocortical and intracortical feedforward synapses suppresses repeated input while preserving strong responses to abrupt changes and temporally irregular features. This implements an input-specific dynamic gain control that automatically emphasizes the unexpected–functionally equivalent to a local, activity-history-dependent filter that highlights prediction-violating transients at the earliest cortical processing stage 6 , 9 , 10 . Dynamic E/I reweighting across a spike train. Because PV-linked pathways have been shown to depress and SST-linked pathways have been shown to facilitate, the balance of soma-targeting versus dendrite-targeting inhibition is itself history-dependent. Over the course of a stimulus, cortical integration shifts from an early regime dominated by fast perisomatic/feedforward inhibition (PV-mediated) toward a later regime in which contextual and dendritic gating (SST-mediated) becomes progressively more influential–changing the cortical integration window from early fast veto toward later contextual/dendritic gating 17 , 18 , 19 . Extended temporal integration in association cortex. Facilitating recurrent and long-range corticocortical synapses allow repeated or sustained activity to become progressively more effective, providing a plausible synaptic substrate for delay-period maintenance and context accumulation in prefrontal and association circuits. Where depressing sensory synapses strip away redundancy and emphasize novelty, facilitating association-cortex synapses do the converse: they accumulate evidence over time, letting sustained or repeated signals build influence—a temporal integration profile well matched to the working-memory and decision-making computations these areas support 2 , 14 , 15 , 11 . In sum, STP is best described as the fastest layer of the cortical adaptive-gain stack : it operates at every synapse, requires no instructive signal, and automatically adjusts the effective weight of each pathway based on its recent activation history. Combined with pathway- and cell-type-specific profiles, STP dynamically reshapes E/I balance, interneuron recruitment order, and the relative weighting of feedforward versus feedback streams on a moment-by-moment basis—complementing the slower neuromodulatory, oscillatory, and structural precision mechanisms covered in the preceding sections.

title: Metaplasticity (The Sliding Threshold and Adaptive Learning Rates)
text: The preceding subsections described what cortical plasticity rules do: voltage/Ca2+-dependent coincidence detection writes compartment-specific eligibility traces, three-factor neuromodulatory gating and intracellular resource allocation determine which of those traces are consolidated, inhibitory co-training keeps learned changes stable and selective, and short-term dynamic filtering reshapes the effective gain of every cortical pathway from spike to spike. This subsection addresses another question: how are those rules themselves regulated over time? Metaplasticity —the activity-dependent modification of the capacity for, or rules governing, future synaptic plasticity (the "plasticity of plasticity")—further ensures that cortical learning remains stable and context-appropriate despite the continual operation of Hebbian and three-factor mechanisms 1 . The Bienenstock–Cooper–Munro (BCM) model provides the canonical theoretical framework. It proposes a modification threshold θ M \theta_M for each synapse that separates LTD-inducing from LTP-inducing activity levels—and θ M \theta_M is not fixed but slides as a superlinear function of the recent time-averaged postsynaptic firing rate 2 . After a period of elevated activity, θ M \theta_M rises, making LTP harder to induce and LTD easier; after a period of reduced activity, θ M \theta_M falls, making LTP easier and LTD harder. This single sliding-threshold mechanism provides intrinsic homeostatic stabilization of Hebbian learning without requiring a separate rate-homeostasis controller: if a neuron’s activity drifts upward, the rising threshold automatically biases subsequent plasticity toward depression, pulling activity back down; if activity drifts downward, the falling threshold biases plasticity toward potentiation, restoring drive 3 , 2 . The BCM framework makes a strong, testable prediction for cortex: manipulations that chronically raise or lower cortical activity should shift the frequency or pattern threshold at which standard induction protocols cross from LTD to LTP territory. This has been supported in visual cortex, as described below. The molecular substrate of the sliding threshold should be stated cautiously, as no single mechanism fully accounts for all metaplastic phenomena. Nevertheless, a major cortical mechanism is activity-dependent regulation of NMDAR subunit composition and kinetics . The Bear laboratory’s work in rodent visual cortex provides a strong source of evidence: dark-rearing increases the GluN2B:GluN2A (NR2B:NR2A) subunit ratio at visual cortical synapses, which lengthens NMDAR-mediated Ca2+ currents and effectively lowers θ M \theta_M —precisely the direction BCM theory predicts for a reduced-activity state 4 , 5 . Restoring normal visual experience reverses this shift. The subunit ratio is thus a slow biophysical variable that "remembers" recent activity history and adjusts the Ca2+ transient profile for any given stimulation pattern, changing which outcomes (LTP, LTD, or no change) result from nominally identical induction protocols. This connects directly to the voltage/Ca2+-dependent plasticity framework: because the sign and magnitude of synaptic change depend on the amplitude and duration of local Ca2+ transients, and because NMDAR subunit composition controls the kinetics of those transients, activity-history-dependent shifts in GluN2B:GluN2A ratio effectively reparameterize the Ca2+-to-plasticity mapping at every synapse that underwent the subunit shift. Metaplasticity is a clean way to express how the slow background constraints described in "Cortical Loss Functions"–homeostatic rate errors, metabolic cost signals–interact with the fast instructive and self-supervised learning rules described in the preceding subsections. A useful interpretation is that metaplasticity acts as an adaptive learning-rate controller layered on top of Hebbian, voltage-dependent, and error-driven plasticity: recent overactivity raises the barrier for further potentiation, while recent underactivity lowers it, preventing runaway positive feedback while preserving sensitivity to new evidence. In this framing, the homeostatic firing-rate error signal ( ⟨ r ⟩ τ − r * \langle r \rangle_\tau - r^* , described in "Neuronal Error Signals") does not directly oppose Hebbian weight changes in real time; instead, it is transduced—over hours to days, via Ca2+-sensing cascades, NMDAR subunit trafficking, and intracellular signaling—into a shift in the metaplastic state that biases future plasticity in the compensatory direction. The result is a two-timescale control system : fast plasticity rules drive learning toward error-minimizing weight configurations, while slow metaplastic drift ensures that the fast rules do not push the system into regimes where further learning is impossible (saturated potentiation) or previously acquired structure is erased (runaway depression). A second major cortical metaplasticity mechanism operates not at the level of individual synapses but at the level of local circuits. Perineuronal nets (PNNs) —specialized extracellular matrix structures that ensheathe primarily PV+ interneurons—do not encode a synapse-specific eligibility trace, but instead regulate whether an entire local circuit remains in a high-plasticity or a stabilized regime. In visual cortex, PNN formation around PV interneurons coincides with critical-period closure and is delayed by dark rearing; enzymatic digestion of PNN components (chondroitinase ABC treatment) in adult V1 reopens ocular-dominance plasticity, and Otx2-PNN interactions help maintain the mature low-plasticity state 6 , 7 , 8 . Because PNNs regulate the excitability and synaptic integration properties of PV interneurons—the same perisomatic-targeting cells whose plasticity was shown in the preceding subsection to gate the sign and capacity of excitatory plasticity—PNN maturation effectively raises the bar for experience-dependent circuit remodeling across all the synapses within the PV cell’s inhibitory domain, not just at a single input. Overall, metaplasticity adds three important dimensions to the cortical optimization architecture developed in the preceding sections: Adaptive learning rate. The sliding threshold implements a biophysically grounded, synapse-local (and, via PNNs, circuit-local) adaptive learning rate. Rather than treating the learning rate as a fixed hyperparameter, cortex continuously adjusts the ease of potentiation and depression based on activity history—preventing saturation, which would abolish further learning, and preventing runaway depression, which would erase useful structure. Interaction with precision-weighting. Metaplasticity adds a slow temporal dimension to the precision-weighting story from "Cortical Error Signals." Fast precision-weighting mechanisms—neuromodulatory gain, oscillatory gating, apical dendritic amplification, population variability suppression—determine which current prediction errors are amplified at any given moment. Metaplasticity determines which synapses are currently in a state where those amplified errors can be converted into lasting change. A synapse in a high- θ M \theta_M metaplastic state will resist potentiation even when a large, high-precision prediction error drives strong local depolarization; conversely, a synapse in a low- θ M \theta_M state will potentiate readily in response to moderate errors. The two mechanisms are therefore complementary: precision-weighting controls the instantaneous gain on error signals, while metaplasticity controls the long-run susceptibility of the substrate to those signals. Critical periods as metaplastic regimes. The opening and closure of developmental critical periods in sensory cortex can be understood as a large-scale metaplastic transition: early high plasticity (low θ M \theta_M , immature PNNs, high GluN2B:GluN2A ratio) gives way to a consolidated adult state (raised θ M \theta_M , mature PNNs, lower GluN2B:GluN2A ratio).

title: Structural Plasticity: Error-Driven Spine Dynamics
text: The plasticity mechanisms developed so far—voltage/Ca2+-dependent coincidence detection, three-factor consolidation, inhibitory co-training, short-term dynamic filtering, and metaplastic threshold adjustment—all operate by modifying the efficacy or induction rules of existing synaptic contacts. But cortex also reshapes its connectivity at a more architectural level: when particular dendritic subtrees repeatedly enter a plasticity-permissive state, cortex does not merely rescale existing weights—it can also add, stabilize, or eliminate synaptic contacts in a branch-specific manner 1 , 2 , 3 . Structural plasticity is therefore the slower architectural consequence of the same branch-local voltage/Ca2+ and three-factor signals described in the preceding subsections. The molecular machinery of spine formation, enlargement, shrinkage, and elimination is covered in greater depth in "The Fundamentals"; here the emphasis is on the logic by which structural remodeling extends the credit-assignment and error-driven learning architecture of the cortex. Some of the clearest evidence linking structural change to the dendritic error-computation framework comes from motor cortex. In mouse motor cortex, different motor tasks evoke branch-specific apical Ca2+ spikes in L5 pyramidal neurons, and spines active during those spikes undergo persistent potentiation and measurable spine-head enlargement, whereas nearby inactive spines do not 4 . This finding is significant because it argues that structural plasticity in cortex is not neuron-global "Hebbian growth"—a uniform increase in synaptic contacts across the entire arbor of an active cell—but a dendritic credit-assignment process tied to the particular branches carrying high-error or high-coincidence events. The same branch-specific Ca2+ spikes that the preceding subsections identified as compartment-local error signals and plasticity gates for functional weight changes also determine where on the dendritic tree new structural capacity is allocated or withdrawn. During motor learning, new cortical spines are not added randomly across the arbor. They preferentially arise near pre-existing, task-related local spine ensembles, and their survival is biased toward inputs that remain co-active with nearby task-related spines 5 , 6 . This suggests that spinogenesis preferentially elaborates dendritic regions already engaged in locally coherent, behavior-related activity, rather than distributing new contacts indiscriminately. Conversely, synapses eliminated during motor learning are not simply inactive or uniformly weak; they are more often poorly co-active with neighboring spines and mistimed relative to postsynaptic output , suggesting that cortical pruning removes inputs that fail local cooperative integration 7 . Structural addition and elimination may therefore governed by principles similar to the branch-local cooperativity principle that shapes functional plasticity in the apical compartment: spines that participate in coordinated dendritic events are retained and reinforced, while those that are temporally or spatially out of register with their local neighborhood are pruned. Structural changes unfold across multiple temporal windows, generally much slower than the fastest efficacy changes that help initiate them. Learning-induced spinogenesis in motor cortex rises over hours to days—with some new spines detectable as early as within 1 hour of training, and additional branch-specific formation continuing over the first 6–48 hours–while post-learning sleep promotes branch-specific formation and the next-day persistence of those new spines 2 , 8 . Over still longer windows, only a subset of newly formed spines are stabilized across weeks to months 2 , 3 . Structural plasticity is therefore best viewed as a long-horizon selection stage of cortical learning: fast synaptic efficacy changes occur over seconds to minutes, consolidation mechanisms stabilize a subset over hours, and structural addition, stabilization, and pruning over days to months determine which changes become enduring features of cortical circuitry. Cortical spine density follows a stereotyped developmental trajectory: rapid synaptogenesis in early postnatal life produces a transient overabundance of excitatory synapses, followed by substantial pruning during childhood and adolescence. Importantly, in human cortex this trajectory is strongly regionally asynchronous . Early quantitative studies showed that auditory cortex reaches peak synaptic density within the first months of life, whereas middle frontal gyrus (prefrontal cortex) peaks substantially later and undergoes pruning over a much more prolonged developmental window 9 . Subsequent work examining identified pyramidal neurons demonstrated that dendritic spine density in human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex remains elevated well beyond adolescence and does not reach stable adult levels until approximately the third decade of life, representing one of the most extended structural maturation trajectories reported for any cortical region in primates 10 . This regional asynchrony is broadly consistent with the hierarchical organization of cortical timescales described in “Cortical Loss Functions”: lower-order sensory areas exhibit faster intrinsic dynamics and mature earlier, whereas higher-order association regions—including prefrontal cortex—operate over longer temporal integration windows and undergo structural refinement much later in development. Whether this developmental gradient reflects a form of curriculum learning , in which lower-level sensory representations must stabilize before higher-order circuits that depend on them can be meaningfully pruned, remains unresolved. Nonetheless, the striking correspondence between the cortical hierarchy of representational abstraction and the hierarchy of structural maturation suggests that the developmental timetable of cortical spine pruning may itself act as a metaplastic variable , regulating when different levels of the cortical generative model are allowed to structurally consolidate.
references: Long-term in vivo imaging of experience-dependent synaptic plasticity in adult cortex

title: Sleep-Dependent Consolidation and Replay
text: A substantial fraction of cortical learning occurs offline , during sleep. The broad theory of sleep-dependent memory consolidation and its inter-system coordination (hippocampal replay driving cortical model updating, reward-biased reactivation, systems-level reorganization) is developed in "Offline Learning"; the emphasis here is on the cortical implementation—the specific mechanisms by which sleep places cortical circuits into an offline plasticity regime and how that regime engages the same synaptic machinery described above. A safe framing is not that sleep computes a wholly new set of learning rules, but that it places cortical circuits into an offline plasticity regime in which recently active ensembles—especially those associated with salient or rewarded experiences—are reactivated under oscillatory conditions that favor stabilization. In motor cortex, learned ensemble patterns replay during post-learning NREM sleep in rodents, and analogous learned motor patterns replay during human sleep 1 . In mouse sensory cortex, selective reactivation of learning-activated cortical ensembles during sleep is not merely correlative but can be causally necessary for later memory expression: disrupting this reactivation impairs subsequent fear-memory retrieval, establishing a direct link between sleep-dependent cortical replay and behavioral consolidation 2 . A predictive-processing interpretation is that replay provides a second, value-weighted offline pass through the same cortical credit-assignment machinery described in the preceding subsections: the dendritic voltage/Ca 2+ rules, three-factor gating, and branch-local consolidation mechanisms do not shut down during sleep but are instead driven by internally generated reactivation patterns rather than external sensory input. A key candidate mechanism by which offline replay becomes plasticity-relevant is the precise temporal coordination of NREM sleep rhythms. Slow oscillations (SO), spindles, and ripples form a nested temporal hierarchy that is thought to organize windows of excitability and interareal communication during consolidation. In rodents, neocortical dendritic Ca2+ activity is elevated and synchronized during spindle-rich sleep, and cortical pyramidal-cell Ca2+ signals are markedly amplified when spindles occur in SO upstates 3 , 4 . In humans, the precision of SO–spindle coupling predicts endogenous memory reactivation strength, and reactivation strength predicts consolidation 5 . Human intracranial work further shows that, under SO upstate control, spindles set a temporal frame in which ripples occur, while cortical ripples during NREM tend to occur near the down-to-upstate transition, often with spindles, and are associated with unit co-firing in an STDP-relevant range 6 , 7 , 8 . Thus, the most defensible claim is that coupled sleep rhythms provide a temporal scaffold that may bias replay toward the biophysical conditions favorable for cortical plasticity and consolidation. Sleep-dependent consolidation of at least some forms of cortical plasticity engages late-phase biochemical machinery overlapping with that described in the three-factor and synaptic-tagging literatures. In visual cortex, sleep consolidates ocular-dominance plasticity through intracortical NMDAR- and PKA-dependent potentiation-related processes, and blocking mTOR-dependent protein synthesis during sleep abolishes consolidation while reducing sleep-dependent translation of plasticity-related mRNAs such as ARC and BDNF 9 , 10 . These findings provide one of the clearest cortical links between offline activity and protein-synthesis-dependent stabilization: sleep is not merely permissive ‘time off’ from sensory processing, but an active state in which waking-induced plasticity can be further consolidated. A reasonable STC-like interpretation is that waking experience sets synapse-specific plasticity states or tags, and subsequent sleep provides molecular conditions favorable for PRP capture and lasting stabilization, although this tag-capture mechanism has not yet been demonstrated directly in cortex during sleep 11 . More broadly, sleep can preferentially reactivate and strengthen salient or rewarded traces, suggesting that neuromodulatory signals during encoding may bias which memories are later replayed and consolidated, though the exact role of neuromodulators during sleep itself remains unsettled 12 , 13 .
