title: Cortical Learning in Action
text:
The three preceding sections decomposed cortical learning into analytically separable components: the normative objectives that define what should be improved, the neural machinery that computes and routes the relevant error signals, and the plasticity mechanisms that convert those signals into lasting change. This section reassembles those components into a single picture. Its aim is to trace the full transduction chain from sensory encounter to durable representational update, showing that cortical loss functions, error signals, and plasticity rules are not three independent stories but three views onto one continuously running optimization process. At the same time, this synthesis should be read with some caution. The overall picture is strongly motivated by the convergences reviewed above, but parts of the mechanistic stitching remain speculative, especially where normative frameworks outrun current circuit-level evidence or where multiple competing implementations remain live; be cautious of absorbing some of the contents of this section as settled/strong claims. The Complete Cortical Update Cycle A useful way to reassemble the cortex into the optimizer language introduced at the start of this chapter is the following: cortical populations propose hypotheses about the causes of current and impending input; laminar and dendritic circuitry compares those hypotheses against bottom-up drive, lateral context, and action-conditioned feedback; compartment-specific voltage/Ca 2 + ^{2+} events, precision weighting, and eligibility traces assign credit for the mismatch to particular synapses and branches; and excitatory, inhibitory, metaplastic, and structural mechanisms update the substrate so that future proposals are better. In cortex, however, these are not cleanly separated stages. The same ongoing activity that carries the current posterior estimate also determines which synapses enter a plasticity-permissive state, and the same precision mechanisms that shape fast inference also scale the effective learning rate of the synapses currently participating in that inference. The cortical update cycle is therefore best understood not as a serial pipeline but as a nested, continuously running optimization in which activity-level inference and weight-level learning are two timescales of one process 1 , 2 , 3 . Consider a single pass through that cycle. A cortical area begins not as a passive recipient of input but as an active generator of predictions. In canonical predictive-coding accounts, deep pyramidal populations in L5/6 encode the current conditional expectations or latent causes and send descending predictions to lower cortical areas, while corticothalamic neurons in L6 help shape the thalamic contribution to the same comparison process 4 . APC assigns some of these roles differently—placing state-transition and policy-related computations across L2/3, L5, and L6—but preserves the same core requirement that a descending prediction stream exist and that it be conditioned not only on latent state but also on action 3 . Thus, before the next sensory sample fully arrives, the column already embodies a hypothesis: a prediction of what lower-level activity, sensory input, or action consequence ought to occur next. Into that prepared state arrives the ascending drive. External input enters principally through thalamocortical afferents terminating in L4, together with ascending corticocortical signals from lower areas. But the first comparison has, in a sense, already begun at the synapse itself, because feedforward contacts are dynamically filtered by short-term plasticity. In sensory pathways, thalamocortical synapses often begin in a depressing regime that suppresses sustained or redundant drive while emphasizing onsets, transients, and pattern irregularities, so novelty is amplified at the very point of cortical entry rather than only after a later explicit subtraction 5 , 6 , 7 . The incoming volley is therefore not a raw copy of the world but an already temporally filtered message about what changed . That temporally filtered ascending drive then meets the descending prediction within the cortical column. Here the literature diverges sharply on implementation while converging on function. Canonical predictive coding frames the operation as an explicit residual computed by superficial populations; predictive routing frames it as pathway-selective oscillatory preparation that renders unpredicted input more effective; APC supplements sensory mismatch with action-prediction-error channels routed through higher-order thalamus; the Thousand Brains framework emphasizes the contrast between sparse predicted responses and burst-like unpredicted responses; and Bio-RCN casts the operation as iterative explaining-away and message passing rather than literal subtraction. Yet across all of these accounts, the deepest invariant is the same: feedforward and feedback streams must converge somewhere locally computable—within layered cortical circuitry, dendritic compartments, or thalamocortical loops—so that the magnitude of some signal scales with the discrepancy between expectation and observation 4 , 8 , 3 . That raw mismatch is not yet the effective teaching signal. It is immediately reshaped by the cortex’s multi-layer precision architecture. At the smallest scale, apical dendritic gating determines whether top-down/contextual input has enough leverage to amplify or suppress a local mismatch. At larger scales, neuromodulators such as acetylcholine, norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin alter gain through receptor-specific effects on interneuron subtypes, intrinsic conductances, and network state. On the tens-of-milliseconds timescale, oscillatory coherence and spectral multiplexing gate which error-like messages are successfully transmitted upward and which feedback/prediction-like messages dominate downward communication. At the population level, suppression or amplification of shared variability determines the effective signal-to-noise ratio of the error-coding ensemble. And at the inter-areal level, TRN- and pulvinar-mediated thalamocortical gating regulates which channels are open at all 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 . These mechanisms are not redundant copies of a single gain signal. They operate on different spatial scales, different temporal scales, and different mathematical aspects of the precision tensor, so the local learning rate is scaled dynamically and specifically, not globally. Once precision-weighted, the mismatch drives fast inference. Activity propagates upward to revise higher-order beliefs and downward to refine lower-level predictions, and recurrent cortical dynamics iteratively relax toward a state of greater internal consistency—an approximate local minimum of free energy, or equivalently an approximate posterior over the latent causes generating the input 1 , 2 , 14 , 15 . This is the cortical Propose-Compare loop in action: the proposal is revised by the comparison, and the comparison itself changes as the proposal changes. Importantly, this relaxation is not purely perceptual. Under APC, action-prediction errors simultaneously update L5 policy-related populations, and some L5 corticofugal neurons can issue commands whose sensory consequences become part of the next round of cortical evidence, thereby closing the active-inference loop within the same general optimization 3 , 16 . While that activity-level inference is unfolding over roughly a few hundred milliseconds, a second process is already underway at every active synapse: voltage and Ca 2 + ^{2+} dynamics write a local eligibility trace. This is where credit assignment becomes genuinely compartment-specific. In basal dendrites, potentiation is better predicted by synaptic activity that coincides with postsynaptic output, whereas in apical dendrites plasticity is better predicted by local coactivity among nearby spines and branch-local nonlinear events 17 . The same neuron therefore implements different effective learning rules in different compartments. Local NMDA conductance, voltage-gated Ca 2 + ^{2+} entry, regenerative dendritic events, and the metaplastic state of the synapse together determine the amplitude and duration of the Ca 2 + ^{2+} transient, and thus whether the synapse enters an LTD-like, LTP-like, or null-update regime 18 . When a suprathreshold dendritic Ca 2 + ^{2+} spike occurs, a graded mismatch can be converted into a discrete, high-SNR branch-level event, sharply increasing the probability that a particular local input cluster is marked as causally relevant 19 . Those eligibility traces do not by themselves guarantee lasting change. In cortex, they typically decay over a behavioral-timescale window of roughly seconds, and whether they are converted into stable synaptic modification depends on the arrival of an appropriate third factor 20 , 21 . Formally, the synapse has registered, "this contact was active when something important may have happened," but it has not yet committed to how that contact should change. The third factor resolves that ambiguity. Phasic dopamine can stamp in reward-contingent changes; acetylcholine can promote learning under attentional relevance; norepinephrine can privilege surprising or high-arousal events; serotonin can alter the sign or gain of the update in receptor- and area-specific ways 22 , 21 . Because cortical dopaminergic innervation is highly heterogeneous, this gating is not spatially uniform. Frontal and motor territories sit nearer the policy-output end of the hierarchy and receive denser dopaminergic teaching signals, making reinforcement-gated consolidation more dominant there; posterior sensory regions, with sparser dopaminergic input, remain more strongly governed by self-supervised predictive error minimization, though reward and attention can still bias plasticity when behaviorally relevant 23 , 24 . The same local pre × \times post coincidence can therefore consolidate differently in different cortical territories because the probability and identity of the third factor differ systematically across the sheet. Even then, excitatory change is not permitted to proceed alone. Inhibitory plasticity is the principal anti-runaway mechanism that lets cortical learning occur safely, and the cleanest way to think about it is not as a secondary repair system but as part of the same local optimization 25 . At I → \to E synapses, inhibitory plasticity is often gated by postsynaptic pyramidal-cell Ca 2 + ^{2+} generated by the surrounding excitatory context, making inhibition sensitive to the same local events that drove excitatory eligibility traces 26 . In auditory cortex, inhibitory inputs can potentiate within an approximately symmetric peri-spike window, tightening E/I timing and improving spike-time fidelity even while nearby excitatory synapses obey a more classical asymmetric STDP rule 27 . At E → \to I synapses, the rules are highly target-cell-specific, so pyramidal recruitment of PV, SST, and other interneuron classes is itself learned in a pathway-specific manner 28 . The resulting picture is one of co-trained E/I microcircuits: excitatory updates alter what the circuit wants to represent, inhibitory updates determine whether those changes can be stably and precisely expressed, and together they maintain the balanced regime in which further learning remains possible 29 . The aftermath of the online episode continues across longer timescales. Over hours, protein-synthesis-dependent mechanisms selectively stabilize some of the tagged synapses and not others. Strong events can self-stabilize; weaker ones can survive only if plasticity-related proteins are made available locally or if subsequent reactivation supplies the needed biochemical support. In "Synaptic Tag and Capture (STC)" terms, waking experience lays down synapse-specific tags, and later biochemical conditions determine which tags capture the resources required for late-phase consolidation 30 . During subsequent sleep, recently active cortical ensembles are replayed under the temporal scaffold provided by slow oscillations, spindles, and ripples, giving the same dendritic credit-assignment machinery a second, offline pass over the experience in a regime that is most favorable for inter-areal integration and plasticity 31 , 32 , 33 . Replay is not a generic recapitulation of waking activity. It is biased toward salient and rewarded traces, coordinated with hippocampal-cortical transfer, and coupled to protein-synthesis-dependent consolidation processes in cortex itself 34 , 35 , 36 . Over days to weeks, the cumulative consequence of repeated branch-local Ca 2 + ^{2+} spikes and consolidated efficacy changes becomes architectural. New spines preferentially form near pre-existing task-related clusters, and spines that are poorly co-active with their neighbors or mistimed relative to postsynaptic output are preferentially eliminated 37 , 38 , 39 . Structural plasticity thus commits what began as a graded efficacy shift into a durable reorganization of the dendritic substrate itself. On still slower timescales, metaplasticity updates the induction rules. Activity history shifts BCM-like modification thresholds through NMDAR subunit trafficking and related signaling, while circuit-level variables such as perineuronal-net maturation regulate whether an entire local network remains plastic or enters a stabilized regime 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 . In this way, cortex not only learns from error but learns how learnable it should remain. The integrative point is that these are not twelve sequential boxes through which experience passes once. They are nested, concurrent processes operating over milliseconds, seconds, hours, days, and developmental epochs, all driven by the same local imperative to reduce precision-weighted free energy. Fast inference and slow learning are therefore not two separate systems superimposed on the same tissue. They are two temporal regimes of one cortical optimizer: the fast regime moves activity toward a better posterior; the slow regime moves synapses, branches, and eventually circuit architecture toward a better generative model. The Multi-Timescale Optimization Stack The preceding subsection traced cortical learning as though it were a single pass through an update loop. But the cortex does not optimize on one timescale. The same sensory encounter simultaneously recruits fast recurrent inference, transient synaptic filtering, delayed credit assignment, neuromodulator-gated consolidation, protein-synthesis-dependent stabilization, offline replay, structural remodeling, metaplastic retuning, and developmental schedule-setting. The cortex is therefore not merely an optimizer; it is a stack of nested optimizers , each operating on a different state variable, over a different temporal horizon, and with a different degree of reversibility 1 , 2 , 21 , 44 . A useful formalization is to treat cortical free-energy minimization as descent along different coordinates of the same objective on different timescales. Let μ \mu denote neural activity / posterior parameters, W W synaptic weights, λ \lambda metaplastic and learning-control variables, and 𝒜 \mathcal{A} the effective circuit architecture. Then the cortex can be viewed as minimizing a shared free-energy objective F ( x ; μ , W , λ , 𝒜 ) F(x;\mu,W,\lambda,\mathcal{A}) through a nested family of updates: μ * ≈ arg ⁡ min μ F , W * ≈ arg ⁡ min W 𝔼 [ F ] , ( λ * , 𝒜 * ) ≈ arg ⁡ min λ , 𝒜 𝔼 [ F ] . \begin{equation}
\mu^{*} \approx \arg\min_{\mu} F,
\qquad
W^{*} \approx \arg\min_{W}\,\mathbb{E}[F],
\qquad
(\lambda^{*},\mathcal{A}^{*}) \approx \arg\min_{\lambda,\mathcal{A}}\,\mathbb{E}[F].
\end{equation} The first term corresponds to fast inference/perception: recurrent activity relaxes toward an approximate posterior for fixed synaptic parameters. The second corresponds to learning proper: synapses are updated so that future encounters incur less precision-weighted prediction error on average. The third corresponds to meta-learning and structural optimization : the cortex gradually retunes its own learning rates, plasticity thresholds, branch allocation rules, inhibitory set points, and architectural commitments so that the learning process itself becomes better matched to the statistics of its niche 1 , 45 , 2 . The key point is that these are not different objectives. They are different timescale-indexed realizations of the same objective . Nested timescales of cortical optimization. Faster processes optimize activity and transient pathway gain; progressively slower processes determine which local discrepancies become durable synaptic change, which changes are stabilized, and what kind of learner the circuit becomes. Timescale Mechanism What is optimized Substrate ∼ \sim 10-200 ms Neural dynamics (recurrent relaxation) Activity patterns (fast inference / perception) Membrane potentials, firing rates ∼ \sim 10 ms - seconds Short-term plasticity Momentary pathway gain (temporal filtering) Vesicle pools, residual Ca 2 + ^{2+} , receptor desensitization ∼ \sim 1-10 s Eligibility trace formation Candidate synaptic changes (credit assignment) CaMKII, voltage/Ca 2 + ^{2+} traces Seconds-minutes Three-factor consolidation Selective weight change (learning) Neuromodulatory gating, early-LTP cascades Hours Protein synthesis / STC Late-phase stabilization PRP synthesis, dendritic translation, Arc/BDNF Hours (offline) Sleep replay + coupled oscillations Systems-level consolidation, interleaving SO–spindle–ripple coupling, cortical reactivation Days-weeks Structural plasticity Architectural commitment Spinogenesis, spine elimination, bouton turnover Weeks-months Metaplasticity Adaptive learning rate NMDAR subunit trafficking, PNN maturation Months-years Developmental maturation Critical-period gating, curriculum Myelination, laminar maturation, PNN closure What matters is not merely that these processes coexist, but that they are nested in a control hierarchy . Read from fast to slow, short-term plasticity shapes which presynaptic patterns are emphasized or attenuated before a mismatch is even fully expressed; the resulting voltage and Ca 2 + ^{2+} events write eligibility traces; three-factor signals determine which of those traces are converted into actual synaptic updates; metaplastic state determines the thresholds and gain with which the same eligibility trace yields LTP versus LTD; and developmental programs determine when these mechanisms are permissive, biased, or effectively closed 20 , 22 , 46 , 40 . Read from slow to fast, the relation is even more revealing: slower timescales constrain faster ones . Metaplastic state sets the BCM-like modification threshold; three-factor gating determines which eligibility traces consolidate; eligibility traces determine which voltage events matter for lasting change; and STP shapes those voltage events themselves. This is a hierarchical control system over the optimization process , not merely over the representations being optimized. The consequence is that “learning rate” in cortex is not a single scalar. It is a distributed object implemented across multiple layers of mechanism. A synapse may experience a large instantaneous mismatch yet undergo no lasting change because STP filtered the drive, because the relevant dendritic compartment failed to enter a plasticity-permissive regime, because neuromodulatory state withheld consolidation, because local inhibitory plasticity opposed excitation, or because the synapse sits in a metaplastic state biased toward stability 9 , 17 , 47 , 48 . Conversely, a relatively small mismatch may produce durable learning if it arrives in a high-precision, behaviorally salient, replay-supported, protein-synthesis-permissive state. The cortex therefore does not merely ask whether a prediction error occurred. It asks, across nested timescales, whether that error is worth remembering . This multiscale optimization stack mirrors the temporal hierarchy of the cortical generative model itself. The "Cortical Loss Functions" section argued that cortical world models are temporally stratified: low levels track rapidly changing sensory variables, while higher levels encode slower latent causes, broader contexts, and temporally extended predictions 44 , 49 , 50 . The learning process exhibits a matching hierarchy. Fast sensory areas, with short intrinsic timescales, strong onset sensitivity, and rapidly adapting feedforward drive, are optimized for quick local inference and fine temporal discrimination; association and prefrontal areas, with stronger recurrence, slower NMDA-weighted dynamics, and longer intrinsic timescales, are optimized for integrating evidence and assigning credit over broader windows 51 , 52 , 53 . Put differently: the temporal structure of the learner mirrors the temporal structure of what it learns. The correspondence is unlikely to be accidental. Areas with slow intrinsic dynamics are not just “thinking for longer”; they are embedded in biophysical regimes that plausibly support slow learning dynamics as well. Stronger recurrence prolongs the effective integration window of error signals; GluN2B-enriched NMDA signaling extends synaptic and dendritic time constants while coupling strongly to CaMKII-dependent plasticity cascades; association cortex exhibits protracted structural maturation and delayed critical-period closure relative to early sensory cortex 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 . The emerging picture is that slow-timescale cortical areas do not merely represent slow latent causes; they are also built to learn them through broader eligibility windows, slower stabilization, and more prolonged architectural refinement. Conversely, early sensory cortex is built to learn rapidly recurring, fine-grained regularities under tighter temporal precision and earlier developmental commitment. A useful intuition is that each timescale answers a different optimization question. Fast recurrent dynamics ask: What latent state best explains the input right now? Short-term plasticity asks: Which pathways should dominate this moment’s comparison? Eligibility traces ask: Which synapses were plausibly causal? Three-factor control asks: Which candidate changes are behaviorally or statistically worth consolidating? Protein synthesis and sleep-dependent replay ask: Which local updates are worth stabilizing and interleaving into the larger model? Structural plasticity and metaplasticity ask: What circuit should this area become so that future learning is better calibrated? Development asks: What curriculum and plasticity regime should be available at this stage of the organism’s life? Same objective, different state variables; same optimizer, different horizons. A useful accompanying figure would depict these mechanisms as concentric or vertically stacked loops around a cortical column. At the center sits the fast Propose-Compare loop of recurrent inference. Surrounding it is a shell of STP that shapes momentary gain. Around that sits the eligibility-trace layer that stores candidate credit assignment. Around that, a neuromodulatory / three-factor layer selects which candidates consolidate. Outside that, protein-synthesis and sleep-dependent replay stabilize selected updates. Still further out, structural and metaplastic processes reshape branch allocation, inhibitory balance, and learning thresholds. The outermost shell is developmental maturation, which changes the operating range of all inner loops. The visual moral is that cortical learning is not a single update rule repeated over time; it is a nested optimization stack in which slower processes regulate the conditions under which faster ones count as evidence, count as causes, and count as change. The overall synthesis is therefore straightforward but deep. Cortical learning is multiscale in the strong sense: not only are different representational levels assigned different temporal horizons, but the optimizer itself is distributed across those horizons. Fast neural dynamics minimize free energy with respect to activity; intermediate plasticity minimizes it with respect to synaptic parameters; slow metaplastic, structural, and developmental processes minimize it with respect to the learning system’s own priors, thresholds, and architecture. The cortex is thus a temporally deep optimizer twice over: in the temporal depth of the generative model it builds, and in the temporal depth of the machinery by which it builds it. Regional Parameterization of the Cortical Algorithm The preceding subsection traced a single cortical update cycle as though one generic columnar algorithm were running everywhere. The next step is to state explicitly how that genericity coexists with the cortex’s enormous regional specialization. The strongest synthesis claim is not that V1, M1, dlPFC, insula, and default-mode cortex implement fundamentally different learning algorithms, but that they instantiate the same canonical cortical algorithm under systematically different parameter settings. Everywhere, cortical tissue proposes latent causes or state trajectories, compares them against incoming evidence and contextual constraints, assigns credit through compartment- and precision-dependent eligibility mechanisms, and updates synapses/branches/circuit state accordingly. What changes from region to region is what counts as evidence , what counts as error , how far in time and state-space the error reaches , how strongly it is precision-weighted , and which plasticity channels are available to convert it into lasting change 1 , 2 , 44 . A useful formal shorthand is to say that each cortical region r r is characterized by a parameter bundle Λ r = ( ℒ r , 𝒩 r , Π r , τ r , 𝒫 r , 𝒎 r ) , \Lambda_r \;=\; \bigl(\mathcal{L}_r,\; \mathcal{N}_r,\; \Pi_r,\; \tau_r,\; \mathcal{P}_r,\; \mathbf{m}_r\bigr), where ℒ r \mathcal{L}_r is the region’s dominant loss term, 𝒩 r \mathcal{N}_r its effective dependency neighborhood / “cognitive lightcone,” Π r \Pi_r its characteristic precision-weighting regime, τ r \tau_r its temporal horizon, 𝒫 r \mathcal{P}_r its dominant balance of plasticity rules, and 𝒎 r \mathbf{m}_r its neuromodulatory regime. The point is not that each area optimizes only one variable or receives only one kind of error signal. Rather, each area sits at a different location in a high-dimensional design space, and that location biases which discrepancies dominate learning on average . This is why the same cortical motif can behave like a fast self-supervised feature learner in V1, a proprioceptive controller in M1, an action-outcome monitor in ACC, an interoceptive regulator in insula, or a narrative/self-model optimizer in the transmodal apex. high structural stability; large revisions require sustained error Strong 5-HT state dependence; diffuse DA/NE/ACh context control The deepest principle illustrated by Table X is that the cortical hierarchy is parameterized along a principal gradient from fast, local, high-bandwidth sensory mismatch toward slow, abstract, temporally deep model mismatch. At one end, the local loss is dominated by high-SNR reconstruction-like discrepancies tightly locked to thalamocortical input. At the other end, the local loss is dominated by violations of long-range contextual, social, autobiographical, or policy-level expectations that may accumulate over seconds, hours, or years before they become strong enough to force revision. Equally important, the dependency neighborhood of the comparison expands along this gradient. A primary sensory column “sees” a narrow, rapidly changing world through its Markov blanket; a prefrontal or default-mode population sees a much broader world, integrating hippocampal context, latent task structure, social inference, interoceptive state, and subcortical teaching signals across longer windows 51 , 52 , 58 . Primary sensory cortex as the self-supervised base. In V1, A1, and S1, the cortical loss is dominated by precision-weighted mismatch between predicted and observed sensory structure. This is the regime in which Eq. 2 is closest to a literal description: local reconstruction-like error terms dominate, the relevant dependency neighborhood is tightly tied to feedforward receptive fields and local lateral context, and learning is driven chiefly by self-generated sensory targets rather than by reward-contingent supervision. Thalamocortical short-term depression provides the fastest adaptation layer, attenuating redundant drive while preserving onsets and deviance, so even the first cortical comparison is already biased toward what changed rather than what merely persisted 5 , 6 , 7 . Developmentally, these regions commit early: activity-history-dependent shifts in NMDAR subunit composition and perineuronal-net maturation progressively narrow the plasticity window, making early sensory cortex the clearest example of a cortical region whose long-run function is to become a stable, high-throughput, self-supervised feature extractor 40 , 42 , 43 . Reward-modulated perceptual learning certainly occurs, but in these areas it is best understood as a secondary modulation layered on top of a primarily self-supervised representational regime. Moving up into secondary and associative sensory cortex, the same algorithm is retained but the dominant error content becomes less about raw local feature mismatch and more about violations of structured combinations 59 of features across larger windows: object identity in inferotemporal cortex, phonemic and syllabic sequence structure in auditory-language pathways, biological motion and socially relevant dynamics in STS, and so on. The dependence neighborhood is broader, the temporal integration window is longer, and the role of attentional precision control becomes more prominent. These regions are still recognizably self-supervised, but they are no longer learning only to reconstruct the next local sensory sample; they are learning to predict mesoscopic structure. Motor cortex as active inference made concrete. M1 is the clearest cortical case in which the APC framing becomes more than a metaphor. On this view, motor cortex does not fundamentally emit “motor commands” in the classic feedforward-control sense; rather, it generates descending proprioceptive predictions about the bodily state that should obtain next, and the spinal/peripheral reflex apparatus acts to minimize the resulting proprioceptive prediction error by moving the body until sensed state matches predicted state 3 . Motor learning is therefore not merely tuning an output controller; it is improving a generative model of the proprioceptive consequences of action. This is precisely why M1 sits at an intermediate point in the cortical hierarchy: its dominant loss is still a prediction-error loss, but the predicted variable is action-conditioned body state rather than exteroceptive input. Here the plasticity regime shifts strongly toward three-factor control. Dopamine in motor cortex is necessary for skill learning and synaptic plasticity, VTA → \rightarrow M1 projections are required for motor-learning-related reorganization, and branch-specific dendritic Ca 2 + ^{2+} events provide a plausible biophysical mechanism by which movement-specific mismatch is converted into spine-specific stabilization during skill acquisition 60 , 61 , 19 . In other words, M1 still runs the cortical algorithm, but it runs it over a sensorimotor blanket in which proprioceptive fulfillment closes the loop. Parietal and premotor cortex occupy the natural bridge between sensory and motor parameterizations. Their dominant errors are action-conditioned but not yet purely proprioceptive: spatial expectation violations, affordance mismatches, trajectory deviations, failures of object permanence in reachable space, and discrepancies between intended and possible state transitions. Computationally, these regions are where predictive coding becomes explicitly embodied . They must bind external scene structure to body-centered coordinates and immediate action possibilities, so their loss is neither pure sensory reconstruction nor pure motor fulfillment, but sensorimotor consistency across near-future horizons. Prefrontal cortex as the slow, abstract, policy-optimizing apex. Prefrontal cortex sits near the top of the cortical temporal hierarchy because the abstract contextual priors it represents must remain stable long enough to constrain all faster levels beneath it. Its long intrinsic timescales, strong recurrent excitation, NMDA dependence, and hierarchy-linked GluN2B enrichment make it especially suited for maintaining latent task states, rules, goals, and other slowly varying contextual variables over delay periods and across behavioral episodes 51 , 53 , 62 . Put differently, PFC predictions are not mostly about the next edge, tone, or joint angle; they are about the context under which lower-level sensory and motor predictions should be interpreted. This makes its dominant error content correspondingly abstract: rule violations, goal disruption, working-memory mismatch, policy-context inconsistency, and failures of longer-run action models. Because these errors often unfold with substantial temporal delay, eligibility traces must remain behaviorally useful for longer here, plausibly aided by persistent activity itself 20 , 21 , 63 . The well-known D1 inverted-U is naturally interpretable in this framework as a precision-control law on abstract priors: too little dopaminergic gain and contextual representations become unstable; too much and they become over-rigid. The very late structural maturation of PFC then acquires a clear computational meaning: among cortical regions, it is the last to architecturally commit because it is the last that should stop learning high-level social, strategic, and self-regulatory structure. ACC and OFC as reinforcement-related regional specializations of the same cortical motif. Medial frontal cortex, especially dACC/mPFC, does not abandon predictive coding in favor of a foreign RL algorithm; rather, it parameterizes cortical prediction around the action-outcome domain. Here the dominant discrepancies are unsigned surprise, unexpected non-occurrence of predicted outcomes, conflict, and volatility–precisely the kinds of signals needed to decide when the current internal model of contingencies is no longer trustworthy 64 , 65 , 66 . OFC complements this by maintaining rich outcome predictions and latent task-state representations against which those medial-frontal discrepancies can be computed. In this sense, OFC is less a pure “error map” than a high-dimensional prediction source for identity-specific expected outcomes, reversal, and devaluation. Together, ACC and OFC show that even reinforcement-related cortical regions remain inside the same canonical logic: build a predictive model, compare outcome against expectation, precision-weight the mismatch, and update only insofar as current contingencies warrant it. Insular cortex as interoceptive inference. The insula extends the cortical algorithm into the body interior. Its dominant loss is not exteroceptive reconstruction or abstract rule consistency, but mismatch between predicted and observed visceral state: heart rate, respiratory effort, gastric state, nociceptive tone, and broader autonomic variables. In active-inference terms, this is a cortical instantiation of visceral free energy . The anterior insula and allied visceromotor circuitry generate interoceptive predictions; ascending bodily signals report the residual; and learning updates the model so that future allostatic control is better calibrated. This is the most direct cortical bridge back to the superordinate-objectives discussion, because interoceptive predictions are constrained by some of the deepest prior preferences in the organism—those specifying viable bodily states in the first place. Emotional experience, under this view, is not added on top of the optimization; it is partly what it feels like for the cortex to infer and regulate the body’s hidden causes through interoceptive prediction error. Thus insular cortex is not a special-purpose “emotion module,” but the regional parameterization of the cortical algorithm over visceral state-space. Default-mode / transmodal apex as narrative and self-model optimizer. At the slowest end of the cortical gradient, the default-mode network and related transmodal apex regions maintain temporally extended latent causes: autobiographical continuity, social-role models, narrative coherence, mental-state models of self and other, and deep priors about “what kind of situation this is” over long horizons. These are the most abstract cortical predictions and therefore the least cheaply revised. A transient sensory anomaly should not rewrite the self-model; only strong, repeated, or sustained multilevel mismatch should be permitted to do so. This is exactly what one would expect if apex-level priors are assigned high default precision and very low online learning rates. Updating here is correspondingly slow and likely depends disproportionately on replay, schema integration, and distributed consolidation, rather than on single-pass online plasticity. In this sense, the default-mode network is the cortical region in which the social-control and narrative-coherence components of the cortical loss become most explicit. The REBUS account of psychedelic action provides a particularly striking perturbational example: 5-HT 2 A _{2A} agonism is proposed to relax the precision of high-level priors, thereby allowing lower-level sensory, affective, and associative signals to invade and destabilize ordinarily rigid self-model structure, producing ego-dissolution and related phenomena 67 . Whether or not one accepts all details of that account, the core computational point is compelling: psychedelic phenomenology looks exactly like what should happen when apex-level prior precision is transiently weakened. Two clarifications are essential. First, these regional descriptions are statements about dominance , not exclusivity. Primary sensory cortex is not devoid of reward signals; PFC is not devoid of sensory prediction; DMN is not devoid of online error; M1 is not devoid of abstract context. The claim is simply that different cortical territories place different terms of the common objective in the foreground. Second, the boundaries are gradient-like rather than box-like. Timescale, precision regimes, neuromodulator receptor expression, recurrent strength, and plasticity thresholds all vary continuously across the cortical sheet 55 , 56 . The table should therefore be read as a schematic cut through a smooth manifold, not as a list of discrete algorithmic species. The overall synthesis is that cortical regionalization is best understood as parameterization rather than pluralism . Evolution and development did not solve the learning problem by inventing one cortical algorithm for sensation, another for motor control, another for emotion, and another for selfhood. They solved it by preserving a common propose–compare–assign-credit–update motif and systematically tuning its loss emphasis, precision deployment, temporal depth, and plasticity regime along the cortical hierarchy. Once seen this way, the diversity of cortical function becomes less mysterious: the cortex is one optimizer whose local objective is reparameterized as its cognitive lightcone expands from edges and tones, to objects and affordances, to actions and outcomes, to rules and goals, to bodies, selves, and social worlds. Developmental Trajectory as Hierarchical Curriculum Learning Cortical development can be understood as the slowest and outermost layer of cortical optimization: a curriculum over which error terms are even available to the learner . Across childhood and adolescence, maturation proceeds roughly along a posterior-to-anterior, sensorimotor-to-association gradient, with primary and unimodal cortices stabilizing earlier and higher-order transmodal association cortices maturing later 68 , 69 . Computationally, this looks less like a simultaneous end-to-end training run than a staged curriculum. Lower-level cortical populations must first acquire relatively stable feature spaces, temporal filters, and precision regimes before higher-order areas that depend on those representations can learn efficiently from them. A high-level circuit cannot infer durable rules about agents, norms, or self if its inputs for objects, events, and action consequences are still themselves high-variance and poorly calibrated. On this view, developmental order follows the dependency structure of the generative model: the cortex learns the world in roughly the order in which the world becomes predictable to it . The metaplastic machinery described above is the biological implementation of this curriculum. In early sensory cortex, critical-period opening and closure are governed by mechanisms such as maturation of local inhibitory circuitry, perineuronal-net (PNN) accumulation around PV interneurons, Otx2 capture, and developmental shifts in NMDAR composition and kinetics 57 , 42 , 40 . Functionally, critical-period closure in circuits such as V1 does not merely reduce plasticity; it stabilizes the training set for the rest of cortex. Once low-level detectors and gain-control regimes are partially consolidated, the prediction errors sent forward become less dominated by noise in the learner itself and more informative about structured regularities in the environment. At the other extreme, association and especially prefrontal cortex retain extended windows of refinement: human cortical development spans multiple decades, PFC synaptic pruning extends into the third decade, and association-cortex maturation remains notably protracted 68 , 70 . The longest structural exploration is thus reserved for the regions tasked with learning the slowest, most abstract, and most socially contingent latent causes. This framing also provides a natural bridge to neo-Piagetian theories. Neo-Piagetian accounts preserve Piaget’s intuition that cognition reorganizes in a staged fashion, but reinterpret those stage-like transitions in terms of graded increases in working-memory capacity, executive control, relational integration, and representational coordination rather than abrupt global rewrites of logic 71 , 72 , 73 . In cortical terms, what appears psychologically as a “stage transition” can be redescribed neurally as a shift in which cortical territories remain open to plastic reorganization, which temporal horizons can be integrated, and which error signals are now sufficiently stable, precise, and behaviorally relevant to drive learning. Thus the rough progression from sensory features → \rightarrow objects → \rightarrow spatial layouts → \rightarrow action-outcome contingencies → \rightarrow social rules → \rightarrow self-models → \rightarrow abstract conceptual structures need not be treated as a sequence of sui generis symbolic stages; it can be understood as recursive bootstrapping up the cortical hierarchy . The broader developmental chronology and its domain-specific variations are deferred to the "Dense Chronological Account," "Principles of Learning," and "Overarching Theories of Cognitive Development" sections. The same framework also helps reconcile the core knowledge debate. The present view does not require either a blank-slate cortex or a library of fully formed innate concepts. A better computational reading is that evolution installs structured early priors , privileged input organizations, and early-available loss landscapes—for example, biases for object persistence, numerosity, agency, or spatial continuity—that constrain the infant’s hypothesis space from the outset 74 , 75 . In that sense, “core knowledge” is not the opponent of developmental learning but its bootstrap condition. Indeed, violations of core expectations appear to create privileged opportunities for learning, suggesting that early priors do not terminate learning; they focus it 76 . Within the present framework, then, the cortical loss function changes qualitatively over development not because the organism adopts a new ultimate objective, but because metaplastic state, structural capacity, and inherited priors determine which components of the standing objective are currently actionable. Early in life, low-level sensory and object-model prediction errors dominate the open-plasticity territories; later, as transmodal cortex matures, social, normative, and self-model prediction errors become the major remaining drivers of cortical reorganization. Architectural Invariants Across Frameworks At the level of mechanistic storytelling, cortical theories disagree substantially. Canonical predictive coding emphasizes explicit residual units; predictive routing emphasizes oscillatory preparation and pathway-specific gain control; DPL and related target-based accounts emphasize local activation differences; APC makes action-conditioned state-transition prediction canonical; Thousand Brains emphasizes location-conditioned sensorimotor modeling; Bio-RCN emphasizes structured message passing and explaining away; Sacramento-style schemes emphasize segregated dendrites and target-based credit assignment; and recent self-supervised predictive frameworks recast laminar roles around temporal prediction targets. But beneath these differences, one claim appears unusually robust: cortex implements local free-energy minimization on a densely recurrent, heterarchical graph . The deepest invariant is not a particular laminar cartoon of “error neurons” and “prediction neurons,” but the fact that each local circuit updates beliefs and synapses using only signals available within its own dependency neighborhood, while the aggregate effect approximates descent on a broader variational objective. In this sense, predictive coding, belief propagation, relaxation dynamics, and arbitrary-graph predictive learning are best understood as different coordinate systems on the same underlying problem of locally computable error-reducing message passing 1 , 15 , 77 , 14 . A second framework-independent conclusion is that feedforward and feedback streams must physically converge for comparison to occur . Whether the resulting mismatch is implemented as literal subtraction, differential gain, burst-vs-singlet coding, explaining away, or target-minus-prediction relaxation, some circuit must place expected and observed causes into a common substrate. The exact locus remains open: superficial layers, deep layers, higher-order thalamus, and cortico-thalamo-cortical loops all likely participate. What appears non-negotiable, however, is dendritic compartmentalization as the substrate that makes multi-stream comparison biologically possible. Basal and perisomatic compartments are preferentially positioned to receive driving/feedforward evidence; apical and tuft compartments are preferentially positioned to receive contextual, predictive, and modulatory signals; and the interaction between these compartments determines the local voltage and Ca 2 + ^{2+} landscape that synapses “read out” during credit assignment. Different frameworks therefore disagree less about whether cortex performs compartment-specific multi-stream integration than about which lamina should be assigned which computational label 4 , 3 , 78 , 79 . A third robust conclusion is that cortex does not simply reduce raw mismatch; it reduces precision-weighted mismatch under a multi-layer gain architecture. Neuromodulators, oscillatory synchrony, dendritic nonlinearities, inhibitory microcircuits, population-level variability, and thalamocortical routing all reshape which discrepancies matter, when they matter, and how strongly they are allowed to drive plasticity. The effective learning rule is therefore best viewed not as Hebbian versus STDP versus dendritic versus three-factor plasticity, but as a single voltage/Ca 2 + ^{2+} -dependent, compartment-specific, three-factor-gated family expressed in different operating regimes. Because this family is embedded in an anatomical hierarchy of recurrent strength, NMDAR composition, spine density, myelination, and long-range connectivity, it inherits a corresponding hierarchy of learning timescales; and because candidate updates must survive branch-local tagging-and-capture, neuromodulatory selection, and offline replay, consolidation is necessarily selective rather than automatic. On this view, the thalamus is not a passive relay but an active participant in cortical optimization: a comparator, precision router, and context-sensitive deviance detector whose exact computational role varies across nuclei and tasks. Across frameworks, then, the most defensible synthesis is that cortex learns by locally computing, precision-weighting, and selectively consolidating mismatches on a heterarchical sensorimotor graph 1 , 9 , 80 . What Cortex Cannot Do Alone: Motivating the Other Optimizers The synthesis above might tempt one to treat cortex as a nearly complete learning system: a massive heterarchical graph that minimizes local free energy, builds temporally deep generative models, integrates multimodal context, and gradually distills experience into robust world knowledge. But the very properties that make cortex such a powerful general-purpose optimizer also impose hard computational limits. Cortical learning is high-dimensional, locally error-driven, statistically interleaved, and stability-constrained. Those features are ideal for extracting slowly varying structure from noisy sensory streams, but they are poorly matched to several other learning problems the organism must solve: storing the details of a single episode after one exposure, assigning delayed reward to the internal states and actions that caused it (a focus of the basal ganglia), and calibrating motor commands at millisecond precision. The multi-optimizer architecture introduced at the start of this section is therefore not a redundancy but a necessity 81 , 82 , 83 . First, cortex likely learns too slowly for episodic memory. The cortical algorithm described in the preceding sections is fundamentally incremental: it averages across many exposures, consolidates selectively, and commits structurally over hours to weeks. This is exactly what one wants from a semantic world model, because it protects previously learned representations from catastrophic overwrite (instead encouraging integration ) and allows common structure to be distilled from variable experience. But it is catastrophically ill-suited for one-shot storage of a unique event. A system that tried to write every individual episode directly into cortical weights at hippocampal speed would immediately run into the stability–plasticity dilemma: the same plasticity regime that allows fast memorization would destroy the distributed statistical structure accumulated over prior experience. This is the central logic of complementary learning systems. The hippocampus solves the problem by acting as a fast-write relational buffer that can bind the conjunctive details of a single experience into a retrievable trace, then gradually teach those traces back to cortex through interleaved replay, allowing cortical learning to remain slow, stable, value-weighted, and structure-extracting rather than episodically brittle 81 , 82 , 84 , 85 , 86 . Second, cortical self-supervised errors cannot by themselves solve the distal reward problem. Cortical prediction errors are rich, structured, and locally available: they tell a circuit what in its current prediction failed, where it failed, and often on what timescale. But they do not, on their own, say whether a sequence of internal states and actions ultimately improved fitness, secured reward, avoided punishment, or satisfied a homeostatic need after a delay of seconds, minutes, or years. The consequence of an action often arrives long after the cortical populations that helped produce it have changed state, so the relevant teaching signal must bridge temporal gaps and compress a vast causal history into a low-bandwidth scalar or distributional value update. That is the computational niche of the basal ganglia dopamine system. Cortex supplies the high-dimensional state representation, model-based predictions, action candidates, and contextual features; basal ganglia circuitry computes and broadcasts reward-prediction-error-like teaching signals that can tag which cortical-striatal trajectories should be strengthened, weakened, gated, or repeated 87 , 88 , 21 , 89 , 90 . In this sense, cortex can represent the world and imagine futures, but it cannot on its own derive the compressed reinforcement signal required to optimize policies over delayed consequences. A related limitation appears even in active-inference framings that embed action within the cortical generative model. Cortex may evaluate candidate futures by expected free energy, but policy selection becomes goal-directed only when the model contains prior preferences over outcomes P ( o τ ) P(o_\tau) . Those preferences cannot be grounded by cortical self-supervision alone. A purely cortical system could still infer, predict, and reduce epistemic uncertainty, but it would lack an endogenous basis for treating some futures as biologically better than others except insofar as value had already been installed into it by other systems. In organisms, those preferences are ultimately anchored in subcortical value and homeostatic circuitry—including hypothalamic, amygdalar, and basal-ganglia loops—that define which sensory and bodily outcomes count as desirable, urgent, threatening, or worth pursuing. Cortex can model and elaborate these preferences; it does not originate their core biological valence 91 , 92 . Thus even a predictive, policy-evaluating cortex still requires external value-setting machinery. Third, cortex likely lacks the temporal precision for rapid sensorimotor calibration. The cortical update cycle traced above unfolds across nested timescales: recurrent relaxation on the order of tens to hundreds of milliseconds, eligibility traces and modulatory consolidation over seconds to minutes, and structural stabilization over hours to weeks. That architecture is powerful for inference, abstraction, and flexible planning, but it is too slow and too temporally diffuse to serve as the sole substrate for fine motor timing, gain adjustment, and submovement calibration. Reaching, saccades, speech articulation, and posture require error correction on millisecond scales with consistent, low-jitter teaching signals. The cerebellum supplies exactly this regime. Its highly regular feedforward architecture, climbing-fiber instructive events, and rapid parallel-fiber → \rightarrow Purkinje-cell plasticity enable precise supervised updating of forward models and motor calibration in a way cortical recurrent dynamics cannot easily reproduce 83 , 93 , 94 , 95 , 96 . Cortex can learn rich sensorimotor structure and long-horizon task models, but cerebellar circuitry is required when the target is precise timing and online calibration rather than slow representational improvement. These limitations are not deficiencies of cortex. They are the reason the brain partitions learning across multiple optimizers. Cortex is the largest and most general-purpose optimizer: it builds the world model, supplies high-dimensional state representations, and supports temporally deep inference over rich heterarchical structure. But it achieves its full computational power only in concert with three complementary systems: hippocampus for rapid episodic binding and replay, cerebellum for fast supervised calibration, and basal ganglia for value-based selection and delayed credit assignment. Having now characterized what cortical optimization can and cannot do on its own, we turn next to the basal ganglia: the system that converts cortical state representations into reinforced policies by supplying the teaching signals that self-supervised cortex alone cannot generate.

title: The Basal Ganglia: Reinforcement Learning
text: The basal ganglia (BG) are the brain’s principal policy optimizer . Each of the brain’s major learning systems occupies a distinct niche in the broader optimization landscape: cortex minimizes precision-weighted prediction error across a deep, recurrent generative model of the world’s causal and statistical structure; hippocampus rapidly encodes one-shot episodic traces that bind context, content, and temporal order into retrievable relational maps; cerebellum performs millisecond-resolution supervised calibration of sensorimotor forward models using climbing-fiber error signals. The basal ganglia solve a complementary problem that none of these systems is designed to handle on its own: selecting, reinforcing, and automating action policies on the basis of delayed, sparse, evaluative feedback . The “actions” subject to this optimization should be understood broadly—not only overt motor outputs such as reaching, saccading, or locomoting, but also covert cognitive and affective operations, including attentional gating, working-memory updating, task-set selection, motivational vigor, and the deployment of abstract decision strategies 1 , 2 , 3 . In active-inference terms, where cortex furnishes much of the state space and predictive structure from which expected free energy is computed, the basal ganglia help convert prior preferences over outcomes into biases over policies, thereby steering both overt and covert action toward preferred states of the world 4 , 5 . Their niche, then, is not world modeling but world acting : to evaluate candidate actions defined over cortical representations, assign credit for outcomes that may arrive seconds or minutes after the decision that produced them, and progressively compile successful action patterns into efficient, automatized routines. What makes the basal ganglia indispensable is precisely what makes them different from cortex: they do not need to reconstruct the high-dimensional structure of the environment, only to learn which cortical computations to gate, energize, suppress, or crystallize—and to do so under the guidance of a teaching signal (dopaminergic prediction error) whose computational logic is fundamentally evaluative rather than reconstructive. This functional specialization is underwritten by an architecture that differs from cortex in almost every computationally relevant dimension . The cortical sheet is built from recurrent excitatory networks organized into a canonical six-layer columnar motif, in which local pyramidal-cell collaterals sustain persistent activity, lateral inhibition sharpens representations, and laminar segregation supports hierarchical message-passing between levels of abstraction. The striatum—the basal ganglia’s principal input nucleus and the largest structure in the subcortical forebrain—is organized according to very different principles. Its principal projection neurons, the spiny projection neurons (SPNs, also called medium spiny neurons or MSNs), are GABAergic and interact through local inhibitory axon collaterals, rather than the recurrent excitatory circuitry that characterizes cortex, making the striatum poorly suited for the kind of recurrent attractor dynamics thought to support cortical persistent activity and self-supervised error computation 6 , 7 . Nor does it possess a hierarchical laminar organization: although the striatum contains compartmental (e.g., striosome/matrix) and topographic organization, it lacks the layered vertical axis that gives cortex its capacity for intracolumnar feedforward and feedback signaling 7 . Likewise, there is no established analogue of the apical-basal comparison or cortical prediction-error circuitry proposed to support local self-supervised error computation within cortex. Instead, the basal ganglia implement a massively convergent, dopamine-modulated architecture specialized for competitive selection, value-based gating, and reinforcement-driven credit assignment. Cortical afferents converge onto striatal SPNs at enormous ratios—each SPN integrates glutamatergic input from thousands of cortical neurons across multiple cortical areas—and the result of this convergence is funneled through the pallidum and substantia nigra to a small set of thalamic and brainstem targets whose tonic inhibition is selectively released to permit action 8 , 9 . The striatum is, accordingly, the largest recipient of dopaminergic innervation in the brain, receiving the densest projection from midbrain dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and ventral tegmental area (VTA)—a fact that reflects the system’s fundamental dependence on dopaminergic teaching signals for synaptic plasticity and credit assignment 10 , 11 . Where cortex is thought to support local error computation through its recurrent hierarchical circuitry, the basal ganglia instead rely on an extrinsic neuromodulatory teaching signal, and the entire architecture is organized around making that broadcast maximally useful for reinforcement learning and credit assignment. Anatomically, the basal ganglia comprise a set of interconnected subcortical nuclei—the striatum (caudate nucleus, putamen, and ventral striatum including the nucleus accumbens), the globus pallidus external and internal segments (GPe and GPi), the subthalamic nucleus (STN), the substantia nigra pars reticulata and pars compacta (SNr and SNc), and the ventral tegmental area (VTA)—whose wiring implements a set of parallel, partially segregated cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops 12 , 8 . The classical three-channel taxonomy distinguishes motor loops (linking sensorimotor cortex through putamen and ventrolateral thalamus), associative/cognitive loops (linking prefrontal and parietal cortex through caudate and mediodorsal thalamus), and limbic loops (linking orbitofrontal, cingulate, and insular cortex through ventral striatum and ventromedial thalamus), though recent whole-brain mapping has refined this into at least six parallel subnetworks, each transducing a specific cortical information channel through every node of the loop in a bona fide closed circuit, with additional open-loop projections—particularly from ventral striatum through medial SNr to motor thalamus—allowing limbic evaluations to exert a unidirectional influence on motor output 8 , 13 . It is this loop architecture that constitutes the skeleton on which the reinforcement-learning optimizer is draped: each loop carries a different cortical state representation into the striatum, subjects it to dopamine-modulated competitive selection, and returns the result to the cortical territory from which it originated—thereby allowing a single computational logic (evaluative gating under dopaminergic credit assignment) to be applied in parallel to qualitatively different behavioral domains, from the vigor of a reach to the selection of an attentional set. Importantly, the basal ganglia resolve their optimization problem through an opponent pathway architecture . The D1-receptor-expressing SPNs of the direct pathway project monosynaptically to GPi/SNr output neurons, whose tonic inhibition of thalamus they suppress, thereby facilitating the selected action; the D2-receptor-expressing SPNs of the indirect pathway project through GPe and STN to the same output neurons, reinforcing tonic inhibition and thereby suppressing competing or contextually inappropriate actions 14 , 15 . The global loss of the system is resolved through the competitive integration of these two channels: the direct pathway learns the expected value of executing an action, the indirect pathway learns the expected cost of that action or the value of withholding it, and their dynamic balance—modulated in opposite directions by phasic dopamine, which excites D1 SPNs and inhibits D2 SPNs—determines whether a candidate action clears the threshold for release 16 , 17 . Greater anatomical detail on the intrinsic circuitry, loop organization, and inter-loop interactions of the basal ganglia is provided in “Systems-Level Architecture and Dynamics”; the present section focuses on how this architecture supports learning —what is optimized, what error signal drives the optimization, how that signal modifies the circuit, and what behavioral competences emerge. The cellular substrate of this optimization is dominated by the spiny projection neuron . SPNs are a specialized class of GABAergic inhibitory neuron constituting approximately 90–95% of the neuronal population within the striatum, with the remaining 5–10% comprising several classes of interneurons—most prominently the tonically active cholinergic interneurons (CINs), fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive interneurons, and several peptidergic GABAergic interneuron types 10 , 18 . SPNs exist in two principal phenotypes that map onto the opponent pathway architecture: D1-type SPNs express the D1 family of dopamine receptors (coupled to G s _s /G o l f _{olf} signaling and adenylyl cyclase activation) and project through the direct pathway, while D2-type SPNs express the D2 family of dopamine receptors (coupled to G i _i /G o _o signaling and adenylyl cyclase inhibition) and project through the indirect pathway. In the dorsal striatum, these two populations are roughly equal in size, largely non-overlapping, and uniformly intermingled, with D1 SPNs comprising approximately 50–52% and D2 SPNs approximately 46–48% of the total SPN population; a small subpopulation (approximately 2% in dorsal striatum, rising to 7–15% in ventral striatum) co-expresses both receptor types, though the functional significance of this co-expressing population remains under active investigation 18 , 19 . The SPN’s electrophysiology—deeply hyperpolarized resting states enforced by inward-rectifying potassium channels, a requirement for convergent cortical drive to reach spike threshold, and dendritic spine architecture that compartmentalizes individual corticostriatal synapses into semi-independent plasticity units—makes it a neuron exquisitely designed to integrate broad cortical context with a dopaminergic teaching signal at the level of the single synapse. It is this integration, repeated across millions of SPNs organized into opponent D1 and D2 channels within each of the parallel cortico-basal ganglia loops, that constitutes the physical substrate of the reinforcement-learning computation whose loss functions, error signals, plasticity rules, and emergent behavioral competences are detailed in the subsections that follow.

title: BG Error Signals
text: We have normative, BG-scale loss functions, now onto the actual hardware that computes and routes error signals The preceding section established the form and structure of the BG loss; we now turn to the neural machinery that computes, weights, and routes the error signals that this loss implies.

title: Dopaminergic nuclei
text: Before turning to the arithmetic of the error itself, it is useful to briefly situate the hardware that computes and distributes it. The basal ganglia’s dopaminergic teaching signals arise principally from two midbrain nuclei, the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) . These should not be understood as wholly separate error calculators, but rather as partially overlapping, differently biased routing hubs within a shared dopaminergic architecture. At a coarse level, VTA dopamine neurons preferentially participate in mesolimbic and mesocortical loops, projecting strongly to ventral striatum, prefrontal cortex, and other limbic-associative targets, whereas SNc neurons are biased toward nigrostriatal loops and project predominantly to dorsal striatum, where they modulate associative and sensorimotor control. This division is only approximate: projection-defined dopamine subtypes cut across classical VTA/SNc boundaries, and both nuclei contain substantial anatomical and functional heterogeneity. Likewise, their afferent organization is biased rather than absolute: SNc receives relatively stronger sensorimotor- and STN-related drive, whereas VTA is more strongly coupled to limbic and hypothalamic inputs. The result is that the same general prediction-error computation can be embedded in partially distinct motivational, cognitive, and motor loops, with different dopamine subpopulations receiving somewhat different mixtures of state, action, sensory, and homeostatic information 1 , 2 , 3 . Just as important, once computed, the error signal is not relayed through a point-to-point “wire” in the manner of a classical fast synapse. Dopamine remains a neuromodulatory broadcast signal whose influence is shaped by sparse release-site architecture, extracellular diffusion, and powerful reuptake, allowing a relatively compact population of midbrain neurons to distribute teaching signals across large regions of striatum and cortex 4 . But this broadcast is not purely volumetric or spatially amorphous. Recent work shows that evoked dopamine secretion in the striatum depends on sparse "active-zone-like" release hotspots with rapid kinetics and high spatiotemporal precision, supported by specialized presynaptic scaffolds present at only a minority of dopaminergic varicosities 5 , 6 ; diffusion and dopamine-transporter-mediated clearance then sculpt the final spatiotemporal profile seen by downstream receptors. Cryo-electron and ultrastructural work further indicates that many dopaminergic varicosities modulate nearby cortico-striatal synapses without forming classical one-to-one synaptic specializations, enabling locally structured yet non-synaptic control 7 . In addition, dopamine neurons in both SNc and VTA can release dopamine somatodendritically within the midbrain itself, engaging D2 autoreceptors and local microcircuits that regulate excitability, burst probability, and pause structure before signals ever reach forebrain axons 8 , 9 . Thus, the dopaminergic nuclei of the basal ganglia are best viewed as projection-specific, multilayered error-routing systems : they integrate heterogeneous inputs in VTA and SNc, interact locally through dendritic and somatic release, convert this integration into phasic burst-pause dynamics, and then broadcast those teaching signals through axonal release mechanisms that are diffuse at circuit scale but highly structured at the level of release hotspots and varicosity-synapse relationships.
