title: How the error is computed: expectation, outcome, and subtraction
text: The preceding section established what the basal ganglia’s error signal represents–a scalar (or population-level) temporal-difference prediction error δ = r + γ V ( s ′ ) − V ( s ) \delta=r+\gamma V(s')−V(s) –and what loss landscape it serves. This section asks the circuit-level question: how is that error actually computed? In the most stripped-down form, computing δ requires three quantities to be available at the right time and combined with the right arithmetic: (i) an expectation signal, V(s), representing the predicted value of the current state; (ii) an outcome signal, representing the reward actually received together with the discounted value of the successor state, r + γ V ( s ′ ) r+\gamma V(s') ; and (iii) a subtraction operation that takes the difference between the two. These three ingredients must converge on the dopamine neuron at the moment an outcome occurs or a prediction is updated, yielding the signed error whose broadcast to striatum drives the plasticity described in subsequent sections. To understand how the midbrain implements this comparison, it is essential to appreciate the input architecture of VTA and SNc dopamine neurons. Whole-brain mapping of direct (monosynaptic) inputs to dopamine neurons reveals an extraordinarily broad afferent landscape: dopamine neurons receive convergent projections from the ventral and dorsal striatum, ventral pallidum, lateral hypothalamus, subthalamic nucleus, lateral habenula, rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg), pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg), dorsal raphe, prefrontal cortex, and other structures 1 , 2 . Each of these inputs can, in principle, convey some component of the information needed for the RPE computation–actual reward, predicted reward, or some mixture of the two. The critical organizing question is which of these afferents carries the expectation term, which carries the outcome term, and how they are combined at the level of the dopamine neuron to yield a subtracted error. A landmark result on the arithmetic of the computation came from Eshel, Bukwich, Rao, and colleagues, who combined optogenetic manipulations with extracellular recordings in the VTA during classical conditioning. By delivering rewards of varying magnitudes that were either temporally unexpected or temporally expected (preceded by an odour cue), they were able to ask a precise question: does temporal expectation suppress dopamine reward responses in a subtractive or divisive fashion? If the operation is division, then the expectation-induced reduction should be proportionally larger for larger reward responses; if it is subtraction, the reduction should be a constant offset regardless of reward size. Light-identified dopamine neurons showed a purely subtractive shift: the dose-response curve for reward responses was displaced downward by a constant amount when reward was expected, with no change in slope 3 . This is exactly the operation required by the TD error equation δ = r + γ V ( s ′ ) − V ( s ) \delta=r+\gamma V(s')−V(s) , in which the predicted value is subtracted from the obtained outcome. Subtraction, though intuitively simple, is rarely observed at the single-cell level in the brain–most forms of inhibitory gain modulation produce divisive rather than subtractive effects–making the dopamine neuron’s implementation noteworthy and important for the fidelity of RL 3 . Having established that the operation is subtractive, the next question is: which input supplies the expectation term that is subtracted from the reward response? A convergent body of evidence identifies GABA neurons local to the VTA as a major source of this signal. Cohen, Haesler, and colleagues used optogenetic tagging to identify VTA GABA neurons during Pavlovian conditioning, and found that these neurons show sustained, ramping activity that increases between cue onset and the expected time of reward delivery, with the magnitude of this sustained activity varying with the probability and size of the predicted reward–precisely the profile expected of a reward-expectation signal 4 . Eshel and colleagues then confirmed the causal role of VTA GABA neurons in the subtraction operation through a complementary pair of manipulations. Optogenetically exciting VTA GABA neurons at the time of reward delivery mimicked the effect of temporal expectation: dopamine reward responses were suppressed in a subtractive fashion, shifting the dose-response curve downward by a constant amount, reproducing the effect of a naturally learned expectation 3 . Conversely, optogenetically inhibiting VTA GABA neurons around the time of expected reward partially reversed expectation-dependent suppression, causing dopamine neurons to respond as though reward was more unexpected than it actually was 3 . Furthermore, bilateral stimulation of VTA GABA neurons paired with a conditioned odour dramatically reduced anticipatory licking, consistent with an important role for these neurons in the reinforcement-learning loop 3 . Together, these results establish a local circuit mechanism: VTA GABA interneurons receive information about predicted reward (from cortical, striatal, and pallidal afferents), produce sustained inhibitory activity proportional to the expectation, and synapse directly onto neighbouring dopamine neurons, where this inhibition implements the subtractive component of the TD error 2 , 3 . A second major pathway by which the expectation term reaches dopamine neurons involves the lateral habenula (LHb) and the rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg) . The LHb is well positioned to represent worse-than-expected outcomes because it sits downstream of an anti-reward forebrain stream, receiving strong input from pallidal structures—especially the GPi/entopeduncular complex–that themselves encode reward omission, non-reward, and aversive contingencies 5 , 6 . Importantly, this pallido-habenular pathway is not a simple inhibitory BG output; it includes excitatory glutamatergic signaling (and in some cases mixed transmitter phenotypes), allowing the LHb to be driven when outcomes are worse than predicted and suppressed when outcomes are better than predicted 6 , 7 . The LHb also receives broader hypothalamic and limbic inputs, enabling it to integrate learned reward expectations with internal-state and aversive information into a unified negative evaluative signal. Its influence on dopamine neurons is powerfully inhibitory despite its own projections being glutamatergic, a paradox resolved by the discovery of the RMTg–a GABAergic nucleus positioned between the LHb and the VTA/SNc that converts LHb excitation into dopamine inhibition 8 , 9 . Ultrastructural evidence confirms a disynaptic pathway: LHb glutamatergic axons synapse onto GABA neurons in the RMTg, which in turn form inhibitory synapses preferentially onto dopamine neurons in the VTA 10 . This LHb->RMTg->dopamine pathway is especially important for the negative component of the TD error—the pause in dopamine firing that occurs when an expected reward is omitted. Habenula lesion experiments dissociate this function from the general RPE computation: after habenula lesions, dopamine neurons retain their ability to signal positive prediction errors (bursts to unexpected reward, transfer of responses to reward-predictive cues), but their response to reward omission is greatly attenuated, indicating that the LHb–RMTg system has a uniquely important role in conveying the signal for worse-than-expected outcomes 11 . In intact animals, LHb neuron activation precedes the inhibition of dopamine neuron firing at a latency consistent with a disynaptic relay, and stimulation of the LHb inhibits virtually all midbrain dopamine neurons at short latency 5 , 12 . If the subtraction is implemented by local VTA GABA neurons and the LHb–RMTg system, what supplies the outcome signal –the excitatory drive that represents r + γ V ( s ′ ) r+\gamma V(s') at the time of reward (or at the time of a reward-predictive cue)? Several afferent systems are positioned to contribute this term, and they do so because each sits downstream of circuitry that already integrates biologically relevant outcomes, learned reward contingencies, and action-relevant motivational state. The pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg) is especially well placed to provide a fast reward-related drive: embedded within the mesopontine locomotor/arousal system and tightly linked to basal-ganglia output, it carries both state-updating salience signals and learned reward information, with separable neuronal populations encoding sustained predicted reward from cue onset to reward delivery and phasic actual reward at outcome time 13 , 2 . The lateral hypothalamus contributes a more physiologically grounded signal. Because it has privileged access to feeding, thirst, arousal, and other homeostatic variables, LH can convey not merely whether an event is externally rewarding, but how valuable it is given the organism’s current internal state; correspondingly, LH projections to dopamine neurons are heterogeneous, with some populations relaying appetitive and reward-predictive information and others carrying aversive or defensive signals 1 , 2 . The ventral pallidum (VP) , meanwhile, acts less like a simple relay and more like a convergent valuation hub: receiving dense input from nucleus accumbens and related mesolimbic structures, it integrates cue value, incentive salience, preference, and action-invigoration variables into a downstream estimate of motivational significance 14 . Thus, PPTg, LH, and VP come to signal "reward" not because any is a dedicated reward wire, but because each occupies a different point in the transformation from raw outcome to subjective utility: PPTg emphasizes fast outcome- and cue-related reward information, LH grounds value in bodily need and internal state, and VP integrates learned motivational value into a format suitable for action selection. Their convergent excitatory drive therefore supplies much of the r + γ V ( s ′ ) r+\gamma V(s') -like signal that, after subtraction by inhibitory expectation pathways, yields the signed TD error. An important insight from recent work, however, is that the RPE computation does not arise from a simple, modular "one input for reward, one input for expectation" architecture. Tian, Huang, Cohen, and colleagues combined rabies-virus-mediated trans-synaptic tracing with optogenetic identification to record from the monosynaptic inputs of dopamine neurons across seven brain areas during classical conditioning. If the textbook modular view were correct, distinct populations of presynaptic neurons should encode pure reward signals or pure expectation signals, and dopamine neurons should combine them. Instead, they found that the information required for RPE computation–actual reward, predicted reward, and mixtures of the two–was distributed and already mixed in monosynaptic input neurons across all brain areas examined, including the striatum, ventral pallidum, lateral hypothalamus, subthalamic nucleus, RMTg, and PPTg 14 . Only ∼5% of input neurons signaled actual reward in a pure fashion, and only ∼13% signaled expectation purely; the majority of task-responsive input neurons encoded mixtures of reward and expectation, and a substantial fraction (∼18%) already showed aspects of RPE coding—expectation-dependent suppression of reward responses—before these signals even reached dopamine neurons 14 . Strikingly, even when the weights assigned to individual input neurons were randomly shuffled, a linear combination of input-neuron activity still approximated the shape of the dopamine RPE, indicating that the activity profiles of monosynaptic inputs are "pre-formatted" such that the downstream dopamine neuron can robustly converge on the correct RPE signal without exquisitely precise synaptic tuning 14 . Despite this redundancy and distribution, the contribution of different input structures is not entirely interchangeable. The LHb-RMTg pathway, as noted above, appears to have a relatively unique role in signaling reward omission 11 . Among identified monosynaptic inputs, the RMTg is distinctive in that its neurons preferentially show negative reward coding (excited by aversive cues, inhibited by reward cues), whereas monosynaptic inputs from most other areas are predominantly excited by reward-predictive stimuli 14 , 8 . Similarly, VTA GABA neurons are enriched for sustained expectation-like activity 4 , and the PPTg for both tonic predicted-value and phasic actual-reward signals 13 . Thus, while the overall computation is distributed and redundant, individual input channels are biased toward particular computational roles–some more excitatory and reward-signaling, others more inhibitory and expectation-signaling–and the dopamine neuron integrates these heterogeneous inputs to construct a more complete RPE than any single input carries on its own. The picture that emerges, then, is of a multi-layered, convergent subtraction rather than a clean two-input comparator. The dopamine neuron sits at the apex of a network in which multiple excitatory and inhibitory afferents carry overlapping, partially pre-computed error signals. At the most local level, VTA GABA interneurons provide a subtractive expectation signal that suppresses reward responses in proportion to predicted value 3 . In parallel, the LHb-RMTg system provides a disynaptic inhibitory pathway that is especially important for signaling the negative component of prediction errors–reward omission and worse-than-expected outcomes 11 , 12 . The reward and outcome signals are delivered by excitatory glutamatergic and cholinergic inputs from the PPTg, lateral hypothalamus, ventral pallidum, and other structures, many of which are themselves partially mixed with expectation signals 14 , 13 . The individual dopamine neuron applies a common response function 15 to the net effect of these converging inputs, yielding a signed, quantitative error whose positive component (burst) or negative component (pause) is then broadcast to striatal and cortical targets via phasic dopamine release. Recent evidence that dopamine neurons exhibit stable heterogeneity in the relative scaling of positive versus negative error responses–consistent with distributional RL–adds the further nuance that even the subtraction itself may be asymmetrically parameterized across individual neurons, allowing the population to encode not just the mean error but a family of asymmetric errors spanning the return distribution 16 , 3 , 15 . The upshot is that the RPE computation, though often written as a single subtraction, is biologically implemented as a distributed, multi-step, and redundantly organized process in which many brain areas partially pre-compute components of the error and the dopamine neuron refines this into a more complete signal 14 , 2 , 17 .

title: Actor–critic architecture
text: The actor–critic decomposition introduced in the loss-function section is best treated, at the level of anatomy, as a biased architectural motif rather than a literal two-box partition . In the clean RL formalism, the critic estimates value and helps generate the teaching signal, whereas the actor converts that teaching signal into policy updates. The basal ganglia appear to implement something close to this logic, but they do so through partially overlapping gradients, loops, and compartments rather than through one anatomically isolated “critic nucleus” and one isolated “actor nucleus” 1 , 2 , 3 . At the coarsest scale, the most important organizing principle is a ventromedial-to-dorsolateral gradient across striatum. As one moves from nucleus accumbens and ventromedial striatum toward dorsomedial and then dorsolateral striatum, neural coding shifts from relatively stronger value, expectation, and motivational variables toward relatively stronger action, associative, and sensorimotor variables. This gradient is exactly what one would expect from an approximate actor–critic architecture: ventral territories are more critic-like because they are more strongly concerned with state and motivational value, whereas dorsal territories are more actor-like because they are more tightly linked to action selection, action chunks, and habit-like control 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 . The ventral striatum is especially well placed to implement the critic side of the architecture. The classical reason is computational: it has access to phasic dopaminergic prediction-error signals and receives convergent limbic, hippocampal, orbitofrontal, medial prefrontal, and thalamic information appropriate for computing state value and expected utility. But the anatomical reason is at least as important: ventral striatum sits in a strategic position to influence the very dopaminergic teaching signals on which both critic and actor depend, via its projections through ventral pallidum and related ventral midbrain circuitry. As van der Meer and Redish emphasized, ventral striatum has unusually good access to prediction-error inputs; and as earlier actor–critic interpretations stressed, it is in a prime position to shape prediction-error learning signals for both systems, not merely to receive them 2 , 7 . More recent projection-specific tracing is broadly consistent with this emphasis: for many dopamine subpopulations, ventral striatum is among the densest input sources, making it a plausible major supplier of critic-like expectation information to the midbrain 8 . The dorsal striatum , by contrast, is better viewed as the actor side of the architecture, though again only in a dominant and not exclusive sense. Recordings in dorsal striatum have repeatedly found action-specific value signals, chosen-action signals, contralateral choice signals, and other variables suitable for policy updating rather than pure state evaluation 4 , 9 . This is especially clear in dorsomedial striatum for flexible, goal-directed action selection, and in dorsolateral striatum for more sensorimotor and habitual control. Projection-specific dopamine measurements sharpen the point: dopamine terminals in ventral striatum respond more strongly to reward consumption and reward-predicting cues, whereas dorsomedial terminals more strongly encode contralateral choice; yet both still carry RPE-like information 5 . Thus the actor is not error-free or critic-free; rather, it is an action-centered substrate trained by regionally tailored error signals 4 , 5 , 9 , 10 . But how does the critic train the actor ? The classical answer is the striato–nigro–striatal spiral . In primates, Haber and colleagues described an ascending spiral in which ventral striatal territories influence progressively more dorsal dopamine-recipient territories through ventral-to-dorsal striatonigral and nigrostriatal connectivity, providing an appealing route by which value learning in ventral loops could progressively tutor action learning in dorsal loops 11 . But this should not be stated as though it were the sole or even a fully established mechanism. More recent circuit dissection finds strong evidence for closed loops , which would allow a striatal subregion to regulate its own dopamine release, alongside evidence for open loops that could support cross-region transfer. Likewise, whole-brain tracing of projection-defined dopamine subpopulations suggests that most dopamine groups receive a fairly common set of inputs rather than being organized as neatly closed, target-by-target reciprocal loops; the major outlier is the posterior/tail striatal system, which receives relatively little ventral-striatal input and more pallidal, subthalamic, and zona incerta drive 12 , 8 . The safest synthesis, then, is that dorsal striatum receives value-relevant information from ventral systems indirectly –through shared dopaminergic broadcasts, ventral-striatal influence on midbrain teaching signals, and open striato–nigro–striatal loops–rather than through a simple monosynaptic “ventral critic to dorsal actor” line. A second, and in some ways deeper, candidate implementation of the actor–critic architecture lies in the patch/striosome versus matrix organization of the striatum. This mapping is attractive because it places the critic-like function not simply in ventral striatum as a whole, but in those striatal compartments that are anatomically specialized to control dopamine neurons directly. Striosomal neurons form the unusual striosome–dendron bouquet arrangements that target dopamine-containing dendrites and clustered nigral cell bodies, strongly suggesting a specialized route by which striatum can regulate the computation and routing of dopaminergic teaching signals 13 . Lazaridis and colleagues then showed that striosomes contain parallel D1- and D2-defined pathways that target dopamine neurons rather than the canonical basal-ganglia motor output nuclei , with net effects opposite to the standard direct/indirect pathways (i.e S-D1 is net inhibitory and S-D2 is net excitatory); and Cai and colleagues showed that patch activation suppresses locomotion and strongly inhibits dopamine release, whereas matrix striatonigral activation promotes locomotion and initially promotes dopamine release 14 , 15 . On this view, the matrix is naturally actor-like because it is more tightly embedded in the canonical action-output channels, whereas striosomes are naturally critic-like because they are disproportionately positioned to compute, gate, and sculpt the dopaminergic teaching signal that trains those channels. The compartment story also clarifies why the actor–critic mapping should remain graded rather than absolute . Striosomes are not pure critics, matrix is not pure actor 16 , ventral striatum can participate in performance and incentive invigoration, and dorsal striatum still carries value signals. Even at the local physiological level, dopamine affects striosome and matrix neurons differently rather than simply exciting one and ignoring the other: dopamine can prolong up-states in matrix D1 neurons while shortening them in striosomal D1 neurons, implying that the microarchitecture is built for differential learning rules , not for a single uniform policy substrate 17 . The right conclusion is therefore not that the BG literally contain one critic and one actor, but that they contain nested actor–critic-like motifs : a ventral-to-dorsal territorial gradient, a striosome-to-matrix compartmental specialization, and a projection-specific dopamine system that broadcasts partly shared but regionally customized teaching signals. In that sense, the potential architectural underpinnings of the dorsal/ventral actor–critic subdivision are now clearer. The critic-like side of the system is implemented by circuits that estimate motivational/state value and that can reach back to the dopamine system—most prominently ventral striatum, ventral pallidum, and striosomal pathways to midbrain dopamine neurons. The actor-like side is implemented by circuits more directly coupled to action competition and policy expression—especially matrix-rich dorsal striatal loops projecting through the canonical basal-ganglia output channels. Dopamine links the two: it is the shared teaching signal, but it is not perfectly homogeneous. Rather, it is routed through topographically organized, partially looping, and compartmentally gated architectures that allow critic-like valuation to train actor-like policy at multiple anatomical scales 18 , 5 , 6 .

title: Distributional and multi-timescale error signals
text: The classical temporal-difference account writes the dopaminergic teaching signal as a single scalar error, δ = r + γ V ( s ′ ) − V ( s ) \delta=r+\gamma V(s')-V(s) . But the emerging physiological picture suggests that this scalar is best understood as an idealization of a structured population code . The basic RPE computation still appears to be shared across dopamine neurons: they retain a common subtractive response function, and the scalar TD formalism remains the right first approximation. Yet the neurons implementing that computation are not perfectly redundant copies of one another. Instead, different dopaminergic channels appear to instantiate different parameterizations of the error computation, allowing the basal ganglia to learn not only the mean of future return but aspects of its full distribution over both reward magnitude and reward time 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . The clearest evidence for a distributional reward code came from Dabney and colleagues, who showed that VTA dopamine neurons differ systematically in their reversal points and in the relative scaling of positive versus negative prediction errors. In other words, the population is not organized around one shared prediction with noise added on top; rather, individual neurons behave as though they are tilted toward more optimistic or more pessimistic slices of the return distribution. That is precisely the pattern expected if different dopamine channels converge toward different expectile-like estimates of future reward. Importantly, this result does not abolish the scalar RPE idea; it refines it. Each neuron still computes an error-like signal, but the population as a whole spans a family of asymmetric error channels whose aggregate activity can represent multimodal reward distributions that mean-based TD learning cannot recover 2 , 5 . What physiological architecture could generate this distributional diversity? The safest answer is: not one mechanism, but several layered together . Part of the heterogeneity likely originates upstream of the dopamine neuron. Dopamine populations are projection-defined, receive different mixtures of sensory, motor, cognitive, and motivational inputs, and can therefore inherit different feature weightings from their afferent circuitry 6 , 7 . This point has been sharpened by recent theory showing that some dopaminergic heterogeneity can be explained by feature-specific prediction errors , in which different neurons compute errors for different aspects of the animal’s state rather than merely different quantiles of one scalar reward variable 8 . The most defensible synthesis, then, is that distributional coding and feature-specific coding are complementary rather than mutually exclusive : one concerns asymmetric weighting of outcomes, the other differential weighting of state features, and both may contribute to the observed diversity of dopamine responses 9 , 8 . Just as important, the distributional code is likely completed downstream in the striatum through opponent receptor and plasticity machinery. Dopamine’s effects are read out through partially segregated D1- and D2-receptor-expressing spiny projection neuron populations with complementary signaling and plasticity rules, giving the striatum a natural substrate for differentially learning from positive versus negative outcomes 10 , 11 , 12 . Recent work makes that idea much more concrete: Lowet and colleagues found that striatum encodes not only reward mean but reward variance, that chronic dopamine ablation disrupts this distributional representation, and that D1- and D2-expressing neurons preferentially encode opposite tails of the learned reward distribution 13 . This suggests that the biological implementation of “distributional RL” is not simply a diverse midbrain population projecting onto a passive striatum; it is a midbrain–striatal composite architecture in which heterogeneous dopaminergic RPE channels are transformed by opponent striatal readout into optimistic and pessimistic learning streams. The same logic extends from reward magnitude to reward time . At the level of dopamine release in striatal targets, Mohebi, Wei, and colleagues showed that dopamine transients obey a robust ventral-to-dorsolateral gradient of time horizons : dynamics become faster from ventral striatum to dorsomedial striatum to dorsolateral striatum, both in spontaneous fluctuation timescales and in the discounting of future rewards 14 . In delay-manipulation experiments, all regions preferred sooner rewards, but DLS discounted delay most steeply whereas VS discounted most shallowly, with DMS intermediate. Computationally, this implies that the effective discount factor in the TD error is not one system-wide constant. Different cortico-basal-ganglia loops appear to receive teaching signals with different implicit γ i \gamma_i values, so that limbic loops learn over longer horizons, associative loops over intermediate horizons, and sensorimotor loops over shorter horizons 14 , 15 . Recent single-neuron work argues that this temporal diversity is not only regional but also cell-specific . Masset, Tano, and colleagues found that individual dopamine neurons encode future rewards over distinct temporal horizons, and that the discount factors inferred from single neurons are correlated across two different behavioral tasks, implying that temporal discounting is a relatively stable property of the neuron rather than a task-by-task reassignment 3 . Published in parallel, Sousa, Bujalski, and colleagues extended this logic to a joint code over reward time and magnitude : in their account, each dopamine neuron is characterized by both a temporal parameter ( γ i \gamma_i ) and an asymmetric error-scaling parameter ( κ i \kappa_i ), allowing the population to encode a two-dimensional probabilistic map of future reward over both “when” and “how much” 4 . Their results further suggest an efficient-coding organization, in which the distribution of temporal sensitivities adapts to the statistics of experienced delays, and show that reward-time predictions decoded from the dopamine population correlate with anticipatory licking, indicating that this code is behaviorally used rather than epiphenomenal 4 . Overall, the BG error signal is best understood not as one homogeneous scalar broadcast, but as a family of partially specialized teaching signals distributed over reward magnitude and temporal horizon. Mechanistically, that family likely arises from several interacting sources: projection-specific input/output architecture, neuron-to-neuron differences in asymmetric error scaling, topographic specialization of dopamine release across striatal territories, and opponent plasticity rules in dopamine-recipient striatal circuits. At present, however, the field has not converged on a single exhaustive implementation. Some observed heterogeneity may reflect true distributional coding; some may reflect feature-specific errors; some may reflect other task variables layered onto canonical RPE computations. The strongest present claim is therefore not that the classical TD account is wrong, but that it is biologically unfolded : what appears in theory as one scalar δ \delta is implemented in the brain as a structured, heterogeneous population of error signals whose collective action supports risk-sensitive, uncertainty-sensitive, and time-sensitive policy optimization 2 , 8 , 14 , 3 , 9 .

title: Generalizing dopamine
text: The preceding subsections characterized dopamine as the biological implementation of a temporal-difference reward prediction error—a signed scalar whose burst-pause dynamics teach the striatum to optimize cumulative discounted reward. That characterization is not wrong, but it is incomplete. A growing body of experimental evidence, synthesized and extended by recent theoretical perspectives 1 , 2 , 3 , reveals that at least some dopaminergic channels carry prediction errors over variables other than reward value: over the sensory identity of expected outcomes, over associative transitions between value-neutral states, over the degree of match between an intended and an executed action, and over the spatial trajectory taken toward a goal. Rather than constituting anomalies that strain the reward-RPE framework, these non-canonical signals are best understood as instances of a deeper engineering principle: the basal ganglia exploit a shared prediction-error architecture to solve multiple, partially distinct learning problems simultaneously, with different dopaminergic channels serving as the specialized teaching signals for each. The result is a system that is, in its functional logic, far closer to a general-purpose credit assignment engine than to a dedicated reward-tracking device. Perhaps the clearest and most extensively documented departure from pure reward-value coding concerns sensory and identity prediction errors . The conventional model-free RPE framework assigns dopamine the task of tracking a scalar cached value; it predicts that dopamine responses to outcome delivery should be sensitive to the amount and probability of reward but indifferent to the sensory identity of the reward so long as value is held constant. This prediction fails. Takahashi and colleagues recorded light-identified dopamine neurons in the VTA of rats while independently manipulating reward quantity (to drive value prediction errors) and reward flavor (to drive identity prediction errors at constant value). The same neurons that showed canonical burst responses to quantity increases also responded to unexpected flavor changes, and critically, the identity-driven changes in firing were not readily explainable as novelty or salience artifacts, nor did they track cached value–the 1st drop of a large reward, which should excite under value-RPE logic, instead did the opposite when its identity was unexpected, consistent with an identity-error signal rather than a value signal 4 . Importantly, these identity- and value-driven responses were not confined to non-overlapping populations; most neurons that encoded value errors also encoded identity errors, suggesting that individual dopamine neurons carry multiplexed teaching signals over multiple outcome dimensions 4 . Stalnaker and colleagues extended this finding by showing that the information about which sensory identity was mispredicted–not merely that a misprediction occurred–is encoded at the ensemble level across dopamine neurons in rats, and that analogous ensemble-level content specificity can be detected in the human midbrain BOLD signal, implicating dopamine in conveying content-rich rather than purely scalar teaching signals 5 . In humans, Howard and Kahnt provided a mechanistic link downstream: identity prediction errors in the midbrain correlated with the updating of reward-identity expectations specifically in the orbitofrontal cortex, and not in areas that track value, suggesting that the OFC is a dedicated downstream recipient of identity-specific dopaminergic teaching signals 6 . Further human work confirmed that these identity-error signals in the midbrain are independent of perceptual distance/similarity–they scale with the violation of identity expectations regardless of how perceptually similar the received and expected outcomes are 7 . Recent circuit-level work has clarified which upstream structures supply the prediction of reward identity that must be subtracted: hippocampal lesions broadly impaired both value and identity error signaling by dopamine neurons, whereas OFC lesions produced a highly selective failure to extinguish identity-error responses despite relatively intact value-error signaling, indicating that OFC normally provides the learned identity expectation that is compared against received identity, while hippocampus is a more general memory supplier for the comparison 8 . At the striatal level, identity-based dopamine signals have been shown to participate in sensory and perceptual decisions: striatal dopamine in the dorsal striatum integrates sensory prediction errors with reward prediction errors to guide perceptual choices, with dopamine release in both nucleus accumbens and dorsomedial striatum tracking errors in predicting value-neutral cues during latent learning as well as errors in predicting reward during reward-conditioning 9 , 10 . The unified implication is that the scope of what dopamine "predicts" is broader than reward magnitude: it can include the full featural content of expected outcomes, and its error signal updates both value and content representations in downstream targets. The identity-error data already stretched the model-free RPE framework to its limits, because even a feature-augmented RPE model can, in principle, be reconciled with dopamine tracking the value of specific sensory events once those features are incorporated into the state representation. A more fundamental challenge comes from evidence that dopamine transients can drive learning about the associative transitions between entirely value-neutral stimuli –a form of learning that requires state prediction errors rather than reward prediction errors of any kind. Sharpe and colleagues delivered a decisive causal test using a sensory preconditioning paradigm designed to isolate associative, value-free learning 11 . The task has three phases. In preconditioning, rats experience repeated C → X C\rightarrow X pairings–two neutral cues presented in succession, with no reward–allowing an associative link between them to form. In conditioning, X X is separately paired with reward (the unconditioned stimulus, U S US ). In a probe test, the rat is presented with C C alone: if it responds, it must be because it stored the C → X C\rightarrow X association during preconditioning and is now chaining it forward through X X to the remembered reward–a C → X → U S C\rightarrow X\rightarrow US inference. This inference is model-based rather than model-free: C C was never directly paired with reward, so any cached value on C C must be zero (this was supported directly by a conditioned reinforcement probe in a parallel experiment, in which preconditioned cues–unlike directly conditioned cues–failed to support conditioned reinforcement, suggesting that they carry no cached value 12 ). Responding to C C in the probe test therefore reveals that the rat built and consulted an internal map of state transitions, not that it retrieved a stored value. Having established the behavioral signature, Sharpe et al. then asked whether dopamine is the teaching signal that writes the C → X C\rightarrow X link. To test sufficiency, they incorporated a blocking design: cue A A was first trained to predict X X ( A → X A\rightarrow X ), then A A and C C were presented together before X X ( A C → X AC\rightarrow X ). Because A A already predicts X X , there is no prediction error at the C → X C\rightarrow X transition, and standard blocking was confirmed– C C -learning was suppressed. The key manipulation then delivered a brief optogenetic burst to VTA dopamine neurons precisely at the moment of the A C → X AC\rightarrow X transition on blocked trials, artificially reinstating a prediction error where none existed. This unblocked C C -learning: rats now responded robustly to C C in the probe test, despite C C being entirely redundant throughout training 11 . To test necessity, halorhodopsin was used to suppress dopamine neurons at the B → Y B\rightarrow Y transition during a standard sensory preconditioning task; this selectively attenuated probe-test responding to B B while leaving a control cue unaffected. Together, these findings provide strong causal evidence that transient VTA dopamine activity is sufficient, and likely necessary, for acquisition of reward-free cue-cue associations that later support model-based behavior. A follow-up study closed the loop on the model-free alternative: using three controlled experiments, Sharpe and colleagues showed that optogenetic dopamine activation in the identical sensory-preconditioning setting enhanced associative (model-based) representations without endowing antecedent cues with cached value, as confirmed by conditioned reinforcement probes 13 . The dopamine transient functioned as an associative credit assignment signal rather than a value signal, contradicting the assumption that dopamine transients are restricted to model-free reinforcement learning. The theoretical framework that best accommodates these findings treats dopamine as a generalized prediction error signal 14 : rather than being restricted to reward predictions, dopaminergic error signals may span the full spectrum of prediction-error-driven learning–from cached reward-value updating at one end to model-based state-transition learning at the other–retaining all the successes of the RPE hypothesis while explaining why dopamine participates in sensory preconditioning and identity unblocking, paradigms that are entirely opaque to pure model-free theories. Kahnt and Schoenbaum’s 2025 review synthesizes this evidence alongside related human findings to conclude that the hypothesis of a strictly value-based dopaminergic teaching signal should be replaced by a framework in which dopamine tracks errors over a richer representational space that includes stimulus identity, associative structure, and contextual transitions 2 . Adding to this story, a distinct functional dimension emerges from the tail of the striatum, which receives dopaminergic input from neurons in the lateral SNc and substantia nigra pars lateralis (SNl) that respond prominently to movement rather than reward. Greenstreet and colleagues used an auditory discrimination task in mice to ask whether the movement-related dopamine activity in this region encodes the theoretical action prediction error (APE) –defined as the discrepancy between the action that was taken and the action that was predicted given the animal’s past actions (regardless of value) 15 . The prediction term here is not a value forecast but an action prior : the degree to which a particular movement was expected given the current sensory context and the animal’s history of state-action associations. On repeated trials, well-practiced actions become strongly predicted by their antecedent sensory states; novel or inconsistent actions remain poorly predicted. The APE is therefore large when the executed action deviates from this internally maintained action prior, and small or zero when the animal does exactly what its prior history leads it to expect of itself. Fiber photometry confirmed that tail-of-striatum dopamine signals behave accordingly: they increased when the executed action deviated from prediction and decreased when actions were well-predicted, independently of reward . Causal manipulations using optogenetic activation and suppression confirmed that this APE signal serves as a value-free teaching signal : stimulation of tail-of-striatum dopamine neurons drove the reinforcement of repeated state-action associations without endowing those actions with reward value, and suppression impaired the learning of stable sound-action mappings 15 . Computational modeling showed that APE and RPE signals are complementary rather than redundant: APE alone cannot support reward-guided learning (because it carries no information about outcome value), but when paired with RPE circuitry it consolidates stable sensorimotor associations in a value-free manner–essentially locking in action mappings that RPE has already established as broadly correct. This constitutes a second dopaminergic learning system operating in parallel with the canonical mesolimbic reward-RPE system, specialized for the formation of habits defined by repetition consistency rather than by reward history 15 . The empirical separation between APE and RPE dopaminergic populations is anatomically precise: RPE is predominantly encoded in VTA and medial SNc projecting to ventral and dorsomedial striatum, while APE resides in lateral SNc and SNl projecting to posterior and tail striatum. In this sense the spatial multiplexing of teaching signals across striatal territories (already emphasized in the distributional and multi-timescale discussion above) extends to include a qualitative division: the posterior striatal axis carries a learning signal defined over the action dimension, not the value dimension. Consistent with this, Brown and colleagues recently showed that cue-evoked dopamine release in the striatum encodes bidirectional trajectory errors –the discrepancy between an animal’s ongoing speed and direction relative to an optimal trajectory toward a goal–entirely independently from simultaneous dopamine signals reflecting learned cue value, with the two signals separable in timing and regional prevalence across the striatum 16 . Computational analysis revealed that a standard RPE algorithm supplied with mixed sensorimotor inputs can simultaneously reproduce both cue-value and trajectory-error coding, suggesting that the error-signal infrastructure is shared but the inputs that drive it differ across dopamine subpopulations, yielding functionally distinct teaching signals from a common algorithmic substrate. Taken together, the evidence reviewed in this section converges on a view that is difficult to reconcile with any narrow interpretation of dopamine as a dedicated reward-value tracker. Recent work by Gershman and colleagues 1 frames three major empirical challenges to the classical RPE theory–ramping dopamine signals during approach to reward, responsivity to sensory and motor features, and influence on action selection–and argue that each can be addressed by suitably generalizing the prediction-error concept rather than abandoning it. In their account, ramps can arise from TD-like prediction errors under realistic assumptions about convex value estimates and state uncertainty; sensory and identity-related responses can be understood either through model-based updating of internal transition/reward models or through generalized, vector-valued prediction errors over non-reward features; and action-related signals may reflect action prediction errors or related control signals embedded within RL architectures for choice, vigor, and average reward. However, Gershman et al. also emphasize that this generalized synthesis is still incomplete: a full theory of dopamine likely must incorporate additional mechanisms related to salience, causal inference, precision, and adaptive learning-rate control. Their proposed direction is therefore not a rejection of prediction-error theory, but an expansion from scalar reward-RPE toward richer, structured prediction-error signals that can update generalized value functions and, potentially, components of a world model 1 . Overall, recent work suggests that the basal ganglia do not implement one optimizer tracking one objective through one teaching signal. Instead, they implement a portfolio of prediction-error channels, anatomically distinguished at the level of projection-defined dopamine subpopulations and their striatal targets, each specialized for a different learning problem: value learning in mesolimbic circuits, identity and associative structure learning in circuits coupling OFC and dorsomedial striatum to midbrain, sensorimotor habit consolidation in lateral SNc-to-posterior striatum channels, and trajectory optimization in SNl-to-tail-striatum channels. What unifies these channels is not a shared objective but a shared computational motif : each computes a prediction error relative to some expected state of the world (defined over different state spaces and different prediction horizons), broadcasts that error via dopaminergic release, and uses it to update the synaptic weights of the circuits that generated the prediction. This implies that dopamine is best understood not as a neurotransmitter synonymous with reward, but as a general-purpose credit assignment signal –one whose reward-value channel is the best-characterized instance of a much larger family of error signals through which the basal ganglia continuously update a distributed, structured model of the agent’s world.

title: Reining dopamine in
text: The preceding subsections have progressively expanded the dopaminergic mandate: from a scalar TD reward-prediction error to a distributed, multi-timescale, multi-domain portfolio of credit assignment channels. Taken at face value, this generalization threatens to make the dopaminergic system appear unconstrained–a universal prediction-error engine capable of updating arbitrary representations across arbitrary cortical state spaces. Here, it is argued that two structural features prevent this from being the case. First, corticostriatal and mesocortical dopaminergic innervation are not evenly distributed across the cortex; they are strategically concentrated in cortical areas that process policy-relevant variables, meaning the BG’s credit assignment machinery is anatomically prohibited from modifying much of the brain’s representations. Second, and more deeply, the inputs that supply the prediction baseline to VTA and SNc dopamine neurons are not drawn from neutral cortical state spaces—they are heavily weighted toward interoceptive and homeostatic channels, which ensures that the dopaminergic system, however broad its learning scope, remains anchored to the organism’s biological preference distribution. The corticostriatal projection is often summarized as involving "all of cortex," and as a first approximation that is broadly correct: classical tract-tracing in primates and modern whole-brain mapping in mice both show that the striatum receives topographically organized input from a very wide range of cortical territories, with corticostriatal neurons arising predominantly from layer V (which is implicated in action prediction 1 ) and, to a lesser extent, deep layer III rather than being uniformly distributed across cortical laminae 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 . Importantly, however, this coverage is highly unequal and functionally structured, not homogeneous: orbitomedial prefrontal, anterior cingulate, amygdalar, and hippocampal inputs are concentrated in ventromedial and ventral striatal territories; associative territories of caudate receive strong projections from dorsolateral and other lateral prefrontal, posterior parietal, and higher-order temporal association cortex; and sensorimotor cortex projects most strongly to dorsolateral putaminal/putamen-like sectors, yielding the familiar limbic-to-associative-to-sensorimotor gradient across the striatum 4 , 7 , 8 . Primary sensory cortex lies at the extreme end of this organization, but not in the sense of simply bypassing the basal ganglia: rather, sensory cortical input is concentrated in specialized caudal/posterior striatal territories—including the tail/posterior striatum in rodents and the visual caudate-tail system in primates—which receive convergent corticostriatal, thalamostriatal, and distinctive nigrostriatal input and are implicated in sensory salience, stable stimulus-value learning, and sensory-guided orienting or action selection 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 . Thus, the strongest version of the claim is not that early perceptual representations are excluded from basal-ganglia learning, but that basal-ganglia credit assignment is anatomically biased toward striatal territories that already integrate sensory, motivational, cognitive, and action-related information, while more direct sensory learning is funneled through specialized posterior channels rather than distributed uniformly across the canonical ventral-to-dorsolateral corticostriatal axis 4 , 5 , 9 . The mesocortical dopaminergic projection appears to impose a complementary bias on the cortical side of the learning loop. In primates, dopaminergic innervation and dopaminoceptive machinery are not distributed uniformly across cortex: frontal association, cingulate, orbitomedial prefrontal, paralimbic, and at least some motor cortical territories receive especially prominent dopamine input, whereas many primary sensory areas tend to show sparser innervation, though not a complete absence of dopaminergic signaling 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 . This gradient should not be overstated into a sensory-versus-nonsensory dichotomy: dopamine receptors are present across cortical regions, including primary sensory cortex, but their regional densities and laminar patterns are heterogeneous, and cortical DARPP-32 expression is correspondingly selective rather than ubiquitous 18 , 19 . Within frontal cortex, D1 receptor signaling has been especially implicated in sculpting persistent delay-period activity and working-memory representations, with the characteristic inverted-U profile indicating that mesocortical dopamine is tuned to stabilize task-relevant representations rather than indiscriminately amplify cortical activity 20 , 21 . Taken together with the unequal corticostriatal projection pattern, the picture is not that the basal ganglia implements a universal learning rule over all cortical content, but that dopamine-dependent credit assignment is anatomically biased toward cortical state spaces that already participate in valuation, working memory, action selection, cognitive control, and policy expression, while exerting weaker and more specialized influence over early sensory representations 4 , 6 , 16 . The deeper constraint on dopaminergic error signaling is not whether dopamine can, in principle, report prediction errors over rich and abstract state spaces, but how the baseline and gain of those signals are conditioned by internal-state circuitry. On this point, the evidence supports a strong homeostatic influence without implying that VTA or SNc dopamine neurons are driven by a purely interoceptive channel: monosynaptic tracing shows that midbrain dopamine neurons integrate inputs from a highly heterogeneous afferent network, but hypothalamic and other autonomic/interoceptive regions are prominent components of that ensemble, and cell-type-specific mapping likewise identifies the lateral hypothalamus as one of the dominant long-range inputs to VTA dopamine neurons 22 , 23 . The lateral hypothalamus is especially important at this interface because LH->VTA circuitry carries information relevant to arousal, feeding, and motivational state through multiple molecularly distinct channels: GABAergic LH inputs can disinhibit dopamine neurons and increase nucleus-accumbens dopamine release, while orexin/hypocretin-, neurotensin-, and melanin-concentrating-hormone-related LH systems also modulate VTA function and reward-related behavior 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 . Arcuate hunger circuitry provides a more direct example of homeostatic state gating dopaminchatergic teaching signals across timescales: metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons is required for normal fasting-dependent increases in motivated sucrose seeking and for normal dopamine dynamics in both nucleus accumbens and dorsal striatum, supporting the view that AgRP neurons regulate the magnitude and temporal profile of striatal dopamine responses as a function of energy state rather than merely shifting tonic baseline activity 28 . Conversely, melanocortin signaling supplies a satiety-linked constraint, but in a circuit-specific way that should not be collapsed into a single "POMC suppresses dopamine" rule: arcuate POMC neurons project to VTA dopamine neurons and can enhance sucrose motivation via MC3R signaling within the VTA, whereas α \alpha -MSH acting at MC4R in nucleus accumbens decreases sucrose motivation 29 , 30 . Thus, even if dopamine is generalized beyond a narrow scalar reward-prediction error, the circuitry that sets its operating point remains strongly tethered to homeostatic state: internal needs do not define the entire dopaminergic error code, but they do help set which prediction errors are amplified, when, and for what behavioral purpose. The influence of homeostatic state on dopaminergic signaling extends beyond caloric balance to fluid and electrolyte regulation. In rats, thirst potentiates phasic VTA and nucleus-accumbens dopamine responses to water-predictive cues, and this effect can be mimicked in euvolemic animals by central angiotensin II, supporting the view that early dehydration signals can selectively amplify mesolimbic teaching signals for balance-restoring outcomes 31 . More generally, this fits a broader principle already established for feeding: hunger augments phasic dopamine responses to food-predictive cues, and the hunger signal ghrelin can enhance cue-evoked mesolimbic dopamine, indicating that internal need states gate dopaminergic responses to predictive stimuli in a domain-specific manner rather than simply shifting a global reward baseline 31 , 32 . The relevant thirst circuitry begins in classic homeostatic structures of the lamina terminalis, especially the subfornical organ, whose neurons detect circulating and osmotic signals and can recruit downstream motivational circuitry to modulate dopamine responses; however, the exact relay from these first-order thirst sensors to VTA dopamine neurons is better described as an emerging circuit motif than as a single fully resolved linear pathway 31 , 33 . Sodium-appetite circuitry provides a parallel, though less fully characterized, route by which electrolyte state may reach midbrain reward systems: aldosterone-sensitive HSD2 neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract are key nodes in sodium-appetite control and send minor direct projections to the VTA, making a VTA interface anatomically plausible even if its functional contribution remains less firmly established than the thirst-related SFO pathway 34 , 33 . Taken together, the strongest claim is not that dopamine is reducible to a single homeostatic signal, but that midbrain dopamine neurons are embedded in a broader interoceptive network carrying information about hunger, hydration, and electrolyte need, such that internal state helps determine which cues and outcomes receive amplified dopaminergic credit assignment at a given moment 35 , 36 . The most defensible computational reading of this architecture is that internal physiological state acts as a context-dependent modifier of outcome value and of the gain placed on dopaminergic teaching signals. In formal terms, this is closely aligned with a state-dependent reward function: in homeostatic reinforcement learning, an outcome is rewarding to the extent that the organism predicts it will reduce the deviation between current internal state and an ideal set point, and recent reviews of dopamine and interoception likewise argue that physiological need acts as an occasion setter or gain-control variable for phasic dopamine responses to cues and outcomes 37 , 38 . Consistent with that view, primary food and fluid rewards are rewarding in part because they correct homeostatic imbalance, and emerging accounts increasingly argue that at least the most basic forms of reinforcement should be understood as depending on interoceptive evaluations of an action’s effect on vital physiological variables rather than on sensory pleasure alone 39 , 40 , 36 . The stronger claim—that general-purpose dopaminergic credit assignment is an evolutionary elaboration of an older homeostatic regulatory architecture—is therefore best presented as a principled hypothesis rather than as settled fact. It is well motivated by current theory and by the anatomy reviewed above, but the available evidence supports most directly the narrower conclusion that generalized prediction-error signaling in dopamine remains strongly constrained by internal-state and interoceptive control systems 40 , 38 . A remaining (open) question is how the dopaminergic system acquires its homeostatic calibration. One compelling answer is developmental: in the neonatal period, the only contexts reliably driving strong positive dopaminergic prediction errors are those that correct acute homeostatic imbalances. In altricial mammals, virtually all early reward structure derives from maternal interaction—milk delivery corrects caloric and fluid depletion, thermal contact resolves cold stress, tactile stimulation regulates the autonomic and hormonal milieu. Because these are the events most reliably available in early postnatal life, and because they are intrinsically coupled to interoceptive repletion signals (gastric stretch, rising blood glucose, skin warming, declining cortisol), the first value functions the corticostriatal system learns are necessarily tethered to homeostatic set points. The predictions that VTA GABA neurons and LH projections encode as the infant’s first conditional expectations are predictions about interoceptive state, not abstract symbolic variables. This process can be understood as a developmental bootstrapping of the preference distribution : the hard-wired hypothalamic-VTA architecture (which ensures homeostatic signals can reach dopamine neurons) provides the structural substrate, while the earliest rounds of corticostriatal learning lock in the value of homeostatic correction as the implicit reference against which subsequent prediction errors are computed. Later-developing secondary rewards—social approval, monetary gain, aesthetic pleasure—acquire their dopaminergic significance through chains of associative and identity prediction errors anchored, ultimately, to that early-established homeostatic baseline. The implication for the computational architecture of the BG is that its "objective function" is not arbitrary: it is inherited from the survival-critical error signals that first activated the system’s teaching machinery, and this origin is preserved in the structural connectivity between hypothalamic homeostatic controllers and the midbrain dopaminergic nuclei that distribute the credit assignment signal. The combined picture that emerges from these two constraints—selective corticostriatal and mesocortical access, and homeostatic grounding of the prediction baseline—is of a credit assignment system that is genuinely capable of generalized learning across a rich state space, but is not free to learn anything. The dopaminergic architecture is, in the relevant engineering sense, a constrained optimizer : its search space is restricted to policy-relevant cortical representations by anatomical connectivity, and its objective function is anchored to biological viability by the interoceptive weighting of its prediction baseline. The generalized prediction-error view of dopamine, far from implying an unconstrained learner, is best interpreted as describing a flexible optimization method operating within hard boundaries set by evolution, development, and anatomy—boundaries whose collective effect is to ensure that however much the dopaminergic system learns about sensory identity, associative structure, and action priors, it remains a tool for keeping the organism within its preference distribution.

title: Cholinergic modulation of error signals
text: Midbrain dopamine is not the only arbiter of the basal ganglia teaching signal. Once a candidate error reaches the striatum, it enters a dense local cholinergic field generated by cholinergic interneurons (CINs, the classical tonically active neurons (TANs)), whose tonic firing is interrupted by task-locked pauses and rebounds. Recent sensor work further shows that dopamine and acetylcholine are coordinated even outside explicitly rewarded events, implying that the striatal terminal field is not a passive sink for a finished RPE but an active layer that temporally structures how that error is delivered to downstream synapses 1 , 2 . Dopamine axons in striatum express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, so local acetylcholine can act directly on the axon terminal rather than only through cell bodies in the midbrain. Classical work established that endogenous nicotinic cholinergic tone regulates striatal dopamine release, and later optogenetic studies showed that selective activation of CINs is sufficient to evoke dopamine release locally in nucleus accumbens, without requiring a change in midbrain spiking 3 , 4 . More recent imaging and modeling sharpen this into a circuit principle: single CINs can induce local dopamine release, nicotinic signaling extends the spatial scale over which dopamine spreads, and acetylcholine–dopamine interactions can support traveling waves and mesoscale neuromodulatory structure within striatum 2 . However, cholinergic modulation is not unidirectionally facilitatory. In dorsal striatum, activation of CINs and axonal nAChRs can impose a short-lived refractory-like suppression on subsequent dopamine release: after nAChR-mediated depolarization, later depolarization events evoke much less dopamine for roughly the next 100 ms, an effect more prominent in dorsal than ventral striatum 5 . By contrast, in nucleus accumbens, the same cholinergic interface can amplify the dopamine response to reward when the reward is earned under high effort; blocking this local cholinergic augmentation selectively blunts the enhanced dopamine signal and impairs effortful behavior while sparing low-effort reward consumption 6 . The right synthesis is therefore not that acetylcholine simply "adds" or "subtracts" dopamine, but that it supplies a state- and territory-dependent gain control over terminal dopamine output. The most conceptually important recent result is that acetylcholine also helps determine what the dopamine transient means . In dorsomedial striatum, simultaneous dopamine and acetylcholine measurements during decision-making showed that dopamine supported different computations depending on its phase relationship to cholinergic dynamics 7 . When a dopamine RPE slightly lagged a cholinergic dip at the offer cue, it predicted subsequent behavioral updating and trial-to-trial changes in striatal firing, consistent with dopamine-dependent plasticity. When a dopamine transient preceded the cholinergic dip at the reward cue, no comparable relationship to learning was observed. At movement-related events, by contrast, acetylcholine appeared as bursts rather than dips, and coincident dopamine predicted the vigor of upcoming movements without evidence for persistent plasticity. This implies that local cholinergic timing can demix multiplexed dopamine into at least two downstream modes: a plasticity-promoting teaching signal and a transient performance/vigor signal. A further possibility is that cholinergic signals are not merely gates placed downstream of dopamine; in some striatal territories they may carry error-like content of their own. During Pavlovian learning and extinction, anterior dorsal striatal acetylcholine exhibited phase-specific prediction-error structure, with positive and negative RPEs expressed in different parts of the ACh waveform, and silencing local ACh release impaired extinction while sparing initial acquisition 8 . In reversal settings, dorsal striatal ACh elevations following unexpected non-reward were causally required for behavioral adaptation 9 . These findings fit naturally with the view that cholinergic circuitry is especially important for negative updating , extinction, and contingency revision–precisely the situations in which cached action values must be weakened rather than strengthened. At the same time, the dopamine–acetylcholine relationship is not a single canonical anti-phase motif repeated everywhere. In ventrolateral striatum, dopamine inhibits acetylcholine transients through CIN D2 receptors, while cortical and thalamic glutamatergic inputs are required to drive acetylcholine release in the first place 10 . In nucleus accumbens, dopamine–acetylcholine correlations vary across task phases rather than obeying one fixed relationship 11 . And across striatal subregions, the alignment between CIN pauses and dopamine RPEs can diverge sharply, with ventral striatum even showing reward-cue-related increases in both signals rather than a simple pause-plus-burst pattern 12 . Thus, cholinergic modulation should be treated as a regionally parameterized local controller , not a universal scalar opponent to dopamine. Taken together, the computational picture is now much richer than “dopamine computes the error, acetylcholine sets general arousal.” A better approximation is that dopamine carries a candidate teaching signal into striatum, and cholinergic circuitry then finalizes its local instructional form : it gates when dopamine becomes plasticity-relevant, rescales terminal release according to current context, helps separate learning from performance-related dopamine, and in some territories contributes its own opponent signal for extinction and behavioral flexibility 7 , 10 , 8 . In reinforcement-learning terms, acetylcholine is not the loss itself and not the canonical TD error either; it is better understood as a fast, state-dependent eligibility and gain controller that determines where, when, and in what effective sign that error is allowed to modify corticostriatal policy. A recent computational model is broadly consonant with this interpretation, showing that cholinergic pauses can solve a structural credit-assignment problem by restricting plasticity to the channels active around action selection 13 .

title: Relationship with cortical error signals
text: The relationship between basal-ganglia and cortical error signals is best understood not as a duplication of one computation in two anatomical locations, but as a division of labor in signal format and function . Cortical circuits compute high-dimensional, content-rich mismatch signals : errors between predicted and observed sensory input, between higher-level beliefs and lower-level evidence, and, in frontal cortex, between expected and obtained action outcomes. These signals are local to particular layers, columns, cell types, and task variables, and they remain tied to the representational geometry of the cortical world model. Basal-ganglia error signals, by contrast, are comparatively low-bandwidth evaluative signals : dopaminergic activity compresses many details of the current inferred state and recent action history into a teaching quantity that indicates whether the selected trajectory, policy, or outcome was better or worse than expected. Put differently, cortical error signals primarily specify what aspect of the model is wrong, whereas BG error signals primarily specify whether recent state-action sampling should be reinforced, weakened, or revised 1 , 2 , 3 . Yet the BG error signal does not float free of cortical computation. A central lesson of recent work is that the “expected” term against which dopamine neurons compare outcomes is often cortically constructed . Orbitofrontal cortex contributes the latent task-state information needed to distinguish externally similar situations with different future consequences; when OFC is damaged, dopaminergic error signals lose precisely this model-based structure rather than simply losing a scalar reward expectation 4 . Likewise, medial prefrontal cortex shapes dopaminergic prediction errors specifically when the environment contains hidden states that must be inferred, but is much less necessary when the relevant state is fully observable 5 . More generally, both theory and experiment now indicate that dopamine errors are computed over belief states rather than over raw sensory surfaces whenever the task demands uncertainty-sensitive inference 6 , 7 . Even outcome identity learning fits this pattern: value-neutral identity prediction errors in the human midbrain are tied to trial-by-trial updating of outcome-identity expectations in OFC 8 . Thus, cortex is not merely a downstream recipient of BG teaching; it provides much of the state-space structure that determines what counts as a dopaminergic error in the first place. The resulting dopaminergic error, however, is not computed over a neutral or unconstrained state space: even when cortex supplies rich latent-state structure, the midbrain channels that evaluate that structure remain strongly biased by interoceptive and homeostatic inputs, so that generalized credit assignment is still anchored to biological preference satisfaction rather than freely ranging over arbitrary cortical discrepancies. The converse is equally important: dopaminergic/BG error signals do not replace cortical comparators, but rather gate which cortical discrepancies become plasticity-relevant and behaviorally consequential . Cortex can generate its own action-outcome and performance-monitoring errors, particularly in medial frontal territories 2 , but these remain distinct from the phasic dopaminergic signal that broadcasts evaluative significance across corticostriatal and mesocortical targets. Mesocortical dopamine operates across multiple temporal and spatial scales, modulating cortical ensembles, oscillatory state, and persistent activity rather than simply delivering a one-shot scalar update to a single synapse 9 , 10 . Functionally, this makes BG error signaling resemble a projection-specific family of third-factor controllers superimposed on a much richer cortical error field: local cortical circuits compute the detailed mismatch, while dopaminergic channels differentially adjust the gain, persistence, consolidation, and policy relevance of those cortical activity patterns according to both the task-defined inferred state and the organism’s current internal-state weighting. The resulting architecture is therefore recurrent rather than serial . Cortical error signals help determine the state representations, transition expectations, and task abstractions over which BG evaluative errors are computed; BG error signals, in turn, bias corticostriatal and mesocortical plasticity, action selection, vigor, and gating; the actions thereby selected alter the organism’s future sensory samples and internal states, which then generate the next wave of cortical prediction errors. The cortex and basal ganglia thus participate in a closed-loop error ecology : cortex supplies the structured, high-dimensional content of the discrepancy, whereas the BG supply a compressed, action-oriented evaluation of its behavioral significance. This is why the two classes of signals are neither redundant nor cleanly separable. Cortical error signals can be exquisitely informative yet behaviorally inert unless some subset is selected for policy updating; BG error signals can strongly reinforce or suppress behavior, but only over the state space that cortex and related forebrain structures have rendered legible to them, and only within the viability-constrained objective landscape imposed by the dopaminergic system’s homeostatic/interoceptive grounding.
