title: BG Plasticity
text: The preceding subsection established the basal ganglia’s error architecture: phasic dopamine as a structured, distributional, multi-timescale evaluative broadcast, sculpted by cholinergic dynamics and routed across parallel cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops. But an error signal does not by itself change policy. For the basal ganglia, learning occurs only when that evaluative signal is converted into persistent changes in synaptic—and, in some cases, intrinsic—gain at the circuit elements that actually participated in action selection. Dopamine, in other words, is not itself the update; it is the teaching variable that opens, biases, or closes plasticity windows at eligible synapses. The central question of BG plasticity is therefore not merely what the error signal means, but where, when, and under what local conditions it can write. The answer is a family of pathway-specific, neuromodulator-gated, multi-factor rules centered above all on glutamatergic inputs to spiny projection neurons, where cortical and thalamic state representations, dopaminergic reinforcement, cholinergic timing signals, postsynaptic depolarization, dendritic nonlinearities, and retrograde signaling are integrated into lasting changes in action value, policy bias, and habit structure. Because the general logic of Hebbian, STDP, three-factor, and related plasticity rules was developed in The Fundamentals , the aim here is narrower: to specify the basal-ganglia-specific biological substrate and learning rules that close the loop from evaluative error to durable policy optimization

title: The canonical substrate: corticostriatal plasticity on SPNs
text: Corticostriatal and thalamostriatal glutamatergic synapses onto spiny projection neurons (SPNs) constitute the dominant site of basal-ganglia learning. Three converging lines of evidence justify this emphasis. First, these synapses are the anatomical convergence point at which cortical state representations meet the dopaminergic teaching signal: the head of an SPN dendritic spine receives an asymmetric glutamatergic contact from a cortical (or, for a subset of spines, thalamic) terminal, while the neck of the same spine or the immediately adjacent dendritic shaft is contacted by a dopaminergic varicosity, providing a subcellular architecture in which the coincidence of a cortical input pattern and a dopaminergic broadcast can be evaluated at the level of a single spine 1 , 2 . Second, corticostriatal synapses are the only basal-ganglia synapse at which long-term plasticity has been shown to be systematically and bidirectionally gated by dopamine in a pathway-specific manner, with D1 and D2 receptor signaling controlling opposite polarities of synaptic change in direct- and indirect-pathway SPNs 3 , 4 . Third, causal manipulations of corticostriatal plasticity–genetic disruption of plasticity-related signaling cascades, optogenetic induction or suppression of dopamine at the moment of corticostriatal coactivation, and pathway-specific pharmacological blockade–produce learning impairments that track closely with the predictions of RL-based accounts of basal-ganglia function 5 , 6 , 7 . The corticostriatal synapse is thus the locus where cortical "what state is the world in?" meets dopaminergic "was that action better or worse than expected?", and where the resulting conjunction is written into synaptic weight changes that update the striatal policy. The neurons that house these synapses are themselves architecturally specialized for this integrative role. Spiny projection neurons–also termed medium spiny neurons (MSNs)–are GABAergic inhibitory neurons that constitute approximately 90-95% of all neurons in the striatum, making them the overwhelmingly dominant cell type and the sole source of striatal output 1 , 8 . Each SPN extends a moderately branched dendritic tree whose initially spine-free proximal segments give way, beyond the first branch point, to dendrites densely studded with dendritic spines—on the order of 5,000 spines per neuron in rodents and likely more in primates 2 , 9 . Each spine head receives, in the typical case, a single asymmetric glutamatergic synapse from a cortical or thalamic afferent. Cortical and non-CM/PF thalamic terminals preferentially contact spine heads, whereas terminals from the centromedian/parafascicular (CM/PF) thalamic complex contact dendritic shafts, establishing two structurally distinct routes of excitatory drive that are subject to different short-term plasticity rules: corticostriatal synapses tend to display short-term facilitation (consistent with a relatively low initial release probability and a role in sustained state-representational input), while thalamostriatal synapses from CM/PF tend to display short-term depression (consistent with a higher release probability and a role in transient salience or state-change signaling) 10 , 11 . Electron microscopic analysis confirms that many corticostriatal and non-CM/PF thalamic boutons are directly apposed by a dopaminergic terminal at the spine neck or adjacent shaft, placing the glutamatergic and dopaminergic inputs in immediate subcellular proximity and providing the structural substrate for dopamine’s modulatory control over glutamatergic efficacy 11 , 12 ; this includes what have been termed "dopamine hub synapses," in which dopaminergic varicosities are physically associated with cortico- or thalamostriatal synapse 13 . Individual SPNs of both direct and indirect pathways receive convergent cortical and thalamic input, with cortical input predominating in both cell types 14 , 15 .

title: Opponent plasticity in the direct and indirect pathways
text: The two principal SPN classes are distinguished less by gross morphology alone than by their molecular markers, projection patterns, neuropeptide content, and–most critically for plasticity–the intracellular signaling cascades dopamine engages within them. Direct-pathway SPNs (dSPNs) express D1-type dopamine receptors along with substance P and dynorphin, and project monosynaptically to the basal-ganglia output nuclei (GPi/SNr), where their activation disinhibits thalamocortical targets and thereby promotes the expression of the selected action 1 , 2 . Indirect-pathway SPNs (iSPNs) express D2-type dopamine receptors along with enkephalin and adenosine A2a receptors, and project to the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe), initiating a polysynaptic cascade through GPe and STN that ultimately increases inhibitory output from GPi/SNr and thereby suppresses competing or undesired actions 1 , 3 . At the level of intracellular readout, opponent plasticity is implemented by opposite biochemical decoding of the same dopaminergic fluctuation. In dSPNs, dopamine increases bias recently eligible corticostriatal synapses toward potentiation through D1-dependent PKA signaling; in iSPNs, by contrast, decreases in dopamine relieve ongoing D2-mediated suppression and permit A2A-receptor- and CaMKII-dependent potentiation and spine enlargement 4 . Thus a phasic dopamine burst and a phasic dopamine dip are not merely opposite motivational events broadcast to a passive striatum; they are interpreted by two distinct molecular substrates, such that positive deviations in dopamine preferentially reinforce direct-pathway representations, whereas negative deviations preferentially reinforce indirect-pathway representations 5 , 6 , 7 . This opponent rule is no longer only an inference from slice physiology; key parts of it have now been observed in vivo. Real-time measurements of striatal signaling show that D1R- and D2R-expressing SPNs exhibit dichotomous, asynchronous PKA modulation during learning, with D1 populations preferentially tracking dopamine increases and D2 populations preferentially tracking dopamine decreases 6 . In ventral striatum, Iino and colleagues further showed that appetitive conditioning initially generalizes through D1R-dependent mechanisms, and that subsequent discrimination learning is sharpened by brief dopamine dips–detectable on the order of hundreds of milliseconds–which disinhibit A2A-dependent spine enlargement in D2-SPNs 7 . Opponent plasticity therefore appears well suited not only to strengthen rewarded actions, but also to refine overgeneralized policies by writing negative-outcome information into indirect-pathway ensembles 7 . A major recent advance is the recognition that the simple slogan "dSPNs learn from positive outcomes, iSPNs learn from negative outcomes" is, in its naive form, computationally inconsistent. In the standard model, dSPNs promoting the chosen action are potentiated when dopamine increases (positive RPE), and iSPNs suppressing unchosen actions are potentiated when dopamine decreases (negative RPE). The difficulty arises from the iSPN side: if iSPNs are active only when suppressing other actions (as in the classical model where active iSPNs suppress non-selected actions), then a dopamine pause after a bad outcome would strengthen iSPN synapses representing those other, non-chosen actions–actions that were not responsible for the negative outcome. This produces a pathological learning signal: the iSPN plasticity rule would reinforce patterns of suppression associated with negative outcomes rather than with the action that actually caused the bad result, effectively punishing the wrong actions 8 . The resolution proposed by Lindsey et al. requires that functionally opponent dSPNs and iSPNs–that is, the dSPN promoting the chosen action and the iSPN also associated with the chosen action (which, when strengthened, would suppress it in the future)–are coactive during and immediately after action selection, so that both populations are eligible for credit assignment by the same dopamine transient. Under this arrangement, a dopamine burst after a good outcome potentiates the dSPN (via D1/LTP) and depresses the co-active iSPN synapse (via D2/eCB-LTD), both changes favoring repetition of the successful action; a dopamine pause after a bad outcome depresses the dSPN synapse and potentiates the co-active iSPN synapse, both changes favoring suppression of the failed action. The model’s central prediction–that functionally opponent dSPNs and iSPNs are simultaneously activated by efferent input following action selection–was confirmed in experimental recordings showing that direct and indirect pathway SPNs are broadly coactive during action initiation, consistent with the findings of Cui and colleagues who first demonstrated concurrent activation of both pathways during movement using fiber photometry 9 , 8 . The model further predicts that this coactivation structure enables multiplexing of action-selection signals and learning signals without interference, and facilitates off-policy learning in which the striatum can learn from actions driven by other neural circuits. The opponent plasticity architecture described above–D1-dependent potentiation after dopamine bursts, D2/A2A-dependent potentiation after dopamine pauses, and the coactivation structure ensuring both pathways are eligible for credit assignment by the same transient–has functional consequences that extend well beyond the reinforcement or punishment of individual actions, spanning distributional value coding, dissociable contributions to decision-making, cortical gating, exploration, and normative advantages in cost-benefit learning. First, opponent plasticity provides a natural substrate for distributional reinforcement learning in the striatum. As discussed in the error-signal section, midbrain dopamine neurons encode a family of asymmetrically scaled prediction errors. Lowet and colleagues showed that D1- and D2-expressing SPNs complete this distributional code downstream by preferentially representing the right (optimistic) and left (pessimistic) tails of the learned reward distribution, respectively; chronic dopamine ablation disorganized these distributional representations without eliminating mean value coding, indicating that opponent plasticity is specifically required for distributional–rather than merely average–value learning 10 . In their computational model, asymmetric plasticity rules operating on opponent SPN populations converge to expectile-like estimates, with D1 SPNs learning expectiles above the median and D2 SPNs below it, thereby harnessing pathway opponency for improved sensitivity to risk and outcome uncertainty 10 . Second, causal manipulations support dissociable pathway contributions to decision-making . Selective inactivation of D1R- versus D2R-expressing dorsal striatal neurons in mice revealed that D1R inactivation selectively impaired value-dependent action selection , whereas D2R inactivation selectively impaired value updating when contingencies changed 11 . Optogenetic stimulation of the two pathways during visual and working-memory tasks further showed that direct-pathway activation increased contralateral responding and globally enhanced cortical activity–including the neural representation of a visual stimulus during a delay period–whereas indirect-pathway activation had the opposite effects, demonstrating that opponent plasticity reshapes not only striatal action probabilities but also thalamocortical representations over which perceptual decisions and working-memory maintenance operate 12 . Third, opponent plasticity endows the indirect pathway with a specific role in exploration, flexibility, and policy revision . In the posterior dorsomedial striatum, direct-pathway neurons are critical for encoding goal-directed action-outcome associations, whereas indirect-pathway neurons are specifically required for updating those associations during reversal–optogenetic inhibition of iSPNs, but not dSPNs, impaired reversal learning while leaving initial acquisition intact 13 . Complementarily, dorsomedial striatal indirect-pathway neurons monitor the unreliability of the current action policy: their late-onset activity following unrewarded suboptimal actions represents lowered policy valuation and a heightened bias to probe alternatives 14 . Lee and Sabatini provided a circuit mechanism for how this suppression of a failed action can simultaneously generate an alternative: iSPN activation suppresses the ipsilateral superior colliculus while exciting the contralateral colliculus via inter-collicular competition, triggering an alternative motor program rather than mere behavioral arrest; inactivation of iSPNs impaired both suppression of devalued actions and exploratory switching 15 . Their recent synthesis proposes that the indirect pathway is governed by a three-factor learning rule in which dopamine dips potentiate iSPN synapses representing the action that caused the negative outcome, enabling learned avoidance while simultaneously–through competitive downstream interactions–facilitating transition to alternative actions; the indirect pathway is thus not merely a "stop" channel but a multifaceted system for avoidance, exploration, and policy updating sculpted by opponent plasticity 16 . Finally, the OpAL* model of Jaskir and Frank formalizes these opponent dynamics as a dual actor-critic system and demonstrates that the architecture confers normative computational advantages, particularly in environments with sparse reward and large action spaces, where separate "benefit" and "cost" actors develop complementary specializations that resolve explore-exploit tradeoffs more efficiently than single-pathway RL 17 . These advantages depend on both opponency and nonlinear three-factor Hebbian plasticity–the biological learning rule–and the model captures patterns of risky choice arising from dopamine manipulations across species, suggesting that risk sensitivity emerges naturally from opponent plasticity rather than from a separate risk-evaluation module 17 .

title: Eligibility traces and temporal credit assignment
text: The most consequential feature of the SPN dendritic spine, from the standpoint of reinforcement learning, is that it provides an architecture for eligibility traces –the molecular memory of recent synaptic coactivation on which a temporally delayed teaching signal can act. The distal reward problem ("how does a dopaminergic burst arriving hundreds of milliseconds to seconds after the action know which synapses participated?") is solved, at the corticostriatal spine, by a cascade of biochemical events that outlast the initial pre-post coincidence and decay on a timescale matched to the physiological delay of the reward signal. The distal reward problem is among the oldest puzzles in learning theory. In neural terms, the difficulty is acute: the firing patterns that represent a sensory cue or motor act occur on a millisecond timescale; these patterns are typically no longer present in the network when the dopaminergic teaching signal arrives seconds later; and that teaching signal is broadcast diffusely across many synapses, most of which did not participate in the relevant action 1 . The theoretical resolution, proposed long before it was experimentally demonstrated, is that nearly coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity leaves behind a slowly decaying synaptic tag–an eligibility trace–that marks recently active synapses as candidates for modification without itself changing synaptic efficacy. Only when a neuromodulatory reinforcement signal arrives during the lifetime of the trace is the tag converted into lasting potentiation or depression. The trace is "silent" in the sense that, absent the third factor, no net synaptic change occurs; the synapse is merely rendered eligible for change 1 , 2 . This three-factor architecture–Hebbian coincidence (factor one), postsynaptic depolarization or calcium (factor two), and delayed neuromodulator (factor three)–maps directly onto the temporal-difference learning rule: the eligibility trace plays the role of the decaying memory e ( s , a ) e(s,a) that allows the scalar error δ \delta to update the weight of the state-action pair that generated it, even when the error arrives after a delay 1 , 2 . A decisive experimental demonstration of a corticostriatal eligibility trace came from Yagishita, Hayashi-Takagi, Ellis-Davies, and colleagues, who used two-photon glutamate uncaging at individual dendritic spines of D1R-expressing SPNs in nucleus accumbens slices, combined with optogenetic activation of dopaminergic fibres via channelrhodopsin-2, to independently control the timing of the glutamatergic and dopaminergic inputs to a single spine 3 . An STDP protocol (repetitive glutamate uncaging paired with postsynaptic action potentials) alone produced only a modest and transient spine enlargement. When dopaminergic fibre stimulation was delivered within a narrow, asymmetric time window of approximately 0.3 to 2 seconds after the glutamatergic input, however, spine enlargement was dramatically and persistently enhanced—a structural correlate of long-term potentiation at the single-spine level 3 . Importantly, dopamine delivered before the glutamatergic input, or more than about 2 seconds after it, had no potentiating effect, confirming that the trace is both temporally asymmetric and sharply bounded. This result constituted the first demonstration of reinforcement plasticity–the conjunction of Hebbian eligibility with delayed neuromodulatory gating–at the resolution of a single corticostriatal spine. Shindou, Shindou, Watanabe, and Wickens provided a complementary and more direct test using whole-cell recordings from identified D1-expressing SPNs in dorsomedial striatum, with phasic dopamine release achieved by photolysis of caged dopamine at precisely controlled delays after pre-post spike-timing protocols 4 . The key finding was that uncaging dopamine selectively at 2 seconds after pre-post pairing converted the outcome from long-term depression into net long-term potentiation, whereas dopamine delivered at earlier or later delays did not. The trace was electrophysiologically "silent"–no change in synaptic efficacy was detectable during the interval between the spike pairing and dopamine arrival–yet the synapse was nonetheless primed for potentiation, confirming the theoretical prediction of a silent eligibility trace 4 . A molecular marker of this silent state was identified: pre-post pairings caused a transient increase in rectification (asymmetric flow of electrical current) consistent with insertion of calcium-permeable AMPA receptors (CP-AMPARs) into the postsynaptic membrane, lasting approximately 2-4 seconds after pairing, and a CP-AMPAR antagonist blocked dopamine-dependent t-LTP without affecting t-LTD 4 . In parallel, Fisher, Reynolds, and colleagues demonstrated the eligibility trace in vivo in intact rats: pairing corticostriatal activity with a reward-conditioned sensory reinforcement signal (which drives dopamine release) induced robust bidirectional STDP at corticostriatal synapses, but only if the reinforcement signal arrived within approximately 2 seconds of the spike-timing pairing; the effect was dependent on both D1 and adenosine A2A receptor signaling 5 . Taken together, the Yagishita, Shindou, and Fisher results converge on a consistent picture: the corticostriatal eligibility trace has a characteristic lifetime on the order of 1-2 seconds, it is synapse-specific in its initial induction but requires a temporally delayed neuromodulatory signal to be converted into lasting change, and it operates through distinct but complementary mechanisms depending on SPN subtype. The molecular mechanism that shapes this narrow temporal window has now been constrained in considerable detail. The critical insight is that the temporal contingency between glutamatergic and dopaminergic inputs is detected by rapid regulation of cAMP in the thin distal dendrites where corticostriatal spines reside, with the effective time window emerging from a competition between calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclase activity and high local phosphodiesterase activity 3 , 6 . Pre-post coincidence drives calcium influx into the spine, primarily through NMDA receptors and voltage-gated calcium channels, which primes calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclase AC1 to produce cAMP. But the high phosphodiesterase activity that characterizes SPN dendrites rapidly degrades cAMP unless D1 receptor activation by dopamine arrives while AC1 is still calcium-primed–that is, within the  0.3-2 s window 3 , 6 . Only when the two signals converge within this interval does the cAMP transient overcome the PDE barrier, activating PKA and its downstream effectors, including DARPP-32-mediated inhibition of PP1, thereby permitting the stabilization of CaMKII-dependent spine enlargement and synaptic potentiation 3 , 6 . If dopamine arrives too late, spine calcium has decayed and the barrier cannot be overcome; if it arrives too early, the calcium signal has not yet occurred. The result is an AC1-centered, PDE-constrained molecular coincidence detector whose time constant defines the eligibility window 3 , 6 . Although calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclases are expressed in dendritic spines across brain regions, and similar logic may operate wherever thin dendrites receive convergent activity-dependent and neuromodulatory signals, the striatum appears to be especially well tuned for this computation. Compared to cortical pyramidal neurons, striatal neurons exhibit much faster, larger, and longer-lasting cAMP/PKA responses to brief D1 stimulation–likely driven by faster cAMP production, lower PDE4-mediated degradation, and the presence of DARPP-32, which prolongs PKA action by inhibiting phosphatases 7 . More broadly, SPNs are unusually dopamine-dependent plasticity substrates: unlike canonical cortical plasticity, which is often inducible through activity-dependent glutamatergic mechanisms alone and only variably gated by dopamine, many of the most behaviorally relevant forms of corticostriatal plasticity depend strongly on dopaminergic receptor activation, particularly in reinforcement-linked settings, even if this dependence is not absolute across every induction protocol or experimental preparation 8 , 9 . Whereas cortical neurons respond much more weakly and sluggishly to brief dopamine transients, striatal neurones are tuned to detect exactly the kind of sharp, phasic signal produced by reward prediction errors: a sub-second dopamine pulse that produces only modest responses in prefrontal pyramidal cells drives a robust PKA response in striatal medium spiny neurons 7 . The implication is that the SPN is not merely a generic neuron that happens to receive dopamine; rather, its intracellular signaling architecture appears specialized for the detection of temporally precise reinforcement signals, making the striatal eligibility-trace mechanism exceptionally well matched to the temporal statistics of the dopaminergic teaching signal it is designed to capture 3 , 6 , 7 , 8 . A behavioral correlate of the synaptic eligibility trace was demonstrated by Yamanaka, Bhatt, and colleagues, who showed that Pavlovian conditioning of head-fixed mice to pure tones depended on a reward-sensitive period of approximately 1 second after tone presentation, and that optogenetically induced presynaptic activity at nucleus accumbens synapses reproduced the same narrow sensitive window 10 . The conditioning depended on plasticity-related signaling in the NAc, and the temporal profile of the behavioural sensitive period closely matched the synaptic eligibility trace measured in slice preparations, providing the first direct link between the subcellular molecular window and the timescale of reinforcement learning at the behavioural level 10 . The eligibility window at corticostriatal synapses, though brief, is broadly matched to the fast temporal profile of phasic dopaminergic teaching signals in reinforcement learning. In key striatal plasticity experiments, dopamine is effective within a narrow window on the order of  0.3–2 s after eligible glutamatergic activity 3 , 4 . Midbrain dopamine responses to unexpected rewards are themselves phasic and brief, and during learning these responses transfer from reward delivery to reward-predictive cues in a manner consistent with temporal-difference accounts 11 , 12 . Accordingly, for many single-step or short-delay tasks, this eligibility window is sufficient to bridge the gap between the corticostriatal activity involved in action selection and the dopaminergic signal that evaluates the outcome. But many real-world learning problems involve delays that substantially exceed 2 seconds–multi-step action sequences, delayed feedback, and extended temporal gaps between choice and consequence. How does the BG solve temporal credit assignment on these longer timescales? The answer is almost certainly not a single mechanism but a layered set of solutions operating at different timescales, of which the synaptic eligibility trace is only the fastest. The first and most important long-range mechanism is temporal-difference learning itself . The TD algorithm does not require that the ultimate reward signal reach back to the first action in a sequence; it requires only that each state’s prediction error update the value of the immediately preceding state. As cues and intermediate states acquire predictive value through experience, the dopaminergic teaching signal transfers backward in time—from reward delivery to the last predictive cue, from that cue to an earlier one, and so on. This backward propagation of value through the chain of states means that, in a well-learned task, the relevant dopaminergic error signal for any given action occurs not at the time of final reward but at the next state transition, which is typically within the 1–2 s eligibility window. TD chaining thus converts a long-horizon credit assignment problem into a series of short-horizon problems, each of which falls within the reach of the synaptic eligibility trace 1 , 13 . It is worth reiterating that the "states" over which this chaining operates are not limited to raw sensory surfaces. As established in the error-signal section, midbrain dopamine neurons compute prediction errors over cortically constructed belief states–latent task representations supplied by orbitofrontal cortex 14 , hidden-state inferences shaped by medial prefrontal cortex 15 , and even identity and associative-structure expectations updated through model-based inference 16 , 17 . This means that the intermediate states through which TD value propagates backward can be abstract, high-dimensional, and context-dependent—a cortical map of inferred task structure, not merely a chain of cached stimulus-response associations. The effective reach of backward chaining therefore reflects the richness of the state representation that cortex makes legible to the dopaminergic system. A second mechanism involves sustained neural activity in prefrontal and striatal circuits that effectively extends the representation of the relevant state across the delay period, keeping the "right" corticostriatal synapses active until the teaching signal arrives. Histed, Pasupathy, and Miller recorded single neurons in primate prefrontal cortex and caudate nucleus during learning of stimulus-response associations and found that both areas contained neurons with sustained, persistent outcome-related responses that lasted well beyond the immediate reward period and predicted the accuracy of subsequent choices 18 . Her and colleagues further showed that dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatal neurons maintained choice-related signals across a delay period in a dynamic foraging task requiring temporal credit assignment, with choice signals appearing sequentially—first in DMS and then in DLS—and being combined with action value and reward signals in DLS at the time of outcome revelation 19 . More recently, Wirt and colleagues demonstrated that medial prefrontal cortex neurons projecting to dorsomedial striatum show elevated activity during the maintenance period of working memory tasks, and that optogenetic inhibition of this projection during the delay selectively impaired performance, indicating that sustained prefrontal-to-striatal input functionally bridges the temporal gap between stimulus encoding and subsequent action 20 . On this view, persistent corticostriatal activity does not replace the eligibility trace; it reactivates or sustains the synaptic input pattern across the delay, ensuring that when the dopaminergic signal finally arrives, the relevant corticostriatal synapses are still (or again) in an eligible state. The eligibility trace mechanism and sustained cortical drive are thus complementary: the trace handles delays up to 2̃ seconds at the synaptic level, while persistent prefrontal and striatal activity extends the effective reach of the same three-factor plasticity rule to longer timescales by maintaining the first factor (corticostriatal coactivation) until the third factor (dopamine) arrives 13 . The picture that emerges is of a multi-timescale credit assignment architecture in which the synaptic eligibility trace, TD-mediated backward chaining of value, and sustained prefrontal-striatal activity jointly solve the temporal binding problem across a range of delays. At the shortest timescales (sub-second to  2 s), the molecular machinery of the SPN spine—calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclase, phosphodiesterase gating, PKA-DARPP-32-PP1 signaling, and transient CP-AMPAR insertion—provides a synapse-autonomous eligibility window that is well matched to the latency of phasic dopamine bursts. At intermediate timescales (seconds to tens of seconds), TD propagation of value through state chains brings the relevant prediction error within reach of the eligibility window at each step. At still longer timescales, or in ambiguous multi-cue environments where eligibility traces alone would credit the wrong synapses, persistent prefrontal activity supplies a network-level "memory bridge" that keeps the relevant corticostriatal ensemble active across the delay. Together, these mechanisms ensure that the dopaminergic teaching signal–however delayed relative to the original action–can be directed to the synapses that actually participated in the behaviorally relevant computation, closing the loop from evaluative error to targeted, temporally precise policy update.

title: Cholinergic modulation and other gates
text: The preceding subsections established the molecular machinery by which dopaminergic prediction errors write into corticostriatal synaptic weights through opponent, pathway-specific plasticity rules operating on eligibility traces. But dopamine is not the only neuromodulatory signal that determines whether a given corticostriatal synapse undergoes lasting change. As emphasized in the error-signal section, cholinergic interneurons (CINs) generate a dense, tonically active acetylcholine field within the striatum whose transient pauses and rebounds are time-locked to behaviorally salient events. This section now revisits the cholinergic system through the lens of plasticity proper, asking: how does acetylcholine gate, sculpt, and in some cases independently drive the synaptic changes that update the striatal policy? A direct demonstration that cholinergic pauses are not merely correlated with but causally required for corticostriatal plasticity came from Zhang, Fisher, and colleagues, who independently manipulated CIN activity and midbrain dopamine neuron activity in two complementary in vivo paradigms. Their central finding was that long-term potentiation at corticostriatal synapses onto SPNs required the triple coincidence of three events: (i) a pause in CIN firing, (ii) phasic activation of dopamine neurons, and (iii) depolarization of the postsynaptic SPN 1 . Neither phasic dopamine alone nor CIN pauses alone were sufficient; only their temporal overlap, combined with ongoing SPN depolarization, produced durable potentiation. This triple-coincidence requirement has important computational consequences. First, the CIN pause defines a temporal window for plasticity: because dopamine neurons fire phasically in response to many behavioral variables beyond reward prediction errors–including salience, novelty, and movement initiation–unrestricted dopamine-dependent plasticity would corrupt stored action values with irrelevant updates. By gating plasticity to epochs in which CIN firing is simultaneously suppressed, the system restricts synaptic modification to those dopaminergic events that co-occur with the particular constellation of thalamostriatal and cortical inputs that drive the CIN pause, thereby implementing a form of contextual credit assignment 1 . Second, the requirement for SPN depolarization provides a spatial constraint: because volume-transmitted dopamine bathes a broad region of striatum, the depolarization criterion ensures that only those spines whose corticostriatal inputs are currently active—and whose parent SPN is therefore depolarized—are eligible for modification. In reinforcement-learning terms, the CIN pause supplies the "when to learn" gate, dopamine supplies the "how much and in what direction" teaching signal, and SPN depolarization supplies the "which synapses" specificity 1 . An important qualification of this picture has emerged from recent work using opto-tagged, positively identified CINs recorded alongside simultaneous dopamine measurements across striatal subregions during decision-making behavior. Duhne, Mohebi, and colleagues found that the classical expectation—CIN pauses temporally aligned with dopaminergic reward prediction errors—did not hold uniformly across the striatum 2 . In dorsolateral striatum, a Go cue evoked a CIN burst-pause sequence followed by a brief dopamine pulse that was unrelated to RPE; in dorsomedial striatum, the same cue evoked a CIN pause that was curtailed by a movement-selective rebound; and in ventral striatum, a reward cue evoked RPE-scaled increases in both dopamine and CIN firing, without a consistent pause. These findings do not invalidate the triple-coincidence principle, but they critically constrain its scope: the simple model in which a uniform CIN pause and a uniform dopamine RPE converge everywhere in striatum to gate learning must be replaced by a regionally parameterized account in which the phase relationship between cholinergic and dopaminergic dynamics varies across striatal territories, implying that different subregions may implement different plasticity regimes under the same behavioral contingency 2 . This regional parameterization has been given a precise functional interpretation by Jang, Ward, Golden, and Constantinople, who simultaneously measured dopamine and acetylcholine release in the dorsomedial striatum of rats performing a decision-making task and found that dopamine served different computational roles depending on its phase relationship to cholinergic dynamics 3 . When a dopamine transient slightly lagged a cholinergic dip at the time of an offer cue, it predicted behavioral updating on subsequent trials and was associated with trial-to-trial changes in dorsomedial striatal firing rates—hallmarks of dopamine-dependent plasticity. When a dopamine transient preceded a cholinergic dip, no comparable relationship to subsequent learning was detected. And when dopamine was coincident with cholinergic bursts rather than dips—as occurred at movement-related events—it predicted the vigor of upcoming contralateral orienting movements without evidence of lasting plasticity 3 . The implication for synaptic learning is direct: local cholinergic timing can demix the multiplexed content of a single dopaminergic signal into at least two downstream modes—a plasticity-promoting mode gated by cholinergic pauses, and a transient performance/vigor mode coincident with cholinergic bursts. In reinforcement-learning terms, acetylcholine determines whether a given dopamine transient functions as a teaching signal that updates corticostriatal weights or as a transient gain signal that modulates the vigor of the currently selected action without modifying the underlying policy. The molecular pathways through which tonic acetylcholine influences corticostriatal plasticity are multiple and partially opposing. At the postsynaptic level, tonic muscarinic M1 receptor activation on SPNs tends to enhance excitability and depolarization, but also inhibits CaV1.3-type L-type calcium channels, which are required for endocannabinoid-dependent long-term depression; the net effect of sustained M1 signaling is therefore to suppress the induction of eCB-LTD 4 , 5 . During a CIN pause, M1 receptor stimulation is transiently relieved, permitting calcium channel activation and eCB mobilization—one route by which the pause can be permissive for depression as well as for potentiation. At the level of direct-pathway SPNs, the Gi-coupled M4 muscarinic receptor plays a particularly important role: M4 is an abundant muscarinic subtype in the striatum and is preferentially expressed in dSPNs, where it is clustered near axospinous glutamatergic synapses 6 . One study showed that endogenous cholinergic signaling through M4 receptors promotes long-term depression at dSPN corticostriatal synapses by suppressing regulator of G-protein signaling type 4 (RGS4) activity, and blocks D1 receptor-dependent LTP; boosting M4 signaling with a positive allosteric modulator was sufficient to block aberrant LTP in dSPNs in a mouse model of L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia and enabled depotentiation of pathologically strengthened synapses 6 . The M4 receptor on dSPNs thus acts as a cholinergic counterweight to D1-mediated potentiation: tonic acetylcholine, via M4, biases dSPN corticostriatal synapses toward depression and away from runaway potentiation, and the CIN pause transiently releases this brake, opening a window in which D1-dependent LTP can proceed 6 , 7 . On the presynaptic side, M2/M4 autoreceptors on cholinergic terminals and M2-like receptors on corticostriatal terminals add further complexity: blockade of presynaptic M2-like receptors enhances striatal LTP by relieving inhibition of glutamate release, and genetic deletion of M2/M4 receptors abolishes both LTD induction and synaptic depotentiation 8 . The picture that emerges is of a cholinergic system that, through multiple receptor subtypes acting at pre- and postsynaptic sites, exerts a tonic bidirectional bias on the plasticity landscape: sustained acetylcholine promotes certain forms of depression (via M4 on dSPNs and eCB-related pathways) and suppresses others (via M1-mediated calcium channel inhibition), while the CIN pause transiently reconfigures this landscape to favor whichever form of plasticity is appropriate to the concurrent dopaminergic and depolarization signals. The molecular pathways through which tonic acetylcholine influences corticostriatal plasticity are multiple, distributed across pre- and postsynaptic sites, and in several cases partially opposing. At the postsynaptic level, tonic muscarinic M1 receptor activation on SPNs tends to enhance excitability and depolarization, increasing dendritic responsiveness to corticostriatal input via mechanisms that include KCNQ potassium-channel regulation and endocannabinoid-related signaling 9 , 10 , 11 . At the same time, M1 signaling can oppose at least some forms of corticostriatal depression by inhibiting CaV1.3-type L-type calcium channels required for endocannabinoid-dependent LTD, so the net contribution of tonic M1 activation is not a simple push toward either potentiation or depression, but a state-dependent reshaping of which plasticity rules are available under current conditions 4 , 5 . Notably, the excitatory effect of M1 stimulation appears especially prominent in D2-expressing indirect-pathway SPNs, suggesting that tonic acetylcholine can differentially regulate pathway excitability even before dopaminergic teaching signals arrive 11 . During a CIN pause, this tonic muscarinic drive is transiently relieved, permitting a rapid reconfiguration of the local plasticity landscape; in that interval, relief of M1-dependent constraints may facilitate calcium-channel activation and endocannabinoid mobilization, making the pause permissive for depression in some contexts and for potentiation in others, depending on the coincident dopaminergic and depolarizing state of the SPN 4 , 5 . At the level of direct-pathway SPNs, the Gi-coupled M4 muscarinic receptor plays a particularly important role. M4 is an abundant striatal muscarinic subtype, densely co-expressed with D1 receptors on MSNs and especially important in D1-linked signaling regimes, where it acts as a functional antagonist of D1 receptor-mediated cAMP-dependent cascades 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 . Consistent with this, endogenous cholinergic signaling through M4 receptors has been shown to promote depression-like plasticity states at dSPN corticostriatal synapses, to suppress regulator of G-protein signaling type 4 (RGS4) activity, and to oppose D1-dependent LTP; boosting M4 signaling with a positive allosteric modulator can block aberrant potentiation and restore depotentiation of pathologically strengthened synapses in models of L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia 6 . M4 receptors on MSNs have also been implicated in prolonged suppression of dopamine release through a cannabinoid CB2-dependent mechanism, further reinforcing the idea that M4 provides a cholinergic counterweight to dopaminergic gain 16 . Mechanistically, this signaling can itself be potentiated by calcium influx, because Ca 2+ /calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II α \alpha binds directly and selectively to M4 and strengthens M4 receptor signaling 17 , 18 . On the presynaptic side, cholinergic control adds yet another layer of regulation. Striatal CINs express Gi-coupled M2 and M4 autoreceptors, whose activation suppresses cholinergic tone and, through a disynaptic mechanism, reduces nicotinic acetylcholine receptor-dependent dopamine transmission 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 . This modulation is not merely inhibitory in a static sense: it also changes the frequency sensitivity of dopamine release, with M2 and M4 contributing in dorsal striatum and M4 appearing to dominate more strongly in ventral striatum/nucleus accumbens 23 , 24 . In parallel, stimulation of presynaptic M4 receptors on corticostriatal terminals depresses glutamatergic transmission itself 25 , 26 , 27 . Consistent with this broader inhibitory role, M4 knockout increases psychostimulant-evoked extracellular dopamine efflux in nucleus accumbens, whereas M2 knockout does not produce the same ventral-striatal phenotype; conversely, M1 knockout elevates extracellular dopamine and exacerbates amphetamine-evoked dopamine efflux despite normal whole-tissue dopamine content 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 . The picture that emerges is therefore of a cholinergic system that exerts a tonic, multi-level, and state-dependent bias on the corticostriatal plasticity landscape : sustained acetylcholine can enhance SPN responsiveness through M1, oppose D1-driven potentiation through M4, suppress glutamate release through presynaptic M4 receptors, and regulate dopamine transmission through M2/M4-dependent control of CIN tone; the CIN pause then transiently releases selected components of this cholinergic constraint, opening a brief window in which the sign and magnitude of plasticity can be more strongly determined by coincident dopaminergic error signals and postsynaptic depolarization. Beyond gating dopamine-dependent plasticity, cholinergic dynamics in some striatal territories appear to carry error-like information of their own that can drive plasticity independently or in opposition to dopamine. During Pavlovian learning and extinction, anterior dorsal striatal acetylcholine exhibited phase-specific prediction-error structure: positive and negative RPE-like signals were expressed in different temporal components of the acetylcholine waveform, and silencing local acetylcholine release impaired extinction while sparing initial acquisition 32 . In reversal-learning paradigms, dorsal striatal acetylcholine elevations following unexpected non-reward were causally required for behavioral adaptation: optogenetic silencing of CINs selectively impaired the ability of mice to switch away from a previously rewarded choice 33 . These findings converge with the opponent-plasticity data reviewed earlier to suggest that cholinergic circuitry is especially important for negative updating, extinction, and contingency revision –precisely the situations in which cached action values must be weakened rather than strengthened. A computational model by Kim and colleagues formalizes and extends these ideas, showing that cholinergic pauses can solve a structural credit-assignment problem that dopamine alone cannot 34 . The model implements a biologically plausible three-factor learning rule requiring presynaptic activity, postsynaptic depolarization, and phasic dopamine, with plasticity gated by cholinergic pauses that temporally align with behaviorally relevant events. In environments with many competing stimuli and actions—where dopamine is broadcast globally and cannot by itself identify which stimulus–action channel was responsible for the outcome—the cholinergic pause restricts plasticity to the channel that was active around action execution, preventing catastrophic interference across channels. Without this cholinergic gate, learning degrades severely as the number of actions increases; with it, the system scales gracefully 34 . This result resonates with earlier computational accounts in which TAN pauses regulate the effective learning rate by modulating SPN excitability and population-level uncertainty 35 , and with models in which the CIN pause protects stored action values from decay during periods of non-reward by suppressing corticostriatal throughput 36 . The local neuromodulatory field in which corticostriatal plasticity is embedded is, however, becoming richer than the dopamine-acetylcholine dyad alone. Serotonin, supplied to the striatum predominantly by dorsal raphe projections, can itself induce a presynaptically mediated long-term depression of corticostriatal glutamate release via 5-HT1b receptors–a form of plasticity (5-HT-LTD) that is mutually occlusive with the canonical dopamine/endocannabinoid-dependent LTD, suggesting that the two forms of depression converge on overlapping, and possibly the same, populations of corticostriatal terminals 37 . Importantly, CINs are now known to shape local striatal serotonin signaling more directly than previously appreciated: Matityahu, Hobel, and colleagues showed that synchronous activation of CINs triggers local serotonin release in the dorsal striatum via nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on serotonergic axons, thereby extending the spatial range of serotonergic signaling; this coupling is exaggerated in the hypercholinergic striatum of Sapap3-/- mice 38 . Thus, CINs can influence corticostriatal plasticity not only through their direct muscarinic and nicotinic actions on dopamine terminals and SPNs, but also by modulating local serotonergic tone–potentially recruiting an additional serotonergic route to synaptic depression under appropriate circuit conditions. Finally, the GABAergic interneuron network within the striatum contributes an additional layer of plasticity control that is only beginning to be characterized. Two interneuron subtypes deserve particular mention. Somatostatin-expressing (SOM) interneurons (also termed low-threshold spiking interneurons, LTSIs) are sparse but tonically active cells that preferentially target SPN distal dendrites and exert especially potent feedforward inhibition in dorsomedial striatum 39 , 40 . Rotariu and colleagues showed that selective manipulation of SOM interneurons disrupted the reorganization of dorsomedial striatal activity during early motor learning–the experience-dependent emergence of a sparse, high-activity SPN ensemble whose size correlates with task performance–whereas manipulation of parvalbumin (PV) interneurons in the same region had no effect 41 . SOM-to-SPN inhibitory connections in dorsomedial striatum proved to be highly plastic: their synaptic strength was significantly enhanced after early training, suggesting that SOM interneurons actively sculpt the representational landscape through learning-dependent changes in their own synaptic output 41 . SOM interneurons also locally gate dopamine release via GABA-B signaling on dopaminergic terminals, providing a mechanism by which this interneuron class can regulate both the excitability of SPN dendritic compartments and the magnitude of the teaching signal that reaches them 42 . Parvalbumin-expressing (PV) fast-spiking interneurons , by contrast, exert especially strong control in DLS, target SPN somata and proximal dendrites, and exert their strongest influence on striatal output during the early phases of associative learning: optogenetic and chemogenetic suppression of PV cells impaired the initial expression of reward-conditioned responses, but their relative contribution to SPN dynamics and behavioral performance diminished with training 43 . In a complementary study, Owen and colleagues showed that PV and cholinergic interneurons have dissociable roles during movement: PV cells facilitate movement execution by refining the activation of SPN networks, while CINs synchronize SPN activity to signal the termination of a movement bout 44 . Together, these results point to a potential division of labor: SOM interneurons are disproportionately important for gating plasticity and shaping representations during early, flexible, goal-directed learning (especially in dorsomedial striatum), whereas PV interneurons are more important for sharpening performance-related output (especially in dorsolateral striatum), with both subtypes operating alongside–and in some cases regulated by–the cholinergic and dopaminergic signals described above. The composite picture is therefore considerably more complex than "dopamine is the teacher, acetylcholine sets the learning window." A more accurate summary is that corticostriatal plasticity is governed by a multi-layered neuromodulatory and interneuronal gating architecture in which: (i) cholinergic pauses define the temporal window within which dopamine can drive plasticity, (ii) the phase relationship between acetylcholine and dopamine transients determines whether a given dopamine event functions as a teaching signal or a vigor signal, (iii) muscarinic receptor signaling biases the plasticity landscape toward depression or potentiation, (iv) cholinergic dynamics carry their own error-like signals that are especially important for extinction and behavioral flexibility, (v) CIN activity recruits parallel serotonergic plasticity pathways through nicotinic activation of raphe-striatal axons, and (vi) GABAergic SOM and PV interneurons provide regionally specialized control over SPN excitability, representational selection, and dopamine release that is itself plastic and learning-dependent. The dopaminergic teaching signal, in other words, does not arrive at a passive synaptic substrate; it arrives at a dynamically configured local circuit whose cholinergic, serotonergic, and GABAergic components collectively determine where, when, and in what effective sign the error is allowed to modify the striatal policy.

title: Up and down states
text: The plasticity rules described above–opponent dopaminergic gating, cholinergic timing, and interneuronal sculpting–all presuppose that the postsynaptic SPN is in an appropriate electrical state to receive and act on those signals. In practice, this state is most often the depolarized "up state" –or a closely related dendritic plateau state–rather than the deeply hyperpolarized down state . Spiny projection neurons are among the most electrically quiescent principal neurons in the mammalian brain: in the absence of convergent excitatory drive, they rest at a deeply hyperpolarized membrane potential (roughly − 80 -80 to − 90 -90 mV), far below action potential threshold, and are effectively silent. This hyperpolarized resting level–the down state –is maintained by a family of strongly expressed inwardly rectifying potassium channels (Kir2 type, principally Kir2.1 and Kir2.3 subunits), whose tonic conductance clamps the membrane near the potassium equilibrium potential and powerfully shunts small or asynchronous depolarizing inputs 1 , 2 , 3 . The computational consequence is stark: a single excitatory synapse, or even a modest number of uncorrelated cortical inputs, is insufficient to bring an SPN anywhere near threshold. Only sufficiently convergent and temporally coordinated glutamatergic afferent activity can drive the membrane into a sustained depolarized regime near threshold, engaging NMDAR-dependent and dendritic plateau mechanisms that support spike generation and corticostriatal plasticity 1 , 4 . This two-state behavior was first described by Wilson and Groves and subsequently characterized in detail by Wilson and Kawaguchi using in vivo intracellular recordings. Their landmark study demonstrated that neostriatal spiny neurons spend most of their time at two preferred membrane potentials, with relatively little time in transition between them, and that the up state is not a consequence of intrinsic membrane bistability but instead reflects a maintained barrage of synaptic excitation, primarily of cortical origin 1 , 5 . Several key manipulations established this conclusion. Blocking sodium and calcium spikes intracellularly with QX314 and D890 did not abolish up-state transitions, ruling out regenerative somatic conductances as their primary cause 1 . In contrast, intracellular cesium strongly depolarized and linearized the membrane response, in some conditions shifting the depolarized level toward roughly − 20 -20 mV, revealing that the synaptic input underlying the up state has a reversal potential consistent with mixed excitatory and inhibitory drive, and that potassium conductances normally clamp the up-state voltage well below that net synaptic reversal potential 1 . Acute cortical lesions abolished striatal up states while sparing monosynaptic responsiveness, confirming that the up state requires ongoing cortical activity rather than an intrinsic striatal oscillation 5 . The up state is therefore best understood not as a bistable switch internal to the SPN, but as a network-imposed depolarizing regime whose onset, duration, and termination are dictated by the spatiotemporal structure of convergent excitatory input and shaped by the SPN’s intrinsic conductance landscape 5 . The transition between states is not a simple linear ramp but is sharpened by a cascade of voltage-sensitive conductances that act as successive thresholds. In the down state, Kir2 channels dominate: they stabilize the membrane near the potassium equilibrium potential and present a large shunting conductance to incoming EPSPs. As depolarization begins to overcome this barrier, rapidly inactivating potassium currents (Kv4-type A-currents) and slowly inactivating potassium currents (Kv1-type) further slow the depolarizing trajectory, producing the characteristic delayed onset to the first action potential that is a hallmark of SPN electrophysiology 1 , 6 , 7 . Once in the up state, outwardly rectifying and non-inactivating potassium conductances buffer the membrane potential in a narrow subthreshold range, where even large slow fluctuations in synaptic drive produce only modest voltage changes; it is brief, fast transients—such as a well-timed cortical volley—that can escape this clamping and trigger an action potential 5 . The result is that the SPN acts as a coincidence detector with two nested thresholds: the first (down-to-up transition) requires convergent, synchronized excitation from a large cortical ensemble; the second (up-state spiking) requires an additional fast excitatory transient superimposed on the already depolarized plateau. Both thresholds are modulated by the neuromodulatory context described in preceding sections. Under anesthesia and during natural slow-wave sleep, cortical networks oscillate at roughly 1 Hz between active and silent phases, and striatal SPNs faithfully inherit this rhythm: they toggle between up and down states in tight synchrony with cortical slow oscillations, with the onset and offset of striatal up states closely tracking periods of cortical ensemble activity 8 , 5 . This sleep/anesthesia pattern—which has dominated the experimental literature on SPN state transitions—should not, however, be taken as the universal operating mode of striatal neurons. During wakefulness, cortical input to the striatum becomes more tonically desynchronized, and the membrane potential distribution of SPNs shifts accordingly: rather than exhibiting a sharply bimodal distribution, SPNs in the awake state spend more time at intermediate and depolarized potentials, with state transitions becoming less stereotyped and more variable in timing and depth 8 . The functional relevance is that in the awake, behaving animal, the up/down framework still applies as a description of the SPN’s intrinsic conductance landscape—the Kir2-mediated down state remains the default, and convergent input is still required for depolarization—but the temporal structure of state transitions is governed by task- and movement-related cortical dynamics rather than by slow oscillatory rhythms. This distinction matters for plasticity: the same cortical stimulation protocol that produces robust long-term potentiation under barbiturate anesthesia (where pronounced up/down cycling concentrates synaptic drive into discrete depolarized epochs) produces long-term depression instead in awake, freely moving animals 9 , demonstrating that behavioral state—and by implication the temporal patterning of up-state occupancy—is a critical regulator of the sign of corticostriatal synaptic change 10 . The relevance of up/down state dynamics for plasticity is direct and mechanistically grounded. In the classical corticostriatal up/down-state regime, SPNs fire action potentials primarily during up states, and the induction of corticostriatal plasticity requires postsynaptic depolarization sufficient to engage the Ca2+-dependent signaling pathways that govern synaptic change. In practice, the up state functions as a powerful permissive gate: it relieves the Mg2+ block of NMDA receptors, enhances dendritic Ca2+ influx, and recruits voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels, thereby restricting plasticity to those SPNs that are genuinely engaged in processing the current cortical state 11 , 12 , 13 . Kerr and Plenz demonstrated that this gating is not merely binary but temporally graded: the magnitude of dendritic calcium transients evoked by single backpropagating action potentials during up states depends sharply on the delay between up-state onset and spike timing, with calcium peaking when the action potential occurs close to the beginning of the up state and declining exponentially with increasing delay ( τ ≈ \tau \approx 47 ms in tertiary dendrites) 14 . In effect, the up state creates a rapidly decaying dendritic eligibility window: synapses active near the onset of a cortical ensemble event receive the largest calcium signal and are therefore most susceptible to the spike-timing-dependent and dopamine-gated plasticity rules described in preceding sections. A more recent and mechanistically deeper understanding of how individual SPNs achieve the up state has come from the discovery of dendritic plateau potentials . Plotkin, Day, and Surmeier showed that convergent activation of a modest cluster of glutamatergic synapses on a distal SPN dendritic segment can trigger a regenerative, NMDA-receptor-dependent dendritic plateau potential that propagates decrementally to the soma and produces a sustained depolarization resembling the classically described up state 15 . Du and colleagues extended this finding by showing that such plateau potentials last tens to hundreds of milliseconds and can be controlled in a cell-type-specific manner by GABAergic inhibition: slow-kinetics dendritic inhibition resembling that of NPY-neurogliaform interneurons is especially effective at regulating plateau duration, whereas fast-spiking perisomatic inhibition primarily regulates output spiking and somatic depolarization rather than switching off the dendritic plateau itself 16 . The implication is that the up state, while still a synaptically imposed event, need not reflect only diffuse aggregate bombardment; it can be initiated efficiently by the coincidence of a modest number of spatially clustered inputs on a single dendritic branch, dramatically raising the importance of synaptic spatial organization and dendritic computation in striatal function. These dendritic nonlinearities have profound implications for learning. The plateau potential requires spatiotemporal clustering of excitatory inputs and strong engagement of dendritic NMDA receptors, molecular machinery that also drives calcium-dependent plasticity. When a plateau potential is triggered, the sustained local depolarization produces large and prolonged NMDA-receptor-mediated calcium influx in the dendritic segment, together with recruitment of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels, creating a calcium regime well suited to engage the opponent plasticity rules described earlier 17 , 18 , 12 . Recent computational work has formalized this link, showing that a biologically grounded learning rule governed by local calcium dynamics from NMDA and L-type channels, gated by dopaminergic reward signals, and stabilized by metaplasticity, can enable single SPNs to solve the nonlinear feature binding problem—a task traditionally attributed to multi-layer networks—by exploiting dendritic plateau potentials as branch-specific computational units 17 . In this framework, learning is not simply a matter of strengthening or weakening an undifferentiated population of corticostriatal synapses; it is a spatially structured process in which different dendritic segments of a single SPN may act as partially independent plasticity subunits, each defined by its local plateau-potential responsiveness to a particular subset of cortical inputs. Dopamine modulates the up-state machinery at multiple levels. D1 receptor activation on direct-pathway SPNs enhances intrinsic excitability on timescales ranging from hundreds of milliseconds to minutes: it reduces the latency to first spike, suppresses depolarization- and calcium-activated potassium currents, and lowers action potential threshold through PKA-dependent mechanisms 7 . At the dendritic level, D1 signaling prolongs the duration of dendritically evoked up states in matrix dSPNs while, strikingly, shortening them in striosome dSPNs, an opposition mediated in part by differences in L-type voltage-gated calcium channel engagement 19 . Conversely, D2 receptor activation in indirect-pathway SPNs attenuates glutamatergic, including NMDA-receptor-mediated, signaling and tends to reduce excitability, making iSPNs less responsive to cortical drive 20 , 21 , 22 . The net effect is that dopamine does not merely deliver an error signal to a passive substrate; it also reshapes the excitability landscape in which cortical inputs are integrated, biasing direct- and indirect-pathway SPNs in opposite directions. This is consistent with the broader principle that dopamine’s modulation of intrinsic excitability and its gating of synaptic plasticity are deeply coupled functions: by regulating how readily particular SPNs enter and sustain depolarized states, dopamine helps determine which corticostriatal synapses become eligible for updating. The composite picture that emerges is of a multi-layered eligibility architecture in which the up state serves as the foundational gate. At the broadest level, Kir2-mediated hyperpolarization ensures that only SPNs receiving sufficiently convergent and synchronized cortical input are promoted to the depolarized state from which plasticity is possible. Within the up state, the timing of action potentials relative to up-state onset determines dendritic calcium amplitude and thus the magnitude of plasticity. At the dendritic level, NMDA-dependent plateau potentials provide branch-specific amplification that can focus plasticity on the particular dendritic segments where input clustering has occurred. Dopamine then modulates all of these levels simultaneously: it adjusts intrinsic excitability to bias which SPN populations reach the up state, it provides the phasic error signal that the three-factor rule requires, and it differentially tunes dendritic plateau dynamics across striatal compartments. The cholinergic pause, operating in parallel, defines the temporal window within which this entire cascade can produce lasting synaptic change. The result is that corticostriatal plasticity is not gated by a single factor but by the conjunction of network state (up-state occupancy), dendritic state (plateau-potential engagement), neuromodulatory state (dopamine burst coincident with cholinergic pause), and spike timing –a conjunction that is fulfilled only when the SPN is genuinely processing a cortically defined state, acting on it, and receiving evaluative feedback about the outcome.

title: Territory-dependent plasticity
text: A crucial point, and one that follows directly from the parallel-loop architecture described in the loss- and error-signal sections, is that the striatum does not instantiate one uniform plasticity rule everywhere. The molecular primitives recur—glutamatergic coincidence, postsynaptic depolarization, dopamine, acetylcholine, endocannabinoids, and local inhibition—but the sign, timing sensitivity, dominant induction regime, and functional consequence of those primitives vary across striatal territories. Territory-specific plasticity is therefore not an incidental modulation layered atop a generic BG learning rule; it is one of the mechanisms by which the same dopaminergic evaluative variable is converted into different forms of policy optimization in associative, sensorimotor, limbic, and posterior striatal loops 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . Some of the clearest evidence comes from dorsomedial versus dorsolateral striatum. Perez and colleagues showed that corticostriatal STDP is itself region-specific: DMS expresses predominantly symmetric anti-Hebbian plasticity, whereas DLS expresses asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP 1 . Their modeling further showed that these two rules have different computational consequences: the symmetric rule favors memory flexibility and rapid updating, whereas the asymmetric rule favors memory maintenance, providing an unusually clean synaptic correlate of the canonical behavioral division in which DMS supports flexible goal-directed control and DLS supports the stabilization of habitual policies. Importantly, during motor-skill learning, plasticity in that study was engaged in DMS and in DLS striatonigral neurons during early learning, whereas DLS striatopallidal neurons were mobilized later, indicating that the locus of corticostriatal modification shifts across training rather than simply scaling uniformly with practice 1 . This DMS-DLS asymmetry is not only descriptive; it plausibly changes what each territory is good at learning. Vignoud and colleagues showed that anti-Hebbian corticostriatal STDP, especially when combined with two classical striatal features–spike latency and collateral inhibition–is well suited for learning spike sequences, and explicitly note that realistic models will need to incorporate the experimentally observed distinction between DMS and DLS anti-Hebbian regimes 5 . In that sense, a DMS-like rule appears well matched to continual policy revision and relearning, whereas a DLS-like rule appears well matched to the chunking and stabilization of repeated sensorimotor sequences into durable habits 5 , 1 . Moving from the dorsal to the ventral striatum , the plasticity landscape changes again, in ways that may reflect the distinct computational demands of the limbic cortico-basal ganglia loops. Ji and Bhatt examined STDP in core nucleus accumbens (NAc) SPNs using spike-timing protocols that more closely approximated in vivo firing patterns than high-frequency stimulation 6 . Relative to the classical anti-Hebbian rule often observed in dorsal striatal slice preparations under intact inhibitory conditions, the same anti-Hebbian pairing protocol (post-before-pre at low frequency) in NAc core SPNs evoked bidirectional long-term plasticity : roughly half of recorded SPNs underwent timing-dependent LTP and the other half underwent timing-dependent LTD, with the two outcomes appearing to segregate into functionally distinct neuronal subpopulations 6 . Moreover, the molecular mechanisms underlying tLTP and tLTD in NAc differed from those in dorsal striatum: tLTP depended on NMDA receptors but not on action potentials (consistent with a purely dendritic induction mechanism), whereas tLTD required action potentials and calcium-induced calcium release from ryanodine-sensitive intracellular stores–a dependence on ryanodine receptors rather than IP3 receptors that contrasts with the dominant LTD mechanisms in dorsal striatum, where endocannabinoid- and IP3-dependent pathways predominate 6 . Even the effects of dopamine receptor agonists on MSN firing diverged from dorsal striatal expectations: a subset of NAc MSNs whose firing was strongly suppressed by dopamine agonists was exclusively associated with tLTP, but the relationship between D1/D2 receptor expression and plasticity polarity was not as cleanly segregated as in dorsal striatum 6 . These findings suggest that NAc core operates under a distinct plasticity regime in which bidirectional plasticity can be generated by a single induction protocol, potentially enabling rapid, flexible reweighting of cortico-accumbal synapses in response to motivational contingency changes. The cholinergic gating of plasticity is also territory-dependent. As described in the error-signal section, recent work suggests that the relationship between striatal cholinergic pauses and dopaminergic reward signals is not uniform across subregions 2 . Complementing that systems-level observation, Marche, Martel, and Apicella showed that cholinergic interneurons (TANs) themselves display region-specific response properties in primates performing a Pavlovian conditioning task 7 . In ventral (limbic) striatum, the fraction of TANs responding to reward was higher than in motor or associative dorsal striatum, and TAN pause responses were generally longer; for reward-predictive stimuli, pause magnitude was also greater in ventral than dorsal territories 7 . Because corticostriatal LTP requires the coincidence of a cholinergic pause, phasic dopamine, and SPN depolarization 8 , these ventral TAN dynamics may permit reward-related teaching signals to influence plasticity over a broader temporal window. This interpretation is broadly consistent with evidence that dopamine signals follow a ventral-to-dorsal striatal gradient of reward time horizons, with slower discounting in ventral striatum than in more dorsal territories 9 . The regional TAN differences likely reflect differences in afferent organization, potentially including regionally heterogeneous midbrain dopamine/glutamate signaling, although the precise circuit basis remains unresolved 7 , 10 . Overlaying the ventral-to-dorsal territorial gradient is the striosome–matrix compartmental axis, which introduces a further dimension of plasticity heterogeneity. As established in the loss-function and error-signal sections, striosomes are disproportionately positioned to regulate dopaminergic teaching signals through their specialized projections to SNc dopamine neurons, whereas matrix SPNs are more tightly embedded in the canonical action-output channels 11 . This anatomical distinction likely has corresponding plasticity consequences. Dopamine transmission itself differs across the two compartments: in dorsal striatal slice preparations, electrically evoked dopamine release is slightly higher in matrix than in striosomes, despite reports that dopaminergic axon density is greater in striosomes 12 . More importantly, the modulatory effects of dopamine on SPN state transitions differ between compartments: D1 signaling prolongs dendritically evoked up states in matrix dSPNs while shortening them in striosomal dSPNs 13 . This suggests that the same class of dopaminergic event could bias the temporal conditions for plasticity induction in opposite directions across the two compartments, though this remains an inference rather than a directly demonstrated learning-rate effect. Combined with evidence that striosomal neurons exhibit stronger representations of reinforcement outcomes—especially large reward and punishment prediction errors—than matrix neurons during cost-benefit foraging 14 , and that in classical conditioning dopamine release in striosomes is especially engaged by aversive-predictive cues 15 , the emerging picture is of a compartmental architecture in which striosomes and matrix may learn under partially different dopaminergic regimes even within the same striatal territory. This organization is consistent with–though does not by itself prove–the compartment-specific critic-versus-actor division of labor proposed in the loss-function section. Taken together, the evidence reviewed in this subsection establishes that the basal ganglia’s plasticity rules are not a single canonical recipe applied uniformly across the striatum, but a family of regionally and compartmentally parameterized learning rules that share a common molecular toolkit—three-factor dopamine-gated Hebbian/anti-Hebbian STDP, endocannabinoid-dependent LTD, eligibility traces, cholinergic gating—but differ in their temporal profiles, polarity biases, pathway selectivity, and effective learning rates across striatal territories. In DMS, symmetric anti-Hebbian STDP, transient synaptic potentiation during early learning, and strong engagement of neuromodulatory gating favor rapid, flexible acquisition of goal-directed contingencies that can be readily overwritten when the environment changes. In DLS, asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP, progressive and long-lasting potentiation concentrated in D2-expressing striatopallidal neurons, and slower formation of spatially clustered ensembles favor the consolidation of stable, extinction-resistant habits and motor skills. In ventral striatum, bidirectional plasticity from a single induction protocol, distinct calcium-signaling mechanisms, longer cholinergic plasticity windows, and morphologically specialized neuronal substrates favor the kind of rapid, flexible value estimation that the critic side of the actor–critic architecture requires. And at the striosome–matrix interface, opposite dopaminergic modulation of up-state dynamics and differential dopamine release produce compartment-specific learning rates that may support the separation of policy evaluation (striosome) from policy expression (matrix). The effective loss function that each territory optimizes is therefore matched, at the level of synaptic plasticity, by a learning rule whose parameterization is tuned to the computational demands of that territory’s position in the cortico-basal ganglia hierarchy. This is the synaptic-level instantiation of the broader principle established throughout this chapter: the basal ganglia do not implement a single optimizer with a single learning rule, but a structured portfolio of interacting optimizers, each with its own objective, its own error signal, and—as this section has shown—its own plasticity regime.
