title: Relationship with cortical plasticity
text: The relationship between basal-ganglia and cortical plasticity is best understood not as a contrast between two wholly different learning principles, but as a contrast between two parameterizations of the same broad three-factor logic deployed for different computational purposes. In both systems, recent pre- and postsynaptic coactivity can write an eligibility-like state that is later converted into lasting synaptic change by additional modulatory or circuit-level signals. But the function of that machinery differs. In cortex, plasticity is comparatively more heterogeneous, compartmentalized, and partly self-supervised: dendritic voltage landscapes, local calcium dynamics, disinhibitory motifs, homeostatic constraints, and longer eligibility windows allow cortical circuits to refine predictive features, latent causes, and internal world models across multiple timescales. In the basal ganglia, by contrast, the same generic primitives are tuned toward evaluative policy updating : eligibility windows are shorter, dependence on phasic dopamine is stronger, and opponent D1/D2 pathway rules translate scalar outcome information into selective strengthening or weakening of action-linked representations 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . The cortex therefore tends to learn what is there and what it means ; the basal ganglia tend to learn what to do about it . Yet these systems are inseparable in operation, because each trains under conditions partly created by the other. Cortical populations provide the high-dimensional state, context, and action representations that converge onto SPN spines and become eligible for dopaminergic credit assignment; basal-ganglia output, in turn, biases thalamocortical traffic, action selection, exploration, and the statistics from which cortex learns. Empirically, skill learning is accompanied by coordinated plasticity across both structures rather than isolated modification in either one alone: corticostriatal plasticity is required for abstract skill learning, corticostriatal coherence and offline coupling increase with practice, and motor learning strengthens the outputs of motor-cortex engram neurons onto striatal SPNs; conversely, direct- and indirect-pathway manipulations can reshape cortical activity and perceptual representations, while motor-cortical and thalamic inputs to striatum make dissociable contributions to acquisition and execution 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 . The most useful synthesis, then, is that cortex and basal ganglia form a nested optimizer pair : cortex learns the representational geometry of the task, whereas the basal ganglia learn which cortical representations should be gated, repeated, suppressed, or consolidated into policy. BG plasticity is thus not an alternative to cortical plasticity, but the evaluative counterpart that closes the loop between world-model construction and action selection.

title: BG Learning in Action
text: The three preceding subsections decomposed BG learning into analytically separable components (loss functions, error signals, plasticity). This section reassembles them into a unified picture. Aim: trace the full transduction chain from action selection through dopaminergic evaluation to durable corticostriatal weight change, showing that BG loss, error, and plasticity are three views onto one continuously running policy-optimization process. Caveat about speculative stitching where normative frameworks outrun circuit-level evidence.

title: Mediating the exploration-exploitation tradeoff
text: A policy optimizer that can only exploit will starve whenever the environment changes; one that can only explore will never consolidate a gain. The exploration-exploitation tradeoff is therefore not an incidental problem the basal ganglia sometimes face but the defining tension of their loss landscape: the policy must be biased toward actions whose values are already estimated to be high (exploitation), yet must simultaneously allocate some fraction of behavior to actions whose values are poorly known (exploration), so that the value estimates on which exploitation depends remain accurate enough to be worth exploiting. Formally, this amounts to a meta-level optimization over the explore-exploit balance itself, and the preceding subsections have already laid out the machinery that makes it possible. Distributional coding gives the system access to the variance, not merely the mean, of expected returns; multi-timescale discounting gives it access to the temporal profile of uncertainty; opponent D1/D2 plasticity gives it asymmetric channels for reinforcing versus suppressing actions; and the indirect pathway’s documented role in policy revision, reversal learning, and collicular competition gives it a dedicated circuit for generating behavioral alternatives when the current policy becomes unreliable. What remains is to show how these components are assembled, in real time, into a coherent exploration-exploitation strategy. The conceptual starting point is that the basal ganglia do not need to solve the exploration-exploitation tradeoff through a single mechanism. Instead, converging evidence suggests that the BG implement a layered portfolio of exploration strategies , each operating at a different computational level and supported by a partially distinct anatomical substrate: (i) uncertainty-driven directed exploration , in which the system biases action selection toward options whose outcome distributions are wide or poorly sampled, likely exploiting the distributional information carried by opponent D1/D2 pathways; (ii) novelty-driven exploration , in which transient dopaminergic responses to novel stimuli act as exploration bonuses or shaping signals that inflate the effective value of unfamiliar options before any reward has been observed; (iii) policy-unreliability-driven switching , in which the indirect pathway of the dorsomedial striatum monitors the accumulating evidence that the current policy is performing below expectation and biases behavior toward probing an alternative; and (iv) homeostatic modulation of exploration scope , in which internal physiological state, conveyed through hypothalamic-midbrain circuitry, globally recalibrates the gain on exploratory behavior by modulating dopaminergic signaling in specialized striatal territories. These are not mutually exclusive channels; they likely operate concurrently, with their relative influence shifting as a function of task phase, environmental volatility, and internal state. Uncertainty-driven directed exploration. The distributional RL framework developed in the loss-function and error-signal sections implies that the D1 and D2 pathways do not merely learn the mean value of an action; they learn something approaching the optimistic and pessimistic tails of its return distribution, with D1 SPNs preferentially encoding expectiles above the median and D2 SPNs encoding expectiles below it 1 . Wang, Lak, Manohar, and Bogacz formalized the computational consequences of this architecture for exploration, showing that direct and indirect striatal pathways acting together can estimate both the mean and the variance of reward distributions associated with each action 2 . In their model, the mean reward estimate is encoded in the difference between D1- and D2-pathway corticostriatal weights, whereas the spread (mean deviation) of the reward distribution is encoded in their sum. The critical insight is that this spread estimate provides a natural uncertainty signal that can be used to implement directed exploration: at the level of action selection, the effective value of an action can be augmented by a term proportional to its estimated uncertainty, biasing choice toward options about which the system knows least–formally, an upper-confidence-bound-like strategy emerging from the opponent architecture rather than being imposed from outside. Wang et al. fitted exploration strategies derived from this basal ganglia model to human behavioral data from multi-armed bandit tasks and found that a hybrid strategy combining both directed (uncertainty-biased) and random exploration components provided the best fit, consistent with the behavioral literature showing that humans use both forms of exploration simultaneously 2 . In simulation, the biologically inspired exploration strategy achieved overall competitive or superior performance relative to classic upper-confidence-bound algorithms, suggesting that the opponent D1/D2 architecture is not merely compatible with efficient exploration but may be well suited to it 2 . This result connects directly to the distributional and opponent-plasticity machinery described in the preceding sections: if D1 SPNs learn the right tail and D2 SPNs learn the left tail of the return distribution, then the system already possesses the information needed to estimate outcome spread, and the basal ganglia’s native architecture for competitive action selection can, in principle, convert that spread estimate into an exploration bonus without requiring a separate dedicated uncertainty-computation module. Novelty-driven exploration. Uncertainty about an action’s value is highest when the action has never been tried at all–that is, when it is novel . Directed exploration based on learned variance estimates, however, cannot operate on truly novel options because no variance estimate yet exists. This creates an initialization problem: how does the system assign an effective value to an action before any outcome has been observed? An influential theoretical proposal, due originally to Kakade and Dayan, is that the dopaminergic system solves this problem by treating novelty itself as a transient reward bonus–an "exploration bonus" or "shaping bonus" that inflates the initial effective value of unfamiliar stimuli or actions, ensuring that they are sampled at least once before the standard TD machinery takes over 3 . The proposal requires that dopamine neurons actually fire to novel stimuli, and they do–but the mechanistic question of why/how they do so deserves careful treatment, because a potential answer connects directly to the generalized prediction-error framework developed in the error-signal section. The classical RPE account offers no obvious reason for dopamine neurons to respond to a stimulus that has never been paired with reward: a novel, unrewarded stimulus should carry zero cached value and therefore generate zero prediction error in a standard model-free TD learner. But the generalized prediction-error view resolves this apparent anomaly. If dopamine neurons compute prediction errors not only over reward but over a broader set of sensory and state features–as argued by Gardner, Schoenbaum, and Gershman, and as supported by the identity, sensory, and associative prediction-error data reviewed in the error-signal section–then a truly novel stimulus is, by definition, maximally unpredicted across many feature dimensions simultaneously 4 , 5 . It violates expectations about what stimulus should appear in this context, what sensory features that stimulus should carry, and what state the world should be in. The resulting burst of generalized prediction-error activity is large precisely because the system has no learned model to predict any aspect of the novel event. As the stimulus becomes familiar–even without ever being paired with reward–these feature-level prediction errors are progressively resolved, and dopamine responses decline. This habituation profile is exactly what is observed: single dopamine neurons show substantial activation on the first presentations of a novel, unrewarded stimulus, and this activation diminishes over tens of trials as the stimulus becomes predictable, in parallel with declining behavioral orienting responses 6 . Beyond correlative evidence, Morrens, Aydin, and colleagues provided a causal demonstration that novelty-evoked dopamine is not epiphenomenal but functionally participates in learning. Using fiber photometry in head-restrained mice, they showed that VTA/SNc dopamine neurons produce robust responses to novel, inconsequential olfactory stimuli that are absent for familiar stimuli of the same sensory modality 7 . Importantly, when these novel cues were subsequently paired with reward in a Pavlovian conditioning task, mice conditioned significantly faster to novel than to pre-exposed (familiar) cues–the classical latent-inhibition effect. Bidirectional optogenetic manipulations then established causality: inhibiting VTA dopamine neurons during novel cue presentation slowed subsequent conditioning to those cues, whereas stimulating dopamine neurons during familiar cue presentation accelerated it, as though the stimulation had artificially restored the novelty-associated dopamine transient 7 . The implication is that cue-evoked dopamine at the moment of first encounter acts as a learning-rate amplifier : it does not itself encode reward value, but by transiently boosting corticostriatal drive it increases the eligibility of newly encountered stimulus-action-outcome mappings for subsequent dopamine-dependent plasticity. Wang et al. integrated this empirical picture into their basal ganglia model of exploration by showing that the transient dopaminergic novelty signal can serve as precisely the kind of initializing exploration bonus that the uncertainty-driven machinery alone cannot provide 2 . In their formalization, when a novel option is first encountered, the dopaminergic novelty transient provides a brief additive boost to the corticostriatal drive representing that option, biasing action selection toward it independently of any learned value. The novelty signal is transient—it decays as the option becomes familiar—so its effect is to kickstart sampling of unfamiliar options rather than to permanently distort the learned value landscape. The dual functionality of fast dopamine transients—carrying generalized prediction errors that encompass novelty at the time of first encounter, and reward prediction errors at the time of outcome—is consistent with the broader view, developed at length in the error-signal section, that dopamine neurons multiplex information across different temporal phases and behavioral epochs. In functional terms, the novelty bonus solves the cold-start problem that uncertainty-based exploration alone cannot handle: it gets the novel option sampled at least once, and with elevated plasticity gain, so that the distributional machinery described above can take over as soon as initial outcome information becomes available, driving subsequent exploration on the basis of learned variance rather than raw novelty. The two mechanisms are therefore not alternative theories of exploration but sequential phases of a single adaptive process: novelty-driven initialization hands off to uncertainty-driven directed exploration as the system acquires distributional knowledge about each option’s returns. Policy-unreliability-driven switching via the indirect pathway. The preceding two mechanisms–uncertainty-driven directed exploration and novelty-driven initialization–operate primarily by modulating the values assigned to alternative actions. But the exploration-exploitation tradeoff can also be resolved at the level of policy monitoring : the system can detect that its current policy is performing poorly and trigger a switch to an alternative, without necessarily computing the value of that alternative in advance. This is the function that recent work assigns to the indirect pathway of the dorsomedial striatum . Isomura and colleagues recorded and optogenetically manipulated indirect-pathway SPNs in the dorsomedial striatum of rats performing a stochastic reversal task, and found that iSPNs exhibited a distinctive late-onset sustained signal following unrewarded trials on which the animal had chosen the suboptimal (lower-value) action 8 . The magnitude of this late-onset iSPN activity scaled with the degree of outcome uncertainty and with the accumulating evidence that the current action policy was unreliable: it was strongest when the animal had experienced a run of failures under high outcome stochasticity, precisely the condition under which the normative explore-exploit balance should shift toward exploration. Optogenetic stimulation of DMS iSPNs at this late-outcome epoch increased the probability of the animal switching to the alternative action on the subsequent trial; inhibition decreased it 8 . Complementarily, early-onset signals from both dSPNs and iSPNs mediated the automatic, outcome-guided persistence of learned action policies for expected rewards: dSPN stimulation following rewarded high-value actions increased the probability of repeating the same action on the next trial. The picture that emerges is of a temporally multiplexed opponent architecture in which early-outcome signals support exploitation (repeat what worked) and late-outcome signals support exploration (probe the alternative when the policy appears unreliable), with the indirect pathway serving as the primary carrier of the exploration-biasing signal. This DMS indirect-pathway mechanism dovetails with two findings described in theplasticity section. First, it is consistent with the broader role of iSPNs inreversal learning and behavioral flexibility: optogenetic inhibition of iSPNs, but not dSPNs, in posterior DMS impairs the updating of goal-directed learning during reversal without affecting initial acquisition 9 , and iSPN activation suppresses the current action while simultaneously exciting alternative motor programs through inter-collicular competition 10 . Second, it connects to the opponent-plasticity logic of the OpAL* model, in which the indirect pathway’s preferential learning from negative outcomes endows it with a cost-sensitive representation that is well suited to detecting when the current policy’s expected returns have deteriorated below a switch threshold 11 . The DMS indirect pathway therefore appears to implement something close to a policy-reliability monitor : it tracks the cumulative evidence of suboptimality, and when that evidence exceeds a threshold it biases the next action toward the less-favored alternative, effectively converting an evaluative signal ("this policy is increasingly unreliable") into an exploratory action ("try the other option"). Territory-specific modulation of exploration: the dorsomedial striatum under uncertainty. The claim that the DMS is specifically engaged under conditions of reward uncertainty, and not merely during any form of action selection, receives support from multiple converging lines of evidence. Rodriguez, Naude, and colleagues used an adapted Iowa Gambling Task in mice combined with chemogenetic manipulation of pathway-specific populations across striatal territories, beginning by showing that decision-making profiles are a combination of archetypal strategies–Optimizers, Risk-averse, and Explorers–that reflect stable individual differences in sensitivity to reward magnitude, risk, and punishment 12 . Among three striatal territories tested (DMS, DLS, NAc), only DMS manipulations substantially altered decision-making strategies. Facilitating DMS dSPN activity decreased risk aversion, whereas facilitating DMS iSPN activity increased seemingly stochastic exploratory choices, an effect the authors link computationally to changes in reward saturation and the perception of outcome variance 12 . These findings reinforce the idea that the DMS is the striatal territory most centrally involved in flexible, uncertainty-sensitive exploration, consistent with its position in associative cortico-basal ganglia loops that receive convergent prefrontal, cingulate, and parietal input and operate on intermediate temporal horizons 13 , 14 . In primates, White and Monosov identified a population of neurons in an internal-capsule-bordering region of the dorsal striatum that selectively signal the uncertainty of object-reward associations 15 . These neurons responded most strongly when monkeys were presented with objects whose reward contingencies were ambiguous or still being learned, and their uncertainty responses evolved rapidly as the animal acquired new object-reward associations, diminishing as uncertainty was resolved. The finding is significant because it demonstrates that the primate dorsal striatum does not merely participate in actions aimed at known rewards, but actively represents the uncertainty of those rewards–precisely the variable that normative exploration strategies require to determine when to explore. Combined with DMS inactivation studies showing that DMS lesions selectively impair flexible decision adjustments under probabilistic, but not certain, reward contingencies 16 , the picture is one in which the dorsomedial striatal loop is preferentially recruited when the policy-optimization problem is not merely to select the best-known action but to manage the second-order problem of how much to trust that knowledge. Homeostatic gating of exploration: hunger and the tail of the striatum. The preceding mechanisms—directed exploration, novelty bonuses, policy-reliability monitoring, and uncertainty signaling—all operate within the domain of learned or learnable reward contingencies. But the most ancient and consequential instances of exploration are not triggered by abstract uncertainty computations; they are triggered by need . A sated animal can afford to exploit a known food source; a starving animal must range more widely, tolerate more risk, and approach novel stimuli that a sated animal would avoid. Recent work by Kamath, Lodder, Sabatini, and colleagues reveals a remarkably specific circuit through which hunger modulates exploration by acting on the dopaminergic system of the tail of the striatum 17 . In their experiments, food-deprived mice showed increased exploration of novel objects and faster habituation to novelty, and these behavioral changes were accompanied by suppression of dopamine signaling in the tail of the striatum (TOS). The causal chain was traced to AgRP neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus–the canonical "hunger neurons"–which polysynaptically project to TOS-projecting dopamine neurons through the lateral hypothalamus, central amygdala, and periaqueductal gray. Optogenetic activation of AgRP neurons in sated mice reproduced the hunger-like increase in exploration and the associated suppression of TOS dopamine transients; conversely, inhibiting AgRP neurons in hungry mice reduced exploration back toward sated levels 17 . The tail of the striatum, as described in the error-signal section, receives input from a distinctive population of lateral SNc/SNl dopamine neurons that respond to novel and salient sensory stimuli and encode something closer to threat prediction errors or action prediction errors than to classical reward RPEs 18 , 19 , 20 . The finding that hunger suppresses dopamine in this territory, rather than amplifying it, is therefore interpretable through the territory-specific loss-function framework developed earlier: TOS dopamine normally promotes avoidance and caution in the face of novel or salient stimuli, functioning as a conservative brake on approach. Hunger, by suppressing this signal, effectively releases the brake, allowing the animal to approach objects and environments that it would otherwise treat as potentially threatening. This is precisely what a homeostatic optimizer should do: when the opportunity cost of caution rises (because the animal is energetically depleted), the system shifts the explore-exploit boundary toward greater exploration by reducing the gain on a dopaminergic channel that normally penalizes approach to uncertain stimuli. The mechanism is not a global increase in dopaminergic tone or a simple amplification of reward signals; it is a targeted suppression of a specific avoidance-promoting dopaminergic channel , leaving reward-related dopamine in ventral and dorsomedial striatum relatively intact. This circuit provides a concrete biological instantiation of the homeostatic constraint on the BG loss function described in the loss-function section. There, it was argued that the dopaminergic system’s operating point is anchored to internal physiological state through hypothalamic and interoceptive inputs, so that the effective objective function is not "maximize reward" in the abstract but "maximize constrained subjective utility relative to current bodily need." The hunger-TOS pathway shows how this constraint operates in practice for exploration: internal need does not simply inflate the value of food-related actions; it restructures the boundary conditions of exploration by selectively modulating a dopaminergic channel that gates approach to novel and potentially dangerous stimuli. The result is an adaptive shift in the exploration-exploitation tradeoff that is not computed by a central explore-exploit controller, but emerges from the interaction between homeostatic circuitry and the territory-specific architecture of the dopaminergic system. The picture that emerges from these converging lines of evidence is not of a single "exploration switch" but of a distributed, multi-channel architecture in which different aspects of the exploration-exploitation tradeoff are handled by different components of the basal ganglia’s loss, error, and plasticity machinery. Distributional coding in opponent D1/D2 pathways provides the substrate for uncertainty estimation; transient dopaminergic novelty signals solve the cold-start problem for truly unfamiliar options; the DMS indirect pathway monitors policy reliability and generates exploratory switches when the current policy becomes unreliable; and hypothalamic-TOS circuitry globally modulates the scope of exploration as a function of internal need. These mechanisms are not independent channels operating in parallel isolation; they are nested within the same cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops, share the same dopaminergic teaching signal (albeit with territory-specific parameterizations), and are subject to the same cholinergic and interneuronal gating that determines where, when, and in what sign that teaching signal can write into corticostriatal weights. From the standpoint of the BG loss landscape, the exploration-exploitation tradeoff is therefore not a separate optimization problem bolted onto the side of policy learning; it is an intrinsic consequence of the loss landscape’s structure. A system that maintains distributional rather than mean-only value estimates has access to uncertainty for free. A system whose indirect pathway preferentially learns from negative outcomes has a built-in detector for policy failure. A system whose dopaminergic channels are heterogeneous across striatal territories—with ventral channels tracking long-horizon reward value, dorsomedial channels tracking intermediate-horizon action-outcome contingencies, and posterior channels tracking sensory salience and threat—can modulate different dimensions of exploration independently, without requiring a single scalar explore-exploit parameter. And a system whose dopaminergic operating point is grounded in homeostatic circuitry can shift the global explore-exploit balance as a function of bodily need without corrupting the learned value estimates on which exploitation depends. The result is a policy optimizer that does not merely select the best-known action, but continuously and adaptively manages the tension between exploiting what it knows and exploring what it does not—a tension that, as the loss-function section argued, is not peripheral to the BG’s computational mandate but central to it.

title: Skill Acquisition: From Goal-Directed to Habitual
text: The exploration-exploitation section described how the basal ganglia manage uncertainty and generate behavioral variability when contingencies are unknown. But the most consequential transformation the BG orchestrate is not a single decision under uncertainty; it is the long-arc process by which a novel, effortful, outcome-sensitive behavior is gradually compiled into a fast, stereotyped, and largely outcome-insensitive skill or habit. This transformation recruits, in sequence and in parallel, virtually every mechanism described in the preceding subsections: ventral striatal critic signals, dorsomedial flexible action-outcome learning, dorsolateral sequence crystallization, territory-specific plasticity regimes, distributional and multi-timescale error signals, opponent D1/D2 pathway dynamics, cholinergic gating, and the progressive remodeling of corticostriatal synaptic architecture. Tracing the full arc from goal-directed exploration to automatized execution therefore serves as the integrative case study for the BG optimization architecture. The process is best described not as a discrete three-stage pipeline but as a continuous, overlapping redistribution of influence across striatal territories and cortico-basal ganglia loops; for clarity, however, it is organized here into three broadly sequential phases that correspond to distinguishable behavioral and neural signatures. Phase 1: Goal-directed acquisition (ventral and dorsomedial dominance) . Early in learning, the organism confronts an environment whose action-outcome contingencies are unknown or poorly estimated. The computational demands at this stage are dominated by two problems: evaluating whether the current state of the world is worth engaging with, and discovering which actions produce which outcomes. These two problems map onto the ventral and dorsomedial striatal loops, respectively, and the neural and synaptic evidence reviewed in preceding sections converges on the conclusion that both are maximally engaged during early acquisition. The ventral striatum, operating as the critic side of the actor-critic architecture, provides the initial value scaffolding. Ventral striatal neurons encode state value and reward expectation, and the dopaminergic prediction errors they help generate are largest and most information-rich during early learning, when outcomes are maximally surprising. Recent primate work by Fujimoto, Bhatt, Bhatt, and colleagues extends this picture by showing that ventral striatal neurons do not merely passively encode value but actively transform value representations into action-selection signals: single-unit activity initially reflects the value of an offered option and then gradually shifts, within a trial, to reflect the monkey’s upcoming choice, as though the ventral striatum itself bridges valuation and commitment 1 . Optogenetic facilitation of dopamine input to the ventral striatum, as well as electrical stimulation of this region, causally altered the monkeys’ action selection, confirming that the ventral striatum is not merely a passive value register but an active participant in the conversion of motivational evaluation into behavioral output 1 . This finding dovetails with the actor-critic analysis in the loss-function section: the ventral striatum is critic-like in its dominant concern with state value, but it is not purely a critic—it contributes directly to the process by which value information is translated into the policy biases that determine which action is actually selected. During early learning, when value estimates are volatile and action-outcome mappings are being established for the first time, this bridging function is presumably at its most consequential. Meanwhile, the dorsomedial striatum supports the flexible, goal-directed component of early learning. DMS neurons encode action-outcome contingencies and are sensitive to outcome devaluation and contingency degradation—the hallmarks of goal-directed control 2 , 3 . At the network level, using in vivo recordings during rotarod skill learning, Yin, Mulcare, and colleagues showed that DMS neural activity is preferentially elevated during the early phase of training, with task-related firing rates in DMS peaking during the first sessions and declining thereafter 4 . Ex vivo recordings from DMS slices of early-trained mice revealed changes in excitatory synaptic transmission consistent with rapid corticostriatal potentiation, confirming that the early DMS engagement has a synaptic substrate 4 . At finer resolution, Badreddine, Bhatt, and colleagues used ex vivo two-photon calcium imaging to show that early training produces a distinctive DMS network signature: overall population activity decreases , but a small, sparsely distributed subset of highly active (HA) neurons emerges, and the size of this HA population correlates with individual learning performance 5 . The sparsity and rapid turnover of DMS ensembles during early learning is consistent with the symmetric anti-Hebbian STDP regime described in the plasticity section, which favors flexible rewriting of corticostriatal weights over durable stabilization 6 . Targeted silencing of these DMS HA cells with the cFos-TRAP strategy strongly impaired individual performance, confirming that the sparse early-phase DMS ensemble is not an epiphenomenon but a functional requirement for skill acquisition 5 . The dopaminergic teaching signal during this phase is large, bidirectional, and information-rich. In DMS-projecting dopamine terminals, prediction errors operate on intermediate temporal horizons and are sensitive to action-outcome contingencies 7 , 8 . The indirect pathway of the DMS is simultaneously active: as described in the exploration section, DMS iSPNs monitor the reliability of the current action policy and generate exploratory switches when outcomes are worse than expected 9 . During reversal or contingency change, iSPN-dependent updating is specifically required 10 . The cholinergic gating regime in DMS is reward-timed: dopamine transients that lag cholinergic dips at the offer cue predict trial-to-trial behavioral updating, consistent with a plasticity-promoting teaching mode 11 . In summary, Phase 1 is characterized by large prediction errors, flexible corticostriatal rewriting in DMS, active ventral striatal value-to-action bridging, indirect-pathway-mediated exploration and policy revision, and behavior that is sensitive to outcome value and contingency structure. Phase 2: Consolidation and the dorsomedial-to-dorsolateral transfer. With continued practice, a progressive shift occurs in which the dorsolateral striatum assumes an increasingly dominant role in behavioral control, while DMS engagement wanes. This shift is among the most replicated findings in basal ganglia neuroscience, having been documented with lesions, recordings, pharmacology, and imaging across species and task types 4 , 12 , 13 . In the Yin et al. rotarod study, in vivo recordings showed that DLS task-related neural activity was low during early training but increased progressively with practice, reaching its highest levels during the late, consolidated phase of skill learning—the temporal inverse of the DMS pattern 4 . Ex vivo recordings confirmed that this late-phase DLS engagement was accompanied by long-lasting potentiation of glutamatergic transmission, and—critically—this potentiation was preferentially expressed in striatopallidal (D2-expressing, indirect-pathway) neurons rather than striatonigral neurons 4 . This pathway-specific finding is notable because it resonates with the opponent plasticity framework: in DLS, progressive D2-pathway potentiation may reflect the stabilization of action-suppression representations that protect the consolidated skill from interference by competing motor programs, consistent with the DLS’s known role in behaviors that are resistant to extinction and insensitive to outcome devaluation 14 . At the network level, the DLS reorganization follows a qualitatively different trajectory than DMS. Whereas DMS produces a sparse, transient ensemble that is rapidly remodeled, DLS develops a progressive and long-lasting formation of spatially clustered highly active cell groups whose size and density increase monotonically with training duration 5 . Importantly, these DLS clusters arise not merely from synaptic strengthening but from anatomical rearrangements—changes in the spatial organization of responsive neurons—suggesting that the consolidation of skill in DLS involves structural remodeling of the corticostriatal network, not merely functional reweighting of existing connections 5 . This structural plasticity extends to the presynaptic side: recent longitudinal two-photon imaging of motor cortical axonal boutons in the DLS of awake mice showed that motor learning induces a transient burst of new bouton formation followed by selective stabilization of boutons responsive to rewarded movements and elimination of those responsive to unrewarded movements 15 . The structural dynamics of DLS learning are therefore bidirectional and functionally selective: the circuit does not merely add connections; it prunes unrewarded pathways while consolidating rewarded ones, yielding a progressively more refined and movement-specific corticostriatal architecture. The anatomical substrate for the DMS-to-DLS transfer has classically been attributed to the spiraling striato-nigro-striatal architecture described by Haber and colleagues, in which ventral striatal territories influence progressively more dorsal dopamine populations through ascending loops 16 . As noted in the error-signal section, the strongest version of this spiral model has been tempered by evidence for both closed loops and more diffuse input organization, but the core principle—that ventral and medial striatal value signals can indirectly shape dopaminergic teaching in dorsolateral territories—remains the best available account of how value learning in one loop can progressively tutor policy learning in another. Complementing this indirect route, the dopamine signal itself changes character across the transfer. In DLS, dopamine dynamics are the fastest of any striatal territory, integrating reward history over the fewest trials and reflecting the steepest temporal discounting 7 . Moreover, dopamine signals in DLS are positively shifted: reward responses remain non-negative even for outcomes worse than expected, and clear inhibitory dips to negative prediction errors are absent or strongly attenuated 8 . This positive bias means that the effective teaching signal in DLS preferentially stamps in actions that were at least minimally successful, without erasing them when outcomes occasionally fall short—a property ideally suited to the consolidation of a well-practiced skill that should be robust to occasional failure. The asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP regime in DLS further supports this stability: as described in the plasticity section, DLS plasticity rules favor memory maintenance over memory flexibility, providing a synaptic correlate of the behavioral transition from outcome-sensitive to outcome-insensitive control 6 . The cholinergic regime in DLS likewise shifts. Whereas DMS cholinergic dynamics are reward-timed and plasticity-promoting, DLS cholinergic interneuron activity is more movement-timed: CIN bursts coincide with movement events rather than reward events, and coincident dopamine predicts the vigor of upcoming movements without evidence of lasting plasticity 11 , 17 . This transition from a learning mode to a performance/vigor mode in the local neuromodulatory environment is consistent with the broader shift from policy updating to policy execution that characterizes the DMS-to-DLS transfer. A crucial point, emphasized in the user’s notes and supported by recent evidence, is that the DMS-to-DLS transfer is not a simple serial handoff . Both territories are simultaneously active throughout learning, but they develop different task-related patterns with different dynamics. The Vandaele, Bhatt, and colleagues study found that, contrary to the canonical expectation, distinct DMS and DLS activity patterns were present during early training but converged with extended training, and performance after extended training was not associated with DMS disengagement 18 . Even more strikingly, Turner and colleagues showed that DMS and DLS can compete for behavioral control: in a five-step heterogeneous action sequencing task optimized for habitual responding, DMS lesions accelerated sequence acquisition—rats became faster, more accurate, and more stereotyped sooner–whereas DLS lesions impeded it 19 . This result is difficult to reconcile with a purely cooperative model and instead supports a competitive-opposition account in which DMS-mediated goal-directed control actively gates or restrains the transition to DLS-mediated automaticity. The implication is that the DMS does not simply hand off control to DLS when its job is done; rather, DMS continuously competes with DLS for behavioral expression, and the shift toward habitual control reflects a change in the balance of this competition–a balance that is itself regulated by the dopaminergic, cholinergic, and cortical inputs that set the relative excitability and plasticity of the two territories. The lateral orbitofrontal cortex, but not medial prefrontal cortex, was found to be critical for this balance, suggesting that cortical evaluation of action outcomes feeds into the competitive dynamics between striatal subregions 19 . Phase 3: Crystallization, chunking, and cortical disengagement. The final phase of the goal-directed-to-habitual arc is the crystallization of individual actions into concatenated sequences that are processed as single behavioral units ("chunks") and the progressive transfer of motor-program specification from cortical to subcortical circuits. This phase represents the endpoint of BG policy optimization for a given skill: the policy is no longer being searched or revised; it is being compiled into a format that minimizes the computational and metabolic cost of execution. The neural signature of chunking in the DLS is the task-bracketing pattern : with extensive training, DLS neurons develop concentrated activity at the initiation and termination of well-learned action sequences, with suppressed or below-baseline activity during the interior of the sequence 12 , 20 . This pattern has been replicated across maze navigation, lever-pressing, and oculomotor tasks in rodents and primates 12 , and it is remarkably durable: reward devaluation after prolonged overtraining hardly changes it, and even extinction (complete reward removal) only temporarily suppresses it–the pattern reappears almost immediately when rewards are reinstated, indicating that the underlying synaptic architecture is latent but not erased 12 . This extinction-resistance is precisely what the DLS plasticity regime predicts: asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP, positively biased dopamine signals, and progressive structural consolidation of corticostriatal ensembles all favor durable, extinction-resistant memory traces 6 , 8 . The task-bracketing pattern is computationally significant because it implies that the DLS treats the entire action sequence as a single macro-action, with explicit representations only at the boundaries. In reinforcement-learning terms, this is hierarchical chunking : instead of selecting each element of a sequence independently (which would require a separate selection-evaluation cycle for every action), the BG select the chunk as a unit, and the internal elements are executed ballistically under local motor-circuit control. This dramatically reduces the computational and metabolic cost of action selection by collapsing a multi-step decision problem into a single policy choice. The start signal disinhibits a cortical or subcortical motor program that itself specifies the temporal sequence of sub-elements; the stop signal terminates it and returns control to the higher-level selection process. The anti-Hebbian STDP rule in DLS is computationally suited for encoding the temporal order within these chunks: Vignoud and colleagues showed that anti-Hebbian plasticity, when combined with the characteristic spike latency and collateral inhibition of SPNs, enables striatal circuits to learn spike sequences, providing a synaptic-level mechanism for how temporal order is written into DLS representations 21 . The DLS does not, however, only mark sequence boundaries. Dhawale, Wolff, Ko, and Ölveczky showed that the sensorimotor arm of the basal ganglia circuit specifies and controls the fine-grained kinematic details of learned motor skills, not merely their initiation and termination 22 . DLS neurons encoded the detailed movement trajectories of well-trained rats on a trial-by-trial basis, and lesioning DLS abolished the idiosyncratic kinematic signatures of the learned skill—the animals could still move, but the specific, stereotyped movement patterns they had acquired through training were lost 22 . Importantly, these DLS representations and the control functions they subserve did not depend on inputs from motor cortex: even after motor cortex lesions, striatal neural activity retained its sequential, kinematic-encoding structure 22 . This result extends the BG’s role beyond action selection and chunking to encompass the continuous, moment-by-moment shaping of movement kinematics during automatized execution. This last finding connects to one of the most striking demonstrations of cortical disengagement during skill consolidation. Kawai, Ölveczky, and colleagues showed that motor cortex is required for learning a skilled motor sequence but not for executing it: motor cortex lesions performed after asymptotic training had no discernible effect on the acquired skill, which was expressed in its distinct pre-lesion form on the very first day of post-lesion testing 23 . Hwang and colleagues extended this by showing that motor cortex gradually disengages from movement control over the course of long-term learning, with optogenetic inactivation of motor cortex producing progressively smaller behavioral deficits as training proceeds 24 . The implication is that motor cortex serves as a "tutor" during skill acquisition–providing the rich, flexible corticostriatal drive that enables DMS-and then DLS-dependent learning–but that the ultimate repository of the learned motor program is subcortical, residing in the corticostriatal and thalamostriatal synaptic weights of DLS and in the downstream brainstem and spinal circuits that DLS modulates through its output via GPi/SNr 23 , 22 , 25 . A recent perspective by Grillner formalizes this endpoint, proposing that the DLS-SNr-parafascicular thalamus-DLS loop, subdivided into many parallel channels with precise cortical input, constitutes the minimal circuit for storing and executing crystallized motor programs once cortical tutoring is complete 26 . The composite picture of the goal-directed-to-habitual arc can now be stated in the vocabulary of the preceding BG subsections. Early in learning, the ventral striatum provides the critic-like value scaffolding that converts motivational state into action-selection biases, while the DMS supports flexible, outcome-sensitive action-outcome learning through rapid corticostriatal rewriting under large, bidirectional dopaminergic prediction errors and cholinergic plasticity gating. With continued practice, the balance of influence shifts toward DLS–not through a discrete handoff but through a competitive rebalancing in which DMS goal-directed control progressively yields to DLS habitual control. The DLS develops spatially clustered, structurally consolidated corticostriatal ensembles under an asymmetric anti-Hebbian plasticity regime, positively biased dopamine signals, and movement-timed cholinergic dynamics. At the endpoint, individual actions have been concatenated into chunks marked by task-bracketing boundary signals, the fine-grained kinematics of the skill are specified by DLS representations operating through subcortical motor circuits, and the motor cortex that originally tutored the learning has largely disengaged from execution. The entire transformation can be read as a progression through the BG’s multi-timescale, territory-specific loss landscape: from a regime dominated by long-horizon, high-uncertainty, outcome-sensitive evaluation (ventral and dorsomedial loops) to a regime dominated by short-horizon, low-uncertainty, execution-optimized control (dorsolateral loops). This is the BG’s version of a curriculum—but where cortical learning curricula are typically organized over representational depth (and over developmental timescales), the BG curriculum is organized over policy type : from flexible, model-informed, goal-directed policies to rigid, stimulus-bound, automatized policies whose computational and metabolic cost of execution is minimized.

title: Cognitive Gating: The BG as a Policy Over Thought
text: The preceding sections described how the basal ganglia manage the exploration-exploitation tradeoff and orchestrate the long-arc transition from goal-directed to habitual motor control. Both accounts treated the "actions" gated by the BG as overt motor outputs—movements, sequences, kinematic trajectories. But the parallel-loop architecture developed throughout this chapter implies something far more general: because the basal ganglia are embedded in limbic, associative, and sensorimotor cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops, they gate not only skeletal movements but also cognitive operations —working-memory updating, attentional set-shifting, task-set selection, strategy deployment, and the retrieval or suppression of internal goals. In this extended sense, the BG implement a policy over thought : they learn, through dopaminergic reinforcement, when to allow new information into prefrontal working memory, when to protect maintained representations from distraction, which cognitive strategy to deploy in a given context, and when to switch from one interpretive frame to another. The same opponent D1/D2 plasticity that trains motor action selection trains these cognitive gating policies; the same distributional and multi-timescale error signals that evaluate motor outcomes evaluate cognitive ones; and the same territory-specific plasticity regimes that distinguish flexible goal-directed motor learning from rigid habitual execution may, in principle, distinguish flexible cognitive strategies from deeply automatized mental routines. This section makes that abstract claim concrete. Working-memory gating: the PBWM framework and extensions. The most fully developed computational account of BG-mediated cognitive gating is the prefrontal cortex basal ganglia working memory (PBWM) model, introduced by O’Reilly and Frank and extended in subsequent work 1 , 2 , 3 . The core insight is architectural: prefrontal cortex maintains information through recurrent excitatory connectivity–sustained firing patterns that persist after a stimulus has been removed–but this very persistence creates a dilemma. If PFC representations are easily overwritten, they cannot serve as a stable working-memory buffer; if they are too stable, they cannot be updated when new task-relevant information arrives. The PBWM model resolves this maintenance-versus-updating tradeoff by assigning the basal ganglia the role of a learned dynamic gate . PFC is organized into separable "stripes"–anatomical clusters of interconnected neurons that are functionally isolated from other stripes–and each stripe is gated by a corresponding basal ganglia channel 1 . When direct-pathway ("Go") neurons in the striatal channel fire, they disinhibit the thalamocortical loop for that stripe, triggering an update of its working-memory contents with whatever cortical input is currently active (in vivo, likely those contents held in cortical regions corresponding to the prefrontal stripe). When indirect-pathway ("NoGo") neurons dominate, the gate remains closed and the existing PFC representation is maintained against distractors. The gating decision itself–whether to open or close–is learned through dopaminergic reinforcement: positive prediction errors (dopamine bursts) potentiate corticostriatal Go synapses that were active at the time of a successful gate, while negative prediction errors (dopamine dips) potentiate NoGo synapses, gradually shaping a gating policy that admits task-relevant information and excludes irrelevant input 1 . This gating architecture is not limited to a single operation. The PBWM model and its descendants distinguish at least three separable gating functions: input gating (whether to encode a new item into a PFC stripe), maintenance (whether to protect the current contents of a stripe from overwriting), and output gating (which of the currently maintained items should be read out to influence downstream processing or response selection) 1 , 2 . The combination of input and output gating decisions made on each trial constitutes the gating policy , and it is this policy–not merely the contents of working memory–that the BG learn to optimize through reinforcement. The computational consequence is that the BG do not simply store or retrieve information; they learn a control program that governs the flow of information through prefrontal circuits, determining what enters working memory, what persists there, and what influences behavior at any given moment. Empirical evidence supports key predictions of this framework. Patients with Parkinson’s disease, whose striatal dopamine depletion produces an exaggerated NoGo bias, show impaired working-memory updating while simultaneously exhibiting increased resistance to distractors—a double dissociation that follows directly from the opponent Go/NoGo architecture applied to the cognitive domain 4 , 5 . Dopaminergic medication reverses these effects, restoring updating at the cost of increased distractibility. Human eye-blink rate, a putative peripheral marker of phasic striatal dopamine, increases on trials that require working-memory updating and on trials that require gate switching, consistent with the PBWM prediction that both operations depend on striatal dopaminergic gating signals 6 . And individual differences in genetic variants affecting striatal D1 and D2 receptor function predict individual differences in Go versus NoGo learning in probabilistic reinforcement tasks, with the effects being specific to striatal genotypes rather than prefrontal dopaminergic genotypes–consistent with the model’s assignment of the gating computation to the striatum rather than to PFC itself 7 , 8 . A recent and theoretically important extension of the PBWM framework concerns adaptive chunking in working memory. This work showed that a neural network model of PFC-BG interactions can learn to reuse the same prefrontal populations to store multiple items, effectively compressing several distinct stimuli into shared PFC representations 9 . This chunking strategy trades precision for capacity: by gating multiple items into the same PFC stripe, the system can hold more items in working memory, but the individual item representations become less precise. Here, the decision of whether and how to chunk is itself learned through dopaminergic reinforcement in the BG gating circuits, making it a task-dependent policy choice rather than a fixed architectural constraint. The model required a dynamic range of dopaminergic signals to adjust striatal gating policies across different working-memory demands, and the authors note that this provides a new interpretation of working-memory difficulties in clinical populations such as Parkinson’s disease, ADHD, and schizophrenia: these disorders may involve not merely a deficit in storage capacity but a failure to adaptively learn the gating policies–including chunking strategies–that determine how effectively the available capacity is used 9 . From the standpoint of the BG loss landscape developed in the preceding subsections, adaptive chunking is a striking example of the BG optimizing not merely which action to take (store this item or not) but how to represent the relevant information–a policy over the format of thought, not merely its content. The "actions" metaphor taken literally: cognitive operations as policy variables. The PBWM model treats working-memory gating as a cognitive "action" that the BG learn to select, but this metaphor can—and arguably should—be taken literally. In the active-inference framework, overt movements and covert cognitive operations are both policies selected under the same variational optimization logic: the agent selects among candidate policies (sequences of state transitions, whether muscular or cognitive) on the basis of expected free energy, which scores both the pragmatic value (reward, goal-satisfaction) and the epistemic value (information gain, uncertainty reduction) of each policy 10 , 11 , 12 . In this formulation, the basal ganglia’s disinhibitory gating mechanism is not merely analogous to motor action selection; it is action selection, operating over a different action space. The ventral and dorsomedial cortico-basal ganglia loops, which receive convergent input from prefrontal, cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortices, are positioned to gate prefrontal representations that determine what cognitive "policy" is currently active–whether to maintain a working-memory trace, shift attentional focus, switch task sets, retrieve a new goal from long-term memory, or deploy a particular reasoning strategy. The dopaminergic δ \delta that evaluates motor outcomes evaluates cognitive outcomes by the same logic: a positive prediction error following a successful working-memory update, a well-timed attentional shift, or a correctly deployed strategy reinforces the corticostriatal weights that produced it, just as it would reinforce the weights that produced a successful grasp. Recent computational work makes this unification especially explicit: they model working-memory maintenance as itself a type of policy selection within an active-inference generative model, casting the decision to hold a percept in working memory as a cognitive action implemented through PFC-basal ganglia loops 12 . The formal parallel with motor gating is precise: in both cases, the BG evaluate candidate policies (gate open versus gate closed; maintain versus update; attend versus ignore) on the basis of expected free energy, and in both cases, the selected policy is executed through disinhibition of thalamocortical circuits. The implication is that the BG’s policy-optimization mandate, as described in the loss-function section, extends without modification to the cognitive domain: the same territory-specific objective functions, the same distributional and multi-timescale error signals, and the same opponent D1/D2 plasticity that optimize motor policies optimize cognitive ones, with the crucial difference being the identity of the cortical state representations over which the optimization operates. Frank and Badre provided one of the most detailed accounts of how this cognitive gating architecture supports hierarchical cognitive control . In their model, nested cortico-striatal circuits at different rostro-caudal levels of frontal cortex each gate cognitive representations at a particular level of abstraction 13 . More anterior (rostral) frontal regions maintain more abstract contextual representations—task rules, category-level goals—and their BG gating circuits learn to selectively admit higher-order contextual information. More posterior (caudal) frontal regions maintain more concrete stimulus-response mappings, and their gating is modulated by the output of the rostral circuits. The result is a hierarchy of learned gating policies in which the BG at each level learn, through dopaminergic reinforcement, which contextual information should be gated into PFC at that level of abstraction. Functional MRI evidence confirmed key predictions: rostral prefrontal and striatal activations tracked the discovery of abstract hierarchical rules in a reinforcement-learning task, and the computational model’s trial-by-trial estimates of latent hypothesis states predicted the BOLD signal in individual cortico-striatal circuits at specific levels of policy abstraction 14 . This finding extends the BG’s domain from simple action selection to the kind of structured, multi-level cognitive control that supports human reasoning, planning, and rule use. Reinforcement learning over strategies: meta-learning and the prefrontal-BG system. The hierarchical gating architecture just described allows the BG to learn which task rules and contextual representations to maintain; but the most powerful form of cognitive gating may be the BG’s role in learning strategies themselves . Collins and Frank showed that human learning on multi-stimulus, multi-response tasks is not well described by a single reinforcement-learning system but instead reflects the interaction of at least two partially dissociable systems: an incremental BG-dependent RL system and a prefrontal working-memory system that can maintain recent stimulus-response mappings in a fast, capacity-limited buffer 15 . The relative contribution of these two systems depends on task demands—set size, delay, interference—and the BG learn not only the stimulus-response mappings themselves but also the task-set structure : which stimuli should be grouped under the same abstract rule, which rules should be created anew versus retrieved from a library of previously learned task sets, and how policies should be transferred and composed across novel situations 16 , 17 . In these models, the BG gating circuitry operates at two levels simultaneously: at the lower level, it gates specific stimulus-response mappings; at the higher level, it gates the selection of the abstract task set under which those mappings are organized. Dopaminergic reinforcement operates at both levels, enabling the system to perform conditional "if-then" hypothesis testing and to discover hierarchical structure through experience 13 . Wang, Kurth-Nelson, Kumaran, and colleagues pushed this logic further, proposing that the dopaminergic system trains prefrontal cortex not merely to implement a fixed policy but to operate as its own free-standing meta-learning system 18 . In their account, slow dopamine-dependent corticostriatal plasticity shapes the recurrent dynamics of PFC over many tasks, such that PFC acquires a general-purpose learning algorithm implemented in its own activation dynamics. This "meta-learned" PFC system can then adapt rapidly to new tasks—within a single episode—without requiring further synaptic change, because the adaptation occurs through the fast dynamics of prefrontal activity rather than through slow weight modification. The BG’s role in this framework is to provide the slow outer-loop optimization that sculpts prefrontal dynamics over the developmental and experiential timescale: dopaminergic prediction errors, broadcasting through corticostriatal loops, gradually tune the recurrent connectivity of PFC until its fast dynamics implement an efficient learning algorithm for the kinds of tasks the organism regularly encounters. This is RL over RL: the BG learn a policy for how to learn , not merely a policy for what to do. The meta-learning framework has a natural interpretation in terms of the territory-specific loss landscape developed earlier. The ventral and dorsomedial striatal loops, which operate on longer temporal horizons and receive convergent input from prefrontal, cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortices, are well positioned to learn the abstract, slowly changing strategic variables—which task set to deploy, which learning rate to use, which information to attend to—that constitute the meta-policy. The dorsolateral loops, operating on shorter horizons, may then implement the concrete motor and cognitive actions dictated by the currently active strategy. In this picture, strategy selection and meta-learning are simply the highest levels of a hierarchical policy that the BG optimize across their full territory-specific gradient, from abstract goals (ventromedial) through intermediate action-outcome contingencies (dorsomedial) to concrete motor execution (dorsolateral). The same dopaminergic teaching signals, parameterized by different discount factors, asymmetric error scalings, and cholinergic gating regimes, operate at each level—but the "actions" they evaluate become progressively more abstract as one ascends the hierarchy. This perspective connects to a broader set of cognitive competences that can be reframed as BG-gated policies over internal operations. Metamemory —the monitoring of one’s own memory confidence and the strategic allocation of encoding effort—can be understood as a gating policy over hippocampal-prefrontal memory encoding: the BG learn when it is worth investing cognitive resources in committing an experience to memory and when those resources are better deployed elsewhere. Metacognition more broadly—the evaluation of one’s own decision-making process, including judgments of confidence, the decision to seek more information, and the decision to commit to a choice—partially maps onto the STN-mediated threshold-adjustment and conflict-monitoring computations described in the loss-function section, but applied to the cognitive rather than the motor domain: the BG regulate how much evidence to accumulate before committing to a cognitive judgment, just as they regulate how much evidence to accumulate before committing to a motor action 19 . Game strategy and social reasoning —choosing which interpersonal or competitive strategy to deploy in a multi-agent setting—likewise require the selection of abstract, context-dependent cognitive policies; the BG’s associative loops, receiving input from prefrontal and cingulate cortices that represent social and strategic variables, are positioned to gate these selections through the same disinhibitory mechanism that gates motor actions. In each of these domains, the formal structure is the same: cortex represents the space of possible cognitive operations, and the BG evaluate, select, and reinforce particular operations on the basis of dopaminergic credit assignment. Speculative extension: cognitive habitization and the rigidity of mental routines. The skill-acquisition section described in detail how the BG orchestrate a progressive transfer of behavioral control from flexible, goal-directed, DMS-dependent policies to rigid, automatized, DLS-dependent habits. The question naturally arises: does a parallel transfer occur for cognitive routines? If the BG gate cognitive operations through the same cortico-basal ganglia loops that gate motor actions, and if these loops are subject to the same territory-specific plasticity regimes that differentiate DMS from DLS, then it is at least plausible that well-practiced cognitive strategies—habitual modes of attention, reflexive interpretive frames, automatic emotional appraisals, default reasoning heuristics—undergo a similar transition from flexible, outcome-sensitive, "goal-directed" cognitive control to rigid, stimulus-bound, "habitual" cognitive control. Several lines of evidence, though none definitive, support this speculation. First, at the behavioral level, cognitive routines clearly become more automatic with practice: expert chess players, experienced clinicians, and fluent readers all deploy complex cognitive operations that were once effortful and deliberate in a rapid, seemingly reflexive manner, with reduced demands on attentional resources and reduced sensitivity to the details of the current context—precisely the behavioral signatures of the goal-directed-to-habitual transition in the motor domain. Second, neuroimaging studies of skill learning across cognitive and motor domains report a common pattern in which prefrontal and parietal attentional-control regions show decreasing activation with practice, while striatal and premotor regions show increasing or reorganized activation—a pattern that is at least consistent with a shift from dorsomedial (associative) to dorsolateral (sensorimotor) cortico-basal ganglia engagement, though the imaging evidence cannot by itself confirm a DMS-to-DLS transfer for cognitive routines 20 , 21 . Third, Graybiel’s influential definition of habits emphasizes that they extend beyond motor behaviors to include cognitive processes, and recent work on "attentional habits" shows that learned attentional biases can exhibit hallmark properties of motor habits—automaticity, insensitivity to outcome devaluation, and inflexibility—suggesting that at least some forms of attention are governed by the same corticostriatal habit machinery that governs motor routines 22 . The critical question, however, is whether the DMS-to-DLS transfer mechanism documented for motor habits operates in the cognitive domain. Here the evidence is more ambiguous. The executive loop connecting lateral prefrontal cortex with the caudate (the primate homolog of DMS) does not have a cleanly established "habitual" counterpart in the sensorimotor putamen (DLS homolog) for purely cognitive routines; the cognitive and motor loops, while sharing architectural principles, involve partially distinct cortical territories and may not be organized in exactly the same hierarchical gradient 21 . Baladron and Hamker’s hierarchical model of multiple BG loops offers one possible resolution: in their framework, each loop learns to select intermediate objectives at a different abstraction level, and a learned "shortcut" pathway that bypasses the higher loops can link stimulus information directly with motor execution, providing the motor loops with less cognitive influence and leading to faster, more habitual behavior 23 . Applied to the cognitive domain, an analogous shortcut might allow well-practiced cognitive operations—initially mediated by the associative (DMS) loop in a flexible, context-sensitive manner—to be triggered more directly by stimuli through cortico-cortical connections that have been trained by BG-dependent learning but no longer require BG gating for execution. This is precisely the mechanism by which Helie, Ashby, and colleagues proposed that the BG train robust cortico-cortical connections during initial learning, which then support automatized performance independently of BG involvement 20 . If cognitive habitization does occur through mechanisms analogous to motor habitization, the implications would be far-reaching. Well-practiced attentional biases—the tendency to interpret ambiguous stimuli in a particular way, to deploy a particular reasoning heuristic by default, or to appraise emotional situations through a particular evaluative frame—might shift from flexible, outcome-sensitive, DMS-mediated control to rigid, stimulus-bound, automatized routines that are resistant to extinction and insensitive to devaluation, just as motor habits are. The asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP regime in DLS, the positively biased dopamine signals, and the progressive structural consolidation of corticostriatal ensembles described in the plasticity section would all favor the durability and inflexibility of these cognitive habits. This could help explain why some cognitive styles—chronic worry patterns, ruminative thinking, rigid interpretive frames in psychopathology, but also adaptive expertise and fluent professional judgment—are so resistant to deliberate revision: they may have been compiled into corticostriatal weight configurations whose plasticity regime actively resists rewriting, just as overtrained motor habits resist extinction even after reward contingencies have changed 24 . The therapeutic difficulty of dislodging deeply practiced maladaptive cognitive habits—a central challenge in cognitive-behavioral therapy and related interventions—may thus reflect not merely a motivational or insight deficit, but a genuine circuit-level rigidity inherited from the same DLS plasticity machinery that makes motor habits durable. This account should be flagged as speculative. The evidence for a complete DMS-to-DLS transfer in purely cognitive routines remains indirect, and the cognitive and motor cortico-basal ganglia loops may differ in ways that preclude a simple isomorphism. Moreover, the degree to which "cognitive habits" are truly BG-dependent—as opposed to being stored in cortico-cortical connections that were initially trained by BG mechanisms but subsequently operate autonomously—remains an open question. What can be said with reasonable confidence is that the BG’s policy-optimization machinery is not confined to the motor domain; that the same opponent D1/D2 plasticity, dopaminergic credit assignment, and hierarchical gating architecture that select and reinforce motor actions also select and reinforce cognitive operations including working-memory updating, task-set selection, strategy deployment, and attentional allocation; and that the territory-specific and training-dependent plasticity regimes that differentiate flexible from habitual motor control provide at least a plausible neural substrate for the analogous distinction between flexible and automatized cognitive control. The BG, on this view, are not merely the brain’s motor optimizer. They are its general-purpose policy optimizer —a system that learns, through dopaminergic reinforcement, which cortical computations to gate, energize, suppress, or automatize, whether those computations produce a movement, a memory update, or a thought.
