title: Developmental Bootstrapping of the BG Optimizer
text: The preceding sections described the BG’s policy-optimization machinery as though it arrives fully formed: distributional error signals, opponent plasticity, territory-specific loss functions, cholinergic gating, and hierarchical cognitive control all operating in concert. But the BG optimizer does not start from a blank slate, nor does it come online all at once. Its objective function, its teaching-signal infrastructure, and its corticostriatal connectivity are themselves bootstrapped over a protracted developmental timescale that spans from the prenatal specification of dopaminergic pathways through adolescent circuit refinement, with different components of the optimization stack maturing at different rates and in a functionally consequential sequence. This developmental ordering is not incidental; it defines which kinds of policy learning are available at each stage of life and, by implication, which aspects of the organism’s value landscape are laid down first and therefore exert the strongest structural constraint on all subsequent learning. The initial preference distribution is anchored to homeostatic correction. The BG optimizer’s first operating environment is the neonatal world, in which the only contexts reliably driving strong dopaminergic prediction errors are those that correct acute homeostatic imbalances. In altricial mammals, virtually all early reward structure derives from maternal interaction: milk delivery corrects caloric and fluid depletion, thermal contact resolves cold stress, tactile stimulation regulates autonomic and hormonal milieu. Because these are the events most reliably available in early postnatal life, and because they are intrinsically coupled to interoceptive repletion signals—gastric stretch, rising blood glucose, skin warming, declining cortisol—the first value functions the corticostriatal system learns are necessarily tethered to homeostatic set points. The mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway, comprising VTA projections to the nucleus accumbens and ventral striatum, is functional relatively early in postnatal development: in rodents, dopaminergic fibers reach the striatum and nucleus accumbens by the late embryonic period (approximately E15-E17), and the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic pathways largely complete their basic wiring during the first postnatal week 1 , 2 . This early functionality means that the mesolimbic system is positioned to generate reward prediction errors in response to homeostatic correction events well before the cortical representations over which those errors are computed have achieved anything approaching adult sophistication. The predictions that VTA GABA neurons and lateral hypothalamic projections encode as the infant’s first conditional expectations are predictions about interoceptive state—about the arrival of milk, warmth, and contact—not about abstract symbolic variables. In this sense, the initial "loss function" of the BG optimizer is defined not by a general-purpose reward-maximization mandate, but by the specific homeostatic error signals that the hypothalamic-VTA architecture is pre-wired to detect. This is not merely a starting condition that is later overwritten; it is a structural constraint that persists throughout life, ensuring that however abstract the BG’s value computations become, they remain tethered to biological viability through the interoceptive grounding of the dopaminergic prediction baseline described at length in the error-signal section 3 , 4 . As the infant’s cortical representations mature, the BG gain access to progressively richer state spaces over which to compute value. The developmental trajectory of corticostriatal functional connectivity reflects this expansion with remarkable clarity. In a large resting-state fMRI study spanning ages 3-42, Bhargava and colleagues showed that dorsal striatal connectivity to sensorimotor cortical regions is established early and remains strong through childhood and adolescence, supporting sensory-seeking behaviors and basic habit formation during these developmental periods 5 . Connectivity to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex emerged only in adolescence, while connectivity to dorsomedial prefrontal and posterior cortical regions belonging to attentional and default-mode networks was not observed until adulthood 5 . This ventral-to-dorsal, sensorimotor-to-associative, and local-to-long-range developmental gradient in corticostriatal connectivity means that the BG’s policy-optimization machinery operates over a progressively expanding cortical state space: early in life, the system can learn policies over sensorimotor and limbic representations (simple stimulus-reward associations, basic approach-avoidance); later, as associative and prefrontal loops come online, it can learn policies over increasingly abstract representations including action-outcome contingencies, task rules, working-memory contents, and strategic variables. Secondary reinforcers–social approval, symbolic reward, abstract goal satisfaction–are not hard-wired but emerge from the same TD learning machinery operating over cortically enriched state representations, constructed through chains of associative and identity prediction errors anchored, ultimately, to the early-established homeostatic baseline. The developmental expansion of the BG optimizer’s computational reach is not driven solely by cortical maturation; it also depends on the maturation of the dopaminergic teaching signal itself, which follows a strikingly pathway-specific timetable. In rodents, the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic dopamine pathways largely complete their basic innervation during the first postnatal week, but the mesocortical dopamine pathway—VTA projections to prefrontal cortex—has a uniquely protracted maturation that continues through adolescence and into early adulthood 1 , 6 , 2 . The density of dopamine fibers in prefrontal regions increases progressively from the late embryonic period through adulthood, a pattern replicated across rodents and primates 2 , 6 . Remarkably, Reynolds, Bhatt, and colleagues showed using dual viral tracing that a significant subset of mesocortical dopamine axons are still physically growing from the nucleus accumbens to the prefrontal cortex during adolescence–the only known case of long-distance axon growth at this developmental stage (based on the 2017 article)–and that the extent of this growth is regulated by the Netrin-1 guidance cue receptor DCC, which determines target recognition events in axons passing through the striatum 7 , 8 . This protracted mesocortical maturation has a direct computational implication for the BG optimizer: the cognitive gating functions described in the preceding section–working-memory updating, attentional control, task-set selection, hierarchical rule learning, and meta-learning–depend on dopaminergic modulation of prefrontal circuits, and these circuits are not fully innervated until early adulthood. The BG’s capacity to learn cognitive policies (the PBWM-style gating of prefrontal representations) therefore comes online substantially later than its capacity to learn basic appetitive and sensorimotor policies, potentially explaining why young children can learn simple stimulus-reward associations and motor skills but struggle with tasks requiring flexible cognitive control and abstract rule use. In parallel with the protracted growth of mesocortical fibers, the dopamine receptor landscape itself undergoes developmental remodeling. In rat dorsal striatum, D1 and D2 receptor densities peak around puberty (approximately postnatal day 28-40) and are subsequently pruned back to adult levels, with reductions of 35-40% from peak values 9 , 10 . In the nucleus accumbens, by contrast, receptor densities plateau without the same pronounced pruning, suggesting territory-specific developmental trajectories that may differentially shape the learning dynamics of ventral versus dorsal loops during adolescence 9 . In prefrontal cortex, the maturation of dopaminergic modulation follows yet another trajectory: before mid-adolescence, D2 receptor stimulation has weak or negligible effects on GABAergic interneuron firing, but after adolescence an excitatory D2 effect on interneurons emerges that creates the inhibitory tone characteristic of the mature prefrontal circuit 2 , 1 . This adolescent shift in dopaminergic regulation of prefrontal excitation-inhibition balance is thought to be a critical step in the developmental calibration of cognitive control, and its disruption may contribute to psychiatric disorders of adolescent onset 2 . The well-documented adolescent profile–heightened reward sensitivity, increased sensation-seeking, greater risk tolerance, and relatively immature cognitive control–can be read, through the framework developed in this chapter, as a developmental mismatch between components of the BG optimization stack that mature at different rates 11 , 12 . The ventral striatal/mesolimbic system, which provides the critic-like value scaffolding and motivational drive described in the loss-function and skill-acquisition sections, is functionally mature by early adolescence and shows peak reward reactivity during this period: fMRI studies consistently report that ventral striatal activation to reward anticipation and receipt follows an inverted-U developmental trajectory, peaking in mid-adolescence and declining toward adult levels 11 , 13 . Meanwhile, the dorsomedial and prefrontal components of the BG optimizer—the associative loops that support goal-directed control, the cognitive gating circuits that implement hierarchical rule use and working-memory management, and the mesocortical dopamine projections that modulate all of these functions—are still maturing, with long-range striatal-prefrontal connectivity not reaching adult patterns until the mid-twenties 5 , 14 . The result, in the vocabulary of this chapter, is a BG optimizer whose ventral/limbic loss functions and error signals are operating at full gain while its dorsomedial/associative policy-learning and cognitive-gating circuits are still being tuned. The territory-specific loss landscape is, during adolescence, temporarily distorted: the long-horizon, motivationally weighted valuation machinery is fully calibrated, but the intermediate-horizon, contingency-sensitive, and cognitively gated control machinery that normally counterbalances it is still being assembled. This imbalance is not a design flaw; it may be an adaptive feature of a system that must, during a specific developmental window, recalibrate its policy repertoire for the demands of independent adult life—a period in which heightened exploration, novelty-seeking, and sensitivity to social reward serve the organism’s transition from parental dependence to autonomous agency. The composite picture is of a BG optimizer whose developmental trajectory mirrors the hierarchical structure of its adult architecture. The system boots from the bottom up: homeostatic anchoring first (hypothalamic-VTA pre-wiring ensures the first prediction errors are about biological need), mesolimbic reward learning second (ventral striatal value functions are established in infancy), sensorimotor habit learning third (dorsolateral corticostriatal connectivity is strong from early childhood), associative/goal-directed policy learning fourth (dorsomedial-prefrontal connectivity emerges in adolescence), and full cognitive gating last (mesocortical dopamine innervation and prefrontal dopamine receptor maturation are not complete until early adulthood). At each stage, the BG can learn policies only over the state spaces that cortex has made legible and that dopaminergic innervation has made teachable. The developmental curriculum of the BG optimizer is therefore not organized over the type and scope of policy : from rigid homeostatic reflexes, through flexible sensorimotor skills, to abstract cognitive strategies and meta-learning–with each successive layer of policy complexity becoming available only as the required cortical, dopaminergic, and corticostriatal infrastructure comes online. This developmental ordering also implies that the earliest-learned value functions—those anchored to homeostatic correction and primary reward—occupy a privileged position in the BG’s loss landscape: they are laid down first, they shape the dopaminergic baseline against which all subsequent prediction errors are computed, and they are encoded in the most structurally mature corticostriatal circuits. In this sense, the BG optimizer’s "objective function" is not a free parameter specified by experience alone; it is inherited from the survival-critical error signals that first activated the system’s teaching machinery, and this developmental origin is preserved in the structural connectivity between hypothalamic homeostatic controllers and the midbrain dopaminergic nuclei that distribute the credit assignment signal throughout life.

title: Grand synthesis
text: The basal ganglia, as described across these four subsections, constitute a structured, multi-objective policy optimizer embedded within–and reciprocally coupled to–a cortical generative model that it does not itself construct. The architecture can be summarized along four interlocking axes: what is optimized, what signal drives the optimization, how that signal writes into the circuit, and what behavioral and cognitive competences emerge from the resulting learning dynamics. What is optimized. The BG do not minimize a single scalar loss. They minimize a family of coupled objectives distributed across parallel cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops, each parameterized by a territory-specific discount factor, a territory-specific state representation inherited from upstream cortex, and a territory-specific behavioral domain. Ventral striatal loops optimize long-horizon motivational valuation; dorsomedial loops optimize intermediate-horizon, flexible action-outcome contingencies; dorsolateral loops optimize short-horizon sensorimotor execution and sequence consolidation; and posterior/tail loops stabilize sensory-action mappings through value-free repetition signals. Within each territory, the objective is not raw reward but constrained subjective utility: the reward term is nonlinearly transformed by the organism’s risk attitude, temporal discounting, effort costs, physiological need, and subjective probability weighting–a utility already expressed in the organism’s internal currency before it enters the TD computation. Layered atop this transformed reward are regularizers–energetic cost balanced through opponent D1/D2 pathway integration, policy complexity penalized in the dopaminergic signal itself, homeostatic and allostatic need defining the objective’s operating point, and STN-mediated commitment thresholds imposing sparse, non-impulsive selection under conflict. The cortical loss and the BG loss are complementary rather than competing: cortex minimizes precision-weighted prediction error to build and refine a high-dimensional generative world model (epistemic adequacy), while the BG minimize evaluative error to select, time, energize, and automatize policies over the state space that model provides (pragmatic adequacy). Together they form a coupled optimizer pair in which world-model learning and policy learning are analytically separable but biologically inseparable — each training under conditions partly created by the other, linked through the recurrent loop of action, sampling, and cortical updating. What signal drives the optimization. The teaching signal is phasic dopamine, but "phasic dopamine" is itself a structured, heterogeneous population code rather than a single scalar broadcast. At the most classical level, midbrain dopamine neurons compute a temporal-difference reward prediction error through a distributed, multi-layered subtraction: VTA GABA interneurons supply a local subtractive expectation signal; the LHb–RMTg disynaptic pathway conveys worse-than-expected outcome information; and excitatory afferents from PPTg, lateral hypothalamus, and ventral pallidum supply the outcome and predicted-value terms–with most monosynaptic inputs already carrying mixed, partially pre-computed error signals rather than clean modular components. This classical RPE is then unfolded along two axes. Along the magnitude axis, individual dopamine neurons display stable heterogeneity in their asymmetric scaling of positive versus negative errors, implementing a distributional code in which different channels converge to different quantiles of the return distribution; downstream, D1 and D2 SPNs complete this code by preferentially encoding the optimistic and pessimistic tails, respectively, yielding an opponent distributional representation that supports risk-sensitive policy optimization. Along the temporal axis, dopamine transients follow a ventral-to-dorsolateral gradient of reward time horizons across striatal territories, and individual dopamine neurons carry stable, cell-intrinsic discount factors that are correlated across tasks, so that the population encodes something approaching the full joint distribution of future reward over both magnitude and time. Beyond reward value, dopamine has been shown to carry prediction errors over sensory identity, associative transitions between value-neutral states, action execution relative to an action prior, and ongoing movement trajectories–each implemented by anatomically distinguishable subpopulations projecting to distinct striatal targets. The unifying principle is not a shared objective but a shared computational motif: each channel computes a prediction error relative to some expected state of the world, broadcasts it via dopaminergic release, and uses it to update the synaptic weights of the circuits that generated the prediction. Dopamine is therefore best understood not as a neurotransmitter synonymous with reward, but as a general-purpose credit assignment signal–one whose reward-value channel is the best-characterized instance of a much larger family of teaching signals. Yet this generality is not unconstrained. Corticostriatal and mesocortical dopaminergic innervation are anatomically biased toward cortical areas processing policy-relevant variables, and the inputs that set the dopaminergic prediction baseline are heavily weighted toward hypothalamic and interoceptive channels, ensuring that the system–however broad its learning scope–remains anchored to the organism’s biological preference distribution. Once the dopaminergic signal reaches the striatum, it enters a cholinergic field that finalizes its local instructional form: cholinergic pauses gate when dopamine becomes plasticity-relevant, the phase relationship between acetylcholine and dopamine demixes multiplexed dopamine into a plasticity-promoting teaching mode versus a transient vigor/performance mode, and in some territories cholinergic dynamics carry their own error-like signals that are especially important for extinction, reversal, and negative updating. How the signal writes into the circuit. The canonical site of BG learning is the corticostriatal glutamatergic synapse onto spiny projection neurons, where the cortical state representation (the "what") meets the dopaminergic teaching signal (the "how good") at the subcellular level of a single dendritic spine. Learning is governed by a three-factor rule: Hebbian (and/or variants of Hebbian) learning establishes a molecularly defined eligibility trace–a silent synaptic tag lasting approximately 1–2 seconds, implemented through calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclase gated by high phosphodiesterase activity in SPN dendrites–that is converted into lasting potentiation or depression only when phasic dopamine arrives within the eligibility window. The sign of plasticity is determined by opponent pathway-specific decoding: D1 receptor activation drives PKA-dependent potentiation in direct-pathway SPNs, while D2 receptor relief and A2A-dependent signaling drive potentiation in indirect-pathway SPNs, such that a dopamine burst simultaneously reinforces the chosen action (via dSPNs) and weakens the representation of suppressing that action (via iSPNs), while a dopamine dip does the reverse. This opponent rule requires–and recent evidence confirms–that functionally opponent dSPNs and iSPNs are coactive during action selection, resolving a long-standing computational inconsistency about which synapses receive credit for negative outcomes. The eligibility window at the synapse is extended across longer delays by two complementary mechanisms: temporal-difference chaining, in which backward propagation of value through learned state sequences brings the relevant prediction error within the synaptic eligibility window at each step; and sustained prefrontal-to-striatal activity, which maintains the corticostriatal input pattern across the delay period until the teaching signal arrives. Cholinergic pauses add a further gating layer, restricting plasticity to epochs when CIN firing is suppressed, dopamine is phasic, and the SPN is depolarized–a triple-coincidence requirement that prevents irrelevant dopaminergic events from corrupting stored action values. The SPN’s intrinsic electrophysiology provides the foundational gate: deeply hyperpolarized down states, enforced by Kir2 channels, render the neuron unresponsive to sparse or uncorrelated input; only convergent, synchronized cortical drive can promote the SPN into the depolarized up state–or, at finer resolution, trigger NMDA-dependent dendritic plateau potentials on individual branches–from which plasticity-relevant calcium dynamics and spiking become possible. These molecular primitives are, however, not uniformly parameterized across the striatum. DMS expresses symmetric anti-Hebbian STDP favoring flexible rewriting; DLS expresses asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP favoring durable stabilization; NAc core shows bidirectional plasticity from a single induction protocol with distinct calcium-signaling mechanisms; and striosomal versus matrix compartments experience opposite dopaminergic modulation of up-state dynamics. The effective learning rule at each territory is thus matched to the computational demands of that territory’s position in the cortico-basal ganglia hierarchy: rapid revision where flexibility is needed, progressive consolidation where stability is needed, and compartment-specific evaluation-versus-execution separation where the critic must be distinguished from the actor. What emerges. From these interacting components–territory-specific losses, structured heterogeneous error signals, and regionally parameterized plasticity rules–emerge the behavioral and cognitive competences that define the BG’s contribution to adaptive behavior. The exploration-exploitation tradeoff is not solved by a single mechanism but by a layered portfolio: opponent D1/D2 distributional coding provides uncertainty estimates that support directed exploration; transient dopaminergic novelty signals solve the cold-start problem for unfamiliar options; the DMS indirect pathway monitors policy reliability and triggers exploratory switching when accumulated negative evidence exceeds a threshold; and hypothalamic-to-tail-of-striatum circuitry globally modulates exploration scope as a function of homeostatic need–each mechanism operating concurrently, with their relative influence shifting as a function of task phase, environmental volatility, and internal state. Skill acquisition unfolds as a progressive redistribution of influence across the territory-specific loss landscape: from ventral striatal value scaffolding and dorsomedial flexible contingency learning during early goal-directed acquisition, through competitive rebalancing toward dorsolateral consolidation under positively biased dopamine and asymmetric plasticity, to crystallized chunking in which task-bracketing boundary signals, fine-grained kinematic control, and cortical disengagement mark the endpoint of policy compilation. This is not a serial handoff but a continuously negotiated competition between territories, with lateral orbitofrontal cortex regulating the balance and DMS actively restraining premature automatization. The same optimization architecture extends without modification to the cognitive domain: through associative and limbic cortico-basal ganglia loops, the BG gate working-memory updating, attentional allocation, task-set selection, hierarchical rule use, and–at the most abstract level–strategy deployment and meta-learning, with opponent D1/D2 plasticity training these cognitive gating policies just as it trains motor ones. The developmental trajectory of the system mirrors its hierarchical adult architecture, booting from the bottom up: homeostatic anchoring first, mesolimbic reward learning second, sensorimotor habit learning third, associative goal-directed policy learning fourth, and full cognitive gating last–each layer becoming available only as the required cortical, dopaminergic, and corticostriatal infrastructure comes online, and the earliest-learned value functions occupying a privileged position that structurally constrains all subsequent learning. The deepest lesson of this chapter, then, is that the basal ganglia are not a reward tracker, not a habit machine, and not a motor controller–though they contribute to all three. They are the brain’s general-purpose policy optimizer : a constrained, biologically grounded, developmentally bootstrapped engine of credit assignment that learns, through a structured population of dopaminergic prediction errors operating on opponent corticostriatal plasticity, which cortical computations to gate, energize, suppress, or automatize–whether those computations produce a movement, a memory update, or a thought. What makes the system powerful is not any single mechanism but their conjunction: distributional coding gives it access to uncertainty; multi-timescale discounting gives it access to temporal structure; opponent pathway plasticity gives it asymmetric channels for reinforcement and suppression; territory-specific parameterization gives it the capacity to learn qualitatively different kinds of policies in parallel; cholinergic gating gives it temporal precision in credit assignment; and homeostatic grounding gives it an objective function anchored to biological viability rather than arbitrary reward maximization. What makes the system constrained is equally important: its teaching signal is anatomically restricted to policy-relevant cortical representations, its prediction baseline is weighted by interoceptive state, its eligibility windows are molecularly bounded, and its developmental ordering ensures that abstract cognitive policies are always built atop–and remain tethered to–the homeostatic value functions that first activated the dopaminergic teaching machinery. The result is a policy optimizer that is genuinely general in scope but not free to learn anything: a flexible optimization method operating within hard boundaries set by evolution, development, and anatomy, whose collective effect is to ensure that however much the basal ganglia learn about sensory identity, associative structure, action priors, cognitive strategies, and abstract goals, they remain a tool for keeping the organism within its preference distribution–a distribution that is itself inherited from the survival-critical error signals that first powered the system’s learning.

title: The Cerebellum: Predictive Calibration
text: FIGURE: 1 Cerebellar contributions to action and cognition: Prediction, timescale, and continuity The cerebellum is the optimizer most naturally described as a system for predictive calibration . If the cortex learns a hierarchical generative model of the world, and the basal ganglia learn which actions, policies, and behavioral programs are worth selecting, the cerebellum learns how to make selected policies run accurately through the physics of a body and the timing constraints of a nervous system. Its canonical domain is movement, but its computational signature is more general: it receives high-dimensional contextual and efference-copy signals, expands them into a very large basis set, uses sparse teaching signals to detect when predicted and actual consequences diverge, and returns precisely timed corrections to downstream motor, autonomic, cognitive, and affective loops 3 , 4 , 1 . In this sense, the cerebellum is not primarily a system for deciding what to do. It is a system for learning the fast internal models that allow an already-selected behavior to be executed smoothly, continuously, and with minimal error. Recent reviews frame the cerebellum’s motor contribution around speed and accuracy, feedforward control, associative learning, and internal model-based prediction rather than simple "coordination" alone 4 . The need for such a system is easiest to see in movement. Motor commands do not act on a simple plant. They act on a many-jointed, nonlinear, noisy, delayed body whose parts mechanically perturb one another. A command to move the shoulder alters the dynamics of the elbow; a rapid reach generates interaction torques; a change in posture changes the mapping from muscle activation to endpoint motion; and sensory feedback arrives too late to be used as a purely reactive controller. A nervous system that waited passively for proprioceptive and visual feedback would always be controlling the body’s past state. The cerebellum appears to solve this problem by learning forward models: internal simulations that use current state, context, and efference copy to predict the sensory consequences of actions before delayed feedback arrives 3 , 4 , 5 . These predictions can be used for state estimation, rapid online correction, cancellation of self-generated sensory input, and anticipatory compensation for the inertial and interaction dynamics of the body 6 , 4 . The cerebellum therefore occupies a niche complementary to both cortex and basal ganglia: cortex can represent goals, policies, body schemas, and world states; basal ganglia can bias selection among candidate actions; but the cerebellum calibrates the timing and gain structure required for those selected actions to land accurately in the physical world 7 , 8 . This division of labor is visible in computational models that combine basal ganglia and cerebellar learning. In one recent systems-level model, the cortex-basal ganglia loop learned to map desired outcomes onto concrete actions, while the cerebellum minimized the remaining aiming error; the authors summarized the distinction by concluding that the cortex-basal ganglia loop learns through a novelty-based motor prediction error to determine concrete actions, whereas the cerebellum reduces the residual error of the selected movement 9 . This is, however, not meant to imply a rigid serial pipeline. The basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus, brainstem, and cortex form interacting loops, and cerebellar outputs can influence both cortical dynamics and basal-ganglia-related circuits. But it does capture a useful computational asymmetry: the basal ganglia are naturally framed around selection, reinforcement, vigor, exploration, and policy commitment, while the cerebellum is naturally framed around supervised calibration, prediction, timing, and error-based refinement 10 , 11 , 7 . Evolutionarily, this computational role is plausible because the cerebellum appears to have expanded with exactly the kinds of control problems that make pure feedback inadequate. As bodies become larger, sensorimotor delays become more consequential: a signal from the periphery takes longer to arrive, the limb may have moved substantially by the time feedback is processed, and destabilizing corrections can arrive out of phase with the state they are meant to fix. As motor repertoires expand, the organism must also handle a larger space of limb configurations, self-generated sensory consequences, and interaction torques. A high-capacity predictive controller is therefore increasingly valuable: it can learn mappings from context and motor command to future sensory state, allowing control to be based on an estimate of what the body will be doing rather than what it was doing tens or hundreds of milliseconds ago 4 , 6 . This does not mean the cerebellum is purely a "millisecond-scale" device. Its most distinctive advantage is temporal precision , especially in the tens-to-hundreds-of-milliseconds range of sensorimotor prediction and conditioned responses, but the same architecture can contribute to longer behavioral sequences, cognitive timing, language, social interaction, and affective regulation when embedded in slower cortical loops 1 , 2 . Diedrichsen’s 2026 account describes a cerebellar circuit in which Purkinje cells learn to predict climbing-fiber input from high-dimensional parallel-fiber patterns, with predictions often timed tens to hundreds of milliseconds before the teaching event 1 . The symptoms of cerebellar disease illustrate what happens when this predictive calibration fails. Cerebellar lesions do not usually paralyze muscles or abolish the desire to move. Instead they produce dysmetria, decomposition of movement, intention tremor, impaired adaptation, poor timing, instability, and a striking loss of smooth coordination. These are the symptoms expected from an engineered control system that has lost its forward model: the controller still issues commands, but it no longer accurately compensates for delay, noise, inertia, multi-joint coupling, or the changing gain of the body across contexts 12 , 4 , 13 . In reaching, speech, posture, eye movements, and locomotion, the deficit is not merely weakness but miscalibration : errors are detected too late, corrections are over- or under-scaled, and movement breaks into a sequence of late feedback corrections rather than unfolding as a continuous feedforward trajectory 14 , 15 . Recent work on corrective submovements further sharpens this view by linking reactive corrections to the training of future anticipatory cerebellar control signals 14 . The same computational motif appears to extend beyond overt movement. Human neuroimaging and anatomical work show that large portions of the cerebellum are coupled not to primary motor cortex but to association networks, including prefrontal, parietal, temporal, default-mode, language, executive-control, salience, social-cognitive, and affective systems 16 , 17 , 18 . Buckner and colleagues’ intrinsic-connectivity work was perhaps especially important, showing that much of the human cerebellum is functionally coupled to cerebral association cortex rather than motor cortex alone 16 . Subsequent task-based and multi-dataset atlases have refined this picture, identifying cerebellar territories associated with sensorimotor control, attention, executive control, language, mentalizing/default-mode function, and small limbic territories 17 , 18 . This non-motor expansion does not require abandoning the forward-model view. It suggests instead that cerebellar modules may learn predictive models for any domain in which temporally structured internal dynamics must be calibrated against delayed consequences. In language, the cerebellum may help predict the timing, sequencing, and sensory consequences of speech and comprehension; in social cognition, it may help anticipate the unfolding of another agent’s behavior; in affect, it may help regulate the timing and gain of autonomic and emotional responses; and in cognition, it may help coordinate distributed cortical communication by shaping thalamo-cortical dynamics 1 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 . The cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome supports this broader view clinically: lesions can impair executive function, visuospatial cognition, language, and affective regulation even when the primary deficit is not a simple motor impairment 23 , 24 . A recent PLOS Biology review emphasizes that many cerebellar regions form loops with non-motor cortical areas and that cerebellar activation is reliable across cognitive tasks, while also warning that the precise cognitive teaching signals carried by climbing fibers remain unresolved 1 . The reward literature further complicates, but also enriches, the simple “supervised motor error” picture. Classical cerebellar theories emphasized climbing fibers as motor-error teaching signals that train parallel-fiber-to-Purkinje synapses 25 , 26 , 27 . Yet recent work shows reward-related signals in granule cells, Purkinje-cell complex spikes and simple spikes, molecular-layer interneurons, and cerebellar nuclei, as well as anatomical interactions between cerebellum, basal ganglia, ventral tegmental area, and prefrontal cortex 28 . This does not make the cerebellum “just another reinforcement-learning system.” Rather, it suggests that the teaching signals available to cerebellar modules can be task-specific: motor errors in motor loops, sensory surprise in perceptual loops, reward or outcome signals in reward-associated loops, and possibly abstract prediction failures in cognitive loops 28 , 1 . The safest generalization is therefore not that the cerebellum always learns motor errors, but that it learns precisely timed predictive mappings from high-dimensional context to future teaching-signal events. A 2024 consensus paper explicitly describes the cerebellum as building internal models, predicting how actions affect state, updating those models when predicted and actual outcomes mismatch, and participating in reward mechanisms alongside basal ganglia and prefrontal systems 28 . Anatomically, the cerebellum is unusually well matched to this algorithm, and each of its components will reappear in the subsections that follow. Its inputs arrive through two excitatory systems that map naturally onto the two halves of a predict–compare loop. Mossy fibers , arising from pontine, spinal, vestibular, reticular, and other precerebellar nuclei, carry contextual, sensory, motor, and cortical information into the granule-cell layer and send collaterals to the deep cerebellar nuclei. They supply the context from which predictions are made. Climbing fibers , arising from the inferior olive, deliver powerful but sparse teaching signals to Purkinje cells and also send collaterals to the nuclei 29 , 4 , 1 . The output of the cerebellar cortex runs through a single cell type: Purkinje cells , which are inhibitory and project to the deep cerebellar and vestibular nuclei. These nuclei in turn send cerebellar output to motor, premotor, prefrontal, parietal, brainstem, vestibular, red-nucleus, and thalamic targets 29 , 30 , 31 . The basic loop is therefore cortico-ponto-cerebellar input, transformation in the cerebellar cortex, integration in the nuclei, and output through cerebello-thalamo-cortical or cerebello-brainstem pathways. These loops are topographically organized, so different cerebellar territories are linked to different body parts and cortical networks 16 , 32 . This anatomy sets up the rest of the section. "Cerebellar Loss Functions" asks what the mossy-fiber context is used to predict. "Cerebellar Error Signals" follows the two input streams in detail: how granule cells recode mossy-fiber input into the Purkinje simple-spike prediction, where the climbing-fiber error is actually computed, and how the olive keeps that error so precisely timed. "Cerebellar Plasticity" turns to how the climbing-fiber signal rewrites parallel-fiber synapses onto Purkinje cells and how the mossy-fiber collaterals allow learning in the nuclei themselves. Finally, "Cerebellar Learning in Action" shows the whole loop at work in vestibulo-ocular reflex adaptation, eyeblink conditioning, reaching, and speech. Internally, the cerebellar cortex is resembles a repeated engineered module. Across lobules and functional territories, the same microcircuit is reused: mossy fibers excite granule cells; granule cells send parallel fibers across Purkinje-cell dendritic arbors; Purkinje cells inhibit nuclear neurons; climbing fibers deliver powerful complex-spike events; and inhibitory interneurons shape timing, sparsity, and gain 27 , 33 , 1 . This architecture performs an enormous expansion of input dimensionality. In humans, the cerebellar cortex contains tens of billions of granule cells, more than half of all neurons in the brain, and each Purkinje cell receives on the order of one million parallel-fiber synapses 1 , 29 . This expansion gives the cerebellum a kernel-like representational geometry: mossy-fiber inputs are projected into a huge, temporally structured granule-cell basis, from which Purkinje cells can learn precisely timed predictions and corrections 34 , 25 , 26 . Diedrichsen’s 2026 review gives the useful modern formulation: the cerebellum looks like a high-capacity learning engine that provides precisely timed predictive signals learned from very high-dimensional input 1 . The feedforward character of this architecture is central. Neocortex is massively recurrent and well suited for persistent latent-state inference, attractor dynamics, sequence modeling, and hierarchical generative modeling. The basal ganglia are looped, inhibitory, and disinhibitory, well suited for gating, policy selection, reinforcement, and vigor control. The cerebellar cortex, by contrast, is largely a fast feedforward expansion-and-readout system: inputs enter through mossy and climbing fibers, are transformed through granule, parallel-fiber, Purkinje, and nuclear stages, and leave through deep nuclei and vestibular nuclei 29 , 4 . Its internal recurrence appears limited compared with neocortex; its computational power comes less from self-sustaining internal dynamics and more from the breadth of its basis expansion, the precision of its timing mechanisms, and the strength of its teaching signals 27 , 33 . This makes the cerebellum an ideal substrate for learning mappings that must be fast, stable, and automatically deployed once learned. The cerebellum is also modular. Rather than one homogeneous controller, it is organized into many partially independent modules or microcomplexes, each defined by a linked set of mossy-fiber inputs, climbing-fiber inputs from inferior olive, Purkinje-cell microzones, and nuclear output neurons 35 , 36 . The modules share a common circuit motif but differ in what they receive and where they project. A vestibulo-ocular module can learn eye-movement calibration; a spinocerebellar module can predict limb dynamics; a cerebro-cerebellar association module can help calibrate prefrontal, language, or social-cognitive dynamics. This repeated-module design makes a single-algorithm account attractive: one conserved circuit, one local computation re-parameterized per territory. But the inference from uniform anatomy to uniform computation is contested. Diedrichsen and Ivry pose a universal transform (one algorithm everywhere) against multiple functionality (the same circuit running distinct computations, each needing its own algorithmic account), and use cerebellar functional heterogeneity as evidence against the former 37 . It is therefore best to treat predictive calibration as an organizing hypothesis, not an established universal transform. Overall, the cerebellum is introduced here as the brain’s high-capacity predictive calibrator : a modular, relatively feedforward, error-trained system that learns how ongoing states will unfold and how selected actions should be corrected before delayed feedback can arrive. It is “motor” in its historical and most clinically obvious role, but not in its full computational scope. Its deeper function is to keep behavior continuous across time: to make action, perception, thought, affect, and social interaction unfold with the right timing, gain, and anticipatory structure 2 , 38 , 1 . The next subsections treat cerebellar learning in the same loss->error->plasticity->learning-in-action sequence used for cortex and basal ganglia, but with a different central question: what losses does a predictive calibration system minimize, what teaching signals carry those errors, and how does its distinctive circuit architecture convert them into precisely timed internal models ?

title: Cerebellar Loss Functions
text:
In computational terms, the cerebellum is the optimizer whose objective is closest to supervised predictive calibration . At the level of a local microzone, the cerebellar circuit does not primarily infer a rich latent state, as cortex does, nor does it primarily estimate the long-horizon value of actions, as the basal ganglia do. Instead, it learns a mapping from high-dimensional contextual input to a sparse, module-specific teaching signal: a future motor error, sensory prediction error, timing error, reward-related outcome signal, or cognitive prediction failure. In the idealized language of machine learning, the local cerebellar loss can therefore be written as a regression-like discrepancy between what the microcircuit predicts or cancels and what the climbing-fiber-linked teaching system actually reports 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . This makes the cerebellar loss both simple and plural. It is simple because the same canonical computation recurs across modules: mossy-fiber inputs are expanded through the granule-cell/parallel-fiber basis, Purkinje cells learn a timed readout, and climbing fibers provide a powerful supervisory signal when prediction and outcome diverge. But it is plural because the content of the target depends on the loop in which the module is embedded. In a vestibulo-ocular module, the target may be retinal slip; in limb control, a kinematic or dynamic error; in eyeblink conditioning, the unexpected presence or omission of an unconditioned stimulus; in reward-linked loops, reward magnitude, omission, or outcome surprise; and in cerebro-cerebellar loops, some still-unresolved form of cognitive or cortical prediction failure 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 . This loss is time-structured . The cerebellum is not merely comparing prediction and target at the same instant. Its distinctive function is to learn predictors that lead their teaching signals by tens to hundreds of milliseconds, or, in some behavioral contexts, by longer task-relevant intervals. A cerebellar module is therefore trained to answer: given the current state, context, and efference copy, what error or outcome signal is likely to arrive next, and what correction should already be in place before delayed feedback returns? This is why the cerebellum is naturally framed as a predictive calibrator: its losses are local discrepancies between expected and actual consequences, but those discrepancies are organized around the temporal demands of control 9 , 10 , 8 . Thus, “the cerebellar loss function” is not one universal biological scalar. It is a family of supervised, module-specific prediction losses: desired versus actual movement state, expected versus actual sensory consequence, predicted versus actual timing, expected versus actual reward or outcome, and perhaps anticipated versus actual cortical or cognitive state. What unifies these cases is not the target’s semantic content, but the learning format: high-dimensional context is used to predict a sparse future teaching event, and the residual error trains the circuit to make the next action, perception, thought, or affective transition unfold with better timing, gain, and continuity 6 , 7 , 10 , 8 . The proximal local loss: predict or eliminate the future teaching signal At the most proximal level, the cerebellar loss is the residual predictability of a future teaching signal from the present parallel-fiber context. The Marr-Albus-Ito tradition already cast the cerebellar cortex as a supervised learning device: mossy fibers are expanded through granule cells and parallel fibers, Purkinje-cell output is modified by learned parallel-fiber weights, and climbing fibers provide the sparse instructive signal that tells the circuit when its current output failed to anticipate the relevant event 1 , 2 , 11 , 12 , 13 . Modern reviews still treat this as the core local algorithm, while emphasizing that Marr, Albus, and Ito differed on the exact meaning of the climbing-fiber signal, the sign of plasticity, and the relation between pattern recognition, control, and internal models 13 . In adaptive-filter language, each Purkinje cell learns a filter from a high-dimensional basis of parallel-fiber signals to an output that removes the predictable component of a later climbing-fiber-linked error. The objective is therefore not literally to silence the inferior olive, but to decorrelate the residual teaching signal from the basis functions that could have predicted it: 𝔼 [ p i ( t − τ ) e ( t ) ] → 0 , \mathbb{E}[p_i(t−\tau)e(t)]\to0, where p i ( t − τ ) p_i(t−\tau) is a parallel-fiber feature active at the relevant lead time and e ( t ) e(t) is the later residual teaching signal. At the optimum, parallel-fiber variations should no longer predict climbing-fiber variations, because all predictable structure has already been absorbed into Purkinje/nuclear output 14 , 15 , 3 , 16 . A useful modern restatement is: Purkinje cells learn timed predictions of their climbing-fiber input. Diedrichsen formulates the circuit this way explicitly: high-dimensional parallel-fiber patterns train Purkinje cells to predict climbing-fiber events, often tens to hundreds of milliseconds before the event arrives; in eyeblink conditioning, for example, the granule-cell layer supplies temporal basis functions that allow Purkinje cells to predict the precise time of the unconditioned stimulus 8 . This phrasing is slightly different from the older adaptive-filter phrasing. “Decorrelation” describes the optimality condition on the residual signal; “prediction” describes the internal model learned by the circuit. They are two views of the same local loss: once the future teaching event is predicted, it is no longer surprising in the same way, and the residual climbing-fiber signal should be reduced, retimed, or stripped of predictable structure. This also prevents an overly narrow interpretation of the loss. In motor loops, the future teaching signal may be retinal slip, limb-state error, dynamic interaction error, or an aversive unconditioned stimulus. In associative learning, recent causal work supports climbing fibers and complex spikes as essential instructive signals for eyeblink conditioning 17 . In reward-linked and cognitive loops, however, climbing fibers can carry task-specific variables such as reward prediction, unexpected reward, reward omission, or other outcome-related signals, so the “error” need not be a simple signed motor error 18 , 6 , 19 , 8 . Thus the proximal cerebellar loss can be summarized as: use the present context to predict the future teaching event well enough that the same event no longer arrives as an unmodeled residual. The cerebellum does not need to know, in global semantic terms, whether the signal means “wrong reach,” “mistimed blink,” “unexpected reward omission,” or “failed cortical transition.” That interpretation is supplied by the microzone’s inputs and outputs. Locally, the rule is simpler: learn a precisely timed readout from parallel-fiber context that reduces the future teaching signal’s predictable component, thereby converting delayed errors into anticipatory calibration. The forward model loss: minimize sensory prediction error The canonical sensory prediction error loss is the cerebellum’s most familiar special case of predictive calibration. A forward model learns the mapping from current state, context, and efference copy to the sensory consequences that should follow from an action. In motor-control terms, the loss is the discrepancy between the sensory feedback that the system predicts and the sensory feedback that actually arrives: ℒ S P E = ∥ s t + Δ t − s ̂ t + Δ t ( x t , u t , c t ) ∥ Σ − 1 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPE}}

    \hat{s}_{t+\Delta t}(x_t,u_t,c_t)
    \right\|^2_{\Sigma^{-1}}, where x t x_t is the estimated current state, u t u_t is an efference-copy or motor-command signal, c t c_t is the relevant context, and s t + Δ t s_{t+\Delta t} is delayed sensory feedback. The precision term Σ − 1 \Sigma^{-1} emphasizes that the loss is not a raw Euclidean mismatch in one sensory channel, but a reliability-weighted prediction error across visual, proprioceptive, vestibular, tactile, and auditory consequences 20 , 21 , 9 . The need for this loss follows from a basic control problem: sensory feedback arrives too late to stabilize fast movement by itself. A reaching arm, moving eye, vocal tract, or postural controller must act on an estimate of what the body is about to do, not merely on what the sensors reported tens or hundreds of milliseconds ago. A forward model solves this by using efference copy to predict the next sensory state before feedback returns. When the prediction is wrong, the resulting sensory prediction error trains the system to anticipate that consequence more accurately next time 20 , 21 , 22 . This makes sensory prediction error different from task error. A task error says that the action failed relative to an external goal: the hand missed the target, the cursor landed off-center, or the eye failed to stabilize the image. A sensory prediction error says that the sensory consequence of the motor command was not what the nervous system expected. In visuomotor adaptation, this distinction is crucial: explicit strategies can reduce task error while implicit recalibration continues to be driven by mismatches between predicted and observed feedback. The cerebellar forward-model loss is therefore closer to "my action produced an unexpected sensory consequence" than to "my goal was not achieved" 23 , 24 , 25 . The vestibulo-ocular reflex provides the cleanest canonical example. The control objective is to keep the retinal image stable while the head moves. If the head turns and the eyes fail to compensate with the correct gain and timing, visual motion remains on the retina as retinal slip. That slip functions as a sensory prediction error for the oculomotor system: the predicted sensory consequence was retinal stability, but the actual consequence was image motion. Cerebellar floccular circuits use vestibular and visual information to calibrate the gain of the reflex, so that future head movements produce anticipatory eye movements that better cancel self-generated retinal motion 26 , 27 , 28 . Reaching adaptation supplies the analogous limb-control case. When a visuomotor rotation or force field perturbs the normal relation between motor command and sensory consequence, the hand or cursor appears somewhere other than expected. Cerebellum-dependent adaptation uses that mismatch to update the internal model of the limb and environment; patients with cerebellar degeneration are especially impaired at this implicit recalibration, even when they can sometimes use explicit strategies to aim around the perturbation. This supports the view that the cerebellum is not simply choosing better actions, but updating a forward model that predicts the sensory consequences of actions 23 , 29 , 30 . The same loss also explains sensory cancellation . If the cerebellum predicts the tactile, auditory, or proprioceptive consequences of one’s own action, then predictable reafference can be attenuated while unexpected input remains salient. This is why self-generated touch feels less intense than externally generated touch, and why self-initiated sounds evoke reduced auditory responses. In these cases the forward model does not merely help control the limb; it helps partition the sensory stream into expected consequences of one’s own action and unexpected events from the outside world 31 , 32 , 33 . At the circuit level, this loss is implemented through the same architecture described above. Mossy fibers carry state, context, sensory, and efference-copy-related information; granule cells expand those signals into a high-dimensional temporal basis; Purkinje cells learn a timed prediction over that basis; and climbing fibers provide sparse teaching events when the predicted and actual sensory consequences diverge. Purkinje-cell simple spikes encode both predictive and feedback-related variables, consistent with the idea that the cerebellar cortex participates in computing the difference between expected and observed consequences 9 , 34 , 35 . The forward-model loss should therefore be treated as the canonical motor-domain cerebellar objective, but not as the only possible cerebellar objective. It is canonical because it explains the cerebellum’s classic roles in rapid movement, VOR adaptation, reaching adaptation, dysmetria, sensory cancellation, and the compensation of feedback delays. But it is still one member of the broader family of cerebellar losses. In other loops, the future teaching signal may concern reward, timing, autonomic consequence, affective state, or cortical dynamics rather than low-level sensory feedback. The general rule is preserved: use high-dimensional context and efference copy to predict a future consequence, then use the residual mismatch to make the next transition smoother, earlier, and more precise 6 , 7 , 8 . Temporal granularity and precision as a cerebellar signature Perhaps the most distinctive cerebellar property is not what is predicted but the temporal regime in which prediction is computed. Cerebellar contributions are repeatedly localized to the subsecond-to-low-second window, with peak sensitivity in the range that spans rapid sensorimotor prediction, conditioned-response timing, and short-interval discrimination 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 . Patients with cerebellar damage show increased variability on tasks that require discrete millisecond-scale event timing, perception of short durations, and precisely timed motor responses, while sparing tasks whose timing emerges continuously from movement dynamics 40 , 41 , 42 . Transient cerebellar disruption with rTMS selectively impairs subsecond, not suprasecond, interval estimation 43 . The pattern suggests that the cerebellum is not a general-purpose clock but a specialized substrate for predictions whose target lead time is short, sparse, and event-anchored. The behavioral hallmark of this regime is anticipatory rather than reactive. In delay eyeblink conditioning, the conditioned response is acquired not as a generic blink but as a movement whose amplitude profile peaks just before the unconditioned stimulus, and accurate timing of this anticipation is the primary thing that cerebellar damage degrades 8 , 44 . Reaching, vestibulo-ocular control, and speech show analogous miscalibration after cerebellar lesions: feedforward correction within a movement is selectively impaired while the slower, feedback-driven scaffolding of the same behaviors is relatively preserved 45 , 30 . Sensory cancellation has the same temporal flavor: the cerebellum predicts the consequences of self-motion accurately enough that they can be subtracted before they dominate perception, which requires the prediction to lead the reafferent signal by exactly the delay-compensation window in which cerebellar circuits operate 33 , 9 . In each case the cerebellum is doing the same kind of work: closing a short, structured gap between a present cue and an upcoming consequence. This grain constrains what the cerebellum can usefully optimize. A predictor whose teaching signal lands tens to hundreds of milliseconds in the future is well matched to the structured, short-latency mismatches generated by movement, sensory cancellation, conditioned associations, and short-interval estimates. It is less obviously matched to outcomes that arrive seconds or minutes later, where basal-ganglia and prefrontal reinforcement-learning systems appear to carry the relevant credit-assignment work 39 , 46 . Recent work extends cerebellar contributions to longer intervals via cerebro-cerebellar loops with association cortex, but the underlying computational primitive is unchanged: convert present context into a precisely timed prediction of a future event 36 , 47 , 10 . Temporal precision is therefore best treated as a signature of the cerebellar loss family rather than a loss in itself: whatever the modality of the teaching signal – retinal slip, limb endpoint error, blink-eliciting stimulus, reward outcome, cortical state transition – the cerebellum preferentially absorbs its predictable structure on the side of the timeline that its circuits are configured to resolve. The architectural and plasticity-rule reasons for that configuration belong in "Cerebellar Error Signals" and "Cerebellar Plasticity" 8 , 9 , 10 . Synthesis Overall, cerebellar losses are locally supervised prediction losses whose learned models support state estimation and anticipatory control: the same predictive calibration that lets a forward model estimate the current state before feedback returns is what lets the system act early rather than react late.
