title: Cerebellar Error Signals
text: Having framed the cerebellar objective as predictive calibration, the physical question is how a microzone actually implements a predict–compare loop: which signals carry the prediction, which carry the error, where the comparison happens, and what makes it temporally precise. The answer is unusually clean, because the cerebellar cortex funnels two anatomically and physiologically distinct input streams onto a single output neuron. The primary output cells of the cerebellar cortex, Purkinje cells (1̃5 million), make kinematic predictions about ongoing movements via high-frequency simple spikes, and encode sensory error information about that movement in low-frequency complex spikes 1 . The first stream is the mossy-fiber (2̃00 million) → \rightarrow granule-cell (4̃0 billion) → \rightarrow parallel-fiber pathway, which drives the Purkinje cell’s high-rate simple-spike discharge (typically tens of hertz) 2 ; the second is the climbing-fiber input from the inferior olive, which drives the sparse complex spike (1̃ Hz): a large, stereotyped burst whose occurrence is near-binary, thanks to the exceptionally reliable climbing-fiber synapse, but whose duration and spikelet count are graded in a way that scales the resulting plasticity 3 . The working hypothesis of this subsection is therefore that the simple-spike stream carries the module’s running prediction while the complex-spike stream carries the teaching signal that reports when that prediction has failed 4 , 5 . The logic of the loop follows directly from the objective established above. On each cycle a microzone emits a prediction through its Purkinje simple spikes; the world, or the rest of the nervous system, returns the actual consequence; a comparison somewhere in the circuit extracts the residual by which prediction and consequence disagree; that residual is delivered back to the same Purkinje cells as a sparse climbing-fiber teaching event; and the resulting plasticity adjusts the prediction so that the next cycle’s residual is smaller. What makes the cerebellar version of this loop unusually tractable to study is that its two limbs are carried by anatomically segregated pathways with opposite statistics — a dense, high-rate prediction stream and a sparse, low-rate error stream — that converge on one output cell whose plasticity binds them. The rest of this part develops this two-signal picture in four steps: the mossy-fiber/simple-spike pathway that carries the prediction; the climbing-fiber/complex-spike pathway that carries the error, together with the circuit that actually computes it; the mechanisms that make the whole loop temporally precise; and the question of whether this machinery is specific to movement or reused across the cerebellum’s non-motor territories. Mossy fibers, granule cells, and simple spikes The prediction limb begins with the mossy fibers , the cerebellum’s dominant afferent system, which collectively provide the information from which a forward model can estimate the consequences of an action: the state of the body and environment, the behavioral context, and motor-related signals indicating the action being generated 6 , 7 , 8 . These variables are not carried in neatly segregated channels; individual mossy-fiber pathways can combine sensory, motor, and contextual information, while convergence within the granule-cell layer constructs high-dimensional, multimodal representations of the current task state 9 , 10 . Mossy fibers arise from numerous precerebellar sources. The largest contingent comes through the pontine nuclei, which relay widespread cerebral-cortical activity—including motor preparation, sensory and association signals, goals, and higher-order behavioral context—into the granule-cell layer 11 , 12 , 6 . Spinocerebellar and cuneocerebellar pathways convey proprioceptive, cutaneous, and integrated spinal-circuit activity; importantly, some spinocerebellar signals reflect the state of spinal premotor networks and therefore function as internal copies of descending or spinally generated motor commands rather than as sensory feedback alone 7 , 13 . Vestibular afferents and vestibular nuclei provide information about head motion, orientation, and balance 14 , 15 . The lateral reticular nucleus integrates descending motor signals with sensory and premotor activity from spinal interneuronal circuits, supplying the cerebellum with a compound representation of the command being implemented and the bodily state in which it is implemented 16 , 7 . Corollary-discharge or efference-copy information reaches the cerebellum through several task-dependent routes, including corticopontine pathways and collateral branches of descending brainstem and spinal motor systems 7 , 6 . Specialized pathways also provide efference-copy signals for particular control domains: for example, the nucleus prepositus participates principally in oculomotor and vestibular circuits and may convey internal signals related to eye and head movement, rather than serving as a general relay for all outgoing motor commands 17 , 18 . Thus, there is no single universal “efference-copy tract”; motor-command information is distributed across multiple mossy-fiber systems 7 . Mossy fibers also issue excitatory collaterals to the cerebellar nuclei , allowing related sensory, contextual, and motor-related input to reach both the cerebellar cortical microcircuit and its nuclear output stage 11 , 19 . Heterogeneous mossy fiber input is then recoded by the granule cells . Each mossy fiber diverges onto hundreds of granule cells, and — contrary to the older assumption of unimodal relay — individual granule cells integrate mossy-fiber inputs from different sources, mixing, for example, basilar-pontine and proprioceptive streams onto the same cell 9 . The result is the expansion recoding anticipated by Marr and Albus and formalized in modern kernel terms: the modest-dimensional mossy-fiber input is projected into an enormous, sparse granule-cell basis, from which a Purkinje cell can approximate a wide range of functions 20 , 21 , 22 , 4 . The learned cortical output is carried by the Purkinje cell’s high-rate simple-spike discharge. Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and their simple spikes provide a continuous inhibitory signal–commonly tens of spikes per second and sometimes exceeding 100 Hz–to the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei 23 , 24 . In the simplified Marr–Albus picture, this discharge is the weighted readout of the parallel-fiber representation. Biophysically, however, it also reflects Purkinje cells’ intrinsic pacemaking, feedforward and lateral inhibition from molecular-layer interneurons, climbing-fiber interactions, and plasticity at several classes of synapse. It is therefore best described as the cerebellar cortex’s learned model-output stream , rather than as a literal linear readout of parallel-fiber weights alone. Nor should the discharge of a single Purkinje cell necessarily be identified with the complete output of a cerebellar module. Neurons within deep cerebellar nuclei integrate convergent inhibition from populations of Purkinje cells with excitatory mossy-fiber and climbing-fiber collaterals; in many cases, the behaviorally relevant estimate or command becomes legible only after population-level convergence onto these downstream neurons 25 , 26 . Several features make the simple-spike stream naturally interpretable as the output of a forward model. Its content is predictive: during movement, simple-spike firing encodes upcoming kinematics — position, velocity, and speed — with components that lead the movement rather than merely reporting it, and the timing distribution is biased toward prediction, with modulation on average preceding movement by roughly 100 ms 27 , 28 . This holds across effectors and tasks: the same predictive coding appears in vermal Purkinje cells during saccades and in intermediate/lateral-zone cells during manual tracking, which is what one would expect if the forward-model computation were a generic mode of cortical processing rather than a quirk of one motor system 29 . And this predictive code is legible at the population level in a form matched to control. In the oculomotor vermis, when Purkinje cells are grouped by their shared climbing-fiber input — that is, by complex-spike directional tuning — the combined simple-spike activity of the bursting and pausing cells predicts the real-time speed and direction of a saccade multiplicatively, as a gain field. Importantly, neither the bursting nor the pausing population alone suffices; the prediction is a property of the convergent input onto a cerebellar nucleus neuron, information no single cell carries 25 . The prediction, in other words, is not an abstraction imposed by the modeller: it is present in the firing of the output cells, timed ahead of the movement, and organized by the very climbing-fiber map that will later teach it. The label "prediction stream," however, requires immediate qualification, and this is the first place the two-signal picture becomes more subtle. Simple spikes do not encode predictions alone; they also encode the errors themselves. Individual Purkinje cells signal performance errors — how far the effector missed — independently of the kinematic signals they carry, and, strikingly, each variable (both kinematic and error) is represented twice : once by a component that leads the movement and once by a component that lags it, with a change in the sign of the modulation between the two 28 , 30 . A leading (predictive) and a lagging (feedback) copy of the same quantity is exactly what a neuron would carry if it were computing a sensory prediction error internally, by holding its own prediction against the feedback that arrives a moment later 5 , 29 . This matters for the architecture: part of the predict–compare operation is already visible in the cortical output, so the residual is not delivered exclusively by the separate error pathway described next. These paired signals span a wide temporal window — from tens of milliseconds to as much as two seconds around the movement in tracking tasks — consistent with a forward model that both anticipates consequences and retains a short memory of recent performance to inform the next action 30 . The classical error limb is carried by the climbing fibers , and its anatomy is as distinctive as its statistics. Every Purkinje cell in the adult cerebellum is innervated by single climbing fiber (with residual multi-innervation in some cells, perhaps more prominently in humans 31 ) from the inferior olive , a brainstem nucleus. That lone input forms one of the most powerful synapses in the nervous system: it wraps the soma and smooth proximal dendrite in anywhere from several hundred to over a thousand contact sites, each with high release probability, while the parallel fibers are confined to the spiny distal branchlets 32 , 3 . A single olivary spike therefore reliably drives a complex spike : a large calcium-based dendritic event consisting of an initial full spike followed by a brief burst of smaller spikelets, occurring at a low rate of roughly one per second against the Purkinje cell’s much faster simple-spike background 33 , 34 . In the Marr–Albus–Ito framework this sparse event is the instructive signal that guides plasticity, and recent causal work confirms the role directly: optogenetically supplied complex spikes are sufficient to serve as the teaching signal for associative cerebellar learning 35 , 4 . For a teaching signal, though, the complex spike has a notorious problem: because the climbing-fiber synapse is so reliable, the postsynaptic response is nearly all-or-none within a given cell, which at first glance makes it a poor instrument for reporting the magnitude or sign of an error 33 . The resolution is that the signal is graded at two levels the binary caricature misses. Within a cell, the complex spike is not truly invariant: the number of spikelets and the duration of the event vary with the size of the underlying olivary burst, and these variations are behaviourally consequential. Longer-duration complex spikes drive larger single-trial depression and stronger learning; a short climbing-fiber burst can bias plasticity toward potentiation while a longer burst drives depression, so the number of spikes even controls the direction of the change; and the dendritic calcium transient the complex spike delivers is itself graded during learning 36 , 37 , 38 . Across cells, the olive grades the signal by which Purkinje cells it drives: each cell responds preferentially to errors in a particular direction — its "CS-on" direction — so a population of Purkinje cells within a microzone collectively encodes a directional error vector, and that vector in sensory space is aligned with the direction of the corrective force the module controls 1 . Recent recordings extend this to reciprocally modulated parasagittal bands whose complex spiking encodes the sign and magnitude of an imposed perturbation 39 . A near-binary event per cell thus becomes a graded, signed, directional teaching signal at the level of the microzone. None of this yet answers where the comparison — the actual subtraction of prediction from consequence — is performed. The classical picture places it implicitly at the Purkinje cell, but the decisive circuit element may lie at the other end of the loop, in the projection from the cerebellar nuclei back to the inferior olive. A subpopulation of small GABAergic nucleo-olivary neurons in the cerebellar nuclei projects to the olive, following the same zonal organization as the climbing fibers and thereby closing a reciprocal loop between olive, cortex, and nuclei 40 , 41 , 42 . This inhibition delivers the cerebellum’s own output back to the source of its teaching signal, where it is subtracted from the incoming sensory error: if the module’s prediction matches the actual consequence, the two cancel and olivary activity stays at its baseline; only an unpredicted consequence drives the olive away from baseline and produces a climbing-fiber event 43 , 44 . This is the circuit-level implementation of two principles invoked in the loss section: the Rescorla–Wagner rule that learning occurs only when events violate expectation, and the adaptive-filter corollary that the cerebellum learns only when the olive is perturbed from baseline 43 , 44 . The consequences are directly demonstrable: a properly timed cerebello-olivary signal is by itself sufficient to drive extinction of a learned response, and omission of an expected outcome drives the olive precisely at the time the outcome was predicted 45 . The comparison, in short, is distributed and recurrent: the cortex already carries paired prediction and feedback signals, while the nucleo-olivary loop performs an explicit subtraction that converts sensory error into a teaching-relevant prediction error before it ever reaches the Purkinje cell. One caveat about the subtraction deserves stating, because it changes what kind of operation we should say the olive is performing. The account above treats the olive computationally as a subtraction node: prediction in, sensory error in, surprise out. Mechanistically, however, the inferior olive is not a simple monotonic firing-rate subtractor. Olivary neurons are electrically coupled through gap junctions concentrated between dendritic spines within the glomeruli (specialized synaptic structures), and many—but not all, and not necessarily continuously—exhibit prominent subthreshold membrane-potential oscillations. Nucleo-olivary inhibition can therefore do more than simply reduce firing probability: it can hyperpolarize the neuron, recruit rebound conductances, reset and alter the amplitude of an oscillation, and regulate electrical coupling and synchrony within the olivary network 42 , 46 , 47 . Excitatory afferents and inhibitory cerebellar terminals frequently converge upon the same electrically coupled dendritic spines within the glomerulus, placing their interaction close to the gap junctions that coordinate neighboring neurons. The olive’s output depends steeply on the relative interval between the two inputs. Excitation delivered shortly after inhibition–approximately 50-70 ms later, near the trough of the inhibitory response–generates almost no spikes, whereas excitation delivered approximately 150 ms later, around one oscillatory cycle and near the rebound peak, drives spiking optimally and can evoke more spikes than excitation alone. The same inhibitory input can therefore suppress or facilitate the ensuing climbing-fiber discharge depending on its timing relative to excitation, the phase of the olivary state, and the neuron’s membrane potential 46 . Inhibition also modulates electrical coupling between olivary neurons and can disrupt or reorganize coherent subthreshold oscillations. The cerebellar feedback carrying the prediction may therefore regulate not only whether an incoming error-related excitation produces climbing-fiber spikes, but also the size and synchrony of the olivary ensemble recruited by it—and hence how broadly and synchronously the resulting error signal is delivered across the corresponding Purkinje-cell population 42 , 47 , 46 . Two qualified conclusions follow. First, cancellation, temporal gating, and ensemble coordination are not cleanly separable stages linked only by anatomy: they are implemented through overlapping interactions among inhibitory input, excitatory input, intrinsic rebound conductances, and electrical coupling in and around the glomerulus. Second, "subtraction" is best understood as a computational description of the closed loop’s net effect, not as literal instantaneous arithmetic performed by an olivary neuron. The proposed biophysical implementation is a state-dependent gate over membrane potential, oscillatory phase, spike probability, and network coupling. Describing that gate as the mechanism of prediction-error subtraction is therefore a plausible synthesis of the evidence, rather than a directly demonstrated identity 42 , 46 , 45 . Two loose ends complete the picture. The first is why an error signal of this form produces the right synaptic change. Because a given microzone’s climbing fibers are tuned to a particular error direction, an error in that direction drives complex spikes selectively in the cells that control the opposing correction; those complex spikes depress the parallel-fiber synapses that were active just before the error, weakening the simple-spike drive that produced the errant command; and because the microzone’s error tuning is anatomically aligned with the correction it exerts through the nuclei, the net change opposes the error and shrinks it on the following trial 1 , 4 . It should be said that the parallel-fiber synapse is not the only site the teaching signal reaches: the same climbing-fiber activity instructs plasticity at molecular-layer interneurons and, via the Purkinje-cell output, at the cerebellar nuclei themselves, where learning is consolidated — so the error signal should not be over-located in the cortex. The second loose end is what defines "error" for a given module in the first place. The inferior olive integrates excitatory drive from its own afferents — sensory information relayed directly from spino-olivary and trigeminal pathways from the lower brainstem, and higher-order signals relayed through the mesodiencephalic junction from cortex, superior colliculus, and red nucleus — against the nucleo-olivary inhibition, so the content of the teaching signal is set by which error-reporting inputs a given olivary subregion happens to receive 42 , 46 , 48 . The temporal precision of the error pathway does not arise from a single clock; it is assembled in stages. Intrinsic membrane dynamics constrain when olivary neurons are most excitable; electrical coupling aligns the firing of neurons belonging to the same functional ensemble; the olivocerebellar axons preserve that alignment despite unequal path lengths; and the exceptionally powerful climbing-fiber synapse converts each arriving olivary spike into a sharply defined Purkinje-cell event. These mechanisms solve different timing problems. Subthreshold oscillations provide a phase-dependent temporal framework on the scale of tens to hundreds of milliseconds, whereas electrical coupling, matched conduction times, and climbing-fiber transmission preserve relative timing on the scale of milliseconds or less. The best-established source of millisecond-scale population precision is regulated electrical coupling within the inferior olive . Olivary neurons are joined dendrite-to-dendrite by connexin36-containing gap junctions concentrated within the glomeruli. These junctions transmit subthreshold voltage fluctuations between neighboring cells, allowing functionally related neurons to approach threshold together. At the cerebellar cortex, the consequence is visible as complex spikes whose onsets are synchronized to within approximately one millisecond, principally among Purkinje cells arranged in the same parasagittal strip 49 , 50 . Optical recordings reveal the same organization at finer spatial scale: climbing-fiber events coactivate narrow microbands of neighboring Purkinje-cell dendrites, commonly tens of micrometres wide, with correlations consistent with synchrony on a timescale of at most a few milliseconds 51 . The causal evidence for this mechanism is unusually strong. Pharmacological reduction of coupling inside the olive decreases both complex-spike synchrony and the associated rhythmic organization 52 , while connexin36 deletion reduces olivary electrical coupling and leaves complex-spike synchrony near chance levels without its normal parasagittal distribution 53 . The behavioral consequence is not necessarily gross ataxia, but a loss of precision when a movement must be learned at a particular time: connexin36-deficient mice show more variable olivary response latencies and poorly timed conditioned locomotor and eyeblink responses 54 . During natural movement, moreover, synchrony is not fixed. It increases and spreads across selected microzones during sharply bounded components of locomotion, whereas the same Purkinje-cell populations are less strongly synchronized at rest 55 . The functionally relevant mechanism is therefore not indiscriminately high coupling, but coupling strong enough to form temporally coherent ensembles and sufficiently regulated to recruit only the microzones appropriate to the current event. Electrical coupling aligns an ensemble, but the temporal state being aligned is supplied partly by the olive’s intrinsic subthreshold membrane-potential oscillations . Olivary neurons possess voltage-dependent conductances that can generate approximately sinusoidal fluctuations in membrane potential 56 . In vivo recordings reveal heterogeneous oscillatory regimes: some neurons express faster oscillations in the several-hertz range, others slower low-threshold calcium oscillations, and oscillatory activity may occur in transient epochs rather than continuously 57 . When fast oscillations are present, olivary spikes occur preferentially near the depolarized phase, so an input arriving at different points in the cycle does not have an equal probability of producing an immediate climbing-fiber discharge 58 . Synaptic inputs and spikes can also reset the phase of the oscillation, allowing an unexpected event to reorganize the timing of subsequent olivary excitability 59 . It is therefore reasonable to describe the oscillation as a temporal scaffold , but not as a universal metronome that assigns every error to a rigid ten-hertz grid. Olivary oscillations are heterogeneous and state-dependent, and rhythmicity can persist in individual neurons after connexin36-dependent coupling has been removed 60 , 61 , 53 . What coupling supplies is principally coherence: uncoupled cells may continue to oscillate at similar frequencies, but their phases and spikes are no longer coordinated across the population. The precision of the teaching signal consequently emerges from the interaction of two properties—intrinsic conductances that create preferred firing phases and gap junctions that align those phases within a temporarily assembled ensemble. Synchrony generated in the olive would nevertheless be lost if unequal axonal distances converted simultaneous olivary spikes into dispersed cortical arrivals. The olivocerebellar pathway appears to solve this problem through approximate isochrony . In the rat, stimulation near the inferior olive produced complex spikes across widely separated cortical regions after a remarkably uniform conduction time of 3.98 ± 0.36 3.98 \pm 0.36 ms, despite substantial differences in measured climbing-fiber length 62 ; longer fibers conducted faster than shorter fibers, thereby compensating for their additional distance. Developmental and dysmyelination experiments further indicate that differential myelination is a major contributor to this compensation: as normal fibers myelinate, the initially larger latency differences across cerebellar regions converge toward a common value, whereas those differences persist in myelin-deficient animals and are accompanied by reduced complex-spike synchrony 63 . Strict isochrony should, however, not be treated as a settled universal property of every olivocerebellar projection. Experiments in the cat 64 and measurements using the climbing-fiber reflex in the rat vermis 65 have reported systematic regional latency differences, although the interpretation of the reflex measurements—and whether they isolate one-way olivocerebellar conduction—has been disputed 66 . The defensible conclusion is therefore narrower: compensatory tuning of conduction velocity is strongly supported in the rat pathways examined directly and provides a plausible means of preserving cortical synchrony, but the degree of compensation may vary across species, cerebellar territories, developmental stages, and measurement paradigms. The final stage is the climbing-fiber–Purkinje-cell synapse , which functions as a high-fidelity temporal relay. A mature Purkinje cell is ordinarily dominated by one climbing fiber whose arbor forms hundreds of release sites over the proximal dendritic tree 67 . Release probability is high, several vesicles can be released simultaneously at an individual site, and the resulting compound excitatory conductance is sufficiently large to trigger a complex spike from a single presynaptic olivary action potential 67 , 68 , 69 . The Purkinje cell therefore does not estimate the timing of an error by slowly integrating many weak afferents: the arrival of one climbing-fiber spike produces a rapid, unitary event with little opportunity for probabilistic transmission failure to blur its onset. Here again, "all-or-none" applies most cleanly to the occurrence and onset of the climbing-fiber response, not to every dimension of the resulting waveform. Complex-spike duration, dendritic calcium entry, and spikelet number vary with olivary burst structure and the state of the Purkinje cell, allowing the same temporally discrete event to carry graded information about teaching strength 36 , 70 . Nor do all later spikelets necessarily propagate faithfully down the Purkinje-cell axon 71 . These qualifications do not undermine the timing mechanism: they separate a relatively reliable event boundary— an olivary spike arrived now —from a graded internal waveform that can determine how strongly that event modifies the circuit. The loop’s precision is therefore hierarchical rather than unitary. Oscillatory membrane dynamics define preferred temporal windows and permit phase resetting; connexin36-mediated coupling coordinates the particular olivary cells that should report the event; approximate isochrony prevents unequal axonal distances from dispersing their output; and the climbing-fiber synapse converts each arrival into a reliable, sharply initiated complex spike. A climbing fiber may fire only about once per second on average, but low rate is not the same as low temporal resolution: each sparse event can be positioned with millisecond-scale precision relative to the other members of its microzone and embedded within a slower, state-dependent phase structure. title: Cerebellar Plasticity
text: From teaching signal to parameter update An error signal becomes a learning signal only when it changes the circuit parameters that produced the erroneous prediction. In the canonical cerebellar-cortical rule, this requires the conjunction of three factors: a pattern of parallel-fiber activity representing the preceding state or context; a local postsynaptic state that marks the active synapses as eligible for modification; and a subsequent climbing-fiber event indicating that the circuit’s output was followed by an unexpected consequence. The foundational experiment demonstrated this conjunction directly: repeated joint stimulation of parallel and climbing fibers in rabbit cerebellar cortex produced a depression of parallel-fiber-evoked Purkinje-cell responses lasting at least an hour, whereas stimulation of either pathway alone did not produce the same effect 1 . Later whole-cell experiments established the required temporal order: depression was strongest when a burst of parallel-fiber activity preceded the climbing-fiber event, peaking when it occurred approximately (80) ms earlier and declining over a broader window of several hundred milliseconds 2 . The climbing fiber therefore does not indiscriminately modify every synapse on the Purkinje cell. It acts on a transient eligibility trace left preferentially at parallel-fiber synapses that were active before the error arrived. Causal behavioral experiments support the interpretation of climbing fibers as instructive rather than merely correlational signals. In mouse delay-eyeblink conditioning, optogenetic activation of climbing fibers could replace the natural air-puff unconditioned stimulus and train a correctly timed conditioned blink even when the stimulation itself produced no reflexive blink. Conversely, temporally selective suppression of the evoked climbing-fiber response blocked learning to the natural stimulus 3 . These findings show that, in this associative-learning circuit, the climbing-fiber-driven complex spike is sufficient to supply the teaching event and is required for normal learning. The conclusion should not, however, be universalized to every cerebellar behavior: rhesus monkeys can show substantial vestibulo-ocular-reflex adaptation under training conditions in which the usual error-related modulation of climbing fibers is absent, implying that simple-spike-related, nuclear, or other instructive mechanisms can sometimes support learning 4 . The defensible generalization is therefore that climbing fibers are the canonical—and in some paradigms essential—teacher for cerebellar cortical plasticity, not that every cerebellar parameter update is caused exclusively by a climbing-fiber error signal. The way that this local synaptic change becomes a corrective behavioral update depends on the sign structure and anatomical organization of the microzone. Parallel fibers excite Purkinje cells, whereas Purkinje cells inhibit cerebellar nuclear neurons. Depression of an eligible parallel-fiber input therefore tends to reduce the Purkinje cell’s simple-spike response to the same context, releasing its nuclear targets from inhibition when that context next occurs. But this sign inversion alone does not guarantee that the change will oppose the error: the relevant Purkinje cell must also belong to a microzone whose climbing-fiber error preference is aligned with the direction of the correction produced through its nuclear output. Recordings from the monkey oculomotor vermis provide direct evidence for this alignment. Complex-spike probability was tuned to the direction of a visual error, and the occurrence of a complex spike was followed on the next trial by depression of the Purkinje cell’s simple-spike response. The resulting change in the next saccade was directed along the cell’s own preferred error axis, regardless of the exact direction of the error that had elicited the complex spike 5 . Thus, the olivocerebellar map does not merely announce that something went wrong; it routes the teaching event to a cortical–nuclear module capable of producing a specifically oriented correction. The complex spike also controls more than the binary decision of whether learning occurs. In monkeys adapting smooth-pursuit eye movements, longer-duration complex spikes were followed by larger trial-to-trial depressions of Purkinje-cell simple-spike activity and by larger changes in behavior. Complex-spike duration was correlated across the relevant Purkinje-cell population, consistent with the underlying olivary burst and network state modulating the strength of instruction delivered to an entire functional ensemble 6 . The effective learning rate is therefore partly encoded in the internal structure of the teaching event: longer climbing-fiber bursts produce longer complex spikes, larger dendritic calcium signals, and stronger updates. This provides a graded learning rule even though the arrival of a climbing-fiber event at an individual Purkinje cell is comparatively sparse and reliable. The transition from teaching signal to parameter update is therefore best understood as a locally gated credit-assignment operation. Recent parallel-fiber activity identifies the candidate synapses; dendritic and biochemical state determines whether they remain eligible; the climbing-fiber event reports a module-specific failure or outcome; its probability, timing, duration, and population distribution regulate the sign and magnitude of learning; and the fixed excitatory–inhibitory geometry of the microzone translates the synaptic change into a downstream correction. Parallel-fiber–Purkinje-cell LTD is the canonical example of this operation, but it is only the first layer of the learning system. The same teaching event can interact with potentiation, inhibitory plasticity, intrinsic excitability, and downstream nuclear plasticity, allowing the cerebellum to distribute an update across several parameter classes and timescales rather than storing the entire correction in one synapse. Parallel-fiber-Purkinje-cell LTD: induction conditions and molecular expression The canonical parameter update in the cerebellar cortex is long-term depression at the parallel-fiber–Purkinje-cell synapse (PF–PC LTD): a persistent reduction in the response of a Purkinje cell to parallel-fiber inputs that were active in association with a climbing-fiber teaching event. Ito and Kano first demonstrated that conjunctive stimulation of parallel and climbing fibers produced a depression of parallel-fiber-evoked Purkinje-cell responses lasting at least an hour, whereas either pathway alone was ineffective 1 . Subsequent electrophysiological, imaging, and molecular studies established that the canonical form is expressed primarily through a postsynaptic reduction in AMPA-receptor-mediated transmission at eligible PF–PC synapses 7 , 8 , 9 . LTD is associative because the parallel fiber and climbing fiber contribute different parts of the induction signal. Parallel-fiber glutamate marks the recently active synapses and initiates a transient local biochemical state, while the climbing-fiber complex spike produces strong dendritic depolarization and calcium entry. Direct Purkinje-cell depolarization capable of evoking dendritic calcium spikes can substitute experimentally for climbing-fiber stimulation when paired with parallel-fiber activity, showing that the climbing fiber’s critical contribution is the postsynaptic instructive signal it normally supplies rather than some unique transmitter 10 , 11 . The rule is also temporally asymmetric . In mouse slices, LTD was strongest when a burst of parallel-fiber activity preceded a climbing-fiber event by approximately (80) ms, with a broader effective window spanning several hundred milliseconds 2 . Single-spine calcium imaging similarly showed that parallel-fiber activation followed tens to hundreds of milliseconds later by climbing-fiber activation produced supralinear local calcium signals and LTD 12 . This ordering solves the local temporal-credit problem: the synaptic pattern that helped generate the prediction occurs first, while the consequence that evaluates it arrives later. The exact eligibility window is not universal. In the flocculus, LTD is narrowly tuned to PF–CF intervals near the delay with which retinal-slip signals reach the circuit during vestibulo-ocular learning; coincident activation can instead induce potentiation. Vermal Purkinje cells exhibit a broader and more heterogeneous range of preferred intervals 13 . Different cerebellar modules therefore appear to tune their plasticity kernels to the sensory and motor delays of the behaviors they control rather than sharing one fixed spike-timing rule. At the biochemical level, recent parallel-fiber activity activates mGluR1-dependent signaling and generates a local eligibility trace, while the climbing fiber supplies the large dendritic calcium signal. Their conjunction produces a supralinear calcium elevation in or near recently active spines, engaging kinase pathways that ultimately remove AMPA receptors from those synapses 12 , 14 , 9 . Genetic and rescue experiments confirm essential roles for mGluR1, intracellular calcium release, protein kinase C, GluA2 phosphorylation, and PICK1-dependent AMPA-receptor trafficking in conventional PF–PC LTD 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 . Calcium does not simply switch plasticity on or off; its magnitude and context help determine the sign of the change. Strong climbing-fiber-associated calcium signals generally bias eligible PF synapses toward LTD, whereas weaker calcium elevations or different activity patterns can produce LTP. Experiments manipulating calcium buffering and stimulation frequency show that there is no single absolute calcium threshold separating depression from potentiation; the boundary shifts with the recent state and activity of the synapse 19 , 20 . The update is therefore better represented as a nonlinear, state-dependent function of eligibility, calcium, inhibition, synaptic weight, and recent activity than as an invariant command to depress. Under sparse activation, LTD can be highly synapse- and branch-specific. PF–CF pairing generates enhanced calcium signals in active spines, and in-vivo optical experiments localized lasting depression to the intersection between the stimulated parallel-fiber beam and the climbing-fiber-defined parasagittal zone 12 , 8 . Stronger stimulation can recruit broader dendritic calcium signals and diffusible messengers, producing heterosynaptic depression beyond the directly activated inputs 21 . LTD is therefore predominantly input-specific under physiological sparse activation, but not obligatorily confined to a single spine. The canonical sequence can be summarized as: [ , , ] [ + . ] When the same context recurs, the Purkinje cell responds less strongly, reducing its inhibition of the corresponding cerebellar nuclear neurons and thereby altering the module’s output. This is the canonical mechanism by which a delayed teaching signal is converted into a selective change in the prediction that preceded it. PF–PC LTD should nevertheless not be equated with the complete cerebellar learning algorithm. Mice in which conventional GluA2/PICK1-dependent LTD is eliminated can retain substantial learning in several cerebellum-dependent tasks, indicating that potentiation, inhibitory plasticity, intrinsic excitability, granular-layer plasticity, and plasticity in the cerebellar nuclei can compensate for or operate alongside the LTD pathway 22 . LTD is therefore best treated as the archetypal cerebellar cortical update—not as the sole substrate of cerebellar memory. PF-Purkinje potentiation and bidirectional weight control If parallel-fiber synapses could only undergo LTD, repeated errors would eventually drive their weights toward a lower bound, erasing useful inputs and leaving the circuit unable to reverse a previously learned calibration. PF-Purkinje synapses therefore possess complementary forms of long-term potentiation (LTP) that increase their effective strength. Postsynaptic PF-PC LTP can reverse previously saturated LTD, while an LTD-inducing protocol can reverse saturated LTP, demonstrating that the two forms provide genuinely bidirectional control over the same synaptic pathway 23 , 19 . Potentiation is consequently not merely an auxiliary form of plasticity: it prevents one-way saturation, permits extinction or reversal of obsolete calibrations, and allows the circuit to continue learning around a useful operating range. In the simplest induction regime, repeated parallel-fiber activity without a coincident climbing-fiber event produces postsynaptic LTP, whereas the same parallel-fiber activity paired with a climbing fiber produces LTD. Manipulating postsynaptic calcium can reverse these outcomes without changing the presynaptic stimulation pattern: partially buffering calcium can convert an LTD-inducing PF–CF protocol into LTP, raising calcium by photolysis can convert a normally potentiating PF-only protocol into LTD, and stronger calcium buffering prevents either change. These experiments indicate that LTP requires calcium, but at a lower effective range than LTD; the climbing fiber acts as a polarity switch largely because its complex spike pushes eligible dendritic compartments into the higher-calcium depression regime 19 . There is, however, not a literal fixed "calcium lookup table". The thresholds depend on stimulation history, dendritic state, inhibition, and cerebellar region, but the central principle is experimentally supported: the climbing-fiber-linked calcium increment biases recently active PF synapses away from potentiation and toward depression 19 , 13 . Postsynaptic LTP is not simply LTD run backward. The two directions recruit partially distinct intracellular mechanisms: LTD is generally associated with stronger calcium and kinase-dominated signaling that reduces AMPA-receptor transmission, whereas LTP occurs in a lower-calcium regime and depends more strongly on phosphatase-mediated signaling 24 , 19 . One experimentally identified form of postsynaptic LTP increases the efficacy of GluA3-containing AMPA receptors already present at the synapse rather than inserting a new population of receptors 25 . The molecular implementations of potentiation and depression are therefore partly separable rather than perfectly symmetric. Genetic experiments show that potentiation contributes directly to cerebellar learning. Purkinje-cell-specific deletion of PP2B abolishes postsynaptic PF–PC LTP while largely sparing LTD and impairs bidirectional vestibulo-ocular-reflex adaptation and delay-eyeblink conditioning 26 . Because PP2B also affects Purkinje-cell intrinsic excitability, these deficits cannot be attributed exclusively to synaptic LTP. More selective evidence comes from Purkinje-cell GluA3 deletion, which disrupts postsynaptic potentiation while preserving basal transmission and LTD and strongly impairs several forms of VOR learning 25 . Potentiation can also be expressed presynaptically. Repeated parallel-fiber activity can produce a lasting increase in glutamate release, and granule-cell-specific disruption of a presynaptic potentiation pathway impairs VOR adaptation [An NMDA receptor/nitric oxide cascade in presynaptic parallel fiber-Purkinje neuron long-term potentiation; cAMP–EPAC–PKC( ϵ \epsilon )–RIM1( α \alpha ) signaling regulates presynaptic long-term potentiation and motor learning]. The effective PF-PC connection is therefore controlled from both sides of the synapse: postsynaptic mechanisms change the response to released glutamate, while presynaptic mechanisms change how reliably and strongly glutamate is released. The PF–PC connection should consequently not be treated as one scalar weight governed by the simple rule “complex spike means depress; no complex spike means potentiate.” Its effective influence depends on presynaptic release, postsynaptic receptor efficacy, intrinsic excitability, and the temporal and inhibitory state of the Purkinje-cell dendrite 27 . These parameters can change independently or together, allowing the circuit to regulate both the mean strength and the reliability of a parallel-fiber input. Bidirectional plasticity gives the cerebellar cortex a way to remain both adaptable and stable. LTD reduces the influence of parallel-fiber patterns associated with subsequent errors; LTP restores or strengthens inputs that remain useful without generating the same teaching signal, reverses obsolete depression, and preserves the dynamic range needed for continued learning 19 , 25 . Which update occurs is determined not by the presence of parallel-fiber activity or a complex spike alone, but by their timing and by the current physiological state of the synapse and dendrite. Temporal credit assignment and eligibility traces A climbing-fiber error normally arrives only after the parallel-fiber activity that contributed to the faulty prediction. The plasticity rule must therefore solve a local temporal credit-assignment problem : when the teaching signal arrives, it must modify synapses that were active when the error-producing command or prediction was generated, rather than only those active at the moment the delayed feedback reaches the cerebellum. PF–PC synapses solve part of this problem by retaining a transient eligibility trace of recent parallel-fiber activity. A subsequent climbing-fiber event can convert this silent trace into lasting plasticity, while synapses that were inactive during the relevant earlier interval remain relatively unaffected 2 , 28 . The existence and temporal shape of this trace are inferred experimentally from the delay between parallel-fiber and climbing-fiber activation that produces LTD. In mouse slices, depression was strongest when a parallel-fiber burst occurred approximately 80 ms before the climbing-fiber event; the effective window was broad, with a fitted half-width of approximately 300 ms 2 . Single-spine imaging similarly showed that sparse PF activation produced especially large local calcium signals and LTD when it preceded the climbing fiber by approximately 50-200 ms 12 . The synaptic state produced by parallel-fiber activity therefore outlasts the electrical event itself and remains available to interact with delayed instruction. Biophysically, recent parallel-fiber activity leaves a local dendritic and synaptic state that can interact supralinearly with the later climbing-fiber calcium signal. Sparse PF activation can confine this interaction to individual active spines, while stronger activation recruits larger dendritic compartments 12 . Metabotropic glutamate signaling, intracellular calcium release, and other short-lived second-messenger processes likely contribute to the timing dependence, but no single molecule has been established as the complete biological eligibility trace. The trace is perhaps best understood as an emergent state of the recently active synapse and its surrounding dendritic compartment. Similar to other brain regions, the shape of the eligibility window is matched to the delays of the circuit in which the synapse operates. In the cerebellar flocculus, long-term and single-trial depression are narrowly tuned to a PF-CF interval of approximately 120 ms, similar to the delay with which visual error information reaches the circuit during vestibulo-ocular learning 13 . Coincident PF and CF activation instead produced LTP, a 100 ms interval also favored potentiation, and a 150 ms interval produced no significant change. In the vermis, by contrast, plasticity was induced by a range of intervals, with individual cells tuned for different intervals 13 . The eligibility trace is therefore not a universal cerebellar hyperparameter: its timing differs across modules in accordance with their characteristic feedback delays. Inhibitory plasticity Inhibition in the cerebellar cortex is not merely a fixed mechanism for limiting Purkinje-cell firing. The parallel-fiber pathway recruits basket and stellate cells, which can change both the excitatory inputs they receive and the strength of the inhibition they deliver to Purkinje cells. Plasticity can therefore modify a mossy-fiber context along two coordinated routes: directly through PF–PC synapses and indirectly through PF–interneuron–PC feedforward inhibition. The learned Purkinje-cell output is the net result of both pathways rather than a readout of excitatory parallel-fiber weights alone 29 , 30 . The clearest evidence for coordinated excitatory and inhibitory learning comes from in-vivo recordings of Purkinje cells and their afferent molecular-layer interneurons. In one study, parallel-fiber stimulation delivered without climbing-fiber activity produced large, persistent expansions of Purkinje-cell receptive fields but contractions of the receptive fields of nearby interneurons. Pairing the same parallel-fiber stimulation with climbing-fiber activity produced the opposite pattern: Purkinje-cell receptive fields contracted while interneuron receptive fields expanded. Mossy-fiber receptive fields did not change, leading the authors to attribute the effects to reciprocal bidirectional plasticity at parallel-fiber synapses onto Purkinje cells and interneurons 29 . Functionally, these reciprocal changes are positioned to reinforce one another. When parallel-fiber stimulation was paired with climbing-fiber activity, Purkinje-cell PF receptive fields contracted while the PF receptive fields of their afferent interneurons expanded; without climbing-fiber pairing, Purkinje-cell receptive fields expanded while interneuron receptive fields contracted 29 . If these receptive-field changes reflect altered PF synaptic efficacy, as the unchanged mossy-fiber receptive fields suggest, the two pathways would change Purkinje-cell output in the same net direction: weaker direct PF excitation together with stronger PF-recruited inhibition would reduce the response to climbing-fiber-paired inputs, whereas stronger excitation together with weaker feedforward inhibition would increase the response to unpaired inputs. This synergistic effect is, however, a functional inference rather than a direct measurement of excitation and inhibition in the same connected circuit. Plasticity has also been shown to occur at the inhibitory synapse itself. Strong Purkinje-cell excitation or climbing-fiber stimulation can produce a long-lasting increase in G A B A A GABA_A -receptor-mediated inhibition, termed rebound potentiation . In the original experiments, climbing-fiber stimulation potentiated inhibitory postsynaptic currents for as long as 75 minutes and similarly increased the Purkinje cell’s response to externally applied GABA. This indicated a predominantly postsynaptic increase in G A B A A GABA_A -receptor responsiveness, triggered by the climbing-fiber-evoked rise in Purkinje-cell calcium 31 . Rebound potentiation allows one teaching event to modify excitation and inhibition in a mutually reinforcing direction. A climbing-fiber complex spike can depress eligible excitatory PF–PC synapses while increasing the Purkinje cell’s sensitivity to inhibitory input. Both changes reduce Purkinje-cell output when the relevant circuit is reactivated, thereby disinhibiting downstream cerebellar nuclear neurons. The two mechanisms nevertheless have different calcium thresholds and induction requirements, so they need not always occur together or in the same proportion [Intracellular Ca(^ 2+ ) Thresholds for Induction of Excitatory Long-Term Depression and Inhibitory Long-Term Potentiation in a Cerebellar Purkinje Neuron; Synaptic Excitation Produces a Long-Lasting Rebound Potentiation of Inhibitory Synaptic Signals in Cerebellar Purkinje Cells]. A recent study suggests that this inhibitory potentiation is more selective than a uniform increase in every GABAergic input. In recordings from individually stimulated interneurons, Purkinje-cell depolarization caused a persistent increase at somatic and proximal-dendritic basket-cell synapses but not at distal stellate-cell synapses; deleting the G A B A A GABA_A -receptor ( β 2 \beta2 ) subunit abolished the basket-cell plasticity 32 . Other preparations have demonstrated rebound potentiation of responses associated with both basket and stellate inputs, indicating that its expression depends on interneuron identity, receptor composition, developmental stage, and induction protocol rather than following one uniform rule across the dendritic tree. The activity of the inhibitory synapse during the teaching event also affects whether it is potentiated: GABA release during Purkinje-cell depolarization can activate postsynaptic G A B A ( B ) GABA(_B) receptors and suppress rebound potentiation 33 . Thus, the climbing-fiber-linked calcium signal preferentially strengthens inhibitory synapses that are permissive under the current activity state rather than automatically strengthening every active GABAergic contact. This gives inhibitory plasticity its own form of synapse-specific gating and prevents a global complex spike from producing completely uniform inhibitory gain. Inhibitory transmission can also undergo long-term depression. In anaesthetized mice, repeated 1 Hz (but not 2 or 4 Hz) facial stimulation caused a lasting reduction in sensory-evoked MLI-PC (MLI = molecular layer interneuron) inhibition and shortened the accompanying pause in Purkinje-cell simple-spike firing. The evoked firing properties of the recorded interneurons did not change significantly, while pharmacological experiments implicated NMDA-receptor and endocannabinoid signaling in the depression 34 . This demonstrates that natural sensory pathways can weaken, as well as strengthen, inhibition onto Purkinje cells in the intact cerebellar cortex. Associative learning can recruit similarly bidirectional changes. in one study, fear conditioning increased both excitatory PF-PC transmission and GABA release from molecular-layer interneurons onto Purkinje cells 35 . Extinction reversed the enhanced inhibitory transmission, and an extinction-like parallel-fiber stimulation pattern produced inhibitory LTD after fear conditioning but not in naïve animals. This learning-dependent inhibitory LTD required GluN2D-containing NMDA receptors. Inhibition also determines whether plasticity is induced at neighboring excitatory synapses. Although inhibition is often assumed simply to reduce dendritic calcium and suppress learning, hyperpolarization can increase the availability of low-threshold calcium channels in Purkinje cells. Under one high-frequency parallel-fiber protocol, intact GABAergic inhibition was required for PF-PC LTP; blocking inhibition eliminated both the relevant calcium signal and potentiation 36 . In other conditions, disinhibition increases climbing-fiber-evoked dendritic calcium and permits climbing-fiber instruction. Inhibition therefore regulates the sign and probability of excitatory plasticity in a state- and protocol-dependent manner rather than serving as an invariant brake on learning. Behavioral experiments confirm that molecular-layer inhibition is necessary for normal cerebellar learning, although they do not assign the resulting deficits to one inhibitory plasticity mechanism. In one major study, selectively removing G A B A A GABA_A -receptor-mediated MLI inhibition from Purkinje cells caused relatively mild baseline motor abnormalities but strongly impaired phase adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex and consolidation of learned gain changes 30 . Purkinje cells also developed abnormal simple-spike patterns, supporting the proposal that feedforward inhibition shapes the output patterns that train plasticity in cerebellar and vestibular nuclei. More direct evidence shows that learning changes interneuron activity itself. After gain-increase VOR adaptation, the population response of floccular molecular-layer interneurons shifted in phase. Acute optogenetic suppression of these interneurons left the baseline reflex largely intact but abolished expression of the newly acquired gain-increase memory. After several days of consolidation, the learned response was no longer sensitive to the same suppression 37 . MLI activity therefore forms a necessary component of the early, labile memory trace, while later expression can become less dependent on that cortical inhibitory pattern—consistent with transfer or redistribution of memory to downstream sites (more on such "memory transfer" below). Cerebellar inhibitory plasticity can therefore operate at several coupled parameters: [ , , . ] Plasticity in the first pathway learns which contexts recruit inhibition; plasticity in the second controls how strongly that inhibition affects Purkinje output; and the inhibitory state of the dendrite determines whether concurrent excitatory inputs undergo LTD, LTP, or no lasting change. These mechanisms make inhibition part of the learned predictive transformation itself, not merely a stabilizer placed around a plastic excitatory circuit. The principal unresolved question is how changes at PF-PC, PF-interneuron, and interneuron-PC synapses are coordinated during natural learning so that they reinforce rather than cancel one another. Plasticity in the granular input layer Classical cerebellar models often treated the mossy-fiber–granule-cell pathway as a fixed expansion recoder, with most learning assigned to PF–Purkinje synapses. But the granular layer is itself plastic: mossy-fiber inputs onto granule cells express LTP and LTD, granule-cell intrinsic excitability changes with synaptic plasticity, and excitatory inputs onto Golgi cells are also modifiable 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 . The cerebellum can therefore adapt not only the readout from its expanded representation, but the representation itself. At mossy-fiber–granule-cell synapses, the direction of plasticity depends on the strength and temporal pattern of input. Strong bursts producing large postsynaptic calcium signals generally induce LTP, whereas weaker patterns favor LTD 39 , 42 . Plasticity alters both neurotransmitter release and granule-cell excitability, changing the probability that a mossy-fiber pattern will generate granule-cell spikes 43 , 40 . These changes affect the gain and temporal structure of the information sent to Purkinje cells. One study showed that MF-granule-cell LTP increases response reliability, advances spike timing, raises transmission gain, and broadens the range of input frequencies represented by granule-cell output; LTD produces the opposite effects 44 . Granular-layer learning can therefore promote selected mossy-fiber features while delaying, attenuating, or suppressing others. Golgi-cell inhibition helps determine where LTP and LTD occur. Strongly excited and weakly inhibited regions tend to potentiate, whereas more strongly inhibited surrounding regions tend to depress, producing spatially organized core-surround patterns of plasticity 45 , 46 . Similar bidirectional changes can be induced by tactile stimulation in vivo, and reducing GABAergic inhibition shifts the balance toward LTP 47 . The granular layer can thus learn a contrast-enhanced filter over related mossy-fiber inputs rather than modifying each channel independently. Golgi cells are themselves part of the learned transformation. Parallel-fiber inputs onto Golgi cells express LTD, while both mossy-fiber and parallel-fiber inputs can undergo state-dependent LTP or LTD 48 , 41 . Their compartmentalized dendritic architecture also allows activity in the two pathways to interact: mossy fibers principally contact basal dendrites in the granular layer, whereas parallel fibers excite apical dendrites extending into the molecular layer. Recent slice experiments showed that a parallel-fiber-evoked Golgi-cell spike can backpropagate into the basal dendrites and determine the sign of plasticity at mossy-fiber synapses. Mossy-fiber activation shortly before the spike produced LTP, whereas the reverse order produced LTD, providing a spike-timing-dependent rule that associates incoming mossy-fiber patterns with temporally related parallel-fiber activity 49 . Plasticity at these convergent inputs can therefore regulate which granule-cell ensembles are inhibited, how long they remain active, and how sparse or temporally precise the resulting parallel-fiber code becomes. The STDP evidence currently comes from acute juvenile mouse slices, so its contribution during natural learning remains to be established. Behavioral evidence is suggestive but not yet conclusive. Disrupting NMDA-receptor-dependent MF–granule-cell potentiation impairs vestibulo-ocular learning, and blocking granule-cell transmission impairs several cerebellum-dependent motor-learning tasks 50 , 51 . Imaging during eyeblink conditioning also shows that granule-cell population activity changes substantially as learning proceeds 52 . These experiments establish that the granular representation is plastic and behaviorally important, but do not yet isolate how much of the learned code arises locally rather than from changing upstream mossy-fiber input. Plasticity in the granular layer is therefore best understood as adaptive representation learning ; it modifies the gain, timing, reliability, sparsity, and spatial contrast of the mossy-fiber features supplied to Purkinje cells. PF–Purkinje plasticity then learns over a feature basis that has already been shaped by experience, rather than over a permanently fixed random expansion. Plasticity in the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei The cerebellar and vestibular nuclei are adaptive output stages rather than passive relays. Their neurons combine excitatory mossy-fiber or vestibular-afferent input with inhibitory Purkinje-cell input, and plasticity occurs in both pathways as well as in intrinsic excitability 53 , 54 , 55 . Excitatory mossy-fiber synapses onto nuclear neurons express LTP when recent mossy-fiber activity is followed by strong Purkinje-cell-like inhibition and subsequent resumption of firing. NMDA-receptor activation marks the active excitatory synapses, while the inhibition-disinhibition sequence supplies a broader postsynaptic signal, allowing recently active inputs to be selectively strengthened 53 , 56 . The important signal appears to be the ordered transition from excitation through inhibition to renewed firing, not necessarily a large stereotyped rebound burst 57 . Mossy-fiber inputs are bidirectional: other activity patterns produce postsynaptic LTD, so nuclear weights can be either strengthened or weakened according to mossy-fiber activity, Purkinje inhibition, and nuclear-cell state 58 . Purkinje-cell inhibitory synapses onto nuclear neurons also express long-term changes, altering how strongly future Purkinje bursts and pauses control nuclear output 54 . Nuclear neurons can additionally undergo persistent increases in intrinsic excitability, causing the same synaptic input to evoke more spikes after induction 55 . A learned nuclear response can therefore reflect stronger excitation, altered Purkinje inhibition, increased cellular responsiveness, or some combination of all three. Related plasticity occurs in the medial vestibular nucleus, the major downstream target of the flocculus. Pairing vestibular-afferent excitation with Purkinje-like inhibition induces LTD at vestibular synapses, providing a mechanism through which learned cortical inhibition can train the brainstem pathway that ultimately generates the vestibulo-ocular reflex 59 . These mechanisms support a distributed account of cerebellar memory. The cerebellar cortex can rapidly learn high-dimensional, context- and time-specific Purkinje-cell patterns, while the nuclei learn a lower-dimensional mapping from recurring mossy-fiber contexts and Purkinje output to the final command. A learned Purkinje pause can therefore both immediately disinhibit nuclear output and help strengthen excitatory inputs that later reproduce part of the response more directly 56 . Much work has supported a teacher–student relationship between the cerebellar cortex and nuclei, where rapidly acquired, context-specific Purkinje-cell activity trains slower plasticity in nuclear excitatory and inhibitory pathways, gradually transferring part of the learned correction into a more stable output-stage representation 56 , 60 , 61 , 62 ; behavioral evidence, however, supports interacting cortical and nuclear learning sites. The interposed nucleus is essential for expression and normal acquisition of eyeblink conditioning, yet animals lacking relevant cerebellar cortex can sometimes acquire slower and poorly timed conditioned responses; imaging also shows cortical and nuclear engagement during learning 63 , 60 , 61 . The cortex-to-nucleus transfer model is therefore plausible, but memories are unlikely to be copied through one universal early-to-late sequence. A recent normative account proposes that the amount and direction of memory transfer likely depend on task difficulty and the relative errors available to the two sites 62 . Plasticity in the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei therefore forms a second adaptive layer downstream of cerebellar cortex. Cortical plasticity learns precisely timed, context-specific modulation of Purkinje output, while nuclear and vestibular plasticity recalibrates how excitatory input, Purkinje inhibition, and intrinsic excitability are combined to generate the final cerebellar command. Developmental construction of the climbing-fiber teaching channel The adult one-climbing-fiber-per-Purkinje-cell arrangement is developmentally constructed rather than present at birth. In one study involving neonatal rodents, each Purkinje cell was initially innervated by roughly five climbing fibers of similar strength 64 . During the first postnatal week, their strengths diverge and one input becomes dominant; the weaker inputs are then removed through successive phases, leaving most Purkinje cells mono-innervated by the end of the third postnatal week 64 , 65 . Winner selection is coupled to a change in synaptic territory. The dominant climbing fiber begins extending from the Purkinje-cell soma onto the dendritic arbor, while competing fibers remain confined to perisomatic regions and are subsequently eliminated 66 . In-vivo two-photon imaging showed that the fiber beginning dendritic translocation almost invariably survived; ablating that fiber allowed a former competitor to translocate and become the new winner, indicating that dendritic occupation stabilizes competitive success rather than merely marking it 67 . The refinement is activity-dependent, but activity has different roles at different stages. Purkinje-cell calcium signaling is required for normal strengthening, dendritic translocation, and elimination, while increasing Purkinje-cell activity accelerates late elimination through an Arc/Arg3.1-dependent postsynaptic program 68 , 69 . Parallel-fiber and granule-cell signaling also contribute to the later removal and spatial restriction of surplus climbing fibers; disrupting mGluR1, GluD2-associated PF synaptogenesis, granule cells, or NMDA-receptor signaling during a brief developmental critical period leaves persistent multiple innervation 70 , 71 , 72 . A recent study qualifies the simple idea that the strongest climbing fiber necessarily wins. Climbing fibers rendered unable to release glutamate could still be selected as winners, although their subsequent dendritic expansion and elimination of competing fibers were impaired 73 . Initial winner identity may therefore involve activity-independent molecular or structural biases, while synaptic transmission is essential for stabilizing, expanding, and refining the selected connection. Synthesis Cerebellar plasticity is not a single climbing-fiber-triggered LTD rule, but a distributed family of state-dependent learning mechanisms. Recent parallel-fiber activity leaves temporally structured eligibility traces; climbing-fiber events provide module-specific instruction; and the timing, magnitude, and circuit context of those events determine whether eligible synapses weaken, strengthen, or remain unchanged. Bidirectional plasticity at PF–Purkinje synapses prevents saturation, while plasticity in inhibitory circuits, the granular layer, and intrinsic excitability changes how inputs are represented, gated, and converted into Purkinje-cell output. Learning also extends beyond the cerebellar cortex. Plasticity in the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei modifies how excitatory afferents, Purkinje inhibition, and cellular excitability are combined into the final output command, providing a second adaptive stage that can stabilize or redistribute corrections initially expressed in cortical activity. The evidence therefore supports interacting learning sites rather than a single memory store or a rigid cortex-to-nucleus transfer sequence. Overall, the cerebellum solves predictive calibration through distributed temporal credit assignment : a developmentally organized climbing-fiber channel routes teaching events to the appropriate microzone, local eligibility mechanisms identify the recent activity relevant to those events, and multiple plasticity sites update complementary parameters across different timescales. The resulting circuit can rapidly correct context-specific prediction errors while retaining the stability, reversibility, and representational flexibility required for continued learning.
