Generate hypotheses (programs) from current library 2. Select actions that maximize expected information gain 3. Observe outcomes 4. Update posterior over programs 5. Cache useful new programs/subprograms to library 6. Refactor library for efficiency Phase 4: Stochastic Search with Annealing From the "theory learning as stochastic search" framework: Start "hot" (high exploration, accept suboptimal proposals) Gradually cool (exploitation, convergence to high-posterior theories) Mirrors developmental trajectory: Children are more exploratory, adults more stable – Sensory/Motor (0-2 yrs): Minimizes error in basic perception. "Burnt in" (myelinated). Parietal/Temporal (2-11 yrs): Minimizes error in concrete spatial/linguistic tasks. "Burnt in." Prefrontal (11-25 yrs): Now that the lower layers are efficient "subroutines" that don’t require conscious monitoring, the Rostrolateral Prefrontal Cortex (RLPFC) wakes up. The RLPFC is the "apex" of the hierarchy. It takes the outputs of the concrete layers (concepts like "mass," "volume," "fairness") as its inputs. It doesn’t process sensory data; it processes representations of representations. – Stage 1 (Analogous to 0-2 years): Embodied Grounding and Intuitive Physics. The initial phase of training should focus on grounding the agent’s representations in physical reality. An agent, equipped with basic architectural priors (e.g., convolutional layers for vision, motor outputs for action) and core knowledge-like principles (e.g., object persistence), would be placed in a physically realistic, interactive simulation. Its learning would be driven not by extrinsic rewards, but by an intrinsic motivation module inspired by the PACE framework, rewarding the agent for exploration that reduces the prediction error of its nascent world model. Goal: Learn a grounded, low-level, causal generative model of the physical world through self-supervised, embodied "play." Be able to render (even though it remains implicit) a full 3D map of a scene, fully segmented and complete with geometry, material properties, affordances, miscellaneous properties, and motion for each segment Stage 2 (Analogous to 2-7 years): The Symbolic and Social Explosion. In the second stage, the agent would be introduced to language and social interaction. This could involve interacting with humans or other AI agents via natural language. The agent’s task would be to ground linguistic symbols in its sensorimotor experience (e.g., learning that the word "cube" corresponds to the visual and tactile properties of cubes it has manipulated). It would engage in more complex, goal-directed "play," both alone and with others, to test hypotheses. It would also begin to build a rudimentary Theory of Mind by learning to predict the actions of other simple agents based on their goals and observable knowledge. Goal: Build a multimodal world model that links language to sensorimotor representations and includes basic predictive models of other agents. Virtuous cycle between language learning and learning in all other modalities Stage 3 (Analogous to 7 years - Adulthood): Abstract and Long-Horizon Reasoning. In the final stage, the agent’s full planning and control architecture (its "PFC") would be enabled. Leveraging its grounded, multimodal world model, the agent would be trained on tasks requiring complex, multi-step planning, counterfactual reasoning ("what if?"), and sophisticated collaboration in multi-agent social dilemmas. Its ToM would mature, allowing it to infer more complex latent states in other agents, facilitating more effective cooperation and competition. Goal: Deploy the fully developed world model for flexible, abstract, and temporally extended goal-directed behavior in complex, open-ended environments. Rule-based inference beyond simple association/co-occurence; proposing rules and testing them

title: From Conception to Birth
text: By birth, the brain’s optimization architecture is already scaffolded: the learning loops are anatomically in place and their teacher channels wired, even if connectivity (including long- and short-range connectivity) is only coarsely specified (all major white matter tracts are, however, identifiable by the end of normal gestation 1 ). Cortico-cerebellar microcomplexes are formed (mossy fibers from pontine relays and climbing fibers from inferior olive converge on Purkinje dendrites and deep nuclei), establishing a supervised-calibration pathway with fractured somatotopy and strong temporal precision. Basal ganglia actor-critic loops are closed: cortex projects to a compartmentalized striatum (D1/D2, patch/matrix), midbrain dopamine reaches striatum and pallidum, and thalamo-cortical return paths exist, yielding an RL substrate with innate action-selection competition and a burst/pause teaching signal. Cortico-thalamo-cortical hierarchies are laminated and topographic-retino-/tono-/somatotopy are present, layer-4 relay and feedback layers are differentiated, and higher-order thalamus (pulvinar/MD) provides the long-range gating needed for predictive-coding-like inference. The hippocampal-entorhinal trisynaptic loop is assembled, and the major long-range conduits (corticospinal tract, corpus callosum, fornix, cingulum) are laid down but lightly myelinated, imposing bandwidth and latency constraints that may act as inductive biases on what can be learned first. Across the brainstem and forebrain, neuromodulatory tone (ACh, NE, DA, 5-HT) is established and the chloride-transport "GABA switch" around birth re-times excitability, effectively opening and closing gates on plasticity. These architectural priors–topography, center-surround inhibition, temporal precision in the olive, winner-take-most competition in BG, hierarchical feedforward/feedback loops in cortex–mean the newborn does not learn with a blank slate; it starts with biased, coarsely wired optimizers that need calibration (a lot of it). Taking it a step further, by late gestation, the brain is not merely a bag of partially-wired modules; it already exhibits a system-level communication scaffold. Macroscale connectivity is organized according to a cost-value compromise: strongly clustered, modular local circuits coupled by a sparse set of long-range routes that disproportionately link hub regions (a core-periphery / rich-club-like backbone; see "The Semantic Memory System") 2 , 3 , 4 . Importantly, this "global graph" is not purely structural: in utero resting-state dynamics already reveal recognizable large-scale functional networks–sensorimotor/visual/thalamic systems appear first and are detectable by mid-gestation, while higher-order association networks (default-mode/frontoparietal/salience-like components) emerge later in the third trimester and remain spatially fragmented and weakly segregated compared to postnatal patterns 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 . So the right way to phrase the "degree" of prenatally identifiable network structure is: the backbone and community structure are already present as a coarse, biased scaffold, with rapidly increasing long-range and interhemispheric coupling late in gestation, but the adult-like sharpness of network boundaries and the reliable, high-bandwidth timing of long-range coordination (and thus fully fledged "global workspace-like" broadcasting) remain immature until postnatal myelination, synaptic/inhibitory stabilization, and continued circuit refinement. Pillars of Gestational Learning Molecular patterning and cell migration can be seen as the "zeroth pillar" of gestational learning. Long before sensory-driven learning, the cortex is "pretrained" by gradients and lineage programs that set where computations will live and how information will flow. Competing-but-compatible frames– protomap (intrinsic areal identity from morphogen gradients) and protocortex (extrinsic refinement via extrinsic (especially thalamic) input)–together explain why early cortex is neither blank nor fully specified: it is biased, scaffolded, and then data-aligned 9 , 10 . Meanwhile, inside-out lamination via radial glial cells and long-range tangential migration (parallel to the brain’s surface) of interneurons from ganglionic eminences supply the canonical cortical microcircuit parts list (projection neurons in layers, inhibitory classes arriving on schedule), with transient populations such as Cajal-Retzius cells (which produce reelin, an extracellular matrix protein) shaping final layer placement 11 , 12 , 13 . This is "initializing" the brain in the literal sense: a structured hypothesis class is built before experience tunes parameters. The first pillar of gestational learning is patterned spontaneous activity : before the senses open to the world, peripheral organs and central circuits generate structured "proto-data" that calibrate maps and controllers. In vision, retinal waves–coherent, spatially local bursts that propagate across the immature retina–drive correlated activity through the optic nerve into downstream relays, where they refine (rather than solely create) topographic organization laid down by molecular guidance cues, sharpening retinotopy in targets such as the lateral geniculate nucleus and superior colliculus and promoting eye-specific segregation and competitive alignment 14 , 15 , 16 . This is not noise; it is a low-dimensional curriculum : the dominant prenatal patterns are constrained (e.g., wavefronts and bursts), meaning that despite rich single-neuron variability, population activity often lies on a small set of recurring spatiotemporal modes (location/phase, direction, speed, amplitude). These modes implicitly implement priors that later perception will rely on: topographic continuity (nearby sensors co-activate), temporal coherence (states evolve smoothly via propagating fronts), and local correlation structure (activity is clustered rather than globally synchronous) 17 , 18 , 19 . Importantly, this does not mean the fetus "learns to detect edges" in the adult sense; rather, it initializes the wiring geometry and gain structure that make oriented, localized receptive fields an easy downstream solution once real images arrive. In vision specifically, wave statistics can bias circuits toward the kinds of anisotropic correlations that later support orientation-/direction-selective organization and map alignment 20 , 19 . Similar low-dimensional spontaneous regimes exist cortically (spindle bursts/early network oscillations, delta brushes) and somatosensorily, where thalamus-subplate-cortex loops rehearse the dialogue they will later run online 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 . Audition shows the same logic. Long before airborne sound is reliably transduced, inner hair cells and supporting epithelial networks in the cochlea fire organized bursts that sweep tonotopic space 25 , 26 , 27 . At the population level this again resembles a low-dimensional generator (a burst packet whose latent variables include position along the tonotopic axis, spatial spread to neighboring channels, and inter-burst timing), which is exactly what map-refinement plasticity needs before high-dimensional natural sound statistics dominate 25 , 27 . These events walk the auditory pathway through its future feature basis (frequency channels and their co-activation patterns) so that, when acoustic input actually arrives near 25-27 gestational weeks for low frequencies and by  29-31 weeks for higher frequencies, the system is already partially tuned 28 , 29 . This staged opening means that much of "auditory pretraining" is self-generated, then smoothly handed off to real sound in late gestation. That handoff produces measurable fetal/neonatal plasticity to structured stimulation (e.g., repeated melodies or speech-like patterns), and the trace persists postnatally 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 . The second pillar is the subplate , a transient but highly active cortical compartment that acts as a timed interface between incoming thalamic drive and an immature cortical plate. Thalamic axons reach the appropriate cortical territory before layer-4 targets are ready; they form provisional synapses and "wait" within the subplate, then invade the cortical plate once targets mature–effectively routing and pacing early sensory drive into nascent circuits 34 , 35 , 36 . Subplate neurons are among the earliest-born cortical neurons and form one of the first functional cortical networks: they receive thalamic input (and are positioned to integrate diffuse neuromodulatory signals) and project into the developing cortical plate, providing a temporary excitatory/organizational scaffold that can amplify weak thalamic signals, synchronize local activity, and bias where thalamic branches stabilize during the waiting-to-invasion transition 37 . During late fetal and early neonatal periods, subplate-coupled circuitry participates in prominent spindle-burst and related early oscillations; these patterned events are thought to supply precisely the kind of structured, repeatable training signal" needed for activity-dependent refinement–guiding axonal branching, target selection, map sharpening, and synaptic stabilization along thalamocortical pathways when peripheral inputs are sparse and cortical microcircuits are still being assembled 38 , 39 . Disruption of subplate development (including injury affecting subplate/white matter compartments) is associated with durable neurocognitive deficits, consistent with the idea that this transient relay exerts lasting control over when and where early instructive signals land–and therefore over the initial conditions from which mature cortical architecture self-organizes 40 , 41 , 42 . A third pillar is fetal motor babbling and reafference . Spontaneous self-generated movements begin in the first trimester (with an expanding repertoire from whole-body to limb-specific actions), ensuring that even before rich exteroceptive input is available, the fetus is bathed in structured proprioceptive, vestibular, and tactile consequences of its own actions–including "double touch" during self-contact (touching hand + touched face) that naturally labels body boundaries and seeds somatotopic organization 43 , 44 , 45 . In late gestation, spontaneous twitches and multi-joint movements are expressed prominently during REM-like (active) sleep, indexed in humans by characteristic eye-movement bouts and embedded within organized ultradian sleep cycling (with active/REM-like sleep comprising a large fraction of fetal state time) 21 , 46 , 47 , 48 . Each twitch is a labeled event: a motor event paired with precisely timed reafferent feedback that calibrates developing spinal/brainstem controllers, builds sensorimotor contingencies, and drives activity-dependent refinement of sensorimotor circuits–including nascent cerebellar computations consistent with forward-model learning 49 , 50 . Importantly, reafferent processing is state dependent : expected reafference is gated during wake-related self-generated movements, but this gating is reduced/absent during active-sleep twitches, allowing twitches–despite being self-generated–to robustly propagate error-like sensory signals upstream and support credit assignment 51 , 50 , 49 . Because active sleep occupies such a high fraction of time in late gestation and the early neonatal period, gestation provides a massive, low-cost reservoir of self-supervised (motor, sensory) tuples that initialize postnatal goal-directed control long before the infant explicitly "intends" an action 21 , 46 . The fourth pillar is a sequential, low-to-high dimensional sensory curriculum whose "stage 0" is internally generated activity. Early gestation is dominated by low-bandwidth, highly redundant streams (visceroceptive rhythms, full-field tactile pressure, vestibular sway) plus patterned spontaneous bursts/waves that act as synthetic "proto-inputs"; only later do higher-entropy, high-dimensional channels (external acoustics, then vision) ramp up and reshape representations 52 , 21 , 28 , 53 . This ordering parcels experience from low- to high-dimensional streams: stable, slowly varying signals (cardiac and respiratory rhythms, visceroceptive cycles, steady contact) can pretrain temporal integrators and priors, while higher-bandwidth channels ramp later to enrich the representational manifold. Only late in gestation do external airborne acoustics become behaviorally salient 28 , 54 (after weeks of primarily low-pass, internally generated sound), and vision may largely be deferred until after birth 53 , 55 , 56 . The result is a curriculum that eases optimization–preventing early representational collapse, minimizing interference, and aligning emerging controllers with reliable state estimation before the sensory firehose opens. A helpful intuition is manifold expansion : early learning happens on a small, stable set of latent modes (waves/bursts/rhythms), and later sensory experience increases dimensionality and specificity without forcing the optimizer to search the full space from scratch 19 , 18 . This curriculum installs statistical structure that the postnatal learner will exploit. Maternal speech prosody and repeated melodies leave durable neural traces; newborns show ERP signatures of having learned specific auditory patterns in utero and even display production biases that mirror native-language intonation in their cries 31 , 32 , 30 . Chemosensory exposure provides another early "real-world" channel: flavors and odors from the maternal diet diffuse into the amniotic fluid, biasing early preferences and anchoring hedonic baselines (i.e value priors tuned to local ecology) 57 , 58 . The fifth pillar is neuromodulatory scheduling and hormonal gating . In early gestation, the placenta converts maternal tryptophan into serotonin and delivers it to the fetal forebrain before raphe inputs arrive, where 5-HT functions as a developmental signal that biases axon growth and sensory map formation (notably via 5-HT1B/1D pathways); this makes the placental-maternal state a plausible lever on the neurochemical context the newborn inherits 59 , 60 . Around birth, inhibitory tone undergoes the canonical NKCC1->KCC2 chloride-transport switch, shifting GABAA action from predominantly depolarizing to hyperpolarizing and retiming network dynamics as giant depolarizing potentials and other synchronous neonatal patterns give way to sparser, adult-like regimes 61 , 62 , 63 . In vivo and review work converge that this maturation of inhibition is a prerequisite for opening and closing classic critical-period windows-i.e., it sets when and where Hebbian changes can be expressed-which justifies reading "plasticity’s sign, gain, and spatial reach" as developmentally scheduled control knobs 64 , 65 . Several of these knobs are also coupled to maternal-placental inputs: the placental serotonin pathway is sensitive to maternal physiology and inflammation, and the 11β-HSD2 barrier in placenta buffers fetal exposure to glucocorticoids that modulate excitability and plasticity thresholds, providing concrete mechanisms by which extrinsic state can tune the initial learning conditions 66 , 67 , 68 , 69 . Sleep is the sixth pillar: by late gestation it occupies the vast majority of time, dominated by active (REM-like) sleep 70 , 71 . This state is saturated with developmental burst patterns, which may coordinate thalamocortical and hippocampo-cortical communication while gating plasticity 72 , 73 . During active sleep, the aforementioned spontaneous twitches and organ-driven rhythms send precisely timed reafferent volleys through spinal cord, brainstem, thalamus, cerebellum, and sensorimotor cortex, supplying labeled motor-sensory tuples that pretrain forward models and calibrate gains well before intentional action. Across these long offline windows, sleep-dependent mechanisms consolidate useful assemblies (those with high inter-neuronal resonance) and prune maladaptive ones 21 , 74 , 75 , 76 , so the system emerges with cleaner, more stable controllers. It is worth emphasizing that gestation doesn’t only add synapses; it also sculpts circuits by deleting cells/branches that fail to integrate. Programmed cell death is widespread in developing brain and participates in morphogenesis, controlling population sizes and removing transient scaffolds 77 , 78 . Interpreted computationally, apoptosis + synapse elimination behave like an L0/L1-style constraint on gestational circuit complexity: overspecify early, then compress toward efficient solutions consistent with spontaneous and peripheral-driven activity statistics (a process that plays out across the lifespan, but is perhaps most present during gestation). On this view, early low-dimensional motifs act like a stabilizing training signal: circuits that resonate with (and can reliably predict / reproduce) the dominant prenatal modes are preferentially stabilized, while branches that fail to participate in coherent assemblies are more likely to be eliminated–compression not just of parameters, but of dynamics 21 , 77 . Conclusion In sum, the prenatal brain is not passively awaiting experience but actively constructing the preconditions for learning. Molecular gradients and migratory programs establish a coarse computational blueprint; patterned spontaneous activity (retinal waves, cochlear bursts, spindle-burst oscillations) provides a low-dimensional synthetic curriculum that sharpens maps and initializes gain structures before the corresponding sensory channels open. The subplate orchestrates when and where thalamic signals first engage cortex, while fetal motor babbling and state-gated reafference supply labeled sensorimotor tuples that pretrain forward models. Layered atop this is a naturalistic curriculum in which low-bandwidth, highly redundant streams (visceroceptive rhythms, vestibular sway, filtered maternal speech) give way to progressively higher-dimensional input, easing optimization by expanding the representational manifold incrementally rather than all at once. Neuromodulatory and hormonal schedules (placental serotonin, the peri-birth GABA polarity switch, glucocorticoid gating) set the when and where of plasticity, while prolonged active sleep provides the offline state in which twitches, bursts, and consolidation mechanisms refine and compress emerging circuits. By birth, therefore, the newborn inherits not a blank slate but a richly biased, coarsely wired optimization engine: learning loops are closed, teaching signals are routed, and statistical priors (topographic continuity, temporal coherence, local correlation structure, and even culture-specific auditory templates) are already written into the hardware, ready to be calibrated by the postnatal world.

title: 0-3 Months
text: Behavioral capabilities Between birth and three months the system shifts from reflex to a minimally controllable learner: quiet-alert bouts lengthen, startle is suppressed, reflexive saccades give way to nascent smooth pursuit 1 , and the notorious optokinetic response (OKR) asymmetry begins to abate 2 , together raising sensory SNR so prediction-error machinery has clean signals to process. Behaviorally, habituation/dishabituation paradigms already show rapid attenuation to predictable repeats with recovery to novelty, providing a direct assay of early surprise-driven model updating 3 . In parallel, perceptual organization accelerates as contrast and motion sensitivity climb 4 , 5 , 6 and face processing pivots from global outline to internal features (eyes/mouth) 7 , 8 , providing a sharper representational basis for learning. Remarkably, even the youngest infants do not merely detect features–they recover stable distal-world properties from variable retinal input. Newborns (1-6 days) exhibit size constancy, responding to the real size of an object rather than its retinal projection across changes in viewing distance 9 . Shape constancy is similarly present at birth: neonates habituated to a shape at one slant treat the same shape at a novel slant as familiar while treating a different shape that produces the same retinal projection as novel 10 . Relatedly, preferential-looking and novelty-preference paradigms indicate that recognition memory is already present in the first months, but remains slow and attention-limited: infants require prolonged exposure (often tens of seconds) to subsequently recognize a stimulus 11 . A further dimension of early abstraction is approximate numerosity: newborns discriminate large-ratio numerosities (e.g., 4 vs. 12) with continuous variables (element size, total area, density) controlled, indicating that the world model encodes set cardinality as an abstract property independent of specific perceptual features 12 . Multisensory binding comes online through temporal synchrony: intersensory redundancy pulls attention to audio-visual events 13 , 14 , early voice<->face 14 matching and oral<->visual shape transfer 15 align codes across senses; the infant starts treating cross-modal coincidences as labels rather than noise. This cross-modal alignment is not limited to audio-visual or mouth-based transfer: newborns can transfer haptically acquired shape information to vision (hand → \rightarrow eye recognition), and by ∼ \sim 3 months infants can use manual exploration to discriminate material properties including weight differences , helping calibrate the visual world model with contact-grounded constraints 16 , 17 . Furthermore, the system begins modeling latent temporal structure immediately. Beyond simple sensory tuning, newborns demonstrate visual statistical learning, detecting violations in transitional probabilities within simple visual sequences 18 , suggesting the brain is acting as a ’prediction machine’ from day one, calculating the likelihood of event B B given event A A to segment continuous visual streams. Prediction in this period is not limited to two-dimensional gaze sequences: infants as young as 2 weeks display an integrated defensive response (head retraction, arm raising, distress) to a looming visual stimulus on a collision course, but not to receding or lateral motion 19 . Subsequent work confirmed that defensive blinking is specific to optical patterns specifying collision trajectory rather than mere optical expansion 20 , implying that the infant extrapolates a three-dimensional trajectory from two-dimensional optic flow and predicts contact with the self–an early form of egocentric spatial prediction. Parallel evidence from audition shows that temporal prediction is domain-general from birth. Sleeping newborns generate mismatch responses when an expected beat is omitted from a rhythmic auditory pattern, with the response time-locked to when the beat should have occurred–demonstrating generative temporal prediction over an absent event 21 . The social channel is biased from the start: newborns ( 2 days old) preferentially attend to faces displaying direct gaze over averted gaze 22 , providing an attentional prior that marks moments of communicative intent and high informational value before any social reward loop is established. Social orientation and proto-communication then structure the data stream: the ≈ \approx 6-8-week "two-month shift" (mutual gaze (locking eyes) and the social smile 23 , 24 ) creates a closed-loop social reward that stabilizes proto turn-taking 25 , 26 , while caregiver-specific recognition for voice/odor/face anchors value to people 27 , 28 , 29 . In live interaction, infants also exhibit anticipatory postural adjustments when being picked up (2-4 months), consistent with predicting others’ imminent actions toward the self rather than purely reacting 30 . By  10 weeks, infants discriminate caregivers’ basic facial affect displays (e.g., happy vs sad/angry), providing early affective labeling of socially salient states 31 Speech isn’t heard as a continuous acoustic soup: classic work shows categorical perception of speech contrasts in very young infants (including  1-month-olds), meaning the auditory front-end is already carving the space into discrete-ish partitions that later map cleanly onto phonemes/words 32 . Even earlier, newborns prefer listening to their native language and discriminate languages using broad rhythmic/prosodic cues, implying early partitioning over long-timescale acoustic structure 33 , 34 . Vocalization shifts from reflex-dominated (cry/grunt) toward increasingly voluntary "protophones" (comfort sounds / early coo-like phonation), effectively giving the agent a controllable action channel into the social environment that can be reinforced by contingent caregiver responses 35 . The model also comes equipped with an ’Animate Prior’: unrelated to face processing, newborns (1-3 days old) show a distinct preference for biological motion (point-light displays of biological kinematics) over rigid or random motion 36 . This allows the infant to instantly segment the visual scene into ’Agents’ (biological dynamics) and ’Objects’ (Newtonian dynamics). Furthermore, the ’Ecological Self’ is established via proprioceptive prediction: newborns distinguish between self-touch and external-touch (rooting significantly less when their own hand touches their cheek), indicating an early form of corollary discharge that filters ’self’ from ’world’ 37 . On the instrumental side, action-outcome contingency learning is reliable by  2-3 months (mobile-conjugate kicking, with retention extendable by reminders 38 , 39 , 40 ); even earlier, newborns can use nonnutritive sucking as an operant control variable to select auditory outcomes (e.g., different sucking patterns produce the mother’s voice versus another voice), and neonates show contingency sensitivity in high-amplitude sucking paradigms that reinforce sucking with auditory stimulation/variation 27 , 41 . Operant shaping is not confined to sucking: head turning can be conditioned in human newborns, demonstrating learnable orienting policies that actively sample the sensory scene 42 . More generally, by 8-10 weeks infants show robust behavioral reactions to response-contingent stimulation , and by ∼ \sim 3 months they differentially allocate gaze/smiles as a function of social contingency (e.g., disruption vs normal vs imitation), indicating that the infant is beginning to explicitly track whether outcomes are contingent on its own actions (and others’) 43 , 44 . Early "control" is bottlenecked by the body: improvements in head/postural control over the first months stabilize gaze and make hand-eye contingencies learnable; posture and reaching co-develop as a coupled control problem (stabilize the platform -> unlock goal-directed limb control) 45 , 46 . Even earlier, newborns exhibit organized hand-to-mouth coordination, and 2-day-old neonates preferentially attend to thumb-to-mouth actions specifically when anticipatory mouth opening predicts the action’s target–suggesting sensitivity to goal-structured body actions and predictive cues 47 , 48 . Meanwhile, spontaneous "general movements" provide rich exploratory variability–usable as motor babbling for learning sensorimotor contingencies (active system identification) 49 . By the end of this window (and clearly in the 2–5 month range), nutritive sucking itself shows online adaptation to external constraints (flow/shape/flexibility of teats), highlighting early closed-loop control over a complex action sequence 50 . Overall, by the end of this window the agent can predict a bit, control a bit, and bind across senses and agents. Training data and optimization Training data How to bootstrap with little-to-no priors 51 Training data in 0-3 months comes from several concurrent streams. Endogenous offline activity (REM twitches and stage-2 spindles) generates labeled sensorimotor tuples for consolidation while the infant still sleeps  14-17 hours/day 52 , 53 . Awake, self-initiated motor babbling produces proprioceptive, vestibular, and visual reafference, yielding dense, signed physical errors (e.g., retinal slip (eye movement errors)) that cortical and cerebellum-brainstem circuits use for supervised calibration 54 , 55 , 56 . Memory dynamics and offline compilation improve: habituation speeds up 57 , novelty preference strengthens, sleep remains abundant ( 14-17 h/day with heavy REM) 58 , and stage-2 spindles emerge over weeks 3-9 53 , so REM twitches and N2 spindles (N2 = stage-two sleep (NREM)) can drive consolidation of the day’s discoveries 59 . Social contingencies (e.g infant-directed speech 60 and mutual gaze 61 ) provide high-SNR, quasi-labeled samples and scalar reward. Ambient physical exafference (e.g gravity, being carried/rocked, textures, temperature, luminance transitions) supplies continuous dynamics that tune feedforward gains and gaze stabilization. Interoceptive cycles (e.g hunger->satiety, thermal discomfort->comfort) set objectives and adjust trial-wise learning rates via neuromodulatory precision and valence. Cross-modal temporal synchrony (e.g mouth-voice, optic-flow-acceleration, visuo-tactile co-events) acts as a self-supervised label for binding and invariances. Circadian and ultradian schedules (e.g light/dark and feeding rhythms) entrain plasticity windows and sampling distributions. Caregiver curation (e.g pose support, swaddling, pacing/rocking, object placement) actively shapes the exploration policy and task difficulty. Optimization Throughout this stage, local predictive learning in sensory cortices runs continuously: newborns exhibit mismatch responses and statistical learning even in sleep 62 , 63 , 64 ; in vision, contrast sensitivity and acuity rise steeply ( 2.4-> 4.0 cyc/deg from 1->3 months) 65 , 4 , motion-selective responses are detectable by  5 weeks 66 , and face-selective N290/P400 components emerge by  3 months 67 , 68 , 69 . These are textbook signatures that early sensory representations are being tuned by prediction errors. The cortex also helps train action: self-generated twitches during active sleep and early quiet-sleep spindles drive somatotopic bursts over S1/M1, refining body maps 70 , 71 . In wake, the rapid improvement of smooth pursuit around 2 months 1 implicates cortical motion perception circuits (e.g MT/MST/FEF) learning basic target dynamics 72 while cerebellar supervised calibration refines reflexes and sensorimotor forward models from dense error streams (retinal slip, vestibular mismatch (balance)), visible behaviorally in the rapid reduction of monocular optokinetic reflex (OKR) asymmetries 2 and the early maturation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) set-point 73 . Concurrently, behavior has the operant fingerprint of cortico-basal-ganglia RL: by 2-3 months, infants in the mobile-conjugate task raise kicking when it produces the sensory reward (mobile motion), stop when the contingency is removed, and show longer retention under spaced reactivation–precisely the acquisition->extinction->retention pattern expected when a dopamine-trained striatal critic updates action values and a cortico-striatal actor adjusts policy 74 , 75 . Neuromodulators schedule these loops, with DA providing distributional value errors 76 , 77 and ACh/NE setting precision and learning rates 78 , 79 , 80 , so updates are strongly gated by arousal and context. Neural development Remarkably, there is substantial evidence indicating that high-level category-selectivity (e.g faces vs. scenes, animate vs. inanimate, object size) is already detectable in the ventrotemporal cortex by 2 months 81 , 82 , suggesting the cortical perceptual hierarchy comes online well before the motor hierarchy can utilize it. Neurally, the 0-3-month trajectory is a fast, lawful handoff from transient, endogenously dominated regimes to thalamo-cortically gated, externally driven ones, marked by rising oscillatory structure and conduction speed. Along with the aforementioned advancements in visual-cortical representations (contrast sensitivity, visual acuity, motion selectivity, and orientation tuning 83 , 5 ), the ascending auditory pathway speeds up: auditory brainstem response wave latencies shorten across the first weeks to months 84 , 85 , indexing myelination/synchrony gains that expand temporal bandwidth for speech envelopes and fine structure 86 . This early agency operates under a ’subcortical constraint’: cortical motor outflow remains functionally disconnected from the brainstem until  3-6 months 87 , meaning the infant’s earliest ’experiments’ are driven by subcortical loops that train the silent cortex–leveraging spontaneous motor babbling to build the first proprioceptive priors without top-down cortical interference. Sleep and oscillations reorganize from neonatal "delta brushes/spindle bursts" to recognizable N2 spindles appearing at  6-8 weeks 88 and increasing through the first months 89 ; spindles plausibly gate plasticity at this stage, but mature SO-spindle-ripple coupling is viewed as a mature mechanism that strengthens across later infancy, childhood, and beyond 90 , 91 . At the systems level, neonatal rs-fMRI already shows dynamic sensorimotor, visual, and auditory networks that reconfigure over weeks, whereas higher-order networks (e.g., DMN) are highly fragmented and strengthen later 92 , 93 ; in parallel, myelin-sensitive MRI metrics (e.g., R1) and diffusion markers rise measurably from 0->3 months, providing the physical substrate for faster, more reliable long-range coupling across the brain 94 , 95 . These coordinated shifts (better SNR, faster conduction, maturing thalamo-cortical timing) directly improve the efficacy of the optimization machinery, so the same error channels operate with sharper precision and higher sample-efficiency by the end of the first quarter. It is worth emphasizing that this stage is made possible by prenatal scaffolds. Prenatal auditory exposure seeds language priors so that, at birth, infants differentiate linguistic rhythms and can exploit infant-directed speech to drive segmentation–hence the striking efficacy of newborn statistical learning in sleep 96 , 97 . Subplate-mediated thalamocortical wiring peaks before birth and then reorganizes through the first months, ensuring that early sensory errors are strongly broadcast and can train cortical hierarchies once the subplate wanes 98 . Fetal and neonatal REM-twitch dynamics pre-calibrate body maps and sensorimotor loops, which the cerebellum then tunes postnatally 99 , 100 . The prenatally-established optimization architecture (predictive coding in cortex, supervised teaching lines in cerebellum, distributional RL in BG, cortico-hippocampal loops (all gain-scheduled by neuromodulators)) means that when the world "turns on" at birth, the infant already has the right error channels and clocks; primary sensorimotor and visual networks are already functioning at birth 101 . The first three months simply flood those channels with structured data: endogenous (REM/spindles) and exogenous (faces/voices/contingencies), driving rapid improvements in representation quality, control fidelity, and social learning.

title: 3-6 Months
text: Behavioral capabilities By ∼ \sim 3-6 months, infants shift from mostly sampling to actively probing the world: the representational repertoire becomes both richer and more structured as infants begin to encode stable, cross-situational regularities that support category, object, and social representations. Stereopsis (binocular disparity; 3D vision) effectively "switches on" around ∼ \sim 3-4 months 1 , 2 , 3 and, together with rapidly improving smooth pursuit 4 , increases access to metric depth and improves foreground–background parsing; stereoacuity then sharpens quickly over the following weeks 5 . Depth is not just static: during 3-6 months infants increasingly maintain dynamically completed object trajectories when a moving object is temporarily hidden. By ∼ \sim 4 months, infants use spatiotemporal continuity constraints to anticipate where and when an occluded object should reappear (sensitive to occlusion duration), rather than treating disappearance as termination 6 , 7 . Even in the absence of continuous motion, infants demonstrate generative prediction over learned event structure: by ∼ \sim 3.5 months, infants viewing a basic spatial-temporal sequence (e.g., stimuli alternating between left and right locations) generate anticipatory saccades to the correct location before stimulus onset, including for asymmetric temporal patterns–providing a direct oculomotor readout of a predictive world model that encodes where and approximately when the next event will occur 8 . These predictions begin to couple to control: infants move from reactive tracking toward predictive pursuit and predictive reaching for moving targets, extrapolating future position to compensate for sensorimotor delays 9 , 10 . In a closely related vein, prediction begins to cover not only translation but also latent transformations : across this window infants can track invisible spatial transformations (e.g., an object rotating or changing orientation behind an occluder) and anticipate the post-occlusion configuration, consistent with early mental rotation / transformation-completion rather than mere reappearance timing 11 , 12 . Strikingly, self-generated object exploration can causally facilitate this capacity (more varied object manipulation → \rightarrow better mental-rotation performance), linking action to the acquisition of viewpoint- and transformation-invariant world models 13 . Basic-level categories emerge: early in this window, infants form category representations that generalize across novel exemplars (e.g., cats, dogs, chairs, couches) 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 . Categorization is not limited to object kinds: early in this window, infants also form basic spatial relational categories , discriminating above from below configurations of a target relative to a reference object and generalizing across changes in the identity and position of both items 21 . Object representations acquire several foundational priors during this window. Early in this window, infants can perceptually complete partly occluded objects (treating disjoint visible fragments as one persisting entity) and use spatiotemporal continuity to individuate objects across disappearances–a precursor to "object files" that support stable reference 22 , 23 . The ’physics engine’ also updates to enforce solidity constraints : by 3.5-4.5 months, infants look significantly longer (dishabituate) when a rotating screen appears to pass through a solid block, suggesting they model objects as substantial entities that cannot occupy the same space 24 . Shortly after (approx. 4.5 months), they begin to factor variable height into these occlusion models, detecting violations when a tall object disappears behind a short occluder, implying a metric calibration of the hidden world 25 By ∼ \sim 4.5 months, they can also use featural differences (e.g., shape/size) to decide whether an occlusion event implies one object or two, strengthening identity tracking beyond pure motion cues 26 , 27 . Correspondingly, physical expectations expand beyond mere tracking: infants respect simple support constraints by ∼ \sim 4.5 months 28 and, toward the end of this window, show increasingly explicit sensitivity to gravity-consistent dynamics , treating violations of gravity-appropriate acceleration as surprising 29 . Importantly, physical expectations are acquired in an event-type-specific manner: infants use a variable like object height to detect violations during occlusion events (e.g., a tall object behind a short occluder) several months before they apply the same variable to containment events (e.g., a tall object lowered into a short container). This "decalage" implies that the infantile physics engine maintains distinct event schemas–occlusion, containment, covering–each independently calibrated through experience, rather than a single general solidity principle 30 , 31 . Causal structure also becomes perceptible as an invariant over kinematics: infants discriminate causal launching from superficially similar noncausal motion (e.g., delayed reaction), implying that the world model is learning event grammars 32 , 33 . In parallel, the model begins sharpening agent/object priors : infants treat humans as solid, persisting entities in occlusion events (i.e., not exempt from material constraints) 34 . Self-propulsion acts as a powerful cue that supports inferences not licensed for inert objects, consistent with early domain-specific expectations about agent-like motion (a precursor to explicit theory-of-mind) 35 . Beyond rigid-body constraints, the physical world model also begins to differentiate ontological kinds : by ∼ \sim 5 months infants use motion cues to distinguish solids vs. liquids and apply different expectations about whether contents will pour vs. tumble , and whether objects will pass through vs. remain on top of a nonsolid substance–extending intuitive physics beyond "blocks and balls" 36 . The action-coupled side of these transitions is scaffolded by a posture-to-reach cascade (rolling, stable midline control, supported sitting) that reorganizes the workspace so reaching becomes reliable and multimodal object exploration becomes more systematic 37 , 38 . Correspondingly, object interaction becomes increasingly epistemic (chosen to reveal information): infants begin to vary exploratory actions (mouthing, rubbing, banging, rotating) as a function of object and surface properties, effectively probing affordances and learning object-action-outcome maps 39 , 40 . Rudimentary preshaping (anticipatory hand shaping for grasping) appears 41 , 42 , and raking grasps (all fingers at the same time) emerge by  6 months 43 . More generally, the hands become a uniquely available near-field effector/object : sustained hand regard (watching their own hand movements) emerges during this window, providing dense closed-loop visuomotor experience with a controllable target before canonical reaching is reliable 44 , 45 . Attention control improves as "sticky fixation" eases and saccadic latencies drop 46 ; and a minimal visual working memory ( 1 item) is measurable by  5 months 47 , 48 , which allows looking and reaching to be more strategic than reactive. Similarly, memory for structured action sequences becomes measurable: by ∼ \sim 6 months, infants can reproduce multi-step action sequences in delayed imitation paradigms (with performance depending on delay and retrieval support), indicating emerging capacity to store and reinstate ordered event models rather than only static percepts 49 , 50 , 51 . In language, representations begin to align with native statistics: by  4.5 months infants recognize the sound pattern of their own name 52 , and by  6 months they can segment word-like units when prosodic edges or distributional cues are favorable 53 ; in parallel, vowel categories show the first signs of perceptual narrowing toward the native phonology 54 . Familiar tokens (especially the infant’s name) act as anchors for speech segmentation 55 , accelerating early lexical learning 56 . In parallel, vocal control becomes more interaction-ready: infants participate in increasingly structured vocal turn-taking across this window, and the approach to ∼ \sim 6 months marks the onset of more syllable-like babbling (e.g "ba-ba" or "ma-ma") in typical development, providing a higher-bandwidth action channel for shaping caregiver responses 57 , 58 , 59 , 60 . On the social side, 4-6-month-olds detect and remember specific face-voice pairings and can match facial and vocal affect, making person-specific, multimodal identity a learnable unit rather than parallel streams 61 , 62 . Towards the end of this window, infants are also able to discriminate expressions of happiness, sadness, and anger from visual or vocal cues alone, passing through stages where less and less temporal synchrony of multimodal cues (i.e face and voice) is required 63 . Social selectivity also sharpens as face-space begins to narrow toward frequently seen categories 64 , 65 , changing who is tracked and imitated, while action understanding begins taking a step beyond kinematics: by  5-6 months infants may even encode the goal object of others’ reaches 66 . Beyond identifying what an agent acts on, infants also evaluate how goals are pursued: by ∼ \sim 6 months, infants expect agents to minimize the cost of their actions (e.g., taking a shorter path when no obstacle is present), and look longer when an agent takes an unnecessarily circuitous route to a goal–even for unfamiliar, non-human agents. This efficiency principle (a nascent "teleological stance") allows the infant’s agent model to generate predictions about action trajectories from goal + context alone, going beyond kinematic pattern matching 67 , 68 . Social learning also becomes increasingly triadic : by ∼ \sim 4.5-6 months infants can follow others’ gaze to external targets, with this behavior being shaped by perceptual cues (motion of the head) as well as social cues (gaze direction) 69 , 70 and combining with an emerging ability to follow others’ pointing 71 . Moreover, gaze following is selectively engaged by ostensive/communicative signals (e.g when preceded by direct gaze or infant-directed speech), implying that infants are learning when another’s attention shift is referential rather than mere motion 72 . Triadic communication allows basic "social referencing" (using caregivers as emotional referents in ambiguous situations) by 6 months 73 , 74 , following the arc of infants’ abilities to discriminate emotions 63 , but potentially remaining limited to stimuli that have both facial and vocal emotional information available for referencing 75 . Also following the arc of emotion discrimination, infants begin evaluating how agents treat other agents : by 6 months, infants prefer an individual who helps another achieve a goal over one who hinders it, prefer a helper over a neutral individual, and prefer a neutral individual over a hinderer. This indicates that the world model assigns social-evaluative valence to observed agent-agent interactions on the basis of behavior toward third parties–a capacity that may serve as a biological foundation for moral cognition 76 . Finally, abstract magnitude codes come online: six-month-olds discriminate numerosities (regardless of modality) at  1:2 ratios (e.g., 8 vs. 16 but not 8 vs. 12), indicating an approximate number system with coarse, ratio-dependent precision that can scaffold later symbolic learning 77 , 78 . Moreover, the approximate number system supports not just static discrimination but transformation-level predictions: by ∼ \sim 5 months, infants look longer at arithmetically impossible outcomes (e.g., one object is placed on stage, a screen occludes it, a second object is added behind the screen, yet only one object is revealed when the screen drops) than at the correct outcome, and analogous results hold for subtraction (2 − - 1). This implies that the world model tracks numerical change across occlusion and generates expectations about resultant quantities—an early form of event-based arithmetic prediction 79 . Predictions also may begin to represent uncertainty rather than only deterministic regularities: by ∼ \sim 6 months infants may form probabilistic expectations from visible population statistics, looking longer at samples that are improbable given proportions–an early signature of "intuitive statistics" / likelihood-sensitive prediction error 80 . Training data and optimization Training data Tactile! At this stage, training data becomes self-generated, closed-loop, and reweighted by posture and pedagogy. As stereopsis and smooth pursuit come online, rolling and early sitting expand the workspace and create rich self-motion (optic flow, motion parallax, head-hand reafference), with each curiosity-driven reach yielding a tightly time-locked packet of retinal slip, proprioception, sound, and haptics that the system can align and learn from. Manual exploration multiplies contingencies: by  5-6 months infants vary mouthing, scratching, shaking, and banging with size, texture, mass, and sound, producing multimodal contingencies that inform proto physics-and-objects models. Concurrently, a vocal-auditory loop spins up: coos, squeals, and marginal babble generate controllable acoustic features that are rife with cheap prediction errors; caregivers mirror, praise, and time turn-taking, converting phonation control into supervised data. Caregivers further shape the input distribution: infant-directed speech and "motionese" (slower, exaggerated actions), name cues, contingent touch, direct gaze, and structured routines (peekaboo, turn-taking) function as high-SNR micro-curricula and increase temporal alignment across modalities; affective touch and cardiorespiratory rhythms supply slow interoceptive/affective structure that gates precision and learning rate. Sticky mittens evidence Causally, experimentally boosting early prehension via the "sticky mittens" paradigm (Velcro mittens that let pre-reaching ∼ \sim 3-month-olds lift objects through contact) has been shown to increase object-directed engagement and manual exploration (e.g., more sustained contact/manipulation and more coordinated looking–acting patterns) relative to matched observational/passive experience, with some reports of downstream carryover; however, recent critical and preregistered work suggests the size/robustness of motor gains can be context-dependent 81 , 82 , 83 , 84 , 85 . pre-reaching 3-month-olds given brief "sticky mittens" experience (Velcro-enabled grasping) subsequently encode the goal object of another person’s reach in violation-of-expectation tasks, whereas age-matched infants without this experience do not—demonstrating that first-person motor competence causally scaffolds the agent model’s capacity to represent others’ action goals 86 . Optimization These rich, time-locked, cross-modal data streams (disparity + pursuit + contact; face-voice; shake->sound) saturate the underlying optimizers, shifting the system’s objective from generic calibration toward controllability and precise perception. Cerebellar microcomplexes run supervised calibration on eyes and arms: each visually guided reach or pursuit episode yields direction- and timing-specific climbing-fiber teaching signals that retune Purkinje output and update forward models; optic flow and fingertip contact provide high-SNR labels. Basal-ganglia actor-critic loops exploit distributional dopamine codes to update policies from sparse successes ("act->auditory/visual consequence"), while tonic dopamine tracks opportunity cost and scales vigor so controllable, information-rich actions are repeated, consolidated, and pursued; eligibility traces ensure the right corticostriatal synapses get credited. Cortical predictive coding becomes cheaper and more specific because error units now receive targeted, tightly synchronized, cross-modal mismatches (mouth motion->expected phoneme; hand motion->expected sound/feel), so local updates discover better representations with fewer samples; acetylcholine up-weights sensory-error precision during focused bouts, noradrenaline raises learning rates or resets policy under volatility, and serotonin lengthens the temporal horizon and lowers subjective effort as manipulation bouts extend. Transthalamic controllers (pulvinar/MD, gated by TRN) set large-scale precision and synchrony for feedback, opening apical dendritic write windows when engagement/attention is high (e.g., ostentive/demonstrative gaze). Overnight, sleep compiles the day’s dataset: growing spindle density and tighter slow-oscillation coupling support abstraction, generalization, and pruning, with replay favoring recent, salient, or socially-tagged episodes. retention of these event models depends on timely sleep consolidation : 6-month-olds who nap within ∼ \sim 4 hours of encoding successfully reproduce the target action sequence 24 hours later, whereas those who remain awake during this window do not, even when total wake time is equated—implying that offline replay during sleep is already integral to stabilizing event-level representations 87 . Net objective weights reallocate accordingly: speech moves from generic acoustic compression toward fidelity for native contrasts (helped by name-anchored segmentation), exploration prioritizes information gain about controllable object properties (size, texture, mass, sound), and social pedagogy increases the value of people-contingent outcomes. Neural development During this stage, the optimizers scale up: oscillations organize, conduction speeds up, networks segregate, and white matter lays down more of the bandwidth that later supports long-range inference. In scalp EEG, a posterior dominant rhythm emerges around  3 months (not the adult 10 Hz but a 3-5 Hz occipital rhythm that gradually accelerates 88 ) alongside a progressive flattening of the aperiodic 1/f slope 89 , both pointing to maturing E/I balance and shorter effective synaptic time constants that support faster, more precisely timed plasticity. Sleep architecture also shifts: classic N2 spindles, which first appear by  6-8 weeks, lengthen and strengthen through month 4-5, while REM proportion drops toward  30% by  6 months–changes that increase offline signal-to-noise as more room is made for replay and thalamo-cortical consolidation 90 , 91 . Structurally, white-matter bandwidth rises rapidly and heterogenously: quantitative MRI shows longitudinal relaxation rate (R1) (a myelin-linked measure) increasing from birth to 6 months across all bundles with faster gains in initially immature segments and along inferior->superior and posterior->anterior gradients (a well-documented progression of myelination that plays out across decades development); myelin-water and T1w/T2w maps replicate the early occipital->parietal->callosal gradient across 3-11 months 92 , 93 . As a convergent, non-MRI readout of conduction speed, visual cortical responses shorten sharply: infant visual N1/P1 latencies drop nonlinearly with rapid change through  6-9 months, consistent with faster afferent and intracortical transmission 94 . At the network level, the connectome shifts from mostly local coupling to more segregated-yet-cohering large-scale systems 95 : thalamocortical connectivity differentiates along sensory-specific motifs and strengthens its overall integration with cortex 96 ; within-network synchrony rises in primary sensorimotor, auditory, and visual systems 97 (although some is present from birth 98 ). The global sensorimotor network splits into mouth and hand submodules by  6 months 99 , the dorsal attention network becomes detectable around 6 months 99 , and default-mode components appear as anterior and posterior nodes that remain relatively segregated rather than an integrated midline core 97 . The salience and fronto-parietal networks remain largely unsynchronized at this stage 97 . Synaptically, V1 is in its exuberant growth phase: classic histology places the most rapid synapse production around  2-4 months, with high density through  8-12 months before prolonged pruning; this transient overparameterization increases representational capacity and sample efficiency before compression 100 , 101 , 102 , a common motif across brain regions which tracks behavioral development (e.g the PFC is the last region to reach full exuberance and then to be fully pruned, taking multiple decades). Key learning gates are open: the sensitive/critical period (sensitive = strong bias in plasticity (best time to learn, but not the only time); critical = hard cutoff (learning must occur within window, or it’s lost forever)) for binocular alignment and stereopsis is most vulnerable around  3-4 months (with susceptibility extending into later childhood) 2 , and the first phonetic reorganization toward native speech begins by  6 months 103 , together shaping the priors for depth and language that downstream circuits will build on. The 3-6-month gains are only possible because 0-3 months pre-trained the whole stack: early sensory codes were already being carved by prediction errors as contrast sensitivity climbed  2.4->4.0 cyc/deg from 1->3 months, motion selectivity appeared by  5 weeks, and face-selective N290/P400 components emerged by  3 months-so by this window, ventral/dorsal representations are not learning from scratch but refining an initialized basis. Offline, REM twitches and the first N2 spindles had already supplied labeled sensorimotor tuples and consolidation windows during  14-17 h/day of sleep, seeding calibrated somatosensory/motor maps that 3-6-month cerebello-cortical loops now exploit for faster forward-model updates. On the control side, the system entered this stage with a working operant channel: by 2-3 months infants showed acquisition->extinction->retention in the mobile-conjugate paradigm, evidence that cortico-basal-ganglia actor-critic machinery had already begun assigning credit to actions, which 3-6-month exploration then scales up into richer policies. The sampling policy itself was bootstrapped by caregivers and social rewards during the "two-month shift": mutual gaze and the social smile turned interactions into high-SNR, quasi-labeled episodes that continue to gate what is learned next in the 3-6-month window (e.g., person-specific face-voice bindings and joint-attention precursors). The systems handoff described for 0-3 months (moving from transient, endogenously dominated regimes to thalamo-cortically gated, externally driven processing) means that by 3-6 months rising oscillatory structure and conduction speed can actually be used: predictive loops run with better signal-to-noise, long-range coupling starts to stabilize, and visuomotor controllers shift from reflex reduction (e.g., OKN asymmetry) toward predictive pursuit.
