title: 6-12 Months
text: Behavioral capabilities Between 6 and 12 months, infants flip from mostly reactive observers to self-propelled epistemic foragers, with capability ramping across motor, manual, social-communicative, and problem-solving domains. Median hands-and-knees crawling lands near 8.3 months, cruising and brief supported steps cluster around 9-10 months, and the window for independent walking is strikingly wide (roughly the 1st-99th percentiles span  8.2 to 17.6 months) so experience, not a fixed schedule, determines the timeline 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . Locomotion rapidly becomes calibrated to environmental affordances : crawlers vs. novice walkers learn posture-specific "can/can’t" boundaries (e.g., which slopes are safely descendable), with famously poor transfer when switching from crawling to walking, and errorful exploration that reflects active estimation of action limits rather than mere clumsiness 5 , 6 . Similarly, many experienced crawlers begin to show wariness of heights (hesitation/avoidance and/or cautious exploration) on drop-off paradigms 7 , 8 . Self-produced locomotion also enables landmark-based spatial orientation and spatial updating : across 6-12 months infants increasingly remember where an object is relative to stable cues in the environment (basic relational landmark use), supporting search and reorientation in a way that goes beyond egocentric reach space 9 . Grasp pre-shaping (adjusting to object shape) and timing (hand closure) become reliable by 12 months 10 . Grasping strategies move from whole-hand grasps to an emerging pincer grasp (ability to use the index finger and thumb only) with voluntary release and basic bimanual coordination (typically evident around 7-9 months 11 ), expanding the space of self-produced object contingencies the brain can sample. These gains unlock constructive, compositional object play : late in this window infants increasingly stack, nest, and affix (join/attach) objects, creating repeatable "part/whole + spatial-relation" scenes that the world model can encode as structured states rather than single-object snapshots 12 (one study, however, estimates that only 15% of 10-month-olds can stack one block on another 13 ). Meanwhile, infants’ percussive "banging" becomes straighter and more force-controlled from across this window, a motor trajectory that may scaffold simple tool use near the end of this period 14 ; near the end of this window, infants begin to acquire proto-tool-use policies under favorable geometries (e.g., early success with rake-like tools when tool-target contiguity is high) 15 but remain largely unable to learn conventional artifact actions by observation (copying demonstrated functional uses of novel objects) 16 , 17 , despite basic delayed imitation being possible before this window. On the perceptual side, the visual system undergoes a qualitative computational shift during this window: whereas 3-4-month-olds can detect subtle image-level luminance changes (due to illumination shifts) that are not salient to adults , this "pre-constancy" sensitivity fades by ∼5 months and is replaced, by ∼7-8 months, with perceptual constancy for surface color and material –the ability to perceive stable distal surface properties despite dynamic variation in the retinal image across viewpoints and illuminations 18 . Unlike size and shape constancy (present at birth), surface-property constancy thus appears to require postnatal calibration, and its emergence implies that object representations increasingly encode distal surfaces rather than proximal images . Similarly, categories become more selective and knowledge-structured across this window: in general, categories increasingly reflect relations among features (e.g., correlations/co-occurrences) and abstraction of invariant structure (e.g dogs have four legs and distinct noses) rather than treating features as independent 19 . By ∼ \sim 7-11 months, object-examination paradigms reveal differentiation of broad conceptual domains such as animals vs. vehicles (often with domain-specific substructure, e.g airplanes vs. cars vs. motorcycles) 20 , and by ∼ \sim 10-11 months infants can show knowledge-based category discrimination that is not well-explained as an ad hoc response to perceptual similarity alone 21 . These categories begin to support inductive inference and object identity tracking . By ∼ \sim 9 months, infants use minimal experience with a single exemplar to draw simple inferences about nonobvious properties (e.g whether an object will float) of novel objects, and these expectations reliably guide exploratory play 22 . Relatedly, 9-11 month-olds can generalize demonstrated properties preferentially within appropriate domains (e.g., animal-appropriate vs. vehicle-appropriate behaviors) 23 , 24 . Moreover, object-individuation paradigms (where multiple objects that are in contact must be segmented suggest a transition between ∼ \sim 10 and 12 months: infants increasingly use object kind/property information to individuate, going beyond spatiotemporal cues (i.e objects moving independently) 25 , 26 ; this is further supported by evidence from manual-search paradigms, where 10-12-month-olds are able to determine whether "one vs. two objects" are inside a container 27 . On the communication front, production advances from canonical babbling (repetitive, speech-like syllables, such as "ba-ba" or "ma-ma") toward the first words 28 , 29 , 30 , and the amount and quality of canonical syllables already forecast later language outcomes. Receptive language is, however, not waiting for production: 6-9-month-olds recognize everyday words in natural scenes 31 , and English-learning infants begin segmenting words from fluent speech by  7.5 months 32 , leveraging additional segmentation cues by  10.5 months 33 , 34 . By ∼ \sim 12 months, infants can also resolve referential ambiguity via cross-situational statistics : when individual naming events are ambiguous (multiple objects present), they track word-object co-occurrence regularities across events to identify the correct referent 35 . In parallel, the perceptual front end specializes as non-native phonetic contrasts that 6-month-olds hear often fade by 10-12 months 36 , while native categories strengthen 28 . This experience-driven narrowing is not unique to speech: face-processing systems undergo a parallel contraction, with 6-month-olds able to discriminate individual faces of other species (e.g., monkeys) but 9-month-olds no longer able to do so unless given intervening individuation training 37 , suggesting a domain-general mechanism that prunes representational distinctions not reinforced by environmental statistics. Social cognition becomes increasingly triadic (include self, other, and a shared referent (an object, event, or location in the environment)) and informational: by 10-11 months infants follow gaze selectively when others can see (eyes open) 38 , and around 12 months many point declaratively to share information, along with making requests 39 , 40 ; pointing is considered a landmark communication skill of the 12-month mark 41 , 42 . 43 . Around the first birthday, pointing can also function as an epistemic request –a way to solicit new information from an adult about an ambiguous referent, not just to share attention or request objects 44 . Another key instance of triadic communication, social referencing becomes a portable, modality-flexible uncertainty resolver. As locomotion and manual exploration make more situations genuinely risky or ambiguous, infants increasingly query caregivers’ affect to set the valence/expected value of a novel referent and to gate approach vs. avoidance policies. In the classic visual-cliff paradigm, 12-month-olds use maternal emotional messages to decide whether to cross an apparent drop-off (positive signals promote crossing; fearful signals sharply suppress it), demonstrating affect-to-action regulation rather than mere mood contagion 45 . In "ambiguous toy" paradigms, 10-13-month-olds’ looks to the parent predict systematic shifts in exploration/withdrawal, consistent with a multi-component skill (referential looking → \rightarrow appraisal → \rightarrow behavior regulation) that consolidates across the first year 46 . Unlike the previous window, by ∼ \sim 12 months the appraisal no longer requires rich intersensory redundancy: infants can use face-only or voice-only emotional information to regulate behavior toward a novel stimulus, with vocal fear sufficient to suppress approach even in the absence of facial cues 47 , 48 . Social-emotional signals also start acting like value tags that persist beyond the immediate moment: 11-month-olds show delayed regulatory effects of an adult’s emotional display on later behavior toward the referent, implying that social referencing is beginning to write longer-lived affective priors into the world model 49 . Referencing is not strictly mother-bound: 1-year-olds can use affect from another (familiarized) adult to guide their response to a novel object even when the mother is present but neutral, broadening the class of "informants" whose appraisals can train action selection 50 . Social cognition also becomes more recursive : whereas 5-month-olds uniformly prefer individuals who act positively toward others regardless of the target’s moral status, by ∼ \sim 8 months infants selectively prefer characters who act positively toward prosocial individuals and characters who act negatively toward antisocial individuals. This implies that the agent model now composes at least two layers of social evaluation–tracking both a target’s prior behavior and a second agent’s response to that target–yielding rudimentary second-order social judgment 51 . Relatedly, by ∼ \sim 9 months, infants react with greater impatience when an adult is unwilling to hand over a toy than when the adult is unable to do so (e.g., clumsy or physically blocked), further indicating that the world model parses others’ behavior in terms of underlying intentions and dispositions 52 . Intention/action understanding also becomes motor-grounded and predictive : by ∼12 months (but not 6 months), infants watching another person reach for an object shift their gaze to the reach target before the hand arrives, and this anticipatory looking correlates with the infant’s own ability to perform the same action 53 . This suggests that by the end of the first year, the observer internally simulates the actor’s movement plan via a shared motor forward model to generate goal predictions–linking the infant’s own visuomotor experience to the prediction of others’ behavior. Perhaps most strikingly, the "agent model" begins tracking not just what others intend, but what others know or have experienced . By 12 months, infants track whether an adult was present or absent during an object’s introduction; if the adult was absent, the infant’s world model treats the object as "new" for the adult and will selectively offer or point to that object over familiar ones 54 . Even earlier, by 7 months, looking-time paradigms indicate that infants automatically encode another agent’s belief about an object’s hidden location, showing altered reaction times when the agent’s belief conflicts with physical reality 55 . This implies a profound architectural upgrade: the infant’s world model now maintains parallel, decoupled state representations–the actual state of the world, and the state of the world as represented within another agent’s internal model. The criteria for classifying an entity as an "agent" also become less tied to morphological cues and more sensitive to behavioral structure . While early in life infants are strongly biased by cues such as face-like configurations and biological motion, by the end of the first year they can attribute goal-directedness and attentional orientation to morphologically unfamiliar, even faceless objects on the basis of cues such as contingent interaction and organized, environment-directed behavior. In classic studies, infants treated an unfamiliar object that had interacted contingently and behaved intentionally as goal-directed, and they also followed the subsequent orientation of non-human faceless agents after contingent interaction, suggesting that temporal contingency and behavioral reciprocity can serve as powerful triggers for instantiating an agent model even in the absence of recognizable biological form 56 , 57 , 58 , 59 . A foundational action-coupled advance is the onset of manual search for fully hidden objects at ∼ \sim 8 months: infants now lift a cloth or reach behind a screen to retrieve a completely invisible object, implying that the world model maintains a spatial representation of the hidden object sufficient to guide goal-directed action toward it–bridging the gap between the looking-time evidence for object permanence measurable months earlier and its expression through the motor system 60 , 61 . Likewise, performance on A-not-B (where infants mistakenly search for a hidden object in a familiar location (A) rather than a new location (B), even after witnessing the object being moved to B) improves though perseveration (repetitive failures) is common across this window 62 . 7-9-month-olds also increasingly solve one-step means-end problems (e.g., pulling a cloth to retrieve a distant object) 63 , and 9-12-month-olds exhibit deferred imitation after 24-hour delays (which is quite rare for 6-month-olds 64 )–an early readout of long-term recall 65 . Importantly, deferred imitation becomes increasingly decontextualized : whereas 6-month-olds’ deferred imitation is tightly bound to the specific demonstration context, experimenter, and stimulus objects, by ∼12 months infants generalize imitated action sequences across changes in background context, demonstrator identity, and object exemplar 66 , 67 , reflecting a shift from episode-locked to more abstract, transferable event representations that can support flexible reuse. Infants’ working memory updating + inhibitory control improves across 9-12 months (visible in reduced perseveration on A-not-B-like demands), and visual working memory shows a marked capacity increase across this window (often reported as rising from  1 item earlier in infancy toward  3 items by  10-12 months in change-detection paradigms) 68 , 69 , 70 , 71 . Core physical priors also sharpen: infants refine rule-like expectations about physical support across this window (i.e accurately predicting how much physical overlap is needed for stability, related to block stacking) 72 , 73 , 74 , 75 , and their approximate number system also increases in precision–from discriminating 1:2 ratios at  6 months to  2:3 by ∼ \sim 9-10 months–yielding quantifiable gains in representational acuity 76 . Exploration also sharpens: by ∼ \sim 9 months, infants finger textured objects more than nontextured ones, shake or bang sounding objects more than nonsounding ones, and press pliable objects more than nonpliable ones 77 ; by ∼11 months, expectation violation does not merely elicit longer looking–it drives targeted hypothesis-testing exploration . Infants who witness a solidity violation (an object appearing to pass through a wall) selectively bang the object against a surface, while those who witness a support violation (an object appearing to hover in mid-air) selectively drop it, as if testing the specific physical property that was violated. Moreover, infants learn novel information (e.g., a hidden squeaker) about expectation-violating objects better than about objects that behaved predictably 78 . This implies that the world model generates structured prediction errors that specify what needs updating, and that exploration is recruited as a corrective inference mechanism rather than an undirected response to surprise. Infants also begin exploring containment and insertion by the end of the first year 79 , 80 , 81 . More generally, by 11 months, after experience with a novel object, infants can transfer their exploration skills to objects with the same novel properties 82 , meaning core physical representations are beginning to crystallize in a disentangled form (in contrast to the 3-6 months window, where core physical priors often fail to generalize 83 , 84 ). Causal reasoning also extends beyond observable events: by 10-12 months, infants who see a beanbag emerge from behind a screen on a self-propelled-looking trajectory infer the existence of a hidden agent behind the screen as the plausible cause–expecting to find an agent (i.e a hand or even a puppet 85 ) when the screen is removed and looking longer when no agent is present. Importantly, this inference is selective: infants draw it when the object’s motion is consistent with having been launched by an agent but not when the object is self-propelled 86 , and use the beanbag’s trajectory to predict the position of a hand, but not a toy block 85 . In sequence-learning paradigms, while 6-month-olds show a preference for novel spatiotemporal sequences containing basic patterns (e.g., stimuli alternating between left and right locations), 11-month-olds show a distinct preference for more complex sequences (e.g those defined by shape/color differences) 87 . In general, sequence learning becomes more abstract and relational across this window. By 8-11 months, infants can generalize certain repetition-based visual rules across novel items (with younger infants succeeding on simpler repetition structures and older infants on harder position-sensitive contrasts), and by ∼ \sim 11 months they detect reversals in ordinal numerical direction (ascending vs. descending numerosities), indicating that the world model is beginning to encode higher-order structure over sequences rather than only local transitions or feature co-occurrences 88 , 89 . Similarly, by ∼ \sim 9 months, infants can also learn statistical structure from passive observation of complex scenes : after exposure to many multi-element displays, they attend more to feature pairs that are not only more frequent co-occurrences but also more predictive (higher conditional probability), implying that the world model is estimating structured joint/conditional statistics over compositional visual features–not merely learning isolated associations 90 ; this can be seen as the scene-level expression of the aforementioned advancements in object categorization. Training data and optimization The onset of self-produced locomotion has been characterized as a developmental cascade that simultaneously reorganizes spatial coding, social referencing, wariness of heights, and aspects of object search–not because crawling directly causes each change, but because it exposes the infant to a qualitatively new distribution of self-generated experience with distance, occlusion, spatial perspective shifts, and the need for distal social-emotional information 91 . By ∼ \sim 9 months, joint attention does not merely redirect looking; it selectively changes how objects are encoded . Infants remember different–and behaviorally more useful–properties of a novel object when it is introduced under eye contact / shared attention than when the same object is encountered in a noncommunicative parallel-attention context, indicating that the world model is beginning to treat socially cued objects as privileged learning targets rather than as ordinary scene items 92 , 93 , 94 . Near the end of the first year, labels begin to actively reorganize object representations rather than merely accompany them. Words (but not matched nonlinguistic tones) facilitate category formation, and by ∼ \sim 12 months infants can use referential labeling cues to decide whether a scene should be represented as containing one object or two , indicating that linguistic signals are beginning to constrain both category structure and object individuation inside the world model 95 , 96 . Explanation-based learning in infancy Do words facilitate object categorization in 9-month-old infants? The infant now becomes a prolific generator of its own training data. A major driver is the embodiment shift: new postures (sitting -> crawling -> cruising) change the mapping between optic flow, vestibular cues, and motor commands, so affordance knowledge is elaborated on in a posture-specific way; locomotion plus posture control let infants generate rich optic-flow/vestibular/proprioceptive tuples on demand, while egocentric studies show that everyday learning episodes are engineered into single-object, centered views dominated by hands (often because adults place and hold targets in the infant’s field), effectively reducing referential uncertainty during naming or demonstration. Manual exploration supplies dense cause-effect samples: banging, shaking, mouthing, throwing, and two-handed manipulation produce repeatable audiovisual-haptic contingencies, with stabilized sitting and the emergence of the pincer grasp (using the thumb and index finger to grasp small objects) turbocharging visual-manual exploration: rotating, transferring, and dropping objects couples haptics with vision and, empirically, is when 3D object completion comes online 99 –evidence that manipulation experience is a key aspect of the curriculum for viewpoint-invariant object models. Exploration is not random: attention follows a "Goldilocks" policy that prefers stimuli of intermediate predictive complexity (demonstrated in 7- and 8-month-olds 100 ), and violations of expectation at  11 months trigger hypothesis-testing play and faster learning–an intrinsic surprise-weighted sampler that concentrates updates where gradients are steep. The vocal system runs a parallel closed-loop generator: on top of producing auditory prediction errors, canonical babbling recruits contingent caregiver feedback that immediately reshapes infant syllable statistics toward speech-like forms, a social reinforcement signal that alters both produced and heard distributions. High-precision supervision comes from joint attention and ostension: "follow-in" labeling when the child already fixates on the physical referent predicts vocabulary growth (especially when paired with "motionese" demonstrations), and by  12 months, gaze following and attention to a talker’s mouth predict later productive vocabulary; these are all powerful cross-modal alignment signals that accelerate learning. Sleep acts as a periodic batch processor for the day’s episodes: a ≥30-min nap within  4 hours preserves novel action memories in 6- and 12-month-olds, and between 9 and 16 months, sleep reorganizes specific word-object traces into more abstract, category-like knowledge. Finally, caregiver-infant biobehavioral synchrony (especially affectionate touch) stabilizes arousal and vagal tone, effectively gating learning rates during play and teaching bouts. Caregivers also gate whether certain (especially dangerous) states are even sampled, avoiding disaster and overall shaping which parts of the environment enter memory. Optimization The internal optimizers now lock to the statistics of a much richer sensorimotor and social world. Cerebellar microcomplexes run high-bandwidth supervised calibration on the rapidly expanding motor repertoire: they calibrate timing and gain for head-trunk stabilization, smooth pursuit during active gaze shifts, visually guided reaching and the emerging pincer grasp, and the first locomotor primitives (belly crawl -> hands-and-knees -> cruising). Climbing-fiber bursts remain the essential, precisely routed teacher, but their "analog" character now matters: larger retinal slip, reach endpoint error, and footfall mistiming yield bigger complex-spike Ca2+ plateaus and faster step sizes, while context arriving on mossy fibers (posture, target motion, effector used) ensures that updates are feature-selective rather than global. Together, this yields rapid gain and timing corrections for oculomotor and limb controllers that infants visibly acquire across this window. Concurrently, cortico-striatal actor-critic loops shift from ventral/limbic dominance to stronger dorsomedial recruitment as goal-directed choice emerges; phasic dopamine broadcasts continue to implement a distributional code over returns, which is especially adaptive in this regime because outcomes are both higher variance (novel objects, surfaces, and people) and increasingly long-horizon (multi-step plans like pull-to-stand). Tonic dopamine tracks rising average reward as mobility and social success raise opportunity cost, boosting vigor (latency and force) and biasing the policy toward faster exploration; phasic bursts/dips commit updates only where recent corticostriatal activity laid seconds-long eligibility traces, solving distal credit assignment for multi-step actions like reach-grasp-transfer. Cortical hierarchies minimize local prediction errors under progressively sharper precision control: feedforward residuals in superficial layers continue to tune invariances for object identity, pose, and occlusion, while apical-tuft feedback carries predictions and plasticity control, opening dendritic plateau-gated plasticity windows when contextual signals warrant; environmentally driven "perceptual narrowing" commits auditory maps to native phonetic contrasts between  6-12 months, while nonnative contrasts decline, a signature of priors sharpening and residuals falling in behaviorally relevant subspaces. Neuromodulatory controllers arbitrate: acetylcholine up-weights expected-uncertainty terms as cues become reliable (e.g., caregiver vocal prosody or graspable affordances), norepinephrine emits brief mode-switch broadcasts at volatility boundaries (novel places, strangers), and serotonin lengthens the integration window for delayed outcomes, supporting patience and effortful control over longer action chains. Objectives themselves become more structured: intrinsic reward tracks learning progress (the "Goldilocks" band drives sampling), while triadic joint attention and pedagogical cues (gaze alternation, pointing, infant-directed speech) act as externally supplied goal pointers that label what variables "matter," effectively installing subgoals into OFC/vmPFC state maps and raising the value of information about others’ intentions. Finally, hippocampal-cortical loops already support sleep-dependent consolidation and generalization: timely naps (≤4 h after learning) stabilize 6- and 12-month-olds’ declarative memories, and spindles relate to infants’ abstraction of word meanings-while canonical slow-oscillation<->spindle coordination is present but still maturing across the first year (with precise ripple coupling better established later), consistent with an offline "compile and train" phase that is functional but not yet adult-like. Neural development From 6-12 months, the macroscale picture of the brain tightens along three interacting axes (rhythms, networks, and substrate) and these shifts have clear computational consequences. Spectrally, infants’ peak-alpha frequency (PAF, the frequency exhibiting maximum power (implicated as a clock on visual temporal processing 101 )) continues its climb (meta-analyses put it near  6.1 Hz at 6 months and rising thereafter), and higher PAF within this window already tracks shorter saccadic latencies and sharper temporal attention 102 , indicating narrower integration windows for selection and prediction. Beyond alpha, sensorimotor mu/beta activity (which, in adults, is strongly associated with sensorimotor processing and higher-order cognitive tasks 103 ) becomes more structured, with a low-beta peak emerging by  6 months and mu rhythm gradually accelerating, signals of maturing thalamo-cortical gain control for movement prediction 104 , 105 . Early gamma responses strengthen as infants maintain multiple occluded objects by  6-8 months 106 , 107 , 108 , foreshadowing faster local assemblies for working memory, while the aperiodic 1/f slope flattens across the first year 109 , consistent with evolving excitation-inhibition balance and better throughput. Cross-frequency coordination is still coarse but detectable: slow-oscillation-spindle coupling becomes more systematic between late infancy and toddlerhood 110 , laying the scaffolding for hippocampo-cortical credit assignment during sleep even as communication channels continues to mature. At the network level, higher-order systems that are patchy earlier consolidate into a more segregated-yet-integrated topology. By around one year, the default-mode network shows rapid increases in regional perfusion (delivery of blood, oxygen, and nutrients) that specifically support the emerging DMN 111 , 112 , marking a nascent internal-modeling system. This system-level refinement sits on a backbone that already exhibits "rich-club"-like organization in infancy 113 and becomes more modular with age, supplying long-range highways for selective exchange while protecting local specialization. Thalamocortical channels (especially pulvinar gateways that gate salience and synchrony) are still tuning but increasingly capable of coordinating cortico-cortical communication essential for selective attention 114 while the frontoparietal control network is quite immature at this stage (and is among the last networks to fully develop) 112 . Insert Figure 2 from "Functional Network Development During the First Year: Relative Sequence and Socioeconomic Correlations") Beneath these dynamics, the physical substrate is racing ahead. White-matter microstructure and myelin-sensitive metrics rise steeply across the first year in major tracts (callosal splenium, optic radiations, corticospinal) 115 , 116 , 117 , and visual/auditory evoked latencies shorten, reflecting faster conduction that supports higher-frequency synchronization and longer-range phase alignment. Synaptically, V1 is in an exuberant state with peak synaptic density roughly between  8-11 months (in line with other primary sensory/motor cortices), while association cortices are still ascending; pruning is increasingly activity- and complement/microglia-mediated 118 , 119 -mechanistically tying experience statistics and sleep slow waves to circuit sharpening and E/I homeostasis 120 , 121 . Relative to its size at birth, the 1-year-old’s brain has doubled in volume, largely accounted for by the growth of neural connections in gray matter (i.e., synapse and dendrites), long-range axons, and myelination 122 . A clean behavioral readout of these shifts in macroscopic structural properties is "perceptual narrowing": discrimination of non-native phonemes and other-race/other-species faces diminishes as top-down priors strengthen over faster, myelinated pathways-exactly what you’d expect when a broad, exuberant code is being sculpted into an efficient, task-contingent world-model.

title: 12-24 Months
text: Behavioral capabilities Between 12 and 24 months, behavior shows sparks of deliberate, multi-step, symbol-guided action. Locomotion becomes an always-on data-collection loop as new walkers cover on the order of two thousand steps and 1̃7 falls per hour during free play 1 , vastly expanding active sampling of objects, surfaces, and affordances for learning. Locomotion shifts from wide-based, fall-prone toddling to efficient, planned movement as thousands of daily steps tune balance, stride, and path control–yielding stiff-legged running, stair-climbing with support, kicking, and furniture climbing by  18-24 months 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . Fine motor control progresses from generic grasps to role-differentiated bimanual manipulation 5 , 6 and basic tool use (spoons, rakes, rails, levers) 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , with strengthening hand preference 13 , organized scribbles 14 , taller block stacks (some can reach up to 8 blocks by 25 months) 15 , and increasingly anticipatory action planning (e.g planning for the most comfortable hand/wrist pose when grasping) 16 , 17 . Tool use and problem solving show emerging analogical transfer : by ∼ \sim 18-24 months, toddlers who learn an effective strategy for retrieving an out-of-reach toy (e.g., choosing the correct tool from several candidates) transfer that strategy to structurally similar but perceptually different problems, indicating that the world model is beginning to extract and reuse abstract relational structure from specific episodes rather than remaining bound to surface features 18 . Similarly, action understanding becomes more latent-goal-based in this period. By 18 months, toddlers can reproduce what an adult intended to do even when the adult visibly fails, indicating that the child’s model distinguishes the observed movement from the unobserved goal state it was meant to achieve 19 . More broadly, selective-imitation findings from the second year show that young children do not simply copy surface behavior; they increasingly treat others’ actions as means chosen under constraints , copying unusual means preferentially when those means appear necessary or rational rather than arbitrary 20 . Mobility feeds language and concept learning: head-mounted camera studies show that naming often occurs during brief, toddler-created "clean views" of a single object, and words learned at those moments stick better than labels delivered in cluttered scenes 21 . Expressive vocabulary and early compositionality accelerate: by 18-24 months toddlers have learned 50-100 words 22 , 23 , and most children are combining two words ("more milk") 24 . This vocabulary acceleration co-occurs with a broader restructuring: it coincides with a categorization spurt –a sharp increase in spontaneous sorting behavior (e.g., exhaustively grouping objects by kind) that emerges around 18 months 25 , 26 . Similarly, toddlers increasingly exploit heuristics such as mutual exclusivity by  17 months (e.g when presented a familiar and a novel object (e.g. car and phototube) and asked to "look at the dax", 17-month-olds increased looking to the novel object (i.e. phototube) above baseline preference) 27 and a growing shape bias (toddlers start to assume that nouns refer to objects of a particular shape rather than to their color, texture, or size) from  18-24 months to generalize names 28 . They also become more "symbol-minded" in a general sense: many can learn from pictures as referential symbols by 18-24 months 29 even as scale-error attempts (e.g., trying to sit in a doll chair) reveal an ongoing integration between perception, action planning, and inhibitory control 30 . Basic pretend play with object substitutions (e.g using a "banana" as a "phone") is also common across this window, further signaling the emergence of symbolic thought while enhancing social sensitivity, emotional regulation, and understanding of multi-step narratives 31 . This capacity to quarantine simulated states from veridical representations is a foundational precursor to generalized forward planning, hypothetical reasoning, and "theory of mind," allowing the agent to run internal forward models using representations that conflict with immediate sensory input 32 , 33 . Language in this window becomes increasingly event-structured and combinatorial , not merely lexically larger. By ∼ \sim 22-24 months, toddlers can use syntax to infer latent event structure: when viewing unseen events paired with spoken sentences, they retain a novel verb’s syntactic frame (e.g "Anna blicked" versus "Anna blicked the baby") over a delay and later use it to constrain their interpretation 34 , and 2-year-olds can use syntax alone to infer whether a novel verb refers to a causative versus synchronous relation (i.e causative versus synchronous events) even before seeing the candidate scenes 35 . Relatedly, by ∼ \sim 18 months infants show evidence of representing abstract nonlocal syntactic dependencies (e.g for "What did the chef burn?" knowing the relationship between "What" and "burn"), indicating that the language model is beginning to support structured relations that extend beyond adjacent words 36 . This matters for world modeling because language is no longer functioning only as an object-labeling system; it is beginning to specify who did what to whom and what kind of relation links event participants 37 . Language in this window also begins to support displaced reference –the capacity to denote entities and events that are not currently perceivable. By ∼ \sim 18–24 months, children spontaneously talk about absent objects, past experiences, and anticipated events in conversation with caregivers 38 , 39 , and even prelinguistic 12-month-olds point to an absent object’s prior location to communicate about it to an uninformed adult, indicating that gestural displaced reference precedes its full linguistic expression 40 . This capacity is significant for world modeling because symbolic vehicles can now access and transmit internal world-model states—past episodes, absent objects, anticipated events—entirely decoupled from the ongoing sensory scene. Moreover, language begins to function as a channel for directly updating the world model, not just labeling it. Towards the end of this window, toddlers who are told about a change to a hidden object (e.g., "the doll got wet") update their mental representation accordingly, expecting the transformed state when the object reappears rather than the last directly observed state 41 . This demonstrates that verbal testimony can write to the internal world model in the absence of any direct perceptual evidence, marking an early transition from purely experiential to partially testimonial world-model construction. A further representational upgrade in the second year is the emergence of an explicit self-model . During this window, toddlers increasingly recognize their own image, use self-referential forms such as personal pronouns, and show more advanced pretend play, suggesting that the world model now includes the self as a stable referential entity rather than merely the default point of view 42 , 43 . Importantly, this self-model is still incomplete and dissociable across levels: even as mirror self-recognition emerges, toddlers often struggle to explicitly represent their own body as a size-constrained object in action planning, and this mismatch likely contributes to classic scale errors and other body-planning failures 44 , 45 . Nonetheless, the emergence of the self-model coincides with the appearance of self-conscious emotions –embarrassment, shame, and pride–which become reliably observable (albeit still rudimentary) around 18-24 months and correlate with the attainment of mirror self-recognition 46 , 47 , 48 , suggesting that the world model now includes not just the self as a referential entity, but a nascent representation of how the self is evaluated by others. In parallel, toddlers begin representing ownership as a social-relational property linking persons to objects. By ∼ \sim 18–24 months, children use possessive language (e.g., "mine," "daddy’s"), protest when their possessions are taken, and track who held an object first as a cue to ownership 49 . This represents a new representational layer in the world model: objects are now encoded not only by their physical properties and functions but by a person-linked relational tag specifying who controls or has prior claim over them—an early step toward modeling social-institutional facts that go beyond physical reality. The agent model’s state-tracking capacity also deepens during this window. Looking-time paradigms show that 15-month-olds represent an agent’s false belief about an object’s location: they look longer when the agent searches where the object actually is (but the agent should not know this) than when the agent searches at the now-empty location consistent with the agent’s outdated belief 50 . This extends the implicit belief-tracking detected earlier (see 6-12 months) to a paradigm in which the infant must predict the agent’s action from a decoupled, counterfactual world state. Complementary evidence from desire understanding shows a parallel advance: 18-month-olds who observe an experimenter expressing disgust toward crackers but delight toward broccoli hand the experimenter broccoli, even though the toddler herself prefers crackers; 14-month-olds, by contrast, egocentrically offer their own preferred food 51 . Together, these results imply that by 18 months the world model can decouple another agent’s value function and belief state from the child’s own, supporting richer social perspective-taking. Leveraging these abilities, prosociality comes online in graded form: 18-month-olds readily perform instrumental helping (helping others achieve concrete, goal-directed actions), while empathic and especially costly (altruistic) helping become more reliable closer to the end of the second year 52 , 53 . Beyond unilateral helping, toddlers also begin engaging in cooperative joint-goal activities : by 18-24 months, pairs of toddlers can coordinate complementary roles to achieve a shared outcome (e.g one child operates one end of a tube apparatus while a partner operates the other), and they actively attempt to re-engage a partner who stops participating—implying a representation of the shared plan and the partner’s necessary contribution 54 , 55 . Visual perspective taking also becomes behaviorally explicit in this window: by ∼ \sim 24 months, toddlers demonstrate Level-1 perspective taking –they can determine what another person can vs. cannot see from a different vantage point and use this to guide their own behavior, such as selectively showing or hiding objects 56 . This complements the implicit belief-tracking measured by looking time at 15 months; here, the child’s own actions reveal an online computation of another agent’s perceptual access to the world. The social world model also becomes more epistemic : toddlers begin tracking not only what other agents want or believe, but also which informants are worth learning from . By 18 months, toddlers are less willing to learn a novel word or imitate a novel action from a speaker who has previously labeled familiar objects inaccurately 57 . By 24 months, this selectivity is more robust: toddlers preferentially learn novel word-object mappings from previously accurate speakers 58 , and can use a third party’s agreement/disagreement gestures (nodding vs shaking) to infer which testimony about an object’s identity or location should be accepted 59 . The world model is thus beginning to represent speaker reliability as a latent variable, filtering socially transmitted information by source quality rather than treating testimony as uniformly trustworthy. Spatial navigation shows robust geometric reorientation by  18-24 months with increasing use of landmarks (any salient environmental cues (like a unique object, building, or tree) that can serve as reference points) 60 , 61 , 62 , indicating early integration of layout geometry and features. Beyond geometric reorientation, spatial cognition in this window also shows the emergence of allocentric coding –the ability to represent object locations relative to environmental landmarks rather than to one’s own body. Towards the end of this window, toddlers can use stable external cues to relocate a hidden object even after being passively moved to a new vantage point, indicating that the spatial world model is no longer locked to an egocentric reference frame 63 , 64 , 65 . Relatedly, locomotion becomes more prospective and detour-capable : by ∼18–24 months, toddlers can select efficient detour routes around barriers to retrieve a goal, integrating spatial layout with action planning rather than relying solely on direct approach 66 , 3 . Numerical cognition shifts from purely pre-verbal magnitude tracking ("approximate number sense") toward emerging exactness: toddlers show nascent ordinal judgments 67 and begin mapping small number words to precise set sizes 68 (often knowing what "one" (and even "two") means around the 24-month mark 69 ) and this growth is measurably shaped by caregiver "number talk" during 14-30-month interactions 70 . Causal learning becomes more probabilistic by the end of this window: by about 24 months, toddlers can watch two candidate causes produce an effect with different probabilities and then preferentially intervene on the object that was more likely to generate the outcome, even when absolute frequency is controlled 71 , suggesting that the world model is no longer restricted to deterministic event schemas or direct trial-and-error learning, but can estimate graded causal strength from noisy evidence. Furthermore, causal modeling in this window builds on the latent-cause inference of the previous window. By 10-12 months infants already infer a hidden agent in certain unseen causal interactions 72 , 73 . What changes across the second year is that causal inference becomes broader, more observational, and more abstract . By ∼ \sim 24 months, toddlers can learn causal structure from watching other people’s interventions , distinguishing genuine cause-effect relations from mere temporal association and then intervening on the causal object themselves 74 . They also infer unobserved causes for apparently spontaneous physical events in contexts that go beyond the specific hidden-agent launching cues emphasized in the first year (e.g searching for a cause after seeing a toy spontaneously light up) 75 . More generally, 18-30-month-olds can extract higher-order relational causal principles from just a few observations and use them to generate or predict novel causal outcomes (e.g understanding that two identical objects must be placed on a toy for it to light up) 76 . The shift, then, is not from “visible causation” to “hidden causation,” but from relatively specific hidden-cause expectations to more flexible observational, probabilistic, and relational causal modeling. Executive functions (working memory, inhibitory control, and flexible goal maintenance) move from fragile to reliably measurable across this window. Goal maintenance/working memory improves: by ∼ \sim 2 years, children can keep track of multiple hidden objects in multilocation search ("Spin-the-Pots") 77 , and 24-month batteries show success not only on classic A-not-B-like demands but on invisible-displacement versions with brief delays, indicating that toddlers can maintain a latent object state across occlusion and distraction rather than relying only on the last visible location 78 . Inhibitory control also strengthens across paradigms: toddlers increasingly succeed on A-not-B/delayed-response 79 and detour/object-retrieval variants (suppressing the direct reach to a visible goal), with performance falling when tasks require arbitrary multi-step means actions and improving when the task structure is more causally transparent or easier to maintain in working memory 80 , 81 . Toddlers also begin to tolerate short, structured delays on snack-delay-style tasks 82 as well as crayon- and tongue-delay tasks (i.e not using crayons until the adult returns, and holding a cracker on the tongue without eating it) 78 . It is best, however, to keep any flexibility claims conservative: near the end of this window, toddlers can maintain a simple sorting rule over several trials and inhibit competing responses, but full rule switching remains limited, which is why 24-month longitudinal batteries typically use pre-switch rather than post-switch sorting as the informative measure 78 . By the end of the second year, then, executive control is still highly task-sensitive, but it is no longer just a collection of isolated successes and failures; it is becoming a coherent, behaviorally expressed control capacity that supports hidden-state maintenance, response suppression, and simple goal-guided action over delay 78 . Episodic memory undergoes major expansion across the second year of life, though retention remains unreliable over long delays. Using elicited-imitation paradigms, 20-month-olds can reproduce multi-step event sequences (including their temporal order) after delays of up to 12 months 83 , 84 , a dramatic increase from the <1-month retention window typical prior to this period 85 , 86 . Memory for locations also improves across this window—though still fragile—with evidence that toddlers can retain spatial information across multi-month delays under favorable conditions 84 . Nonetheless, retention remains highly incomplete: retrospective studies suggest that even salient events from around 19 months are remembered only ∼40% of the time when children are tested years later (which is, however, likely explained by encoding and forgetting) 87 . Consistent with the emerging self-model described above, between ∼ \sim 18–24 months children also begin referencing themselves in past events, indicating that episodic memory is starting to incorporate the self as a participant in remembered scenes rather than merely storing perceptual episodes 88 . Even so, fully autobiographical, narratable recollection remains rudimentary in this period and develops substantially later, helping explain why most episodic memories from the second year of life ultimately fail to persist into later childhood 89 , 90 , 85 . Training data and optimization sleep increasingly stabilizes and abstracts episodes into nascent semantic/generalized knowledge 91 , 92 , 93 . From 12-24 months, the optimizer pursues a tight bundle of implicit objectives that each come with distinctive training data and error signals, and together they explain the aforementioned behavioral step-changes. A locomotor calibration objective continuously minimizes sensory prediction error across vestibular, proprioceptive, and visual channels: every footfall, sway, and retinal-slip event supplies supervised error to cerebellar forward models and cortical mismatch units, yielding fewer falls, narrower bases of support, and lawful gains in path planning, stairs, kicking, and early running as "teacher" spikes gate plasticity at co-active synapses. A manipulation/tool-use objective minimizes end-state and trajectory costs: mismatches between intended end-states and achieved configurations (orientation, torque, force) produce vector-like errors on each attempt, while success-contingent dopaminergic bursts stamp in the policies that led to scooping with a spoon, raking, levering, and role-differentiated bimanual coordination; over repetitions, anticipatory grasps emerge because forward models begin to predict the distal pose required for comfort at movement’s end. These motor objectives double as a system-identification loop: by driving down trajectory and end-state errors across thousands of self-generated interactions, the learner is forced to infer latent physical parameters-mass, friction, rigidity/compliance, centers of mass and graspable axes-and to encode affordance constraints like hinges and slots, yielding object concepts that transfer across contexts. In parallel, minimizing locomotor prediction errors over optic flow, vestibular, and proprioceptive cues stabilizes body- and world-centered coordinate frames and carves metric structure for distance, slope, and boundaries, seeding landmark/layout codes and the "intuitive physics" priors that support reorientation and increasingly abstract reasoning about objects. As sensorimotor primitives solidify, the bottleneck shifts to maintaining latent task state over longer, branchier action sequences while suppressing prepotent reaches; accordingly, a control-and-working-memory objective optimizes cortical-basal ganglia gating so that the right rule stays "on line" and incorrect motor programs are paused. Each failure on a control-reliant task yields conflict signals in dACC and negative TD-errors in striatum that penalize the impulsive policy; the hyperdirect STN pathway transiently raises decision thresholds, while MD-thalamus-PFC loops amplify and stabilize the active goal representation. With practice, neuromodulatory precision control (ACh/NE) reduces distractor gain and sharpens gating selectivity, producing reliable multi-step deferred imitation and short, rule-bound delays by the end of the window. A symbol-grounding objective maps word-forms to latent causes in the scene, not just pairing "sounds to things" but also exploiting social and perceptual structure to manufacture informative cross-modal contingencies. Joint-attention bouts (adult gaze/point/name) and child-initiated "clean views" create high-confidence alignments between short acoustic tokens and single object files; the learner effectively runs cross-situational expectation-maximization, updating a sparse lexicon that penalizes overlapping mappings (mutual exclusivity) and regularizes by shape-stable visual invariants, yielding the classic shape bias. Pragmatic inference functions as a noisy-channel prior-speaker intent, common ground, and naming timing steer credit assignment-while distributional frames ("more _", "kick the _", "grab two _") provide syntactic-bootstrapping signals that constrain verb meanings and enable early composition despite telegraphic production. Gains in phonological working memory and sleep-dependent spindle-ripple coupling increase retention and interference-resistance, consolidating single-trial labelings into anterior-temporal conceptual codes that transfer across views and media (objects <-> pictures). A spatial reorientation objective reduces discrepancy between predicted layout geometry and landmark relations ("toddler SLAM"): self-motion updates from path integration and head-direction cells are "closed" against extended surfaces whenever predicted pose drifts, forcing the system to anchor geometry (walls, corners, junctions) as the most reliable basis for an allocentric map. Through repeated experience and replay, these geometric codes are combined with feature-based inputs, with stability and distinctiveness determining their weight such that, by  18-24 months, toddlers can fuse geometry and landmarks to recover proper heading direction, recognize locations across viewpoints, and navigate through a sparse graph of corners and gateways transformed between egocentric and allocentric representations. As the learner’s agent model matures, the objective widens from "reduce my error" to "reduce another’s control error." Observed need or a stalled goal generates other-referenced prediction errors; STS/TPJ parse agents and intentions, ACCg/insula register the gap between expected and achieved states, and vmPFC-striatal critics fold vicarious value into a common currency. Contingent approval and task success provide dense scalar supervision that credits policies which minimize another’s error, shifting behavior from instrumental assistance toward state-oriented empathic responses and, as cost representations sharpen, toward costlier altruistic choices when expected social value outweighs self-cost. A declarative-binding objective incentivizes the system to preserve the structure of experiences rather than just isolated traces. Every retrieval failure or partial reinstatement acts as supervised feedback, driving hippocampo-cortical updates that sharpen links between items, places, and temporal order. The same comparators that stabilize reorientation maps (e.g entorhinal grid, boundary codes aligned with hippocampal place codes) also provide the coordinate frame for binding "what-where-when" into coherent episodes. Across waking replay and dendritic plateau tagging, recently co-activated representations are selected for offline consolidation, gradually transforming fragile sequences into durable, relationally indexed memories. By late in the second year, this system will support month-scale retention of event sequences and increasingly flexible transfer, as relational bindings become less scene-bound and more transportable across contexts. Imitation learning functions as a meta-learned objective that amortizes control, perception, and language priors across domains. By repeatedly optimizing to match the outputs of competent demonstrators, toddlers acquire hierarchical action sketches, causal scripts, and pragmatic templates that initialize policy search in new tasks, effectively few-shot policy cloning. One interesting example of this dynamic is 15-month infants’ imitation of adults’ persistence during task execution 94 . In general, frontoparietal ’mirror’ circuitry, BG gating, and cerebellar inverse models jointly compress observed sequences into reusable motor-cognitive programs, so subsequent learning starts closer to the optimum and needs only small, task-specific prediction-error adjustments. Threading these objectives is an intrinsic "learning-progress" objective that steers internalized objectives towards the Goldilocks zone (where prediction errors fall fastest); phasic NE resets policies when models fail, ACh raises the precision on trustworthy sensory errors, and distributional DA calibrates risk and vigor-together scheduling when the system exploits a just-learned controller (e.g., a spoon grip) versus when it perturbs policies to discover cleaner labels or new affordances. Neural development Cognitively, this stage of development marks a shift in the child’s world model from mostly sensorimotor predictions to increasingly abstract, relational, and symbolic representations that support flexible generalization and planning. Word learning accelerates and becomes more "model-based": toddlers begin forming a denser lexical-semantic network and adopt efficient inductive biases like the shape bias (organizing objects by shape instead of size, color, or texture), enabling rapid category extension from few exemplars and seeding the classic vocabulary spurt for many children 95 , 96 . Sleep starts playing a measurable role in consolidating these new words into the lexicon (e.g., emergence of lexical competition only after sleep), consistent with fast hippocampal capture and slower neocortical integration 97 . At the same time, probabilistic expectations about events become richer and more coherent (12-month-olds already integrate multiple cues to form Bayesian-like predictions 98 ) so by the second year children treat causes, agents, and object dynamics as structured variables in a causal model rather than isolated facts. The toddler’s "physics engine" also becomes more structured: beyond simple contact/no-contact rules, they encode graded support constraints (proportion- and position-of-contact, and by  13 months proportional distribution of mass) 99 , begin exploiting material/weight cues for planning 100 , and continue to use violations of expectation as catalysts for targeted exploration 101 . Object representations extend from visible displacements to robust solutions of invisible-displacement problems by  18-24 months 102 , signaling genuine mental tracking of occluded trajectories. Action planning folds advanced physics models back into control: by  14-19 months many children anticipate end-states (e.g., spoon reorientation and efficient grips) 16 , 103 , and imitation becomes selective and constraint-sensitive (i.e toddlers copy strange actions when they appear rational given the actor’s constraints, otherwise defaulting to more efficient actions 20 ). Yet characteristic limits still reveal what’s under construction, such as the gravity bias in tube-trajectory tasks near age two, where expectations of straight-down motion can override accurate path visualization 104 . Overall, these changes reflect a physics model that is increasingly relational, predictive, and action-useful, tightly coupled to symbolic growth in language and pretend play, and already operating as a compact causal model that supports multi-step, foresighted interaction with the world. The brain’s large-scale dynamics and wiring take major steps toward fast, high-bandwidth, "segregated-yet-integrated" control over this period. Cortically, oscillatory timing quickens and stabilizes: peak-alpha frequency continues its early rise into the lower alpha range 105 and the aperiodic (1/f) slope flattens nonlinearly through 24 months 106 , both pointing to shorter integration windows and tighter excitation-inhibition balance for local selection and prediction. Sleep spindles are bilaterally synchronous by  12-18 mo 107 and slow-oscillation<->spindle coupling that is weak/unsystematic in late infancy becomes reliably positive in toddlers 108 , strengthening the hippocampo-cortical channel that abstracts from episodes. Behavior-network coupling reorganizes from sensorimotor-anchored to control-network-anchored: at 12 months, walking covaries mainly with motor and posterior default-mode connectivity, but by 24 months it shifts toward dorsal attention and posterior cingulo-opercular (salience/monitoring) circuits 109 , evidence that action control is becoming top-down and distributed rather than local and reflexive. Default-mode hubs continue to ramp regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF) faster than primary systems, and rCBF increases are tightly coupled to strengthening DMN functional connectivity 110 , an explicit perfusion-network link that helps explain the toddler’s DMN consolidation, emerging self-awareness 111 , and growing antagonism (and perhaps arbitration) between internal modeling (DMN) and attention systems 112 . The substrate keeps pace: association pathways show steep myelination and axonal-organization gains during the first two years (fractional anisotropy (FA) rises; radial diffusivity (RD) falls; quantitative myelin metrics like R1 increase) 113 , with dedicated 1- and 2-year-old DTI/MRI atlases now resolving tract-specific maturation 114 , 115 ; limbic highways critical for spatial (and perhaps non-spatial) navigation and declarative binding (e.g the fornix, parahippocampal cingulum, and uncinate) are among the bundles upgrading conduction and phase-locking fidelity. Macroscopically, total brain volume continues to expand from year one to year two by roughly fifteen percent (about  948 cm³ ->  1072 cm³ in one longitudinal MRI cohort, now at 80% of adult brain size 116 ), which raises global signaling capacity and energy budget even as white-matter efficiency improves. Synaptic quantities shift in a region-specific way that matches the behavioral profile: in primary visual cortex, the post-natal synaptogenesis burst has already peaked by  8-12 months and the 12-24 month window is dominated by the early phase of pruning (density remains above adult levels but is declining) 117 , while in prefrontal cortex synaptic density is still rising beyond  15 months, climbing toward the well-known childhood overshoot that later prunes back 118 ; dendritic-spine counts in human PFC reach 2-3x adult values in childhood before protracted elimination that may last well into the third decade of life 119 . In parallel, hippocampal machinery grows and plugs in: human MRI shows a rapid hippocampal volume increase up to  2 years 120 , and resting-state work across infancy into early childhood finds the hippocampus strengthening its coupling to posterior midline DMN nodes that anchor scene/context models 121 , aligning with toddlers’ improving allocentric guidance and episodic binding. Thalamo-cortical gateways also mature, with longitudinal infant studies showing system-specific thalamic connectivity (including later-emerging links to DMN) becoming more adult-like by the end of year two 122 , complete with cognitive correlations.
