title: 2-3 Years
text: Behavioral capabilities Between 2 and 3 years, behavior shifts from mostly reactive, here-and-now routines to planned, symbolic, and increasingly rule-governed performance across domains. Around 24 months, children often speak in telegraphic two-word phrases (e.g. "mommy go"); soon after, they undergo a vocabulary burst. Expressive vocabulary grows from on the order of tens of words at age 2 to hundreds by age 3. By 30 months, most toddlers know at least  50 words (some know many more), and by 36 months vocabularies of several hundred to 1000 words are common. Toddlers begin combining words into longer utterances–by three years they routinely use 3-4 word sentences. Their grammar is still immature (omitting or misusing some particles and tenses), but they start using basic pronouns and plurals correctly. Receptive language also expands: two-year-olds can follow one-step commands; by 3 they understand two- to three-step instructions and spatial terms like "in," "on," and "under" 1 . They can name familiar objects and even tell you their own name and gender. Three-year-olds typically ( 75% of the time 2 ) speak clearly enough that unfamiliar adults understand most of what they say, and they can carry on a simple conversation with a few back-and-forth exchanges. Although far from fully mature, the roots of executive function are increasingly observable during this stage. Between 2-3 years, children show improvements in attention span and working memory, enabling them to hold in mind and follow multi-step (typically 2-step but often 3-step 1 ) commands and simple routines. They also begin exerting inhibitory control over impulses in certain contexts; a two-year-old might grab a treat as soon as they see it, whereas a three-year-old is slightly more likely to wait when told "not yet". Caregivers still provide crucial external regulation (reminders, rules, distraction), but toddlers internalize some of these rules over time. By the end of this period, many children can plan a multi-step play activity (like building a specific tower out of blocks) with minimal adult help, showing emerging ability to organize actions towards a goal 3 . By 2 years, most children walk and run with ease; over the next year their mobility and coordination improve markedly. By around 36 months, toddlers can run and climb confidently, jump in place, and even pedal a tricycle. They also begin walking up and down stairs with an alternating foot pattern (one foot per step) instead of the earlier one-step-at-a-time method 4 . Hand-eye coordination and dexterity also advance. A 1- to 2-year-old can usually stack a few blocks; by 3 years, children build towers of more than six blocks and manipulate small objects with greater precision; they can coordinate both hands to string large beads, turn book pages one at a time, and start to copy simple shapes (e.g. drawing a circle). Improved fine motor control allows for more self-care (e.g. feeding with a spoon/fork, beginning to dress/undress) and tool use. One of the hallmark changes in this period is the blossoming of symbolic thought (the ability to let one thing represent another in the mind). Around the second birthday, toddlers begin to engage in pretend play: for example, using a block as a "phone" or "feeding" a doll with an empty spoon; as they approach 3 years, pretend play becomes more elaborate and imaginative 5 . Children start acting out scenarios with themes and roles, such as playing house or pretending to be animals and characters. They also demonstrate early visual-artistic symbolism: for example, a three-year-old can copy a circle or cross with crayon, and will often ascribe meaning to their drawings ("This is Mommy") even if abstract. It should be noted that at this age the line between fantasy and reality can be blurry; a 3-year-old may believe their pretend monsters are real and become afraid, since the cognitive ability to reliably distinguish imagination from reality will develop closer to age 4 5 . Alongside pretend play, causal, numerical, and spatial reasoning all take practical leaps. A toddler at 2 might trial-and-error with simple cause-and-effect toys; by 3 they confidently operate toys with buttons, levers, and moving parts to produce intended effects 1 . In "blicket detector"-style tasks, 2-3-year-olds infer novel causal relations from sparse covariation and interventions 6 and explore more when evidence is confounded 7 . They can also work on easy puzzles (3-4 pieces) 1 and, numerically, many children move from rote counts to being "subset-knowers" who can map small number words onto exact set sizes, with full grasp of the cardinality principle emerging for many slightly after this window; still, by  3 years they often answer "how many?" correctly for small sets. Socially, 2-to-3-year-olds move beyond solitary and parallel play into more interactive engagements. Imitation is a powerful tool at this age - children copy the actions of adults and peers, learning social routines and basic cultural behaviors 1 . They show emerging empathy and attachment: a toddler may spontaneously show affection to friends (e.g. hugging a playmate) and express concern if a peer is crying or upset, reflecting the beginnings of reliable social perspective-taking 1 . By 3 years, children start to engage in simple cooperative play. They can take turns in games (though patience is limited) and are learning to share, at least in structured situations 5 . Possessiveness peaks during the "terrible twos" ("mine!" is a favorite word), but gradually they come to understand the property rights of others. Emotionally, toddlers display a wide range of feelings and quick mood shifts. Frustration and inability to communicate effectively at age 2 often lead to temper tantrums (screaming, crying, even breath-holding). By around 3, as language and self-control improve, many children handle emotions slightly better - they may use words to protest or seek comfort from adults instead of only throwing fits. They also separate more easily from parents at this age, showing that secure attachment and confidence in exploring have increased. Still, changes in routine can upset a 3-year-old, and they thrive on consistency and reassurance as they develop coping skills. Development of episodic and autobiographical memory: The importance of remembering forgetting Training data and optimization In the 2-3 year window, the brain is effectively pursuing a handful of coupled optimization problems at once, and each has a characteristic stream of "training data" and error routing that drives the aforementioned behavioral gains. For language, the objective is to compress and generalize lexical-syntactic regularities while minimizing pragmatic failure; dense child-directed speech and joint-attention episodes generate layer-by-layer cortical prediction errors (surprisal at the next phoneme/word/morpheme) that reshape representations, while communicative success/failure yields dopaminergic reward-prediction errors (approval, repair, being understood vs not) that reinforce production choices and conversational policy; apical dendritic plateaus gate when those local errors "write," and offline replay consolidates them, resulting in the vocabulary burst and first combinatorial grammar. Building directly on the 12-24-month spatial learning algorithm, the 2-3 year objective shifts from merely reorienting to actively stabilizing and extending a queryable scene-graph that binds who-what-where-when across delays, viewpoints, and displacements. The optimizer still closes self-motion drift against extended surfaces, but now it reliability-weights multiple cues (geometry, gateways/corners, and distinctive landmarks) by their stability and distinctiveness, so that boundary-anchored grids reset phase, item features attach to LEC-like codes, and retrosplenial/AG hubs improve the egocentric-allocentric transform at room transitions. Training data are the errors that arise at loop closure and displacement: returning to a start point and being "off," failing to predict which doorway leads to a hidden target, misbinding an object to a look-alike corner, or retrieving an episode and landing at the wrong heading. These mismatches drive novelty/comparator signals in DG-CA3-CA1, tag active assemblies (including large apical Ca2+ plateaus/BTSP-like events), and prioritize them for offline replay, which stitches short trajectories into longer routes and cements landmark-geometry conjuncts. With each tagged-and-replayed episode, objects, corners, and gateways consolidate as graph nodes, transitions as edges, and place codes become more viewpoint-invariant; language labels for relations ("in/on/under," "by the door") begin to cue retrieval, further reducing search entropy. For social valuation, the toddler is tuning a composite objective that weighs self-reward, concern for others’ outcomes, and compliance with simple rules. The data stream is dense and scalar: praise, smiles, touch, approving words, and access to peers act as positive reward-prediction errors; reprimands, withdrawal of attention, and brief "time-outs" act as negative ones; witnessing another’s need or failed goal generates vicarious errors. These signals train orbitofrontal/vmPFC-ventral striatum loops to recalibrate the value of social actions, while dACC/insula register others’ distress and norm conflict to engage control. TPJ/STS sharpen inverse-planning over others’ goals so credit assignment lands on the right features (who needed help, which rule applied). Serotonin lengthens the time horizon and raises the subjective cost of impulsive grabs, promoting patience and turn-taking; norepinephrine adjusts learning rates in volatile settings (new peer, new room); oxytocin/vasopressin increase the gain on affiliative cues so approval becomes a stronger teacher. Language supplies crisp rule tokens ("share," "wait," "no hitting"), letting basal-ganglia gates cache deontic policies that generalize. During sleep, hippocampal-cortical replay prioritizes episodes where helping or fair play yielded rich approval, strengthening other-regarding and norm weights. The readout between 2-3 years (more spontaneous helping, proto-fairness, emerging reputation sensitivity, longer turn-taking without prompts) falls out naturally from this training loop. For tool use, the objective is learning controllable cause-effect structure to achieve a comfortable, functional end state. Toddlers aren’t just repeating motor synergies; they’re discovering which interventions on objects (and on their own joints) reliably produce the desired distal outcome while leaving the body in a viable final posture. When a reach-grasp-transport ends in an awkward or unstable configuration (e.g wrist over-rotated, elbow locked, handle oriented wrong), the proprioceptive and vestibular mismatch, elevated effort, and micro-failures at contact yield large cerebellar teaching signals (climbing-fiber spikes) plus fronto-striatal negative TD-errors. Those errors update inverse models toward anticipatory pre-shaping and correct grip selection, and they also reshape the "policy over interventions" so the child chooses levers, rakes, or handles that make the end state easy. Conversely, successful, low-effort end states deliver positive TD-errors and lower cerebellar error, reinforcing the whole action sequence and the specific causal belief ("this action with this orientation causes that outcome"). Over weeks of practice, the system shifts from brute force to planning: the hand rotates before contact, the body chooses a stance that affords the terminal wrist angle, and the child selects the right implement geometry on the first try because the causal model now predicts which action will yield a high-comfort terminal pose. The gross motor objective factorizes into precision, efficiency, and vigor. Dense, self-initiated practice yields tightly time-locked error that cerebellar complex spikes use to train forward/inverse models, cutting endpoint variance, anticipating load, and pre-shaping grasp; in parallel, corticospinal myelination and synergy pruning (the process by which broad, overlapping motor patterns (or "synergies") are gradually refined into more precise, independent control of muscles and joints) increase bandwidth to distal musculature. Basal ganglia learn an effort-time trade-off, with tonic dopamine setting average vigor as opportunity cost so movements become quicker yet smoother, with fewer corrective submovements and earlier anticipatory postural adjustments. The altered nature of motor objectives is reflected behaviorally as step-to stair climbing gives way to alternating gait, running and pedaling stabilize, hand aperture scales with object size before contact, and utensil trajectories straighten, approaching Fitts-like speed-accuracy efficiency (i.e. movements converge toward the law that faster actions require reduced accuracy, and accuracy requires slower, more carefully controlled movements) in everyday reaches. For emerging executive control, the objective is to maintain a task state and suppress prepotent actions, which is common across tasks regardless of domain; multi-step instructions, turn-taking games, and A-not-B/detour-like conflicts deliver negative and positive TD errors into cortico-striatal loops, tuning working-memory gating and inhibitory policy, with ACh/NE adjusting precision and learning rates under stable vs volatile contexts-so toddlers get noticeably better at waiting, following 2-3-step routines, and organizing play toward a goal. Pretend play is the toddler’s sandbox: it trains event schemas by having the child actively compose agents, roles, goals, and causal contingencies into coherent episodes. By staging counterfactuals ("the block is a phone," "I’m the doctor"), hippocampal-DMN-PFC loops practice event segmentation, role binding, and temporal ordering, yielding reusable narrative priors (scripts with slots for agents, tools, locations, and goals) that later scaffold narrative comprehension and multi-step planning (along with providing a fruitful activity to engage in with other agents). This synergizes with imitation: demonstrations supply grounded action sketches, while pretense expands them combinatorially, so policy search in new tasks starts with both a motor scaffold and a narrative scaffold for predicting who does what, when, and why; this speaks to a deeper truth about human learning: humans’ capacity for generalization is perhaps largely due to the uniquely human propensity to take what information/episodes are available and to generate expansive learning signals based on counterfactual simulations. Fundamental drives for curiosity/uncertainty resolution sit over all of this: toddlers continue to preferentially sample the "Goldilocks" band where prediction errors are informative yet tractable, and neuromodulators schedule when to exploit a stable model (ACh-weighted precision), reset it under volatility (NE), or invest effort/patience (5-HT) while distributional dopamine supplies signed updates. Imitation also remains an underlying meta-objective that accelerates learning curves. Neural development From a neurocomputational standpoint, ages 24-36 months mark the high-plasticity summit of the human cortex precisely as the system retools for efficiency. Regionally staggered synaptogenesis has pushed association cortex to its most exuberant state: classic quantitative work shows that primary sensory cortices peak earlier (within the first year), whereas prefrontal association cortex crests around  3-3.5 years at nearly double adult synaptic density before protracted pruning ensues 9 . Converging cellular evidence shows that dendritic spine densities in human prefrontal cortex during childhood exceed adult values by roughly two- to three-fold and only begin their prolonged decline during puberty, continuing to remodel through the third decade 10 . The metabolic footprint matches this exuberance: developmental PET work demonstrates a marked rise to a childhood hypermetabolic plateau, with cortical glucose utilization around early preschool years substantially above ( 2x) adult levels 11 . Morphometrically, absolute gray-matter expansion has largely crested by  18-24 months; after that point, "apparent thinning" of cortex reflects intracortical myelination and pruning rather than degeneration per se. Longitudinal infant/toddler MRI shows cortical thickness and volume rising rapidly in year one, flattening by year two 12 , and then trending downwards in early childhood 13 , while quantitative and biophysical MRI link the thickness decline specifically to increasing myelin within the cortical ribbon 13 . Functionally, this shortens local integration windows and reduces energy per transmitted bit, shifting the system from diffuse local coupling to more selective, gated interactions that favor policy stabilization over reflexive responses. White-matter organization continues its steep, tract-specific efficiency gains through toddlerhood. Longitudinal diffusion work across birth-to-6 years shows rising fractional anisotropy with falling radial diffusivity across major association bundles, indicating thicker sheaths and tighter axonal packing 14 ; individual differences by age one are already predictive of microstructure at six, implying early-established "throughput budgets". In perisylvian language-control loops, these microstructural improvements are especially salient: dorsal (arcuate) and lateral frontoparietal (SLF II/III) segments show measurable maturation across the preschool window 14 , and independent studies linking the richness of early conversational turn-taking through age two to stronger myelination in language tracts by toddlerhood 15 . These changes lengthen the brain’s effective communication radius at a roughly fixed energy budget, enabling faster top-down selection and tighter perception-action coupling. At the systems level, large-scale networks continue to be more recognizable and less spatially diffuse than in infancy. During natural sleep, 1.5-3.5-year-olds already express a familiar set of intrinsic networks; within this window, posterior default-mode components become more reliable and track developmental skills, and language/salience networks sharpen in children with stronger behavioral scores 16 . Anticorrelation between default-mode and dorsal attention networks (characteristic of adult "internal-model vs. control" arbitration) remains weak but trends in the expected direction 17 , supported by increasing perfusion to posterior midline hubs and ongoing tuning of thalamocortical relays that coordinate cortico-cortical communication. The net effect between 24-36 months is more stable event-modeling at rest and quicker, more selective recruitment of control networks during tasks. Spectrally, the system continues to point towards tighter excitation-inhibition control and faster sampling. Across  24-36 months there is a continued shift from dominant theta toward rising alpha/mu power, a flattening of the aperiodic 1/f slope, and a gradual increase of peak-alpha frequency 18 . Sleep physiology gives a concordant readout of thalamocortical maturity: between age two and three, spindles lengthen and densify and slow/fast spindle topographies begin to differentiate 19 . Pulling these threads together, the 2-3 window is a hinge point where exuberant synaptic resources meet rapidly improving conduction and gating, under a metabolic regime that is generous but beginning a multi-year transition towards adult-level efficiency. The macro-result is a brain that can sustain more selective, longer-range, lower-cost communication; stabilize latent event models at rest; and pivot control more quickly during tasks, all of which shows up behaviorally as sharper turn-taking and articulation planning, longer working-memory spans for action sequences, and more deliberate tool-mediated manipulation.

title: 3-4 Years
text: Behavioral capabilities Between the ages of 3 and 4, children see substantial gains in observable behavior across multiple domains. This one-year span often marks the transition from toddlerhood to early childhood, bringing new competencies in motor coordination, language use, social understanding, self-control, emotional management, memory, and problem-solving. By age 4, children display significantly improved balance, strength, and coordination compared to age 3. Notably, a 4-year-old can hop on one foot and maintain one-foot balance for a few seconds, feats that a 3-year-old generally cannot perform 1 . Four-year-olds also run and climb with greater agility; they can confidently walk up and down stairs one foot per step and ride a tricycle with better steering control 2 . Running control shifts from simply moving fast to regulating pace and direction changes; you see quicker starts/stops and smoother forward-backward transitions 3 . Four-year-olds can also catch a large ball (using the whole body) and walk on their tip toes 3 . Fine motor control also advances between 3 and 4. Three-year-olds can scribble and stack a few blocks, but four-year-olds achieve new precision in hand-eye tasks. For example, a 4-year-old can cut paper with child-safe scissors, a skill uncommon at 3 1 . Drawing and writing skills progress from basic shapes to more complex forms: a typical 3-year-old might draw a simple circle, whereas a 4-year-old can copy geometric shapes (like crosses or squares) and even draw a person with 2-4 body parts 1 . They begin holding crayons or pencils with better control, allowing them to trace letters or write some characters by age 4 2 . Such fine motor milestones (which also includes turning pages one at a time and unscrewing jar lids) illustrate the new dexterity and planning in hand movements that emerge during this period. Relatedly, 4-year-olds display a basic ability to categorize objects according to their functions 4 , suggesting a emerging integration between semantic and motor systems. Children’s language ability grows explosively between 3 and 4 years, in vocabulary, grammar, and communicative skills. Vocabulary size roughly doubles during this interval: the average expressive vocabulary expands from about 900-1,000 words at age 3 to roughly 1,500-1,600 words by age 4 5 . This larger lexicon enables four-year-olds to express themselves on a wider range of topics. In addition to nouns and verbs, they regularly use adjectives and basic feeling words by age 4 (e.g. "long," "happy," "sad"), which are seldom heard from 3-year-olds 2 . Sentence structure and grammar become substantially more complex; a 3-year-old typically speaks in telegraphic sentences of 3-4 words, but by 4 years children form longer sentences of  5-6 words or more 2 . Four-year-olds reliably use grammatical markers that were just emerging at 3; for instance, they correctly use plurals, basic prepositions ("in," "on"), and present progressive "-ing" verbs 6 . They also begin to grasp more complex grammar: by 4, most children understand basic past tense and can recite simple songs or nursery rhymes with correct phrasing 1 . In fact, many 4-year-olds enjoy playing with language: they love poems or absurd phrases and can appreciate simple jokes (e.g. understanding the silliness of asking "Is that an elephant on your head?"). Furthermore, whereas strangers can catch only  75% of a 3-year-old’s speech on average, a 4-year-old’s speech is almost fully intelligible to unfamiliar adults 6 . They also become more active conversationalists. Four-year-olds express ideas and feelings, not just labeling objects or needs 6 . They can answer simple questions ("What do you do when you’re hungry?") and even start asking the endless "why" questions themselves as their curiosity blossoms 2 . This ability to engage in back-and-forth dialogue and provide descriptions or narratives (for example, telling a brief story about their day) is a new capability that sets 4-year-olds apart from younger preschoolers. Overall, the transition from age 3 to 4 is marked by flourishing linguistic competence: more words, longer and grammatically richer sentences, and far more effective communication with others. Three-year-olds largely play side-by-side (parallel play) with minimal coordination, but by 4 years old children can begin truly playing together in cooperative and imaginative ways, marking a shift from simply being near other children to engaging with them toward shared goals 7 . A 4-year-old is more likely to play games with rules with peers, negotiate roles in pretend play ("I’ll be the doctor, you be the patient"), and collaborate on a common project (building a fort of blocks together) than a 3-year-old. Along with this, sharing and turn-taking improve noticeably by age 4. Three-year-olds can take turns for short periods but often struggle with impulses to grab or hog toys. By 4, children better understand the concepts of "mine" versus "yours" and show emerging fairness; they are more willing to share and have learned basic turn-taking norms 2 . Early friendships also form in this period. Although preschoolers’ friendships are still quite fluid, studies show that children of 3-4 can name particular peers as friends and maintain those preferences over a span of months. Four-year-olds often exhibit touching moments of empathy and loyalty in these friendships - for example, comforting a friend who is crying or declaring "I love my friend" - behaviors that are just beginning to appear at this age. By contrast, 3-year-olds are less consistent: they may play with others but are just as likely to abruptly say "You’re not my friend" over minor conflicts. The increased social stability and kindness at 4 reflect growth in understanding others’ feelings. The fourth year also brings an expansion in imaginative play and the understanding of fantasy vs. reality. Around age 4, children’s pretend play scenarios become far more elaborate and story-driven; they enjoy inventing characters and narratives (playing house, pirates, superheroes, etc.) with peers or imaginary friends 2 . Many 4-year-olds have imaginary companions and can engage in lengthy make-believe play, yet they typically can distinguish pretend from real by this age 2 . This contrasts with 3-year-olds, who are only beginning to engage in simple pretend roles and may be more easily confused by fantasy. By 4, children also develop a sense of humor and trickery in social play. A common delight at this age is trying to fool others with playful deceptions (e.g. a child might giggle that they "tricked Mom into thinking I was asleep") 2 . The fact that a 4-year-old can intentionally deceive playfully (and also start to realize others might trick them) signals a new level of social cognition, reflecting a major cognitive-social milestone that typically occurs around 4 years: children begin to grasp that others have independent thoughts and can hold false beliefs (basic "theory of mind"); decades of developmental research using "false-belief" tests (like the classic Sally-Anne task) show a sharp transition in this age range. In one meta-analysis, the vast majority of 3-year-olds could not ascribe a false belief to someone else, whereas 4-year-olds reliably succeeded 8 . In other words, a 3-year-old assumes everyone knows what they know, but a 4-year-old can begin to appreciate that another person might be unaware of certain facts or might be fooled by a situation. For example, at 3 a child will insist that a friend looking for a toy will check where the child knows the toy really is, even if the friend didn’t see it moved. By 4, the child is more likely to anticipate that the friend will have a false belief and look in the toy’s original location. This emerging theory of mind also manifests in everyday interactions: four-year-olds start lying or bluffing in simple ways. The preschool years are a time of rapid growth in executive functions, with many executive abilities that are fragile or absent at 3 becoming reliably present by age 4. Four-year-olds exhibit much better impulse control compared to three-year-olds, showing signs of successful performance on both simple (i.e., pure response inhibition) and complex inhibition tasks (i.e., response inhibition plus alternative response) 9 . For example, in the "Simon Says"-type Bear/Dragon game (where children must only follow commands given by a "nice bear" puppet and ignore a "naughty dragon" puppet), young 3-year-olds understand the rule but cannot resist mimicking the dragon’s commands. In contrast, most 4-year-olds can inhibit their impulses and successfully "freeze" for the dragon 10 . Likewise, parents often notice that by age 4, children can handle simple instructions like "don’t touch that yet" or can wait a short time for a treat, skills that were very hard at 2-3. Around age 4, children achieve a milestone in mental flexibility (the ability to shift to a new rule or perspective). A classic test is the Dimensional Change Card Sort (DCCS). A 3-year-old can sort cards by an initial rule (say, by color), but when the rule changes (sort by shape), the child perseverates (they keep sorting by the old rule even though they know it changed). By contrast, 4-year-olds can switch to the new rule and sort correctly after a rule change 11 ; researchers characterize this 3-to-4-year shift from perseveration to flexibility as a fundamental cognitive development 12 . This newfound flexibility at 4 allows children to handle multi-step routines and adjust when rules or expectations change (for example, a 4-year-old can learn that at school they must line up quietly after playtime, even if at home playtime has no such rule, whereas a 3-year-old has difficulty with such context shifting). Working memory capacity and the ability to follow complex directions also improve by age 4. A three-year-old can hold in mind and follow about two simple related commands in sequence, but by 4 years children can handle 2-3 step instructions reliably (especially if the steps relate to familiar contexts) 2 . For instance, a 4-year-old can understand: "Close the book and give it to Mommy" or "Go to your room, find your shoes, and bring them here," whereas a 3-year-old might forget one of those steps or get confused after the first action; one study showed that when tasked with recalling and executing a sequence of actions (opening a series of drawers in the correct order to retrieve prizes), 3-year-olds could successfully remember two-step sequences, whereas 4-year-olds managed three- and four-step sequences reliably 13 . This reflects both better attention span and memory. Educators note that four-year-olds can sustain attention on a single activity for longer periods than toddlers (often engaging in a task for 10+ minutes 14 ) and can shift focus under adult guidance without melting down. By 4 years, episodic memory shifts from mostly gist- (what happened) and script-based (basic steps) recall at 3 to more episodic, source- and context-tagged remembering. Four-year-olds recall personally experienced events with more of the "what-where-when" bound together (e.g. they can tell you not just that they went to the lab but which room particular activities happened in) and they outperform younger preschoolers on memory for the locations of events and on conjunctions between event content and place, although performance is still far from adultlike 15 . Temporal information becomes more recoverable: across early childhood, memory for the order of past events shows pronounced gains, with preschoolers around four beginning to succeed on temporal-order tasks that would most three-year-olds 16 , 17 . Source monitoring also improves: by four, children are better able than three-year-olds to report where they learned something, though "source amnesia" errors remain common relative to older children 18 . This richer episodic recall co-develops with more coherent autobiographical narratives; four-year-olds include more relational details and evaluative commentary than three-year-olds, consistent with sociocultural accounts of autobiographical memory emerging across the preschool years 19 , 20 . Four-year-olds also begin to pass tasks tapping episodic future thinking (projecting themselves into a specific future event), a capacity that typically emerges between ages 3 and 4 and reflects more explicit, self-referential episodic representations 21 . Development of episodic and autobiographical memory: The importance of remembering forgetting Spatial reasoning also shows a clear inflection. One study involving classic mental-rotation puzzles with 2D "ghost" figures showed that the proportion of children performing above chance rises steeply from 3-4 years; only about 10% of 3-year-olds perform above chance while 40% of 4-year-olds do 23 . Reorientation also improves qualitatively: whereas 3-year-olds search essentially at random in a rectangular layout, 4-year-olds begin to encode and use the room’s geometry to find hidden targets, although their feature/landmark use is still fragile and error-prone 24 . In larger rooms after disorientation, 4-year-olds reliably use geometry but typically fail to exploit a salient landmark unless given brief spatial wording 25 . They are also on the cusp of Level-2 visual perspective-taking: with simple scenes some 4-year-olds can reason about how an array looks from another viewpoint, but with multi-object arrays they still default to egocentric choices far more than older children 26 , 27 . Finally, gains in spatial language and construction play scaffold these abilities: richer command of relational terms (e.g., in front/behind/between) correlates prospectively with better number skills, and puzzle/block play between ages 2-4 predicts stronger spatial transformation performance by  4.5 years 28 , 29 . Causal reasoning gets more principled: children start relying less on mere co-occurrence and more on temporal order, probabilities, and hidden mechanism. In temporal-priority tasks, far more four-year-olds than three-year-olds pick the earlier event as the cause; in one study, 41/50 four-year-olds performed perfectly across four trials versus 22/50 three-year-olds 30 . Their inferences also incorporate abstract rules 31 : in certain experiments, they can recognize basic rules 31 and resolve ambiguity by considering how likely each (usually implicit) explanation is, something three-year-olds struggle with 32 , 31 . This shift shows that by four, children are not only noticing patterns but also weighing probabilities when deciding what caused what, an ability that researchers see in simple ’blicket detector’ tasks where kids must infer which objects activate a machine 32 . They also begin to link causal powers to hidden mechanisms: four-year-olds infer that an object’s internal parts explain its efficacy and track that causal property when parts move between objects, whereas three-year-olds more often lean on surface appearance 33 . Four-year-olds more also selectively seek and remember satisfying "why" answers than younger peers 34 , 35 , supporting their own causal inductions. Finally, nascent counterfactual reasoning emerges in some basic tasks by four 36 , 37 , though it remains highly fragile and task-dependent 38 , 39 . These causal feats do, however, remain confined to the most basic systems and still appear to be subserved by fast, largely automatic processing (System 1) rather than fully reflective, System 2 reasoning, which comes online in forthcoming years 39 . Training data and optimization In the 3-4 year window, the brain continues to pursue a handful of coupled optimization problems, each having a characteristic stream of "training data" and error routing that drives the aforementioned behavioral gains. The motor system keeps optimizing the same objective laid out for 2-3 (accurate terminal states with comfortable biomechanics under an energy/vigor budget) but the weights further tilt towards precision as opposed to adding new basic skills; efficiency rises, brute-force corrections drop, and vigor is better scheduled. Practically, this looks like a tighter feedforward controller trained by denser, more precisely timed errors. Cerebellar climbing-fiber teaching spikes remain the vector-valued supervisor calibrating forward/inverse models, now clearly necessary for learning to natural stimuli 40 and capable of grading step size via complex-spike dynamics; that supervision reduces endpoint variance, anticipates load, and improves anticipatory postural adjustments as tasks get faster and more coordinated. In parallel, basal ganglia keep converting practice into policy: distributional dopamine encodes multiple "expectiles" of return, letting the actor learn risk-sensitive action timing and effort allocation so movements become quicker yet smoother with fewer submovements. Corticospinal bandwidth is rising rapidly with early-childhood myelination (especially along the corticospinal tract 41 ) so distal control and bimanual coordination can be decomposed more finely, and cortical predictive controllers can pre-shape hand orientation earlier in the reach. Fine-motor trajectories reflect this optimization: grip aperture scaling and pre-shaping become more anticipatory, and everyday pointing/aiming begins to follow cleaner speed-accuracy tradeoffs 42 . Offline, preschool naps consolidate: spindles upregulated by learning enhance retention 43 , helping compile practiced subroutines into smoother, chunked skills. The linguistic system is optimizing four coupled objectives: mapping new forms to meanings, compressing grammar into predictive rules, stabilizing an efficient speech motor code, and using pragmatics to choose informative utterances. Lexical growth (especially verbs) leans on cross-situational statistics 44 and syntactic bootstrapping 45 : children track co-occurrence structure across episodes 44 and use context clues (especially the grammatical frame of the sentence (who is doing what to whom)) to narrow a novel verb’s meaning, so prediction errors in word-scene mappings and mismatches between syntax and event structure drive belief updates that yield faster, more accurate verb use 46 . Grammar advances because the learner increasingly prefers rules that best predict the input; overregularization is the signature of that generalization pressure (e.g using "mouses" instead of "mice") 47 , while caregiver recasts supply tightly time-locked contrastive feedback that reduces future surprisal for the same message 48 . Behaviorally this shows up as Brown-stage IV-V morphemes (articles, regular past, third-person -s, copula/aux "be") entering spontaneous speech 49 . In comprehension, children begin to anticipate upcoming words; processing difficulty tracks probabilistic prediction error (surprisal) 50 , and better producers predict more 51 , feeding a virtuous cycle between production and comprehension. Production itself is tuned by auditory-somatosensory error: controllers compare expected with heard speech and adapt articulatory commands 52 ; altered-feedback studies show robust, error-driven adaptation in young children 53 , aligning with the observed jump in intelligibility and longer, morphologically richer utterances. Social learning is dominated by three coupled objectives: predicting minds, internalizing norms, and becoming an informative, cooperative partner. For mind‐prediction, children prioritize learning how desires, beliefs, and especially knowledge access ("seeing leads to knowing") drive others’ actions; errors arise whenever behavior contradicts their current model (e.g a listener acts confused or a partner chooses unexpectedly) and these social prediction errors, plus caregivers’ frequent mental-state talk 54 , update belief attributions and yield the observed jump in mental-state vocabulary and success on early ToM tasks 55 . For norm acquisition, pedagogy and play supply dense, labeled data 56 : demonstrations flag that an action is conventional, children then "overimitate" even causally irrelevant steps 57 , 58 , and third-party norm violations elicit protest; these tightly time-locked signals train a normative policy that shows up behaviorally as rule-following in games and explicit corrections of others 59 . For cooperative pragmatics, the objective is to choose utterances that uniquely identify referents and maintain common ground; when messages are ambiguous, peers’ clarification requests function as error signals that drive rapid adjustments in referential specificity and repair skill across trials, producing more informative, partner-sensitive talk by age four 60 , 61 . Finally, prosocial choice is tuned by reputational and fairness feedback: children increasingly weight others’ helpfulness and simple equity rules when sharing 62 , so approval, gratitude, and allocation outcomes reinforce selective generosity and early inequality aversion (which is quite unreliable at this stage 63 ). The episodic system is optimizing three coupled objectives: segmenting continuous experience into discrete events, binding those events’ elements into a detailed and retrievable "what-where-when" code, and imposing temporal order that supports coherent retelling and planning. Training data arrive as prediction errors at event boundaries: when the next state in a viewed or enacted sequence deviates from the child’s event model, boundary-linked surprise sharpens the model and boosts encoding, a mechanism formalized in Event Segmentation Theory and shown to enhance later recall at boundaries 64 , 65 . Hippocampal maturation and connectivity then translate these boundary-tagged signals into stronger bindings: across early childhood, better episodic recall covaries with hippocampal structure/function, and preschoolers’ performance on naturalistic what-where-when searches improves over this window 66 , 67 , 68 . Errors in temporal and source attributions during retrieval (e.g., telling events out of order or misremembering "who told me") generate corrective feedback from adults and tasks. Caregiver elaborative reminiscing provides densely labeled supervision (wh-questions, confirmations, recasts) that fills gaps and tunes narrative structure, producing richer, more temporally organized autobiographical reports 69 , 70 . Everyday life trains executive control through three practical objectives: executing multi-step scripts under distraction (morning routines, clean-up, "get your shoes then your jacket"), inhibiting prepotent responses to meet rules ("wait your turn," "don’t touch the stove"), and flexibly switching goals and roles across activities (ending play to eat; shifting from "doctor" to "patient" in pretend). Naturalistic errors are dense and well-timed: missed steps, spills, or social corrections act as salient feedback, and adult scaffolding (prompting, modeling, graded hints) tightens children’s working-memory maintenance and response inhibition, yielding fewer prompts needed, smoother transitions, and better compliance across weeks 9 , 71 . Self-generated "private speech" becomes a key control signal: children label steps aloud ("first socks, then shoes"), which reduces off-task behavior and frustration by converting language into top-down guidance 72 . Mechanistically, everyday successes and slip-ups gate what is held vs. updated in working memory via basal-ganglia-PFC loops 73 , while conflict and anticipated payoffs tune how much control to deploy ("expected value of control" in dACC 74 ), so routines progressively compress into chunked scripts with faster, more reliable initiation. Practice matters: repeated rule-governed play, movement classes, and classroom routines deliver the kind of structured, incremental demands that measurably strengthen preschool executive function 75 . Social pretend play adds powerful set-shifting and perspective-keeping pressure, improving flexibility in natural dialogue and cooperative tasks 76 . Finally, sleep stabilizes the day’s control policies (naps and good nighttime sleep enhance attention and emotion regulation the next day 77 ) so children arrive at four with longer on-task stretches, quicker regrouping after errors, and more adaptive switching. Spatial learning in the wild pursues four everyday objectives: making stable structures, transforming shapes mentally, navigating to goals, and mapping symbols to real space; each objective delivers dense error that sharpens the system. Block and track building optimize "stability under load" and "fit/alignment": sagging bridges, topples, and mis-joins generate salient physical mismatches that drive revisions to part-whole geometry and support the jump from stacks to bridged spans and simple enclosures; the same assembly practice is predictive of later spatial and even math skill, indicating that these error streams translate into generalizable spatial programs 78 , 79 . Puzzle play optimizes "shape-pose correspondence": every piece is a supervised trial where non-fit and rotated-fit act as labeled negatives/positives, and the frequency and quality of puzzle play in the 2-4 window predict children’s spatial-transformation performance months later 80 , 23 ; the need for effective tool use further incentivizes mental rotation. Wayfinding in homes, classrooms, and playgrounds optimizes "place finding under disorientation" and incentivizes cognitive map formation: wrong-door searches and detours supply navigation prediction errors; at this age children can reorient by the extended geometry of rooms but still struggle to use the geometry of freestanding objects, so boundary-based cues yield more reliable success than isolated beacons 81 . Throughout, caregiver spatial talk and gesture ("under the bridge," "rotate it," "left of the red door") act like high-information recasts: they focus attention on diagnostic relations and reduce future surprisal in similar scenes, and longitudinal data show that richer spatial language in this period predicts children’s later spatial performance 82 . Neural development During this window, the brain is still "overprovisioned" while continuing its long shift toward faster, cheaper, and more selective computation. At the cellular-mesoscale, association cortex is at or just past its maximum synaptic density; classic quantitative work places a prefrontal crest roughly around 3-3.5 years before protracted pruning begins 83 , which is consistent with the well-described childhood hypermetabolic plateau where cortical glucose use approaches roughly twice adult levels near age four 84 . This combination (dense circuit substrate plus high energy availability) lets the system explore large hypothesis spaces while it starts to tighten control. Apparent "cortical thinning" is now visible on MRI across much of the mantle, not because tissue is vanishing but because intracortical myelin is increasing and redundant synapses are slowly being removed. Longitudinal early-childhood imaging shows thickness/volume rising rapidly in year one, flattening by year two, then trending downward into the preschool years 85 ; quantitative MRI and biophysical analyses tie this specifically to myelin accumulation within the cortical ribbon rather than degeneration 86 . Functionally, those microstructural changes continue to shorten local integration windows and reduce the energy per transmitted bit, shifting dynamics from diffuse local coupling toward gated, policy-stabilizing interactions. White-matter bandwidth continues its steep, tract-specific gains. Diffusion MRI across birth->6 years shows rising fractional anisotropy with falling radial diffusivity in major association bundles, including dorsal perisylvian language pathways (arcuate) and lateral frontoparietal segments (SLF II/III), which are measurably maturing across the preschool window 87 . This means longer effective communication radius at roughly fixed power, enabling faster top-down selection and tighter perception-action coupling.

title: 4-5 Years
text: This period (which bridges the late preschool years and the start of formal schooling) sees rapid gains in language complexity, social understanding, motor coordination, and cognitive control, along with a generally-enhanced understanding of the causal forces underlying everyday experience (and the means to learn them).

title: Language
text: By age 4, most children are already chatty and use multi-word sentences, but their language grows noticeably more sophisticated by age 5. Vocabulary expands from a few hundred or early thousand words at 3-4 years to an active lexicon of several thousand words by age 5 1 . Five-year-olds frequently learn new words through fast-mapping and can name basic colors, shapes, and common objects; they also start using words for more abstract concepts (e.g. words for feelings like "confused", "decide", or "remember", or spatial relations like "between" and "above") 2 , 3 . Syntax and grammar show clear advancements: a 4-year-old’s sentences often average 4-5 words, whereas a 5-year-old commonly speaks in sentences of 6+ words 4 . By 5, children reliably form complex sentences with conjunctions ("and," "because") and even basic subordinate clauses. They begin to use different sentence types; for example, many 5-year-olds can produce in both active and passive sentence constructions to convey the same meaning (e.g. "The dog chased the cat" vs. "The cat was chased by the dog") 2 . Grammatical morphemes are largely in place: five-year-olds correctly use plural -s, past -ed, and even comparatives/superlatives (adding -er or -est to adjectives) 2 . They still make the occasional overregularization error (saying "runned" or "sheeps"), but such errors become less frequent. Pragmatic and conversational skills undergo refinement between four and five. Four-year-olds are enthusiastic conversationalists but may provide either too little or too much information when telling a story, and they often assume the listener knows the context. By age 5, children are better at tailoring their language to the listener’s perspective 2 . This reflects gains in social cognition that allow a child to, for instance, explain an idea more simply to a younger child or supply relevant background information to an unfamiliar listener. Five-year-olds also improve in turn-taking and narrative coherence. They can recount past events in a (somewhat) logical sequence, and their stories include more details about who was involved, where it happened, and when (e.g. "We went to the park yesterday and my friend Alice and I fed the ducks") 2 ; by five, many children can narrate a simple setting->problem->resolution storyline and use temporal/causal connectives ("then… because…") and pronoun reference more consistently, reflecting improved coherence and making self-explanation and planning through language feasible. Their storytelling is still imperfect (endings might be abrupt or chronology jumbled) but compared to 4-year-olds, five-year-olds include more temporal and causal language and are beginning to grasp the basics of plot structure 2 . Another leap in this period is the understanding of non-literal language and humor. Four-year-olds enjoy silly words and simple jokes, but they often interpret language very literally. By five, many children start to appreciate figurative expressions and wordplay. For example, a 5-year-old might giggle at idioms or understand common metaphors, realizing that "pulling someone’s leg" is a joke and not an act of aggression 1 . They also use language socially to tease or tell simple jokes, and they love absurd rhymes or playing with "naughty" words (it’s common for 4-5-year-olds to experiment with so-called "bathroom words" for shock value, reflecting their burgeoning sense of humor). Pragmatically, five-year-olds are learning social conventions of speech: they modulate volume and tone to suit the setting and use more polite forms ("could I have...?") in requests 2 . Overall, the typical five-year-old is a confident user of language, being able to carry on extended conversations and narrate events while continuing to use language as a tool for learning (by asking endless "Why?" questions).

title: Social
text: By age 5, theory of mind (everyday understanding of mental states (e.g., beliefs, intentions, knowledge) and the links between these unobservable states and action 1 ) is more firmly established and underpins more advanced social cognition. Five-year-olds not only understand false beliefs, but also grasp that people can have different knowledge or viewpoints on the same event. They start to comprehend that others can be fooled or surprised by things that the child himself/herself knows. They also show budding awareness of "hidden feelings"; for instance, a 5-year-old may understand that someone who is smiling could actually feel sad inside, a concept younger preschoolers struggle with. This lays the groundwork for empathy: while even toddlers exhibit basic empathic concern (e.g. distress when another child cries), 4- to 5-year-olds develop cognitive empathy (the ability to infer how someone else might feel in a given situation and why) 2 . A five-year-old might say, "She’s sad because her ice cream fell," demonstrating an understanding of the connection between an event and another’s emotional state. They also start responding to others’ emotions in more appropriate ways (like offering to help or giving comfort spontaneously). Furthermore, one reputable study showed that some 5-year-olds are capable of holding meaningful values (i.e desirable goals that serve as guiding principles in a person’s life, like "having fun" or "caring for others") and can set them within a hierarchy of importance 3 . Peer interactions evolve in tandem with these cognitive advances. Around 4 years, children engage in associative and cooperative play: they don’t just play side-by-side (parallel play), but actually cooperate on shared goals (building a fort together) or act out complementary roles in pretend play ("You be the doctor, I’ll be the patient"). By 5, these social play scenarios become more elaborate and governed by agreed-upon "rules" or narratives, indicating better understanding of others’ intentions and the norms of group activity. Five-year-olds are generally more cooperative and responsible than four-year-olds, often eager to please peers and adults 4 . They form friendships based on shared interests and can verbalize who their "friends" are. Positive peer relationships are supported by their improved theory of mind and emotion understanding; children who can empathize and take turns tend to be well-liked, and indeed research finds that gains in ToM between 4 and 5 correlate with more positive peer interactions 5 .

title: Semantic and episodic memory
text: Young children’s memory abilities also improve qualitatively between ages four and five; both semantic and episodic memory show rapid development during this period as the brain’s memory systems (especially the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex) become more efficient. By age 4, children already remember plenty of factual information: for instance, a 4-year-old knows the names of many everyday objects, familiar people, perhaps some letter or number names, and so on (this is their semantic memory store). Over the next year, semantic memory expands in breadth and depth. Five-year-olds have accrued more general knowledge: they often know basic facts like the days of the week, some months, their address and phone number, and can name common coins or animals 1 . They ask innumerable "Why?" and "How?" questions at this age, which fuels their semantic learning. They begin to form simple schemas and taxonomic knowledge, for example understanding that a tiger and an elephant are both animals (knowledge of categories). This is reflected in vocabulary growth and the ability to give simple definitions (e.g "what’s a fork?" -> "it’s something you eat with."). Between four and five, episodic memory (a reflection of event modeling abilities) becomes less "gists with tags" and more truly recollective ; five-year-olds bind item-context relations more reliably at encoding and retrieve those bindings after delay and interference, reflecting a shift from the retrieval limits typical at four toward recollection-based remembering. Laboratory tests that require remembering combinations (e.g., what happened with which background/room) show clear improvement from 4 to 6 years, with the biggest early gains emerging right in the preschool window 2 , and follow-ups indicate that much of the four-year-old deficit is a retrieval (not encoding) bottleneck 3 . Five-year-olds also show better memory for temporal order (e.g. if asked to recount the day’s events in order, a 5-year-old is more likely to correctly sequence two or three events than a 4-year-old). Source monitoring also becomes sturdier: compared to four-year-olds, five-year-olds are better at reporting where or from whom they learned something (and at keeping sources distinct), marking a step away from the "source amnesia" errors common earlier in preschool 4 . Overall, the episodic memory system can (unreliably) carry out its basic functions while continuing along a steep trajectory of improvement. These gains in episodic memory manifest in autobiographical memory; by 5, children provide more detailed and organized narratives of past events than at 3 or 4, often spontaneously including emotional or evaluative comments (e.g. "That was fun!") 5 . At this age they also begin to treat "remembering" as a mental act (using verbs like "I remember..." appropriately and showing early meta-memory/subjective-recollection abilities 6 , 7 , 8 ), reflecting a growing understanding that memories are internal representations of past experiences. Consistent with that, five-year-olds can recount events from a year or more earlier 9 , 10 , reflecting emerging maturity of hippocampo-cortical loops. title: Fine and gross motor
text: Motor skills see noticeable refinement between ages 4 and 5, as children gain strength, balance, and dexterity. Gross motor abilities of a typical 4-year-old include running and jumping with confidence and the emerging ability to hop on one foot a few times in a row. By 4, most children can skip or gallop in an uneven rhythm and can navigate stairs one foot per step (alternating feet) when going down as well as up 1 . They can also catch a large ball (though trapping it against the body is more common than a clean catch with hands at this age) and throw overhand with improved aim 1 . Balance improves dramatically around this time: a four-year-old might manage to stand on one foot for about 4-5 seconds. By age 5, these gross motor skills become more advanced and integrated. Five-year-olds can typically balance on one foot for at least 5-10 seconds and walk heel-to-toe along a line 1 . Many can skip with a smoother alternating gait and even attempt activities like jumping rope by the end of the fifth year 1 . They also learn to hop forward on one foot and can walk backwards with balance 1 . This improved coordination lets them start participating in group games and sports appropriate for preschoolers. Indeed, the transition to age 5 often corresponds with the ability to learn basic movement sequences (for example, a simple children’s dance or an obstacle course) and to adjust movements in response to obstacles or changes in terrain. Fine motor skills also undergo important advances. At 4, children have sufficient fine motor control to draw basic shapes (circles, squares) and perhaps a very simple human figure (often a "tadpole" person with just a head and limbs). They can build tall block towers (8-10 blocks high) and are beginning to use child-safe scissors to snip paper 1 . Four-year-olds can dress and undress with minimal help - for example, they can fasten large buttons and zip up a jacket if the zipper is started for them 1 . By age 5, fine motor precision and hand-eye coordination have improved such that children can cut along a line with scissors and draw more recognizable objects. A five-year-old typically can draw a person with  6 body parts (head, body, arms, legs, etc.), whereas a 4-year-old’s drawing might only include 3 or 4 parts 1 . Five-year-olds also master copying more complex geometric shapes: in addition to circles and squares, they can copy triangles and even basic diamonds by the end of this age 1 . Age 5 is also when many children learn to write some letters and numbers. It’s common for 5-year-olds to be able to write their first name legibly and draw some letter forms (even if not perfectly formed) 1 . They also often know how to hold a pencil with a proper tripod grasp, whereas a 4-year-old might still use a fisted or four-finger grasp for drawing. Five-year-olds enjoy crafts and construction play that challenge their fine motor skills: bead stringing, simple origami, small Lego assembly, etc., become easier and more enjoyable as their dexterity increases. By contrast, a 4-year-old can do puzzles and Duplo blocks, but a 5-year-old’s longer attention span and finer control often allow completion of more intricate puzzles (20+ pieces) and even basic Lego models.

title: Physics and objects
text: Gross and fine motor advancements clearly reflect developments in executive function and the child’s ability to control/coordinate/predict their own body; however, these advancements also reflect advancing (although still basic) knowledge of object-level properties such as physics, kinematics, and affordances. In construction and stacking, some five-year-olds start to move beyond a naive "support the middle" rule and, especially brief guided play, can reason about stability in terms of mass distribution and center of mass 1 . They also get better at using hidden properties like weight to plan actions: by 4-5, children can consistently leverage weight to cause specific physical outcomes, categorize objects by weight, and transfer that knowledge to novel objects, supporting more appropriate force selection and tool choice 2 . By age five, children’s kinematic models are "online" enough to guide prediction, but they’re still being tuned. In eye-tracking tasks where a target briefly disappears, 5-year-olds already sustain predictive pursuit and generate anticipatory saccades (qualitatively adult-like strategies) but with weaker gain and larger errors than adults 3 . Their memory-based extrapolations are also advancing: the forward-displacement bias (representational momentum) reliably shrinks between ages 5 and 6, indicating more precise estimation of post-occlusion position and velocity 4 . Explicit reasoning about motion remains fragile, however. In horizontal-projectile problems (predicting the path of an object released from a moving carrier), five-year-olds’ judgments are easily pulled by salient spatial context rather than inertial constraints, showing that correct trajectory rules are not yet robust 5 . Classic gravity-inertia dissociations also narrow at this age: in predictive-judgment tasks, sensitivity to inertia (combining forward motion with downward acceleration) emerges around 5-6 years, marking a transition from a gravity-only bias to integrating both constraints in unseen motion 6 . Functionally, predictive timing for interceptive actions (e.g., catching/striking) shows measurable improvement by five and continues to strengthen across childhood, supporting the cleaner ball catches and early jump-rope attempts described earlier; this capability does clearly trail older children and adults, though 7 . Research on force dynamics shows that 3.5-5.5 year-olds mostly understand single forces impacting object movement, but only the oldest can integrate two contradictory forces 8 , suggesting their physics engine runs single-threaded rather than computing multiple simultaneous influences. Taken together, five-year-olds have kinematic models that work for implicit prediction and motor control but remain undertrained and single-threaded-unable to robustly support explicit reasoning or integrate multiple simultaneous forces, requiring further calibration across childhood before the architecture that drives anticipatory eye movements can also generate reliable trajectory judgments. This reveals a critical insight: humans don’t develop kinematics understanding through pure physics simulation-instead, we start with heuristic principles that work most of the time, then spend years debugging edge cases where perceptual salience misleads our intuitive physics engine.

title: Spatial
text: Between ages 4 and 5, children make significant strides in understanding and using spatial terms to describe relationships. They typically begin to grasp basic prepositions like above, below, in front of, behind, and between, applying them not just egocentrically (relative to themselves) but also to describe object-to-object relations in a scene 1 . For example, a 5-year-old can follow instructions such as "put the toy between the boxes" or "stand behind me," whereas a 3- or 4-year-old might still confuse these terms. By this age children also begin to grasp left vs. right on their own bodies (e.g. identifying their left hand) and use these terms in context, though consistently applying left/right remains challenging; true mastery of left/right generally comes between 5 and 7 years 1 . Improvements in spatial vocabulary are directly tied to improvements in spatial problem solving (e.g block design tests) 2 . At 4-5 years old, children show rapid gains in their ability to mentally manipulate spatial information, although these skills are still developing and error-prone. One key milestone is the emergence of mental rotation ability (the capacity to imagine objects turning in space and recognize how they would look from different angles). Classic experiments have demonstrated that by around 5 years of age children start to perform above chance on simplified mental rotation tasks. For instance, when shown a shape and asked to pick which of two holes it would fit into (with the shape presented at various rotated angles), 5-year-olds’ error rates and reaction times increase systematically with the degree of rotation, much like adults who take longer for larger mental rotations 3 , 4 . This linear increase in difficulty with angle suggests that the 5-year-old is indeed mentally rotating the figure to align it, rather than randomly guessing. In contrast, 4-year-olds often perform at chance on such tasks, not yet showing a reliable increase in response time with angle and frequently resorting to guessing 3 . Another data point lies in the mental rotation study mentioned earlier; in this task (where pairs of asymmetrical ghost figures and a hole are presented; the child must determine which ghost fits in the hole by mentally rotating it), 10% of 3-year-olds and 40% of 4-year-olds perform above chance, while 95% of 5-year-olds do 5 . In tandem with object rotation skills, spatial perspective-taking (the ability to imagine how the world looks from another viewpoint) improves notably by age 4-5. At earlier ages, children are notoriously egocentric in the spatial sense: they tend to assume others see what they see. By 4, however, children show the first signs of overcoming this egocentrism. Researchers distinguish Level 1 perspective-taking (understanding what another person can or cannot see) and Level 2 perspective-taking (understanding how another person sees something, i.e. the appearance from their angle) 6 . Level 1 develops in infancy and toddlerhood (see the 12-24 months section). Level 2 perspective-taking first appears around 4-5 years of age 6 , but remains nascent. They can understand that a person sitting opposite them sees a picture "upside down" relative to their own view, or that a toy hidden behind a screen is visible to them but not to someone on the other side; conversely, when a 4- to 5-year old is shown a tabletop display and asked to choose a photograph that depicts what a doll would see from a different position, their performance is typically at chance level, frequently defaulting to their own viewpoint 6 . The ability to mentally rotate scenes (especially those with mutiple objects) continues to develop across the ensuing years, suggesting that 4- to 5-year-olds are still laying the groundwork for mental rotation (by learning to recognize basic spatial relationships and expanding their knowledge of objects/places). At this stage, children become better at forming mental representations of and navigating their environment, allowing more flexible travel beyond simple habit or trial-and-error; their navigation is, however, still not nearly as efficient or flexible as that of older children and adults. One major development is the child’s increasing use of landmarks to orient and navigate; younger children (toddlers) navigate mostly egocentrically (e.g they might remember a route as a series of body turns (go left, then right) or actions ("pass the sofa then the door")), while four- and five-year-olds begin to encode the environment in relation to external cues (allocentrically; e.g "the playground is next to the big red house"). After disorientation, both 4- and 5-year-olds can reliably reorient by extended surface geometry (e.g if the room is rectangular/irregular) 7 , but five-year-olds are more likely to recruit landmarks in the kinds of "large-room" or ecologically valid settings where four-year-olds often fail unless scaffolded by language 8 , 9 (although 3- and 4-year-olds have been shown to reliably use landmarks in straightforward scenarios where they remain oriented towards the goal 10 ). In everyday terms, a 5-year-old might start saying, "We turn at the big oak tree to go home" (using that landmark in conjunction with a sense of left/right) whereas a 3-year-old might only retrace the route without explicitly referencing the tree. The progression is from landmark-as-beacon (toddler will go straight to an object in view) to using landmark configurations and spatial layouts (older child can keep track of where things are even when not in view, by remembering how landmarks are arranged around them). Another emerging navigational skill at this age is path integration (the ability to update one’s position by tracking self-movement (the distances and turns traveled) even without obvious external cues); in one study, blindfolded 5-year-olds who were led along a path with a couple of turns could successfully orient back to the start point on their own on the majority of trials, though often not as precisely as adults 11 . Moreover, some children at this age can go beyond simple homing and begin to form a rudimentary cognitive map of the space using path integration; in the same study, a substantial subset of 5-year-olds could even use their path integration-derived knowledge to take novel shortcuts between locations (mapping rather than just retracing routes) 11 . Five-year-olds also begin to grasp symbolic spatial representations like maps and models. The famous "scale model" experiments by DeLoache showed that 2½-year-olds struggle to relate a model room to a larger room, but by 3 years they start to understand it when helped, and by 4-5 years most children can use a small model or a simple map to find an object in a real space. By age 5, many children find it exciting to follow a basic treasure map or use a picture diagram to locate something, demonstrating that they can translate between abstract spatial representations and real-world locations 12 . Overall, the 4-5 age range is a period of rapid improvement in navigational cognition. Children move from an almost purely egocentric and trial-and-error approach toward using external references and internal cues in concert. They do, however, still rely on salient structures (like room shape or a prominent landmark) to reorient when disoriented, highlighting a continuing bias for geometric framework at this age (which can be framed as prefrontal/premotor networks not yet discovering better strategies).

title: Causal learning and simulation
text: Preschoolers are often called "little scientists," and indeed between four and five years of age, children’s causal reasoning becomes more sophisticated and rule-governed. A 4-year-old can understand simple cause-and-effect relationships and frequently asks explanatory "Why?" questions; by age 5, these abilities expand into a more systematic intuitive grasp of how the physical and social world operates (albeit with some naïve misconceptions that will be corrected in later childhood). By five, children parse causal structure more reliably than at four: they more consistently distinguish causation from correlation, notice when evidence is confounded, and actively intervene to resolve it during play 1 . They can integrate probabilistic evidence with the results of their own actions to estimate causal strength, rather than relying on raw co-occurrence 2 . They choose targeted "what if I change this?" actions (the "conditional intervention" principle; manipulating objects to isolate variables) to test a system and tell whether events form a chain, share a single cause, or require two causes together, an ability that’s noticeably less consistent at four 3 ; in general, children this age now have a measurable degree of metacognitive awareness of confounded evidence 4 , 5 and can disambiguate the causal structure of simple systems, reflecting the emergence of scientific reasoning (in a largely implicit and context-specific manner). Classic theory held that counterfactual reasoning didn’t emerge until age 6 or later. But newer findings suggest the beginnings appear during the 4- to 5-year window under the right conditions. In one study using an over-determined outcome (two blocks made a box light up), children were asked to mentally remove one block and predict the effect: four-year-olds answered correctly significantly more often than not, and five-year-olds were nearly perfect, while three-year-olds struggled to do better than guessing 6 . This shows that by 4 or 5, kids can simulate a simple "what if" scenario in their minds, holding one factor constant and mentally undoing another to see the hypothetical result. That said, their counterfactual thinking is still fragile and very task-dependent. They often appear to skip the actual "counterfactual simulation" step 7 , 8 or to maintain/alter variables inaccurately (often systematically 8 ); if the narrative is even slightly more complicated than the most basic presentations or the question phrased subtly, younger children often err by either overwriting reality with fantasy or failing to keep track of what changed versus what stayed the same 9 , 7 . For example, one study used multi-step food chains to probe 5- and 7-year-olds’ capacity for counterfactual simulation, finding that 5-year-olds typically perform at chance while 7-year-olds are accurate 10 . Another study used a basic doubly-determined physical outcome to probe counterfactual reasoning, finding that 4- and 5-year-olds performed at chance levels 11 . Overall, children this age can imagine a basic "what if" outcome, but, even in basic scenarios, they do not always choose the most relevant or correct one or may not even initiate a simulation in the first place. Nonetheless, the capacity to entertain alternative causal worlds (even nascently) is a huge step; it underpins their understanding of why something happened (by thinking of what would happen otherwise) and even moral/emotional concepts like guilt or relief ("If I hadn’t broken the vase, Mom wouldn’t be upset."). Along with basic scientific reasoning and counterfactual simulation, four- to five-year-olds link hidden internal parts to causal powers, prefer common-mechanism matches over superficial similarity for generalization, and allow causal properties to "transfer" with the mechanism (e.g., moving an inner component) 12 . Similarly, 4- to 5-year-olds see advancements in producing and understanding explanations of causal structures; they not only prefer satisfying explanations but also remember them better than weak ones, showing a clearer memory advantage for "good" explanations across naturalistic tasks (e.g they find "The paddle moves the boat because it pushes water backwards" more satisfying than "It moves because it moves") 13 . When prompted to explain, older preschoolers increasingly privilege causally rich, inductive features over surface similarity and even boost memory for hidden (internal) properties (a tendency that strengthens as children are prompted to explain their actions/beliefs) 14 . They also become more willing to revise earlier explanations in light of discrepant evidence, a flexibility that strengthens from 4 to 5 years and helps them integrate cross-domain information 15 . In step with these cognitive gains, their causal language sharpens: 4-5-year-olds succeed more often at matching "because/so" to event structure and, in constrained production tasks, show markedly fewer cause-effect inversions than younger preschoolers, signaling more adult-like deployment of "because" and "so" in explanations 16 . Around this age, there is also evidence that children weigh others’ explanations based on their verifiability (whether the child can verify the explanation) 17 , 18 , further signaling epistemic vigilance. In summary, between ages four and five, children’s understanding of causality and physical logic becomes more principled. A 5-year-old is less fooled by mere coincidence and more interested in underlying reasons than a 4-year-old. They experiment actively and learn from interventions, embodying the scientific method in their play. Their intuitive theories about how things work (from machines to natural phenomena) are still simplistic, yet increasingly they incorporate concepts of unseen causes (germs make you sick, wires carry power, etc.).
