title: Executive function
text: Executive functions undergo rapid improvement during the preschool years. Many executive abilities that are fragile or inconsistent in 3-year-olds become reliably measurable by age 4, and they strengthen further by age 5. This means that between 4 and 5, children become noticeably better at focusing attention, following multi-step rules, controlling impulses, and switching flexibly between different tasks or mental sets. Five-year-olds can play games that involve withholding an action (like "Red Light, Green Light" or "Freeze dance") and typically follow rules like "wait your turn" in group settings with only occasional reminders. Experimental tasks such as the Day-Night Stroop (where children must say "night" when shown a sun card, and "day" for a moon card) illustrate the improvement: 4-year-olds often struggle to maintain accuracy throughout the task, whereas 5-year-olds show markedly better interference control and can sustain the rule for more trials 1 , reflecting maturation of frontal-striatal circuits supporting response inhibition. Working memory also expands between 4 and 5. A 3-year-old can typically keep  2 items in mind (e.g. simple instructions like "touch your nose and clap your hands"), and a 4-year-old about 3 items. By age 5, children can often manage 4-step instructions or remember a sequence of 4 digits or words, especially if they practice some informal strategies like self-repetition 2 . In practical terms, a five-year-old can more reliably follow complex directions such as, "Go to your room, get your shoes, then come to the kitchen and put them on," while a 4-year-old might get sidetracked or forget one of the steps. Five-year-olds increasingly recruit verbal self-instructions to keep rules active ("say the rule to do the rule"), which is a known strategy to boost working memory and cognitive control (and helps explain why linguistic advances at this age amplify executive performance) 3 . Cognitive flexibility also undergoes a step change; here, we continue referring to the classic Dimensional Change Card Sort (DCCS) task. Three-year-olds will perseverate on the first rule given (e.g., sorting cards by color) and struggle to switch to a new rule (sorting by shape) even when they know the rule changed; they’ll verbally acknowledge the new rule but still sort cards wrongly according to the old rule 4 . By 4 years old, children can successfully switch to the new sorting rule after a few reminder trials 4 (considered a fundamental cognitive milestone). By age 5, cognitive flexibility is more robust: five-year-olds not only switch rules, but can sometimes handle a more complex sequence of switches or hierarchical rules (for instance, sorting by shape only if a border on the card is a certain color) 5 , 4 . They still cannot match the flexibility of older children (for example, 5-year-olds will struggle with switching rules on every trial, a level of flexibility seen around 7-8 years 5 ), but they are clearly more adaptable than preschoolers just a year younger. In everyday life, this translates to coping better with changing plans or contexts: a 5-year-old is more likely than a 4-year-old to handle a sudden schedule change with only minor upset or to understand that "at school we do it this way, even if at home we do it that way". This age is sometimes termed an "executive function sweet spot" in that children make noticeable gains that parents and teachers can see: they become better at cleaning up with a routine, following classroom rules, and verbalizing strategies (like saying "I have to wait, so I’m counting to 10") 6 . Not coincidentally, many interventions to promote school readiness target executive skills at this age, using games and play to strengthen self-control and flexibility 7 . Overall, five-year-olds can hold more information in mind, resist more impulses, and shift rules more readily than they could a year prior, forming the cognitive foundation for the structured learning environment of kindergarten.

title: Training data and optimization
text: Language/semantic The linguistic system continues to optimize the same four coupled objectives from 3-4 years but with escalating demands and widening scope. Lexical learning accelerates through increasingly efficient fast-mapping and extends into abstract domains: children now track cross-situational co-occurrences not just for concrete nouns and action verbs but for mental-state terms ("decide," "remember," "confused"), spatial relations ("between," "above"), and emotion words, so prediction errors in word-concept mappings now span both observable referents and internal/relational states that require deeper theory-of-mind and spatial inference to ground. Syntactic bootstrapping sharpens as grammatical frames become more reliable cues: children exploit the full argument structure of complex sentences (including subordinate clauses and conjunctions like "because" and "when") to narrow verb meanings and infer abstract event relations, and syntactic prediction errors (mismatches between the child’s current grammar and heard input) drive the consolidation of Brown-stage V morphemes (articles, auxiliaries, third-person -s) and the emergence of passive constructions and comparative/superlative forms, though overregularization (e.g saying "runned" or "sheeps") persists at a lower rate as the learner balances rule generalization against stored exceptions. Caregiver recasts remain a high-precision teaching signal, supplying immediate contrastive feedback that reduces surprisal for morphosyntactic and pragmatic errors, while richer child-directed narrative input (story-telling, event recounting with temporal/causal connectives) trains hierarchical event schemas and coherence constraints that feed back into production. Comprehension increasingly relies on anticipatory processing: children generate strong predictions over upcoming words and morphemes, and violations of those predictions (surprisal) drive updates to both lexical probabilities and syntactic templates, tightening the production-comprehension loop as better predictors become better producers. Production itself continues to be tuned by auditory-somatosensory error under the DIVA framework, but the speech motor targets are now longer, morphologically complex utterances that demand finer articulatory sequencing and prosodic planning. Pragmatics adds a new optimization layer: children begin explicitly modeling the listener’s knowledge state and pick referring expressions and clause packaging that raise expected listener recovery (informativeness under effort/ambiguity costs), so communicative failures (ambiguous references, listener confusion, requests for clarification) generate pragmatic prediction errors that update both the child’s partner model and their utterance planning/selection policy, yielding more informative, repaired, and socially appropriate speech by age five. Finally, semantic memory is "semanticizing": repeated word-world pairings and narrative discourse are replayed offline, shifting from hippocampal episode traces to mPFC/temporal cortex category structure, which lowers prediction error for taxonomic and thematic generalizations and supports more coherent, causally linked narratives in speech Social Social learning from 4-5 keeps the three objectives (predicting minds, internalizing norms, and becoming a cooperative, informative partner) but the dominant error signals now come from failures over longer social horizons: mistaken belief-tracking across multi‐turn interactions, norm violations in group play, unreliable testimony, and audience-dependent payoffs. Children track not just what others know but what they think others know (nascent second-order ToM), infer hidden feelings that contradict expressions (understanding appearance-reality dissociations in emotion), and distinguish intentional deception from honest mistakes, so social prediction errors now include subtler mismatches (e.g a peer’s unexpected emotional response, a failed persuasion attempt, or misjudging whether someone is pretending versus believing) and these errors, amplified by richer mental-state discourse and explicit emotion coaching, refine the child’s generative model of minds to include epistemic states (knowledge, ignorance, certainty), affective states (felt vs. displayed emotion), and intentional stance (trying to fool vs. being mistaken). This expanded model drives the observed leap in cognitive empathy: five-year-olds reliably pass standard false-belief tasks and increasingly succeed on appearance-reality emotion tasks, and longitudinal data confirm that gains in ToM and emotion understanding across this window predict more positive peer interactions as children become better at inferring why a peer is upset or how to adjust their behavior to match a partner’s goals. Norm acquisition shifts from rigid overimitation to context-sensitive rule deployment: children now parse when norms are conventional (arbitrary but binding within a group) versus instrumental (causally necessary), so they overimitate less in instrumental contexts while maintaining or increasing normative conformity in social rituals, and they begin to grasp that rules can vary by setting (the "school rule" vs. "home rule" distinction), with errors arising when context boundaries are misjudged; explicit rule instruction, observed norm violations with varied consequences (punishment, praise, indifference), and participation in rule-negotiated pretend play supply dense labels that train flexible normative policies, producing the five-year-old’s ability to enforce rules on peers, adjust behavior across contexts, and articulate simple justifications ("because that’s the rule" or "it’s not fair"). Prosocial choice becomes more reputation-sensitive and principle-guided: five-year-olds preferentially share with helpful over unhelpful peers, show nascent indirect reciprocity (rewarding those who helped others), and increasingly invoke fairness principles ("everyone should get the same") even when costly, indicating that the value function now includes reputational terms (how my actions affect others’ models of me) and simple deontic rules; errors include social disapproval for stinginess, peer rejection after selfish acts, and occasional explicit fairness violations by adults or peers that generate contrastive "ought" signals, together training a prosocial policy that still leans heavily on external reinforcement but is beginning to internalize equity and reciprocity norms as stable goal weights rather than purely situational responses. Gross/fine motor From 4-5 years, the motor objective remains accurate, biomechanically efficient terminal states under an energy/vigor budget, but now the bottleneck shifts toward integrating multiple degrees of freedom in real time (e.g role-differentiated bimanual control) and sequencing longer action chains with predictive rather than reactive control. The documented advances-sustained one-foot balance, heel-to-toe walking, smoother skipping, scissors control along curved paths, tripod pencil grip, and 20+ piece puzzles-reflect a system that has moved from correcting errors after they happen to anticipating them before contact. Cerebellar climbing-fiber teaching continues to calibrate forward/inverse models but now operates over richer, multiarticular synergies: complex-spike bursts encode vectorized error for trunk-limb coordination during dynamic balance (hopping, jumping rope), wrist-finger coupling during scissor cuts, and grip-aperture timing for small-piece manipulation. Basal ganglia loops convert repeated practice into chunked, time-locked policies: distributional dopamine keeps teaching multiple expectiles of return, so action timing and effort are tuned for both accuracy and time-cost (children will "spend" vigor when the task is time-critical, but downshift when precision dominates), and dorsal striatal consolidation reduces online search, yielding smoother velocity profiles and fewer pauses between subskills (grasp-stabilize-cut, draw-rotate-trace). Cortico-parietal controllers contribute by improving state estimation and feedforward reach planning (earlier peak velocity, later corrections), while rising corticospinal bandwidth and finger individuation let the child settle into a tripod grasp, trace within boundaries, follow curved paths, cut along a line while the other hand stabilizes the page, button/zip with bimanual role asymmetry, and string small beads, all signatures that distal controllers now run with higher resolution and better predictive calibration. Training data are dense and naturally labeled: rhythmic games (skipping, clapping), ballistics with binary outcomes (catch/miss), tool use with tight haptic error (scissors "chatter," pencil drag), and vestibular-visual dephasing during spinning/rough-and-tumble play; these generate cerebellar kinematic mismatch signals, scalar RPEs for success/vigor tradeoffs, and phasic NE "model-failure" bursts that transiently raise learning rates when predictions break. Precision control from ACh sharpens sensory prediction errors during fine work, while tonic 5-HT stretches the horizon for slow, effortful sequences (lace, zip) so the child finishes longer chains before abandoning. Imitative learning supplies high-SNR supervised data: adult demonstrations of tool grip, letter formation, and multi-step sequences (tying, folding) function as vector-valued targets that children approximate through observational motor learning, with visual prediction errors (mismatch between observed and self-produced kinematics) driving rapid policy updates that generalize across similar manual tasks. Object-level (physics, kinematics, affordances) Object-level learning from 4-5 years pursues a compound objective: minimize surprise in physical interactions while (increasingly) building transferable, compositional models of mass, support, and motion that can guide both implicit prediction and explicit reasoning. The primary training stream comes from dense, self-generated manipulation and construction errors: every toppled tower, mis-weighted throw, failed catch, and misjudged jump supplies tightly time-locked physical prediction errors that update both forward models and causal beliefs. In construction tasks, stability failures-blocks sliding, bridges sagging, towers collapsing-generate salient mismatches between expected and observed outcomes; these errors initially train heuristic rules ("heavier on bottom," "support near center") but, especially under guided play or scaffolded exploration around age five, children begin extracting deeper principles like center-of-mass constraints and mass distribution, evidenced by their newfound ability to stabilize asymmetric structures and transfer weight reasoning to novel objects. You see this in classic torque and gravity problems: on balance beams many five-year-olds still operate a weight-only heuristic (Rule I), ignoring distance unless it is extreme, which yields systematic errors but also dense, label-rich feedback for learning torque (τ = wxd) and for gating when to invoke a richer model 1 . Cerebellar forward models remain a core substrate for implicit physical prediction: climbing-fiber teaching signals driven by kinematic mismatches (unexpected object motion, failed interceptions, trajectory deviations under occlusion) continuously calibrate internal simulators. Cortical hierarchies run a parallel, slower optimization over explicit physical reasoning: prediction errors in verbal and pictorial physics tasks (e.g., "which way will it fall?") update symbolic causal models, but these updates are sparse and high-variance because explicit tasks lack the dense, motor-coupled feedback of manipulation, explaining why five-year-olds reliably catch balls (cerebellar implicit prediction works) yet fail horizontal-projectile reasoning when spatial context misleads (cortical explicit reasoning remains fragile); cerebellar learning is supervised by vector-valued, millisecond-locked reafference during action, while cortical reasoning learns from delayed, often ambiguous verbal/visual feedback during passive observation or questioning, so the cerebellum compiles thousands of labeled catching trials into tight priors on parabolic motion, whereas cortex sees dozens of varied, under-constrained "what if" queries and builds noisier, more context-dependent heuristics. Force and weight learning similarly benefits from action-contingent error: systematic mismatches between applied force and achieved outcome (object doesn’t move, moves too far, feels unexpectedly light/heavy) train both feedforward force scaling (cerebellar inverse models) and object property inference (cortical weight/material categories), yielding five-year-olds’ reliable weight-based planning in simple tasks while they still default to single-force reasoning in multi-cause scenarios because integrating simultaneous forces requires cortical models to compose multiple additive predictions, a computational demand that stresses working memory and exceeds the current representational bandwidth of preschool PFC. Imitation and pedagogy inject high-confidence labels: adult demonstrations of tool use, throwing techniques, and balance strategies supply action trajectories with known-good outcomes, functioning as supervised targets that children approximate through observational motor learning, while explicit physical explanations ("It falls because it’s heavier on one side") provide sparse but high-value semantic constraints that bias cortical hypothesis search toward mechanistic over perceptual features. Episodic/autobiographical/event modeling The episodic (event modeling) system keeps optimizing the same three objectives (cleaner segmentation, stronger what-where-when bindings, and preserved temporal order) but now pushes toward "narrativized precision": boundaries are detected more reliably in the stream of experience, bindings carry more contextual detail, and sequences are organized into retellable stories that can be used for planning. Event boundary prediction errors are still the core training signal, but the child now experiences richer, more structured events (multi-step classroom routines, rule-governed games, extended pretend narratives) that supply denser temporal structure and causal scaffolding while being annotated by a richer internal script library, so violations of internal expectations are are more diagnostic and produce bigger updates. Hippocampal maturation (rising volume, strengthening functional connectivity with key cortical regions, and increasingly reliable place-code stability 2 , 3 ) translates these tagged episodes into durable, context-rich traces: CA3 auto-associative dynamics bind arbitrary conjunctions (which toy, which room, which friend) into a coherent index, while CA1 comparators detect mismatches between predicted and actual context during retrieval attempts, generating errors that tune pattern-completion thresholds and reduce false alarms. Caregiver elaborative reminiscing remains a high-bandwidth supervision channel that increasingly scaffolds not just "what happened" but also temporal connectives ("first… then… because…"), emotional/evaluative commentary ("you felt proud"), and source attributions ("remember, Grandma showed you that"), effectively providing labeled supervision for narrative coherence, causal structure, and source monitoring 4 . It is worth noting that episodic retrieval and future thinking are domain-general capabilities, implying that they are not only optimized while they are directly/obviously at hand (e.g when mother asks "do you remember what happened this morning?"), but also when the child pursues objectives that are not recollection-/simulation-focused (e.g motor or social objectives). Executive Building directly on the 3-4 foundation, everyday routines between 4-5 years scale up in length and branching structure, transforming the executive objective from "hold a short script" to "maintain and flexibly update simple plans." Morning sequences now involve 4-5 conditionally ordered steps ("if your shirt is dirty, get a new one from the drawer, then brush teeth"), classroom transitions require inhibiting one activity set while loading another ("put away blocks, line up quietly, remember your folder"), and rule-governed games explicitly demand online rule switching ("now sort by shape, not color"); the DCCS is the laboratory distillation of this everyday pressure. These longer, branch-heavy scripts generate richer error structure: children now fail not just by skipping a step or grabbing impulsively, but by perseverating on an outdated rule despite verbal acknowledgment of the switch. Each perseveration error, missed transition, or mid-routine derailment acts as a negative prediction error that trains cortico-basal-ganglia loops to better arbitrate between maintaining the current goal and flushing it when context changes, while adult scaffolding shifts from step-by-step prompts at 3-4 ("now get your shoes") to higher-level reminders that cue retrieval of the whole cached routine ("remember the morning steps?"), effectively training children to internally reinstantiate multi-step policies rather than rely on external working-memory prosthetics. Structured preschool and kindergarten environments deliver dense, graded practice: circle-time routines, wait-your-turn games, multi-step art projects, and explicit "freeze/go" activities function as naturalistic cognitive training, with incremental difficulty that measurably strengthens inhibition, shifting, and working-memory span across this window, while social pretend play continues to add set-shifting pressure as children negotiate and update roles mid-narrative ("now you’re the patient, I’m the doctor… wait, let’s switch"). Under the hood, basal-ganglia-PFC gating policies learn when to open the "update gate" versus hold the current contents, so fewer irrelevant items intrude and relevant cues trigger timely refreshes. Which gate to deploy (and how forcefully) is tuned by a cost-benefit controller in dorsal ACC that learns the expected value of exerting control in each context, so practice and token economies raise the inferred payoff for sustained attention and timely switching 5 . Thalamocortical relays then make the policy stick over seconds to tens of seconds: mediodorsal thalamus amplifies and stabilizes rule-specific PFC dynamics, while pulvinar routes behaviorally relevant information between visual areas according to the current task set, together reducing switch costs and improving selective attention in naturalistic settings typical of pre-K 6 . Neuromodulators act as adaptive gain controllers over these loops: acetylcholine increases the precision (gain) on sensory prediction-error units when noise is expected, sharpening cue use during rule maintenance, whereas noradrenaline broadcasts an unsigned "model-failure" pulse when the environment turns volatile, transiently resetting state and hiking learning rates so children abandon the old rule and adopt the new one more quickly; pupil-linked arousal readouts track and causally influence these learning-rate adjustments 7 . Spatial The same four spatial objectives (making stable structures (in the general sense), transforming shapes (and scenes) mentally, navigating to goals, and mapping symbols to real space (especially spatial relationships)) upgrade and tighten their teaching signals. In construction, "stability under load" expands into symmetry, span, and bracing: children’s assemblies become more regular, multi-unit, and enclosed, and the salient errors are buckling, shear, and asymmetric sag, all dense physical mismatches that refine part-whole geometry and correlate prospectively with math and later spatial scores, indicating that this error stream keeps training (or at least reflects) generalizable spatial programs 8 , 9 . Mental rotation and perspective-taking are trained by multiple prediction-error streams converging on parietal circuits. Seeing objects from multiple angles generates cross-view mismatches, with each view-transition supplying a labeled sample tightening the allocentric-structure-to-appearance mapping; a similar training loop takes place at the level of scenes. Puzzle play delivers dense binary trials: every rotated piece yields a fit/no-fit outcome with motor-efference coupling, and hundreds of attempts compile a generalized mental-rotation routine. Fine motor objectives add parallel training pressure: tool use and manipulation requiring comfortable terminal grips (scissors, spoons, pencils) generate end-state prediction errors when the child grasps without pre-rotating, forcing awkward wrist angles or mid-action adjustments; each proprioceptive mismatch trains the system to mentally preview the final pose and select the initial grip angle accordingly, with these action-coupled rotation demands strengthening the same parietal transformation circuits that puzzles engage. Perspective-taking errors (defaulting to egocentric view when needing to determine what another person sees) further incentivize scene rotation, with adult corrections supplying explicit labels that prune search space. Rotation and perspective-taking likely improve in parallel because they share a parietal viewpoint-transformation substrate operating domain-generally across "how does this look rotated?" and "how does this look from there?" For navigation, the objective moves towards maintaining stable, query-able cognitive maps that bind extended surfaces (room shape, walls) with distinctive features (colored landmarks, furniture) and support novel shortcuts. Training data come from everyday search errors: wrong-turn penalties, detours, and disorientation episodes that generate place-prediction mismatches. Additionally, the same multi-view prediction errors that train mental rotation-seeing rooms, landmarks, and layouts from different approach angles during locomotion-drive hippocampal place cells and retrosplenial cortex to build viewpoint-invariant place representations, with each novel viewpoint of a familiar location generating a mismatch between predicted and actual visual features that strengthens the binding between allocentric spatial structure and appearance, making landmarks recognizable from multiple directions and rooms navigable from arbitrary entry points. At 3-4, children could reorient by geometry but failed to use landmarks unless verbally cued; by 4-5, they spontaneously weight landmarks when they are stable and distinctive, and language continues to scaffold ("turn at the big oak tree"), indicating that linguistic labels reduce the dimensionality of the landmark space and make features more retrievable. Errors in path integration (arriving at the wrong heading, distance miscalibration) are corrected by loop closure: when the child returns to a known location and the predicted position drifts from the actual sensory match (boundary cells fire, visual scene recognition succeeds), hippocampal theta sequences replay and credit-assign back along the trajectory, tightening the gain on grid-cell updates and vestibular integration. Spatial relational concepts are learned through coupled physical and linguistic error streams. During manipulation and navigation, children generate dense action-outcome errors (e.g toppled stacks, failed "between" placements, wrong-side searches) that update parietal representations of geometric configurations like vertical alignment, containment, and relative position. Language then compresses these continuous spatial features into discrete, transferable categories: when caregivers say "put it between the boxes" and the child’s action mismatches the instruction, the resulting comprehension error plus explicit corrections ("between means in the middle of both") sharpen category boundaries by clustering similar arrangements under linguistic tokens. These spatial skills all reinforce one another. As children learn spatial words, they can encode and communicate spatial relationships more effectively, which supports tasks like puzzle-solving or map reading. Improvements in mental rotation and perspective-taking allow them to better align maps with reality and to navigate by imagining different viewpoints. Better navigation experiences (e.g. successfully finding a shortcut or reorienting by a landmark) provide feedback that sharpens their spatial concepts and confidence. Overall, most activities in the physical world generate data that the developing brain uses to calibrate distances, learn spatial frameworks, and link verbal concepts to spatial experiences. Causal Causal learning from 4-5 years optimizes a dual objective: build compositional models of hidden mechanisms that both predict observations and guide effective interventions. The core training stream is dense, action-contingent surprise from exploratory play and everyday problem-solving: when a child manipulates toys, machines, or natural systems, each intervention yields a tightly time-locked outcome (block topples, drawer opens, toy activates) that either confirms or violates their current causal hypothesis, generating signed prediction errors that update both "what causes what" beliefs and "how to make X happen" policies. Children increasingly deploy conditional interventions (isolating variables by holding others constant or testing specific combinations), and the resulting pattern of successes/failures across varied manipulations supplies the high-information data needed to distinguish confounded from unambiguous causal structure, infer whether events form chains or share a common cause, and estimate causal strength probabilistically rather than from raw co-occurrence. Cortical hierarchies run predictive coding over these causal sequences: each violated expectation (object moves without contact, expected outcome fails to occur, hidden mechanism produces surprising result) generates a mismatch signal that propagates up the hierarchy and, when precision is high (acetylcholine up-weights the error during focused exploration), drives representational updates toward models that privilege mechanism over surface similarity and allow causal properties to "transfer" with internal parts rather than appearance. Hippocampal-cortical loops bind event structure (agent-action-object-outcome) into retrievable episodes, with replay during naps and night sleep consolidating interventions that yielded clear causal information, while striatal RL learns which exploratory policies (vary one thing, repeat successful probes, abandon unresponsive objects) maximize information gain about hidden structure, with distributional dopamine signaling not just scalar reward but uncertainty reduction itself as an intrinsic return. The cerebellum supplies supervised, vector-valued teaching signals for temporal causality (exactly-timed E-M mismatches) that calibrate generative forward models of contact, delay, and continuous dynamics, tightening judgments about necessity vs. sufficiency. Language acts as a high-bandwidth teaching channel and compression layer: adult explanations supply sparse but high-value supervision that prunes hypothesis space ("It works because the gear turns the wheel"), causal discourse (especially "because"/"so" and mechanistic talk) sharpens children’s ability to verbalize and generalize their intuitive theories. Children also become more selective consumers of causal testimony, preferring verifiable explanations and revising beliefs when new evidence contradicts prior accounts, indicating that they’re not just memorizing claims but evaluating them against an internal causal-coherence criterion. Counterfactual reasoning emerges as a natural byproduct of this architecture: once forward models can simulate "what happens if I do X," running them with hypothetical rather than actual states (mentally removing a block, imagining an alternative action) yields counterfactual predictions, though these simulations remain fragile and single-threaded at five because prefrontal working memory hasn’t learned to load/maintain multiple contradictory premises or reliably backchain through multi-step causal chains.

title: Neural development
text: Building directly on the 3-4 year profile of "overprovisioned substrate + high energy + tightening control," the 4-5 window keeps the energy budget elevated 1 while decisively retooling the machinery for speed and selectivity: intracortical myelination and targeted pruning push the MRI-observed "thinning" 2 into a regime of more selective communication, shorter local integration windows, and lower energy per transmitted bit; association tracts such as arcuate and SLF continue their climb on key metrics 3 , effectively extending the cortex’s communication radius at roughly fixed power so long-range communication (incl. top-down selection) can run at higher sampling rates; large-scale graphs continue becoming more "segregated yet integrated," with clearer default-mode <-> dorsal-attention competition and a rapidly strengthening frontoparietal control ensemble 4 , 5 , yielding more reliable state arbitration; spectrally, peak alpha and sensorimotor rhythms speed up 6 and the aperiodic 1/f background flattens 7 , consistent with briefer synaptic time constants and tighter E/I gain; and sleep spindles and slow-oscillation coupling get more coordinated 8 , improving hippocampo-cortical write-back. Overall, a similar exploratory capacity rides on faster clocks, longer-reach white-matter highways, and crisper gating, so policies stabilize sooner without sacrificing the rich hypothesis search that the preschool hyper-metabolic plateau affords. title: Language
text: Between ages 5 and 7 children’s language explodes in both breadth and complexity. Receptive vocabulary on the order of ten thousand words is typical by age five and children learn thousands more words each year 1 , with expressive repertoires expanding to include not just concrete nouns and action verbs but metacognitive verbs (remember, conclude, decide) and metalinguistic verbs (explain, confirm) that describe thinking and communication itself 2 , 3 , alongside abstract descriptive terms (carefully, slowly, surprised) and relational words that go beyond the basic spatial prepositions of earlier years 3 . Vocabulary growth reflects not just breadth but richer semantic networks (e.g., learning multiple related senses of the same word) that support inference during reading 4 . Children this age also transition from predominantly concrete word learning to systematic acquisition of abstract terms (love, freedom, success), reflecting the cognitive demands of formal schooling. Syntactic complexity undergoes a measurable inflection: whereas five-year-olds produce mostly simple sentences punctuated by coordinate clauses joined with "and" or "but", six- and seven-year-olds show steep increases in subordination, with conditional clauses (if) appearing reliably by ages 6-7, relative pronouns (e.g the scientist "who discovered penicillin") and embedded subordinate clauses (e.g she believes "that the experiment will succeed") rising between 7-8, and the proportion of utterances containing subordinate clauses climbing roughly 0.2% per month across the elementary years 5 , 6 , 7 ; children increasingly deploy advanced conjunctions (because, so, while, although, unless) to link ideas causally and temporally within single utterances, yielding longer, hierarchically structured sentences that can express conditionality, contrast, and multi-clause logical relations 6 , 3 , 7 . Receptive sophistication keeps pace: children reliably follow multi-step unrelated commands, understand that words can have multiple meanings (e.g orange the fruit vs. the color) and that different words can mean the same thing (e.g minus and take away), and track stories told over multiple days without losing the thread 3 , all while their processing speed for familiar words accelerates and their ability to extract meaning from increasingly complex syntactic frames improves markedly. Narrative capabilities also transform dramatically. Five-year-olds produce primitive narratives with basic story grammar elements but limited temporal sequencing and causal coherence, relying heavily on "and" as their primary connector. By age 7, children consistently include 5+ story grammar elements (character, setting, initiating event, action, consequences, resolution) 8 with logical temporal ordering and appropriate causal markers, although the inclusion of multiple episodes with reliable causal chaining and rich "inner state" descriptions of agents appears to remain mostly out of reach.

title: Social
text: Between ages 5 and 7, social cognition undergoes a marked qualitative shift from understanding isolated mental states to basic reasoning about nested social representations and navigating increasingly complex peer ecologies. Theory of mind advances beyond first-order false belief (what another person thinks) toward second-order reasoning (what one person thinks another person thinks), with most children passing classic second-order false-belief tasks (e.g understanding that "John thinks Mary thinks the ice cream van is in the park") between 6 and 7 years 1 , 2 , a capacity that requires holding and manipulating nested propositional attitudes and predicts more sophisticated social problem-solving and peer acceptance (and continues to develop for many more years). Children also develop basic interpretive theory of mind: they come to understand that two people witnessing the same event can form different beliefs about it depending on their prior knowledge, attention, or interpretive frameworks 3 , 4 , 5 , moving beyond the simpler realization that people can hold false beliefs to grasping that beliefs are actively constructed rather than passively received (which relates to the emergence of metalinguistic awareness at this stage). This supports more nuanced social navigation, as six- and seven-year-olds increasingly recognize that disagreements can stem from differing interpretations rather than one party simply being wrong, and they begin to adjust their communication strategies accordingly (e.g explaining more when they detect that a listener lacks relevant background or holds a different construal). Emotion understanding deepens in parallel, with children gaining firmer mastery of display rules (the social norms governing when and how to express or mask feelings) and applying them more flexibly across contexts: whereas five-year-olds show emerging awareness that people can hide feelings, six- and seven-year-olds can reliably predict when someone would display a false emotion (e.g smiling when receiving a disappointing gift) and can articulate the social motivations behind such regulation 6 , 7 , 8 , indicating integration of emotion knowledge with normative and strategic reasoning. They also develop more sophisticated causal models of emotion, moving from simple situational attributions ("she’s sad because her toy broke") to incorporating beliefs, desires, and past history ("he’s angry because he thought his friend would save him a seat, and they’ve had arguments before") 9 , and they begin to understand self-conscious emotions like pride, shame, embarrassment, and guilt as distinct from basic emotions, recognizing that these require an evaluative self-representation and tracking others’ judgments. Peer relationships undergo structural and functional reorganization during this window. Friendships shift from activity-based and relatively transient ("we’re friends because we play together") toward more stable, psychologically grounded bonds; six- and seven-year-olds increasingly cite personality traits, shared interests, and reciprocal liking as friendship criteria 10 , 11 , and friendship stability (maintaining the same best friend over months) rises relative to preschool. Cooperative play becomes more rule-governed and competitive-cooperative, with games involving explicit turn-taking, scorekeeping, and negotiated rule modifications 12 , 13 , 14 , and children show heightened sensitivity to fairness violations and procedural justice within peer interactions 15 , 16 , both protesting unfair treatment (and unfair group norms 17 , 18 ) more vigorously and invoking equity norms to resolve disputes (although still unreliably). Moral and prosocial reasoning also advance. While five-year-olds show strong fairness preferences in simple allocation tasks, some six- and seven-year-olds integrate multiple moral dimensions: they consider not only equality but also merit (rewarding harder work), and need (giving more to those who lack), and they increasingly balance self-interest against group welfare when these conflict 19 , 20 , 15 , 21 , 22 (though this behavior is far from robust/solidified; it is strictly emerging at this stage, which most children either being fully self-interested or using "equal shares" heuristics). Prosocial behavior becomes more strategic and reputation-sensitive: helping and sharing increase in public relative to private contexts 23 , 24 , and children selectively assist peers who have helped others (indirect reciprocity) or who might reciprocate in the future 25 , 26 , indicating that prosocial acts are now partly governed by reputational and reciprocal incentives rather than purely empathic motivation. Group dynamics become more salient and hierarchically structured. By early elementary school, peer networks exhibit clear social hierarchies, with some children consistently preferred as playmates and leaders, and children are acutely aware of their own and others’ social standing, actively working to maintain or improve their position through strategic affiliation, selective disclosure, and sometimes exclusion or relational aggression 27 , 28 , 29 . Gender segregation typically intensifies across this period, with children increasingly preferring same-gender playmates and engaging in gender-typed activities, driven by a combination of identity development, peer enforcement of gender norms, and differential socialization pressures. Friendship networks also begin to cluster into stable cliques or groups with shared norms and coordinated activities, and being accepted into a desirable peer group becomes a central social goal 30 . Collectively, these shifts reflect a social-cognitive system that is no longer merely tracking individual minds but is beginning to actively model the social field (its reputational dynamics, normative structures, relational networks, and emergent hierarchies), preparing children to navigate the increasingly complex and competitive social ecologies of middle childhood.

title: Physics and objects
text: Between five and seven, physics and object understanding shifts from single-rule heuristics to integrating mass, support, and motion, producing a paradox: rich implicit know-how alongside systematic explicit errors. Early on, many still show pre-operational biases (appearance-based judgments, animistic force reasoning); by six to seven, concrete-operational logic emerges: conservation of number and mass, multi-factor causal reasoning, and impersonal physical rules (unsupported objects fall, solids don’t interpenetrate). This is not a threshold but a long tuning phase: everyday manipulation, construction, and sport supply dense error signals that refine context-bound heuristics into nascent, rule-governed reasoning. By age six, children reason above chance when multiple forces act along a single dimension, marking the first reliable step beyond the single-force regime documented at four to five years, yet most elementary-school children still consider either the direction or the magnitude of both force vectors but not both simultaneously, with their preferred strategy varying by problem context 1 . When two force vectors are not parallel, five- and six-year-olds focus on a single dominant cause 2 , and predictions remain significantly less accurate when forces are placed on two dimensions, with perpendicular "Prevent" relations (where one force opposes or deflects another at ninety degrees) proving especially difficult compared to simpler "Cause" or "Enable" configurations 3 , 4 . The developmental progression moves from understanding a single force toward grasping enabling forces and ultimately preventative relations 2 , but throughout the five-to-seven window, children’s physics engine remains functionally single-threaded for non-aligned forces: they serially process the most salient influence rather than computing a true vector sum, only beginning to compose forces into net effects when those forces are collinear, equally weighted, and presented in low-complexity contexts. Five- to seven-year-olds increasingly bind appearance and dynamics to hidden material properties. They read weight from others’ actions (e.g., lift kinematics) 5 , though judgments still lag adults’ accuracy, and their own anticipatory grip/load control shows shorter-latency, more adult-like scaling to expected weight and surface resistance 6 , supporting gentler handling of "fragile" vs. "sturdy" objects in practice. For flexibility/softness, children begin to exploit deformation and optical cues, yet material perception remains single-cue biased: optimal visuo-haptic combination for texture/softness and shape-from-touch typically does not mature until  8-10, so 5-7-year-olds’ judgments can shift with the sensing modality 7 , 8 . Relatedly, school-age material categorization from images relies more on local/textural features (instead of global features) and only gradually becomes adult-like over later childhood 9 , reflecting immature material-to-object-class mappings. Based on naturalistic observations, however, by age seven children do possess an extensive, largely implicit database of object-property associations accumulated through years of manipulation and observation (e.g knowing that ceramic mugs shatter when dropped, blankets are soft and flexible, rubber balls bounce, paper tears easily, and metal is hard) though this knowledge remains action-grounded and context-dependent rather than organized into explicit material-science categories; for example, 5-7-year-olds have been documented as having the core of their "weight" concept being felt/experienced weight and as having material kinds defined in terms of properties of large scale objects (as opposed to objects’ constituent parts) 10 . Essentially, their everyday "material intuition" guides force selection, grip configuration, and risk assessment during handling, effectively functioning as a look-up table indexed by object identity rather than a compositional model that predicts novel material behaviors from first principles. Conservation understanding (recognizing that quantity remains invariant despite perceptual transformation) follows a hierarchical acquisition sequence, with number conservation typically mastered around age six 11 , 12 , followed by mass and length around age seven, weight around age nine, and volume not until roughly age ten 13 . Mechanistically, success at this age reflects two linked advances: children can mentally reverse the change (reversibility/compensation) and they can inhibit the misleading "longer = more" heuristic; neuroimaging of number-conservation shows parietal circuits for reversibility (intraparietal sulcus) coupled with right inferior frontal engagement for inhibitory control 14 , 15 , 16 . This new control generalizes: brief embodied participation in the transformation (pouring/spreading it themselves) boosts 6-7-year-olds’ conservation 17 , suggesting that dense action-coupled error continues to be the primary teaching signal even as explicit logical reasoning begins to emerge. Kinematic prediction continues its dual-track development: implicit, cerebellum-mediated anticipatory control improves steadily (supporting cleaner catches, better batting timing, and smoother interceptive actions across childhood), yet explicit trajectory reasoning remains error-prone and context-dependent. In occluded-target pursuit, 5-7-year-olds already generate anticipatory saccades and sustain predictive smooth eye movements qualitatively like adults (albeit lower gain, higher error) 18 . Sensitivity to inertia emerges around 5-6 years in predictive-judgment tasks 19 , and while explicit projectile-motion predictions remain vulnerable to salient context 20 , children’s estimates become more constraint-consistent than a year earlier, aligning their explicit judgments with the improving implicit controllers described for the 4- to 5-year window. The same calibration shows up in perception-action coupling: judgments of "can I fit/reach through this opening?" become much more adult-like by  7, with fewer unsafe attempts and tighter action scaling to aperture size 21 , evidence that affordance perception is being recast in body- and task-scaled coordinates rather than visual salience alone. Tool use and understanding in the 5-7 window shifts from reactive grip selection toward prospective, efficiency-driven planning, though tool innovation remains severely limited. By  7 many children now plan grasps for end-state comfort reliably when tasks impose competing demands (e.g., orientation + precision/force), a capacity that is weak or inconsistent at 5 and that first emerges under multi-constraint loads around 7 22 , 23 . Four- to five-year-olds exhibit high intra-individual variability (Siegler’s "overlapping waves"), simultaneously deploying infantile, transitional, and adult-like strategies within single sessions, whereas seven-year-olds consolidate toward the efficient solution and rarely revert 23 , suggesting that five-to-seven marks the period when sensitivity to implementation costs drives competitive displacement of immature strategies. Yet important limits remain at 7: spontaneous tool innovation (e.g., bending a pipe-cleaner into a hook, or coordinating two tools concurrently) is still rare despite competent tool use and learning from demonstration, underscoring that abstract means-end synthesis lags behind improved affordance calibration 24 , 25 , 26 . Seven-year-olds thus possess reliable prospective planning for known tool-object pairings and efficient grip implementation but lack the flexible reshaping and mechanical problem-solving that characterizes later childhood tool cognition. The capabilities emerging during this stage point to a broader representational shift: by six to seven, children are learning that objects possess abstract, invariant properties (volume, mass, material kind) that persist across perceptual changes, but they still frequently default to appearance- and experience-based heuristics when task demands are high or contextual cues mislead, revealing that these emerging concepts are probabilistic priors being tuned by dense naturalistic error rather than crisp, rule-governed modules; their intuitive physics is transitioning from purely perceptual-motor prediction toward nascent explicit, depersonalized reasoning, but the explicit layer remains shallow, domain-specific, and easily overridden by salient perceptual features, a learning regime where everyday manipulation, construction play, and sports continue to generate the dense, action-coupled error streams that will eventually compile fragile heuristics into robust, generalizable physical models. We can say, however, that by about age six, most children maintain an implicit, globally consistent 3D scene representation with object individuation, coarse (and unreliable) material/affordance labels, and simple physical dynamics sufficient for planning and re-planning, while adult-like metric precision, cue-combination, and multi-object dynamics mature later (likely from  7-12).

title: Spatial
text: By 7, spatial cognition looks qualitatively more flexible than at 5. Mental rotation is both faster and more reliable: classic speed-angle functions show markedly higher rotation rates by the early school years (e.g.,  67deg/s at 5 vs.  167deg/s by 8 in one study 1 ), with overall performance on standardized mental-rotation batteries steeply increasing from 5-7 2 . Mental folding (imagining an object after it has been folded, a non-rigid spatial transformation) develops similarly to rotation across this window 3 . Perspective-taking undergoes substantial refinement between ages 5 and 7, transitioning from fragile, context-dependent success to more systematic (though still developing) competence in coordinating conflicting viewpoints. At age 5, most children still perform at or near chance level on multi-object Level 2 perspective-taking tasks, and when they do err, they systematically choose their own egocentric perspective rather than responding randomly 4 . This represents a qualitative shift from the near-random performance typical of four-year-olds: five-year-olds have begun to grasp that the task requires considering another’s viewpoint, but they cannot yet reliably execute the transformation, especially when spatial complexity is high. By age 7, performance increases steeply and egocentric errors decrease dramatically 2 , 4 , though even at age 8 children show considerable individual variability. Seven-year-olds reliably coordinate multiple perspectives across moderate angular disparities (90°, 180°) and can mentally rotate arrays of two to four objects to determine which photograph matches an observer’s viewpoint, a capacity that was "virtually non-existent" in four-year-olds and inconsistent in five- and six-year-olds. This improvement is part of a broader developmental shift in extrinsic-dynamic spatial skills (visualizing environments from different positions) that shows relatively slow, late development compared to intrinsic spatial transformations, with extrinsic skills continuing to improve steadily from ages 5 through 8 and beyond 5 . Across this period, children’s drawings and spatial constructions increasingly incorporate ideas of perspective and projective geometry: whereas five-year-olds’ drawings remain topological (features are enclosed but lack coordinated viewpoint), seven-year-olds begin to represent objects "from a side" and acknowledge occlusion ("we can’t see the other eye because it’s on the other side") 6 , mirroring their improving performance on explicit perspective-taking tasks. This convergence across production and judgment suggests a domain-general shift in how children mentally represent and manipulate spatial layouts, moving from viewer-independent topological relations toward viewer-dependent projective and Euclidean frameworks that support flexible viewpoint transformation. Between five and seven years, children’s navigation shifts from fragmentary landmark-based homing toward more systematic use of allocentric spatial representations, though full cognitive mapping proficiency remains years away. The advances are quantitative rather than qualitative: seven-year-olds navigate with measurably greater metric precision, recruit landmarks more reliably under challenging conditions, and show emerging capacity to integrate geometric layout with feature cues, all capabilities that five-year-olds possess in only rudimentary form or fail to deploy consistently outside highly scaffolded contexts. Landmark use becomes substantially more precise and flexible across this window. While five-year-olds can use salient landmarks to reorient after disorientation in large-room or ecologically valid settings (especially when scaffolded by spatial language), their representations remain coarse and context-bound 7 , 8 . By seven, children show improvements in both categorical performance (correctly identifying that a location has changed based on landmark shifts) and metrical performance (precisely estimating distances and angles relative to landmarks), with seven-year-olds significantly outperforming five- to six-year-olds on both measures in virtual navigation tasks 9 . Importantly, this development is not uniform across landmark types: throughout this window, children rely more heavily on directional landmark information (cues that specify which way to turn) than on positional landmarks (cues that mark fixed locations), and this directional bias persists even as overall landmark use strengthens 9 . The improvement in metrical precision relates primarily to age itself, whereas categorical landmark understanding at five is already above chance and correlates with visuospatial working memory and the ability to produce left/right labels 9 , suggesting that the 5-7 transition reflects both domain-general cognitive maturation (better working memory, faster processing) and domain-specific tuning of spatial metric codes. Allocentric navigation (encoding locations relative to external environmental features rather than one’s own body) undergoes a protracted emergence across this period. At five, allocentric strategies are nascent: children show some capacity to use geometry and landmarks in simplified reorientation tasks, but performance is fragile, highly task-dependent, and often requires explicit verbal cues to succeed 7 . Empirical evidence places the reliable onset of allocentric navigation somewhere between five and eight years, with substantial individual variation 9 , 10 . By seven, more children deploy allocentric strategies spontaneously, and those who do show better metric resolution and can handle mild viewpoint changes, yet even at seven performance lags notably behind nine- to ten-year-olds, who show adult-like precision and flexibility in many paradigms 9 . Path integration continues to improve from its five-year baseline. Blindfolded five-year-olds led along multi-turn paths can return to the start point on the majority of trials, though less precisely than adults, and a subset can even use path-integration-derived knowledge to take novel shortcuts between locations, demonstrating rudimentary cognitive map formation without vision 11 . However, across the 5-9 age range, performance on both egocentric homing (returning to start) and allocentric cognitive mapping (navigating novel routes between previously visited locations) shows continuous, graded improvement, with five- to seven-year-olds occupying the lower end of this developmental curve 11 . Nonetheless, by seven children are more accurate in estimating cumulative distance and angular displacement during blind navigation, and they can integrate path-integration-derived spatial knowledge with visual landmark information more reliably than at five, though the resulting cognitive maps remain sparse and error-prone compared to those of nine-year-olds and adults. The integration of geometric and landmark cues (a hallmark of mature allocentric navigation) strengthens gradually across this window but remains incomplete at seven. Five-year-olds reliably reorient by extended surface geometry (e.g., rectangular room boundaries) but often fail to conjoin geometric and featural information unless explicitly cued by spatial language ("turn at the red wall"); by seven, spontaneous conjunction improves, with children more consistently weighting both room shape and distinctive landmarks when both are available 12 , 13 . Yet even at seven, children show a persistent geometric bias: when geometry and features conflict, many default to geometric cues, and their landmark use remains less systematic and more error-prone than that of older children, who by nine to ten routinely fuse geometry and features into unified spatial representations 9 , 10 . Shortcut-taking and flexible route planning (cardinal signatures of true cognitive mapping) do, however, remain largely out of reach for five- to seven-year-olds. In virtual navigation paradigms designed to assess cognitive map formation, seven- and eight-year-olds are significantly less effective than nine-year-olds and adults at identifying and using novel shortcuts, marking a clear developmental discontinuity around age nine when children begin to proficiently navigate using survey-like, map-based representations 14 , 15 ; at seven, children can learn specific routes and recognize familiar landmarks along those routes, but they struggle to infer spatial relations between locations that were learned via separate paths. Spatial language continues to scaffold navigation across this period, though its role evolves. At five, explicit verbal cues (e.g., "in the middle," "turn at the oak tree") can significantly boost performance on tasks where children would otherwise fail, effectively directing attention to task-relevant spatial relations and reducing the dimensionality of the search space 16 , 17 . By seven, children’s spontaneous production and comprehension of relational spatial terms (above, between, next to) have expanded and become more context-appropriate, and their ability to use left/right productively (not just receptively) correlates with better egocentric navigation 9 . However, the relationship between language and navigation is not merely one of verbal labeling enabling spatial memory; rather, spatial language appears to function as an attention-directing and category-forming tool that helps children encode task-relevant geometric and featural structure more efficiently, a mechanism that operates across both spatial and non-spatial linguistic frames 17 . The developmental progression from five to seven thus reflects not only better spatial working memory and faster processing but also more strategic, language-mediated deployment of attention during encoding and retrieval.

title: Executive function
text: Executive functions undergo continued refinement between 5 and 7 years, transitioning from the "sweet spot" gains of the preschool period toward more robust, flexible, and strategically deployed control. While five-year-olds can reliably switch rules, follow multi-step instructions, and sustain attention in structured settings, seven-year-olds show qualitatively stronger performance: they maintain executive control across longer sequences, deploy it more selectively based on task demands, and recover more quickly from errors or rule changes. Working memory broadens from short, concrete strings at 5 to longer, more manipulable representations by 7; asks that produce floor effects at 5 (e.g., complex spans and backward spans 1 ) become tractable by 6-7, and by 7 most children can maintain and operate on rule strings with an extra dependency (e.g., "if there’s a border, sort by color; else by shape"). Normative studies for the n-back task (a continuous recognition task) show reliable 1-back performance from 7 upward with age-graded improvements thereafter 2 . In classrooms, these working-memory gains support executing four-plus-step instructions, keeping a future subgoal active while finishing the current one, and using silent verbal rehearsal in place of out-loud self-talk 3 . Cognitive flexibility undergoes a critical transition across this window, moving from basic rule-switching to handling hierarchical and rapidly alternating rule structures. On the standard Dimensional Change Card Sort (DCCS), most 5-year-olds pass the post-switch phase (sorting by a new rule after sorting by an initial rule), marking the well-documented 3-to-5 developmental shift 4 . However, the more challenging border version (which requires sorting by shape when cards have a border and by color when they don’t, demanding trial-by-trial rule selection rather than block-wise switching) is failed by most 4-year-olds, passed by approximately half of 5-year-olds, and mastered by age 7 4 . This progression reflects a shift from simply switching between two rule sets to flexibly deploying a higher-order conditional rule ("if border, then shape game; if no border, then color game"), which requires formulating and maintaining a hierarchical rule structure in working memory while inhibiting the now-irrelevant dimension on each trial 5 . In everyday contexts, this translates to seven-year-olds handling rapid context shifts (such as switching from "inside voice" to "outside voice" to "library voice" based on location cues) with minimal cognitive load, whereas five-year-olds show visible effort and occasional perseveration when rules change frequently or depend on subtle contextual signals. Inhibitory control shows continued improvement from 5 to 7. On Stroop-like interference tasks, the sharpest reduction in interference occurs between ages 3.5 and 5, with another period of sharp improvements occuring through age 7-8, followed by more gradual declines thereafter through age 11 6 . In the classic Day-Night task, whereas 4-year-olds struggle to maintain accuracy across trials and 5-year-olds show better interference control, 7-year-olds perform with near-ceiling accuracy and significantly faster response times, though some errors persist even at this age 7 , 8 . Planning abilities show measurable gains across the 5-7 window, though full maturity remains years away. By 7, children plan multiple steps ahead on Tower-of-London-type problems more efficiently than 6-year-olds (also increasing the amount of planning time systematically with problem difficulty 9 ), reflecting better prospective maintenance and fewer impulsive first moves 10 ; however, even at 7, planning remains effortful and context-dependent; children succeed on well-structured problems with clear subgoals but struggle when problem structure is ambiguous or when subgoal ordering is non-obvious, limitations that persist into later childhood 11 . In naturalistic settings, however, seven-year-olds can plan and execute multi-step morning routines with minimal adult scaffolding, organize materials for a craft project, and anticipate obstacles in simple games, capabilities that five-year-olds possess only in fragmented form or under close supervision. Seven-year-olds also show emerging metacognitive monitoring: they can report when a task is "hard" or "easy," adjust effort allocation accordingly 9 , and sometimes recognize their own errors mid-task and self-correct 10 , capacities largely absent in five-year-olds who plow ahead with the same strategy regardless of feedback. This metacognitive layer transforms executive function from a set of reactive control mechanisms into a more proactive, self-regulated system that can anticipate demands, allocate resources strategically, and learn from control failures, a progression that continues through adolescence but shows its first clear signs during the 5-7 window.

title: Causal learning and simulation
text: Across 5-7 years, causal cognition shifts from "rule-of-thumb scientists" to beginning model-builders: children move from noticing confounds and running simple tests to representing small causal systems explicitly, selecting diagnostic interventions in more complex systems, and keeping basic counterfactuals consistent with their models. This is a qualitative change in how evidence is represented more than a mere speed-up. It is visible in interventional learning on multi-variable systems, in counterfactual reasoning about indirect effects, and in an emerging grasp of necessity/sufficiency and mechanistic explanation, all capacities that are fragile or task-dependent at 5 but reliably present by 7. Recent synthesis work frames this as a move toward more "depersonalized, decontextualized" causal representations that support science-like reasoning 1 . During this window, children can use their own interventions to disambiguate the structure of three-variable systems (common-cause vs causal chains) 2 and they reliably exploit temporal dependence to infer causal direction 3 , abilities only inconsistently deployed at 5. Development improves both the efficiency with which children produce the interventions needed to disambiguate causal structure and the informativeness of those interventions (children increasingly resemble "idealized Bayesian learners" 2 ), with intervention quality serving as a significant predictor of children’s correct causal inferences 2 . In general, children this age begin to integrate prior theories with new evidence in a principled way, and this integration reorganizes their exploration itself. Another study shows that 5-7-year-olds with competing "center" vs. "mass" balance theories explore the very same apparatus differently as evidence confirms or violates their priors, and they update explanations accordingly 4 ; younger "no-theory" children display a simpler novelty preference. This marks a qualitative shift from the 4-5 pattern (where explanation already boosts attention to inductively rich features) toward a genuinely Bayesian trade-off between prior belief and likelihood that shapes which interventions they perform next. Evidence evaluation becomes more explicitly meta-cognitive between 5 and 7. During this window, children begin to represent indeterminacy ("the data don’t decide") and confounding as distinct epistemic states and use that representation to guide further testing 5 , 6 , 7 ; this understanding predicts later mastery of control-of-variables strategies (i.e holding all variables constant except for the variable being investigated) in the upper-elementary years 8 and couples to more skeptical, evidence-seeking behavior: compared with 4-5-year-olds, 6-7-year-olds are more likely to interrogate surprising claims, ask for missing evidence, and propose targeted checks, rather than accepting assertions at face value 9 . Explanatory practice also shifts from teleological defaults toward mechanism. Classic findings show broad "promiscuous teleology" (i.e describing phenomena according to their functions instead of the causes by which they arise) in younger children 10 , but by 6-7 most children reliably favor mechanistic over merely functional or categorical explanations when both are available 11 , and they begin to privilege informants who know underlying mechanisms 12 . This mechanistic tilt supports better causal generalization and more adult-like evaluation of explanations as evidential arguments. There is parallel growth in reasoning about necessity and sufficiency. Compared with five-year-olds, seven-year-olds are far more likely to treat a factor as necessary only when removing it abolishes the effect, and as sufficient only when its presence produces the effect across relevant conditions, an explicit logical framing that supports correct diagnoses in multi-cause settings and reduces over-attribution to single salient causes 13 . Sensitivity to causal complexity (e.g., recognizing when multiple interacting causes must be considered or when expert help is needed to decompose a system) also becomes measurable around this age 14 . Counterfactual reasoning undergoes substantial maturation across this window. Recent research using sufficiently simple and clear physical causation tasks finds that 4- and 5-year-olds can demonstrate mature counterfactual reasoning in over-determined scenarios (where two blocks both make a box light up), with four-year-olds answering correctly significantly more often than chance and five-year-olds performing nearly perfectly when asked to mentally remove one block and predict the effect 15 . Five-year-olds can entertain simple "what-ifs," (including in singly-determined scenarios like "Susie walked into the house with muddy shoes; would the floor be dirty if she did not walk into the house?" or in singly-determined physical tasks 16 which can be solved with basic conditional reasoning 17 ) but they often fail when complexity increases or when a change propagates through a dynamic system; by seven, children see higher success rates in more complex tasks 16 , 18 and begin to accurately project both direct and indirect consequences of hypothetical changes (for example, removing a species from a food chain and predicting downstream effects 19 ). This counterfactual upgrade reorganizes social evaluation: by 6-7, children experience and use counterfactual emotions (regret/relief) to guide choices and learning 20 , 21 , and they increasingly weight whether an agent "could have done otherwise," judging benevolence more positively when helpful acts reflect choice rather than constraint 22 . Related work on developing intuitions of free will shows that around this age children explicitly endorse the idea that agents can select among alternatives, aligning with their counterfactual social judgments 23 . Overall, seven-year-olds see substantial improvements on tasks probing counterfactual simulation and are starting to project indirect downstream effects in dynamic systems; their success does, however, remain fragile and highly task-dependent, with performance dropping quickly as complexity or hidden constraints continue to increase 24 , 17 . Overall we can say that, by seven, the foundational architecture for scientific reasoning is largely in place. What began at five as fragile, context-dependent hypothesis testing has crystallized into an integrated causal inference engine: children now maintain explicit models of multi-variable systems, run diagnostic interventions to disambiguate structure, simulate counterfactual trajectories through those models, and represent epistemic states like indeterminacy and confounding that guide further evidence-seeking. This is a qualitative shift in representation, from perceptually-bound heuristics towards abstract, depersonalized models that can be interrogated, updated, and applied across contexts. The result is a reasoning system that is beginning to look strikingly Bayesian: priors shape exploration, evidence is weighed mechanistically rather than teleologically, and necessity/sufficiency logic replaces simple association.
