title: Training data and optimization
text: Language Between ages five and seven, the language system’s objective function shifts from mostly local form-meaning mapping to constructing and querying generative, event-structured models that forecast upcoming words, clauses, and story beats; behaviorally, this shows up as faster on-line anticipation during sentences and more coherent, causally linked narratives, consistent with probabilistic prediction at multiple representational levels [What do we mean by prediction in language comprehension?; Prediction during language comprehension: what is next?]. The densest training signals come from dialogic book-reading 1 , 2 , movie- and TV show-watching, classroom discourse, caregiver-child conversational turns, and narrative retell with adult recasts. For lexical learning, the training signal shifts from predominantly concrete cross-situational co-occurrence toward systematic syntactic bootstrapping, where children exploit the grammatical frame of a sentence to narrow a novel verb’s meaning 3 . Caregiver recasts supply dense, tightly time-locked contrastive feedback: reformulations that immediately follow a child’s morphosyntactic or lexical error provide models of correct usage that the child can compare against their just-produced utterance 4 , reducing future surprisal for the same message and consolidating Brown-stage IV-V morphemes (articles, regular past tense, third-person -s, copula/auxiliary "be") alongside emerging subordinate and conditional clauses, though overregularization persists at lower rates as the learner balances rule generalization against stored exceptions. Narrative discourse itself becomes training data: stories with explicit temporal connectives and causal markers train children to encode not just sequential "and then" structures but hierarchical causal networks 5 , 6 , where events are bound by enabling, motivational, and consequence relations, with the shift from five-year-olds’ primitive, "and"-heavy sequences to seven-year-olds’ inclusion of 5+ story grammar elements (character, setting, initiating event, attempt, consequence, resolution) reflecting integration of theory of mind (understanding that listeners need contextual information), semantic memory, and executive function (coordinating multiple elements under working-memory load). Under the hood, cortical predictive-coding hierarchies minimize local surprisal in superior temporal (phonological/lexical) and inferior frontal (syntactic) areas, with theta-band activity proposed to carry prediction-error signals 7 that update representations when heard input violates expectation. Hippocampal-cortical loops continue their episode-to-semantic transition: repeated word-world pairings and narrative episodes are replayed during sleep, shifting from hippocampal traces to medial prefrontal and anterior temporal category structures that support richer semantic networks and enable inference during reading and discourse. Basal ganglia implement procedural learning of grammatical sequences and morphological rules through dopaminergic reinforcement, while cerebellar forward models calibrate speech-motor timing and articulatory sequencing under auditory-somatosensory error (children compare expected versus heard speech and adapt motor commands, yielding the observed jump in intelligibility and morphologically complex, fluent production). Neuromodulators act as adaptive gain controllers: acetylcholine up-weights the precision of linguistic prediction errors during focused classroom instruction, noradrenaline raises learning rates and resets representations when linguistic volatility is detected (novel constructions, ambiguous contexts), and together they ensure that the most informative mismatches (those arising from syntactic bootstrapping, contrastive recasts, and communicative failures) drive the steepest updates, compounding into the vocabulary burst, syntactic inflection, and narrative coherence that distinguish seven-year-olds from their five-year-old selves. Social Across 5-7 years, the child’s social optimizer is trained by a dense stream of belief-mismatch, norm-violation, and reputation-update signals that arise in classrooms, multi-party play, narratives, and rule-governed games. The dominant objectives are to minimize prediction error about others’ beliefs (now including recursive, interpretive beliefs), to maximize long-run social inclusion and reputation under local group norms, and to communicate efficiently under audience constraints. Practically, this means that mentalizing networks learn from social prediction errors (beliefs/behavior that contradict the child’s current model of another’s mind); these errors drive representational updates in ToM circuitry (TPJ/STS for agentive parsing, mPFC for trait/disposition models) and engage striatal evaluative learning when advice, trustworthiness, or cooperation pay off differently than expected. Interpretive theory-of-mind is further scaffolded by language: mastery of complementation and pragmatic competence provides the representational format for embedding "X thinks that Y thinks…", and meta-analyses link language growth to ToM gains around school entry, while experiments show that six-year-olds selectively trust pragmatically competent informants 8 . Core advanced theory-of-mind development follows a nonlinear trajectory with children reaching a critical milestone around age 7 when they attain the conceptual insight that mental states can be recursive 9 , and this recursive capacity is scaffolded by dense caregiver mental-state discourse that supplies high-bandwidth supervision; parents’ frequent use of belief/desire/knowledge language predicts children’s ToM performance months later by labeling the unobservable variables children must learn to track. For emotion understanding, the objective is building causal models that link situations, beliefs, desires, and past history to affective states while learning display rules as context-dependent mappings from felt to expressed emotion; inhibitory control and socioemotional knowledge jointly support emotion regulation 10 , and conceptual knowledge about emotions plays an increasingly important role in emotion understanding as perceptual discrimination of facial cues becomes less influential with age 11 , reflecting a shift from purely perceptual-motor emotion recognition toward model-based inference that integrates context, norms, and interpersonal history. Training data are dense and multimodal: mismatches between predicted and actual emotional displays (a peer smiles despite losing, someone cries without visible cause), explicit coaching on when to mask feelings ("thank Grandma even if you don’t like the gift"), vicarious observation of others’ display-rule violations and their social consequences, and the child’s own experience of managing felt-versus-shown emotion under social monitoring; these errors update both the forward emotion model (situational felt state) and the strategic display policy (felt vs shown expression given audience/norm), with acetylcholine up-weighting precision on reliable caregiver feedback and noradrenaline raising learning rates when norms shift across contexts. Norm acquisition moves from rigid overimitation to flexible, principle-guided deployment: children now distinguish conventional (arbitrary but group-binding) from instrumental (causally necessary) rules and grasp that norms vary by setting, with errors arising when they misjudge context boundaries or violate an implicit rule; explicit rule instruction, observed norm violations with varied consequences (punishment, praise, indifference), and participation in rule-negotiated pretend play supply labeled supervision, while peer enforcement (protest, exclusion, reputation damage) delivers immediate negative feedback that trains normative policies via striatal actor-critic loops: violations generate negative TD-errors, compliance with approval yields positive bursts, and distributional dopamine encodes the reputational-risk profile so children learn both the expected payoff and its variance across social partners. Prosocial learning is driven by prediction errors for others’ outcomes processed in ventral striatum, sgACC, dACC, and DLPFC-regions that receive dopaminergic input and code reward-prediction errors not just for self but for rewards delivered to others 12 , with oxytocin release in nucleus accumbens promoting serotonin release that filters excitatory inputs and modulates social reward, while dopamine neurons in VTA that project to NAc produce rewarding effects and mediate prosocial behavior 13 ; empathy modulates these prosocial prediction errors, with both cognitive and affective aspects of empathic processing motivating prosocial behaviors 12 . Prosocial choice itself becomes reputation-sensitive and principle-guided: children preferentially share with helpful peers, show indirect reciprocity (rewarding those who helped others), and increasingly invoke fairness principles even when costly; the value function now includes reputational terms (how my actions affect others’ models of me) and deontic rules (equity, reciprocity), trained by social approval for generosity, peer rejection after selfish acts, and occasional fairness violations that generate contrastive "ought" signals. Together, these update a prosocial policy that still leans on external reinforcement but is internalizing equity norms as stable goal weights. Across all four objectives, neuromodulators act as adaptive controllers: serotonin lengthens the temporal horizon and lowers subjective cost of prosocial acts, supporting patience in turn-taking and sustained helping; noradrenaline adjusts learning rates and resets representations when social volatility is detected (new peer group, novel norm structure); acetylcholine increases precision on reliable social-error signals during focused interactions; and dopamine supplies distributional, feature-aware prediction errors whose risk profile and learning rate depend on striatal target (ventral for fast motivation updates, dorsomedial for goal-directed social policy, dorsolateral for habitual prosocial scripts). Hippocampalâ€"cortical loops consolidate the day’s social episodes during sleep, with replay prioritizing interactions that yielded rich approval, surprising norm violations, or reputational consequences, gradually abstracting from specific encounters into stable person models, norm schemas, and strategic social policies that generalize across partners and settings, producing the observed jump in friendship stability, recursive mind-reading, flexible display-rule deployment, and strategic prosociality that distinguish seven-year-olds from their five-year-old selves. Physics and affordance perception Building directly on the 4-5 year foundation, physics learning from 5-7 years continues pursuing the same compound objective (minimize surprise in physical interactions while building transferable, compositional models) but the optimization bottleneck shifts from extracting basic principles (center of mass, support constraints) to composing multiple factors under working-memory load and making those compositions explicit enough to guide verbal reasoning. The training stream remains dense self-generated manipulation and construction errors, but now children encounter systematically more complex physical scenarios: organized sports (catching, batting, dodging), multi-constraint construction tasks (bridges that must span and support load), classroom science demonstrations (balance beams, ramps, pendulums), and tool use demanding prospective planning across competing biomechanical demands. Each failed catch, toppled asymmetric tower, mis-predicted balance, or awkward tool grip supplies a tightly time-locked physical prediction error, but whereas 4-5 year errors primarily trained single-variable heuristics, 5-7 year errors increasingly expose interactions: a block that falls despite being "heavy enough" (because it wasn’t centered), a thrown ball that curves unexpectedly (because spin and gravity combine), a lever that doesn’t budge despite strong pushing (because the fulcrum placement matters). Cerebellar forward models continue their vector-valued supervised calibration via climbing-fiber instructive signals triggered by kinematic mismatches (unexpected object motion, failed interceptions, trajectory deviations under occlusion), continuously update Purkinje-cell outputs, tightening predictive gains for parabolic motion, contact dynamics, and reafferent timing. This explains the paradox at the heart of 5-7 year physics: children reliably catch balls, time jumps to moving targets, and generate anticipatory saccades that extrapolate occluded motion with qualitatively adult-like strategies (albeit lower gain and higher error), all signatures that cerebellum-mediated implicit prediction works robustly for single-object, continuous dynamics. Yet the same children fail explicit horizontal-projectile reasoning when spatial context misleads, cannot reliably integrate perpendicular forces in pictorial problems, and default to single-factor explanations in verbal tasks. This split maps onto partially distinct optimization substrates: dense, action-coupled reafference during every reach, catch, and throw, continuously calibrate forward/inverse models and motor predictions through tightly time-locked error signals, whereas a dorsal fronto-parietal ’physics’ network (with lateral prefrontal involvement) supporting verbal/pictorial physics reasoning learns from sparse, delayed, often noisy/ambiguous verbal/visual feedback during passive observation or questioning (dozens of varied, under-constrained "what if" queries), resulting in more context-dependent heuristics that remain vulnerable to perceptual salience and framing effects. Cortical hierarchies run their parallel, slower optimization over symbolic causal models: prediction errors in verbal reasoning tasks ("which way will it fall?", "what happens if we add weight here?") and pictorial physics problems propagate up temporal-parietal-frontal networks as mismatches between expected and observed outcomes, updating representations when precision is high (acetylcholine up-weights errors during focused classroom instruction). But these updates face a bandwidth constraint that doesn’t bind the cerebellum: integrating multiple simultaneous forces (especially non-parallel ones) requires PFC working memory to maintain and compose multiple additive predictions, a computational demand that exceeds the current capacity of 5-7 year dorsolateral circuits. This is why children at six can reason above chance when forces act along a single dimension (collinear composition is cheap: just add/subtract scalars), yet fail dramatically when forces are perpendicular or when "Prevent" relations require computing a deflected resultant vector; their physics engine remains functionally single-threaded, serially processing the most salient influence rather than computing a true vector sum, only composing forces into net effects when alignment, salience, and working-memory load are all favorable. The system is learning the right compositional architecture but hasn’t yet scaled the parameters (PFC representational bandwidth, parietal vector integration) to run it under general conditions, so explicit multi-factor reasoning remains fragile and task-dependent while implicit control soars. Force and weight learning similarly reflect this dual-track dynamic: systematic mismatches between applied force and achieved outcome (object doesn’t move, moves too far, feels unexpectedly light/heavy) continue training both feedforward force scaling via cerebellar inverse models (supporting the observed improvements in anticipatory grip/load control) and object property inference via cortical weight/material categories. By 5-7 years, children possess an extensive, largely implicit database of object-property associations accumulated through years of manipulation: ceramic mugs shatter when dropped, blankets are soft and flexible, rubber balls bounce, paper tears easily, metal is hard. This "material intuition" functions as an action-grounded lookup table indexed by object identity, guiding force selection, grip configuration, and risk assessment during handling with increasing reliability. Yet optimal visuo-haptic integration for material properties (combining visual texture cues with haptic deformation to infer softness, or fusing appearance with lift kinematics to estimate weight) does not mature until roughly 8-10 years; throughout 5-7, material perception remains single-cue biased, with judgments shifting depending on whether the child sees or touches first, revealing that the system is still learning the reliability weights for cross-modal cues rather than having solved the integration problem. Training data come from dense prediction errors at contact: every squeeze, lift, drop, and throw where expected feel/sound/outcome mismatches reality generates a labeled sample that tunes both the within-modality property models and the cross-modal integration policy, but because these errors are distributed across thousands of object types and contexts, and because PFC-parietal circuits that compute precision-weighted cue combination are still maturing, the consolidation into adult-like Bayesian fusion lags behind the raw lookup-table knowledge. Across all these streams, basal ganglia actor-critic loops learn which exploratory and goal-directed actions yield informative physical feedback: distributional dopamine trains striatal policies to preferentially sample interactions that reveal hidden properties (shaking unfamiliar objects, testing weight before lifting, probing stability before stacking), while tonic dopamine scales vigor and shapes the fast-ballistic versus slow-careful tradeoff based on expected task payoff and error cost. Together, cerebellar supervised calibration of forward/inverse models, cortical predictive coding over symbolic causal representations, and striatal reinforcement learning of exploration and control policies constitute a coupled, multi-timescale optimizer that explains the 5-7 window’s signature profile: robust implicit physical competence in familiar sensorimotor loops, rapidly expanding but still-fragile explicit reasoning under working-memory and inhibitory demands, and an emerging capacity to verbalize physical principles that nevertheless remains vulnerable to perceptual misleads and cannot yet compose multi-factor interactions reliably. Spatial The same four spatial objectives (making stable structures (in the general sense), transforming shapes (and scenes) mentally, navigating to goals, and mapping symbols to real space (especially spatial relationships)) continue but with substantially upgraded teaching signals and tightening precision demands that push the system from fragile, context-dependent success toward more systematic, generalizable spatial reasoning. Mental rotation and perspective-taking remain trained by converging prediction-error streams (experiencing multiple views of objects/scenes; puzzle/structure play; tool use), but the density and complexity of those streams escalate dramatically: whereas 4-5 year olds encounter cross-view mismatches primarily during object manipulation and simple puzzle play, 5-7 year olds face systematic multi-view prediction errors during organized sports (tracking spinning balls, anticipating teammates’ viewpoints, coordinating plays), classroom geometry activities (folding paper, rotating drawn shapes, imagining 3D solids from 2D nets), and increasingly complex construction tasks (LEGO models with branching subassemblies, multi-level block structures, simple machines with gears and levers), all of which generate denser, more precisely time-locked visuospatial mismatches that refine parietal transformation circuits. Each failed catch of a spinning ball, each puzzle piece that doesn’t fit despite looking correct, each construction that collapses because a support was misaligned from the mental preview, delivers a vector-valued error signal that updates both the allocentric-structure-to-appearance mapping (what does this look like rotated 90°?) and the viewer-dependent projective transformation (what does this array look like from there?). Fine motor objectives continue adding parallel training pressure through tool use and bimanual manipulation, but now with longer action chains and tighter biomechanical constraints: writing implements must be pre-rotated for efficient letter formation, scissors must be oriented correctly before cutting curves, sports equipment (bats, rackets) must be gripped with anticipatory pose adjustments, each proprioceptive mismatch between planned and achieved grip angles trains the same parietal circuits to preview terminal states more accurately and select initial configurations accordingly, with these action-coupled rotation demands strengthening mental transformation abilities that generalize across both object manipulation and pure imagery tasks. Perspective-taking errors shift from simple egocentric defaults at 5 (choosing one’s own view when asked what another sees) toward more systematic yet still-imperfect coordination at 7, with the key training signal (along with multi-view prediction errors, which are likely foundational) being repeated failures during social play, collaborative tasks, and explicit instruction where children must reconcile their viewpoint with others’: board games where piece visibility matters, hide-and-seek where occlusion from another’s position determines success, classroom activities requiring description of scenes "as the teacher sees them," and peer communication breakdowns when spatial descriptions assume shared viewpoints. Adult corrections and peer feedback supply explicit labels ("that’s what you see, but from her side...") that prune egocentric search strategies, while the sheer volume of viewpoint-coordination demands in school and structured play-hundreds of trials per week versus occasional scaffolded episodes at 4-5-drives the steep improvement in Level 2 perspective-taking. For navigation, objectives move further away from learning route fragments and towards actively maintaining query-able, viewpoint-invariant place codes that bind room geometry to stable features, though true shortcut-taking remains out of reach. Training data continue to come from everyday search errors and disorientation episodes, but these now occur in larger, more complex environments with richer featural structure: school buildings with multiple rooms and hallways, playgrounds with varied landmarks and boundaries, neighborhoods traversed during walks or bike rides, all generating denser place-prediction mismatches than the home-dominated 4-5 year ecology. The densest teaching signal for landmark use comes from systematic failures in landmark-based search tasks: children predict a target’s location based on a landmark configuration, approach it, and discover a mismatch (either categorical (the target moved relative to landmarks) or metrical (distance/angle estimates were wrong)) which generates a prediction error that updates both the reliability weight assigned to that landmark type (directional vs. positional) and the precision of the distance/angle estimate. Across hundreds of such episodes during hide-and-seek, treasure hunts, classroom activities, and everyday navigation, seven-year-olds accumulate enough labeled data to shift from coarse, binary landmark use ("it’s near the red door") toward metrical estimates that approach adult precision in familiar environments. The integration of geometric and landmark cues (the hallmark of mature allocentric navigation) does, however, remain incomplete at seven, with persistent geometric bias revealing that the system is still learning the conditional reliability of featural versus geometric information: when geometry (room shape, extended boundaries) and features (colored walls, furniture) conflict, many seven-year-olds default to geometry, indicating that boundary-based codes remain the most trusted basis for reorientation. This bias is rational under current evidence statistics: boundaries are stable and viewpoint-invariant, whereas individual features can be ambiguous, moveable, or viewpoint-dependent, so the optimizer continues heavily weighting geometric cues while slowly accumulating evidence about which featural configurations are stable and distinctive enough to override geometry. Training pressure to integrate comes from naturalistic search errors where geometry alone is insufficient (symmetrical rooms, multiple similar corners) and successful searches that required weighting both sources, with language continuing to provide high-bandwidth supervision: caregivers and teachers supply explicit landmark-geometry conjunctions ("it’s in the far corner by the blue cabinet") that function as labeled training samples, directing attention to relevant conjunctive features and compressing the hypothesis space. Each successful landmark-guided search after disorientation, each corrected geometric-only error, and each adult-scaffolded integration episode incrementally raises the precision weight on landmark cues and trains the hippocampal-retrosplenial-parietal circuits to bind featural and geometric codes into unified place representations, yielding the observed improvement in spontaneous conjunction by age seven while explaining why systematic, adult-like fusion remains years away-the system needs more data to overcome its geometric prior, and shortcut-taking (the ultimate test of true cognitive mapping) requires inferring spatial relations between locations learned separately, a capacity that demands robust place-to-place associations that seven-year-olds’ still-sparse cognitive maps cannot reliably support. Spatial relational concepts continue being learned through coupled physical and linguistic error streams, but the bottleneck shifts from initial category formation to refining metric precision and extending to more abstract, hierarchical relations. During construction, sports, and classroom activities, children generate increasingly complex action-outcome errors involving multi-object spatial configurations: stacking blocks "between" two boundaries and having them topple (alignment error), placing objects "above" a reference and misjudging height (metric error), arranging items "around" a center and achieving asymmetric distribution (radial-distribution error), each mismatch updating parietal representations of geometric relations with finer granularity than the coarse success/failure signals of 4-5 years. The key advance is that spatial language shifts from merely labeling static configurations to serving as an active computational tool: children increasingly use verbal encoding ("left of the door, then right at the tree") to compress navigation routes, rehearse spatial sequences during problem-solving, and communicate procedures to peers, with production errors (miscommunicating a route and having a peer get lost, using "left" when they meant "right" and having to repair) supplying immediate, tightly time-locked feedback that tunes both the spatial-to-linguistic mapping and the pragmatic deployment of spatial terms. The optimizers co-train on these spatial streams: cerebellar supervised calibration keeps end-state previews and saccade/hand trajectories aligned as transforms get larger and faster; hippocampal-retrosplenial loops use view-change and loop-closure errors (discovering that predicted position disagrees with boundary/scene matches) to harden allocentric codes; corticothalamo-cortical hierarchies minimize prediction residuals for view and scene transforms; and basal-ganglia actor-critic loops shape exploratory routing and strategy selection under distributional value signals. Executive Building directly on the 4-5 foundation, everyday routines between 5-7 years scale up not just in length but in hierarchical depth and conditional branching, transforming the executive objective from "maintain and flexibly update simple plans" to "construct, monitor, and adaptively reweight multi-level goal hierarchies under competing task demands." Morning sequences now involve 5-7 conditionally nested steps with explicit if-then-else logic ("if it’s gym day, pack sneakers and water bottle; otherwise just your lunch; then check your folder for homework to return"), classroom activities require maintaining a lesson-level goal (complete the worksheet) while dynamically selecting and sequencing multiple sub-procedures (read instruction, retrieve correct operation, check work, raise hand for help if stuck), and rule-governed games demand rapid, hierarchical switching where the active rule depends on higher-order context ("in this round, sort by shape only if the card has a border; track your score; rotate who goes first after each round"). Organized sports and group projects add parallel demands: children must hold their assigned role in working memory (defense vs. offense, their part in the group task), update it when the coach/teacher signals a switch, inhibit interference from nearby peers’ different instructions, and monitor their own performance to detect errors mid-execution. These longer, branch-heavy, hierarchical scripts generate qualitatively richer error structure than the 4-5 window: children now fail not just by perseverating on an outdated rule or skipping a step, but by loading the wrong level of the hierarchy (executing a sub-goal out of sequence), failing to refresh a conditional premise when context shifts (continuing the "no-border" rule after seeing a border), losing track of which meta-rule is active (forgetting whether it’s "shape game" or "color game" block), or failing to recognize that their current strategy is producing systematic errors. Each hierarchical confusion, mid-sequence derailment, failed conditional branch, or undetected error acts as a structured, multi-dimensional prediction error that trains cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamic loops to better partition goal space into stable sub-policies, gate updates at the appropriate hierarchical level, and allocate monitoring resources to track progress and detect deviations. Under the hood, basal-ganglia-PFC gating policies graduate from binary hold-vs-update to hierarchically organized, precision-weighted state maintenance: striatal circuits (especially dorsomedial caudate projecting to cognitive regions of PFC) learn not only when to open the "update gate" but which level of the goal stack to refresh (flush the current sub-goal but preserve the overarching task rule, or reset the entire hierarchy), with distributional dopamine supplying signed, multi-timescale prediction errors that credit both immediate sub-goal completion and longer-horizon primary-goal progress, while tonic dopamine continues tracking average reward rate (opportunity cost) to set vigor and persistence thresholds across nested action sequences. The cost-benefit controller in dorsal ACC becomes more sophisticated: it learns the expected value of deploying control as a function of hierarchical depth, task volatility, and error history, inferring when to invest effort in proactive goal maintenance (rehearsing the rule before each trial, pre-loading the next sub-step) versus when to rely on reactive retrieval or external cues, and it begins tracking prediction-error sequences to detect systematic failures (repeatedly choosing wrong on bordered cards signals "I’m applying the rule incorrectly" rather than random noise), generating confidence-weighted signals that bias toward error-checking and strategy revision when internal models drift. Thalamocortical relays scale up their stabilization function: mediodorsal thalamus amplifies and sustains increasingly complex, multi-clause rule representations in lateral PFC ("if border -> shape; else -> color"), maintaining them across longer sequences of trials (10-20 cards rather than 3-5) and against stronger distractor interference (irrelevant dimensions, peer actions, teacher instructions), while pulvinar routes task-relevant visual features (border presence, shape identity) with higher selectivity and lower latency, together reducing switch costs on hierarchical DCCS and enabling the rapid, context-sensitive shifts described in naturalistic settings where seven-year-olds toggle between "inside voice," "outside voice," and "library voice" based on location cues with minimal visible effort, a capacity that required sustained concentration and frequent prompts at five. Neuromodulators refine their roles as adaptive, context-sensitive gain controllers. Acetylcholine up-weights the precision (inverse variance) on task-relevant sensory prediction errors during rule maintenance, effectively sharpening the contrast between target features (border/no-border) and irrelevant dimensions (color, shape) so that noisy or ambiguous cues are less likely to trigger spurious updates; this precision boost is now modulated by learned task statistics (ACh release ramps higher in volatile blocks where rules change frequently, lower in stable blocks) and coupled to attentional orienting, so children at seven show tighter stimulus-locked pupil responses and faster RT adjustments after rule switches than at five, signatures of more finely tuned cholinergic filtering. Noradrenaline broadcasts model-failure signals with greater specificity: rather than a uniform "reset everything" pulse, phasic LC bursts are increasingly targeted to task-relevant networks (PFC for rule updates, parietal for attentional reorienting), triggered not just by unexpected outcomes but by volatility detection (the second or third consecutive error signals "the rule changed" rather than "I made a mistake"), transiently hiking learning rates in frontostriatal synapses so outdated rules are abandoned faster and new ones stamped in with fewer trials, explaining why seven-year-olds recover from rule switches within 1-2 trials on average compared to 3-5 trials at five. The 5-7 window sees the emergence of metacognitive monitoring as an explicit optimization objective layered over reactive control: children begin tracking their own confidence, effort expenditure, and error likelihood, and they use those internal signals to adjust strategy mid-task (slowing down when a problem feels hard, asking for help when stuck, double-checking work when uncertain). This metacognitive capacity is trained by a distinct error stream: mismatches between subjective confidence and actual performance (feeling certain but getting it wrong, or feeling unsure but succeeding) generate metacognitive prediction errors that tune the mapping from internal cognitive states (processing fluency, experienced effort, memory vividness) to calibrated confidence and appropriate regulatory responses. Anterior prefrontal cortex (especially rostrolateral PFC) and posterior medial cortex track these metacognitive signals, with dACC monitoring the discrepancy between expected and actual task difficulty, and these regions output to cognitive-control networks to adjust resource allocation (working-memory refreshing, inhibitory gating, exploratory search) on subsequent trials. Overall, the 5-7 executive advance is not merely more of the 4-5 gains but a qualitative architectural upgrade: hierarchical goal representations, multi-level gating, confidence-weighted monitoring, and metacognitive regulation, all trained by the denser, more complex, and more cognitively demanding routines, games, and academic tasks that define early elementary school life. Causal Building directly on the 4-5 year foundation, causal learning from 5-7 continues pursuing the dual objective of building compositional models that both predict and guide intervention, but the optimization bottleneck shifts from extracting basic mechanism-over-correlation principles to representing and querying explicit multi-variable causal structures, integrating those structures with prior theories, and using them to simulate counterfactual trajectories that propagate through dynamic systems. The training stream remains centered on dense, action-contingent surprise from exploratory play (in the general sense), but now children encounter systematically more complex causal scenarios: classroom science demonstrations with three-plus interacting variables (circuits with switches and bulbs in series/parallel, balance beams with weight and distance, ramps with angle and surface friction), structured games where outcomes depend on conjunctions of causes, and everyday problem-solving that requires disambiguating common-cause from chain structures (does flipping both switches activate the toy, or must one enable the other?). Each intervention yields a tightly time-locked outcome (and linguistically packaged explanations that compress mechanisms into manipulable variables), but whereas 4-5 year errors primarily trained single-mechanism beliefs ("this block makes it go"), 5-7 year errors increasingly expose structural ambiguities: the same observed pattern (A and B both correlate with E) can arise from chains, common causes, or interactive conjunctions, and only systematic conditional interventions ("what if I remove A but keep B?", "what if I manipulate A while holding everything else constant?") supply the high-information data needed to resolve these confounds. The key architectural advance is that children now bring explicit prior theories to the data 14 , 15 , and this changes the optimization itself: rather than passively absorbing correlations, the learner runs a Bayesian update where strong priors about causal structure (from past experience, pedagogy, or analogy) are weighed against the likelihood of new evidence, with exploration policy actively shaped by this trade-off; children preferentially test interventions that maximally distinguish competing theories, abandon fruitless exploration sooner when priors are strong, and reorganize their search when evidence overwhelmingly contradicts expectations, behaviorally visible as 5-7-year-olds with competing theories exploring the same apparatus differently as evidence confirms or violates their beliefs. Striatal RL continues learning exploratory policies, but the objective function now includes epistemic value more explicitly: distributional dopamine signals not just scalar reward from "making it work" but also uncertainty reduction from resolving structural ambiguity, with phasic bursts following informative interventions (those that disambiguate common-cause from chain) being larger than those following redundant tests; this intrinsic information-seeking reward, combined with rising PFC working-memory capacity that can now maintain multiple competing hypotheses simultaneously, drives the documented improvement in intervention quality where children produce more efficient, more diagnostic probes and increasingly resemble idealized Bayesian learners. Counterfactual reasoning upgrades from fragile single-step simulation to propagating changes through dynamic causal models, enabled by tighter hippocampal-PFC coupling and stronger executive control: the cerebellum’s forward models, trained by years of action-outcome mismatches, can now be "run offline" with hypothetical initial conditions (mentally removing one block from an over-determined scenario, imagining an alternative action, simulating species removal from a food chain), and at 5-7, better PFC working memory can maintain the counterfactual premise ("if X had not happened") alongside actual state while hippocampal pattern-completion retrieves relevant event structure and cortical predictive loops propagate the change forward through the causal graph, yielding predictions about both direct and indirect downstream effects and reorganizing social cognition as counterfactual emotions (regret, relief) emerge and vmPFC-striatal loops learn to credit actions not just by actual outcomes but by counterfactual value (what would have happened if I’d chosen differently), driving the shift where 6-7-year-olds use regret to guide choices and increasingly judge benevolence by whether helpful acts reflected free choice versus constraint. Language continues acting as high-bandwidth supervision but now also provides representational scaffolding for meta-cognitive awareness of evidence quality: adult explanations still compress hypothesis space, but 5-7-year-olds increasingly evaluate those explanations for verifiability and mechanistic depth, preferring testable claims over unverifiable assertions and favoring mechanistic over teleological accounts when both are available, while causal discourse (especially "because"/"so" and necessity/sufficiency language) not only labels relations but makes epistemic states explicit, with terms like "we don’t know yet," "it could be either," and "we need to test both" teaching children to represent indeterminacy and confounding as distinct states demanding further investigation rather than forcing premature closure. Hippocampal-cortical loops continue binding and consolidating causal episodes, but replay now prioritizes interventions that yielded high information gain: during sleep, sequences where conditional tests resolved ambiguity or where surprising outcomes violated strong priors are preferentially reactivated, with dopamine-dependent tagging ensuring that the most diagnostic evidence gets written into long-term causal schemas rather than being treated as isolated anomalies, gradually abstracting from specific episodes (this blicket detector, this balance beam) to generalized principles (necessity vs sufficiency, common-cause vs chain structures) that support the shift from perceptually-bound heuristics toward depersonalized, transferable causal models. The net result by age seven is an integrated causal inference engine: children maintain explicit multi-variable models, deploy diagnostic interventions shaped by theory-evidence trade-offs, simulate counterfactual trajectories through those models with improving fidelity, and represent their own epistemic states (indeterminacy, confounding, verifiability) as explicit variables that guide further exploration-a reasoning system that looks strikingly Bayesian in its weighing of priors against evidence, privileging of mechanism over correlation, and principled handling of necessity and sufficiency.

title: Neural development
text: Neural perspectives on cognitive control development during childhood and adolescence Structurally, factor-analytic work shows the classic phonological, visuospatial, and "central executive" components of working memory are already separable from  6 years Neurally, the scene/navigation network that supports map-based navigation continues to specialize across 5-7. The retrosplenial complex (RSC) underpins using landmark configurations to link viewpoints and supports "map-like" transformations; developmental imaging shows that the three scene systems-OPA for visually guided navigation, PPA for scene categorization, and RSC for map-based navigation-are present but still functionally maturing across early school years, with 5-7-year-olds recruiting these regions less selectively and efficiently than adults. Together, these findings locate the qualitative step from 5 to 7 in greater viewpoint-invariance, more consistent landmark-configuration coding, better (though still non-optimal) cue use, and improved map alignment-setting the stage for the later transition to robust survey knowledge around  10-12. 2 Looking closely at frontal activity, Jonkman (2006) found a linear increase in no-go P3 amplitude (a positive wave 300 - 500 ms after stimulus presentation) across development: Children ages 6-7 showed no P3 activity, children ages 9-10 showed limited P3 activity in frontal-central electrodes, and young adults showed broad P3 activity across frontal and frontal-central electrodes (see also Jonkman el al., 2003). P3 activity has been interpreted to index the allocation of attentional resources during stimulus engagement, with greater activity representing greater resource allocation (Polich, 1987). In contrast, the no-go N2 response (a negative wave 150 - 400 ms after stimulus presentation) decreased across the same age span, with the largest decrease in amplitude occurring between ages 6 and 10.

title: Language
text: Between ages 7 and 9, language development continues its steep trajectory with measurable advances across all domains, shifting from foundational competence toward increasingly sophisticated, context-sensitive deployment. Vocabulary acquisition accelerates: typical children add roughly three new base (root) words a day 1 ; if you count derived forms (prefixes/suffixes creating new words), the effective intake is closer to 8-12 items a day. By this stage their core lexicon averages about 6-7.5k root words (roughly  6k by the end of Grade 2 and  7k by mid-late Grade 3 2 ) with wide spread by experience. Age  8 is also when the child’s phonological repertoire is complete 3 , 4 . During this window, vocabulary growth becomes explicitly derivative: children start using derivational morphology (i.e forming new words by adding prefixes or suffixes to a base word) as a productive tool, parsing and composing prefixes/suffixes to infer meanings and part-of-speech shifts (happy->unhappy, govern->government), a skill that accelerates towards the end of the 7- to 9-year window and contributes substantially to the surge of new words learned during the middle-elementary years 5 , 6 , 7 ; this skill does, however, remain immature through age 9. By age eight, children also understand jokes and riddles that play on sounds (e.g "what do you call a fake noodle?" -> "an impasta") 8 and start to grasp that words can carry multiple meanings (e.g literal and psychological meaning of "cold") 9 , reflecting richer semantic networks that support inference and abstract reasoning; relatedly, figurative language production emerges and accelerates between ages 7-9 10 , reflecting developing metalinguistic awareness, which is a strong predictor of understanding figurative language 11 , though adult-like comprehension of idioms in off-line metalinguistic tasks doesn’t emerge until years later 12 . Syntactic complexity continues its nonlinear climb: between ages 7-8, use of relative pronouns (e.g who, whom, whose, which, that, whoever) and subordinate clauses (e.g "when it rang" in "she answered the phone when it rang") increases and children start using gerunds (a verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun in a sentence, e.g "running") more frequently, while towards the end of this window, subordination increases further with more advanced conjunctions such as "meanwhile", "unless", "even if", or "although" 13 . Their sentences, measured properly as T-units (a main clause plus all its subordinate material), average about 7 words 14 , reflecting a broad expansion of clause chaining and embedded structure beyond the mostly coordinate/"because/so" scaffolds typical at seven. During this window, children’s stories shift from the single-episode, locally ordered tales common at seven towards sustained, multi-episode narratives that keep a global plot in view 15 , chain causes and consequences explicitly (albeit in a basic and unreliable manner 16 ), and deploy temporal previews and summaries 17 ; they also attribute protagonists’ inner states far more often to motivate actions, marking a clear step up in evaluative (i.e interpreting events as a narrator would) and causal coherence 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 (although there appears to be a tension between evaluative comments and narrative coherence at this age, likely reflecting immature semantic working memory 19 ). Relatedly, their narratives show richer perspective-taking: primary-school children coordinate the "landscapes" of action and consciousness more effectively, using mental-state language to explain goals and beliefs 22 . In autobiographical narration, nine-year-olds’ accounts are typically more specific, temporally ordered, and causally linked than at seven, even though the most interpretive, identity-building commentary continues to rise mainly from late childhood into adolescence 23 , 24 , 16 . In comprehension, nine-year-olds more reliably generate and integrate both bridging and elaborative inferences (i.e "bridging" events or "elaborating" on them with prior/world knowledge), capacities tightly tied to overall comprehension and increasingly supported by growth in vocabulary, working memory, and the ability to handle embedded clause structures 25 , 26 .

title: Social
text: By nine, the social mind has shifted from the 5-7 window’s budding second-order belief tracking, display-rule mastery, and emerging reputation sensitivity into a genuinely well-informed, strategic, and norm-aware social reasoner. Nine-year-olds now succeed far more often on "advanced" mentalizing that requires embedding beliefs within beliefs and reading pragmatic intent: some 9-year-olds can distinguish sarcasm from literal criticism and from irony, recover what the speaker really meant, and even attribute why a speaker used a non-literal form (teasing, mitigation) rather than just noticing incongruity 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . Their epistemic vigilance also sharpens: rather than trusting by default (or using basic heuristics to evaluate speakers), nine-year-olds weigh informants’ past accuracy, expertise, benevolence, and potential conflicts of interest, showing a more adult-like "knowing when to doubt" stance than seven-year-olds 5 . In emotion understanding, nine-year-olds enter the "reflective" phase on the Test of Emotion Comprehension 6 : they coordinate mixed and even conflicting emotions within a single person (e.g being happy and disappointed at the same time), differentiate inner feelings from outward displays with meta-representational justifications, and can explain how beliefs and perspectives drive affect (including in themselves) 7 , 6 , 8 , capacities that are only nascent at seven. Knowledge about cognitive regulation also becomes explicit: they can articulate and begin to deploy cognitive reappraisal (not merely suppression) and understand that different strategies alter emotional intensity and expression, capacities that show strong gains across late childhood and are measurable in 9-12-year-olds 9 , 10 . Moral emotion attributions shift as well: whereas many seven-year-olds still show traces of the "happy-victimizer" pattern, nine-year-olds more reliably predict guilt or shame for wrongdoers and begin to differentiate these emotions in terms of internal standards and self-evaluation 11 , 12 . Prosocial behavior shifts from predominantly sympathy-based motivation toward increasingly strategic deployment: while five-to-seven-year-olds show emerging reputation sensitivity, children aged seven to nine become proficient at instrumentally using prosocial acts to achieve self-serving goals including reputation enhancement, eliciting reciprocity, and securing future social partnerships, balancing altruistic and selfish motives with growing sophistication. This strategic capacity extends to deception, where semantic leakage control improves substantially; one study showed that, by age 8, approximately half of children can maintain consistency between initial lies and subsequent statements (feigning ignorance when asked follow-up questions), compared to the majority of younger children who immediately betray their deception 13 , and children increasingly tell white lies in politeness situations despite viewing them as technically dishonest 14 , demonstrating emergent capacity to navigate conflicting social rules and make strategic trade-offs between honesty norms and relationship maintenance. Peer relationship structures become more differentiated and hierarchically organized, with stable cliques forming around shared interests and coordinated activities rather than mere proximity, sociometric hierarchies solidifying such that children show strong consensus about popular and rejected peers and actively work to improve social standing through strategic affiliation and self-presentation, and friendship conceptions shifting from "fair-weather cooperation" (expecting immediate reciprocity) toward more psychologically grounded bonds emphasizing loyalty, trust, and genuine care for the other’s welfare independent of transactional exchange 15 . Children also develop more nuanced understanding of social influence and peer dynamics, becoming increasingly aware that they are being evaluated by others and that different peers hold different social perspectives (extending the simpler "audience effects" of younger ages) 16 , enabling more sophisticated navigation of the reputational landscape while simultaneously making them vulnerable to heightened social anxiety as they track their standing within increasingly complex peer networks. Across major theoretical frameworks, nine-year-olds sit at the cusp of "big-kid" social cognition. In Piagetian terms they are firmly in the concrete-operational period and, in Piaget’s moral theory, begin the shift toward autonomous morality ( 9-10 y): they begin to decenter from outcomes to intentions (moral judgements are outcome-based until  8 17 ) and treat rules as human agreements rather than absolutes 18 , 19 . In Selman’s role-taking model they are characteristically at Level 2 (reciprocal, self-reflective;  8-10 y), able to reason about how the other sees them and how they appear to the other, though not yet to coordinate multiple perspectives from a generalized third party 20 . Social-domain theory finds that by this age children reliably treat moral norms as authority-independent and generalizable while viewing conventional rules as context-bound 21 ; meanwhile, Kohlberg’s accounts place many at the boundary between preconventional self-interest and emerging conventional concern for interpersonal expectations and norm maintenance 22 . From sociocultural and information-processing views, the internalization of private speech into inner speech together with middle-childhood gains in executive control makes social reasoning more planful and strategic, improving encoding/interpretation of social cues, generation of response options, and evaluation of consequences with affect integrated 23 , 24 .

title: Physics and objects
text: Intro and conservation laws By age nine, midway through Piaget’s concrete operational stage, children exhibit qualitative advances in intuitive and explicit physics reasoning that are not yet seen in seven-year-olds. Weight conservation (the flagship achievement of this age) emerges around age nine 1 , representing the fourth conservation concept to crystallize (following number, mass, and length) and reflecting the child’s growing capacity to mentally reverse transformations while inhibiting overlearned heuristics (like "length-equals-number") 2 , 3 . What emerges is decentration (the ability to coordinate multiple dimensions simultaneously (e.g height and width) rather than fixating on one salient feature) and reversibility (enabling mental operations that reverse transformations); between 7 and 9, children increasingly select and verbalize the correct reversible/compensatory strategies over naive height/length rules. These capacities reflect the concrete operational stage’s hallmark: logical thinking about tangible objects, constrained to concrete (not yet abstract) domains 4 . Force understanding and kinematics Nine-year-olds also begin attempting to coordinate multiple variables in physical problems. At age 7, children demonstrate functional single-force reasoning and begin composing collinear forces, but struggle profoundly with non-parallel force vectors. The transition to age 9 brings attempted integration of multiple force dimensions: on balance-scale problems most 8-9-year-olds have shifted from a weight-only rule to considering distance (Rule II) and, for a minority, to partial (Rule III) and even full (Rule IV) torque integration 5 , 6 , yielding much better predictions on conflict items than 7-year-olds. Although true proportional integration of forces (i.e. computing torque) does not emerge until adolescence 6 , a multi-factor logic is evident by nine, marking a clear step beyond the preoperational single-rule approach. Similarly, their predictions of object motion become more constraint-consistent and less dominated by perceptual bias: younger children’s trajectory judgments are easily misled by salient context (e.g. assuming an object dropped from a moving carrier will fall straight down beneath it), but by nine children more consistently anticipate the physical path, having largely overcome such context-bound errors 7 . They have not yet achieved an adult-like theory of motion (systematic but non-Newtonian notions like "impetus" only begin to appear around age 11 7 ), but a 9-year-old’s explicit kinematic reasoning is noticeably more aligned with actual dynamics than a 7-year-old’s. Conversely, the implicit online control stack needed to intercept moving objects is already close to mature by nine: most children can reliably catch fly balls under ordinary conditions, doing so with time-to-contact-based guidance and predictive eye-hand coordination even though smooth-pursuit precision and general predictive motor ability continue to fine-tune into early adolescence 8 , 9 , 10 . This implies the continuation of a clear implicit-explicit gap: nine-year-olds’ actions are often Newton-consistent in interception tasks while their verbal explanations still show straight-down/impetus-like errors on diagrammatic judgments, implying that procedural forward models of dynamics consolidate years before declarative theories do. Material properties of objects By nine, children’s material ontology has been reworked enough that material kind and density become usable causal primitives rather than fragmented perceptual cues. Whereas many seven-year-olds still fold "heavy-for-size" into an undifferentiated weight notion, nine-year-olds typically articulate weight and density as distinct concepts and treat "material" as the constituent substance of an object (not just its surface look), enabling generalizations like "steel is heavy for its size" or knowing that a small steel object can be heavier than a larger aluminum object because steel is a heavier kind of stuff (which hold across changes in shape) 11 . This conceptual differentiation (documented in tasks that probe judgments about size, weight, density, and what counts as "matter") emerges clearly by 8-9 years, alongside a reconstrual of weight as a property of matter per se 11 . Relatedly, buoyancy judgments shift from one-dimension heuristics toward implicit multi-variable integration: compared with 7-year-olds, nine-year-olds more reliably combine mass with volume (and often material kind) when predicting float/sink outcomes for unfamiliar objects, even if their verbal explanations still default to simple rules (another implicit-explicit gap) 12 . Another example of decentration (coordinating multiple dimensions) lies in cross-modal integration: visual-haptic integration for object properties (e.g size or pose) transitions from modality-dominance (where either vision or touch completely overrides the other) to statistically optimal, adult-like cue combination by around 9 years 13 , enabling more accurate and flexible material property judgments; before this age, children show strong single-cue biases even when the dominant modality provides less reliable information than the ignored sense. This emerging cross-modal integration supports more sophisticated material understanding: eight- to nine-year-olds begin extracting material properties from distributed cues rather than relying on isolated features, though their material categories likely remain grounded in familiar exemplars/experiences rather than compositional physical principles. Rule-based taxonomic understanding, part-whole relationships, and identifying defining features of objects/scenes By nine, children’s category system has shifted from the seven-year-old’s heavy reliance on thematic links (e.g dog-leash) and salient superficial/perceptual cues toward explicitly rule-based, taxonomic organization: nine-year-olds are more likely to group by kind and to justify those choices with superordinate relations, not co-occurrence or function (which draws on superficial associations), reflecting the broader developmental tilt toward taxonomic processing in middle childhood 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 (this is, however, not to say that thematic or perceptual categorization are useless abilities 15 ). They now succeed far more reliably on class-inclusion problems (e.g treating "dogs" as a subset of "animals" and reasoning over the hierarchy) whereas younger children rarely solve these consistently under standard task phrasing 19 , 20 ; performance improves as pragmatic confounds (the child misunderstanding the question/task) are controlled 21 . Their concept definitions show the classic characteristic-to-defining shift: compared with seven-year-olds, nine-year-olds increasingly privilege necessary features over merely typical ones ("a triangle has three straight sides," not "looks pointy") and can use those defining rules to classify borderline or appearance-violating cases 4 , 22 , in line with the ongoing shift towards rule-based inference. These children do, however, still appear to struggle on complex categorization tasks (e.g they are adult-level on implicit similarity-based tasks ("All objects that look similar belong to Category A") and single-dimension rule-based tasks ("All red objects belong to Category A") but struggle on tasks with disjunctive rules ("All red OR square objects belong to Category A") 23 ), reflecting persistent logical/abstract difficulties. Tool use/innovation; affordance perception Between ages seven and nine, children see major advancements in tool use and innovation capabilities, moving from simple tool selection to nascent mechanical problem-solving. While technical reasoning appears partially operative from age six onward (allowing children to understand basic means-end relationships in tool use), the ability to spontaneously solve mechanical problems by innovating novel tools emerges in a basic form around age eight, with approximately half of eight-year-olds, for example, succeeding on the canonical hook-making task (requires bending a pipe cleaner into a hook to retrieve an out-of-reach reward) 24 . This is, however, despite these same children demonstrating reliable end-state comfort planning and efficient tool use with familiar implements; this "innovation gap" suggests that prospective motor planning and affordance perception, both present by nine years 10 , are necessary but insufficient for flexible mechanical problem-solving, which additionally requires abstract means-end analysis, causal model manipulation, and systematic hypothesis testing that do not mature until later childhood.

title: Spatial
text: Mental rotation of objects and scenes Relative to the 7-year baseline (faster, more reliable object rotation and emerging but still fragile Level-2 perspective taking) nine-year-olds add measurable speed, scale, and compositionality to spatial transformations. From 7-9, performance on mental rotation tasks (including both objects and scenes) continues to sharply increase 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ; in the classic (and relatively challenging) Mental Rotation Test (MRT), some studies put 9-years-old as the age when children begin performing above chance levels 5 . Beyond improved accuracy, a critical transition toward automatization emerges around age 9: one study demonstrated that motor-mental rotation interference effects present in children younger than 9 years (including 5- and 8-year-olds) disappear around age 9 and in adults 1 , suggesting that mental rotation processes become functionally decoupled from concurrent motor activity at this developmental juncture, which is consistent with studies showing that the rate of improvement in object-based mental rotation tasks may begin to decrease towards the end of this window 2 , 4 . The rate of improvement in the ability to mentally rotate objects appears to begin slowing down towards the end of this age window, while mental rotation of scenes ("perspective taking") is in the midst of its most rapid improvements 6 , 2 , 7 . Overall, these changes mark age nine as a pivot point where children’s spatial computations begin to resemble a genuinely internalized and flexibly deployable transformation system rather than a motor-anchored skill still in the process of consolidation. Navigation, path integration, and cognitive mapping The 7-9 year window marks a critical inflection point in navigation development, defined most saliently by the emergence of proficient cognitive mapping (allocentric spatial representations) and shortcut-taking capabilities that were largely absent at seven. Around age nine, children exhibit a distinct developmental change in their ability to orient and navigate using cognitive maps, demonstrated most clearly by their newfound capacity to identify and use novel shortcuts and detours spontaneously when navigating virtual environments to reach target locations quickly 8 , a cardinal signature of true survey knowledge that seven- and eight-year-olds notably lack when tested under identical conditions (performance does, however, remain far from adult-like 9 ). Starting from age nine, children’s navigational capabilities also expand to encompass large-scale spaces, with metric information being used more frequently and systematically than ever before, and children showing emerging ability to switch between egocentric and allocentric strategies during navigation tasks 10 , 11 , whereas seven-year-olds remain confined primarily to demonstrating competence in small, simplified environments and continue to default to egocentric strategies even when allocentric approaches (viewpoint-independent localization rather than "this-way-then-that-way") would be more efficient. Fundamentally, the capacity for route integration (mentally relating separately learned routes to form a unified spatial representation) shows significant age-related improvement during this window, with within-route knowledge (knowing locations along a single path) developing more rapidly than between-route knowledge (inferring spatial relations between locations learned via different paths), and the latter showing the strongest gains during this window 12 . Overall, the period from 7 to 9 years marks a transition from the piecemeal, route-bound navigation of early childhood to a far more flexible, map-like spatial competence by age nine, characterized by robust allocentric representations, integrated geometric-landmark cues, novel shortcut taking, and greatly enhanced spatial planning and path integration accuracy; performance does, however, remain limited in terms of the rate of errors, the speed of exploration/learning, and in the fusion of self-motion and visual cues 13 .

title: Causal learning and simulation
text: Relational and analogical reasoning During the 7-9 year window, relational and analogical reasoning undergo a qualitative reorganization. These children are undergoing the classic "relational shift": when faced with a conflict between a tempting object/scene match and a relational match (especially a higher-order relational match (e.g., the similarity between an apple falling from a tree, permitting a cow to reach it and a book falling from a shelf, permitting a child to reach it)), featural errors drop sharply across this age range as children increasingly suppress surface lures and map the higher-order relation instead (e.g., in scene analogies and A:B::C:? tasks), whereas seven-year-olds are still frequently captured by perceptual similarity (e.g similar color/shape) or, especially, semantic similarity (e.g dress-closet and milk-cow instead of dress-closet and milk-fridge 1 ) 2 , 3 , 1 ; this shift does, however, appear to often occur before this window but usually in a simpler, domain-specific, or language-scaffolded form 4 , 3 , 5 . On Raven-like relational-integration tasks (similar to those seen in IQ tests), nine-year-olds outperform seven-year-olds (often by a large margin 1 ) and show the developmental signature of greater recruitment of prefrontal systems implicated in selecting task-relevant relations (anterior/rostrolateral PFC), further placing this age at the inflection where controlled relational retrieval and integration start to become reliable 1 , 6 . Inductive and deductive reasoning Closely related to classification abilities, inductive reasoning (drawing generalizations from specific observations; "bottom-up") is a hallmark of Piaget’s concrete operational stage and becomes increasingly sophisticated across this window (while remaining tied to concrete observations). In line with the "relational shift", inductive reasoning shifts from featural similarity toward principled generalization with explicit attention to the informativeness of evidence: by nine, children are more likely than seven-year-olds to prefer diverse over narrow samples when projecting a property within a kind, especially when within-category variability has been highlighted 7 , and they begin to treat larger samples as more reliable 8 , 9 , 10 ; before this window, it is rare to observe sensitivity to sample size and diversity 11 . In naturalistic settings, 7- to 9-year-olds reliably generate inferences from repeated instances (e.g concluding "dinosaurs are big" after observing multiple big dinosaurs), detect regularities in concrete data, and use similarity and typicality (how typical an instance is compared to other category members) to induce properties and transfer them across categories 12 , 13 . Deductive reasoning (drawing specific conclusions from general principles; "top-down") shifts from piecemeal, premise-by-premise responding towards coordinated, model-based inference that integrates multiple premises and actively searches for counterexamples. This window sees a classic inflection point in performance on transitive inference tasks 14 ; seven-year-olds often treat each premise (e.g A>B) locally while nine-year-olds more reliably coordinate the ordered set (e.g., five-term A>B>C>D>E 15 ) and succeed on conflict items that require integrating across premises rather than recalling a single link 16 , 17 , 18 . In conditional reasoning, nine-year-olds show a clear shift from predominantly biconditional interpretations of "if-then" statements (e.g the child assumes it rained if the street is wet) toward genuinely conditional reasoning driven by counterexample search (e.g searching for other explanations for why the ground is wet); this shift is arguably the most robust effect in the developmental conditional reasoning literature and is a signature of the logical, abstract cognition that fully emerges during ensuing developmental windows 19 . Behaviorally, this appears as a rise in "uncertainty" responses on the uncertain conditional forms (e.g understanding the street being wet does not mean it certainly rained) and the first reliable spontaneous production of "disabling conditions" (counterexamples) that block modus ponens (modus ponens: "if P then Q" and "P," conclude "Q") in causal problems (e.g., "the rock hit the window but there was unbreakable film"), with both effects tightly tied to the child’s ability to retrieve alternative causes from memory 20 , 21 . Counterfactual reasoning and episodic future thinking Relative to the 7-year-old baseline, 9-year-olds’ counterfactual reasoning is notably more "causal-structure respecting": instead of solving "what if P had happened?" by simply discarding inconvenient story facts (basic conditional reasoning), they increasingly preserve the actual sequence of events and make the minimal change needed to accommodate the antecedent (the "nearest-possible-world" constraint), which is the hallmark of genuine counterfactual reasoning. Behaviorally, this shows up as near-ceiling, robust performance on singly-determined problems and a rising success rate on classic over-/doubly-determined problems that require holding an alternative cause fixed and knowing "it would still have happened because…". Performance on these problems does, however, vary broadly, in one instance between chance levels 22 and 90-100% success rates 23 . One study involving a real-world, memory-scaffolded task showed that 6- to 7-year-olds could solve doubly-determined questions at a  70% success rate while 8- to 9-year-olds were near-perfect, suggesting that by 9 they can preserve the actual structure and selectively negate just the targeted cause 23 (i.e they are no longer solving via "basic conditional" shortcuts). This task was "memory-scaffolded" in comparison to an earlier design 24 where the child would have to spontaneously retrieve the second cause from memory at test, with no visual cues (e.g the full end-state of the system 25 ) available and even control questions steering attention back to the main actor (e.g children saw Carol and Max dirtying a clean floor, then were asked "If Carol had taken her dirty shoes off, would the floor be clean or dirty?" 22 ); this earlier design saw 9-year-olds falling to chance-level performance 22 , suggesting that counterfactual reasoning is still not a fully-internalized or reliably-deployed cognitive function but is nonetheless becoming more principled/robust in real time. A breakthrough does, however, appear to occur during the next developmental stage (9-12 years). Scientific reasoning Following these advancements in domain-general pattern recognition and reasoning, across the 7-9-year window, children’s scientific reasoning begins to reorganize from largely outcome-driven tinkering toward more explicitly hypothesis- and evidence-guided experimentation, but remains fragile, context-sensitive, and strongly constrained by pragmatic goals. Seven- to nine-year-olds rarely deploy a genuine control-of-variables strategy (VOTAT) spontaneously: left on their own, they typically vary several factors at once, treat any successful outcome as confirming their hunch, and only reliably use unconfounded comparisons when these are modeled, heavily scaffolded, or made highly salient in the task structure 26 , 27 , 28 . Yet when asked to design and reflect on their own investigations, most 2nd graders ( 7-8 years) and an even larger fraction of 4th-5th graders ( 9-11 years) can already conceptualize multiple "spheres" of uncertainty in an inquiry-uncertainty about how to produce the outcome, about the data themselves, about the reliability of an apparent trend, about whether it generalizes, and about which theory best explains it-and can propose concrete modifications (e.g., collecting more trials, refining measures, or changing the manipulation) to reduce the particular uncertainty they notice 29 . In everyday causal scenarios that invite experimentation (e.g., why a cake failed or a paper airplane flew well), 7- to 9-year-olds flexibly choose among vary-one-thing-at-a-time (VOTAT), hold-one-thing-at-a-time (HOTAT), and change-all strategies, but their strategy selection is still governed more by a desire to preserve good outcomes and eliminate bad ones than by a norm of unconfounded testing: even by nine, they tend to hold the suspected causal factor constant when the outcome was positive and only selectively shift toward diagnostic VOTAT experiments for negative outcomes 30 . In structured discovery tasks that explicitly pit plausible against implausible hypotheses (e.g., inferring what a "mystery key" does on a programmable robot), children in this age range can generate rival hypotheses but mainly use experiments to confirm the most plausible one (confirmation bias); only occasionally do they adopt the more advanced, adult-like heuristics of restricting their search to informative experiments that discriminate between alternatives and systematically attending to one feature at a time 31 . Limitations aside, the capacity to generate conclusive tests of concrete hypotheses (including a search for disconfirming or falsifying evidence) is rarely found before this developmental window, reflecting intensifying abstraction of information-seeking behaviors 32 , 33 . Conclusion By around nine years of age, a child’s causal learning and simulation abilities form a genuinely generative, but still concrete-bound, world model. They can track higher-order relational structure across events, use both inductive and deductive constraints to narrow down plausible causes, and increasingly treat "if-then" claims as genuinely conditional, searching for counterexamples rather than automatically accepting a favored story. Their counterfactual simulations tend to respect the actual causal skeleton of events and make minimal changes ("it still would have happened because…"), especially when the situation is well supported by memory or external cues, and they can project the downstream consequences of alternative actions in ways that guide everyday decision-making. At the same time, their experimentation remains outcome-driven and pragmatically biased: they can talk about uncertainty, imagine informative interventions, and occasionally design near-normative tests, but their internal control-of-variables strategy is fragile, unevenly deployed, and heavily scaffolded by the task context. Overall, the nine-year-old’s causal system is best characterized as an emerging, partially explicit "intuitive scientist": capable of structured causal simulation and evidence-based revision in familiar domains, but still limited in how reliably and abstractly those skills are recruited and coordinated.
