title: Executive function
text: Inhibitory control (response inhibition and interference control) During the 7-9 year window, children exhibit strong improvements in inhibitory control capabilities across multiple domains, with this period marking the steepest developmental gains in several key measures. Response times in the flanker task (where a target stimulus is "flanked" by distractors) show their most rapid developmental decline (within the 7- to 12-year window) between ages 7 and 9 1 . This result matches large-sample "stop-signal" data, which show that the capacity to cancel an initiated response sees the same steep trajectory of improvement 2 . Antisaccade work (which measures the ability to inhibit reflexive saccades toward peripheral targets) likewise shows a rapid decline in direction errors across this window, with voluntary response suppression continuing to strengthen from late childhood into adolescence; nine-year-olds commit fewer reflexive saccades than seven-year-olds but are still well short of adult levels, suggesting this is a period of rapid but incomplete consolidation 3 , 4 . Planning Closely related to inhibitory control, this period marks a qualitative shift towards proactive control: nine-year-olds increasingly maintain task goals in advance and pre-configure responses, rather than relying primarily on reactive, late correction, and they modulate that proactive stance with context (e.g cue reliability) more flexibly than younger children 5 , 6 ; children show clear improvements in pre-move deliberation and multi-step look-ahead in both standardized planning tasks and in naturalistic settings. Across tasks designed to measure planning abilities (e.g Tower of London, Stockings of Cambridge), children in this window invest initial thinking time before the first move and, in turn, make fewer extra moves and rule violations, an pattern that is much weaker at seven and becomes reliable (but still far from adult-like) towards the end of this window 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 . In everyday scenarios, the emergence of planning abilities manifests in children making weekend plans with friends 11 , reading with an explicit goal of learning about something of interest 11 , 12 , and fundamental advancements in prospective memory 13 (ability to take previously-planned actions, which predicts planning abilities 14 ). Working memory By nine, working memory is not just "bigger" than at seven; it’s more controllable, precise, and strategically maintained. Capacity and fidelity both improve: visual WM holds more detailed feature information and retains it with higher precision than at age seven, with school-age gains well documented across elementary years 15 . This is reflected in change-detection and delayed-reproduction work showing sharper representations and less misbinding, and in broader syntheses arguing that capacity growth during the school years is genuine rather than an encoding artifact 16 , 17 . At nine, children also cope better with concurrent processing: the "refreshing" of items (attention briefly switching back to revive decaying traces) becomes efficient after about age seven and continues to strengthen 18 , so nine-year-olds maintain lists under distraction more successfully than seven-year-olds. Updating metrics show the same shift: on n-back, 2-back accuracy rises meaningfully from 7-9 even as 1-back nears ceiling, indicating a newly robust ability to monitor, drop, and replace items online 19 . Interference control is another emergent difference: nine-year-olds are less derailed by proactive interference and show a clearer capacity to actively remove outdated contents from WM, reducing intrusion errors that are common at seven 20 , 21 . Verbal maintenance also becomes more "adult-like": forward and backward digit span shows rapid growth across childhood 22 , and by nine children are measurably better at maintaining and manipulating sequences (including on complex/listening span tasks) than at seven; in parallel, rehearsal processes become more consistently deployed and faster, with classic work 23 , 24 placing the emergence and consolidation of spontaneous verbal rehearsal within this developmental window. More sophisticated organizational memory strategies (including chunking and visual imagery that reduce memory load by forming associations) also emerge during this window 25 , fundamentally changing how information is encoded. Underlying these behavioral capabilities is maturation of goal maintenance and attentional control: 7- and 9-year-olds tested on complex span tasks requiring mental arithmetic show that the ability to coordinate storage and processing improves substantially across this window 26 , reflecting developing central executive function. Overall, working memory expansion during this period reflects not merely increased storage capacity, but the acquisition of active maintenance mechanisms, strategic encoding operations, and executive control over the coordination of multiple concurrent cognitive processes. Metacognition Metacognition (which can be broken down into monitoring (confidence/uncertainty and related self-evaluations) and control (regulatory actions conditional on those evaluations)) sees a similarly steep improvement across the 7- to 9-year window, essentially emerging as an operative control system rather than a vague feeling: children not only gauge how certain they are, they use those internal signals to regulate behavior. On paired-associate learning (remembering associations between two items, often stimulus-response) and test-taking paradigms, nine-year-olds show sharper retrospective monitoring than seven-year-olds (their confidence judgments discriminate correct from incorrect answers more reliably, and they are more willing to withdraw low-confidence responses) 27 . Prospective monitoring (thinking about future performance), in contrast, develops far more slowly and remains relatively inaccurate across the 7-9 year range, with children continuing to show overconfidence in predicting future recall performance even as their retrospective judgments become well-calibrated 28 ; converging "metamemory" work, however, indicates that during this window children begin to monitor not only familiarity but also expected memorability 29 and the absence of memory at retrieval 30 , supporting more calibrated decisions about when to restudy, to seek help, or to change an answer. A qualitative step that is typically absent at seven but present by nine is uncertainty monitoring: when items are literally unanswerable, nine-year-olds depress confidence and differentiate "guesses" from ordinary errors, whereas seven-year-olds tend to treat difficult and unanswerable items similarly, evidence that meta-level representations of "I don’t know" have become actionable 31 , 32 , 33 . Similarly, work on children’s understanding of inference as a source of knowledge finds that, relative to 7-year-olds, 9-year-olds become more consistent in judging knowledge gained by valid deduction as more certain than knowledge gained by perception in noisy conditions or by guessing, and they begin to explicitly justify this in terms of the structure of the argument rather than the vividness of the evidence 34 . In reading, nine-year-olds engage in more effective comprehension monitoring: they allocate time to inconsistencies and better detect contradictions in text, and individual differences in this monitoring explain unique variance in comprehension beyond vocabulary and working memory 35 , marking a real behavioral gain in this period; this performance-monitoring loop also shows up in arithmetic tasks, where 7- to 9-year-olds show measurable error detection and adjustment signatures (e.g., post-error slowing/accuracy improvements) that correlate with arithmetic accuracy 36 . Fine-grained feedback appears to be a potent tool for encouraging accurate self-evaluations (and self-regulation) in children and adults 37 . Conclusion Collectively, 7- to 9-year gains in executive function cohere into a single control stack: planning becomes viable precisely because working memory can buffer subgoals and constraints, response inhibition can suppress prepotent or distractor-driven moves, and metacognitive monitoring can track uncertainty and trigger strategy shifts midstream. By nine, executive function is still capacity-limited and not yet adult-like, but the core infrastructure for flexible, goal-directed control is operational: children maintain goals proactively, rehearse and update task-relevant information, inhibit counterproductive impulses, and use confidence signals to decide whether to proceed, pause, or seek more information. That integrated control noticeably lifts non-EF abilities: in language, better goal maintenance and error monitoring support comprehension checks and repair when texts conflict; in social cognition, improved inhibitory control and self-monitoring enable perspective-taking, turn-taking, and reputation-aware restraint; in mental rotation, stronger maintenance and interference control stabilize intermediate transforms and dampen egocentric pull; and in navigation/cognitive mapping, proactive planning plus flexible set-shifting supports route planning, detours, and switching between landmark-based and survey-like strategies. Closing paragraph for what theories of cognitive development say about this age (9) and connect to above capabilities Bring it all together "In this stage, the child is no longer limited to making judgements solely based on the perceptual properties of stimuli, but can instead use logic and perform purely mental operations to make inferences."

title: Neural development
text: Chart hippocampal maturation; relate back to behavioral capabilities acquired Taxonomic classification depends on prefrontal regions and arrives late, while thematic classification arises earlier and depends on X Thus, both forms of categorization-taxonomic and thematic-explain different classes of phenomena and are activated in different contexts, contributing in unique ways to cognition. The general consensus is that these two modes of conceptual organization are functionally different but complementary. This decoupling has been reported in behavioral studies (Borghi & Caramelli, 2003; Coane, McBride, Termonen, & Cutting, 2016; Landrigan & Mirman, 2018; Lin & Murphy, 2001; Masuda & Nisbett, 2001; Mirman & Graziano, 2012; Pluciennicka, Coello, & Kalenine, 2016), neuroimaging studies (Chen et al., 2013, Lewis, Poeppel, & Murphy, 2015; Sachs, Weis, Krings, Huber, & Kircher, 2008; Schwartz et al., 2011), and neuropsychological studies (Davidoff & Roberson, 2004; Kalenine, Mirman, & Buxbaum, 2012). Retrosplenial cortex (a subregion of the posterior cingulate cortex; responsible for egocentric-allocentric transforms), a transmodal hub sitting atop the principal gradient, has likely benefited from its input regions finally maturing/stabilizing and has now begun to mature itself, along with other higher-order, transmodal regions; for example, the emergence of reliable class inclusion marks the growing maturity of the anterior temporal cortex, which must integrate disparate object-centric information (e.g visual appearance, tactile memories, tool-use memories) to provide a full characterization of objects. Neuroimaging studies by Houdé et al. (2011) reveal that 9-10-year-old conservers show bilateral parietofrontal network activation, particularly in the right inferior frontal gyrus associated with inhibitory control, while 5-6-year-old non-conservers show no such activation 1 . Looking closely at frontal activity, Jonkman (2006) found a linear increase in no-go P3 amplitude (a positive wave 300 - 500 ms after stimulus presentation) across development: Children ages 6-7 showed no P3 activity, children ages 9-10 showed limited P3 activity in frontal-central electrodes, and young adults showed broad P3 activity across frontal and frontal-central electrodes (see also Jonkman el al., 2003). P3 activity has been interpreted to index the allocation of attentional resources during stimulus engagement, with greater activity representing greater resource allocation (Polich, 1987). In contrast, the no-go N2 response (a negative wave 150 - 400 ms after stimulus presentation) decreased across the same age span, with the largest decrease in amplitude occurring between ages 6 and 10. Complementing these behavioral gains, EEG studies using child-friendly flanker paradigms report more differentiated N2/P3 signatures of conflict detection and resolution by this window, consistent with a more reliable recruitment of control when distractors must be filtered 2 Taxonomic signatures in semantic memory Rostrolateral PFC coming online?

title: Language
text: Vocabulary Between ages 9 and 12, children’s vocabulary grows explosively, both in size and in depth of understanding. A 9-year-old’s lexicon, though large, is still rooted in everyday conversational words and concrete terms. By 12, children have acquired thousands of new words, including the academic and abstract vocabulary needed for school learning 1 . This reflects the mid-childhood shift from "learning to read" to "reading to learn," which typically occurs by 4th grade (around age 9-10) 2 . As 12-year-olds read textbooks and broader literature, they encounter and master specialized terms in science, math, and social studies (e.g. photosynthesis, fraction, government), words rarely found in casual conversation at age 9 1 . Morphological sophistication continues to accelerate as derivational morphology becomes increasingly productive, allowing children to parse and generate novel forms with greater facility than at nine 3 , 4 , 1 ; they parse unfamiliar words into bases plus affixes, use Greek/Latin combining forms to triangulate meanings (photo-/bio-/-logy, electro-/-magnet-/-ism), and flexibly shift parts of speech via nominalizations and adjectival derivations that saturate textbooks (predict->prediction; molecule->molecular) 3 . This shift goes beyond the robust 7-9 surge: knowledge of derived forms and multi-morphemic items becomes a principal driver of vocabulary expansion through late elementary and into middle school 5 , and performance on derived-word tasks and CALS (Core Academic Language Skills) assessments increasingly predicts reading comprehension in informational text. Syntax Children’s sentence structures also undergo a marked increase in complexity. By age 9, most children command the fundamental grammar of their language and produce complex sentences in conversation; however, their sentences tend to be relatively short (on the order of 7 words; e.g "I went to the pool and swam") and tied to familiar structures. By age 12, children can reliably comprehend and generate much more elaborate syntax 6 , 1 , including subordinate clauses, conditional sentences, and varied word orders 1 that were challenging at 9. There is a clear rise in the use of multi-clause sentences 7 : for example, a 12-year-old might say or write, "I did my homework after I ate dinner because I wanted to watch TV later," comfortably embedding adverbial and causal clauses. In fact, one study notes that persuasive essays written by children this age heavily employ subordinate clauses and causal connectors as key linguistic resources 8 , illustrating how syntax becomes a tool for organizing complex ideas. Comparatively, a 9-year-old’s persuasive attempt might rely on simpler coordination (e.g. stringing ideas with "and") rather than such embedded structures. Dual meanings Semantic development between 9 and 12 years is characterized by a shift from concrete, literal interpretations toward a richer understanding of abstract and non-literal meaning. One important change is the handling of multiple-meaning words. A 9-year-old might recognize that some common words have more than one meaning (for example, "cold" as a temperature vs. "a cold" illness) and find simple jokes about homophones funny; however, by 12, children not only understand many polysemous words but can also explain the different meanings and how context determines the interpretation (e.g a 12-year-old can clarify that a "tie" you wear versus "to tie a knot" are related by a notion of joining but are used differently as noun and verb 1 ). They also become proficient in providing superordinate and subordinate relations among concepts (e.g. knowing that sparrow is a type of bird, which is a type of animal, etc.), and in understanding metaphorical categorizations (e.g. that "school can be a second home" is not literal but conveys an abstract relationship). Figurative language Perhaps the most noticeable leap in this age range is in figurative language comprehension and production. Children around age 9 are beginning to "get" some figurative expressions; they laugh at basic puns, enjoy simple similes or metaphors (like "as busy as a bee"), and may understand common idioms if given enough context. Yet, their interpretations can still be literal or incomplete. By age 12, many figurative forms that baffled younger children become intelligible (tracking with an overall "less literal understanding of language" 9 ). For example, 12-year-olds generally understand common idioms such as "knocked my socks off" or "in hot water", even if they might not articulate exactly why the phrases mean what they do 9 , 1 . Learning idioms and metaphors is certainly a gradual process, but by the end of childhood most kids can interpret at least the common idioms in context 1 . They also start to grasp proverbs and more culturally bound figurative sayings by early adolescence; a 12-year-old may not fully explain a proverb like "A picture paints a thousand words" in the abstract, but can often interpret its meaning within a given context, a capability that typically solidifies in the years shortly after 12 1 . Narratives and autobiography Reflecting broader linguistic advancements, this window marks a significant transition in narrative and autobiographical memory, shifting from foundational storytelling (i.e acquisition of the abilities to include multiple episodes, evaluative comments, and causal chaining by age 9) to more organized, analytical, and integrated narrative comprehension and construction 10 , 11 , 12 . Surfacing in both autobiographical and fictitious accounts, their narratives see substantial maturation both in terms of their coherence (i.e proposing a story structured in several steps at the temporal, causal and thematic levels; at the level of the overall macrostructure) 13 , 14 , 15 and cohesion (i.e the creation of links between two statements; at the microstructure level) 16 , with some suggesting that these abilities begin to plateau (reaching near adult levels) around age 12 16 , but other evidence suggesting that these abilities continue to grow more sophisticated/strategic well past this window (which aligns with naturalistic observations) 17 , 18 . Likewise, the specificity of remembered and imagined events increases, and children’s narratives become more semantically rich (i.e more consistently answering who-what-where-when-why and approaching greater "completeness") as shown longitudinally 19 , 20 . Despite these gains, 9-12-year-olds remain less likely than older adolescents and adults to fully integrate trait descriptors, second-order beliefs 21 , and other social-cognitive information into their stories, with performance still sensitive to social-cognitive processing demands and the structural importance of that information 22 . Overall, by age 12 there is a convergence between broad world knowledge (cause-effect relations, event schemas, protagonists’ goal-directed behavior) and knowledge of narrative conventions (e.g story grammar 23 ) to yield the ability to construct and revise multi-episode situation models that maintain global coherence while flexibly integrating local details during both comprehension and production. This window also foreshadows the adolescent turn toward identity/self-conceptual development, as youths increasingly leverage autobiographical memory and burgeoning narrative reasoning to assemble more coherent self-stories and explore commitments 24 ; by the midpoint of this window, children can understand periods in history, seem to have a fully developed ability to reason about time on an abstract level 25 , and their tendency to group their life stories into coherent periods or "chapters" is increasing rapidly 26 .

title: Social
text: Perspective taking / ToM + moral reasoning Between 9 and 12, moral cognition shifts towards coordinated, principle-based reasoning that recruits third-person perspective taking (while remaining anchored in rule-following and appeals to authority). By 12, most children can simultaneously represent the perspectives of multiple actors (including a neutral observer) and use this coordination to adjudicate conflicts between motives, duties, and consequences (Selman’s "mutual/third-person" level that typically emerges across roughly 10-12+ years) 1 , 2 . This social-cognitive upgrade scaffolds several moral advances in this window, with "third-order" theory of mind supporting reasoning about nested beliefs and reputation management 3 , and cognitive empathy showing rapid gains that make it easier to forecast how different parties will evaluate the same act 4 . Applied to resource and fairness dilemmas, children around 10-11 often rectify group-level inequalities with no in-group bias and a tendency to allocate more to disadvantaged out-groups 5 , and by the end of the window many endorse equity when effort or productivity differs (even if outcomes are unequal) while also becoming more capable of jointly weighing need and effort 6 , 7 . Their judgments also grow more permissive of necessary harms to prevent greater harms, reflecting increased tolerance for trade-offs and side-effects in complex scenarios 8 . In Kohlberg’s framework, most children here sit in the conventional stage, prioritizing shared norms and perceived expectations (especially of authorities) when justifying moral choices, even as perspective-taking and principle-based reasoning begin to loosen a strict dependence on authority pronouncements 9 . Pragmatics Pragmatics becomes adult-like in ways that nine-year-olds typically cannot yet sustain. By twelve, children reliably infer speaker intent in nonliteral language, distinguishing ironic compliments from sarcastic criticisms, tracking attitude and politeness goals, and using prosody and context to recover "what was really meant" 10 ; they can now modulate their interpretation of irony based on what the listener knows 11 , meaning they model common ground and adjust their pragmatic readout accordingly (something far weaker before this age window). Relatedly, faux-pas detection (recognizing when someone unintentionally says something socially inappropriate) improves across late childhood; nine-year-olds succeed in simple stories, but by  11-12 performance is robust across subtler narratives, indicating more reliable access to second-order beliefs ("she didn’t know he didn’t know…") 12 . Self identity These children also undergo a fundamental shift in how they conceptualize themselves, moving from concrete, role- and behavior-bound descriptions toward a more abstract, integrative identity that explains actions in terms of enduring motives, principles, and trade-offs. Their value descriptions become more abstract, more likely to transcend specific situations, and more motivation-based rather than behavior-based 13 : a child who once said "I help my mom with dishes" now articulates "I care about being helpful to people." Across this same window, children develop the capacity to increasingly resolve value conflicts and take stances that reflect their value priorities, such as when the desire to "care for others" conflicts with the desire for status or power 14 . This represents a shift from holding multiple, potentially contradictory self-concepts in separate mental compartments to actively integrating them into a coherent hierarchy. In parallel, they move beyond compartmentalizing different "selves" across home, school, and peer contexts, learning to compare and reconcile contrasting self-descriptions ("I’m outspoken with friends but cautious in class") into higher-order traits and conditional rules that preserve coherence across settings, rather than treating them as disconnected identity fragments 15 . This integration process essentially builds a value-based operating system for identity, where abstract motivational states govern behavior across contexts rather than context-specific behavioral scripts. title: Physics, objects, motor control, and tools
text: Physics, and mechanics of objects Between ages 9 and 12, children see significant progress in their understanding of intuitive and explicit physics, along with related advancements in their understanding of objects and their utilization of tools. In "physics" per se, a landmark is that by roughly age 11 most children succeed on conservation-of-volume problems (e.g same amount of a liquid but in a taller glass), recognizing that quantity remains constant despite perceptual changes in appearance 1 . On balance-beam problems, the modal strategy shifts from the weight-only or distance-only rules common around age 9 (Rule I/II) to Rule III, where weight and distance are jointly coordinated; by the end of this window the distribution of rule use approaches the adult profile, reflecting reliable multi-dimensional integration in physical problem solving 2 , 3 . In trajectory prediction, younger children are easily captured by salient but irrelevant contextual features (e.g the relative location of objects), whereas by 1̃2 performance is much improved and, more importantly, a substantial fraction of responses reflect engagement of an "impetus" conception, applying rudimentary physics principles rather than purely perceptual strategies 4 . In terms of applied physics, the same shift from percept-bound to principle-based reasoning is visible when children explain and predict the behavior of familiar mechanical artifacts. Direct evidence is surprisingly sparse, but where it exists it points to clear structural change. When asked "how a bicycle works," children’s explanations between 6 and 8 years are relatively flat and largely descriptive (naming parts, focusing on visible motion), with a noticeable step-wise improvement around 8-9 and continued gains through 9-10 as they begin to invoke hidden force-transmission mechanisms (e.g., chains transferring pedal force to wheels, the role of gears in trading off speed and torque) 5 . Similarly, across this window their reasoning about simple gear trains becomes more principled and generalizable: rather than treating each configuration as a new visual puzzle, older children increasingly extract and apply abstract rules about motion transmission (e.g., "adjacent gears rotate in opposite directions") and can justify speed differences in terms of gear-size ratios rather than surface features 6 . Speculatively, these advances in mechanical reasoning are mirrored in tool choice and tool sequencing during problem solving: by  12, many children can pick or improvise tools based on leverage, force redirection, and mechanical advantage rather than trial-and-error exploration alone, and can mentally "run" simple mechanisms forward to anticipate downstream consequences. Taken together with the more formal understanding of conservation, balance, and trajectories described above, these developments suggest that between 9 and 12 the child’s mechanical world model is upgraded from a patchwork of local heuristics about specific devices at age 9 to something closer to a compact, compositional physics engine by age 12-one that can be flexibly deployed to explain, predict, and manipulate novel physical systems in a way that begins to resemble an adult’s principled grasp of the physical world. Multisensory cue integration Another interesting capability reflecting decentration in late childhood is multisensory (multimodal) cue integration, where children begin to move from relying on a single, salient cue to combining multiple, partially redundant cues in something like an uncertainty-weighted, Bayesian way. For example, one study found that no participants younger than 12 were able to optimally integrate binocular visual disparity and surface texture information to reduce their uncertainty in judging the slant of a surface 7 , with 12-year-olds clearly remaining below adult levels. Similarly, in another study the integration of multiple cues for depth perception (integrating visual disparity and relative motion) does not emerge (as measured both in terms of task accuracy and associated sensory-fusion activity in cortex) until roughly age 11, and then shows protracted development thereafter 8 . By contrast, size and orientation prediction for objects may become statistically optimal, approaching adult-like weighting of visual and haptic information, during this age window (perhaps during the first half) 9 . Thus, compared to 9-year-olds who still tend to treat individual modalities or cues in isolation, 12-year-olds are beginning to construct a more integrated, reliability-sensitive, and uncertainty-aware multisensory world model, even though their cue fusion remains less efficient and less automatic than in adults. Knowledge of object taxonomies and classification abilities Between ages 9 and 12, the rule-based (explicit) categorization system undergoes a critical maturation phase ("maturation" as in the system’s efficiency and consistency of deployment) 10 ; while 9-year-olds often default to guessing when faced with complex classification tasks, 10- to 11-year-olds reach near-adult levels of consistency in applying rule-based strategies 11 . This same period appears to mark the emergence of strategic flexibility, for instance the ability to switch between thematic and taxonomic classification modes based on task demands. Children begin distinguishing when to use associative clustering (associating dog-bone because they co-occur in stories) versus categorical clustering (associating dog-cat because both are mammals) 12 , selecting the appropriate strategy for contexts like creative writing versus biology study; this is essentially the development of meta-cognitive control over different classification algorithms, allowing task-appropriate deployment of different representational schemes. The nature of the features children use for taxonomic classification also transforms dramatically across this window. Between 9 and 12, there’s a steep increase in children’s tendency to classify objects based on intensive properties (intrinsic characteristics like material composition or state of matter) rather than extensive properties like shape or size 13 . So a 12-year-old is much more likely than a 9-year-old to group a metal fork and metal can together as "metal objects" rather than grouping by superficial perceptual features. However, even the older children often rely on salient prototypes (like identifying "air" as the basis for grouping gases) rather than true abstract concepts, suggesting they’re still transitioning from instance-based to principle-based causal models, particularly in complex conceptual domains like matter and substance. Viewed through multiple-systems accounts of category learning, late childhood is the period when the explicit, rule-based route reliably wins the arbitration against the implicit, similarity-based route, although the discovery of optimal rules for classification sees continued development. When irrelevant dimensions are salient or feedback is noisy, these children can still be captured by perceptual similarity or revert to guessing: compared with adults, 8-12-year-olds remain less able to suppress an irrelevant dimension during rule application and are more brittle when the correct rule requires coordinating multiple cues or switching midstream 14 . Motor control and tool use Predictive manipulation shows a clear step-change. In precision grip-lift tasks (e.g lifting something with only the thumb and index finger), children progressively shift from corrective, feedback-heavy lifts to anticipatory grip-force scaling that matches object weight and friction before contact, with classic longitudinal work indicating that the core feedforward capacity reaches an adult-like range by about 8-11 15 ; related work on predictive motor ability indicates that performance is in the adult range by about 12 on tasks requiring forecasting and acting on a forthcoming state 16 . In practical terms, 12-year-olds can time interceptive actions (e.g., catching, striking) with far less over-reliance on late feedback than 9-year-olds (with interceptive actions, for example, being near adult-level at 12 16 ), who are more easily derailed by occlusion, acceleration, or context shifts. Complementing predictive manipulation, online corrections also improve rapidly across this window: studies of constant isometric force (where muscular force perfectly matches resistance, e.g when holding a heavy object steady) show reductions in output noise and much more adult-like reweighting of visual and somatosensory feedback 17 , and evidence from developmental movement-perturbation paradigms shows that the speed and accuracy of rapid online corrections continue to improve rapidly across this window 18 . Graphomotor control (handwriting) also crosses an important threshold. Cross-sectional analyses show handwriting speed climbs steeply from 8 to 10 and then stabilizes through 12, while "graphic" drawing speed (non-word writing speed) continues to improve from 10 to 12 19 , evidence that by 12 the motor program itself has become more fluent even when central linguistic load is held constant. Consistent with that picture, the influence of lexical frequency on stroke timing is prominent at 8 but largely disappears by  11 19 , indicating reduced central bottlenecks and greater automatization of the peripheral motor routine. Consistent with these advancements, the ability to use tools develops rapidly between 9 and 12, reflecting advance mechanical reasoning abilities 20 ; 12-year-olds can independently and proficiently use simple tools such as hammers, scissors, and screwdrivers, engage in complex crafts like jewelry-making and model building, and execute intricate drawing tasks with spatial precision that was not consistently achievable at age 9. Again reflecting rapidly advancing mechanical reasoning skills, tool use innovation (making a new functional tool to complete a task) moves from nascent (classically nascent at age 8) to reliable by 12 20 , although age effects on tool innovation tasks persist until around young adulthood. Essential for everyday function and skilled tool use, bimanual coordination becomes meaningfully more independent. At 12, children show smaller "circles-lines" interference (drawing different figures simultaneously with each hand) 21 and can better sustain asymmetric/rhythmic patterns without one hand being captured by the other’s dynamics, reflecting improved interhemispheric coordination and higher-level control policies. Nine-year-olds, by contrast, still exhibit strong spatial coupling and phase-locking in dual tasks. By around age 12, the motor system has achieved near-adult precision and fluidity under familiar conditions: children can anticipate object dynamics, stabilize posture under shifting sensory inputs, and coordinate multi-joint and bimanual movements smoothly and deliberately. Fine motor sequences like handwriting or instrument fingering are automated and resilient to cognitive distraction, while gross motor actions like running, turning, and balancing are supported by mature cerebellar feedforward control and executive oversight. Yet some limitations remain. Under novel or highly time-critical conditions, predictive models are still less stable and adaptable than in adults, leading to greater variability in unpracticed coordination, fatigue-sensitive endurance, and fine force scaling. In essence, the 12-year-old possesses a well-calibrated, efficient control architecture, but one whose internal models and strength parameters are still fine-tuning toward the adult brain’s precision and robustness. Conclusion Inferred capabilities Fully "decentralized" (can coordinate multiple dimensions at once); can now simulate multiple interacting material and geometric properties at once (e.g a bowling ball falling on top of a paper object, then rolling down a hill) in a way that is functionally relevant (e.g a pencil is thin and sturdy so it can fit in my hand and won’t bend) Large repository of objects’ materials, components, and mechanicsm which are now explicitly defined (including causally and functionally defined) and reasoned against ?? Devising novel uses for objects (e.g using a mug to hold pens) ?? Fully concrete operational: now essentially operating with the core architecture for flexible and robust concrete/physical simulation ("physical common sense") semantic categories of physical entities, causal schemas for interaction types, and probabilistic priors over outcomes have all become both densely populated and dynamically linked by 12, many children can (a) infer latent mechanical structure (center of mass, torque, friction), (b) run counterfactuals on that latent structure ("what if it were heavier / what if there was no friction?"), (c) select and even manufacture tools to exploit that structure, and (d) physically execute the required manipulation with anticipatory control rather than trial-and-error brute force Limitations Quantitative precision and dynamic parameter estimation: their internal physics engine has the correct architecture but suboptimal parameters; needs some fine-tuning still. Extracting hidden constraints from minimal data: adults can watch a complex mechanism briefly and infer latent degrees of freedom, friction properties, or load-bearing limits. This requires not just simulation but meta-learned priors about what physical variables matter in novel contexts. Kids overgeneralize or miss subtle cues. Predicting edge cases and failure modes: Adult physical intuition shines in knowing when things will break, slip, or behave unexpectedly under stress. This comes from accumulated prediction errors (including long-horizon prediction errors); a 12-year-old hasn’t debugged their models on enough corner cases or long-horizon projects/observations. Compositional generalization to novel physical systems: Consider how adults quickly grasp unfamiliar tools, sports equipment, or mechanical systems by composing known physical principles. This requires rich, well-factorized representations that transfer flexibly. Kids’ models are more brittle and context-bound. Overall, 11-12 is when you have a functioning forward model but nowhere near the prediction accuracy, generalization bandwidth, or error-corrected priors of an adult; essentially the difference between a high-fidelity but narrowly trained simulator and a fully generalizable world model.

title: Spatial
text: Mental rotation of objects and scenes Between 9 and 12 years of age, children’s mental rotation of both objects and scenes becomes faster, more accurate, and more automatic, pushing their spatial transformations closer to an adult-like regime. For object-based tasks, one recent study using 3D cube aggregates (i.e 4-6 connected colored cubes) found roughly 10% higher mental-rotation accuracy in 10-11-year-olds than in 8-9-year-olds, suggesting a meaningful boost in how efficiently children can encode, chunk, and transform multi-part configurations in working memory 1 . Over the same age range, scene rotation (perspective-taking) tasks show parallel improvements: when asked to imagine another person’s viewpoint across a range of angular disparities, 12-year-olds produce faster, more reliable judgments about what the other person sees and how left-right relations change with viewpoint, reflecting a growing ability to use genuine mental rotation of the whole scene (rather than ad hoc visual matching or rule-based guessing) to solve these problems 2 , 3 . Overall, these trends suggest that between 9 and 12, children’s overall spatial cognitive repertoire consolidates into a more unified, high-capacity "3D workspace" in which objects and viewpoints can be rapidly and flexibly transformed, supporting more sophisticated navigation, tool use, and social perspective taking. Navigation and cognitive mapping By 9 years of age, children possess a rudimentary cognitive map that lets them handle large-scale spaces, identify shortcuts using metric information, and switch between egocentric and allocentric reference frames; between 9 and 12, navigation performance on top of this scaffold improves rapidly and mostly smoothly rather than via sharp qualitative jumps. Across this window, the quantity and quality of landmarks and directions that children can produce and recognize in both verbal and visuospatial tasks increase, they more reliably select decisional landmarks (those at choice points), and they become better at binding landmarks to the directions that follow them 4 . They also show higher accuracy in learning a new environment after a single exposure, particularly in large virtual environments 5 , and they more spontaneously switch between egocentric and allocentric strategies rather than sticking rigidly to a single frame of reference 6 , 7 . Exploration becomes faster and more efficient across a variety of environments 8 , 6 , 9 , while susceptibility to confusion under rotations or rearrangements of landmarks and other navigational cues decreases, indicating more stable underlying spatial reference frames 10 , 11 . By around 12 years, several studies indicate that overall navigation performance is broadly similar to adults but still noticeably slower and more error prone 12 , 13 . For instance, in large-scale virtual navigation tasks, 12-year-olds can reach adult levels of performance 14 , 15 , and can even be categorized into the same three adult-like groups: imprecise navigators (who form only imprecise ideas of routes), non-integrators (who represent routes more accurately but are imprecise in relating two routes), and integrators (who relate the two routes and, thus, form cognitive maps) 15 . At the level of cue integration and environmental structure, 10-11-year-olds are already near-optimal in combining visual and self-motion information when reproducing a walked path, especially under challenging conditions such as darkness 16 , and by 11 they can "regularize" irregular environments whose layout must be inferred from the inclination and angle of maze walls, matching adult performance 17 . Overall, these findings suggest that 12-year-olds operate with a fast, flexibly updatable, near-adult cognitive map in which landmarks, routes, metrics, and multiple reference frames are tightly integrated, meaning that their world model for large-scale space has become a richly structured, inferential map that can support efficient navigation and planning in complex environments. Essentially, these children are "zooming out" and beginning to abstract from their immediate environments to derive efficient, reusable strategies for long-horizon tasks; one way this is apparent in the spatial domain is in the more-rapid advancement of extrinsic (between-object relationships) spatial cognition relative to intrinsic (within-object relationships) during this window 18 .

title: Causal learning and simulation
text: Abstract thinking (11+ years): Thinking shifts from being tied to physical objects to operating on abstract ideas. Adolescents can reason about concepts that are not directly experienced. this is effectively where the agent transitions from a system that optimizes known policies within a familiar state space to a system capable of hypothesis testing and zero-shot generalization via structural mapping; there is movement from analyzing things to analyzing the relations between things. Inductive, deductive, counterfactual, and scientific reasoning; generating and deploying abstract world models Between 7 and 9, children effectively shift from "piecemeal, premise-by-premise responding" toward "coordinated, model-based inference". They can integrate multiple premises into a coherent whole and have begun to actively search for counterexamples in conditional reasoning tasks. However, these capabilities remain fragile. They are "memory-scaffolded" (mental encoding of relevant states and transitions is unreliable) and heavily reliant on the semantic content of the problem matching the agent’s prior experience. Overall, the 9-year-old is a master of the actual ; they reason well about what is, or what is likely to be based on what has been (what has directly presented itself; the concept of "democracy", for instance, tends to escape them). The 12-year-old, conversely, begins their emergence as a master of the possible : the primary computational gain during the 9-12 year window is the decoupling of the internal world model from empirical inputs. This decoupling allows them to perform valid logical operations on hypothetical, indeterminate, and even belief-contradicting premises (including simulating their implications). It is essentially the birth of the "virtual laboratory" within the mind, where variables can be isolated, history can be rewritten (counterfactuals), and future branches can be rigorously stress-tested without the interference of current sensory data or strong semantic priors. As a result, the window between ages 9 and 12 marks a transition from largely instance-bound, association-driven generalization over concrete regularities to increasingly explicit, hypothesis-guided coordination of evidence with abstract causal theories. Inductive reasoning In terms of inductive reasoning, performance on classic inductive reasoning tasks (often abstract, relational, and IQ-test-like 1 , 2 ) shows steep gains across this period, with the broader developmental curve suggesting that some of the fastest improvements in induction occur from late childhood ( 10-12) into early adolescence ( 12-14), starting in earnest here and accelerating into the 12-14 range 1 , 3 , 1 , 4 . These gains are driven in part by better evidence evaluation: children become more sensitive to whether a sample is diverse, representative, and large enough to justify a generalization 5 , 6 . They also become better at detecting meaningful subcategories within a kind, reflecting advanced conditional modeling ("X is true for this subtype, but not necessarily for all members") 6 . These gains are not confined to matrix puzzles and figure analogies; they are increasingly visible in everyday reasoning. Inductive ability in this window is strongly coupled to improvements in fluid intelligence, scientific reasoning, and school achievement in mathematics and science, such that older children’s higher induction scores partly mediate their advantage in STEM learning and complex problem solving 1 , 7 , 8 , 9 . In everyday contexts, we can go down the list of behavioral/cognitive advancements that are driven by advanced inductive reasoning. In language, stronger figurative/idiom/proverb understanding reflects causal-pragmatic hypothesis testing about speaker intent and non-literal mappings, and the shift from episodic storytelling to detailed narratives with causal chaining and "global coherence" demonstrates an ability to structure information logically, integrate evidence from real-world episodes, and link events through cause-and-effect frameworks. Reading comprehension also benefits, with 12-year-olds more reliably extracting thematic patterns and inferring character traits from samples across contexts 10 . Socially, moral reasoning shifts toward coordinating multiple perspectives (including third-person viewpoints), indicating improved causal attribution across interacting agents and rule-based evaluation of conflicts; the ability to simulate a "neutral observer" view to adjudicate conflicts reflects a detached, quasi-scientific capability to weigh evidence objectively outside of one’s own bias. Self-concept shifts from concrete behaviors to abstract traits/values and children start resolving value conflicts, reflecting principled causal reasoning about motives that generalize across contexts. In the domain of physical objects, the transition to weighting multisensory cues (visual, haptic) based on reliability suggests the brain is adopting a probabilistic, uncertainty-aware approach to inferring latent variables, while strategic switching between thematic and taxonomic classification shows metacognitive control over which inductive scheme fits the causal structure of the task. Spatially, navigation gains (better decisional landmarks, landmark-direction binding, one-trial learning) reflect inductive construction and refinement of causal cognitive maps; the capacity to integrate distinct routes into a survey-like map reflects the logical synthesis of fragmented spatial experiences into a unified global model. Metacognitively, 12-year-olds show a more adult-like ability to evaluate the quality of everyday arguments, for example judging a friend’s decision not to study as a "bad way of thinking" even if it happened to lead to a good grade and explicitly justifying their judgment by appeal to the unreliability of the reasoning process rather than the outcome, reflecting a shift toward process-based, metacognitively monitored induction in everyday scenarios 11 , 12 . By age 12, then, the typical child’s inductive reasoning has moved from the largely concrete, episodic, and outcome-focused profile of a 9-year-old to a qualitatively more adult-like, explicit, abstract, and process-based system that can monitor sample quality, consider alternative hypotheses, and track causal coherence, even though it still falls short of mature adult induction in reliability, capacity, speed, and domain-generality. Deductive reasoning Deductive reasoning between ages 9 and 12 shifts from a fragile, content-bound competence into the early stages of "true" logical reasoning, where children begin to coordinate multiple premises, detach from immediate belief, and explicitly track logical necessity versus mere plausibility. While younger children rely heavily on heuristic processing, 12-year-olds are much more likely to suppress an immediately compelling but invalid response and instead work through the premises analytically 13 , allowing them to construct and test multiple mental models of a problem rather than settling on a single, salient interpretation 14 . In conditional reasoning, this shows up as a reduced tendency to "collapse" one-way rules into biconditionals: 12-year-olds are much less likely than 9-year-olds to affirm the consequent (e.g., inferring from "If something is a car, then it has a motor; it has a motor" that it must be a car), with this improvement being particularly noticeable in cases where the antecedent and consequent are strongly associated in semantic memory 15 , 16 . Across this window, children show a steady increase in their ability to retrieve counterexamples ("things with motors that are not cars") and disabling conditions ("reasons why the usual cause would not produce the effect here") when evaluating "if-then" rules 17 , 18 . Belief-bias effects are correspondingly weakened: 12-year-olds are more willing to endorse logically valid but factually strange conclusions and to reject believable but invalid ones, indicating that they can let the internal causal/schematic model be constrained by the stipulated premises rather than by their default world knowledge. The same pattern appears in syllogistic reasoning: 12-year-olds are less susceptible to belief bias in classic syllogism tasks, and they are better able to construct and test multiple mental models of the premises ("All A are B; some B are C; what about A and C?"), rather than relying on a single content-driven image 19 , 14 . On transitive inference and linear-ordering problems with five-term series, performance between 9 and 12 begins to approach ceiling under manageable memory demands: by 12, many children reliably build an ordered internal representation (A>B>C>D>E) and query it flexibly, instead of computing each comparison in isolation, and age differences now look more like differences in strategy and representational load than in basic logical competence 20 , 21 . Meta-logically, 12-year-olds display a far more explicit grasp of the various "flavors" of inference, including those based in logical necessity: they differentiate necessary truths (e.g., simple tautologies and arithmetic identities) from empirical regularities and social conventions, judge them as universally and unchangeably true, and increasingly report that they "cannot imagine" a genuine violation, capturing the idea that some conclusions follow in all possible worlds compatible with the premises 22 . They are also much better at distinguishing deduction from guessing and from mere perception, at grading the certainty of different knowledge sources, and at explaining in words that "you know that because you figured it out from the rule," not because you saw it; judgments that deduction is more certain than guessing are now backed by explicit reference to inferential structure rather than surface cues 23 . Functionally, this makes deduction start to operate as a general-purpose "constraint engine" over internal simulations: given a hypothesis space specified by premises, the 12-year-old can construct and compare alternative possible states of the world, apply abstract if-then rules to those simulated states, and privilege conclusions that are logically necessary within the stipulated model even when they conflict with prior belief or perceptual salience. This competence is, however, still emerging rather than fully mature: belief-bias effects remain robust in many paradigms, especially when propositions are emotionally or socially loaded 24 , and 12-year-olds still find it much more demanding to reason with counterfactual causal premises than with familiar factual ones 25 . Broadly, conditional reasoning with categorical premises is solid by around 7-8 years, but reliable logical treatment of familiar causal conditionals only becomes typical in the 10-12 range; extending the same level of competence to counterfactual and fully abstract conditionals is more characteristic of mid-adolescence and adulthood 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 . In everyday life, the upshot is that a 12-year-old can increasingly treat rules, promises, and causal claims as operators over a space of possibilities, probing "what follows if we all obey this rule?", "what if this assumption is wrong?", or "could both of these stories be true at the same time?", and can call out a peer’s argument as "not making sense" even when the conclusion is attractive, because they are now evaluating the structure of the reasoning rather than just its outcome; a 12-year-old might catch a parent in a contradiction not just by pointing to facts, but by highlighting the flaw in the logic itself ("You said we couldn’t go because of the rain, but now that it’s stopped, you’re changing the rule"), effectively treating the conversation as a system of premises that must remain consistent. Counterfactual reasoning Counterfactual reasoning, a form of reasoning in which one contemplates a change to a mental representation and tracks the causal implications of that change 30 , is the natural test case for this emerging "virtual laboratory": it is where deductive, causal, and simulational capacities have to be tightly integrated. Structurally, a good counterfactual inference is a constrained deductive inference over an altered world model ("if P had been different, then Q would/would not have occurred"), but computationally it is much harder than the factual cases described above, because the child must maintain at least two models in parallel (the actual and the imagined), decide what to hold fixed, and then propagate the consequences of the stipulated change in a way that respects the underlying causal structure, ultimately allowing the agent to debug past errors and anticipate future regret. Between 7 and 9, children can already answer simple "what if" questions when the story is short, the critical dependency is highlighted, and there is a single, salient causal chain; but they frequently default to basic conditional reasoning (ignoring parts of the actual sequence or overwriting it wholesale) rather than respecting the "nearest-possible-world" constraint, especially when there are multiple potential causes or non-trivial temporal orderings 31 . By contrast, during the 9-12 window there is a clear consolidation: counterfactual reasoning starts to look like a general-purpose nearest-world operator rather than a fragile, task-specific strategy; around 12 years, the modal pattern in classic paradigms flips: children now systematically change only those events that are causally downstream of the counterfactual antecedent, keep background conditions fixed, and correctly judge that outcomes with back-up causes would still have occurred if the actual cause were removed, often explicitly justifying their answers with "it would still have happened because …" explanations 32 . Mechanistically, 9- to 12-year-olds become markedly better at keeping the real and imagined worlds apart: whereas many younger children allow counterfactual assumptions to "leak" into their memory for what really happened or confuse actual and imagined details, 11-12-year-olds can track which facts belong to which branch and update only the relevant antecedent in the counterfactual model, a clear sign that the underlying world representation has been decoupled from immediate experience and can be manipulated in a controlled, meta-representational way 33 . In everyday life, this manifests as a sophisticated grasp of fault, regret, and relief; a 12-year-old can say "If I had started studying earlier, I would have done better, even if I still passed," or articulate "close calls" ("If I had left one minute later, I would have missed the bus"), utilizing this reasoning to refine future behavior rather than just learning from immediate outcomes. At the same time, important limitations remain. Performance is still highly sensitive to processing load, with long, multiply-caused event chains, deeply counter-to-fact premises, or emotionally charged content leading to systematic errors and outcome-based judgments that resemble those of adults under heavy cognitive load 24 , 25 . Even by 12, many children focus on a single salient change and neglect less obvious but causally relevant alterations, struggle with nested or iterated counterfactuals ("If she had not believed that…"), and rely heavily on familiar content and story structure. Thus, counterfactual reasoning between 9 and 12 undergoes a qualitative shift from a brittle, context-bound approximation that often collapses back into simple conditional reasoning to an increasingly domain-general, nearest-possible-world operation that can be deployed as a core tool of causal learning and hypothesis testing, but its full flexibility, abstraction, and resistance to belief and emotion-driven distortions continue to develop into mid-adolescence and adulthood. Scientific reasoning Scientific reasoning is not a single skill but a coordinated suite of operations over the internal world model: generating hypotheses, designing interventions, representing and aggregating data, evaluating the fit between predictions and outcomes, and regulating all of this with meta-level goals ("what am I trying to find out?") and epistemic norms ("what counts as good evidence?"). Between 9 and 12 these components develop asynchronously and with large individual differences, but the overall profile is clear. Inductive, deductive, and counterfactual reasoning provide the computational "micro-operations" (generalizing from samples; enforcing logical constraints; simulating alternatives); scientific reasoning is the emerging orchestrator that uses those operations intentionally to answer questions about how the world works. This window sees the rapid emergence of the tendency to perform experiments with explicit hypotheses in mind 34 , 35 , 36 , especially in a manner that is cleanly separated from evidence/data (the crucial disentanglement of "theory" and "evidence" 37 ). On classic paradigms, 9-year-olds may happily manipulate an apparatus and notice regularities, but they typically do so in a way that is driven by curiosity or performance goals without a clearly verbalized "If X, then Y should happen" structure. By 12, a substantial fraction of children will describe their activity in epistemic terms ("I want to see whether this variable matters"), and there is a detectable shift from treating experiments as demonstrations of what one already believes to treating them as tools for inquiry 38 . In the words of Deanna Kuhn: "It is the intention to seek knowledge that transforms implicit theory revision into scientific thinking. Theory revision becomes something one does, rather than something that happens to one outside of conscious awareness. To seek knowledge is to acknowledge that one’s existing knowledge is incomplete, possibly incorrect – that there is something new to know." 36 At the level of concrete strategies, the 9-12 window is foremost marked by visible improvements in the control of variables, including in its spontaneous application. Piaget’s classic pendulum problem captures the inflection: while 9- to 10-year-olds typically change string length, bob weight, and release height together and then infer period from the resulting blur of outcomes, around 11-12 years many children begin to systematically vary one factor at a time, holding the others constant, and to reason hypothetico-deductively about which variable the period "must" depend on 39 , 40 . This control-of-variables strategy is present in rudimentary form much earlier (a 4-year-old can, for example, disambiguate which blocks activate a blicket detector), but the class of systems to which it can be applied expands dramatically: by 12-years-old, children can, say, debug the causal forces in an RC car or a simple aerodynamic system (e.g a kite or a plane) 41 , 42 and, overall, 12-year-olds are much better than 9-year-olds at designing controlled, unconfounded experiments, with more demanding assessments often failing to find robust evidence of such competence until around 12 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 . Children also become much more sensitive to sample diversity and size; instead of treating "three examples" as intrinsically compelling, they increasingly attend to whether the examples are varied and representative, and they start to articulate why a homogeneous but larger sample may be less informative than a small but diverse one for generalizing to a whole category 5 , 6 . These strategic gains are scaffolded by advances in meta-memory and representational infrastructure. Young children tend to view all strategies in memory tasks as roughly equivalent, and to underestimate both the limits and the malleability of their own cognitive resources. During the first half of this age window ( 9-10), they begin to discriminate between strategies; by age 12, children tend to not only know which strategies (e.g., categorization, rehearsal, external note-taking) are more effective, but also increasingly deploy them spontaneously 47 , 48 . This period is often described as a qualitative shift in "meta-memory": children come to appreciate that memory is limited and fallible, and that external representational aids (notebooks, tables, diagrams) can and should be used to offload storage and support systematic data recording 49 . Concurrent gains appear in their ability to read and construct simple tables and graphs. By 12, most children can interpret basic line graphs and bar charts ("this line goes up, so…") and use them to support inferences, connecting trends or differences in the visualization to underlying causal stories 50 , 51 . Yet variability and noise remain deeply problematic: children frequently over-interpret single data points, ignore sampling error, and underappreciate the need for repeated trials or larger samples, especially when the data are messy or conflict with their expectations. Against this backdrop of real progress, the limitations of 9- to 12-year-olds’ scientific reasoning are equally telling. When faced with systems of intermediate or high complexity (multiple variables that combine additively or interactively) most 12-year-olds struggle to generate unconfounded experiments, to disconfirm their own hypotheses, to keep accurate and systematic records, and to integrate results across trials 52 , 53 , 54 , 55 . They often test a new idea without checking its compatibility with earlier results 56 , or fail to keep records at all, relying instead on noisy impressions of "what seemed to work" 57 , 41 , 58 . Exclusion inferences ("this variable does not have an effect") and judgments of indeterminacy ("this experiment is inconclusive") are especially rare 57 , 52 . Children in this window, much like adults under strong motivational or cognitive load, tend to treat such outcomes as "failures" rather than as informative constraints on the hypothesis space. Prior beliefs, goals, and affective stakes continue to exert a strong pull. Although 12-year-olds are markedly better than 9-year-olds at separating theory and evidence as distinct sources of knowledge 59 , 49 , 60 , their experimentation remains highly sensitive to whether they hold strong prior theories and whether the outcomes can be interpreted as positive or negative 60 , 61 . In many studies, they proceed as though the causal status of a focal variable is already certain and construe the task either as producing the best possible outcome (e.g., building the fastest car) or as accumulating demonstrations that their favored variable "works" across a range of conditions 41 , 62 , 63 , 29 , 64 . In other words, they readily treat experiments as engineering optimization procedures or as rhetorical tools in service of a prior belief, and only slowly come to view them as impartial tests that could just as well reveal the irrelevance of a cherished factor as its importance. Genuine theory revision (explicitly acknowledging that "what I thought before was wrong" because "the data show something else" and drawing out the downstream implications) remains relatively rare and fragile when it clashes with entrenched prior knowledge 65 . Sophisticated scientific reasoning involves both a toolbox of strategies for hypothesis testing, induction, inference, and evidence evaluation, and a meta-level awareness of when , how , and why to deploy those strategies in the service of knowledge-seeking goals 49 . Between 9 and 12, children make major strides across the board: they acquire and refine control-of-variables strategies, become more attuned to diversity, sample size, and subcategories, start to read and construct simple external representations of data, and begin to frame their activity as testing explicit hypotheses rather than merely "trying things out." At the same time, these skills are still highly context-dependent, skewed by prior beliefs and outcome valence, and heavily reliant on scaffolding and relatively simple task structures. By age 12, then, the "virtual laboratory" in the mind has become a partially explicit, self-directed system: children can deliberately set up interventions in their internal and external world models, monitor the resulting data with some appreciation of evidential quality, and use this to revise (or defend) their theories. But the system is still far from adult-like in generality, robustness, or epistemic rigor; what the 9-12 window inaugurates is not mature scientific reasoning, but the onset of formal scientific thought.
