title: Graeme Halford: Relational Complexity
text: Graeme Halford’s theories introduced some interesting objections to Case’s theory. His core objection to Case is that "working memory capacity" isn’t a single executive resource you can read off from task difficulty, because two people can face the same task yet represent it differently (different goals, chunking, latent variables). So he shifts the explanation of cognitive growth from "how much executive capacity do you have?" to "what relational structure can you hold and map into a coherent mental model?" Essentially, he argued that development is less about raw buffer size and more about the maximum relational arity (how many entities/relations) your internal simulator can bind at once without collapsing into heuristics or memorized templates. His central mechanism is structure mapping : you understand new problems by translating them into a familiar relational schema (an internal model) via analogy, suggesting that intelligence scales with the ability to align incoming data with high-dimensional internal graphs. What limits you, then, is relational complexity : the number of distinct entities/dimensions that must be simultaneously represented for the relations to be understood (not just recognized). A simple comparison like "A is larger than B" is a binary relation (two entities + one relation). A transitive inference like "A > B and B > C, so A > C" forces you to coordinate three entities and two relations at once; if you can’t keep that whole structure active, you won’t reliably derive the implied relation. Halford’s four levels are basically a ladder of "how many slots in the relational graph can you bind simultaneously," often linked to  1, 3, 5, and  10 years (and aligning roughly with Piaget/Case stage labels): Unary / element mappings ( 1y; sensorimotor) are about single-attribute matches In perception/objects, "this is an apple" from shape or color; in social, "smiling face = happy," "loud voice = scary." Actions at this stage are basic stimulus-response mappings. Case Equivalent: Sensorimotor Stage (The "unit" is a raw input/output). The agent binds a specific attribute to an entity. It validates existence but not relation. Binary / relational mappings ( 3y; preoperational) add dyadic relations In space/physics, "the block is on the box," "this door is bigger than that opening"; in social, "Mom likes me," "he is meaner than her," or simple ownership ("that’s mine"). Case Equivalent: Interrelational Stage (The "unit" is a relationship between sensorimotor units). This is the minimum complexity required for simple feedback loops where S t a t e c u r r e n t State_{current} is compared to S t a t e g o a l State_{goal} . System mappings ( 5y; concrete operational) handle ternary structure or the integration of two relations In math, solving "3 + ? = 8" requires coordinating (3, ?, 8) under one operation; in causal/spatial reasoning, transitivity and constraints like "if A blocks B and B blocks C, moving B frees C," or "A fits in B, B fits in C ⇒ A fits in C" (containment chains). This corresponds to Case’s Dimensional stage, where the "unit" is a quantitative variable This is the first stage where variables are abstract Multiple-system mappings ( 10y; formal operational / vectorial) support quaternary structure-relations between relations: in math/physics, proportionality and ratios ("gear A:B = 2:1 and B:C = 3:1 ⇒ A:C = 6:1"), or balancing two unknowns under constraints; in social/strategy, reasoning about "what I believe you believe she intends" (nested mental-state models) or coordinating multiple interacting rules ("if we choose plan X, it helps goal G but violates constraint K unless we add step S"). This level of complexity is required for abstract analogy and proportionality. Halford is basically proposing a capacity metric for model-based reasoning that’s not "tokens in a buffer," but "maximum relational complexity of the latent graph you can stably instantiate and manipulate." Scaling up cognition then looks like (1) learning better schemas to map into (better priors / reusable world-model fragments), and (2) increasing the system’s ability to bind higher-arity relations (more simultaneous variables/constraints) without losing coherence-exactly the difference between a model that recognizes patterns and a model that can do robust planning, counterfactuals, and multi-constraint control across domains. It may seem that Halford’s theory is redundant with respect to Case’s theory; however, Halford adds a sharper task-analytic metric for what "capacity" must actually support: the maximum relational arity (unary -> binary -> ternary -> quaternary) that can be simultaneously bound for a concept to be intelligible. Where Case explains developmental growth via practice-driven compilation of ECS components (freeing resources to build higher-order units like dimensions and vectors), Halford tells you how to count the minimal structure the world model must co-instantiate (how many entities, relations, and relations-between-relations must be live at once) independent of domain content or strategy. Essentially, Case is the growth mechanism (compression/automation increases effective bandwidth), while Halford is the constraint and measurement lens: it predicts exactly which problems will collapse into heuristics or memorization when relational complexity exceeds the agent’s current binding capacity, and it lets you compare "difficulty" across domains by the structure of the underlying graph, not by superficial features of the task. Halford argues that "number of items" (storage) is irrelevant if they aren’t interacting. He cares about the dimensionality of the active graph, which is about parallelism . It doesn’t matter if you can store 10 variables; if you can only compute the interaction of 3 at a time, you literally cannot represent a quaternary relation (like a proportion of proportions) without collapsing the waveform. Another way of putting it: Halford provides the architecture (the "what"; the data structures): he tells you that "intelligence" is the ability to process higher-rank tensors (relations of relations). Case provides the learning rule (the "how"; the optimization process): he tells you that the only way to afford those expensive higher-rank tensors is by compressing the lower-rank ones into efficient sub-routines. Practice compresses "Search" (high compute) into "Lookup" (low compute); from high- to low-dimensional. Structure mapping is a key mechanism for such compression.

title: Kurt Fischer: Dynamic Skill Theory
text: Kurt Fischer’s Dynamic Skill Theory is a "skills-in-context" account of cognitive development. Instead of treating development as one global stage that applies everywhere, it says people build skills (coordinated control structures for thinking/acting) in particular domains/contexts, and those skills grow through hierarchical integration: you construct a new skill by coordinating multiple earlier skills into a single, more powerful unit. Two key consequences are (1) development looks jagged and task-dependent (you can be "advanced" in one domain and "earlier" in another), and (2) performance has a range: with support/scaffolding (which makes success barely attainable), you often show a higher "optimal" level than you show spontaneously in everyday conditions ("functional" level). For a world-modeling lens, it’s basically a theory of how internal models become more compositional, more decoupled from the here-and-now, and more rule/principle-governed over time. Fischer organizes growth into broad tiers (often described as stages): reflex -> sensorimotor actions -> representations -> abstractions. Within each tier, skills progress through four recurring, structurally identical levels: single set (agent can control one "unit" in the tier), mappings (relations between units), systems (relations between mappings), systems of systems (relations between systems; is the "single set" of the next tier). Stages and substages (similar to Case) The below age ranges represent approximate boundaries for the child’s optimal performance (the upper limits of their abilities, which often only arise under high scaffolding (e.g., a researcher demonstrating the task, removing distractions, and explicitly prompting the child)). In everyday life (i.e without a researcher scaffolding them), children typically operate one or two levels below their optimal age.

title: Tier 0: Reflexive (~0–4 months)
text: The building blocks are hard-wired reflexes (e.g rooting, grasping, startle); during this stage, the infant gains control over involuntary movements. Skills in this tier consist of innate actions that require direct physical or socio-emotional stimulation for their evocation. Fischer treats this as a corollary/starting point: the infant begins with single reflexes then coordinates them into reflex mappings, then reflex systems, then systems of reflex systems, which can yield a flexible single sensorimotor action (like robust "looking"). Level 1: Single Reflexes ( 3-4 weeks) The infant has a single, specific reflex in response to a stimulus. Example 1: Hold the infant upright with feet touching a surface and you see alternating step-like leg movements (the stepping reflex) Example 2: A baby closes their hand when a finger touches their palm (the palmar grasp reflex). This is an isolated action, not yet coordinated with looking or reaching. Example 3: A baby turns their head and opens their mouth towards a touch on the cheek to find a breast or bottle, helping them feed (the rooting reflex) Example 4: Something touches the lips/roof of the mouth and you get rhythmic sucking (the sucking reflex) Example 5: A sudden loud noise or movement makes the baby throw their arms out and then pull them back in, as if to embrace someone (the Moro (startle) reflex) Level 2: Reflex Mappings ( 7-8 weeks) The infant coordinates two distinct reflexes into a single action pattern. Example 1: The infant hears a sound (auditory reflex) and turns their eyes toward it (visual reflex). They have "mapped" hearing to looking. Example 2: visual swiping (Visually Elicited Reaching); the infant coordinates visual fixation with arm extension. Upon locking eyes on an interesting object (visual reflex), the infant immediately flings their arm toward it (motor reflex). This is distinct from Level 3 because it is ballistic: they "swipe" at where they see the object, but they cannot yet correct their hand’s path mid-flight if they miss. Example 3: The Traction Response (Grasp-Pull Mapping); the infant coordinates the palmar grasp with arm flexion. When an adult’s finger touches the infant’s palm, they grasp it (reflex 1). Once the grip is secure, they automatically tense and flex their biceps (reflex 2) to pull their torso up. The two reflexes are now mapped into a single "pulling" unit. Level 3: Reflex Systems ( 10-11 weeks) Multiple reflex mappings are integrated into a complex, continuous feedback loop. The infant can now vary their action to maintain a specific result. This effectively generates the first Single Sensorimotor Actions (which become the single "units" of Tier 1). Example 1: Tracking a moving object. The infant sees an object (vision), turns their head (motor), and adjusts their focus (accommodation) continuously as the object moves. Example 2: Visually-guided reaching. This is the evolution of the "Visual Swipe" (Level 2). The infant sees the object, moves the hand, sees the hand’s position relative to the object , and corrects the trajectory mid-air. It integrates vision, proprioception, and motor control into a loop: L o o k → R e a c h → C o m p a r e → A d j u s t → G r a s p Look \rightarrow Reach \rightarrow Compare \rightarrow Adjust \rightarrow Grasp . Example 3: Suck-Swallow-Breathe (The Feeding System). This requires the precise, rhythmic sequencing of three distinct reflexes: sucking (extracting liquid), swallowing (transporting liquid to the esophagus), and breathing (protecting the airway). Unlike a simple mapping, this is a system: if the milk flow is too fast, the infant adjusts the breathing/swallowing ratio. If they need air, they pause the sucking. The components work together dynamically.

title: Tier 1: Sensorimotor (~4–18 months)
text: The "Reflex System" (Level 3) becomes a smooth, voluntary "Single Sensorimotor Action"; the skill is one coherent perception-action (sensorimotor) routine, like sustained looking or a simple grasp. Fischer’s example is an infant who can keep her gaze on a swinging doll-effective control of a single action, but not relations between actions. The child now operates on the physical world; Piaget noted that this is where infants become environmentally focused. Level 1: Single Sensorimotor Set ( 3-4 months) The child can perform a single, voluntary action on an object. They cannot yet coordinate two voluntary actions simultaneously. If they are busy looking at something, they might stop listening. If they are busy grasping, they might stop looking. A "set" refers to a cohesive, voluntary behavior pattern (a scheme) that the infant applies to a specific object or event. Example 1: The Voluntary Grasp (The "Power Grip") The infant sees a block, reaches for it, and wraps their fingers around it firmly. In the Palmar Reflex, the hand closed only because the palm was touched; in this Sensorimotor Set, the infant initiates the grasping to hold the object. The infant grasps the object but cannot manipulate it (turn it over, pass it to the other hand) while holding it. The hand simply "holds." Example 2: Visual Inspection (The "Stare") The infant locks their gaze onto a face or a high-contrast toy and studies it intently for several seconds. This is not just the Visual Tracking Reflex (following movement). This is active information gathering. The infant controls the duration and focus of the gaze. The infant often seems "stuck" staring at the object (sometimes called "sticky fixation"). Because they are in a Single Set, they often cannot easily break their gaze to look at something else until the stimulus changes or they become exhausted. Example 3: The "Bat" (Ballistic Striking) The infant sees a mobile hanging above them and excites their arm to strike it, causing it to spin. This is a constructed action used to make an interesting event continue (a precursor to the "Secondary Circular Reactions" noted by Piaget; intentionally repeating actions that produce interesting effects in the external world, shifting focus from self (primary) to the environment). The action is not fine-tuned. The infant cannot hit the mobile gently versus hard on command; they just run the "Hit" program. Example 4: Non-Social Babbling (Vocal Practice) The infant lies in the crib and produces a string of vowel sounds ("ooo-aaa") for the sheer sensation of making noise. This is often done when the infant is alone or not focusing on anything else. If a parent enters and waves (visual stimulus), the infant often stops vocalizing immediately because they cannot maintain the Vocal Set while processing the new Visual Set . Level 2: Sensorimotor Mappings ( 7-8 months) The child coordinates two actions to achieve a goal. This is the beginning of "means-end" behavior; the dawn of intentionality . Example 1: Pulling a blanket (Action A) to bring a toy resting on it within reach (Action B). Action A: Pulling the blanket (Motor action). Action B: Grasping the toy (Motor action). Mapping: The child wants the toy but cannot reach it. They realize that "pulling the blanket" (Action A) causes the toy to come closer, allowing "grasping the toy" (Action B). They map the means to the end. Example 2: Two-Handed Coordination (Container Play) Action A: Stabilizing an object. Action B: Manipulating the object. Mapping: The child holds a box steady with the left hand (Action A) so the right hand can pull the lid off (Action B). In Level 1, the hands acted independently or mirrored each other; now they have distinct, complementary roles. Example 3: Auditory-Motor Localization (The "Name Call") Action A: Auditory processing (Identifying a specific meaningful sound, e.g., their name). Action B: Motor orientation (Turning the body). Mapping: The child hears their name spoken, processes the meaning, and maps it to the voluntary action of turning to look at the speaker. Level 3: Sensorimotor Systems ( 11-13 months) The child coordinates two or more Sensorimotor Mappings into a meaningful system. This allows them to compare multiple variables (e.g., "If I do X, Y happens; but if I do Z, Q happens") and vary their actions to solve new problems. This is the stage of active experimentation, corresponding to Piaget’s "Tertiary Circular Reactions" (i.e deliberately experimenting with objects and actions through trial-and-error to discover new outcomes and understand cause-and-effect). The child can hold Action A constant while varying Action B to see how the outcome (C) changes ( A + Δ B → Δ C A + \Delta B \rightarrow \Delta C ). Example 1: The "High Chair Physicist" The child is sitting in a high chair with a handful of peas or a spoon. They don’t just drop the object; they drop it differently each time. Mapping A (Release): The mapping of opening the hand to letting the object fall (vertical drop). Mapping B (Thrust): The mapping of arm extension force to horizontal distance. The System: First, they simply open their hand (Mapping A) and watch the spoon hit the floor directly below. Next, they push the spoon gently (Mapping A + Low B) and watch it land a few inches away. Finally, they throw it hard (Mapping A + High B). They are testing the relationship between Force and Landing Position. They are systematically varying the initial velocity to learn the rules of trajectory. Example 2: The "Sound Engineer" (Acoustics) The child has a wooden spoon and is crawling around the kitchen hitting different surfaces. Mapping A (The Strike): The motor action of swinging the arm to hit a surface. Mapping B (Auditory Feedback): The processing of the resulting sound (pitch, timbre, volume). The System: The child hits the carpet (Mapping A applied to Surface 1) → \rightarrow Result: Dull thud (Low auditory feedback). The child hits the metal pot (Mapping A applied to Surface 2) → \rightarrow Result: Loud clang (High auditory feedback). The child hits the family dog or a parent (Mapping A applied to Biological Agent) → \rightarrow Result: Reaction/Noise. The child is holding the action constant but varying the target surface to classify objects based on their material properties (acoustic resonance). Example 3: The "A-not-B" Success (Object Permanence) An object is hidden under Cloth A, then moved (while the child watches) under Cloth B. Mapping A (The "Search A" Habit): The child remembers the object was at A and knows how to pull Cloth A to reveal it. Mapping B (The "Visual Track"): The child visually tracks the object moving to location B. The System: In Level 2, these mappings compete. The child sees the object go to B, but the "Search A" mapping is so strong they look under A anyway (A-not-B Error). Now, the child integrates them. The visual tracking (Mapping B) updates the search target. The child suppresses Mapping A and executes the search at B. Example 4: The "Container" Fit (Volume & Orientation) The child has a large container (like a bucket) and several smaller objects (a ball, a square block, a long stick). Mapping A (Insertion): The motor action of placing an object inside a boundary. Mapping B (Object Rotation): The manipulation of the object’s orientation in 3D space. The System: They drop the ball in (Easy fit). They try to put the long stick in sideways (Mapping A). It hits the rim (Failure). Instead of giving up, they rotate the stick vertically (Mapping B) and try Mapping A again (notice the coordination of mappings). It slides in. They then try to put the bucket inside the cup (Size inversion). They are testing spatial containment . They are learning the rules of "big vs. small" and how orientation affects whether one object can contain another. Example 5: Social Referencing (The "Visual Cliff") The child crawls toward a drop-off (or a scary toy) but pauses to look at their mother’s face. Mapping A (Exploratory Drive): The child sees an interesting goal and initiates crawling toward it. Mapping B (Emotional Interpretation): The child sees the mother’s fearful facial expression and maps it to "danger/stop." The System: The child does not just react to the toy or just react to the face. They treat the mother’s face as information about the environment . They construct a system: "The toy is desirable (Mapping A), BUT Mom looks scared (Mapping B), therefore the toy is dangerous." The child halts based on the synthesis of these two inputs. Example 6: Sequential Tool Use The child uses a stick to retrieve a toy, but there is a barrier in the way requiring a maneuver. Mapping A (The "Pull"): Mapping the stick movement toward the body to bring the toy closer. Mapping B (The "Push/Slide"): Mapping the stick movement sideways or away to navigate around the obstacle. The System: A child in Level 2 creates a simple cause-effect: Pull Stick → \rightarrow Get Toy. If a barrier blocks the straight path, they fail. Now, the child coordinates the mappings into a sequence: First Push/Slide (Mapping B) to clear the obstacle, then transition smoothly to Pull (Mapping A). They understand that an action moving away from the goal is sometimes necessary to achieve the goal. Example 7: Complex Imitation (Gesture + Vocalization) The parent claps their hands while saying "Yay!" and the child imitates the full performance. Mapping A (Motor Imitation): Mapping the visual sight of clapping to the motor action of clapping hands. Mapping B (Vocal Imitation): Mapping the sound of "Yay" to the vocal action of saying "Yay." The System: A child in Level 2 typically does one or the other. If they clap, they stop talking. If they talk, they stop clapping. Now, they integrate the two mappings into a single performance. They can coordinate the rhythm of the hands (Mapping A) with the timing of the voice (Mapping B).

title: Tier 2: Representational (~2–10 years)
text: This marks the first major restructuring : the child’s coordinated sensorimotor systems are internalized into stable representations, concrete concepts tied to specific objects, events, or roles that no longer require the child to be actively manipulating the object to "hold the idea." Fischer emphasizes that at this point children can begin to treat things as having properties more independent of their immediate actions, and he uses pretend/social role play as a clean example of representational skill (e.g., enacting a "doctor" role with instruments). By the end of this tier, thought is still concrete (tied to specific objects or events), yet the child can reflect on actions rather than merely perform them. Level 1: Single Representations ( 18-24 months) The child can hold a single concrete idea in their mind without the object being present. This is the birth of symbols and language (the "vocabulary explosion"). They can focus on one property or category at a time (e.g., "This is a dog," "That is a toy"). If you try to tell a 2-year-old, "This is a dog, AND it is a toy," they often get confused. It is either a DOG (real) or a TOY (fake). They struggle to coordinate two contradictory representations of the same object simultaneously. They also tend to represent a toy as "Mine." They cannot simultaneously represent it as "Yours" or "Shared." The concept of sharing requires Level 2 (Representational Mappings), where two people’s ownerships are coordinated. Example 1: Pretend Play (The "Symbolic" Representation) The child picks up a banana, holds it to their ear, and says "Hello?" The child is representing the banana as a telephone. They are overriding the sensorimotor reality (it looks/tastes like fruit) with a mental representation (it is a phone). They can hold this single symbolic identity in their mind to execute the action. Example 2: Deferred Imitation (The "Memory" Representation) A child watches their father shave in the morning. The child does nothing at that moment. Hours later, the child picks up a toy block, rubs it on their face, and makes a buzzing sound. Previously, the child would have to imitate immediately while watching. Now, the child has formed a mental representation of "shaving." They held this concept in memory for hours and then "played it back" later. The action is now independent of the stimulus. Example 3: Naming Explosion (The "Label" Representation) The child points to a Golden Retriever and says "Dog!" Later, they point to a Chihuahua and also say "Dog!" The child has formed a single, stable category: "dog". They understand that this sound ("dog") represents a specific type of thing in the world, regardless of size or color. This is the leap from "words as triggers" (previous level) to "words as symbols". Example 4: Agency (The "Agent" Representation) The child sees a wind-up toy stop moving. Instead of banging it (Sensorimotor), they hand it to an adult and look expectantly at the adult’s hands. The child represents the adult as an Agent , a being who can make things happen. They have a single concept: "Adults fix things." They are treating the adult as a tool for solving the problem. Level 2: Representational Mappings ( 3.5-4.5 years) The child coordinates two distinct Single Representations into a functional relationship. Instead of activating just one independent concept at a time, the child can now hold two concepts in mind simultaneously and compute the specific link between them; one representation stands for, predicts, or constrains the other-e.g., "the idea of the ball being behind the couch" guiding search, or "the remembered rule of a game" shaping what move is allowed. It’s characterized by mental-to-mental linking: using a representation as an input to transform/update another representation (often in simple if-then, analogy, or role-rule form), so behavior can be guided by what’s absent, hypothetical, or socially defined rather than only what’s currently perceived. This level is characterized by: Causality ( A → B A \rightarrow B ): The understanding that one concrete event or object acts upon another (e.g., "The rain caused the puddle"). Comparison: The ability to relate two objects along a single dimension. A younger child knows "Big," while a child at this level understands "Bigger than" (mapping Object A against Object B). Social Reciprocity: The coordination of complementary social roles. The child understands that their role (e.g., "Hider") is defined by its relationship to another person’s role (e.g., "Seeker"). Example 1: The "Theory of Mind" Breakthrough (False Belief) The classic "Sally-Anne" test. Sally puts a marble in a basket and leaves. Anne moves the marble to a box. You ask the child: "Where will Sally look for her marble?" Previously, the child points to the box (reality). They can only represent one reality-the current one where the marble is in the box. Now, the child points to the basket. They can map the Real State (marble is in the box) against Sally’s Mental State (Sally thinks it is in the basket). They coordinate two distinct representations of the same event. Example 2: The "Because" Justification (Causal Reasoning) The child explains their behavior or a physical event. "I am crying (Representation A) because I scraped my knee (Representation B)." A younger child might cry and say "Knee!" (single concept). Now, the child constructs the bridge: the scrape is the cause of the tears. This allows for the first true excuses and explanations. Example 3: Past & Future (Temporal Mapping) The child says "after dinner, I get cookie." (sentences are now 5-6 words long) The child is mapping an event that is happening to an event that will happen . They are constructing a timeline in their head. A sensorimotor child might cry for a cookie, but they cannot understand the conditional logic of "First X, then Y." Example 4: "Who done it?" (Causal Mapping) When asked who broke a lamp, the child explains that "The cat broke it" despite not witnessing the event. They see the broken pieces, access their mental representation of the cat’s behavior, and construct a causal link between the two. They are inferring an invisible history. Example 5: Socio-Dramatic Scripts (Role Reciprocity) A child might hold a toy stethoscope (Single Representation: "I am Doctor"). Now, they force you to join the simulation (e.g "I am the teacher, so you have to sit down."). The child isn’t just acting; they are holding a mental script of how two abstract categories relate. If you stand up, they get mad-not because you physically blocked them, but because you broke the logical rule of the relationship they are representing. Level 3: Representational Systems ( 6-7 years) The child integrates multiple Representational Mappings into a complex, interacting system. They can now control two or more sources of information (relations) simultaneously. This level is characterized by: Multivariate Control: The ability to focus on two changing dimensions at once (e.g., Height and Width) rather than being captured by the single most obvious feature. Reversibility: The understanding that mental operations can be done in reverse to return to the starting point (e.g., knowing that subtraction "undoes" addition, or that pouring water back into the original glass restores the original level). Integration of Contradictions: The capacity to synthesize opposing traits into a single concept (e.g., a person can be "nice" generally but "strict" about homework), moving beyond the black-and-white splitting of the previous level. Remember that " 6-7 years" indicated these abilities are coming online (in Fischer’s terms, they represent "optimal" performance), meaning they are usually only reached with high support (scaffolding, prompts, familiar materials, practice). Example 1: Conservation of Liquid (The Classic Test) The child understands that the amount of liquid is conserved after you pour water from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass. Mapping A: Height (The water level went up); Mapping B: Width (The glass got thinner). A younger child focuses on just one mapping. "It has more water because it is taller." They cannot compensate for the width. Now, the child coordinates both mappings into a system of compensation; they understand that the change in one dimension cancels out the change in the other. Example 2: Social Complexity (The "Nice & Mean" Integration) When asked to describe a parent or friend, the child is able to integrate traits that are superficially contradictory. Previously, the child may say "Mommy is nice," then, if Mommy yells, the child switches: "Mommy is mean." They struggle to understand how she can be both. Now, the child might say "Mommy is nice, but she gets mean if I don’t clean my room." The child constructs a system where a person can possess multiple, distinct attributes simultaneously depending on the context. They understand nuance . Example 3: Double Classification (The Matrix) You give the child a pile of shapes: Red Squares, Blue Squares, Red Circles, Blue Circles. You ask them to sort them into a grid (Matrix); the child now sorts by shape and color, processing two symbolic categories simultaneously. Example 4: The Arithmetic System (Reversibility) The child understands that subtraction is the inverse of addition. Whereas a younger child can count, these children understand the logical system of numbers. Example 5: Intersecting Social Roles The child understands that a person can hold two roles at once. Previously, if you say, "Grandpa is also my Daddy’s daddy," the child gets confused ("No, he’s not a Daddy, he’s a Grandpa!"). Now, the child understands that one person can be Grandpa (to me) AND Father (to Dad) simultaneously. They can map the single individual into two different slots in the family system .

title: Tier 3: Abstract (~10–25 years)
text: This is the next major restructuring : the child’s coordinated representational systems are internalized into stable abstractions-intangible, generalizable concepts that transcend any particular concrete instance. Where representational thought remained anchored to specific objects, events, or roles (this doctor, that act of sharing, my mother’s anger yesterday), abstract thought captures what is common across many such instances, yielding concepts like "honesty," "justice," or "addition" as a general operation rather than a collection of specific arithmetic facts. Fischer emphasizes that at this point individuals can reason about hypothetical and counterfactual situations, manipulating ideas that have never been directly experienced and may never exist in concrete form. A paradigmatic example is the emergence of abstract moral concepts: rather than simply knowing that "sharing my toy with Sam was nice" and "hitting my sister was mean," the young adolescent can now grasp "fairness" as a general principle-an invisible entity that organizes and explains diverse concrete situations without being reducible to any one of them.

title: Level 1: Single Abstractions (~10–12 years)
text: The individual becomes capable of constructing single abstractions -general concepts that are built by identifying what is common across multiple representational systems. Fischer emphasizes that abstractions constitute a qualitatively different kind of cognitive structure, one that is extracted from concrete instances but no longer reducible to them. What characterizes this level is that the abstraction functions like a new mental variable ("the same kind of thing is happening here") that can organize judgments and actions, but it’s usually still one-at-a-time: you can deploy one abstract dimension robustly without yet coordinating multiple abstractions into a larger structure. Example 1: Variables and Arithmetic Operations The child understands a "variable" as a thing they can operate on: understanding that x x stands for "any number" and using that idea across different problems, without needing a concrete number each time. The child constructs "multiplication" as an abstract operation , a general procedure that applies to any two quantities, including quantities she has never encountered and quantities too large to visualize (e.g., 347x892). The abstraction captures the structure of the operation independent of any particular content (i.e a x b = a + a + a + . . . + a axb=a+a+a+...+a ). These abstractions can now be applied to novel problems, manipulated symbolically, and reasoned about as entities in their own right ("multiplication makes numbers bigger... except when one number is less than one"). At the Representational level, the child might understand that 3x4=12 by thinking of it as "three groups of four objects," perhaps visualized as three rows of four apples. She can solve specific multiplication problems and may even recognize patterns across several problems. However, her understanding remains tied to these concrete instantiations-she is manipulating mental images of grouped objects. Example 2: Moral Abstractions The child starts using fairness as a general principle rather than a case-by-case preference: they can look at splitting candy, taking turns in a game, or sharing chores and say (and act as if) "it should be equal" or "it should match contribution," even when the surface details differ. The key is that "fairness" is no longer "what we did last time" or "what mom said," but an abstract property they can carry across situations. The child extracts the abstraction honesty as a general property that people can possess and that characterizes a category of actions. Honesty becomes an intangible entity -it cannot be seen or touched, it is not identical to any single act of truth-telling, yet it is understood as something real that organizes and explains diverse behaviors. A younger child at the representational tier understands specific instances of honesty and dishonesty: "I told Mom I didn’t eat the cookie, but I did-that was lying" or "Sarah said she liked my drawing even though she didn’t." These are concrete representational systems tied to particular events, actors, and contexts. At this level, however, the child holds their moral abstractions in isolation. They cannot yet systematically coordinate "honesty" with other moral abstractions like "kindness" or "loyalty". For instance, reasoning about what to do when being honest would hurt someone’s feelings (which requires coordinating "honesty" and "kindness"). Example 3: Personality Traits Previously, a child might say "My friend gave me his lunch, and he helped me with homework, and he always waits for me." The child describes a system of behaviors. Now, the child might say "My friend is kind" or "He is generous." The child extracts a single, abstract personality trait ("Kindness") that explains all the disparate concrete behaviors. "Kindness" isn’t an action you can see; it’s an invisible internal quality that causes the actions. At this level, however, the abstraction is often rigid. A person is "Kind." If they do something mean, the 10-year-old is confused (similar to the Level 7 "dog vs. toy" confusion when seeing a toy dog). They cannot yet coordinate "Kindness" with "Stress". Example 4: Theme Identification (Literature) Previously, a child writes a book report summarizing the plot: "The boy went to the mountain, fought the dragon, and came back home." They track the complex sequence of events. Now, the student identifies the theme : "This story is about courage." "Courage" is not an event in the book. It is an abstract concept that summarizes the emotional weight of the concrete events. The student has moved from "what happened" to "what it means. Example 5: Energy In elementary science, children learn concrete examples: a ball rolling down a ramp, a battery powering a light bulb, food giving you strength to run. These are representational systems-specific scenarios understood in terms of their particular objects and actions. Now, the student constructs energy as a single abstraction: an invisible quantity that exists in different forms, can be transferred between objects, and explains why things happen. Energy is not any particular instance of "stuff that makes things go"-it is the general concept that unifies all such instances. The student can now: Identify energy in novel situations ("the wind has energy") Discuss energy without reference to any specific system Understand that energy is conserved as a general principle

title: Level 2: Abstract Mappings (~14–16 years)
text: The individual becomes capable of constructing abstract mappings -systematic coordinations of two abstractions that specify how they relate to one another. The adolescent can now think relationally about abstract concepts, asking not just "what is honesty?" but "how does honesty relate to kindness?" or "what is the connection between freedom and responsibility?" They move beyond defining terms to constructing logical arguments, linking intangible concepts through causality, correlation, or comparison. This level is characterized by stable cross-situational "law-like" reasoning (i.e tradeoffs, conditional rules, and monotonic relations (e.g., "as X increases, Y changes," "X overrides Y under condition C")) rather than applying a single abstraction in isolation. This is where people start forming portable relations like incentives -> behavior, constraints -> feasible actions, or information quality -> decision quality; each is a mapping between abstractions that can be reused across wildly different concrete scenarios. The individual is no longer simply categorizing the world using abstract concepts; they are building theories about how abstract concepts interact. However, these theories remain limited to two-variable relationships : the adolescent can map abstraction A onto abstraction B, but cannot yet integrate multiple such mappings into a coherent system that coordinates A, B, C, and D simultaneously. Some common limitations of this level: Two-Variable Thinking in a Multi-Variable World Perhaps the most pervasive limitation is that these individuals restrict reasoning to dyadic relationships while real-world problems almost always involve three, four, or more interacting abstractions. For example, they might frame a career decision in terms of a single mapping: "Do I follow the money or follow my heart?" This framing captures something real, but it omits other crucial abstractions: job security, work-life balance, geographic location, social status, skill development, family obligations. The individual is not unaware that these factors exist, but she struggles to reason about how they all jointly constrain the decision. They may oscillate between different two-variable framings (sometimes thinking about income vs. passion, other times about security vs. growth) without integrating them into a coherent multi-factor analysis. The result is often: Decisions that optimize for one trade-off while neglecting others Feeling "blindsided" when an unconsidered variable becomes important Difficulty explaining decisions in a way that accounts for all relevant factors Isolated Mappings Without Integration These individuals may possess multiple abstract mappings but hold them in separate mental compartments, failing to recognize when they apply simultaneously or how they constrain each other. For example, a parent at this level might understand several mappings: Freedom <-> Responsibility: "Give children freedom as they show responsibility" Discipline <-> Warmth: "Balance firmness with affection" Protection <-> Independence: "Keep them safe but let them grow" The limitation is that these mappings exist in isolation . When a complex parenting situation arises-say, a teenager wants to go to an unsupervised party-the parent may invoke one mapping without considering how it interacts with the others. They might think purely in freedom-responsibility terms ("Has she earned this freedom?") without integrating protection-independence considerations ("What are the actual risks?") and discipline-warmth considerations ("How do I enforce a decision while maintaining connection?"). The result is often: Inconsistent parenting that shifts between different two-variable framings Children who perceive the parent as unpredictable or hypocritical Post-hoc rationalization using whichever mapping supports the decision already made False Dilemmas and Either/Or Thinking Abstract mappings often take the form of trade-offs: more of A means less of B. While this is sometimes accurate, it can also create false dilemmas that obscure creative solutions requiring multi-variable thinking. For example, when considering "work-life balance" the framing might be: Career Success <-> Family Time; "The more I work, the less I’m home." This mapping treats the relationship as a zero-sum trade-off. What it misses is that the relationship between career and family is mediated by other variables: job flexibility, efficiency, outsourcing of tasks, quality vs. quantity of time, spousal support, career stage, and so forth. An individual at the Abstract Systems level might recognize: High efficiency at work could increase both career success and family time Quality of family time may matter more than quantity, altering what "balance" means Career success might provide resources (money, status, security) that benefit the family Someone at the Abstract Mappings level, locked into the two-variable trade-off, may agonize over an either/or choice that a more systematic analysis would dissolve. Intolerance of Ambiguity Some sophisticated ideas require holding multiple mappings in productive tension, recognizing that apparent contradictions resolve at a higher level of integration; individuals at this level often crave clear, logical consistency, getting frustrated by "it depends" answers. If a rule is "Honesty is the best policy," they view "white lies" not as social nuance, but as Hypocrisy. They struggle to understand that two opposing truths (Honesty vs. Kindness) can be valid at the same time depending on the context. Another example involves the two Abstract Mappings of "Accepting myself as I am brings peace" and "Striving to be better leads to growth." At this level, these can feel contradictory: "Should I accept myself or try to change myself? If I accept myself, why improve? If I need to improve, how can I accept myself?" A thinker in the Abstract Systems level can integrate these mappings into a system: self-acceptance and self-improvement are not opposites but complementary-acceptance provides the secure base from which genuine growth becomes possible, while growth expresses (rather than contradicts) self-acceptance. The paradox dissolves when the two mappings are coordinated within a larger framework. The Abstract Mappings thinker, unable to achieve this integration, may oscillate between frames-sometimes practicing radical acceptance, other times berating herself for not improving-without finding stable ground. Ideological Rigidity (Politics & Beliefs) This is the "Zealot" phase (fanatical and uncompromising). Once these thinkers map two concepts together, the connection feels absolute and becomes "the" lens through which they form beliefs. For example: "Capitalism (A) leads to Freedom (B)." They act as if this relationship is a universal law. If someone argues, "But Capitalism can also lead to Inequality," the individual often rejects it entirely. They cannot hold both mappings simultaneously ( A → B A \rightarrow B AND A → C A \rightarrow C ). This results in "Black and White" thinking; you are either with them (logical) or against them (illogical). This generates the familiar phenomenon of people "talking past each other" in political discussions, with each person applying a different Abstract Mapping and being unable to construct an Abstract System that coordinates multiple mappings. The "Silver Bullet" Error (Problem Solving) In the workplace or personal improvement, they tend to over-apply a single abstract principle. For example: "The problem with our company is a lack of Transparency." They apply "Transparency" to everything-salaries, strategy, private conflicts. They fail to see the boundary conditions -the situations where transparency might actually destroy trust or competitive advantage. They have the tool (the mapping), but not the wisdom (the system) to know when not to use it. Fragile Self-Esteem (Identity) They map their identity to specific abstract traits. For example: "I get good grades, therefore I am Smart." ( S u c c e s s → I n t e l l i g e n c e Success \rightarrow Intelligence ). This mapping is brittle. If they fail a test, the logic breaks: "I failed, therefore I am Stupid." They struggle to integrate contradictions (e.g., "I am a smart person who sometimes struggles"). This often leads to perfectionism or crushing imposter syndrome, because they cannot mentally stabilize the conflict between their ideal self and their real performance. Example 1: Effort and Ability A straightforward example is linking effort and ability to explain outcomes: "performance depends on both; if ability is low, more effort can compensate up to a point." That’s not just having the abstractions of effort and ability; it’s mapping them into a relation that supports predictions across domains (sports, school, work). Example 2: Moral Mapping (Honesty and Kindness) During the previous stage, the individual possesses the abstractions "honesty" and "kindness" as separate concepts. She understands that honesty involves telling the truth and that kindness involves caring for others’ feelings. But these abstractions exist in isolation: she has not yet systematically considered what happens when they conflict. Now, the adolescent constructs a mapping between honesty and kindness: she recognizes that these two moral values can trade off against each other. Being completely honest sometimes requires being unkind ("Your painting isn’t very good"), while being kind sometimes requires shading the truth ("I love what you made!"). This mapping enables the adolescent to: Recognize situations as involving a honesty-kindness trade-off Reason about when honesty should take priority and when kindness should Understand "white lies" as a phenomenon arising from this tension Evaluate others’ behavior in terms of how they navigate this trade-off What this individual cannot yet do is integrate this mapping with other moral mappings into a coherent ethical framework. For instance, she might separately understand honesty-kindness trade-offs and loyalty-fairness trade-offs, but she cannot yet coordinate all four abstractions into a unified moral system that specifies how honesty, kindness, loyalty, and fairness jointly constrain ethical action. Example 3: Political Mapping (Freedom and Responsibility) At the previous level, the adolescent can grasp "freedom" and "responsibility" as separate abstractions. Freedom is understood as the ability to make one’s own choices without external constraint; responsibility is understood as the obligation to fulfill duties and accept consequences. Now, the adolescent maps these two abstractions onto each other, recognizing their reciprocal relationship : greater freedom entails greater responsibility, and accepting responsibility earns greater freedom. This is not merely knowing both concepts; it is understanding their systematic connection. This mapping enables reasoning such as: "If I want my parents to give me more freedom, I need to show I can be responsible" "Having the freedom to drive means being responsible for others’ safety" "A society that maximizes freedom must also cultivate responsibility in its citizens" The adolescent can now evaluate situations, policies, and arguments in terms of this freedom-responsibility relationship. However, she cannot yet integrate this mapping with other political mappings (e.g., liberty-equality, rights-duties, individual-collective) into a coherent political philosophy; that systematic integration is a forthcoming achievement. Example 4: Scientific Mapping (Energy and Force) At the previous level, the student possesses "energy" and "force" as separate scientific abstractions. Energy is understood as the capacity to do work or cause change; force is understood as a push or pull that can change an object’s motion. Now, the student constructs a mapping between these abstractions, understanding how they systematically relate: F o r c e x D i s t a n c e = W o r k = Δ E n e r g y ForcexDistance=Work=\Delta Energy This mapping captures the insight that force and energy are not independent concepts-applying a force over a distance transfers energy. The student can now: Explain why pushing harder (more force) transfers more energy Understand why the same force applied over a longer distance does more work Reason about mechanical advantage: how machines trade off force and distance while conserving energy Connect kinetic energy to the forces that produced it However, this student holds this mapping in relative isolation. They cannot yet integrate force-energy relationships with other abstract mappings (e.g., energy-entropy, force-momentum, energy-mass) into a unified physical framework. Understanding how energy, force, momentum, and entropy all jointly constrain physical systems is a forthcoming achievement. Example 5: Psychological Mapping (Introversion and Social Anxiety) At the previous level, the adolescent has constructed "introversion" and "social anxiety" as separate psychological abstractions. Introversion is a preference for lower stimulation and solitary activities; social anxiety is fear and discomfort in social situations. Now, the adolescent can map these abstractions onto each other. They recognize both their similarities and their differences , noticing they have overlapping behaviors but different causes. This mapping enables sophisticated psychological reasoning: "Someone might avoid parties because they’re introverted (preference) or because they’re anxious (fear). These look similar but are different" "An introvert can enjoy social situations but finds them draining; an anxious person finds them threatening" "I might be both introverted and anxious, and I need to figure out which is driving my behavior in different situations" The adolescent is now thinking about how two psychological abstractions relate -where they overlap, where they diverge, and how to distinguish them. This is qualitatively more complex than simply possessing both concepts separately. Example 6: Psychological Mapping (Self-Esteem and Narcissism) At the previous level, the adolescent possesses "self-esteem" and "narcissism" as separate abstractions. Self-esteem is understood as positive self-evaluation (feeling worthy, capable, and valuable). Narcissism is understood as excessive self-focus, grandiosity, and need for admiration. Now, the adolescent maps these abstractions onto each other, recognizing a superficial similarity that masks a structural difference (both involve positive self-view, but differ in stability and source). This mapping generates insights such as: "Both the person with high self-esteem and the narcissist appear confident, but their confidence has different foundations" "Self-esteem is stable ; it doesn’t depend on constant external validation. Narcissism is fragile ; it requires continuous admiration from others to be maintained" "Self-esteem allows acknowledging flaws without feeling threatened. Narcissism requires defending against any perceived criticism" "High self-esteem correlates with genuine confidence; narcissism may mask underlying insecurity" The adolescent can now make subtle psychological distinctions: "He seems really confident, but notice how he reacts when someone disagrees with him. That defensiveness suggests it might be narcissism rather than genuine self-esteem." Example 7: Psychological Mapping (Fear and Anxiety) At the previous level, the adolescent understands "fear" and "anxiety" as separate negative emotional states. Both involve feeling bad, worried, threatened. Now, the adolescent maps these abstractions onto each other, recognizing structural differences : both involve aversive arousal, but differ in object and time-orientation. This mapping enables reasoning such as: "Fear has a specific object -you’re afraid of something identifiable (a snake, a mugger, a test). Anxiety is more diffuse -a general sense of dread without a clear target" "Fear is usually about the present -an immediate threat. Anxiety is usually about the future -something bad that might happen" "Fear has a clear action tendency-fight, flight, or freeze in response to the threat. Anxiety involves vigilance and worry without a clear action to take" "Fear resolves when the threat passes. Anxiety can persist indefinitely because there’s no specific threat to resolve" "Fear is often proportionate -the fear matches the actual danger. Anxiety is often disproportionate -the distress exceeds any realistic threat" "Fear is adaptive-it protects you from real dangers. Chronic anxiety is often maladaptive-it creates suffering without protecting you" "Treatment differs: fear responds to removing or mastering the specific threat; anxiety requires addressing the underlying cognitive patterns" The adolescent can now analyze emotional experiences: "I thought I was afraid, but I realize I’m actually anxious. There’s nothing specific threatening me right now-I just have this constant sense that something bad is going to happen. That’s why I can’t ’solve’ it by avoiding something specific." Example 8: Psychological Mapping (Intelligence and Wisdom) At the previous level, the adolescent understands "intelligence" and "wisdom" as separate positive cognitive attributes. Intelligence is the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems; wisdom is... something about being wise, making good decisions, having good judgment. Now, the adolescent maps these abstractions onto each other, discovering they are distinct capacities that can dissociate and exist independently . This mapping enables reasoning such as: "Someone can be highly intelligent but not wise-brilliant at solving problems but making poor life decisions" "Someone can be wise without being exceptionally intelligent-having good judgment about life even without high IQ" "Intelligence is about processing power -how quickly and effectively you can manipulate information. Wisdom is about judgment -knowing what matters, what to do, how to live" "Intelligence peaks relatively early; wisdom may continue developing throughout life" "Intelligence without wisdom can be dangerous-the capacity to achieve goals without the judgment to choose good goals" "Wisdom might require intelligence as a foundation, but intelligence alone doesn’t produce wisdom-something else is needed (experience? reflection? values?)" The adolescent can now make more nuanced evaluations: "My professor is clearly brilliant-one of the smartest people I’ve met. But I’m not sure he’s wise. He makes poor decisions about relationships and seems unable to see beyond his narrow expertise." Example 9: Psychological Mapping (Loneliness and Solitude) At the previous level, the adolescent understands "loneliness" and "solitude" as separate abstractions related to being alone. Loneliness is a painful feeling of isolation; solitude is the state of being by oneself. Now, the adolescent maps these abstractions onto each other, recognizing they are independent dimensions : one is subjective suffering, the other is objective circumstance. This mapping generates insights such as: "Loneliness is a feeling ; solitude is a situation . They often co-occur but don’t have to" "You can be lonely in a crowd-surrounded by people but feeling disconnected. You can be alone without being lonely-in solitude but feeling content and connected" "Solitude can be chosen and restorative -time alone to recharge, reflect, create. Loneliness is always unwanted and painful " The adolescent can now reason about social situations more precisely: "She’s always at parties, always surrounded by friends, but I think she might actually be lonely. All those social contacts seem shallow-she doesn’t seem to have anyone she can really talk to."
