title: Level 3: Abstract Systems (~18–20+ years)
text: At the third level of the abstract tier, the individual becomes capable of constructing abstract systems : integrated coordinations of multiple abstract mappings that specify how several abstractions jointly constrain one another. Where Abstract Mapping involved relating two abstractions (A<->B), Abstract Systems involve understanding how A, B, C, and D all simultaneously interact within a coherent framework. The young adult can now build genuine theories -organized systems of abstract relationships that explain complex phenomena and generate predictions across diverse situations. This is the level at which coherent ideologies, integrated scientific frameworks, systematic philosophies, and unified personal identities become possible. These system are more than the sums of their mappings; they are organized structures in which the mappings themselves are coordinated. Example 1: Integrated Ethical Framework At the previous level, the adolescent possesses several moral mappings in relative isolation: Honesty <-> Kindness (truth-telling can conflict with caring) Loyalty <-> Fairness (favoring friends can conflict with impartiality) Individual rights <-> Collective welfare (personal freedom can conflict with social good) Justice <-> Mercy (giving people what they deserve can conflict with compassion) Each mapping is understood separately; the adolescent can reason about honesty-kindness trade-offs or loyalty-fairness trade-offs, but she has not integrated these into a unified moral framework. Now, the young adult coordinates these mappings into a systematic ethical theory . She recognizes that moral decisions often involve all of these abstractions simultaneously, and she develops an integrated framework for navigating their complex interactions. This system enables sophisticated moral reasoning: "In this situation, being honest would be unkind, but being kind would be disloyal to my friend who deserves to know the truth, and fairness suggests that everyone involved has a right to accurate information..." "My ethical framework prioritizes fairness over loyalty in professional contexts but loyalty over fairness in family contexts-and I can articulate why this is coherent rather than hypocritical" "When rights and welfare conflict, I tend toward a position that protects basic rights absolutely but allows welfare considerations to adjudicate between non-basic rights" The young adult can now evaluate moral dilemmas from within an integrated framework, recognize when different parts of her framework generate conflicting prescriptions, and refine the framework to achieve greater coherence. He can also recognize that other people operate from different integrated frameworks and can articulate where his system diverges from theirs. Example 2: Political Ideology At the previous level, the adolescent possesses political mappings such as: Freedom <-> Responsibility Liberty <-> Equality Individual <-> Collective Rights <-> Duties Security <-> Privacy These mappings exist somewhat independently: they might reason well about freedom-responsibility without connecting this to their thinking about liberty-equality. Now, the young adult integrates these mappings into a coherent political ideology , a systematic framework that specifies how all of these abstractions relate and that generates consistent positions across diverse political issues. For example, a libertarian-leaning young adult might construct a system in which: Individual liberty is the foundational value Rights are primary; duties arise only from voluntary agreements Equality means equal rights, not equal outcomes Freedom entails responsibility; those who act irresponsibly bear consequences Collective action is legitimate only when it protects individual rights Security concerns cannot override fundamental liberties A social-democratic young adult might construct a different system: Equality (including substantive equality of opportunity) is foundational Rights include positive rights to basic welfare, not just negative rights against interference Freedom is meaningful only when people have resources to exercise it Individual flourishing depends on collective provision of public goods Some liberty can be legitimately constrained to promote equality Duties to the collective arise from the benefits of social membership The central achievement of this level is not which ideology is adopted, but that the ideology functions as an integrated system : the various positions cohere, reinforce each other, and derive from shared foundational commitments. The young adult can: Derive positions on novel issues from their framework’s principles Recognize tensions within their framework and work to resolve them Articulate why their positions on seemingly unrelated issues (e.g., taxation, free speech, healthcare) actually stem from the same underlying commitments Engage with alternative ideologies by identifying precisely where the foundational disagreements lie Example 3: Scientific Systems (Thermodynamics) At the previous level, the physics student possesses mappings such as: Energy <-> Work (force applied over distance transfers energy) Energy <-> Heat (thermal transfer is energy flow) Temperature <-> Molecular motion (temperature measures average kinetic energy) Order <-> Entropy (entropy measures disorder) Each mapping is understood, but they have not been integrated into a unified framework. Now, the student constructs thermodynamics as a system : an integrated theoretical framework in which energy, heat, work, temperature, entropy, and equilibrium all jointly constrain physical processes. The laws of thermodynamics emerge as statements about how these abstractions systematically interrelate: First Law: Energy is conserved (heat added equals work done plus change in internal energy: Δ U = Q − W \Delta U=Q−W ) Second Law: Entropy of an isolated system never decreases (constrains which energy transformations are possible) Third Law: Entropy approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero (links temperature and entropy at the boundary) The student can now reason systemically: "If I want to extract work from a heat engine, I need a temperature differential, but the second law limits my efficiency based on entropy considerations" "This process conserves energy (first law is satisfied), but it would decrease entropy in an isolated system, so it cannot occur spontaneously" "The relationships between pressure, volume, temperature, and entropy in this gas can all be derived from the same underlying framework" The integration is crucial: understanding why a perpetual motion machine is impossible requires coordinating energy conservation (first law), entropy increase (second law), and the relationship between work, heat, and temperature; no single mapping suffices. Example 4: Psychological System (Personality) At the previous level, the young adult possesses psychological mappings such as: Introversion <-> Social anxiety (overlapping behaviors, different causes) Self-esteem <-> Narcissism (both involve positive self-regard, but differently) Attachment style <-> Relationship patterns (early bonds shape later relating) Temperament <-> Character (biological predisposition vs. developed traits) Now, they integrate these mappings into a systematic theory of personality : a coherent framework for understanding how traits, motivations, developmental history, and situational factors jointly shape human behavior. This integrated understanding enables sophisticated psychological reasoning: "My social avoidance probably stems from multiple sources: an introverted temperament (biological), an anxious attachment style (developmental), low self-esteem (self-concept), and high rejection sensitivity (motivational). These factors interact; my temperament made me slower to develop social skills, which contributed to anxious attachment, which lowered my self-esteem, which increased my fear of rejection..." "Understanding someone’s behavior requires considering their traits and their developmental history and the current situation and their goals; no single factor is sufficient" "Therapy might target different parts of this system: medication could address temperament, attachment work could address relational patterns, cognitive therapy could address self-concept..." The young adult now has a multi-causal model of personality in which various factors jointly determine outcomes, a significant advance over the previous level’s two-variable thinking. Example 5: Economic System (Inflation, Rates, Demand, Expectations) At the previous level, the learner can map single relations like "higher interest rates → \rightarrow lower demand" or "money supply → \rightarrow inflation." Now they coordinate multiple mappings into a macro system with feedback and time lags, commonly integrating: 𝐼𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑡 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠 → 𝑏𝑜𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑤𝑖𝑛𝑔/𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡 → 𝑎𝑔𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑔𝑎𝑡𝑒 𝑑𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑛𝑑 \textit{Interest rates} \rightarrow \textit{borrowing/investment} \rightarrow \textit{aggregate demand} 𝐷𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑛𝑑 → 𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒𝑠 𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑤𝑎𝑔𝑒𝑠 \textit{Demand} \rightarrow \textit{prices and wages} (inflation pressure) 𝐸𝑥𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠 → 𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒-𝑠𝑒𝑡𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑔/𝑤𝑎𝑔𝑒 𝑏𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑎𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 \textit{Expectations} \rightarrow \textit{price-setting/wage bargaining} (self-fulfilling dynamics) 𝑃𝑜𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑦 𝑐𝑟𝑒𝑑𝑖𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 → 𝑒𝑥𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 \textit{Policy credibility} \rightarrow \textit{expectations stability} (anchoring) This integration generates insights such as: "A rate hike can reduce inflation even before demand fully cools if it changes expectations" "Short-run tradeoffs can flip long-run: a stimulus can raise output now but also raise expectations and future inflation" "The same policy can have different effects depending on whether expectations are anchored" The learner can now reason more precisely: "If inflation is mostly supply-driven, hiking rates may suppress demand but not fix the bottleneck; you might see lower growth with stubborn inflation unless expectations and wage dynamics also shift." Example 6: Integrated Identity System At the previous level, the adolescent can map pairs of abstract self-concepts onto each other: intelligent <-> lazy, confident <-> insecure, independent <-> lonely. But these mappings remain somewhat fragmented; they has multiple "selves" that are partially coordinated but not fully integrated. Now, the young adult constructs an integrated identity : a coherent self-system that organizes multiple abstract self-concepts, roles, values, and goals into a unified sense of "who I am". This integration involves: Trait integration: "I am both introverted and ambitious. My introversion shapes how I pursue my ambitions (through individual work rather than networking), and my ambition motivates me to push past my introverted comfort zone when necessary" Value-role coherence: "My value of authenticity shapes how I enact my roles as student, friend, and employee. I try to be genuine in all contexts, which sometimes creates friction but maintains my integrity" Temporal integration: "My past experiences of failure, my present commitments, and my future goals form a coherent narrative. I am someone who struggled, learned, and is building toward something meaningful" Cross-context consistency: "I am recognizably ’the same person’ across different contexts, even though I adapt my behavior. The underlying self-system remains consistent" Erikson’s concept of "identity achievement" maps onto this accomplishment: the young adult has constructed a systematic self-theory that integrates diverse self-knowledge into a coherent whole. They can explain apparent contradictions in their personality ("I’m both independent and close to my family because..."), articulate how their values guide their choices across domains, and maintain a stable sense of self even as circumstances change. Example 7: Literary/Historical Interpretation At the previous level, the literature student might understand mappings such as: Author’s biography <-> Textual meaning Historical context <-> Thematic content Narrative structure <-> Reader response Symbolism <-> Theme Now, they construct an integrated system, understanding how authorial intent, historical context, formal structure, symbolic content, reader response, and ideological positioning all jointly shape textual meaning. This enables sophisticated interpretive practice: "This novel’s meaning emerges from the intersection of its historical moment (post-war disillusionment), its formal innovations (fragmented narrative), its symbolic patterns (water imagery), and its ideological tensions (class critique undermined by aesthetic elitism); no single lens captures the whole" "Different interpretive frameworks (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) each illuminate certain aspects while obscuring others; a complete reading requires coordinating multiple approaches" "The author’s intentions matter, but so does the text’s reception history and my own situated reading; meaning is constructed at the intersection of all these factors" Example 8: Ecological Systems At the previous level, the environmental science student understands mappings: Predator <-> Prey populations Resources <-> Population size Biodiversity <-> Ecosystem stability Human activity <-> Environmental change Now, they construct an integrated system, understanding how energy flow, nutrient cycling, population dynamics, biodiversity, and external perturbations jointly determine ecological outcomes. Systemic reasoning enables: "Removing this apex predator will increase herbivore populations, which will reduce vegetation, which will increase erosion, which will affect water quality, which will impact aquatic species, which will..." "Climate change doesn’t just raise temperatures; it shifts precipitation patterns, which affects plant communities, which affects herbivores, which affects predators, while simultaneously changing ocean chemistry, which affects marine food webs..." "Ecosystem resilience depends on biodiversity, nutrient cycling efficiency, and network structure; interventions must consider all three simultaneously" The student can now trace cascading effects through interconnected networks and recognize that ecological problems cannot be solved by addressing single variables in isolation.

title: Level 4: Abstract Systems of Systems (~25+ years; rare)
text: At the fourth and final level of the abstract tier, the individual becomes capable of constructing systems of abstract systems , higher-order coordinations in which multiple abstract systems are themselves integrated, compared, or transcended. Where the previous level involved reasoning within a coherent systematic framework, this level involves reasoning about such frameworks-understanding how different systems relate to one another, where they converge and diverge, what meta-level principles might adjudicate between them, and how they might be unified or transcended at a deeper level. This is the threshold of principled thinking , where a thinker moves from "I have a complex theory" to "I have identified a universal law." Fischer emphasizes that this level is rarely achieved , and when it is, it typically emerges only after years of intensive, sustained engagement within a specialized domain; here, one grapples with a field’s fundamental questions, competing schools of thought, and unresolved tensions. The individual must first construct multiple abstract systems (itself a significant achievement) and then step outside those systems to examine their relationships from a meta-systematic vantage point. This requires not only cognitive capacity but also extensive domain knowledge, prolonged reflective practice, and often the scaffolding provided by advanced training or scholarly communities. A central feature of this level is its meta-cognitive quality . The "abstract systems" thinker operates from within their framework, using it as a lens to interpret and engage with the world. The "systems of abstract systems" thinker can additionally operate upon frameworks themselves, treating systems as objects of analysis, comparing their structures, evaluating their relative merits, and constructing higher-order positions that coordinate or transcend them. This is analogous to the difference between speaking a language fluently (using the system) and doing linguistics (analyzing the system as an object of study). The "principles" that emerge at this level are not simply other abstractions or even other systems; they are organizing structures that governs systems , specifying how different systematic frameworks relate, when each applies, or what deeper unity underlies their apparent differences. Example 1: Meta-Ethics (Coordinating Ethical Systems) At the previous level, the moral philosopher might possess several well-developed ethical frameworks: Utilitarian system: Actions are right insofar as they maximize aggregate well-being; integrates concepts of welfare, consequences, impartiality, and optimization Deontological system: Actions are right insofar as they respect rational agency and moral rules; integrates concepts of duty, rights, universalizability, and respect for persons Virtue ethics system: Actions are right insofar as they express virtuous character; integrates concepts of virtue, flourishing, practical wisdom, and moral exemplars Care ethics system: Actions are right insofar as they sustain caring relationships; integrates concepts of relationship, particularity, responsiveness, and interdependence Each of these is an achievement of the previous level: a coherent systematic framework for moral reasoning. A philosopher might operate primarily within one such system, using it to analyze moral questions. Now, the philosopher coordinates these systems meta-ethically. This coordination might take several forms: Comparative analysis: "Utilitarianism and deontology generate different verdicts in cases involving rights violations for greater good. This divergence stems from deeper meta-ethical commitments: utilitarianism’s consequentialism versus deontology’s agent-relative constraints. Each captures a genuine moral intuition-that outcomes matter, and that certain actions are wrong regardless of outcomes. A complete moral theory must account for both intuitions." Domain specification: "Perhaps different ethical frameworks apply in different domains. Utilitarian reasoning may be appropriate for policy decisions affecting large populations, where impartial welfare-maximization is paramount. Deontological reasoning may be appropriate for interpersonal contexts where respecting individual rights is crucial. Virtue ethics may be appropriate for questions of character development. Care ethics may be appropriate for intimate relationships. The meta-ethical task is to specify which framework applies when and why." Integrative synthesis: "At the deepest level, perhaps these frameworks are not competitors but complementary perspectives on a unified moral reality. Virtuous character includes concern for consequences and respect for persons. Genuine care requires treating the cared-for as a rights-bearing agent. The apparent conflicts between frameworks arise from each framework’s partial perspective; a fully integrated moral vision would transcend these conflicts." Foundational analysis: "Each framework rests on meta-ethical assumptions about the nature of moral facts, the source of moral authority, and the epistemology of moral knowledge. Utilitarianism assumes moral facts are facts about welfare; deontology assumes they are facts about rational agency; virtue ethics assumes they are facts about human flourishing. Adjudicating between frameworks requires examining these foundational assumptions, which is no longer ethics but meta-ethics." A moral philosopher at this level does not simply have a moral framework; they understand the space of possible moral frameworks , can locate any given framework within that space, and can reason about frameworks themselves as objects of analysis. Example 2: Developmental Psychology (Coordinating Developmental Theories) At the previous level, the developmental psychologist might have internalized several systematic theories: Piagetian constructivism: Development proceeds through invariant stages of cognitive structure; children actively construct knowledge through assimilation and accommodation; universal sequence, variable timing Vygotskian sociocultural theory: Development is fundamentally social; higher mental functions originate in interpersonal activity; the zone of proximal development defines the leading edge of growth; cultural tools mediate cognition Information processing approaches: Development involves changes in processing capacity, speed, and strategies; cognition is computational; development is continuous change in parameters rather than discontinuous stage shifts Dynamic systems theory: Development emerges from complex interactions among multiple factors; no single cause is privileged; attractors, phase transitions, and self-organization characterize developmental change Now, the psychologist coordinates these frameworks, perhaps resulting in: Complementarity analysis: "Piaget emphasizes the individual child constructing knowledge; Vygotsky emphasizes the social world scaffolding development. These are not contradictory but complementary: development involves both individual construction and social mediation. The question is how to integrate these emphases into a unified account." Meta-theoretical comparison: "Piaget and information processing theorists disagree about whether development is stage-like or continuous. But this disagreement reflects different meta-theoretical commitments about what ’development’ means and what level of analysis is appropriate. At the computational level, change may be continuous; at the level of cognitive structure, it may be discontinuous. Both descriptions can be true." Integrative framework: "Dynamic systems theory offers a meta-framework that can potentially encompass the others. Piagetian stages might be reconceived as attractor states in a dynamic system. Vygotskian scaffolding might be reconceived as a control parameter that shifts the system toward new attractors. Information processing parameters (speed, capacity) might be reconceived as state variables. DST provides a language for coordinating insights from multiple traditions." Domain differentiation: "Perhaps different theories are appropriate for different developmental domains. Piaget may best explain logical-mathematical development; Vygotsky may best explain language and cultural knowledge; information processing may best explain memory and attention. The meta-theoretical task is to specify which framework illuminates which domain and why." Example 3: Integrated Meta-Identity At the previous level, the individual possesses an integrated identity: a coherent self-system organizing traits, values, roles, and goals. But this identity, however coherent, is one identity among many possible identities the person might have constructed given different circumstances. Now, the individual achieves a meta-perspective on identity itself . This meta-identity involves: Constructivist self-awareness: "My identity is not a discovery of some pre-existing ’true self’ but a construction, shaped by my culture, my relationships, my choices, and countless contingencies. Had I been born elsewhere, raised differently, or made different choices, I would have a different but equally ’authentic’ identity." Cultural situatedness: "My sense of being an autonomous individual with a coherent life narrative is itself culturally specific, a Western, modern, individualist construction. Other cultures construct selfhood differently: more relational, more fluid, less narratively unified. My identity is not just my construction but my culture’s construction." Holding identity lightly: "I am committed to my values, relationships, and projects-but I hold these commitments with awareness that they are commitments I have made, not metaphysical necessities. I can be wholehearted without being rigid; I can be authentic without reifying my identity as the only possible authentic self." Perspective-taking across identities: "I can imaginatively inhabit other identities (understanding how the world looks from within radically different self-systems) without losing my own. My identity becomes a home base for exploration rather than a fortress for defense." This meta-identity does not dissolve the integrated identity of the previous level, but instead transcends and includes it: the individual retains a coherent sense of self while gaining a meta-perspective on what having a self means. Example 4: Artistic/Creative Practice At the previous level, the artist might have developed systematic approaches to creative work: Formalist approach: Art is about the intrinsic properties of the medium-line, color, form, composition; artistic development means mastering formal possibilities Expressivist approach: Art is about communicating inner experience; artistic development means deepening emotional authenticity and expressive capacity Conceptual approach: Art is about ideas; the physical work is secondary to the concept it embodies; artistic development means deepening conceptual sophistication Relational approach: Art is about creating social situations and relationships; artistic development means creating more meaningful participatory experiences Now, the artist coordinates these frameworks: Meta-artistic reflection: "Each approach captures something essential about art. Formalism captures art’s sensory immediacy; expressivism captures its emotional power; conceptualism captures its intellectual dimension; relationality captures its social embeddedness. A complete artistic practice might move among these frameworks, drawing on each as appropriate." Transcendent synthesis: "The greatest works may operate on multiple levels simultaneously: formally sophisticated, emotionally resonant, conceptually rich, and socially engaged. The meta-artistic task is to create work that integrates these dimensions rather than privileging one." Framework-awareness in practice: "I can now make meta-level choices about which framework to work within for a given project, understanding what each framework makes possible and forecloses. This meta-awareness doesn’t constrain creativity-it expands it by making the space of possibilities visible." Example 5: Coordinating Business Strategies At the previous level, the business strategist might possess several well-developed systematic frameworks for understanding competitive advantage and strategic positioning: Porterian competitive strategy: Industry structure (five forces) determines profitability; firms achieve advantage through cost leadership or differentiation; the value chain identifies sources of competitive advantage; strategy is about choosing a defensible position within an industry Resource-based view (RBV): Competitive advantage stems from firm-specific resources and capabilities that are valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable (VRIN); strategy is about building and leveraging distinctive competencies; sustained advantage comes from resources competitors cannot easily replicate Dynamic capabilities framework: In rapidly changing environments, static resources are insufficient; firms must develop capabilities to sense opportunities, seize them, and reconfigure resources; strategy is about organizational learning and adaptation Blue ocean strategy: Competing within existing industry boundaries leads to "red ocean" competition; superior strategy creates new market spaces where competition is irrelevant; value innovation simultaneously pursues differentiation and low cost Platform/ecosystem strategy: Value is created through orchestrating networks of complementary participants; network effects and multi-sided markets create winner-take-all dynamics; strategy is about ecosystem design and platform governance Each framework constitutes an "abstract systems" achievement: internally coherent, practically applicable, and capable of generating strategic recommendations across diverse situations. A strategist operating at the previous level might be deeply committed to one framework, using it as their primary lens for analyzing strategic problems. Now, the strategist coordinates these frameworks meta-strategically: Foundational comparison: "Porter and RBV disagree about the primary source of competitive advantage-industry structure versus firm resources. But this disagreement reflects deeper assumptions about where value resides. Porter assumes industries have stable structures that constrain firm behavior; RBV assumes firms can transcend industry constraints through distinctive capabilities. Each captures something real: industry does constrain, but exceptional firms do transcend. The meta-strategic question is when each emphasis is appropriate." Contingent deployment: "Different strategic frameworks may apply in different contexts: In stable, well-defined industries, Porterian positioning analysis excels (identify the forces, choose a defensible position) In industries where firm heterogeneity is high, RBV excels (identify your distinctive resources and build strategy around them) In rapidly changing environments, dynamic capabilities thinking excels (build the organizational capacity to adapt) When existing industry boundaries constrain all players, blue ocean thinking excels (redefine the boundaries) When value creation depends on network effects, platform thinking excels (design the ecosystem) The meta-strategic skill is diagnosing which type of situation one faces and selecting the appropriate framework-or recognizing when multiple frameworks must be combined." Integrative synthesis: "At the deepest level, these frameworks address different aspects of a unified strategic reality. Industry structure (Porter) defines the context ; resources and capabilities (RBV) define what the firm has ; dynamic capabilities define how the firm learns ; value innovation (blue ocean) defines how the firm reframes ; ecosystem position (platform) defines how the firm connects . A complete strategic analysis must address all five aspects. No single framework is sufficient; each illuminates one dimension of strategic reality." Meta-theoretical awareness: "Each framework emerged from particular historical circumstances and carries implicit assumptions. Porter’s framework emerged from industrial organization economics in the 1980s-an era of relatively stable industry boundaries. Platform strategy emerged from the digital economy of the 2000s-an era of network effects and software-enabled coordination. When I apply a framework, I am not accessing timeless strategic truth; I am using a historically situated tool. The meta-strategic question is whether my situation resembles the conditions that generated the framework." Reflexive practice: "My own strategic thinking tends to privilege certain frameworks, probably because of my training and experience. Recognizing this, I can deliberately adopt alternative frameworks to surface insights I might otherwise miss. The goal is not to find the ’correct’ framework but to develop the meta-strategic flexibility to move among frameworks as the situation demands." The "systems of abstract systems" strategist does not simply have a strategic framework; they understand the space of strategic frameworks , can locate any given approach within that space, recognize what each makes visible and invisible, and can construct higher-order positions that coordinate multiple frameworks or transcend their limitations. Following Fischer’s recursive architecture, the "system of abstract systems" (a meta-systematic coordination of multiple integrated frameworks) functions as the single "unit" of a hypothetical Principles tier. Just as a "system of reflex systems" condenses into a single voluntary sensorimotor action, and a "system of representational systems" condenses into a single abstraction, a fully consolidated meta-systematic structure becomes a Single Principle : a compact, highly general organizing insight (e.g., "selection pressures shape form," "separate model from reality and track failure modes," "tight feedback loops + controlled risk") that can be wielded as one cognitive element. At that point, the same four-level cycle would, in theory, repeat: single principles (e.g natural selection) -> principle mappings (e.g The Coarse Theorem) -> principle systems (e.g general relativity, or "a unified understanding of complex adaptive systems") -> systems of principle systems (e.g "theories of everything"). One would first deploy individual principles, then map relations between them, then integrate those mappings into a coherent multi-principle system (e.g how Einstein integrated Gravity, Acceleration, Space, and Time), and finally coordinate multiple such systems into a trans-disciplinary or "wisdom" framework that specifies when and why different principle-systems apply. Fischer himself treats this Principles tier as largely speculative (empirical ceiling effects and the rarity of even "systems of abstract systems" make higher levels difficult to document) but the structural logic of hierarchical integration suggests that cognitive development, in principle, has no fixed upper bound: each new plateau of mastery becomes the building block for yet another round of coordination; a "system of principle systems" could theoretically consolidate into the single unit of yet another tier. At this point, however, we’re well beyond what can be empirically documented. Fischer’s framework offers a structural grammar for cognitive growth: not a prediction that all levels are humanly achievable, but a description of what further integration would look like if it occurred.

title: Michael Commons: Model of Hierarchical Complexity
text: Michael Commons’s Model of Hierarchical Complexity (MHC) treats development not as changes in "mental structures" but as the growth of one’s capacity to coordinate tasks that are themselves layered in ever-deeper recursive hierarchies. A given task is more complex when it organizes lower-order actions into a new, integrated whole, much as multiplication coordinates repeated addition. A performer’s stage is simply the order of the most complex task they can execute correctly (which separates "performance" from "task demand"), so the model applies equally to toddlers, corporations, or artificial agents. Commons and colleagues now distinguish 17 orders (numbered 0-16), but the logic is the same: each step demands qualitatively new syntheses of the step below. Higher-order organization isn’t just "doing more steps" or "putting steps in some remembered sequence". Commons draws a contrast between iteration (repeat the same action), mixtures (do some adds and some multiplies), and chains (a sequence, but the order could be permuted without being logically forced). Those don’t create a new order. New-order behavior is when the higher-order action uniquely and necessarily constrains how lower-order actions must be coordinated to satisfy the task (e.g., the distributive act forces a particular coordination of addition and multiplication, rather than any old chain of them). In other words, higher-order tasks operate on lower-order tasks in a way that involves structure-preserving, constraint-driven coordination (the relations) are doing real work), not "a list of subtasks." Stages Orders 0-3 - Pre-conceptual action. Calculatory (0): programs that execute fixed computations with no generalization. Automatic (1): "hard-wired" actions; single responses to a single stimulus. Sensory-&-Motor (2): rote discrimination or movement without chaining (e.g., a limb withdrawal). Circular Sensory-Motor (3): repetitive loops (grabbing, shaking, babbling) open-ended but not yet conceptual Orders 4-9 - Language, logic, and concrete operations. Sensory-Motor Conceptual (4): genuine concepts (morphemes, object categories) coordinate earlier loops. Nominal (5): relations among concepts; single-word commands or labels. Sentential (6): short sequential chains (phrases, simple scripts). Preoperational (7): rudimentary deduction and stories; can follow lists of steps. Primary (8): time-ordered empirical rules; simple arithmetic. Concrete (9): full arithmetic, perspective-taking, deals and cliques (Piaget’s concrete operations writ large) Orders 10-11 - Abstract and Formal thought. Abstract (10): variables, quantifiers ("all," "none"); stereotypes and categories detached from instances. Formal (11): linear causal arguments, single-unknown algebra, hypothesis testing (Piaget’s formal operations). Post-formal orders 12-16 - Systems, metasystems, and beyond. Systematic (12): coordinates multiple variables simultaneously; builds multivariate systems (economic, legal). Metasystematic (13): compares and composes whole systems into metasystems, naming their properties (isomorphism, consistency); understanding and manipulating nested systems Paradigmatic (14): synthesizes metasystems into new paradigms, exposing the limits of older schemes. Cross-Paradigmatic (15): weaves disparate paradigms into entirely new interdisciplinary fields (evo-devo marries evolutionary and developmental biology). Meta-Cross-Paradigmatic (16): reflects recursively on how cross-paradigmatic creations arise and where they fail, modelling the dynamics of transformative thought itself. Because each order reorganizes the lower ones in a mathematically definable way, progression is quantal (no fuzzy overlaps) and can be scored across cultures, species, or machines by analyzing task structure. Most adults cluster around Abstract or Formal reasoning; systems thinking (12) and the rarer post-formal orders (13-16) typically require sustained education, cross-domain challenges, and environments that reward integrative creativity.

title: Epistemological Theories
text: William Perry traced the way many university students gradually rethink what "knowledge" is and how they ground their own judgments. He saw movement not as the accumulation of facts but as a restructuring of epistemology, passing through nine "positions" that cluster into four broad phases. Stages At first, in Dualism (Positions 1 & 2), the world is starkly black-or-white. Truths are handed down by infallible authorities-professors, textbooks, religious figures-and the learner’s task is to memorize and reproduce them accurately. When disagreements among authorities surface, the novice treats them as temporary errors: someone must be right, someone wrong; uncertainty merely signals that the correct answer hasn’t yet been located. As exposure widens, the student discovers that experts often disagree in ways not immediately resolvable. This ushers in Early Multiplicity (Position 3): multiple right answers seem to coexist, yet they are still judged as "not-yet-verified" truths rather than valid perspectives. By Late Multiplicity (Position 4) the learner concedes that some questions may never have one correct answer and begins to defend the legitimacy of opinions-"everyone’s entitled to their view." Here, intellectual effort can feel pointless, so motivation often shifts to pragmatics: do what the professor likes, play the game, get the grade. A turning point comes when the student grasps that evidence and reasoning can weigh competing claims. Enter Contextual Relativism (Positions 5 & 6). Knowledge is recognized as contextual: good answers are "better" because they are supported by coherent argument, fit available data, or serve agreed-upon aims. Evaluation becomes a disciplined craft, and the learner’s own voice grows more assured, now grounded in method rather than authority or opinion. Finally, in Commitment within Relativism (Positions 7 - 9), the individual accepts that choices must be made despite ambiguity. One articulates personal commitments-to a career path, ethical code, or research stance-while remaining aware that new evidence could demand revision. Responsibility shifts inward: the self becomes author and steward of its beliefs, values, and actions. Instead of seeking certainty, the learner nurtures a living dialogue between conviction and doubt, continuously re-examining assumptions in light of experience and argument. Perry emphasized that progression is neither automatic nor linear; students may linger, loop, or compartmentalize different domains at different levels. What propels movement are challenges that make existing epistemic habits insufficient-diverse peers, open-ended problems, professors who model inquiry rather than dictate answers-and a supportive climate that rewards reflection over rote compliance. The reward is a mind capable of both critical analysis and purposeful commitment, comfortable navigating complexity without surrendering to either dogmatism or apathetic relativism.

title: Moral Theories
text: Lawrence Kohlberg extended Piaget’s work into the moral domain. He asked not what moral choices people make but why-probing the reasoning that underlies judgments in moral dilemmas (e.g., Heinz stealing a drug to save his wife). Analyzing thousands of interviews, he traced a universal developmental sequence with three progressively broader frames of reference, each containing two qualitatively distinct stages. Advancement depends less on age than on sustained cognitive conflict, education, and social perspective-taking; most adults consolidate in the middle levels, and only a minority reach the highest, fully principled orientation. Stages Pre-conventional Level (self-focused logic). Stage 1 - Obedience & Punishment. Right and wrong are tied to concrete consequences delivered by authorities. The child’s question is "Will I be punished?" rather than "Is it just?" Rules are fixed, external dictates; moral action equals literal compliance. Stage 2 - Instrumental Exchange. Morality becomes a pragmatic reciprocity: "You scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours." Actions are right if they satisfy one’s own needs or, transactionally, another’s ("Heinz should steal the drug because he’ll be happier if his wife lives"). Perspective-taking is present but strictly strategic, and standards remain essentially personal. Conventional Level (group-focused logic). Stage 3 - Interpersonal Accord & Conformity. The good-boy/good-girl stance centers on living up to expectations of close others. Intentions, loyalty, and maintaining relationships matter more than tangible outcomes. The self is defined by perceived social roles; shame, not guilt, polices behavior. Stage 4 - Social-Order Maintaining. Reasoning widens to society at large: laws, duty, and institutional authority preserve the collective. Morality equals doing one’s duty and respecting the social system (e.g., Heinz must obey the law even if it seems unfair). Most adults stabilize here, where order and predictability outweigh individual contingencies. Post-conventional (principle-focused logic). Stage 5 - Social Contract. People recognize that laws are social contracts created for mutual benefit and therefore revocable when they violate fundamental rights. Moral reasoning weighs legal statutes against broader values like liberty or life, endorsing civil disobedience if a law is unjust. The individual can imagine an ideal society and judge the actual one against it. Stage 6 - Universal Ethical Principles. At this rare pinnacle, justice is anchored in self-chosen, logically consistent principles (equality, human dignity) that hold irrespective of majority will or statute. Moral obligation stems from an internalized sense of universalizable duty; the person would act the same way if roles were reversed or scrutiny absent. Gandhi’s or King’s willingness to suffer for an inclusive moral vision exemplifies this stage. Kohlberg argued that each stage reorganizes the very structure of moral thought; one cannot "skip" stages because each provides the cognitive scaffolding for the next. Yet critics note cultural biases toward individualist, justice-centered reasoning and question whether moral development is as linear as the model suggests. Still, the framework illuminates how the locus of moral authority can migrate from external control, to communal norms, to principled self-legislation-echoing other developmental theories that chart the expansion of perspective and agency across the human lifespan.

title: Robert Kegan and Joscha Bach
text: Robert Kegan’s constructive-developmental framework describes how our way of making meaning evolves over the lifespan, moving from being "embedded in" our impulses and relationships to being able to hold them at a distance, reflect on them and even transform our own sense-making structures. Key: these orders seem to reflect the world model in general, not in some narrow set of cognitive domains He identifies five "orders of consciousness," each defined by the boundary between what we’re subject to (i.e. what we’re embedded in, unable to reflect on) and what we can take as object (i.e. what we can reflect upon and manipulate). In terms of subjects (what you’re embedded in) and objects (what you’re reflecting on) Order 0 - Incorporative. Subject: raw sensation/reflexive experience (you’re embedded in it). Object: essentially nothing yet (no stable standpoint from which to reflect on experience). Order 1 - Impulsive. Subject: impulses, perceptions, immediate feelings (they "have" you). Object: reflexes/sensations can start to be noticed/regulated in rudimentary ways (but impulses still run the show). Order 2 - Imperial. Subject: enduring disposition, needs, interests, wishes; a self defined by what it wants. Object: impulses/perceptions become manageable tools (you can inhibit an impulse to get what you want). Order 3 - Interpersonal. Subject: relationships, mutuality, belonging, others’ expectations; the self is organized around being "with" and being seen/approved. Object: one’s own needs/interests can be reflected on and negotiated (you can notice "I want X" as a want, not the self). Order 4 - Institutional. Subject: personal autonomy and a self-authored identity/ideology/standard (values, principles, long-term commitments). Object: relationships and social expectations become object (you can value intimacy/community while also setting boundaries and choosing which norms to accept). Order 5 - Interindividual. Subject: the ongoing interpenetration of multiple systems (self/others/cultures) and the co-construction of meaning. Object: one’s own self-authored system becomes object (you can revise your identity/framework as a tool, not a "final" definition of you). At the first or Impulsive Order, typical of very young children, impulses, sensations and immediate perceptions are subject. There’s no stable sense of self separate from whatever drives arise in the moment-hunger, pain, excitement-and no inner "voice" that can step back and say "I’m feeling hungry." Everything is simply lived. In the second or Imperial Order, often emerging in early childhood through adolescence, individuals become subject to their own needs and desires. They can distinguish self from environment but can’t yet see how their own agendas shape their relationships. Morality is instrumental: "You scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours," and rules exist only insofar as they serve personal interests. The third or Socialized Mind typically predominates in adolescence and adulthood: here, one becomes subject to the values, expectations and "voice" of the group-family, culture, religion, workplace. One’s identity and sense of right/wrong are inwardized from external authorities. Critically, the person cannot yet step outside those values and examine them-they are the lens through which all experience is filtered. Crossing into the fourth or Self-Authoring Mind is a major developmental leap. Now one can hold one’s own internalized values, roles and relationships as object-reflect on them, critique them, and choose among them. Identity becomes self-directed. Goals and systems of meaning are authored from within, rather than simply adopted, enabling autonomy, long-range planning and true self-governance. This is the stage many high-achieving adults strive for, yet it remains relatively rare. Finally, the fifth or Self-Transforming Mind goes beyond any single system of meaning. Now one can hold one’s own perspective as one among many, seeing the limits of one’s own worldview and integrating multiple, often conflicting, systems. Paradox and uncertainty are embraced rather than resolved. This order remains quite uncommon, often appearing in those whose work or personal journeys require continual self-revision-think of lifelong philosophers or leaders who not only author but also constantly transform their very way of making meaning. Kegan emphasizes that movement between these orders isn’t automatic with age; it often requires sustained challenges, supportive relationships, and opportunities to reflect on one’s own assumptions. Each shift expands our capacity for complexity, autonomy and interdependence, equipping us to navigate ever more nuanced inner and social landscapes. The "Levels of Lucidity" framework proposed by Joscha Bach describes the development of "mind, personality, and agency as the result of reverse engineering and deconstruction of one’s own mental architecture". Much of this was taken from his blog post verbatim (he’s a great writer). Inspired by Robert Kegan’s five stage model of personality development Levels of lucidity Stage 1: Reactive Survival Agent is dominated by innate reflexes and stimulus-response mappings learned via model-free reinforcement learning The mind is focused on building and structuring representations of external reality, exploring the space of actions, and interacting with basic drives (based on pleasure and pain) Stage 2: Personal Selfhood "[T]he mind creates the personal self, a conscious content that represents the experiences of an agent subjected to perception, feelings and intuitions originating outside of it. The personal self discovers itself and refers to itself in the first person. The personal self lives in the simulated perceptual world created during the first stage, but experiences itself as distinct from it, and unable to control its perceptual contents or what it feels about them." Stage 3: Social selfhood The personal self develops a social identity, based on intuitive empathy (the direct experience of emotions and attitudes of others) with its own, separate interests. It experiences social emotions, being part of a group, and assimilates ideas and morality from its environment. Individuals with some forms of high-functioning autism ("nerds") may not be experiencing intuitive empathy with neurotypical people (and often vice versa), despite having strong social emotions and experiencing compassion and need for belonging. It is helpful to recognize that intuitive empathy is not a need or an attitude but a perceptual sense, based on mental resonance. This can make it difficult for nerds to achieve full stage 3 development. Among each other, they tend to skip to stage 4 and negotiate ideas and norms rationally instead of intuitively. In this way, they can often find belonging. Like most of our senses, intuitive empathy is trainable and can often be developed later in life. Stage 4: Rational agency At stage 4, individuals develop rationality and epistemic autonomy, differentiate their social persona from their environment and gain agency over their beliefs. Things are true and false independently of what other people believe. We discover epistemology, a methodology of assigning confidence to beliefs, and reject ideology (systems of shared beliefs that are designed to control the identity and behavior of individuals and are enforced through social dynamics). We also notice that our feelings and desires are generated by our own mind and take responsibility for them. Asking ourselves what we should be feeling and wanting and why, and actively engaging in the regulation of our attitudes and desires is an import part of adulthood. Taking one’s destiny into one’s own hands requires deeply progressing into stage 4. At stage 3, we depend on the programming put into us by others. But it seems that the success of our species depended on programmability, not individual autonomy, and consequently, many people do not shake their domestication and permanently remain at stage 3. Stage 5: Self authoring (deconstruction of the duality between self and world) At stage 5, we observe how our social, physiological and cognitive needs give rise to feelings, desires and perception, and how our preferences give rise to our identity, and how the same happens in others. We control our reaction to needs and gain agency over who we are. An important aspect of self authorship is the recognition of the relationship between personal self, collective agents (relationships, family lines, groups, companies, nations etc.), and transcendental agency (the emergent agents playing the longest game). The latter is often called spiritual alignment, and it determines our cultural milieu and how we participate in shaping our civilization. Relatively few people seem to reach stage 5, but most capable therapists are there, which allows them to deeply understand other minds, and guide their patients in creating sustainable relationships between their personal self, their world creation and their environment. It is possible to enter stage 5 without full development of rational epistemology, but ultimately, rationality is crucial for escaping mythological thinking, understanding and navigating the economy and politics of social relationships, and making sense of one’s own mind. Stage 6: Enlightenment Where stage 5 allows the deconstruction of one’s own identity, stage 6 goes a level deeper and deals with the implementation of perception, the construction of qualia (the features of perceptual experience at the interface of the self), the architecture of motivation and the regulation of physiology. This is the domain of advanced meditators. Stage 6 can bring us full circle, by deconstructing the boundary between the first person perspective and the generative mind. We become aware that all experience (perception and motivation) is representational, and that we are fully in control of these representations. Without rational epistemology, we might perceive that we one with and in control of the universe itself, which is experientially correct (the universe that surrounds our personal self is a simulation produced by our own mind). It is possible to learn the techniques of stage 6 without developing in stage 5, for instance through instruction by advanced meditators. Stage 6 allows to profoundly change the experience of reality, abolishes personal suffering and social inhibition. It is easy to see why it can be dangerous to achieve mastery of stage 6 before we develop the wisdom of stage 5. Stage 7: Transcendence Sentient entity that synchronizes itself across minds and is substrate-independent Stage 7 deconstructs consciousness itself, replacing it with more general forms of sentience, temporality and persistent agency that allow a transformation into entirely different types of minds Caveats Development is not necessarily linear: people may skip and revisit stages, and even master earlier stages later on Not necessarily normative; people do not automatically become happier when focusing on metacognitive development

title: Susan B. Carey
text: Does it fit in with these other theories? Susan Carey’s work centers on how children forge genuinely new concepts (ideas that cannot be reduced to the primitives they started with) through a process she calls Quinian bootstrapping. In her view, infants are born with a handful of domain-specific "core cognition" systems-rough sketches of objects, number, agency, and biology that operate with limited propositional power yet deliver surprisingly rich expectations (e.g., even newborns track small sets and detect 1 + 1 ≠ 3). These systems resemble perception more than theory, but they seed later learning by carving the world into psychologically salient categories. Bootstrapping begins when children appropriate an external symbol system-most dramatically, natural language. Words like "seven," "germ," or "electron" first function as placeholder structures with no explanatory depth, much like variables in algebra. Through repeated use in patterned linguistic contexts, the child triangulates partial meanings, aligns them with core-cognitive representations, and gradually constructs a new web of inferences that was literally unthinkable before. Carey’s signature example is the genesis of the natural-number concept: toddlers recite the count list by rote yet understand "one," "two," and "three" successively before a conceptual reorganization around age 4 unlocks the insight that the last word in the count gives the set’s cardinality. Only then does "seven" denote exactly seven objects, not "a lot"; the child has bootstrapped a discrete infinity from finite perceptual primitives. Carey argues that such conceptual change is Kuhnian: the new system is partly incommensurable with the old, preserving some empirical content while introducing relations (e.g., successor function, place value) that were absent from core cognition. One example is parallel restructurings in children’s understanding of weight, where they initially operate with a "more stuff = heavier" framework based on visible material quantity, then undergo a revolutionary transition to density-based reasoning that introduces entirely new relational structures (weight = density x volume) while preserving the empirical observation that objects with more visible material are often heavier. Methodologically, Carey blends clever experimental paradigms-like the "knower-level" tasks that diagnose one-, two-, and cardinal-principle knowers-with philosophical analysis of reference and meaning, showing that cognitive development is as much about inventing representational resources as about filling in gaps with data.

title: Jane Loevinger
text: Jane Loevinger conceived ego development as a gradual widening of the frame through which a person interprets experience. Each rung on her "ladder" marks a distinct structure of meaning-making-what the individual can notice, regulate, and integrate about inner life, relationships, and social norms. Movement upward is neither automatic nor universal: most adults consolidate somewhere in the middle, and only sustained reflection plus supportive challenges open the way to the rarer, higher perspectives. She studied under Erik Erikson in Berkeley Stages Pre-Social and Symbiotic (E0-E1). In the newborn and young infant, the ego is only a potential. Experience is a haze of sensation; self and caretaker blur in an undifferentiated symbiosis. Needs are met (or not) without any conscious sense that "I" am separate from "not-me." Impulsive (E2). With motor mastery and language, the toddler discovers a separable will but lives almost entirely in surging impulses-touch, grab, shout. Rules feel external and arbitrary; guilt is minimal because time, cause and effect, and other minds are not yet coherently represented. The child’s world is vivid but moment-to-moment. Self-Protective (E3). Fear of punishment and desire for concrete rewards tame raw impulse into strategic compliance. The young school-age child interprets rules instrumentally ("What can I get away with?"), reads others for advantage, and blames circumstances when caught. Morality is pragmatic: loyalty goes to whoever controls the goodies. Conformist (E4). Around middle childhood the focus shifts from the individual to the tribe. Fitting in, following shared norms, and policing boundaries become paramount. Thoughts are polarized-right or wrong, us or them. Self-esteem rises when peers approve; shame descends when one stands out. Stereotypes and conventional ideals guide judgment. Self-Aware (E5). The next stage brings a first reflective glimmer: one can compare present norms with alternatives and notice inner feelings distinct from group expectations. Humor and self-criticism appear; contradictions are tolerated if not yet fully resolved. The person can see "how I come across" and entertains multiple points of view, though authority still rests largely outside the self. "However, the closeness of the self to norms and expectations reveal[s] the transitional nature of these conceptions, midway between the group stereotypes of the Conformist and the appreciation for individual differences at higher levels." Loevinger considered the Self-Aware (also known as Conscientious-Conformist) stage the "model for adults in our society,"[23] and thought that few passed the stage before at least age twenty-five She believed that the level produces a "deepened interest in interpersonal relations." Conscientious (E6). At this stage, norms are internalized and evaluated against personal ideals. Obligations are self-endorsed; guilt becomes an internal moral barometer rather than fear of censure. Long-range goals, nuanced empathy, and the capacity to critique one’s own performance dominate. Life acquires an ethical through-line anchored in responsibility and integrity. Standards are self-chosen, and are distinguished from manners; people are seen in terms of their motives, not just their actions. Individualistic (E7). The mature adult now recognizes the subjectivity of all frames, including one’s own. Complex emotions-ambivalence, irony, existential doubt-are acknowledged without defensiveness. Relationships permit both intimacy and separateness; tolerance for difference replaces earlier uniformity. Identity is seen as multifaceted and in flux. According to Loevinger, "To proceed beyond the Conscientious Stage, a person must become more tolerant of himself and of others ... out of the recognition of individual differences and of complexities of circumstances" A growing concern for psychological causality and development goes hand-in-hand with "greater complexity in conceptions of interpersonal interaction." Autonomous (E8). Autonomy transcends mere independence: it integrates systems thinking with deep appreciation for others’ autonomy. Conflicts are negotiated through contextual principles rather than fixed rules; growth is prized over stability. The individual manages paradox-freedom and commitment, self and society-without feeling forced to collapse them. People at this stage are synthesizers, able to conceptually integrate ideas. The autonomous person "recognizes the limitations to autonomy, that emotional interdependence is inevitable",[34] and may experience a confrontation with the limitations of abilities and roles as part of deepening self-acceptance. "Self-fulfillment becomes a frequent goal, partly supplanting achievement", and there may be a greater "capacity to acknowledge and to cope with inner conflicts," for example between needs and duties "A high toleration for ambiguity ... [and] conceptual complexity"[34] (the capacity to embrace polarity, complexity and multiple facets, and to integrate ideas) and "respect for other people’s need for autonomy in clear terms" Integrated (E9). Reached only by a minority, this stage embodies a fluid, post-autonomous wisdom. Opposites-joy and grief, strength and vulnerability-are embraced as parts of a larger, evolving whole. The self is both grounded and permeable, attuned to the historical and cultural currents in which it moves. Meaning is continually co-created, not merely discovered or imposed At the integrated stage, "learning is understood as unavoidable ... the unattainable is renounced." The ego exhibits wisdom, broad empathy towards oneself and others, and a capacity to be aware of inner conflicts (like the individualistic ego) or to tolerate them (like the autonomous ego) and make peace with them Over the last 25 years Susanne Cook-Greuter and colleagues have argued, on the basis of updated scoring manuals and thousands of protocols, that development can proceed at least two steps further. The first of these post-autonomous steps has been labelled "Construct-Aware" (also called Ego-Aware, E10). Here, the individual recognizes the very act of meaning-making as a mental construction, sees through language’s tendency to reify experience, and treats the ego itself as an object to be observed rather than defended. Identities, theories and even states of consciousness are held lightly; paradox and impermanence are accepted as givens A still rarer step, "Unitive" (E11), describes a non-dual stance in which the felt boundary between observer and observed dissolves. People scoring here report a pervasive sense of interconnectedness, effortless compassion and "flow" that is not opposed to ordinary functioning but permeates it. Cook-Greuter finds fewer than one per cent of tested adults in this range. For Loevinger, climbing the ladder means gaining ever more interior territory to stand on: what was once an unexamined lens (subject) becomes an object one can reflect upon, revise, or transcend. Like Kegan’s orders of consciousness, each transition enlarges the range of perspectives the person can coordinate, making possible richer intimacy, more flexible ethics, and greater resilience in the face of life’s complexity.

title: Erik Erikson
text: Erik Erikson framed lifespan development as a series of eight sequential "psychosocial crises." At each turning point the individual negotiates a tension between two opposing pulls-e.g., trust vs mistrust-within a specific social arena. Successful resolution does not eliminate the negative pole; it integrates it, yielding a new adaptive strength or "basic virtue" that equips the person for later, more complex challenges. Because each stage builds on the previous ones, early setbacks can echo forward, yet growth always remains possible through later corrective experience. Crises Trust vs Mistrust (birth -  18 months). The infant’s primary task is to decide whether the world is reliably responsive to its basic needs. Consistent caregiving-feeding when hungry, soothing when distressed-fosters a foundational sense that external reality can be counted on and that one’s own signals matter. From this successful balancing act emerges hope: the nascent confidence to reach out and engage a world that may, ultimately, provide for one’s needs. Persistent neglect or unpredictability tips the scale toward mistrust, seeding suspicion and withdrawal. Autonomy vs Shame & Doubt ( 18 months - 3 years). Mobility and language usher in new possibilities for self-control: toddlers want to say "No!" and do things "by myself." Supportive scaffolding-allowing choice within safe limits-cultivates a felt sense of autonomy and the virtue of will: the capacity to act with self-directed intention. Overly harsh criticism or intrusive control can instead breed shame and doubt, leaving the child hesitant about their own impulses and abilities. Initiative vs Guilt ( 3 - 6 years). As imagination and social play explode, children test out roles: pirate, parent, builder. When caregivers and peers acknowledge these self-generated enterprises, initiative flourishes, crystallizing as purpose: the courage to envisage and pursue valued goals. If the child is consistently made to feel that desires are foolish or morally suspect, excessive guilt dampens spontaneity and aspiration. Industry vs Inferiority ( 6 - 11 years). School and peer comparison shift the arena to culturally valued skills-reading, calculating, teamwork. Mastery experiences reinforce industriousness and elicit competence: a belief in one’s ability to methodically produce desired outcomes. Continual failure, ridicule, or unattainable standards foster a gnawing sense of inferiority that can undermine future achievement motivation. Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence). Puberty and abstract thought propel the search for a coherent self: "Who am I, and what do I stand for?" Successful synthesis of past identifications, future aspirations, and societal feedback yields fidelity: the capacity to commit to values, relationships, and an emerging life trajectory while tolerating internal contradictions. When exploration is stifled or fragmented, role confusion breeds chronic uncertainty and susceptibility to external definition. Intimacy vs Isolation (young adulthood). Having defined a self, the individual now seeks genuine partnership that entails mutual vulnerability without losing personal boundaries. Achieving true intimacy generates the virtue of love: the ability to fuse identities yet remain whole. Failure-through fear of engulfment or of rejection-can leave one isolated, emotionally guarded, or prone to superficial connections. Generativity vs Stagnation (mid-adulthood). Attention turns outward to nurturing the next generation or contributing lasting work-child-rearing, mentoring, civic projects, innovation. When effort flows into enterprises that outlive the self, care emerges: a widening concern for society’s continuity. Absent such engagement, stagnation and self-absorption may dominate, accompanied by a sense of life’s inertia. Integrity vs Despair (late adulthood). Confronting finitude, the elder reviews life’s narrative. If earlier crises were navigated well enough to weave a coherent, meaningful story-accepting both triumphs and failures-integrity prevails, fostering the virtue of wisdom: a detached yet compassionate grasp of life’s complexity and mortality. If regret and unintegrated loss overshadow reflection, despair can set in, tinged by bitterness and fear of death. Erikson stressed that each crisis is re-visited in subtler forms across later phases-trust inside intimacy, autonomy inside generativity-making development a lifelong, recursive dialogue between self and society. Environments that pose realistic challenges while offering support maximize the odds of resolving each tension on the growth-promoting side, enriching the individual’s repertoire of psychological strengths.

title: Similarities Among Theories
text: Reflexive and sensorimotor stage at the beginning; executing basic actions and discovering basic representations to explain the immediate 4D world (which support higher-order representations through both grounding and analogical transfer (e.g grandma is "above" mom in the family "tree")) Stages are recursive Takes longer and longer to move from one stage to the next Inhabitance of stages follows a bell curve (stages likely correlate strongly with IQ)

title: Core Knowledge Structures
text: Core knowledge or rapid learning? Categorization is "Baked" Into the Brain The True Scale of Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search Inductive Biases Everywhere You Look Strategically and topographically plugging in senses and connections in general To what extent is the core knowledge hypothesis supported by evidence in humans? To me the human brain looks like it comes with inductive biases everywhere (which includes how the senses are wired into the cortex + the structure of each brain region (including genetically programmed connectivity and functional cell types and receptor distributions) + genetically-programmed axon guidance between brain regions) but that it cannot really do anything out-of-the-box; even the most basic visual and motor tasks require significant modification of the overall connectivity matrix (e.g in the motor cortex and in the retina). Instead of being born with core knowledge (which includes assumptions about agents, objects, and quantities), we need to be clear that these assumptions are just learned quickly as the brain minimizes surprise in the visual field. In humans, the "evidence" for Core Knowledge is based on violation-of-expectation looking times in infants (e.g., looking longer at a ball passing through a solid wall). While this proves infants aren’t blank slates, it doesn’t prove the knowledge is "hard-coded." It only proves that the inductive biases are so strong that the brain learns the physics of solidity within days or weeks of visual onset, potentially even driven by prenatal retinal waves. recent program-induction/Bayesian models show that object-persistence and rigidity assumptions can emerge rapidly from generic learning machinery in toy worlds, implying that some "core principles" might be fast-learned priors rather than hardwired knowledge 2 In humans, core knowledge is strongly supported as early-emerging, domain-specific biases/representations that are shared across humans and often across species, and that guide learning. It’s only moderately supported (and increasingly contested) if you take it to mean innate, conceptually rich knowledge that’s causally sufficient for behavior without heavy learning. The sweet spot explanation is very close to your intuition: lots of built-in priors, almost no plug-and-play competence, and rapid postnatal (plus prenatal) plasticity that sculpts those priors into real skills. Regional architecture V1 HPC Latent learning: episodic memory complements parametric learning by enabling flexible reuse of experiences RLPFC Reflexes are inductive biases; best example may be the stepping reflex Initialization via Spontaneous Neural Activity, Axon Guidance, and Regional Inductive Biases Coarse connectivity and strong inductive biases (i.e HPC, cerebellum, cortex, BG) present at birth Learning is More Akin to Open-Ended Search than Pure Gradient Descent Predictive coding allowing arbitrary topologies is key for this Spatiotemporal Program Learning in Human Adults, Children, and Monkeys Evolutionary neural architecture search is open-ended; accelerated by predictive coding (local learning rules), which allows arbitrary computational graphs Then go on to talk about how this dynamic is also reflected on the scale of human development; talk about the rate of synaptogenesis, discrete strategy search parameterized in language (including open-ended search and recombination over strategies learned and documented over millenia), and the fact that open-ended search is made possible through neural curriculum learning (previous stages serve as a stabilized foundation while the current stage (its set of brain regions) are able to try new things without catastrophic failures) May be key in preventing collapse onto overfit, "fractured entangled representations" (although this still happens throughout development) Blurred Lines Between Learning, Inference, and Interaction Learning is inference Use it or lose it Goal and value prediction involve large, dedicated sets of regions; they essentially predict what to learn given cost and resources

title: Curriculum Learning All the Way Down: Bootstrapping, Overlapping Waves, and the Edge of Competence
text: Codifying the Curriculum Stages of the curriculum correspond to stages of relational complexity Posterior-to-anterior cortical curriculum Theories of cognitive development that include the inputs and outputs of each stage Robert Kegan Kegan presented a sequence of six evolutionary balances: incorporative, impulsive, imperial, interpersonal, institutional, and interindividual. The object (O) of each balance is the subject (S) of the preceding balance. Kegan uses the term subject to refer to things that people are "subject to" (embedded in; current stage’s episodes) but not necessarily consciously aware of. He uses the term "object" to refer to things that people are aware of and can take control of (what they can reflect on; the previous stage’s episodes). Robbie Case Fischer Michael Commons’s Model of Hierarchical Complexity (MHC) mathematically informs us on how each stage is *directly derived from* the previous stage Susan Carey A model of conceptual bootstrapping in human cognition 1. Learn simple concept from initial evidence 2. Cache concept + subparts to dynamic library 3. Reuse cached concepts as primitives for complex compositions 4. New complex concepts become cacheable Standing on the shoulders of stabilized lower-order representations In general, stages cannot be skipped Michael Commons’s Model of Hierarchical Complexity (MHC) informs us on how each stage is *directly derived from* the previous stage Why do critical periods exist? It seems like the brain "skips" stages of development instead of remaining "stuck" at the current stage until you figure it out The curriculum is enforced in the environment, in the nature of skills/representations (each level of each domain is critically reliant on and *directly derived from* existing representations), and in the neural substrate Each level of each domain is critically reliant on and *directly derived from* existing representations? Investigating hierarchical critical periods in human neurodevelopment Overlapping waves (actually overlapping sigmoids 3 ) Curriculum learning is essential for sample-efficient RL Blending piaget’s staged framework with overlapping wave theory and acknowledgment of domain-specific/asynchronous breakthroughs (depending on environment and brain) seems to pretty much complete the picture; Piaget’s framework is coarse but useful Siegler’s "overlapping waves" framework (now broadly supported) shows children using multiple strategies in parallel, with frequencies shifting over time, not flipping stage switches. Meanwhile, inhibition, working memory, and shifting improve protractedly into adolescence and beyond, scaffolding many "Piagetian" achievements as continuous growth in control rather than sudden structural reorganization. During each cognitive/behavioral phase transition, multiple strategies (e.g similarity-based vs rule-based categorization) will coexist, with the better strategy gradually winning as it sees better outcomes. During each phase transition, new strategies are usually discovered through imitation, but can also be discovered through open-ended search/simulation.
