title: Strategy Induction: Control Primitives as Emergent Properties of Sufficiently Hierarchical World Modeling
text: The previous section fleshed out the nature of reasoning and argued that it relies on and is directly derived from lower- and middle-order representations. This section collapses the "representational" and "control" distinction (without claiming the distinction is useless/invalid) since it will allow us to more clearly explain how humans learn to design, pursue, and attain long-term goals whole responding flexibly and adaptively to changes in the environment. We show that attention control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory are distinct but they share a common factor. This factor is completely identical with an integral construct standing for relational integration and awareness, suggesting that executive function does not have much beyond this construct 1 Control primitives are definitely enabled by sufficiently hierarchical world modeling (since they involve abstract representations) but are they actually an emergent phenomenon or were abstract representations evolutionarily optimized to have a high "control coefficient" (influence on the rest of the brain)? Or, given the nature/constraints of the brain (the learning rules and architecture), would abstract representations have to have a high control coefficient to exist in the first place? Thinking is another form of control Learning by thinking in natural and artificial minds From skills to strategies Cognitive control a family of top-down mental processes needed when you have to concentrate and pay attention, when going on automatic or relying on instinct or intuition would be ill-advised, insufficient, or impossible 4 a set of processes enabling us to design, pursue, and attain short- and long-term goals while responding flexibly and adaptively to changes in the environment 5 We can (partially) collapse the distinction between cortical regions underlying "representation" and those underlying "control", making every cortical region a "representation of the environment that is necessarily action-oriented, with information integration occurring across varying timescales". While "control" and "representational" regions certainly have their distinctions besides their intrinsic timescales and representational contents (e.g region-specific connectivity to subcortical regions and neuromodulatory hubs), by seeing cognitive control as the natural dynamics of the most abstract, temporally extended layers of the hierarchical world model, this allows us to better explain how executive functions are learned 6 . This is what the active inference folks argue; they unify perception and action under one objective: Minimizing Free Energy. All cognition is "goal-directed" because the brain is always trying to minimize the divergence between its model and reality, contrasting popular definitions of executive functions as cognitive processes that underlie "goal-directed behavior" 7 ; labeling EFs as those cognitive functions underlying goal-directed behavior. The field of active inference still uses the term to distinguish between Model-Based (calculating the path to a goal state) and Habitual/Amortized (reflexive S t a t e → A c t i o n State \rightarrow Action mappings), but they still are just two ways of doing the same thing (minimizing surprise). If the brain is a hierarchical generative model, the higher layers must encode slower, more stable latent variables (context, rules, plans). Mapping each executive function Inhibitory control: involves being able to control one’s attention, behavior, thoughts, and/or emotions to override a strong internal predisposition or external lure, and instead do what’s more appropriate or needed 4 Inhibition maps to Action Selection/Policy Arbitration: The competition between the high-level policy and the low-level policy. "Inhibition" is not a force that pushes back; it is the act of assigning extremely high precision (confidence) to a top-down prior ("I am a person who remains calm") relative to the bottom-up sensory/proprioceptive prediction error ("I am about to punch this person"). Shifting (Flexibility): one aspect is being able to change perspectives spatially (e.g., "What would this look like if I viewed it from a different direction?") or interpersonally (e.g., "Let me see if I can see this from your point of view"). To change perspectives, we need to inhibit (or deactivate) our previous perspective and load into WM (or activate) a different perspective. It is in this sense that cognitive flexibility requires and builds on inhibitory control and WM. Another aspect of cognitive flexibility involves changing how we think about something (thinking outside the box). For example, if one way of solving a problem isn’t working, can we come up with a new way of attacking this or conceiving of this that hadn’t been considered before? Cognitive flexibility also involves being flexible enough to adjust to changed demands or priorities, to admit you were wrong, and to take advantage of sudden, unexpected opportunities. Suppose you were planning to do X, but an amazing opportunity arose to do Y: Do you have the flexibility to take advantage of serendipity? maps to State Transition/Inference: The ability of the high-level model to rapidly switch its belief about which "context" (latent state) is currently active. If your model is "sticky" (low flexibility), it over-predicts the previous context. Working memory: involves holding information in mind and mentally working with it (or said differently, working with information no longer perceptually present 4 Updating (WM) maps to State Maintenance: The stability of the active high-level representation over time. Lower levels of the brain (sensory cortex) encode fast-changing variables (milliseconds). Higher levels (PFC) encode slow-changing latent variables (seconds/minutes). When you "hold" a thought, you aren’t storing it; your high-level model is stuck in a stable state that predicts a sequence of lower-level dynamics. The "maintenance" is just the natural inertia of a high-level representation that has a slow time constant. Metacognition = Hyperpriors (Beliefs about Beliefs): This is the system estimating its own uncertainty. It’s not just predicting the world; it’s predicting how precise its predictions are likely to be. It is abstracting over learning episodes and thought processes themselves. It’s not just predicting the world; it’s predicting how precise its predictions are likely to be. Reasons why removing the distinction between "representational" and "control" regions is useful The same machinery (i.e cortical columns) that comes to be used to discover hierarchical representations requiring low and middling abstraction (e.g basic fine/gross motor control, classification, and navigation) can to some extent be naively extended and give rise to abstract representations (and executive functions) Labeling certain regions as "control" or "executive" regions is still useful: Calling certain regions "working memory regions" (i.e dlPFC) is useful because these are indeed the regions that maintain their activity over the longest time periods and contain the variables that most directly correlate with our behaviors; however, these regions can equivalently be seen as the regions that simply model the most higher-order/low-frequency (abstract) variables, which leads to particularly auto-correlated representations over time and just so happen to be the representations that maximize cumulative rewards (explaining their acquired "top-down influence" across development). Executive functions are not control primitives but emergent properties of high-level generative models constraining lower-level perception, valuation, and action; it simply turns on when higher order patterns/rules/representations are present, especially those that haven’t been fully internalized into ventral striatal policies Can I conceptualize executive functions essentially as the most abstract portion of the world model? Each executive fucntion just seems like the natural behavioral/cognitive signature of higher-order pattern recognition. For example, "inhibition" is recognized when you realize the more concrete parts of your brain are incorrect in their valuation of an action due to them missing some higher-order pattern ("I shouldn’t call her a bitch cause I have X higher-order goal to reach"). Working memory maintanence is merely a reflection of the fact that abstract patterns/rules/representations necessarily have "slots" that lower-order patterns fit into. Metacognition is the highest-order abstract knowledge, where self and thought are themselves abstracted (other executive functions + internal states are abstracted). The label of executive function being "goal-directed" seems like a useless label, as all cognition is goal-directed (used to think this, but "goal-directed" needs to be altered to "long term goal-directed" to make sense as a classifier for EFs). It is quite integrative, and therefore quite costly to run. Consciousness is expensive! Prefrontal cortex sits at the apex of a representational hierarchy: long temporal receptive fields, high abstraction, multimodal integration, and weak coupling to immediate sensory input. When a high-level latent variable becomes active - a long-horizon goal, social rule, identity constraint, or abstract task structure - it necessarily re-weights downstream value functions, policies, and attentional priorities. What psychologists label as "executive function" is just what this re-weighting looks like behaviorally. Planning, skills, and hierarchical control Executive function (expressed component-wise) can be seen as the principal limiter from an early age; develops extremely slowly and is both a key enabler of and a key beneficiary of post-training The competence system is concerned with understanding or knowing, whereas the procedural system makes success possible on particular problems (Overton, 1990; Overton & Dick, 2007). Performance or procedural factors cannot substitute for competence, and the latter cannot be reduced to some set of procedures. The competence system for formal reasoning in Overton’s account is assumed to consist of a mental logic that resembles standard propositional logic. see Overton and colleague’s "competence-procedural" theory executive function as a bottleneck on conceptual change. Susan B Carey and collaborators show that the ability to update intuitive theories depends on working memory, inhibition, and cognitive flexibility: children must hold competing representations in mind, inhibit default interpretations, and switch between explanatory frameworks as they test new hypotheses Planning, Skills, and Hierarchical Control Reward shaping (hierarchical, dense rewards) Skill learning in the developing brain: Interactions of control and representation systems Looking deeper into the algorithms underlying human planning ; a mechanistic theory of planning in prefrontal cortex ; cognitive maps in prefrontal cortex Language-parameterized skill library Treat skill acquisition as the control-theoretic side of abstraction. Start with corticostriatal loops as a library builder: dorsomedial circuits learn flexible, goal-directed policies; dorsolateral circuits slowly crystallize habits/options; ventral loops set vigor and motivation. Explain how subgoal discovery arises from bottlenecks in the state-transition graph (frontoparietal discovery, striatal consolidation) and how chunking shows up in neural population dynamics as low-dimensional, reusable trajectories. Fold in the cerebellum as a supervised calibrator of forward/inverse models for each skill, emphasizing vector-valued teaching lines from inferior olive that tune timing and gains. End with the robotics-ready pattern: discover options via graph bottlenecks or successor-eigenoptions, pretrain cerebellum-like inverse models with dense supervised traces, and use BG-like distributional critics to stitch skills together with risk-aware arbitration. Planning as inference; heavily discuss how biological agents learn how to plan Long-horizon planning Learning Reasoning and Rationality from Everyday Experiences: Discovering Strategies and Abstractions Derive a full spec for how reasoning is learned From skills to strategies; from strategies to systems of strategies Awake replay: off the clock but on the job Learning by thinking in natural and artificial minds Embodied cognition perspectives within early executive function development How is reasoning learned? It seems like humans may never learn them without cultural technology (which allows humans across millenia to essentially function as a super-organism, increasing the sample efficiency of each successive generation), but that there is also a strong RL component (mostly on-policy but also offline/off-policy) First, there are some proto-strategies that you probably get "for free" from generic learning machinery. If you drop a kid in a rich environment with no schooling, they still discover things like "try another way if the first attempt fails," "compare this situation to a remembered similar one," "mentally test a few steps ahead before acting," and "look for where the difference is between two conditions." You can think of these as primitive internal options over a world model. The brain’s RL system is not just tuning motor outputs; it’s tuning policies over internal computations: where to attend, whether to simulate, how many steps to roll out, whether to check an alternative hypothesis. When a particular mini-procedure reliably improves reward (solving puzzles faster, avoiding scolding, getting praise, experiencing that "aha" intrinsic reward), it gets reinforced as a reusable pattern. Second, there’s an explicit RL story over strategies, not just actions. Take "try a counterexample" as a reasoning mode. Initially a child might occasionally think, "wait, is there a case where this doesn’t work?" by accident. When that move pays off-by catching an error on homework, impressing a teacher, winning an argument-it gets value. Over many episodes, the control system learns something like: in states with features abstract claim, high stakes, moderate time, prior conflict , launch the "search for counterexample" routine. That’s on-policy meta-RL over their own reasoning: each episode is "I tried strategy S in context C and got reward R." Offline/off-policy kicks in when they replay episodes in memory or imagine how things could have gone ("if I’d checked both cases, I wouldn’t have been wrong") and assign credit or blame retroactively; hippocampal replay plus prefrontal evaluation is doing gradient steps on a policy over internal operations rather than just overt behavior. Now add culture, and everything explodes in richness and sample efficiency. Other people literally present you with high-performing internal policies: "When you’re stuck, draw a diagram"; "Consider the opposite hypothesis"; "Prove it by contradiction"; "Control one variable at a time." Instruction, worked examples, and even casual language ("what if everyone did that?", "in the extreme case…") are all ways of shipping pre-discovered reasoning modes into your head. Mechanistically, that looks like a mix of imitation learning (copying external verbalized chains of thought), supervised learning (matching teacher solutions), and RL (praise, grades, not-looking-stupid in front of peers). Crucially, culture doesn’t just give you strategies, it gives you meta-tags and cues: "this is a proof by induction," "this is a thought experiment," which helps the control system learn a mapping from problem features -> appropriate mode much faster than unguided exploration would. There’s also a strong offline/off-policy component via text, lectures, and examples. When you read a proof or watch someone debug, you’re seeing a trajectory in "reasoning space" that you didn’t generate. You can still update your own policy: "In problems of type T, the experts open with step X, not step Y." That’s off-policy learning over internal actions: you’re adjusting which mental steps you would take in a state, based on someone else’s trace. This is exactly why cultural technology (writing, notation, diagrams, formal logic, algebra, probability theory) is so powerful: it externalizes sequences of internal operations so they can be observed, copied, tweaked, and recombined by others. Over time, repeated use and reward turn some of these modes from slow, effortful System-2 procedures into fast, semi-automatic System-1 patterns. Early on, "do a case split" is a deliberate choice; later, the space of cases just pops into mind. The basal ganglia-PFC loop is basically learning which internal option to gate in which context and how long to run it. Additionally, metacognition itself becomes a learned strategy library: "If my confidence is low but stakes are high, escalate to a more expensive mode (formal check, external calculation, ask for help)." That’s reflective-system RL over which algorithmic patterns to deploy.

title: Socially-Acquired Priors: The Tradeoffs of Pedagogical, Collaborative, and Cultural Learning
text: This section talks about how culture, peers, and language allows humans to learn faster (discover strategies faster) and deeper each generation, culminating in the present "information age", then dives into the specific benefits and roles of language as a representational medium Cover Kieran Egan’s cultural toolkits Benefits of language as a representational medium Language discretizes continuous spaces. Before you have a word for something, your representation of it may be fuzzy and gradient. Once labeled, it becomes a discrete, manipulable object. Is this seen in nominalization? Besides its communicative benefits, language is effective because language is compressive and compositional. You can bind together many concepts into a structured chunk ("the failure mode is distribution shift + sloppy evaluation + motivated reasoning"), and that chunk can steer perception, memory retrieval, and action selection without re-deriving everything from first principles or storing many high-dimensional, redundant vectors (i.e without simulating every detail). Words become handles for high-dimensional bundles of (non-verbal) experience: saying "I’m procrastinating because the task is ill-defined" can immediately trigger an action template (define success criteria -> reduce scope -> first small step). This is like calling a library function instead of rewriting code or simulating: fast, reusable, and easier to inspect. This means language serves as an efficient yet expressive medium for controlling mental simulations Language also serves as a substrate for cross-modal integration; by 25, language becomes a common currency that links otherwise semi-separate "apps" (emotion, planning, social inference, memory search, moral norms). The developmental punchline is integration: language becomes the standardized API that lets these modules call each other reliably; more of cognition becomes addressable, inspectable, and cross-module composable via linguistic pointers. How much did language (compressive, symbolic, mutually interpretable) and social interaction (parallel, collaborative, multi-generation) influence the structure of and accelerate our acquisition of robust, abstract world modeling? Abstractions are largely inherited (although they of course must be constructed from the ground up and (in most cases) must be error-corrected online to reach full robustness) "We emphasize that the language network works closely with, but is distinct from, both lower-level - perceptual and motor - mechanisms and higher-level systems of knowledge and reasoning. The perceptual and motor mechanisms process linguistic signals, but, in contrast to the language network, are sensitive only to these signals’ surface properties, not their meanings; the systems of knowledge and reasoning (such as the system that supports social reasoning) are sometimes engaged during language use but are not language-selective." 1 The precise relationship between language and human thought is hotly debated 2 Language as a modulator to cognitive and neurological systems ; Situating language in higher-order cognition ; The Language of Thought Hypothesis ; A language of episodic thought? ; Is language necessary for thought? Benefits of language as a representational medium, especially relative to visuospatial The system definitely recruits and combines different kinds of representations for specific tasks Is it fair to say that language serves primarily as a compressive interface/API for the self and other agents (expressive/communicative) and system of representational priors (the structure of language informs the structure of non-verbal representations/networks 8 , 9 ) for the brain? Relate to working memory model Overall, however, visuospatial representations are likely more central and more fundamental to human thought, especially when you consider that visuo-spatial (and sensorimotor) representations serve as a necessary foundation from which linguistic representations are derived. Really drill into this Language as the operating system and controller The "pointer" architecture Childhood (The Label): The word "force" is just a label associated with pushing a toy. It’s a direct associative map. Adulthood (The Handle): The word "force" becomes a low-dimensional "handle" that allows the brain to manipulate a high-dimensional sensorimotor simulation. The Mechanism: When a 20-year-old engineer thinks "torque," they aren’t just retrieving a dictionary definition. The word triggers a compressed, non-linguistic simulation of rotational physics. The word is the address in memory; the "meaning" is the sensorimotor state it points to. Developmental Shift: The 12-25 window is when the brain learns to trust the pointers enough to perform operations on them directly (algebraic manipulation of concepts) without having to fully unpack the sensorimotor simulation at every single step. This is cognitive efficiency. Language as the control system The Base Layer: The brain is a predictive engine constantly generating a "World Model" based on physics, geometry, and social dynamics (the non-linguistic layer). The Language Layer: Language acts as the control signal for this simulation. Example: If I say, "Imagine a blue elephant jumping over a fence," your language center parses the syntax and sends a top-down command to your visual cortex to construct that scene. In a breakup, this is why "talking it out" (linguistic) helps process emotion (non-linguistic). You are using the linguistic OS to structure, bound, and make sense of raw, high-dimensional emotional data that otherwise feels overwhelming. Language allows us to decouple from the immediate sensory stream, providing the stable tokens required to hold that future goal in place against the wash of immediate sensory data. In Vygotsky’s theory, mediation is the central process where humans use tools and signs (especially language), provided by their culture, to transform basic mental functions into complex, higher-order thinking Does feedback-related brain response during reinforcement learning predict socio-motivational (in-)dependence in adolescence? The role of language in human and machine intelligence Another modern angle asks what reasoning is for evolutionarily. Mercier and Sperber’s "argumentative theory of reasoning" claims its primary adaptive function isn’t solitary truth-seeking but producing and evaluating arguments in a social context-justifying one’s actions, persuading others, and guarding against being misled. This helps explain why reasoning alone is so prone to confirmation bias and motivated reasoning, yet small groups engaged in critical discussion can be surprisingly good at solving logic and inference tasks. On this picture, the development of reasoning is also the development of argumentation skills and epistemic norms-learning to give reasons, challenge others, handle disagreement, and use language and external notations (diagrams, equations, experiments) as scaffolds. Education then shows up not just as "adding content" but as installing socially shared procedures for how to reason. The hot/cold distinction is not purely biological; cultural and environmental factors modulate the landscape . Cultures differ in how much they scaffold adolescent decision-making (supervision, structured environments, graduated autonomy) versus allowing autonomous hot-context exposure. They also differ in norms around emotional expression, reward structures for risk-taking, and the social and material consequences of failure. An adolescent in a tightly supervised environment with strong recovery support and tolerance for mistakes may rationally take exploratory risks that would be maladaptive for an adolescent facing permanent consequences for failure (criminal records, loss of educational opportunity, reputational damage in small communities). The developmental question is not just "how robust is hot EF?" but "how well calibrated is hot EF to the actual contingencies of the environment?"–and environments differ enormously in their forgiveness. Pitfalls Imitation without understanding; overimitation The double-edged sword of pedagogy; direct instruction can speed learning but reduce spontaneous exploration and discovery. So a good curriculum for AGI is often interleaved: phases of unguided play/exploration to build broad affordance models, followed by short bursts of instruction/demos that compress the hypothesis space, followed again by play to re-expand and test Language fundamentally shapes our cognition + allows us to communicate with other agents. In our situation, it is probably necessary for the development of higher-order cognition. How instruction, joint attention, and cultural transmission massively compress search by providing shaped targets and curricula Instruction, joint attention, and imitation act like strong priors and KL regularizers that compress search, with language serving as a high-bandwidth index into shared schemas Learning with language Language/culture as inductive biases Humans have the privileged capacity to perceive and act upon shared symbolic (linguistic) spaces 12 , 13 Undoubtedly enables efficient communication of culture and concepts (both atomic concepts and the structure of conceptual networks which is encoded in language structure) between agents Linguistic and physical sensorimotor experiences are fundamentally entangled and cooperative modes of learning and representation 14 , 12 , 15 , 16 ; linguistic patterns are compact representations of the physical world while sensorimotor patterns act as the ultimate source of linguistic patterns and knowledge in general. They are representing the same universe of patterns but differ in information density and precision; language often trades specificity for efficiency while sensorimotor learning often does the opposite Desirable properties of language Discrete, compositional structures Recursive hierarchies Role-filler independence A less obvious benefit of our linguistic capacity is that resulting from the grammatical and amodal structure of languages Information learned through linguistic communication use allows language to serve as a cognitive "scaffold" for nonlinguistic, semantic cognition 17 , expanding our knowledge bases while generally enhancing our ability to relate and compose concepts, or, as Dove puts it, generally enhancing our "cognitive reach". Languages act as a sort of operating system for individual brains, providing abstractions for organizing and accessing knowledge. Language facilitates intermodal connectivity thanks to the coordination of modalities required by linguistic learning and action Capacity for language may enhance capacity for fine-grained categorization; evidence from aphasia patients 18 , 19 , 20 ; implies that atomic semantic representations are incentivized by the atomic structure of language, allowing humans to quickly latch onto defining characteristics of stimuli Language is particularly beneficial for learning abstract concepts Measures of abstraction: degree of appeal to the senses, relational vs individual, context specificity, potential for body-object interaction, etc These measures directly imply that abstract concepts are more often encountered and more readily processed given linguistic capacity; abstract patterns acquire embodiment through the communication of distributional-linguistic and low-level sensory regions of the brain 16 Discrete conceptual labels present in languages particularly benefit abstract concept learning 21 ; labels anchor and index categories with highly variable members 16 In line with "cognitive reach" quote; language may allow us to reach higher levels of the conceptual hierarchy In brains, abstract concepts are stored adjacent to and interact preferentially with linguistic regions The nature and extent of the influence of language on cognition remains controversial Semantic memory literature is most likely biased towards the benefits of language, since studies most often use language as a window into semantic memory systems External scaffolding Imitation learning Things learned through imitation must be stamped in through on-policy RL/SSL, no matter the domain; internal inconsistencies must be "wrung out" through rollouts Mirror neurons In the premotor and parietal cortices, neurons have been found that fire not only when an individual executes an action, but also when they observe someone else performing that same action. These aptly named mirror neurons (originally discovered in macaques) provide a clear example of embodied representation: the observer’s brain activates its own motor representation of the action as if simulating it This mirroring mechanism is thought to underlie action understanding and imitation - the brain makes sense of others’ actions by referencing its own motor programs. In humans, brain imaging confirms a similar mirror system engaged during action observation (e.g. watching someone kick a ball engages one’s own motor cortex for leg movements). Such findings support theories of embodied cognition in social contexts: understanding others’ behaviors and intentions is grounded in one’s own embodied action representations

title: Offline Learning: Replaying, Restructuring, and Branching
text: This section talks about the role offline (non-interactive) learning in human learning, especially relative to online (interactive) learning The "Offline Learning" section should be pruned and sharpened. It currently reads as a comprehensive review of sleep and replay literature. For the Principles section, what matters is: what does offline learning accomplish that online learning cannot, and why? The answer is: (1) prioritized replay for sample efficiency, (2) model-based imagination for counterfactual training, (3) representational reorganization for interference reduction, (4) synaptic homeostasis as complexity regularization. Make those four points crisply and defer the detailed neurophysiology to the Systems Architecture section. Credit assignment via offline branching sim "Planning" in the broadest sense; it is meant to convey that offline learning is squarely future-oriented There is constantly a queue of memories to be processed, which are augmented many times over artificially/synthetically. Does this explain human "generalization"? New structure Compression/abstraction Consolidation/reorganization Synthetic data generation and planning Counterfactual simulation is critical for generating new knowledge Carvalho’s work 1 Data pipeline: observe, explore, and narrate; sleep; repeat Offline learning is both retrospective and prospective We often spend time escaping the present by remembering events from the past (episodic memory), imagining how those past events might have turned out differently (episodic counterfactual thinking), thinking about how the future will unfold (episodic future thinking), or daydreaming about events that we know will never transpire (fictional thinking) 2 Replay as a Basis for Backpropagation Through Time in the Brain Episodic memory consolidation by reactivation of human concept neurons during sleep reflects contents, not sequence of events A complementary learning systems model of how sleep moderates retrieval practice effects Neural replay is connected to latent cause inference and supports fast generalization The role of neural replay in structure learning and value generalization Prioritizing replay when future goals are unknown Awake replay: off the clock but on the job Learning by thinking in natural and artificial minds Slow semantic learning in the cerebral cortex, and its relation to the hippocampal episodic memory system Sufficient conditions for offline reactivation in recurrent neural networks Frame offline learning as the other half of the optimizer. Give a mechanistic pass first: during NREM, hippocampal ripples coordinated by slow-oscillation->spindle nesting replay tagged episodes; dopaminergic salience biases which traces are selected; REM then delivers dendritic plateaus that prune and stabilize structural changes. Tie this to three algorithmic payoffs. First, sample efficiency via prioritized replay that focuses updates on states with high temporal-difference error or high epistemic value. Second, model-based imagination: generative world models (hippocampus-DMN) produce synthetic rollouts that let the actor/critic learn from counterfactuals it never executed. Third, representational reorganization: replay "remixes" features so that neocortical codes become sparser and more linearly separable, reducing interference. Make it pragmatic for AGI/robotics: separate an online learner (fast, low-variance, small steps, strict safety budget) from an offline learner (large-batch, distributional-RL critics, conservative policy updates from logged data, heavy model-based imagination), and add a targeting mechanism analogous to targeted memory reactivation to steer which skills/episodes are consolidated after each deployment day. Since the seminal work of Marr in 1971 [], the notion that offline replay plays a key role in learning has received a wealth of supporting evidence. Progress has been made in identifying the key characteristics and functions of replay in the context of the three "offline" behavioral states: NREM sleep, also called "slow wave" and "deep" sleep; REM sleep; and wakeful rest. Each of these states contributes uniquely to behavior, facilitating the construction and transformation of generalized representations in the brain []. In this section, the characteristics and functions of replay are mostly described in the context of each offline behavioral state independently, then are synthesized into key takeaways. History of systems consolidation theories Standard model of systems consolidation posits that episodic memories are converted into semantic memories, implying they are transferred from the hippocampus to the cortex. Under this model, it has been assumed that remote episodic memories reflect semanticized versions of the original memories (personal semantics) that are independent of the hippocampus. Multiple trace theory (MTT) posited that episodic memories, no matter how remote, always depend on the hippocampus, while semantic memories are supported by cortical modules. Trace Transformation Theory (TTT) took these ideas a step further and proposed that memories’ substrates are adaptively determined according to task demands, emphasizing that semantic and episodic memories continually communicate, can coexist, and cooperate at retrieval-time. This model emphasizes the concept of "neural-psychological correspondence", which states that neural transformations directly reflect psychological transformations (e.g transforming a perceptually detailed episodic memory into a "gist-like" episodic memory means going from posterior HPC to anterior HPC and mPFC) Credit assignment, counterfactual planning Unified view: replay according to expected utility of computing trajectories Mattar and Daw 2018 produce a model that accounts for forward and reverse replay Condition replay on expected utility of visiting each state; reverse replay for propagating new information to previous locations and forward replay for prospection based on past trajectories Sequential neural activity in humans has similarly been observed to exhibit orderings consistent with sampling based on future need. Using a statistical learning task with graphlike dependencies between visual cues (Schapiro et al., 2013; Garvert et al., 2017; Lynn et al., 2020), Wittkuhn et al. (2022) showed participants a series of animal images drawn from a ring-like graph structure in either a uni- or bi-directional manner. Using fMRI data recorded during 10s pauses between trials, Wittkuhn et al. (2022) found forward and reverse sequential activity patterns in visual and sensorimotor cortices, a pattern well-captured by an SR model learnt from the graph structure participants experienced. Goal-conditioned traversal of past, present, and future environments according to information gain More on this in NREM section Replay During NREM Sleep Qualities of NREM sleep brain-wide synchronization [] hippocampal excitability [] cortical plasticity [] regularly occurring sharp wave ripple (SWR) events, which are bursts of activity in the hippocampus that have been shown to implement replay on a compressed timescale [] Sharp wave ripples often coincide with "sleep spindles", which are bursts of thalamo-cortical activity that further coincide with the "up" states of slow waves; slow waves provide a global temporal framework for the coordination of nested oscillatory programs [] SWRs and sleep spindles have repeatedly and reliably been causally linked to memory performance across all memory types [], with their disruption during NREM sleep often leading to the complete prevention of learning [] History of replay during NREM sleep first observed during NREM sleep in the 1994 work of Wilson and McNaughton [], where the authors demonstrated that populations of hippocampal cells which fired together during a spatial navigation task were more likely to fire together during subsequent NREM sleep In 1996, it was then shown that these cells were reactivated in an order matching the original, waking experience [] These findings provided evidence for longstanding theories of systems consolidation, which posited that newly acquired information is transferred from short-term (hippocampal) to long-term (cortical) storage during sleep [] (Figure [fig:transfer] ). Today, it is widely held that NREM sleep represents the most focused and vigorous period of replay [], which is known to be goal-directed (see "Selective Replay"), abstractive (see "Generalization and Abstraction"), and generative [] Recent work also scrutinizes the notion of memories being "transferred" from short-term memory to long-term memory during NREM replay, instead opting for a model which posits that memories’ neural substrates are proactively determined in response to and in anticipation of task demands (see "Beyond ...") Modern functional view of NREM replay All fall under the umbrella of preparing for the future by processing the past; basic need to prevent ill-preparedness at inference-time 13 ; also results in less compute overall if you trade sleep-time compute for inference-time compute Basic need for repetition for robust integration 14 ; synaptic consolidation Interleaved learning Not bound by ongoing experience Humans and neural network models learn faster (especially in terms of conceptual relatedness) when diverse concepts are interleaved instead of blocked 15 , 16 , 17 Supports all kinds of representations Structural abstraction, in the general case Extraction of "gist" representations of experiences [] Packaging/compressing them for retrieval and generalization Semantic memories Integrating distant experiences into new knowledge Schematic memories Schemas are superordinate knowledge structures that reflect abstracted commonalities across several experiences []. A cognitive structure must satisfy the following criteria to be considered a schema: abstraction over several experiences; associative structure; lack of unit detail; and adaptability []. One example of a schema is a network of neural representations encoding the usual behaviors and events of a typical birthday party (an event schema) [], and another is the usual layout of a modern city (a spatial schema) []. The associative, abstract, and adaptive nature of schemas make them uniquely positioned to benefit from the offline, replay-based learning Offline replay allows brains to perform focused reasoning over new experiences in tandem with any of the cognitive structures and experiences held in the vast repositories supported by biological brains (Figure [fig:transfer] ) Biomarkers for the abstraction and integration of experiences include reduced hippocampal activation during a task [] and increased functional connectivity among distributed memory traces Schemas gradually develop with repeated exposure and consolidation [] NREM assimilates new info into existing schemas 18 Maps of specific events and environments 19 ; reduced similarity between hippocampal representations measured during task exposure and across NREM sleep 20 Model-free policies 21 and task representations 22 ; forging a generalizable representation of the world can be seen as creating a model-free policy or as caching results for reuse Selective and generative Most informative experiences are simulated, including synthetic experiences; can be seen as planning 21 "rank order correlation between neuronal firing sequences during slow-wave sleep or awake rest and future novel place-cell sequences on a previously unexplored linear context" 23 Waking offline replay as dynamic consolidation Selectivity Perhaps the most well-studied and predictable aspect of selective replay is its preference for experiences including large rewards Large reward prediction errors 21 Recency (which accounts for the observed "transfer" of memories from the hippocampus to the cortex) []; however, a large fraction of offline replay’s contents appear to not be recency-biased 24 ; remote replay is especially clear in dreaming 25 Number of times an experience/task was repeated or was apart of waking replay NREM replay has also been shown to be less sequential and more fragmented/partial than waking replay Potential balancing effect via replay?: "Another study of goal oriented navigation showed that while animals spent the most time physically in the proximity of a reward location in real time, replay reduces this behavioral bias by upsampling regions of space in which less time was spent (Grosmark et al. 2021)" Initial replay builds a rough draft, later replays fill in the gaps: Berners-Lee et al. (2022) found that replays appear after single exposures and slow down while increasing in resolution with repeated experience One intriguing proposition is that, during offline replay, the hippocampus implements a sort of similarity-weighted retrieval over abstract cortical representations []. Such selectivity could minimize the degree to which new representations interfere with overlapping representations, along with maximizing learning speed []. On top of the computational evidence presented in the original work [], recent work has bolstered the original claim with more sophisticated modeling techniques [] Replay should support generalization of world models and therefore should focus on "predictable" episodes; may be actualized in brains and has seen success in ML Can show this computationally 26 Predictable stimuli vs random are replayed in mice 27 Maybe the appearance of selective replay being geared towards emotional experiences is correlational; replay should focus on revealing environmental dynamics Although the extent to which similar, remote, and "predictable" memories are retrieved during offline replay remain open questions, existing demonstrations of selective replay tease out another one of the main benefits of offline, replay-based learning: the high degree of cortical plasticity afforded during offline learning is utilized by the most relevant and information-dense experiences, as a purely online learning algorithm would need to constantly update synaptic connections since the learner would always be unsure of whether previous or future experiences will carry the most (or any ) information regarding the world’s latent structure []; without carefully optimizing the "training data" fed into the cortex, overfitting and inefficiency take hold []. As the saying goes, hindsight is 20/20. REM Sleep Especially useful for rare/counterfactual experiences Intro REM is paradoxical; matches the oscillatory profiles of waking behavior; majority of dreams happen here High cortical plasticity and low hippocampal synchrony Implicated in creative problem solving through the flexible recombination, extrapolation, and disintegration 28 of cortical world models through goal-directed simulation, which manifests as dreams While the hippocampus likely contributes to these simulations, classifying them as "replay" seems misguided since they are far from recapitulations of waking experiences, altough substantial evidence implies that the contents of dreams are strongly biased towards recent events (Daytime exp..) Mixed evidence for REM sleep’s role in general consolidation, but lots of support for emotional Dreams can depict remote experiences and events that cannot be traced to specific experiences 25 Net optimization/pruning of synapses "synaptic homeostasis hypothesis" (SHY) Synapses net pruned Reduced cortical excitability in humans after sleep Overall May still involve HPC-supported compositional replay of the like seen in planning (future work) Foreshadow interaction with NREM via interleaving Interleaving NREM and REM: Reinforcement and Refinement NREM replay is accompanied by a exploratory, creative reorganization period during REM sleep Reinforcement and refinement. Reflects respective *emphases*, not sole purposes 29 , 18 NREM first and (70/30) Related to SIT theory Open questions How does a REM period alter the following NREM period Waking Replay Also supported by SWRs, although these are shorter and smaller amplitude + do not have the same coordination enabled by slow waves and spindles? Reverse (hindsight) after, forward (planning) before ( , new Nico Schuck) NREM versus Waking Replay in Offline Learning Most studies have been focused on either wake or sleep Greater "sequenceness" and locality [] than NREM Lack of sequenceness in sleep may reflect active transformation of memories or the simultaneous activation of multiple memories undergoing integration May also reflect greater selectivity Waking replay: local, exploratory, initiation, and substantial work + actual novel planning which overlaps in nature and function with online replay -> NREM replay: continued consolidation + nonlocal + system integration Substrate of rapid memory integration? Waking SWRs tag experience for offline replay; related to repetition bias (Wannan Yang, Selection of exp...) What is the training data / training pipeline of the DMN?: Complementary learning systems and online/offline learning regimes The learning problem, stated cleanly: the DMN is not trained on a continuous sensory stream. It is trained on a curated , temporally restructured , value-tagged set of internal "replays" and "simulations" whose job is to turn (i) a long tail of idiosyncratic episodes into (ii) a small set of predictive latent variables (schemas, narratives, social models, self-model) that generalize. This is why "rest" and sleep are not idling–they are the brain’s dataset construction + optimization loop for high-level generative structure 30 . Architectural precondition: the DMN is already a memory-simulation composite (core + medial temporal + dorsal-medial subsystems), i.e., it is physically interleaved with the very machinery that provides its training samples (hippocampus/MTL) and the machinery that stores abstractions (mPFC/PCC/AG). 31 . Complementary learning systems The brain’s architecture reflects a split between "raw data buffering" and "compressed model storage," codified in the Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) framework. The hippocampus acts as a fast-learning buffer for episodic details (high fidelity, low compression), while the neocortex (specifically the DMN apex) acts as a slow-learning repository for statistical regularities (lossy, high compression). Systems consolidation is the off-line optimization process where the brain distills the chaotic log of daily experience into the structured, low-dimensional manifold of the cortical model 32 , 33 . The human brain utilizes a dual-store architecture to manage the accuracy/complexity trade-off over time: The Fast/High-Complexity Store (Hippocampus) : Rapidly encodes episodic experiences with high fidelity via pattern separation . This minimizes immediate prediction error but carries a high "description length" or complexity cost. The Slow/Compressed Store (Neocortex/DMN) : Over time, these high-dimensional episodes are "replayed" and interleaved with existing knowledge to extract invariants. By the time information reaches the DMN, it has been stripped of idiosyncratic noise and integrated into schemas 34 , 35 . The DMN’s learning is not a single mechanism–it is an alternation between online data acquisition and offline dataset distillation, i.e., a true online/offline regime split. Training data: what actually "feeds" the DMN? Indexed episodes (high-fidelity tokens) from hippocampus : sparse bindings of "what/where/when" plus relational structure; these are the seed points for later semanticization. 36 , 37 . Event-structured transitions (state sequences rather than static snapshots) : what matters for compression is predictive structure –how latent states evolve. Replay often appears sequential, as if the brain is rehearsing trajectories through a learned state graph. 38 , 39 . Schema priors and "explanation frames" from mPFC/DMN core : existing concepts, scripts, and social models that new episodes must either be assimilated into or force accommodation (schema update / creation). This makes learning conditional: the same episode trains different hypotheses depending on the current schema. 40 , 41 . Value/affect tags attached to episodes (salience-weighting): reward, threat, curiosity/uncertainty, goal relevance–these act like sample weights that change replay probability and plasticity gain. 42 , 43 . Self-generated "synthetic data": counterfactuals, future events, social rehearsals, narrative recombinations. These samples are not veridical, but they are structurally consistent with learned priors and therefore useful for training a generative model (data augmentation / regularization). 44 , 45 . The DMN’s learning is not a single mechanism–it is an alternation between online data acquisition and offline dataset distillation, i.e., a true online/offline regime split. Stage 1 – Online (wake): acquisition + tagging (construct the replay buffer) Encode : hippocampus rapidly indexes episodes; cortex/DMN extracts coarse gist online (enough to guide behavior), but defers heavy compression. 37 . Tag : neuromodulators assign priority labels (reward, novelty, uncertainty, threat, goal relevance), determining what will be replayed and with what plasticity gain. Think of this as "importance sampling" for the offline learner. 46 , 43 . Early integration when schemas exist : mPFC can bias encoding/retrieval toward schema-consistent features (rapid assimilation) or highlight prediction-violating features (schema update). This is a key inductive bias: the DMN is trained to prefer explanations that reuse existing latent factors when possible. 40 , 41 . Stage 2 – Offline (quiet wake / rest): replay-driven "mini-batch updates" Offline learning is not only sleep. During awake rest, hippocampus expresses replay and the cortex expresses reinstatement; importantly, there is direct evidence that hippocampal sharp-wave ripples are followed by increased DMN (BOLD) activity, consistent with ripples acting like "commit events" that write episodic minibatches into DMN-level representations. 47 , 48 . Replay during rest is selective : it often prioritizes weaker or high-utility memories (not simply the most recent), consistent with a learning system that is actively reducing uncertainty / improving generalization. 39 . Computationally, this is where the DMN can run controlled internal rollouts : hippocampus provides the state sequence; DMN provides the generative "world model" and tries to compress it into reusable latent causes; control networks can gate which rollouts are pursued. Stage 3 – Offline (NREM sleep): high-bandwidth transfer + schema writing NREM is the canonical regime for active systems consolidation : hippocampal replay events (sharp-wave ripples) are temporally coordinated with cortical slow oscillations and thalamocortical spindles, creating windows where hippocampal patterns can effectively train cortical networks. 49 , 50 , 51 . This tri-oscillation choreography is a structure-preserving bottleneck –it compresses time (replay is time-compressed), sparsifies updates (discrete ripple events), and interleaves new episodes with old knowledge (spindle/slow-oscillation mediated cortical context), which is exactly what you want for extracting invariants without overwriting. The DMN’s role here is plausibly: (i) integrate across modalities (transmodal hub property), (ii) map episodes onto schemas (mPFC), and (iii) update narrative/social/self latents that require long temporal integration. Recent work explicitly discusses DMN-hippocampus involvement in consolidation across sleep/wake regimes. 52 . Stage 4 – Offline (REM sleep) : generative recombination + affective reweighting REM shifts the optimization profile: rather than faithful replay, REM is well-positioned for hyperassociative recombination (dream-like simulation), abstraction, and emotional retagging–useful for training a generative model to capture broader structure and for updating value priors. 53 , 54 . The neuromodulatory milieu differs sharply across stages (e.g., acetylcholine/norepinephrine/serotonin dynamics), changing both what gets replayed and how plasticity is expressed, i.e., the brain effectively changes its optimizer settings across sleep stages. 46 , 55 . Global regularization: synaptic homeostasis as "compression pressure" In parallel to targeted replay-based updates, sleep may implement a cortex-wide normalization/downscaling that acts like a complexity penalty (prevent runaway growth of synaptic strength; improve SNR; keep representational capacity usable). This pairs naturally with the "drive for compression" framing: replay writes useful structure; downscaling removes diffuse, low-utility potentiation. 56 , 57 . text: Evolution seems to have built a generic "continuous quantity module" for guiding action in space and then later re-used it for counting, arithmetic, and eventually symbolic math. All that said, mathematics is not just spatial. Symbolic math and proof recruit a broader fronto-parietal network that includes prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and language/semantic regions like angular gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus, especially for exact, verbally mediated arithmetic and algebra. So a decent summary is: basic quantity/magnitude and a lot of mental arithmetic are heavily grounded in spatial systems, but higher mathematics is a hybrid of those with symbolic, linguistic, and executive systems.

title: Philosophical Theories of Brains
text: Long before the first electrode was lowered into cortex, philosophers were asking the questions that define computational neuroscience: Where does the mind reside? Is perception a passive reception or an active construction? Could thought be a form of computation? What is the relationship between the model and the modeled? This section traces the long arc of these questions from antiquity to the present day, highlighting the ideas that most directly anticipate—or challenge—the framework of the brain as a world-modeling engine.

title: The Ancient World — c. 3000–600 BCE
text: The philosophical traditions of Greece did not emerge from nothing. For millennia before Alcmaeon, physicians in Egypt, diagnosticians in Mesopotamia, and sages in Vedic India grappled with the organ of thought, the nature of awareness, and the reliability of perception. Their answers—sometimes startlingly empirical, sometimes embedded in cosmology and ritual—established many of the terms of debate that Greek philosophy would inherit and transform. The Edwin Smith Papyrus The Edwin Smith Papyrus (c. 1600 BCE, likely transcribed from a source dating to c. 2500 BCE) is the earliest known document to describe the brain—and contains the first recorded use of a word for “brain” in any surviving language 1 . Across forty-eight case studies of traumatic injuries, organized systematically from head to spine, the anonymous Egyptian physician documented the meninges, cerebrospinal fluid, and cranial sutures, and noted that injuries to the brain produce symptoms in distant parts of the body, including contralateral motor and sensory deficits. Each case is classified with remarkable clinical discipline as “an ailment I will treat,” “an ailment I will contend with,” or “an ailment not to be treated.” The papyrus represents a strikingly naturalistic, empirical approach to the brain as the organ that governs bodily experience—an approach that, as we shall see, was not shared by its own broader culture. The Egyptian Cardiac Doctrine Despite the clinical insights of their physicians, Egyptian civilization as a whole located the mind not in the brain but in the heart ( ib ) 2 , 3 . The heart was the seat of intelligence, memory, emotion, and moral character—so central to personal identity that mummification practices carefully preserved it while the brain was extracted through the nostrils with hooks and discarded. In the weighing-of-the-heart scene depicted in the Book of the Dead, the deceased’s heart is placed on a scale against the feather of Ma’at (truth and cosmic order); if the heart is heavy with wrongdoing, the soul is devoured. The dominance of cardiac doctrine in a culture that simultaneously produced the Edwin Smith Papyrus’s brain observations is instructive for world-modeling theories: it demonstrates how powerfully prior beliefs—the generative model of a culture—can resist updating in the face of disconfirming evidence. Esagil-kin-apli and the Mesopotamian Diagnostic Tradition In Mesopotamia, the physician Esagil-kin-apli (c. 11th century BCE) compiled the Sakikkû (Diagnostic Handbook), the most systematic ancient compendium of disease classification prior to Hippocrates [Sakikkû]. Its forty tablets catalog neurological and psychiatric symptoms—seizures, paralysis, speech disturbances, altered states of consciousness, and what appear to be descriptions of stroke—organized by affected body region. However, unlike the Egyptian surgical tradition, the Sakikkû ’s explanatory framework was overwhelmingly supernatural: symptoms were attributed to the actions of specific deities or demons. The Mesopotamian tradition thus embodies a paradox relevant to the philosophy of scientific modeling: meticulous empirical observation can coexist with a causal framework that, by modern lights, entirely misidentifies the generative process. Yajnavalkya The sage Yājnavalkya (c. 8th–7th century BCE), whose dialogues form the philosophical core of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upanishad 4 , produced what may be the earliest sustained analysis of consciousness as such. In his account of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, dreaming is especially revelatory: the mind, cut off from external sensation, “takes along the material of this all-encompassing world” and “tears it apart and builds it up again” from its own light. In deep dreamless sleep even this self-generated world dissolves, yet the self (Ātman) persists as pure awareness. For Yājnavalkya, the dream state demonstrates that the mind is fundamentally a world-generating system; the external environment merely constrains a process that would otherwise produce experience spontaneously—an insight whose resonance with the predictive processing view of perception as “controlled hallucination” is difficult to miss. Uddalaka Aruni Uddālaka Āruṇi (c. 8th–7th century BCE), the central teacher of the Chāndogya Upanishad 5 , approached consciousness from a more naturalistic direction. In a celebrated passage, he instructs his son Śvetaketu that the mind depends on material nourishment: fast for fifteen days and thought degrades; eat again and it recovers. The mind ( manas ), on Uddālaka’s account, is composed of the subtlest portion of food—a substance-based theory of cognition that grounds mental life in metabolism. His teaching culminates in the mahāvākya “ tat tvam asi ” (“thou art that”): the deepest self and the fundamental reality of the world are identical. Where Yājnavalkya emphasized the self-generating autonomy of consciousness, Uddālaka emphasized its material dependence—a tension between internalist and externalist accounts of mind that persists in contemporary debates between predictive processing and enactivism. Ptahhotep Ptahhotep (c. 2400 BCE), vizier to the pharaoh Djedkare Isesi, composed the oldest surviving work of philosophical instruction 6 . His thirty-seven maxims elaborate a cognitive psychology centered on the heart ( ib ): the heart is the organ of knowledge, judgment, intention, and moral reasoning, and its proper functioning determines the quality of a life. The cardinal intellectual virtue is sedjem —conventionally translated as “hearing” but denoting something closer to receptive, evaluative comprehension. The fool is defined not by ignorance but by a heart that “does not hear”: it receives sensory and social information but fails to integrate it correctly. The wise person’s heart hears, weighs, and responds with calibrated precision. For a world-modeling framework, Ptahhotep’s insistence that the same organ can receive identical input yet produce wise or foolish output—depending on the quality of its internal processing—is an early, if implicit, recognition that cognition is determined less by the data than by the model that interprets it. The Nasadiya Sukta The Nāsadīya Sūkta (Rig Veda X.129, c. 1200–1000 BCE), the celebrated Hymn of Creation, is among the most philosophically radical texts of the ancient world 7 . “Then there was neither being nor non-being … Darkness was hidden by darkness in the beginning; all this was an indistinguishable sea.” From this undifferentiated void, the hymn declares, kāma (desire, or primordial intentionality) arose as “the first seed of mind.” Desire—a directedness toward something not yet actual—is placed metaphysically prior to both the world and the consciousness that knows it. The hymn ends in radical epistemic humility: perhaps even the gods do not know how creation came about. For the philosophy of world modeling, the Nāsadīya Sūkta poses a question that modern enactivism inherits: does the world give rise to the mind that models it, or does something like mind (intentionality, directedness, the capacity for modeling) precede and condition the world? Kapila and Early Samkhya Kapila (traditionally c. 7th century BCE, though dating remains deeply uncertain) is credited as the founder of Sāṁkhya , one of the oldest systematic philosophies of mind and matter 8 , 9 . Sāṁkhya draws a sharp ontological line between puruṣa (pure consciousness—passive, unchanging, contentless awareness) and prakṛti (material nature—active, evolving, and encompassing not only the physical world but also the mind, senses, intellect, and ego). Cognition, perception, and every form of information processing belong entirely to prakṛti ; puruṣa merely witnesses. This may be the oldest systematic mind–body dualism, but it inverts the Cartesian version: here it is consciousness , not matter, that is inert, and it is matter , not mind, that thinks. For computational neuroscience, Sāṁkhya sharpens a question that remains unresolved: is consciousness identical with information processing (as functionalism holds), or is it something that merely accompanies it—a witness to the computation rather than the computation itself? Zarathustra Zarathustra (Zoroaster; c. 1000–600 BCE, dating highly uncertain) articulated a cosmic and cognitive dualism in the Gāthās , the oldest stratum of the Avesta [Gāthās]. Reality is structured by the opposition between aša (truth, order, the way things are) and druj (falsehood, disorder, the way things are not), and the human mind is the arena in which this opposition plays out. Central to Zarathustra’s teaching is vohu manah (“good mind” or “right thinking”)—a cognitive and moral capacity to perceive and align with the true structure of reality. The human task is the exercise of vohu manah : discriminating truth from falsehood, real pattern from deceptive appearance, signal from noise. Embedded in cosmological and ethical language is what amounts to a proto-epistemological program: the mind’s fundamental operation is the separation of veridical models (those aligned with aša ) from misspecified ones (those corrupted by druj )—a framing that resonates, at a considerable distance, with the Bayesian imperative to maintain accurate generative models of the world’s causal structure.

title: Ancient Greek Philosophy — c. 600–300 BCE
text: Alcmaeon of Croton The brain hypothesis begins with Alcmaeon of Croton (c. 500 BCE), a physician-philosopher who declared that the brain, not the heart, is the seat of understanding. By tracing sensory channels (most likely the optic nerves) from the sense organs to the brain, Alcmaeon inferred that perception is a process that terminates in a central organ capable of integrating disparate signals—a claim that would not be universally accepted for another two millennia. Democritus Democritus (c. 460–370 BCE) offered the first thoroughgoing materialist account of perception. Objects shed thin films of atoms called eidola , which travel through the air and impinge on the sense organs, where they interact with the atomic structure of the perceiver. Mind itself is composed of fine, spherical, highly mobile atoms distributed through the body but concentrated in the brain. Every mental event—thought, sensation, emotion—is atomic motion, and nothing more. Hippocrates The Hippocratic text On the Sacred Disease 1 mounted a vigorous defense of the brain doctrine against cardiocentrism: “Men ought to know that from nothing else but the brain come joys, delights, laughter and sports, and sorrows, griefs, despondency, and lamentations.” By arguing that epilepsy is a brain disorder rather than a divine affliction, Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BCE) established that pathologies of experience are pathologies of the organ that produces experience. Plato Plato (c. 428–348 BCE) was less interested in the brain per se than in the epistemic situation of any perceiving mind. The Allegory of the Cave 2 depicts prisoners who mistake projected shadows for reality—an image that resonates strikingly with the modern view of perception as an internally generated model constrained by incomplete sensory data. In the Timaeus [Timaeus], Plato located the rational soul in the head, the spirited soul in the chest, and the appetitive soul in the abdomen, producing an early—if speculative—functional neuroanatomy. Aristotle Aristotle (c. 384–322 BCE) produced the most systematic ancient treatment of the mind in De Anima 3 . He introduced phantasia (imagination), the faculty that produces internal images persisting after sensation ceases—a precursor to the concept of endogenous neural representation. His sensus communis (common sense) is a faculty that binds inputs from the individual senses into a unified percept, anticipating the binding problem. Ironically, Aristotle was a committed cardiocentrist who assigned the brain the role of a cooling organ for the blood, a reminder that even the most rigorous thinkers can be led astray when anatomical evidence is sparse. Empedocles Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE) proposed that all matter is composed of four roots—earth, water, air, fire—driven by two cosmic forces: Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion) 4 , 5 . Perception operates through a system of pores: effluences streaming from objects enter pores of matching size and shape in the sense organs, so that “like perceives like.” Crucially, Empedocles located thought and consciousness not in the brain but in the blood around the heart—a cardiocentrist position that Aristotle would later adopt. His model of perception as structural matching between emitted patterns and receiving channels is a proto-mechanistic account that reduces representation to physical correspondence between object and organ. Anaxagoras Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) introduced Nous (Mind, Intellect) as a fundamental cosmic principle: the finest and purest of all substances, unmixed with the matter it organizes, which initiates and governs the rotation of the cosmos from primordial chaos [fragments; reported in Plato’s Phaedo and Aristotle’s Metaphysics ]. Unlike the material elements, Nous “has knowledge of all things and the greatest power.” While later philosophers—most notably Socrates, as Plato reports him—were disappointed that Anaxagoras then used Nous merely as a mechanical trigger rather than a purposive intelligence, the concept marks a critical philosophical step: the identification of an ordering, information-processing principle ontologically distinct from the material substrate it organizes—a separation of the “program” from the “hardware” that anticipates functionalism by two and a half millennia.

title: Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy — c. 300 BCE–400 CE
text: Epicurus Epicurus (c. 341–270 BCE) refined Democritean atomism and introduced a concept of striking relevance to Bayesian accounts of cognition: prolepsis , or preconception 1 . A prolepsis is a general mental pattern formed from repeated sensory encounters—a kind of learned prior—that allows the mind to categorize and anticipate new experiences before full sensory evidence arrives. Perception, on this view, is never raw; it is always shaped by what the mind already expects. Chrysippus The Stoic philosopher Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BCE) developed a sophisticated theory of mental content centered on phantasia (impression or representation). Sensory impressions are stamped into the hegemonikon (ruling faculty), which Chrysippus located in the brain. Crucially, not every impression compels belief: the mind must give synkatathesis (assent) to an impression before it becomes a commitment about the world. This two-stage architecture—automatic sensory representation followed by evaluative acceptance—prefigures modern dual-process theories and the distinction between perceptual inference and decision. Lucretius Lucretius (c. 99–55 BCE) rendered Epicurean physics into Latin verse in De Rerum Natura 2 , producing the most detailed surviving ancient account of materialist perception. Simulacra —films of atoms continually shed by objects—enter the sense organs and produce experience through physical impact. Thought, dreaming, and hallucination arise from residual or recombined simulacra, establishing a single mechanistic framework for veridical and non-veridical experience alike. Galen Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 CE) transformed the study of the brain from speculation into experimental science 3 , 4 . Through systematic dissection and vivisection of animals, he traced cranial nerves, identified the cerebrum and cerebellum as functionally distinct, and demonstrated—by ligating nerves and compressing brain regions—that the brain controls sensation and voluntary movement. His ventricular doctrine, which localized perception, reasoning, and memory to the fluid-filled cerebral ventricles, would dominate neuroscience for over a thousand years. Augustine Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE) turned philosophical attention inward. Book X of the Confessions 5 contains an extraordinary phenomenology of memory: a “vast palace” of stored experiences that the mind can search, recombine, and deploy in the production of expectations. His analysis of time perception in Book XI—where the present is a vanishing knife-edge between expectatio (anticipation of what is coming) and memoria (retention of what has passed)—describes the temporal structure of experience in terms strikingly compatible with predictive processing: the mind lives perpetually in the gap between prediction and recollection. Sextus Empiricus Sextus Empiricus (c. 160–210 CE) compiled the most systematic surviving statement of Pyrrhonian skepticism 6 , 7 . His ten modes ( tropoi ) demonstrate that every perception is relative—to the species of the perceiver, to the individual, to the sense organ, to the circumstances, to the position and distance, to the admixtures, to the quantity and composition, to the frequency of encounter, and to the cultural context. Since one can never step outside perception to compare a representation with how things “really are,” one ought to suspend judgment ( epochē ) about the nature of external reality. For world-modeling neuroscience, Sextus articulates in philosophical terms the fundamental epistemic predicament of any brain: locked behind its sensory surfaces, a brain has access only to its own representations, never to the world those representations purport to describe—a predicament later formalized as the “evidentiary boundary” of the Markov blanket. Plotinus Plotinus (c. 204–270 CE), the founder of Neoplatonism, described reality as a cascade of emanations from a unitary source: the One gives rise to Nous (Intellect), which gives rise to Psychē (Soul), which gives rise to the material world [Enneads]. Consciousness occupies an intermediary position, oriented simultaneously toward the intelligible realm and the sensible realm below. Most remarkably for present purposes, Plotinus argued that the soul does not passively receive sensory impressions but actively generates its own awareness: external objects are occasions for the soul’s activity, not causes of its states. This top-down, generative picture of awareness—in which the mind’s own productive activity takes priority over bottom-up sensory input—has a strikingly modern resonance with hierarchical predictive models in which perception is driven more by descending predictions than ascending signals.

title: Medieval Philosophy — c. 500–1400
text: Alhazen / Ibn al-Haytham No medieval thinker is more important to the computational neuroscience of perception than Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, c. 965–1040). In his monumental Kitāb al-Manāẓir 1 , he established that vision works by light entering the eye (refuting the extramission theory) and, crucially, that perception involves unconscious judgment and inference . The optical image on the crystalline humor is insufficient to determine the scene: the mind must draw on prior experience, comparison, and recognition to construct a percept. This is, in all but mathematical formalism, the hypothesis that perception is inference—the core of the Helmholtzian and Bayesian traditions—articulated seven centuries before Helmholtz. Avicenna / Ibn Sina Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) elaborated Aristotle’s brief remarks on inner sense into a detailed faculty psychology 2 , 3 . Between raw sensation and abstract intellection, he posited a cascade of internal senses : the common sense (integrating modalities), retentive and compositive imagination (storing and recombining images), wahm (estimation—the immediate, pre-rational detection of significance, as when a sheep perceives danger in a wolf’s form), and memory. His celebrated floating man thought experiment—a person created in midair, deprived of all sensation, who would nonetheless know that he exists—argues that self-awareness is prior to and independent of any world model. Averroes / Ibn Rushd Averroes (Ibn Rushd, c. 1126–1198) produced the most influential medieval commentaries on Aristotle’s De Anima 4 , which shaped European scholastic psychology for centuries. His most provocative thesis was that the agent intellect —the faculty that renders sensory particulars into universal concepts—is a single, supra-individual entity shared by all humans. Whatever its metaphysical plausibility, this raises a question that computational neuroscience still grapples with: to what extent are the abstract representational structures of cognition universal across brains? Thomas Aquinas Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274) synthesized Aristotelian psychology with Christian theology to produce a theory of cognition as abstraction 5 , 6 . The intellect does not know material objects directly; it abstracts intelligible species (structural forms) from phantasms (sensory images) produced by the internal senses. This process—from high-dimensional sensory data to compressed, abstract, category-level representations—is a medieval description of what we would now call hierarchical feature extraction. William of Ockham William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) contributed two ideas of lasting relevance. First, his famous razor— entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem —is a parsimony principle that, reformulated in information-theoretic terms, is central to Bayesian model selection and the free energy principle: the best model is one that explains the data with minimal complexity. Second, his theory of mental language ( oratio mentalis ) 7 proposed that thought occurs in an internal combinatorial language with its own syntax—anticipating Fodor’s language of thought hypothesis by six centuries. Al-Farabi (c. 872–950), known in the Latin West as Alpharabius, developed an emanationist theory of intellect that doubles as a hierarchical model of cognitive processing 8 , 9 . Cognition proceeds through successive stages: from sensation, through imagination, to the various levels of intellect (potential, actual, acquired, and agent). Each stage abstracts further from the material particulars of sensation, progressively approaching purely intelligible form. This ascending hierarchy of abstraction—from low-level sensory features to increasingly general, amodal representations—maps with surprising precision onto the deep hierarchical architecture of modern generative models, where each layer learns progressively more abstract representations of its inputs. Roger Bacon Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1294) synthesized Alhazen’s optics with Aristotelian natural philosophy in his Opus Majus 10 , insisting that scientia experimentalis —knowledge grounded in systematic observation and experiment—must take priority over purely deductive reasoning. His theory of the multiplication of species described how causal influence propagates from objects through intervening media to the sense organs: every natural agent emits species (likenesses of itself) that are transmitted through the medium in straight lines, weakening with distance and undergoing refraction at boundaries. This is, in effect, a medieval theory of information propagation—an account of how structured signals from the distal environment are transmitted, transformed, and finally received by the brain’s sensory interfaces.
