title: Renaissance and Scientific Revolution — c. 1450–1630
text: Leonardo da Vinci Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) brought the empirical ethos of the Renaissance to neuroanatomy. He injected molten wax into ox brain ventricles to produce accurate three-dimensional casts—the first experimental modeling of brain structure. His anatomical sketches, though unpublished in his lifetime, revealed a commitment to observation over ancient authority that would define the scientific revolution to come. Andreas Vesalius Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564) dismantled Galenic neuroanatomy through direct dissection in De Humani Corporis Fabrica 1 . His detailed illustrations of the brain, cranial nerves, and spinal cord established that brain structure is an empirical question, not a matter of philosophical deduction. By revealing how much Galen had gotten wrong by relying on animal dissection, Vesalius demonstrated that the accuracy of any model depends on the quality of the data it is built from. Michel de Montaigne Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) deployed radical skepticism against the pretensions of human reason 2 , 3 . Our senses are unreliable, our judgments are shaped by custom and bodily states, and introspection is not transparent self-knowledge but a further act of interpretation. For a world-modeling framework, Montaigne is a reminder that the model is not merely of the external world—it includes a model of the modeler, and that self-model is no less fallible. Francis Bacon Francis Bacon (1561–1626) catalogued the systematic ways in which the human mind distorts its picture of reality 4 . His four idols —of the Tribe (species-wide perceptual and cognitive biases), Cave (individual biases from experience), Marketplace (distortions from imprecise language), and Theater (distortions from received theories)—constitute a proto-taxonomy of the ways a generative model can be misspecified. Science, for Bacon, is the disciplined correction of the mind’s default model. Galileo Galilei Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) drew a distinction between primary qualities (size, shape, number, motion—objective and mathematical) and secondary qualities (color, taste, warmth—subjective and perceiver-dependent) 5 . This distinction implies that the world as we experience it is not the world as it is: much of perceptual content is generated by the perceiver, not simply received from the world. The mechanistic philosophy Galileo championed would provide the conceptual framework within which the brain itself could be understood as a physical mechanism. Juan Luis Vives Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540) produced one of the most remarkably modern psychological works of the Renaissance in De Anima et Vita 6 . Rather than speculating about what the soul is , Vives proposed to investigate what it does —its operations, and in particular the associative mechanisms of memory. He described how sensory experiences become linked through contiguity, resemblance, and emotional salience, forming networks of association that determine recall and shape the flow of thought. This operational, mechanistic approach to mental processes—investigating function rather than metaphysical essence—anticipates the functionalist turn by four centuries, and his emphasis on learned associative structure presages connectionist models of memory. Bernardino Telesio Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588) broke with Aristotelian scholasticism through a radical empiricism in De Rerum Natura iuxta Propria Principia 7 . All knowledge, he insisted, originates in sensus (sensation), which is not a passive reception but an active response of the spiritus —a subtle material substance pervading the nervous system—to external stimulation. The soul itself is material, a warm, thin substance housed in the brain’s ventricles, and cognition is the spiritus ’s capacity to detect similarities and differences among sensory impacts. In grounding all mental life in the reactive dynamics of a material nervous substance, Telesio sketched a picture of the mind as a physical system whose fundamental operation is the discrimination and classification of sensory patterns—a pattern recognizer built from matter.

title: The Age of Reason — c. 1630–1720
text: René Descartes René Descartes (1596–1650) is the watershed figure. In the Meditations 1 , he established the mind as the one indubitable reality ( cogito ergo sum ) while casting the entire external world into doubt—including the possibility that a malicious demon fabricates all sensory experience, a thought experiment that maps directly onto the brain-in-a-vat scenarios of modern philosophy. His dualism of res cogitans (thinking substance) and res extensa (extended substance) created the mind–body problem that neuroscience has been trying to dissolve ever since. Yet Descartes was also a mechanist: in L’Homme 2 and the Dioptrics 3 , he modeled the body as hydraulic machinery, tracing sensory signals along nerve tubes to the pineal gland, producing a genuine (if wrong) mechanistic theory of the reflex arc. Thomas Hobbes Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) proposed the first explicitly computational theory of mind: “By ratiocination , I mean computation ” 4 . Thought is nothing but the addition and subtraction of internal names. Sensation is motion propagated from external objects through the sense organs to the brain, producing phantasms (internal representations) whose sequential processing constitutes reasoning. Where Descartes preserved a non-physical mind, Hobbes was an uncompromising materialist—there is nothing to the mind beyond matter in motion, and cognition is mechanical reckoning. Baruch Spinoza Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) dissolved Cartesian dualism by proposing that mind and body are not two substances but two attributes of a single substance [Ethics]. Every physical event in the brain has a corresponding mental description, and vice versa, but neither causes the other—they are one process described under two aspects. His concept of conatus , the striving of every being to persist in its own existence, has been noted as a philosophical antecedent of the free energy principle’s formalization of adaptive self-maintenance. John Locke John Locke (1632–1704) countered rationalist innatism with a systematic empiricism 5 . The mind begins as “white paper,” devoid of content; all ideas arise from sensation (external experience) or reflection (the mind’s observation of its own operations). Complex ideas are built from simple ideas through combination, comparison, and abstraction. Locke’s further distinction between primary qualities (intrinsic to objects: solidity, extension, motion) and secondary qualities (produced by the object’s powers acting on the perceiver: color, sound, taste) reinforced the implication that much of experience is constructed, not copied. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) argued against Locke that the mind possesses innate structure: “Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses— except the intellect itself ” 6 . His concept of petites perceptions —tiny, unconscious perceptions that individually fall below the threshold of awareness but collectively shape conscious experience (as the roar of the sea is composed of individually inaudible waves)—is a remarkable anticipation of subliminal processing and hierarchical sensory integration. The mill argument 7 anticipates the hard problem: if one could walk through a brain enlarged to the size of a mill, one would find only mechanical parts pushing against each other, and nowhere would one find perception. Thomas Willis Thomas Willis (1621–1675) effectively founded the discipline of neurology. In Cerebri Anatome 8 , illustrated by Christopher Wren, he produced the most detailed neuroanatomy of his era, identifying and naming structures including the arterial circle that bears his name, the striate body, and the corpus striatum. More consequential than his anatomy was a theoretical revolution: Willis relocated mental functions from the ventricular fluid—where Galenic tradition had housed them for over a millennium—to the brain’s solid tissue, its cortical convolutions and subcortical nuclei. Imagination and memory, he argued, reside in the cerebral gyri; involuntary and instinctive motion is governed by the cerebellum. With Willis, the brain ceased to be a passive container of animal spirits and became an active, structurally differentiated organ whose regional architecture maps onto distinct cognitive operations. Nicolas Malebranche Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715) developed his theory of perception in De la recherche de la vérité 9 , a work that is simultaneously a systematic epistemology and a remarkably thorough catalog of perceptual error, sensory illusion, and cognitive bias. The senses, he argued, are systematically unreliable guides to the nature of things; they were designed by God for the preservation of the body, not the discovery of truth, and must be corrected by reason at every turn. His occasionalism—the doctrine that God is the sole true cause of every event, with physical and mental occurrences serving merely as “occasions” for divine action—can be read, if one substitutes the generative model for God, as a striking early intuition that the proximate cause of perceptual experience lies not in the external stimulus but in the internal system that generates the percept.

title: The Enlightenment — c. 1720–1800
text: George Berkeley George Berkeley (1685–1753) radicalized empiricism into idealism: esse est percipi —to be is to be perceived 1 . There is no “matter” behind our perceptions; the world just is the structure of experience. More concretely, his Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision 2 argued that visual depth is not directly given but inferred from cues such as ocular convergence, blur, and learned associations with touch—a constructive account of spatial perception that anticipates the cue-integration models of modern vision science. David Hume David Hume (1711–1776) pushed empiricism to its skeptical limits 3 , 4 . There is no substantial self, only a “bundle” of perceptions in constant flux. Causation is not observed in the world but projected onto it by the mind through custom or habit : having repeatedly experienced event A A followed by event B B , we come to expect B B upon seeing A A . This is, in modern terms, a description of learned predictive association—and Hume’s problem of induction (why should past regularities predict future ones?) remains the foundational challenge that Bayesian inference addresses but does not fully resolve. La Mettrie Julien Offray de La Mettrie (1709–1751) wrote what is arguably the most radical materialist text of the Enlightenment: L’Homme Machine 5 . Humans differ from animals only in the complexity of their organization, not in kind. The soul is merely the brain in action; thought is a property of organized matter as surely as electricity is a property of certain materials. This thoroughgoing materialism—scandalous in its day—is the implicit metaphysics of modern neuroscience. Condillac Étienne Bonnot de Condillac (1714–1780) devised the celebrated statue thought experiment 6 : imagine a marble statue endowed with a single sense, say smell. From this single channel, Condillac argued, the statue would gradually develop attention (by having one sensation more vivid than others), memory (by retaining faded sensations), comparison, judgment, desire, and eventually all the faculties of mind. This is a constructivist thought experiment in building a mind from sensory atoms—a philosophical precursor to the modern project of understanding how hierarchical world models are learned from raw sensory input. Immanuel Kant Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) produced the deepest philosophical foundation for the view of the brain as a world-modeler 7 . Against the empiricists, Kant argued that the mind does not passively receive sensory impressions; it actively structures them through a priori forms of intuition (space and time) and categories of the understanding (causality, substance, unity, and others). Experience is always already a construction: what we perceive is not the world as it is in itself ( Ding an sich ) but the world as filtered through the mind’s own organizational principles ( Erscheinung , appearance). The Kantian insight—that the mind brings structure to sensation rather than extracting it from a pre-given world—is arguably the single most important philosophical ancestor of predictive processing and the Bayesian brain. Thomas Reid Thomas Reid (1710–1796) mounted the most formidable 18th-century challenge to the “way of ideas” shared by Locke, Berkeley, and Hume 8 , 9 . Against the view that we perceive only our own mental representations, Reid argued that perception yields direct , non-inferential awareness of the external world. Sensation (a subjective feeling in the perceiver) and perception (a direct apprehension of an external object) are distinct acts that occur simultaneously but must not be conflated. For world-modeling theories, Reid articulates a perennial challenge: if perception is truly Bayesian inference over a generative model, why does it phenomenologically present itself as immediate, transparent contact with reality—rather than as the output of a laborious computation? David Hartley David Hartley (1705–1757) was the first philosopher to ground the laws of association in an explicit neural mechanism 10 . Sensory stimuli produce vibrations in the nerves and brain substance; these vibrations leave behind diminished traces ( vibratiuncles ) that constitute ideas and memories. Ideas become associated when their corresponding vibrations co-occur, producing compound vibrations of increasing complexity from which all higher cognition is constructed. Hartley’s system—sensation as neural oscillation, memory as attenuated reactivation, and learning as temporal co-occurrence of neural events—is a recognizable ancestor of Hebbian synaptic plasticity and oscillatory neural coding, articulated more than a century before either.

title: Post-Kantian and Early 19th Century — c. 1800–1850
text: Fichte Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814) radicalized the Kantian program: the ego does not merely structure experience—it posits both itself and the not-self (the world) through its own activity 1 . The world model, on this view, is not imposed on a passively received sensory stream; it is spontaneously generated by the agent itself. This emphasis on the constitutive activity of the subject resonates with active inference, where the organism enacts its world through the interplay of prediction and action. Hegel G.W.F. Hegel (1770–1831) described consciousness as a developmental process in the Phenomenology of Spirit 2 . Each stage of awareness—from raw sensory certainty through perception, understanding, self-consciousness, and onward—discovers the inadequacy of its current model and is driven, through contradiction, to a richer one. The result is a dialectical, self-correcting hierarchy of representations, making Hegel an unexpected precursor to iterative, hierarchical inference. Schopenhauer Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) opened The World as Will and Representation 3 with a sentence that could serve as an epigraph for this book: “The world is my representation.” Everything we experience—objects, space, time, causality—is the brain’s representational construction. Behind the representation lies the blind, purposeless Will (the thing-in-itself), forever inaccessible to the modeling apparatus. Schopenhauer thus articulated, more starkly than any predecessor, the condition of an organism that can never step outside its own world model. Herbart Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776–1841) was the first to insist that psychology must be a mathematical science 4 . Ideas have quantitative strengths; they compete for access to consciousness, with weaker ideas being inhibited below a threshold (the Schwelle ). His “statics and mechanics of mind”—systems of differential equations governing the rise and fall of ideas through mutual inhibition and reinforcement—constitute a remarkably early neural-network-like dynamics of mental representation. Lotze Hermann Lotze (1817–1881) addressed a puzzle that remains central to computational neuroscience: how does the brain construct spatial perception from non-spatial neural signals 5 , 6 ? His theory of local signs ( Localzeichen ) proposed that each retinal point contributes a qualitatively distinct signal; spatial layout is then reconstructed by learning the lawful relationships among these signals and their motor consequences. This is the insight that the brain must decode its own neural code—that representation and the interpretation of representation are equally necessary. Johannes Müller (1801–1858) established the law of specific nerve energies : each sensory nerve, regardless of how it is stimulated, produces only its own characteristic quality of sensation 7 . Press on the closed eye and you see flashes of light, not pressure; electrically stimulate the auditory nerve and you hear a tone, not a tingle. The implication is profound and extends Kant’s philosophy into physiology: the brain has no direct access to the external world—it receives only the qualitatively idiosyncratic signals of its own nerves, and the character of experience is determined by which nerve fires, not by the physical nature of the external stimulus. Müller thus provided the physiological bridge between Kant’s claim that the mind imposes form on experience and Helmholtz’s subsequent theory of perception as unconscious inference: if all the brain ever receives is its own neural activity, then the perception of a coherent world “out there” must be a construction. Maine de Biran Maine de Biran (1766–1824) argued that the most fundamental datum of consciousness is not passive sensation but effort —the volitional, motor sense of exerting force against bodily and environmental resistance 8 , 9 . The self is not discovered through Cartesian meditation on thought but through the lived experience of willed bodily action: I move, therefore I am . Furthermore, habit progressively automates what was once effortful, transforming deliberate voluntary acts into transparent, nearly reflexive operations that withdraw from conscious awareness. For active inference, Maine de Biran is a remarkable precursor: his insistence that the self is constituted through motor engagement with the world, and that consciousness emerges precisely where prediction meets resistance, anticipates the primacy of action in the free energy framework.

title: Birth of Scientific Psychology — c. 1850–1900
text: Hermann von Helmholtz Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894) is, for the purposes of this book, the pivotal figure in the entire philosophical tradition. By measuring the speed of nerve impulses (and finding them surprisingly slow), he demonstrated that neural processing takes time—perception is not instantaneous contact with reality but the output of a process. He then proposed that perception is unconscious inference ( unbewusster Schluss ): the brain does not receive the world directly but infers the most likely external causes of its sensory signals, drawing on prior experience to resolve the inherent ambiguity of sensory data 1 , 2 . This is the direct ancestor of the Bayesian brain hypothesis, predictive processing, and the free energy principle. When Helmholtz wrote that “the sensations of the senses are tokens for our consciousness, it being left to our intelligence to learn how to comprehend their meaning,” he was describing the brain as a probabilistic inference engine. Gustav Fechner Gustav Fechner (1801–1887), in Elemente der Psychophysik 3 , founded psychophysics by demonstrating that the relationship between physical stimulus intensity S S and perceived sensation P P follows a lawful mathematical function—the Weber–Fechner law: P = k ln ⁡ ( S / S 0 ) P = k \ln(S/S_0) . This was the first successful quantitative bridge between the physical world and the world model, establishing that the mapping from reality to representation is compressive and can be precisely characterized. Franz Brentano Franz Brentano (1838–1917) reintroduced intentionality as the defining characteristic of mental phenomena: every mental act (perceiving, believing, desiring, imagining) is directed at an object —it is about something 4 . This “aboutness” is what any neural theory of world modeling must ultimately explain: how do patterns of electrochemical activity come to be about objects, events, and states of affairs in the external world? Brentano’s question has never gone away. William James William James (1842–1910) produced the most influential English-language psychology of the 19th century 5 . Consciousness is not a chain of discrete ideas but a continuous stream —a dynamic, contextually rich flow. Neural habit is the physiological substrate of cognition: well-worn pathways of activity that free higher processes for novel situations. The James–Lange theory of emotion—that we are afraid because we run, not the reverse—casts emotion as the perception of the body’s own physiological response, a form of interoceptive inference that modern predictive processing has embraced. Ernst Mach Ernst Mach (1838–1916) argued in The Analysis of Sensations 6 that science should abandon the metaphysical distinction between “physical” and “mental” and deal only with elements (sensations) and the functional relations among them. The task of any good model, whether scientific or cognitive, is to describe regularities among elements with maximal economy of thought ( Denkökonomie ). This principle of descriptive parsimony is a qualitative forerunner of the variational free energy principle’s mandate to minimize model complexity. Wilhelm Wundt Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920) founded the first formal laboratory of experimental psychology in Leipzig in 1879, marking the institutional separation of psychology from philosophy 7 . His method of trained experimental introspection —in which observers reported the elementary components of conscious experience under rigorously controlled stimulus conditions—was an attempt to decompose the world model into its basic constituents through systematic observation. Central to Wundt’s theory was apperception : the active, volitional process by which the mind synthesizes disparate sensory elements into a unified, attended experience. This concept—attention as an active, selective, integrative process that shapes what enters consciousness—anticipates the role of precision-weighting and attentional gain modulation in predictive processing, where not all prediction errors are treated equally, and the mind must actively select and weight its inputs. Charles Sanders Peirce Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) introduced abduction —inference to the best explanation—as a third fundamental mode of reasoning alongside deduction and induction 8 , 9 , 10 . Where deduction unfolds consequences from premises and induction generalizes from observed instances, abduction generates hypotheses that would, if true, explain the data at hand. This is precisely the inferential move that Helmholtz attributed to unconscious perception—-and that the Bayesian brain formalizes as posterior inference over a generative model. Peirce’s broader semiotics (theory of signs) provides an additional philosophical resource: neural states can be understood as signs of their external causes, related to those causes through interpretants (further neural states that specify how the sign is to be read), producing an inferential cascade with no foundational, uninterpreted terminus—representations all the way down.

title: Early 20th Century — c. 1900–1940
text: Edmund Husserl Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) founded phenomenology as a rigorous method for investigating the structures of conscious experience 1 , 2 . Every conscious act has a noetic aspect (the act of perceiving, judging, remembering) and a noematic aspect (the content perceived, judged, remembered). His analyses of internal time-consciousness —how the mind holds together the just-past ( retention ), the living present ( primal impression ), and the about-to-come ( protention )—describe the temporal microstructure of experience in terms deeply compatible with predictive processing’s account of temporal prediction. John Dewey John Dewey (1859–1952), in his landmark critique of the reflex arc concept 3 , argued that perception and action are not separate stages in a linear chain but phases of a continuous organism–environment loop . The stimulus does not precede the response; the organism’s ongoing activity determines what counts as a stimulus. This circular causality between perception and action is a core motif of modern active inference and enactivism. Martin Heidegger Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) rejected the entire framework of a subject representing an external world. In Being and Time 4 , human existence ( Dasein ) is always already being-in-the-world —embedded, practical, and engaged. We encounter objects primarily as ready-to-hand ( zuhanden )—tools transparently integrated into purposive action—rather than as present-at-hand ( vorhanden )—detached objects of theoretical scrutiny. The latter arises only in breakdown. For world-modeling theories, Heidegger poses a challenge: if our primary mode of engagement is skilled, transparent coping, is an internal model always involved, or only when things go wrong? Ludwig Wittgenstein Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951) offered two profoundly different philosophies of mind. The Tractatus 5 proposed a picture theory of meaning: propositions are logical pictures of states of affairs, their structure mirroring the structure of the world. The later Philosophical Investigations 6 dismantled this image: meaning is constituted by use within social language games , not by correspondence between inner representations and outer facts. His discussion of seeing-as (the duck–rabbit figure), and the private language argument —which challenges the coherence of a purely internal, first-person mental vocabulary—raises deep difficulties for any theory that grounds world modeling in private neural representations alone. Rudolf Carnap Rudolf Carnap (1891–1970), in Der logische Aufbau der Welt 7 , attempted to rationally reconstruct all concepts of science from a base of elementary experiences ( Elementarerlebnisse ) using purely logical relations. The project is, in effect, a formal blueprint for building a hierarchical world model from sensory primitives—and its partial failure is instructive: Carnap discovered that logical construction from experience alone is insufficient without structural priors, an insight consonant with the Kantian foundations of predictive processing. Bertrand Russell Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) developed a form of neutral monism that dissolved the mind–body divide 8 , 9 . Both mental and physical events, he argued, are composed of the same underlying neutral “stuff”; the distinction between mind and matter is one of arrangement , not of intrinsic nature. A given event is “mental” when placed in the context of a particular biography (a chain of experiences) and “physical” when placed in the context of a causal group radiating from a spatial location. Russell also drew the influential distinction between knowledge by acquaintance (direct, non-inferential awareness of sense-data) and knowledge by description (indirect knowledge mediated by concepts and inference)—a divide that maps suggestively onto the difference between the brain’s raw sensory prediction errors and the high-level, structured world model that interprets them. Wolfgang Köhler (1887–1967), together with Max Wertheimer and Kurt Koffka, founded Gestalt psychology on the principle that perceptual experience is organized into structured wholes ( Gestalten ) that are irreducible to the sum of their sensory elements 10 , 11 . The laws of perceptual grouping—proximity, similarity, closure, good continuation, common fate, Prägnanz—describe the structural priors the visual system brings to the organization of sensory input, segmenting the retinal image into objects, surfaces, and events before any deliberate analysis. Köhler’s principle of psychophysical isomorphism proposed that the structural relations within perceptual experience faithfully mirror the structural relations within the underlying brain dynamics—a hypothesis that finds modern expression in topographic cortical maps, representational similarity analysis, and the geometry of neural population codes.

title: Mid-Century: Cybernetics and the Mind — c. 1940–1965
text: Kenneth Craik Kenneth Craik (1914–1945) may have been the first thinker to state the central thesis of this book in explicit terms. In The Nature of Explanation 1 , he proposed that the brain constructs “small-scale models” of external reality that it uses to try out alternatives, anticipate events, and select among possible actions. “If the organism carries a ‘small-scale model’ of external reality and of its own possible actions within its head, it is able to try out various alternatives, conclude which is the best of them, react to future situations before they arise.” Craik died in a cycling accident at thirty-one; his vision would take decades to be realized in computational form. Alan Turing Alan Turing (1912–1954) provided the formal foundation for any computational theory of the brain. His 1936 paper 2 showed that a simple abstract machine (the Turing machine ) can compute anything that is computable. In “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” 3 , he posed the question of whether machines can think and proposed the imitation game (Turing test) as a pragmatic criterion. The question that computational neuroscience inherits from Turing is precise: what does the brain compute, and how ? Maurice Merleau-Ponty Maurice Merleau-Ponty (1908–1961) mounted the most influential philosophical challenge to disembodied, representationalist accounts of the mind 4 , 5 . Perception is not the brain’s construction of an internal replica; it is the body’s active engagement with the world. The body schema—a pre-reflective, motor understanding of the body’s capabilities and position—is the medium through which the world shows up as meaningful. Pathological cases (phantom limbs, spatial neglect, apraxia) reveal that perception and action are inseparable. His work is the primary philosophical source for the embodied cognition movement and remains a standing challenge to purely internalist world-modeling accounts. Gilbert Ryle Gilbert Ryle (1900–1976) attacked Cartesian dualism in The Concept of Mind 6 as a “category mistake”—the error of treating the mind as a “ghost in the machine,” a hidden inner theater where experience is privately screened. Mental predicates (knowing, believing, intending) are not reports of inner episodes but descriptions of dispositions to behave in certain ways. Though few neuroscientists accept full-blown behaviorism, Ryle’s critique sharpened the question: what explanatory work does an “internal model” do that cannot be captured by the organism’s dispositions to act? Wilfrid Sellars Wilfrid Sellars (1912–1989) demolished the Myth of the Given in “Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind” 7 : there is no level of experience that is simply “given” to the mind, raw and uninterpreted. All perceptual experience is already theory-laden —structured by concepts, expectations, and inferential commitments. His distinction between the manifest image (the world as it appears to everyday experience) and the scientific image (the world as described by physics and neuroscience) defines the central tension of the field: the brain’s world model produces the manifest image, but the scientific image tells us that the manifest image is a construction of neural processes that are nothing like how the world appears. Norbert Wiener Norbert Wiener (1894–1964) named and defined the field of cybernetics : the study of “control and communication in the animal and the machine” 8 . The foundational insight is that organisms and engineered systems share a common architecture of negative feedback : a system continuously compares its current state to a reference state and acts to minimize the discrepancy. Purposive behavior, on this view, is not metaphysically mysterious; it is any behavior governed by feedback toward a set-point. Wiener’s framework—in which the brain is a self-regulating, stochastic, information-processing system that acts to minimize the divergence between expected and actual states—is a direct intellectual ancestor of the free energy principle’s account of action as the minimization of prediction error. W. Ross Ashby W. Ross Ashby (1903–1972) asked, more precisely than anyone before him, what it takes for a physical system to be genuinely adaptive 9 , 10 . His homeostat —an electromechanical device with randomly connected feedback loops that settles, through a process of trial and ultra-stability, into configurations maintaining essential variables within survival-compatible bounds—was a physical proof of concept that self-organizing, adaptive behavior requires neither a designer nor explicit goal representations. His law of requisite variety states that a regulator must possess at least as many distinguishable internal states as the system it controls—a formal lower bound on the complexity of any viable world model. In the idiom of the free energy principle, the brain’s generative model must be rich enough to account for the variability of its sensory input; Ashby’s law specifies the minimum complexity this demands.

title: Cognitive Revolution and Functionalism — c. 1960–1985
text: J.J. Gibson James J. Gibson (1904–1979) posed the most radical alternative to the world-modeling framework 1 , 2 . Perception does not require internal representations, inference, or models. The structured ambient light array (optic flow, texture gradients, occlusion patterns) already contains sufficient information to specify the layout of the environment directly. Organisms do not build models; they pick up affordances —possibilities for action offered by the environment. Gibson’s ecological approach remains a powerful critique: any computational theory of world modeling must explain what it can do that direct specification cannot. Hilary Putnam Hilary Putnam (1926–2016) introduced functionalism , the thesis that mental states are individuated not by their physical substrate but by their functional roles —their causal relations to sensory inputs, behavioral outputs, and other mental states 3 , 4 . Multiple realizability —the argument that the same mental state could in principle be implemented in neurons, silicon, or any other medium with the right functional organization—licenses computational neuroscience’s focus on algorithms over hardware. Putnam later turned against his own position, arguing in Representation and Reality 5 that computational functionalism cannot adequately capture meaning. Jerry Fodor Jerry Fodor (1935–2017) articulated the classical computational theory of cognition. The Language of Thought 6 argued that thinking is computation over structured symbolic representations in an innate mental language (“Mentalese”). The Modularity of Mind 7 proposed that perceptual systems are informationally encapsulated, domain-specific, fast, and mandatory modules —a claim that continues to shape theories of cortical functional architecture, even as strict encapsulation is challenged by the top-down predictions of predictive processing. David Marr David Marr (1945–1980) provided the methodological framework that computational neuroscience still largely operates within. In Vision [Vision], he argued that any information-processing system must be understood at three levels: the computational level (what problem is being solved and why?), the algorithmic level (what representations and processes are used?), and the implementational level (how are these physically realized?). Before asking how the brain builds a world model, one must first specify what a world model is for . Thomas Nagel Thomas Nagel (1937–) raised a challenge that no computational theory has fully met. “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” 8 argues that an organism has conscious experience if there is something it is like to be that organism. Even a complete physical, functional, and computational description of a bat’s sonar system would not convey what echolocation feels like from the bat’s own point of view. This explanatory gap between objective description and subjective experience haunts every world-modeling theory: does the model fully constitute experience, or does something remain left over? Noam Chomsky Noam Chomsky (1928–) precipitated the cognitive revolution with the argument that language acquisition cannot be explained by learning from environmental input alone 9 , 10 . The poverty of the stimulus holds that the linguistic data available to a child massively underdetermines the grammar the child reliably acquires; therefore, the mind must bring rich innate structure—a universal grammar —to the learning task. This rationalist nativism ended the dominance of behaviorism and reintroduced the Kantian insight in a new key: the brain does not learn from data alone but brings powerful structural priors that constrain and enable acquisition. In the language of predictive processing, Chomsky’s universal grammar is a highly informative prior over the space of possible generative models of language—biology’s answer to the poverty of the sensory stream. Fred Dretske Fred Dretske (1932–2013) developed the most influential information-theoretic account of mental representation 11 , 12 . A neural state represents an external condition, Dretske argued, if it carries information about that condition: that is, if there is a lawful, counterfactual-supporting dependency such that the neural state would not have occurred (during the relevant learning period) had the external condition not obtained. This naturalized intentionality by grounding the “aboutness” of mental states in objective statistical relations rather than in semantic primitives taken as given. For computational neuroscience, Dretske provides a principled criterion for what makes a pattern of neural activity a representation of something in the world: the reliable, learned covariance between internal state and external cause—precisely the kind of dependency that a well-trained generative model exploits.

title: Neurophilosophy and the Consciousness Debates — c. 1985–2000
text: John Searle John Searle (1932–) attacked the computational theory of mind with the Chinese Room thought experiment 1 : a person who follows rules to manipulate Chinese characters can produce correct outputs without understanding a word of Chinese. Syntax (computation) is not sufficient for semantics (meaning). His alternative, biological naturalism , holds that consciousness is a real, causally efficacious biological phenomenon produced by specific neurobiological processes—not by the abstract formal structure that any computer might share with a brain. Daniel Dennett Daniel Dennett (1942–2024) rejected the Cartesian theater—the assumption that there is a single place in the brain where “it all comes together” for a conscious observer 2 . Instead, he proposed the Multiple Drafts model: at any moment, multiple parallel streams of content are being revised and edited throughout the brain, and there is no sharp line between conscious and unconscious processing. His intentional stance 3 treats the attribution of beliefs and desires as a predictive strategy: we model systems as if they have beliefs and goals because doing so lets us predict their behavior, regardless of their internal architecture. Patricia Churchland Patricia Churchland (1943–) coined neurophilosophy and argued that traditional philosophical categories—belief, desire, intention—may not carve the brain at its joints 4 . As neuroscience matures, these folk-psychological concepts may be revised or eliminated entirely in favor of neuroscientific categories ( eliminative materialism ). Philosophy of mind, on this view, must be continuous with and constrained by brain science. Her work has been instrumental in breaking down disciplinary barriers between philosophy and neuroscience. David Chalmers David Chalmers (1966–) drew the sharpest contemporary distinction between what a computational theory of the brain can and cannot explain 5 , 6 . The easy problems —explaining discrimination, integration, reportability, attentional control—are hard in practice but easy in principle: they are functional problems amenable to computational explanation. The hard problem is why and how any of this functional processing is accompanied by subjective experience ( qualia ). A perfect Bayesian world model running in a brain would solve all the easy problems; whether it would thereby solve the hard problem remains the deepest open question in the field. Francisco Varela Francisco Varela (1946–2001), with Humberto Maturana, introduced autopoiesis : a living system is a self-producing network of processes that generates and maintains its own boundary 7 . With Evan Thompson and Eleanor Rosch, he then developed enactivism : cognition is not the construction of a representation of a pre-given world but the enactment of a world through the organism’s embodied activity 8 . His program of neurophenomenology 9 called for first-person phenomenological reports to be used as data constraining third-person neuroscientific models—a bridge between the manifest and scientific images. Paul Churchland Paul Churchland (1942–) argued that cognition is best understood not as logical inference over sentence-like representations but as the learned transformation of high-dimensional activation patterns across neural populations 10 , 11 . His state-space semantics proposes that a concept is not a symbol but a region in a high-dimensional neural activation space, and that semantic similarity is geometric proximity in that space. Learning is the sculpting of synaptic weights so that the network’s activation landscape comes to mirror the statistical structure of the environment—a view that harmonizes with both modern deep learning and with the predictive processing claim that the brain’s generative model is a learned mapping from hidden causes to expected sensory states. If Patricia Churchland argued that philosophy must become neuroscience, Paul Churchland showed what a neurocomputational philosophy of mind might look like in practice. Alva Noë (1964–) developed a radically anti-representationalist enactivism 12 , 13 . Perception, he argued, is not something that happens inside the brain; it is something the whole organism does —a skillful, exploratory activity governed by the perceiver’s implicit mastery of sensorimotor contingencies : the lawful ways in which sensory stimulation changes as a function of the organism’s own movement. We do not need a rich internal world model, on this view, because the world is perpetually available to be sampled through action; the brain’s role is not to build a detailed internal replica but to facilitate ongoing, dynamic access to environmental structure. Noë’s enactivism poses the sharpest form of the question that every predictive processing theorist must answer: if the brain is a prediction machine that models the world, does it genuinely represent the world, or does it merely anticipate the sensory consequences of its own actions—and is there, in the end, a difference?

title: Predictive Processing, Free Energy, and 4E Cognition — c. 2000–Present
text: Karl Friston Karl Friston (1959–) has developed the most comprehensive mathematical framework for the brain-as-world-modeler thesis 1 , 2 , 3 . The free energy principle states that any self-organizing system that persists in a changing environment must minimize variational free energy —an information-theoretic quantity that bounds the surprise ( surprisal ) of sensory observations given the system’s internal generative model. This single imperative subsumes perception (updating the model to reduce prediction error), action (changing sensory input to match predictions), learning (optimizing model parameters), and attention (adjusting the precision of prediction errors). The brain, on this account, is a hierarchical generative model, and everything it does—from saccadic eye movements to abstract reasoning—is variational inference. The mathematical apparatus of the free energy principle, including the role of Markov blankets in defining the boundary between agent and environment, provides the formal backbone of much of this textbook. Andy Clark Andy Clark (1957–) has been the most prominent philosophical interpreter and champion of the predictive processing framework 4 , 5 . He argues that the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine : a system that proactively generates top-down expectations about incoming signals and updates itself only when those predictions fail. Perception, on this view, is “controlled hallucination”—an ongoing, largely successful attempt to predict the sensory stream from the inside out. Clark’s earlier work with Chalmers on the extended mind thesis 6 argued that cognitive processes can extend beyond the skull into notebooks, tools, and digital devices, raising the question of whether the world model has a fixed boundary. Jakob Hohwy Jakob Hohwy (1974–) has provided the most sustained philosophical analysis of predictive processing as a theory of mind 7 . If the brain is a prediction engine locked behind the sensory surfaces—what Hohwy calls the “evidentiary boundary” of the skull—then all it ever has access to are its own prediction errors. The world model is the brain’s best hypothesis about the hidden causes of its sensory states. This leads to an inferential seclusion : the brain never contacts the world directly, only its own best guess about the world—an updated, formally precise rehabilitation of the Kantian predicament. Thomas Metzinger Thomas Metzinger (1958–) offers a theory of subjectivity grounded in self-modeling 8 . The conscious self is not an entity but a transparent self-model —the phenomenal self-model (PSM)—generated by the brain. “Transparent” means that we do not experience the model as a model; we look through it and experience it as unmediated reality. Consciousness is an “ego tunnel” 9 : a low-dimensional, integrated self-world model that the organism cannot see the edges of. This account connects directly to the hierarchical generative model: the self is just another layer of the brain’s world model—the layer that models the modeler. Evan Thompson Evan Thompson (1962–) has extended and deepened the enactivist tradition into the era of predictive processing 10 , 11 . Cognition, he argues, is not a brain process but a relational process involving brain, body, and environment—a view that is continuous with Varela’s autopoietic framework and Merleau-Ponty’s embodied phenomenology. Thompson offers a critical counterpoint to internalist versions of predictive processing: if the world model is understood as an internal neuronal structure, then the embodied, embedded, environmentally coupled character of actual cognition may be lost. The tension between the skull-bound generative model and the world-involving enactive agent is one of the most productive open questions in the field, and it runs through every chapter that follows. Anil Seth Anil Seth (1972–) has extended the predictive processing framework inward, from exteroceptive perception to interoception and affect 12 , 13 . His “beast machine” thesis holds that the most fundamental layer of conscious selfhood arises not from the brain’s model of the external world but from its predictions about the body’s own internal physiological states—visceral, hormonal, and autonomic signals that constitute the felt sense of being alive. Perception, on Seth’s account, is “controlled hallucination” not only of the external scene but of the embodied self that inhabits it. He has also urged a pragmatic reorientation of consciousness science away from Chalmers’s “hard problem” and toward what he calls the “real problem”: explaining, predicting, and experimentally controlling the specific, fine-grained correspondences between neural mechanisms and particular qualities of conscious experience. Giulio Tononi Giulio Tononi (1960–) has developed Integrated Information Theory (IIT), the most mathematically ambitious attempt to identify consciousness with a measurable physical quantity 14 , 15 . IIT proposes that a system is conscious to the extent that it possesses integrated information , denoted Φ \Phi : a measure of how much the system’s current state is simultaneously differentiated (capable of occupying a vast repertoire of distinct states) and integrated (such that the whole generates more information than the sum of its independently considered parts). A system with high Φ \Phi is conscious; one with Φ = 0 \Phi = 0 is not, regardless of its behavior or functional organization. IIT offers an instructive contrast to the free energy principle: where predictive processing characterizes what the brain does (minimize prediction error through inference), IIT attempts to characterize what a conscious system is (a structure with high integrated information)—and to derive the quality and content of experience from the intrinsic geometry of that structure rather than from its input–output relations. Lisa Feldman Barrett Lisa Feldman Barrett (1963–) has extended predictive processing into the domain of affect and emotion with the theory of constructed emotion 16 , 17 . Against the classical view that emotions are triggered reactions mediated by dedicated neural circuits (a “fear circuit,” a “disgust circuit”), Barrett argues that the brain constructs emotional experiences through the same domain-general, predictive, categorization-based machinery it uses for all perception. Interoceptive signals from the body are inherently ambiguous—a racing heart may signify fear, excitement, or exercise—and the brain resolves this ambiguity by predicting the most probable cause given the current context and the organism’s learned conceptual repertoire. The resulting emotion is a prediction, not a detection. Barrett’s concept of the “body budget” (allostasis) reframes the brain’s deepest function: before it is a perceiver or a thinker, the brain is an organ of metabolic regulation, continuously predicting and managing the body’s energetic needs. Her work demonstrates that the world model is not limited to the external scene; it encompasses the affective and physiological interior, and that the felt quality of experience—whether the world seems threatening, welcoming, or dull—is itself a construction of the generative model, shaped as much by visceral prediction as by sensory input. Michael Graziano Michael Graziano (1967–) has proposed Attention Schema Theory (AST), a mechanistic account that treats consciousness as a specific variety of self-modeling 18 , 19 . Just as the brain constructs a body schema —a simplified internal model of the body’s geometry, posture, and capabilities—it constructs an attention schema : a simplified, schematic model of its own attentional processes. When the brain directs attention to a stimulus, the attention schema represents this process as a mental possession of the stimulus—an internal, subjective experience of it. This schema is what we introspectively report as “awareness.” AST thus reframes consciousness not as a metaphysical mystery but as a modeling problem with a specific computational function: by representing its own attentional states, the brain can monitor, predict, and control where and how it allocates processing resources. The theory also provides a natural account of social cognition—because we model attention in others using the same schema machinery, we readily attribute consciousness to other minds, to animals, and even to animated objects. For the world-modeling framework of this book, Graziano’s contribution is the insight that the model is recursive: the brain models the external world, the body within it, and—crucially—the very process of modeling itself, and it is this last, self-referential layer that generates the felt sense of being a conscious subject.
