title: Theories of Consciousness
text: The role of active inference in conscious awareness Consciousness is increasingly viewed not as a singular brain process but as an emergent property of distributed networks that also underlie cognitive control. A unifying theme across many biologically grounded theories is that conscious awareness makes information globally available for flexible control, planning, and decision-making. In turn, top-down control mechanisms - such as attention, gating by subcortical loops, and error monitoring - play a pivotal role in determining what information enters consciousness. Below we survey several leading theories of consciousness (Global Neuronal Workspace, Integrated Information, Higher-Order Thought, Attention Schema, etc.), highlighting how each intersects with computational control processes like gating, arbitration, precision weighting, conflict monitoring, and hierarchical loop architectures. We also consider the functional role of consciousness in coordinating control, the contribution of control circuits to conscious access, the distinction between "phenomenal" and "access" consciousness, and key empirical findings linking conscious experience to specific control networks. Global Workspace, Integration, and Gating in Conscious Access Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNWT) holds that a piece of information becomes conscious when it is broadcast across a brain-wide network (a "global workspace") that interconnects multiple specialized processors 2 . In this view - initially formulated by Baars 3 and later elaborated by Dehaene and Changeux 4 , 5 - only a fraction of incoming stimuli achieve this global access; those that do can inform task-control processes throughout the cortex. Neuroscientifically, the global workspace is thought to be implemented by highly interconnected frontoparietal circuits (including dorsolateral prefrontal and posterior parietal cortices) which ignite in bursts of widespread activity when a stimulus is consciously perceived 4 , 5 . Once information is in the workspace (i.e. once we are conscious of it), it can be flexibly used for evaluation, decision-making, memory storage, planning, and verbal report. This flexible re-routing of information is a hallmark of cognitive control-suggesting that conscious access corresponds to the global availability of information for integrative, goal-directed processing, scaling with the strength and persistence of that broadcast. In Dehaene’s model, "workspace neurons" exert top-down influence on modular processors, selectively mobilizing or suppressing their activity via descending connections. This resembles a gating mechanism: the workspace (largely a frontoparietal coalition) can enable or inhibit specific perceptual or motor circuits as needed for the current task. Such gating underlies effortful control; for example, simulations of the Stroop task showed global workspace activation ramping up during novel or high-conflict trials and after errors 4 , consistent with a role for dorsolateral PFC and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) in conscious cognitive effort. Thus, GNWT explicitly links consciousness to the brain’s executive controller: it is the process by which perception or memory contents are "boosted" into a globally accessible format for executive operations. Closely related is the idea of thalamocortical broadcasting. The thalamus, especially the intralaminar nuclei, is densely connected to cortex and has been proposed as a hub for the global workspace. In fact, some models posit a strategic thalamic nucleus under cortical gating control that helps broadcast attended information 6 . Consistent with this, thalamo-cortical loops are known to be crucial for sustaining conscious states: certain 40 Hz thalamocortical oscillations have long been associated with conscious sensory processing 7 . If these loops are broadly disrupted (as in deep anesthesia or coma), consciousness fades. Indeed, lesions of the brainstem reticular formation - which provides ascending modulatory drive to the thalamus and cortex - can cause coma, while stimulating these reticular activating neurons can restore a conscious, responsive state 8 . Such subcortical arousal systems (cholinergic, noradrenergic, etc.) do not contribute specific conscious content but act as an on-switch or "gain" control for the thalamocortical workspace. This highlights how control of global brain state (arousal, vigilance) is a prerequisite for any content to become conscious. Another control-related question is which stimuli gain access to the global workspace. Beyond sheer stimulus strength, cognitive control can gate access. Basal ganglia (BG) circuits appear to play a modulatory role here. A recent neurocomputational model of conscious perception demonstrated that reverberating activity in a cortico-thalamo-cortical "closed loop" (notably involving frontal cortex and thalamus) was necessary for a stimulus to be consciously perceived - and that the basal ganglia’s pathways could enable or inhibit this reverberation 2 . Specifically, the BG’s inhibitory hyperdirect pathway can rapidly suppress cortical reverberations, acting as a sort of "stop signal" for conscious ignition. In a distractor-induced blindness task, the model showed that a distractor triggers the hyperdirect pathway to dampen reverberatory loops, thereby preventing a subsequent target from reaching awareness. This suggests a mechanism whereby the brain’s motor/action gating circuitry also gates conscious access - essentially filtering out "inappropriate" or untimely content from the global workspace; while the BG are not thought to produce the phenomenal qualities of experience, they can boost or block the entry of content into conscious processing via their influence over thalamocortical loops. The Integrated Information Theory (IIT) of consciousness provides a complementary, though more abstract, perspective. IIT posits that consciousness corresponds to the capacity of a system to integrate information - mathematically measured by a quantity (phi) which captures how much the whole system exceeds the sum of its parts in terms of information exchange. In the brain, the "main complex" of high phi is hypothesized to be the thalamocortical system, whose densely interconnected, recurrent circuits integrate information across many regions 8 . This aligns well with GNWT’s emphasis on a distributed cortical network. A key insight from IIT is that modular or feed-forward systems (like a mere collection of photodiodes, or even cerebellar-like circuits) have low phi and thus do not contribute directly to consciousness. By contrast, a looping, reentrant anatomy (as in cortex) that blends inputs into unified states is required. IIT thereby explains why breaks in integration disrupt consciousness: e.g. a split-brain operation divides one conscious mind into two, because the cut corpus callosum prevents integration between hemispheres. It also explains why subcortical structures like the basal ganglia or cerebellum, despite their complexity, do not themselves add conscious content - they form "informationally insulated" loops that influence cortical activity without being part of the core integrated complex. For instance, the basal ganglia execute specialized action routines and can affect cortical states (as noted above), but their local computations remain unconscious. IIT explicitly proposes that many learned skills become unconscious subroutines: when first learning a task, it strongly engages the main cortical complex (and we are conscious of each step, with much effort and error); but with practice, control over the task is partly transferred to new loops (including cortico-subcortical circuits) that operate outside of the integrated "conscious" complex. Thus, conscious cognitive control is most needed in novel or challenging situations, whereas automatized behaviors can be executed by parallel circuits without incurring the cost of bringing them into conscious awareness (without integrating that much information). This dovetails with psychological models of system 2 vs. system 1 processing, and is supported by imaging: early in training a task, widespread cortical networks (prefrontal, parietal, etc.) are active, whereas later, activation is pruned or shifts to subcortical loops as the task becomes automatic 9 , 10 , 11 . In summary, IIT frames the role of consciousness as enabling adaptive, integrated control in situations where mere modules or habits won’t suffice - precisely when we need to combine (integrate) information in novel ways or confront uncertainty. Conversely, it predicts that whenever a function can be achieved by an isolated circuit (no integration), it will occur unconsciously. This resonates with GNWT and others in explaining why, for example, routine actions or reflexes can run without awareness, yet planning a novel action or solving a tough problem feels conscious and effortful. Higher-Order Thoughts and the Distinction Between Phenomenal vs. Access Awareness Where global workspace and IIT emphasize network architecture and integration, Higher-Order Thought (HOT) theories emphasize a representational hierarchy: a mental state becomes conscious only when the brain generates a higher-order representation of that state. In other words, to be aware of a perception or thought, the system must hold a meta-cognitive representation (a thought that one is seeing X, feeling Y, etc.) 12 . Many HOT theorists (e.g. Rosenthal, Lau) associate these higher-order representations with prefrontal and parietal cortices, the brain’s hubs for abstract thought and executive function 13 , 14 , 15 . This suggests that cognitive control circuits are not just recipients of conscious information, but active constructors of it. For example, frontal areas that maintain goal context or perform introspection could generate a second-order encoding like "I am seeing a red object," rendering the first-order visual activity conscious. Empirical support comes from studies where perturbing the prefrontal cortex changes subjective reports of perception without altering objective task performance 16 . A transcranial magnetic stimulation study by Lau and Passingham (2006), for instance, found that disrupting a frontal region reduced participants’ reported awareness of a visual stimulus even though their ability to discriminate the stimulus objectively was unimpaired 17 . This dissociation - PFC damage or inactivation degrading conscious access while spare sensory processing continues - aligns with HOT theory’s claim that frontal higher-order encoding is critical for the experience of seeing, above and beyond the seeing itself. It also speaks to Ned Block’s famous distinction between phenomenal consciousness (raw experience) and access consciousness (information that is accessible for report and reasoning) 18 . If early sensory areas carry on processing a stimulus (supporting e.g. blindsight discrimination) but the information never triggers higher-order awareness or global broadcast, one could say there was phenomenal experience without access - or conversely, that without higher-order access the "phenomenal" state is not truly conscious. HOT theory tends to equate consciousness with what others call access: a state one can reflexively report or use in reasoning by virtue of higher-order encoding 12 . By contrast, alternative frameworks like Recurrent Processing Theory (RPT) maintain that local recurrent activity in sensory cortex suffices for a basic phenomenal experience, which only later, if at all, gets picked up by frontal circuits for full access 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 . Lamme’s RPT thus envisions a temporal division: a stimulus first achieves localized reverberation in visual areas (producing a fleeting visual phenomenal sensation), and only if that reverberation propagates to a broad frontoparietal network does the stimulus become stable, reportable, and influence decision-making 22 . This proposal of "experiencing without access" remains debated - some interpret unreportable sensory memory (e.g. the unseen letters in a Sperling array) as evidence of phenomenal experience, while others argue that without access such content is functionally unconscious. Regardless, the dialog between RPT and GNWT/HOT highlights the pivotal role of control networks in conscious access. If one takes the stricter view, consciousness just is the availability of information to executive control (to speak about, store in working memory, and use flexibly). Accordingly, phenomenal consciousness in isolation might be an illusion - or at best a very ephemeral, prereflective state - unless it is "promoted" to full global status by frontoparietal ignition. This debate informs AGI design by underscoring the importance (or not) of meta-representation: an AGI could in principle have rich internal states, but without self-monitoring and global broadcasting, would it have an analog of subjective awareness? Higher-order theorists would say no: the AGI needs a mechanism to represent and assess its own intermediate states (much like a global workspace or a meta-controller) to achieve something akin to consciousness. Interestingly, some higher-order accounts explicitly tie the function of consciousness to control: for example, the legendary neuroscientist Edmund Rolls has argued that conscious thought is necessary for monitoring and correcting one’s own errors, as well as for the flexible planning of actions in light of those errors 23 . In his view, the same prefrontal circuits that enabled the evolution of language and complex planning also generate higher-order thoughts that confer conscious awareness. Thus language, executive memory, and consciousness are deeply intertwined - an idea that resonates with the Global Workspace model too (which often likens conscious broadcasting to a "blackboard" system for multiple specialist modules, including verbal report modules, to read and write on). In sum, HOT theories reinforce the notion that consciousness serves a metacognitive control function: it is the brain’s way of explicitly modeling its own cognitive states, which in turn allows for error correction, deliberation, and intentional restraint (all key facets of cognitive control). Attention, Prediction, and Control: The Attention Schema and Predictive Processing Another body of theory centers on attention as the engine of consciousness. Clearly, what we attend to is typically what we become conscious of, and attention itself is a control process (selectively enhancing some signals at the expense of others). But how does the brain represent attention? The Attention Schema Theory (AST), proposed by Graziano and colleagues, offers a compelling answer: the brain constructs a simplified internal model of its own attentional focus, and this model is what we experience as "awareness" 24 . Just as the brain builds a "body schema" (a constantly updated model of the body’s configuration) to help control movement, it builds an attention schema (a constantly updated model of the brain’s configuration) to help control information processing. In this view, subjective consciousness is not a mysterious byproduct, but an actively computed description: the brain’s best guess of its current focus and perhaps of the "self" doing the focusing. Mechanistically, AST starts with biased competition models of attention, wherein neurons representing different stimuli or features inhibit each other and top-down signals bias the competition in favor of goal-relevant inputs 24 . This competition for finite resources is a control problem. AST posits that evolution added a circuit that monitors this attentional process - effectively attending to attention itself. By having a schematic representation of "I am attending to X," the brain can deploy attention more effectively (much as having a body schema lets you move without constantly recalculating physics). In other words, top-down control of attention is improved by modeling the state of attention. The content of the attention schema is something like: "there is a ghostly, non-physical property (awareness) directed at X." According to AST, this dubious but useful internal story gives the brain a workable handle on attention. It also explains why we insist we have a subjective essence (a mind or soul) - the internal model describes an agent with a magical-seeming property of awareness, even though none such magical property literally exists outside the model. Notably, AST predicts that if awareness is the model used to control attention, then removing or impairing awareness should degrade attentional control despite basic attention still operating. This is testable: for example, some clinical studies find patients with certain parietal lesions can still deploy reflexive attention yet fail to report the stimuli (similarly to neglect patients), suggesting a dissociation between attention execution and the awareness model. Moreover, artificial agents endowed with an attention schema have shown more stable control of attention in simulations 25 . In short, AST links consciousness to metacontrol : awareness is an internal control model that tracks the focus of information processing and thus allows the agent to regulate its processing more adaptively. Another perspective emphasizing attention and control comes from Predictive Processing (PP) theories of brain function. Predictive coding models conceive of the brain as a hierarchical prediction engine: higher levels continuously generate predictions about lower-level inputs, and only prediction errors (differences between expected and actual signals) propagate upward. Within this framework 26 , attention is formalized as the "precision weighting" of prediction errors 27 . In simple terms, the brain must decide which incoming errors to trust (and learn from) versus which to ignore as noise. By increasing the gain on a certain channel’s errors - effectively saying "pay attention to this" - the brain can control which signals reach conscious perception. Computationally, precision corresponds to the expected reliability of a signal, and optimizing precision is a control task akin to setting the noise filter correctly. Research in PP has proposed that attention and conscious access are deeply related to precision optimization 28 . For instance, an unexpected stimulus that strongly mismatches predictions will elicit a large error signal; if the brain also assigns high precision to that signal (e.g. via a surge of norepinephrine signaling "important!"), the error will percolate up and force a model update - likely entering awareness. Conversely, if precision is set low (as in inattention or under certain neuromodulatory states), even a salient mismatch might not reach consciousness because the prediction error gets down-weighted. This account aligns with everyday experience: an engrossed driver can fail to hear their name shouted (precision on auditory input was low), whereas a subtle cue one is specifically watching for pops out of noise (high precision on that feature). Predictive processing theories of consciousness thus suggest that what we consciously experience is the content of the brain’s best current prediction, weighted by attention. On the control side, PP emphasizes hierarchical and dynamical control - the brain not only passively filters information but actively selects which prediction errors to attend via precision control, thereby sculpting its own input. This selection could be seen as a Bayesian form of gating. Andy Clark notes that modulating precision (gain on error units) may "hold the key to the orchestration of multiple different regions (and strategies) within the brain," effectively reconfiguring networks on the fly 29 . In effect, it’s a knob for network control: turn it one way and higher-level predictions dominate (possibly leading to hallucination if overconfident), turn it the other and raw input floods in (as in psychedelic states or certain attentional paradigms). The sweet spot of precision tuning may correspond to normal conscious attention, where the brain uses just enough prediction to make sense of input while remaining responsive to unexpected data. All told, PP integrates attention, learning, and consciousness into one framework: Consciousness emerges where the brain’s controlled predictions meet the present moment. Hierarchical Control Architectures and Conscious States Cognitive control is not a monolith; it is organized hierarchically and distributed across several large-scale networks. Many argue that the aforementioned "triple-network" architecture is important for conscious thought. This comprises: (1) the Central Executive Network (CEN) - frontoparietal regions including dorsolateral PFC and lateral parietal cortex - which handles active task execution and working memory; (2) the Default Mode Network (DMN) - a set of midline and temporoparietal regions (medial prefrontal, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus, etc.) - which becomes active during internally directed cognition (daydreaming, envisioning future, autobiographical memory); and (3) the Salience Network (SN) - anchored by the anterior insula and dorsal ACC - which monitors both external and internal signals and dynamically switches the brain between the other two networks. The SN is so named because it helps detect what is salient (important) in the moment and trigger appropriate network transitions: for example, if an unpredictable stimulus arises, the SN may attenuate DMN activity (mind-wandering) and ramp up CEN activity (focused attention). This toggle function is thought to be mediated by the anterior insula/ACC’s connections to both networks, possibly via fast neuromodulatory signals. The SN has been linked to aspects of self-awareness and subjective feeling, as it integrates sensory, emotional, and visceral information. Some researchers even argue that the DMN might constitute a core "workspace" for conscious self-related thought, while the CEN underlies conscious goal-directed perception, and the SN decides where consciousness should reside at any given time. In disorders of consciousness (like vegetative state), as well as psychiatric conditions, disruptions in the connectivity or switching of these networks are commonly observed. For instance, severely brain-injured patients who regain consciousness show restored communication between frontoparietal (CEN) and insular (SN) hubs, suggesting that integrating executive and salience processing is necessary for conscious awareness of self or environment. The anterior insula in particular has been proposed as a critical region for the subjective aspect of consciousness - the fusion of attention to the external world with interoceptive, embodied context (sometimes called the "sentient self"). One might interpret the triple-network model as a blueprint for a system that needs to balance internal modeling and external input, with a top-level arbitrator for context-sensitive mode switching. The human solution to this appears to involve the salience network acting as a high-level controller that can enforce cognitive set switching (between internally oriented and externally oriented processing). This is another example of how control and consciousness entwine: the ability to flexibly switch modes in response to salient changes feels like a hallmark of conscious volition (e.g. "snapping out" of mind-wandering when something demands attention), and indeed this process has identifiable neural drivers. On a more mechanistic loop level, we have already noted cortico-striatal-thalamic loops in gating conscious contents. We should also mention cortico-hippocampal interactions in conscious memory. The hippocampus (in the medial temporal lobe) is essential for forming and retrieving episodic memories, which are typically accompanied by a conscious recollective experience ("mental time travel"). Neuroimaging indicates that conscious recollection specifically activates the hippocampal formation, beyond what is seen in mere familiarity or implicit memory tasks 30 . When one vividly remembers a past event, one is likely engaging a PFC-hippocampal circuit: the prefrontal cortex provides strategic search control and verifies retrieved information, while the hippocampus reinstates the cortical patterns representing the memory. Indeed, right prefrontal cortex has been repeatedly found to activate during explicit memory retrieval attempts. This fronto-hippocampal dialogue exemplifies how higher-order control regions interface with content-specific modules to produce conscious experience - here, the experience of remembering. If either partner is compromised (hippocampus lesion or frontal executive dysfunction), conscious recollection suffers: hippocampal damage yields amnesia (inability to bring memories to conscious awareness), whereas frontal damage can yield confabulation or failures to suppress irrelevant memories (awareness becomes filled with erroneous content because control over retrieval is lost). We see similar principles in working memory, often dubbed the "workbench" of consciousness. The prefrontal cortex and connected posterior areas sustain active representations that we are conscious of (e.g. holding a number in mind) and allow us to manipulate them. These rely on recurrent loops between PFC and other regions (including mediodorsal thalamus) to keep the information online. If those loops are interrupted - say via TMS or dopamine depletion - the information may fade from both working memory and conscious awareness. Consistent with this, recent studies highlight the mediodorsal thalamus as a key regulator of prefrontal cortex in tasks requiring cognitive set maintenance, uncertainty resolution, and memory buffering. Deep in the brain’s hierarchy, we again encounter thalamic regulation of cortical dynamics as a determinant of conscious cognitive function. Bringing these pieces together: consciousness appears to arise from the coordinated activity of a tiered control architecture. At the top level, large-scale networks (frontoparietal, default-mode, salience) interact to allocate resources either outwardly or inwardly and perhaps to maintain the unified sense of self in context. At a mid-level, recurrent loops between the cortex and subcortical hubs (basal ganglia, thalamus, hippocampus) implement gating, sustaining, and routing of information - processes that decide which perceptions, thoughts, or memories enter our awareness and for how long. At the micro-level, mechanisms like synaptic plasticity modulated by dopamine (teaching signals) and competitive inhibition in cortical microcircuits ensure that the content of consciousness is both selected by relevance and capable of driving behavior. Notably, reinforcement learning signals intersect with conscious control in this architecture: for example, in the basal ganglia, phasic dopamine marks the outcomes of actions, which can gradually delegate a task from conscious, careful learning to automatic habit. Conversely, when a habitual response fails or a reward expectation is violated, a surprise signal (prediction error) can engage frontal control to reevaluate and bring the issue to conscious attention. Experiments on humans performing dual tasks show that model-based (planning) strategies give way to model-free (habitual) strategies under high cognitive load, implying that the brain deploys conscious cognitive resources (the "central executive") only when necessary. In one study, taxing working memory caused participants to fall back on simpler trial-and-error learning, consistent with the idea that full-blown planning (which likely involves mental simulation and conscious foresight) requires those limited PFC resources 31 . This kind of result underscores a plausible functional role for consciousness: it is expensive but powerful. The brain should only "upshift" to conscious, model-based control when lower-level systems or cached routines cannot handle the situation. When it does upshift, the global workspace or higher-order circuits come online, integrating information from various modules and offering the opportunity for global evaluation, imagination of alternatives, and intentional re-routing of behavior. Functional Roles of Consciousness and Supporting Evidence Considering all the above, we can outline several interlocking roles for consciousness in relation to control. First, consciousness enables broad integration of information, which is crucial for coordination among specialized processes. This lets an agent handle novel problems: one can consciously see a problem and mentally try out different solutions (thanks to global broadcasting to working memory, etc.), whereas an unconscious system would be stuck in stimulus-bound reactions. In neural terms, conscious states (especially those involving frontoparietal ignition) allow brain regions that normally work in isolation to synchronize and share information. This is supported by neuroimaging of conscious perception, which finds that, for example, a seen stimulus triggers activity in occipital, parietal, and frontal cortices in a coherent episode, whereas an unseen stimulus (presented below threshold) yields only localized sensory activation. Second, consciousness allows intentional control and planning: Because conscious content is accessible to the executive, the agent can form explicit goals and strategies about it. For instance, one can consciously recollect a past event and then decide, "I will not repeat that mistake" - effectively using a memory to guide future action, a step that requires both the memory and the decision to be present in the global workspace together. Without conscious recall, only implicit habit learning would prevent the mistake, which is slower and less flexible. A concrete computational exemplar is the difference between model-based and model-free reinforcement learning, as mentioned. Conscious simulation (imagination) of future possibilities is a form of model-based evaluation that likely relies on fronto-hippocampal loops and attentional control (to mentally walk through a scenario). This is an essential ingredient for higher intelligence and is closely tied to what we subjectively experience as "deliberating" or "daydreaming." Indeed, the default-mode network’s activation during imagined navigation or future planning correlates with conscious mentation, and damage to it or the hippocampus impairs the richness of conscious foresight. Third, consciousness contributes to error monitoring and adaptive control. The feeling of surprise, conflict, or error tends to be conscious (we notice it). The ACC, our brain’s conflict monitor, generates an error-related negativity (ERN) within milliseconds of a mistake, and typically the person becomes aware of having erred when this system is engaged. If an error is made without ACC engagement (say, if attention was elsewhere), we often go unaware of it. Thus, conscious awareness of conflict may be crucial for recruiting remedial actions (like adjusting strategy or slowing down after an error). Stimulating or recording from ACC supports this: people with ACC lesions sometimes have difficulty sensing conflicts or errors in real time, and deep brain stimulation of ACC can alter the conscious experience of urge or effort. Another example: in conscious decision-making, especially difficult choices, we experience a feeling of effort or indecision, which reflects the deliberation of multiple options by frontoparietal circuits. That subjective tension corresponds to detectable neural signatures of competition (perhaps in frontal cortex or BG loops), and once a decision is reached and conscious, the system can commit to it and implement top-down bias to carry it out. Finally, an important functional role of consciousness might be training the unconscious. As IIT and others suggest, conscious practice can wire in new routines that later run unconsciously. When we learn a new skill (driving, playing piano, speaking a language), initially we must pay close conscious attention to each sub-act (often via verbal self-instruction). Over time, those control sequences get encapsulated into subconscious programs (in cortical-subcortical loops) that execute without need for global workspace supervision. Consciousness thus has a pedagogical role for the brain’s many sub-systems - it shapes plasticity by bringing together the right information at the right time (and often by triggering neuromodulatory signals when something is found important or rewarding). Supporting evidence comes from experiments on attention and learning: attended (hence likely conscious) stimuli are learned and remembered far better than unattended ones 24 . Also, conscious feedback and error awareness during training greatly enhance skill acquisition compared to learning purely by trial and error without awareness of what went wrong. Overview of neural evidence linking consciousness to control circuits Lesions to areas of the frontoparietal "multiple-demand" network (which underlies fluid intelligence and executive function) tend to also impair conscious report and flexibility. Conversely, lesions to primary sensory cortex can remove specific sensations but leave consciousness per se intact (one simply perceives nothing in that modality), whereas lesions to frontal or parietal hubs can cause more profound syndromes (neglect, anosognosia, or even global loss of conscious responsiveness as in coma if widespread). This suggests the content of consciousness is localized (each modality in its cortex) but the access to consciousness - the ability to be aware of and act on that content - depends on distributed control networks. Stimulation studies are particularly striking: electrical stimulation of a tiny region deep in the brain, the claustrum, was reported to induce immediate loss of consciousness in an awake human (anecdotally by Koubeissi et al. 2014). The claustrum is a thin sheet of neurons connecting to many cortical areas; Crick and Koch hypothesized it might act like a "conductor" synchronizing cortical ensembles. While more research is needed, this hints at a specific substrate for integrating activity across disparate regions - a role very much about control and coordination. Likewise, clinically, stimulating the central thalamus (intralaminar nuclei) in patients with disorders of consciousness has led to improvements in arousal and interaction 32 . These nuclei are known to project broadly and are thought to help orchestrate cortical rhythms; by electrically biasing them toward an "awake" firing mode, one can apparently facilitate a global ignition in a brain that was on the edge of awareness. Neuroimaging of various conscious states aligns with control network involvement. In general anesthesia, for example, studies have found that the functional connectivity between frontal and parietal regions breaks down as patients become unconscious, and that frontoparietal and thalamic activity markedly diminishes (while primary sensory areas may still respond somewhat to stimuli). In contrast, as patients recover consciousness, connectivity between the PFC and midline regions re-emerges even before behavioral signs of consciousness, suggesting that reactivation of the executive-global workspace network is a precursor to regaining conscious awareness 32 . PET studies comparing conscious vs unconscious perception show that frontal and parietal association areas "light up" only for conscious stimuli, not for subliminal ones. Similarly, alertness fluctuations (as in drowsiness or microsleeps) correlate with activity in brainstem arousal nuclei and the integrity of the salience network (notably locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system coupling with anterior insula)-reinforcing that maintaining consciousness is an active, neuromodulated process tied to those control circuits. Pathologies provide natural experiments: in unilateral neglect, a stroke to right parietal/insular cortex leads the patient to lose conscious awareness of the left side of space, essentially because the attention-control circuitry for that side is damaged. In schizophrenia or certain hallucination disorders, there may be overactivity of midbrain dopamine or underactivity of frontal monitoring, leading to internally generated content (voices, etc.) being uncontrolled and experienced as external - a failure of the normal conscious control filters. And in locked-in syndrome (where brainstem output pathways are lesioned but cortex is intact), patients are fully conscious (by all subjective and EEG measures) despite near-total paralysis; interestingly, such patients often show preserved frontoparietal metabolism, again underscoring that consciousness depends more on integrative brain networks than on ability to move or respond. Overall, modern theories of consciousness richly illuminate its intimate relationship with cognitive control systems. Global Workspace theory portrays consciousness as the enabling medium for control - the blackboard on which the brain’s specialists write and read flexibly. Integrated Information theory adds that the capacity for unified control (and thus consciousness) arises from tight informational coupling (especially in thalamocortical loops), and that control can become unconscious when segregated into encapsulated loops. Higher-Order theories remind us that awareness itself may be a metacognitive stance - the brain’s self-monitoring of its own states - closely tied to executive reflection and planning. The Attention Schema theory explicitly frames subjective awareness as a control model - a computed feature that helps allocate attention willfully. Predictive processing accounts cast conscious perception as the brain’s controlled best-guess, emphasizing attentional precision as a lever for what pops into awareness. These perspectives converge on a view of the brain (and by extension, a future AGI) as employing layered control: low-level automatic controllers handle routine cases, while a high-level, conscious controller intervenes for novel, complex, or significant situations. Consciousness is what it feels like from the inside when that high-level control is engaged - when information is globally broadcast, integrated, and scrutinized by an agent aware of itself. The evidence from lesions, stimulation, and neuroimaging substantiates that without the neural substrates for such global integration and self-monitoring (frontoparietal assemblies, thalamic and basal ganglia regulators, insular and cingulate gateways, etc.), consciousness diminishes or disappears. Thus, any biologically inspired AGI aiming for human-like general intelligence (and perhaps human-like sentience) will likely need to reproduce these control architectures: a global workspace for information exchange, hierarchical loops for gating and sustaining representations, an attention mechanism guided by an internal model, and a meta-cognitive layer that monitors and directs the whole. On this synthesis, consciousness is a software state of a physical inference engine: a transient control regime in which a deep generative model of world and body (including a compact self-model of attention and interoception) is placed into a high-gain, globally broadcast configuration. Mechanistically, thalamo-cortical relays and long-timescale frontoparietal hubs supply the broadcast ("ignition"), salience-network nodes (AI/dACC) arbitrate entry by routing precision-weighted prediction errors, basal-ganglia loops gate or quench the reverberation that sustains access, and oscillatory coherence opens the communication channels needed for rapid integration. When this regime is active, selected variables in the world/self model become available for flexible report, working-memory maintenance, planning, counterfactual simulation via PFC-hippocampal loops, and model-based control; when it collapses, processing persists locally but loses global availability and authorship. Framed this way, phenomenal "what-it-is-likeness" tracks the system attributing those selected variables to itself ("I am seeing/feeling X") within the self-schema, while access corresponds to their broadcast utility for control. The view yields testable consequences and an engineering checklist: disrupt broadcast, precision control, or self-model and conscious reportability degrades; conversely, in artificial agents, adding a broadcast layer, precision/attention control, and an attention/self-schema should improve instruction following, verbal report, metacognition, and deliberate reconfiguration-hallmarks of conscious processing.
